lessons.title: Mathematical logic
lessons.summaryHtml: Mathematical logic gives exact rules for deciding when a statement is true and when an argument is correct. Propositional logic combines true/false statements with connectives (¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔) and checks them with truth tables, laws of equivalence and normal forms (CNF, DNF and their principal forms). Rules of inference such as modus ponens, modus tollens and resolution tell you which conclusions follow from given premises, and which tempting patterns are fallacies. Predicate logic adds variables, predicates and the quantifiers ∀ and ∃, so you can express statements such as “every student has a friend” and negate or reorder them correctly. NTA tests this unit through tautology checks, equivalences, “which is the correct translation” questions and nested-quantifier reasoning. Fast methods, such as hunting for the one falsifying row, win most of these marks.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Logic studies the form of an argument rather than its topic. A proposition is a declarative sentence that is either true (T) or false (F), not both: “7 is prime” is a proposition, while “Close the door” and “x + 2 = 5” are not (the second becomes one once x is fixed). Small propositions are joined by connectives into compound ones, and a truth table lists the value of a compound for every combination of values of its parts. Two formulas are equivalent when their truth tables match, and an argument is valid when its conclusion can never be false while all its premises are true. Predicate logic goes further: it talks about objects with variables, predicates such as P(x), and the quantifiers “for all” (∀) and “there exists” (∃).

Why it matters for NET

Mathematical logic is the first topic of Unit 1 and gives a steady supply of short questions. The recurring patterns are: identifying a tautology or contradiction; picking the formula equivalent to a given one; converse, inverse and contrapositive; the English reading of “only if”, “unless” and “necessary”; functionally complete sets; valid arguments and named rules of inference; and, most often in recent papers, translating English into predicate logic and negating or reordering quantifiers. The same ideas return in Unit 10 (resolution and first-order logic in AI) and Unit 7 (SAT and NP-completeness), so time spent here pays twice.

Concepts in depth: connectives and the conditional

ConnectiveSymbolRead asFalse exactly when
Negation¬pnot pp is true
Conjunctionp ∧ qp and qat least one is false
Disjunctionp ∨ qp or q (inclusive)both are false
Exclusive orp ⊕ qp or q but not bothp and q have the same value
Conditionalp → qif p then qp is true and q is false
Biconditionalp ↔ qp if and only if qp and q differ
NANDp ↑ qnot bothboth are true
NORp ↓ qneitherat least one is true

The conditional causes most errors. p → q promises only that q holds whenever p holds; when p is false the promise cannot be broken, so the conditional is true (“vacuously true”). English has many ways to say p → q: “if p, q”, “q if p”, “p only if q”, “p is sufficient for q”, “q is necessary for p”, “q whenever p”. “p unless q” means ¬q → p, which is equivalent to p ∨ q.

From p → q we form the converse q → p, the inverse ¬p → ¬q and the contrapositive ¬q → ¬p. The contrapositive is equivalent to the original; the converse and inverse are equivalent to each other but not to the original. The usual precedence is ¬, then ∧, then ∨, then →, then ↔. The conditional is not associative: (p → q) → r and p → (q → r) differ at p = F, r = F, so always keep the brackets.

Concepts in depth: truth tables and classification

A formula with n variables has 2n rows. Because each row can be T or F independently, there are 22n different truth functions of n variables: 16 binary connectives, 256 functions of three variables. A formula is a tautology (valid) if it is true in every row, a contradiction (unsatisfiable) if it is false in every row, and a contingency otherwise. It is satisfiable if at least one row makes it true. Three links are worth memorising: A is a tautology exactly when ¬A is a contradiction; A ≡ B exactly when A ↔ B is a tautology; and A logically implies B (A ⇒ B) exactly when A → B is a tautology.

The fastest test for a tautology is the falsifying-row method. Suppose the formula is false and follow the consequences. An implication is false only with a true left side and a false right side, and a conjunction on the left forces every conjunct to be true. If the assumptions force a variable to be both T and F, no falsifying row exists and the formula is a tautology. If they succeed, you have found a counterexample in seconds.

Concepts in depth: laws of equivalence

LawEquivalence
Identity and dominationp ∧ T ≡ p, p ∨ F ≡ p; p ∨ T ≡ T, p ∧ F ≡ F
Idempotent, double negationp ∨ p ≡ p, p ∧ p ≡ p; ¬¬p ≡ p
Complement (negation)p ∨ ¬p ≡ T, p ∧ ¬p ≡ F
Commutative, associativefor ∧, ∨, ⊕ and ↔ (not for →)
Distributivep ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r); p ∨ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r)
De Morgan¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q; ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q
Absorptionp ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p; p ∧ (p ∨ q) ≡ p
Conditionalp → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q ≡ ¬q → ¬p; ¬(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q
Biconditionalp ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q); ¬(p ↔ q) ≡ p ⊕ q ≡ p ↔ ¬q
Exportation(p ∧ q) → r ≡ p → (q → r)
Common antecedent(p → q) ∧ (p → r) ≡ p → (q ∧ r); (p → q) ∨ (p → r) ≡ p → (q ∨ r)
Common consequent(p → r) ∧ (q → r) ≡ (p ∨ q) → r; (p → r) ∨ (q → r) ≡ (p ∧ q) → r

The last row is the favourite trap: with a common consequent, “and” outside becomes “or” inside, and “or” outside becomes “and” inside. The duality principle says that if an equivalence uses only ¬, ∧, ∨, T and F, swapping ∧ with ∨ and T with F on both sides gives another valid equivalence. The dual of (p ∧ T) ∨ q is (p ∨ F) ∧ q.

Concepts in depth: functional completeness

A set of connectives is functionally complete if every truth function can be built from it. {¬, ∧, ∨} is complete because every truth function has a DNF. De Morgan then removes one of ∧ and ∨, so {¬, ∧} and {¬, ∨} are complete; {¬, →} is complete because p ∨ q ≡ ¬p → q; {→, F} is complete because ¬p ≡ p → F; and the single connectives NAND and NOR are each complete (¬p ≡ p ↑ p). A set is not complete if all its members share a property that composition preserves. {∧, ∨, →, ↔} can never produce F when all inputs are T, so it cannot express ¬. {∧, ∨} is also monotone. {¬, ↔, ⊕} only builds linear functions (XORs of variables plus a constant), so it cannot express ∧. These five properties (preserving F, preserving T, self-dual, monotone, linear) are Post’s criteria: a set is complete exactly when, for each property, some member lacks it.

Concepts in depth: normal forms

A literal is a variable or its negation. A DNF is an OR of ANDs of literals; a CNF is an AND of ORs of literals (each OR is a clause). Every formula has both. The principal (canonical) forms use full terms. A minterm contains every variable once and is true in exactly one row; the PDNF (sum of products) is the OR of the minterms of the true rows. A maxterm is an OR of every variable and is false in exactly one row; the PCNF (product of sums) is the AND of the maxterms of the false rows. For a false row, a variable that is 0 appears plain and a variable that is 1 appears negated. With n variables, the number of minterms in the PDNF plus the number of maxterms in the PCNF is always 2n, and the PCNF indices are exactly the indices missing from the PDNF.

Two facts connect normal forms to complexity. A CNF is a tautology exactly when every clause contains a complementary pair (easy to check), and a DNF is satisfiable exactly when some term has no complementary pair (also easy). Checking whether a CNF is satisfiable is the NP-complete SAT problem.

Concepts in depth: rules of inference

RuleFromInfer
Modus ponensp, p → qq
Modus tollens¬q, p → q¬p
Hypothetical syllogismp → q, q → rp → r
Disjunctive syllogismp ∨ q, ¬pq
Additionpp ∨ q
Simplificationp ∧ qp
Conjunctionp, qp ∧ q
Resolutionp ∨ q, ¬p ∨ rq ∨ r
Constructive dilemmap → q, r → s, p ∨ rq ∨ s

Each rule corresponds to a tautology; modus ponens is (p ∧ (p → q)) → q. Two invalid patterns look similar: affirming the consequent (from p → q and q, conclude p) and denying the antecedent (from p → q and ¬p, conclude ¬q). An argument whose premises are inconsistent is valid for every conclusion, because no row makes all premises true. Proof by resolution negates the conclusion, converts everything to clauses, and resolves until it reaches the empty clause, which shows the premises plus the negated conclusion are unsatisfiable.

Concepts in depth: predicates and quantifiers

A predicate P(x) becomes a proposition when x is given a value from the domain (universe of discourse). ∀x P(x) is true when P holds for every element; ∃x P(x) when it holds for at least one. Over a finite domain {a₁, …, aₙ}, ∀x P(x) is P(a₁) ∧ … ∧ P(aₙ) and ∃x P(x) is P(a₁) ∨ … ∨ P(aₙ). A variable inside the scope of a quantifier is bound; otherwise it is free, and a formula with free variables is not a proposition. Quantifiers bind more tightly than the connectives, so ∀x P(x) ∧ Q(x) has a free x in Q(x).

De Morgan for quantifiers: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). To negate a long formula, move ¬ to the right across each quantifier, flipping it, then negate the inner formula. ∀ distributes over ∧ and ∃ over ∨, but only one direction holds for the other pairs: ∀x P(x) ∨ ∀x Q(x) implies ∀x (P(x) ∨ Q(x)), and ∃x (P(x) ∧ Q(x)) implies ∃x P(x) ∧ ∃x Q(x); the converses fail. When x is not free in A: ∀x (A → P(x)) ≡ A → ∀x P(x), but a quantifier in the antecedent flips: ∀x (P(x) → A) ≡ ∃x P(x) → A and ∃x (P(x) → A) ≡ ∀x P(x) → A.

Nested quantifiers. Quantifiers of the same kind commute (∀x∀y ≡ ∀y∀x). Mixed ones do not: ∃y∀x P(x, y) says one y works for every x, which is stronger than ∀x∃y P(x, y), where y may depend on x. So ∃y∀x P(x, y) → ∀x∃y P(x, y) is valid, and the converse is not. Over the integers, ∀x∃y (x + y = 0) is true (take y = −x), but ∃y∀x (x + y = 0) is false. The four quantifier rules are universal instantiation (∀x P(x) ⊢ P(c) for any c), universal generalisation (P(c) for an arbitrary c ⊢ ∀x P(x)), existential instantiation (∃x P(x) ⊢ P(c) for some new c) and existential generalisation (P(c) ⊢ ∃x P(x)).

Concepts in depth: translating English

EnglishFormulaCommon wrong form
All S are P∀x (S(x) → P(x))∀x (S(x) ∧ P(x)) says everything is S and P
Some S are P∃x (S(x) ∧ P(x))∃x (S(x) → P(x)) is true if anything is not S
No S is P∀x (S(x) → ¬P(x)) ≡ ¬∃x (S(x) ∧ P(x))¬∀x (S(x) → P(x)) means “not all”
Not all S are P∃x (S(x) ∧ ¬P(x))∀x (S(x) → ¬P(x)) means “none”
Only S are P∀x (P(x) → S(x))∀x (S(x) → P(x)) is the converse
Exactly one x has P∃x (P(x) ∧ ∀y (P(y) → y = x))∃x P(x) allows many

The rule of thumb is: ∀ goes with →, and ∃ goes with ∧.

Worked examples

Example 1: prove hypothetical syllogism is a tautology. Show that F = [(p → q) ∧ (q → r)] → (p → r) is a tautology.

Falsifying-row method. For F to be false we need p → r false, so p = T and r = F. We also need (p → q) true, which with p = T forces q = T, and (q → r) true, which with q = T forces r = T. But r = F, a contradiction. No row falsifies F, so it is a tautology.

Check with the truth table (L = (p → q) ∧ (q → r)):

pqrLp → rF
FFFTTT
FFTTTT
FTFFTT
FTTTTT
TFFFFT
TFTFTT
TTFFFT
TTTTTT

L is true in 4 rows, and p → r is true in each of them, so the last column is all T.

Example 2: simplify with the laws. Simplify ¬(p ∨ (¬p ∧ q)).

  1. De Morgan: ¬p ∧ ¬(¬p ∧ q).
  2. De Morgan again and double negation: ¬p ∧ (p ∨ ¬q).
  3. Distribute: (¬p ∧ p) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q).
  4. Complement and identity: F ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q) = ¬p ∧ ¬q.

Result: ¬p ∧ ¬q, which is ¬(p ∨ q) and also p ↓ q. The inner p ∨ (¬p ∧ q) had simplified to p ∨ q.

Example 3: PDNF and PCNF. Find both principal forms of (p ∨ q) → r, with rows numbered in the order p q r (p is the most significant bit).

The formula is false only when p ∨ q is true and r is false: rows 010 (2), 100 (4) and 110 (6). All other rows are true: 0, 1, 3, 5, 7.

PDNF = Σm(0, 1, 3, 5, 7) = (¬p ∧ ¬q ∧ ¬r) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q ∧ r) ∨ (¬p ∧ q ∧ r) ∨ (p ∧ ¬q ∧ r) ∨ (p ∧ q ∧ r).

PCNF = ΠM(2, 4, 6). For row 010 the maxterm is (p ∨ ¬q ∨ r); for 100 it is (¬p ∨ q ∨ r); for 110 it is (¬p ∨ ¬q ∨ r). So PCNF = (p ∨ ¬q ∨ r) ∧ (¬p ∨ q ∨ r) ∧ (¬p ∨ ¬q ∨ r).

Check: 5 minterms + 3 maxterms = 8 = 2³. A shorter CNF is (¬p ∨ r) ∧ (¬q ∨ r), which is the common-consequent law (p → r) ∧ (q → r).

Example 4: test an argument. Premises: “If the server is patched (p), the audit passes (q). If the logs are complete (r), the report is signed (s). The server is patched or the logs are complete. The audit did not pass.” Conclusion: “The report is signed.”

  1. Premises: p → q, r → s, p ∨ r, ¬q. Conclusion: s.
  2. From p → q and ¬q: ¬p (modus tollens).
  3. From p ∨ r and ¬p: r (disjunctive syllogism).
  4. From r → s and r: s (modus ponens).

The argument is valid. Now change the last premise to “The audit passed (q)” and conclude “The server was patched (p)”. That is affirming the consequent: p = F, q = T, r = T, s = T makes every premise true and the conclusion false, so it is invalid.

Example 5: nested quantifiers on a finite domain. Domain D = {1, 2, 3, 4} and P(x, y): “x divides y”. Decide each statement.

  1. ∀x∃y P(x, y): true, take y = x.
  2. ∃y∀x P(x, y): we need a y in D divisible by 1, 2, 3 and 4, that is a multiple of 12. None exists, so false.
  3. ∃x∀y P(x, y): x = 1 divides everything, so true.
  4. ∀y∃x (x ≠ y ∧ P(x, y)): y = 1 has no divisor other than itself in D, so false.

Two are true and two are false. Statements 1 and 2 use the same predicate with the quantifiers swapped and get different answers, which is the whole point of nested-quantifier questions.

Example 6: translate and negate. “Every aspirant who revises daily clears the exam.” Let A(x): x is an aspirant, R(x): x revises daily, C(x): x clears the exam.

Formula: ∀x ((A(x) ∧ R(x)) → C(x)).

Negation: ∃x ¬((A(x) ∧ R(x)) → C(x)) = ∃x (A(x) ∧ R(x) ∧ ¬C(x)), “some aspirant revises daily and does not clear the exam”. It is not “every aspirant who revises daily fails”, which is the contrary, not the negation.

NTA traps

  • Converse for contrapositive. Wrong: “p → q is the same as q → p.” Fix: only ¬q → ¬p is equivalent; the converse and the inverse are equivalent to each other.
  • Reading “only if” backwards. Wrong: “p only if q” is q → p. Fix: “only if” introduces the consequent: p → q. “p if q” is q → p.
  • Common consequent. Wrong: (p → r) ∧ (q → r) ≡ (p ∧ q) → r. Fix: it is (p ∨ q) → r; the “or” form (p → r) ∨ (q → r) is (p ∧ q) → r.
  • Treating → as associative. Wrong: p → q → r means (p → q) → r. Fix: the two bracketings differ (p = F, r = F); NTA writes the brackets, so read them.
  • Negating a conditional into a conditional. Wrong: ¬(p → q) = ¬p → ¬q. Fix: ¬(p → q) = p ∧ ¬q.
  • ∀ with ∧, ∃ with →. Wrong: “All S are P” as ∀x (S(x) ∧ P(x)). Fix: ∀ pairs with →, ∃ pairs with ∧.
  • Swapping mixed quantifiers. Wrong: ∀x∃y ≡ ∃y∀x. Fix: only ∃y∀x ⇒ ∀x∃y holds.
  • Quantifier in an antecedent. Wrong: ∀x (P(x) → A) ≡ ∀x P(x) → A. Fix: it is ∃x P(x) → A.
  • Fallacies accepted as valid. Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are invalid; test them with the row p = F, q = T.
  • Counting rows instead of functions. Three variables give 8 rows but 256 functions.

How NTA asks this

  • Direct MCQ: which formula is a tautology, contradiction or equivalent to a given one; the negation of a quantified sentence; the correct translation of an English sentence. Use the falsifying-row method, and test equivalence by finding one row where the two formulas differ.
  • Match the following: rules of inference with their forms, connectives with equivalent expressions, English sentence types with formulas, laws with their names.
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: contrapositive and converse, functional completeness, validity of quantifier laws, CNF/DNF facts.
  • Multiple select: which formulas are equivalent, which sets are functionally complete, which formulas are tautologies.
  • Order: steps of CNF conversion or of a resolution proof.

Mini-example (match). List I: A. p → q, B. p ↔ q, C. p ⊕ q, D. p ↓ q. List II: I. ¬p ∧ ¬q, II. ¬p ∨ q, III. (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q), IV. (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ (¬p ∧ q). Answer: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I. Fix the easiest pair first (NOR = “neither” = I), then eliminate every option that disagrees.

Mini-example (A-R). A: ∃y∀x P(x, y) → ∀x∃y P(x, y) is valid. R: Swapping ∀ and ∃ never changes the meaning. A is true (one y that works for all x certainly gives each x a y), but R is false (∀x∃y does not imply ∃y∀x). Answer: option 3.

Elimination trick: for “which is equivalent” questions, test every option at the row p = F, q = T (and r = F). That single row separates a conditional from its converse, inverse and most distractors.
Watch out: in quantifier questions, check whether the domain is stated. “∃x∀y (x ≤ y)” is true over the natural numbers (x = 0) but false over the integers.

terms.definition: A declarative sentence that is either true or false, but not both. “x + 2 = 5” is not a proposition until x is fixed.
A formula that is true in every row of its truth table, such as p ∨ ¬p. Its negation is a contradiction.
A formula that is true in some rows and false in others; it is satisfiable but not valid.
For p → q, the contrapositive is ¬q → ¬p. It is logically equivalent to p → q; the converse q → p is not.
A set of connectives that can express every truth function, such as {¬, ∧}, {¬, →}, {NAND} or {NOR}.
Principal (canonical) normal forms: the OR of the minterms of the true rows, and the AND of the maxterms of the false rows.
An argument in which the conclusion is true in every row where all premises are true; equivalently (P₁ ∧ … ∧ Pₙ) → C is a tautology.
The rule that from (p ∨ q) and (¬p ∨ r) infers (q ∨ r); the basis of automated proof by refutation.
∀x P(x) is true when P(x) is true for every x in the domain; over a finite domain it is a long conjunction.
∃x P(x) is true when P(x) is true for at least one x in the domain; over a finite domain it is a long disjunction.

lessons.examTip: To test whether a formula (or an argument) is a tautology, do not draw the whole truth table. Try to make it false: an implication is false only when its left side is true and its right side is false. If no row can do that, it is a tautology.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For each tautology, equivalence or validity problem, write the single row you used to accept or reject each option.
Check every answer with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (converse taken as equivalent, “only if” reversed, ∀ paired with ∧, mixed quantifiers swapped).
Write the 12 equivalence laws, the 9 rules of inference, the two fallacies and the quantifier negation and distribution rules on one page from memory; compare with the fact sheet.
Translate five English sentences of your own into predicate logic and negate each one, then check the negation by testing it on a three-element domain.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then take the lesson quiz and bank questions at 60–90 seconds per question.
check: At least 12 of 15 practice problems correct.
Problems 9–15 solved within 12 minutes.
Any “is it a tautology” question settled in under 60 seconds with the falsifying-row method.
The negation of any sentence with two nested quantifiers written correctly on the first attempt.

quiz.question: Which of the following formulas is a tautology?
quiz.explanation: (p ∧ (p → q)) → q is modus ponens written as a formula. To falsify it we need q false and p ∧ (p → q) true; but p true and q false make p → q false, so no row falsifies it. The others fail: (p → q) → (q → p) is false at p = F, q = T; (p ∨ q) → (p ∧ q) is false at p = T, q = F; and (p → q) ↔ (¬p → ¬q) compares a conditional with its inverse, which differ at p = F, q = T.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Modus ponens affirms the antecedent (IV). Modus tollens denies the consequent (III). Disjunctive syllogism removes a false disjunct (II). Hypothetical syllogism chains two conditionals (I). The distractors swap one pair each: ponens and tollens, or the two syllogisms.

b: I. p → q, q → r ⊢ p → r
II. p ∨ q, ¬p ⊢ q
III. p → q, ¬q ⊢ ¬p
IV. p → q, p ⊢ q

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: In how many of the 16 rows of the truth table of (p ∨ q) → (r ∧ s) is the formula true?
quiz.explanation: The implication is false only when p ∨ q is true and r ∧ s is false. p ∨ q is true in 3 of the 4 (p, q) rows; r ∧ s is false in 3 of the 4 (r, s) rows. False rows = 3 × 3 = 9, so true rows = 16 − 9 = 7. Choosing 9 counts the false rows instead.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: ¬q → ¬p ≡ q ∨ ¬p ≡ p → q, so Statement I is true. The converse q → p is false at p = F, q = T, where p → q is true, so Statement II is false. The converse is equivalent to the inverse (¬p → ¬q), not to the original.

stmts: Statement I: p → q is logically equivalent to its contrapositive ¬q → ¬p.
Statement II: p → q is logically equivalent to its converse q → p.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: {¬, ∧, ∨} is complete because every truth function has a DNF (one minterm per true row). De Morgan’s law removes ∨: p ∨ q ≡ ¬(¬p ∧ ¬q). So {¬, ∧} can express everything, and R is exactly the reason.

stmts: Assertion (A): The set of connectives {¬, ∧} is functionally complete.
Reason (R): Every truth function can be written in DNF using ¬, ∧ and ∨, and p ∨ q ≡ ¬(¬p ∧ ¬q).
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Which of the following formulas are logically equivalent to p → (q → r)?
options: A, B, C and D only
quiz.explanation: p → (q → r) ≡ ¬p ∨ (¬q ∨ r) = D. By exportation this is (p ∧ q) → r = A, and since ∨ is commutative it also equals q → (p → r) = B. C is different: at p = F, r = F it is false (p → q is true, r false) while the original is true. E is (p ∨ q) → r, which is false at p = T, q = F, r = F, where the original is true.

stmts: A. (p ∧ q) → r
B. q → (p → r)
C. (p → q) → r
D. ¬p ∨ ¬q ∨ r
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Which of the following is the negation of ∀x (P(x) → ∃y Q(x, y))?
quiz.explanation: Push ¬ inward step by step: ¬∀x(…) = ∃x ¬(P(x) → ∃y Q(x, y)). ¬(a → b) = a ∧ ¬b, so we get ∃x (P(x) ∧ ¬∃y Q(x, y)) = ∃x (P(x) ∧ ∀y ¬Q(x, y)). The negation of an implication is never an implication, which removes options 2 and 4; option 3 forgot to flip ∀x.

quiz.question: Let G(x): “x is a graduate” and E(x): “x is eligible”. Which formula expresses “Only graduates are eligible”?
quiz.explanation: “Only graduates are eligible” means that anyone eligible is a graduate: E(x) → G(x). ∀x (G(x) → E(x)) says every graduate is eligible, the converse and the most common trap. ∀x (G(x) ∧ E(x)) claims everyone is a graduate and eligible, and the existential form only says some eligible graduate exists.

quiz.question: How many distinct truth functions (different truth tables) of three propositional variables are there?
quiz.explanation: Three variables give 2³ = 8 rows. Each row can independently be T or F, so there are 2⁸ = 256 truth functions. 8 is only the number of rows; in general there are 2^(2^n) functions of n variables.

quiz.question: Arrange the following steps of converting a propositional formula to CNF in the correct order.
quiz.explanation: First remove → and ↔ (B), because De Morgan’s laws only apply to ∧ and ∨. Then push ¬ down to the variables (D), giving negation normal form. Then distribute ∨ over ∧ to get an AND of ORs (A). Finally simplify the clauses (C); a clause containing p and ¬p is always true and can be dropped.

stmts: A. Distribute ∨ over ∧
B. Eliminate ↔ and → using p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q
C. Delete repeated literals and any clause that contains a complementary pair
D. Push negations inward using De Morgan’s laws and double negation

lessons.title: Sets, relations and functions
lessons.summaryHtml: Sets, relations and functions are the vocabulary of every other unit. This lesson covers set operations and identities, power sets and Cartesian products, and relations with their properties (reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive) and closures. It then covers equivalence relations and the partitions they create, and partial orders drawn as Hasse diagrams, with maximal and minimal elements, bounds and lattices. It ends with functions (injective, surjective, bijective), composition and inverses. NTA’s favourite questions here are counting questions: how many relations of a given type, how many functions, onto functions or equivalence relations. Each has a formula with a one-line reason, so learn the reason and you can rebuild the formula in the exam hall.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A set is a collection of distinct objects. A relation records which pairs of objects are linked, such as “divides”, “is a prerequisite of” or “lives in the same city as”. Some relations sort objects into groups of equals (equivalence relations); others rank them (partial orders). A function is a special relation that gives each input exactly one output. These ideas are the language of databases (a table is a relation), compilers (dependency orders), algorithms (hash functions) and much of Unit 1.

Why it matters for NET

This topic yields direct questions almost every cycle. The dominant sub-topics are: counting relations with a property (reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric and combinations); counting functions, injections and surjections; equivalence relations and partitions (Bell and Stirling numbers); identifying properties of a given relation; Hasse diagrams with maximal, minimal, greatest and least elements; lattices, complements and distributivity in divisor lattices; and composition and inverses of functions. The questions are short, and the options are close numbers, so you need the exact formula.

Concepts in depth: sets and operations

For sets A and B inside a universe U: union A ∪ B, intersection A ∩ B, difference A − B (in A, not in B), complement A′ = U − A, and symmetric difference A ⊕ B = (A − B) ∪ (B − A) = (A ∪ B) − (A ∩ B). The identities mirror the logic laws of lesson 1.1: De Morgan ((A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′), distributive, absorption (A ∪ (A ∩ B) = A). Useful difference laws are A − (B ∪ C) = (A − B) ∩ (A − C) and A − (B ∩ C) = (A − B) ∪ (A − C).

The power set P(A) has 2|A| elements, since each element is either in or out of a subset. P(A ∩ B) = P(A) ∩ P(B), but P(A ∪ B) is usually larger than P(A) ∪ P(B). The Cartesian product A × B = {(a, b)} has |A|·|B| elements, and it distributes over ∪, ∩ and −. For two sets, |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| and |A ⊕ B| = |A| + |B| − 2|A ∩ B|. A set is countable if it is finite or can be listed as a sequence: ℕ, ℤ, ℚ, ℤ × ℤ and the set of finite strings over an alphabet are countable, while ℝ and P(ℕ) are not (Cantor’s diagonal argument).

Concepts in depth: relations and their properties

A relation R on A is a subset of A × A, written a R b when (a, b) ∈ R. It can be drawn as a 0–1 matrix M (rows and columns indexed by A) or as a directed graph.

PropertyDefinitionMatrix test
Reflexivea R a for every aevery diagonal entry is 1
Irreflexivea R a for no aevery diagonal entry is 0
Symmetrica R b ⇒ b R aM = Mᵀ
Antisymmetrica R b and b R a ⇒ a = bno off-diagonal pair has both entries 1
Asymmetrica R b ⇒ not b R aantisymmetric and irreflexive

Two points cause most errors. First, antisymmetric is not “not symmetric”: the identity relation {(a, a)} is both symmetric and antisymmetric, and {(1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 3)} is neither. Second, properties that are “if … then” statements hold vacuously when nothing triggers them: the empty relation on a non-empty set is symmetric, antisymmetric, asymmetric and transitive, but not reflexive.

Concepts in depth: counting relations

Think of the n × n matrix as n diagonal cells plus n(n − 1)/2 unordered off-diagonal pairs {(a, b), (b, a)}. Each property restricts each part independently, so the count is a product.

From an m-set to an n-set there are 2mn relations. On an n-set there are nn² binary operations and nn(n+1)/2 commutative ones (only the diagonal and one cell of each off-diagonal pair are free).

Concepts in depth: closures and composition

The closure of R under a property is the smallest relation containing R that has the property. The reflexive closure is R ∪ Δ (add the diagonal); the symmetric closure is R ∪ R⁻¹; the transitive closure R⁺ is R ∪ R² ∪ R³ ∪ … ∪ Rⁿ, the pairs (a, b) joined by a path of length at least 1 in the digraph. Warshall’s algorithm computes R⁺ in O(n³): for each k, set M[i][j] = 1 whenever M[i][k] and M[k][j] are 1. Composition: (a, c) ∈ S ∘ R when a R b and b S c for some b; with matrices, M(S∘R) = M(R) ⊙ M(S) (Boolean product). There is no “antisymmetric closure”, because adding pairs can never remove a violation.

Concepts in depth: equivalence relations and partitions

An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. The equivalence class [a] = {x : x R a}. Classes are either identical or disjoint and together cover A, so they form a partition; conversely “in the same block” is an equivalence relation. Congruence modulo m on ℤ has exactly m classes [0], [1], …, [m − 1]. The number of partitions of an n-set into exactly k non-empty blocks is the Stirling number S(n, k), with S(n, k) = S(n − 1, k − 1) + k·S(n − 1, k) (element n either forms its own block or joins one of k blocks). The Bell number Bₙ = Σₖ S(n, k) counts all partitions: 1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 52, 203, 877 for n = 0 to 7. Useful values: S(n, 2) = 2^(n−1) − 1 and S(n, n − 1) = C(n, 2).

Concepts in depth: partial orders and Hasse diagrams

A partial order ⪯ is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive; (A, ⪯) is a poset. Examples: ≤ on numbers, ⊆ on sets, divisibility on positive integers. Elements a and b are comparable if a ⪯ b or b ⪯ a. A total order (chain) makes every pair comparable. A Hasse diagram draws the poset without clutter: remove the loops (reflexivity), remove every edge implied by transitivity, and draw each remaining “covering” edge upward, so b sits above a when b covers a (a ≺ b with nothing in between).

  • Maximal: nothing is strictly above it. Greatest: above every element. A finite poset always has a maximal element; a greatest element exists only if there is exactly one maximal element that sits above everything. The same holds for minimal and least.
  • Upper bound of a subset S: an element ⪰ every element of S. The least upper bound (lub, supremum, join ∨) is the least of the upper bounds, if it exists; the greatest lower bound (glb, infimum, meet ∧) is defined dually.
  • A topological sort lists the elements in a total order compatible with ⪯; every finite poset has one.

Concepts in depth: lattices

A lattice is a poset in which every pair has a join and a meet. In (P(S), ⊆) join is ∪ and meet is ∩; in the divisor lattice (Dn, |) join is lcm and meet is gcd. Every finite lattice is bounded, with a least element 0 and greatest element 1. A lattice is distributive if a ∧ (b ∨ c) = (a ∧ b) ∨ (a ∧ c); P(S), Dn and every chain are distributive. The two smallest non-distributive lattices are the diamond M₃ and the pentagon N₅; a lattice is distributive exactly when it contains neither as a sublattice. A bounded lattice is complemented if every a has some b with a ∨ b = 1 and a ∧ b = 0. In a distributive lattice a complement, if it exists, is unique. A complemented distributive lattice is a Boolean algebra; every finite one is isomorphic to some P(S) and has 2k elements. For divisor lattices, Dn is a Boolean algebra exactly when n is square-free (for example D30), and then the complement of a is n/a.

Concepts in depth: functions

A function f : A → B assigns to every a ∈ A exactly one f(a) ∈ B. A is the domain, B the codomain, f(A) the range. f is injective (one-to-one) if different inputs give different outputs, surjective (onto) if the range is all of B, and bijective if both, in which case the inverse f⁻¹ : B → A exists. For finite sets with |A| = |B|, injective ⇔ surjective ⇔ bijective. This fails for infinite sets: n ↦ n + 1 on ℕ is injective but not onto.

Composition (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)) is associative but not commutative. Compositions of injections are injective, of surjections surjective. If g ∘ f is injective, then f is injective; if g ∘ f is surjective, then g is surjective. For bijections, (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹ (“socks and shoes”).

Worked examples

Example 1: counting relations on A = {a, b, c}. Find the number of antisymmetric relations and the number of relations that are reflexive and antisymmetric.

  1. The matrix has 3 diagonal cells and 3 off-diagonal pairs: {ab, ba}, {ac, ca}, {bc, cb}.
  2. Antisymmetric: each diagonal cell is free (2 ways). Each pair may hold neither, only the first, or only the second (3 ways), but not both. Count = 2³ × 3³ = 8 × 27 = 216.
  3. Reflexive and antisymmetric: the diagonal is forced to 1 (1 way), the pairs still have 3 ways: 3³ = 27.

A brute-force count over all 512 relations gives the same numbers.

Example 2: equivalence relations on a 4-element set. Count the equivalence relations on {1, 2, 3, 4} by the shape of the partition.

Block sizesHow many partitions

2 + 2C(4, 2)/2 = 3
2 + 1 + 1C(4, 2) = 6
1 + 1 + 1 + 11

Total B₄ = 1 + 4 + 3 + 6 + 1 = 15. Grouped by the number of blocks: S(4, 1) = 1, S(4, 2) = 4 + 3 = 7, S(4, 3) = 6, S(4, 4) = 1. The relation with blocks {1, 2}, {3}, {4} has 2² + 1 + 1 = 6 ordered pairs.

Example 3: the Hasse diagram of D36. Draw it, count the edges, and find the extremal elements of the subset {4, 6, 9}.

            36
           /  \
         12    18
        /  \  /  \
       4    6     9
        \  / \   /
         2     3
          \   /
            1

The 9 divisors 2i3j (0 ≤ i, j ≤ 2) form a 3 × 3 grid. Covering edges multiply by one prime: 6 edges for “× 2” and 6 for “× 3”, 12 in all. D36 has least element 1 and greatest element 36. For S = {4, 6, 9}: the upper bounds are the common multiples inside D36, which is only 36, so lub(S) = 36; the lower bounds are the common divisors, only 1, so glb(S) = 1. Inside S itself all three elements are both maximal and minimal (no two are comparable), so S is an antichain.

Example 4: onto functions. Count the surjections from A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} onto B = {x, y, z}.

  1. All functions: 3⁵ = 243.
  2. Functions missing a given element of B: 2⁵ = 32; there are C(3, 1) = 3 such elements.
  3. Functions missing two given elements: 1⁵ = 1; C(3, 2) = 3 choices.
  4. Inclusion–exclusion: 243 − 3 × 32 + 3 × 1 − 0 = 150.

Check: S(5, 3) = 25 partitions of A into 3 blocks, and 3! = 6 ways to assign the blocks to x, y, z: 25 × 6 = 150. The common wrong answer 243 − 3 = 240 subtracts only the constant functions.

Example 5: transitive closure with Warshall. R = {(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)} on {1, 2, 3, 4}.

  1. k = 1: no pair ends at 1, nothing changes.
  2. k = 2: (1, 2) and (2, 3) give (1, 3).
  3. k = 3: (1, 3), (2, 3) with (3, 4) give (1, 4) and (2, 4).
  4. k = 4: no pair starts at 4, nothing changes.

R⁺ = {(1, 2), (1, 3), (1, 4), (2, 3), (2, 4), (3, 4)}: 6 pairs, exactly the strict order 1 < 2 < 3 < 4. Its reflexive-transitive closure adds the 4 loops and has 10 pairs.

Example 6: complements in divisor lattices. Compare D30 and D12.

D30: 30 = 2·3·5 is square-free. Each divisor a has complement 30/a: 2 and 15, 3 and 10, 5 and 6, 1 and 30. Every complement is unique, and D30 is isomorphic to P({2, 3, 5}): a Boolean algebra with 8 elements and a cube-shaped Hasse diagram (12 edges).

D12 = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12}: 3 and 4 are complements (gcd 1, lcm 12), and 1 and 12 are complements, but 2 and 6 have none, because any b with lcm(2, b) = 12 is a multiple of 4 and then gcd(2, b) = 2. D12 is distributive but not complemented.

NTA traps

  • Antisymmetric as “not symmetric”. Wrong: a symmetric relation cannot be antisymmetric. Fix: the diagonal relation is both; 2^n relations are both.
  • Forgetting vacuous truth. Wrong: the empty relation is not transitive. Fix: there are no pairs to break transitivity; it is symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive, but not reflexive on a non-empty set.
  • Onto count. Wrong: n^m − n. Fix: use the full inclusion–exclusion or n!·S(m, n).
  • Maximal versus greatest. Wrong: a poset with maximal elements 8, 9 and 12 has greatest element 12. Fix: a greatest element must be above everything; with several maximal elements there is none.
  • Complement in Dn. Wrong: every element of D12 has complement 12/a. Fix: n/a is a complement only when gcd(a, n/a) = 1.
  • Composition order. Wrong: (f ∘ g)(x) = g(f(x)). Fix: f ∘ g applies g first.
  • Inverse of a composition. Wrong: (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹. Fix: f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹.
  • Power sets. Wrong: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) ∪ P(B). Fix: only the intersection law holds.

How NTA asks this

  • Numerical MCQ: the number of relations, functions, onto functions or equivalence relations; |P(…)|; Hasse-diagram edges; lub and glb in Dn. Write the formula, then substitute; the distractors are usually the neighbouring formulas (2^(n²) instead of 2^(n²−n)).
  • Match the following: relation types with their counts, example relations with their properties, functions with injective/surjective/bijective.
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: complemented and distributive lattices, equivalence classes and partitions, finite versus infinite injections.
  • Multiple select: properties of a given relation, set identities, composition facts.
  • Order: ranking counts for a small n.

Mini-example (A-R). A: Every function from a finite set A to itself that is injective is also surjective. R: Every injective function from ℕ to ℕ is surjective. A is true (n distinct images inside an n-set fill it). R is false (n ↦ n + 1 misses 0). Answer: option 3.

Elimination trick: test any counting option at n = 1 or n = 2, where you can list everything by hand. On a 2-element set there are 16 relations, 4 reflexive, 8 symmetric, 12 antisymmetric and 2 equivalence relations. An option that fails at n = 2 is wrong.
Watch out: “relations from A to B” (2^(mn)) and “relations on A” (2^(n²)) are different questions; so are “functions from A to B” (n^m) and “functions from B to A” (m^n). Read which set is the domain.

terms.definition: P(A), the set of all subsets of A; |P(A)| = 2^|A|.
A subset of A × B; a relation on A is a subset of A × A, so an n-element set has 2^(n²) relations.
Whenever (a, b) and (b, a) are both in R, a = b. It is not the opposite of symmetric: a relation can be both or neither.
A relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; its classes form a partition of the set.
A relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive; the set with it is a poset, drawn as a Hasse diagram.
A poset in which every pair of elements has a least upper bound (join) and a greatest lower bound (meet).
A bounded lattice in which every a has some b with a ∨ b = 1 and a ∧ b = 0.
A function onto its codomain: every element of B is an image. From an m-set onto an n-set there are n!·S(m, n) of them.
Bₙ, the number of partitions (equivalently, equivalence relations) of an n-element set: 1, 2, 5, 15, 52, 203.

terms.term: Stirling number of the second kind
terms.definition: S(m, k), the number of ways to partition an m-element set into exactly k non-empty blocks.

lessons.examTip: For every “how many relations” question, think of the n × n relation matrix: n diagonal cells and n(n − 1)/2 pairs of off-diagonal cells. Each property just restricts what each diagonal cell or each off-diagonal pair may hold, and the count is the product of the choices.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For every counting problem, write “diagonal: … choices, each off-diagonal pair: … choices” before multiplying.

Check every answer with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (antisymmetric read as not symmetric, onto functions counted as n^m − n, maximal confused with greatest).
Verify one formula by hand at n = 2: list all 16 relations on {a, b} and count the reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric and equivalence relations (expect 4, 8, 12 and 2).
Draw the Hasse diagrams of D24, D30 and D36, and mark every complement or write “none”.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then take the lesson quiz and bank questions at 60–90 seconds per question.

quiz.question: How many reflexive relations are there on a set with 3 elements?
quiz.explanation: The relation matrix has 9 cells. Reflexivity forces the 3 diagonal cells to 1, and the other 9 − 3 = 6 cells are free: 2⁶ = 64. 512 = 2⁹ counts all relations.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Symmetric: n diagonal cells free and one choice (both or neither) per off-diagonal pair: 2^n · 2^(n(n−1)/2) = 2^(n(n+1)/2) (II). Reflexive: diagonal fixed, n² − n cells free (III). Antisymmetric: diagonal free, and each off-diagonal pair has 3 allowed states (neither, only (a, b), only (b, a)): 2^n · 3^(n(n−1)/2) (IV). Symmetric and antisymmetric: no off-diagonal pairs at all, only the diagonal is free: 2^n (I).

h: List I (Relations on an n-element set)
b: I. 2^n
III. 2^(n² − n)

quiz.question: How many onto (surjective) functions are there from a set of 5 elements to a set of 3 elements?
quiz.explanation: By inclusion–exclusion, subtract the functions that miss some element: 3⁵ − C(3, 1)·2⁵ + C(3, 2)·1⁵ = 243 − 96 + 3 = 150. Equivalently 3!·S(5, 3) = 6 × 25 = 150. 243 counts all functions.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Equivalence relations and partitions are in one-to-one correspondence (“same block” is the relation), so Statement I is true. The number of partitions of a 4-set is the Bell number B₄ = S(4,1) + S(4,2) + S(4,3) + S(4,4) = 1 + 7 + 6 + 1 = 15, so Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: Every equivalence relation on a set A determines a partition of A into its equivalence classes, and every partition of A determines an equivalence relation on A.
Statement II: The number of equivalence relations on a 4-element set is 15.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: In Dn, join is lcm, meet is gcd, 0 = 1 and 1 = n. A complement b of a needs gcd(a, b) = 1 and lcm(a, b) = n. If gcd(a, n/a) = 1 then b = n/a works, so R is true. But in D12, a = 2 needs lcm(2, b) = 12, so 4 | b, and then gcd(2, b) ≥ 2: 2 (and likewise 6) has no complement, so A is false. Dn is complemented exactly when n is square-free.

stmts: Assertion (A): The lattice D12 of positive divisors of 12 under divisibility is a complemented lattice.
Reason (R): In the divisor lattice Dn, n/a is a complement of a whenever gcd(a, n/a) = 1.

quiz.question: Let f : A → B and g : B → C be functions. Which of the following statements are always true?
quiz.explanation: A: if f(x) = f(y) then g(f(x)) = g(f(y)), so x = y. C: every c ∈ C is g(f(a)) for some a, so it is an image of g. D: undoing “f then g” means undoing g first, then f. B fails: A = {1}, B = {1, 2}, C = {1}, g maps both to 1; g ∘ f is injective but g is not. E fails with the same kind of example: f hits only one element of B, but g ∘ f can still cover C.

stmts: A. If g ∘ f is injective, then f is injective.
B. If g ∘ f is injective, then g is injective.
C. If g ∘ f is surjective, then g is surjective.
D. If f and g are bijections, then (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹.
E. If g ∘ f is surjective, then f is surjective.

quiz.question: How many edges does the Hasse diagram of the poset (D36, |), the positive divisors of 36 under divisibility, have?
quiz.explanation: 36 = 2²·3², so D36 has (2 + 1)(2 + 1) = 9 elements arranged as a 3 × 3 grid of exponents (i, j). An edge joins two divisors whose exponent pairs differ by 1 in one coordinate: 2 × 3 edges in each direction per row or column, 6 + 6 = 12. 9 is the number of vertices.

lessons.title: Counting and recurrences
lessons.summaryHtml: Combinatorics answers “how many?” without listing. This lesson builds the toolkit step by step: the sum and product rules; permutations and combinations, with and without repetition (including stars and bars); the pigeonhole principle; inclusion–exclusion and its most famous use, derangements; recurrence relations and how to solve linear ones with the characteristic equation; generating functions; and the Catalan numbers. NTA uses this unit for short numericals, where the options are close and one wrong model (ordered or unordered, repetition allowed or not) gives a wrong option. Decide the model before you touch a formula, and check small cases when you can.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Counting problems ask how many objects of some kind exist: passwords, committees, seatings, bit strings, routes. Listing them all is too slow, so we split the problem into steps (product rule), into cases (sum rule), or count the opposite and subtract (complement and inclusion–exclusion). When the answer for size n depends on the answers for smaller sizes, we write a recurrence and solve it. Generating functions turn a sequence into a single algebraic object, so that counting becomes multiplying polynomials. The same tools estimate the running time of algorithms in Unit 7.

Why it matters for NET

Counting gives quick numericals in almost every Paper 2. The dominant patterns are: arrangements of letters with repeated symbols; committees with conditions; stars and bars (integer solutions, identical objects into distinct boxes); pigeonhole “minimum number to guarantee” questions; inclusion–exclusion for divisibility and bounded solutions; derangements; the closed form of a linear recurrence; the coefficient of a term in a binomial or generating-function expansion; and Catalan numbers disguised as binary trees, stack permutations or bracket sequences. Most distractors come from using the wrong model, so train the modelling step, not just the formulas.

Concepts in depth: the basic rules

Sum rule: if a task can be done in one of two disjoint ways, with m and n options, there are m + n options. Product rule: a sequence of two independent steps with m and n options gives m × n. Subtraction rule: for overlapping cases, |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. Complement: it is often easier to count what you do not want: 4-digit strings with at least one repeated digit = 10⁴ − 10·9·8·7 = 4960.

Concepts in depth: permutations and combinations

Choosing r from nOrder mattersOrder does not matter
No repetitionP(n, r) = n!/(n − r)!C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n − r)!)
Repetition allowedn^rC(n + r − 1, r)
  • Circular arrangements of n distinct objects: (n − 1)!, because rotations are the same. If a flip is also the same (a necklace or garland), (n − 1)!/2 for n ≥ 3.
  • Permutations of a multiset with n₁ copies of one kind, n₂ of another, …: n!/(n₁!·n₂!·…·nₖ!). MISSISSIPPI gives 11!/(4!·4!·2!·1!) = 34650.
  • Useful identities: C(n, r) = C(n, n − r); Pascal’s rule C(n, r) = C(n − 1, r − 1) + C(n − 1, r); Σ C(n, r) = 2ⁿ; Vandermonde Σ C(m, k)C(n, r − k) = C(m + n, r).
  • Binomial theorem: (x + y)ⁿ = Σ C(n, k) x^k y^(n−k). The general term is T(k+1) = C(n, k) x^(n−k) y^k; keep the sign and coefficient of each part, since (2x − y)⁷ has the x³y⁴ term C(7, 3)(2x)³(−y)⁴ = 280x³y⁴.

Stars and bars. To count non-negative solutions of x₁ + … + xₖ = n, write n stars and k − 1 bars in a row; the bars cut the stars into k groups. Choosing the positions of the bars among n + k − 1 symbols gives C(n + k − 1, k − 1). For positive solutions, give each variable 1 first: C(n − 1, k − 1). For a lower bound xᵢ ≥ a, substitute xᵢ = yᵢ + a and reduce the total. Upper bounds need inclusion–exclusion.

Distributing n objects into k boxesAny number per boxNo box empty
Distinct objects, distinct boxeskⁿk!·S(n, k)
Identical objects, distinct boxesC(n + k − 1, k − 1)C(n − 1, k − 1)
Distinct objects, identical boxesS(n, 1) + … + S(n, k)S(n, k)
Identical objects, identical boxesinteger partitions of n (no simple formula)

Concepts in depth: the pigeonhole principle

If N objects go into k boxes, some box holds at least ⌈N/k⌉ objects; otherwise the total would be at most k(⌈N/k⌉ − 1) < N. The “guarantee” form: to be sure that some box has r objects, you need k(r − 1) + 1 objects, since k(r − 1) can be spread with r − 1 in every box. The art is choosing the boxes. Examples: choosing 11 numbers from {1, …, 20} guarantees two that sum to 21 (boxes are the 10 pairs {1, 20}, …, {10, 11}); among any n + 1 integers two have the same remainder mod n; in any group of people two have the same number of friends inside the group. A deeper consequence (Erdős–Szekeres) is that every sequence of n² + 1 distinct numbers has a monotone subsequence of length n + 1.

Concepts in depth: inclusion–exclusion

For three sets, |A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A| + |B| + |C| − |A ∩ B| − |A ∩ C| − |B ∩ C| + |A ∩ B ∩ C|. In general, add the single sets, subtract the pairwise intersections, add the triple ones, and so on with alternating signs. An element that lies in exactly m of the sets is counted C(m,1) − C(m,2) + … = 1 time, which is why the formula works. The number of elements in none of the sets is the total minus the union. Standard applications are divisibility counts (the count of multiples of d up to N is ⌊N/d⌋, and a multiple of both a and b is a multiple of lcm(a, b)); Euler’s φ(n) = n·Π(1 − 1/p); onto functions (lesson 1.2); integer solutions with upper bounds; and derangements.

Concepts in depth: derangements

A derangement of n objects is a permutation with no fixed point. Let Aᵢ be the permutations that fix i. |Aᵢ| = (n − 1)!, the permutations fixing a given set of k points number (n − k)!, and there are C(n, k) such sets. Inclusion–exclusion gives Dₙ = Σₖ (−1)^k C(n, k)(n − k)! = n! Σₖ (−1)^k/k!. The values are D₁ = 0, D₂ = 1, D₃ = 2, D₄ = 9, D₅ = 44, D₆ = 265, D₇ = 1854. Two recurrences help with checking: Dₙ = (n − 1)(Dₙ₋₁ + Dₙ₋₂) and Dₙ = nDₙ₋₁ + (−1)ⁿ. Because the series is that of e⁻¹, Dₙ is the integer nearest to n!/e for n ≥ 1, and the probability that a random permutation is a derangement tends to 1/e ≈ 0.368. Permutations with exactly k fixed points number C(n, k)·Dₙ₋ₖ.

Concepts in depth: recurrence relations

A recurrence expresses aₙ through earlier terms, plus initial conditions. Classic models: Tower of Hanoi Hₙ = 2Hₙ₋₁ + 1 (so Hₙ = 2ⁿ − 1); binary strings with no two consecutive 0s, bₙ = bₙ₋₁ + bₙ₋₂; regions made by n lines in general position, Rₙ = Rₙ₋₁ + n, so Rₙ = (n² + n + 2)/2; compound interest aₙ = (1 + r)aₙ₋₁.

Linear homogeneous with constant coefficients: aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + … + cₖaₙ₋ₖ. Try aₙ = rⁿ to get the characteristic equation r^k − c₁r^(k−1) − … − cₖ = 0. If its roots r₁, …, rₖ are distinct, aₙ = α₁r₁ⁿ + … + αₖrₖⁿ. A root r of multiplicity m contributes (α₀ + α₁n + … + αₘ₋₁n^(m−1))rⁿ. The constants come from the initial conditions.

Non-homogeneous: aₙ = (homogeneous part) + F(n). The general solution is the homogeneous solution plus one particular solution.

F(n)Try as particular solution
constant dconstant A (if 1 is a root of multiplicity m, use A·n^m)
polynomial of degree tgeneral polynomial of degree t (times n^m if 1 is a root of multiplicity m)
d·sⁿA·sⁿ, or A·n^m·sⁿ if s is a root of multiplicity m

The first-order case aₙ = c·aₙ₋₁ + d (c ≠ 1) has the closed form aₙ = cⁿ(a₀ − p) + p, where p = d/(1 − c) is the fixed point. For example, aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ + 4 with a₀ = 1 has p = −2, so aₙ = 3·3ⁿ − 2 = 3ⁿ⁺¹ − 2. Divide-and-conquer recurrences such as T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n are solved by the master theorem in lesson 7.4.

Concepts in depth: generating functions

The ordinary generating function of a₀, a₁, a₂, … is G(x) = Σ aₙxⁿ, treated as a formal power series.

G(x)aₙ
1/(1 − x)1
1/(1 − ax)aⁿ
1/(1 − x)²n + 1
1/(1 − x)^kC(n + k − 1, k − 1)
(1 + x)^mC(m, n)
(1 − x^(m+1))/(1 − x)1 for n ≤ m, else 0
x/(1 − x − x²)Fibonacci Fₙ (F₀ = 0)

The key rule is that multiplying generating functions convolves the sequences: the coefficient of x^n in A(x)B(x) is Σ aₖbₙ₋ₖ. So the number of solutions of x₁ + x₂ + x₃ = n with each xᵢ in a set Sᵢ is the coefficient of xⁿ in the product of the polynomials Σ_{s∈Sᵢ} x^s. To solve a recurrence, multiply it by xⁿ, sum over n, solve for G(x) and split it into partial fractions. Exponential generating functions Σ aₙxⁿ/n! do the same job when the objects are labelled (arrangements rather than selections).

Concepts in depth: Catalan numbers

Cₙ = C(2n, n)/(n + 1) = C(2n, n) − C(2n, n + 1): 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, 429, 1430, 4862 for n = 0 to 9. They satisfy C₀ = 1 and Cₙ₊₁ = Σᵢ CᵢCₙ₋ᵢ, because a structure of size n + 1 splits into a “left part” of size i and a “right part” of size n − i. Cₙ counts: balanced strings of n pairs of parentheses; binary trees with n nodes (so binary search trees on n distinct keys); full binary trees with n + 1 leaves; triangulations of a convex (n + 2)-gon; monotone lattice paths from (0, 0) to (n, n) that never go above the diagonal; ways to parenthesise a product of n + 1 factors; and stack permutations of 1, …, n. The second formula comes from the reflection principle: of the C(2n, n) paths, exactly C(2n, n + 1) touch the line one step above the diagonal.

Worked examples

Example 1: letters with repetition. How many arrangements of MISSISSIPPI are there, and in how many are the four S’s together?

  1. Counts: M 1, I 4, S 4, P 2; total 11. All arrangements: 11!/(1!·4!·4!·2!) = 39916800/1152 = 34650.
  2. Glue SSSS into one block. Now arrange 8 items (the block, M, IIII, PP): 8!/(4!·2!) = 40320/48 = 840.

A common error is to multiply by 4! for the order inside the block; the S’s are identical, so there is only one internal order.

Example 2: stars and bars with bounds. (a) Count the integer solutions of x₁ + x₂ + x₃ + x₄ = 20 with x₁ ≥ 2, x₂ ≥ 3, x₃ ≥ 0, x₄ ≥ 0. (b) Count the solutions of x₁ + x₂ + x₃ = 10 with 0 ≤ xᵢ ≤ 4.

(a) Put x₁ = y₁ + 2, x₂ = y₂ + 3. Then y₁ + y₂ + x₃ + x₄ = 15 with all variables ≥ 0: C(15 + 3, 3) = C(18, 3) = 816.

(b) No upper bounds: C(12, 2) = 66. One variable ≥ 5: total drops to 5, C(7, 2) = 21, for each of 3 variables. Two variables ≥ 5: total drops to 0, C(2, 2) = 1, for each of 3 pairs. Three variables ≥ 5 is impossible. Answer: 66 − 63 + 3 = 6. As a generating function, this is the coefficient of x¹⁰ in (1 + x + x² + x³ + x⁴)³.

Example 3: inclusion–exclusion for divisibility. How many integers in 1 to 1000 are divisible by none of 2, 3, 5?

TermSetsCount
Singles⌊1000/2⌋ + ⌊1000/3⌋ + ⌊1000/5⌋500 + 333 + 200 = 1033
Pairs⌊1000/6⌋ + ⌊1000/10⌋ + ⌊1000/15⌋166 + 100 + 66 = 332
Triple⌊1000/30⌋33

At least one: 1033 − 332 + 33 = 734. None: 1000 − 734 = 266. Sanity check: 1000 × (1/2)(2/3)(4/5) ≈ 266.7, and the exact count is close.

Example 4: derangements. Five students hand in their phones and get them back at random. (a) How many ways does no one get their own phone? (b) Exactly two get their own?

(a) D₅ = 120(1 − 1 + 1/2 − 1/6 + 1/24 − 1/120) = 60 − 20 + 5 − 1 = 44. The probability is 44/120 ≈ 0.367, close to 1/e.

(b) Choose the two lucky students, C(5, 2) = 10, and derange the other three, D₃ = 2: 10 × 2 = 20.

Example 5: distinct and repeated roots. (a) Solve aₙ = 5aₙ₋₁ − 6aₙ₋₂, a₀ = 1, a₁ = 4. (b) Solve aₙ = 4aₙ₋₁ − 4aₙ₋₂, a₀ = 1, a₁ = 4.

(a) r² − 5r + 6 = 0, r = 2, 3. aₙ = α2ⁿ + β3ⁿ; α + β = 1, 2α + 3β = 4, so β = 2, α = −1: aₙ = 2·3ⁿ − 2ⁿ. Terms: 1, 4, 14, 46.

(b) r² − 4r + 4 = 0, r = 2 twice. aₙ = (α + βn)2ⁿ; α = 1, 2(1 + β) = 4, so β = 1: aₙ = (n + 1)2ⁿ. Terms: 1, 4, 12, 32, and indeed 4·12 − 4·4 = 32.

Example 6: a non-homogeneous recurrence. Solve aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ + 2ⁿ with a₀ = 1.

  1. Homogeneous part: r = 3, so A·3ⁿ.
  2. F(n) = 2ⁿ and 2 is not a root, so try C·2ⁿ: C·2ⁿ = 3C·2ⁿ⁻¹ + 2ⁿ. Divide by 2ⁿ⁻¹: 2C = 3C + 2, so C = −2, and the particular solution is −2ⁿ⁺¹.
  3. aₙ = A·3ⁿ − 2ⁿ⁺¹; a₀ = A − 2 = 1 gives A = 3: aₙ = 3ⁿ⁺¹ − 2ⁿ⁺¹.

Check: a₁ = 3 + 2 = 5 = 9 − 4, and a₂ = 15 + 4 = 19 = 27 − 8.

Example 7: a recurrence from a counting problem, solved with a generating function. Let aₙ be the number of moves for the Tower of Hanoi with n discs: a₀ = 0, aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ + 1.

  1. Multiply by xⁿ and sum for n ≥ 1: G(x) − a₀ = 2xG(x) + x/(1 − x).
  2. So G(x) = x/((1 − x)(1 − 2x)) = 1/(1 − 2x) − 1/(1 − x).
  3. Read off the coefficients: aₙ = 2ⁿ − 1. For 10 discs, 1023 moves.

Example 8: Catalan numbers. How many binary search trees can be built from the keys 1, 2, 3, 4?

The root k splits the keys into k − 1 on the left and 4 − k on the right, so the count is C₀C₃ + C₁C₂ + C₂C₁ + C₃C₀ = 5 + 2 + 2 + 5 = 14 = C₄. The closed form agrees: C(8, 4)/5 = 70/5 = 14, and by reflection C(8, 4) − C(8, 5) = 70 − 56 = 14.

NTA traps

  • Wrong model. Wrong: using C(n, r) when order matters, or nPr for a committee. Fix: ask “would swapping two chosen items give a different outcome?”
  • Positive versus non-negative. Wrong: C(n + k − 1, k − 1) for “each gets at least one”. Fix: C(n − 1, k − 1).
  • Circular arrangements. Wrong: n! seatings at a round table. Fix: (n − 1)!; halve it only when mirror images are the same.
  • Stopping inclusion–exclusion early. Wrong: subtracting the pairs and forgetting to add back the triple. Fix: write all 2³ − 1 = 7 terms for three sets.
  • Pigeonhole off by one. Wrong: 4 grades and “5 with the same grade” needs 20 students. Fix: 4 × 4 + 1 = 17.
  • Repeated roots. Wrong: aₙ = α2ⁿ + β2ⁿ for a double root 2. Fix: (α + βn)2ⁿ.
  • Resonance. Wrong: trying A·3ⁿ as a particular solution of aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ + 3ⁿ. Fix: 3 is a root, so try A·n·3ⁿ.
  • Catalan index. Wrong: n + 2-gon triangulations = Cₙ₊₂. Fix: a convex (n + 2)-gon has Cₙ triangulations; an octagon has C₆ = 132.

How NTA asks this

  • Numerical MCQ: arrangements, committees, solutions, divisibility counts, derangements, the n-th term of a recurrence, a binomial coefficient, a Catalan count. Estimate first (the answer to “none of 2, 3, 5 up to 1000” must be near 1000 × 4/15), then compute.
  • Match the following: special numbers with their values, generating functions with sequences, recurrences with closed forms, counting models with formulas.
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: pigeonhole statements, derangement formulas, characteristic roots, Catalan interpretations.
  • Multiple select: which problems a given formula counts; which structures are counted by Catalan numbers.
  • Order: ranking several counts (nPr, C(n, r), Dₙ, Cₙ, Bₙ) by size.

Mini-example (A-R). A: The number of onto functions from a 4-set to a 3-set is 36. R: By inclusion–exclusion it equals 3⁴ − 3·2⁴ + 3·1⁴. Both are true, and R is the computation that proves A: option 1.

Elimination trick: check a recurrence’s closed-form options at n = 0 and n = 1 against the initial conditions. Usually only one option survives both, without solving anything.
Watch out: Fibonacci indexing differs between books (most start F₀ = 0, F₁ = 1; some start F₀ = F₁ = 1, which shifts every index by one). When a question states the indexing, use it; when it does not, compute the first few terms of the counting problem directly.

terms.definition: If a task is a sequence of two steps with m and n ways, the whole task can be done in m × n ways.
Choosing r items from n types when repeats are allowed and order does not matter: C(n + r − 1, r) ways (stars and bars).
If N objects go into k boxes, some box holds at least ⌈N/k⌉ objects.
|A₁ ∪ … ∪ Aₙ| = Σ|Aᵢ| − Σ|Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ| + Σ|Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ ∩ Aₖ| − … with alternating signs.
A permutation with no fixed point. Dₙ = n!(1 − 1/1! + 1/2! − … + (−1)ⁿ/n!): 0, 1, 2, 9, 44, 265.
For aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + … + cₖaₙ₋ₖ, the equation r^k = c₁r^(k−1) + … + cₖ; its roots give the general solution.
The power series G(x) = Σ aₙxⁿ that stores a whole sequence; products of generating functions count combined choices.
Cₙ = C(2n, n)/(n + 1): 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132. Counts binary trees, balanced parentheses, triangulations and more.

lessons.title: Induction and discrete probability
lessons.summaryHtml: This lesson joins two tools that NTA tests together under discrete mathematics. Mathematical induction proves that a statement holds for every natural number: prove a base case, then prove that the truth of one case forces the truth of the next. Strong induction and the well-ordering principle are equivalent variants that let you lean on all earlier cases. Discrete probability starts from the three axioms and builds conditional probability, independence, the total probability rule and Bayes’ theorem, which is the single most-asked numerical here. It ends with random variables, expectation (and its linearity), variance, and the four distributions you must know cold: Bernoulli, binomial, geometric and Poisson.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Induction is a way to prove infinitely many statements with a finite amount of work. Picture an endless row of dominoes. If you knock over the first one, and every domino is close enough to knock over the next, then every domino falls. The first push is the base case; the spacing rule is the inductive step. You never have to check the millionth domino directly.

Probability measures uncertainty with numbers between 0 and 1. In discrete probability the outcomes can be listed (coin tosses, dice, cards, bits, keys in a hash table), so most questions reduce to careful counting plus a few rules: the complement rule, the addition rule, conditional probability, and Bayes’ theorem for reasoning backwards from an effect to its cause. A random variable turns outcomes into numbers, and its expectation and variance summarise it.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 1 contributes a steady share of Paper 2 questions, and this lesson feeds it regularly. Induction appears mostly as concept questions: which principle is equivalent to which, what a valid inductive step needs, where a flawed proof breaks, and the smallest n from which an inequality holds. Probability appears as short numericals: Bayes’ theorem (machines, boxes, medical tests), dice and card counting, “at least one” questions via the complement, independence versus mutual exclusion, and the mean and variance of standard distributions. The same ideas return in other units (expected probes in hashing, randomised quicksort, Bayesian networks in AI, ALOHA in networks), so time spent here pays twice.

Concepts in depth: mathematical induction

Ordinary (weak) induction. To prove P(n) for all n ≥ n₀: (1) base case: prove P(n₀); (2) inductive step: for an arbitrary k ≥ n₀, assume P(k) (the inductive hypothesis) and deduce P(k + 1). Both parts are essential. Without the base case, “n = n + 1” has a perfectly valid inductive step and is still false. Without a valid step, checking many cases proves nothing: n² + n + 41 is prime for n = 0, 1, …, 39 but fails at n = 40, where it equals 1681 = 41².

Why it works. Suppose P fails somewhere. The set of failures is a non-empty set of integers ≥ n₀, so by well-ordering it has a least element m. m ≠ n₀ because the base case holds, so m − 1 ≥ n₀ and P(m − 1) is true (m is the least failure). The inductive step then gives P(m), a contradiction. This argument shows that well-ordering implies induction; the converse also holds, and so do both directions with strong induction. The three principles are equivalent.

Strong (complete) induction. The hypothesis is that P(n₀), P(n₀ + 1), …, P(k) are all true, and you prove P(k + 1). Use it when k + 1 depends on a case further back than k. Standard examples: every integer n ≥ 2 is a product of primes (if k + 1 is composite, it is a × b with both factors smaller); Fibonacci bounds such as Fn < 2n (Fk+1 = Fk + Fk−1 needs two earlier cases); and postage problems. When the step reaches back j cases, you need j base cases.

Well-ordering and minimal counterexample. The well-ordering principle says every non-empty set of non-negative integers has a least element. It is false for the integers (no least element) and for the positive rationals (1/n gets smaller forever). A proof by minimal counterexample assumes a smallest failure and derives a smaller one, a contradiction.

Structural induction proves properties of recursively defined objects (strings, lists, binary trees, well-formed formulas): prove it for the basis objects, then show every construction rule preserves it. For example, a full binary tree with i internal nodes has i + 1 leaves.

Where flawed proofs break. The classic “all horses are the same colour” argument removes one horse, then another, from a group of k + 1 and relies on the two groups of k overlapping. For k + 1 = 2 the two groups of size 1 do not overlap, so the step P(1) → P(2) fails. NTA likes to ask exactly where such a chain breaks.

Concepts in depth: probability axioms and basic rules

A sample space S is the set of all outcomes; an event is a subset. Kolmogorov’s axioms: (1) P(E) ≥ 0; (2) P(S) = 1; (3) for mutually exclusive events, P(E₁ ∪ E₂ ∪ …) = P(E₁) + P(E₂) + …. Everything else follows:

  • P(Ē) = 1 − P(E), and P(∅) = 0.
  • If A ⊆ B then P(A) ≤ P(B).
  • Addition rule: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). For three events add back the triple intersection (inclusion–exclusion).
  • Boole’s inequality: P(A ∪ B) ≤ P(A) + P(B).

With equally likely outcomes, P(E) = |E| / |S|, so counting techniques from Lesson 1.3 do the work. “At least one” is almost always easier through the complement: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).

Concepts in depth: conditional probability, independence and Bayes

Conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) restricts the sample space to B. Rearranged, it is the multiplication rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(B) P(A | B). For draws without replacement, multiply along the sequence: P(two aces) = 4/52 × 3/51 = 1/221.

Independence means P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A | B) = P(A). If A and B are independent, so are A and B̄, Ā and B, and Ā and B̄. Do not confuse it with mutual exclusion (P(A ∩ B) = 0): two exclusive events with positive probabilities are always dependent. For three events, pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence. Toss two fair coins; let A = first is heads, B = second is heads, C = both show the same face. Each has probability ½, each pair intersects with probability ¼, but P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = ¼ ≠ ⅛.

Total probability. If B₁, …, Bₙ partition S (disjoint, covering S), then P(A) = Σ P(A | Bᵢ) P(Bᵢ). Bayes’ theorem reverses the conditioning:

P(Bi | A) = P(A | Bi) P(Bi) / [ P(A | B1) P(B1) + ... + P(A | Bn) P(Bn) ]

P(Bᵢ) is the prior, P(A | Bᵢ) the likelihood, and P(Bᵢ | A) the posterior. The practical method is a tree: first-level branches are the causes with their priors, second-level branches are the observation with its likelihoods; multiply along each path, then divide the path you want by the sum of the paths that show the observation.

Concepts in depth: random variables, expectation and variance

A discrete random variable X has a PMF p(x) = P(X = x) with p(x) ≥ 0 and Σ p(x) = 1, and a CDF F(x) = P(X ≤ x), which is non-decreasing and rises from 0 to 1. The expectation is E[X] = Σ x p(x), and more generally E[g(X)] = Σ g(x) p(x).

Linearity of expectation, E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y], holds for any random variables, dependent or not. Combined with indicator variables (I = 1 if an event happens, else 0, so E[I] = P(event)), it solves problems that look hard:

  • Expected fixed points of a random permutation of n items: n × (1/n) = 1, for every n.
  • Expected inversions of a random permutation: each of the C(n, 2) pairs is inverted with probability ½, so n(n − 1)/4.
  • Expected number of heads in n tosses with bias p: np.
  • Coupon collector: expected draws to see all n types is n(1 + ½ + … + 1/n); for a die, 6 × 49/20 = 14.7 rolls.

Variance measures spread: Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − μ². The standard deviation is its square root. Rules: Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X) (shifting does not change spread, scaling squares); Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) only when X and Y are independent (in general add 2 Cov(X, Y)). Likewise E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] for independent variables.

The geometric distribution is memoryless: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t). The Poisson approximation replaces Binomial(n, p) by Poisson(λ = np) when n is large and p is small: for 100 bits with error rate 0.02, P(no error) is exactly 0.98100 ≈ 0.1326, and e−2 ≈ 0.1353. The sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson with the rates added; the sum of independent binomials with the same p is binomial.

Worked examples

Example 1 (weak induction). Prove that 6 divides n³ − n for every n ≥ 1.

Base case: n = 1 gives 1 − 1 = 0, and 6 divides 0.

Step: assume 6 | k³ − k. Then (k + 1)³ − (k + 1) = k³ + 3k² + 3k + 1 − k − 1 = (k³ − k) + 3k(k + 1). The first term is divisible by 6 by the hypothesis. k(k + 1) is a product of consecutive integers, so it is even, and 3k(k + 1) is divisible by 6. Hence 6 divides the sum, which is P(k + 1). By induction the claim holds for all n ≥ 1.

Example 2 (strong induction). Show that every amount n ≥ 12 can be paid exactly with 4-unit and 5-unit stamps.

Base cases: 12 = 4 + 4 + 4, 13 = 4 + 4 + 5, 14 = 4 + 5 + 5, 15 = 5 + 5 + 5.

Step: for k ≥ 15, assume every amount from 12 to k can be paid. Then k + 1 − 4 = k − 3 ≥ 12 can be paid by hypothesis; add one 4-unit stamp. Because the step reaches back 4 places, four base cases are needed. The amount 11 cannot be paid, so 12 is the least starting point (11 = 4 × 5 − 4 − 5, the Frobenius number).

Example 3 (Bayes with three causes). Machines A, B and C make 50%, 30% and 20% of a factory’s bolts, with defect rates 3%, 4% and 5%. A bolt is found defective. Which machine most likely made it?

MachinePriorP(defective | machine)Path productPosterior
A0.50.030.01515/37 ≈ 0.405
B0.30.040.01212/37 ≈ 0.324
C0.20.050.01010/37 ≈ 0.270
Total0.0371

P(defective) = 0.037 by total probability. Machine A is the most likely source (15/37), even though C has the highest defect rate: its larger share of production outweighs its lower rate.

Example 4 (binomial, complement, geometric). A fair coin is tossed 5 times.

  • P(exactly 3 heads) = C(5, 3)/2⁵ = 10/32 = 5/16.
  • P(at least one head) = 1 − (½)⁵ = 31/32.
  • E[heads] = np = 5/2; Var = np(1 − p) = 5/4.

A die is rolled until the first six. P(first six on roll 3) = (5/6)² × (1/6) = 25/216. Expected number of rolls = 1/p = 6.

Example 5 (Poisson). Packets reach a router at an average of 2 per millisecond (Poisson). Find P(no packet), P(at most one) and P(at least two) in a millisecond.

P(0) = e−2 ≈ 0.1353. P(1) = 2e−2 ≈ 0.2707. P(X ≤ 1) = 3e−2 ≈ 0.4060. P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − 3e−2 ≈ 0.5940. Mean and variance are both 2.

Example 6 (expectation and variance from a PMF). X takes values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3.

E[X] = 0 + 0.5 + 0.6 = 1.1. E[X²] = 0 + 0.5 + 1.2 = 1.7. Var(X) = 1.7 − 1.21 = 0.49, so the standard deviation is 0.7. For Y = 3X − 2: E[Y] = 3(1.1) − 2 = 1.3 and Var(Y) = 9 × 0.49 = 4.41; the −2 does not affect variance.

Formula and fact sheet

NTA traps

  • Reversing the conditional. Wrong: “the test is 99% accurate, so a positive person is 99% likely to be ill.” Fix: 99% is P(+ | D). The posterior P(D | +) depends on the prior; with 1% prevalence and a 5% false-positive rate it is only 1/6.
  • Exclusive = independent. Wrong: “they cannot happen together, so they do not affect each other.” Fix: exclusive events with positive probabilities are dependent: one happening forces the other not to.
  • Adding probabilities of overlapping events. Wrong: P(at least one six in 4 rolls) = 4/6. Fix: use 1 − (5/6)⁴ = 671/1296.
  • Pairwise = mutual. Fix: check every sub-collection; the two-coin example is pairwise but not mutually independent.
  • Variance of a sum. Wrong: Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y always, or Var(2X) = 2 Var X. Fix: additivity needs independence; scaling by a multiplies variance by a².
  • Geometric convention. Fix: read whether X counts trials (mean 1/p) or failures (mean (1 − p)/p). Both have variance (1 − p)/p².
  • Induction without a base case, or with too few. Fix: a step that uses P(k − 3) needs four base cases.
  • Checking cases is not a proof. n² + n + 41 is prime for n = 0 to 39 and fails at 40.
  • Ordered vs unordered outcomes. With two dice, (4, 6) and (6, 4) are different outcomes; the sample space has 36, not 21, equally likely points.

How NTA asks this

  • Direct numericals: Bayes (two or three causes), dice and card probabilities, “at least one”, binomial probabilities, the mean and variance of a given PMF or distribution, Poisson values with e−λ. Draw the tree, keep fractions, and compare with the options only at the end; distractors are usually the reversed conditional, the prior, or P(observation).
  • Match the following: distributions with means or variances, event types with their defining equations, induction variants with their hypotheses.
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: exclusive versus independent, pairwise versus mutual independence, linearity of expectation without independence, equivalence of well-ordering and induction, why a flawed induction proof fails.
  • Multiple select and ordering: which rules always hold, which functions are valid PMFs, arranging events by probability, or arranging the steps of an induction proof.

Mini-example (A-R). A: E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] for any two random variables with finite means. R: If X and Y are independent, Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). Both statements are true, but R is about variance under independence and does not explain A, which needs no independence at all: option 2.

Remember: eliminate fast with sanity checks. A probability above 1 or below 0 is impossible; a posterior must move from the prior in the direction the evidence points; a variance can never be negative, and it is unchanged by adding a constant.

terms.definition: If P(n₀) is true and P(k) → P(k+1) for every k ≥ n₀, then P(n) is true for every n ≥ n₀.
The inductive step may assume P(n₀), P(n₀+1), …, P(k) all together to prove P(k+1). Logically equivalent to ordinary induction.
Every non-empty set of non-negative (or positive) integers has a least element. Equivalent to induction; used in proofs by minimal counterexample.
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), defined only when P(B) > 0.
P(A ∩ B) = P(A) · P(B). For three or more events, mutual independence needs the product rule for every sub-collection, not just every pair.
P(Bᵢ | A) = P(A | Bᵢ) P(Bᵢ) / Σⱼ P(A | Bⱼ) P(Bⱼ) for a partition B₁, …, Bₙ of the sample space.
A function from the sample space to real numbers. A discrete one has a probability mass function p(x) = P(X = x) with Σ p(x) = 1.
E[X] = Σ x · p(x). It is linear: E[aX + bY + c] = aE[X] + bE[Y] + c for any X, Y, independent or not.
Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − (E[X])². Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X).
P(X = k) = e^(−λ) λ^k / k!, k = 0, 1, 2, …; mean = variance = λ. The limit of Binomial(n, p) when n → ∞ and np = λ stays fixed.

quiz.question: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test detects it in 99% of people who have it, but also gives a positive result for 5% of healthy people. A randomly chosen person tests positive. What is the probability that the person has the disease?
quiz.explanation: Tree: P(D ∩ +) = 0.01 × 0.99 = 0.0099; P(D̄ ∩ +) = 0.99 × 0.05 = 0.0495. P(+) = 0.0594 (total probability). P(D | +) = 0.0099 / 0.0594 = 1/6 ≈ 0.167. 0.99 is P(+ | D), the reversed conditional (the classic trap). 0.0594 is P(+), not the posterior. 5/6 is P(healthy | +).

quiz.explanation: Bernoulli: E[X²] = p, so Var = p − p² = p(1 − p) (III). Binomial is a sum of n independent Bernoullis, so Var = np(1 − p) (II). Geometric (trials): mean 1/p, variance (1 − p)/p² (IV); the same variance holds for the “failures before success” version. Poisson: mean = variance = λ (I).

quiz.question: A fair die is rolled 4 times. What is the probability of getting at least one six?
quiz.explanation: Use the complement: P(no six in 4 rolls) = (5/6)⁴ = 625/1296. So P(at least one six) = 1 − 625/1296 = 671/1296 ≈ 0.518. 2/3 comes from wrongly adding 1/6 four times (the events are not exclusive). 625/1296 is the complement itself.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Statement I is a standard result: each principle can be derived from the others. Statement II is false: the base case(s) must still be proved (for example the postage proof checks 12, 13, 14 and 15 separately). A formally stated strong induction can hide the base case inside the step for k = n₀, but it must still be argued; skipping it is exactly how false “proofs” arise.

stmts: Statement I: Over the natural numbers, the well-ordering principle, ordinary (weak) induction and strong induction are logically equivalent.
Statement II: A proof by strong induction never needs a base case, because the hypothesis already assumes all earlier cases.

quiz.question: X is the number shown by a fair six-sided die. What are E[X] and Var(X)?
Which of the following statements are correct for any events A and B with P(B) > 0?
options: A, C, D and E only
A, B, C and D only
quiz.explanation: A follows from P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) (Boole’s inequality). C holds because A ∩ B ⊆ A. D is the complement rule. E: P(A | B) = P(A) means P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). B is false in general: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) and P(B | A) = P(A ∩ B)/P(A), equal only if P(A) = P(B) (or P(A ∩ B) = 0).

stmts: A. P(A ∪ B) ≤ P(A) + P(B)
B. P(A | B) = P(B | A)
C. P(A ∩ B) ≤ P(A)
E. If P(A | B) = P(A), then A and B are independent
