lessons.title: Group theory
lessons.summaryHtml: Group theory studies sets with one operation that behaves well. Add axioms one at a time and you climb a ladder: a groupoid (closure), a semigroup (associativity), a monoid (identity) and a group (inverses); if the operation also commutes, the group is abelian. The key numbers are the order of a group and the order of an element. Lagrange’s theorem ties them together: the order of every subgroup, and of every element, divides the order of the group. Cyclic groups are fully described by their order: ℤₙ has φ(n) generators and exactly one subgroup for each divisor of n. The lesson also covers cosets, normal subgroups, homomorphisms and isomorphisms, permutation groups, and the basics of rings, integral domains and fields.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Think of a Rubik’s cube. Each move scrambles it, doing two moves in a row is again a move, every move can be undone, and “do nothing” is a move too. Group theory captures exactly this pattern: a set of actions or values, one way of combining them, a neutral element, and an undo for everything. The same pattern shows up in clock arithmetic (ℤₙ), in shuffles of cards (permutations), in rotations of a square, and in the non-zero numbers under multiplication. Once you know a structure is a group, a handful of theorems tell you a great deal about it with almost no calculation.

Why it matters for NET

Algebraic structures are a regular part of the discrete-structures questions in Paper 2. The recurring question types are: is a given set and operation a semigroup, monoid or group; find the identity or an inverse for an unusual operation; the order of an element; the number of generators or subgroups of a cyclic group; which subgroup orders Lagrange allows; the order of a permutation; the definitions of normal subgroups and homomorphisms; and whether a given ℤₙ is a field or has zero divisors. Nearly all of them are solved by a formula or a single counterexample, so they reward exact definitions.

Concepts in depth: binary operations and the structure ladder

A binary operation on a set S is a rule * that combines any two elements of S into an element of S. “Into S” is the closure property, and it is the first thing to check: subtraction is a binary operation on ℤ but not on ℕ (3 − 5 ∉ ℕ); division is not one on ℤ.

StructureAxiomsExampleNon-example (fails)
Groupoid (magma)closure(ℤ, −)(ℕ, −): not closed
Semigroup+ associativity(ℤ⁺, +), strings under concatenation without ε(ℤ, −): (5 − 3) − 1 ≠ 5 − (3 − 1)
Monoid+ identity(ℕ ∪ {0}, +), (ℤ, ×), strings with ε(ℤ⁺, +): no 0
Group+ inverses(ℤ, +), (ℚ \ {0}, ×), (ℤₙ, +ₙ), Sₙ(ℤ, ×): 2 has no inverse
Abelian group+ commutativity(ℤ, +), (ℤₙ, +ₙ), U(n)S₃, invertible 2 × 2 matrices

Basic facts in every group. The identity is unique, and each element has exactly one inverse. (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹ (reverse order, like taking off socks and shoes). Left and right cancellation hold: ab = ac ⟹ b = c. The equations ax = b and ya = b have unique solutions x = a⁻¹b and y = ba⁻¹, so every row and column of a finite group’s Cayley table contains each element exactly once (a Latin square). If every element satisfies a² = e, the group is abelian, because ab = (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹ = ba. Every group of order at most 5 is abelian; the smallest non-abelian group is S₃, of order 6.

Checking an unusual operation. For a * b defined by a formula, test closure, associativity, then solve a * e = a for the identity and a * b = e for the inverse. Two common families: a * b = a + b + k on ℤ (identity −k, inverse −a − 2k) and a * b = ab/k on ℚ⁺ (identity k, inverse k²/a).

Concepts in depth: order, subgroups and Lagrange

The order of a group |G| is its number of elements. The order of an element a is the least n ≥ 1 with aⁿ = e; if no such n exists the order is infinite. The identity is the only element of order 1. In ℤₙ, o(k) = n / gcd(n, k). In any group, if o(a) = n, then o(aᵏ) = n / gcd(n, k), and aᵐ = e exactly when n divides m.

A subgroup H ≤ G is a non-empty subset that is a group under the same operation. The one-step test: H is a subgroup if a, b ∈ H implies ab⁻¹ ∈ H. For a finite non-empty subset, closure alone suffices, because the powers of any element eventually cycle back to e. Every group has the trivial subgroups {e} and G; the intersection of two subgroups is a subgroup, but a union usually is not (in ℤ, 2ℤ ∪ 3ℤ contains 2 and 3 but not 5).

Lagrange’s theorem. If H ≤ G and G is finite, then |H| divides |G|. The proof: the left cosets gH all have |H| elements (the map h ↦ gh is a bijection), and any two cosets are equal or disjoint, so the cosets cut G into [G : H] equal blocks, giving |G| = [G : H] × |H|. Corollaries:

  • The order of every element divides |G| (apply Lagrange to ⟨a⟩), so a|G| = e.
  • A group of prime order is cyclic, abelian, and generated by any non-identity element.
  • Fermat’s little theorem: ap−1 ≡ 1 (mod p) for p ∤ a, from the group ℤₚ \ {0} of order p − 1; Euler’s theorem aφ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n) comes from U(n).

The converse is false: a divisor of |G| need not be the order of a subgroup. The alternating group A₄ has order 12 but no subgroup of order 6. (For cyclic groups the converse does hold.)

Concepts in depth: cyclic groups

G is cyclic if G = ⟨a⟩ = {aᵏ : k ∈ ℤ} for some generator a. Up to isomorphism, the only cyclic groups are ℤ (infinite, generators ±1) and ℤₙ. Facts for a cyclic group of order n:

  • aᵏ is a generator exactly when gcd(k, n) = 1, so there are φ(n) generators.
  • For each divisor d of n there is exactly one subgroup of order d, and it is cyclic. So the number of subgroups is the number of divisors of n.
  • The number of elements of order d (for d | n) is φ(d). Summing over all divisors gives Σ φ(d) = n.
  • Every cyclic group is abelian; every subgroup and every quotient of a cyclic group is cyclic.
  • ℤₘ × ℤₙ is cyclic exactly when gcd(m, n) = 1 (then it is isomorphic to ℤₘₙ). In general, the order of (a, b) is lcm(o(a), o(b)).

U(n), the integers in 1 … n − 1 coprime to n under multiplication mod n, is an abelian group of order φ(n). It is cyclic for n = 1, 2, 4, pᵏ and 2pᵏ (p an odd prime) and not otherwise: U(10) = {1, 3, 7, 9} is cyclic (generated by 3), while U(8) = {1, 3, 5, 7} is the Klein four-group. For a prime p, U(p) = ℤₚ \ {0} is cyclic of order p − 1.

Concepts in depth: permutation groups

The symmetric group Sₙ is the set of all bijections of {1, …, n} under composition; |Sₙ| = n!. It is non-abelian for n ≥ 3. Write permutations as products of disjoint cycles; disjoint cycles commute. The order of a permutation is the lcm of its cycle lengths, so the largest order in S₅ is lcm(2, 3) = 6 and in S₇ it is lcm(3, 4) = 12. A k-cycle is a product of k − 1 transpositions; a permutation is even or odd by the parity of that count. The even permutations form the alternating group Aₙ, of order n!/2. Composition convention in this course: (στ)(x) = σ(τ(x)), so apply the right-hand permutation first; check which convention a question uses, because it changes the answer.

Cayley’s theorem: every group of order n is isomorphic to a subgroup of Sₙ. Other standard small groups: the Klein four-group V₄ (order 4, every non-identity element of order 2), and the dihedral group of symmetries of a regular n-gon (order 2n, non-abelian for n ≥ 3).

Concepts in depth: cosets, normal subgroups and homomorphisms

For H ≤ G, the left coset gH and right coset Hg need not be equal. The number of left cosets is the index [G : H] = |G|/|H|. A subgroup N is normal (N ⊴ G) when gN = Ng for every g, equivalently gng⁻¹ ∈ N for all g ∈ G, n ∈ N. Then the cosets form the quotient group G/N with (aN)(bN) = abN and |G/N| = |G|/|N|. Quick facts: every subgroup of an abelian group is normal; every subgroup of index 2 is normal (the two cosets are H and the rest, on either side); {e} and G are always normal; Aₙ ⊴ Sₙ. In S₃, the subgroup A₃ = {e, (1 2 3), (1 3 2)} is normal but {e, (1 2)} is not.

A homomorphism f: G → G′ satisfies f(ab) = f(a)f(b). It automatically maps e to e′ and a⁻¹ to f(a)⁻¹, and o(f(a)) divides o(a). The kernel ker f = {a : f(a) = e′} is a normal subgroup, and f is one-to-one exactly when ker f = {e}. A bijective homomorphism is an isomorphism; isomorphic groups have the same order, the same number of elements of each order, and are both abelian or both not. Examples: n ↦ n mod k from (ℤ, +) onto ℤₖ (kernel kℤ); x ↦ eˣ from (ℝ, +) onto (ℝ⁺, ×) (an isomorphism, with inverse ln); det from invertible matrices onto (ℝ \ {0}, ×). The first isomorphism theorem: G / ker f ≅ f(G), so |G| = |ker f| × |image| for finite G.

Concepts in depth: rings and fields

A ring (R, +, ·) is an abelian group under +, a semigroup under ·, with both distributive laws. It may be commutative and may have a unity 1. A zero divisor is a non-zero a with ab = 0 for some non-zero b. An integral domain is a commutative ring with unity and no zero divisors (ℤ). A field is a commutative ring with unity in which every non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse (ℚ, ℝ, ℂ, ℤₚ).

  • ℤₙ: the non-zero elements not coprime to n are zero divisors; the ones coprime to n are units. So ℤₙ is a field ⟺ integral domain ⟺ n is prime. ℤ₁₂ has φ(12) = 4 units and 11 − 4 = 7 zero divisors.
  • Every field is an integral domain; every finite integral domain is a field. ℤ is an integral domain that is not a field.
  • The 2 × 2 real matrices form a non-commutative ring with unity and with zero divisors.
  • The characteristic of an integral domain is 0 or a prime; ℤₙ has characteristic n. Finite fields exist exactly for prime-power orders.

Worked examples

Example 1 (everything about ℤ₆). Orders: o(0) = 1, o(1) = o(5) = 6, o(2) = o(4) = 3, o(3) = 2 (all from 6 / gcd(6, k)). Generators: 1 and 5 (φ(6) = 2). Subgroups, one per divisor of 6: {0}, {0, 3}, {0, 2, 4}, ℤ₆, which is 4 subgroups. The cosets of H = {0, 3} are {0, 3}, {1, 4}, {2, 5}: index 3 = 6/2, as Lagrange predicts. Elements of order 3: φ(3) = 2 (namely 2 and 4).

Example 2 (is it a group?). On G = ℚ \ {−1}, define a * b = a + b + ab.

  1. Closure: 1 + a * b = (1 + a)(1 + b), which is non-zero when a, b ≠ −1, so a * b ≠ −1.
  2. Associativity: 1 + (a * b) * c = (1 + a)(1 + b)(1 + c) = 1 + a * (b * c).
  3. Identity: a + e + ae = a ⟹ e(1 + a) = 0 ⟹ e = 0.
  4. Inverse: a + b + ab = 0 ⟹ b = −a/(1 + a), defined because a ≠ −1. The inverse of 1 is −½.

It is commutative too, so (G, *) is an abelian group. The trick “1 + a * b factorises” turns the check into ordinary multiplication.

Example 3 (U(10) versus U(8)). U(10) = {1, 3, 7, 9} under ×₁₀. Powers of 3: 3, 9, 27 ≡ 7, 21 ≡ 1, so o(3) = 4 and U(10) = ⟨3⟩ is cyclic (≅ ℤ₄). U(8) = {1, 3, 5, 7} under ×₈: 3² = 9 ≡ 1, 5² = 25 ≡ 1, 7² = 49 ≡ 1. No element has order 4, so U(8) is not cyclic; it is the Klein four-group. Both have order 4, but they are not isomorphic.

Example 4 (S₃: non-abelian, subgroups, normality). S₃ has 6 elements: e, three transpositions (1 2), (1 3), (2 3) of order 2, and two 3-cycles (1 2 3), (1 3 2) of order 3. Applying the right factor first, (1 2)(1 3) = (1 3 2) but (1 3)(1 2) = (1 2 3), so S₃ is non-abelian.

Subgroups: {e}; {e, (1 2)}, {e, (1 3)}, {e, (2 3)}; A₃ = {e, (1 2 3), (1 3 2)}; S₃. That is 6 subgroups, with orders 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 6, all dividing 6. Normal ones: {e}, A₃ (index 2) and S₃, which is 3. {e, (1 2)} is not normal: conjugating (1 2) by (1 3) gives (2 3), which is outside it.

Example 5 (orders of permutations). In S₈, σ = (1 3 5)(2 4 6 7 8) has disjoint cycles of lengths 3 and 5, so o(σ) = lcm(3, 5) = 15. Its parity: a 3-cycle is 2 transpositions and a 5-cycle is 4, total 6, so σ is even. In S₇ the maximum order is 12, from a 3-cycle and a disjoint 4-cycle.

Example 6 (Lagrange in use). A group G has order 20. Possible subgroup orders: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20; a subgroup of order 6 is impossible. If H ≤ G has order 4, it has 20/4 = 5 left cosets. If G is cyclic, it has exactly one subgroup for each of these 6 orders, φ(20) = 8 generators, and φ(5) = 4 elements of order 5.

Concepts in depth: products and quotients of algebraic structures

The syllabus phrase “product and quotients of algebraic structures” comes from the standard discrete-mathematics treatment (Kolman, Busby and Ross): build a bigger structure from two small ones (the product), or a smaller one by gluing equivalent elements together (the quotient).

Direct product. If (S, *) and (T, ∘) are semigroups, then S × T with the componentwise operation (s1, t1)(s2, t2) = (s1 * s2, t1 ∘ t2) is a semigroup. Every property that is checked coordinate by coordinate carries over:

  • product of monoids: a monoid with identity (eS, eT);
  • product of groups: a group with |G × H| = |G| · |H| and inverse (a, b)−1 = (a−1, b−1); it is abelian iff both factors are abelian;
  • the order of (a, b) is lcm(o(a), o(b)), so ℤm × ℤn is cyclic iff gcd(m, n) = 1. ℤ2 × ℤ3 ≅ ℤ6 (generated by (1, 1)), but ℤ2 × ℤ2 is the Klein four-group;
  • product of rings, operated componentwise: a ring, but never an integral domain when both factors are non-zero, since (1, 0)(0, 1) = (0, 0). So ℤ2 × ℤ2 is a product of two fields that is not a field.

Congruence relations and quotient semigroups. An equivalence relation R on a semigroup (S, *) is a congruence if a R a′ and b R b′ imply (a * b) R (a′ * b′). Then the equivalence classes form the quotient semigroup S/R with [a] ⊛ [b] = [a * b]. The definition is well defined precisely because R is a congruence: the answer does not depend on which representatives you pick. The natural map a ↦ [a] is an onto homomorphism. Example: congruence mod n on (ℤ, +) gives the quotient ℤ/nℤ, which is ℤn. The fundamental homomorphism theorem says that if f : S → T is an onto homomorphism, then “a R b iff f(a) = f(b)” is a congruence and S/R ≅ T.

Quotient groups and rings. For groups, the congruences come from normal subgroups: G/N is the set of cosets gN with (aN)(bN) = abN, and |G/N| = |G|/|N|. The order of gN in G/N is the least k ≥ 1 with gk ∈ N. For rings, the congruences come from ideals: ℤ/nℤ is the ring ℤn, which is a field exactly when n is prime.

Example. (a) In ℤ12, let H = ⟨4⟩ = {0, 4, 8}. The quotient ℤ12/H has 12/3 = 4 cosets: H, 1 + H, 2 + H, 3 + H. The coset 1 + H has order 4 (1, 2, 3 ∉ H but 4 ∈ H), so ℤ12/H ≅ ℤ4, and 2 + H has order 2. (b) ℤ2 × ℤ4 has order 8. Its elements of order 2 are (1, 0), (0, 2) and (1, 2), which is three of them. Its largest element order is lcm(2, 4) = 4 < 8, so it is not cyclic.

Concepts in depth: automorphisms

An automorphism of a group G is an isomorphism from G onto itself. Under composition, the automorphisms form a group, Aut(G), and the identity map is always one of them. An automorphism preserves everything structural: the order of every element, and therefore it sends generators to generators; it also maps the centre to itself and subgroups to subgroups of the same order.

  • Inner automorphisms. For each g, φg(x) = gxg−1 (conjugation by g) is an automorphism. The inner automorphisms form a normal subgroup Inn(G) of Aut(G), and Inn(G) ≅ G/Z(G), where Z(G) is the centre. In an abelian group every inner automorphism is the identity. A normal subgroup is exactly a subgroup that every inner automorphism maps onto itself.
  • Cyclic groups. An automorphism of ℤn is fixed by the image of the generator 1, which must again be a generator. So the automorphisms are x ↦ kx with gcd(k, n) = 1, and Aut(ℤn) ≅ U(n), of order φ(n). For example, Aut(ℤ10) = {x ↦ x, 3x, 7x, 9x} is cyclic of order 4, while Aut(ℤ8) ≅ U(8) is not cyclic. Aut(ℤ) has only 2 elements, x ↦ x and x ↦ −x.
  • Other standard facts. Aut(ℤ2 × ℤ2) ≅ S3, of order 6: any permutation of the three non-identity elements works. Aut(S3) ≅ S3, and every automorphism of S3 is inner (its centre is trivial). The map x ↦ x−1 is an automorphism iff G is abelian. In a finite abelian group, x ↦ x2 is an automorphism iff |G| is odd.

A homomorphism from G to itself is not automatically an automorphism. On ℤ10, f(x) = 2x is a homomorphism, but its kernel is {0, 5}, so it is neither one-to-one nor onto.

Concepts in depth: applications of group theory

Group codes (error detection and correction). Messages are binary words. Bⁿ = {0, 1}ⁿ under bitwise XOR (⊕) is an abelian group in which every element is its own inverse. An encoding function e : Bᵐ → Bⁿ (n > m) adds check bits, and the code is a group code when its set of codewords is a subgroup of Bⁿ. The weight w(x) is the number of 1s in x, and the Hamming distance is d(x, y) = w(x ⊕ y).

  • In a group code, x ⊕ y is again a codeword, so the minimum distance equals the minimum weight of a non-zero codeword. This is much quicker to find than checking every pair.
  • A code with minimum distance d detects up to d − 1 errors and corrects up to ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋ errors.
  • The simple parity-check code (m, m + 1) has d = 2: it detects any single error but corrects none.
  • Decoding with cosets: the received word lies in some coset of the code. Choosing a word of least weight in that coset (the coset leader) as the error pattern gives maximum-likelihood decoding. This is the idea behind syndrome decoding of Hamming codes.

Other applications.

  • Cryptography: RSA works in the group U(n) and relies on Euler’s theorem aφ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n); Diffie–Hellman key exchange works in the cyclic group ℤp*; elliptic-curve cryptography uses the group of points of a curve.
  • Counting under symmetry (Burnside’s lemma): the number of essentially different objects is (1/|G|) Σg∈G fix(g), the average number of objects left unchanged by the symmetries.
  • Automata and formal languages: strings under concatenation form the free monoid Σ*, and the transition functions of a finite automaton form a monoid.
  • Symmetry groups in geometry, graphics and chemistry, and puzzles such as the Rubik’s cube, are permutation groups.

Example. (a) C = {00000, 01110, 10101, 11011}. Closure: 01110 ⊕ 10101 = 11011, and the other sums are also in C, so C is a group code. Its non-zero weights are 3, 3 and 4, so the minimum distance is 3: the code detects up to 2 errors and corrects 1. (b) Necklaces of 4 beads, each black or white, counted up to rotation. The rotation group has 4 elements, fixing 16, 2, 4 and 2 colourings (identity, quarter turn, half turn, three-quarter turn). Burnside gives (16 + 2 + 4 + 2)/4 = 6 different necklaces.

NTA traps

  • Converse of Lagrange. Wrong: “12 is divisible by 6, so a group of order 12 has a subgroup of order 6.” Fix: A₄ has none. The converse holds for cyclic groups (and, by Sylow, for prime-power divisors), not in general.
  • Abelian ⟹ cyclic. Wrong. Fix: the Klein four-group (U(8), ℤ₂ × ℤ₂) is abelian but not cyclic. The true direction is cyclic ⟹ abelian.
  • Forgetting 0 under multiplication. (ℤₙ, ×ₙ) including 0 is never a group (0 has no inverse). Remove 0, and it is a group only for prime n.
  • Wrong inverse for a custom operation. Wrong: “the inverse of 5 under a * b = a + b − 1 is −5.” Fix: find the identity of * first (here 1), then solve a * b = e (b = 2 − a = −3).
  • Order of a permutation = sum of cycle lengths. Fix: it is the lcm, and only after writing the permutation as disjoint cycles.
  • Number of generators = n − 1. Fix: φ(n). Only for prime n does every non-identity element generate.
  • (ab)⁻¹ = a⁻¹b⁻¹. This holds only in abelian groups; in general reverse the order.
  • Union of subgroups. An intersection of subgroups is always a subgroup; a union is one only if one contains the other.
  • Integral domain vs field. ℤ has no zero divisors but 2 has no inverse, so it is an integral domain, not a field.

How NTA asks this

  • Direct numericals: the order of an element in ℤₙ, U(n) or Sₙ; the number of generators, subgroups or elements of a given order in a cyclic group; the identity or inverse under a custom operation; the number of cosets; the number of zero divisors or units in ℤₙ. Use the formulas and verify with one quick check.
  • Match the following: structures with examples (semigroup, monoid, group, abelian group), groups with their orders, permutations with their orders, ring types with examples.
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: the converse of Lagrange, cyclic versus abelian, prime order ⟹ cyclic, index-2 subgroups are normal, “a² = e for all a ⟹ abelian”.
  • Multiple select: which of several (set, operation) pairs are groups, which groups are cyclic, which ℤₙ are fields. A single failing axiom (closure, identity, inverse) eliminates an item; find it fast.

Mini-example (A-R). A: U(8) is not cyclic. R: Every non-identity element of U(8) has order 2. Both are true, and R explains A: a generator of a group of order 4 would need order 4. Option 1.

Remember: to reject a claim, one counterexample is enough. Keep four in your pocket: (ℤ, −) is not associative, (ℤ, ×) has no inverses, S₃ is non-abelian, and U(8) is abelian but not cyclic.

terms.definition: A set G with a binary operation * that is closed and associative, has an identity e, and gives every element an inverse.
A group in which a * b = b * a for all a, b.
The least positive n with aⁿ = e (na = 0 in additive notation). In ℤₙ the order of k is n / gcd(n, k).
A non-empty subset H that is itself a group under the same operation. Test: a, b ∈ H ⟹ ab⁻¹ ∈ H; for finite H, closure alone is enough.
In a finite group G, the order of every subgroup H divides |G|, and the index [G : H] = |G|/|H| is the number of cosets.
A group generated by one element: G = ⟨a⟩. A cyclic group of order n has φ(n) generators and one subgroup of each order d dividing n.
For a subgroup H and g ∈ G, the left coset gH = {gh : h ∈ H}. The cosets partition G into equal-sized blocks.
A subgroup N with gN = Ng (equivalently gNg⁻¹ = N) for every g ∈ G. Only normal subgroups give quotient groups G/N.
A map f: G → G′ with f(ab) = f(a)f(b). Its kernel {a : f(a) = e′} is a normal subgroup; a bijective homomorphism is an isomorphism.
A commutative ring with unity 1 ≠ 0 in which every non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse. ℤₙ is a field exactly when n is prime.

lessons.examTip: In ℤₙ, never list elements to find orders: the order of k is n / gcd(n, k), the generators are the k coprime to n (φ(n) of them), and the number of subgroups is the number of divisors of n.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For every “is this a group?” check, write the four axioms as a checklist and tick them.

Check every answer against solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (for example: assumed the converse of Lagrange, forgot that 0 has no inverse under ×, or composed permutations in the wrong order).
Make a one-page sheet: the structure ladder, order formulas in ℤₙ, φ(n) for n up to 30, order of a permutation, and the ring ladder (ring → integral domain → field).
Redo the problems you got wrong after 24 hours, without looking at the solutions.
Finish with the lesson quiz and bank questions at 60–90 seconds per question.
check: At least 12 of 15 problems correct.
Problems 9–15 solved within 12 minutes.
The order of any element of ℤₙ, and the number of generators and subgroups of ℤₙ, found in under 30 seconds each.
Four standard counterexamples (non-associative, no inverses, non-abelian, abelian but not cyclic) written from memory.

quiz.question: How many generators does a cyclic group of order 12 have?
quiz.explanation: If G = ⟨a⟩ has order n, then aᵏ generates G exactly when gcd(k, n) = 1, so there are φ(n) generators. φ(12) = 12 × (1 − ½)(1 − ⅓) = 4: in ℤ₁₂ they are 1, 5, 7 and 11. 11 counts all non-identity elements; 6 is the number of subgroups (divisors of 12).

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: (ℤ⁺, +) is closed and associative but has no identity (0 is missing): semigroup only (III). (ℤ, ×) has identity 1, but 2 has no integer inverse: monoid (I). S₃ is the smallest non-abelian group (II). (ℤ₆, +₆) is cyclic and therefore abelian (IV).

a: A. Semigroup but not a monoid
B. Monoid but not a group
b: II. (S₃, composition)
IV. (ℤ₆, +₆)

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: R is precisely the proof of A: the cyclic subgroup ⟨a⟩ has order dividing p, and since a ≠ e its order is p, so ⟨a⟩ = G. Consequences: every group of prime order is abelian, and it is isomorphic to ℤₚ.

stmts: Assertion (A): Every group of prime order p is cyclic.
Reason (R): By Lagrange’s theorem, the order of any non-identity element divides p and is not 1, so it equals p and that element generates the group.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: What is the order of the element 8 in the group (ℤ₁₂, +₁₂)?
quiz.explanation: Order of k in ℤₙ = n / gcd(n, k) = 12 / gcd(12, 8) = 12/4 = 3. Check: 8, 16 ≡ 4, 24 ≡ 0, so three additions reach 0. The value of the element (8) is not its order; 4 is the gcd.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Statement I is a standard theorem: a subgroup of ⟨a⟩ is generated by aᵐ for the least positive m with aᵐ in it. Statement II is false: the Klein four-group {e, a, b, ab} (for example U(8) = {1, 3, 5, 7}) is abelian, but every non-identity element has order 2, so no element generates all 4 elements. Cyclic ⟹ abelian, not the converse.

stmts: Statement I: Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic.
Statement II: Every abelian group is cyclic.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Which of the following are groups?
options: A, B, C and E only
B, C, D and E only
quiz.explanation: B: non-zero rationals under × form a group (inverse 1/x). C: ℤ₇ \ {0} under ×₇ is a group because 7 is prime. E: the fourth roots of unity form a cyclic group of order 4 generated by i. A fails associativity: (5 − 3) − 1 = 1 but 5 − (3 − 1) = 3; there is also no two-sided identity. D fails closure: 2 ×₈ 4 = 0, which is not in the set (and 2 has no inverse mod 8).

stmts: A. (ℤ, −) (integer subtraction)
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: How many subgroups does the group (ℤ₁₂, +₁₂) have (including the trivial subgroup and the whole group)?
quiz.explanation: A cyclic group of order n has exactly one subgroup of order d for each divisor d of n. 12 has divisors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12, so there are 6 subgroups: {0}, ⟨6⟩, ⟨4⟩, ⟨3⟩, ⟨2⟩ and ℤ₁₂. 4 is φ(12), the number of generators.

quiz.question: In the symmetric group S₅, what is the order of the permutation (1 2 3)(4 5)?
quiz.explanation: Written as disjoint cycles, the order of a permutation is the lcm of the cycle lengths: lcm(3, 2) = 6. Check: after 6 applications both the 3-cycle and the 2-cycle are back to the identity, and no smaller power works. 5 adds the lengths; 3 and 2 are the individual cycle orders.

quiz.question: Arrange the following algebraic structures from the one requiring the fewest axioms to the one requiring the most.
quiz.explanation: Groupoid: closure only. Semigroup: + associativity. Monoid: + identity. Group: + inverses. Abelian group: + commutativity. So C, B, E, A, D. Each structure in the chain is a special case of the ones before it.

stmts: A. Group
B. Semigroup
C. Groupoid (magma: a closed binary operation)
D. Abelian group
E. Monoid
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: On the set of integers, define a * b = a + b − 1. (ℤ, *) is a group. What are its identity element and the inverse of 5?
quiz.explanation: Identity e: a + e − 1 = a gives e = 1. Inverse b of a: a + b − 1 = 1 gives b = 2 − a, so the inverse of 5 is −3. Check: 5 * (−3) = 5 − 3 − 1 = 1 = e. Options with −5 wrongly use the ordinary additive inverse; 0 is the identity of +, not of *.

lessons.title: Graph theory
lessons.summaryHtml: A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges. It is the model behind networks, circuits, maps, schedules and almost every algorithm in Unit 7. This lesson builds the vocabulary (simple graphs, multigraphs, complete, bipartite, regular, cycle, wheel and hypercube graphs) and the counting results that NTA turns into one-line numericals: the handshake lemma, edge counts, components and connectivity. It then covers the big named theorems: Euler circuits and paths, Hamiltonian cycles (Dirac and Ore), trees and Cayley’s n^(n−2) formula, planarity through Euler’s formula v − e + f = 2 and the forbidden graphs K₅ and K₃,₃, and colouring with chromatic numbers and polynomials. It ends with matchings, isomorphism invariants and bipartite graphs.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Draw some dots and join some pairs of them with lines: that is a graph. The dots (vertices) can be cities, computers, people or tasks; the lines (edges) are roads, cables, friendships or conflicts. Graph theory asks structural questions. Can you walk every road exactly once? Can you visit every city exactly once? Can the drawing avoid crossings? How few colours keep neighbours different? How many pairs can you match up? Remarkably, many of these questions are answered by counting degrees, edges and faces.

Why it matters for NET

Graph theory is one of the most dependable sources of Unit 1 questions, and it also underpins the graph algorithms of Unit 7 and the network topics of Unit 9. The recurring questions are: the handshake lemma (find the number of vertices or edges); edge counts of standard graphs; whether a degree sequence is graphic; Euler circuits and paths; Hamiltonian facts; tree counts and Cayley’s formula; regions from Euler’s formula; planarity of K₅, K₃,₃ and friends; chromatic numbers and chromatic polynomials; the number of non-isomorphic graphs or trees; and bipartite properties. Most are two-line calculations once the right theorem is recalled.

Concepts in depth: types of graphs and degrees

A simple graph has no loops and no multiple edges; a multigraph allows parallel edges; a pseudograph also allows loops. In a directed graph each edge has a direction, and each vertex has an in-degree and an out-degree. Standard families:

GraphVerticesEdgesNotes
Complete graph Kₙnn(n − 1)/2(n − 1)-regular; χ = n
Cycle Cₙ (n ≥ 3)nn2-regular; χ = 2 (n even) or 3 (n odd)
Path Pₙnn − 1a tree
Wheel: Cₙ plus a hubn + 12nχ = 3 (n even) or 4 (n odd)
Complete bipartite Kₘ,ₙm + nmnχ = 2; Kₙ,ₙ is n-regular
Hypercube Qₙ2ⁿn·2ⁿ⁻¹n-regular, bipartite, Hamiltonian for n ≥ 2
Petersen graph10153-regular, girth 5, χ = 3, non-planar, non-Hamiltonian

Textbooks write the wheel as Wₙ with n counting either the rim vertices or all vertices, so read the question’s definition. The handshake lemma Σ deg(v) = 2e holds because every edge contributes two edge-ends. Consequences: the number of odd-degree vertices is always even; a k-regular graph on n vertices has nk/2 edges, so nk must be even (no 3-regular graph on 7 vertices exists). In a digraph, Σ in-degree = Σ out-degree = e. The complement Ḡ of a simple graph on n vertices has n(n − 1)/2 − e edges. A graph isomorphic to its complement is self-complementary; it has n(n − 1)/4 edges, so n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4). There are 2^(n(n−1)/2) labelled simple graphs on n vertices.

Graphic sequences (Havel–Hakimi). A non-increasing sequence is the degree sequence of a simple graph if and only if the sequence obtained by deleting the first term d and subtracting 1 from each of the next d terms is graphic. Repeat until all zeros (graphic) or a negative number or too few terms appears (not graphic). Quick rejections: an odd sum, or a degree ≥ n.

Concepts in depth: walks, paths and connectivity

A walk is a sequence of vertices joined by edges, with repeats allowed. A trail repeats no edge; a path repeats no vertex. A closed trail is a circuit, and a closed path is a cycle. (Some books, such as Rosen, say “path” for any walk and “simple path” for no repeated vertex, so read the options carefully.) The number of walks of length k from i to j is the (i, j) entry of Aᵏ, where A is the adjacency matrix.

A graph is connected if every pair of vertices is joined by a path; its maximal connected pieces are components. Useful bounds for simple graphs on n vertices:

  • Connected ⟹ at least n − 1 edges.
  • With k components, at most (n − k)(n − k + 1)/2 edges (one big complete component plus isolated vertices).
  • More than (n − 1)(n − 2)/2 edges forces connectivity.
  • If G is disconnected, its complement Ḡ is connected.

A cut vertex (articulation point) or a bridge (cut edge) is one whose removal increases the number of components. The vertex connectivity κ and edge connectivity λ are the minimum numbers of vertices or edges whose removal disconnects the graph; Whitney’s inequality says κ ≤ λ ≤ δ (the minimum degree). A digraph is strongly connected if every vertex can reach every other along directed edges, and weakly connected if its underlying undirected graph is connected.

Concepts in depth: Euler and Hamilton

Euler’s theorem. A connected graph (ignoring isolated vertices) has an Euler circuit iff every vertex has even degree, and an Euler path that is not a circuit iff exactly two vertices have odd degree; the path must start at one odd vertex and end at the other. The reason is that every pass through a vertex uses two edges. Königsberg’s four land masses had degrees 3, 3, 3 and 5, so no walk crosses every bridge once. For digraphs: an Euler circuit exists iff in-degree = out-degree at every vertex and the graph is connected. Examples: Kₙ has an Euler circuit iff n is odd; Kₘ,ₙ iff m and n are both even; Qₙ iff n is even.

Hamiltonian cycles visit every vertex exactly once. There is no neat characterisation; the decision problem is NP-complete. Sufficient conditions for n ≥ 3: Dirac, δ(G) ≥ n/2; Ore, deg(u) + deg(v) ≥ n for every pair of non-adjacent u, v. Kₙ has (n − 1)!/2 distinct Hamiltonian cycles (fix a start, order the rest, and divide by 2 for direction), which is the number of tours in a symmetric TSP. Kₘ,ₙ is Hamiltonian iff m = n ≥ 2. The Petersen graph is the standard non-Hamiltonian 3-regular graph (it has a Hamiltonian path). A graph with a cut vertex has no Hamiltonian cycle.

Concepts in depth: trees and spanning trees

For a graph T on n vertices, the following are equivalent: T is a tree (connected and acyclic); T is connected with n − 1 edges; T is acyclic with n − 1 edges; there is a unique path between every pair of vertices; T is minimally connected (every edge is a bridge); T is maximally acyclic (adding any edge creates exactly one cycle). Every tree with n ≥ 2 vertices has at least two leaves. A forest with k trees has n − k edges. A full m-ary tree with i internal vertices has mi + 1 vertices and (m − 1)i + 1 leaves.

A spanning tree is a subgraph that is a tree and includes every vertex; a graph has one iff it is connected. Counts: Cayley’s formula gives nⁿ⁻² labelled trees on n vertices, which is also τ(Kₙ); τ(Kₘ,ₙ) = mⁿ⁻¹nᵐ⁻¹; τ(Cₙ) = n; and for any graph, Kirchhoff’s matrix-tree theorem says τ(G) equals any cofactor of the Laplacian L = D − A. Up to isomorphism (unlabelled), the number of trees on 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 vertices is 2, 3, 6, 11, 23.

Concepts in depth: planarity

A graph is planar if it can be drawn without crossings; a drawing splits the plane into faces (regions), including the unbounded outer face. Euler’s formula for a connected planar graph: v − e + f = 2; with k components, v − e + f = k + 1. Since every face of a simple graph (v ≥ 3) is bounded by at least 3 edges and each edge borders at most 2 faces, 3f ≤ 2e, which gives e ≤ 3v − 6. If there are no triangles (for example, bipartite graphs), each face has at least 4 edges and e ≤ 2v − 4. Consequences:

  • K₅ (v = 5, e = 10 > 9) and K₃,₃ (v = 6, e = 9 > 8) are non-planar.
  • Every simple planar graph has a vertex of degree at most 5 (otherwise 2e ≥ 6v).
  • The bounds are necessary, not sufficient: K₃,₃ passes e ≤ 3v − 6 (9 ≤ 12) and is still non-planar.

Kuratowski’s theorem: a graph is planar iff it contains no subdivision of K₅ or K₃,₃ (Wagner’s version uses minors). K₅ and K₃,₃ are the smallest non-planar graphs; deleting any edge from either leaves a planar graph. Kₙ is planar iff n ≤ 4; Kₘ,ₙ iff min(m, n) ≤ 2; all trees, cycles, wheels and Q₁–Q₃ are planar, while Q₄ and the Petersen graph are not. The dual of a plane graph swaps faces and vertices (edges correspond one-to-one).

Concepts in depth: colouring

A proper colouring gives adjacent vertices different colours; χ(G) is the minimum number of colours. Bounds: ω(G) ≤ χ(G) ≤ Δ(G) + 1, where ω is the largest clique. Brooks’ theorem sharpens the upper bound to Δ for connected graphs other than complete graphs and odd cycles. χ(G) ≤ 2 iff G is bipartite iff G has no odd cycle. The four colour theorem says every planar graph has χ ≤ 4 (the five colour theorem is the easier proof). Colouring models scheduling: exams as vertices, clashes as edges, time slots as colours; register allocation in compilers uses the same idea.

The chromatic polynomial P(G, k) counts proper colourings with at most k colours. P(Kₙ, k) = k(k − 1)…(k − n + 1); for a tree on n vertices, k(k − 1)ⁿ⁻¹; for the cycle, P(Cₙ, k) = (k − 1)ⁿ + (−1)ⁿ(k − 1). χ(G) is the least positive integer k with P(G, k) > 0. The deletion–contraction rule P(G) = P(G − e) − P(G / e) computes the rest. Edge colouring: Vizing’s theorem says χ′(G) is Δ or Δ + 1; χ′(Kₙ) = n − 1 for even n and n for odd n; χ′ of a bipartite graph is Δ (König).

Concepts in depth: matching, covers, isomorphism and bipartite graphs

A matching is a set of pairwise disjoint edges. It is maximal if no edge can be added, and maximum if it has the largest possible size; every maximum matching is maximal but not conversely. A perfect matching covers all vertices and needs an even number of them; K₂ₙ has (2n − 1)!! = (2n − 1)(2n − 3)…1 of them, and Kₙ,ₙ has n!. Hall’s theorem: a bipartite graph with parts X, Y has a matching saturating X iff |N(S)| ≥ |S| for every S ⊆ X. König’s theorem: in a bipartite graph, the maximum matching size equals the minimum vertex cover size. For any graph, α(G) + β(G) = n, where α is the independence number and β the vertex-cover number (a set is independent iff its complement is a vertex cover).

Isomorphism. G ≅ H if a bijection of vertices preserves adjacency. To prove non-isomorphism, find an invariant that differs: numbers of vertices and edges, degree sequence, number of cycles of each length, connectivity, bipartiteness, or the degrees of the neighbours of a vertex. Equal degree sequences do not prove isomorphism: C₆ and two disjoint triangles are both 2-regular on 6 vertices. The number of non-isomorphic simple graphs on 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 vertices is 1, 2, 4, 11, 34.

Bipartite graphs: characterised by having no odd cycle, checked by a BFS 2-colouring. A bipartite graph on n vertices has at most ⌊n²/4⌋ edges (reached by K⌊n/2⌋,⌈n/2⌉), which is also Turán’s bound for triangle-free graphs.

Worked examples

Example 1 (handshake and Havel–Hakimi). (a) A graph has 15 edges; three vertices have degree 4 and the rest degree 3. Then 2 × 15 = 30 = 12 + 3(n − 3), so n = 9. (b) Is (4, 3, 3, 2, 2) graphic?

4 3 3 2 2
  drop 4, −1 from next 4: 2 2 1 1
2 2 1 1
  drop 2, −1 from next 2: 1 0 1
  sort: 1 1 0
1 1 0
  drop 1, −1 from next 1: 0 0
all zeros: graphic

By contrast, (4, 4, 4, 1, 1) reduces to (3, 3, 0, 0) and then to (2, −1, −1): not graphic, even though its sum 14 is even.

Example 2 (Euler circuit or path?). A connected graph has degrees 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2. Exactly two vertices are odd, so it has an Euler path (from one degree-3 vertex to the other) but no Euler circuit. K₅ (all degrees 4) has an Euler circuit; K₄ (all degrees 3, four odd vertices) has neither. K₂,₄ has degrees 4, 4, 2, 2, 2, 2, so it has an Euler circuit, and it is not Hamiltonian because its parts are unequal.

Example 3 (Euler’s formula and planarity). (a) A connected planar graph has 20 vertices, all of degree 3. Then e = 30 and f = 2 − 20 + 30 = 12 (this is the dodecahedron). (b) A planar graph has 12 vertices, 15 edges and 3 components: f = k + 1 − v + e = 4 − 12 + 15 = 7. (c) Is a simple graph with 8 vertices and 19 edges planar? 3v − 6 = 18 < 19, so no. With 18 edges the test is inconclusive: the bound only rules graphs out.

Example 4 (chromatic polynomial of C₄). P(C₄, k) = (k − 1)⁴ + (k − 1) = k⁴ − 4k³ + 6k² − 3k. Then P(C₄, 1) = 0, P(C₄, 2) = 2 and P(C₄, 3) = 18. The least k with P > 0 is 2, so χ(C₄) = 2. For the path on 4 vertices (a tree), P = k(k − 1)³, which gives 24 colourings with 3 colours; adding the closing edge removes the 6 colourings where the ends match.

Example 5 (counting spanning trees). K₄ has 4² = 16 spanning trees (Cayley). Remove one edge, say {1, 2}: the spanning trees of K₄ that avoid it number 16 − 8 = 8, because each of the 6 edges lies in 16 × 3 / 6 = 8 spanning trees (each tree has 3 edges, and by symmetry every edge is equally used). Kirchhoff’s theorem on K₄ − e gives the same 8. K₂,₃ has 2² × 3¹ = 12.

Example 6 (matchings and covers). C₇: a maximum matching has ⌊7/2⌋ = 3 edges, the independence number is 3, and so the minimum vertex cover is 7 − 3 = 4. C₇ is not bipartite, and König fails here (matching 3 ≠ cover 4). K₆ has 5 × 3 × 1 = 15 perfect matchings, and K₈ has 7 × 5 × 3 × 1 = 105.

Concepts in depth: multigraphs, weighted graphs and shortest paths

Degrees in multigraphs and pseudographs. Each parallel edge counts separately, and a loop adds 2 to the degree of its vertex (it has two ends there). With this convention the handshake lemma Σ deg(v) = 2e holds for every multigraph and pseudograph. Euler’s theorem also holds unchanged: the Königsberg problem is really a multigraph with 4 vertices and 7 edges (bridges), with degrees 3, 3, 3 and 5, so the degree sum is 14 = 2 × 7. All four degrees are odd, so there is no Euler path. In an adjacency matrix of a multigraph, entry aij is the number of edges between i and j.

Weighted graphs. A weighted graph attaches a number w(e) to each edge: a distance, cost or delay. The length of a path is the sum of its weights, not its number of edges, and a shortest path minimises that sum. Road maps, network routing (OSPF runs Dijkstra’s algorithm) and the travelling-salesperson problem all use weighted graphs. In an unweighted graph, “shortest” means fewest edges, and breadth-first search finds it.

Dijkstra’s algorithm (non-negative weights, single source s):

  1. Set d(s) = 0 and d(v) = ∞ for every other vertex; no vertex is final yet.
  2. Pick the non-final vertex u with the smallest label and make it final (permanent).
  3. For each neighbour v of u that is not final, relax the edge: d(v) = min(d(v), d(u) + w(u, v)).
  4. Repeat until all vertices are final. With an adjacency matrix it takes O(V²) time; with a binary heap, O((V + E) log V).

The greedy choice is safe only because weights are non-negative: once u has the smallest label, no detour through other vertices can reach u more cheaply. With a negative edge that argument fails, and Bellman–Ford (V − 1 rounds of relaxing every edge, O(VE)) is used instead. If a negative cycle is reachable, no shortest path exists. Floyd–Warshall finds all-pairs shortest paths in O(V³). Unit 7 (lesson 7.6) covers these algorithms in detail.

Example (Dijkstra trace). Edges: S–A 4, S–B 1, B–A 2, A–C 5, B–C 8, B–D 6, C–D 1, C–T 3, D–T 7. Source S. Each row shows the labels after the vertex in the first column is made final.

FinalSABCDT
S041∞∞∞
B03197∞
A03187∞
D0318714
C0318711
T0318711

The vertices become final in the order S, B, A, D, C, T. The shortest S–T distance is 11, along S–B–A–C–T. The direct-looking route S–A–C–T costs 12, and S–B–D–T costs 14: fewest edges is not least weight.

Concepts in depth: rooted trees and tree traversals

A rooted tree is a tree with one vertex chosen as the root, so every edge points away from it. Terms: parent, child, siblings (same parent), ancestors and descendants, leaf (no children), internal vertex (has children), and subtree. The level of a vertex is the length of its path from the root (the root is at level 0), and the height is the largest level. A tree is m-ary if every internal vertex has at most m children, and full m-ary if every internal vertex has exactly m. It is balanced if all leaves are at level h or h − 1.

  • A full m-ary tree with i internal vertices has n = mi + 1 vertices and l = (m − 1)i + 1 leaves. A full binary tree therefore has l = i + 1 and n = 2l − 1.
  • An m-ary tree of height h has at most mʰ leaves, so a tree with l leaves has height at least ⌈logm l⌉. A binary tree of height h has at most 2h+1 − 1 vertices.

Mind the convention: some books start levels at 1 or measure height in vertices, so read the stem.

Traversals of an ordered rooted tree (for binary trees, left subtree before right):

  • Preorder: root, then each subtree in preorder.
  • Inorder (binary trees): left subtree, root, right subtree. The inorder of a binary search tree lists the keys in sorted order.
  • Postorder: each subtree in postorder, then the root.
  • Level order: level by level, left to right (breadth-first).

For an expression tree (operators inside, operands at the leaves), preorder gives prefix (Polish) notation, inorder gives infix (brackets needed), and postorder gives postfix (reverse Polish). Reconstruction: preorder + inorder, or postorder + inorder, determine a binary tree uniquely: the first preorder (or last postorder) symbol is the root, and it splits the inorder list into the left and right subtrees. Preorder + postorder do not, because they cannot tell whether a lone child is a left or a right child (they do determine a full binary tree).

Example. The tree below has preorder A B D E G C F, inorder D B G E A C F, postorder D G E B F C A and level order A B C D E F G.

        A
      /   \
     B     C
    / \     \
   D   E     F
      /
     G

For (a + b) × c − d ÷ e the root is −, with left subtree × (whose children are + and c) and right subtree ÷. Preorder gives − × + a b c ÷ d e, and postorder gives a b + c × d e ÷ −.

Concepts in depth: prefix codes and Huffman coding

A prefix code is a set of codewords in which no codeword is a prefix of another. Such a code can be decoded left to right without separators, because the moment the bits read so far form a codeword, that codeword must be the one intended. Every binary prefix code is a binary tree: label left edges 0 and right edges 1, and put the symbols at the leaves. A symbol at an internal vertex would make its codeword a prefix of those below it. The Kraft inequality Σ 2−li ≤ 1 holds for every binary prefix code, and conversely any lengths that satisfy it can be realised by a prefix code. So lengths {1, 1, 2} are impossible, since ½ + ½ + ¼ > 1.

Huffman’s algorithm builds an optimal prefix code (minimum average length Σ pili) for given frequencies:

  1. Make each symbol a one-vertex tree weighted by its frequency.
  2. Repeatedly merge the two trees of smallest weight under a new root whose weight is their sum.
  3. Stop when one tree remains; read each codeword along the path from the root.

Ties can be broken either way. The codewords may differ, but the average length is always the same minimum.

Example. Frequencies (per 100 symbols): A 30, B 25, C 20, D 15, E 10. The merges are D + E = 25; then C + (B or DE) = 45; then the other 25 + A = 55; then 45 + 55 = 100. Every symbol then gets length 2 or 3: A, B and C get 2 bits, and D and E get 3 bits. Average length = (2 × 75 + 3 × 25)/100 = 2.25 bits per symbol, against 3 bits for a fixed-length code for 5 symbols (⌈log2 5⌉ = 3). One valid code is A = 10, B = 00, C = 01, D = 110, E = 111. Check Kraft: 3 × ¼ + 2 × ⅛ = 1.

Concepts in depth: cut-sets and fundamental circuits

In a connected graph, a cut-set is a set of edges whose removal disconnects the graph, and which is minimal: putting back any one of its edges reconnects it. A bridge is a cut-set with one edge. The edge connectivity λ(G) is the size of a smallest cut-set, for example λ(Kₙ) = n − 1 and λ(Q3) = 3. Some books use “cut” or “edge cut” for any disconnecting set; a cut-set in the strict sense is minimal.

Fix a spanning tree T of a connected graph with n vertices and e edges. Its n − 1 edges are branches, and the other e − n + 1 edges are chords.

  • Adding a chord to T creates exactly one cycle, a fundamental circuit. There are e − n + 1 of them, the circuit rank (cyclomatic number, also written μ = e − n + k for a graph with k components).
  • Removing a branch splits T into two parts. The edges of G joining those parts form a fundamental cut-set, and there are n − 1 of them.
  • Every cut-set shares at least one edge with every spanning tree (otherwise the tree would survive the cut and keep the graph connected). Every circuit shares an even number of edges with every cut-set.

Example. G has vertices 1–5 and edges 12, 23, 34, 41, 13 and 45 (a square with a diagonal and a pendant edge), so n = 5 and e = 6. Any spanning tree has 4 branches and 2 chords, giving 2 fundamental circuits and 4 fundamental cut-sets. {45} is a cut-set of size 1 (a bridge), so λ(G) = 1. {12, 23} is a cut-set that isolates vertex 2. {12, 23, 13} also disconnects G, but it is not a cut-set, because it is not minimal: putting 13 back still leaves 2 isolated.

NTA traps

  • Euler vs Hamilton. Wrong: “all degrees even, so there is a Hamiltonian cycle.” Fix: the degree test is for Euler (edges). Hamiltonicity has only sufficient conditions (Dirac, Ore).
  • Using e ≤ 3v − 6 as a proof of planarity. Fix: it is necessary only. K₃,₃ satisfies it; use e ≤ 2v − 4 for triangle-free graphs, or find a K₅ or K₃,₃ subdivision.
  • Forgetting the outer face. Fix: f in Euler’s formula includes the unbounded region.
  • Same degree sequence ⟹ isomorphic. Fix: C₆ versus two triangles. Invariants can only prove non-isomorphism.
  • n edges on n − 1 vertices is a tree. Fix: n − 1 edges makes a tree only together with connectivity or acyclicity.
  • χ of a cycle. Fix: even cycle 2, odd cycle 3. For a wheel, add 1 to the rim’s chromatic number.
  • Hamiltonian cycles in Kₙ. Fix: (n − 1)!/2 undirected distinct cycles, not n! or (n − 1)!.
  • Maximal vs maximum matching. Fix: maximal means “cannot be extended”; maximum means “largest possible”.
  • Wheel notation. Fix: check whether Wₙ counts the hub; the edge count is twice the number of rim vertices.

How NTA asks this

  • Direct numericals: vertices from degree data, edges of standard graphs, regions from Euler’s formula, labelled trees or spanning trees, Hamiltonian cycles in Kₙ, perfect matchings, maximum edges with k components, chromatic polynomial values. Write the one identity, substitute, and check parity (2e must be even).
  • Match the following: graphs with chromatic numbers, edge counts or spanning-tree counts; named theorems (Euler, Dirac, Kuratowski, König, Cayley) with their statements.
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: planarity of K₅ and K₃,₃ and the reason, Euler versus Hamilton, bipartite ⟺ no odd cycle, degree sequence versus isomorphism, necessary versus sufficient conditions.
  • Multiple select and ordering: which graphs are planar, bipartite, Eulerian or Hamiltonian; order graphs by edges, spanning trees or chromatic number.

Mini-example (A-R). A: The Petersen graph has no Hamiltonian cycle. R: The Petersen graph is non-planar. Both statements are true, but planarity has nothing to do with Hamiltonicity (K₅ is non-planar and Hamiltonian), so R does not explain A: option 2.

Watch out: when an option list mixes necessary and sufficient conditions, test each claim against a small counterexample graph: the bow-tie, C₆ versus two triangles, K₃,₃, K₂,₄ and the Petersen graph cover almost every trap.

terms.definition: The number of edge-ends at a vertex (a loop counts 2). Handshake lemma: Σ deg(v) = 2|E|.
Every vertex has the same degree k; a k-regular graph on n vertices has nk/2 edges.
Vertices split into two sets with every edge going across. A graph is bipartite exactly when it has no odd cycle.
A closed trail using every edge exactly once. A connected graph has one iff every vertex has even degree.
A cycle through every vertex exactly once. No simple degree test exists; deciding it is NP-complete.
A connected acyclic graph. With n vertices it has n − 1 edges and a unique path between any two vertices.
A graph that can be drawn in the plane without edge crossings. Connected planar graphs satisfy v − e + f = 2.
The least number of colours for a proper vertex colouring (adjacent vertices get different colours).
A set of edges with no shared endpoint. A perfect matching covers every vertex.
A bijection between vertex sets that preserves adjacency. Isomorphic graphs share every invariant (degree sequence, cycle lengths, and so on).

lessons.examTip: For every numerical, reach for one identity first: Σ deg = 2e for degree questions, v − e + f = 2 for regions, e ≤ 3v − 6 (or 2v − 4 without triangles) for planarity, n^(n−2) for labelled trees, and (n − k)(n − k + 1)/2 for the most edges with k components.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For every Euler or planarity question, write the degree list or the e ≤ 3v − 6 check before choosing.

Check every answer against solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (for example: used e ≤ 3v − 6 as a proof of planarity, confused Euler and Hamilton, or forgot that an odd cycle needs 3 colours).
Make a one-page sheet: edge counts of Kₙ, Kₘ,ₙ, Qₙ, wheels and cycles; chromatic numbers of standard graphs; spanning-tree formulas; the Euler, Dirac, Ore, Kuratowski and König statements.
Redo the problems you got wrong after 24 hours, without looking at the solutions.
Finish with the lesson quiz and bank questions at 60–90 seconds per question.
check: At least 12 of 15 problems correct.
Problems 9–15 solved within 12 minutes.
Handshake, Euler-formula and Cayley numericals solved in under 60 seconds each.
Six counterexample graphs (bow-tie, C₆ versus two triangles, K₃,₃, K₂,₄, Petersen, K₅) drawn from memory with the fact each one disproves.

quiz.question: A simple graph has 21 edges. Three of its vertices have degree 4 and every other vertex has degree 3. How many vertices does the graph have?
quiz.explanation: Handshake lemma: Σ deg = 2e = 42. With n vertices: 3 × 4 + (n − 3) × 3 = 42, so 12 + 3n − 9 = 42 and n = 13. Check: 12 + 30 = 42. 14 comes from forgetting to subtract the three degree-4 vertices; 7 halves the wrong way.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Kₙ needs n colours: χ(K₅) = 5 (IV). An odd cycle needs 3 (II). Any bipartite graph with an edge needs 2 (I). The wheel’s rim is an odd cycle (3 colours) and the hub is adjacent to all rim vertices, so it needs a fourth colour (III). With an even rim the wheel needs only 3.

a: D. Wheel: a 5-cycle plus a hub vertex adjacent to all five
b: II. 3
III. 4
IV. 5

options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: K₃,₃ is bipartite, so it has no triangles and every face of a planar drawing would need at least 4 edges: 4f ≤ 2e. With Euler’s formula this gives e ≤ 2v − 4 = 8 < 9, a contradiction. So R is exactly the proof of A. (The usual bound e ≤ 3v − 6 = 12 would not detect it.)

Reason (R): A connected simple planar graph with v ≥ 3 vertices and no triangles satisfies e ≤ 2v − 4, but K₃,₃ has 9 edges and 2 × 6 − 4 = 8.

quiz.question: How many different labelled trees can be formed on 5 distinct vertices (equivalently, how many spanning trees does K₅ have)?
quiz.explanation: Cayley’s formula: nⁿ⁻² labelled trees on n vertices, so 5³ = 125. It is also the number of spanning trees of Kₙ (Prüfer sequences of length n − 2 over n symbols). 120 = 5! and 60 = 5!/2 are permutation counts; 25 = 5² uses the wrong exponent.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Statement I is Euler’s theorem. Statement II is false: the “bow-tie” (two triangles sharing one vertex) has all degrees even (2, 2, 4, 2, 2), so it has an Euler circuit, but any cycle through all vertices would pass the shared vertex twice, so it has no Hamiltonian cycle. Euler is about edges, Hamilton about vertices; neither implies the other.

stmts: Statement I: A connected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree.
Statement II: Every graph that has an Euler circuit also has a Hamiltonian cycle.

quiz.question: A connected planar simple graph has 10 vertices, each of degree 3. Into how many regions (faces, including the outer one) does any planar drawing divide the plane?
quiz.explanation: Edges: e = 10 × 3 / 2 = 15. Euler’s formula v − e + f = 2 gives f = 2 − 10 + 15 = 7. The outer (unbounded) face is included. 15 is the edge count; 5 forgets the +2; 17 adds instead of subtracting.

quiz.question: What is the maximum number of edges in a simple graph with 10 vertices and exactly 3 connected components?
quiz.explanation: Edges are maximised by making two components isolated vertices and the third a complete graph on the remaining n − k + 1 = 8 vertices: C(8, 2) = 28 = (n − k)(n − k + 1)/2 = 7 × 8 / 2. 45 = C(10, 2) is the connected maximum; 21 = C(7, 2) uses one vertex too few; 36 = C(9, 2) is for 2 components.

quiz.explanation: Vertex 1 can be matched to any of 5 others, then the smallest unmatched vertex to any of 3, then the last pair is forced: 5 × 3 × 1 = 15 = (2n − 1)!! for K₂ₙ. 720 = 6! counts orderings, not matchings; 30 double-counts by ordering the pairs partly.

lessons.title: Boolean algebra
lessons.summaryHtml: Boolean algebra works on two values with OR, AND and NOT, obeys the Huntington postulates (including the second distributive law x + yz = (x + y)(x + z)), and pairs every identity with its dual. Any Boolean function can be written in canonical form as a sum of minterms (Σm) or a product of maxterms (ΠM), and then minimised with a Karnaugh map or the Quine–McCluskey table, using don't-cares to enlarge groups. NTA tests this through near-identical minimisation options, dual versus complement, counting formulas such as 2^(2^n) functions and 2^(2^(n−1)) self-dual functions, and functional completeness decided by Post's five classes. Learn the Gray-code layout of the map, the essential-prime-implicant rule and Post's table, and these become fast, safe marks.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Boolean algebra is the algebra of two values, 0 and 1, with three basic operations: OR (written +), AND (written · or by putting letters side by side) and NOT (written with a prime, A′). It is the mathematics behind every logic circuit and every condition in a program. A Boolean function is just a rule that gives 0 or 1 for each combination of its inputs, so it can always be written as a truth table.

Most of this lesson is about one practical job: taking a function and writing the cheapest correct expression for it. Fewer terms and fewer literals mean fewer gates. Karnaugh maps (K-maps) do this by eye for up to 4 or 5 variables. The Quine–McCluskey (QM) method does the same job as a table procedure that a computer can follow. The lesson closes with functional completeness: which small sets of operations can build every Boolean function.

Why it matters for NET

Boolean algebra sits in Unit 1 (Discrete Structures and Optimization) and overlaps with digital logic in Unit 2. That overlap makes it one of the most reliable scoring areas in Paper 2. Expect questions of these kinds:

  • K-map minimisation, often with don't-cares, where the four options are four expressions that look almost the same.
  • Identity checking: which of several equations are valid.
  • Duality and complement, which students often confuse.
  • Counting: how many Boolean functions, self-dual functions or neutral functions exist on n variables.
  • Canonical form conversions between Σm and ΠM.
  • Functional completeness of sets such as {→, ¬} or {⊕, ∧}.

These questions are quick if you work systematically. They are also easy to lose to one careless adjacency or one wrongly applied rule.

Postulates and theorems

A Boolean algebra is a set B with two binary operations + and ·, a unary operation ′, and two distinct elements 0 and 1. The Huntington postulates are the minimum rules everything else follows from:

  1. Closure: x + y and x · y are in B.
  2. Identity: x + 0 = x and x · 1 = x.
  3. Commutativity: x + y = y + x and xy = yx.
  4. Distributivity, both ways: x(y + z) = xy + xz, and also x + yz = (x + y)(x + z). The second law has no counterpart in ordinary arithmetic, and it is the one students forget.
  5. Complement: x + x′ = 1 and x · x′ = 0.
  6. There are at least two distinct elements.

Associativity is not in the list. It can be proved from the other postulates. The theorems you must be able to use without thinking are these:

TheoremOR formAND form (dual)
Idempotencex + x = xx · x = x
Null (dominance)x + 1 = 1x · 0 = 0
Involution(x′)′ = x
Absorptionx + xy = xx(x + y) = x
Redundant literalx + x′y = x + yx(x′ + y) = xy
De Morgan(x + y)′ = x′y′(xy)′ = x′ + y′
Consensusxy + x′z + yz = xy + x′z(x + y)(x′ + z)(y + z) = (x + y)(x′ + z)

Why is the consensus term yz redundant? Whenever yz = 1, x is either 1 or 0. If x = 1, the term xy = y = 1. If x = 0, the term x′z = z = 1. So yz never produces a 1 that the other two terms miss. The same argument, with the variable split into its two cases, proves most of these theorems quickly. Formally this is Shannon's expansion: f = x·f(1, …) + x′·f(0, …).

Duality, complement and self-dual functions

Principle of duality. If an identity holds, the identity obtained by swapping + with · and 0 with 1 also holds. Variables and their primes are left alone. For example, x + x′y = x + y is true, so its dual x(x′ + y) = xy is also true. This works because the postulates themselves come in dual pairs.

The dual of a function F, written Fd, is obtained the same way: swap + and ·, and swap 0 and 1. The complement F′ does that and also primes every literal. For F = AB′ + C:

  • the dual is Fd = (A + B′)C;
  • the complement is F′ = (A′ + B)C′.

Keep the brackets. Operator precedence changes when + and · swap. In terms of truth tables, Fd(x1, …, xn) = [F(x1′, …, xn′)]′.

A function is self-dual when Fd = F. Equivalently, complementing all the inputs complements the output. For example, the majority function AB + BC + CA and the XOR of three variables are self-dual. A self-dual function is fixed by its values on half of the input combinations, one from each complementary pair. So there are 22n−1 self-dual functions of n variables: 4 for n = 2 and 16 for n = 3.

Counting Boolean functions

An n-variable truth table has 2n rows, and each row can independently output 0 or 1. So there are 22n Boolean functions of n variables: 16 for n = 2, 256 for n = 3 and 65,536 for n = 4. Other counts NTA asks:

  • Neutral functions (equal numbers of 0s and 1s): C(2n, 2n−1). For n = 3 this is C(8, 4) = 70.
  • Symmetric functions (the output depends only on how many inputs are 1): 2n+1.
  • Functions with a fixed value at one input, for example F(0, …, 0) = 0: 22n−1.
  • Linear (affine) functions c0 ⊕ c1x1 ⊕ … ⊕ cnxn: 2n+1.

Minterms, maxterms and canonical forms

A minterm is an AND term containing every variable once, primed or unprimed. It equals 1 for exactly one input row. Minterm mi uses the binary form of i, with 0 giving a primed variable. For A, B, C: m5 = 101 = AB′C.

A maxterm is an OR term containing every variable once. It equals 0 for exactly one row, and the rule is reversed: 0 gives the plain variable and 1 gives the primed one. So M5 = A′ + B + C′. In general Mi = (mi)′.

  • The canonical SOP (sum of minterms) ORs the minterms where F = 1: F = Σm(…).
  • The canonical POS (product of maxterms) ANDs the maxterms where F = 0: F = ΠM(…).

The two index lists are complements of each other within {0, …, 2n − 1}. For F(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 4, 5, 6), the canonical POS is ΠM(0, 2, 3, 7), and F′ = Σm(0, 2, 3, 7). Every term in a canonical form has all n literals. A standard (non-canonical) SOP only needs to be a sum of products.

Karnaugh maps

A K-map is a truth table folded into a grid whose rows and columns are labelled in Gray-code order (00, 01, 11, 10). Two cells next to each other then differ in exactly one variable. The map also wraps around: the left edge is adjacent to the right edge, and the top edge to the bottom edge. So in a 4-variable map, the four corner cells m0, m2, m8 and m10 form one group, B′D′.

4-variable map (cell = minterm number)      AB\CD  00   01   11   10
                                            00      0    1    3    2
                                            01      4    5    7    6
                                            11     12   13   15   14
                                            10      8    9   11   10

Grouping rules:

  • A group is a rectangle of 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells, always a power of two. Wrap-around counts.
  • A group of 2k cells removes k variables. In a 4-variable map, a pair leaves 3 literals, a quad leaves 2 and an octet leaves 1.
  • Make every group as large as possible. A group that cannot be enlarged is a prime implicant (PI).
  • An essential prime implicant (EPI) is a PI that covers some 1-cell no other PI covers. Every minimal SOP must contain all EPIs.
  • After taking the EPIs, cover the remaining 1s with as few PIs as possible, preferring larger ones.

Don't-cares (X, written d(…)) are inputs that never occur or whose output does not matter, like the codes 1010–1111 in a BCD circuit. Treat an X as 1 if that enlarges a group and as 0 otherwise. You never have to cover an X.

Minimal POS. Group the 0-cells instead, which gives a minimal SOP for F′. Then apply De Morgan to get F as a product of sums.

Five variables. Use two 4-variable maps, one for A = 0 and one for A = 1, placed side by side. A cell in one map is also adjacent to the same position in the other map. A group that appears in the same place on both maps drops A.

A function can have several different minimal SOPs. The standard example is the cyclic function Σm(0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7) of three variables. It has six PIs, all pairs, and no EPI. Two different 3-term covers, B′C + A′C′ + AB and BC′ + A′B′ + AC, are both minimal.

Quine–McCluskey (tabulation) method

QM is the K-map idea turned into a table procedure. It works for any number of variables and is guaranteed to find all PIs.

  1. Write every minterm, and every don't-care, in binary. Group them by the number of 1s.
  2. Compare each term with every term in the next group. If two terms differ in exactly one bit, combine them, put a dash in that position and tick both.
  3. Repeat on the new list. Only terms with dashes in the same positions can combine. Remove duplicates, since the same quad appears twice.
  4. Terms that were never ticked are the prime implicants.
  5. Build the PI chart, with PIs as rows and the true minterms (not the don't-cares) as columns. Select the EPIs: any column with a single cross.
  6. Cover the remaining columns using row and column dominance, or Petrick's method, which writes the covering condition as a product of sums and multiplies it out.

The number of PIs can grow exponentially with n, and choosing a minimum cover is NP-hard (it is set cover). So QM is exact but not fast. That is why tools such as Espresso use heuristics for large functions.

Functional completeness (Post's theorem)

A set of operations is functionally complete if every Boolean function can be built from it. {AND, OR, NOT} is complete because every function has a canonical SOP. {AND, NOT} and {OR, NOT} are also complete, because De Morgan rebuilds the missing operation. NAND alone and NOR alone are complete: NOT x = x NAND x, and AND is NAND followed by NOT.

Post's theorem gives an exact test. There are five classes of functions, each closed under composition:

  1. T0, 0-preserving: F(0, …, 0) = 0.
  2. T1, 1-preserving: F(1, …, 1) = 1.
  3. S, self-dual.
  4. M, monotone: raising an input from 0 to 1 never lowers the output.
  5. L, linear (affine): an XOR of some variables, possibly with 1.

A set is complete if and only if, for each of the five classes, at least one operation in the set lies outside it. If every operation stays inside one class, whatever you compose also stays inside it, so the set is stuck.

OperationT0T1SML
AND, ORyesyesnoyesno
NOTnonoyesnoyes
XORyesnononoyes
XNOR (↔)noyesnonoyes
→ (implication)noyesnonono
NAND, NORnonononono
majority(x, y, z)yesyesyesyesno

Reading the table: {→} alone is incomplete because it preserves 1. {→, ¬} and {→, 0} are complete. {⊕, ¬} is incomplete because both operations are linear. {⊕, ∧} is incomplete because both preserve 0, but {⊕, ∧, 1} is complete. {majority, ¬} is incomplete because both are self-dual.

Worked examples

Example 1: 4-variable K-map with don't-cares

Problem. Minimise F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(2, 3, 7, 9, 11, 13) + d(1, 10, 15).

AB \ CD00011110
000X11
010010
1101X0
10011X
  1. Column CD = 11 holds m3, m7, m15 (X) and m11. Taking X15 as 1 gives the quad CD. It is the only PI that covers m7, so it is essential.
  2. The cells m2, m3, m10 (X) and m11 form the quad B′C, rows 00 and 10 with columns 11 and 10. It is the only PI that covers m2, so it is essential.
  3. The cells m9, m11, m13 and m15 (X) form the quad AD. It is the only PI that covers m13, so it is essential.
  4. The fourth PI, B′D (m1, m3, m9, m11), is not needed. Every 1 is already covered.

Answer: F = CD + B′C + AD, with 3 terms and 6 literals. An exhaustive search over all prime-implicant covers confirms that no 2-term cover exists.

Example 2: Quine–McCluskey on Σm(0, 1, 2, 5, 8, 9, 10)

Number of 1sMintermsPairs (first combination)Quads
00 = 0000 ✓(0,1) 000−, (0,2) 00−0, (0,8) −000(0,1,8,9) −00−, (0,2,8,10) −0−0
11, 2, 8 ✓(1,5) 0−01, (1,9) −001, (2,10) −010, (8,9) 100−, (8,10) 10−0(each quad is formed twice; keep one copy)
25, 9, 10 ✓all pairs except (1,5) combine further

Prime implicants.

  • (1,5) 0−01 = A′C′D: this pair was never ticked.
  • −00− = B′C′.
  • −0−0 = B′D′.

PI chart.

  • m5 is covered only by A′C′D.
  • m9 is covered only by B′C′.
  • m2 and m10 are covered only by B′D′.

All three PIs are essential.

Answer: F = B′D′ + B′C′ + A′C′D, with 7 literals.

Minimal POS. The 0-cells give F′ = CD + BD′ + AB. So F = (C′ + D′)(B′ + D)(A′ + B′), with 6 literals. Both forms agree with the truth table on all 16 inputs.

Example 3: Canonical forms, dual and complement

Problem. F(A, B, C) = A + B′C. Find Σm, ΠM, Fd and F′.

  • A = 1 gives the rows 4, 5, 6 and 7. B′C = 1 with A = 0 gives row 1. So F = Σm(1, 4, 5, 6, 7) = ΠM(0, 2, 3).
  • For the dual, swap + and · while keeping the literals: Fd = A(B′ + C).
  • For the complement, also prime the literals: F′ = A′(B + C′) = A′B + A′C′. As a check, F′ = Σm(0, 2, 3): A′B gives rows 2 and 3, and A′C′ gives rows 0 and 2. This is correct.

Is F self-dual? No. Fd = AB′ + AC = Σm(4, 5, 7) with the same three variables. That is not equal to F.

Example 4: Is {→, 0} functionally complete?

Apply Post's test:

  • → is outside T0, because 0 → 0 = 1.
  • The constant 0 is outside T1.
  • → is not self-dual: (x′ → y′)′ = (x + y′)′ = x′y, which is not x′ + y.
  • → is not monotone: raising x from 0 to 1 with y = 0 drops the output from 1 to 0.
  • → is not linear: x′ + y = 1 ⊕ x ⊕ xy has a product term.

Every class is escaped, so the set is complete. Constructively:

  • NOT x = x → 0.
  • x + y = (x → 0) → y.

{NOT, OR} is complete, so {→, 0} is too. Without the 0, the set {→} can never produce 0 when all its inputs are 1, so it is not complete.

Example 5: A 5-variable map

Problem. F(A, B, C, D, E) = Σm(0, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15, 16, 18, 21, 23, 24, 26, 29, 31).

  1. Split the minterms by A. For A = 0 they are 0, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15. For A = 1 they are the same numbers plus 16. So the two 4-variable maps (in B, C, D, E) are identical, and A drops out.
  2. On one map, the cells 0, 2, 8, 10 form the four corners, which is C′E′ in the variables B, C, D, E. The cells 5, 7, 13, 15 form the centre quad, CE.
  3. With A dropped as well, each quad becomes a 16-cell group across both maps.

Answer: F = C′E′ + CE, which is C XNOR E. Exhaustive search confirms that this is the only minimal SOP.

NTA traps

  • Dual taken as complement. Wrong: “the dual of AB′ + C is (A′ + B)C′.” Fix: the dual keeps the literals, (A + B′)C. Only the complement primes them.
  • Forgetting brackets when dualising. Wrong: A + BC becomes A · B + C. Fix: A(B + C). Bracket every sum before you swap.
  • Maxterm rule reversed. Wrong: M5 = A + B′ + C. Fix: in a maxterm a 1 bit is primed, so M5 (101) = A′ + B + C′.
  • Binary-order K-map. Wrong: labelling columns 00, 01, 10, 11, which makes m1 and m2 look adjacent. Fix: always use Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10. Minterms 2 and 8 are never adjacent (they differ in two bits), but 0 and 8 are, through the wrap.
  • Groups of 6 or 3. A 2 × 3 block is a rectangle but not a power of two, so it cannot be a group.
  • Covering don't-cares. You never need to cover an X. A group made only of Xs is never part of a minimal answer.
  • Not every PI is essential. In Σm(1, 5, 6, 7, 11, 12, 13, 15), BD is a prime implicant but it is not used in the minimal answer.
  • Assuming a unique minimum. Cyclic functions have two or more equally good answers. Check every option against the truth table, not against the one answer you found.
  • Counting functions as 2n. That is the number of rows. The number of functions is 22n.
  • {→} called complete. It needs ¬ or the constant 0. {⊕, ¬} and {↔, ¬} are never complete, because they are linear.

How NTA asks this

Formats.

  • Direct minimisation, with four near-identical expressions as options.
  • Match List I (laws, sets or counts) with List II.
  • Assertion–Reason on duality or completeness.
  • Statement I/II on minterm and maxterm facts.
  • “Which of the following are valid identities” (multi-select).
  • Ordering the steps of QM.

Mini-example (Assertion–Reason).

  • A: {NOR} is functionally complete.
  • R: NOR is neither monotone nor linear.

Both statements are true. But completeness also needs NOR to escape T0, T1 and the self-dual class. So R is only part of the reason, and the answer is “both true, R is not the correct explanation.”

Mini-example (Match). Pair each set with the Post class that traps it:

  • {∧, ∨, 0, 1} → monotone;
  • {⊕, ¬} → linear;
  • {majority, ¬} → self-dual;
  • {→} → 1-preserving.

Elimination tricks.

  • For a minimisation question, test each option on two or three minterms and one 0-cell. One wrong cell eliminates the option.
  • Count literals: the minimal answer has the fewest literals among the options that are correct.
  • Check that each option contains every EPI. An option without the obvious EPI is wrong.
  • For counts, remember the powers-of-powers: 16, 256 and 65,536.

terms.definition: Every valid Boolean identity stays valid when + and · are swapped and 0 and 1 are swapped; variables are not complemented.
A product of all n variables that equals 1 for exactly one input row i; a 0 bit gives a primed variable (m5 = AB′C).
A sum of all n variables that equals 0 for exactly one input row i; a 1 bit gives a primed variable (M5 = A′ + B + C′). M_i = (m_i)′.
An implicant (group of 1s and don’t-cares) that cannot be enlarged into a bigger implicant.
A prime implicant that alone covers at least one true minterm; it must appear in every minimal SOP.
An input combination whose output does not matter; it may be taken as 1 or 0, whichever makes the groups larger, and need not be covered.
A function equal to its own dual, i.e. complementing all inputs complements the output. There are 2^(2^(n−1)) of them.
xy + x′z + yz = xy + x′z: the consensus term yz is redundant.
A set of operations that can express every Boolean function, e.g. {NAND}, {NOR}, {→, ¬}.
T0 (0-preserving), T1 (1-preserving), self-dual, monotone, linear. A set is complete iff it has an operation outside each class.

lessons.examTip: Before choosing a minimisation option, test it on one or two 1-cells and one 0-cell of the map: a single mismatch eliminates it, and among the options that survive, the one with the fewest literals that still contains every essential prime implicant is the answer.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace). Draw each K-map in Gray order before grouping.
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes.

Check every answer against solutions.md. Record each mistake in your error log with the trap behind it (binary-order map, dual versus complement, redundant prime implicant, don’t-care forced into the cover).
For every minimisation you got right, test your expression on two 1-cells and one 0-cell to build the checking habit.
Write Post’s five-class table and the counting formulas (2^(2^n), 2^(2^(n−1)), C(2^n, 2^(n−1))) from memory.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.
check: At least 12 of 15 problems correct.
Problems 9–15 solved within 12 minutes.
Every K-map answer contains all essential prime implicants and no group of a non-power-of-two size.
Post’s table and the three counting formulas reproduced from memory without an error.

quiz.question: What is the minimal sum-of-products form of F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15)?
quiz.explanation: The four corners m0, m2, m8, m10 form the quad B′D′ (the map wraps both ways), and the centre m5, m7, m13, m15 forms the quad BD. Both are essential and cover all eight 1s, so F = B′D′ + BD (B XNOR D). B′D + BD′ is the complement (the XOR). A′B′D′ is only a pair, not the largest group, and A′D′ includes m4 and m6, which are 0s.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Absorption: x + xy = x (III). Consensus: the term yz is redundant in xy + x′z + yz (IV). De Morgan: (x + y)′ = x′y′ (I). The second distributive law, special to Boolean algebra, is x + yz = (x + y)(x + z) (II). So A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II. The other options swap one or two of these pairs.

b: II. x + yz = (x + y)(x + z)
III. x + xy = x
IV. xy + x′z + yz = xy + x′z

stmts: Assertion (A): Since x + x′y = x + y is a valid Boolean identity, x(x′ + y) = xy is also a valid identity.

quiz.question: How many Boolean functions of 3 variables are self-dual?
quiz.explanation: A self-dual function satisfies F(x′) = F(x)′, so the value on one input of each complementary pair fixes the value on the other. 3 variables give 8 rows in 4 complementary pairs, so there are 2^4 = 16 self-dual functions (formula 2^(2^(n−1))). 256 is the count of all functions of 3 variables, and 70 = C(8, 4) is the count of neutral functions.

Both Statement I and Statement II are false
