quiz.explanation: NAND gives NOT (x NAND x) and AND (NOT of NAND), so {NAND} is complete. Implication preserves 1 (1 → 1 = 1), so every expression built only from → outputs 1 when all inputs are 1; it can never produce NOT. So {→} is incomplete; it needs ¬ or the constant 0.

stmts: Statement I: The set {NAND} is functionally complete.
Statement II: The set {→} containing only the implication operation is functionally complete.

quiz.explanation: Prime implicants: BD (5, 7, 13, 15) and five pairs: B′C′D′ (0, 8), A′C′D′ (0, 4), A′BC′ (4, 5), AC′D (9, 13), AB′C′ (8, 9). That is 6. Only BD is essential (it alone covers m7 and m15); every other 1 lies in two pairs. A minimal cover is BD + A′C′D′ + AB′C′.

quiz.question: Arrange the following steps of the Quine–McCluskey method in the correct order.
quiz.explanation: First tabulate by number of 1s (B), then combine repeatedly (C), then the unticked terms are the prime implicants and form the chart (E), then pick essentials (A), then cover what is left (D): B, C, E, A, D. Essentials cannot be chosen before the chart exists.

stmts: A. Select the essential prime implicants from the prime implicant chart
B. List the minterms and don’t-cares in binary, grouped by the number of 1s
C. Combine terms of adjacent groups that differ in exactly one bit, repeating until no more combinations are possible
D. Cover the remaining minterms with the fewest additional prime implicants (dominance or Petrick’s method)
E. Take the unticked terms as prime implicants and build the prime implicant chart over the true minterms

quiz.question: The canonical product-of-maxterms form of F(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 4, 5, 6) is:
quiz.explanation: The maxterms are the rows where F = 0, i.e. the indices missing from the minterm list: {0,…,7} − {1, 4, 5, 6} = {0, 2, 3, 7}. So F = ΠM(0, 2, 3, 7). ΠM(1, 4, 5, 6) would be a completely different function (it is 0 exactly where F is 1).

lessons.title: Optimization
lessons.summaryHtml: Linear programming maximises or minimises a linear objective over a convex feasible region defined by linear constraints, and an optimum, if one exists, is always at a corner point. The graphical method checks corners for two variables; the simplex method moves between basic feasible solutions using the entering-variable rule and the minimum ratio test, with slack, surplus and artificial (Big-M or two-phase) variables. Every LPP has a dual with the same optimal value, linked by weak and strong duality and complementary slackness. Transportation problems start from NWCR, least cost or VAM and are optimised by MODI; assignment problems use the Hungarian method; integer programs use branch and bound or cutting planes because rounding is unsafe. NTA asks quick numericals (corner optimum, IBFS cost, assignment cost, basic-variable counts) and concept checks on unbounded, infeasible, degenerate and alternative-optimum cases.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Optimization means choosing the best decision within given limits. In a linear programming problem (LPP), both the goal and the limits are linear. We maximise or minimise an objective such as Z = 3x + 5y, subject to constraints such as x + y ≤ 8 and x, y ≥ 0.

The feasible choices form a convex polygon, or a polyhedron in higher dimensions. The best value is always found at a corner of it. The graphical method checks these corners by hand for two variables. The simplex method walks from corner to corner algebraically for any number of variables.

Every LPP also has a mirror problem, the dual, with the same optimal value. Three special structures have their own shortcut methods:

  • the transportation problem, which ships goods from sources to destinations;
  • the assignment problem, which pairs n workers with n jobs;
  • integer programming, where the variables must be whole numbers.

Why it matters for NET

Optimization is the “O” in Unit 1 (Discrete Structures and Optimization). The syllabus lists LPP, simplex, duality, transportation, assignment and integer programming. NTA questions here are mostly quick numericals. For example:

  • the optimum of a two-variable LPP;
  • the initial cost by NWCR, least cost or VAM;
  • the minimum assignment cost;
  • the number of basic variables.

These are mixed with concept checks:

  • what an unbounded, infeasible or degenerate tableau looks like;
  • primal–dual correspondence rules;
  • which method ignores costs.

The arithmetic is simple, but the options are built from the usual slips. Typical ones are stopping VAM at a wrong penalty, forgetting to check a corner, or treating a degenerate solution as non-degenerate.

Interactive solvers

Enter any problem, including the ones in your practice set, and the solver works it out step by step with the conventions stated. Use it to check your answers, not to replace doing them by hand: the exam gives you no solver.

Interactive solver: Linear programming solver

The solver runs in your browser. Turn on JavaScript to use it.

Interactive solver: Transportation problem solver

The solver runs in your browser. Turn on JavaScript to use it.

Interactive solver: Assignment problem: Hungarian method

The solver runs in your browser. Turn on JavaScript to use it.

Formulating an LPP

Every LPP has three parts:

  • decision variables, the quantities you control;
  • a linear objective function;
  • linear constraints, including non-negativity.

The key assumptions are proportionality and additivity, which together make it linear, and also divisibility and certainty. Divisibility means variables may take fractional values. Dropping divisibility is exactly what turns an LPP into an integer program.

Some terms:

  • A feasible solution satisfies all the constraints.
  • The feasible region is the set of all feasible solutions. It is always convex, because it is an intersection of half-planes.
  • An optimal solution is a feasible solution with the best objective value.

Fundamental theorem. If an LPP has an optimal solution, at least one optimal solution is a corner point (extreme point) of the feasible region. A linear objective over a convex polygon cannot peak in the interior. Moving in the improving direction keeps improving until you hit the boundary, and then a corner.

The graphical method

  1. Draw each constraint as a line and shade the side that satisfies it.
  2. Find the corner points of the feasible region by solving pairs of boundary lines.
  3. Evaluate Z at every corner, or slide an iso-profit line, and pick the best.

Four special outcomes are read straight from the picture:

  • Unique optimum: one best corner.
  • Alternative (multiple) optima: the objective line is parallel to a binding edge, so every point on that edge is optimal.
  • Unbounded solution: the region is open in the improving direction, so Z can grow forever. An unbounded region alone is not enough; the objective must also improve in the open direction.
  • Infeasible: the constraints have no common point, for example x + y ≤ 4 together with x + y ≥ 6.

A redundant constraint is one whose removal does not change the feasible region.

The simplex method

Standard form. Every constraint becomes an equation with a non-negative right-hand side:

  • For a ≤ constraint, add a slack variable: x + y + s1 = 8.
  • For a ≥ constraint, subtract a surplus variable and add an artificial variable: x + y − s2 + A1 = 6. The artificial variable is needed because a surplus variable cannot start the basis: it would equal −6.
  • An = constraint needs an artificial variable only.

With m equations and n variables in total, a basic solution sets n − m variables to zero and solves for the other m. There are at most C(n, m) basic solutions. Those with all variables ≥ 0 are the basic feasible solutions (BFS), and they correspond exactly to the corners of the feasible region.

Iteration (maximisation). Write the objective row as Z − Σcjxj = 0.

  1. Entering variable: the most negative entry in the Z-row. In the cj − zj convention this is the most positive cj − zj.
  2. Leaving variable: the minimum ratio test. Take RHS ÷ pivot-column entry, over positive entries only. The smallest ratio leaves, because it is the first constraint to become tight.
  3. Pivot: divide the pivot row by the pivot element, then clear the pivot column in every other row, including the Z-row.
  4. Stop when no Z-row entry is negative. The solution is then optimal.

Artificial variables. Big-M gives each artificial variable a huge penalty: −MA in a maximisation, +MA in a minimisation. This forces them out of the basis. The two-phase method instead first minimises the sum of the artificials (Phase I). If that minimum is positive, the problem is infeasible. Otherwise it drops them and optimises the real objective (Phase II).

SituationHow it shows in the simplex tableau
OptimalNo negative Z-row entry (max), i.e. all cj − zj ≤ 0
Alternative optimaAt optimality, some non-basic variable has a zero Z-row entry
UnboundedThe entering column has no positive entry, so the ratio test is impossible
InfeasibleAn artificial variable is still positive in the optimal tableau (Big-M), or Phase I ends with a positive value
DegenerateA basic variable equals 0, caused by a tie in the minimum ratio test; the next iteration may not improve Z and cycling is possible (Bland’s rule prevents it)

Reading the final tableau. The Z-row entries under the slack variables are the shadow prices, also called dual values. Each one is the increase in optimal Z per extra unit of that resource, within the range where the basis stays optimal.

Duality

Every LPP (the primal) has a dual. For a primal of the form “max cTx, Ax ≤ b, x ≥ 0”, the dual is “min bTy, ATy ≥ c, y ≥ 0”. In words:

  • constraints become variables, and variables become constraints;
  • the right-hand sides become the objective coefficients, and the objective coefficients become the right-hand sides;
  • A is transposed.
Primal (max)Dual (min)
i-th constraint ≤yi ≥ 0
i-th constraint =yi unrestricted in sign
i-th constraint ≥yi ≤ 0
xj ≥ 0j-th constraint ≥
xj unrestrictedj-th constraint =
m constraints, n variablesn constraints, m variables

The main theorems:

  • The dual of the dual is the primal.
  • Weak duality: for any feasible x and y, Z = cTx ≤ bTy = W. Every dual-feasible W is therefore an upper bound on the primal. So if the primal is unbounded, the dual must be infeasible, and vice versa.
  • Strong duality: if either problem has a finite optimum, so does the other, and Z* = W*.
  • Both problems can also be infeasible at the same time. So “primal infeasible ⇒ dual unbounded” is not a valid rule.
  • Complementary slackness: at optimality, yi × (slack of primal constraint i) = 0 and xj × (surplus of dual constraint j) = 0. A resource that is not fully used has a shadow price of 0.

Transportation problem

The model. There are m sources with supplies ai, n destinations with demands bj, and unit costs cij. We minimise Σcijxij subject to row sums = ai and column sums = bj.

Balance. The problem is balanced when Σai = Σbj. Otherwise, add a dummy source or destination for the difference, with zero cost (or a penalty cost if stated). A balanced problem always has a feasible solution. If all supplies and demands are integers, some optimal solution is integral.

Basic cells. Of the m + n equations, only m + n − 1 are independent, because one is implied by balance. So a basic feasible solution has m + n − 1 basic cells. If an IBFS has fewer positive allocations, it is degenerate. Put a tiny ε in a suitable empty cell (one that forms no loop) so that MODI can run.

Initial solution methods.

  • North-West Corner Rule (NWCR): start at the top-left cell and allocate min(supply, demand). Move right if the column is exhausted, and down if the row is exhausted. It ignores costs completely.
  • Least Cost Method (LCM): allocate as much as possible to the cheapest remaining cell, cross out the exhausted row or column, and repeat.
  • Vogel's Approximation Method (VAM): for every row and column, compute the penalty, the difference between its two smallest remaining costs. Pick the line with the largest penalty and allocate to its cheapest cell. Recompute the penalties and repeat. VAM usually gives the best starting solution, often the optimum, but it is not guaranteed to.

Optimality test: MODI (u–v) method.

  1. For every basic cell set ui + vj = cij, taking u1 = 0, and solve for the rest.
  2. For every empty cell, compute dij = cij − (ui + vj).
  3. If all dij ≥ 0, the solution is optimal. It is unique if all are > 0.
  4. Otherwise, the most negative cell enters. Trace its closed loop with alternate + and − corners. Shift θ = the smallest allocation on a − corner, and repeat.

The stepping-stone method computes the same dij by tracing a loop for every empty cell.

Assignment problem

The model. Assign n workers to n jobs, one each, at minimum total cost. It is a transportation problem with every supply and demand equal to 1. So each BFS has 2n − 1 basic cells but only n of them positive: it is always highly degenerate. That is why the special Hungarian method is used instead of MODI. There are n! possible assignments.

Hungarian method.

  1. Subtract each row's minimum from that row.
  2. Subtract each column's minimum from that column.
  3. Cover all zeros with the minimum number of horizontal and vertical lines.
  4. If the number of lines is n, an optimal assignment exists among the zeros. Pick rows or columns with a single zero first.
  5. If fewer than n lines are needed, find the smallest uncovered entry k. Subtract k from every uncovered entry, add k to entries at line intersections, and go back to step 3.

Variants.

  • Maximisation: subtract every entry from the largest entry (or negate the entries), then minimise.
  • Unbalanced: add a dummy row or column of zeros.
  • Forbidden pair: give that cell the cost M (a very large number).

Integer programming

An integer program (IP) is an LPP in which some variables (a mixed IP) or all variables (a pure IP) must be integers. In a 0–1 IP the variables are binary; 0–1 knapsack and capital budgeting are examples. Dropping the integer requirement gives the LP relaxation. For a maximisation, its optimum is an upper bound on the IP optimum, since the relaxation has more choices.

Rounding is not safe. The rounded LP optimum may be infeasible, or feasible but not optimal.

Branch and bound.

  1. Solve the LP relaxation.
  2. If some xj = f is fractional, split into two subproblems: xj ≤ ⌊f⌋ and xj ≥ ⌈f⌉.
  3. Solve each subproblem. Prune a node if it is infeasible, if its bound is no better than the best integer solution found so far (the incumbent), or if its LP solution is already integral, which may give a new incumbent.

Gomory's cutting-plane method. It adds a constraint built from the fractional parts of a tableau row. The cut removes the current fractional optimum but no integer point. General IP is NP-hard, unlike LP, which is solvable in polynomial time by interior-point methods, although simplex is exponential in the worst case.

Dual simplex method

The ordinary (primal) simplex keeps every tableau feasible (all right-hand sides ≥ 0) and works towards optimality. The dual simplex method does the opposite. It starts from a tableau whose Z-row is already optimal (the tableau is “dual feasible”) but whose basic solution is infeasible (some right-hand side is negative), and it works towards feasibility. Each of its iterations is a primal simplex iteration on the dual problem, which is where the name comes from.

When it is used.

  • A minimisation with non-negative costs and ≥ constraints. Multiply each ≥ constraint by −1 and add a slack. The slacks form the starting basis with negative values, so no artificial variables and no Big-M are needed.
  • Re-optimising after an optimal tableau is disturbed: a new constraint is added (sensitivity analysis, branch and bound, Gomory cuts), or a right-hand side changes so that a basic variable turns negative.

Rules (Z-row written so that “optimal” means every Z-row entry is ≥ 0):

  1. Leaving variable first: the basic variable with the most negative right-hand side. If no right-hand side is negative, stop: the tableau is optimal and feasible.
  2. Entering variable: look only at columns with a negative entry in the leaving row, and take the smallest ratio |Z-row entry ÷ row entry|. This ratio test keeps every Z-row entry ≥ 0.
  3. If the leaving row has no negative entry, the problem is infeasible: that row says “a sum of non-negative terms equals a negative number”.
  4. Pivot exactly as in the primal simplex.

The mirror image is worth memorising. Primal simplex: entering variable first (from the Z-row), then the leaving variable by a ratio test on the right-hand sides. Dual simplex: leaving variable first (from the right-hand sides), then the entering variable by a ratio test on the Z-row.

Example (dual simplex from the start). Minimise Z = 3x1 + 2x2 subject to x1 + x2 ≥ 4, 2x1 + x2 ≥ 6, x ≥ 0. Multiply by −1 and add slacks: −x1 − x2 + s1 = −4 and −2x1 − x2 + s2 = −6. The Z-row holds the costs 3 and 2, which are ≥ 0, so the start is dual feasible.

Sensitivity analysis (post-optimality analysis)

Sensitivity analysis asks how much the data of an LPP (the right-hand sides bi, the objective coefficients cj, or the constraint matrix) can change before the current optimal basis stops being optimal. It is done on the final tableau, without re-solving. The key object is B−1, which can be read from the final tableau under the columns that were the initial slack variables.

Take Example 2 (maximise Z = 6x1 + 5x2, x1 + x2 ≤ 5, 3x1 + 2x2 ≤ 12, optimum (2, 3) with Z = 27). Under s1 and s2 the final rows are x2: (3, −1) and x1: (−2, 1), and the Z-row has shadow prices (3, 1).

  • Right-hand-side ranging (feasibility). The basic values are B−1b. With b1 = 5 + Δ: x2 = 3 + 3Δ ≥ 0 and x1 = 2 − 2Δ ≥ 0, so −1 ≤ Δ ≤ 1, that is 4 ≤ b1 ≤ 6. With b2 = 12 + Δ: x2 = 3 − Δ and x1 = 2 + Δ, so 10 ≤ b2 ≤ 15. Inside its range each extra unit changes Z by the shadow price (3 and 1). Outside it the basis becomes infeasible, and the dual simplex restores feasibility.
  • Cost ranging (optimality). If a basic variable’s coefficient changes by δ, each non-basic Z-row entry changes by δ × (that variable’s row entry). For c1 = 6 + δ: s1 gives 3 − 2δ ≥ 0 and s2 gives 1 + δ ≥ 0, so 5 ≤ c1 ≤ 7.5. For c2 = 5 + δ: 3 + 3δ ≥ 0 and 1 − δ ≥ 0, so 4 ≤ c2 ≤ 6. Graphically, the objective line stays between the slopes of the two binding constraints. For a non-basic variable, its coefficient can rise by its Z-row entry (its reduced cost) before it becomes worth entering.
  • Adding a new variable (a new product). “Price it out” with the shadow prices. A product x3 using 1 unit of each resource costs 3 × 1 + 1 × 1 = 4 in forgone profit. If its profit is 7, its Z-row entry is 4 − 7 = −3 < 0, so the current solution is no longer optimal and x3 should enter (primal simplex).
  • Adding a new constraint. If the current optimum satisfies it, nothing changes. Otherwise append it as a row, express it in terms of the non-basic variables, and apply the dual simplex. For example, add x1 ≤ 1. Substituting x1 = 2 + 2s1 − s2 gives the row 2s1 − s2 + s3 = −1. Then s3 leaves and s2 enters (the only negative entry), and one pivot gives the new optimum (1, 4) with Z = 26.

PERT and CPM: network representation

A project is a set of activities (jobs that take time) with precedence relations such as “D can start only after A finishes”. CPM (critical path method, du Pont, 1957) treats durations as known and is used for time–cost trade-offs. PERT (program evaluation and review technique, US Navy Polaris programme, 1958) treats durations as uncertain, with three time estimates. Both draw the project as a network.

  • Activity on arrow (AOA), the classic PERT/CPM drawing: arrows are activities and nodes are events (the instants when activities start or finish). A node where several arrows end is a merge event; one where several start is a burst event.
  • Activity on node (AON): nodes are activities and arrows show precedence. No dummies are ever needed.

Rules for an AOA network.

  1. One start event and one end event.
  2. Each activity is exactly one arrow, and no two activities may share both the same tail and the same head event.
  3. No loops (a cycle would mean an activity precedes itself) and no dangling arrows (every activity except the last leads somewhere).
  4. Events are numbered by Fulkerson’s rule, so that every arrow goes from a smaller to a larger number (i < j).

A dummy activity is a dashed arrow with zero duration and zero resources. It is used (i) to keep rule 2 when two activities run in parallel between the same events, and (ii) to show a logical dependency that no real arrow can show. The textbook case: C needs only A, but D needs both A and B. Then a dummy from the end of A to the end of B is required.

Fragment: A, B start; C after A; D after A and B

  (1) --A--> (2) --C--> (4)

   |          v
   +---B---> (3) --D--> (5)

The example network used below has six activities: A (3 days) and B (4) start the project; C (1) and D (5) follow A; E (3) follows B and C; F (4) follows D and E. In AOA form: A = 1→2, B = 1→3, C = 2→3, D = 2→4, E = 3→4, F = 4→5. No dummy is needed here, because no two activities share both end events.

Critical path calculations

Forward pass. ES (earliest start) = the largest EF of the predecessors, with 0 at the start; EF = ES + duration. The project duration T is the largest EF. Backward pass. LF (latest finish) = the smallest LS of the successors, with T at the end; LS = LF − duration.

Floats. Total float TF = LS − ES = LF − EF: how long an activity can slip without delaying the project. Free float FF = (earliest ES of the successors) − EF: how long it can slip without delaying any successor. Independent float IF = (earliest ES of the successors) − (latest LF of the predecessors) − duration, taken as 0 if negative. Always IF ≤ FF ≤ TF. In AOA terms, the slack of an event is its latest time TL minus its earliest time TE.

PERT times. Each activity has an optimistic time a, a most likely time m and a pessimistic time b (a beta distribution). Then te = (a + 4m + b) ÷ 6 and σ2 = ((b − a) ÷ 6)2. The project time is taken as normal, with mean Te = Σte and variance Σσ2 along the critical path only, and P(T ≤ D) = Φ((D − Te) ÷ σ).

Example (PERT probability). A critical path has three activities with (a, m, b) = (1, 4, 7), (2, 5, 14) and (2, 8, 14). Their te values are 24/6 = 4, 36/6 = 6 and 48/6 = 8, so Te = 18 days. Their variances are 1, 4 and 4, so σ2 = 9 and σ = 3. The probability of finishing within 21 days is Φ((21 − 18)/3) = Φ(1) ≈ 0.8413. Within 18 days it is exactly 0.5. For about 97.7% confidence (Z = 2), quote 18 + 2 × 3 = 24 days. The trap is adding standard deviations (1 + 2 + 2 = 5) instead of variances.

Resource levelling and resource allocation

The ES schedule is often uneven: many people are needed on some days and few on others. Two related problems follow.

  • Resource levelling (smoothing): the project duration is fixed. Non-critical activities are shifted within their floats to reduce the peak demand and the day-to-day fluctuation. A common measure is Burgess’s method: minimise the sum of the squares of the daily requirements. The total resource-days never change, so a smaller sum of squares means a flatter profile.
  • Resource allocation (resource-constrained scheduling): the resource limit is fixed. Activities are scheduled so the daily demand never exceeds the limit, which may extend the project duration. Heuristics give priority to the activity with the least float (critical activities first).

Example (levelling the example network). Daily worker needs: A 2, B 3, C 2, D 1, E 3, F 2. Scheduling every activity at its ES gives the first profile below: a peak of 6 on day 4, where B, C and D overlap, and a sum of squares of 176. Now delay C by its one day of float (to day 5). E must then start on day 6, which uses E’s one day of float, so the project still ends on day 12. The peak falls to 5 and the sum of squares to 164.

Cost considerations: time–cost trade-off (crashing)

Project cost has two parts. Direct costs (labour, materials, equipment) rise when an activity is speeded up. Indirect costs (overheads, supervision, penalties) rise with the project duration. Total cost is therefore U-shaped in the duration, and the aim is the duration of minimum total cost.

Each activity has a normal time and cost and a crash time and cost (the shortest possible time, at a higher cost). Assuming linearity between them, the cost slope is:

cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost) ÷ (normal time − crash time), the extra cost per unit of time saved.

Crashing procedure.

  1. Find the critical path(s) with normal times.
  2. Crash the critical activity with the lowest cost slope by one unit (only critical activities shorten the project).
  3. Recompute the paths. When several paths are critical, one unit must be cut from every critical path, so compare the cheapest combinations.
  4. Stop when the cheapest cut costs more than the indirect cost it saves, or when a critical path cannot be shortened further.

NTA traps

  • Checking only some corners. Wrong: evaluating only the intercepts. Fix: list every corner, including the intersections of pairs of constraints, and evaluate Z at each.
  • Unbounded region confused with unbounded solution. A minimisation over an open region, like Example 3's dual, can still have a finite optimum.
  • Ratio test with negative or zero entries. Only positive entries in the pivot column count. If there are none, the problem is unbounded, not “pick the smallest”.
  • Surplus used as a starting basic variable. For ≥ constraints you need an artificial variable. The surplus would be negative.
  • “Primal infeasible ⇒ dual unbounded”. This is not a theorem. Both can be infeasible. Only “unbounded ⇒ the other infeasible” is guaranteed.
  • Counting basic cells as m × n or m + n. The correct count is m + n − 1, for example 6 for a 3 × 4 problem. NWCR can give fewer when a row and a column are exhausted together. Such a solution is degenerate.
  • VAM penalty as largest minus smallest. The penalty is the difference of the two smallest costs in the line, recomputed after every allocation.
  • Assuming VAM or LCM is optimal. In Example 4, VAM gives 505 but the optimum is 500. Always run MODI if the question asks for the optimum.
  • Hungarian on a maximisation problem directly. Convert first, by subtracting from the largest entry, or you will minimise profit.
  • Rounding an LP answer for an IP. The rounded point may violate a constraint, as (3, 1) does in Example 6.

  • A direct numerical: the optimum Z, the IBFS cost or the minimum assignment cost.
  • Match List I (special case, method or primal element) with List II (its tableau symptom, description or dual element).
  • Statement I/II on duality theorems or degeneracy.

Mini-example (A–R).

  • A: If the primal has an unbounded objective, the dual is infeasible.
  • R: By weak duality, every dual-feasible W is an upper bound on every primal Z.

Both are true, and R is the reason: a dual-feasible point would cap the unbounded Z. So the answer is option 1.

  • MODI → optimality test with ui + vj = cij.

Speed tricks.

  • For a graphical LPP, compute Z only at corners that satisfy all the constraints. Options often list an infeasible corner with a higher Z.
  • For transportation, check that the options' costs are ordered as NWCR ≥ LCM ≥ VAM ≥ optimum in the usual case.
  • For assignment, a quick lower bound is the sum of the row minimums. Any option below it is impossible.

terms.definition: The set of points satisfying all constraints; for an LPP it is always convex.
A solution with n − m variables set to zero and the rest, found from the m equations, all non-negative; BFSs are the corner points.
Slack is added to a ≤ constraint; surplus is subtracted from a ≥ constraint; an artificial variable is added to ≥ and = constraints to get a starting basis.
RHS ÷ positive pivot-column entry; the smallest ratio decides the leaving variable, keeping the solution feasible.
A BFS in which some basic variable is zero (in transportation: fewer than m + n − 1 positive allocations). It can cause cycling in simplex.
Each LPP (primal) has a dual whose variables correspond to primal constraints; weak duality gives Z ≤ W, strong duality gives Z* = W*.
The optimal dual value of a constraint: the change in optimal Z per unit increase of that resource.
An IBFS method that allocates in the row or column with the largest penalty (difference of its two smallest costs).
Optimality test for transportation: u_i + v_j = c_ij on basic cells; d_ij = c_ij − u_i − v_j must be ≥ 0 on empty cells.
Assignment algorithm: reduce rows and columns, cover zeros with minimum lines, adjust by the smallest uncovered entry until n lines are needed.
IP method that solves LP relaxations and splits on a fractional variable (x ≤ ⌊f⌋, x ≥ ⌈f⌉), pruning by bound, infeasibility or integrality.

lessons.examTip: For any graphical LPP, list every corner of the feasible region (including the intersection of each pair of binding constraints), confirm each satisfies all constraints, and only then compare Z. For transportation, count the allocations: exactly m + n − 1 means non-degenerate.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 14 minutes without notes (these are longer numericals; about 100 seconds each).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes.

Check every answer against solutions.md. Record each mistake in your error log with the trap behind it (missed or infeasible corner, VAM penalty from the wrong pair of costs, maximisation not converted, rounded IP answer).
For problems 5–8, recount the allocations (must be m + n − 1 = 6) and recompute each total cost cell by cell.
Write the primal–dual correspondence table and the simplex special-case table from memory.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.
check: At least 12 of 15 problems correct.
Problems 9–15 solved within 12 minutes.
NWCR, LCM and VAM costs for problems 5–7 correct on the first attempt.
Primal–dual table and simplex special cases reproduced without an error.

quiz.question: Maximise Z = 3x + 5y subject to x + y ≤ 8, x + 3y ≤ 18, 2x + y ≤ 14, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. What is the optimal value of Z and where is it attained?
quiz.explanation: Corners: (0, 0), (7, 0), (6, 2) from 2x + y = 14 and x + y = 8, (3, 5) from x + y = 8 and x + 3y = 18, and (0, 6). Z = 0, 21, 28, 34, 30. Maximum 34 at (3, 5). (7, 0) gives only 21, not 35; the 35 option miscalculates Z there.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: No positive entry in the entering column means no ratio limits the increase: unbounded (III). A zero Z-row entry for a non-basic variable at optimality means it can enter without changing Z: alternative optima (IV). A positive artificial at the end: infeasible (I). A ratio tie leaves a basic variable at 0: degeneracy (II).

h: List II (What the simplex tableau shows)
b: I. An artificial variable remains positive in the optimal tableau
II. A tie in the minimum ratio test, so a basic variable becomes zero
III. The entering column has no positive entry
IV. A non-basic variable has a zero net evaluation (Z-row entry) at optimality

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: (R) is the weak duality theorem: Z ≤ W for any feasible pair. If the dual had even one feasible point, its W would cap the primal Z, contradicting unboundedness. So the dual must be infeasible: (A) is true and follows directly from (R).

stmts: Assertion (A): If a maximisation LPP has an unbounded objective value, its dual has no feasible solution.
Reason (R): By weak duality, the objective value of any feasible solution of the dual (minimisation) is an upper bound on the objective value of every feasible solution of the primal.

quiz.question:
For the transportation problem below, what is the total cost of the initial basic feasible solution given by Vogel’s approximation method (VAM)?
Costs (rows S1–S3, columns D1–D4):
S1: 4 9 6 9 | supply 45
S2: 11 3 5 1 | supply 70
S3: 8 12 7 9 | supply 20
Demand: 35 35 15 50
quiz.explanation: Penalties: column D4 (9 − 1 = 8) is largest, allocate S2D4 = 50. Then D2 (penalty 6): S2D2 = 20. Then D1 (4): S1D1 = 35. Then row S3 (12 − 7 = 5): S3D3 = 15. Finally S1D2 = 10, S3D2 = 5. Cost = 50 + 60 + 140 + 105 + 90 + 60 = 505. 590 is NWCR, 525 is least cost and 500 is the true optimum (MODI improves VAM by one unit on 5 items).

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Only m + n − 1 of the m + n equations are independent, so a non-degenerate BFS has m + n − 1 positive cells (Statement I true). In an assignment problem a BFS needs 2n − 1 basic cells but only n cells can be positive (each row and column has a single 1), so it is always degenerate (Statement II true).

stmts: Statement I: A non-degenerate basic feasible solution of a balanced transportation problem with m sources and n destinations has exactly m + n − 1 positive allocations.
Statement II: Every basic feasible solution of an n × n assignment problem, viewed as a transportation problem, is degenerate.

quiz.question:
Four workers W1–W4 must be assigned to four jobs J1–J4, one each. The cost matrix (rows W1–W4, columns J1–J4) is:
W1: 9 19 13 11
W2: 11 6 8 15
W3: 7 13 20 14
W4: 16 8 15 9
What is the minimum total cost?

Assignment: W3→J1 (7), W1→J4 (11), W4→J2 (8), W2→J3 (8): total 34. 30 is the sum of row minimums, only a lower bound; it is not achievable because W3 and W1 both have their minimum in J1.

quiz.question: Which of the following statements about duality in linear programming are correct?
options: A, B, C and D only
A, B, C and E only
B, C, D and E only
quiz.explanation: A, B, C and E are standard results (E is strong duality: both feasible implies both have finite, equal optima). D is false: the primal and the dual can both be infeasible, so primal infeasibility does not force the dual to be unbounded.

stmts: A. The dual of the dual is the primal.
B. The number of dual variables equals the number of primal constraints.
C. An equality constraint in the primal corresponds to an unrestricted (free) dual variable.
D. If the primal is infeasible, the dual must be unbounded.
E. If both the primal and the dual have feasible solutions, their optimal objective values are equal.

quiz.question: Maximise Z = 6x1 + 5x2 subject to x1 + x2 ≤ 5, 3x1 + 2x2 ≤ 12, x1, x2 ≥ 0, by the simplex method with slack variables s1 and s2 as the initial basis. In the first iteration, which variable enters, which leaves, and what is the pivot element?
options: x1 enters, s1 leaves, pivot element 1
x2 enters, s1 leaves, pivot element 1
x1 enters, s2 leaves, pivot element 2
x1 enters, s2 leaves, pivot element 3
quiz.explanation: x1 has the most negative Z-row entry (−6), so it enters. Ratios: 5/1 = 5 for s1 and 12/3 = 4 for s2; the minimum is 4, so s2 leaves and the pivot element is 3. After this iteration Z = 24; one more iteration (x2 enters, s1 leaves) gives the optimum Z = 27 at (2, 3).

quiz.question: Arrange the following steps of the Hungarian method (minimisation) in the correct order.
quiz.explanation: Row reduction (B), column reduction (D), cover zeros (A), adjust if fewer than n lines (C), and finally assign (E): B, D, A, C, E. The adjustment step cannot come before the lines are drawn, because it depends on which entries are uncovered.

stmts: A. Cover all zeros with the minimum number of horizontal and vertical lines
B. Subtract the smallest entry of each row from every entry of that row
C. If fewer than n lines are needed, subtract the smallest uncovered entry from uncovered entries and add it at intersections
D. Subtract the smallest entry of each column from every entry of that column
E. When n lines are needed, make the assignment on zeros, one per row and column

quiz.question: Maximise Z = 6x1 + 8x2 subject to 5x1 + 2x2 ≤ 15, 4x1 + 6x2 ≤ 17, x1, x2 ≥ 0 and integer. The LP relaxation optimum is x = (28/11, 25/22) with Z ≈ 24.36. What is the optimal integer solution?
quiz.explanation: Rounding gives (3, 1), but 5·3 + 2·1 = 17 > 15, so it is infeasible. Branch and bound (or listing all integer points) gives the best feasible point (1, 2): 5 + 4 = 9 ≤ 15, 4 + 12 = 16 ≤ 17, Z = 6 + 16 = 22. (2, 1) is feasible but gives only 20, and (0, 2) gives 16.

lessons.title: Digital logic circuits and components
lessons.summaryHtml: Digital logic is the hardware layer under every computer: gates combine bits, combinational circuits (adders, multiplexers, decoders, encoders, comparators) compute outputs from present inputs only, and sequential circuits (latches, flip-flops, registers, counters) add memory by feeding outputs back. NTA tests this unit through gate counts (how many NAND gates for XOR), multiplexer and decoder trees, flip-flop characteristic and excitation tables, counter sequences and moduli, and speed numericals for ripple counters and ripple-carry adders. Every one of these is mechanical once you know the standard tables and the few formulas in this lesson. Learn the tables cold, practise tracing a counter state by state, and you will collect these marks quickly and reliably.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A computer is built from switches that are either on (1) or off (0). A logic gate takes one or more such bits and produces an output bit: AND is 1 only when all inputs are 1, OR is 1 when any input is 1, NOT flips a bit, and XOR is 1 when the inputs differ. Wire gates together and you get combinational circuits, whose outputs depend only on the inputs at this instant: an adder, a multiplexer, a decoder. Add feedback, so that an output is fed back as an input, and the circuit can remember a bit. That gives sequential circuits: latches, flip-flops, registers and counters.

Think of a combinational circuit as a calculator that shows the answer for whatever you type now, and a sequential circuit as a scoreboard that keeps its value until the next event (the clock edge) changes it.

Why it matters for NET

Digital logic sits at the start of Unit 2 and usually yields a small but steady number of questions each paper. Some come directly from this unit and some are hidden inside computer-organisation questions. The recurring sub-topics are: gate counts with universal gates; implementing a function with a multiplexer or a decoder; building large MUXes and decoders from small ones; flip-flop characteristic and excitation tables; flip-flop conversions; counter analysis (find the sequence or the modulus); ripple versus synchronous counter speed; and matching circuits to their properties. Most are either quick facts or short, mechanical numericals, which makes them high-value marks.

Concepts in depth: gates and universal gates

The basic gates are AND, OR, NOT, NAND (NOT-AND), NOR (NOT-OR), XOR and XNOR. XOR is AB′ + A′B; XNOR is its complement, AB + A′B′, and acts as a 1-bit equality detector. Two useful XOR facts: A ⊕ 0 = A and A ⊕ 1 = A′, so XOR is a controlled inverter, which is why it appears in adder–subtractors and in parity circuits.

A set of gates is functionally complete if it can build every Boolean function. {AND, OR, NOT} is complete by definition of sum-of-products. {AND, NOT} and {OR, NOT} are complete because De Morgan’s laws let you make the missing operation. NAND alone is complete: NOT A = NAND(A, A); AND = NOT of NAND; OR = NAND(A′, B′). NOR is complete by the dual argument. That is why NAND and NOR are called universal gates. Sets such as {AND, OR} (cannot invert) or {XOR} (cannot build AND) are not complete.

FunctionMinimum 2-input NAND gatesMinimum 2-input NOR gates
NOT11
AND23
OR32
XOR45
XNOR54
Half adder (sum and carry)55
Full adder99

Notice the symmetry: NAND is naturally good at AND-type functions and XOR; NOR is naturally good at OR-type functions and XNOR. A half adder with NAND is the 4-gate XOR plus one more NAND to invert the shared first gate (NAND(A,B)) into the carry AB.

Concepts in depth: adders and subtractors

A half adder adds two bits: S = A ⊕ B, C = AB. A full adder adds three bits (A, B and carry-in): S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin and Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B), which equals the majority function AB + BCin + ACin. Two half adders plus one OR gate make a full adder; two half adders alone do not, because the two partial carries must be ORed.

A half subtractor computes D = A ⊕ B and borrow Bout = A′B. A full subtractor computes D = A ⊕ B ⊕ Bin and Bout = A′B + A′Bin + BBin. The difference output has the same XOR form as the sum; only the borrow differs from the carry.

An n-bit ripple-carry adder chains n full adders. The carry must travel through every stage, so with carry delay tc per stage and sum delay ts, the worst-case delay is (n − 1)tc + ts (some books simplify this to n × tc; read the question). A carry-lookahead adder removes the chain: define generate Gi = AiBi and propagate Pi = Ai ⊕ Bi; then Ci+1 = Gi + PiCi. Expanding, C2 = G1 + P1G0 + P1P0C0, and so on: every carry is a two-level sum of products of G, P and C0. Within one lookahead block all carries are ready after a fixed number of gate levels, independent of position. The price is gate count and fan-in, so real designs use 4-bit lookahead blocks. An adder–subtractor uses XOR gates on the B inputs with a mode line M that is also fed to C0: M = 0 adds, M = 1 computes A + B′ + 1 = A − B.

Concepts in depth: multiplexers, demultiplexers, decoders, encoders, comparators

A multiplexer (data selector) has 2n data inputs, n select lines and one output. A 4-to-1 MUX computes Y = S1′S0′I0 + S1′S0I1 + S1S0′I2 + S1S0I3. A demultiplexer does the reverse: one input, n select lines, 2n outputs. A decoder with an enable input is the same circuit as a demultiplexer (the enable acts as the data input).

Function implementation with a MUX. A 2n-to-1 MUX implements any function of n + 1 variables: put n variables on the select lines, and connect each data input to 0, 1, the remaining variable, or its complement. If instead all n variables go on the select lines, the MUX is simply a look-up table: tie each data input to the function value 0 or 1 for that row. Because it can build any function of its select inputs (given the constants 0 and 1), even a 2-to-1 MUX is a universal logic element.

A decoder with n inputs has 2n outputs, each one a minterm. So any function in sum-of-minterms form is one decoder plus one OR gate per output. A full adder needs a 3-to-8 decoder and two OR gates: S = Σm(1, 2, 4, 7) and C = Σm(3, 5, 6, 7).

Building large blocks from small ones. A tree of k-to-1 MUXes forming an N-to-1 MUX needs (N − 1)/(k − 1) MUXes when N is a power of k: 16-to-1 from 4-to-1 needs 4 + 1 = 5; 32-to-1 from 2-to-1 needs 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 31. A 4-to-16 decoder from 2-to-4 decoders with enable needs 4 output decoders plus 1 decoder driving their enables = 5.

An encoder does the inverse of a decoder: 2n input lines, one of which is active, give an n-bit code. A plain encoder gives nonsense when two inputs are active at once, so a priority encoder outputs the code of the highest-priority active input and adds a valid bit V that is 0 when no input is active. A magnitude comparator compares two n-bit numbers and produces three outputs A > B, A = B and A < B. Equality uses XNOR per bit: (A = B) = x3x2x1x0, where xi = Ai ⊙ Bi.

Concepts in depth: latches and flip-flops

Two cross-coupled NOR gates form an SR latch: S = 1 sets Q to 1, R = 1 resets it, S = R = 0 holds, and S = R = 1 is forbidden because it forces both Q and Q′ to 0 and the state is unpredictable when both inputs return to 0. (With cross-coupled NAND gates the inputs are active-low and S′ = R′ = 0 is forbidden.) Adding a clock or enable gives a gated latch; a gated D latch removes the forbidden case by setting S = D and R = D′.

A latch is level-triggered: it follows its inputs while the enable is high. A flip-flop is edge-triggered (or master–slave): it samples its inputs at one clock edge only. This matters for the JK flip-flop: with J = K = 1 it toggles, and a level-triggered JK would keep toggling while the clock stays high if the pulse is longer than the propagation delay. That is the race-around condition. Master–slave construction (the master follows the inputs while the clock is high, the slave copies the master when it goes low) or true edge triggering removes it.

Flip-flopBehaviourCharacteristic equation
SR00 hold, 01 reset, 10 set, 11 not allowedQ(t+1) = S + R′Q, with SR = 0
JK00 hold, 01 reset, 10 set, 11 toggleQ(t+1) = JQ′ + K′Q
DQ(t+1) = D; no hold inputQ(t+1) = D
T0 hold, 1 toggleQ(t+1) = T ⊕ Q

Excitation tables answer the reverse question: which inputs cause the transition Q → Q(t+1)? X means “don’t care”.

Q → Q(t+1)S RJ KDT
0 → 00 X0 X00
0 → 11 01 X11
1 → 00 1X 101
1 → 1X 0X 010

The many don’t-cares are why JK flip-flops often give the simplest counter logic. Conversions follow from the equations: JK to T by J = K = T; JK to D by J = D, K = D′; D to T by D = T ⊕ Q; SR to D by S = D, R = D′. Timing terms: setup time is how long the input must be stable before the active edge, hold time is how long after it, and propagation delay is the time from the edge to the output change.

Concepts in depth: registers and counters

A register is a group of flip-flops sharing a clock, one per bit. Shift registers move data one position per clock: serial-in serial-out (SISO), serial-in parallel-out (SIPO), parallel-in serial-out (PISO) and parallel-in parallel-out (PIPO). Loading n bits serially takes n clock pulses. A universal shift register can hold, shift left, shift right and load in parallel, selected by two mode lines.

A counter is a register that steps through a fixed sequence of states. A mod-N counter has N states and needs at least ⌈log₂ N⌉ flip-flops, leaving 2k − N unused states when it uses k flip-flops. The output of the last stage has frequency f/N, so counters are also frequency dividers; cascaded mod-M and mod-N counters divide by M × N.

  • Ripple (asynchronous) counter: only the first flip-flop gets the clock; each later flip-flop is clocked by the previous output. It is simple but slow: the worst-case settling time is n × tpd, and intermediate wrong states (glitches) appear while the change ripples. fmax = 1/(n × tpd).
  • Synchronous counter: all flip-flops share the clock, and gates compute which ones must toggle (for a binary up-counter, Ti = Q0Q1…Qi−1). The minimum clock period is one flip-flop delay plus the gate delay (plus setup time, if given), independent of n for parallel carry gating.
  • Ring counter: a circular shift register holding a single 1; n flip-flops give n states and each state is already decoded (no gates needed to detect it).
  • Johnson (twisted-ring) counter: the complement of the last output is fed back; n flip-flops give 2n states, and each state can be decoded with one 2-input gate.
  • Mod-N by reset: a binary ripple counter can be truncated by detecting state N (for example 1010 for a decade counter) and clearing all flip-flops, so the counter goes 0 … N − 1.

Counter analysis method. Write the input equation for each flip-flop, substitute into the characteristic equation to get Q(t+1), and trace from the start state until a state repeats. Counter design is the reverse: state diagram, number of flip-flops, state table with the required transitions, excitation-table columns for the chosen flip-flop, K-map for each input, then the circuit.

Concepts in depth: integrated circuits and logic families

By integration level, ICs are SSI (a few gates, e.g. a quad NAND package), MSI (functional blocks such as decoders, multiplexers, counters, registers), LSI (processors, memories) and VLSI (complete processors and large memories). The gate-count boundaries differ between textbooks, so learn the order and a typical example of each. Logic families differ in technology: TTL (bipolar, multi-emitter input transistor, long the standard family), ECL (bipolar, transistors kept out of saturation, fastest but high power), MOS (high density) and CMOS (complementary MOS, very low static power, dominant in VLSI). The parameters used to compare them are fan-out, power dissipation, propagation delay and noise margin.

Worked examples

Example 1: XOR from four NAND gates, and a full adder from a decoder.

Step 1. n1 = NAND(A, B) = (AB)′.

Step 2. n2 = NAND(A, n1) = (A(AB)′)′ and n3 = NAND(B, n1) = (B(AB)′)′.

Step 3. Y = NAND(n2, n3) = A(AB)′ + B(AB)′ = A(A′ + B′) + B(A′ + B′) = AB′ + A′B = A ⊕ B. Four gates.

Step 4 (decoder adder). The full-adder truth table has S = 1 for inputs (A B Cin) = 001, 010, 100, 111, so S = Σm(1, 2, 4, 7), and C = 1 for 011, 101, 110, 111, so C = Σm(3, 5, 6, 7). A 3-to-8 decoder gives all eight minterms; one 4-input OR gate for S and one for C finish the adder.

Example 2: implement F(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 3, 5, 6) with a 4-to-1 MUX (select lines A, B).

A B (select)Minterms in this rowF when C = 0F when C = 1Data input
00 → I0m0, m101C
01 → I1m2, m301C
10 → I2m4, m501C
11 → I3m6, m710C′

Result: I0 = I1 = I2 = C and I3 = C′. Rule: if F is 0 and 0 connect 0; 1 and 1 connect 1; 0 then 1 connect C; 1 then 0 connect C′.

Example 3: analyse a counter. JK flip-flops A (MSB) and B, with JA = B, KA = 1, JB = A′, KB = 1. Start at AB = 00.

Step 1. With K = 1, Q(t+1) = JQ′ + K′Q = JQ′. So A(t+1) = B·A′ and B(t+1) = A′·B′.

Present ABA(t+1) = A′BB(t+1) = A′B′Next AB
000101
011010
100000
11 (unused)0000

Step 2. The sequence is 00 → 01 → 10 → 00: a mod-3 counter. The unused state 11 goes to 00, so the counter is self-starting.

Example 4: speed of counters and adders.

(a) A 4-bit ripple counter with tpd = 20 ns per flip-flop: worst-case settling = 4 × 20 = 80 ns, so fmax = 1/80 ns = 12.5 MHz.

(b) A synchronous counter with flip-flop delay 20 ns and AND-gate delay 10 ns: minimum period = 20 + 10 = 30 ns, so fmax = 1/30 ns ≈ 33.33 MHz.

(c) An 8-bit ripple-carry adder with full-adder carry delay 12 ns and sum delay 15 ns: worst case = (8 − 1) × 12 + 15 = 99 ns.

Example 5: trace a JK flip-flop and a shift counter.

(a) Q starts at 0. The (J, K) inputs at six successive edges are (1,0), (1,1), (1,1), (0,1), (0,0), (1,1).

EdgeJ KActionQ after
11 0set1
21 1toggle0
31 1toggle1
40 1reset0
50 0hold0
61 1toggle1

(b) A 4-bit Johnson counter starting at 0000 (shift right, complement of the last bit enters on the left) goes 0000 → 1000 → 1100 → 1110 → 1111 → 0111 → 0011 → 0001 → 0000: 8 states. After 5 pulses it shows 0111.

Example 6: building blocks.

(a) 16-to-1 from 4-to-1 MUXes: level 1 has 16/4 = 4 MUXes, level 2 has 1, total 5 = (16 − 1)/(4 − 1).

(b) 4-to-16 decoder from 2-to-4 decoders with enable: 4 decoders produce the 16 outputs (driven by the two low bits), and 1 decoder (driven by the two high bits) enables one of them. Total 5.

(c) A 1 MHz clock through a mod-5 counter, then a mod-4 counter, then a mod-2 counter: 1 MHz / (5 × 4 × 2) = 25 kHz.

Concepts in depth: Boolean algebra and map simplification (recap for Unit 2)

The official Unit 2 list repeats “Boolean algebra, map simplification” because every circuit in this lesson is designed from a simplified Boolean expression. Lesson 1.7 teaches the full method; here is the part you need at circuit level. A digital computer works on two-valued signals, so every output is a Boolean function of its inputs, and the cost of a two-level circuit is roughly the number of product terms plus the number of literals. A Karnaugh map arranges the minterms so that neighbouring cells differ in exactly one variable (rows and columns follow Gray code order 00, 01, 11, 10, and the edges wrap round). Grouping 2, 4, 8 … adjacent 1s removes 1, 2, 3 … variables from the term.

  • Make every group as large as possible (a prime implicant) and use as few groups as possible.
  • First take the essential prime implicants (the only group covering some 1), then cover what is left with the fewest extra groups.
  • Don’t-care cells (X) may be included in a group when they make it bigger, and ignored otherwise. They never need to be covered.
  • For a product-of-sums answer, group the 0s and complement.

Example: a K-map with don’t-cares. Simplify F(W, X, Y, Z) = Σm(2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 14) + d(11, 15).

Step 1. The 1s are all cells with Y = 1 except 11 and 15, which are don’t-cares.

Step 2. Treat 11 and 15 as 1s: the eight cells 2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 11, 14, 15 are exactly the cells with Y = 1, one group of 8.

Step 3. A group of 8 in a 4-variable map removes 3 variables, so F = Y. Without the don’t-cares the best cover would be W′Y + YZ′, which needs two gates more.

Concepts in depth: the memory unit (RAM, ROM and programmable logic)

In Mano’s list of digital components, the memory unit is a collection of storage cells with the circuits that move information in and out. It stores binary information in groups of bits called words. A memory with k address lines and n data lines holds 2k words of n bits, written 2k × n, and its capacity is 2k × n bits. For example, a 64K × 16 memory needs 16 address lines and 16 data lines. Two control inputs (read and write, or a single R/W line plus a chip select) choose the operation.

  • Write: put the address on the address lines, the word on the data-input lines, then activate write. The decoder selects one word and the bits are stored.
  • Read: put the address on the address lines and activate read. The selected word appears on the data-output lines; the stored word is not changed.

Internal construction. Each bit is a binary cell (a latch with select, read/write and input lines). A k-to-2k decoder turns the address into one active word line. A single decoder for a large memory is expensive, so real chips use coincident (two-dimensional) decoding: the cells form a square array, half the address bits drive a row decoder and half a column decoder, and a cell is selected where the two active lines cross. For 1K words, a single 10-to-1024 decoder needs 1024 AND gates, but two 5-to-32 decoders need only 32 + 32 = 64.

RAM is read-write and volatile. Static RAM keeps each bit in a latch; dynamic RAM keeps it as charge on a capacitor and must be refreshed (details, chip counts and address maps are in lesson 2.8). ROM is read-only and non-volatile. Because its output depends only on its present address, a ROM is a combinational circuit: a 2k × n ROM is a k-to-2k decoder followed by n OR gates whose connections are fixed when it is programmed. So a ROM can implement any n functions of k variables directly from the truth table, with no minimisation. ROM kinds: mask ROM (programmed at the factory), PROM (programmed once by the user, by blowing fuses), EPROM (erased by ultraviolet light), EEPROM (erased electrically), flash (erased in blocks).

Programmable logic devices differ in which array is programmable:

DeviceAND arrayOR arrayRemark
PROMFixed (full decoder: all 2k minterms)ProgrammableTruth table stored as is
PALProgrammableFixedEach output gets a fixed number of product terms
PLAProgrammableProgrammableProduct terms can be shared between outputs; most flexible

Example: sizing a ROM and a memory unit.

(a) A ROM must add two 4-bit numbers and a carry-in. Inputs = 4 + 4 + 1 = 9, so it needs 29 = 512 words. Outputs = 4 sum bits + 1 carry = 5. Size 512 × 5 = 2560 bits.

(b) A memory unit of 4M × 32: 4M = 222 words, so 22 address lines, plus 32 data lines: 54 lines in all (control lines extra).

(c) A 4K-word RAM with coincident decoding: 12 address bits split 6 + 6, two 6-to-64 decoders = 128 AND gates, against 4096 for one 12-to-4096 decoder.

Watch out: the size of a ROM that implements functions depends on the number of inputs (2inputs words) and outputs (bits per word). Do not try to minimise the functions first; a ROM stores every row of the truth table.

Interactive solver

Enter any problem, including the ones in your practice set, and the solver works it out step by step with the conventions stated. Use it to check your answers, not to replace doing them by hand: the exam gives you no solver.

Interactive solver: K-map minimiser

The solver runs in your browser. Turn on JavaScript to use it.

Formula and fact sheet

NTA traps

  • “J = K = 1 holds the state.” Wrong: J = K = 1 toggles, J = K = 0 holds. Say the JK table aloud: hold, reset, set, toggle.
  • Using n × tpd for a synchronous counter. That formula is for ripple counters only. A synchronous counter’s period is one flip-flop delay plus the steering-gate delay.
  • Forgetting the second level of a MUX or decoder tree. A 16-to-1 MUX from 4-to-1 MUXes needs 5, not 4. Use (N − 1)/(k − 1).
  • Ring versus Johnson. Ring: n states. Johnson: 2n states. Neither uses all 2^n states.
  • “Mod-6 needs 6 flip-flops.” It needs ⌈log₂ 6⌉ = 3 flip-flops.
  • Assuming a counter’s modulus from its size. A 3-flip-flop counter can be mod-3, mod-5 or mod-6. Always trace the states.
  • Two half adders make a full adder. Only with an extra OR gate for the two partial carries.
  • Mixing up the forbidden input. For a NOR SR latch it is S = R = 1; for a NAND latch (active-low inputs) it is S′ = R′ = 0.
  • Latch versus flip-flop. Latches are level-sensitive; flip-flops are edge-triggered. Race-around is a problem of level-triggered JK circuits.

How NTA asks this

  • Direct numerical (MCQ): gate counts, number of MUXes or decoders in a tree, flip-flops for mod-N, unused states, fmax, adder delay, the state after k clock pulses. Memorise the formula sheet; do the arithmetic on paper.
  • Sequence tracing: “Starting from 000, the counter goes through …” Build a next-state table; eliminate options by checking only the first two transitions.
  • Match the following: flip-flops with equations or excitation entries, circuits with functions, logic families with properties.
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: race-around and its cure, ripple versus synchronous speed, ring versus Johnson state counts, functional completeness.

Mini-example (A-R). A: A ripple counter is slower than a synchronous counter of the same size. R: In a ripple counter each flip-flop is clocked by the previous flip-flop’s output, so the delays add up. Both are true, and R is exactly why A holds: answer option 1.

Elimination trick: in a match question, fix the pair you are surest of (for example D flip-flop → Q(t+1) = D). Usually only one or two options survive; then check a single remaining pair.
Watch out: when a counter question gives flip-flop input equations, the “obvious” binary sequence is almost always a distractor. Trace at least three transitions before choosing.

terms.definition: A gate from which every Boolean function can be built. NAND and NOR are each universal on their own.
A circuit whose outputs depend only on the present inputs; it has no memory and no feedback. Examples: adder, multiplexer, decoder.
A circuit whose outputs depend on present inputs and on stored state. Examples: flip-flop, register, counter.
A data selector: 2^n data inputs, n select lines, one output. The select lines choose which input reaches the output.
A circuit with n inputs and up to 2^n outputs; exactly one output (one minterm) is active for each input combination.
The next-state equation of a flip-flop, e.g. Q(t+1) = JQ′ + K′Q for the JK flip-flop.
For each required transition Q → Q(t+1), the flip-flop inputs that cause it. Used when designing counters.
In a level-triggered JK flip-flop with J = K = 1, the output toggles repeatedly while the clock stays high. Removed by master–slave or edge-triggered designs.
A counter in which each flip-flop is clocked by the previous flip-flop’s output, so delays add up stage by stage.
The number of distinct states a counter passes through before repeating. A mod-N counter needs ⌈log₂ N⌉ flip-flops.

lessons.examTip: For any counter question, do not guess from the name: write the flip-flop equations, then trace the states one clock at a time from the given start state until a state repeats. The number of distinct states is the modulus.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For every counter or flip-flop problem, write the state trace as a table, not in your head.
Check every answer against solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (for example: counted J=K=1 as hold, or used n×tpd for a synchronous counter).
Redraw the four flip-flop excitation tables and the MUX/decoder tree formulas from memory on one sheet of paper.
Redo the problems you got wrong after 24 hours, without looking at the solutions.
Finish with the lesson quiz and bank questions, timing yourself at 60–90 seconds per question.
check: At least 12 of 15 problems correct.
Problems 9–15 solved within 12 minutes.
All four excitation tables (SR, JK, D, T) reproduced from memory without an error.
Every counter answer backed by a written state trace.

quiz.question: What is the minimum number of 2-input NAND gates needed to implement a 2-input XOR function (inputs A and B available only in true form)?
quiz.explanation: XOR needs 4 NAND gates: n1 = NAND(A,B); n2 = NAND(A,n1); n3 = NAND(B,n1); output = NAND(n2,n3) = AB′ + A′B. Three gates are not enough, and 5 is the count for XNOR with NAND gates (or XOR with NOR gates), which is the usual distractor.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: SR: set wins when S = 1, otherwise the flip-flop holds unless R = 1, giving S + R′Q. JK: JQ′ + K′Q (J sets, K resets, both toggle). D: the next state equals D. T: toggles when T = 1, giving T ⊕ Q. The distractors swap one or two of these pairs.

b: I. Q(t+1) = JQ′ + K′Q
II. Q(t+1) = D
III. Q(t+1) = S + R′Q
IV. Q(t+1) = T ⊕ Q

quiz.question: What is the minimum number of 4-to-1 multiplexers needed to build a 16-to-1 multiplexer?
quiz.explanation: Four 4-to-1 MUXes select one of 4 inputs each (first level, using S1 S0), and a fifth 4-to-1 MUX picks one of those four outputs (using S3 S2). General formula for k-to-1 building blocks: (N − 1)/(k − 1) = 15/3 = 5. The answer 4 forgets the second level.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: (A) describes the race-around condition and is true. (R) is also true, but it explains how the master–slave design removes race-around, not why race-around occurs. The cause is feedback of the toggled output while the clock is still high. So both are true but (R) does not explain (A).

stmts: Assertion (A): In a level-triggered JK flip-flop with J = K = 1, the output can toggle more than once during a single clock pulse if the pulse width is greater than the flip-flop’s propagation delay.
Reason (R): In a master–slave JK flip-flop, the slave copies the master only after the master has been isolated from the inputs, so the output changes at most once per clock pulse.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: A 4-bit ripple (asynchronous) up-counter uses flip-flops with a propagation delay of 20 ns each. Ignoring all other delays, what is the maximum clock frequency at which the counter can be read reliably?
quiz.explanation: In a ripple counter the worst case is a change that ripples through all n stages (for example 0111 → 1000). Total settling time = n × tpd = 4 × 20 ns = 80 ns. f(max) = 1/80 ns = 12.5 MHz. 50 MHz uses one flip-flop delay, which is the rule for a synchronous counter, not a ripple counter.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: A Johnson counter feeds the complement of the last flip-flop back to the first, giving 2n states (for example 8 states with 4 flip-flops). A ring counter circulates a single 1, so it has only n states; the other 2^n − n states are unused. Statement I is true, Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: A Johnson (twisted-ring) counter built with n flip-flops has 2n distinct states in its normal sequence.
Statement II: A ring counter built with n flip-flops uses all 2^n possible states.

quiz.question: Which of the following sets are functionally complete, that is, able to implement every Boolean function?
options: A, B, C and D only
A, B, D and E only
quiz.explanation: NAND alone and NOR alone are universal. {AND, NOT} is complete because OR = (A′B′)′ by De Morgan. {XOR} cannot produce constants or AND and {AND, OR} cannot produce complement (both sets are missing a way to invert or to build non-linear functions), so C and E are not complete.

stmts: A. {NAND}
B. {NOR}
C. {XOR}
D. {AND, NOT}
E. {AND, OR}

quiz.question: F(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 3, 5, 6) is implemented with a 4-to-1 multiplexer whose select lines are A (MSB) and B. What must be connected to the data inputs I0, I1, I2, I3 respectively?
quiz.explanation: Group minterms by AB. AB = 00: minterms 0,1; only m1 (C = 1) is present, so I0 = C. AB = 01: m2, m3; only m3, so I1 = C. AB = 10: m4, m5; only m5, so I2 = C. AB = 11: m6, m7; only m6 (C = 0), so I3 = C′. Answer: C, C, C, C′.

quiz.question: A synchronous counter uses two JK flip-flops A (MSB) and B with inputs JA = B, KA = 1, JB = A′, KB = 1. Starting from AB = 00, which state sequence does it follow?
quiz.explanation: Use Q(t+1) = JQ′ + K′Q. With K = 1 for both, A(t+1) = B·A′ and B(t+1) = A′·B′. From 00: A+ = 0, B+ = 1 → 01. From 01: A+ = 1·1 = 1, B+ = 1·0 = 0 → 10. From 10: A+ = 0, B+ = 0·1 = 0 → 00. So 00 → 01 → 10 → 00, a mod-3 counter. State 11 is never reached from 00.

quiz.question: Arrange the following IC integration levels in increasing order of the number of gates per chip.
quiz.explanation: Small-scale (SSI, a few gates) < medium-scale (MSI) < large-scale (LSI) < very-large-scale (VLSI). The exact gate-count boundaries differ between textbooks, but the order never changes, which is what NTA tests.

stmts: A. LSI
B. SSI
C. VLSI
D. MSI

lessons.title: Data representation
lessons.summaryHtml: Everything a computer stores is a pattern of bits, and data representation is the set of rules that gives those patterns meaning. This lesson covers number-system conversions, radix and diminished-radix complements, the three ways to store signed integers (sign-magnitude, 1’s complement, 2’s complement) with their ranges and overflow rules, fixed-point and IEEE 754 floating point, and the character and decimal codes (BCD, excess-3, Gray, ASCII, Unicode). It ends with error-detecting and error-correcting codes: parity and the Hamming code. NTA asks many direct numericals here (convert, complement, encode a float, count Hamming check bits, find the base), so speed and exactness pay off. Practise each conversion until you can do it in under a minute.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A memory cell holds only 0s and 1s. The same eight bits 11011011 can mean the unsigned number 219, the signed number −37, part of a floating-point value, or a character, depending on the rule used to read them. Data representation is the study of those rules. For integers the rules are positional number systems and complements; for real numbers they are fixed point and floating point; for text and decimal digits they are codes such as ASCII, Unicode and BCD; and for reliability they are extra bits that detect or correct errors.

Why it matters for NET

This topic reliably gives direct, calculation-based questions. The recurring ones are: converting between bases and finding an unknown base; r’s and (r−1)’s complements; ranges of signed representations; detecting overflow; encoding and decoding IEEE 754 single-precision numbers, including the special values; BCD, excess-3 and Gray conversions; and the number of Hamming check bits or the position of an error. Each is a two-minute calculation if you know the method, and a common source of careless mistakes if you do not write the bits down.

Concepts in depth: number systems and conversion

In base r, the number dn−1…d1d0.d−1d−2 means Σ di × ri. To convert to decimal, expand with powers. To convert a decimal integer to base r, divide repeatedly by r and read the remainders from last to first. To convert a decimal fraction, multiply repeatedly by r and read the integer parts from first to last. A fraction terminates in base r only if its denominator (in lowest terms) has no prime factor that r lacks: 0.625 = 5/8 terminates in binary (0.101), but 0.1 = 1/10 does not (0.000110011…), because 10 contains the factor 5.

Binary, octal and hexadecimal convert by grouping: 3 bits per octal digit and 4 bits per hex digit, grouping outwards from the binary point. To go from octal to hex, expand to binary first: (7654)8 = 111 110 101 100 = 1111 1010 1100 = (FAC)16. An unsigned integer N needs ⌈log₂(N + 1)⌉ bits, so 1000 needs 10 bits.

Finding an unknown base. Expand both sides as polynomials in the base and solve. Every digit must be smaller than the base, which rules out some options at once: (211)b needs b ≥ 3.

Concepts in depth: complements

For an n-digit number N in base r, the (r−1)’s complement (diminished radix complement) is (rn − 1) − N: subtract every digit from r − 1. The r’s complement (radix complement) is rn − N: the (r−1)’s complement plus 1. In decimal, the 9’s complement of 2830 is 7169 and the 10’s complement is 7170. In binary, the 1’s complement inverts every bit and the 2’s complement inverts and adds 1. A quick way to get the 2’s complement: copy bits from the right up to and including the first 1, then invert the rest.

Subtraction with complements. To compute M − N with r’s complements, add M and the r’s complement of N. If there is an end carry, discard it: the result is positive. If there is no end carry, the result is negative, and its magnitude is the r’s complement of the sum. With (r−1)’s complements, an end carry is not discarded but added back to the least significant digit (end-around carry).

Concepts in depth: signed integers and overflow

Representation (n bits)RangeZeros−5 in 4 bits
Sign-magnitude−(2^(n−1) − 1) to 2^(n−1) − 1two (+0, −0)1101
1’s complement−(2^(n−1) − 1) to 2^(n−1) − 1two (0000, 1111)1010
2’s complement−2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1one1011
Excess-2^(n−1) (biased)−2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1one0011

For 8 bits the 2’s complement range is −128 to 127; for 16 bits, −32768 to 32767. The pattern 1000…0 is the most negative number and is its own 2’s complement. Sign extension copies the sign bit into the new high-order bits, so the 4-bit −5 (1011) becomes 11111011 in 8 bits with the same value.

Overflow means the true result lies outside the range. In 2’s complement addition it can happen only when both operands have the same sign, and it shows up as a result with the opposite sign. The hardware test is V = Cn ⊕ Cn−1: the carry out of the sign bit differs from the carry into it. The carry out alone does not indicate signed overflow; it is the overflow indicator for unsigned addition.

Concepts in depth: fixed point and IEEE 754 floating point

A fixed-point number places the binary point at a fixed position. With 4 integer bits and 4 fraction bits (often written Q4.4), 1011.0110 = 11.375 and the resolution is 2−4 = 0.0625. Fixed point is simple and exact within its range, but the range is small.

A floating-point number stores a sign, an exponent and a significand: value = (−1)s × 1.f × 2e − bias. IEEE 754 defines these formats:

FormatTotal bitsSignExponentFractionBias
Half (binary16)16151015
Single (binary32)321823127
Double (binary64)64111521023
Quadruple (binary128)12811511216383

Because a normalized binary significand always starts with 1, that hidden bit is not stored, which gives one extra bit of precision (24 significant bits in single precision). The biased exponent lets hardware compare floats almost like unsigned integers. Two exponent patterns are reserved:

Exponent fieldFractionMeaning (single precision)
00±0 (two zeros, by sign)
0≠ 0Denormal: (−1)^s × 0.f × 2^−126
1 to 254anyNormalized: (−1)^s × 1.f × 2^(e − 127)
255 (all 1s)0±∞
255 (all 1s)≠ 0NaN (not a number)

So in single precision the largest finite value is (2 − 2−23) × 2127 ≈ 3.4 × 1038, the smallest positive normalized value is 2−126 ≈ 1.18 × 10−38, and the smallest positive denormal is 2−149 ≈ 1.4 × 10−45. Denormals give gradual underflow: the spacing near zero stays even instead of jumping from 2−126 to 0. Floating point trades exactness for range: most decimal fractions (0.1, 0.2) are stored only approximately.

Concepts in depth: decimal and character codes

BCD (8421) stores each decimal digit in 4 bits: 95 = 1001 0101. It wastes 6 of 16 patterns and needs more bits than pure binary, but converts easily to and from decimal displays. When two BCD digits are added and the 4-bit sum exceeds 9 or produces a carry, add 0110 (6) to skip the six invalid patterns and pass a carry to the next digit.

Weighted codes give each bit position a weight: 8421, 2421, 5211, and 84−2−1 (with negative weights). Excess-3 is non-weighted: each digit is written as its value plus 3 (5 → 1000). Excess-3, 2421 and 84−2−1 are self-complementing: inverting the bits of a digit’s code gives the code of its 9’s complement, which simplifies decimal subtraction.

Gray code is a unit-distance code: consecutive values differ in one bit, so a mechanical position encoder never shows a wildly wrong value mid-transition. Binary to Gray: gn−1 = bn−1 and gi = bi+1 ⊕ bi (in one step, g = b ⊕ (b >> 1)). Gray to binary: bn−1 = gn−1 and bi = bi+1 ⊕ gi, so each binary bit is the XOR of all Gray bits to its left, inclusive.

ASCII is a 7-bit code (128 characters, usually stored in a byte): space = 32, ‘0’ = 48, ‘A’ = 65, ‘a’ = 97. Upper and lower case differ by 32, that is, by bit 5. EBCDIC is IBM’s 8-bit code. Unicode assigns a code point to every character; UTF-8 encodes code points in 1 to 4 bytes and is backward compatible with ASCII (ASCII text is valid UTF-8); UTF-16 uses 2 or 4 bytes; UTF-32 always uses 4. For example, U+00E9 (é) takes 2 bytes in UTF-8 and U+20AC (€) takes 3.

Concepts in depth: error detection and correction

A parity bit makes the number of 1s even (even parity) or odd (odd parity). It detects any odd number of bit errors but no even number, and it cannot locate an error.

The Hamming distance between two words is the number of positions in which they differ (the number of 1s in their XOR). If the minimum distance of a code is d, it can detect up to d − 1 errors and correct up to ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋. So correcting t errors needs d ≥ 2t + 1, and detecting s errors needs d ≥ s + 1.

The Hamming code reaches distance 3 (single-error correction) with few extra bits. With m data bits and r check bits, the r-bit syndrome must name any of the m + r positions or “no error”, so 2r ≥ m + r + 1. Positions numbered from 1 that are powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8, …) hold check bits; check bit pk covers every position whose binary index has bit k set. At the receiver, recompute each check; the checks that fail, read as a binary number, give the position of the error (0 means no error). Adding one overall parity bit gives SEC-DED (single-error correction, double-error detection).

Data bits mCheck bits rCode word m + r
