quiz.question: What is the main weakness of the one-wire strobe method of asynchronous transfer?
options: It needs a common clock between the units
The source cannot know whether the destination actually received the data
It cannot transfer more than one bit at a time
It works only for destination-initiated transfers
quiz.explanation: A strobe is a single control line. When the source strobes, nothing comes back, so the source cannot tell whether the destination took the data. Handshaking adds the second, reply signal to fix exactly this. Strobe needs no common clock and can be source- or destination-initiated.

lessons.title: Memory hierarchy
lessons.summaryHtml: No single memory is fast, large and cheap at once, so computers stack several levels: registers, cache, main memory (RAM and ROM chips) and auxiliary memory (disks). The hierarchy works because programs show locality of reference: they reuse recent data and touch nearby addresses. A cache keeps copies of recently used blocks, found by splitting the address into tag, index and offset under direct, associative or set-associative mapping. Virtual memory lets programs use a large address space, translated page by page through a page table, with a TLB to make translation fast. NET asks bit-split numericals, chip counts and address maps, hit-ratio and access-time calculations, hit/miss traces, write and replacement policies, and virtual-memory effective access time.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A student keeps today’s notes on the desk, this term’s books on a shelf, and old books in a store room. The desk is small but instant; the store room is huge but slow. A computer does the same: registers and cache are the desk, main memory is the shelf, and disks are the store room. The hardware and the operating system move data between levels so that, most of the time, what the CPU needs is already close.

This works because of locality of reference. Temporal locality: an item used now is likely to be used again soon (loop variables, instructions of a loop). Spatial locality: items near a used address are likely to be used soon (array elements, sequential code). So copying a whole block near the CPU pays off.

Why it matters for NET

Memory hierarchy is one of the most heavily tested areas of Unit 2, and it overlaps with memory management in Unit 5. Expect cache questions nearly every paper: tag/index/offset splits, which line or set an address goes to, hit or miss counts for a reference string, AMAT and hit-ratio calculations, and write or replacement policies. Chip-count and address-map questions, associative memory, and virtual-memory (page table size, TLB effective access time) questions appear regularly too.

Concepts in depth

The hierarchy and its measures

LevelTechnologyTypical accessManaged by
RegistersFlip-flopsUnder 1 nsCompiler
Cache (L1, L2, L3)SRAMAbout 1–20 nsHardware
Main memoryDRAM, ROMTens of nsOS
Auxiliary memoryMagnetic disk, SSD, tapeMicroseconds to millisecondsOS

Going down, capacity grows and cost per bit falls; access time grows. The key measure is the hit ratio h = hits ÷ total references. If level 1 has access time T1 and level 2 has T2, there are two standard formulas:

  • Hierarchical (look-through) access: the CPU checks the cache first and goes to memory only on a miss. Tavg = h·T1 + (1 − h)(T1 + T2) = T1 + (1 − h)T2.
  • Simultaneous (look-aside) access: both levels start together, and a miss costs only T2. Tavg = h·T1 + (1 − h)T2.

The modern form is AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. With two cache levels: AMAT = TL1 + mL1 × (TL2 + mL2,local × Tmem). The local miss rate of L2 is misses in L2 ÷ accesses to L2; the global miss rate is mL1 × mL2,local.

Main memory: RAM and ROM chips, address maps

RAM is read-write and volatile. Static RAM stores bits in flip-flops (fast, used for cache); dynamic RAM stores charge in capacitors that must be refreshed (dense, cheap, used for main memory). ROM is non-volatile and holds bootstrap code; variants are mask ROM, PROM (programmed once), EPROM (erased by ultraviolet light), EEPROM (erased electrically, byte by byte) and flash (erased electrically in blocks).

A chip of size W × b has log₂W address lines and b data lines, plus chip-select inputs. To build a bigger memory of size Wtotal × B from W × b chips:

  • chips per row = B ÷ b (to widen the word), rows = Wtotal ÷ W (to add words), total chips = rows × chips per row;
  • the low log₂W address lines go to every chip; the next log₂(rows) lines go to a decoder that selects a row.

An address map is a table of which addresses each chip occupies. Example: four 256 × 8 RAM chips and one 1K × 8 ROM in an 11-bit address space.

ComponentHex rangeA10A9 A8A7–A0
RAM 1000–0FF00 0x…x
RAM 2100–1FF00 1x…x
RAM 3200–2FF01 0x…x
RAM 4300–3FF01 1x…x
ROM400–7FF1x xx…x

A10 chooses RAM (0) or ROM (1); A9 A8 feed a 2-to-4 decoder that selects one RAM chip; A7–A0 go to every RAM chip; A9–A0 go to the ROM.

Interleaved memory splits memory into modules so that consecutive words are in different modules (low-order interleaving: module = address mod number of modules). Sequential accesses can then overlap.

Auxiliary memory

A magnetic disk has platters with surfaces, each divided into concentric tracks, each divided into sectors; the same track on all surfaces forms a cylinder. Capacity = surfaces × tracks per surface × sectors per track × bytes per sector. Access time = seek time (move the head to the track) + rotational latency (on average half a revolution) + transfer time. Magnetic tape is sequential access. Solid-state drives use flash and have no seek or rotation.

Associative memory

An associative memory or content-addressable memory (CAM) finds a word by content, not address. It has an argument register A (the pattern), a key register K (a mask: 1 marks the bit positions to compare) and a match register M with one bit per word. All words are compared in parallel: word j matches if, in every position where K = 1, its bit equals A’s bit. It is fast but expensive, because every cell has compare logic. It is used for TLBs and fully associative caches.

Cache memory: mapping

Memory is divided into blocks; the cache holds lines (block frames), each with a tag, a valid bit and, under write-back, a dirty bit. For a byte-addressed memory with block size B, cache size C and associativity k:

  • offset bits = log₂B; lines = C ÷ B; sets = lines ÷ k;
  • Direct mapping (k = 1): index = log₂(lines); line = block number mod lines. One comparator. Cheap, but two hot blocks with the same index keep evicting each other (conflict misses).
  • Fully associative (one set): no index; tag = address bits − offset. Every tag is compared in parallel. No conflict misses, but costly.
  • k-way set-associative: set bits = log₂(sets); set = block number mod sets; k comparators, each as wide as the tag.
| tag | index (line or set) | offset |
tag = address bits - index bits - offset bits

Tag directory size = number of lines × (tag bits + valid bit + dirty bit if any). Doubling associativity at fixed size halves the sets, so the index loses one bit and the tag gains one.

Misses fall into three kinds (the 3 Cs): compulsory (first touch of a block; bigger blocks help), capacity (the working set exceeds the cache; a bigger cache helps) and conflict (too many blocks map to one set; more associativity helps).

Cache writes and replacement

  • Write-through: every write updates cache and memory. Memory is always current (simple coherence, good for DMA), but traffic is high; a write buffer hides the delay.
  • Write-back (copy-back): writes update only the cache and set the dirty bit; the block is written to memory when it is replaced. Less traffic, but a miss that evicts a dirty block costs two block transfers.
  • Write-allocate (fetch the block on a write miss) usually pairs with write-back; no-write-allocate (write straight to memory) usually pairs with write-through.

When a set is full, a replacement policy chooses the victim: LRU (least recently used), FIFO (oldest loaded), random, or LFU. Direct mapping needs no policy since there is only one choice.

Virtual memory

Programs use virtual (logical) addresses in a large address space; memory hardware uses physical addresses in a smaller memory space. Both are divided into equal pieces: pages (virtual) and frames (physical). A virtual address = page number + offset. The page table maps page number to frame number, with a presence (valid) bit, dirty bit and protection bits. The offset passes through unchanged.

  • Number of pages = 2virtual bits ÷ page size; page table size = pages × PTE size.
  • Large tables are split into multilevel page tables or replaced by an inverted page table (one entry per frame, searched associatively or by hashing).
  • A TLB caches recent translations. With TLB time t, memory time m, hit ratio h and a single-level table: EAT = h(t + m) + (1 − h)(t + 2m). With an n-level table the miss term is t + (n + 1)m.
  • A reference to a page not in memory causes a page fault; the OS loads it from disk, maybe replacing a page (FIFO, LRU, optimal). With fault rate p: EAT = (1 − p)·m + p·(fault service time).

Memory management hardware also handles segmentation (variable-size logical units such as code, data and stack, each with base and limit) and segmented paging (logical address = segment + page + word). It enforces protection: each segment or page has access rights such as full read-write, read only, execute only or system only.

Worked examples

Example 1: Building memory from chips

Build a 2K × 16 memory from 256 × 8 chips.

  1. Chips per row = 16 ÷ 8 = 2. Rows = 2048 ÷ 256 = 8. Total = 16 chips.
  2. Each chip needs log₂256 = 8 address lines. Rows need a 3-to-8 decoder.
  3. Total address lines = log₂2048 = 11 (8 to the chips, 3 to the decoder).

Example 2: Address split for three mappings

32-bit byte addresses, a 64 KB cache and 32-byte blocks.

  1. Offset = log₂32 = 5. Lines = 65,536 ÷ 32 = 2048.
  2. Direct: index = 11, tag = 32 − 11 − 5 = 16. Tag directory = 2048 × (16 + 1 valid) = 34,816 bits.
  3. 4-way: sets = 512, set bits = 9, tag = 18; four 18-bit comparators.
  4. Fully associative: tag = 32 − 5 = 27.
  5. Address 0x1234ABCD in the direct cache: tag = 0x1234, line = (0x1234ABCD ÷ 32) mod 2048 = 1374, offset = 13.

Example 3: Hits and misses for one reference string

A cache of 4 lines, initially empty, receives block references 0 4 8 0 4 1 5 0 8 1. Compare direct mapping, 2-way set-associative (LRU) and fully associative (LRU).

Ref0480415081
Direct (mod 4)MMMMMMMMMM
2-way (mod 2)MMMMMMMHMH
Fully assoc.MMMHHMMHMH
  1. Direct: 0, 4 and 8 all map to line 0 and evict each other; 1 and 5 fight over line 1. 0 hits.
  2. 2-way: even blocks share set 0 (two lines). The pair 0, 4, 8 still thrashes, but after 1 and 5 settle in set 1, block 0 hits and block 1 hits. 2 hits.
  3. Fully associative: four lines hold 0, 4, 8, 1; then 5 evicts the LRU block 8, and 8 later evicts 4. 4 hits, hit ratio 0.4.

More associativity removed conflict misses. Every scheme still pays the compulsory misses.

Interactive solvers

Enter any problem, including the ones in your practice set, and the solver works it out step by step with the conventions stated. Use it to check your answers, not to replace doing them by hand: the exam gives you no solver.

Interactive solver: Cache mapping solver

The solver runs in your browser. Turn on JavaScript to use it.

Interactive solver: Memory access time calculator

The solver runs in your browser. Turn on JavaScript to use it.

Example 4: Access-time formulas

  1. Cache 10 ns, memory 100 ns, h = 0.95. Hierarchical: 10 + 0.05 × 100 = 15 ns. Simultaneous: 0.95 × 10 + 0.05 × 100 = 14.5 ns.
  2. Hit ratio needed for 16 ns hierarchical: 10 + (1 − h) × 100 ≤ 16, so h ≥ 0.94.
  3. Two levels: L1 1 ns, miss rate 5%; L2 8 ns, local miss rate 25%; memory 80 ns. AMAT = 1 + 0.05 × (8 + 0.25 × 80) = 2.4 ns. Global L2 miss rate = 0.05 × 0.25 = 1.25%.
  4. Write-back: hit 2 ns, miss rate 10%, block transfer 100 ns, and 40% of evicted blocks are dirty. Miss penalty = 100 + 0.4 × 100 = 140 ns; AMAT = 2 + 0.1 × 140 = 16 ns.

Example 5: Virtual memory and the TLB

  1. 32-bit virtual address, 4 KB pages, 4-byte entries: pages = 2³²⁻¹² = 2²⁰, table = 2²⁰ × 4 B = 4 MB. With 30-bit physical addresses, frame number = 30 − 12 = 18 bits.
  2. Split 10 | 10 | 12 in two levels: the outer table has 2¹⁰ × 4 B = 4 KB, exactly one page.
  3. TLB 10 ns, memory 80 ns, hit 90%, one-level table: EAT = 0.9 × 90 + 0.1 × 170 = 98 ns. With a two-level table the miss costs 10 + 3 × 80 = 250 ns, so EAT = 81 + 25 = 106 ns.
  4. Memory 100 ns, fault service 10 ms. For EAT ≤ 200 ns: (1 − p)100 + p × 10⁷ ≤ 200, so p ≤ 100 ÷ 9,999,900 ≈ 1 fault in 100,000 references.

Example 6: Disk and associative memory

  1. A disk spins at 7200 rpm with 500 sectors of 512 bytes per track and a 4 ms average seek. One revolution = 60 ÷ 7200 s = 8.33 ms, so average latency = 4.17 ms. One sector transfers in 8.33 ÷ 500 = 0.0167 ms. Average access for one sector ≈ 4 + 4.17 + 0.017 = 8.18 ms.
  2. With 8 surfaces and 20,000 tracks per surface: capacity = 8 × 20,000 × 500 × 512 = 40,960,000,000 bytes (40.96 GB).
  3. CAM: A = 1011 0110, K = 1111 0000. Only the upper four bits are compared. Words 1011 1001 and 1011 0000 match; 1001 0110 and 0011 0110 do not.

Formula and fact sheet

QuantityFormula
Offset bitslog₂(block size)
Index bits (direct)log₂(cache size ÷ block size)
Set bits (k-way)log₂(lines ÷ k)
Tag bitsaddress bits − index/set bits − offset bits
Hierarchical accessT₁ + (1 − h)T₂
Simultaneous accesshT₁ + (1 − h)T₂
AMAT (two levels)TL1 + m1(TL2 + m2Tmem)
Chips needed(Wtotal ÷ W) × (B ÷ b)
Page table size2VA bits − offset bits × PTE size
TLB EATh(t + m) + (1 − h)(t + 2m)
Page-fault EAT(1 − p)m + p × fault service time
Rotational latency½ × 60 ÷ rpm seconds
Comparatorsdirect 1; k-way k; fully associative = number of lines

NTA traps

  • Hierarchical versus simultaneous. If the question says the cache is checked first, a miss costs T₁ + T₂. If both are accessed in parallel, a miss costs T₂. Read the wording before choosing a formula.
  • Words or bytes. In word-addressable machines, offset bits count words in a block, not bytes.
  • Using lines instead of sets. In a k-way cache, the index is log₂(lines ÷ k), not log₂(lines).
  • Local versus global miss rate. AMAT multiplies L1’s miss rate by L2’s local miss rate.
  • TLB miss counted as one memory access. A single-level page table on a TLB miss costs two memory accesses: one for the entry, one for the data.
  • “LRU always beats FIFO.” False for particular reference strings; LRU is better on average, not always.
  • “Write-through needs a dirty bit.” No; only write-back needs it.
  • Decoder size. The decoder selects rows of chips, so its outputs = rows, not total chips.

How NTA asks this

  • Numericals: tag/index/offset bits, number of chips and address lines, AMAT or hit ratio, TLB and page-fault EAT, page table size, disk latency.
  • Match the following: mapping techniques with properties, write policies with behaviour, the 3 Cs with remedies, ROM types with erasing method.
  • Order: the hierarchy by speed or cost, or the steps of address translation.
  • Assertion–Reason and two statements: locality, conflict misses, write-back and dirty bits, TLB behaviour.

Mini-example: Match the following

List I: A. Compulsory miss, B. Capacity miss, C. Conflict miss. List II: I. Increase associativity, II. Increase block size (prefetch more), III. Increase cache size.

Answer: A-II, B-III, C-I. Fix C first (conflict is about mapping, so associativity), and the rest follows.

Elimination tricks. Check that tag + index + offset equals the address width: options that fail are wrong. Doubling associativity moves one bit from index to tag. For AMAT, the answer must lie between the hit time and the memory time. For chip counts, the product rows × columns must give the total capacity.

terms.definition: Programs tend to reuse recently accessed items (temporal) and access items near recent ones (spatial). It is why caches work.
Fraction of memory references found in the cache: hits ÷ total references.
Each memory block can go into exactly one cache line: line = block number mod number of lines.
The cache is split into sets of k lines; a block maps to one set (block mod sets) and may occupy any line in it.
A write updates only the cache; the block is written to memory when it is replaced, if its dirty bit is set.
Content-addressable memory (CAM): words are found by comparing their contents in parallel with an argument, under a key mask.
Translation lookaside buffer: a small associative cache of recent page-table entries.
A reference to a page that is not in main memory; the OS must bring it from disk.
Average memory access time = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty.

lessons.examTip: For any cache question, first write the address split: offset = log₂(block size), index = log₂(number of lines or sets), tag = the rest. Most options fall at once.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. Draw the tag | index | offset boxes for every cache question before calculating.
Check with solutions.md and write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (for example, hierarchical versus simultaneous access, or local versus global miss rate).
Redo problem 9 by hand with a small table of cache contents after each reference.
Redo the wrong ones after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.
Write the five formulas of the fact sheet from memory and check them.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct on the first attempt.
Problems 2–8 solved within 10 minutes, each with its formula written first.
Tag + index + offset adds up to the address width in every cache answer.
Problem 9 traced with no slips in either policy.

quiz.question: A 16 KB direct-mapped cache uses 64-byte blocks. The processor issues 32-bit byte addresses. How many bits are in the tag, index and offset fields?
quiz.explanation: Offset = log₂ 64 = 6. Lines = 16384 ÷ 64 = 256, so index = 8. Tag = 32 − 8 − 6 = 18. Option 3 uses 1024 lines (as if the block were 16 bytes).

quiz.question: Match List I with List II

b: I. A block may occupy any line of the cache, so every tag is compared
II. A block has exactly one possible line; one comparator suffices

quiz.question: A cache has a hit time of 1 ns, a miss rate of 4% and a miss penalty of 50 ns. What is the average memory access time (AMAT)?
quiz.explanation: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty = 1 + 0.04 × 50 = 3 ns. 2 ns forgets the hit time; 51 ns is the time of a single miss.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Conflict misses happen when blocks compete for the same line or set while other lines are free. If any block can go anywhere, that competition cannot happen; only compulsory and capacity misses remain. R explains A.

stmts: Assertion (A): A fully associative cache has no conflict misses.

quiz.question: A system has a TLB lookup time of 5 ns and a main memory access time of 50 ns, with a single-level page table in memory. The TLB hit ratio is 80%. What is the effective memory access time?
quiz.explanation: Hit: 5 + 50 = 55 ns. Miss: 5 + 50 (page table) + 50 (data) = 105 ns. EAT = 0.8 × 55 + 0.2 × 105 = 44 + 21 = 65 ns. 105 ns is the miss case alone.

quiz.question: How many 256K × 8 RAM chips are needed to build a 1M × 32 memory, and what size of decoder selects the chip rows?
quiz.explanation: Rows = 1M ÷ 256K = 4; chips per row = 32 ÷ 8 = 4; total = 16 chips. Four rows need a 2-to-4 decoder. The decoder selects rows, not individual chips, so 4-to-16 is wrong.

quiz.question: An associative memory is best described as memory that is
options: accessed by address in a fixed sequence
accessed by comparing the stored contents with a given argument
accessible only by the operating system
quiz.explanation: Associative (content-addressable) memory compares the argument register, masked by the key register, with every stored word in parallel and sets the match register. Sequential access describes tape.

lessons.title: Multiprocessors
lessons.summaryHtml: A multiprocessor is a single computer with two or more CPUs that share memory and I/O under one operating system. It is a MIMD machine. Tightly coupled systems share main memory; loosely coupled systems give each processor its own memory and exchange messages. Processors and memories are joined by an interconnection structure: a time-shared bus, multiport memory, a crossbar switch, a multistage network such as the omega network, or a hypercube. When many processors want the bus, arbitration picks one; when they share data, synchronisation (semaphores built on test-and-set) and cache coherence (snooping, directories, the MESI protocol) keep it correct. Amdahl’s law limits the speedup any number of processors can give. NET asks match questions on networks and arbitration, MESI state questions, and speedup, switch-count and hypercube numericals.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

One cook can only chop so fast. A restaurant hires several cooks who share one pantry (memory) and one serving hatch (the bus). Now new problems appear: who uses the hatch next (arbitration), how two cooks avoid grabbing the same pan (synchronisation), and how each cook knows that the recipe card on his bench is still the latest version (cache coherence). A multiprocessor is this kitchen: two or more CPUs, shared memory and I/O, controlled by one operating system.

Why it matters for NET

Multiprocessors close Unit 2 and link to parallel processing (lesson 2.6) and to operating-system synchronisation (Unit 5). Questions are mostly conceptual matches: interconnection structures and their properties, arbitration schemes, coupling types, and coherence protocols. The numericals are few but reliable: Amdahl’s law, switch and crosspoint counts, hypercube links and routes, and MESI state traces.

Concepts in depth

Characteristics of multiprocessors

In Flynn’s taxonomy a multiprocessor is MIMD: many instruction streams on many data streams. It differs from a multicomputer network in that all processors are coordinated by one operating system that manages shared resources. Benefits are reliability (if one processor fails, others can take over its work) and performance, through either job-level parallelism (independent programs run on different processors) or program-level parallelism (one program split into parallel tasks).

FeatureTightly coupledLoosely coupled
MemoryShared main memory (each CPU may also have a cache)Local memory per processor
CommunicationThrough shared memoryMessages over channels or a network
Best forHigh degree of interaction between tasksLittle interaction between tasks
Also calledShared-memory multiprocessorDistributed-memory system, multicomputer

Shared-memory machines are further described as UMA (uniform memory access: every processor sees the same access time), NUMA (non-uniform: local memory is faster than remote memory) and COMA (cache-only memory architecture: local memories act as caches).

Interconnection structures

Time-shared common bus. All processors and memory modules sit on one bus. Only one processor can transfer at a time, so the others wait; the bus limits the total transfer rate. Improvements: a dual-bus design in which each processor has a local bus with local memory and I/O, plus a system bus to shared memory through a system bus controller.

Multiport memory. Each memory module has a separate port (bus) for each CPU, and the module resolves conflicts by giving the ports fixed priorities. Transfer rate is high because paths are separate, but the memory control logic, cables and connectors are expensive.

Crossbar switch. A grid with a crosspoint at each intersection of a processor bus and a memory-module path. Each crosspoint has switching and arbitration logic. Simultaneous transfers to different modules are possible. An n × m crossbar needs n × m crosspoints, which grows as N² for N processors and N memories.

Multistage switching network. Built from 2 × 2 interchange switches, each able to connect either input to either output. In an omega network of size N × N there are log₂N stages of N/2 switches, joined by perfect shuffles, so it needs (N/2)log₂N switches in total. Routing uses the destination address: at stage i the switch looks at bit i of the destination (most significant first) and sends the message to the upper output for 0 and the lower output for 1. Some combinations of source–destination pairs cannot be connected at once: the network is blocking.

Hypercube (binary n-cube). 2ⁿ nodes, each a processor with its own memory, labelled with n-bit addresses. Each node is linked to the n nodes whose addresses differ in exactly one bit. So the degree is n, the number of links is n × 2ⁿ⁻¹, and the diameter is n. To route from a source to a destination, XOR their addresses: the number of 1s is the number of hops, and each 1 names a dimension to cross.

3-cube (8 nodes)
      110-------111
     / |       / |
  010-------011  |
   |  100-----|-101
   | /        | /
  000-------001

Route 010 to 111:
  010 XOR 111 = 101, two 1s
  = 2 hops: 010 -> 011 -> 111
Network (N processors)Switching costSimultaneous transfersDiameter
Single busLowest (one bus)One at a time1 (shared medium)
Crossbar N × NN² crosspointsUp to N, if all modules differ1 (one crosspoint)
Omega N × N(N/2)log₂N switchesMany, but blockinglog₂N stages
Hypercuben × 2ⁿ⁻¹ linksManyn = log₂N
2D mesh k × k2k(k − 1) linksMany2(k − 1)
RingN linksMany⌊N/2⌋

Interprocessor arbitration

A system bus has data lines, address lines and control lines (including bus request, bus grant, bus busy and the arbitration lines). Each processor’s bus arbiter decides, with the others, who becomes bus master.

  • Serial (daisy-chain) arbitration. Arbiters are chained with priority-in (PI) and priority-out (PO). The first arbiter’s PI is 1. An arbiter whose processor is not requesting passes PO = PI; a requesting arbiter with PI = 1 sets PO = 0. The winner waits until the bus busy line is inactive, then activates it and uses the bus. Priority is fixed by position.
  • Parallel arbitration. Each arbiter drives a request line into a priority encoder; the encoder output goes to a decoder that raises the acknowledge of the highest-priority requester. Faster than the chain.
  • Dynamic arbitration algorithms change priorities while the system runs, so that no processor starves: time slice (fixed round-robin slots, independent of position), polling (a controller polls processors in a programmable sequence), LRU (the processor that has not used the bus for the longest time gets top priority), FIFO (requests served in arrival order) and rotating daisy chain (the chain is closed into a loop, and the processor that last used the bus becomes the lowest priority).

Interprocessor communication and synchronisation

In a shared-memory system processors communicate through a common message area in memory; the sender may also interrupt the receiver to tell it a message is waiting. The operating system can be organised as master–slave (one master runs the OS; others run user programs and ask the master for service), separate operating system (each processor has its own copy; suits loosely coupled systems) or distributed (floating) operating system (OS routines are shared and may run on any processor).

Shared resources need mutual exclusion. A binary semaphore in memory marks a critical section as busy (1) or free (0). Testing and setting it must be one indivisible action, or two processors could both see 0 and both enter. Hardware provides a test-and-set (TSL) instruction that reads the semaphore and writes 1 in a single locked bus cycle. A processor leaves the critical section by clearing the semaphore to 0.

Cache coherence

If each processor has a private cache, several copies of one memory word can exist. When one processor writes its copy, the others become stale. Write-through keeps memory current but does not fix the other caches. Solutions:

  • Software approaches: allow only non-shared or read-only data in private caches; shared writable data is marked non-cacheable, or a shared cache is used for it. Simple, but slow for shared data.
  • Snoopy protocols (hardware, bus-based): every cache controller watches (snoops) the bus. In write-invalidate, a write makes all other copies Invalid; in write-update (write-broadcast), a write sends the new value to all copies.
  • Directory protocols (hardware, scalable): a directory entry per memory block records which caches hold it, often as a full bit vector (one presence bit per processor) plus state bits. Messages go only to the caches listed, so no broadcast bus is needed; this suits large NUMA machines.

MESI is the standard write-invalidate protocol:

StateValid?Same as memory?Other copies?
M (Modified)YesNo (dirty)None
E (Exclusive)YesYes (clean)None
S (Shared)YesYesPossibly
I (Invalid)No––
  • Read miss: go to E if no other cache has the block, else to S (a cache holding it in M flushes and drops to S; E drops to S).
  • Write: from M stay M; from E go to M silently (no bus traffic, the main benefit of E); from S send an invalidate (upgrade) and go to M; from I read-with-intent-to-modify, invalidating the others.
  • Snooped invalidate or read-for-ownership: go to I (flushing first if in M).

False sharing occurs when two processors write different words that happen to lie in the same block, so the block bounces between caches though no data is truly shared.

Speedup: Amdahl and Gustafson

If a fraction f of the work can be parallelised over n processors and 1 − f must run serially:

Amdahl (fixed problem size):  S(n) = 1 / ((1 - f) + f/n)
Upper limit as n grows:       S = 1 / (1 - f)
Efficiency:                   E = S(n) / n
Gustafson (scaled size):      S = n - s(n - 1),  s = serial fraction of the parallel run

Amdahl’s law says the serial part dominates as n grows. Gustafson’s law observes that larger machines usually run larger problems, where the serial fraction shrinks, so scaled speedup grows almost linearly. The Karp–Flatt metric e = (1/S − 1/n) ÷ (1 − 1/n) estimates the experimentally observed serial fraction.

Worked examples

Example 1: Amdahl’s law

  1. f = 0.9, n = 10: S = 1 ÷ (0.1 + 0.09) = 5.26; efficiency = 5.26 ÷ 10 = 52.6%.
  2. n = 100: S = 1 ÷ (0.1 + 0.009) = 9.17. Ten times more processors gave less than twice the speed.
  3. Limit: 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10, whatever n is.
  4. With f = 0.95, how many processors for S = 8? 1 ÷ (0.05 + 0.95/n) = 8 gives 0.95/n = 0.075, so n = 12.67: at least 13 processors (12 gives less than 8).
  5. Gustafson with s = 0.1 and n = 64: S = 64 − 0.1 × 63 = 57.7.

Example 2: Switch counts

  1. 16 × 16 crossbar: 16 × 16 = 256 crosspoints.
  2. 16 × 16 omega: log₂16 = 4 stages × 8 switches = 32 switches (each 2 × 2).
  3. 8 processors and 4 memory modules in a crossbar: 8 × 4 = 32 crosspoints.
  4. Route to destination 6 = 110 in an 8 × 8 omega: bits 1, 1, 0 give lower, lower, upper at stages 1, 2, 3, whatever the source.

Example 3: Hypercube

  1. 4-cube: 16 nodes, degree 4, links = 4 × 2³ = 32, diameter 4.
  2. Route 0101 → 1110: XOR = 1011, three 1s, so 3 hops, for example 0101 → 0100 → 0110 → 1110.
  3. A hypercube of 1024 nodes: n = 10, so each node has 10 links, and there are 10 × 2⁹ = 5120 links.

Example 4: MESI trace

Three processors; the block starts Invalid everywhere. Operations: P0 read, P1 read, P1 write, P0 read, P2 write.

OperationP0P1P2Bus action
P0 readEIIRead; no other copy
P1 readSSIRead; P0 drops E to S
P1 writeIMIInvalidate (upgrade)
P0 readSSIRead; P1 flushes the dirty block
P2 writeIIMRead-exclusive; others invalidated

One flush and one upgrade occurred. Had P0 written right after its first read, E would have moved to M with no bus traffic.

Example 5: Directory overhead and bus capacity

  1. 32 processors, 64-byte blocks, full bit vector plus 2 state bits: 34 bits per 512-bit block = 6.64% overhead. With 64 processors and 1 state bit: 65 ÷ 512 = 12.7%. The full-map directory grows with the number of processors.
  2. A bus delivers 1600 MB/s and each processor, after its cache, needs 200 MB/s. The bus saturates at 1600 ÷ 200 = 8 processors. This is why buses do not scale.
  3. Karp–Flatt: a speedup of 6 on 8 processors gives e = (1/6 − 1/8) ÷ (1 − 1/8) ≈ 0.048, about a 4.8% serial fraction.

Multicore processors

A multicore processor (chip multiprocessor, CMP) places two or more complete processor cores on one integrated-circuit die. Each core has its own control unit, registers, ALUs and usually private L1 (and often L2) caches; the cores normally share a last-level cache (L3), the memory controller and the connection to the rest of the system. To software it looks like a small shared-memory (tightly coupled, MIMD) multiprocessor on one chip, so everything earlier in this lesson applies: the cores need an on-chip interconnect (a shared bus, a ring or a mesh), arbitration, synchronisation instructions and cache coherence (usually a MESI-style snoopy or directory protocol inside the chip).

Why the industry moved to multicore. Dynamic power of CMOS logic is P = αCV2f. Raising the clock also needs a higher supply voltage, so power and heat grow much faster than speed (the power wall), and extra instruction-level parallelism inside one core gives diminishing returns (the ILP wall). Two cores at a somewhat lower voltage and frequency can deliver more total throughput than one core pushed harder, for about the same power. The price is that programs must be written as multiple threads or processes to use the extra cores, and Amdahl’s law still limits the speedup of any single program.

TermMeaning
Homogeneous multicoreAll cores identical (most desktop and server chips)
Heterogeneous multicoreDifferent cores on one chip, e.g. big (fast) and little (low-power) cores, or CPU cores plus GPU cores
Simultaneous multithreading (SMT, hyper-threading)One core runs several hardware threads that share its execution units; not extra cores
Logical processorscores × hardware threads per core, the number the OS schedules on
ManycoreTens to thousands of simpler cores, for highly parallel work (GPUs, accelerators)

Example: multicore throughput and power. One core runs at voltage V and frequency f with dynamic power P. A dual-core chip runs each core at 0.8V and 0.8f.

Step 1. Power per core = (0.8)2 × 0.8 × P = 0.512P, so two cores use 1.024P, almost the same as before.

Step 2. For perfectly parallel work, throughput = 2 × 0.8 = 1.6 times the single core.

Step 3. For a program that is only 50% parallel, Amdahl gives time = 0.5 + 0.5/2 = 0.75 of the single-thread time at 0.8f, i.e. speedup 0.8/0.75 ≈ 1.07. Multicore pays only when the software is parallel.

Step 4. An 8-core chip with 2-way SMT shows 8 × 2 = 16 logical processors to the operating system.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFormula or fact
Dynamic powerP = αCV2f
Logical processorscores × hardware threads per core
Amdahl speedup1 ÷ ((1 − f) + f/n); limit 1 ÷ (1 − f)
Partial enhancement1 ÷ ((1 − f) + f/k) for a part sped up k times
Gustafsonn − s(n − 1)
Efficiencyspeedup ÷ n
Crossbarn × m crosspoints
Omega N × Nlog₂N stages, N/2 switches each, (N/2)log₂N total
Hypercube n-cube2ⁿ nodes, degree n, n·2ⁿ⁻¹ links, diameter n; hops = ones in XOR
Mesh k × k / ring Ndiameter 2(k − 1) / ⌊N/2⌋
Full-map directoryN presence bits + state bits per block
Dynamic arbitrationtime slice, polling, LRU, FIFO, rotating daisy chain
OS organisationsmaster–slave, separate OS, distributed (floating) OS
MESIE → M silently; S → M needs an invalidate; snooped read turns M/E into S

NTA traps

  • “Speedup can reach n.” Only if f = 1. With any serial part, the ceiling is 1 ÷ (1 − f) whatever n is.
  • “Write-through solves cache coherence.” It keeps memory current, but other caches still hold stale copies unless they are invalidated or updated.
  • Invalidate versus update. Write-invalidate removes other copies; write-update (broadcast) sends new data to them.
  • E versus S after a read. A read miss goes to E only if no other cache holds the block.
  • Omega switch count. It is (N/2)log₂N switches, not N log₂N; each switch has two inputs.
  • Hypercube links. n × 2ⁿ counts each link twice; divide by 2.
  • Crossbar and module conflicts. A crossbar removes path conflicts, not memory conflicts: two processors cannot use the same module at once.
  • Tight versus loose coupling. Shared memory means tight coupling; message passing means loose coupling.

How NTA asks this

  • Match the following: interconnection structures with properties, dynamic arbitration algorithms with descriptions, MESI states with meanings, OS organisations with descriptions.
  • Assertion–Reason and two statements: crossbar concurrency, bus limits, coherence protocols, Amdahl’s ceiling.
  • Numericals: Amdahl or Gustafson speedup, processors needed, crosspoint and switch counts, hypercube links, diameter and hops, directory overhead.
  • Order: arbitration steps, or networks by diameter or cost.

Mini-example: Assertion–Reason

A: Adding processors to a single shared bus eventually stops improving performance. R: A time-shared bus allows only one transfer at a time.

Both true, and the one-transfer limit is exactly why the bus saturates. Answer: both true, R explains A.

Elimination tricks. In an Amdahl question, strike any option above 1 ÷ (1 − f). In a switch-count question, the crossbar must be the largest number and a single bus the smallest. In a MESI question, any answer with M in one cache and a valid copy in another is impossible. For hypercube routing, count the 1s in the XOR before anything else.

terms.definition: Processors share a common main memory and communicate through it. Also called a shared-memory multiprocessor.
Each processor has its own local memory; processors communicate by passing messages. Also called a distributed-memory system.
A grid of crosspoints joining every processor to every memory module, allowing simultaneous transfers to different modules.
A multistage network of log₂N stages of N/2 two-by-two switches, routed by the bits of the destination address.
A network of 2ⁿ nodes where each node links to the n nodes whose binary addresses differ in one bit.
Deciding which requesting processor gets the shared system bus next.
Making sure that all cached copies of a shared memory word show the same, latest value.
A write-invalidate coherence protocol with four line states: Modified, Exclusive, Shared and Invalid.
Speedup with n processors = 1 ÷ ((1 − f) + f/n), where f is the parallelisable fraction; the limit is 1 ÷ (1 − f).

lessons.examTip: In any speedup question, find the serial fraction first. Amdahl’s ceiling is 1 ÷ serial fraction, which removes impossible options before you calculate.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For MESI problems, keep a row of states for every processor after every operation.
Check with solutions.md and write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (for example, the Amdahl limit, or E versus S after a read).
Draw an 8 × 8 omega network and route one message by its destination bits.
Redo the wrong ones after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.
Write the switch counts for crossbar, omega and hypercube from memory for N = 16 and check them.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct on the first attempt.
Every Amdahl answer checked against the 1 ÷ (1 − f) ceiling.
Problem 10 traced with all five state rows correct.
Problems 2–9 solved within 12 minutes.

quiz.question: 90% of a program can be parallelised perfectly; the rest is serial. What speedup does Amdahl’s law predict on 10 processors?
quiz.explanation: S = 1 ÷ ((1 − 0.9) + 0.9/10) = 1 ÷ (0.1 + 0.09) = 1 ÷ 0.19 ≈ 5.26. Even with infinitely many processors the speedup cannot pass 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10, so 10.00 is only the ceiling.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: A single shared bus allows one transfer at a time (II). Multiport memory puts the switching inside each module, with one port per CPU (IV). A crossbar has a crosspoint for every pair (I). A hypercube links nodes whose addresses differ in one bit (III). Option 2 swaps B and C.

b: I. A crosspoint for every processor–memory pair; simultaneous transfers to different modules
II. Only one transfer at a time over a single path
III. 2ⁿ nodes, each linked to the nodes differing in one address bit
IV. Each memory module has a separate port for every CPU and resolves conflicts internally

quiz.question: In a 4-dimensional hypercube (16 nodes), how many bidirectional links are there, and what is the diameter?
quiz.explanation: Each of the 2⁴ = 16 nodes has 4 links, and each link joins two nodes: 16 × 4 ÷ 2 = 32. The farthest pair differs in all 4 bits, so the diameter is 4. 64 counts each link twice.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false

quiz.explanation: E means “only copy, same as memory” (I true). A write-invalidate protocol makes other copies Invalid; sending the new data to them describes a write-update (write-broadcast) protocol (II false).

Statement II: In a write-invalidate protocol, a write sends the new data to every other cache that holds the block.

quiz.question: Arrange the steps of serial (daisy-chain) bus arbitration for a processor that wants the system bus.
quiz.explanation: The request comes first; the arbiter wins the chain (PI = 1, PO = 0); it must still wait for the current bus user to finish (bus busy inactive); then it takes the bus and finally releases it. Taking the bus before bus busy is inactive (option 2) would collide with the current master.

B. Its arbiter receives PI = 1 and sets PO = 0, blocking lower-priority arbiters
C. The arbiter waits until the bus busy line is inactive
D. It activates bus busy and the processor uses the bus
E. When the transfer ends it releases bus busy

quiz.question: Three processors P0, P1 and P2 use MESI. A block starts Invalid in all caches. The operations are: P0 writes, P1 reads, P2 reads, P0 writes. What are the states of the block in (P0, P1, P2) at the end?
quiz.explanation: P0 write: (M, I, I). P1 read: P0 flushes, (S, S, I). P2 read: (S, S, S). P0 write on a Shared line: it invalidates the others, (M, I, I). (M, S, S) is impossible because M means the only valid copy.

quiz.question: An 8 × 8 omega network is built from 2 × 2 switches. How many stages and how many switches does it need?
quiz.explanation: Stages = log₂8 = 3; each stage has 8 ÷ 2 = 4 switches; total = 3 × 4 = 12. An 8 × 8 crossbar would need 64 crosspoints. 24 counts ports instead of switches.

quiz.question: In a tightly coupled multiprocessor, processors communicate mainly through
options: message passing over communication channels only
quiz.explanation: Tightly coupled systems share main memory, so processors exchange data by reading and writing shared locations (with synchronisation). Message passing is the loosely coupled (distributed-memory) style.

lessons.title: Language design and translation issues
lessons.summaryHtml: This lesson is about how programming languages are built and run, not about any one language. You will see the main paradigms (imperative, object-oriented, functional, logic), the criteria used to judge a design, and how syntax (BNF, EBNF, parse trees, ambiguity) differs from semantics (operational, axiomatic, denotational). It then covers how programs are translated and run: compilers, interpreters and hybrid systems, and the stages of translation. The core of the lesson is binding and binding times, scope (static and dynamic), lifetime and storage allocation. It ends with parameter passing: by value, reference, value-result and name. NTA gives output questions on scope and parameter passing, so you will learn to trace them step by step.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A programming language is a notation for describing computations, and a language implementation is the software that makes the notation run on a machine. This lesson looks at languages from the designer’s and implementer’s side. The questions are: what does a program mean (syntax and semantics), how is it translated (compiler, interpreter or both), and when does each name get its type, its memory cell and its value (binding)? It also asks which declaration a name refers to (scope), how long a variable lives (lifetime), and how arguments reach a procedure (parameter passing).

Think of a play. The script is the syntax. What the actors do is the semantics. The casting decisions are bindings: some are made when the play is written (design), some when a theatre company stages it (implementation), and some only on the night (run time). Scope is the rule for which actor answers when a character’s name is called.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 3 of Paper 2 starts with this topic (it follows the textbook by Pratt and Zelkowitz, with ideas that Sebesta also covers). Questions come every cycle, usually a few per paper. Three kinds dominate. First, trace questions: “what is printed under call by reference / value-result / name” and “what is printed under static / dynamic scoping”. Second, match questions on binding times, paradigms with languages, and kinds of semantics. Third, statement questions on compilers versus interpreters, lifetime versus scope and aliasing. Trace questions are pure marks if you use a disciplined table. Guessing them from intuition is where most candidates lose marks.

Concepts in depth

1. Language concepts, paradigms and design criteria

A paradigm is a style of computation that a language supports.

ParadigmCentral ideaTypical languages
Imperative (procedural)State held in variables and changed by assignment, step by step; mirrors the von Neumann machineFORTRAN, COBOL, Pascal, C
Object-orientedObjects combine data and operations; classes, inheritance, dynamic bindingSmalltalk, C++, Java, C#
Functional (applicative)Programs are functions applied to arguments; no or little assignment; recursion instead of loopsLISP, Scheme, ML, Haskell
Logic (declarative, rule-based)Facts and rules; execution is a search for proofs (resolution, unification, backtracking)Prolog
Scripting / markup and othersGlue and text processing; concurrency; event-drivenPerl, Python, JavaScript; Ada tasks for concurrency

The imperative style is shaped by the von Neumann architecture: memory holds both data and instructions, and the path between CPU and memory limits speed (the von Neumann bottleneck). Variables model memory cells, assignment models the store, and loops model repeated fetch–execute.

Languages are judged by readability (how easily a program can be understood), writability (how easily it can be written), reliability (whether it behaves as specified) and cost (of training, writing, compiling, running and maintaining). Readability depends on simplicity (a small set of features and little feature multiplicity: C has four ways to add 1 to a variable), orthogonality (a small set of primitive constructs that can be combined in all ways, and every combination is legal and meaningful) and good support for data types and syntax design. Reliability depends on type checking, exception handling and limited aliasing. Too much orthogonality (ALGOL 68) can hurt, because strange combinations become legal.

Pratt’s notion of a virtual computer is also examined. The hardware computer is wrapped in layers of software: the operating system, then the language implementation. Together they present a virtual computer whose “machine language” is the programming language itself. A C program runs on a C virtual computer, whatever the hardware below it.

A programming environment is the set of tools that support program development: editors, compilers, linkers, debuggers, profilers, test tools and version control. Integrated into one tool they form an IDE. Environments also affect language design. Separate compilation of modules needs a linker and interface declarations, and interactive testing favours interpreted languages.

2. Syntax and semantics

Syntax is the form of programs; semantics is their meaning. The lexical level fixes the tokens (identifiers, literals, operators). The grammar fixes how tokens combine.

  • BNF (Backus–Naur Form) writes context-free productions such as <expr> ::= <expr> + <term> | <term>. It was introduced to describe ALGOL 60.
  • EBNF adds [ ] for an optional part, { } for zero or more repetitions and ( | ) for a choice inside a rule. EBNF describes exactly the same class of languages (the context-free languages); it is only more compact.
  • Syntax diagrams (railroad diagrams) draw the same rules as graphs.
  • A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two different parse trees (equivalently, two leftmost derivations). With E → E + E | E * E | id, the string id + id * id has 2 parse trees. The standard fixes are precedence levels (E → E + T, T → T * F) and associativity (left recursion for left-associative operators). The dangling else is the classic statement-level ambiguity.

Context-free grammars cannot express rules like “declare a variable before use” or “types must match”. These are called static semantics, and attribute grammars describe them by attaching attributes and rules to productions. The meaning of running a program (dynamic semantics) is described in three ways.

MethodHow it gives meaningUsed for
OperationalBy the state changes the construct causes on an abstract machine or interpreterLanguage manuals, implementers
AxiomaticBy logical assertions: preconditions and postconditions ({P} S {Q}, Hoare logic, weakest preconditions)Program correctness proofs
DenotationalBy mapping each construct to a mathematical object, usually a function from states to statesRigorous language definitions

For example, the weakest precondition of x = x + 1 {x > 5} is x + 1 > 5, that is, x > 4: replace x by the right side in the postcondition.

3. Translation: compilers, interpreters and hybrids

A compiler translates the whole source program into target code (machine code or assembly) before it runs. An interpreter executes the source (or a simple internal form) statement by statement, decoding each statement every time it is reached. A hybrid system compiles to an intermediate code and then interprets it. Java is the standard example: javac produces platform-independent bytecode, and the JVM interprets it or JIT-compiles hot methods to native code at run time.

AspectCompilerPure interpreter
Unit translatedWhole program, onceEach statement, each time it runs
Execution speedFastSlow (often 10 to 100 times slower)
Error reportsAll syntax errors after compilationStops at the first error it reaches, with source-level detail
OutputObject file / executableNo object file
Memory at run timeOnly the executableInterpreter plus source (and symbol table)
ExamplesC, C++, FORTRAN, COBOLEarly BASIC, shell scripts, early JavaScript engines

Other translators you should know: an assembler (assembly to machine code), a preprocessor (source to source, such as the C preprocessor expanding #include and #define), a linker (joins object modules and libraries and resolves external references) and a loader (places the program in memory and relocates addresses). A cross-compiler produces code for a machine other than the one it runs on.

Stages of translation. Analysis comes first: lexical analysis (characters to tokens), syntax analysis (tokens to parse tree), semantic analysis (type checking, symbol table, intermediate code). Synthesis follows: optimisation, then code generation. Linking and loading come last. The symbol table and error handler are used by all phases. Formal translation models underlie the front end: regular expressions and finite automata for tokens, and context-free grammars with pushdown automata for syntax (the Chomsky hierarchy is covered in Unit 8).

4. Binding and binding times

A binding is an association between an entity and an attribute: a variable and its type, a name and its address, an operator symbol and its operation. The binding time is when the association is made. Pratt’s classes, from earliest to latest:

Binding timeExamples
Language definition (design) timeThe meaning of * as multiplication; the set of primitive types; the structure of statements
Language implementation timeThe number of bits in an int, the range of float, how integers are represented
Translation (compile) timeA C or Java variable to its declared type; a static variable to its relative address; the meaning of an overloaded operator chosen by operand types
Link timeA call to a library function to that function’s code
Load timeA C global or static variable to its absolute memory address (in a system without later relocation)
Execution (run) timeA local variable to its stack cell; a variable to its current value; a pointer to a heap block; a formal parameter to its actual; a Python variable to its type

A binding is static if it happens before run time and stays the same throughout execution. It is dynamic if it happens during execution or can change. Early binding gives efficiency (the compiler can check types and generate direct code). Late binding gives flexibility (Python variables can hold any type, and a C++ virtual call picks its method at run time).

Type binding can be explicit (a declaration, as in C), implicit (a naming rule, as in FORTRAN, where names starting with I–N are integers), or dynamic (the type comes from the value assigned, as in Python and JavaScript).

5. Variables: attributes, lifetime and storage allocation

Sebesta describes a variable by six attributes: name, address, value, type, lifetime and scope. The address is the l-value and the contents are the r-value. In x = x + 1 the left x stands for its l-value and the right x for its r-value. Two names bound to the same address are aliases. Aliases arise from reference parameters, pointers, C unions and FORTRAN EQUIVALENCE. They hurt readability and reliability.

Lifetime is the time during which a variable is bound to a cell. There are four storage categories.

CategoryBound to storageExamplePro / con
StaticBefore execution, until the endC globals and static localsFast, history-sensitive; no recursion
Stack-dynamicWhen its declaration is elaborated (at call), freed at returnC / Java local variablesSupports recursion; small allocation cost; no history
Explicit heap-dynamicBy explicit instructions (malloc/new), freed by free/delete or GCC malloc, C++ and Java newDynamic structures; dangling pointers and leaks possible
Implicit heap-dynamicWhenever a value is assignedJavaScript arrays, Python lists and stringsVery flexible; slowest, weak error detection

Scope and lifetime are different ideas. A C static local variable has a small scope (its function) but a lifetime of the whole program. A local variable of a function that calls another function is still alive during that call, but it is not in scope inside the callee.

Each call gets an activation record (frame) with parameters, local variables, the return address, a dynamic (control) link to the caller’s record, and, in languages with nested procedures, a static (access) link to the record of the textually enclosing procedure. FORTRAN 77 used one static record per subprogram, so it had no recursion. ALGOL-like languages use a run-time stack. Heap blocks that are no longer reachable are reclaimed by garbage collection. Reference counting is incremental but cannot free cycles; mark-and-sweep handles cycles but pauses the program. A dangling pointer points to storage that has been freed. A memory leak is storage that can no longer be reached but was never freed.

6. Scope: static versus dynamic

The scope of a variable is the range of statements in which it is visible. A variable is local to the block that declares it. It is non-local in an inner block that uses it without declaring it. The whole question is how a non-local name is resolved.

  • Static (lexical) scope: look in the enclosing text: the current block, then the block or procedure that textually contains it, and so on out to the globals. This is fixed at compile time. At run time it is implemented with the static chain (follow access links; a reference from depth d to a variable declared at depth k follows d − k links) or a display (an array of pointers, one per nesting level, giving constant-time access). C, C++, Java, Pascal, Ada and Scheme use it.
  • Dynamic scope: look in the current procedure, then in its caller, then the caller’s caller, following the dynamic chain. The answer depends on the calling sequence. Early LISP, APL, SNOBOL4 and Perl’s local variables work this way. Dynamic scope makes programs hard to read and type-check, and non-local access is slower.

A declaration in an inner block hides (shadows) an outer declaration of the same name. The referencing environment of a statement is the set of all names visible there.

7. Parameter passing

Formal parameters are the names in the procedure header; actual parameters (arguments) are the expressions at the call. Semantically, a parameter can be in mode (data flows into the procedure), out mode (data flows back) or in-out mode (both). The implementation models are these.

MethodWhat is passedEffect on the actualWhere you meet it
Call by valueThe r-value, copied into a new local cellNoneC (all parameters), Java primitives, Pascal value parameters
Call by resultNothing in; the formal is copied to the actual at returnSet at returnAda out (conceptually)
Call by value-result (copy-in/copy-out, copy-restore)The r-value in; the final value copied back at returnChanged only at returnALGOL W, Ada in out scalars, Fortran (some implementations)
Call by referenceThe l-value (address)Changed at once, because the formal is an aliasC++ & parameters, Pascal var, Fortran, C through pointers
Call by nameThe unevaluated expression plus its environment (a thunk)Re-evaluated at every use; can hit different cellsALGOL 60
Call by need (lazy)A thunk evaluated at most once, then cached–Haskell

Rules for tracing:

  1. Value: the formal is a private copy. Only globals changed inside the procedure matter to the caller.
  2. Reference: replace the formal by the actual’s cell fixed at the call. For a[i], compute i once, at the call.
  3. Value-result: private copy during the call. Globals changed inside are changed at once. At return, copy each formal back into its actual. The last copy wins if two formals share an actual, so the order of copy-back matters (a question must state it; left to right is the usual assumption). Whether the address of an actual such as a[i] is fixed at the call or recomputed at return must also be stated; at the call is the usual assumption.
  4. Name: textually replace every use of the formal by the actual expression, then evaluate in the caller’s environment at that moment. An actual such as a[i] can refer to a different element after i changes. If the actual is an expression such as m * 2, it is recomputed at each use.

A C function always receives values. When you pass an array, the value passed is the address of its first element, so the function can change the elements. That behaves like reference for the elements, but the pointer itself is still passed by value. Jensen’s device uses call by name to make one formal act like a whole expression over a changing index: sum(a[i]) with i as the loop variable adds all elements.

Worked examples

Example 1: one program, four passing methods

int x = 2, y = 5;
void p(int a, int b) { a = a + b; b = a - b; x = x * 10; }
main() { p(x, y); print(x, y); }

Value: a = 2 and b = 5 are copies. a = 7, b = 2 (local only). x = x × 10 changes the global to 20. Printed: 20 5.

Reference: a is x and b is y. a = a + b gives x = 7. b = a − b gives y = 7 − 5 = 2. x = x × 10 gives x = 70. Printed: 70 2.

Value-result: copies a = 2 and b = 5. a = 7, b = 2. x = x × 10 changes the global to 20. At return, copy back: x = a = 7, y = b = 2. The copy-back overwrites the 20. Printed: 7 2.

Name: a means x and b means y, re-evaluated each time. With plain variables as actuals, name behaves like reference: 70 2.

Example 2: static versus dynamic scope

int n = 1;
void a() { n = n + 1; }
void b() { int n = 5; a(); print(n); }
main() { b(); print(n); }

Static: a is declared at the outer level, so its n is the global n. The call a() makes the global n = 2. b prints its own local n = 5, then main prints the global 2. Output: 5 2.

Dynamic: a has no local n, so it searches its caller b and finds b’s n = 5, which becomes 6. b prints 6. The global is untouched, so main prints 1. Output: 6 1.

Example 3: swap by name fails

int i = 1;
int a[3] = {2, 0, 9};
void swap(int x, int y) { int t = x; x = y; y = t; }
main() { swap(i, a[i]); print(i, a[0], a[1], a[2]); }
Step (by name)Rewrittenia
t = xt = i1{2, 0, 9}, t = 1
x = yi = a[i] = a[1]0{2, 0, 9}
y = ta[i] = t, now a[0]0{1, 0, 9}

By name: 0 1 0 9. The intended swap would set i = 0 and a[1] = 1. By reference the element a[1] is fixed at the call, and you get exactly that: 0 2 1 9. This is the standard proof that a general swap cannot be written with call by name.

Example 4: Jensen’s device

int i = 0, s = 0;
int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4};
int sum(int e) { s = 0; i = 0; while (i < 4) { s = s + e; i = i + 1; } return s; }
main() { print(sum(a[i])); print(sum(i * i)); }

By name, e is re-evaluated at every use with the current i. The first call adds a[0] + a[1] + a[2] + a[3] = 10. The second adds 0 + 1 + 4 + 9 = 14. Output: 10 14. By value, e is computed once at the call: a[0] = 1 gives 4 × 1 = 4. At the second call i is 4 (left over from the first call), so e = 16 and the sum is 64. Output: 4 64.

Example 5: value-result with a global

int k = 3;
void q(int x) { x = x + 10; k = k * 2; print(x); }
main() { q(k); print(k); }

Value: x = 13, k becomes 6; prints 13 6. Reference: x is k, so k = 13 and then k = 26; x shows 26; prints 26 26. Value-result: x = 13 privately, the global k becomes 6, and at return k = x = 13; prints 13 13. The global change is lost at the copy-back.

Example 6: the same idea in real C

#include <stdio.h>
int x = 5;
void show(void) { printf("%d ", x); }
int main(void) {
    int x = 7;
    show();
    { int x = 9; printf("%d ", x); }
    printf("%d", x);
    return 0;
}

Output: 5 9 7. C is statically scoped, so show uses the global x even though main’s local x = 7 is alive during the call. The inner block’s x = 9 hides main’s x only inside that block.

8. Formal transition models

Pratt and Zelkowitz end their chapter on syntax and translation with formal transition models. These are abstract machines that move from state to state as they read the input, one symbol at a time. They explain why the front end of a translator can be both correct and fast, because each class of grammar has a matching class of machine.

Grammar (Chomsky type)Production formMachine that recognises itUse in a translator
Type 3, regularA → aB or A → aFinite-state automaton (FSA)Tokens: identifiers, numbers, operators (the scanner)
Type 2, context-freeA → αPushdown automaton (PDA)Nested structure: expressions, blocks, if–else (the parser)
Type 1, context-sensitiveαAβ → αγβ, γ not emptyLinear-bounded automatonRules such as “declare before use”; in practice checked by semantic analysis instead
Type 0, unrestrictedα → βTuring machineAnything computable; membership can be undecidable

A finite-state automaton has a finite set of states, one start state, a set of final (accepting) states and a transition function. It has no memory apart from its current state. In a deterministic FSA (DFA) each state has exactly one next state for each input symbol. A nondeterministic FSA (NFA) may have several, or ε-moves that read nothing. Every NFA can be converted into an equivalent DFA by the subset construction, so both recognise exactly the regular languages. A transition table or a state diagram describes the machine completely. Regular expressions describe the same class of languages, which is why a tool such as LEX can turn token patterns into a table-driven DFA scanner. The scanner runs in time proportional to the length of the input.

A finite automaton cannot count without limit. To check that parentheses balance it would need a different state for every nesting depth, and it has only finitely many. A pushdown automaton adds a stack: push on “(”, pop on “)”, and accept if the stack is empty at the end. That is exactly the power needed for context-free syntax, so every parser is, in effect, a PDA. General context-free parsing (CYK, Earley) costs O(n³) time. Programming-language grammars are therefore designed to be LL(1) or LR(1), and these are parsed deterministically in O(n) time. Pratt also notes the limits of the theory: some questions about grammars have no algorithmic answer. For example, whether an arbitrary context-free grammar is ambiguous is undecidable.

Example 7: a DFA scanner for identifiers and integers. States: S (start), I (inside an identifier), N (inside an integer) and D (dead, the error state). “letter” means a–z, A–Z or _; “digit” means 0–9.

StateletterdigitAccepting?
SINno
IIIyes: identifier
NDNyes: integer
DDDno
  1. x12: S –x→ I –1→ I –2→ I. It ends in the accepting state I, so the token is an identifier.
  2. 407: S → N → N → N, so it is an integer.
  3. 4ab: S –4→ N –a→ D, and D is never left. An identifier cannot start with a digit, so the string is rejected.

The complete DFA has 4 states, counting the dead state. If you leave out D, the table has blank entries and the machine is a partial DFA.

9. Virtual computers and programming environments

Pratt describes a running program as executing on a layered virtual computer. From the bottom, the layers are:

  1. the actual hardware computer;
  2. on many machines, a firmware (microprogram) layer that interprets the machine instructions;
  3. the operating system, which adds files, processes and input–output services;
  4. the language implementation (translator plus run-time library), which gives a virtual computer for that language. The data objects of a C virtual computer are C objects, and its operations are C operators;
  5. the application program, which in turn defines a virtual computer for its own users.

Each layer is built from the one below it, either by translation (converting a program into an equivalent program in a lower-level language, then running that) or by software simulation (interpretation: a program on the lower machine carries out each operation). A computer can therefore be realised in three ways: as hardware (physical circuits), as firmware (a microprogram in control memory interprets the instruction set) or by software simulation (the Java Virtual Machine interpreting bytecode is the standard example). Binding times depend on this layering. “Implementation time” means the time the language’s virtual computer was built, and the same language can have different implementation-time bindings (such as the size of an int) on different machines.

A programming environment is the set of tools used while a program is written, tested and run. Pratt lists the features that also shape language design:

  • Separate compilation. Modules are compiled independently, so the language needs a way to declare names that are defined in other modules (C’s extern declarations and header files). The compiler of one module does not see the source of the others; the linker resolves the references.
  • Testing and debugging features. Execution traces, breakpoints and assertions. C’s assert(cond) stops the program with a message when cond is false, and compiling with NDEBUG defined removes every assert.
  • Environment frameworks. The support environment of services that a program can use: the file system, window system, libraries and communication facilities.
  • Job control and process languages. Languages that run programs and connect them, such as Unix shell scripts with pipes (ls | wc -l). They are usually interpreted.

An IDE (integrated development environment) bundles the editor, compiler, debugger, profiler and version control into one tool.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemRemember
Binding times (early → late)Language design → implementation → compile → link → load → run
Variable attributesName, address (l-value), value (r-value), type, lifetime, scope
Storage categoriesStatic, stack-dynamic, explicit heap-dynamic, implicit heap-dynamic
Static chain linksReference from nesting depth d to a variable at depth k: d − k links
DisplayOne pointer per nesting level; constant-time non-local access

NTA traps

  • “Value-result is the same as reference.” Wrong when there is aliasing: the same variable passed twice, or a global that is also an argument. Fix: during the call the formal is a private copy; apply the copy-back only at return.
  • Forgetting the copy-back order. With p(n, n), left-to-right copy-back leaves the second formal’s value. Fix: read which order the question states.
  • Treating name as reference for a[i]. Under reference, a[i] is fixed at the call. Under name, a[i] is recomputed each time i changes. Fix: rewrite each use of the formal as the actual text.
  • Using the caller’s variable under static scope. Static scope looks at where the procedure is written, not where it is called. Fix: find the textually enclosing block first.
  • Mixing up scope and lifetime. A C static local has local scope but whole-program lifetime. A caller’s locals are alive but not visible in the callee.
  • Binding-time swaps. The size of int is language implementation time, not compile time. The type of a C variable is compile time, not run time. The value of a variable is always run time.
  • “C passes arrays by reference.” C has only call by value; for an array, the value passed is a pointer to the first element.
  • “EBNF is more powerful than BNF.” Both describe exactly the context-free languages. EBNF is only shorter.
  • “Interpreters produce object code.” A pure interpreter produces no object file. Java is a hybrid: a compiler to bytecode plus a JVM that interprets or JIT-compiles.

How NTA asks this

  • Trace (code) questions: a short program and “what is printed if parameters are passed by …” or “under dynamic scoping”. Draw one box per variable. Under value-result, write the copy-back line. Under dynamic scope, write the call chain main → r → q → p and search it backwards.
  • Match the lists: binding with binding time; paradigm with language; semantics with description; passing method with mechanism. Anchor the easiest pair (Prolog ↔ logic, thunk ↔ name), then eliminate every option that contradicts it.
  • Assertion–Reason: for example, A: “A general swap procedure cannot be written using call by name.” R: “Under call by name the actual parameter is re-evaluated at every use, so a[i] can denote a different element after i changes.” Both are true and R explains A, so the answer is option 1. Check the truth of each statement separately before you judge the “because”.
  • Statement I/II and multi-select: statements on compilers versus interpreters, static versus dynamic scope, and aliasing. One false keyword (“always”, “never”, “compile time”) usually decides it.
Remember: write the call chain and the variable boxes before you look at the options. Trace questions are designed so that each wrong method gives one of the other options.

A non-local name is resolved in the most recent active caller that declares it, following the chain of calls at run time.
The period of execution during which a variable is bound to a memory cell. It is a run-time idea; scope is a textual idea.

quiz.question: Consider the pseudo-code below (C-like syntax, static scoping; print writes its values separated by spaces). What is printed if all parameters are passed by name?
