quiz.explanation: Copy in: x = 5 and y = 5 (two separate local cells). In p: x = 6 and y = 10. Copy out from left to right: n = x = 6, then n = y = 10. The last copy wins, so 10 is printed. By reference both formals alias n: n = 6, then n = 12 (12). By value nothing changes (5). If copies went right to left, the answer would be 6.

quiz.question: A programming language allows recursive procedures. Which storage-allocation scheme must it use (at least) for the local variables of those procedures?
options: Purely static allocation, fixed at load time
Stack-dynamic allocation, a new activation record for each call
Allocation only in the code segment
quiz.explanation: Each active call of a recursive procedure needs its own copy of the locals, and the number of active calls is not known until run time. A run-time stack of activation records gives that. Purely static allocation (FORTRAN 77 style) gives one record per procedure, so it cannot support recursion. The heap could also work, but the stack is the minimum standard answer.

lessons.title: Elementary data types and programming in C
lessons.summaryHtml: This lesson covers elementary data types (data objects, variables and constants, declarations, type checking and conversion, enumerations, characters and strings) and then C programming in depth. You will work through tokens, types and their sizes, and the integer promotions and usual arithmetic conversions that decide many outputs. Then come operators with precedence and associativity, short-circuit evaluation and sequence points, and storage classes. The later sections cover control flow, functions and recursion, pointers and pointer arithmetic, arrays and strings, structures and unions (with padding), the preprocessor, dynamic memory, files and command-line arguments. NTA asks many “what is the output” questions on C. Every program in this lesson was compiled with gcc using -Wall -Wextra and run under the address and undefined-behaviour sanitizers, so the outputs shown are real.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A data type is a set of values together with the operations allowed on them. An int is a range of whole numbers with +, −, *, / and %; a char is a small integer that holds a character code. Elementary types are built into the language, and structured types (arrays, structures, unions) are built from them. C gives you direct access to memory through pointers, so it is fast but unforgiving. For NET you must predict exactly what a short C program prints: know the conversion rules, the precedence table, how pointers move and where behaviour is undefined.

Why it matters for NET

C is the language NTA uses for most programming questions in Paper 2, and it also appears in other units. Expect several output questions per paper. The recurring themes are operators and precedence, integer division and conversions, pointers with arrays and strings, macros, static variables, recursion, switch fall-through and struct/union sizes. There are also statement questions on storage classes, type conversion and the preprocessor. If a question depends on sizes, NTA usually states them (older papers assumed a 16-bit compiler with a 2-byte int, and newer ones often assume 4 bytes), so always use the sizes given in the question.

Concepts in depth

1. Data objects, types and type checking

A data object is a run-time container for values: a variable (its value can change) or a constant (a literal such as 42, or a const int). A declaration gives a name’s type, assignment changes an existing object’s value, and initialisation gives a value when the object is created. Pratt’s elementary types are numeric, enumeration, boolean and character; strings sit between elementary and structured types.

Type checking makes sure each operation gets operands of acceptable types: statically by the compiler (C, Java) or dynamically at run time (Python, Lisp). A strongly typed language detects all type errors; C is not one, because casts, unions and unchecked pointers bypass the type system and array bounds are never checked. A conversion is explicit (a cast, (double)a) or implicit (a coercion). Widening (int to double) keeps the value; narrowing can lose it: int t = 3.99; stores 3, because conversion to an integer truncates toward zero.

2. C tokens, constants and basic types

The C compiler’s tokens are keywords, identifiers, constants, string literals, operators and punctuators. An identifier starts with a letter or underscore, continues with letters, digits and underscores, is case-sensitive, and cannot be a keyword (int, while, sizeof, typedef, …). The name main is not a keyword.

  • Integer constants: decimal 10, octal with a leading 0 (010 is 8), hexadecimal with 0x (0x1F is 31). Suffixes: 10u, 10L.
  • Floating constants are double by default (3.5); 3.5f is float.
  • A character constant such as 'A' has type int in C (value 65 in ASCII). So 'A' + 2 is 67, printed with %c as C. The difference 'a' − 'A' is 32.
  • A string literal "exam" is an array of 5 chars, because the terminating '\0' counts. Modifying a string literal is undefined behaviour.
TypeTypical size on x86-64 Linux (LP64)Guaranteed by the standard
char1exactly 1 byte (at least 8 bits); plain char may be signed or unsigned
short2at least 16 bits
int4at least 16 bits (Turbo C used 2 bytes)
long8at least 32 bits
long long8at least 64 bits
float / double4 / 8IEEE 754 in practice
any pointer8implementation-defined

The guaranteed ordering is sizeof(char) ≤ sizeof(short) ≤ sizeof(int) ≤ sizeof(long) ≤ sizeof(long long). Unsigned arithmetic is modular (unsigned char 255 + 1 = 0; unsigned int 0 − 1 = 4294967295 for 32 bits). Signed overflow is undefined behaviour.

Enumerations give names to int constants. Values start at 0 and each name is one more than the previous one unless you assign a value: in enum {RED, GREEN = 5, BLUE, WHITE = 2, BLACK} the values are 0, 5, 6, 2, 3. Duplicate values are allowed.

3. Conversions in expressions

Two rules decide most “surprising” outputs:

  1. Integer promotions. Before arithmetic, char and short (signed or unsigned) are converted to int. So with unsigned char a = 200, b = 100; the sum a + b is the int 300. Storing it back in an unsigned char keeps it modulo 256: 300 − 256 = 44.
  2. Usual arithmetic conversions. For a binary operator, the “lower” operand is converted to the type of the “higher” one: long double > double > float > the integer types. Among integers of the same rank, unsigned wins. So in -1 < 1u the −1 becomes a huge unsigned value and the comparison is false. sizeof yields size_t, which is unsigned, so if (-1 < sizeof(int)) is also false.

Integer division truncates toward zero: 7 / 2 = 3 and −7 / 2 = −3. The identity (a / b) * b + a % b == a then fixes the remainder, so its sign follows the dividend: −7 % 2 = −1 and 7 % −2 = 1. Only if one operand is floating is the division real: (double)7 / 2 is 3.5, but (double)(7 / 2) is 3.0, and float f = 7 / 2; stores 3.0.

4. Operators, precedence and evaluation order

Level (high to low)OperatorsAssociativity
1() [] -> . postfix ++ --left to right
2unary + - ! ~ prefix ++ -- * (dereference) & (address) sizeof (type)right to left
3* / %left to right
4+ -left to right
5<< >>left to right
6< <= > >=left to right
7== !=left to right
8, 9, 10& then ^ then |left to right
11, 12&& then ||left to right
13?:right to left
14= += -= *= /= %= <<= >>= &= ^= |=right to left
15, (comma)left to right

So 2 + 3 << 1 = 10, x == 3 & 2 is (x == 3) & 2, *p++ is *(p++), and a > b ? a : b > c ? b : c groups as a > b ? a : (b > c ? b : c).

Short-circuit evaluation: in a && b, b is evaluated only if a is non-zero; in a || b, only if a is zero. So with a = 0, a && ++b does not change b, but a || b++ does. Bitwise operators work on bits: 5 & 3 = 1, 5 | 3 = 7, 5 ^ 3 = 6, ~5 = −6 (two’s complement), 5 << 2 = 20.

Precedence is not evaluation order. Precedence only groups operands. The order in which the operands of + or the arguments of a function are evaluated is unspecified. Modifying a variable twice, or reading and modifying it, without an intervening sequence point is undefined behaviour: i = i++ + 1, a[i] = i++ and printf("%d %d", i, i++) have no correct answer. The sequence points you must know are the end of a full expression (;), &&, ||, the ?: condition, the comma operator, and the moment just before a function is called (after its arguments are evaluated). Keep increments in separate statements: after int x = 5; int y = x++ * 2; int z = ++x * 2; x is 7, y is 10 and z is 14.

sizeof works at compile time (except for variable-length arrays), so sizeof(i++) does not increment i. The comma operator yields its right operand: b = (a++, a + 5) with a = 1 gives a = 2, b = 7.

5. Storage classes

ClassStorageDefault valueScopeLifetime / linkage
auto (default for locals)StackIndeterminate (garbage)BlockUntil the block ends
registerCPU register if possibleGarbageBlockUntil the block ends; & is not allowed
static (local)Data segmentZeroBlockWhole program; initialised once
static (global)Data segmentZeroFileWhole program; internal linkage (hidden from other files)
extern / globalData segmentZeroFile (and other files via extern)Whole program; external linkage

A static local is initialised once, so a counter returns 1, 2, 3 on successive calls, while an auto local restarts each time. An extern declaration inside a block refers to the global object, even when a local of the same name hides it.

6. Control flow

  • An else belongs to the nearest unmatched if, whatever the indentation (the dangling-else rule).
  • switch jumps to the matching case and falls through into the following cases until a break. default can appear anywhere; control jumps to it only if no case matches, although a case above it without a break can still fall through into it.
  • for (i = 0; i < 5; i++); has an empty body because of the semicolon. The loop just leaves i = 5.
  • do … while runs its body at least once. continue in a for loop jumps to the increment; in a while loop it jumps to the test. break leaves only the innermost loop or switch.
  • if (x = 0) assigns 0 and tests 0, so the else branch runs. This is legal C, and gcc only warns.

7. Functions and recursion

C passes every argument by value; to change a caller’s variable you pass its address, so swap(int *a, int *b) works and swap(int a, int b) does not. Each recursive call gets its own activation record. Code before the recursive call runs on the way down; code after it runs on the way back, in reverse order. Naive fib(n) (fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1) makes 2·fib(n + 1) − 1 calls: 41 calls for fib(7) = 13. A function pointer such as int (*f)(int, int) = add; is called as f(3, 4).

8. Pointers and pointer arithmetic

A pointer holds an address. &x gives the address of x, and *p gives the object p points to. For T *p, p + n points n elements further, that is, n × sizeof(T) bytes. If an int is 4 bytes and p holds 2000, then p + 3 holds 2012. Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of elements between them (type ptrdiff_t, printed with %td). Pointer arithmetic outside an array (other than one past the end) is undefined.

DeclarationMeaningAllowedNot allowed
const int *p (= int const *p)Pointer to a constant intp = &y*p = 5
int *const pConstant pointer to an int*p = 5p = &y
const int *const pBoth constantreading onlyboth
int **ppPointer to a pointer to int**pp = 5–
int (*p)[4]Pointer to an array of 4 intsp++ moves 4 ints–
int *p[4]Array of 4 pointers to int––
int (*f)(int)Pointer to a function taking and returning intf(3)–

Read declarations with the right-left rule: start at the name, go right while you can (arrays, functions), then left (pointers), and let brackets change the order. Increment forms: *p++ uses *p and then moves p; *++p moves p first; ++*p increments the pointed-to value; (*p)++ also increments the value, but yields the old value.

Never dereference a NULL pointer, a wild (uninitialised) pointer or a dangling pointer (to freed memory or to a dead local). void * holds any object address but cannot be dereferenced or used in arithmetic in standard C.

9. Arrays and strings

An array is a contiguous block of elements, indexed from 0. a[i] is defined as *(a + i), so i[a] is also legal. In an expression an array decays to a pointer to its first element, except in sizeof and &. So sizeof(a) is the whole array, but inside a function, an “array parameter” is really a pointer, and sizeof gives the pointer size (8 on x86-64). Partially initialised arrays are zero-filled: int a[5] = {1, 2}; gives {1, 2, 0, 0, 0}. An array name is not a modifiable lvalue, so a++ is a compile error.

A 2D array int m[R][C] is stored in row-major order: m[i][j] is at base + (i × C + j) × size (column-major, as in FORTRAN: base + (j × R + i) × size). *(*(m + i) + j) is m[i][j], and sizeof(m[0]) is one row.

A C string is a char array ended by '\0'. char s[] = "exam"; makes a modifiable 5-byte array, so sizeof(s) = 5 and strlen(s) = 4. const char *p = "exam"; is a pointer to a read-only literal, and sizeof(p) is the pointer size. The key string.h functions: strlen (length without '\0'), strcpy(dest, src), strcat(dest, src) (the destination must be large enough), strcmp (returns a value < 0, 0 or > 0; only the sign is defined), strchr and strstr. Adding to a char pointer skips characters: if p points to "program", p + 3 is "gram".

10. Structures, unions and typedef

A structure groups members of different types, each at its own offset. The compiler adds padding so that each member starts at a multiple of its alignment, and pads the end so that the size is a multiple of the largest alignment. On x86-64, struct {char c; int i; char d;} is 12 bytes, but {char c; char d; int i;} is 8. A union overlays all members at offset 0; its size is the largest member rounded up to the alignment, and only the member stored last is meaningful. p->x means (*p).x. A self-referential structure (one holding a pointer to its own type) builds linked lists. typedef only gives a new name to an existing type.

11. The preprocessor

The preprocessor runs before compilation and works on text. #include inserts a file. #define defines object-like macros (#define N 10) and function-like macros. Macro arguments are substituted textually, so always bracket each parameter and the whole body: with #define SQ(x) x * x, SQ(a + 2) is a + 2 * a + 2. An argument with a side effect may be evaluated twice: with MAX(i++, j) and i = 4, j = 3, i is incremented twice (once in the test and once in the chosen branch), so m = 5 and i = 6. The # operator turns an argument into a string literal (STR(3 + 4) gives "3 + 4"), and ## pastes two tokens into one (JOIN(x, y) gives xy). Conditional compilation uses #if, #ifdef, #ifndef, #else, #elif and #endif (used for include guards). Predefined macros include __FILE__, __LINE__, __DATE__ and __STDC__.

12. Dynamic memory, files and command-line arguments

  • malloc(n) returns n uninitialised bytes, or NULL on failure. calloc(k, size) returns k × size bytes set to zero. realloc(p, n) resizes the block (it may move it, and it keeps the old contents up to the smaller size). free(p) releases it. Forgetting free causes a leak; using p after free is a dangling pointer; freeing twice is undefined.
  • Files: fopen(name, mode) with "r" (must exist), "w" (create or truncate), "a" (append), "r+" (read/write, must exist), "w+", "a+", plus "b" for binary. Then fprintf/fscanf, fgetc/fputc, fgets/fputs, fread/fwrite, fseek/ftell, fclose. fscanf returns the number of items converted, or EOF.
  • int main(int argc, char *argv[]): argc counts the arguments including the program name, argv[0] is the program name, and argv[argc] is NULL. For ./prog red green, argc = 3 and argv[2] is "green".

Worked examples

Example 1: promotions and narrowing

#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) {
    unsigned char a = 200, b = 100;
    int s = a + b;
    unsigned char c = a + b;
    printf("%d %d", s, c);
    return 0;
}

Output: 300 44. Both operands are promoted to int, so a + b = 300 exactly. Storing 300 in an unsigned char reduces it modulo 256: 300 − 256 = 44. When c is passed to printf it is promoted to int again, so %d is correct.

Example 2: a pointer trace

#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) {
    int a[] = {5, 10, 15, 20};
    int *p = a;
    int x = *p++;
    int y = *++p;
    int z = ++*p;
    printf("%d %d %d %d", x, y, z, a[2]);
    return 0;
}

Output: 5 15 16 16. Trace: x = *p++ reads a[0] = 5 and then moves p to a[1]. y = *++p first moves p to a[2] and reads 15. z = ++*p increments the value at a[2] to 16 and yields 16. So a[2] is now 16. Each statement changes p or *p only once, so there is no undefined behaviour.

Example 3: pointer to an array versus pointer to an element

#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) {
    int a[3][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}, {7, 8, 9}};
    int (*r)[3] = a;
    int *e = &a[0][0];
    r++;
    e += 4;
    printf("%d %d %d", (*r)[0], *e, r[1][2]);
    return 0;
}

Output: 4 5 9. r points to a whole row, so r++ moves one row (3 ints) to row 1, whose first element is 4. e points to one int, so e += 4 moves 4 ints in row-major order, to a[1][1] = 5. r[1][2] is two rows after row 0, that is a[2][2] = 9.

Example 4: a macro with a side effect

#include <stdio.h>
#define MAX(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))
int main(void) {
    int i = 4, j = 3;
    int m = MAX(i++, j);
    printf("%d %d", m, i);
    return 0;
}

Output: 5 6. The line expands to ((i++) > (j) ? (i++) : (j)). The test compares 4 > 3 and makes i = 5. The ?: has a sequence point after the test, so the chosen branch i++ then yields 5 and makes i = 6. A function max(i++, j) would give 4 and 5, because a function evaluates each argument once.

Example 5: arrays decay in function parameters

#include <stdio.h>
int f(int *p, int n) {
    int i, s = 0;
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) s += p[i];
    p[0] = s;
    return (int)sizeof(p);
}
int main(void) {
    int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4};
    int k = f(a, 4);
    printf("%d %d %zu", a[0], k, sizeof(a));
    return 0;
}

Output: 10 8 16. The function receives only the address of a[0], so writing p[0] changes the caller’s array (a[0] = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10). Inside f, sizeof(p) is the size of a pointer (8 on x86-64), while in main sizeof(a) is 4 × 4 = 16 bytes. That is why C functions need the length as a separate parameter.

Example 6: writing and reading a file

#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) {
    FILE *fp = fopen("t.txt", "w");
    int a, b, n;
    if (fp == NULL) return 1;
    fprintf(fp, "%d %d\n", 12, 30);
    fclose(fp);
    fp = fopen("t.txt", "r");
    if (fp == NULL) return 1;
    n = fscanf(fp, "%d %d", &a, &b);
    fclose(fp);
    printf("%d %d", n, a + b);
    return 0;
}

Output: 2 42. Mode "w" creates (or empties) the file. fscanf returns the number of items it converted, 2, and a + b = 42. Always check fopen’s result against NULL, and close each file.

13. Elementary data types: specification, implementation, scalar and composite

The syllabus takes this topic from Pratt and Zelkowitz. A data object is a run-time container (a block of storage) for data values. Its attributes are its type, name, location (l-value), value and lifetime, and each of these is bound at some binding time. A data type is a class of data objects together with the operations on them. The book separates what a type is (its specification) from how it is built (its implementation).

  • Specification has three parts: the attributes that distinguish objects of the type (for an array: the number of dimensions, the subscript ranges and the component type); the values the objects may take; and the operations. Each operation is described by its signature, for example integer addition: integer × integer → integer, square root: real → real and less-than: integer × integer → Boolean. An operation can be undefined for some arguments (division by zero), have implicit arguments or side effects, and even change itself (a random-number generator keeps a hidden seed).
  • Implementation has two parts: the storage representation (often the hardware’s own format, sometimes simulated in software) and the way each operation is carried out (a hardware instruction, a subprogram, or inline code). Attributes are either kept only by the compiler, as in C, where the type is not stored with the object, or kept at run time in a descriptor. An array descriptor (a dope vector) holds the bounds, so subscripts can be checked at run time.
CategoryTypesNotes
Scalar (one value, no components)Numeric: integers, subranges, floating-point real, fixed-point real, complex, rationalA subrange such as 1..10 allows range checks and compact storage; fixed-point keeps a fixed number of decimal places (money in COBOL and Ada)
ScalarEnumerations, Booleans, charactersAn enumeration is an ordered list of distinct named values (C enum); a Boolean needs only 1 bit but usually takes a byte or a word; characters follow a character set (ASCII, Unicode)
Composite (structured storage, but treated like elementary data)Character stringsThree designs: fixed declared length (padded); variable length up to a declared bound; unbounded length (heap storage, as in Java). C uses char arrays ended by '\0'
CompositePointers and programmer-constructed objectsA pointer may be restricted to one type (C, Pascal) or point to any type; the risks are dangling references and garbage
CompositeFilesSequential, text, direct-access, indexed-sequential; a file outlives the program that creates it

Structured types built from these (arrays, records, unions, sets, lists) come next; for C they are covered in sections 9 and 10.

Example 7: storage for a subrange. A subrange with k values needs ⌈log₂ k⌉ bits. The subrange 1..10 has 10 values, so it needs ⌈log₂ 10⌉ = 4 bits. The subrange −5..10 has 10 − (−5) + 1 = 16 values, so it also needs 4 bits (stored as an offset from −5). The subrange 0..16 has 17 values and needs 5 bits. A general integer needs a full word, which is why subranges save space and let the compiler insert range checks.

14. File handling and command-line arguments in depth

A C program works with a file through a FILE * stream returned by fopen. Three streams are already open when main starts: stdin, stdout and stderr. Output is buffered; fflush(fp) or fclose(fp) writes the buffer out. A text stream may translate line endings (on Windows, "\n" becomes "\r\n"); a binary stream ("rb", "wb") copies bytes exactly.

ModeIf the file existsIf it does not existAccess
"r"open at the startfopen returns NULLread
"w"truncate to length 0createwrite
"a"keep contents; every write goes to the endcreatewrite
"r+"open at the startNULLread and write
"w+"truncatecreateread and write
"a+"keep; reads anywhere, writes at the endcreateread and write
  • Character I/O: fgetc/getc return the next character as an int, or EOF (−1); fputc writes one. Line I/O: fgets(buf, n, fp) reads at most n − 1 characters, stops after a newline (and keeps it), and adds '\0'. Formatted I/O: fprintf, fscanf (returns the number of items converted, or EOF). Block I/O: fread(ptr, size, count, fp) and fwrite return the number of whole items transferred.
  • Random access: fseek(fp, offset, whence) with whence = SEEK_SET (from the start), SEEK_CUR (from the current position) or SEEK_END (from the end); ftell(fp) gives the current offset; rewind(fp) is fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_SET) that also clears the error indicator. On a stream opened for update ("r+", "w+", "a+"), you must call fseek, fsetpos, rewind or fflush between a write and a following read.
  • End of file: feof(fp) becomes true only after a read has tried to go past the end. So the loop while (!feof(fp)) { ch = fgetc(fp); … } runs one extra time and processes EOF as if it were data. The correct idiom is while ((ch = fgetc(fp)) != EOF), with ch declared as int, not char.
  • remove(name) deletes a file and rename(old, new) renames it; both return 0 on success.

Command-line arguments. With int main(int argc, char *argv[]), the shell splits the command line into words; a quoted string is one word. argc counts the words including the program name, argv[0] is the program name, argv[1] … argv[argc − 1] are the arguments, and argv[argc] is a null pointer. Every argument is a string, so numbers must be converted with atoi, atof or, with error checking, strtol. char **argv is the same parameter type as char *argv[]. The idiom while (--argc > 0) printf("%s ", *++argv); prints the arguments without the program name.

Example 8: random access in a file. A file opened with "w+" receives the 7 characters NETEXAM (offsets 0 to 6). Then:

fseek(fp, 3, SEEK_SET);   c = fgetc(fp);    /* offset 3: 'E', position becomes 4 */
fseek(fp, -2, SEEK_END);  d = fgetc(fp);    /* 7 − 2 = offset 5: 'A', position 6  */
pos = ftell(fp);                            /* 6 */
fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_END);   size = ftell(fp); /* 7, the file size in bytes         */

So c = 'E', d = 'A', pos = 6 and size = 7. For ./prog red green, argc = 3, argv[1] = "red", argv[argc − 1] = "green", and *argv[argc − 1] is the character 'g'.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemRule
Integer division / remainderTruncate toward zero; the sign of % follows the dividend; (a/b)*b + a%b == a
Signed vs unsignedSame rank: the signed operand is converted to unsigned (−1 becomes UINT_MAX)
Promotionchar and short become int before arithmetic
Unsigned wrapModulo 2^n; signed overflow is undefined
Pointer + naddress + n × sizeof(*p)
Pointer − pointerNumber of elements (ptrdiff_t, %td)
Row-major a[R][C]base + (i × C + j) × size
Column-majorbase + (j × R + i) × size
String sizessizeof("abc") = 4, strlen("abc") = 3
Struct sizeMembers aligned, total rounded up to the largest alignment
Union sizeLargest member, rounded up to the alignment
enumStarts at 0, each next = previous + 1 unless assigned
Octal / hex010 = 8, 0x1F = 31
'a' − 'A'32 in ASCII; 'A' = 65, 'a' = 97, '0' = 48
Bitwise~x = −x − 1; x << k = x × 2^k for small non-negative x
Sequence points; && || ?: , and before a function call
printfReturns the number of characters printed
argcCounts the program name too
Type specificationAttributes, values, operations (signature op: type × type → type)
Subrange storagek values need ⌈log₂ k⌉ bits (1..10 → 4 bits; −5..10 → 16 values → 4 bits)
fseek originsSEEK_SET (start), SEEK_CUR (current), SEEK_END (end); ftell = current offset; rewind = fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_SET) + clear error
End of filefeof is true only after a read fails; loop on (ch = fgetc(fp)) != EOF with int ch
argvargv[0] program name, argv[argc] NULL; a quoted string is one argument; convert numbers with atoi/strtol

NTA traps

  • Integer division. Wrong: 7 / 2 = 3.5. Fix: both operands are int, so the result is 3; float f = 7 / 2 stores 3.0.
  • Mixed signed/unsigned comparisons. Wrong: −1 < 1u is true. Fix: −1 becomes a large unsigned value, so it is false. The same happens with sizeof, which is unsigned.
  • Unbracketed macros. Wrong: SQ(a + 2) = 25. Fix: substitute the text first, then apply precedence.
  • Missing break. Wrong: only the matching case runs. Fix: execution falls through until a break or the end of the switch.
  • Stray semicolon. for (…); and if (…); have empty bodies; the next statement runs once.
  • sizeof of an array parameter. It is the pointer size, not the array size.
  • Precedence of == and &. x == 3 & 2 is (x == 3) & 2.
  • Treating undefined behaviour as an output question. If the code modifies a variable twice without a sequence point (i = i++, a[i] = i++), the only correct answer is “undefined behaviour”, whatever one compiler printed.
  • char s[] versus char *s. The first is a modifiable array (sizeof = length + 1), the second a pointer to a read-only literal (sizeof = pointer size).

How NTA asks this

  • Output (code) questions: 5–15 lines of C. Trace with a box per variable and an arrow per pointer, after checking for the traps above. When the options include “compile error” or “undefined”, first ask whether the code is legal at all.
  • Match the lists: storage classes with properties, format specifiers with types (%d, %u, %ld, %zu, %c, %s, %x, %o, %e), file modes with meanings, declarations with meanings (int *p[4] versus int (*p)[4]).
  • Assertion–Reason: for example, A: “sizeof(arr) inside a function whose parameter is int arr[] gives the pointer size.” R: “An array parameter is adjusted to a pointer to its element type.” Both are true and R explains A (option 1).
  • Statement and multi-select: which expressions are undefined, which identifiers are valid, which statements about static/extern are true. A single word such as “always”, “global” or “zero” decides these.
  • Numericals: array addresses, pointer + n, struct sizes, recursive call counts.
Watch out: an output that one compiler happens to print is not the answer when the code has undefined behaviour. NTA’s key follows the C standard.

terms.definition: A run-time container for data values, such as a variable or constant; it has a type, a location (l-value) and a value (r-value).
Checking that each operation receives operands of the right type. Static checking is done at compile time and dynamic checking at run time. A strongly typed language detects all type errors.
An implicit type conversion inserted by the compiler, for example int to double in 2 + 3.5.
In C, char, short and bit-fields are converted to int (or unsigned int) before arithmetic.
Rules that bring both operands of a binary operator to a common type; if one is unsigned int and the other int, the int is converted to unsigned.
A point where all side effects of earlier evaluations are complete (for example at ;, &&, ||, ?: and the comma operator). Modifying a variable twice between sequence points is undefined behaviour.
auto, register, static or extern: it fixes a variable’s lifetime, default initial value, scope and linkage.
Adding n to a T* pointer moves it by n × sizeof(T) bytes; subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of elements between them.
In most expressions an array name becomes a pointer to its first element; sizeof and & are the main exceptions.
Unused bytes the compiler inserts so that each member is aligned; sizeof(struct) can be larger than the sum of the member sizes.

lessons.examTip: In an output question, first look for the “trick line”: a mixed signed/unsigned comparison, a macro without brackets, a missing break, a stray semicolon after for, integer division, or sizeof on a pointer. Once you find it, three options usually fall away.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace). Predict each output on paper first.
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For 11 and 12, draw the memory layout byte by byte.
Type each program into a file and compile it with gcc -Wall -Wextra -fsanitize=address,undefined; compare the real output with your prediction.
Check every answer against solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (for example: stray semicolon, sign of %, or padding).
Change one line in three of the programs (remove a break, add brackets to a macro, swap two struct members) and predict the new output before you run it.
Redo the problems you got wrong after 24 hours, without looking at the solutions.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct on the first attempt.
Problems 1–8 finished within 12 minutes.
Struct sizes in problem 12 correct, with the padding bytes marked.
You can explain in one sentence why each expression in problem 14 is or is not undefined.

lessons.title: Object-oriented programming and C++
lessons.summaryHtml: Object-oriented programming (OOP) builds a program from objects: bundles of data and the functions that act on that data. This lesson covers the four principles (encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism) and how C++ supports them with classes, access specifiers, constructors and destructors, copy constructors, static and const members, and friends. You will then study inheritance and its access rules, multiple inheritance with the diamond problem and virtual base classes, and virtual functions with dynamic binding, abstract classes and virtual destructors. The last part covers overloading of functions and operators, templates, exceptions and the basics of the Standard Template Library. NTA asks many “what is the output” questions on construction order, virtual calls and overloading. Every program in this lesson was compiled with g++ using -Wall -Wextra and run under the address and undefined-behaviour sanitizers, so every output shown is real.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A procedural program is a list of functions that pass data around. An object-oriented program is a set of objects, and each object keeps its own data together with the functions allowed to change it. A bank account object, for example, holds a balance and offers deposit and withdraw; nobody outside can set the balance directly. A class is the blueprint and an object is one thing built from it. C++ adds classes to C, so you get all of C plus constructors, destructors, inheritance, virtual functions, overloading, templates and exceptions.

Four ideas carry the whole subject. Encapsulation keeps data private behind a public interface. Abstraction shows only what an object does, not how. Inheritance lets a new class reuse and extend an existing one. Polymorphism lets one call behave differently depending on the object that receives it.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 3 regularly carries several questions on OOP and C++. The theory questions ask about OOP terms, access rules under inheritance, what can and cannot be virtual or overloaded, and the kinds of polymorphism, often as Match the List or Assertion–Reason items. The output questions, like those on C, test the order of constructor and destructor calls, virtual versus non-virtual calls, copy construction versus assignment, overload resolution, default arguments, static members and exceptions. Templates and the STL appear less often and at a basic level. If you can trace construction order and dynamic binding without error, you will get most of these marks.

Concepts in depth

1. OOP principles and the C++ class

A class declares data members and member functions. Access specifiers control who may use each member: private members are usable only inside the class and by its friends, protected members also inside derived classes, and public members everywhere. The only difference between class and struct in C++ is the default: members and base classes are private by default in a class and public by default in a struct. Data hiding is enforced at compile time; access to a private member from outside is a compile error, not a run-time error.

Every non-static member function receives a hidden pointer this to the object it was called on. In a const member function (declared with const after the parameter list), this points to a const object, so the function cannot change ordinary data members. A member declared mutable is the exception: it may be changed even inside a const function, which is useful for counters and caches.

2. Constructors and destructors

A constructor has the class name and no return type, not even void. It runs automatically when an object is created and may be overloaded. A default constructor takes no arguments (or has defaults for all of them); the compiler supplies one only if you declare no constructor at all. A destructor, ~X(), takes no arguments, cannot be overloaded, and runs when the object’s lifetime ends: at the end of its block for a local, at the end of the program for a global or static, and at delete for a heap object.

The member-initialiser list (X() : a(1), b(2) {}) initialises members before the body runs. It is the only way to initialise const members, reference members and base classes that lack a default constructor. Members are always initialised in the order in which they are declared in the class, not the order written in the list; g++ warns with -Wreorder when the two differ.

The construction rule for an object of a derived class: (1) virtual base classes, (2) direct non-virtual base classes in the order of the base list, (3) data members in declaration order, (4) the constructor body. Destruction is always the exact reverse. Locals in one block are destroyed in reverse order of their creation; globals are created before main and destroyed after it ends.

3. Copy constructor, assignment and deep copy

The copy constructor X(const X&) makes a new object from an existing one. It is called for X b = a; and X b(a);, when an object is passed by value, and when one is returned by value (although the compiler may elide the copy in that last case). The copy assignment operator X& operator=(const X&) runs only when the left side already exists: b = a;. The parameter of a copy constructor must be a reference, because passing it by value would require a copy, which would call the copy constructor again without end.

If you do not write them, the compiler generates both, and they copy member by member. For a pointer member this is a shallow copy: both objects then point to the same heap block, a change through one shows in the other, and both destructors delete the same block (undefined behaviour). A class that owns a resource needs a deep copy: allocate new memory and copy the contents. This leads to the rule of three: if a class needs a user-defined destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, it almost always needs all three (C++11 adds the move constructor and move assignment, giving the rule of five).

4. Static members, const members and friends

A static data member has one copy shared by all objects; it exists even when no object exists. Before C++17 a non-const static data member declared in the class must also be defined once outside it (int C::n = 0;). A static member function has no this pointer, so it can use only static members directly, and it is called as C::f(). It cannot be virtual or const. A static counter incremented in constructors and decremented in the destructor counts the live objects.

A friend function or friend class is granted access to the private and protected members. A friend function is not a member: it has no this pointer and is called like an ordinary function. Friendship is granted by the class, never taken; it is not inherited, not transitive (a friend of a friend is not a friend) and not mutual. Friends are the usual way to write operator<< for output, because its left operand is an ostream, not the class.

5. Inheritance and access

Inheritance models an is-a relationship. The kinds are single (one base), multiple (several bases), multilevel (a chain A → B → C), hierarchical (several classes derived from one base) and hybrid (a mixture, typically giving a diamond). The mode of derivation limits the access of inherited members: under public inheritance, public stays public and protected stays protected; under protected inheritance, both become protected; under private inheritance, both become private. Private members of the base are inherited (they take space in the object) but are never accessible by name in the derived class, whatever the mode. The default mode is private for a class and public for a struct.

Base memberpublic inheritanceprotected inheritanceprivate inheritance
publicpublicprotectedprivate
protectedprotectedprotectedprivate
privatenot accessiblenot accessiblenot accessible

Constructors, the destructor, the copy assignment operator and friendships are not inherited in the ordinary sense; the derived class gets its own. A derived class constructor calls a base constructor through its initialiser list, for example D(int x) : B(x) {}.

6. Multiple inheritance, ambiguity and virtual base classes

If B and C both derive from A and D derives from both B and C, a D object contains two separate A subobjects. Using an A member through a D is then ambiguous and a compile error; you must write d.B::x or d.C::x. Declaring the inheritance as class B : virtual public A and class C : virtual public A makes A a virtual base class: D contains only one shared A, the ambiguity disappears, and A’s constructor runs once, called by the most-derived class. Ambiguity also arises when two unrelated bases have members with the same name; the scope resolution operator :: settles it.

7. Polymorphism: overloading, overriding and dynamic binding

Compile-time (static) polymorphism is function overloading, operator overloading and templates. Overloaded functions share a name but differ in the number or types of parameters; the return type alone cannot distinguish them. The compiler picks the best match in stages: exact match, then promotion (char, short and bool to int, float to double), then standard conversion (int to double, long to int, and so on), then user-defined conversion. If two candidates tie at the best stage, the call is ambiguous and does not compile; f(10L) with f(int) and f(double) is the classic example, because both need a standard conversion.

Run-time (dynamic) polymorphism needs three things: a virtual function, a derived class that overrides it with the same signature, and a call through a base pointer or reference. The call then goes to the version for the object’s dynamic type. Compilers normally implement this with a vtable (one table of function pointers per class) and a hidden vptr in each object. A function declared virtual stays virtual in all derived classes; the keyword override (C++11) asks the compiler to check that it really overrides.

Three details trap students. A non-virtual function with the same name in the derived class hides the base version; it does not override it, so a call through a base pointer still goes to the base. A derived function with the same name but different parameters hides all base overloads of that name. Default arguments are taken from the static type, even when the body comes from the dynamic type. Finally, a virtual call made inside a constructor or destructor goes to the class being constructed, not to the derived class, because the derived part does not exist yet (or no longer exists).

8. Abstract classes and virtual destructors

A pure virtual function is declared with = 0. A class with at least one is an abstract class: you cannot create objects of it (a compile error), but you can use pointers and references to it, and it can have constructors, data members and ordinary functions. A derived class that does not override every pure virtual function is also abstract. An abstract class with only pure virtual functions plays the role of an interface. When objects are deleted through a base pointer, the base must have a virtual destructor; otherwise the behaviour is undefined, and in practice usually only the base destructor runs.

9. Operator overloading

An operator is overloaded by writing a function named operator@, as a member (the left operand is this) or as a non-member, often a friend. At least one operand must be of a class or enumeration type, the precedence, associativity and number of operands cannot change, and new operators cannot be invented. The operators ::, ., .*, ?:, sizeof and typeid cannot be overloaded. The operators =, (), [] and -> must be members. Prefix ++x is written operator++(); postfix x++ is operator++(int), where the int is a dummy parameter used only to tell them apart. A constructor with one argument also acts as a conversion from that argument type unless it is marked explicit.

10. Templates

A function template template <typename T> T big(T a, T b) is a pattern. At each call the compiler deduces T from the arguments (or takes it from explicit arguments such as big<int>(3, 'A')) and generates an instantiation at compile time. Deduction needs a consistent T, so big(3, 2.5) does not compile without an explicit argument. A class template such as Stack<T, N> can take type and non-type parameters; each distinct set of arguments is a separate class with its own static members. An explicit specialisation (template <>) provides a different body for one particular type. Templates are the basis of the STL.

11. Exceptions

throw raises an exception object; try marks the monitored block; catch handlers are tried in order and the first whose type matches runs. A handler for a base class also catches derived-class exceptions, so derived handlers must come first. catch (...) catches anything and must be last. No conversions such as int to double are applied when matching, apart from derived-to-base and pointer conversions. While control leaves functions on the way to the handler, all fully built local objects are destroyed in reverse order: stack unwinding. A bare throw; inside a handler rethrows the current exception. If no handler is found, std::terminate is called. A function marked noexcept promises not to throw; if it does, terminate is called. Standard exceptions derive from std::exception, whose what() returns a message.

12. STL basics

The Standard Template Library has containers, iterators and algorithms. Sequence containers are vector (dynamic array, random access, amortised O(1) push_back), deque and list (doubly linked list, no [] operator). Associative containers are set and map (sorted, unique keys, usually a red–black tree, O(log n)) and their multi versions, which allow duplicates. The unordered containers use hash tables with average O(1) look-up. stack, queue and priority_queue are container adaptors built on other containers. Iterators connect containers to algorithms such as sort, find and reverse. In a map, m[key] inserts a value-initialised element (0 for int) if the key is missing.

Worked examples

Example 1: construction and destruction with members

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
struct Part {
    char c;
    Part(char x) : c(x) { cout << "P" << c << " "; }
    ~Part() { cout << "~P" << c << " "; }
};
struct Base {
    Base() { cout << "B "; }
    ~Base() { cout << "~B "; }
};
struct Car : Base {
    Part e, w;
    Car() : e('e'), w('w') { cout << "Car "; }
    ~Car() { cout << "~Car "; }
};
int main() {
    Car c;
    cout << "| ";
    return 0;
}

Output: B Pe Pw Car | ~Car ~Pw ~Pe ~B. The base comes first (B). Then the members in declaration order: e before w. Then the body of Car. The | is printed at the end of main, and then c goes out of scope. The destructor body runs first (~Car), then the members in reverse order (~Pw, ~Pe), then the base (~B). If the initialiser list were written as w('w'), e('e'), the order would still be e then w, and g++ would give a -Wreorder warning.

Example 2: which function does a call reach?

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;
struct Animal {
    void intro() const { cout << name() << ":" << sound() << " "; }
    string name() const { return "animal"; }
    virtual string sound() const { return "..."; }
    virtual ~Animal() {}
};
struct Dog : Animal {
    string name() const { return "dog"; }
    string sound() const override { return "woof"; }
};
struct Puppy : Dog {
    string sound() const override { return "yip"; }
};
int main() {
    Animal a;
    Dog d;
    Puppy p;
    Animal *arr[3] = {&a, &d, &p};
    for (Animal *q : arr) q->intro();
    Dog &r = p;
    cout << r.name() << " " << r.sound();
    return 0;
}

Output: animal:... animal:woof animal:yip dog yip. intro is not virtual, and inside it the call name() is bound at compile time to Animal::name, so every line starts with animal. sound() is virtual, so inside intro it follows the dynamic type of the object: ..., woof and yip. Through the reference Dog &r = p, r.name() is bound statically to Dog::name (dog), while r.sound() goes to Puppy::sound (yip). Make a two-column table, static type and dynamic type, for every call.

Example 3: deep copy and the rule of three

#include <iostream>
#include <cstring>
using namespace std;
class Text {
    char *p;
public:
    Text(const char *s) {
        p = new char[strlen(s) + 1];
        strcpy(p, s);
        cout << "N ";
    }
    Text(const Text &o) {
        p = new char[strlen(o.p) + 1];
        strcpy(p, o.p);
        cout << "C ";
    }
    Text &operator=(const Text &o) {
        cout << "A ";
        if (this != &o) {
            char *q = new char[strlen(o.p) + 1];
            strcpy(q, o.p);
            delete[] p;
            p = q;
        }
        return *this;
    }
    ~Text() { delete[] p; }
    void up() { p[0] = p[0] - 32; }
    const char *str() const { return p; }
};
int main() {
    Text a("ugc");
    Text b = a;
    Text c("net");
    c = a;
    b.up();
    cout << a.str() << " " << b.str() << " " << c.str();
    return 0;
}

Output: N C N A ugc Ugc ugc. Text a("ugc") prints N. Text b = a creates b, so the copy constructor prints C. Text c("net") prints N. c = a assigns to an existing object: A. Because both copy operations allocate fresh memory, b.up() changes only b. With the compiler-generated shallow copy, a, b and c would share one array, a would also print Ugc, and the destructors would delete the same memory twice. The self-assignment check and the “copy first, then delete” order make the assignment safe.

Example 4: the diamond, with and without virtual bases

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
struct A { static int made; int v = 0; A() { made++; } };
int A::made = 0;
struct B1 : A {};
struct C1 : A {};
struct D1 : B1, C1 {};
struct B2 : virtual A {};
struct C2 : virtual A {};
struct D2 : B2, C2 {};
int main() {
    D1 x;
    int n1 = A::made;
    A::made = 0;
    D2 y;
    int n2 = A::made;
    x.B1::v = 1;
    x.C1::v = 2;
    y.v = 7;
    cout << n1 << " " << n2 << " ";
    cout << x.B1::v << x.C1::v << " " << y.B2::v << y.C2::v;
    return 0;
}

Output: 2 1 12 77. D1 inherits A through B1 and through C1 without virtual, so a D1 object holds two A subobjects and A’s constructor runs twice. x.B1::v and x.C1::v are different variables (1 and 2); writing x.v would not compile because it is ambiguous. D2 uses virtual bases, so only one A exists, A’s constructor runs once, and y.B2::v and y.C2::v are the same variable (7 and 7).

Example 5: a class template that throws

#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
using namespace std;
template <typename T, int N> class Stack {
    T a[N];
    int top = 0;
public:
    void push(T x) {
        if (top == N) throw overflow_error("full");
        a[top++] = x;
    }
    T pop() {
        if (top == 0) throw underflow_error("empty");
        return a[--top];
    }
};
int main() {
    Stack<int, 2> s;
    try {
        s.push(1);
        s.push(2);
        s.push(3);
        cout << "no ";
    } catch (const overflow_error &e) {
        cout << e.what() << " ";
    }
    int x = s.pop();
    int y = s.pop();
    cout << x * 10 + y << " ";
    try {
        s.pop();
    } catch (const exception &e) {
        cout << e.what();
    }
    return 0;
}

Output: full 21 empty. Stack<int, 2> holds two values; the third push throws overflow_error, so “no” is never printed and the handler prints full. The two pushes stay in the stack, and popping gives 2 then 1, so x × 10 + y = 21. The last pop throws underflow_error, which is caught by the base-class handler const exception & and prints empty. Each different pair of template arguments would be a different class.

13. C++ essentials: tokens, types, references and parameter passing

C++ keeps C’s tokens (keywords, identifiers, literals, operators, punctuators) and C’s rules for identifiers: a letter or underscore first, then letters, digits and underscores, case-sensitive, and no keywords. It adds keywords such as class, new, delete, this, bool, true, false, namespace, template, virtual, try, catch and throw. A name valid in C, such as new or class, can therefore be illegal in C++.

  • Data types. The built-in types of C, plus bool (true/false), wchar_t, reference types and user-defined classes. A character literal such as 'A' has type char in C++ (int in C), so sizeof('A') is 1 in C++ and usually 4 in C.
  • Variables and constants. Declarations can appear anywhere in a block. A const object must be initialised and cannot be changed; in C++ a const int initialised with a constant can size an array. constexpr (C++11) demands a compile-time value.
  • Operators added to C’s set: the scope resolution operator :: (reach a global hidden by a local, ::x, or a class member, A::f), new and delete for the heap (new int[5] must be freed with delete[]), the member-pointer operators .* and ->*, and the stream operators << and >> (the shift operators, overloaded).
  • Control statements are those of C, plus the range-based for (int v : arr) of C++11.

Functions and parameter passing. In C++ a function must be declared before it is called. Functions can have default arguments, which must be the trailing ones: void f(int a, int b = 2, int c = 3); is legal and allows f(1), f(1, 5) and f(1, 5, 7), but void g(int a = 1, int b); is an error. An inline function is a request to expand the body at the call site; the compiler may ignore it. Parameters can be passed three ways:

MethodDeclarationCan the callee change the caller’s variable?Call looks like
By valuevoid f(int x)No; x is a copyf(n)
By pointer (address)void f(int *p)Yes, through *pf(&n)
By referencevoid f(int &r)Yes; r is another name for nf(n)

A reference must be initialised when it is declared and can never be re-seated to another object. A non-const reference cannot bind to a literal or a temporary, so with void f(int &r) the call f(5) does not compile, while void g(const int &r) accepts g(5). Passing large objects by const reference avoids the copy that pass by value makes. A function can also return a reference, so a call can appear on the left of an assignment (max(a, b) = 0;), but it must never return a reference to one of its own local variables.

Example 6: three ways to pass the same variable.

void byValue(int x)  { x = x + 10; }
void byPtr(int *p)   { *p = *p + 10; }
void byRef(int &r)   { r = r + 10; }
/* in main: int n = 5; byValue(n); byPtr(&n); byRef(n); cout << n; */

byValue changes only its copy, so n stays 5; byPtr makes n 15; byRef makes n 25. The program prints 25. The call byRef(5) would not compile, because a non-const reference needs an lvalue.

14. Streams and files

C++ input and output use streams: a stream is a sequence of bytes flowing from a source to a destination. The classes form a hierarchy. ios_base and ios hold the state and format flags; istream (input, operator >>) and ostream (output, operator <<) derive from ios; iostream derives from both. For files, <fstream> gives ifstream (derived from istream), ofstream (from ostream) and fstream (from iostream). The predefined objects are cin (standard input), cout (standard output), cerr (standard error, unbuffered) and clog (standard error, buffered).

  • Formatted I/O: >> skips leading white space and stops at the next white space, so reading "Ada Lovelace" into a string gives only "Ada". Unformatted I/O: get(), put(), getline(cin, s) (reads a whole line and discards the newline), read() and write() for binary blocks.
  • Manipulators (<iomanip>): endl writes '\n' and flushes; setw(n) sets the field width for the next item only (right-justified by default); setfill(c) sets the padding character; setprecision(n) sets significant digits, or digits after the point when combined with fixed. setfill, setprecision and fixed stay in force until changed.
  • Opening files: ofstream out("a.txt"); or out.open("a.txt", mode);. The modes are flags of ios: in (read), out (write, truncates by default), app (every write at the end), ate (open and move to the end, but writes may go anywhere), trunc (discard contents) and binary. They are combined with |, for example ios::in | ios::out. The destructor closes the file automatically, so close() is optional.
  • Stream state: good(), eof(), fail() (a format error or failed open) and bad() (a serious error). A stream converts to false when it has failed, so while (in >> x) reads until end of file or bad input, and if (!in) tests a failed open.
  • Random access: seekg/tellg move and report the get (read) position; seekp/tellp do the same for the put (write) position. The origins are ios::beg, ios::cur and ios::end.

Example 7: formatting and file reading.

cout << setw(5) << 42 << '|';                 // "   42|"  (3 spaces: width 5)
cout << setfill('*') << setw(4) << 7 << '|';  // "***7|"
cout << fixed << setprecision(2) << 3.14159; // "3.14"
ifstream in("marks.txt");   // contains: 40 35 50
int x, sum = 0, n = 0;
while (in >> x) { sum += x; n++; }         // stops when extraction fails at end of file

The three output lines give 42|***7|3.14. The loop adds 40 + 35 + 50, so sum = 125 and n = 3; unlike the C feof loop, it does not run an extra time, because the failed extraction ends it.

15. Multifile programs and event handling

A real C++ program is split into several files. A header file (.h or .hpp) holds declarations: class definitions, function prototypes, extern declarations of global variables, inline functions and templates. A source file (.cpp) holds the definitions: function bodies, member function bodies and global variables. Each .cpp file, together with the headers it includes, is one translation unit and is compiled on its own into an object file; the linker then joins the object files and resolves the names used in one file but defined in another.

// counter.h
#ifndef COUNTER_H          // include guard (or: #pragma once)
#define COUNTER_H
extern int total;          // declaration: defined elsewhere
class Counter { public: void add(int k); int get() const; private: int n = 0; };
#endif
// counter.cpp             // definitions
#include "counter.h"
int total = 0;
void Counter::add(int k) { n += k; total += k; }
int Counter::get() const { return n; }
// build: g++ -c counter.cpp; g++ -c main.cpp; g++ counter.o main.o -o app
  • One definition rule (ODR): a variable or non-inline function may be declared many times but defined only once in the whole program. Defining int total = 0; in a header included by two .cpp files gives a linker error (multiple definition). Calling a function that is declared but never defined gives “undefined reference”, also at link time.
  • Include guards stop the same header from being processed twice in one translation unit (which would redefine the class). They do not help across translation units: that is the ODR’s job.
  • Linkage: a global name has external linkage (visible to other files through extern). static at file scope, or an unnamed namespace, gives internal linkage: the name is private to its file. Templates and inline functions are defined in headers, because the compiler needs their bodies wherever they are used.
  • Build tools such as make recompile only the files whose sources or headers have changed, which is the main practical benefit of separate compilation.

Event handling. In event-driven programs (GUIs, games, servers) the flow is decided by events such as a click, a key press or a timer tick. An event loop waits for events and dispatches each one to the handler registered for it. C++ has no event syntax of its own, so handlers are callbacks: function pointers, function objects (classes with operator()), lambdas, or std::function, which can hold any of these. The observer (publish–subscribe) pattern keeps a list of listeners and notifies each one when the event occurs; Qt’s signals and slots are a well-known version. Exception handling and event handling are different: an exception is raised by the program itself for an error and unwinds the stack to a matching catch, while an event comes from outside (user or system) and is handled by a registered handler, after which the program carries on normally. At the operating-system level, signal(SIGINT, handler) from <csignal> registers a handler for an asynchronous signal such as Ctrl+C.

Formula and fact sheet

NTA traps

  • Members before bases. Wrong: the member objects of D are built before D’s base class. Fix: bases always come first, then members, then the body.
  • Initialiser-list order. Wrong: members are initialised in the order written in the list. Fix: they follow the declaration order in the class.
  • X b = a is assignment. Wrong: it calls operator=. Fix: it creates b, so the copy constructor runs.
  • Hiding treated as overriding. Wrong: a non-virtual derived function with the same name is called through a base pointer. Fix: without virtual, the static type decides.
  • Hiding treated as overloading. Wrong: d.f(2) picks B::f(int) when D declares f(double). Fix: D’s f hides every B::f; only D::f(double) is considered.
  • Default arguments with virtual functions. Wrong: the default comes from the overriding function. Fix: the body is dynamic, the default is static.
  • Virtual calls in constructors. Wrong: the derived override runs while the base constructor executes. Fix: the base version runs.
  • Abstract class cannot have a constructor. Wrong. Fix: it can, and derived constructors call it; only objects of the abstract class itself are forbidden.
  • Friendship is inherited. Wrong. Fix: it is not inherited and not transitive.
  • A base-class catch placed first. The derived handler after it is never reached; g++ warns, and the base handler runs.

How NTA asks this

  • Output (code) questions: 10–20 lines with a small class hierarchy. Mark each class’s constructor and destructor message, write the construction order (bases, members, body) and reverse it for destruction. For every call, write the static and the dynamic type.
  • Match the lists: OOP concept with C++ feature, base member with its access after derivation, container with its data structure, special member function with when it is called.
  • Assertion–Reason: for example, A: “A constructor cannot be virtual.” R: “A constructor has no return type.” Both are true, but R is not the reason (the reason is that no complete object exists to dispatch on), so the answer is option 2.
  • Statement and multi-select: which functions cannot be virtual, which operators cannot be overloaded, which statements about static members or templates are true. Words such as “always”, “inherited” and “run time” usually decide them.
  • Elimination: in an order question, the option that does not start with the (virtual) base is out; in a destructor question, the option that is not the mirror image of construction is out.
Remember: a call is dynamic only when the function is virtual, it is called through a pointer or reference, the call is not qualified with a class name (p->B::f() is always static), and it is not made from a constructor or destructor. Everything else is decided by the compiler from the static type.

terms.definition: A class is a user-defined type that bundles data members and member functions; an object is an instance of a class with its own copy of the non-static data members.
Keeping data and the code that works on it together, and hiding the data behind private or protected access so that other code uses only the public interface.
A member function with the class’s name and no return type that runs automatically when an object is created; it may be overloaded but cannot be virtual.
A constructor of the form X(const X&) that creates a new object as a copy of an existing one; it is called for copy-initialisation, pass by value and return by value.
A data member shared by all objects of the class, or a member function without a this pointer that can use only static members directly.
A non-member function or another class that has been granted access to a class’s private and protected members; friendship is not inherited, not transitive and not mutual.
A member function declared virtual whose call through a base pointer or reference is resolved at run time according to the dynamic type of the object (dynamic binding).
A class with at least one pure virtual function (declared = 0); objects of it cannot be created, but pointers and references to it can.
A base class inherited with the keyword virtual, so that only one shared subobject exists in a diamond-shaped hierarchy.
A pattern for a function or class written in terms of type (or value) parameters; the compiler generates a separate instantiation for each set of arguments at compile time.

lessons.examTip: In a C++ output question, first identify the static type and the dynamic type of every pointer or reference. A virtual function follows the dynamic type; a non-virtual function, a default argument and a hidden name follow the static type. Then apply the construction rule: bases first, then members in declaration order, then the body; destruction runs in exactly the reverse order.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace). Predict each output on paper first.
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For problems 5, 6 and 12, draw the object layout (base subobjects and members) before you trace.
Type each program into a file, compile it with g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra and run it; compare the real output with your prediction.

Check every answer against solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (for example: members before bases, hiding taken for overriding, or X b = a taken for assignment).
Change one line in three programs (remove virtual, make a copy constructor take its argument by value, or swap two catch handlers) and predict what g++ will do before you compile.
Redo the problems you got wrong after 24 hours, without looking at the solutions.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct on the first attempt.
Problems 1–8 finished within 12 minutes.
Problem 12 answered with both the output and the reason for the ambiguity.
You can state from memory the construction order rule and the six operators that cannot be overloaded.

quiz.question: What is the output of this C++ program?
quiz.explanation: An object of a derived class is built in this order: base class subobjects first, then the data members in their declaration order, and last the body of the derived constructor. So B, then the member M, then D. Destruction is the exact reverse: the body of ~D runs first, then the members are destroyed (~M), then the base (~B). Output: B M D ~D ~M ~B. Option 2 puts the member before the base, which is the most common trap.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Encapsulation hides data behind an interface (IV). Run-time (dynamic) polymorphism is a virtual function called through a base pointer or reference (III). Compile-time (static) polymorphism is overloading, resolved by the compiler from the argument types (II). Generic programming, one piece of code for many types, is done with templates (I). Option 1 swaps the two kinds of polymorphism, which is the usual trap.

b: I. Templates
II. Function and operator overloading
III. Virtual functions called through a base pointer or reference
IV. Private data members reached only through public member functions

quiz.question: What is the output of this C++ program?
quiz.explanation: p and r have static type B but refer to a D object. f is virtual, so p->f() and r.f() use the dynamic type: Df. g is not virtual, so p->g() is bound at compile time from the static type: Bg. B b = d copies only the B part of d into a new B object (object slicing), so b.f() is Bf; a virtual call on an object (not through a pointer or reference) uses the object’s own type. Output: Df Bg Df Bf.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Both are true and R explains A. delete p calls the destructor chosen from the static type Base; without virtual, ~Derived is skipped (the standard calls this undefined behaviour), so resources owned by the Derived part leak. Declaring virtual ~Base() makes the call dynamic: ~Derived runs first and then ~Base. Rule: any class meant to be used polymorphically needs a virtual destructor.

stmts: Assertion (A): If Base has a non-virtual destructor, then Base *p = new Derived; delete p; has undefined behaviour, and in practice Derived’s destructor is usually not run.
Reason (R): A destructor call made through a base-class pointer is bound statically, to the static type of the pointer, unless the destructor is declared virtual.

quiz.question: What is the output of this C++ program?
quiz.explanation: f creates r(f), calls g, which creates r(g) and throws 42. The throw leaves g and then f; while leaving, the local objects are destroyed in reverse order of construction (stack unwinding): -g and then -f. Only then does the handler in main run: caught 42. The line printing never is skipped. Output: +f +g -g -f caught 42.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Statement I is true: the parameter is a new object initialised from the argument, so X(const X&) runs (the program for this lesson prints c for the call f(p)). Statement II is false: passing the argument by value would itself need a copy, which would call the copy constructor again without end. C++ therefore rejects X(X other) as a copy constructor; g++ gives a compile error. The parameter must be a reference, usually const X&.

stmts: Statement I: When an object is passed by value to a function, the copy constructor of its class is called to create the parameter.
Statement II: The parameter of a copy constructor may be declared as a plain object passed by value, for example X(X other).

quiz.question: Which of the following can NOT be declared virtual in C++?
options: A, C, D and E only
quiz.explanation: A constructor cannot be virtual: when it runs, the object’s dynamic type is still being built and there is no object to dispatch on. A static member function has no this pointer and so no object whose type could be looked up. A friend is not a member at all, and only members can be virtual. A destructor can and often should be virtual. An inline function can be virtual; the call is simply not inlined when it is dispatched at run time. g++ accepts B and E and rejects A, C and D.

stmts: A. A constructor
B. A destructor
C. A static member function
D. A friend function (a non-member)
E. An inline member function

quiz.explanation: The postfix form is the overload with the dummy int parameter; here it saves a copy, adds 1 and returns the old copy. So a = c++ gives a = 5 and c becomes 6. The prefix form adds 10 (this class defines it that way) and returns the object itself, so b = ++c makes c = 16 and b a copy with 16. Output: 5 16 16. Then the non-virtual direct bases in the order of the base list (B1), then the members in declaration order (m), and last the constructor body. The program prints V B1 M D, so the order is D, C, B, A.

quiz.explanation: A p; is default construction: d. A q = p; looks like assignment but creates a new object, so it is copy-initialisation: c. A r(p); is direct copy construction: c. r = q; assigns to an object that already exists: a. f(p) passes by value, so the parameter x is copy-constructed: c. Output: dccac.
