lessons.title: Web programming
lessons.summaryHtml: Web programming is how a browser (the client) and a web server work together over HTTP. HTML gives a page its structure, CSS gives it its look, and JavaScript makes it respond to the user by changing the DOM. Dynamic HTML (DHTML) is simply these three working together, not a separate language. XML carries data rather than showing it: every XML document must be well-formed, and it is valid only if it also obeys a DTD or an XML Schema. On the server side, Java servlets handle requests through a fixed life cycle (init once, service per request, destroy once), and JSP pages are translated into servlets. Applets were Java programs that ran inside the browser; they are now obsolete but still appear in NET questions. Every JavaScript and Java output in this lesson was produced by actually running the code.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

When you open a web page, your browser (the client) sends a request to a web server using HTTP. The server sends back a document, usually HTML. The browser builds a tree of objects from it, called the DOM, applies CSS rules to decide how each part looks, and runs any JavaScript, which can change the tree later. If the page must be built from a database (your marks, your cart), a program on the server builds the HTML first. In Java, that program is a servlet or a JSP page. XML is a cousin of HTML used to describe and exchange data, and its rules are much stricter.

Think of a restaurant: HTML is the food on the plate, CSS the plating, JavaScript the waiter who changes things at your table, the servlet the kitchen, and HTTP the order slip.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 3 is shared between programming languages and computer graphics, and web programming usually gives a small but steady number of questions. They are mostly factual and fast: the life cycle of a servlet, JSP or applet, JSP element syntax and implicit objects, well-formed versus valid XML, DTD syntax, CSS selectors and precedence, HTTP methods and status codes, and client-side versus server-side technologies. Match-the-list and statement questions dominate. JavaScript output questions on type coercion and scope are now also common.

Concepts in depth: the web, the client and the server

A URL such as https://ugcnet.nta.ac.in:443/notice/list.html?year=2026#top has parts: the scheme (https), the host, an optional port (80 is the HTTP default and 443 the HTTPS default), the path, the query string after ? and the fragment after #. The fragment is never sent to the server; the browser uses it to scroll.

HTTP is a request–response, application-layer protocol that normally runs over TCP. It is stateless: the server keeps no memory of earlier requests, which is why cookies and sessions were invented. HTTP/1.0 opened a new TCP connection per object by default (non-persistent). HTTP/1.1 keeps the connection open by default (persistent) and allows pipelining. A request has a request line (GET /index.html HTTP/1.1), headers (Host, User-Agent, Cookie …), a blank line and an optional body. A response has a status line (HTTP/1.1 200 OK), headers (Content-Type, Content-Length, Set-Cookie …), a blank line and the body.

MethodUseSafe?Idempotent?
GETFetch a resource; data goes in the URL query stringYesYes
HEADLike GET but returns headers onlyYesYes
POSTSend data in the body to be processed (forms, uploads)NoNo
PUTStore or replace the resource at this URLNoYes
DELETERemove the resourceNoYes
OPTIONS / TRACEAsk which methods are allowed / echo the requestYesYes

A safe method does not change server state. An idempotent method has the same effect whether you send it once or ten times. Status codes come in five classes: 1xx informational, 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), 3xx redirection (301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified), 4xx client error (400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed) and 5xx server error (500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable).

Client-side code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, formerly applets) is downloaded and runs in the browser: it can validate a form instantly but cannot be trusted and cannot touch the server database directly. Server-side code (servlets, JSP, PHP, ASP.NET, Node.js) runs on the server: it can read databases and keep secrets, but every action costs a round trip.

Concepts in depth: HTML

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes structure with elements: a start tag, content and an end tag, with attributes in the start tag. A document starts with <!DOCTYPE html>, then <html> containing <head> (title, meta, link, script) and <body>. HTML is not case-sensitive and browsers forgive missing end tags, which XML never does. Void (empty) elements have no end tag: br, hr, img, input, meta, link.

  • Links and images: <a href="url" target="_blank"> opens in a new tab; <img src="a.png" alt="text">, where alt is shown if the image fails and is read aloud by screen readers.
  • Lists: ul (unordered), ol (ordered, with type="A", "a", "I", "i", "1" and start), dl with dt/dd (definition list).
  • Tables: table, tr (row), th (header cell), td (data cell), caption; colspan merges cells across columns and rowspan down rows.
  • Forms: <form action="url" method="get|post">. The default method is GET. Controls: input (type text, password, radio, checkbox, submit, hidden, file, email, number, date …), select/option, textarea, button. Only controls with a name are sent.
  • Block versus inline: block elements (div, p, h1–h6, ul, table, form) start on a new line and take the full width; inline elements (span, a, img, strong, em) flow inside a line.
  • HTML5 added semantic elements (header, nav, section, article, footer), audio, video, canvas and new input types.

Concepts in depth: CSS

A CSS rule is selector { property: value; }. Styles can be inline (a style attribute), internal (a <style> element in the head) or external (a .css file linked with <link rel="stylesheet" href="…">). External sheets are the best for reuse and caching.

When several rules set the same property on an element, the cascade decides. First, !important declarations beat normal ones. Then the specificity of the selectors is compared as a four-part number (a, b, c, d): a = 1 for an inline style, b = number of IDs, c = number of classes, attribute selectors and pseudo-classes, d = number of element names and pseudo-elements. The universal selector * and combinators count zero. The numbers are compared column by column, not added in base 10, so one ID beats any number of classes. If specificity is equal, the rule that appears later wins. Some properties (color, font) are inherited by children; others (border, margin, padding) are not.

Selectors: p (type), .note (class), #menu (ID), div p (descendant), div > p (child), h2 + p (adjacent sibling), a[href] (attribute), a:hover (pseudo-class), p::first-line (pseudo-element).

The box model: every element is a box of content, then padding, then border, then margin. With the default box-sizing: content-box, the width property is the content width only, so the visible box is width + 2 × padding + 2 × border, and the space it takes adds 2 × margin. With box-sizing: border-box, width already includes padding and border. Vertical margins of adjacent blocks collapse: the gap is the larger margin, not the sum. The position property takes static (default), relative (offset from its normal place), absolute (placed relative to the nearest positioned ancestor), fixed (relative to the viewport) and sticky.

Concepts in depth: DHTML, the DOM and JavaScript

DHTML is the combination of HTML, CSS, a scripting language and the DOM that lets a page change after it has loaded: menus that open, content that is replaced, styles that change on hover. It is a marketing term for a technique, not a new language or standard. The DOM, standardised by the W3C, represents the document as a tree of nodes (document, element, attribute, text, comment). Scripts use methods such as document.getElementById(), getElementsByTagName(), querySelector(), createElement() and appendChild(), and properties such as innerHTML and style.

When a user clicks a nested element, the event travels in three phases: capturing (from the window down to the target), target, and bubbling (from the target back up). addEventListener(type, handler, true) listens in the capturing phase; the default, false, listens while bubbling. event.stopPropagation() stops the journey, and event.preventDefault() cancels the default action, such as following a link.

JavaScript (standardised as ECMAScript) is interpreted or JIT-compiled, dynamically and weakly typed, and prototype-based. Its primitive types are number (one type for all numbers, 64-bit floating point), string, boolean, undefined, null, bigint and symbol; everything else is an object, including arrays and functions. Key behaviour for output questions:

  • typeof null is "object" (a historical bug), typeof NaN is "number", typeof [] is "object", and typeof of a function is "function".
  • Binary + concatenates if either operand is a string, working left to right: 1 + 2 + "3" is "33" but "1" + 2 + 3 is "123". The operators − * / % always convert to numbers.
  • == converts types before comparing; === does not. 0 == "0" is true, 0 === "0" is false, null == undefined is true, and NaN is not equal to anything, even itself.
  • var is function-scoped and hoisted with the value undefined; let and const are block-scoped and in the "temporal dead zone" until their line runs, so reading them early throws a ReferenceError.
  • A closure is a function that remembers the variables of the scope in which it was created, even after that scope has returned.
  • Dialogs: alert() shows a message, confirm() returns true or false, prompt() returns the typed string or null.

Concepts in depth: XML, DTD and XML Schema

XML (eXtensible Markup Language, a W3C recommendation) lets you invent your own tags to describe data. HTML is about how data looks; XML is about what data is. A document is well-formed when it follows the syntax rules:

  1. There is exactly one root element that contains all others.
  2. Every start tag has a matching end tag, or the element is written self-closed as <br/>.
  3. Elements are properly nested: <b><i>x</i></b>, never <b><i>x</b></i>.
  4. Names are case-sensitive: <Name> cannot be closed by </name>. Names cannot start with a digit.
  5. Attribute values are always quoted, and an attribute cannot repeat in one tag.
  6. The characters < and & in text must be written as entities. The five predefined entities are <, >, &, ' and ". A CDATA section, <![CDATA[ … ]]>, holds text that the parser does not parse.
  7. The XML declaration <?xml version="1.0"?> is optional, but if present it must be the very first thing in the file.

A document is valid when it is well-formed and obeys a grammar given by a DTD or an XML Schema. A DTD (Document Type Definition) can be internal (<!DOCTYPE note [ … ]>) or external (<!DOCTYPE note SYSTEM "note.dtd">). It declares elements and attributes:

<!ELEMENT book (title, author+, price?)>   sequence: title, one or more authors, optional price
<!ELEMENT title (#PCDATA)>                  parsed character data (text)
<!ELEMENT shelf (book*)>                    zero or more books
<!ELEMENT item (pen | pencil)>              choice: exactly one of them
<!ELEMENT hr EMPTY>
<!ATTLIST book isbn ID #REQUIRED
               lang CDATA "en"
               kind (print | ebook) #IMPLIED>

Occurrence symbols: none = exactly once, ? = zero or one, * = zero or more, + = one or more. A comma means sequence and | means choice. Attribute defaults are #REQUIRED (must appear), #IMPLIED (optional, no default), #FIXED "v" (always v) or a literal default value. Attribute types include CDATA, ID (unique in the document), IDREF, NMTOKEN and enumerations.

An XML Schema (XSD) is itself written in XML, supports namespaces, and has real data types (xs:integer, xs:date, xs:decimal …) with ranges, lengths and patterns, and occurrence counts through minOccurs and maxOccurs. A DTD has its own non-XML syntax, no data types beyond text, and no namespace support. Related technologies: XSLT transforms XML into HTML or other XML, XPath selects nodes (/library/book[1]/title), and namespaces (xmlns) avoid name clashes. Parsers are of two kinds: a DOM parser builds the whole tree in memory (random access, more memory), and a SAX parser fires events (startElement, characters, endElement) as it reads (fast, little memory, forward-only).

Concepts in depth: Java for the web

Applets were small Java programs, compiled to bytecode, downloaded with a page and run by the browser’s Java plug-in inside a security sandbox (no access to local files, network only to the host it came from). An applet extends java.applet.Applet (or javax.swing.JApplet) and has no main(). The browser calls init() once, then start() (and again each time the page is revisited), paint(Graphics g) whenever it must draw, stop() when the page is left, and destroy() once at the end. Calling repaint() asks for update(), which calls paint(). It was embedded with the <applet> tag (code, width, height) and tested with appletviewer. The Applet API was deprecated in Java 9 and removed in JDK 26 (JEP 504), and modern browsers have removed plug-in support, so applets are only of historical and exam interest.

Servlets are Java classes that run inside a web container (Apache Tomcat, Jetty) on the server. Most extend HttpServlet (which extends the protocol-independent GenericServlet) and override doGet() and doPost(). The packages were javax.servlet and are jakarta.servlet since Jakarta EE 9. The life cycle is fixed:

  1. The container loads the class and creates one instance (at first request, or at start-up with load-on-startup).
  2. init(ServletConfig) is called once.
  3. service(request, response) is called for every request, usually on a separate thread, and dispatches to doGet(), doPost() and so on.
  4. destroy() is called once before the instance is removed.

Because one instance serves many threads, instance variables are shared and must be protected. Mappings from URL to servlet are given in web.xml (the deployment descriptor) or with the @WebServlet annotation. RequestDispatcher.forward() passes the same request to another resource on the server (the browser URL does not change), whereas response.sendRedirect() makes the browser send a new request (the URL changes). Since HTTP is stateless, session tracking uses cookies, URL rewriting, hidden form fields or HttpSession. Servlets beat old CGI programs on speed because one loaded instance serves requests on threads, instead of a new process per request.

JSP pages mix HTML with Java. The first request (or a changed file) triggers translation into a servlet source file, then compilation, loading, jspInit(), and _jspService() per request; jspDestroy() runs at the end. JSP elements:

ElementSyntaxWhere it ends up
Directive<%@ page import="java.util.*" %>, <%@ include file="h.jsp" %>, <%@ taglib … %>Instructions to the translator
Declaration<%! int count = 0; %>Class members of the servlet
Scriptlet<% count++; %>Statements inside _jspService()
Expression<%= count %>out.print(count) inside _jspService()
JSP comment<%-- … --%>Removed; never sent to the browser
Standard action<jsp:include page="x.jsp"/>, jsp:forward, jsp:useBean, jsp:setPropertyExecuted at request time

The nine implicit objects are request, response, out (a JspWriter), session, application (the ServletContext), config, pageContext, page (this) and exception (only in error pages). The include directive pastes the file text in at translation time (static), while the jsp:include action includes the output of the other page at request time (dynamic). Modern JSP uses Expression Language (${user.name} style expressions) and JSTL tags, and follows the MVC pattern: a servlet is the controller, JavaBeans are the model and JSP is the view.

Worked examples

Example 1: CSS specificity. Three rules set the colour of a link inside <nav id="top"><ul class="menu"><li><a class="item">.

  1. #top a gives (0,1,0,1).
  2. .menu li a.item gives (0,0,2,2).
  3. nav ul li a gives (0,0,0,4).

Compare the ID column first: only rule 1 has an ID, so rule 1 wins, even though rule 2 has more selectors in total. Adding ten more classes to rule 2 would not change this. If an inline style="color:red" were on the link, (1,0,0,0) would beat all three; only a !important declaration in a stylesheet could override an inline style.

Example 2: box model. .card { width: 240px; padding: 12px; border: 3px solid; margin: 16px; }

Content-box (default): border box = 240 + 2 × 12 + 2 × 3 = 270 px; space taken including margins = 270 + 2 × 16 = 302 px.

Border-box: the border box is exactly 240 px, so the content shrinks to 240 − 24 − 6 = 210 px; space with margins = 272 px.

Two such cards stacked vertically: the 16 px bottom margin and 16 px top margin collapse into one 16 px gap, not 32 px.

Example 3: tracing JavaScript output.

console.log(1 + 2 + "3", "1" + 2 + 3);
console.log(0 == "0", 0 === "0", null == undefined, NaN == NaN);
var a = [1, 2, 3]; a[5] = 6; console.log(a.length, a[4]);
console.log(parseInt("12px"), Number("12px"));

Line 1: 1 + 2 = 3 first, then 3 + "3" = "33"; "1" + 2 = "12", then "12" + 3 = "123". Output 33 123.

Line 2: == converts "0" to 0 (true), === sees number versus string (false), null == undefined is a special true, and NaN never equals anything. Output true false true false.

Line 3: assigning index 5 makes the length 6 and leaves holes at 3 and 4. Output 6 undefined.

Line 4: parseInt reads digits until the first non-digit, giving 12; Number needs the whole string to be numeric, giving NaN. Output 12 NaN. All four lines were run with node.

Example 4: well-formed or valid?

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE shelf [
  <!ELEMENT shelf (book+)>
  <!ELEMENT book (title, price?)>
  <!ELEMENT title (#PCDATA)>
  <!ELEMENT price (#PCDATA)>
  <!ATTLIST book id ID #REQUIRED>
]>
<shelf>
  <book id="b1"><title>Graphics</title></book>
  <book id="b2"><price>450</price><title>Web</title></book>
</shelf>

Syntax: one root (shelf), all tags closed and nested, attributes quoted, so it is well-formed. Against the DTD: book 1 is fine (price is optional). Book 2 has price before title, but the content model is the sequence (title, price?), so the order is wrong and the document is not valid. Swapping the two child elements fixes it. Changing the second id to "b1" would also make it invalid, because ID values must be unique. A validating parser (lxml with the DTD) reports exactly this.

Example 5: servlet life cycle count. A servlet is deployed without load-on-startup. Three users send 2, 3 and 4 requests to it, and then the server is shut down. How many times is each method called?

The instance is created at the first request, so init() runs 1 time. service() runs once per request: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 times (a GET request goes on to doGet()). destroy() runs 1 time at shutdown. Neither the number of users nor the number of threads changes the init and destroy counts.

Formula and fact sheet

JSP life cycletranslate → compile → load → instantiate → jspInit() → _jspService() → jspDestroy()

JSP elements<%@ %> directive, <%! %> declaration, <% %> scriptlet, <%= %> expression, <%-- --%> comment

NTA traps

  • "Valid means well-formed, so well-formed means valid." Wrong. Validity needs a DTD or schema and is a stronger condition. Fix: valid ⇒ well-formed, never the reverse.
  • "init() runs for every request." Wrong. init() and destroy() run once per servlet instance; only service() runs per request.
  • "The include directive is dynamic." Wrong. The directive merges source text at translation time. The jsp:include action is the dynamic one.
  • "Specificity is a decimal number, so 11 classes beat 1 ID." Wrong. The columns never carry over; one ID always beats any number of classes.
  • "width is the size of the visible box." Only with border-box. Under the default content-box, add padding and border, and add margins for the space taken.
  • "JavaScript is a lighter version of Java." Wrong. They are separate languages: JavaScript is dynamically typed and prototype-based; Java is statically typed, class-based and compiled to bytecode.
  • "DHTML is a new version of HTML." Wrong. It is the combined use of HTML, CSS, JavaScript and the DOM.
  • "An applet has a main() method." Wrong. The browser drives it through init/start/paint/stop/destroy. A servlet has no main() either.
  • "GET is safer for passwords because it is safe." "Safe" only means it does not change server state. GET puts data in the URL, where it is logged and cached; forms with passwords should use POST over HTTPS.

How NTA asks this

  • Match the lists: JSP tags ↔ purpose, HTTP codes ↔ meaning, life-cycle methods ↔ when called, DTD symbols ↔ occurrence, technology ↔ side (client/server). Fix the pair you are surest of first.
  • Statement I/II and Assertion–Reason: well-formed versus valid, DOM versus SAX, directive versus action, GET versus POST.
  • Output questions: short JavaScript snippets on coercion, typeof, equality, hoisting and closures. Write the type of each operand before evaluating.
  • Sequence questions: servlet, JSP or applet life cycle; the steps of an HTTP request.

Mini-example (A–R). A: Instance variables of a servlet are not thread-safe. R: The container normally creates a single instance of a servlet and calls its service() method from many threads at once. Both are true, and R explains A, so the answer is option 1.

Elimination trick: in a life-cycle ordering question, the method called once at the start (init/jspInit) must come right after the instance exists, and the method called once at the end (destroy/jspDestroy) must be last. That alone usually leaves one option.

terms.definition: HyperText Transfer Protocol: a stateless, request–response application-layer protocol. The client sends a method (GET, POST …) and a URL; the server answers with a status code and a body.
Dynamic HTML: HTML + CSS + JavaScript + the DOM used together so that a page changes after loading without a new request. It is a technique, not a language.
Document Object Model: a platform- and language-neutral tree of objects that represents a document, so scripts can read and change its content, structure and style.
The weight of a CSS selector, compared as (inline, IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, elements/pseudo-elements). The higher weight wins; on a tie, the later rule wins.
XML that obeys the syntax rules: one root element, every start tag closed, proper nesting, quoted attribute values, case-sensitive names.
A well-formed XML document that also conforms to the rules of a DTD or an XML Schema (XSD).
A Java class that runs inside a web container and answers requests. The container calls init() once, service() for every request and destroy() once.
JavaServer Pages: an HTML page with embedded Java elements. The container translates it into a servlet the first time it is requested (or when it changes).

A Java program embedded in a web page and run by a browser plug-in, with life cycle init, start, paint, stop, destroy. The API was deprecated in Java 9 and removed in JDK 26, and browsers no longer support it.
Ways of keeping state across stateless HTTP requests: cookies, URL rewriting, hidden form fields and the HttpSession object.

lessons.examTip: Sort every option into client side (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, applet) or server side (servlet, JSP, PHP, ASP). Then remember three orders: servlet init → service → destroy; applet init → start → paint → stop → destroy; CSS weight inline > ID > class > element.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in 10 minutes. For each JavaScript problem, write the type of every operand before evaluating.
Check with solutions.md and write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (string +, typeof null, margin collapse, directive vs action).
Open the browser console (F12) and run the JavaScript of problems 3, 4 and 11 to see the outputs for yourself.
Write the XML of problem 9 with a fix that makes it valid, and a second version that is not even well-formed.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.

lessons.title: Computer graphics: output primitives
lessons.summaryHtml: Every picture on a screen is finally a grid of pixels. This lesson covers how display devices show that grid (raster and random scan, CRT, refresh, the frame buffer) and how the basic shapes are turned into pixels: lines with DDA and Bresenham, circles and ellipses with the midpoint method, and filled polygons with scan-line, boundary-fill and flood-fill algorithms. It also covers antialiasing, which smooths the jagged edges, and 2D viewing: mapping a window to a viewport and clipping lines (Cohen–Sutherland, Liang–Barsky) and polygons (Sutherland–Hodgman) to the window. NET asks for frame-buffer sizes, pixel sequences, decision parameters, region codes and clipped endpoints. Every number below was computed by a program, and the C outputs were produced with gcc.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A monitor cannot draw a "line" or a "circle". It can only light up a grid of tiny dots called pixels. So the computer must decide, for every shape, exactly which pixels to light. That job is called scan conversion (or rasterisation), and the algorithms that do it for lines, circles, ellipses and filled areas are the output primitives of graphics. Before drawing, we also decide which part of the scene is shown and cut away everything outside it; that is viewing and clipping. Finally, since pixels are square, slanted edges look like staircases, and antialiasing softens them.

Why it matters for NET

Computer graphics shares Unit 3 with programming languages, and output primitives are its most numerical part. Expect frame-buffer size and refresh-time numericals, DDA and Bresenham pixel sequences or decision parameters, midpoint circle steps, Cohen–Sutherland region codes and clipped endpoints, and Liang–Barsky parameters. Display technology (raster versus random scan, CRT terms, flat panels) and fill algorithms come as Match and Statement questions. The numericals are short if you know the update formulas cold, so this topic rewards practice more than reading.

Concepts in depth: display devices

In a cathode-ray tube (CRT), an electron gun (heated cathode, control grid) emits a beam that is focused and then deflected (electrostatically or magnetically) to hit a spot on a phosphor-coated screen, which glows. The glow fades, so the picture must be redrawn many times per second: this is refresh. A refresh rate below about 25–30 frames per second causes visible flicker. Persistence is how long the phosphor keeps glowing (time to fall to 1/10 of its initial intensity); low persistence needs a higher refresh rate but suits animation. Resolution is the maximum number of distinguishable points (for a raster, pixels across × pixels down). Aspect ratio is defined by Hearn and Baker as the ratio of vertical points to horizontal points needed to produce equal-length lines in both directions (for displays it is also commonly quoted as width : height, such as 4 : 3 for 1024 × 768).

FeatureRaster scanRandom scan (vector)
How the beam movesAcross every scan line, top to bottom, with horizontal and vertical retraceOnly along the lines of the picture
Stored pictureFrame buffer (refresh buffer): a value for every pixelDisplay file (display list): line-drawing commands
RefreshFixed rate (60–80 Hz or more), independent of picture complexityDepends on the number of lines; typically 30–60 times a second
Line qualityJagged (aliasing) on slanted linesSmooth lines, high resolution
Filled areas, shadingEasy, realisticNot practical
ExamplesTV, monitors, most modern displaysEarly CAD systems, oscilloscope-style displays

Interlacing refreshes odd scan lines in one pass and even lines in the next, so a 30 frame/s picture is swept 60 times a second and flickers less. For colour, beam penetration (red and green phosphor layers; the beam speed sets how deep it goes, giving only about four colours) is used with random scan, and the shadow-mask method (three guns and a mask with holes, in delta or in-line arrangement) is used with raster displays and gives millions of colours. The direct-view storage tube (DVST) stores the picture on a charge grid, needs no refresh and shows no flicker, but it cannot erase part of a picture and has poor contrast. Flat-panel displays are emissive (plasma panels, LED, thin-film electroluminescent: they produce light) or non-emissive (LCD: it controls light from another source).

Frame-buffer numericals. With n bits per pixel, a pixel can show 2ⁿ colours or grey levels, and the frame buffer needs W × H × n bits (divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1024 for KB and 1024² for MB). A system with n bit planes has n bits per pixel. A colour lookup table (palette) stores full colours such as 24-bit values; the frame buffer holds only an n-bit index, so 2ⁿ colours can be on screen at once out of 2²⁴ possible. The LUT size is 2ⁿ × 24 bits. The time available per pixel is 1 ÷ (frames per second × number of pixels), ignoring retrace.

Concepts in depth: line drawing

A line from (x₀, y₀) to (x₁, y₁) has Δx = x₁ − x₀, Δy = y₁ − y₀ and slope m = Δy/Δx. We step one pixel at a time along the major axis (x if |m| ≤ 1, y otherwise), so the line has max(|Δx|, |Δy|) + 1 pixels and no gaps.

DDA. steps = max(|Δx|, |Δy|); xinc = Δx/steps and yinc = Δy/steps, so one of them is ±1 and the other is the slope (or 1/slope). Start at (x₀, y₀), add the increments steps times, and plot (ROUND(x), ROUND(y)) each time. It is simple and faster than evaluating y = mx + c directly (no multiplication), but it uses floating-point addition and rounding, and the error from adding a rounded slope accumulates on long lines.

Bresenham (0 < m < 1). At column xₖ + 1, the candidate pixels are yₖ and yₖ + 1. Let d₁ and d₂ be the vertical distances from the true line to the lower and upper candidate. Their difference is d₁ − d₂ = 2m(xₖ + 1) − 2yₖ + 2b − 1. Multiplying by Δx (positive) removes the fraction and gives the decision parameter pₖ = Δx(d₁ − d₂) = 2Δy·xₖ − 2Δx·yₖ + c, whose sign tells which pixel is closer. Subtracting successive values gives the update:

  • p₀ = 2Δy − Δx.
  • If pₖ < 0: plot (xₖ + 1, yₖ) and pₖ₊₁ = pₖ + 2Δy.
  • If pₖ ≥ 0: plot (xₖ + 1, yₖ + 1) and pₖ₊₁ = pₖ + 2Δy − 2Δx.

Everything is integer, and 2Δy and 2Δy − 2Δx are constants computed once. For |m| > 1 the roles of x and y are swapped (step in y, decide x), and for negative slopes one coordinate decreases. When p = 0 both pixels are equally close; the standard form (≥ 0) picks the upper pixel.

Concepts in depth: circles and ellipses

A circle is symmetric in all eight octants, so from one computed point (x, y) we plot (±x, ±y) and (±y, ±x) about the centre. The midpoint circle algorithm starts at (0, r) and moves x by 1 while x < y (the octant from 90° to 45°, where the slope is between 0 and −1). It uses the circle function f(x, y) = x² + y² − r², which is negative inside, zero on and positive outside the circle, and evaluates it at the midpoint (xₖ + 1, yₖ − ½) between the two candidates:

  • p₀ = f(1, r − ½) = 5/4 − r, taken as 1 − r for an integer radius.
  • If pₖ < 0 (midpoint inside): next pixel (xₖ + 1, yₖ); pₖ₊₁ = pₖ + 2xₖ₊₁ + 1.
  • If pₖ ≥ 0: next pixel (xₖ + 1, yₖ − 1); pₖ₊₁ = pₖ + 2xₖ₊₁ + 1 − 2yₖ₊₁.

An ellipse with radii rₓ and ry has only 4-way symmetry, so one quadrant is computed, in two regions. In region 1 (slope magnitude below 1) x steps by 1, starting at (0, ry) with p1₀ = ry² − rₓ²ry + rₓ²/4. Region 1 ends when 2ry²x ≥ 2rₓ²y. In region 2, y steps down by 1 until y = 0, starting with p2₀ = ry²(x₀ + ½)² + rₓ²(y₀ − 1)² − rₓ²ry².

Concepts in depth: filling polygons

The scan-line algorithm fills a polygon one scan line at a time. For each line y, find where it crosses the polygon edges, sort the x-intersections, and fill between pairs (1st to 2nd, 3rd to 4th …). It uses an edge table (edges sorted by their lower y, each with ymax, x at the lower end and 1/m) and an active edge list of the edges that cross the current line; moving to the next line adds 1/m to each active x (edge coherence). A vertex where both edges go the same way (one up, one down, a "pass-through" vertex) is counted once, and a local maximum or minimum is counted twice, so the pairs always match up. Horizontal edges are ignored. The inside test can be the odd–even (parity) rule: a point is inside if a ray from it crosses the boundary an odd number of times; or the non-zero winding rule: inside if the signed count of edge crossings is not zero. The two differ for self-intersecting polygons.

Seed fills start from an interior pixel. Boundary fill spreads until it meets pixels of a given boundary colour, so the boundary must be one colour. Flood fill replaces every connected pixel that has a given interior (old) colour, so it works when the boundary has several colours. Both can be 4-connected (left, right, up, down) or 8-connected (also the four diagonals). An 8-connected fill can "leak" through a boundary drawn diagonally, and the recursive versions need a deep stack; filling whole horizontal spans reduces this.

Concepts in depth: antialiasing

Aliasing is the distortion caused by low-frequency sampling: jagged staircase edges, small objects that vanish between pixels, and moiré patterns. Remedies are: supersampling (post-filtering: compute the picture at a higher resolution, several samples per pixel, and average them), area sampling (pre-filtering: set the pixel intensity in proportion to the area of the pixel covered by the object), filtering with weighting masks, and pixel phasing (micro-positioning the electron beam by a fraction of a pixel). Raising the resolution also helps but costs memory and bandwidth.

Concepts in depth: 2D viewing and clipping

The viewing pipeline takes modelling coordinates → world coordinates → viewing coordinates → normalised coordinates → device coordinates. The window (in world coordinates) is mapped onto the viewport (on the device) so that relative positions are kept:

xv = xvmin + (xw − xwmin) · sx, with sx = (xvmax − xvmin) / (xwmax − xwmin), and similarly for y. If sx ≠ sy, shapes are stretched.

Cohen–Sutherland line clipping. Each endpoint gets a 4-bit region code, written here as T B R L: bit 4 = above (y > ymax), bit 3 = below (y < ymin), bit 2 = right (x > xmax), bit 1 = left (x < xmin). The nine regions get the codes 1001, 1000, 1010 / 0001, 0000, 0010 / 0101, 0100, 0110. If both codes are 0000, the line is trivially accepted. If the bitwise AND of the codes is not 0000, both ends are outside the same edge, so it is trivially rejected. Otherwise, take an outside endpoint, intersect the line with the edge its code names (y = ymax: x = x₀ + (ymax − y₀)/m; x = xmax: y = y₀ + m(xmax − x₀)), replace the endpoint, recompute its code, and repeat. A line can need up to four intersection calculations.

Liang–Barsky uses the parametric form x = x₀ + uΔx, y = y₀ + uΔy with 0 ≤ u ≤ 1. The four inequalities are written as u·pₖ ≤ qₖ with p₁ = −Δx, q₁ = x₀ − xmin; p₂ = Δx, q₂ = xmax − x₀; p₃ = −Δy, q₃ = y₀ − ymin; p₄ = Δy, q₄ = ymax − y₀. If pₖ = 0 and qₖ < 0, the line is parallel to and outside that edge: reject. For pₖ < 0 the line enters: u₁ = max(0, qₖ/pₖ). For pₖ > 0 it leaves: u₂ = min(1, qₖ/pₖ). If u₁ > u₂, reject; otherwise the visible part runs from u₁ to u₂. It computes fewer intersections than Cohen–Sutherland. (The Nicholl–Lee–Nicholl algorithm reduces the work further by examining regions around one endpoint.)

Sutherland–Hodgman polygon clipping clips the whole polygon against one window edge at a time, passing the output vertex list to the next edge. For each polygon edge from S to E: in → in outputs E; in → out outputs the intersection; out → out outputs nothing; out → in outputs the intersection and then E. It works for convex clip windows; for a concave polygon it may leave extra edges joining separate pieces, which the Weiler–Atherton algorithm avoids by following the window boundary. Text can be clipped all-or-none by string, all-or-none by character, or by individual character components. Point clipping just keeps xmin ≤ x ≤ xmax and ymin ≤ y ≤ ymax.

Worked examples

Example 1: frame buffer and timing. A raster system is 1024 × 768 with 24 bits per pixel, refreshed at 60 frames per second.

  1. Frame buffer = 1024 × 768 × 24 bits = 18,874,368 bits = 2,359,296 bytes = 2.25 MB.
  2. Colours per pixel = 2²⁴ = 16,777,216.
  3. Pixels per second = 60 × 786,432 = 47,185,920, so the time per pixel, ignoring retrace, is 1 ÷ 47,185,920 s ≈ 21.2 ns.
  4. If instead the buffer holds an 8-bit index into a lookup table of 24-bit colours, the buffer shrinks to 768 KB, 256 colours can be shown at once out of 16,777,216, and the table needs 256 × 24 bits = 768 bytes.

Example 5: Cohen–Sutherland. Window (10, 10) to (50, 40); line P(0, 20) to Q(60, 50); m = 30/60 = 0.5.

  1. Codes: P is left → 0001; Q is above and right → 1010. AND = 0000 and neither is 0000, so clip.
  2. P is outside on the left: x = 10 gives y = 20 + 0.5 × 10 = 25. P becomes (10, 25), code 0000.

For comparison, the line (5, 45) to (30, 60) has codes 1001 and 1000; their AND is 1000, so it is trivially rejected with no arithmetic.

Example 7: Sutherland–Hodgman. Clip the triangle (3, 3), (15, 3), (3, 15) to the window (0, 0)–(10, 10).

  1. Left edge (x = 0): all vertices inside; 3 vertices pass.
  2. Right edge (x = 10): edge (3,3)→(15,3) leaves at (10, 3); edge (15,3)→(3,15) enters at (10, 8). Output: (3,3), (10,3), (10,8), (3,15): 4 vertices.
  3. Bottom edge (y = 0): all inside; 4 vertices.

Example 8: window to viewport. Window (0, 0)–(100, 50) is mapped to viewport (200, 100)–(400, 300). sx = 200/100 = 2 and sy = 200/50 = 4. The point (30, 20) maps to (200 + 30 × 2, 100 + 20 × 4) = (260, 180). Since sx ≠ sy, a circle in the window would appear as an ellipse.

Concepts in depth: graphics monitors, workstations and input devices

Graphics monitors and workstations. Almost all graphics monitors today are raster-scan displays, CRT in older systems and flat panels now. A general-purpose system has one colour monitor. A graphics workstation adds a high-resolution screen (or several monitors side by side), a large frame buffer in its own video memory, and a display processor (graphics controller). The display processor does scan conversion: it turns picture definitions such as lines and polygons into pixel values in the frame buffer, and it performs raster operations such as filling and moving blocks of pixels. This frees the CPU. The video controller reads the frame buffer and refreshes the screen. Large-screen systems use projection displays or a wall of monitors driven together.

Three kinds of 3D viewing systems are examined:

  • A varifocal (vibrating) mirror display: a flexible mirror vibrates in step with the CRT, so each point of an object is reflected at a different apparent depth. The viewer sees a true 3D volume, which is used for medical data (CT, ultrasound) and geological data.
  • Stereoscopic systems show a different view to each eye. The left-eye and right-eye views are displayed alternately, and LCD shutter glasses, synchronised with the display, block the other eye each time.
  • A head-mounted display (HMD) for virtual reality has a small screen in front of each eye, and sensors track the head so the view changes as the user turns.

The light pen needs a scanning CRT beam, so it works only with refreshed CRT displays. Its drawbacks are arm fatigue, the pen hiding part of the screen, and false triggering by background light. Graphics standards (GKS, PHIGS) classify input by the kind of data delivered, as logical input devices: locator (one coordinate position), stroke (a sequence of positions), string (text), valuator (one real number, such as a dial setting), choice (a menu option) and pick (a part of the picture). A device is used in one of three input modes: request (the program waits until the input arrives), sample (the program reads the device’s current value at once, without waiting) and event (inputs are placed in an event queue, and the program takes them from the queue).

Concepts in depth: viewing coordinate frame, window-to-viewport mapping and viewing functions

The full 2D viewing pipeline is: build the scene in modelling coordinates, place it in world coordinates with modelling transformations, convert world coordinates to viewing coordinates, map the window to a viewport in normalised coordinates (0 to 1, where clipping is usually done), and finally apply the workstation transformation to reach device coordinates.

The viewing coordinate reference frame. Choose a view origin P₀ = (x₀, y₀) in world coordinates and a view-up vector V that gives the direction of the viewing y axis. Normalise it: v = V / |V|. The viewing x axis is perpendicular to v and points to the right: u = (v_y, −v_x). World coordinates are converted to viewing coordinates by translating P₀ to the origin and then rotating the frame onto the axes:

MWC,VC = R · T(−x₀, −y₀), where R has the rows (uₓ, u_y, 0), (vₓ, v_y, 0), (0, 0, 1).

So a point’s viewing coordinates are the dot products x_v = u · (P − P₀) and y_v = v · (P − P₀). A tilted window lets us view the scene at an angle.

Window-to-viewport mapping. The mapping keeps relative positions: (x_v − x_vmin)/(x_vmax − x_vmin) = (x_w − x_wmin)/(x_wmax − x_wmin), and the same for y. As a composite transformation it is: translate the window corner to the origin, scale, and translate to the viewport corner:

M = T(x_vmin, y_vmin) · S(sₓ, s_y) · T(−x_wmin, −y_wmin) = [sₓ 0 x_vmin − sₓx_wmin; 0 s_y y_vmin − s_y y_wmin; 0 0 1], with sₓ = (x_vmax − x_vmin)/(x_wmax − x_wmin) and s_y = (y_vmax − y_vmin)/(y_wmax − y_wmin).

If sₓ ≠ s_y, the aspect ratio changes and objects are stretched. With the viewport fixed, a smaller window zooms in (objects look bigger, less of the scene is shown) and a larger window zooms out; moving a window of fixed size across the scene is panning. Mapping several windows to several viewports shows different parts of a scene, or different views, on one screen.

Example 9: viewing frame and window-to-viewport mapping.

  1. View origin P₀ = (2, 1) and view-up vector V = (−1, 1). Then v = (−1/√2, 1/√2) and u = (v_y, −v_x) = (1/√2, 1/√2). For the world point P = (4, 3): P − P₀ = (2, 2), x_v = (2 + 2)/√2 = 2√2 ≈ 2.83 and y_v = (−2 + 2)/√2 = 0. The point lies on the viewing x axis.
  2. Window (−10, 0) to (30, 20), viewport (100, 50) to (300, 250). sₓ = 200/40 = 5 and s_y = 200/20 = 10, so M = [5 0 100 − 5(−10); 0 10 50 − 10(0); 0 0 1] = [5 0 150; 0 10 50; 0 0 1]. The window point (6, 8) goes to (5 × 6 + 150, 10 × 8 + 50) = (180, 130). Because sₓ ≠ s_y, a circle in the window becomes an ellipse (compare Example 8, where the scale factors were 2 and 4).
  3. Window (10, 10) to (50, 30) mapped to the normalised viewport (0, 0) to (1, 1): sₓ = 1/40, s_y = 1/20. The point (30, 25) goes to (20/40, 15/20) = (0.5, 0.75).

Viewing functions. Hearn and Baker describe the 2D viewing functions of a PHIGS-style graphics package:

GKS offers the simpler setWindow, setViewport and selectNormalizationTransformation. In OpenGL, gluOrtho2D(xwmin, xwmax, ywmin, ywmax) sets the 2D clipping window and glViewport(x, y, width, height) sets the viewport on the display window.

NTA traps

  • Bits versus bytes. 1280 × 1024 × 24 is in bits. Divide by 8 for bytes and by 2²⁰ for MB. Options often include the bit value labelled as bytes.
  • Rounding versus truncation in DDA. A tie such as y = 5.5 goes up with ROUND(v) = ⌊v + 0.5⌋; truncation gives a different pixel list. Use the rule the question states.
  • Wrong Bresenham update. After p ≥ 0 you add 2Δy − 2Δx, not 2Δx − 2Δy, and not just −2Δx. Check: the last pixel must be exactly the endpoint.
  • Starting the circle with p₀ = 5/4 − r and then comparing with fractions. For integer r use 1 − r; the signs, and therefore the pixels, are the same.
  • AND versus OR in Cohen–Sutherland. OR = 0000 means accept; AND ≠ 0000 means reject. AND = 0000 does not mean the line is visible: it may still miss the window.
  • Liang–Barsky signs. Negative p is "entering" (it raises u₁), positive p is "leaving" (it lowers u₂). Mixing them gives u₁ > u₂ and a wrong rejection.
  • Boundary fill versus flood fill. Boundary fill needs a single boundary colour; flood fill looks at the interior colour, so it handles multi-coloured boundaries.
  • Random scan and frame buffers. Random-scan systems have a display file, not a frame buffer. Raster systems have a frame buffer.

How NTA asks this

  • Numerical (most common): frame-buffer size in KB/MB, colours from bits, time per pixel, pixels plotted by DDA or Bresenham, a particular pₖ, midpoint-circle points, a region code, clipped endpoints, u₁ and u₂.
  • Match the lists: device ↔ property, algorithm ↔ purpose, fill method ↔ feature, term ↔ definition.
  • Statements and Assertion–Reason: DDA versus Bresenham, raster versus random scan, symmetry of circles and ellipses, trivial acceptance and rejection.
  • Sequence: the viewing pipeline, the steps of scan-line filling.

Mini-example (Match). List I: A. Cohen–Sutherland, B. Liang–Barsky, C. Sutherland–Hodgman, D. Weiler–Atherton. List II: I. clips concave polygons into separate pieces, II. line clipping with 4-bit region codes, III. parametric line clipping with u₁ and u₂, IV. polygon clipping one window edge at a time. Fix A-II first (region codes are unique), then B-III; only one option will have both, giving A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

Elimination trick: for a pixel-sequence option list, check only the last pixel (it must be the endpoint) and the first changed coordinate (DDA: ROUND of the first increment; Bresenham: sign of p₀). That usually leaves one option without drawing the whole line.

terms.definition: The memory (refresh buffer) that stores one intensity or colour value per pixel of a raster display. Size in bits = horizontal pixels × vertical pixels × bits per pixel.
The beam sweeps the whole screen row by row (scan lines) and each pixel is lit according to the frame buffer. Used by TVs and monitors.
Vector display: the beam draws only the lines of the picture, taken from a display file of drawing commands. Smooth lines, but no realistic filled areas.
How long a phosphor keeps glowing after the beam leaves it, usually measured as the time for the light to fall to one tenth of its original value.
Digital Differential Analyzer: steps one unit along the major axis and adds the slope (a floating-point increment) to the other coordinate, then rounds.
An integer line algorithm that chooses between two candidate pixels with the sign of a decision parameter pₖ; it uses only integer additions, subtractions and doublings.
Tests whether the midpoint between two candidate pixels lies inside or outside the circle, with p₀ = 1 − r, and uses 8-way symmetry to plot one octant only.
The 4-bit code of Cohen–Sutherland clipping that records whether a point is above, below, right of or left of the clip window.
Staircase ("jaggies") and other distortions caused by sampling a continuous shape at discrete pixel positions; reduced by antialiasing such as supersampling or area sampling.
The window is the part of the world-coordinate scene chosen for display; the viewport is the area of the device where it is shown.

lessons.examTip: For every scan-conversion question, first compute Δx, Δy and decide which axis is the major axis. Then: DDA adds the slope and rounds; Bresenham starts with p₀ = 2Δy − Δx and adds 2Δy (if p < 0) or 2Δy − 2Δx (if p ≥ 0); the midpoint circle starts with p₀ = 1 − r.
