lessons.title: Database concepts, architecture and ER modelling
lessons.summaryHtml: A database management system (DBMS) stores shared data once, describes it in a catalog, and controls who reads or changes it. It fixes the classic file-system problems: redundancy, inconsistency, isolated data, weak integrity, lost updates and poor security. The three-schema architecture separates the internal (storage), conceptual (whole database) and external (user view) levels, which gives physical and logical data independence. The ER model describes a design with entities, attributes and relationships, plus cardinality ratios, participation and weak entities; EER adds specialisation and generalisation. Finally, a fixed set of mapping rules turns an ER diagram into tables, and NTA loves asking for the minimum number of tables.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A database is a collection of related data. A database management system (DBMS) is the software that defines, stores, retrieves and protects that data for many users at once. Before DBMSs, each department kept its own files and wrote its own programs to read them. The same customer address lived in three files, and they soon disagreed.

A DBMS keeps one shared copy, describes it in a catalog, and lets programs ask for data by meaning, not by file layout. Designing the database starts with a picture: the entity–relationship (ER) diagram. It shows the things we store (entities), their properties (attributes) and how they are connected (relationships). A mechanical set of rules then turns that picture into tables.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 4 is one of the most dependable scoring units in Paper 2. This lesson’s part of it usually yields a few questions per paper. The favourites are: the three-schema architecture and data independence (often as Assertion–Reason), ER notation symbols (Match the lists), weak entities, participation and cardinality, generalisation versus specialisation, and the minimum number of tables for a described ER diagram. Table-count questions are quick marks if you know the rules and deadly if you count a 1:N relationship as a table.

Concepts in depth

1. File system versus DBMS

Korth lists seven problems of file-processing systems. Remember them as a set, because Multiple-select questions pick from them:

  • Data redundancy and inconsistency: the same data in several files, with copies that drift apart.
  • Difficulty in accessing data: every new query needs a new program.
  • Data isolation: data scattered over files in different formats.
  • Integrity problems: rules such as “balance ≥ 0” are buried in program code.
  • Atomicity problems: a failure half way through a transfer leaves one account debited and the other not credited.
  • Concurrent-access anomalies: two clerks updating the same balance lose one update.
  • Security problems: hard to give each user access to only part of the data.

A DBMS also has costs: extra software and hardware, overhead for security, concurrency and recovery, and staff such as a DBA. For a small, single-user, fixed application, plain files can be cheaper.

2. Schema, instance and data abstraction

The schema is the design of the database (its intension). It changes rarely. The instance or database state is the data at one moment (its extension). It changes with every insert. DBMSs hide complexity through three levels of abstraction: the physical level (how data is stored, as blocks, files and indexes), the logical level (what data is stored and how it is related) and the view level (only the part one user needs).

3. Three-schema (ANSI/SPARC) architecture

   External level    view 1    view 2   ...   view n
                         \        |         /
             external/conceptual mappings
                              |
   Conceptual level     one conceptual schema
                              |
               conceptual/internal mapping
                              |
   Internal level       one internal schema
                              |
                       stored database
  • The internal schema describes physical storage: record layouts, file organisation, indexes and access paths.
  • The conceptual schema describes the whole database for all users: entities, data types, relationships, constraints. It hides storage details.
  • Each external schema (user view) describes the part one user group needs.

There is exactly one internal schema and one conceptual schema, but there can be many external schemas. Requests pass down through the mappings, and results pass back up. The mappings are what give independence.

4. Data independence

Physical data independence is the ability to change the internal schema without changing the conceptual schema. Examples are adding an index, moving a file to another disk or changing a file organisation. Only the conceptual/internal mapping changes.

Logical data independence is the ability to change the conceptual schema without changing external schemas or application programs. Examples are adding a column or splitting a table. Only the external/conceptual mappings change. It is harder to achieve, because programs refer directly to tables and columns.

5. Data models, languages and users

A data model is a set of concepts for describing data, relationships, semantics and constraints. Elmasri groups them as high-level or conceptual (ER), representational or implementation (relational, network, hierarchical) and low-level or physical. The hierarchical model stores records as trees of parent–child links (IBM’s IMS). The network model stores them as a graph of owner–member sets (CODASYL/DBTG). The relational model (Codd, 1970) stores everything as tables. Object-based and semi-structured (XML, JSON) models complete the list.

Languages: a DDL defines schemas, and its output is stored in the data dictionary (system catalog), which holds metadata. A DML retrieves and changes data. A procedural DML says what data is needed and how to get it. A declarative (non-procedural) DML, such as SQL, says only what. Elmasri also names an SDL (storage definition) and a VDL (view definition).

The database administrator (DBA) defines the schema, defines storage structures and access methods, modifies the schema and physical organisation, grants authorisation, and does routine maintenance such as backups and space monitoring. Korth’s users are naive users (use forms and apps), application programmers, sophisticated users (write queries) and specialised users (CAD, knowledge bases).

Inside the DBMS, the query processor contains the DDL interpreter, the DML compiler (which also optimises queries) and the query evaluation engine. The storage manager contains the authorisation and integrity manager, the transaction manager, the file manager and the buffer manager. In a two-tier architecture the client application talks to the database server directly (through ODBC or JDBC). In a three-tier architecture the client talks to an application server, which holds the business logic and talks to the database.

6. The ER model

An entity is a thing with independent existence, such as one student. An entity set is all entities of one type. Attributes come in pairs of kinds:

KindMeaningChen symbol
Simple vs compositeName = (First, Middle, Last) is compositeellipse with sub-ellipses
Single-valued vs multivaluedPhone numbers of a studentdouble ellipse
Stored vs derivedAge derived from DateOfBirthdashed ellipse
Key attributeuniquely identifies an entityunderlined name
Partial key (discriminator)identifies a weak entity within one ownerdashed underline

Other symbols: rectangle = entity set, double rectangle = weak entity set, diamond = relationship set, double diamond = identifying relationship, double line = total participation.

A relationship associates entities. Its degree is the number of entity sets taking part: unary (recursive), binary or ternary. In a recursive relationship, such as EMPLOYEE supervises EMPLOYEE, role names (supervisor, subordinate) tell the two ends apart. Relationships can have descriptive attributes, such as the Grade of ENROLS.

Two structural constraints apply to binary relationships:

  • Cardinality ratio (the maximum): 1:1, 1:N, N:1 or M:N. In DEPARTMENT 1—N EMPLOYEE, one department has many employees and each employee works for one department.
  • Participation (the minimum): total if every entity must take part (double line), partial otherwise. Total participation is also called an existence dependency.

The (min, max) notation writes a pair on each line. (min, max) next to entity set E means each entity of E takes part in at least min and at most max relationship instances. For WORKS_FOR, EMPLOYEE gets (1,1) and DEPARTMENT gets (0,N). Notice that the “N” now sits next to DEPARTMENT, the opposite end from the 1:N labels. This reversal is a classic trap. In Korth’s arrow notation, an arrow from the relationship to an entity set means “one”: each entity on the other side relates to at most one entity there.

Counting relationship instances. With |A| = m and |B| = n, a binary relationship has at most m × n instances if it is M:N. If it is 1:N with the N side B, each B appears at most once, so there are at most n instances. If it is 1:1, there are at most min(m, n). Total participation raises the minimum: in 1:N with B total, each B appears exactly once, so there are exactly n instances.

7. Weak entity sets

A weak entity set has no key of its own. DEPENDENT (Name, Relationship) is the textbook case: two employees can each have a dependent named Anu. A weak entity is identified by its owner (identifying) entity set through an identifying relationship, which is always 1:N (owner to weak) or 1:1, with total participation of the weak side. Its partial key (discriminator) is unique only within one owner, so the weak entity’s key = owner’s primary key + partial key. A weak entity set can itself own another weak entity set.

8. Enhanced ER (EER)

  • Superclass/subclass: every subclass entity is also a superclass entity and inherits its attributes and relationships.
  • Specialisation (top-down): define subclasses of an entity set, such as EMPLOYEE into SECRETARY, ENGINEER and TECHNICIAN. Generalisation (bottom-up): merge the shared features of CAR and TRUCK into VEHICLE.
  • Disjointness constraint: disjoint (an entity is in at most one subclass, marked d) or overlapping (it can be in several, marked o).
  • Completeness constraint: total (every superclass entity is in some subclass, double line) or partial.
  • Predicate-defined (condition-defined) subclasses are decided by an attribute value, such as JobType = ‘Engineer’. User-defined ones are decided by the user.
  • A lattice has a shared subclass with more than one superclass (multiple inheritance). A category or union type is a subclass of the union of different superclasses, such as OWNER being a PERSON, a BANK or a COMPANY.
  • Aggregation (Korth) treats a relationship set as a higher-level entity so that it can take part in another relationship.

9. ER-to-relational mapping

The Elmasri–Navathe algorithm runs in this order:

  1. Strong entity: one relation with all its simple attributes. Composite attributes are flattened into their components, and derived attributes are usually not stored.
  2. Weak entity: one relation with its attributes plus the owner’s key as a foreign key. Primary key = owner key + partial key. The identifying relationship needs no table.
  3. Binary 1:1: the foreign-key approach puts the other side’s key in one relation, preferably the side with total participation. The merged-relation approach puts both into one relation, which is valid when both sides are total. The cross-reference approach adds a third relation (rarely used).
  4. Binary 1:N: add the 1-side key as a foreign key in the N-side relation, along with the relationship’s attributes. No new table.
  5. Binary M:N: a new relation holding both keys as foreign keys. Their combination is the primary key, plus the relationship’s attributes.
  6. Multivalued attribute: a new relation (entity key, value), with both columns forming the key.
  7. n-ary relationship (n ≥ 3): a new relation with the keys of all participants.

EER specialisation adds step 8, with four options. 8A: one relation for the superclass and one for each subclass (subclass key = superclass key). This works for any constraint. 8B: one relation per subclass only, each with all inherited attributes. Use it only for total specialisation, preferably disjoint. 8C: a single relation with one type attribute, for disjoint subclasses (it creates NULLs). 8D: a single relation with one Boolean flag per subclass, for overlapping subclasses.

Minimum-table convention used in NET keys: one table per entity set (strong or weak) + one per M:N relationship + one per multivalued attribute + one per relationship of degree ≥ 3. A 1:N or ordinary 1:1 relationship adds nothing. A 1:1 with total participation on both sides lets two entity tables merge into one. A recursive 1:N adds a self-referencing foreign key and no table; a recursive M:N adds one table.

Worked examples

Example 1: minimum tables for a library

Entity sets BOOK, MEMBER and PUBLISHER. PUBLISHER–BOOK is 1:N. MEMBER–BOOK (BORROWS, with attribute IssueDate) is M:N. MEMBER has a multivalued attribute Email and a derived attribute Age.

  1. Entities: BOOK, MEMBER, PUBLISHER, so the running count is 3.
  2. PUBLISHER–BOOK is 1:N: put PublisherID as a foreign key in BOOK. The count stays 3.
  3. BORROWS is M:N: BORROWS(MemberID, BookID, IssueDate), so the count is 4.
  4. Email is multivalued: MEMBER_EMAIL(MemberID, Email), so the count is 5.
  5. Age is derived, so it is not stored. Answer: 5 tables.

Example 2: the 1:1 cases

E1(a, b) and E2(c, d) are joined by a 1:1 relationship R.

ParticipationMinimum tablesDesign
partial on both sides2E1(a, b, c) with c UNIQUE and nullable, E2(c, d)
E1 total, E2 partial2E1(a, b, c) with c UNIQUE NOT NULL, E2(c, d)
total on both sides1E(a, b, c, d); key a, and c is also a candidate key

Why not merge in the second case? E2 entities without a partner would need NULL in a, but a is E1’s key and cannot be NULL. So a merged table fails whenever any entity can be unpaired.

Example 3: a weak entity chain

EMPLOYEE(Ssn, Name) owns the weak entity DEPENDENT(Dname, Relation) through DEPENDENTS_OF. DEPENDENT has a multivalued attribute Allergy.

  1. EMPLOYEE(Ssn, Name): the primary key is Ssn.
  2. DEPENDENT(Essn, Dname, Relation), with Essn referencing EMPLOYEE. The primary key is {Essn, Dname}.
  3. DEPENDENT_ALLERGY(Essn, Dname, Allergy), whose foreign key is (Essn, Dname), referencing DEPENDENT. A multivalued attribute of a weak entity carries the weak entity’s full key.
  4. DEPENDENTS_OF gets no table. Answer: 3 tables, and the allergy table has 3 columns, all in its key.

Example 4: EER mapping options

EMPLOYEE(Eid, Name, Salary) is specialised, disjoint and total, into SECRETARY(TypingSpeed), ENGINEER(EngType) and TECHNICIAN(TGrade).

  • 8A: EMPLOYEE plus 3 subclass relations, each keyed by Eid, gives 4 tables.
  • 8B: 3 relations, each carrying Eid, Name and Salary, gives 3 tables. This is allowed only because the specialisation is total. Otherwise an employee in no subclass would be lost.
  • 8C: EMPLOYEE(Eid, Name, Salary, JobType, TypingSpeed, EngType, TGrade) gives 1 table, with NULLs in the non-matching columns.

So the “minimum” is 1 if a single table is allowed, 3 with no NULLs, and 4 for the general method. Read the question’s conditions.

Example 5: relationship-instance counts

|A| = 40 and |B| = 25.

  • R is M:N: at most 40 × 25 = 1000 instances.
  • R is 1:N (A one, B many): at most 25, since each B is used once. If B is total, there are exactly 25.
  • R is 1:1: at most min(40, 25) = 25. If A is total, every A needs a distinct B, which is impossible with only 25 B entities. The constraint cannot be satisfied.

Database interfaces and system architectures

The syllabus pairs "database languages" with interfaces: the ways different users reach the DBMS. Elmasri’s list is the one NET draws on.

InterfaceHow it worksTypical user
Menu-based (including web and mobile apps)The user picks options from menus step by step; no query syntax to rememberCasual users who browse
Forms-basedA form is filled in to insert data or to state what to retrieveNaive users; data-entry staff
Graphical user interface (GUI)The schema is shown as a diagram; the query is built by pointing and clickingCasual users
Natural languageAn English request is interpreted against the schema and a dictionary of words; the system asks for clarification when unsureCasual users
Keyword-based searchLike a web search engine: keywords are matched and results rankedCasual users
Speech input and outputSpoken queries and spoken answers (enquiry lines, bookings)Casual users on the phone
Interfaces for parametric usersA small, fixed set of operations bound to function keys or short commands, repeated all dayBank tellers, reservation clerks
Interfaces for the DBAPrivileged commands: create accounts, set system parameters, grant authorisation, change the schemaDBA staff

Alongside these sit the DBMS utilities: loading data files, backup, database reorganisation (for example rebuilding a file with a new organisation) and performance monitoring.

Centralised architecture. In early systems, the DBMS, the application programs and the user-interface processing all ran on one mainframe. Users worked at terminals that only displayed output. As hardware became cheap, the display and application work moved to the user’s PC, but the DBMS itself stayed on one machine.

Basic client/server architecture. Specialised servers (file server, printer server, web server, e-mail server, database server) offer services to client machines over a network. A client is a machine with a user interface and local processing that uses a server when it needs a service it does not have.

  • Two-tier. The user interface and application programs run on the client. The DBMS runs on the server, which is often called the query server or SQL server. The client sends SQL through a standard API: ODBC (C and most languages) or JDBC (Java). The design is simple, but every client carries the application logic and connects to the database directly.
  • Three-tier (and n-tier). An application server (or web server) sits in the middle. The client (often a browser) holds only the presentation layer. The middle tier holds the business rules, checks credentials and sends SQL to the database server, and it can pool connections and balance load. Adding more layers, for example a separate web server and application server, gives an n-tier design.
NTA trap: "three-tier is faster because it has fewer hops" is false: it adds a hop. Its gains are security (the database is not exposed to end-user machines), easier maintenance (business logic lives in one place) and scalability. Also, the ODBC/JDBC link from the client straight to the database is the mark of two-tier, not three-tier.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemRule / fact
Strong or weak entity set1 table each
1:N relationship0 tables (FK on the N side, with the relationship’s attributes)
1:1 relationship0 tables; both sides total means the two entities merge into 1 table
M:N relationship1 table; PK = both keys together
n-ary relationship (n ≥ 3)1 table
Multivalued attribute1 table (owner key + value)
Composite / derived attributeflattened / not stored
Weak entity PKowner PK + partial key
Max instancesM:N: m × n; 1:N: n (the N side); 1:1: min(m, n)
Schemas1 internal, 1 conceptual, many external
Physical independenceinternal changes; conceptual/internal mapping absorbs it
Logical independenceconceptual changes; external/conceptual mappings absorb it (harder)
Specialisation / generalisationtop-down / bottom-up
EER constraintsdisjoint (d) or overlapping (o); total or partial
Two-tier / three-tierclient ↔ DB server (ODBC/JDBC) / client ↔ application server ↔ DB server
Parametric-user interfacefixed operations on function keys (bank tellers, booking clerks)

NTA traps

  • Counting a 1:N relationship as a table. Wrong reasoning: “every diamond is a table”. Fix: only M:N and n-ary diamonds (and recursive M:N) become tables.
  • Merging a 1:1 with one side total. Wrong: “1:1 always merges”. Fix: merge only if both sides are total; otherwise a key would need NULL.
  • Weak entity key = partial key. Fix: the key is owner key + partial key.
  • Reading (min,max) as a cardinality ratio. Fix: (1,1) next to EMPLOYEE means each employee is in exactly one instance, which makes EMPLOYEE the N side.
  • Swapping the data independences. Fix: adding an index is physical; adding a column is logical. Logical is harder.
  • Forgetting the multivalued attribute table, or giving a derived or composite attribute a table.
  • Calling generalisation top-down. Fix: generalisation goes bottom-up, from existing entity sets up to a superclass.
  • “There is one external schema.” Fix: there are many external schemas but one conceptual and one internal schema.

How NTA asks this

  • Match the lists: ER symbols ↔ meanings; schema levels ↔ descriptions; data models ↔ products (IMS is hierarchical, IDMS/CODASYL is network). Memorise the symbol table above.
  • Assertion–Reason: data independence, weak entity participation, why M:N needs a table.
  • Numerical: minimum tables, and maximum or minimum relationship instances. Write a running count.
  • Multiple-select: file-system disadvantages, DBA duties, mapping facts.
  • Sequence: the mapping algorithm steps, or the flow of a query through the levels (external → conceptual → internal).

Mini-example: Assertion–Reason

(A): An M:N relationship cannot be represented by a foreign key in either entity table. (R): A foreign-key column holds one value per row.

A is true. R is true and it explains A: each student row would need several course keys in one column. Answer: option 1.

Elimination trick: in table-count questions, the answer options usually differ by one. Recount only the items that are commonly miscounted: 1:N diamonds (add 0), multivalued attributes (add 1) and 1:1 total-total (subtract 1). That settles the answer in seconds.

terms.definition: ANSI/SPARC design with internal, conceptual and external levels, linked by two mappings.
Changing the internal schema (files, indexes) without changing the conceptual schema or programs.
Changing the conceptual schema without changing external views or programs; harder to achieve.
Entity set with no key of its own; identified by an owner entity plus its partial key (discriminator).
Maximum number of relationship instances an entity can take part in: 1:1, 1:N or M:N.
Every entity of the set must take part in the relationship (double line); an existence dependency.
Attribute with a set of values for one entity (double ellipse); maps to its own table.
Attribute computed from others, such as Age from DateOfBirth (dashed ellipse); not stored.
Top-down definition of subclasses / bottom-up merging of entity sets into a superclass.
System catalog holding metadata: schemas, constraints, users and storage details.

lessons.examTip: For “minimum tables” count one table per entity set (strong or weak), add one per M:N relationship, one per multivalued attribute and one per relationship of degree three or more; 1:N and ordinary 1:1 add nothing, and a 1:1 with total participation on both sides merges two tables into one.

steps: Download practice-set.md and solutions.md. Keep solutions.md closed.
Attempt problems 1–8 in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace). For every table-count problem, write the running count entity by entity.
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes.
Check with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (for example “counted a 1:N relationship as a table”).
Redraw the ER diagrams of problems 1 and 12 from the text, using Chen notation, and map each one to table schemas with primary and foreign keys.
Redo the wrong ones after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct.
All five table-count problems (1, 2, 3, 12, 13) correct.
Problems 9–15 solved within 12 minutes.
Your error log names the trap for every mistake.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Internal = physical storage (I); conceptual = the whole logical database for all users (IV); external = one user group’s view (III); the conceptual/internal mapping relates stored data to the logical structure (II). Option 2 swaps conceptual and external, a common slip. Option 3 swaps the internal level with its mapping.

b: I. How records, files and indexes are stored
II. How the stored data corresponds to the logical structure of the whole database
III. The part of the database one user group sees
IV. Entities, data types, relationships and constraints of the whole database

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: An ER diagram has entity sets STUDENT, COURSE, DEPARTMENT and INSTRUCTOR. STUDENT–COURSE (ENROLS) is M:N. DEPARTMENT–INSTRUCTOR is 1:N and INSTRUCTOR–COURSE (TEACHES) is 1:N, both with partial participation. STUDENT has one multivalued attribute Phone. What is the minimum number of relational tables needed?
quiz.explanation: Entities give 4 tables. The M:N relationship ENROLS needs its own table (+1). Each 1:N relationship is absorbed as a foreign key in the N-side table (+0). The multivalued attribute Phone needs a separate table (+1). Total = 4 + 1 + 1 = 6. Answer 7 comes from wrongly giving a 1:N relationship a table; 5 comes from forgetting the multivalued attribute.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Both are standard textbook statements, and R is exactly why A holds: programs name tables and columns, so changing the conceptual schema tends to break them, while a new index or file organisation does not. So option 1.

stmts: Assertion (A): Logical data independence is harder to achieve than physical data independence.
Reason (R): Application programs depend much more heavily on the logical structure of the data they access than on how that data is stored.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Statement I is true: a weak entity cannot exist without its owner, so its participation is total (existence dependency). Statement II is false: the partial key (discriminator) is unique only within one owner, so the key is the owner’s primary key plus the partial key.

stmts: Statement I: A weak entity set always has total participation in its identifying relationship.
Statement II: The primary key of a relation that represents a weak entity set is its partial key alone.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: In Chen’s ER notation, a double ellipse represents:
quiz.explanation: Double ellipse = multivalued attribute. A derived attribute uses a dashed ellipse, a composite attribute is an ellipse joined to its component ellipses, and a key attribute is underlined.

quiz.question: Which of the following statements are correct about mapping a binary M:N relationship R between entity sets E1 and E2?
options: A, B, C and D only
quiz.explanation: A, B and D are true. C is false: an attribute of an M:N relationship (such as Grade of ENROLS) describes a pair, so it cannot live in either entity’s table. E is false: a single foreign key column can hold only one related entity, which works only for 1:1 or 1:N.

stmts: A. R needs a separate relation.
B. The primary key of R’s relation is the combination of the primary keys of E1 and E2.
C. The descriptive attributes of R can be moved into E1’s relation.
D. Each component of R’s key is a foreign key.
E. R can be absorbed by adding a foreign key to E2’s relation.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Entity set A has 40 entities and entity set B has 25 entities. Relationship R between them is 1:N (one A to many B) and B has total participation in R. How many relationship instances does R contain?
quiz.explanation: In a 1:N relationship each B entity is linked to at most one A. Total participation of B means each B is linked to at least one A. So each of the 25 B entities appears in exactly one instance: 25. 1000 = 40 × 25 would be the maximum for M:N; 40 wrongly counts the one side.

quiz.question: Arrange the following steps of the standard ER-to-relational mapping algorithm (Elmasri–Navathe) in the correct order.
quiz.explanation: The algorithm maps strong entities first (B), then weak entities, which need the owner’s key (C), then 1:1 and 1:N relationships (E), then M:N relationships (A), then multivalued attributes (D), and finally n-ary relationships. Weak entities cannot come before strong ones because they borrow the owner’s key.

stmts: A. Map binary M:N relationship types
B. Map regular (strong) entity types
C. Map weak entity types
D. Map multivalued attributes
E. Map binary 1:N relationship types
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Merging the common features of entity sets CAR and TRUCK into a higher-level entity set VEHICLE is called:
quiz.explanation: Combining existing lower-level entity sets into a superclass is generalisation, a bottom-up process. Specialisation is the top-down opposite (start from VEHICLE and define subclasses). Aggregation treats a relationship as an entity.

quiz.question: Entity sets E1 (key a, attribute b) and E2 (key c, attribute d) are linked by a 1:1 relationship R with total participation on BOTH sides. R has no attributes. What is the minimum number of tables required, with no NULL allowed in any key?
quiz.explanation: With a 1:1 relationship and total participation on both sides, every E1 entity is paired with exactly one E2 entity and vice versa, so both can be stored in one table (a, b, c, d) with a (or c) as the key and no NULLs. With partial participation on either side you would need 2 tables.

lessons.title: Relational model, algebra and calculus
lessons.summaryHtml: The relational model stores data as relations (tables): a set of tuples over named attributes, each drawn from a domain. Keys identify tuples: a superkey is any identifying set, a candidate key is a minimal one, the primary key is the chosen candidate key, and a foreign key points to another relation’s key. Integrity constraints (domain, key, entity and referential integrity) keep the data valid. Relational algebra is a procedural query language built from σ, π, ∪, −, × and ρ, with joins, intersection and division derived from them. Tuple and domain relational calculus are declarative equivalents: every safe calculus query has an algebra equivalent (Codd’s theorem).
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

The relational model says: store everything as tables, and describe every question as an operation on tables. A relation is a table, a tuple is a row, and an attribute is a named column. Relational algebra gives you operators, such as “filter rows” or “join two tables”, that take tables in and give a table out, so you can chain them. Relational calculus describes the result you want as a logical condition and leaves the steps to the system. SQL is built on both ideas.

Why it matters for NET

Expect a few questions from this lesson in most papers. The dominant patterns are output questions (“how many tuples does this expression return?”), division and “for all” queries, superkey and candidate-key counting, bounds on the size of a join, integrity-constraint violations and cascading deletes, and statements about relational calculus, safety and equivalence. Output questions reward slow, careful work: write each intermediate relation.

Concepts in depth

1. Relations and terminology

A domain is a set of atomic values, such as the set of 10-digit phone numbers. A relation schema R(A1, …, An) names the relation and its attributes. A relation instance r(R) is a set of n-tuples, each value drawn from its attribute’s domain. Formally, r(R) ⊆ dom(A1) × … × dom(An). The degree (arity) is the number of attributes. The cardinality is the number of tuples.

Because a relation is a set, it has no duplicate tuples and no order of tuples. Values are atomic, which is first normal form. A NULL means unknown, not applicable or missing.

2. Keys

  • Superkey: any set of attributes that no two distinct tuples can share. The set of all attributes is always a superkey.
  • Candidate key: a minimal superkey. No proper subset is a superkey.
  • Primary key: the candidate key chosen by the designer. The others are alternate keys. A relation has one primary key, which may be composite.
  • Prime attribute: an attribute that belongs to some candidate key. The others are non-prime. This matters in normalisation.
  • Foreign key: attributes of R whose values must equal the primary key of some tuple of S (the referenced relation), or be NULL. R and S can be the same relation.

Counting superkeys. With n attributes and one candidate key of k attributes, any superset of the key is a superkey, so there are 2n−k superkeys. With several candidate keys, use inclusion–exclusion on the “contains key Ki” sets. The sets containing both K1 and K2 are the supersets of K1 ∪ K2, so |S1 ∪ S2| = 2n−|K1| + 2n−|K2| − 2n−|K1 ∪ K2|.

Maximum number of candidate keys. No candidate key can contain another, so the keys form an antichain of subsets. By Sperner’s theorem the largest antichain has C(n, ⌊n/2⌋) sets. For n = 4 that is 6, and for n = 6 it is 20.

3. Integrity constraints

  • Domain constraint: each value comes from the attribute’s domain.
  • Key constraint: candidate-key values are unique.
  • Entity integrity: no primary-key attribute is NULL.
  • Referential integrity: every non-NULL foreign-key value exists as a primary key in the referenced relation.
OperationCan violate
Insertdomain, key, entity integrity, and referential integrity (in the referencing relation)
Deleteonly referential integrity (when a referenced tuple is deleted)
Updateof a non-key attribute: only domain. Of a key or foreign key: the same as a delete followed by an insert

When a delete would break referential integrity, the DBMS can restrict (reject it), cascade (also delete the referencing tuples, recursively) or set null / set default in the referencing tuples.

Codd’s rules for a relational DBMS are sometimes matched in NET: rule 1 information (all data in tables), rule 2 guaranteed access (table + key + column), rule 3 systematic treatment of NULLs, rule 4 an active online catalog, rule 8 physical data independence, rule 9 logical data independence, rule 10 integrity independence, rule 12 non-subversion. Rule 0, the foundation rule, sits above the twelve.

4. Relational algebra

Every operator takes one or two relations and returns a relation. This closure is why expressions can be nested.

OperatorNotationResult degreeNotes

ProjectionπL(R)|L|removes duplicates; πL1(πL2R) = πL1R if L1 ⊆ L2
Union, differenceR ∪ S, R − Ssameneed union compatibility; − is not commutative

RenameρS(B1,…)(R)sameneeded for self-joins

The fundamental (complete) set is {σ, π, ∪, −, ×} plus ρ. Everything else is derived: R ∩ S = R − (R − S); a join is σ over ×; and division is:

R(X, Y) ÷ S(Y) = π_X(R) − π_X( (π_X(R) × S) − R )
  T1 = π_X(R)              every candidate X
  T2 = T1 × S              every X paired with every required Y
  T3 = T2 − R              the (X, Y) pairs that are missing
  T4 = π_X(T3)             X values missing at least one Y
  result = T1 − T4

Outer joins keep unmatched tuples, padded with NULLs. The left outer join (⟕) keeps every tuple of the left relation, the right outer join (⟖) every tuple of the right, and the full outer join (⟗) both. The semijoin R ⋉ S keeps the R tuples that have a match, and the anti-join keeps those that do not. The extended algebra adds aggregation GγF(A)(R) (grouping with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) and generalised projection with arithmetic. Basic relational algebra cannot express aggregation or transitive closure (for example, all ancestors of a person), because each expression has a fixed number of joins.

6. Relational calculus

Tuple relational calculus (TRC) has the form {t | P(t)}, where t is a tuple variable and P is a formula. Atoms are t ∈ R, t.A θ s.B and t.A θ c. They are combined with ∧, ∨, ¬, → and the quantifiers ∃ and ∀. A variable is bound if a quantifier introduces it and free otherwise. Only the result variable may be free. Useful identities: ∀t P ≡ ¬∃t ¬P, and P → Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q.

Domain relational calculus (DRC) has the form {⟨x1, …, xn⟩ | P(x1, …, xn)}, where the variables range over attribute values, not tuples. QBE is based on DRC, and SQL’s SELECT–FROM–WHERE is closest to TRC.

A calculus expression is safe if its result is finite and every value in it appears in the database or the query (the domain of the expression). {t | ¬(t ∈ R)} is unsafe. Codd’s theorem: relational algebra, safe TRC and safe DRC have the same expressive power. A language with that power is called relationally complete. Algebra is procedural (it gives an order of operations); calculus is non-procedural.

“For all” in TRC. Students enrolled in every core course:

{ s.Sid | s ∈ ENROL ∧ ∀c ( c ∈ CORE → ∃e ( e ∈ ENROL ∧ e.Sid = s.Sid ∧ e.Cid = c.Cid ) ) }

This is ENROL ÷ CORE in algebra, and a double NOT EXISTS in SQL.

Worked examples

Examples 1 and 2 use these relations:

EMP                                DEPT
Eid  Name    Dno  Salary            Dno  Dname  Loc
1    Asha    10   50000             10   Sales  Kochi
2    Bala    20   40000             20   HR     Delhi
3    Chitra  10   60000             40   R&D    Pune
4    Deepak  30   45000
5    Esha    20   40000

Example 1: joins and outer joins

  1. EMP ⋈ DEPT joins on Dno. Employees with Dno 10 or 20 match: Asha, Bala, Chitra and Esha, so there are 4 tuples. Deepak (Dno 30) and department 40 have no partner. The degree is 4 + 3 − 1 = 6.
  2. EMP ⟕ DEPT adds Deepak with NULL Dname and Loc: 5 tuples.
  3. EMP ⟗ DEPT also adds department 40 with NULL Eid, Name and Salary: 6 tuples.
  4. EMP × DEPT has 5 × 3 = 15 tuples of degree 7.
  5. πDname(EMP ⋈ DEPT) = {Sales, HR}: 2 tuples, because duplicates are removed.

Example 2: highest salary without MAX

Rename EMP twice, as E1 and E2. The pairs where E1.Salary < E2.Salary identify every employee who earns less than someone:

Lower  = π_E1.Eid( σ_E1.Salary < E2.Salary ( ρ_E1(EMP) × ρ_E2(EMP) ) )  = {1, 2, 4, 5}
Result = π_Eid(EMP) − Lower                                          = {3}

Only Chitra (Eid 3, 60000) is never beaten. This “all minus those beaten by someone” pattern is how basic algebra expresses MAX.

Example 3: division step by step

ENROL = {(S1,C1), (S1,C2), (S1,C3), (S2,C1), (S2,C3), (S3,C1), (S3,C2), (S3,C3), (S4,C2)} and CORE = {C1, C3}.

  1. T1 = πSid(ENROL) = {S1, S2, S3, S4}.
  2. T2 = T1 × CORE has 8 pairs.
  3. T3 = T2 − ENROL = {(S4, C1), (S4, C3)}, the missing pairs.
  4. T4 = πSid(T3) = {S4}.
  5. Result = T1 − T4 = {S1, S2, S3}.

If CORE = {C1, C2, C3}, S2 is missing C2, so the result is {S1, S3}. Division has at most ⌊9/2⌋ = 4 tuples here, and it has 3.

Example 4: counting superkeys

R(A, B, C, D, E) has candidate keys AB and CD.

  1. Supersets of AB: 25−2 = 8.
  2. Supersets of CD: 25−2 = 8.
  3. Supersets of both, which means supersets of ABCD: 25−4 = 2.
  4. Total = 8 + 8 − 2 = 14 superkeys.

With a single key A in R(A, B, C, D, E) there are 24 = 16.

Example 5: cascading delete

NODE(Id, Parent) has Parent as a foreign key referencing Id, with ON DELETE CASCADE. The tuples are (10, NULL), (11, 10), (12, 11), (13, 11), (14, 12), (15, 10) and (16, 15). Delete (11, 10):

  1. The children of 11, which are 12 and 13, are deleted.
  2. The child of 12, which is 14, is deleted. 13 has no children.
  3. In total 4 tuples go (11, 12, 13 and 14), and 3 remain: 10, 15 and 16.

Example 6: size bounds

|R| = 20 and |S| = 30, union compatible: R ∪ S has between 30 (R ⊆ S) and 50 tuples (disjoint). R − S has between max(0, 20 − 30) = 0 and 20. For R(X, Y) with 12 tuples and S(Y) with 4 tuples, R ÷ S has at most ⌊12/4⌋ = 3 tuples, because each result X needs 4 distinct tuples in R.

Codd’s twelve rules in full

In 1985 E. F. Codd published twelve rules (plus a foundation rule 0) that a DBMS must follow to be called fully relational. No commercial product meets all of them, but NET matches rule numbers with names and asks which rule a situation breaks. Learn the whole list, not only the famous ones.

RuleNameWhat it demands
0Foundation ruleThe system must manage its databases entirely through its relational capabilities.
1Information ruleAll information, including the catalog, is stored as values in tables.
2Guaranteed access ruleEvery value can be reached by table name + primary-key value + column name.
3Systematic treatment of null valuesNULL represents missing or inapplicable data, separately from zero or blank, for every data type.
4Dynamic online catalog based on the relational modelThe catalog (metadata) is itself tables that users query with the same language.
5Comprehensive data sublanguage ruleAt least one language supports data definition, view definition, manipulation, integrity constraints, authorisation and transaction boundaries.
6View updating ruleEvery view that is theoretically updatable must be updatable by the system.
7High-level insert, update and deleteInsert, update and delete work on sets of rows, not only one row at a time.
8Physical data independenceChanging storage or access methods does not change applications.
9Logical data independenceInformation-preserving changes to base tables do not change applications.
10Integrity independenceIntegrity constraints are defined in the relational language and stored in the catalog, not in application programs.
11Distribution independenceUsers need not know whether, or how, the data is distributed over sites.
12Non-subversion ruleA low-level (record-at-a-time) interface must not be able to bypass the integrity rules and constraints.

A quick memory chain: 1–4 are about how data and metadata are represented (tables, access, NULLs, catalog); 5–7 are about the language (one complete sublanguage, view updates, set-level changes); 8–11 are the four independences (physical, logical, integrity, distribution); 12 guards the back door.

NTA trap: rule 6 is view updating, not "views must exist", and rule 11 is distribution independence, not data independence. Counting questions also trap students: there are twelve numbered rules (1–12), or thirteen if rule 0 is included.

NTA traps

  • Keeping duplicates after π. Wrong: “5 rows in, so 5 rows out”. Fix: algebra works on sets, so count distinct values.
  • Natural join with no common attributes. Wrong: “no match, so an empty result”. Fix: it equals R × S.
  • Join size equals |S|. Wrong: counting the referenced side. Fix: with a NOT NULL FK in R referencing S’s key, the result has exactly |R| tuples.
  • Superkey double counting. Fix: subtract the supersets of K1 ∪ K2.
  • Division reversed. Wrong: returning the Y values. Fix: R ÷ S returns X values paired with all of S.
  • “Delete can violate entity integrity.” Fix: a delete can only break referential integrity.
  • Calling ∩ or ⋈ fundamental. Fix: both are derived.
  • “DRC variables are tuples.” Fix: DRC variables range over domain values.

How NTA asks this

  • Output: small relations and an expression, asking for the result or its tuple count. Work operator by operator from the innermost.
  • Numerical: superkeys, maximum candidate keys, join or division bounds, degree after a join.
  • Match the lists: operators ↔ purposes, languages ↔ bases (SQL ↔ TRC, QBE ↔ DRC), joins ↔ definitions, Codd’s rule numbers ↔ names.
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: derived operators, safety, set semantics, NULLs in keys.
  • Sequence: the division steps, or expressions arranged by result size.

Mini-example: Match the lists

List I: A. R ⋈ S, B. R ⟕ S, C. R ⋉ S, D. R × S. List II: I. all pairs of tuples, II. matched pairs only, III. matched pairs plus unmatched R tuples padded with NULL, IV. R tuples that have a match, with R’s columns only.

Answer: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I. Elimination: fix the easiest pair first (× = all pairs), then strike every option that does not contain D-I.

Speed trick: for output questions, first cross out tuples that can never match (for example, an FK value missing from the other table). Most options then die at once.

terms.definition: Set of attributes whose values are unique for every tuple of every legal instance.
A minimal superkey: remove any attribute and it stops being a superkey.
An attribute that belongs to at least one candidate key.
Attributes whose values must match the primary key of the referenced relation, or be NULL.
No primary-key attribute may be NULL.
Every non-NULL foreign-key value must exist in the referenced relation.
Two relations have the same degree and matching domains, so ∪, ∩ and − are defined.
R(X,Y) ÷ S(Y) returns the X values paired in R with every Y value of S; used for “for all” queries.
A calculus expression guaranteed to give a finite result drawn from values in the database.
A language can express every query of relational algebra; safe TRC and DRC are relationally complete.

lessons.examTip: Before answering any algebra output question, write the intermediate relation of each operator on paper and remember set semantics: π removes duplicates, so count distinct rows only.

steps: Download practice-set.md and solutions.md. Keep solutions.md closed.
Copy the SP and P relations of the practice set onto paper. For problems 1–5, write every intermediate relation, not just the final answer.
Attempt problems 1–8 in 12 minutes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes without notes.
Check with solutions.md and write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (for example “kept duplicates after π”).
Rewrite the division in problem 1 using only π, × and −, and check you get the same answer.
Redo the wrong ones after 24 hours.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct.
Problems 1–5 (algebra output) all correct.
Superkey problems 6 and 7 solved with inclusion–exclusion in under 2 minutes each.
Your error log names the trap for every mistake.

lessons.title: SQL
lessons.summaryHtml: SQL is the standard language of relational databases. It has sublanguages for defining structure (DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE), changing data (DML: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), controlling access (DCL: GRANT, REVOKE) and ending transactions (TCL: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT). A query is processed logically as FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY, and unlike relational algebra it keeps duplicates unless you say DISTINCT. Most exam traps come from NULL: comparisons with NULL are UNKNOWN, aggregates skip NULLs, and NOT IN over a list containing NULL returns nothing. Subqueries (IN, EXISTS, ANY, ALL, correlated), set operations, views, constraints, triggers and stored procedures complete the syllabus.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

SQL (Structured Query Language) is how people and programs talk to a relational database. You describe the table you want, and the DBMS works out how to build it. One language covers defining tables, loading and changing rows, asking questions, controlling who may do what, and grouping changes into transactions. SQL is declarative, like relational calculus, but it works on bags (multisets) and has NULLs. Those two differences create most of the exam traps.

Why it matters for NET

SQL is one of the most tested topics in Unit 4. The questions come in three shapes. Output questions give two small tables and a query and ask for the result: NULL, GROUP BY/HAVING, NOT IN, ALL/ANY and correlated subqueries dominate. Classification questions ask which commands are DDL, DML, DCL or TCL, or what DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP differ in. Concept questions cover views and their updatability, triggers, constraints, and equivalences such as IN = “= ANY”.

Concepts in depth

1. The sublanguages

GroupCommandsPurpose
DDLCREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAMEdefine and change schema objects
DMLSELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGEread and change rows
DCLGRANT, REVOKEprivileges
TCLCOMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINTtransaction control

DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP. DELETE is DML. It removes chosen rows (WHERE is allowed), logs each row, fires DELETE triggers and can be rolled back. TRUNCATE is DDL. It removes all rows by deallocating pages, has no WHERE and fires no row triggers, and in most systems (such as Oracle) it commits implicitly. DROP removes the table itself: its structure, data, indexes and constraints.

2. Constraints

CREATE TABLE EMP (
  eid    INT PRIMARY KEY,                     -- NOT NULL + UNIQUE
  ename  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  dept   VARCHAR(10) REFERENCES DEPT(dname)
                     ON DELETE SET NULL,      -- or CASCADE / RESTRICT
  salary INT CHECK (salary > 0),             -- NULL passes a CHECK
  email  VARCHAR(40) UNIQUE,                  -- several NULLs allowed in most DBMSs
  joined DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE
);

A table has one PRIMARY KEY but may have many UNIQUE constraints. A FOREIGN KEY may reference a primary key or any UNIQUE column. A CHECK constraint rejects a row only when its condition is FALSE; UNKNOWN (because of a NULL) passes. ALTER TABLE ADD/DROP CONSTRAINT changes constraints later. CREATE ASSERTION defines a database-wide condition, which standard SQL supports but few products implement.

3. The SELECT statement

SELECT [DISTINCT] columns / expressions / aggregates     -- 5, then 6 DISTINCT
FROM   tables and joins                                    -- 1
WHERE  row condition                                       -- 2
GROUP BY grouping columns                                  -- 3
HAVING group condition                                     -- 4
ORDER BY columns [ASC | DESC]                              -- 7

The numbers give the logical evaluation order. It explains several rules: WHERE cannot use aggregates or SELECT aliases, HAVING can use aggregates, and ORDER BY can use aliases. Unlike relational algebra, SQL keeps duplicate rows unless you write DISTINCT. So SELECT dept FROM EMP returns 6 rows, while πdept returns distinct values.

GROUP BY rule: every non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY. All NULLs in a grouping column form one group. Useful predicates: BETWEEN a AND b (inclusive), IN (list), LIKE with % (any string) and _ (exactly one character), and IS [NOT] NULL.

4. Joins

  • INNER JOIN … ON keeps matching pairs. Rows whose join column is NULL never match.
  • NATURAL JOIN joins on all same-named columns and shows each of them once. USING (col) names the columns explicitly.
  • LEFT / RIGHT / FULL OUTER JOIN keep the unmatched rows of the left, right or both sides, padded with NULL.
  • CROSS JOIN (or FROM A, B with no condition) gives the Cartesian product.
  • A self-join uses two aliases of one table, for example to pair each employee with their manager.

A classic trap: in a LEFT JOIN, a WHERE condition on the right table (WHERE m.dept = 'CS') throws away the NULL-padded rows and turns it back into an inner join. Put such a condition in the ON clause to keep them.

5. NULL and three-valued logic

pqp AND qp OR qNOT p
TRUEUNKNOWNUNKNOWNTRUEFALSE
FALSEUNKNOWNFALSEUNKNOWNTRUE
UNKNOWNUNKNOWNUNKNOWNUNKNOWNUNKNOWN
  • Any arithmetic or comparison with NULL gives NULL or UNKNOWN, even NULL = NULL. Test with IS NULL.
  • WHERE, HAVING and ON keep only TRUE. CHECK rejects only FALSE.
  • COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(col), SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN ignore NULLs. So AVG(col) = SUM(col)/COUNT(col), not SUM(col)/COUNT(*).
  • On an empty set, COUNT returns 0 and SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN return NULL.
  • DISTINCT, GROUP BY, UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT treat two NULLs as duplicates. Comparisons do not.
  • COALESCE(a, b, …) returns the first non-NULL argument, and NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a = b.

6. Subqueries

FormTRUE whenEquivalent
x IN (S)x equals some value of Sx = ANY (S)
x NOT IN (S)x differs from every value; UNKNOWN if S contains NULL and there is no matchx <> ALL (S)
x > ANY (S) (or SOME)x beats at least one valuex > MIN(S) when S has no NULL
x > ALL (S)x beats every valuex > MAX(S) when S has no NULL
EXISTS (S)S returns at least one rownever UNKNOWN

Empty set: x > ALL (empty) is TRUE, x > ANY (empty) is FALSE. A NULL in S can make ALL/NOT IN UNKNOWN, but EXISTS only asks whether a row exists, so NOT EXISTS is the safe way to write “no matching row”.

A correlated subquery mentions a column of the outer query (s.sid in the query below), so it is logically evaluated once per outer row. A scalar subquery must return at most one value. Standard SQL has no division operator, so “for all” is written with a double NOT EXISTS: “there is no required course that this student has not taken”.

SELECT s.sname FROM STUDENT s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM COURSE c WHERE c.credits = 4
        AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM ENROLL e
                        WHERE e.sid = s.sid AND e.cid = c.cid));

7. Set operations

UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT (Oracle’s MINUS) need union-compatible SELECT lists and remove duplicates. UNION ALL, INTERSECT ALL and EXCEPT ALL keep multiplicities: if a row occurs m times on the left and n times on the right, UNION ALL gives m + n copies, INTERSECT ALL gives min(m, n) and EXCEPT ALL gives max(m − n, 0). Only one ORDER BY is allowed, at the very end.

8. Views

CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT … stores the query, not the data. Every use of v runs against the current base tables, which gives logical data independence and security (show only some columns). A view is generally updatable when it is defined on one base table, has no DISTINCT, GROUP BY, HAVING, aggregate or set operation, and includes enough columns (the key and NOT NULL columns without defaults) for an insert to make sense. WITH CHECK OPTION rejects changes made through the view that would produce rows the view cannot see. A materialised view stores the result and must be refreshed.

9. Triggers, procedures and privileges

  • A trigger follows the event–condition–action model. The event is INSERT, UPDATE [OF col] or DELETE on a table. The timing is BEFORE, AFTER or INSTEAD OF (for views). The granularity is FOR EACH ROW (fires once per affected row and can use OLD and NEW) or FOR EACH STATEMENT (fires once, even when no row is affected). Triggers cannot be called directly; the event fires them.
  • A stored procedure is precompiled code stored in the server, invoked with CALL, with IN, OUT and INOUT parameters. A stored function returns a value and can be used inside expressions. Both reduce network traffic and centralise business rules. Cursors let procedural code walk a result row by row. Embedded SQL places SQL inside a host language, while dynamic SQL builds statements at run time.
  • GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE(col), DELETE, REFERENCES ON table TO user [WITH GRANT OPTION]. REVOKE … FROM user CASCADE also removes the privileges the user passed on, and RESTRICT refuses if such grants exist.

Worked examples

All examples use these tables. Note the two NULLs: Dev’s salary and Faiz’s department.

EMP                                   DEPT
eid  ename  dept  salary  mgr         dname  loc
1    Anil   CS    70000   NULL        CS     Kochi
2    Beena  CS    50000   1           IT     Pune
3    Charu  IT    60000   1           HR     Kochi
4    Dev    IT    NULL    3           EC     Delhi
5    Ella   HR    40000   1
6    Faiz   NULL  45000   3

Example 1: aggregates and NULL

  1. COUNT(*) = 6, COUNT(salary) = 5, COUNT(dept) = 5, COUNT(DISTINCT dept) = 3.
  2. SUM(salary) = 70000 + 50000 + 60000 + 40000 + 45000 = 265000.
  3. AVG(salary) = 265000 / 5 = 53000, not 265000 / 6.
  4. SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM EMP GROUP BY dept gives 4 rows: CS 2, IT 2, HR 1 and a NULL group with 1 row (Faiz).

Example 2: WHERE before GROUP BY, HAVING after

SELECT dept, SUM(salary) FROM EMP
WHERE salary > 45000 GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
  1. WHERE keeps Anil, Beena and Charu. Dev’s condition is UNKNOWN, and Ella and Faiz fail it.
  2. The groups are CS {Anil, Beena} and IT {Charu}.
  3. HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 keeps CS. Output: CS, 120000.

Example 3: NOT IN versus NOT EXISTS

Which departments have no employees?

  • WHERE dname NOT IN (SELECT dept FROM EMP) returns no rows, because the subquery contains Faiz’s NULL and EC <> NULL is UNKNOWN.
  • WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM EMP e WHERE e.dept = d.dname) returns EC.
  • SELECT dname FROM DEPT EXCEPT SELECT dept FROM EMP also returns EC, because set operations do not use = on NULLs.

Similarly, salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM EMP WHERE dept = 'IT') returns no rows because of Dev’s NULL.

Example 4: correlated subquery and the Nth highest

SELECT ename FROM EMP e1
WHERE 2 = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT salary) FROM EMP e2
           WHERE e2.salary > e1.salary);

For each e1, count the distinct salaries above it. The distinct salaries are 70000, 60000, 50000, 45000 and 40000. Exactly two are above 50000, so the result is Beena, the third highest. For Dev, e2.salary > NULL is never TRUE, so his count is 0. The second-highest salary is SELECT MAX(salary) FROM EMP WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM EMP) = 60000.

Example 5: join counts

  • EMP JOIN DEPT ON dept = dname: Faiz (NULL) matches nothing, so there are 5 rows.
  • LEFT JOIN: Faiz is kept with a NULL loc, giving 6. RIGHT JOIN: EC is kept, giving 6. FULL JOIN: both, giving 7. CROSS JOIN: 6 × 4 = 24.
  • GROUP BY loc over the inner join: Kochi 3 (Anil, Beena, Ella) and Pune 2.

Example 6: a row-level trigger

CREATE TABLE LOG(eid INT, oldsal INT, newsal INT);
CREATE TRIGGER t_sal AFTER UPDATE OF salary ON EMP
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO LOG VALUES (OLD.eid, OLD.salary, NEW.salary);
END;
UPDATE EMP SET salary = salary + 1000 WHERE dept = 'IT';

The UPDATE touches 2 rows (Charu and Dev), so the row trigger fires twice and LOG gets 2 rows: (3, 60000, 61000) and (4, NULL, NULL), because NULL + 1000 is NULL. A statement-level trigger would fire once. This is SQLite/MySQL-style syntax; Oracle uses :OLD and :NEW inside the body.

SQL data types and domains

Every column in CREATE TABLE gets a data type, and the type decides which values, operators and storage apply. The standard groups are:

GroupTypesPoints NET asks about
Exact numericINTEGER (INT), SMALLINT, BIGINT, NUMERIC(p, s), DECIMAL(p, s)p = total significant digits (precision), s = digits after the point (scale). NUMERIC(6, 2) holds −9999.99 to 9999.99.
Approximate numericFLOAT(p), REAL, DOUBLE PRECISIONBinary floating point: 0.1 is not stored exactly, so never use them for money.
CharacterCHAR(n), VARCHAR(n), CLOBCHAR(n) is fixed length and pads with blanks; VARCHAR(n) stores only the characters given, up to n.
Binary and large objectsBINARY, VARBINARY, BLOBBLOBs hold images, audio and video.
BooleanBOOLEANValues TRUE, FALSE and UNKNOWN (because of NULL).
Date and timeDATE, TIME, TIMESTAMP, INTERVALDATE is YYYY-MM-DD; TIMESTAMP adds the time of day with fractions of a second; DATE − DATE gives an INTERVAL.

A domain is a named type with optional constraints that many columns can share: CREATE DOMAIN MARKS AS NUMERIC(5, 2) CHECK (VALUE BETWEEN 0 AND 100). Changing the domain changes every column that uses it.

Example 7: precision, scale and padding

For NUMERIC(p, s), the largest value is 10p−s − 10−s. NUMERIC(6, 2) allows 6 − 2 = 4 digits before the point, so the largest value is 104 − 0.01 = 9999.99, and 12345.6 is rejected. NUMERIC(5, 5) has no integer digits, so it stores only values below 1, up to 0.99999.

'SQL' stored in CHAR(8) occupies 8 positions (3 letters and 5 blanks); in VARCHAR(8) it occupies 3 characters plus a small length field.

Stored procedures, functions and SQL inside programs

SQL/PSM (persistent stored modules) is the standard for code kept inside the database server. A stored procedure is invoked with CALL and passes values through parameters in three modes: IN (caller to procedure), OUT (procedure to caller) and INOUT (both ways). A stored function declares RETURNS <type>, returns one value and can be used inside expressions and SELECT lists.

CREATE FUNCTION grade(m INT) RETURNS CHAR(1)
BEGIN
  IF m >= 75 THEN RETURN 'A';
  ELSEIF m >= 50 THEN RETURN 'B';
  ELSE RETURN 'C';
  END IF;
END;
SELECT sname, grade(marks) FROM STUDENT;

CREATE PROCEDURE raise_pay(IN d VARCHAR(10), IN pct INT, OUT n INT)
BEGIN
  UPDATE EMP SET salary = salary * (100 + pct) / 100 WHERE dept = d;
  SET n = ROW_COUNT();
END;
CALL raise_pay('IT', 10, @cnt);

The syntax above is MySQL-style; Oracle PL/SQL and SQL Server T-SQL differ in detail but not in idea. Benefits: one network call runs many statements; the logic is shared by all applications; the plan can be compiled once; and security improves, because a user can be granted EXECUTE on the procedure without being granted direct access to the tables (the usual definer-rights mode).

SQL in a host language. SQL works on sets of rows, while C or Java work on one variable at a time. This clash is the impedance mismatch. Three approaches handle it:

  • Embedded SQL: statements start with EXEC SQL, host variables are written with a colon (:roll), and a precompiler turns them into library calls. SQLCODE or SQLSTATE reports success or error.
  • Cursors: a cursor walks a multi-row result one row at a time: DECLARE the cursor for a query, OPEN it (the query runs), FETCH rows in a loop into host variables until no row is left, then CLOSE it.
  • Call-level APIs and dynamic SQL: ODBC and JDBC send SQL strings at run time (Connection, Statement, PreparedStatement, ResultSet in JDBC). Dynamic SQL builds a statement at run time with PREPARE and EXECUTE.

SQL injection

SQL injection is an attack in which user input is pasted into an SQL string, so that the input changes the structure of the query instead of acting as a plain value. It is the classic web-application attack on databases, and Elmasri covers it in the security chapter.

Example 8: a login page that can be injected

USERS has five rows: admin, ravi, sneha, joel and meera, each with a password. The application builds the query by string concatenation:

q = "SELECT * FROM USERS WHERE uname = '" + u + "' AND pwd = '" + p + "'"
  • Password typed as ' OR '1'='1 (user ravi) gives WHERE uname = 'ravi' AND pwd = '' OR '1'='1'. AND binds tighter than OR, so this is (FALSE) OR TRUE, and all 5 rows come back. The attacker logs in.
  • User name typed as admin'-- gives WHERE uname = 'admin'--' AND pwd = '…'. Everything after -- is a comment, so the password test disappears and 1 row (admin) is returned.
  • With a prepared statement, SELECT * FROM USERS WHERE uname = ? AND pwd = ?, the same inputs are compared as ordinary strings and 0 rows match.

Kinds of injection. A tautology makes the WHERE clause always true (OR 1=1). A UNION-based attack appends UNION SELECT to read another table. A piggy-backed (stacked) query adds a second statement after a semicolon, such as ; DROP TABLE USERS. Error-based attacks read data from database error messages. Blind injection gets no output, so it infers data from true/false page changes (boolean-based) or from delays such as SLEEP(5) (time-based). Second-order injection stores the malicious text first and triggers it later, when other code reuses it. Elmasri also names SQL manipulation, code injection and function-call injection.

Defences. The main defence is parameterised queries (prepared statements with bind variables). The statement is parsed first and the input is bound later as data, so the input can never change the query’s structure. Add allow-list validation (an ID must be digits), least-privilege database accounts, generic error pages instead of raw database errors, and stored procedures that do not build dynamic SQL from their inputs.

NTA trap: escaping quotes or checking input in client-side JavaScript is not enough, since an attacker can bypass the browser. A stored procedure protects only if it avoids concatenating input into dynamic SQL. And in the login example, injecting the user name with OR '1'='1 while a wrong password follows returns 0 rows, because the AND with the password test binds first.

Database security and authorization

Security protects against three losses: integrity (improper change), availability (legitimate users cannot get data) and confidentiality (unauthorised disclosure). The four control measures are access control, inference control, flow control and encryption. The DBA uses a privileged account for account creation, privilege granting, privilege revocation and security-level assignment. An audit trail (the log extended with user and operation) records who did what.

Discretionary access control (DAC). Owners grant privileges at their own discretion with GRANT and REVOKE. Privileges exist at the account level (CREATE TABLE, CREATE VIEW) and the relation level (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE(col), DELETE, REFERENCES). The owner of a relation holds all privileges on it. WITH GRANT OPTION lets the receiver pass a privilege on, which is propagation. Views give column-level and row-level security: grant SELECT on a view, not on the base table. The grants form a grant graph. After a REVOKE … CASCADE, a user keeps a privilege only if some chain of grants from the owner still reaches that user.

Example 9: revocation in a grant graph

The DBA grants SELECT on EMP WITH GRANT OPTION to A and to B. A and B each grant it WITH GRANT OPTION to C, and C grants it to D.

  • A revokes from C with CASCADE. C still holds the grant from B, so C and D keep it. Holders: A, B, C, D = 4.
  • Then B also revokes from C with CASCADE. No chain from the DBA reaches C now, so C loses it and so does D. Holders: A, B = 2.

Mandatory access control (MAC). Every subject (user, program) and object (relation, tuple, attribute) gets a security class: TS ≥ S ≥ C ≥ U (top secret, secret, confidential, unclassified). The Bell–LaPadula model has two rules. The simple security property: subject S may read object O only if class(S) ≥ class(O), so there is no read up. The star (*) property: S may write O only if class(S) ≤ class(O), so there is no write down, and secret data cannot leak into a lower class. In a multilevel relation, polyinstantiation means several tuples with the same apparent key exist at different classification levels.

Role-based access control (RBAC). Privileges go to roles (CREATE ROLE clerk; GRANT SELECT ON ACCOUNT TO clerk; GRANT clerk TO ravi). Users get privileges through roles, so a change of job needs only a change of role. RBAC supports least privilege and separation of duties.

Statistical database security. Users may run only aggregate queries (COUNT, SUM, AVG). Several aggregates can still be combined to infer one person’s value. Inference control blocks this by refusing queries whose query set is too small, or too close to the whole table, by controlling overlap between query sets and by adding random noise. Flow control stops information from flowing into objects that less-privileged users can read. Encryption protects stored and transmitted data.

NTA trap: in Bell–LaPadula, writing up is allowed and writing down is forbidden. Students often reverse the star property. In a grant graph, a cycle of grants (C grants to D and D back to C) does not keep a privilege alive once no path from the owner reaches it.

NTA traps

  • NOT IN with a NULL in the subquery. Wrong: “EC is not in the list, so it is returned”. Fix: EC <> NULL is UNKNOWN, so no rows come back. Use NOT EXISTS.
  • AVG over all rows. Wrong: 265000 / 6. Fix: divide by the non-NULL count, 5.
  • salary = NULL. Fix: use IS NULL.
  • “x > 45000 OR x ≤ 45000 is always true.” Fix: for a NULL x both parts are UNKNOWN, so that row is dropped (5 rows here, not 6).
  • dept <> 'CS' includes the NULL department. Fix: it gives UNKNOWN for Faiz, so 3 rows, not 4.
  • Using an aggregate in WHERE. Fix: move it to HAVING or a subquery.
  • Forgetting the NULL group in GROUP BY row counts.
  • UNION counts. UNION removes duplicates (including repeated NULLs), UNION ALL keeps them: 5 versus 10 rows for SELECT dept FROM EMP UNION SELECT dname FROM DEPT.
  • TRUNCATE is DML. Fix: it is DDL.
  • A CHECK constraint blocks NULL. Fix: only NOT NULL blocks NULL.

How NTA asks this

  • Output: tables plus a query. Circle the NULLs first, then work in the logical order FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT.
  • Match the lists: commands ↔ categories; subquery operators ↔ meanings; constraints ↔ effects.
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: NULL behaviour, view updatability, TRUNCATE vs DELETE, UNION vs UNION ALL, triggers.
  • Sequence: the logical clause order.
  • Which query is correct: four SQL texts, only one of which answers the English question. Check NULL handling and GROUP BY columns first.

Mini-example: Assertion–Reason

(A): COUNT(*) and COUNT(salary) can return different values on the same table. (R): COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values.

Both are true, and R explains A (6 and 5 on EMP). Answer: option 1.

Elimination trick: when an option list contains “no rows” or an “empty result”, check at once whether the query uses NOT IN or ALL over a column that has a NULL. If it does, that option is almost always the answer.

terms.definition: Data Definition Language: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME; defines and changes schema objects.
Data Manipulation Language: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE (and MERGE).
Data Control Language: GRANT and REVOKE privileges.
SQL conditions evaluate to TRUE, FALSE or UNKNOWN; WHERE and HAVING keep only TRUE.
A subquery that refers to a column of the outer query, so it is logically re-evaluated for each outer row.
Filters groups after GROUP BY; it may use aggregates, which WHERE cannot.
A named, stored query (a virtual table); its rows are computed from the base tables when used.
Event–condition–action rule that runs automatically BEFORE, AFTER or INSTEAD OF an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE.
Named block of SQL and procedural code stored in the server and run with CALL/EXECUTE; can have IN, OUT and INOUT parameters.
View clause that rejects inserts or updates through the view whose rows would not satisfy the view’s WHERE condition.

lessons.examTip: In every output question, first mark the NULLs in the tables. Then apply three rules: WHERE keeps only TRUE, aggregates except COUNT(*) skip NULLs, and NOT IN against a subquery that returns a NULL gives no rows.
