lessons.title: Normalization
lessons.summaryHtml: Normalization splits a badly designed table into smaller tables so that each fact is stored once. The tool is the functional dependency (FD) X → Y: equal X values force equal Y values. With Armstrong’s axioms and the attribute closure X+ you find every candidate key, test any FD and build a minimal cover. The normal forms 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF remove partial and transitive dependencies step by step; 4NF handles multivalued dependencies and 5NF handles join dependencies. A decomposition must be lossless (the natural join gives back exactly the original table) and should be dependency preserving. 3NF synthesis always gives both properties; BCNF decomposition is always lossless but may lose a dependency.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Imagine one big table that stores student, course, instructor and the instructor’s phone number in every row. The phone number of an instructor who teaches 200 students is written 200 times. Change it once and forget one row, and the database now holds two different phone numbers. That is an update anomaly. You also cannot store a new instructor who has no students yet (insertion anomaly), and deleting the last student of an instructor deletes the instructor’s phone number too (deletion anomaly).

Normalization is the disciplined way to split such a table. The rule we use to decide how to split is the functional dependency: “instructor determines phone”. Each normal form (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, 4NF, 5NF) forbids one more kind of bad dependency. The split must never lose information (lossless join) and ideally should keep every rule checkable inside one table (dependency preservation).

Why it matters for NET

Normalization is the most reliably tested DBMS topic in Paper 2. Almost every paper has at least one question here and often two or three. The dominant patterns are: find the candidate keys (or count them), compute a closure, name the highest normal form, decide whether a decomposition is lossless and/or dependency preserving, pick a minimal cover, and count superkeys. Statement-type questions test the facts “BCNF is lossless but not always dependency preserving” and “3NF synthesis gives both”. 4NF and 5NF appear mainly as definition and matching questions. Every one of these is mechanical once you can compute a closure quickly.

Functional dependencies

For a relation R and attribute sets X and Y, the FD X → Y holds if, in every legal instance, any two tuples that agree on all attributes of X also agree on all attributes of Y. X is the determinant.

  • Trivial FD: Y ⊆ X, for example AB → A. It holds in every relation.
  • Non-trivial: Y ⊄ X. Completely non-trivial: X ∩ Y = ∅.
  • An FD is a property of the schema (all legal instances). One sample instance can disprove an FD (two rows agree on X but differ on Y) but can never prove it.

Armstrong’s axioms derive new FDs from a set F:

  1. Reflexivity: if Y ⊆ X then X → Y.
  2. Augmentation: if X → Y then XZ → YZ.
  3. Transitivity: if X → Y and Y → Z then X → Z.

They are sound (they derive only FDs that really hold) and complete (every FD implied by F can be derived). Useful derived rules: union (X → Y, X → Z give X → YZ), decomposition (X → YZ gives X → Y), pseudotransitivity (X → Y, WY → Z give WX → Z) and composition (X → Y, Z → W give XZ → YW). There is no rule that lets you split a left side: AB → C does not give A → C. The set of all FDs implied by F is the closure F+.

Attribute closure: the one algorithm you need

Computing F+ is exponential, so in practice we compute the closure of an attribute set: X+ = all attributes A with X → A in F+.

result := X
repeat
  for each FD  L → R  in F:
     if L ⊆ result then result := result ∪ R
until result does not change

Uses: (1) X → Y holds iff Y ⊆ X+; (2) X is a superkey iff X+ = R; (3) two FD sets are equivalent iff each FD of one is implied by the other; (4) extraneous attributes and redundant FDs are found with closures.

Keys, prime attributes and counting superkeys

A superkey is any set whose closure is R. A candidate key is a minimal superkey. The primary key is the candidate key the designer chooses. An attribute is prime if it belongs to some candidate key, otherwise non-prime.

Fast key-finding method used by toppers:

  1. Classify each attribute. Never on a right-hand side (including attributes that appear in no FD at all): it must be in every key. Only on right-hand sides: it is in no key. Appears on both sides: it may or may not be in a key.
  2. Let the core be the “must” set. If core+ = R, the core is the only key.
  3. Otherwise add “both-side” attributes one at a time, then in pairs, keeping only minimal sets.
  4. Check for more keys: if a key contains attribute A and some FD X → A exists, replace A by X and test. This finds keys such as AB, AC, AD in a chain.

Counting superkeys. With n attributes and a single candidate key of k attributes, every superset of the key is a superkey: 2n−k. With several keys, use inclusion–exclusion on the sets “supersets of K1”, “supersets of K2” and so on. The intersection “supersets of K1 and K2” has 2n−|K1 ∪ K2| members. The largest possible number of candidate keys for n attributes is C(n, ⌊n/2⌋).

Minimal cover

F and G are equivalent if F+ = G+. A minimal (canonical) cover of F is an equivalent set with three properties, produced in this order:

  1. Single right side: split X → AB into X → A and X → B.
  2. No extraneous left-side attribute: in XB → A, B is extraneous if A ∈ X+ computed with the full current F. Then replace the FD by X → A.
  3. No redundant FD: X → A is redundant if A ∈ X+ computed with F minus that FD. Remove it.

Do step 2 before step 3; reversing them can leave a non-minimal result. A minimal cover is not unique. For example {A → B, B → A, A → C, B → C} has the minimal covers {A → B, B → A, B → C} and {A → B, B → A, A → C}. (The canonical cover of Korth then merges FDs with the same left side using union.)

The normal forms

Normal formConditionWhat it removes
1NFEvery attribute value is atomic (no repeating groups or multi-valued attributes)Nested or list values
2NF1NF, and no non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of any candidate keyPartial dependencies
3NFFor every non-trivial X → A: X is a superkey or A is primeTransitive dependencies of non-prime attributes
BCNFFor every non-trivial X → A: X is a superkeyEvery FD whose determinant is not a superkey
4NFBCNF, and for every non-trivial MVD X →→ Y: X is a superkeyIndependent multi-valued facts in one table
5NF (PJNF)Every non-trivial join dependency is implied by the candidate keysRedundancy that only a 3-way (or larger) split removes

Quick test for the highest normal form (assume 1NF). Take each FD X → A of a minimal cover:

  • X is a superkey: fine for BCNF.
  • X is not a superkey but A is prime: violates BCNF, allowed in 3NF.
  • A is non-prime and X is a proper subset of a candidate key: partial dependency, so not 2NF.
  • A is non-prime and X is not part of a key in that way: transitive dependency, so 2NF at best.

The weakest verdict over all FDs is the answer. For 2NF, the safest check is: for each proper subset of each candidate key, compute its closure; if it contains any non-prime attribute outside the subset, 2NF is violated. Useful shortcuts: a relation whose candidate keys are all single attributes is automatically in 2NF; a relation in which every attribute is prime is automatically in 3NF; a relation with two attributes is always in BCNF.

Decomposition: lossless join and dependency preservation

Replacing R by R1, …, Rn is lossless if R1 ⋈ … ⋈ Rn equals R for every legal instance. A lossy decomposition does not lose tuples; it adds spurious tuples, so information about which combinations were real is lost.

Binary test (Heath’s theorem): {R1, R2} is lossless iff R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2 is in F+, that is, the common attributes form a superkey of at least one side. Also R1 ∪ R2 must equal R. For more than two relations, either merge pairs step by step with the binary test, or use the chase (tableau): one row per Ri, symbol aj in the columns of Ri and a distinct bij elsewhere; repeatedly apply each FD by equating right-side symbols of rows that agree on the left side (prefer the a symbol). The decomposition is lossless iff some row becomes all a’s.

Dependency preservation: let Fi be the projection of F+ on Ri. The decomposition preserves dependencies if (F1 ∪ … ∪ Fn)+ = F+. The quick test: every FD of F whose attributes all fit inside one Ri is preserved directly; for any other FD X → Y, grow a set Z from X using only the fragments (Z := Z ∪ ((Z ∩ Ri)+ ∩ Ri) for each i) and check whether Y ⊆ Z.

3NF synthesis (Bernstein): compute a minimal cover; make one relation for each left side X, holding X and all attributes it determines; if no relation contains a candidate key, add one relation that is a key; drop relations contained in others. Result: every relation in 3NF, lossless and dependency preserving.

BCNF decomposition: while some Ri has a violating FD X → Y (X not a superkey of Ri), replace Ri by (X ∪ Y) and (Ri − Y). Every step is lossless because the common part X determines X ∪ Y. The result is always lossless but may not preserve dependencies.

Multivalued dependencies, 4NF and 5NF

An MVD X →→ Y in R(X, Y, Z) says: for each X value, the set of Y values is independent of the Z values. If (x, y1, z1) and (x, y2, z2) are in R, then (x, y1, z2) and (x, y2, z1) must be too. Facts: every FD is an MVD (X → Y implies X →→ Y); complementation (X →→ Y implies X →→ R − X − Y); the MVD is trivial if Y ⊆ X or X ∪ Y = R. A decomposition {R1, R2} is lossless iff R1 ∩ R2 →→ R1 − R2 (or →→ R2 − R1). 4NF requires every non-trivial MVD to have a superkey on the left.

A join dependency *(R1, …, Rn) says R always equals the join of its projections. An MVD is a join dependency with two components. 5NF (project-join normal form) requires every non-trivial join dependency to be implied by the candidate keys. It is needed when a table can be split losslessly into three parts but not into any two.

Denormalization is the deliberate reverse step: merging tables to speed up frequent joins in reporting systems, accepting some redundancy.

Worked examples

Example 1: attribute closure. R(A, B, C, D, E, F, G), F = {A → B, BC → DE, E → G, AD → F}. Find (AC)+ and the candidate keys.

  1. Start: {A, C}.
  2. A → B fires: {A, B, C}.
  3. BC → DE fires: {A, B, C, D, E}.
  4. E → G fires: {A, B, C, D, E, G}.
  5. AD → F fires: {A, B, C, D, E, F, G} = R.

So AC is a superkey. A and C appear on no right-hand side, so both are in every key, and since AC already determines R, AC is the only candidate key. Note A+ = AB, so A → B is a partial dependency of the non-prime B: R is only in 1NF.

Example 2: several candidate keys. R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A}.

  1. Every attribute appears on some right-hand side, so there is no forced core. Try single attributes: A+ = A, B, C, then B → D gives D, CD → E gives E: ABCDE, so A is a key. E+ = E, A, then everything: E is a key. B+ = BD, C+ = C, D+ = D.
  2. Replace keys through FDs: E is determined by CD, so test CD: (CD)+ = CDEAB. CD is a key. A is determined by E and E by CD; A is also reachable from BC: (BC)+ = BCD, then CD → E, E → A: all. BC is a key.
  3. Remaining pairs without A or E: BD+ = BD. So the candidate keys are A, E, BC, CD (four).
  4. All five attributes are prime. B → D has a non-superkey left side, so R is not in BCNF; D is prime, so R is in 3NF.

Example 3: minimal cover. F = {A → BC, B → C, AB → D, D → E}.

  1. Split right sides: A → B, A → C, B → C, AB → D, D → E.
  2. Extraneous left attributes: in AB → D, compute A+ with the full set: A, B, C, D, E contains D, so B is extraneous. The FD becomes A → D.
  3. Redundant FDs: A → C is redundant because without it A+ = A, B, C (via B → C), D, E still contains C. The others are needed: without A → B, A+ = A, D, E lacks B; without B → C, B+ = B; without A → D, A+ = ABC; without D → E, D+ = D.
  4. Minimal cover: {A → B, B → C, A → D, D → E}.

Example 4: highest normal form of four relations.

Relation and FKeysCritical FDHighest NF
R(A,B,C,D): AB → C, C → DABC → D, D non-prime, C not a superkey: transitive2NF
R(A,B,C,D,E): AB → C, C → D, B → EABB → E, B is part of key AB: partial1NF
R(A,B,C): AB → C, C → BAB, ACC → B, C not a superkey but B prime3NF
R(A,B,C,D): A → BCD, BC → ADA, BCBoth left sides are keysBCNF

Example 5: lossless and dependency preserving, with the chase. R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {A → B, C → D, B → E}, decomposition {AB, CD, ACE}.

        A    B    C    D    E
R1=AB   a1   a2   b13  b14  b15
R2=CD   b21  b22  a3   a4   b25
R3=ACE  a1   b32  a3   b34  a5
  1. A → B: rows 1 and 3 agree on A, so row 3 gets B = a2.
  2. C → D: rows 2 and 3 agree on C, so row 3 gets D = a4.
  3. B → E: rows 1 and 3 now agree on B, so row 1 gets E = a5.
  4. Row 3 is a1 a2 a3 a4 a5: lossless.

Dependencies: A → B lives in AB and C → D lives in CD. B → E: B appears only in AB, and B+ inside AB is just B, so E can never be reached. B → E is lost: not dependency preserving.

Example 6: BCNF decomposition that loses an FD, and a 3NF synthesis.

(a) R(Student, Course, Teacher) with SC → T (a student has one teacher per course) and T → C (each teacher teaches one course). Keys: SC and ST. T → C violates BCNF (T is not a superkey) but C is prime, so R is in 3NF. Decompose on T → C: R1(T, C), R2(S, T). Common attribute T determines C, so the split is lossless. SC → T spans both tables and cannot be derived from T → C alone: lost.

(b) R(A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H), F = {AB → C, A → DE, B → F, F → GH}. The only key is AB. Minimal cover: AB → C, A → D, A → E, B → F, F → G, F → H. Group by left side: ABC, ADE, BF, FGH. ABC contains the key AB, so no extra relation is needed. All four are in BCNF here, and the decomposition is lossless and dependency preserving.

Example 7: counting superkeys. R(A, B, C, D, E, F) has candidate keys AB and C.

  1. Supersets of AB: the other 4 attributes are free: 24 = 16.
  2. Supersets of C: 25 = 32.
  3. Supersets of both (contain A, B, C): 23 = 8.
  4. Superkeys = 16 + 32 − 8 = 40.

Interactive solver

Enter any problem, including the ones in your practice set, and the solver works it out step by step with the conventions stated. Use it to check your answers, not to replace doing them by hand: the exam gives you no solver.

The solver runs in your browser. Turn on JavaScript to use it.

NTA traps

  • Stopping at the first key. Wrong: “AB is a key, so the answer is 1.” Fix: after finding a key, replace each of its attributes by any left side that determines it and test again.
  • Splitting the left side. Wrong: AB → C, so A → C. Fix: only the right side may be split (decomposition rule). The left side can only be reduced if the attribute is proven extraneous with a closure.
  • Calling a transitive dependency on a prime attribute a 3NF violation. Wrong: “C → B with C not a key, so not 3NF.” Fix: if B is prime, 3NF allows it; only BCNF forbids it.
  • Checking partial dependency against the primary key only. Fix: 2NF is about every candidate key, and only about non-prime attributes.
  • Thinking a lossy join loses rows. Fix: a lossy join produces extra (spurious) tuples.
  • Believing BCNF is always dependency preserving. Fix: the Student–Course–Teacher example loses SC → T. 3NF synthesis is the one that guarantees both.
  • Counting superkeys by adding. Fix: use inclusion–exclusion; the supersets of two keys overlap.
  • Removing redundant FDs before extraneous attributes. Fix: remove extraneous left-side attributes first, then redundant FDs.
  • Proving an FD from a sample instance. Fix: an instance can only show that an FD does not hold.

How NTA asks this

  • Numerical/MCQ: “number of candidate keys”, “closure of AB”, “highest normal form”, “number of superkeys”. Memorise the key-finding steps and the superkey formula.
  • Decomposition MCQ: four decompositions, pick the lossless (or lossless and dependency-preserving) one. Eliminate first any option whose parts share no attribute or whose union is not R.
  • Match the lists: axioms with names, normal forms with conditions, dependency types with the normal form they violate.
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: BCNF ⊂ 3NF, two-attribute relations, lossless versus dependency preserving, soundness versus completeness.
  • Multiple statements: “which FDs are in F+”, “which statements about R are correct”.
Mini-example (A-R): A: “R(A, B) with A → B is in BCNF.” R: “In a two-attribute relation, the left side of any non-trivial FD is a single attribute that determines the other one, so it is a key.” Both are true and R explains A: choose option 1.
Elimination trick: in a candidate-key question, any option containing an attribute that appears only on right-hand sides is wrong, and any option missing an attribute that never appears on a right-hand side is wrong. This often removes two or three options before you compute a single closure.

terms.definition: Any two tuples that agree on X must agree on Y, in every legal instance of the relation.
The set of all attributes that X determines under F. X is a superkey exactly when X⁺ contains every attribute.
A minimal superkey: its closure is the whole relation, and no proper subset has that property.
An attribute that belongs to at least one candidate key.
An FD set equivalent to F with single-attribute right sides, no extraneous left-side attribute and no redundant FD.
A non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a candidate key. This violates 2NF.
A non-prime attribute depends on the key through another attribute set that is neither a superkey nor part of a candidate key (key → X → A). This violates 3NF.
For every non-trivial FD X → Y that holds, X is a superkey.
Joining the decomposed relations always returns exactly the original relation, with no spurious tuples.
For each X value, the set of Y values is independent of the other attributes. 4NF requires the left side of every non-trivial MVD to be a superkey.

lessons.examTip: Find keys with closures before anything else: an attribute that never appears on a right-hand side must be in every key. Then test each FD X → A: X superkey means fine; A prime means 3NF but not BCNF; X a proper part of a key with A non-prime means not even 2NF.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 14 minutes without notes (about 100 seconds each, the real exam pace for FD problems).
For every closure you compute, write the order in which FDs fired, exactly as in worked example 1 of the lesson.
Attempt problems 9–15 in 12 minutes, then check all 15 with solutions.md.
Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for: missed key, wrong prime set, lost FD or wrong normal form.
Recompute one decomposition question with the chase (tableau) method, even if you used the binary shortcut.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct.
Problems 2, 5 and 10: every candidate key found, with none missing.
Problems 9–15 solved within 12 minutes.
You can state from memory which decomposition method guarantees dependency preservation and which does not.

quiz.question: R(A, B, C, D, E, F) has F = {A → C, C → D, BD → E, E → F}. What is the closure (AB)⁺?
quiz.explanation: Start with {A, B}. A → C adds C. C → D adds D. BD → E fires because B and D are now present, adding E. E → F adds F. So (AB)⁺ = ABCDEF, and AB is a superkey (in fact the only candidate key, because A and B appear on no right-hand side). ABCD is what you get if you forget that BD → E can fire once D has been added.

quiz.question: R(A, B, C, D, E) has F = {AB → C, C → D, D → B, D → E}. How many candidate keys does R have?
quiz.explanation: A appears on no right-hand side, so A is in every key, but A⁺ = A. Try A with one more attribute: (AB)⁺ = ABCDE, (AC)⁺ = ACDBE = ABCDE, (AD)⁺ = ADBEC = ABCDE, (AE)⁺ = AE. So the keys are AB, AC and AD: 3 candidate keys. Stopping at AB and answering 1 is the usual mistake.

quiz.question: R(A, B, C, D, E) has F = {AB → CD, D → E}. What is the highest normal form of R?
quiz.explanation: The only key is AB (A and B never appear on the right). Non-prime attributes: C, D, E. AB → CD comes from the key, so there is no partial dependency: A⁺ = A and B⁺ = B. D → E is a transitive dependency (D is not a superkey and E is non-prime), so R is not in 3NF. Highest normal form: 2NF.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Transitivity chains two FDs (A-IV). Augmentation adds the same attributes to both sides (B-I). Pseudotransitivity replaces Y inside WY by X (C-II). Decomposition splits the right side (D-III). Reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity are the three axioms; union, decomposition and pseudotransitivity are derived rules.

a: A. X → Y and Y → Z give X → Z
B. X → Y gives XZ → YZ
C. X → Y and WY → Z give WX → Z
D. X → YZ gives X → Y
b: I. Augmentation
II. Pseudotransitivity
III. Decomposition
IV. Transitivity

quiz.question: R(A, B, C, D, E) has exactly two candidate keys, A and BC. How many superkeys does R have?
quiz.explanation: Superkeys containing A: fix A, the other 4 attributes are free: 2⁴ = 16. Superkeys containing B and C: 2³ = 8. Both A and BC: 2² = 4 (counted twice). By inclusion–exclusion: 16 + 8 − 4 = 20. Adding 16 + 8 = 24 without subtracting the overlap is the trap.

quiz.question: R(A, B, C, D, E) has F = {A → B, C → D, B → E}. Which decomposition of R is both lossless-join and dependency preserving?
quiz.explanation: {AB, BE, ACD}: AB keeps A → B, BE keeps B → E, ACD keeps C → D, so every FD is preserved. Lossless: AB ∩ BE = B and B → E, so AB ⋈ BE = ABE is lossless; ABE ∩ ACD = A and A → B, E, so the final join is lossless. {AB, CD, ACE} is lossless but loses B → E. {ABE, CD} and {AB, BE, CD} share no attribute with the CD part, so they are lossy.

quiz.question: Arrange the following normal forms from the weakest to the strongest.
quiz.explanation: 1NF ⊃ 2NF ⊃ 3NF ⊃ BCNF ⊃ 4NF ⊃ 5NF. So the order is 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, 4NF, 5NF: B, D, A, E, C. Putting 4NF before BCNF is wrong because 4NF requires BCNF plus the MVD condition.

stmts: A. BCNF
B. 2NF
C. 5NF
D. 3NF
E. 4NF

lessons.title: Transactions, concurrency, recovery and indexing
lessons.summaryHtml: A transaction is a unit of work that must be atomic, consistent, isolated and durable (ACID). When transactions interleave, a schedule is correct if it is serializable: you test conflict serializability with a precedence graph (no cycle means serializable), and view serializability additionally accepts some schedules with blind writes. Schedules are also classified as recoverable, cascadeless or strict. Concurrency is controlled by two-phase locking (basic, conservative, strict, rigorous) or timestamp ordering (with the Thomas write rule), and deadlocks are handled by wait-die, wound-wait or wait-for-graph detection. The log with checkpoints (and the ARIES algorithm) lets the system undo losers and redo winners after a crash. Finally, indexes (primary, clustering, secondary, multilevel, B-tree and B+-tree) and hashing make data access fast; their order, height and block-access numericals are exam favourites.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A bank transfer reads one balance, subtracts, reads another balance and adds. If the power fails halfway, money vanishes; if two transfers run at the same moment, one update can overwrite the other. A transaction wraps such steps so that they behave like one indivisible action. The DBMS then lets many transactions run at once for speed, but makes the result look as if they had run one after another (serializability), and it keeps a log so that after a crash it can finish what was committed and cancel what was not. The last part of this lesson is about finding data quickly: files, indexes, B+-trees and hashing.

Why it matters for NET

This topic gives several questions in almost every Paper 2. The favourites are: is this schedule conflict or view serializable, how many equivalent serial schedules exist, is it recoverable, cascadeless or strict, which 2PL variant has which property, what happens under timestamp ordering or wait-die, which transactions are undone or redone after a crash, and B/B+-tree order, height and block-access numericals. Indexing numericals reward a clean formula sheet; schedule questions reward drawing the precedence graph every time.

Transactions and ACID

PropertyMeaningWho ensures it
AtomicityAll operations happen or none doRecovery manager (undo using the log)
ConsistencyA correct transaction takes a consistent database to a consistent databaseApplication programmer and integrity constraints
IsolationConcurrent execution looks like some serial executionConcurrency-control manager
DurabilityCommitted changes survive failuresRecovery manager (redo from the log on stable storage)

States: active → partially committed (last statement executed) → committed → terminated; or active/partially committed → failed → aborted (then restart or kill).

Concurrency problems: lost update (W–W: one write overwrites another based on a stale read), dirty read (W–R: reading uncommitted data that is later rolled back), unrepeatable read (R–W: reading the same item twice gives different values) and phantom (a re-run query sees new rows that were inserted meanwhile).

Schedules and counting

A schedule is an interleaving of the operations of several transactions that keeps each transaction’s own order. With transactions of n1, n2, …, nk operations, the number of schedules is (n1 + … + nk)! / (n1! n2! … nk!), and exactly k! of them are serial. Two transactions of 3 and 4 operations give 7!/(3! 4!) = 35 schedules, 2 serial and 33 non-serial.

Conflict serializability

Two operations conflict if they belong to different transactions, touch the same item and at least one is a write. Swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations does not change the result; if such swaps turn S into a serial schedule, S is conflict serializable.

Precedence graph test: one node per transaction; an edge Ti → Tj whenever an operation of Ti conflicts with a later operation of Tj. S is conflict serializable iff the graph is acyclic, and every topological order of the graph is an equivalent serial schedule. The number of conflict-equivalent serial schedules is the number of topological orders.

View serializability

S and S′ are view equivalent if (1) each transaction that reads the initial value of X in S also does so in S′, (2) each read of X that reads the value written by Tj in S also does so in S′, and (3) the transaction that performs the final write of each X is the same. S is view serializable if it is view equivalent to some serial schedule. Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable. The extra schedules that are view serializable but not conflict serializable always contain a blind write (a write of X by a transaction that has not read X). Testing view serializability is NP-complete, which is why real systems enforce conflict serializability.

Recoverability

  • Recoverable: if Tj reads a value written by Ti, then Ti commits before Tj commits.
  • Cascadeless (avoids cascading aborts): transactions read only committed values.
  • Strict: no transaction reads or writes X until the last writer of X has committed or aborted. Undo then only needs the before-image.

Hierarchy: strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable. Serializability and recoverability are independent: a schedule can be serializable and not recoverable.

Lock-based protocols

A shared (S) lock allows reading; an exclusive (X) lock allows reading and writing. Only S with S is compatible. Two-phase locking: a growing phase (acquire, no release) and then a shrinking phase (release, no acquire). The moment of the last lock acquisition is the lock point; ordering transactions by lock point gives the equivalent serial order.

VariantRuleSerializableCascadelessDeadlock-free
Basic 2PLGrowing then shrinkingYesNoNo
Conservative (static)Acquire all locks before startingYesNot by itselfYes
Strict 2PLHold X locks until commit/abortYesYes (strict)No
Rigorous 2PLHold all locks until commit/abortYes (commit order)Yes (strict)No

2PL is sufficient but not necessary: some conflict-serializable schedules cannot be produced by 2PL. Lock conversion (upgrade S to X in the growing phase, downgrade in the shrinking phase) is allowed. Graph-based (tree) protocols are deadlock-free without being two-phase.

Timestamp ordering

Each transaction gets a timestamp TS(T) when it starts (older = smaller). Each item X keeps R-TS(X) and W-TS(X), the largest timestamps that read and wrote it.

  • Read(X) by T: if TS(T) < W-TS(X), a younger transaction already overwrote X: roll back T. Otherwise read and set R-TS(X) = max(R-TS(X), TS(T)).
  • Write(X) by T: if TS(T) < R-TS(X), a younger transaction already read the old value: roll back T. If TS(T) < W-TS(X): roll back T in basic TO; under the Thomas write rule, simply ignore this obsolete write. Otherwise write and set W-TS(X) = TS(T).

Basic TO gives conflict-serializable, deadlock-free schedules (no transaction ever waits), but they may not be recoverable and may starve long transactions. The Thomas write rule also admits some view-serializable schedules that are not conflict serializable.

Deadlock handling

  • Wait-die (non-preemptive): an older requester waits; a younger requester dies (is rolled back and restarted with its original timestamp).
  • Wound-wait (preemptive): an older requester wounds (rolls back) the younger holder; a younger requester waits.
  • In both schemes the older transaction is favoured and a restarted transaction keeps its old timestamp, so there is no starvation.
  • Detection: build a wait-for graph (Ti → Tj if Ti waits for a lock held by Tj); a cycle means deadlock; choose a victim (least cost) and roll it back. Timeouts are a simple alternative.

Isolation levels (SQL standard)

LevelDirty readUnrepeatable readPhantom
READ UNCOMMITTEDPossiblePossiblePossible
READ COMMITTEDPreventedPossiblePossible
REPEATABLE READPreventedPreventedPossible
SERIALIZABLEPreventedPreventedPrevented

Recovery

Failures: transaction failure (logical error, deadlock victim), system crash (main memory lost, disk intact) and disk failure (needs backups). The log on stable storage holds <T start>, <T, X, old value, new value>, <T commit> and <T abort> records.

  • Deferred update (NO-UNDO/REDO): nothing is written to the database before commit, so after a crash only committed transactions are redone.
  • Immediate update (UNDO/REDO): updates may reach disk before commit. After a crash, transactions with a commit record are redone (new values, forward), and transactions with a start but no commit or abort are undone (old values, backward).
  • Write-ahead logging: the log record must reach stable storage before the data page, and all log records of T before T commits.
  • Checkpoint: flush log and dirty buffers, then write <checkpoint L> with the list L of active transactions. At restart, transactions that committed before the checkpoint need no redo; the scan starts at the last checkpoint (going back only far enough to undo the transactions in L).
  • ARIES: uses WAL, a log sequence number (LSN) on every page, and three restart passes: analysis (from the last checkpoint, rebuild the transaction table and dirty page table), redo (repeat history from the smallest recLSN, including losers), and undo (roll back losers, writing compensation log records, CLRs, so that undo is never repeated). It supports steal/no-force buffer policies and fuzzy checkpoints.
  • Shadow paging: keeps a shadow page table and switches to the new one at commit; it needs no undo/redo log but fragments data and makes commit expensive.

File organisation and indexing

Records are packed into blocks: blocking factor bfr = ⌊B / R⌋ for unspanned records, and a file of r records needs b = ⌈r / bfr⌉ blocks. A heap file needs b/2 accesses on average for a key search (b if absent); an ordered file allows binary search in ⌈log₂ b⌉ accesses; a hashed file needs about one access.

IndexBuilt onDense or sparseHow many per file
PrimaryOrdering key fieldSparse: one entry per data block (block anchor)At most one
ClusteringOrdering non-key fieldSparse: one entry per distinct valueAt most one (and not together with a primary index)
SecondaryAny non-ordering fieldDense on a key field (one entry per record)Many

With index blocking factor fo (the fan-out), binary search on a single-level index costs ⌈log₂ bi⌉ + 1 accesses. A multilevel index indexes the index until one block remains; with t levels a search costs t + 1 accesses, where t = ⌈logfo (first-level entries)⌉.

B-trees and B+-trees

Using the Navathe convention, the order p is the maximum number of tree pointers in a node. With block size B, key size V, block (tree) pointer P and record (data) pointer Pr:

  • B-tree node: p·P + (p − 1)(V + Pr) ≤ B. Keys and data pointers live in every node.
  • B+-tree internal node: p·P + (p − 1)·V ≤ B. No data pointers, so the fan-out is larger.
  • B+-tree leaf: pleaf(V + Pr) + P ≤ B (one next-leaf pointer).

Every node except the root is at least half full: a non-root internal node has at least ⌈p/2⌉ children and the root at least 2. All leaves are at the same level. For a B-tree of order m with h levels, the maximum number of keys is mh − 1 and the minimum is 2⌈m/2⌉h−1 − 1. In a B+-tree, keys in internal nodes are copies that also appear in the leaves, and the leaves are chained for range queries. Some books define order as the minimum number of keys (d, so a node holds d to 2d keys); read the question’s definition carefully.

Hashing

Static hashing maps a key to one of M buckets (for example h(K) = K mod M), with overflow chains when a bucket is full. Extendible hashing keeps a directory of 2d entries (d = global depth); each bucket has a local depth d′ ≤ d. When a bucket with d′ = d overflows, the directory doubles; when d′ < d, only the bucket splits. Linear hashing grows one bucket at a time in a fixed order without a directory. Hash indexes are excellent for equality search but useless for range queries, where B+-trees win.

Worked examples

Example 1: precedence graph and serial orders. S: R1(A) R2(B) W1(A) R3(A) W2(B) R4(B) W3(C) R4(C).

  1. Conflicting pairs (different transactions, same item, at least one write, in schedule order): W1(A) … R3(A) gives T1 → T3; W2(B) … R4(B) gives T2 → T4; W3(C) … R4(C) gives T3 → T4. R1(A) and R3(A) are both reads, so no edge.
  2. Graph: T1 → T3 → T4 and T2 → T4. No cycle: conflict serializable.
  3. Topological orders: T1 T2 T3 T4, T1 T3 T2 T4, T2 T1 T3 T4. 3 equivalent serial schedules.

Example 2: view serializable but not conflict serializable. S: R2(B) W1(B) W2(B) W3(B).

  1. R2(B) … W1(B) gives T2 → T1, and W1(B) … W2(B) gives T1 → T2: a cycle, so not conflict serializable.
  2. View test against T2 T1 T3: T2 reads the initial B in both; there are no other reads; the final write is by T3 in both. View equivalent to T2 → T1 → T3.
  3. T1 and T3 write B without reading it: blind writes, as expected.

Example 3: recoverable, cascadeless, strict.

ScheduleAnalysisClass
R1(A) W1(A) R2(A) W2(B) C2 C1T2 reads A from uncommitted T1 and commits firstNot recoverable
R1(A) W1(A) R2(A) C1 W2(A) C2Dirty read, but T1 commits before T2Recoverable, not cascadeless
W1(A) R2(B) W2(A) C1 C2No dirty read, but T2 overwrites A before T1 commitsCascadeless, not strict
R1(A) W1(A) R2(B) C1 R2(A) W2(A) C2T2 touches A only after C1Strict

Example 4: timestamp ordering. TS(T1) = 10, TS(T2) = 20, TS(T3) = 30. S: R1(A) W2(A) R3(B) W1(A) W2(B). Initially all R-TS and W-TS are 0.

  1. R1(A): 10 ≥ W-TS(A) = 0, allowed; R-TS(A) = 10.
  2. W2(A): 20 ≥ R-TS(A) = 10 and ≥ W-TS(A) = 0, allowed; W-TS(A) = 20.
  3. R3(B): allowed; R-TS(B) = 30.
  4. W1(A): 10 ≥ R-TS(A) = 10, but 10 < W-TS(A) = 20. Basic TO: roll back T1. Thomas write rule: ignore the write, T1 continues.
  5. W2(B): 20 < R-TS(B) = 30, a younger transaction already read B: roll back T2 (under both rules).

Example 5: wait-die and wound-wait. T5 (TS 5) is older than T9 (TS 9).

SituationWait-dieWound-wait
T5 requests an item held by T9T5 waitsT5 wounds T9 (T9 rolled back)
T9 requests an item held by T5T9 dies (rolled back, restarts with TS 9)T9 waits

Example 6: recovery with a checkpoint (immediate update, crash after the last record).

 1  <T1 start>
 2  <T1, A, 100, 150>
 3  <T2 start>
 4  <T2, B, 200, 250>
 5  <T1 commit>
 6  <checkpoint {T2}>
 7  <T3 start>
 8  <T3, C, 300, 350>
 9  <T2, D, 400, 450>
10  <T4 start>
11  <T4, A, 150, 175>
12  <T3 commit>
  1. T1 committed before the checkpoint: its changes are already on disk, no action.
  2. T3 committed after the checkpoint: redo, C = 350.
  3. T2 (active at the checkpoint) and T4 have no commit record: undo, scanning backward: A = 150 (record 11), D = 400 (record 9), B = 200 (record 4).
  4. Database after recovery: A = 150, B = 200, C = 350, D = 400.

Example 7: B-tree and B+-tree order and capacity. Block B = 1024 bytes, key V = 10, block pointer P = 6, record pointer Pr = 8.

  1. B+-tree internal: 6p + 10(p − 1) ≤ 1024, so 16p ≤ 1034 and p = 64.
  2. B+-tree leaf: 18 pleaf + 6 ≤ 1024, so pleaf ≤ 56.6 and pleaf = 56.
  3. B-tree: 6p + 18(p − 1) ≤ 1024, so 24p ≤ 1042 and p = 43. The B+-tree fans out more because internal nodes carry no record pointers.
  4. A completely full B+-tree with a root, one more internal level and a leaf level: 64 × 64 = 4,096 leaves, holding 4,096 × 56 = 229,376 record pointers.

Example 8: index block accesses. r = 30,000 records of R = 100 bytes, B = 1024, ordered on a 9-byte key; block pointer 6 bytes.

  1. bfr = ⌊1024/100⌋ = 10, b = 3,000 blocks. Binary search on the file: ⌈log₂ 3000⌉ = 12 accesses.
  2. Index entry 9 + 6 = 15 bytes, fo = ⌊1024/15⌋ = 68. Primary index: 3,000 entries, ⌈3000/68⌉ = 45 blocks. Search: ⌈log₂ 45⌉ + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7.
  3. Multilevel: 45 blocks, then ⌈45/68⌉ = 1 block: 2 levels, so 2 + 1 = 3 accesses.
  4. A dense secondary index on another key field: 30,000 entries, ⌈30000/68⌉ = 442 blocks, ⌈log₂ 442⌉ + 1 = 10 accesses (still better than 1,500 on average for a linear search on that field).

Example 9: B+-tree insertion (each node holds at most 3 keys; a full leaf of 4 keys splits 2 + 2 and copies the first key of the right leaf up). Insert 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80.

10,20,30        [10 20 30]
40  -> split    root [30]         leaves [10 20] [30 40]
50              root [30]         leaves [10 20] [30 40 50]
60  -> split    root [30 50]      leaves [10 20] [30 40] [50 60]
70              root [30 50]      leaves [10 20] [30 40] [50 60 70]
80  -> split    root [30 50 70]   leaves [10 20] [30 40] [50 60] [70 80]

Final tree: 2 levels, 4 leaves, 5 nodes. One more split of a leaf would overflow the root and create a third level.

Query processing and optimization

Indexes and file organisations exist to make queries fast. Query processing is the path from an SQL string to its result, in three steps:

  1. Parsing and translation. The parser checks the syntax, checks names against the catalog and translates the query into an internal form, usually a relational-algebra expression drawn as a query tree.
  2. Optimisation. The optimiser picks the cheapest evaluation plan: an algebra tree in which every operator is annotated with an algorithm and an access path (for example "use the B+-tree on dept").
  3. Evaluation. The query-execution engine runs the plan. Results are passed between operators either by materialisation (write each intermediate result to a temporary relation) or by pipelining (pass tuples on to the parent operator as soon as they are produced).

Cost measure. Disk access dominates, so cost counts block transfers and seeks: cost = b × tT + S × tS. The notation used below: nr = tuples of r, br = blocks of r, M = memory buffer blocks, V(A, r) = distinct values of attribute A in r.

Selection. A linear scan reads all br blocks, or br/2 on average for an equality test on a key. Binary search on a file sorted on A costs about ⌈log2 br⌉. A B+-tree primary index of height hi finds a key in hi + 1 accesses. A secondary index on a non-key attribute may cost one access per matching record, so for many matches it can be worse than a scan.

External sort-merge (for ORDER BY, merge join, duplicate removal and grouping) first creates ⌈br/M⌉ sorted runs. It then merges M − 1 runs at a time, which needs ⌈logM−1(br/M)⌉ merge passes. Total block transfers are br(2⌈logM−1(br/M)⌉ + 1), not counting the final write.

Join algorithm (r outer, s inner)Worst-case block transfersNotes
Nested-loopnr × bs + brAny join condition; br + bs if both relations fit in memory
Block nested-loopbr × bs + brAny condition; use the smaller relation as the outer; with M buffers, ⌈br/(M − 2)⌉ × bs + br
Indexed nested-loopbr + nr × cUses an index on the inner relation’s join attribute; c = cost of one index lookup
Merge (sort-merge) joinbr + bs (+ sorting cost)Equi-joins and natural joins; inputs sorted on the join attribute
Hash joinabout 3(br + bs)Equi-joins only; both inputs are partitioned with the same hash function, then each pair of partitions is joined (a 4nh term for partly filled blocks is often ignored)

Heuristic (rule-based) optimisation rewrites the query tree with equivalence rules. Elmasri’s outline:

  1. Break a selection with a conjunctive condition into a cascade of single selections.
  2. Push every selection as far down the tree as possible.
  3. Rearrange the leaf relations so that the most restrictive selections run first, avoiding Cartesian products.
  4. Combine a Cartesian product followed by a selection into a join.
  5. Push projections down, keeping only the attributes needed higher up.
  6. Identify subtrees that can be pipelined.

Cost-based optimisation estimates the cost of alternative plans from catalog statistics (nr, br, V(A, r), index heights) and chooses the cheapest. The estimates assume a uniform distribution: σA=v(r) returns about nr / V(A, r) tuples, and r ⋈ s on A returns about nr × ns / max(V(A, r), V(A, s)). The join order matters a great deal. n relations can be joined in (2(n − 1))! / (n − 1)! different orders, of which n! are left-deep trees, so System R-style optimisers use dynamic programming and often search only left-deep trees.

Example: join costs, sort passes and join orders

r has nr = 8,000 tuples in br = 400 blocks; s has ns = 20,000 tuples in bs = 1,000 blocks. Worst-case block transfers:

  • Nested-loop, r outer: 8,000 × 1,000 + 400 = 8,000,400; s outer: 20,000 × 400 + 1,000 = 8,001,000.
  • Block nested-loop, r outer: 400 × 1,000 + 400 = 400,400; s outer: 1,000 × 400 + 1,000 = 401,000. The smaller relation should be the outer.
  • Hash join: 3 × (400 + 1,000) = 4,200. Merge join on inputs that are already sorted: 400 + 1,000 = 1,400.

Sorting a 12,000-block file with M = 21 buffers creates ⌈12,000/21⌉ = 572 runs and needs ⌈log20 571.4⌉ = 3 merge passes (202 = 400 < 572 ≤ 8,000), so 12,000 × (2 × 3 + 1) = 84,000 transfers.

Four relations can be joined in 6!/3! = 120 orders, of which 4! = 24 are left-deep. If EMP has 10,000 tuples and 50 distinct dept values, σdept='CS'(EMP) is estimated at 10,000/50 = 200 tuples.

NTA trap: hash join and merge join work only for equality conditions; a θ-join such as r.a < s.b needs a nested-loop variant. In block nested-loop the smaller relation goes outside. Heuristic optimisation pushes selections down (earlier), not up.

NTA traps

  • Adding edges for read–read pairs. Fix: only pairs with at least one write conflict.
  • Drawing the edge backwards. Fix: the edge goes from the transaction whose operation comes first.
  • “Cycle, so not serializable at all.” Fix: a cycle rules out conflict serializability only; check for blind writes and test view serializability.
  • Confusing recoverable with cascadeless. Fix: recoverable is about commit order; cascadeless forbids the dirty read itself.
  • Thinking 2PL prevents deadlock. Fix: only conservative 2PL does; basic, strict and rigorous 2PL can deadlock.
  • Swapping wait-die and wound-wait. Fix: in both, the older transaction never dies; wait-die kills the young requester, wound-wait kills the young holder.
  • Applying the Thomas rule to reads or to the R-TS test. Fix: it only ignores a write whose TS is below W-TS(X); a write below R-TS(X) still aborts.
  • Redoing transactions that committed before the checkpoint. Fix: those changes were flushed at the checkpoint.
  • Using the B-tree inequality for a B+-tree internal node. Fix: B+ internal nodes have no record pointers.
  • Forgetting +1 for the data block in index-search questions, or using the number of records instead of blocks for a sparse primary index.

How NTA asks this

  • Schedule MCQ/numerical: CSR or not, number of equivalent serial schedules, which schedule is VSR but not CSR, recoverability class.
  • Match the lists: 2PL variants with properties, ACID with subsystems, anomalies with conflict types, index types with their fields, isolation levels with anomalies.
  • Assertion–Reason: conservative 2PL and deadlock, cascadeless implies recoverable, TO and deadlock freedom.
  • Numericals: B/B+-tree order, capacity, minimum/maximum keys, index block accesses.
  • Sequence: ARIES passes, transaction states.
Mini-example (match): Wait-die, older requests → waits; wait-die, younger requests → dies; wound-wait, older requests → wounds the holder; wound-wait, younger requests → waits. Remember “older is never killed”, and the rest follows.
Elimination trick: in “which schedule is conflict serializable”, first strike every option where two transactions both read X and then both write X (R1(X) R2(X) W1(X) W2(X) pattern): that is a guaranteed 2-cycle.

terms.definition: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the four guarantees of a transaction.
Two operations of different transactions on the same item where at least one is a write (R–W, W–R, W–W).
A graph with an edge Ti → Tj for each conflict where Ti’s operation comes first. The schedule is conflict serializable iff this graph has no cycle.
Equivalence to a serial schedule with the same initial reads, the same reads-from pairs and the same final writes.
Every transaction reads only values written by already committed transactions, so one abort never forces another.
No transaction reads or writes an item until the last transaction that wrote it has committed or aborted.
Every transaction acquires all its locks (growing phase) before releasing any (shrinking phase). It guarantees conflict serializability.
In timestamp ordering, an outdated write (by an older transaction after a younger one already wrote the item) is ignored instead of causing a rollback.
The log record of an update must reach stable storage before the updated data page is written to disk.
The maximum number of child pointers in an internal node. All records are reached through the leaves, which are linked for range queries.

lessons.examTip: For a serializability question draw the precedence graph first: only R–W, W–R and W–W pairs on the same item by different transactions give edges. A cycle means not conflict serializable; then look for blind writes before you decide on view serializability.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 14 minutes without notes (about 100 seconds each).
For every schedule, write the list of conflicting pairs and draw the precedence graph before answering.
Attempt problems 9–15 in 12 minutes, writing the inequality you solved for each B/B+-tree order question.
Check all 15 with solutions.md and write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for.
Redo the timestamp-ordering and recovery problems with the other convention (Thomas write rule on, or redo-first) and see what changes.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct.
Every precedence-graph edge in problems 1 and 2 drawn in the right direction.
Problems 10–13 solved within 6 minutes in total.

quiz.question: Consider the schedule S: R1(A) R3(B) W2(A) W4(B) R2(C) R4(D). How many serial schedules are conflict equivalent to S?
quiz.explanation: Conflicts: R1(A) before W2(A) gives T1 → T2; R3(B) before W4(B) gives T3 → T4. C and D are only read. The graph is two separate chains, T1 → T2 and T3 → T4. Each topological order is a merge of the two chains: C(4, 2) = 6 orders (for example T1 T2 T3 T4, T1 T3 T2 T4, T3 T1 T4 T2). 24 = 4! would be correct only with no conflicts at all.

quiz.question: Which of the following schedules is view serializable but NOT conflict serializable?
quiz.explanation: Option 3: R1(X) → W2(X) gives T1 → T2 and W2(X) → W1(X) gives T2 → T1, a cycle, so it is not conflict serializable. But the serial order T1 T2 T3 has the same initial read (T1 reads the initial X) and the same final write (T3), and nobody else reads, so it is view equivalent. The blind writes of T2 and T3 make this possible. Option 1 is the lost update (not view serializable), option 2 is conflict serializable, and in option 4 T2 reads the initial X (so T2 must precede T1) but T2 also makes the final write (so T1 must precede T2), which is impossible.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Basic 2PL only enforces growing then shrinking, so it is serializable but not cascadeless (A-III). Conservative (static) 2PL predeclares and acquires all locks first, so it is deadlock-free (B-I). Strict 2PL keeps exclusive locks until the end (C-IV). Rigorous 2PL keeps all locks until the end (D-II).

b: I. Locks every item it needs before execution begins, so it cannot deadlock
II. Holds all locks, shared and exclusive, until commit or abort
III. Guarantees conflict serializability but may cause cascading rollbacks
IV. Holds only exclusive locks until commit or abort

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Deadlock needs hold-and-wait. A conservative 2PL transaction either gets all its locks at once or holds none and waits, so hold-and-wait never occurs. R explains A.

stmts: Assertion (A): Conservative 2PL is free from deadlock.
Reason (R): A transaction under conservative 2PL acquires all the locks it needs before it starts executing, so it never waits while holding a lock.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Conflict equivalence implies view equivalence, so CSR ⊆ VSR (I is true). Without blind writes, view serializability and conflict serializability coincide, so a VSR-but-not-CSR schedule must contain a blind write (II is true).

stmts: Statement I: Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable.
Statement II: A schedule that is view serializable but not conflict serializable must contain at least one blind write.

quiz.question: A B+-tree is stored in blocks of 512 bytes. A search key takes 8 bytes and a block pointer 4 bytes. What is the order p (maximum number of child pointers) of an internal node?
quiz.explanation: An internal node holds p pointers and p − 1 keys: 4p + 8(p − 1) ≤ 512, so 12p ≤ 520 and p ≤ 43.3. Order p = 43. The option 64 comes from 512 ÷ 8, ignoring pointers.

quiz.question: Consider the schedule S: R1(A) W1(A) R2(A) C1 W2(A) C2. Which statement is correct?
options: S is cascadeless but not strict
S is recoverable but not cascadeless
quiz.explanation: T2 reads A written by T1 before T1 commits: a dirty read, so S is not cascadeless (and not strict). But T1 commits (C1) before T2 commits (C2), so S is recoverable: if T1 aborted, T2 could still be rolled back.

quiz.question: Which of the following are guaranteed for every schedule produced by strict 2PL?
options: A, B, C and E only
A, B, C, D and E
quiz.explanation: Strict 2PL is still 2PL, so it is conflict serializable (A). Holding exclusive locks until commit makes the schedule strict (E), hence cascadeless (B) and recoverable (C). It does not prevent deadlock (D): two transactions can each hold a lock the other wants.

stmts: A. Conflict serializable
B. Cascadeless
C. Recoverable
D. Free from deadlock
E. Strict

quiz.question: Arrange the states of a transaction that finishes successfully in the order it passes through them.
quiz.explanation: A transaction is active while it executes, partially committed after its last statement, committed once its log records are safely on stable storage, and then terminated. The failed and aborted states belong to the unsuccessful path.

stmts: A. Committed
B. Active
C. Partially committed
D. Terminated
