quiz.question: An ordered file has 20,000 records of 128 bytes on a disk with 2,048-byte blocks (unspanned). A primary index uses 10-byte keys and 6-byte block pointers. How many block accesses does a search using binary search on the primary index need?
quiz.explanation: Data: bfr = ⌊2048/128⌋ = 16 records per block, b = 20000/16 = 1,250 blocks. Index entry = 10 + 6 = 16 bytes, so 2048/16 = 128 entries per block. A primary index is sparse: one entry per data block, so ⌈1250/128⌉ = 10 index blocks. Binary search on the index: ⌈log₂ 10⌉ = 4 accesses, plus 1 for the data block = 5. Binary search on the data file itself would need ⌈log₂ 1250⌉ = 11.

lessons.title: Enhanced data models, data warehousing and data mining
lessons.summaryHtml:
This lesson covers the databases that go beyond flat relational tables.

  • Object-oriented databases add object identity, complex objects, encapsulation and inheritance.
  • Object-relational databases add user-defined types, REF and nested tables to SQL.
  • Temporal databases track valid time and transaction time.
  • Spatial databases index geometry with R-trees and quadtrees.
  • Multimedia databases retrieve images, audio and video by their content.
  • Deductive databases derive new facts with Datalog rules.

A distributed database spreads data over sites. It uses horizontal and vertical fragmentation, replication with quorums, semijoins to cut network cost, and two-phase commit to commit atomically (2PC can block). A data warehouse is subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile. It is modelled as a star or snowflake schema and queried with OLAP operations: roll-up, drill-down, slice, dice and pivot. Data mining is one step of KDD. It finds association rules (support, confidence, lift, Apriori, FP-growth), builds classifiers (ID3 entropy and gain, Gini, Naive Bayes, k-NN) and forms clusters (k-means, hierarchical, DBSCAN).
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

The relational model stores flat rows of simple values. Some applications need more. A CAD system stores parts made of other parts. A map asks "which schools lie within 2 km of this road?". A hospital must know what a patient’s address was in March. A bank wants each city to own its own data. A retail chain asks "how did tea sales change quarter by quarter?" and "which items are bought together?".

Enhanced data models (object-oriented, object-relational, temporal, spatial, multimedia, deductive) extend what a database can store. Distributed databases spread one database over many sites. A data warehouse collects history for analysis, and data mining finds patterns in it.

Why it matters for NET

This is the "breadth" corner of Unit 4. Most questions are conceptual and easy marks if you know the vocabulary: OLAP vs OLTP, star vs snowflake, roll-up vs drill-down, fragmentation types, what 2PC guarantees and which clustering algorithm belongs to which family. Match-the-list and statement questions dominate. The few numericals are reliable: support, confidence and lift, Apriori candidate counts, cuboid counts, entropy and gain, and precision and recall.

Object-oriented databases (OODB)

An OODB stores objects as an object-oriented program sees them:

  • Object identity (OID). Every object gets a system-generated identifier that never changes and does not depend on attribute values. Two objects can hold identical values and still be different objects.
  • Complex objects and type constructors. Types are built with constructors: atom, tuple (struct), set, bag, list and array. An attribute can hold a set of references to other objects, so no join table is needed.
  • Encapsulation. An object has state (attributes) and behaviour (methods). The class defines the interface; the implementation stays hidden.
  • Inheritance and polymorphism. Classes form hierarchies. An operation name can be overloaded, and the right method is chosen at run time (late binding).
  • Persistence. An object is persistent by naming (given a name the DB knows) or by reachability (reachable from a persistent object). Other objects are transient and vanish when the program ends.

The ODMG standard (Object Data Management Group) defines the object model, ODL (Object Definition Language, for schemas) and OQL (Object Query Language, SQL-like with path expressions such as d.manager.name). OODBs suit CAD/CAM and other deeply nested data.

Object-relational databases (ORDBMS)

An ORDBMS keeps tables and SQL but lets columns hold richer types. SQL:1999 added user-defined structured types, typed tables, REF types (a column that points to a row object), type and table inheritance (UNDER) and arrays; SQL:2003 added multisets. The result can model nested relations (non-first-normal-form, NF²), where an attribute value is itself a relation. PostgreSQL and Oracle follow this approach.

Stonebraker’s 2×2 classification is a favourite match question:

No query language neededQuery language needed
Simple dataFile systemRelational DBMS
Complex dataObject-oriented DBMSObject-relational DBMS

Temporal, spatial and multimedia databases

Temporal databases record time explicitly. Valid time is when a fact is true in the real world (Anu lived in Thrissur from 2019 to 2023). Transaction time is when the fact was stored in the database, and the system sets it. A database with both is bitemporal; one with neither is a snapshot database. Time can be a point (an event) or an interval (a period), and interval comparisons use Allen’s relations: before, meets, overlaps, during, starts, finishes and equals. SQL:2011 added period definitions and system-versioned tables.

Spatial databases store geometry: points, lines and polygons, usually in 2D or 3D. Queries are range queries (all hospitals inside this district), nearest-neighbour queries (the nearest petrol pump) and spatial joins (pairs of rivers and roads that cross). Ordinary B+ trees index one dimension, so spatial data uses the R-tree (nested minimum bounding rectangles), the quadtree (recursively splits space into four quadrants) and the k-d tree (alternates the splitting axis). GIS is the classic application.

Multimedia databases hold images, audio, video and documents. Metadata-based retrieval searches captions and tags. Content-based retrieval extracts features, such as colour histograms, texture and shape for images, or shots and key frames for video, and then finds items with similar feature vectors. Large items are stored as BLOBs.

Deductive databases and Datalog

A deductive database combines stored facts (the extensional database, EDB) with rules (the intensional database, IDB) that derive new facts. The language is Datalog, a Prolog-like language without function symbols, built on Horn clauses:

parent(asha, binu).   parent(binu, chitra).
ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Y).
ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Z), ancestor(Z, Y).

The recursive rule computes a transitive closure, which plain relational algebra cannot express. Evaluation is bottom-up (apply rules until no new fact appears: the least fixed point; semi-naive evaluation joins only the new facts of each round) or top-down (backward chaining from the query, as in Prolog). A rule is safe when every variable in its head, and every variable in a negated or comparison literal, also appears in a positive body literal; this keeps answers finite. Negation is allowed when the program is stratified, so that no predicate depends negatively on itself through recursion.

Distributed databases

A distributed database is one logical database stored at several sites linked by a network. Distribution transparency hides where data lives: location transparency (no site names in queries), fragmentation transparency (no fragment names) and replication transparency (no awareness of copies). A homogeneous system runs one DBMS everywhere; a heterogeneous (federated) one mixes autonomous products.

Fragmentation splits a relation:

  • Horizontal: a subset of rows chosen by a selection, σcity='Kochi'(EMP). You rebuild the relation with UNION. With m simple predicates there are at most 2m minterm fragments.
  • Vertical: a subset of columns chosen by a projection. Every fragment must keep the primary key, and you rebuild the relation with a JOIN on that key.
  • Derived horizontal: rows of a member relation are split to follow the fragments of its owner, using a semijoin.
  • Mixed (hybrid): horizontal and vertical splits applied together.

A correct fragmentation satisfies completeness (every data item lands in some fragment), reconstruction (the original can be rebuilt) and disjointness (no row sits in two horizontal fragments; for vertical fragments the key is repeated by design and is the exception).

Replication can be full (every site has everything), partial, or none. It improves availability and read speed but makes updates costlier. Updates are propagated eagerly (synchronously, inside the transaction) or lazily (asynchronously, afterwards). With N copies, quorum voting keeps reads correct when the read quorum R and write quorum W satisfy R + W > N and 2W > N.

Distributed query processing tries to minimise data shipped across the network. The semijoin R ⋉ S returns only the rows of R that have a match in S. You ship the join column of S to R’s site, reduce R there, and ship only the matching rows.

Two-phase commit (2PC) makes a distributed transaction atomic at every site:

  1. Phase 1, voting. The coordinator writes a prepare record in its log and sends PREPARE to every participant. Each participant force-writes <ready T> and replies YES, or writes <abort T> and replies NO.
  2. Phase 2, decision. If every vote is YES, the coordinator force-writes <commit T> and sends COMMIT; otherwise it sends ABORT. Participants act on the decision and acknowledge.

The weakness is blocking. A participant that voted YES may neither commit nor abort on its own. If the coordinator crashes before it sends the decision, that participant waits and keeps its locks. Three-phase commit (3PC) adds a pre-commit phase and avoids blocking when sites crash, provided there is no network partition and message delays are bounded. Distributed deadlocks are found with a global wait-for graph.

Data warehousing

Inmon’s definition is the one to memorise: a data warehouse is a subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile collection of data that supports management decisions. Subject-oriented means it is organised around sales or customers, not around applications. Integrated means codes and units from different sources are made consistent. Time-variant means it keeps history, with time in the key. Non-volatile means data is loaded and read, not updated in place.

Data reaches the warehouse through ETL (extract, transform, load). A data mart is a department-level warehouse: dependent if fed from the enterprise warehouse (Inmon, top-down), independent if fed from sources. Kimball works bottom-up from conformed marts.

FeatureOLTP (operational DB)OLAP (warehouse)
UsersClerks, customers, many at a timeAnalysts and managers, fewer
WorkShort read/write transactionsLong, complex, read-mostly queries
DataCurrent, detailedHistorical, summarised and detailed
DesignNormalised (3NF), ER-basedDimensional: star or snowflake
MetricTransactions per secondQuery response time
SizeGBTB and more

Schemas. A star schema has one central fact table that holds foreign keys to each dimension plus numeric measures (quantity, amount), surrounded by denormalised dimension tables (time, item, store). A snowflake schema normalises the dimensions into sub-tables (item → brand → category). This saves space but needs more joins. A fact constellation (galaxy) has several fact tables that share dimensions. The grain is the level of detail of one fact row. A factless fact table records events, such as attendance, and has no numeric measure.

The data cube and OLAP operations. A cube views measures across n dimensions. Every subset of dimensions gives one cuboid (one group-by), so a cube with n dimensions and no hierarchies has 2n cuboids. The top of this lattice is the apex cuboid (0-D, the grand total) and the bottom is the base cuboid (n-D). If dimension i has a concept hierarchy with Li levels, the total is Π(Li + 1), where the +1 is the level "all".

  • Roll-up (drill-up): climb a hierarchy (city → state) or drop a dimension, so the data becomes more summarised.
  • Drill-down: the reverse (quarter → month), so the data becomes more detailed.
  • Slice: fix one dimension to a value (time = Q1), which gives a sub-cube with one dimension fewer.
  • Dice: select on two or more dimensions (time in Q1 or Q2 and city in Kochi or Chennai), which gives a smaller sub-cube.
  • Pivot (rotate): swap axes for a different view.
  • Drill-across queries more than one fact table. Drill-through goes down to the operational rows behind a cube cell.

Storage options are ROLAP (relational tables, which scale well), MOLAP (multidimensional arrays, which answer fast but can be sparse) and HOLAP (detail kept in ROLAP and aggregates in MOLAP). Measures are distributive (sum, count, min, max: they can be computed from partitions), algebraic (avg, standard deviation: built from a fixed number of distributive values) or holistic (median, mode, rank: they need all the data).

Data mining and the KDD process

Data mining is one step of knowledge discovery in databases (KDD). Han and Kamber list the steps as: data cleaning → data integration → data selection → data transformation → data mining → pattern evaluation → knowledge presentation. Fayyad’s shorter version is: selection → preprocessing → transformation → data mining → interpretation/evaluation. Tasks are descriptive (association, clustering) or predictive (classification, regression).

Association rules and Apriori

For a rule X → Y over N transactions:

  • support(X → Y) = count(X ∪ Y) / N, the fraction of transactions that contain every item of X and Y;
  • confidence(X → Y) = count(X ∪ Y) / count(X), the estimate of P(Y | X);
  • lift(X → Y) = confidence / support(Y) = support(X ∪ Y) / (support(X) × support(Y)). A lift above 1 means positive correlation, 1 means independence and below 1 means negative correlation.

A rule is strong if it meets both the minimum support and the minimum confidence. Mining has two steps: find all frequent itemsets, then generate rules from each one. A frequent k-itemset gives 2k − 2 candidate rules, and d items give 3d − 2d+1 + 1 possible rules in total, which is why brute force fails.

Apriori (Agrawal and Srikant) relies on the Apriori property: every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent. Equivalently, support is anti-monotone, so any superset of an infrequent itemset is infrequent. Level k works like this:

  1. Join: combine two frequent (k−1)-itemsets that share their first k−2 items (in sorted order) to form candidates Ck.
  2. Prune: delete any candidate that has an infrequent (k−1)-subset. No scan is needed.
  3. Count: scan the database once and keep the candidates that meet minimum support; they form Lk.

Apriori scans the database once per level. FP-growth (Han, Pei and Yin) scans only twice. It compresses the data into an FP-tree and mines it recursively without candidate generation. A frequent itemset is closed if no proper superset has the same support, and maximal if no proper superset is frequent. Every maximal itemset is closed, but not the other way round.

Classification

Classification is supervised: it learns from labelled records and predicts the class of new ones.

  • Decision trees. ID3 (Quinlan) splits on the attribute with the highest information gain: Gain(A) = Entropy(S) − Σ (|Sv|/|S|) Entropy(Sv), where Entropy(S) = −Σ pi log2 pi. Information gain favours attributes with many values, so C4.5 uses the gain ratio. CART uses the Gini index, 1 − Σ pi2, and makes binary splits. Pruning (before or after growth) controls overfitting.
  • Naive Bayes applies Bayes’ theorem and assumes the attributes are independent given the class.
  • k-nearest neighbour is a lazy learner: it stores the training data and does its work at prediction time. Decision trees and Naive Bayes are eager learners.
  • Evaluation uses a confusion matrix: accuracy = (TP+TN)/total, precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall (sensitivity) = TP/(TP+FN), specificity = TN/(TN+FP), and F1 = 2PR/(P+R). Holdout and k-fold cross-validation estimate accuracy.

Clustering

Clustering is unsupervised: it groups unlabelled records by similarity.

FamilyAlgorithmsKey idea
Partitioningk-means, k-medoids (PAM, CLARA)Fix k; move points to the nearest centre until stable. k-means uses the mean and is sensitive to outliers; k-medoids uses an actual point and is robust.
HierarchicalAGNES (agglomerative), DIANA (divisive), BIRCH, CURE, CHAMELEONBuilds a dendrogram. Single link = minimum distance, complete link = maximum, average link = mean of all pairs.
Density-basedDBSCAN, OPTICSClusters are dense regions with parameters ε and MinPts; finds arbitrary shapes and labels noise.
Grid-basedSTING, CLIQUE, WaveClusterQuantises space into cells; fast.
Model-basedEM (Gaussian mixtures), COBWEB, SOMFits a statistical or neural model.

In DBSCAN, a core point has at least MinPts points (itself included) within distance ε. A border point is within ε of a core point but is not itself core. Every other point is noise.

Worked examples

Examples 1 and 2 use this nine-transaction database D, with minimum support count 3 (3/9, about 33%) and minimum confidence 70%.

TIDItemsTIDItems
T1Milk, SugarT6Milk, Sugar
T2Biscuit, Milk, Sugar, TeaT7Biscuit, Tea
T3Biscuit, Bread, Sugar, TeaT8Bread, Milk
T4Biscuit, Bread, Milk, TeaT9Biscuit, Sugar
T5Biscuit, Milk, Tea

Example 1: Apriori, level by level.

L1. The counts are Biscuit 6, Bread 3, Milk 6, Sugar 5 and Tea 5. All five items reach 3, so all are frequent.

C2 has C(5,2) = 10 pairs. Counting them gives Biscuit–Bread 2, Biscuit–Milk 3, Biscuit–Sugar 3, Biscuit–Tea 5, Bread–Milk 2, Bread–Sugar 1, Bread–Tea 2, Milk–Sugar 3, Milk–Tea 3 and Sugar–Tea 2.
So L2 = {Biscuit,Milk}, {Biscuit,Sugar}, {Biscuit,Tea}, {Milk,Sugar}, {Milk,Tea}: 5 itemsets.

Join for C3. Combine pairs of L2 itemsets that share their first item.
The prefix Biscuit gives {Biscuit,Milk,Sugar}, {Biscuit,Milk,Tea} and {Biscuit,Sugar,Tea}.
The prefix Milk gives {Milk,Sugar,Tea}.
That makes 4 candidates.

Prune. {Biscuit,Sugar,Tea} and {Milk,Sugar,Tea} both contain {Sugar,Tea}, which is not in L2, so both are deleted without a scan. Two candidates remain.

Count. {Biscuit,Milk,Sugar} = 1, so it is not frequent. {Biscuit,Milk,Tea} = 3 (T2, T4, T5), so it is frequent.
So L3 = {Biscuit,Milk,Tea}. C4 cannot be formed, and Apriori stops.

In total there are 5 + 5 + 1 = 11 frequent itemsets.

Example 2: rules from {Biscuit, Milk, Tea}, with support 3/9 = 33.3%. A 3-itemset gives 23 − 2 = 6 rules.

RuleConfidenceLiftStrong at 70%?
{Biscuit, Milk} → Tea3/3 = 100%1.0 / (5/9) = 1.8Yes
{Milk, Tea} → Biscuit3/3 = 100%1.0 / (6/9) = 1.5Yes
{Biscuit, Tea} → Milk3/5 = 60%0.6 / (6/9) = 0.9No
Tea → {Biscuit, Milk}3/5 = 60%0.6 / (3/9) = 1.8No
Biscuit → {Milk, Tea}3/6 = 50%0.5 / (3/9) = 1.5No
Milk → {Biscuit, Tea}3/6 = 50%0.5 / (5/9) = 0.9No

Look at the rule Tea → {Biscuit, Milk}. Its lift is 1.8, which shows positive correlation, yet it is not strong, because its confidence is only 60%. Lift and confidence answer different questions.

Example 3: counting cuboids. A sales cube has three dimensions. Time has the hierarchy day < month < quarter < year (4 levels), item has item < type (2 levels) and location has city < state < country (3 levels).

Without hierarchies there are 23 = 8 cuboids.
With hierarchies there are (4+1)(2+1)(3+1) = 5 × 3 × 4 = 60 cuboids, because each dimension can also be at the level "all".

A related sizing question: at daily grain, with 365 days, 200 items and 30 stores, the fact table has at most 365 × 200 × 30 = 2,190,000 rows, one per cell of the base cuboid if every combination occurs.

Example 4: information gain (ID3). A bank has 10 loan applicants: 6 were approved (Yes) and 4 were refused (No).

  • Income = High: 5 applicants (4 Yes, 1 No). Income = Low: 5 applicants (2 Yes, 3 No).
  • Owns house = Yes: 4 applicants (4 Yes, 0 No). Owns house = No: 6 applicants (2 Yes, 4 No).

Entropy of the whole set. Entropy(S) = −0.6 log2 0.6 − 0.4 log2 0.4 = 0.971.

Gain for Income.
The High branch has entropy H(4,1) = 0.722 and the Low branch has H(2,3) = 0.971.
Weighted entropy = 0.5(0.722) + 0.5(0.971) = 0.846, so Gain = 0.971 − 0.846 = 0.125.

Gain for Owns house.
The Yes branch has H(4,0) = 0 (it is pure) and the No branch has H(2,4) = 0.918.
Weighted entropy = 0.6(0.918) = 0.551, so Gain = 0.971 − 0.551 = 0.420.

Result. ID3 splits on Owns house. The Gini index agrees. The root Gini is 1 − 0.36 − 0.16 = 0.48. After the house split the weighted Gini is 0.6 × (1 − 1/9 − 4/9) = 0.267, and after the income split it is 0.400. The lower value is better.

Example 5: one k-means iteration. The points are A(1,1), B(2,1), C(4,3), D(5,4), E(1,2) and F(6,5), with k = 2 and initial centres A and D.

Squared distances to (1,1) and to (5,4):
B: 1 vs 18. C: 13 vs 2. E: 1 vs 20. F: 41 vs 2.
So the clusters are {A, B, E} and {C, D, F}.

New centres.
((1+2+1)/3, (1+1+2)/3) = (1.33, 1.33)
((4+5+6)/3, (3+4+5)/3) = (5, 4)

Second pass. Nobody changes cluster, so the algorithm has converged.

Example 6: semijoin in a distributed query. Site 1 holds EMP: 10,000 tuples of 100 bytes each. Site 2 holds DEPT, already filtered to 20 departments, and the query result is needed at site 2. The join attribute DeptNo is 4 bytes, and 2,000 employees work in those 20 departments.

Plan A: ship all of EMP to site 2.
10,000 × 100 = 1,000,000 bytes.

Plan B: semijoin.
Ship πDeptNo(DEPT) to site 1: 20 × 4 = 80 bytes.
Compute EMP ⋉ DEPT at site 1 and ship it: 2,000 × 100 = 200,000 bytes.
Total = 200,080 bytes, a saving of 799,920 bytes.

Other distributed quick counts.
2PC with 5 participants, counting PREPARE, vote, decision and ACK, uses 4 × 5 = 20 messages.
With N = 7 replicas and W = 4, the smallest read quorum is R = 4, since R + W > 7.

XML and Internet databases

XML is the semi-structured data model of the web. A document is an ordered, labelled tree: elements (which may nest), attributes, and text. Data carries its own tags, so the schema is partly inside the data. A document is well-formed if it follows the syntax (one root, properly nested and closed tags, quoted attribute values). It is valid if it also conforms to a schema. The schema can be a DTD (element nesting written in its own non-XML notation; almost no data types) or an XML Schema (XSD) (written in XML, with data types such as xs:integer and xs:date, and with keys and cardinalities).

Querying. XPath selects nodes with path expressions: / is a child step, // is a descendant step at any depth, @ selects an attribute, and [ ] holds a predicate. XQuery builds on XPath with FLWOR expressions, whose clauses run in the order for, let, where, order by, return.

<library>
  <book id="b1"><title>DBMS</title><price>450</price><author>Korth</author></book>
  <book id="b2"><title>Networks</title><price>300</price></book>
  <book id="b3"><title>Compilers</title><price>520</price>
                <author>Aho</author><author>Ullman</author></book>
  <book id="b4"><title>Graphics</title><price>280</price></book>
</library>

for $b in doc("lib.xml")//book
where $b/price > 300
order by $b/title
return $b/title

//book[price > 300]/title returns 2 nodes (DBMS and Compilers; 300 is not greater than 300). count(//author) is 3. /library/book[author]/@id returns b1 and b3, the books that have at least one author child. The FLWOR query returns Compilers and then DBMS, in title order.

Storing XML. A native XML database stores and indexes the tree itself (BaseX, eXist-db). An XML-enabled relational DBMS either shreds documents into tables (a schema-based mapping, where elements become rows and columns) or keeps each document whole in an XML-typed or CLOB column. SQL/XML adds functions such as XMLELEMENT and XMLAGG that publish relational rows as XML. XML is also used to exchange data between applications, for example in web services.

Internet (web) databases sit behind web sites in a three-tier layout. The browser sends an HTTP request, the web or application server runs server-side code (PHP, JSP/servlets, ASP.NET) that connects through JDBC/ODBC or a native driver, and the result comes back as HTML, XML or JSON. The server programs must keep the database safe from injection and must manage many short sessions with connection pooling.

NTA trap: every valid document is well-formed, but a well-formed document need not be valid. A DTD cannot declare that a price is an integer; XSD can.

Mobile databases

In mobile computing, mobile units (laptops, phones, hand-held terminals) move between cells. Each cell is served by a base station, also called a mobile support station (MSS), which is a fixed host with a wireless interface. The base stations sit on a fixed wired network with the database servers. When a unit crosses into another cell, its connection is handed off to the new base station.

What makes mobile data management hard:

  • Disconnection is frequent and often voluntary (to save battery or money), so a client must keep working on local data.
  • Bandwidth is low and asymmetric: the downlink from the server is far wider than the uplink from the client.
  • Battery power is limited, so query processing and communication must save energy (for example by dozing while waiting).
  • Data location changes: answers can depend on where the user is (location-dependent queries), and the system must track users.

Techniques. Clients cache data, and the server sends invalidation reports so that stale copies are dropped. Popular data is broadcast on a repeating cycle (a broadcast disk) so that any number of clients can listen without sending uplink requests. Air indexes tell a client when its item will arrive, so it can sleep until then. Replicas on the device are synchronised with the server when connected, and conflicts are resolved by rules (last writer wins, or application logic). Mobile transactions are long-lived, may run partly while disconnected and may move from one base station to another. Models such as Kangaroo transactions split them into sub-transactions per base station. Small embedded databases such as SQLite run on the device itself.

NTA trap: in a broadcast, clients listen without sending requests, so the uplink is spared. Adding more clients does not add server load; it is the broadcast schedule, not the number of listeners, that decides the waiting time.

Geographic information systems (GIS)

A GIS captures, stores, analyses and displays data that is tied to locations on the earth. It is the largest application of spatial databases. GIS data has two parts. Spatial data gives geometry and position. Non-spatial (attribute) data describes each feature: the name of a road, the population of a ward.

Data modelRepresentationSuits
VectorPoints, lines (polylines) and polygons with coordinates; topology records what touches or contains whatDiscrete objects: wells, roads, land parcels
RasterA grid of cells, each holding one valueContinuous fields and images: elevation, rainfall, satellite pictures
TIN (triangulated irregular network)Terrain as connected triangles over sample pointsSurfaces and slopes

Typical operations: buffer (the zone within a set distance of a feature: all houses within 500 m of a river); overlay (combine layers: flood zone ∩ land parcels); network analysis (shortest route, service areas on a road network); interpolation (estimate values at unsampled points, such as rainfall between gauges); measurement (length, area, distance); and spatial queries using topological relations such as contains, within, touches, overlaps and disjoint. Spatial indexes (R-tree, quadtree, k-d tree, grid files) make these fast.

Example: raster storage

An elevation raster of 4,000 × 3,000 cells with 2 bytes per cell needs 4,000 × 3,000 × 2 = 24,000,000 bytes = 24 MB (106 bytes per MB) before compression. Halving the cell size in both directions multiplies the cell count, and the storage, by 4.

Genome data management

Bioinformatics produces huge sets of sequence data: DNA and RNA are strings over four bases (A, C, G, T; U replaces T in RNA), and proteins are strings over 20 amino acids. With them come 3D structures, gene expression data, pathways and literature. Elmasri lists why biological data is hard to manage:

  • it is highly complex compared with most other applications, and definitions must be rich enough to represent it;
  • the amount and range of variability is high, so the system must tolerate variation;
  • schemas change rapidly as knowledge grows, so schema evolution must be easy;
  • the same data is represented differently by different biologists and databases;
  • most users need only read access, and they want context (provenance) and links between databases;
  • the ability to answer complex queries across sources is critical.
DatabaseHolds
GenBank (NCBI, USA), ENA/EMBL (Europe), DDBJ (Japan)Nucleotide sequences; the three exchange data daily as the INSDC
UniProtKB/Swiss-ProtManually curated protein sequences with functional annotation
PDB (Protein Data Bank)3D structures of proteins and nucleic acids
OMIMCatalogue of human genes and genetic disorders
Gene Ontology (GO), KEGGControlled vocabulary of gene functions; metabolic pathways

Sequence search does not use exact equality. BLAST and FASTA are heuristic similarity (local alignment) searches that rank database sequences by alignment score. Because there are only four bases, DNA packs into 2 bits per base: a genome of 3.1 × 109 bases needs 3.1 × 109 × 2 / 8 ≈ 775 MB in packed form, against about 3.1 GB at one byte per base.

Regression, support vector machines and k-nearest neighbour

Regression is the predictive task for a continuous target, where classification predicts a class label. Simple linear regression fits y = a + bx by least squares, which minimises Σ(y − ŷ)2:

b = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) / Σ(x − x̄)2, a = ȳ − b x̄. The fitted line always passes through (x̄, ȳ). Multiple regression uses several predictors. Logistic regression, despite its name, predicts a probability for a binary class and is used for classification.

Example: least-squares line

Data (x, y): (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 5). x̄ = 3 and ȳ = 4. The deviations of x are −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 and those of y are −2, 0, 1, 0, 1. Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = 4 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 6 and Σ(x − x̄)2 = 10, so b = 0.6 and a = 4 − 0.6 × 3 = 2.2. The prediction at x = 6 is 2.2 + 3.6 = 5.8.

Support vector machine (SVM). For two linearly separable classes, an SVM finds the maximum-margin hyperplane w·x + b = 0, the separating boundary farthest from the nearest points of both classes. Those nearest points lie on w·x + b = ±1 and are the support vectors. Only they decide the boundary. The margin width is 2/‖w‖, so maximising the margin means minimising ‖w‖. A soft margin with penalty C allows some points inside the margin or on the wrong side (a large C gives fewer violations and a narrower margin). The kernel trick (polynomial, RBF/Gaussian kernels) computes inner products in a higher-dimensional space without mapping the points there, so a non-linear boundary can be learned. Example: w = (3, 4) gives ‖w‖ = 5 and a margin of 2/5 = 0.4.

k-nearest neighbour (k-NN) is a lazy, instance-based learner. Training just stores the records. To classify a new point, it finds the k closest training points (usually by Euclidean distance) and takes a majority vote; for regression it averages their values. Odd k avoids ties between two classes. Attributes should be normalised, or a large-scale attribute such as salary will swamp one such as age. Prediction is slow for big data, since every query compares against all stored points.

Example: k-NN changes with k

Training points: class A at (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 1); class B at (4, 3), (5, 4), (6, 5). Classify (3, 3). The distances in order are (4, 3) B = 1, (2, 2) A = √2 ≈ 1.41, (3, 1) A = 2, (5, 4) B = √5 ≈ 2.24, and so on. With k = 1 the answer is B. With k = 3 the neighbours are B, A, A, so the answer is A.

Hidden Markov models

A hidden Markov model (HMM) describes a system that moves between hidden states by a Markov chain and emits a visible observation from each state. It is written λ = (A, B, π). A holds the state-transition probabilities, B the emission probabilities P(observation | state), and π the initial state distribution. HMMs model sequences: speech, part-of-speech tagging, gene finding, and customer behaviour over time. The three classic problems are:

ProblemQuestionAlgorithm
EvaluationP(O | λ): how likely is this observation sequence?Forward (or backward) algorithm, O(N2T)
DecodingMost likely hidden-state sequence for OViterbi (dynamic programming with max instead of sum)
LearningEstimate A, B, π from observationsBaum–Welch (an EM algorithm)

Example: forward algorithm

States H and C; π = (0.6, 0.4). Transitions: H→H 0.7, H→C 0.3, C→H 0.4, C→C 0.6. Emissions: H gives X with 0.8 and Y with 0.2; C gives X with 0.3 and Y with 0.7. Observed O = X, Y.

α1(H) = 0.6 × 0.8 = 0.48 and α1(C) = 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.12. α2(H) = (0.48 × 0.7 + 0.12 × 0.4) × 0.2 = 0.0768 and α2(C) = (0.48 × 0.3 + 0.12 × 0.6) × 0.7 = 0.1512. So P(O) = 0.228. Viterbi keeps the maximum instead of the sum, and the best path is H, C with probability 0.48 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.1008. Brute force would list NT state sequences, which is exponential in T.

Summarization, dependency modelling, link analysis, sequence analysis and social network analysis

Fayyad’s list of primary data-mining tasks is classification, regression, clustering, summarization, dependency modelling, and change and deviation detection. The syllabus adds link, sequence and social-network analysis.

  • Summarization finds a compact description of a subset of data: the mean and standard deviation of each field, a characteristic rule for a class ("most defaulters are under 25 with two or more loans"), or roll-up views of a cube. It is descriptive and is often used in exploratory analysis and report generation.
  • Dependency modelling finds a model of the significant dependencies between variables. At the structural level it states, often as a graph, which variables depend locally on which. At the quantitative level it gives the strengths of those dependencies on a numerical scale. Bayesian networks are the standard example. If P(Rain) = 0.2, P(Wet | Rain) = 0.9 and P(Wet | no Rain) = 0.1, then P(Wet) = 0.2 × 0.9 + 0.8 × 0.1 = 0.26. Association rules are a simple form of dependency model.
  • Change and deviation detection finds the most significant changes from earlier or expected values, as in fraud and fault detection.

Link analysis mines the relationships (links) between objects rather than the objects alone: web pages and hyperlinks, calls between phone numbers, money transfers. PageRank scores a page by the rank flowing in from pages that link to it: PR(p) = (1 − d)/N + d Σ PR(q)/L(q), where q ranges over pages linking to p, L(q) is the out-degree of q and the damping factor d is usually 0.85. A page’s rank is split equally among its out-links. HITS gives every page two scores: a good hub points to many good authorities, and a good authority is pointed to by many good hubs. Link analysis also finds fraud rings and suggests friends.

Example: one PageRank iteration

Links: A→B, A→C, B→C, C→A; N = 3, d = 0.85, and every page starts at 1/3. PR(A) = 0.05 + 0.85 × (1/3)/1 ≈ 0.333; PR(B) = 0.05 + 0.85 × (1/3)/2 ≈ 0.192; PR(C) = 0.05 + 0.85 × (1/6 + 1/3) = 0.475. Iterating to convergence gives about A 0.388, B 0.215 and C 0.397.

Sequence (sequential pattern) analysis finds frequent ordered patterns: "customers who buy a phone then buy a cover within a month". A sequence is an ordered list of itemsets, written <(a)(b c)(d)>. A customer sequence supports a pattern if the pattern’s itemsets appear, each inside some element, in the same order. GSP uses Apriori-style level-wise candidate generation. PrefixSpan grows patterns in projected databases without candidates. SPADE uses vertical id-lists. For biological sequences, alignment tools (BLAST) and HMMs do the job. Example: with customer sequences <(a)(b c)(d)>, <(a b)(c)(b)>, <(b)(a)(c)> and <(a)(d)(b)>, the pattern <(a)(b)> has support 3 (the third sequence has b before a), while <(b)(a)> has support 1.

Social network analysis (SNA) models people or organisations as nodes and their ties as edges, then measures structure:

  • degree centrality: the number of direct ties (normalised by n − 1);
  • closeness centrality: the inverse of the average shortest distance to all others;
  • betweenness centrality: how often a node lies on shortest paths between other pairs (brokers and bridges);
  • clustering coefficient: the fraction of a node’s neighbour pairs that are themselves linked;
  • density = 2m / (n(n − 1)) for an undirected graph with n nodes and m edges.

Community detection finds dense groups, and influence analysis finds nodes that spread information fastest. In two triangles {A, B, C} and {D, E, F} joined by the edge C–D, n = 6 and m = 7, so the density is 14/30 ≈ 0.467. C and D each have betweenness 6: C lies on every shortest path from A or B to D, E or F.

NTA trap: regression predicts numbers and classification predicts labels, so logistic regression is a classifier. k-NN is lazy and decision trees are eager. Only the support vectors fix an SVM’s boundary. Viterbi decodes the state path and the forward algorithm evaluates P(O). In sequence mining, <(a)(b)> and <(a b)> are different patterns: two separate events versus two items bought together.

Formula and fact sheet

NTA traps

  • Confidence is not symmetric. Wrong: conf(A→B) = conf(B→A). Fix: the denominator is the count of the left-hand side. Only support and lift are symmetric.
  • High confidence does not mean a useful rule. If Y is in 90% of baskets, conf(X→Y) = 90% can still mean lift = 1. Check the lift.
  • Apriori property direction. Wrong: "supersets of a frequent set are frequent". Fix: subsets of a frequent set are frequent, and supersets of an infrequent set are infrequent.
  • Slice vs dice. A slice fixes one dimension. A dice selects on two or more dimensions. Neither changes the level of detail.
  • Snowflake is the normalised one. Star dimensions are denormalised. Snowflake saves space but costs joins.
  • "Non-volatile" does not mean "never changes". The warehouse grows by periodic loads. It simply is not updated transaction by transaction.
  • Vertical fragments must repeat the key. Without it you cannot rebuild the relation by a join, so disjointness is relaxed for the key.
  • 2PC is atomic but blocking. 3PC is the non-blocking protocol. A statement that says "2PC is non-blocking" is false.
  • OID is not a primary key. An OID is system-generated, immutable and independent of values. A key is a value.
  • k-means vs k-medoids. Mean-based k-means is outlier-sensitive; medoid-based PAM is robust. k-NN is a classifier, not a clustering method.
  • Valid time vs transaction time. The real world vs the database log. Mixing them is the classic temporal trap.

How NTA asks this

  • Match the lists: OLAP operations to descriptions, clustering algorithms to families, schema types to features, temporal terms to meanings, Stonebraker’s quadrants.
  • Assertion–Reason: the Apriori property, 2PC blocking, why snowflake needs more joins, why k-NN is lazy.
  • Statements I/II and "which are correct": OODB features, warehouse characteristics, fragmentation rules.
  • Order: the KDD steps, the 2PC steps, Apriori’s join → prune → count.
  • Short numericals: support/confidence/lift from a 5–10 row table, cuboid counts, entropy/gain, precision/recall.

Mini A-R. A: If {tea, sugar} is infrequent, {tea, sugar, milk} need not be counted. R: Support is anti-monotone. Both are true, and R explains A, so the answer is the first option.

Mini match. Roll-up, drill-down, slice and dice go with "city → state", "year → quarter", "time = 2025" and "time in {Q1,Q2} and city in {Kochi, Pune}". Anchor the one you are sure of (a single fixed value = slice), then eliminate every option that breaks it.

Speed trick: for support and confidence questions, write each itemset’s count once, in a small tally, before you look at the options. Every ratio in the options then takes seconds.

terms.definition: A system-generated, immutable identity for an object, independent of its attribute values.
Valid time is when a fact is true in the real world; transaction time is when it was recorded in the database.
Splitting a relation into row subsets by selection; the relation is rebuilt with UNION.
A voting phase (PREPARE, YES or NO) and then a decision phase (COMMIT or ABORT). It is atomic but can block if the coordinator fails.
A central fact table of measures and foreign keys joined to denormalised dimension tables.
Moving up a concept hierarchy to summarise, or down to see more detail.
Selecting on one dimension, or on two or more dimensions, of a cube.
count(X∪Y)/N; count(X∪Y)/count(X); confidence divided by support(Y).
Every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent, so any superset of an infrequent itemset can be pruned.
A density-based clustering method with ε and MinPts; it finds clusters of any shape and labels noise.

lessons.examTip: For any support/confidence question, first tabulate the count of every itemset the options mention; confidence divides by the LEFT side’s count, lift then divides by the right side’s support.

steps: Download practice-set.md and attempt problems 1–8 in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For every numerical, write the count tally or the formula first, then calculate.
Check your answers with solutions.md and write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for.
Close the solutions and redo problem 2 (the Apriori trace) on paper: L1, C2, L2, join, prune, count, L3.
Write a one-page revision sheet: OLAP operations, the schema types, the clustering families, the KDD order and the 2PC steps.
Redo every wrong problem after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct on the first attempt.
Problems 1–5 and 8–12 (the numericals) solved within 15 minutes in total.
The Apriori trace for problem 2 reproduced without error, including the prune step.
Zero mistakes on confidence direction (dividing by the left-hand side).

quiz.question: A transaction database has 5 transactions: T1 {A, B, C}, T2 {A, C}, T3 {A, D}, T4 {B, E}, T5 {A, C, E}. What are the support and confidence of the rule A → C?
quiz.explanation: {A, C} appears in T1, T2 and T5, so support = 3/5 = 60%. A appears in 4 transactions, so confidence = 3/4 = 75%. 100% is the confidence of C → A (count of C is 3); 80% is the support of A alone. Confidence always divides by the count of the left-hand side.

b: I. Sub-cube chosen by selecting on two or more dimensions
II. Climbing up a concept hierarchy, such as city to state
III. Selection on one dimension, such as time = Q1
IV. Stepping down a hierarchy, such as quarter to month

lessons.title: Big data systems and NoSQL
lessons.summaryHtml:
Big data is data that is too large (Volume), too fast (Velocity) or too varied (Variety) for traditional tools; later lists add Veracity and Value. Hadoop scales out on commodity machines.

  • HDFS stores files as 128 MB blocks, replicated 3 times with rack awareness. The NameNode holds the metadata and the DataNodes hold the blocks.
  • MapReduce runs split → map → combine → partition → shuffle/sort → reduce.
  • YARN (ResourceManager, NodeManager, ApplicationMaster) shares the cluster between MapReduce, Spark and other engines.
  • Spark keeps data in memory as RDDs. Its transformations are lazy and its actions trigger jobs.

The CAP theorem forces a choice between consistency and availability during a network partition. Many NoSQL stores follow BASE (eventual consistency) instead of ACID and use quorums (R + W > N) to tune it. The four NoSQL families are key-value (Redis, DynamoDB), document (MongoDB, CouchDB), column-family (Cassandra, HBase) and graph (Neo4j). MongoDB queries use JSON-like filters such as {marks: {$gt: 80}}, plus projection, sort, limit and the aggregation pipeline.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A single database server has limits. There is only so much disk, memory and CPU in one box, and buying a bigger box ("scaling up") gets very expensive. Big data systems take the other road, "scaling out". They spread data and computation over hundreds of cheap machines and assume that some of those machines will fail every day. Hadoop stores files across the cluster (HDFS) and runs batch jobs next to the data (MapReduce, scheduled by YARN). Spark does the same kind of work mostly in memory, so it is much faster for repeated passes over the data. NoSQL databases give up some relational guarantees, such as fixed schemas, joins and strict consistency, to gain horizontal scale and flexible data models. The CAP theorem explains the price they pay.

Why it matters for NET

This is newer syllabus material, and the questions are mostly factual. The favourites are: the Vs of big data, which component does what in the Hadoop ecosystem, HDFS NameNode and DataNode roles, block size and replication, the MapReduce phases in order, YARN’s daemons, CAP and BASE, and matching NoSQL databases to their type. Expect match-the-list and order questions. Small numericals appear too: block counts, raw storage with replication, the number of map tasks, and MapReduce outputs for a tiny input.

Big data and its Vs

"Big data" means data sets too large, too fast or too varied for traditional tools to capture, store and analyse in acceptable time. Doug Laney’s original three Vs (2001) are:

  • Volume: the scale of data, from terabytes to petabytes and beyond.
  • Velocity: the speed at which data arrives and must be processed (streams, clickstreams, sensors).
  • Variety: structured tables, semi-structured JSON/XML/logs, and unstructured text, images and video.

Later lists add Veracity (trustworthiness, noise and bias) and Value (useful insight), which makes five Vs. Some add Variability (changing meaning or flow rates) and Visualization as well. Size units rise by factors of 1024: KB, MB, GB, TB, PB, EB, ZB, YB.

The Hadoop ecosystem

Apache Hadoop is an open-source framework, inspired by Google’s GFS and MapReduce papers, for storing and processing huge data sets on commodity clusters. Its core is HDFS (storage), YARN (resource management, from Hadoop 2) and MapReduce (the batch processing model), plus Hadoop Common (shared libraries). Around the core sit many tools:

HDFS: the Hadoop Distributed File System

HDFS is designed for very large files, streaming reads and commodity hardware. Its access model is write-once, read-many: files can be appended to, but not edited in the middle. It is a poor fit for many small files and for low-latency random access.

  • Blocks. A file is cut into large blocks, 128 MB by default in Hadoop 2 and 3 (64 MB in Hadoop 1). The size is configurable. A file smaller than a block uses only the space it needs on disk, but it still costs one block entry in memory.
  • NameNode (master). It holds the namespace, meaning the directory tree, file-to-block mapping and permissions, in memory. It persists this as an fsimage plus an edit log. It knows where each block’s replicas are from the block reports that DataNodes send. No file data ever flows through it.
  • DataNodes (workers). They store blocks on local disks, serve reads and writes, and send a heartbeat every 3 seconds by default. A DataNode that misses heartbeats for a timeout (about ten minutes by default) is declared dead, and its blocks are re-replicated elsewhere.
  • Secondary NameNode. It periodically merges the edit log into the fsimage (a checkpoint). Despite its name, it is not a hot standby. Hadoop 2 added NameNode high availability (an active and a standby NameNode) and federation (several independent namespaces).
  • Replication. The default replication factor is 3. With rack awareness, the first replica goes on the writer’s node, the second on a node in a different rack, and the third on another node in that same remote rack. A whole rack can fail without losing data, while write traffic between racks stays low.
  • Reading and writing. A client asks the NameNode for block locations, then streams data directly to or from the DataNodes. Writes flow through a pipeline of the replica DataNodes.

MapReduce

MapReduce expresses a batch job as two functions:

map:    (k1, v1)          -> list(k2, v2)
reduce: (k2, list(v2))    -> list(k3, v3)

A job runs in these phases:

  1. Input splits. The input is divided into logical splits, normally one per HDFS block. One map task runs per split, preferably on a node that holds that block (data locality: move computation to the data).
  2. Map. A RecordReader turns the split into records; for text these are (byte offset, line). The mapper emits intermediate (key, value) pairs, which are written to the local disk, not to HDFS.
  3. Combine (optional). A "mini-reducer" runs on each mapper’s output to shrink the data before it crosses the network. It is safe only for operations that are commutative and associative, such as sum, count and max.
  4. Partition. Each key is assigned to a reducer, by default with hash(key) mod R. All values of one key go to the same reducer.
  5. Shuffle and sort. Reducers fetch their partitions from every mapper, and the framework merges and sorts them by key, grouping the values.
  6. Reduce. Each reduce call receives one key with all its values and writes the final output to HDFS, one file per reducer (part-r-00000, part-r-00001, …).

The number of reducers is set by the job; the default is 1. With zero reducers you get a map-only job, whose map output is written straight to HDFS. Failed tasks are simply re-executed on another node. Slow "straggler" tasks can be duplicated (speculative execution).

YARN

In Hadoop 1, a single JobTracker did both resource management and job scheduling, while TaskTrackers ran tasks in fixed map and reduce slots. This limited scale, and only MapReduce could run. YARN (Yet Another Resource Negotiator, Hadoop 2) splits these duties:

  • ResourceManager (one per cluster). It has a Scheduler, which allocates resources (FIFO, Capacity or Fair scheduler), and an ApplicationsManager, which accepts jobs and starts their ApplicationMasters.
  • NodeManager (one per node). It launches and monitors containers (bundles of CPU and memory) and reports to the ResourceManager.
  • ApplicationMaster (one per application). It negotiates containers for its job and tracks its tasks.

Because YARN is generic, MapReduce, Spark, Tez and others can share one cluster.

Spark basics

Apache Spark (from UC Berkeley’s AMPLab) is a general cluster-computing engine. Its core abstraction is the RDD (resilient distributed dataset): an immutable, partitioned collection that remembers its lineage, the chain of operations that built it. A lost partition is recomputed from the lineage instead of being restored from a replica. DataFrames and Datasets add a schema on top and are optimised by Spark SQL’s Catalyst optimiser.

  • Transformations (map, filter, flatMap, union, distinct, groupByKey, reduceByKey, join) are lazy. They only record the plan.
  • Actions (count, collect, reduce, first, take, saveAsTextFile, foreach) trigger execution. Each action launches a job. The DAG scheduler splits the job into stages at shuffle boundaries.
  • Narrow dependencies (map, filter) keep each output partition tied to one input partition, so no shuffle is needed. Wide dependencies (groupByKey, reduceByKey, most joins) need a shuffle. reduceByKey is preferred to groupByKey because it combines values on the map side first.
  • Architecture: a driver program (holding the SparkContext/SparkSession) plans the work. A cluster manager (standalone, YARN or Kubernetes) allocates resources. Executors on the worker nodes run tasks and cache data.
  • Libraries: Spark SQL, Structured Streaming (micro-batches), MLlib and GraphX.

Why is Spark faster than MapReduce for iterative work such as machine learning and graph algorithms? MapReduce writes to disk between every job. Spark keeps intermediate data in memory and plans the whole DAG at once.

CAP theorem, ACID and BASE

Brewer’s CAP theorem (conjectured in 2000 and proved by Gilbert and Lynch in 2002) says that a distributed data store cannot guarantee all three of these at the same time:

  • Consistency: every read sees the most recent write, as if there were a single copy.
  • Availability: every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response.
  • Partition tolerance: the system keeps working even when the network drops or delays messages between nodes.

Networks do partition, so the real choice is made during a partition. A CP system refuses or delays some requests to stay consistent; HBase and MongoDB (with default settings) are usually placed here. An AP system answers every request but may return stale data; Cassandra, CouchDB and Amazon’s Dynamo are usually placed here. A single-site RDBMS is often called "CA", because it has no partitions to tolerate. The PACELC extension adds that, else (with no partition), a system trades latency against consistency.

ACID (traditional RDBMS)BASE (many NoSQL stores)
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, DurabilityBasically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency
Strong consistency after every commitReplicas converge if updates stop
Pessimistic: locking and strict isolationOptimistic: availability first
Usually scales upScales out

Many NoSQL stores let you tune consistency with quorums. With N replicas, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read contacts R replicas. If R + W > N, every read quorum overlaps the latest write quorum, which gives strong consistency; otherwise the store is eventually consistent. Data is spread over nodes by sharding (range or hash partitioning), often with consistent hashing. Nodes and keys are placed on a hash ring, and each key belongs to the first node clockwise. Adding or removing a node moves only the keys of one arc.

NoSQL means "not only SQL". These stores are usually schema-less (or schema-on-read), scale horizontally, replicate automatically and avoid joins by denormalising, which means storing together the data that is read together.

MongoDB query basics

MongoDB is a document database. A database holds collections (like tables) of documents (like rows), which are stored as BSON (binary JSON) up to 16 MB each. Every document has a unique _id; by default this is a 12-byte ObjectId. Documents in one collection may have different fields.

db.students.insertOne({name: "Anu", dept: "CS", marks: 82})
db.students.find({dept: "CS", marks: {$gt: 80}})          // AND of conditions
db.students.find({$or: [{city: "Kochi"}, {marks: {$gte: 88}}]})
db.students.find({}, {name: 1, _id: 0}).sort({marks: -1}).limit(2)
db.students.updateMany({dept: "EC"}, {$inc: {marks: 5}})
db.students.deleteOne({name: "Binu"})
db.students.countDocuments({skills: {$exists: false}})
db.students.aggregate([
  {$match: {marks: {$gte: 60}}},
  {$group: {_id: "$dept", avg: {$avg: "$marks"}}},
  {$sort: {_id: 1}} ])

The comparison operators are $eq, $ne, $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $in and $nin. The logical operators are $and, $or, $not and $nor. The element and array operators are $exists, $size, $all and $elemMatch. The update operators are $set, $unset, $inc and $push. In sort, 1 means ascending and −1 descending. In a projection, 1 includes a field and 0 excludes it; _id is included unless you exclude it. The aggregation pipeline chains stages such as $match, $group, $project, $sort, $limit, $unwind and $lookup (a left outer join). For scale, a replica set has one primary and several secondaries with automatic failover by election. Sharding splits a collection by a shard key, with mongos routers and config servers.

Worked examples

Example 1: HDFS blocks and storage (block size 128 MB, replication factor 3).

(a) A 500 MB file.
⌈500/128⌉ = 4 blocks: 128 + 128 + 128 + 116 MB.
Block replicas = 4 × 3 = 12.
Raw disk used = 500 × 3 = 1,500 MB, not 4 × 128 × 3 = 1,536 MB, because the last block occupies only 116 MB.

(b) A 1 GB file (1,024 MB).
1,024/128 = 8 blocks, giving 24 replicas and 3,072 MB of raw storage.
On Hadoop 1, with 64 MB blocks, the same file would need 16 blocks.

(c) Cluster capacity. A cluster has 24 DataNodes with 10 TB each, so raw capacity is 240 TB.
With replication 3, usable capacity is about 240/3 = 80 TB (ignoring temporary space).

(d) The small-files problem. 1,000,000 files of 1 MB each need 1,000,000 blocks, each tracked in NameNode memory.
The same 1,000,000 MB stored as large files needs only ⌈1,000,000/128⌉ = 7,813 blocks.

Example 2: MapReduce word count with a combiner and 2 reducers.

Input. The input has two splits. Split 1 holds the lines "tea coffee tea" and "milk tea". Split 2 holds "coffee milk" and "tea milk coffee coffee".

PhaseMapper 1Mapper 2
Map output(tea,1) (coffee,1) (tea,1) (milk,1) (tea,1): 5 pairs(coffee,1) (milk,1) (tea,1) (milk,1) (coffee,1) (coffee,1): 6 pairs
After combiner(coffee,1) (milk,1) (tea,3): 3 pairs(coffee,3) (milk,2) (tea,1): 3 pairs

The combiner's effect. The network now carries 6 pairs instead of 11.

Partitioning. Suppose hash(coffee) = 7, hash(milk) = 4 and hash(tea) = 9. With R = 2, milk goes to reducer 0 (4 mod 2 = 0), and coffee and tea go to reducer 1.

Shuffle and sort. Reducer 0 receives milk → [1, 2]. Reducer 1 receives coffee → [1, 3] and tea → [3, 1].

Output. part-r-00000 contains "milk 3". part-r-00001 contains "coffee 4" and "tea 4". That is 3 output records in total, one per distinct word.

Example 3: when a combiner gives the wrong answer. The job is to find the average temperature of Kochi. Mapper 1 sees the readings 30 and 32. Mapper 2 sees 34.

Wrong way. Each combiner computes a local average, 31 and 34, and the reducer averages those: (31 + 34)/2 = 32.5.

Correct answer. (30 + 32 + 34)/3 = 32.

The fix. The mapper or combiner emits (sum, count) pairs, here (62, 2) and (34, 1). The reducer adds them to get (96, 3) and divides: 96/3 = 32. Average is algebraic, not distributive.

Example 4: consistent hashing and quorums. A ring runs from 0 to 99, with nodes at N1 = 10, N2 = 45 and N3 = 80.

Placing keys. Each key goes to the first node clockwise:
5 → N1
30 → N2
44 → N2
50 → N3
85 → N1 (it wraps past 99)

Adding a node. Add N4 at 60. Only the keys in the arc (45, 60] move from N3 to N4, so here only key 50 moves. With simple hash mod n, changing n from 3 to 4 would remap most keys.

Quorums. With N = 3 replicas:
R = 2, W = 2: 4 > 3, so it is strongly consistent.
R = 1, W = 3: also strong.
R = 1, W = 1: 2 ≤ 3, so it is eventually consistent (fast but may be stale).
R = 1, W = 2: 3 is not greater than 3, so it is not guaranteed.

Example 5: MongoDB queries. The collection students holds these documents:

{_id:1, name:"Anu",    dept:"CS", marks:82, city:"Kochi",    skills:["python","sql"]}
{_id:2, name:"Binu",   dept:"EC", marks:67, city:"Thrissur", skills:["c"]}
{_id:3, name:"Chitra", dept:"CS", marks:91, city:"Kochi",    skills:["java","python"]}
{_id:4, name:"Deepak", dept:"ME", marks:58, city:"Palakkad"}
{_id:5, name:"Esha",   dept:"CS", marks:74, city:"Thrissur", skills:["sql"]}
{_id:6, name:"Farhan", dept:"EC", marks:88, city:"Kochi",    skills:["python"]}

The queries and their results:

  • find({dept:"CS", marks:{$gt:80}}) → Anu and Chitra (2).
  • find({skills:"python"}) → Anu, Chitra and Farhan (3). An equality test on an array field matches if any element is equal.
  • find({skills:{$ne:"python"}}) → Binu, Deepak and Esha (3). Deepak has no skills field at all, and $ne also matches documents where the field is missing.
  • find({$or:[{city:"Thrissur"},{marks:{$gte:88}}]}) → Binu, Chitra, Esha and Farhan (4).
  • find({},{name:1,_id:0}).sort({marks:-1}).limit(2) → {name:"Chitra"} and {name:"Farhan"}.
  • The aggregation from the code block above ($match marks ≥ 60, $group by dept with $avg) gives CS → (82+91+74)/3 = 82.33 and EC → (67+88)/2 = 77.5. ME disappears, because Deepak’s 58 is filtered out before grouping.

Example 6: Spark laziness.

lines  = sc.parallelize(["tea milk", "tea sugar tea"])
words  = lines.flatMap(lambda l: l.split())       # transformation
pairs  = words.map(lambda w: (w, 1))              # transformation
counts = pairs.reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b)    # transformation (wide)
print(counts.count())                             # action -> 3
print(sorted(counts.collect()))                   # action -> [('milk', 1), ('sugar', 1), ('tea', 3)]

Nothing runs until count() is called. There are 3 transformations and 2 actions, so 2 jobs are launched. In each job, the shuffle caused by reduceByKey splits the work into two stages.

Types of big data and big data architecture

By structure, big data has three types:

  • Structured: a fixed schema of rows and columns, such as relational tables, transaction records and spreadsheets.
  • Semi-structured: self-describing tags or keys but no rigid schema, such as JSON, XML, CSV with varying fields, e-mail headers and log lines of key=value pairs.
  • Unstructured: no predefined model, such as free text, PDFs, images, audio and video. This is most of the world’s data.

By source, it is human-generated (social posts, e-mails), machine-generated (sensor and IoT readings, server logs, clickstreams) or business/transactional (sales, payments).

Layers of a big data architecture. Data sources feed an ingestion layer: batch loads (Sqoop from RDBMSs) or streams (Kafka, Flume). A storage layer holds the raw and processed data: HDFS, a cloud data lake or NoSQL stores. A processing layer runs batch jobs (MapReduce, Spark) and stream jobs (Spark Streaming, Flink, Storm). An analytics and serving layer (Hive, data warehouses, serving databases) answers queries, and a visualisation layer (dashboards, BI tools) presents results. Orchestration (Oozie, Airflow), security and governance run across all of them.

Lambda architecture (Nathan Marz) runs two paths side by side. The batch layer keeps the immutable, append-only master dataset and recomputes accurate batch views. The speed layer processes only recent data to give low-latency real-time views. The serving layer indexes the batch views so they can be queried, and queries merge batch and real-time views. Kappa architecture (Jay Kreps) drops the batch layer: everything is a stream, kept in a replayable log, and reprocessing means replaying the log through new code. Lambda is accurate and fault-tolerant but means maintaining two code bases; Kappa has one code base.

Indexing, ordering and query optimization in NoSQL

NoSQL stores have no general-purpose join optimiser, so most "query optimisation" happens when you design the data model around the queries (query-driven or access-pattern modelling). You denormalise, duplicate data into one table or collection per query pattern, and choose keys so that each query reads from as few nodes as possible.

Keys decide placement and order. In Cassandra the partition key is hashed to choose the node, and the clustering columns set the sorted order of rows inside the partition. A query must restrict the partition key, and ORDER BY is allowed only on clustering columns. Queries that scan every node need ALLOW FILTERING, which is a warning sign. HBase keeps rows sorted by row key in byte order. Monotonic keys, such as timestamps, send all writes to one region (a hotspot), so designers salt or reverse such keys. Redis sorted sets keep members ordered by score, so a top-N leaderboard takes O(log n) per update. DynamoDB uses a partition key plus an optional sort key, and items that share a partition key are stored in sort-key order.

MongoDB indexes. Every collection has a unique index on _id. Other types are single-field; compound (several fields, in order); multikey (on an array field, with one index entry per element); text; 2dsphere (geospatial queries on an earth-like sphere); hashed (supports hash-based sharding and equality matches); TTL (documents expire after a set time); and unique, partial and sparse variants.

  • Prefix rule: a compound index on {a, b, c} also serves queries on its prefixes {a} and {a, b}, but not on {b} or {c} alone.
  • Sort rule: a compound index can return a sort in its own direction pattern or in the exact reverse of it. {a: 1, b: −1} supports sort({a: 1, b: −1}) and sort({a: −1, b: 1}), but not sort({a: 1, b: 1}), which needs an in-memory sort. An in-memory sort of a large result is slow and is capped by a memory limit.
  • ESR guideline for ordering the fields of a compound index: Equality fields first, then Sort fields, then Range fields.
  • explain() shows the winning plan. IXSCAN means an index was used and COLLSCAN means a full collection scan. A good plan has totalDocsExamined close to nReturned. A covered query is answered from the index alone, so it examines 0 documents; that needs every queried and returned field in the index, with _id excluded from the projection. MongoDB’s planner runs candidate plans briefly against each other, caches the winner for that query shape, and re-plans when performance changes.

Example: choosing and reading an index

Query: db.orders.find({status: "A", qty: {$gt: 10}}).sort({date: 1}). By ESR, the index is {status: 1, date: 1, qty: 1}. Before the index, explain() showed COLLSCAN with 200,000 documents examined for 50 returned, a ratio of 200,000 / 50 = 4,000. With the index it shows IXSCAN, with no in-memory SORT stage and a ratio near 1.

An index on {dept: 1, marks: −1, age: 1} serves sorts on {dept: 1}, {dept: −1}, {dept: 1, marks: −1}, {dept: −1, marks: 1} and the full key in either direction. Its prefixes are {dept}, {dept, marks} and the full key: 3 in all.

NoSQL in the cloud

Cloud providers offer NoSQL as a fully managed database-as-a-service (DBaaS). The provider runs the servers, patches, replication, backups and failover. The customer gets elastic scaling (often serverless), multi-region replication, pay-per-use billing and an availability SLA. The customer still designs keys and access patterns.

ServiceModelPoints to remember
Amazon DynamoDBKey-value and documentPartition key + optional sort key. On-demand or provisioned capacity. Reads are eventually consistent by default, with strongly consistent reads as an option. Global tables replicate across regions.

Google Cloud BigtableWide-columnHBase-compatible API; suited to time-series and analytics at scale.

DynamoDB provisioned capacity. One read capacity unit (RCU) is one strongly consistent read per second of an item up to 4 KB, or two eventually consistent reads per second. One write capacity unit (WCU) is one write per second of an item up to 1 KB. Item sizes are rounded up to the next 4 KB (reads) or 1 KB (writes).

Example: sizing DynamoDB capacity

80 strongly consistent reads per second of 6 KB items need ⌈6/4⌉ = 2 RCU each, so 80 × 2 = 160 RCU. If the same reads are eventually consistent, they need half as much: 80 RCU. 10 writes per second of 2.5 KB items need ⌈2.5/1⌉ = 3 WCU each, so 30 WCU.

NTA trap: "managed" does not mean "schema-free design": a bad partition key still creates hot partitions in the cloud. Session, not Strong, is the middle level in Cosmos DB’s list. DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent unless you ask for strong consistency.

NTA traps

  • The Secondary NameNode is not a backup NameNode. It only checkpoints the fsimage. Failover needs the HA standby NameNode (Hadoop 2 and later).
  • The NameNode stores no file data. Clients read and write blocks directly with DataNodes. The NameNode serves only metadata.
  • Map output goes to local disk. Only reducer (or map-only) output goes to HDFS. Options that say "mappers write to HDFS" are wrong.
  • The number of mappers is not chosen freely. It follows the number of input splits. The number of reducers is what the programmer sets.
  • A combiner is an optimisation, not a guarantee. Hadoop may run it zero, one or many times, so it must not change the result. That rules out a plain average.
  • CAP is not "pick any two, any time". The trade-off applies when a partition happens, and consistency in CAP means linearisability, not the C of ACID.
  • Type confusions. HBase and Cassandra are column-family stores, not relational column stores. Redis is key-value. MongoDB and CouchDB are document stores. Neo4j is a graph store.
  • Size is not the only V. A question about "unstructured social-media text and images" is testing Variety, not Volume. "Real-time sensor streams" means Velocity.
  • Spark transformations do not execute. The count of jobs equals the count of actions, not of lines.
  • The $ne and missing-field trap. {field: {$ne: x}} also returns documents that lack the field. {field: {$gt: x}} does not.

How NTA asks this

  • Match: ecosystem tools to roles (Pig, Hive, Sqoop, Flume, ZooKeeper, Oozie); NoSQL products to types; YARN components to duties; Vs to meanings.
  • Order: the MapReduce phases (split → map → combine → partition → shuffle/sort → reduce), and data-size units.
  • A-R and statements: the Secondary NameNode, CAP under partition, BASE vs ACID, why Spark is faster, why rack awareness places replicas on two racks.
  • Numericals: blocks, replicas, raw storage and map-task counts; the output of a word-count job; the result of a MongoDB query.

Mini match. The tools are Sqoop, Flume, Oozie and ZooKeeper. The roles are "RDBMS ↔ HDFS bulk transfer", "streaming log ingestion", "workflow scheduling" and "coordination". Anchor Sqoop (SQL-to-Hadoop), and the rest follow.

Mini A-R. A: With rack awareness, a block with replication factor 3 survives the loss of an entire rack. R: The replicas are spread over two racks. Both are true and R explains A.

Speed trick: for block questions, divide and round up, then multiply by the replication factor. But use the file size, not blocks × 128, when the question asks for raw bytes.

quiz.question: A 500 MB file is stored in HDFS with a block size of 128 MB and a replication factor of 3. How many blocks does the file have, and how many block replicas are stored in the cluster?
quiz.explanation: ⌈500/128⌉ = 4 blocks (128 + 128 + 128 + 116 MB). Each block is stored 3 times: 4 × 3 = 12 replicas. The raw space used is 500 × 3 = 1,500 MB, because the last block uses only 116 MB. The first option drops the partial last block.
