lessons.title: System software
lessons.summaryHtml:
System software turns what a programmer writes into a program that runs. An assembler translates assembly language into machine code, a macro processor expands macro calls, a compiler or interpreter handles high-level languages, and linkers and loaders join object modules, fix their addresses (relocation) and place them in memory. Editors and debuggers support the programmer around this chain.

NET asks about location-counter (LC) numericals, symbol and literal tables, one-pass versus two-pass assembly, macro expansion (including C preprocessor output), the four loader functions, loader schemes and relocation arithmetic. Learn the tables each pass builds, and practise assigning addresses line by line.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A computer runs only machine code: binary instructions at fixed addresses. People write assembly language or high-level languages, split programs into many files and use libraries. System software is the set of programs that closes this gap. The assembler and compiler translate, the macro processor expands shorthand, the linker joins pieces, the loader puts the result in memory, and the editor and debugger help the programmer write and fix code. Think of a publishing house: the author writes (editor), translators convert the text (assembler or compiler), an editor-in-chief merges chapters and fixes cross-references (linker), and the printer places the pages in the final book (loader).

Why it matters for NET

This topic usually gives a question or two in Unit 5. The favourites are: the address of a symbol or literal (LC processing), the tables built by each assembler pass, one-pass versus two-pass assembly, macro expansion and C preprocessor output, the four functions of a loader, matching loader schemes, and relocation or linking arithmetic. The questions are short but full of precise terms, so learn the vocabulary exactly.

Concepts in depth

Machine, assembly and high-level languages

Machine language is binary opcodes and addresses, specific to one processor. Assembly language replaces them with mnemonics (ADD, MOVER), symbolic labels and directives, but it is still one statement per machine instruction and machine-dependent. High-level languages are machine-independent, and one statement can generate many instructions. An assembler translates assembly language, while a compiler or interpreter handles a high-level language.

Assembly statements and the location counter

In the hypothetical machine used in Indian textbooks (Dhamdhere), statements fall into three classes:

  • Imperative statements (IS) such as MOVER, MOVEM, ADD, SUB, MULT, COMP, BC, READ, PRINT and STOP. Each becomes one machine instruction and takes one word.
  • Declaration statements (DL): A DS 3 reserves 3 words, and B DC '5' reserves one word holding 5.
  • Assembler directives (AD): START (set the LC), END (finish and place the pending literals), ORIGIN (set the LC to an expression), EQU (define a symbol’s value without using storage) and LTORG (place the current literal pool here).

The location counter holds the address of the next word. Each label gets the current LC value, except an EQU label, which gets the value of its expression. Literals such as ='5' are collected in a literal table. When LTORG or END appears, each distinct pending literal gets one word at the current LC and the LC advances. The pool table records where each pool begins in the literal table.

The SIC machine (Beck) is byte-addressed and uses hexadecimal addresses. Each instruction is 3 bytes and WORD is 3 bytes. RESW n takes 3n bytes and RESB n takes n bytes. BYTE C'EOF' takes one byte per character, and BYTE X'F1' takes one byte per two hex digits.

Two-pass and one-pass assemblers

The difficulty is the forward reference: an instruction can use a label that is defined later.

  • A two-pass assembler solves this simply. Pass 1 scans the source, processes the LC, builds the symbol table (SYMTAB), literal table (LITTAB) and pool table, and writes intermediate code. Pass 2 uses these tables to generate the machine code. In Donovan’s IBM 360 design, pass 1 uses the machine-op table (MOT), pseudo-op table (POT), symbol table (ST) and literal table (LT); pass 2 uses the MOT, POT, ST and a base table (BT).
  • A one-pass assembler generates code as it reads. For a forward reference, it leaves the operand address blank and records the instruction in a table of incomplete instructions (TII). When the symbol is defined, it goes back and fills in the address. This is backpatching. One-pass assemblers are faster and suit load-and-go systems.

Dhamdhere’s intermediate code writes each statement as class and code pairs, such as (IS,04)(1)(S,01). Variant I also processes constants and literals in pass 1, while variant II leaves more of the work for pass 2.

Macros and macro processors

A macro is a named sequence of statements defined once between MACRO and MEND. The first line after MACRO is the prototype (the name and formal parameters such as &X and &Y), and the lines that follow are model statements. A macro call is replaced by the model statements with the actual arguments substituted. This is macro expansion, and it happens at translation time.

  • Parameters: positional (matched by position) and keyword (&REG=AREG, matched by name, which allows default values).
  • Nested macro calls: a model statement can itself be a macro call. Expansion is done recursively, innermost call first (last in, first out).
  • Conditional expansion: AIF and AGO jump between sequencing symbols, and ANOP marks a place. Expansion-time variables (LCL and GBL, changed with SET) let one macro generate different code for different arguments.
  • Data structures (Donovan’s two-pass macro processor): the Macro Name Table (MNT) holds each name and a pointer into the Macro Definition Table (MDT), which holds the body. The Argument List Array (ALA) maps formal parameters to index markers (#1, #2) at definition time and to actual arguments at call time. MDTC and MNTC are the counters.
  • A macro preprocessor expands macros and passes the output to the assembler. A macro assembler does both jobs in one program.

Macro versus subroutine. A macro inserts a copy at every call. That means more memory but no run-time linkage, so it is faster. A subroutine keeps one copy entered by call and return. It uses less memory but pays linkage overhead. The C preprocessor’s #define is a macro facility. Because it substitutes text, operator precedence can surprise you, so always put brackets around parameters and around the whole body.

Compilers, interpreters and hybrids

A compiler translates the whole program into object code before it runs. Errors are reported for the whole program and execution is fast. An interpreter analyses and executes the program statement by statement, without producing a stored object program. Execution is slower, but interpreters are simple, portable and easy to debug. Hybrid systems compile to an intermediate code (for example Java bytecode) that a virtual machine interprets or compiles just in time (JIT). The phases of a compiler are covered in Unit 8.

Loaders and linkers

Donovan lists four loader functions:

  1. Allocation: reserve memory for the program.
  2. Linking: resolve symbolic references between object modules.
  3. Relocation: adjust address-dependent locations to match the allocated space.
  4. Loading: physically place the instructions and data into memory.

The loader schemes differ in who performs these functions:

  • Compile-and-go (assemble-and-go): the translator writes the code straight into memory and jumps to it. It is simple, but memory is wasted on the translator, the program must be retranslated on every run, and modules in different languages are hard to combine.
  • Absolute loader: the programmer does allocation and linking, the assembler effectively does relocation (the addresses are already fixed), and the loader only loads. It is simple and fast, but the programmer must know the memory layout.
  • Relocating loader, for example the BSS loader: it uses relocation bits (one per word, or a bit mask per text record) to mark the address-sensitive words, and a transfer vector for linking to subroutines.
  • Direct linking loader: a general two-pass relocating loader. The object deck carries ESD records (external symbol dictionary: SD, LD and ER entries), TXT (text), RLD (relocation and linkage directory) and END. Pass 1 allocates segments and builds the global external symbol table (GEST); pass 2 loads the text and applies the RLD entries.
  • Dynamic loading (load-on-call) brings a routine into memory only when it is called. Overlays are the programmer-planned version of the same idea.
  • Dynamic linking postpones linking until run time. A stub finds the shared library routine, so one copy in memory serves many programs and library updates need no relinking.
  • Linkage editor versus linking loader: a linkage editor produces a linked load module that is stored and loaded later (link once, load many times). A linking loader links and loads on every run.
  • Bootstrap loader: a tiny loader in ROM or firmware that loads the operating system at power-on.

Relocation and linking arithmetic

If a program was translated for origin to and is placed at lo, then the relocation factor is r = lo − to, and every address-sensitive word is increased by r. The factor can be negative. Words that are not address-sensitive (constants, opcodes, register numbers) are left alone. That is why the object code must say which words to relocate: relocation bits, RLD entries, or a relocation table. In the linking arithmetic, a symbol at translated address a in a module with translated origin to gets the link address lo + (a − to) when the module is linked at lo. Modules are normally placed one after another, so the next module’s link origin is the previous link origin plus the previous size.

A program that can run anywhere without relocation is position-independent (it uses only relative addressing or base registers). A program containing its own relocation code is self-relocating.

Debuggers and editors

A debugger lets the programmer set breakpoints, single-step through code, set watchpoints on variables, trace execution, and inspect or change memory and registers. It can also examine core dumps. Symbolic debugging needs symbol-table information from the compiler (for example gcc -g). Debuggers are machine-level or source-level.

Editors come in several types:

  • Line editors (ed) work on numbered lines.
  • Stream editors (sed) treat the text as a stream of characters and apply commands non-interactively.
  • Screen editors (vi) show a screenful and let you edit anywhere with the cursor.
  • Word processors add formatting.
  • Structure (syntax-directed) editors know the language grammar and edit the program as a tree.

In Beck’s model, an editor has a command language processor, and editing, travelling, viewing and display components. The travelling component moves the current editing pointer.

Worked examples

Example 1: LC processing with LTORG and EQU

        START   300          LC
        READ    X            300
        MOVER   AREG, X      301
        ADD     AREG, ='4'   302
        MOVEM   AREG, Y      303
LOOP    SUB     AREG, ='1'   304
        BC      GT, LOOP     305
        LTORG                ='4' at 306, ='1' at 307
        PRINT   Y            308
        MOVER   BREG, ='2'   309
BACK    EQU     LOOP         (no LC; BACK = 304)
        STOP                 310
X       DS      2            311-312
Y       DC      '7'          313
        END                  ='2' at 314

SYMTAB: LOOP 304, BACK 304, X 311, Y 313. LITTAB: ='4' 306, ='1' 307, ='2' 314. POOLTAB: pool 1 starts at literal 1 and pool 2 at literal 3. The program occupies 300–314, which is 15 words.

Example 2: ORIGIN

        START   200
        MOVER   AREG, ='3'   200
L1      ADD     AREG, B      201
        ORIGIN  L1+5         LC becomes 206
L2      MOVEM   AREG, C      206
        LTORG                ='3' at 207
B       DS      2            208-209
C       EQU     L2+1         C = 207
        STOP                 210
        END

ORIGIN sets the LC to the value of the expression (201 + 5 = 206). It does not add 5 to the current LC. So B = 208, C = 207, and the next free word after STOP is 211.

Example 3: SIC addresses in hexadecimal

COPY    START   1000      1000
FIRST   LDA     ALPHA     1000
        ADD     INCR      1003
        STA     BETA      1006
        RSUB              1009
ALPHA   WORD    5         100C
INCR    RESW    1         100F
BUF     RESB    100       1012
TEXT    BYTE    C'NET'    1076
HEXV    BYTE    X'F1A2'   1079
BETA    RESW    2         107B
        END     FIRST     (next free 1081)

RESB 100 is 100 decimal bytes, which is 64 in hex: 1012 + 64 = 1076. C'NET' takes 3 bytes and X'F1A2' takes 2. The program length is 1081 − 1000 = 81 in hex, or 129 bytes.

Example 4: relocation and linking

Module P was translated with origin 0 and has a size of 42 words; it is linked at 900. Module Q was translated with origin 300 and defines the entry point ALPHA at 312; it is placed right after P.

  1. Q’s link origin = 900 + 42 = 942.
  2. Q’s relocation factor = 942 − 300 = 642.
  3. The link address of ALPHA = 312 + 642 = 954. Every word of P that refers to ALPHA (declared EXTRN in P) is set to 954.

Relocation bits: a 64 KB program with 4-byte words has 16384 words. One relocation bit per word gives 16384 bits = 2048 bytes = 2 KB of relocation information.

Example 5: nested macro calls

        MACRO
        LDADD   &R, &P, &Q
        MOVER   &R, &P
        ADD     &R, &Q
        MEND
        MACRO
        SUM3    &A, &B, &C, &T
        LDADD   AREG, &A, &B
        ADD     AREG, &C
        MOVEM   AREG, &T
        MEND

The call SUM3 U, V, W, Z expands to LDADD AREG, U, V, which expands again to MOVER AREG, U and ADD AREG, V. Then come ADD AREG, W and MOVEM AREG, Z, so one SUM3 call gives 4 statements and one LDADD call gives 2. Two SUM3 calls and one LDADD call therefore generate 4 + 4 + 2 = 10 statements.

Example 6: C preprocessor traps (all verified with gcc)

  • #define SQ(x) x*x, then SQ(a+1) with a = 3 becomes a+1*a+1 = 7, not 16.
  • #define CUBE(x) (x)*(x)*(x), then 54 / CUBE(3) becomes 54/(3)*(3)*(3) = 162, because / and * associate left to right. The whole body needs outer brackets.
  • #define ABS(x) x < 0 ? -x : x, then ABS(2 - 5) becomes 2 - 5 < 0 ? -2 - 5 : 2 - 5 = −7.
  • #s turns an argument into a string and a##b pastes tokens: with int xy = 5;, CAT(x, y) is xy, which is 5.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemRule
Imperative statement, DC1 word each (hypothetical machine)
DS nn words
EQUno storage; symbol = value of the expression
ORIGIN exprLC = value of expr
LTORG / ENDplace the pending literals, one word each
SICinstruction 3 B, WORD 3 B, RESW n = 3n B, RESB n = n B, BYTE C'..' = number of chars, X'..' = digits/2
Program sizelast LC + 1 − start (or the next free address − start)
Relocation factorr = load (link) origin − translated origin
Relocated addresstranslated address + r
Next module link originprevious link origin + previous size
Expanded sizesource lines − definition lines − calls + Σ(statements generated per call)
Pass 1 tables (assembler)SYMTAB, LITTAB, POOLTAB (Donovan: MOT, POT, ST, LT)
Macro processor tablesMNT, MDT, ALA (+ MNTC, MDTC)
Direct linking loader recordsESD, TXT, RLD, END
Loader functionsallocation, linking, relocation, loading

NTA traps

  • Giving EQU a word. EQU never advances the LC.
  • Forgetting LTORG. Literals seen before an LTORG are placed there, not at END. Duplicate literals in one pool take one word.
  • Reading ORIGIN as “add”. ORIGIN L1+5 sets the LC to L1 + 5; it does not add 5 to the current LC.
  • Mixing decimal and hex in SIC. RESB 100 adds 100 decimal, which is 64 hex.
  • Using the relocation factor with the wrong sign, or adding the whole load origin. Relocate by the difference of the origins.
  • Thinking macro and subroutine differ only in syntax. The macro is expanded at translation time; the subroutine is called at run time.
  • Mixing up dynamic loading and dynamic linking. Loading on call is about memory; linking at run time is about resolving references to shared code.
  • Getting the absolute loader’s division of work wrong. The programmer allocates and links, and the loader only loads.

How NTA asks this

  • Numerical: “What address is assigned to symbol X?”, “What is the size of the program?”, “Where is the literal placed?”, or relocated and link addresses. Write the LC column and do not skip a line.
  • Code: the output of a C program with a macro. Expand the text by hand, then apply C precedence.
  • Match: loader scheme ↔ feature, table ↔ purpose, editor type ↔ example, or statement ↔ class (IS, DL, AD).
  • A–R and statements: two-pass versus one-pass, macro versus subroutine, compiler versus interpreter, dynamic linking.
  • Sequence: the order of records in an object deck (ESD, TXT, RLD, END) or the order edit–translate–link–load–execute.

Mini example (match). MNT ↔ macro names with MDT pointers, MDT ↔ macro bodies, ALA ↔ formal-to-actual argument mapping, SYMTAB ↔ label addresses. Elimination trick: fix the pair you are surest of (for example ESD ↔ external symbols) and strike every option that disagrees before reading the rest.

terms.definition: A counter the assembler keeps to assign an address to each statement. START sets it, each instruction or DC adds one word, and DS n adds n.
A table of labels and their addresses (or EQU values), built in pass 1 and used in pass 2.
An operand written as a constant, such as ='5'. The assembler stores it in a literal pool, placed by LTORG or END.
The use of a symbol before the statement that defines it. A two-pass assembler handles it naturally; a one-pass assembler needs backpatching.
A one-pass technique: leave the address blank, record the instruction in a table of incomplete instructions, and fill it in when the symbol is defined.
A named group of statements. Each call is replaced by a copy of the body with the arguments substituted, at translation time.
Adjusting address-sensitive words when a program is loaded somewhere other than the address it was translated for. Relocation factor = load (link) origin − translated origin.
Resolving references between separately translated modules (EXTRN / ENTRY, or public and external symbols).
Postponing linking of a routine (for example a shared library) until run time, when it is first needed.
A small loader, usually in ROM or firmware, that loads the operating system when the machine starts.

lessons.examTip: In LC questions, walk the program line by line and write the LC beside every statement. EQU uses no LC. LTORG and END place the pending literals, one word each. ORIGIN resets the LC. Most wrong options come from forgetting one of these four rules.

Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours.
Do the cs31 quiz and bank in exam mode and aim for 85% or more.

quiz.question: A program was translated with origin 500 and is loaded into memory starting at 900. An address constant in the program holds the translated address 540. What value must it hold after relocation?
quiz.explanation: Relocation factor = load origin − translated origin = 900 − 500 = 400. Each address-sensitive word is increased by 400: 540 + 400 = 940. 1440 wrongly adds the whole load origin, and 400 is only the factor.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: In compile-and-go, the assembler loads and runs the code itself (A-II). An absolute loader only loads code whose addresses the programmer has already fixed (B-III). The direct linking loader works from the ESD, TXT, RLD and END cards (C-I). Dynamic linking resolves references at execution time (D-IV).

b: I. Uses ESD, TXT, RLD and END records to relocate and link modules
II. The translator places code directly in memory and starts it; the translator itself occupies memory
III. The programmer fixes load addresses; the loader only copies the object code into memory
IV. External references are resolved at run time, typically to shared libraries

quiz.question: In Dhamdhere’s scheme for a hypothetical assembler, which of the following are assembler directives (class AD)?
options: A, B, D and E only
quiz.explanation: START, END, ORIGIN, EQU and LTORG are assembler directives. MOVER is an imperative statement (IS), and DS and DC are declaration statements (DL). A common slip is to call DS a directive.

stmts: A. START
B. LTORG
C. MOVER
D. ORIGIN
E. DS

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of dynamic linking with shared libraries?
options: Programs no longer need a loader
A single copy of a library routine in memory can be shared by many programs, and executables are smaller
All external references are resolved at compile time
quiz.explanation: With dynamic linking, a stub locates the shared routine at run time. One memory copy serves many processes, and library updates need no relinking. Linking is postponed, not moved to compile time, and a loader is still needed.

quiz.question: Arrange the following in the order in which they act on a program, from writing it to running it.
quiz.explanation: Edit (C), translate (D), link (B), load (A), execute (E). With a linking loader, B and A happen in one step, but the order stays the same.

stmts: A. The loader places the executable in memory
B. The linker combines object modules and library routines
C. The programmer writes the source in an editor
D. The assembler or compiler produces object code
E. The program executes

lessons.title: Processes, threads and synchronization
lessons.summaryHtml:
A process is a program in execution. It has its own address space, its state (new, ready, running, waiting, terminated) and a PCB that the OS saves and restores on a context switch. Threads are lighter units of execution inside a process. They share its code, data and open files, but each has its own stack, registers and program counter.

When processes or threads share data, a race condition can corrupt it, so each critical section must satisfy mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting. The tools are Peterson’s algorithm, hardware instructions (test-and-set, compare-and-swap), semaphores and monitors. NET tests fork() counts, semaphore arithmetic, which algorithm violates which requirement, and the classic producer–consumer, readers–writers and dining-philosophers problems.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A program is a file on disk. A process is that program while it runs: its code, its data, its stack, the CPU registers and the files it has open. The operating system juggles many processes on a few CPUs, so it must remember exactly where each one stopped. That memory is the process control block. A thread is a lighter worker inside a process. Several threads share one kitchen (code, data, files), but each has its own recipe card and hands (stack, registers, program counter). When workers share a kitchen they can collide, and synchronization is the set of rules that stops them spoiling the dish.

Why it matters for NET

This lesson feeds several question types in Unit 5. You will see fork() counting and output questions, semaphore value calculations, “which requirement does this algorithm violate?”, Peterson’s algorithm, the classic problems, thread models, and process-state transitions. Many questions are Assertion–Reason or match-the-list on definitions, so precise wording matters as much as calculation.

Concepts in depth

Operating system structures

  • Simple and monolithic (early UNIX, MS-DOS): the whole kernel is one program in one address space. It is fast but hard to maintain.
  • Layered: layer i uses only layer i − 1. It is easy to verify but adds overhead, and choosing the layers is hard.
  • Microkernel (Mach, QNX): only the essentials (IPC, basic scheduling, low-level memory) run in the kernel. Services run in user space and talk by message passing. It is more reliable and extensible, but the messages cost performance.
  • Modular (loadable kernel modules in Linux) and hybrid designs (Windows, macOS) combine these ideas.

Programs request OS services through system calls. The CPU has dual mode operation (user mode and kernel mode, shown by a mode bit), and privileged instructions run only in kernel mode.

Process states and the PCB

The five-state model has new, ready, running, waiting (blocked) and terminated. The legal transitions are:

  • new → ready (admitted);
  • ready → running (dispatched);
  • running → ready (interrupt, quantum expiry, or pre-emption);
  • running → waiting (an I/O request or an event wait);
  • waiting → ready (I/O or the event completes);
  • running → terminated (exit).

A waiting process never goes straight to running. With swapping, suspended ready and suspended blocked states are added (the seven-state model). The PCB stores the state, program counter, CPU registers, scheduling information (priority, queue pointers), memory-management information (base/limit registers or page tables), accounting information, and I/O status (open files, devices). On a context switch, the kernel saves the old process’s context into its PCB and loads the new one’s. The time taken is pure overhead and depends on hardware support (for example, several register sets).

At most one process per CPU is running. So with n processes and m CPUs, at most m are running and the rest are ready or waiting.

Process creation: fork, exec, wait

In UNIX, fork() creates a child that is a copy of the parent. It returns 0 in the child and the child’s PID (> 0) in the parent, or −1 on failure. After the fork, parent and child have separate address spaces (implemented with copy-on-write), so a change in one is not seen by the other. exec() replaces the process image with a new program, and wait() makes the parent wait for a child. A child that has exited but not been waited for is a zombie; a child whose parent exited first is an orphan and is adopted by init/systemd.

Counting rule: n forks executed one after another unconditionally give 2n processes, which is 2n − 1 children. With conditions or short-circuit operators, draw the tree. A classic trap is stdio buffering: text printed without a newline before a fork sits in the buffer and is copied into the child, so it can appear twice.

Threads

The threads of one process share code, data, heap and open files, but each thread has its own thread ID, program counter, register set and stack. The benefits are responsiveness, resource sharing, economy (creating and switching threads is much cheaper than for processes) and use of multicore processors.

  • User-level threads are managed by a library without the kernel knowing. They are fast to create and switch, but one blocking system call blocks the whole process, and they cannot run in parallel on several cores.
  • Kernel-level threads are scheduled by the kernel.

The mapping models are:

  • Many-to-one: many user threads map to one kernel thread. There is no parallelism, and a blocking call blocks all (for example, the old Green threads).
  • One-to-one: each user thread gets its own kernel thread. There is full concurrency, but many kernel threads cost resources (Linux, Windows).
  • Many-to-many: many user threads are multiplexed onto a smaller or equal number of kernel threads.
  • Two-level: many-to-many that also allows some one-to-one bindings.

Many-to-many systems use scheduler activations and upcalls to keep the right number of kernel threads (LWPs).

Inter-process communication

There are two basic models. With shared memory, the processes map a common region. It is fast after setup, but the processes must synchronize themselves. With message passing (send and receive), the kernel is involved in each message. It is easier to get right and works across machines.

  • Messages can be direct (naming the process) or indirect (through mailboxes or ports).
  • They can be blocking (synchronous) or non-blocking. A blocking send with a blocking receive is a rendezvous.
  • Buffering can have zero capacity, bounded capacity or unbounded capacity.

Other mechanisms are pipes (ordinary pipes are one-way and parent–child only; named pipes, or FIFOs, work between unrelated processes), signals, sockets and remote procedure calls (RPC).

The critical-section problem

A race condition happens because a statement such as x = x + 1 is really three machine steps: load, add, store. If two processes interleave these steps, one update can be lost. Each process’s code that touches shared data is its critical section, surrounded by an entry section and an exit section. A correct solution must satisfy:

  1. Mutual exclusion: at most one process is in its critical section at a time.
  2. Progress: if none is inside, only processes that want to enter decide who goes next, and the decision cannot be postponed forever. A process in its remainder section must not block others.
  3. Bounded waiting: after a process asks to enter, others can enter only a bounded number of times before it does. This rules out starvation.

A solution must also assume nothing about the relative speeds of the processes or the number of CPUs. Deadlock freedom is implied by progress.

Software solutions for two processes

  • Strict alternation (a shared variable turn): it gives mutual exclusion but violates progress, because a process cannot enter twice in a row even if the other does not want to enter.
  • Flags, set then check (flag[i] = true; while (flag[j]);): it gives mutual exclusion, but if both set their flags together, both wait forever. That is a deadlock, which violates progress.
  • Flags, check then set: mutual exclusion itself fails, because both can pass the check before either sets its flag.
  • Peterson’s algorithm combines flags and turn. It satisfies all three requirements.
/* process i; j = 1 - i; shared: bool flag[2] = {false,false}; int turn; */
flag[i] = true;          /* I want to enter            */
turn = j;                /* but you may go first       */
while (flag[j] && turn == j)
    ;                    /* busy wait                  */
/* critical section */
flag[i] = false;         /* exit section               */

On modern CPUs that reorder memory operations, Peterson’s algorithm needs memory barriers. The theory questions ignore this. The generalisation to n processes is the bakery algorithm (Lamport), in which each process takes a number and the lowest number enters, with ties broken by process ID.

Hardware support

  • Disabling interrupts works on a uniprocessor for short kernel code. It fails on multiprocessors, because other CPUs continue running, and it is dangerous to let user code do it.
  • TestAndSet(&lock) atomically returns the old value and sets lock to true. while (TestAndSet(&lock)); gives mutual exclusion and progress, but not bounded waiting (an unlucky process may always lose). Adding a waiting[] array and passing the lock around in cyclic order fixes this.
  • CompareAndSwap(&v, expected, new) sets v to new only if v equals expected, atomically. It is the basis of lock-free code.
  • A mutex lock offers acquire() and release(). If implemented by busy waiting, it is a spinlock. Spinlocks waste CPU time but avoid a context switch, so they suit short critical sections on multiprocessors.

Semaphores

A semaphore S is an integer accessed only by two atomic operations. wait(S) (also called P, down or acquire) waits until S > 0 and then decrements it. signal(S) (also called V, up or release) increments it. A counting semaphore ranges over any integers ≥ 0 and controls access to k identical resources (initialise it to k). A binary semaphore is 0 or 1 and acts like a mutex (initialise it to 1).

In the blocking implementation, wait decrements first and blocks the caller if the value becomes negative. The caller goes on the semaphore’s queue. signal increments the value and wakes one process if the value is still ≤ 0. So a negative value −k means k processes are blocked. After any complete set of operations, value = initial − waits + signals.

  • Ordering: to make S2 in P2 run after S1 in P1, use a semaphore initialised to 0. P1 does S1; signal(s), and P2 does wait(s); S2. A precedence graph needs one such semaphore per edge.
  • Dangers: deadlock (P0 does wait(S); wait(Q) while P1 does wait(Q); wait(S)), starvation (a LIFO semaphore queue), and priority inversion, which is solved by priority inheritance. A missing or extra signal breaks mutual exclusion.

Monitors

A monitor is an abstract data type whose procedures run with automatic mutual exclusion: only one process can be active inside at a time. Condition variables provide x.wait(), which suspends the caller and releases the monitor, and x.signal(), which resumes exactly one waiting process or does nothing if none is waiting. Unlike a semaphore’s signal, a condition’s signal has no memory. After a signal, either the signaller waits (signal-and-wait, Hoare) or the signalled process waits (signal-and-continue, Mesa, used in Java and pthreads, which is why waits are written in a while loop).

Classic synchronization problems

  • Bounded buffer (producer–consumer): mutex = 1, empty = n, full = 0. The producer does wait(empty); wait(mutex); add; signal(mutex); signal(full). The consumer does wait(full); wait(mutex); remove; signal(mutex); signal(empty). Swapping the two waits in the producer (wait(mutex) before wait(empty)) can deadlock when the buffer is full.
  • Readers–writers: rw_mutex = 1, mutex = 1, read_count = 0. The first reader locks rw_mutex and the last reader releases it. In the first readers–writers problem, writers may starve. The second version gives writers priority, and then readers may starve.
  • Dining philosophers: chopstick[5], all initialised to 1. If everyone picks up the left chopstick at the same moment, the system deadlocks. The remedies are: allow at most n − 1 philosophers at the table, pick up both chopsticks only if both are free (inside a critical section or monitor), or use an asymmetric order (odd philosophers pick left first, even ones right first). With n philosophers, at most ⌊n/2⌋ can eat at the same time.
  • Sleeping barber: semaphores customers = 0, barbers = 0, mutex = 1, plus a count of waiting customers.

Worked examples

Example 1: counting fork() processes

(a) for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) fork(); printf("X");: the number of processes goes 1 → 2 → 4 → 8, so X is printed 8 times, and 7 of those processes are children.

(b) fork() && fork() || fork();:

P  --fork1-->  child C1 gets 0  : "0 && ..." is false  -> runs fork3 -> 2 processes
P  (non-zero)  -> fork2 -> child C2 gets 0 : "0 || fork3" -> runs fork3 -> 2 processes
P  (non-zero)  after fork2: "1 || ..." short-circuits          -> 1 process
Total = 2 + 2 + 1 = 5

(c) if (fork() == 0) fork();: only the child forks again, giving 3 processes.

(d) printf("A"); fork(); printf("B"); prints ABAB. The A is still in the stdio buffer when fork copies the process, so both processes flush “AB”. Checked with gcc on Linux.

Example 2: semaphore arithmetic

  • S = 10, then 6 waits and 4 signals: 10 − 6 + 4 = 8.
  • S = 2, then 5 processes execute wait with no signal. In the blocking implementation, S = 2 − 5 = −3, so 3 processes are blocked and 2 are inside.
  • S = 1 guards a critical section for 9 processes, each running wait(S); CS; signal(S) once. A tenth, faulty process runs signal(S); CS; signal(S). Exhaustive search over all interleavings gives a maximum of 3 processes inside at once. With S = 2 and one faulty process, the maximum is 4.

Example 3: enumerating a race

x = 1. P1 runs x = x + 1 (load r1; r1 = r1 + 1; store) and P2 runs x = 2 * x (load r2; r2 = 2 × r2; store).

InterleavingFinal x
P1 completely, then P24
P2 completely, then P13
Both load 1; P2 stores 2; P1 stores 22
Both load 1; P1 stores 2; P2 stores 22

The possible final values are {2, 3, 4}. A program that checked all 20 interleavings confirms that no other value occurs. For two processes that each run x++ three times from x = 0, the possible final values are 2 to 6, so the minimum is 2, not 3.

Example 4: checking the entry protocols

An exhaustive state-space search of the two-process protocols gives:

ProtocolMutual exclusionDeadlock possible
Peterson (flag + turn)YesNo
Set own flag, then wait while the other’s flag is setYesYes (both flags set)
Wait while the other’s flag is set, then set own flagNoNo

The deadlock in the second protocol arises when both processes execute flag[i] = true before either tests, so each waits for the other forever.

Example 5: producer–consumer values

The buffer size is n = 5, starting empty (empty = 5, full = 0). After 4 productions and 1 consumption: full = 0 + 4 − 1 = 3 and empty = 5 − 4 + 1 = 2. If the producer then tries to produce 3 more items, the third finds empty = 0 and blocks at wait(empty). Because it has not yet taken the mutex, the consumer can still get in. If the producer had done wait(mutex) first, it would block holding mutex, and the consumer could never remove an item: a deadlock.

Example 6: dining philosophers and precedence graphs

  • With 7 philosophers, at most ⌊7/2⌋ = 3 can eat simultaneously, because no two neighbours can eat together. This is the maximum independent set of a 7-cycle.
  • Suppose statements S1 to S5 must obey S1 → S2, S1 → S3, S2 → S4, S3 → S4 and S4 → S5. That needs 5 semaphores, one per edge, each initialised to 0.

Operating-system services and operations

An OS offers two groups of services. The first group helps the user: a user interface (command line, GUI, touch screen), program execution, I/O operations, file-system manipulation, communication (shared memory or message passing) and error detection. The second group keeps the system itself running well: resource allocation, accounting (logging who used what) and protection and security.

Operations. A modern OS is interrupt driven: it sits idle until a hardware interrupt, a trap (a software-generated interrupt caused by an error such as division by zero) or a system call arrives. To protect itself it needs:

  • Dual-mode operation. A mode bit in hardware records kernel mode (0) or user mode (1). At boot the machine is in kernel mode; the OS switches to user mode before running a user program; every interrupt, trap or system call switches back to kernel mode. Privileged instructions (I/O, timer management, interrupt control, changing the mode bit) run only in kernel mode; in user mode they trap to the OS. CPUs with virtualisation add a third mode for the VMM, and many CPUs have more rings (x86 has four).
  • A timer. The OS sets a timer to interrupt after a fixed or variable period, so a user program in an infinite loop cannot keep the CPU forever. Loading the timer is privileged.

System calls in depth

A system call is the programmed entry into the kernel. Programmers rarely call it directly; they use an API (the POSIX API on UNIX, Linux and macOS, the Windows API, the Java API), and the run-time library’s system-call interface turns each API call into a trap. Each system call has a number, and the kernel uses it to index a table of handlers. The caller needs to know nothing about how the call is implemented.

Passing parameters to the kernel is done in three ways: (1) in registers (fastest, but there are few of them); (2) in a block or table in memory, whose address is passed in a register (Linux uses registers for up to five parameters and a block for more); (3) pushed on the stack by the program and popped by the OS. Methods 2 and 3 do not limit the number or length of parameters.

System calls fall into six groups. NET often matches the Windows and UNIX names:

TypeWindowsUNIX
Process controlCreateProcess(), ExitProcess(), WaitForSingleObject()fork(), exit(), wait()
File managementCreateFile(), ReadFile(), WriteFile(), CloseHandle()open(), read(), write(), close()
Device managementSetConsoleMode(), ReadConsole(), WriteConsole()ioctl(), read(), write()
Information maintenanceGetCurrentProcessID(), SetTimer(), Sleep()getpid(), alarm(), sleep()
CommunicationCreatePipe(), CreateFileMapping(), MapViewOfFile()pipe(), shm_open(), mmap()
ProtectionSetFileSecurity(), InitializeSecurityDescriptor(), SetSecurityDescriptorGroup()chmod(), umask(), chown()

Note that printf() is a library function, not a system call: it formats text in a user-space buffer and eventually calls write().

Example 7: counting system calls. A copy program reads a 1 MB (1,048,576-byte) file with read(fd, buf, 4096) until read() returns 0, and writes each block with write(). How many read() calls are made, and how many user-to-kernel mode switches do all the reads and writes cause?

Full blocks: 1,048,576 ÷ 4,096 = 256 reads that return data. One more read returns 0 (end of file), so there are 257 read() calls. There are 256 write() calls. Each system call enters the kernel once, so 257 + 256 = 513 switches into kernel mode (and as many back). The trap: forgetting the final read that detects end of file.

Operating-system design and implementation

Design goals come in two sets. User goals: the system should be convenient, easy to learn and use, reliable, safe and fast. System goals (for the people who design and maintain it): easy to design, implement and maintain, flexible, reliable, error-free and efficient. The goals are vague and often conflict, so there is no single "best" design; requirements depend on the hardware and on the type of system (batch, time-shared, real-time, distributed, mobile).

The key principle is to separate policy from mechanism. The mechanism decides how to do something; the policy decides what will be done. The timer is a mechanism for CPU protection; how long the timer is set for a given user is a policy. Separating them lets a policy change (say, favouring I/O-bound jobs) with only a parameter change, not a rewrite. Microkernels push this to the limit: the kernel provides mechanisms, and policies live in user-level servers. Solaris lets scheduling policy be changed through loadable tables.

Implementation. Early systems were written in assembly language. Today the kernel is mostly in C (with some C++), the lowest levels (context switch, interrupt entry) in assembly, and system programs in C, C++, and scripting languages. A high-level language makes the code faster to write, easier to understand and debug, and portable (Linux runs on many CPUs). The cost is some speed, which modern compilers largely recover; the real performance gains come from better data structures and algorithms, and only the few critical routines (the bottlenecks) are hand-tuned. Because it is written in a high-level language, an OS can also be emulated on other hardware.

System boot

Booting starts the computer by loading the kernel. The sequence on a typical PC:

  1. At power-on, the CPU starts executing the bootstrap program stored in firmware (ROM or EEPROM, historically the BIOS, today usually UEFI). It runs diagnostics (the power-on self-test), initialises the hardware, and finds a boot device. Firmware is used because RAM contents are unknown at power-on, and ROM cannot be infected by a virus.
  2. With BIOS, the firmware reads the boot block (the master boot record, sector 0 of the disk) into memory and runs it. A simple bootstrap in the boot block loads a more complex one; this is the two-step (multistage) boot. UEFI is a single, complete boot manager that understands file systems and GPT disks, so it is faster.
  3. A boot loader such as GRUB (Linux) or the Windows Boot Manager lets the user pick a kernel and parameters, then loads the kernel image (and on Linux an initramfs, a temporary root file system with the drivers needed to reach the real one).
  4. The kernel initialises itself and the devices, mounts the root file system and starts the first user process (init or systemd, PID 1), which starts the system services. Only then is the system running.

A disk that has a boot partition is a boot disk (system disk). Mobile systems keep the boot loader in firmware and the whole OS image in flash.

Example 8: the MBR layout. The classic MBR is one 512-byte sector. It holds a partition table of 4 entries of 16 bytes and a 2-byte boot signature (0x55AA). How many bytes are left for bootstrap code?

Partition table = 4 × 16 = 64 bytes. 512 − 64 − 2 = 446 bytes. So the MBR can hold at most 4 primary partitions, and its code is too small to understand a file system; that is why it only loads a second-stage loader.

Communication in client–server systems

Besides shared memory and message passing on one machine, processes on different machines use sockets, remote procedure calls and (locally) pipes.

Sockets. A socket is an endpoint for communication, identified by an IP address and a port. A connection is a pair of sockets, one at each end. Servers listen on well-known ports (below 1024: SSH 22, FTP 21, HTTP 80); a client’s port is an arbitrary number above 1024 chosen by its host, so every connection is unique. The loopback address 127.0.0.1 refers to the machine itself. Java provides connection-oriented (TCP) Socket, connectionless (UDP) DatagramSocket and MulticastSocket classes. Sockets are low level: they exchange an unstructured stream of bytes, and the applications must impose structure.

Remote procedure calls raise the level: a call looks like a local procedure call. A client-side stub locates the server port and marshals the parameters into a message; the server-side stub unmarshals them, calls the procedure, and returns results the same way. Three issues:

  • Data representation. Machines differ (big-endian versus little-endian), so parameters are converted to a machine-independent form such as XDR (external data representation).
  • Call semantics. Messages can be lost or repeated. At most once is implemented by attaching a timestamp to each message and having the server ignore duplicates. Exactly once also needs the server to send an ACK and the client to resend until it receives it.
  • Binding. The client must learn the server’s port: either a fixed port compiled in, or dynamically by asking a matchmaker (rendezvous daemon) on a fixed RPC port.

Android’s Binder and Windows’ ALPC are RPC-style mechanisms between processes on one machine.

Multicore programming

On a single core, threads are only interleaved: that is concurrency (more than one task making progress). On several cores they can truly run at the same time: that is parallelism. So a system can be concurrent without being parallel, but not the other way round.

  • Data parallelism distributes subsets of the same data across cores, each doing the same operation (summing halves of an array).
  • Task parallelism distributes different tasks (threads) across cores, each doing a unique operation, possibly on the same data. Most applications mix both.

Programmers face five challenges: identifying tasks that can run independently, balance (tasks of equal value), data splitting, data dependency (which forces synchronisation) and testing and debugging (many possible execution paths).

Amdahl’s law bounds the gain. If a fraction S of the program is serial and N cores are used, speedup ≤ 1 ÷ (S + (1 − S) ÷ N). As N → ∞, the speedup tends to 1 ÷ S.

Example 9: Amdahl’s law. An application is 80% parallel (S = 0.2). Speedup on 4 cores = 1 ÷ (0.2 + 0.8 ÷ 4) = 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5. On 8 cores = 1 ÷ (0.2 + 0.1) = 3.33. No number of cores can beat 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5. Doubling the cores from 4 to 8 gave only 33% more speed: the serial part dominates.

Thread libraries

A thread library gives the programmer an API for creating and managing threads. It is either entirely in user space (calls are local function calls, no system calls) or a kernel-level library supported by the OS (each call usually becomes a system call). The three main libraries:

LibraryCreate / waitNotes
POSIX Pthreadspthread_create(), pthread_join()A specification (IEEE 1003.1c), not an implementation; may be user- or kernel-level; used on Linux, macOS and other UNIX systems. pthread_attr_init() sets default attributes; the thread ends by returning or calling pthread_exit().
Windows threadsCreateThread(), WaitForSingleObject() / WaitForMultipleObjects()Kernel-level library; data shared through global variables
Java threadsExtend Thread or implement Runnable; start(), join()Implemented on top of the host OS library (Pthreads or Windows); calling start() allocates memory, creates a JVM thread and calls run(). Java has no global data, so shared data is passed by reference. The Executor framework separates creating threads from running tasks.

Two styles are common. In asynchronous threading, the parent creates a child and continues concurrently, with little data sharing (a multithreaded server). In synchronous threading (fork–join), the parent waits for all its children to finish before continuing, typically because it combines their results.

Example 10: fork–join with Pthreads. Two threads sum 1..5 and 6..10 into part[0] and part[1]; main joins both and prints part[0], part[1] and the total: 15 40 55 (verified with gcc). Because each thread writes its own array slot and main reads only after pthread_join(), there is no race. Without the joins, main could print before the threads finish.

Implicit threading

With hundreds of threads, getting creation and synchronisation right by hand is hard. Implicit threading moves the creation and management of threads from the programmer to compilers and run-time libraries. The programmer identifies tasks; the library maps them onto threads.

  • Thread pools. A number of threads are created at start-up and wait in a pool. A request is handed to a free thread, which returns to the pool when done; if none is free, the task waits in a queue. Benefits: servicing a request with an existing thread is faster than creating one; the pool bounds the number of threads, so the system is not overwhelmed; and separating the task from the mechanics allows strategies such as delayed or periodic execution. The pool size can be set from the number of CPUs, the memory and the expected load, and can grow and shrink. Examples: Windows QueueUserWorkItem(), Java ExecutorService.
  • Fork–join. The parent forks tasks and joins them; the library decides the actual number of threads. Java’s ForkJoinPool uses recursive divide-and-conquer with work stealing: an idle thread steals tasks from another thread’s queue.
  • OpenMP. Compiler directives for C, C++ and Fortran on shared-memory systems. #pragma omp parallel marks a parallel region: OpenMP creates as many threads as there are processing cores and all of them run the block. #pragma omp parallel for divides loop iterations among the threads.
  • Grand Central Dispatch (GCD) (Apple macOS and iOS): the programmer submits blocks (closures) to dispatch queues. A serial queue runs one block at a time in FIFO order (each process has a main queue); a concurrent queue removes blocks in FIFO order but may run several at once. GCD manages a pool of POSIX threads underneath.
  • Intel Thread Building Blocks (TBB): a C++ template library with a task scheduler that load-balances and is cache-aware (parallel_for).

Threading issues

  • fork() and exec(). If one thread calls fork(), does the child duplicate all threads or only the calling thread? Some UNIX systems offer both versions. If the child calls exec() at once, duplicating only the caller is enough, because exec() replaces the whole process (all threads) with the new program.
  • Signal handling. A signal is generated by an event, delivered to a process, then handled (by the default or a user-defined handler). Synchronous signals (illegal memory access, division by zero) go to the thread that caused them. For asynchronous signals (Ctrl+C, a timer) the options are: deliver to the thread the signal applies to, to every thread, to certain threads, or to one thread assigned to receive all signals. POSIX pthread_kill() sends a signal to a specific thread; Windows emulates signals with asynchronous procedure calls (APCs).
  • Thread cancellation. Terminating a thread (the target) before it finishes. Asynchronous cancellation terminates it at once, which may leave resources unreclaimed or data half-updated. Deferred cancellation (the Pthreads default) sets a flag; the target checks it only at cancellation points (such as read() or pthread_testcancel()), where it can clean up safely using a cleanup handler. On Linux, cancellation is implemented with signals.
  • Thread-local storage (TLS). Data of which each thread has its own copy (for example a transaction ID in a thread pool). Unlike local variables, TLS lives across function calls; it is like static data that is unique to each thread (__thread in gcc, ThreadLocal in Java).
  • Scheduler activations. In the many-to-many and two-level models, an intermediate structure, the lightweight process (LWP), appears to the user-thread library as a virtual processor, and each LWP is attached to a kernel thread. The kernel informs the library of events (such as a thread about to block) through an upcall; the library’s upcall handler then runs another user thread on a new virtual processor. This keeps the right number of kernel threads for the application.

NTA traps

  • “n forks create 2n child processes.” They create 2n processes in total, including the original, so there are 2n − 1 children.
  • Ignoring short-circuit evaluation in fork() && fork() || fork(). Evaluate for each branch separately.
  • Assuming the child shares globals with the parent. After fork, the address spaces are separate. Threads, by contrast, do share globals.
  • Treating busy waiting as a violated requirement. It is inefficient, not incorrect.
  • Mixing up progress and bounded waiting. Strict alternation fails progress, while plain TestAndSet fails bounded waiting.
  • Getting the waits in the producer in the wrong order. wait(mutex) before wait(empty) can deadlock.
  • Believing a semaphore value can never be negative. In the classic busy-wait definition it cannot; in the blocking implementation a negative value counts the waiters. Read which definition the question uses.
  • Treating a monitor signal like V. A signal on a condition variable with no waiter is lost.

How NTA asks this

  • Code: “How many times is … printed?” with fork(). Draw the tree, and watch for &&, ||, if (fork() == 0) and buffered output.
  • Numerical: the final semaphore value, the number of blocked processes, the maximum number in the CS with a faulty process, the minimum or maximum value of a shared variable, and buffer counts.
  • Match: state transitions ↔ causes, thread models ↔ properties, primitives ↔ descriptions, classic problems ↔ semaphores.
  • A–R and statements: Peterson, TestAndSet and bounded waiting, disabling interrupts on multiprocessors, user threads and blocking calls.

Mini example (A–R). A: “Disabling interrupts is not a suitable critical-section solution on a multiprocessor.” R: “Disabling interrupts on one processor does not stop other processors from accessing shared memory.” Both are true and R explains A. Elimination trick: in requirement questions, first strike any option that lists “no busy waiting” or “known speeds” as a requirement.

Saving the state of the running process into its PCB and loading another process’s saved state. It is pure overhead.
A situation where the result depends on the order in which concurrent processes access shared data.
Code that accesses shared data and must not be executed by two processes at once.
If no process is in the critical section, only processes wanting to enter take part in choosing who enters next, and the choice cannot be postponed forever.
There is a limit on how many times others can enter the critical section after a process has requested entry.
An integer variable accessed only through the atomic operations wait (P) and signal (V). It is counting or binary.
A language construct in which only one process can be active at a time. Condition variables (wait, signal) inside it handle ordering.
A lock where the waiting process busy-waits in a loop. It is useful on multiprocessors for short critical sections.
A high-priority process waits for a lock held by a low-priority process, which is itself pre-empted by medium-priority work. The fix is priority inheritance.

quiz.question: How many times is X printed by this program (assume every fork succeeds)?
quiz.explanation: Each fork doubles the number of processes: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8. All 8 processes reach the printf, so X is printed 8 times. 7 is the number of child processes created (2³ − 1), which is a different question.

quiz.question: A counting semaphore S is initialised to 7. Then 20 wait (P) operations and 15 signal (V) operations are completed on it. What is the final value of S?
quiz.explanation: Each wait subtracts 1 and each signal adds 1: 7 − 20 + 15 = 2. The order does not matter for the final value, as long as all operations complete.

b: I. The I/O operation or event the process was waiting for completes
II. The scheduler dispatches the process
III. A timer interrupt ends its time slice, or a higher-priority process arrives

lessons.title: CPU scheduling
lessons.summaryHtml:
CPU scheduling decides which ready process gets the processor next. You judge an algorithm by CPU utilisation, throughput, turnaround time, waiting time and response time. The core algorithms are FCFS, SJF, SRTF, priority (preemptive and non-preemptive, with aging), HRRN, round robin, and multilevel queue and feedback queue.

Almost every NET paper has at least one scheduling numerical. You draw a Gantt chart, read off completion times, and use TAT = CT − AT and WT = TAT − BT. Most wrong options come from a broken convention, so this lesson fixes them: ties go to the earlier arrival, then the lower process number. In round robin, a process that arrives at the same instant a quantum expires joins the queue before the pre-empted process. Response time is first run minus arrival.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Many processes are ready to run, but a single CPU can run only one at a time. The CPU scheduler (the short-term scheduler) picks the next one, and the dispatcher actually hands over the CPU. Picture a single ticket counter with a queue. The counter can serve people in arrival order, serve the quickest customers first, give each person two minutes in turn, or let VIPs go first. Each rule is fair to some people and unfair to others. Scheduling algorithms are these rules, and NET tests whether you can apply them precisely by drawing a Gantt chart.

Why it matters for NET

CPU scheduling is one of the most reliable scoring areas of Unit 5. A typical paper has one or two questions from it, and the most common is a numerical: “find the average waiting time (or turnaround time) under SRTF / RR / priority”. Around it come conceptual questions on which algorithm starves, which is preemptive, what happens to RR when the quantum grows, and matching algorithms to properties. The numericals are easy marks if your conventions are fixed, and costly if they are not, because the distractors are built from the classic slips.

Concepts in depth

CPU–I/O burst cycle and when scheduling happens

A process alternates between CPU bursts (computing) and I/O bursts (waiting for a device). I/O-bound processes have many short CPU bursts; CPU-bound processes have a few long ones. Scheduling decisions occur when a process (1) goes from running to waiting, (2) goes from running to ready (an interrupt or quantum expiry), (3) goes from waiting to ready (I/O completion), or (4) terminates. If scheduling happens only in cases 1 and 4, the scheme is non-preemptive (cooperative): a process keeps the CPU until it blocks or ends. If it can also happen in cases 2 and 3, it is preemptive.

The dispatcher switches context, switches to user mode and jumps to the right place in the user program. The time it takes is the dispatch latency. Do not confuse the three schedulers: the long-term (job) scheduler controls the degree of multiprogramming by admitting jobs, the medium-term scheduler swaps processes out and in, and the short-term (CPU) scheduler picks from the ready queue many times a second.

Interactive solver

Enter any problem, including the ones in your practice set, and the solver works it out step by step with the conventions stated. Use it to check your answers, not to replace doing them by hand: the exam gives you no solver.

Interactive solver: CPU scheduling solver

The solver runs in your browser. Turn on JavaScript to use it.

Scheduling criteria and the formulas

  • CPU utilisation: busy time ÷ total time. Maximise it.
  • Throughput: processes completed per unit time. Maximise it.
  • Turnaround time: TAT = CT − AT (completion minus arrival). Minimise it.
  • Waiting time: WT = TAT − BT, the total time spent in the ready queue. Minimise it. The scheduler affects only this part; the burst itself is fixed.
  • Response time: RT = (first time on CPU) − AT. It matters for interactive systems. For any non-preemptive algorithm, RT = WT, because a process that starts never waits again.

If a process also does I/O, then WT = TAT − (CPU time) − (I/O time).

The conventions used in this course

Remember: (1) Ties go to the process that arrived earlier, then to the lower process number. (2) Preemptive algorithms pre-empt only when the newcomer is strictly better; on an exact tie, the running process continues. (3) In round robin, a process that arrives at the same instant a quantum expires is queued before the pre-empted process. (4) In priority questions, a smaller number is a higher priority unless the question says otherwise. (5) Context-switch time is zero unless given. NET questions normally state their own conventions; always obey the question.

FCFS (first come, first served)

FCFS is a FIFO queue and is non-preemptive. It is simple, but its average waiting time depends heavily on the order. If one long CPU-bound job arrives first, all the short ones wait behind it: this is the convoy effect, and it also leaves I/O devices idle. FCFS never starves a process. It is poor for time-sharing because a process can hold the CPU for a long time.

SJF and SRTF

Shortest Job First runs the ready process with the smallest next CPU burst. The non-preemptive version lets it finish. SRTF (Shortest Remaining Time First) is the preemptive version: when a new process arrives, compare its burst with the remaining time of the running process and switch only if the newcomer is strictly shorter.

Why is SJF optimal? Take two adjacent jobs with bursts s < l. If s runs first, the extra waiting it causes is s (l waits s). If l runs first, the extra waiting is l. Putting the short one first always saves l − s, so repeated swaps sort the jobs shortest-first. For jobs all present at time 0, SJF gives the minimum average waiting time. SRTF is optimal for average waiting time when arrivals are staggered.

The catch is that the length of the next burst is not known. It is predicted by exponential averaging: τn+1 = α·tn + (1 − α)·τn, where tn is the actual length of the last burst and 0 ≤ α ≤ 1. With α = 0, the history alone decides (the prediction never changes); with α = 1, only the last burst counts. Both SJF and SRTF can starve long jobs.

LJF and LRTF are the opposites (longest first). They are poor for waiting time and appear only as numerical traps. In LRTF, ties are frequent, so the question always states a tie rule: follow it exactly, because it changes completion times.

Priority scheduling and aging

Each process has a priority and the highest-priority ready process runs. SJF is a special case in which priority is the (predicted) burst length. The preemptive version pre-empts the running process when a higher-priority one arrives. Priority scheduling can cause indefinite blocking (starvation). The cure is aging: raise the priority of a waiting process by a fixed step at fixed intervals. For example, if priorities run from 60 (lowest) down to 0 (highest) and aging improves priority by 1 every 5 seconds, even the lowest process reaches the top within 60 × 5 = 300 seconds.

HRRN (highest response ratio next)

HRRN is non-preemptive. When the CPU becomes free, compute the response ratio for every waiting process: RR = (W + S) ÷ S, where W is the time it has waited so far and S its burst. The highest ratio runs. Short jobs start with a high ratio, but the ratio of a long job grows as it waits, so HRRN favours short jobs without starving long ones.

Round robin (RR)

The ready queue is a circular FIFO. Each process gets at most one time quantum q, then goes to the tail of the queue if it is not finished. RR is preemptive and designed for time-sharing. With n ready processes, no process waits more than (n − 1)·q for its next slice (ignoring switch overhead). If q is larger than every burst, RR behaves exactly like FCFS. As q becomes very small, RR approaches processor sharing (each of n processes seems to run at 1/n speed), but the context-switch overhead dominates. With switch time s and long bursts, the fraction of CPU time spent on useful work is q ÷ (q + s). Average turnaround time does not necessarily improve as q grows. Response time does get worse with a larger q.

Multilevel queue and multilevel feedback queue

A multilevel queue splits the ready queue permanently into classes (for example system, interactive, batch). Each queue has its own algorithm (often RR for foreground, FCFS for background), and the queues are scheduled among themselves by fixed priority or by time slicing (for example 80% to foreground). A process never moves between queues, so low queues can starve. A multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ) lets processes move. A typical design is Q0 with RR q = 8, Q1 with RR q = 16, and Q2 with FCFS. A new process enters Q0, and a process that uses its whole quantum is demoted one level. A lower queue runs only when all higher queues are empty, and aging can promote a process that has waited too long. MLFQ is the most general scheme, defined by the number of queues, each queue’s algorithm, and the rules for promotion, demotion and entry.

Other points NET touches

  • Number of possible schedules: n processes, all at time 0, run non-preemptively, can be ordered in n! ways.
  • CPU utilisation with multiprogramming (a probabilistic model): if each process waits for I/O a fraction p of the time, the CPU is busy with probability 1 − pn for n processes in memory.
  • Thread and multiprocessor scheduling: process-contention scope versus system-contention scope, processor affinity (soft or hard), load balancing (push and pull migration), and symmetric versus asymmetric multiprocessing.
  • Real-time: rate-monotonic (static priority by shorter period) and EDF (earliest deadline first, dynamic).

Worked examples

The running example for these worked examples uses times in ms, with a smaller priority number meaning higher priority:

Example 1: FCFS and non-preemptive SJF

FCFS. Run the processes in arrival order.

| P1 | P2 |    P3    | P4 |  P5  |
0    6    9          17   19     23

CT = 6, 9, 17, 19, 23. TAT = CT − AT = 6, 8, 15, 16, 18, which sums to 63, so the average TAT is 12.6. WT = TAT − BT = 0, 5, 7, 14, 14, which sums to 40, so the average WT is 8.

SJF. Only P1 is ready at 0, so it runs to 6. At 6 the ready bursts are P2 3, P3 8, P4 2 and P5 4, so SJF picks P4, then P2, P5 and P3.

| P1 | P4 | P2 |  P5  |    P3    |
0    6    8    11     15         23

TAT = 6, 10, 21, 5, 10, which sums to 52, so the average TAT is 10.4. WT = 0, 7, 13, 3, 6, which sums to 29, so the average WT is 5.8. Check: the last CT (23) equals the sum of the bursts (23), so there was no idle time.

Example 2: SRTF, step by step

  1. At t = 0 only P1 (6) is ready, so it runs.
  2. At t = 1 P2 arrives with 3, which is less than P1’s remaining 5, so P2 pre-empts P1.
  3. At t = 2 P3 (8) arrives, but P2 has 2 left, so P2 continues. At t = 3 P4 (2) arrives; P2 has 1 left, so P2 continues and finishes at 4.
  4. At t = 4 the ready processes are P1 5, P3 8 and P4 2, so P4 runs 4–6. At t = 5 P5 (4) arrives, but P4 has 1 left.
  5. At t = 6 the choice is P1 5, P3 8 or P5 4, so P5 runs 6–10. Then P1 runs 10–15 and P3 runs 15–23.
|P1| P2 | P4 |  P5  |  P1  |    P3    |
0  1    4    6      10     15         23

CT: P1 15, P2 4, P3 23, P4 6, P5 10. TAT = 15, 3, 21, 3, 5 (sum 47), so the average TAT is 9.4. WT = 9, 0, 13, 1, 1 (sum 24), so the average WT is 4.8. Response times = 0, 0, 13, 1, 1, so the average RT is 3. There are 5 context switches between different processes (P1→P2→P4→P5→P1→P3).

Example 3: preemptive and non-preemptive priority

Preemptive. P1 runs 0–1. P2 (priority 1) arrives and pre-empts, running 1–4. At 4 the ready processes are P1 (3), P3 (4) and P4 (2), so P4 runs 4–6. Then P1 (3) runs 6–11, P3 (4) runs 11–19 and P5 (5) runs 19–23.

|P1| P2 | P4 |  P1  |    P3    |  P5  |
0  1    4    6      11         19     23

WT = 5, 0, 9, 1, 14 (average 5.8). TAT = 11, 3, 17, 3, 18 (average 10.4).

Non-preemptive. P1 runs 0–6, then the highest-priority ready process each time: P2 6–9, P4 9–11, P3 11–19, P5 19–23. WT = 0, 5, 9, 6, 14, so the average is 34/5 = 6.8.

Example 4: round robin, q = 3, and the tie convention

At t = 3, P1’s quantum expires and P4 arrives at the same instant. With our convention, P4 enters the queue first.

  1. t = 0: queue [P1]. P1 runs 0–3 (3 left). Arrivals up to 3: P2, P3, P4. Queue: P2, P3, P4, P1.
  2. P2 runs 3–6 and finishes. P5 arrived at 5, so the queue is P3, P4, P1, P5.
  3. P3 runs 6–9 (5 left), then P4 runs 9–11 and finishes. P1 runs 11–14 and finishes.
  4. P5 runs 14–17 (1 left), P3 runs 17–20 (2 left), P5 runs 20–21 and finishes, and P3 runs 21–23.
| P1 | P2 | P3 | P4 | P1 | P5 | P3 |P5| P3 |
0    3    6    9    11   14   17   20 21   23

CT = 14, 6, 23, 11, 21. WT = 8, 2, 13, 6, 12, which sums to 41, so the average WT is 8.2. Response times = 0, 2, 4, 6, 9, so the average RT is 4.2.

Other convention (pre-empted process first): at t = 3 the queue is P2, P3, P1, P4. P1 then finishes at 12 and P4 at 14, and the average WT becomes 8.4. The same data gives two different answers, so always read which rule the question fixes.

Example 5: HRRN

P1 runs 0–6 (it is alone at 0). At t = 6, the ratio (W + S)/S is: P2 (5 + 3)/3 = 2.67, P3 (4 + 8)/8 = 1.5, P4 (3 + 2)/2 = 2.5 and P5 (1 + 4)/4 = 1.25. P2 runs 6–9. At t = 9: P3 (7 + 8)/8 = 1.875, P4 (6 + 2)/2 = 4 and P5 (4 + 4)/4 = 2, so P4 runs 9–11. At t = 11: P3 (9 + 8)/8 = 2.125 and P5 (6 + 4)/4 = 2.5, so P5 runs 11–15, then P3 runs 15–23. WT = 0, 5, 13, 6, 6, so the average WT is 6. Note that at t = 9 the long job P3 has already gained on P5.

Example 6: multilevel feedback queue

Q0 uses RR with q = 8, Q1 uses RR with q = 16 and Q2 uses FCFS. P1 (arrival 0, burst 30) and P2 (arrival 4, burst 10) enter Q0.

  1. P1 runs 0–8 in Q0 and uses its full quantum, so it is demoted to Q1 with 22 left. P2 arrived at 4 into Q0, the same level, so it did not pre-empt.
  2. P2 runs 8–16 in Q0 and uses its full quantum, so it is demoted to Q1 with 2 left.
  3. Q0 is empty. P1 runs 16–32 in Q1 and uses its full 16, so it is demoted to Q2 with 6 left. P2 runs 32–34 and finishes.
  4. P1 runs 34–40 in Q2 and finishes.

CT: P2 34, P1 40. TAT: P1 40, P2 30. P2’s waiting time is 30 − 10 = 20.

Example 7: overhead and prediction numericals

  • FCFS with switch overhead. Four jobs with bursts 5, 3, 6 and 2 are present at 0, and each switch between jobs costs 1 ms. There are 3 switches, so the total time is 16 + 3 = 19 and the utilisation is 16/19 ≈ 84.21%.
  • RR efficiency. With q = 40 ms and s = 10 ms, the useful fraction is 40/50 = 80%.
  • Exponential averaging. With α = 0.5, τ0 = 12 and actual bursts 8, 6, 10: τ1 = 0.5·8 + 0.5·12 = 10, τ2 = 0.5·6 + 0.5·10 = 8, and τ3 = 0.5·10 + 0.5·8 = 9.

Thread scheduling

On systems with kernel threads, it is kernel-level threads, not processes, that the OS schedules. User threads are managed by a library and must be mapped onto a kernel thread (possibly through an LWP) before they can run. This gives two contention scopes:

  • Process-contention scope (PCS): in the many-to-one and many-to-many models, the thread library schedules user threads onto the available LWPs. Competition is only among threads of the same process. PCS is usually priority based and preemptive, with priorities set by the programmer and not adjusted by the library.
  • System-contention scope (SCS): the kernel decides which kernel thread gets a CPU, so competition is among all threads in the system. Systems using the one-to-one model (Windows, Linux) schedule threads using only SCS.

Pthreads lets a program choose with pthread_attr_setscope(): PTHREAD_SCOPE_PROCESS or PTHREAD_SCOPE_SYSTEM (pthread_attr_getscope() reads it). Linux and macOS allow only PTHREAD_SCOPE_SYSTEM. Scheduling a user thread onto an LWP does not mean it is running on a CPU; the kernel must still schedule that LWP’s kernel thread.

Multiple-processor scheduling

"Multiprocessor" now covers multicore CPUs, multithreaded cores, NUMA systems and heterogeneous (big.LITTLE) systems.

  • Asymmetric multiprocessing (AMP): one master processor makes all scheduling decisions and does the system work; the others run only user code. Simple (only one processor touches kernel data) but the master can become a bottleneck.
  • Symmetric multiprocessing (SMP): each processor schedules itself. Threads can sit in one common ready queue (which needs locking and can be contended) or in per-processor private queues (the usual choice: no contention and better cache use, but loads must be balanced). Windows, Linux and macOS use SMP.
  • Load balancing keeps the workload even when each processor has its own queue. In push migration a periodic task checks the loads and pushes threads from overloaded to idle processors; in pull migration an idle processor pulls a waiting thread from a busy one. Linux CFS and FreeBSD ULE use both.
  • Processor affinity. A thread that ran on a processor has warmed that processor’s cache; migrating it means invalidating and repopulating caches. So systems try to keep a thread on the same processor. Soft affinity: the OS tries but does not guarantee it. Hard affinity: the thread specifies a set of processors it may run on (Linux sched_setaffinity()). On NUMA systems, affinity also keeps a thread near its memory. Load balancing works against affinity, so tuning is a trade-off.
  • Multicore and hardware threads. When a core accesses memory it may wait a long time (a memory stall). Chip multithreading (CMT), which Intel calls hyper-threading, gives each core two or more hardware threads; when one stalls, the core switches to another. Each hardware thread appears to the OS as a logical CPU, so a 4-core chip with 2 hardware threads per core shows 8 logical CPUs. Coarse-grained multithreading switches threads only on a long-latency event (and must flush the pipeline); fine-grained (interleaved) multithreading switches at the boundary of each instruction cycle. This gives two levels of scheduling: the OS chooses which software thread runs on each hardware thread, and the core decides which hardware thread runs next.
  • Heterogeneous multiprocessing (HMP), such as ARM big.LITTLE, mixes fast big cores with energy-efficient little cores; interactive work goes to big cores and background work to little ones.

Real-time CPU scheduling

A soft real-time system gives critical tasks preference but no guarantee on when they run. A hard real-time system must meet deadlines; a result after the deadline is as bad as no result.

Minimising latency. Event latency is the time from an event to its service. Two kinds matter: interrupt latency (from the arrival of an interrupt to the start of its service routine; interrupts must be disabled only briefly) and dispatch latency (the time to stop one process and start another). Dispatch latency has a conflict phase (preempting any process running in the kernel, and making low-priority processes release resources a high-priority one needs) and a dispatch phase. A preemptive kernel keeps it small.

Priority-based scheduling with preemption gives only soft real-time. For hard real-time we model periodic tasks: each has a processing time t, a deadline d and a period p, with 0 ≤ t ≤ d ≤ p; its rate is 1 ÷ p and its CPU utilisation is t ÷ p. With admission control the scheduler admits a task only if it can guarantee its deadline.

  • Rate-monotonic (RM) scheduling: static priorities, preemptive; the shorter the period, the higher the priority. It is optimal among static-priority schemes: if RM cannot schedule a task set, no static-priority algorithm can. The Liu–Layland bound: n tasks are guaranteed schedulable if total utilisation U = Σ ti/pi ≤ n(21/n − 1). The bound is 1 for one task, 0.828 for two, 0.780 for three, and tends to ln 2 ≈ 0.693. The test is sufficient, not necessary: a set above the bound may still be schedulable, which must then be checked by simulation over the hyperperiod (the LCM of the periods).
  • Earliest-deadline-first (EDF): dynamic priorities; whichever ready task has the earliest deadline runs. It does not require periodic tasks or constant bursts. In theory it can schedule any periodic set with U ≤ 1 (100% utilisation), though context switching and interrupts prevent that in practice.
  • Proportional share: T shares are divided among the applications; an application with N shares gets N ÷ T of the processor time. Admission control refuses a request for more shares than remain.
  • POSIX real-time: SCHED_FIFO (FCFS within a priority, no time slicing) and SCHED_RR (round robin among equal priorities); SCHED_OTHER is implementation defined.

Example 8: RM succeeds. T1 has period 40 and burst 10; T2 has period 60 and burst 24. U = 10/40 + 24/60 = 0.25 + 0.40 = 0.65 ≤ 0.828, so RM is guaranteed to meet every deadline. The RM schedule: T1 0–10, T2 10–34, idle 34–40, T1 40–50, idle 50–60, T2 60–80, T1 80–90 (T1 preempts T2 at 80), T2 90–94, idle 94–120. Hyperperiod = LCM(40, 60) = 120, and no deadline is missed.

Example 9: RM fails, EDF succeeds. T1 has period 40 and burst 20; T2 has period 70 and burst 35. U = 20/40 + 35/70 = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0, above the two-task bound 0.828, so RM is not guaranteed.

RM : T1 0-20 | T2 20-40 | T1 40-60 | T2 60-70 ... deadline 70: T2 has run 30 of 35  -> MISS
EDF: T1 0-20 | T2 20-55 | T1 55-75 | T2 75-80 | T1 80-100 | ...  no miss in 0-280

Under RM, T1 (shorter period) preempts T2 at 40 and runs until 60, so T2 gets only 20 + 10 = 30 units before its deadline at 70. Under EDF, at t = 40 T2’s deadline (70) is earlier than the new T1 job’s deadline (80), so T2 keeps the CPU and finishes at 55; T1’s second job then finishes at 75, before its deadline 80. A simulation over the hyperperiod LCM(40, 70) = 280 finds no miss, as the EDF condition U ≤ 1 predicts.
