quiz.question: A process has 4 frames, all initially empty. It references the pages 4 2 0 2 6 1 2 4 0 6 1 3 2 1 4. How many page faults does the optimal (OPT) algorithm produce?
quiz.explanation: Four compulsory faults load 4, 2, 0, 6. At 1 (position 6), the next uses are 2 → 7, 4 → 8, 0 → 9 and 6 → 10, so 6 is replaced (5 faults). 2, 4 and 0 hit. At 6 (position 10), 0 is never used again, so 0 is replaced (6). 1 hits. At 3 (position 12), 6 is never used again, so 6 is replaced (7). 2, 1 and 4 hit. Total = 7, the minimum possible.

lessons.title: File systems and I/O
lessons.summaryHtml: A file system turns a disk, which is just a long array of blocks, into named files and directories that programs can create, read and protect. The key design choices are the access method, the directory structure, how blocks are allocated to a file (contiguous, linked, FAT or indexed, as in the UNIX inode) and how free blocks are tracked. Below the file system, the OS schedules disk requests to cut head movement (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK and C-LOOK), and RAID combines disks for speed and safety. NET asks head-movement numericals, inode maximum-file-size numericals, bitmap and disk-capacity sums, RAID capacities, and many concept questions in Match, Assertion–Reason and Statement formats. Every number below was checked by a program.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A disk is like a huge warehouse of numbered shelves (blocks). Programs do not want to think about shelf numbers; they want to say "open report.txt". The file system is the warehouse catalogue: it names files, remembers which shelves hold each file, keeps a list of empty shelves and enforces who may touch what. The I/O system is the loading dock: it decides the order in which the forklift (the disk arm) visits shelves, and it moves data between devices and memory efficiently.

Why it matters for NET

Expect one or two questions from this lesson in most papers. Disk-scheduling head-movement numericals are the single most common item. Inode maximum-file-size calculations, disk capacity and access time, bit-vector size and RAID capacity are the other numericals. Concept questions match allocation methods, directory structures, RAID levels and I/O techniques with their properties, often in Match and Statement formats.

Concepts in depth: files, attributes and operations

A file is a named collection of related information on secondary storage. Its attributes are name, identifier, type, location, size, protection, and time and user data. They live in the file control block (the inode in UNIX), and the directory entry points to it.

The basic operations are create, write, read, reposition (seek), delete and truncate. Because searching the directory on every call would be slow, open() copies the FCB into memory and returns an index into the open-file table. The system-wide table holds the FCB copy and an open count. The per-process table holds the file pointer and access mode. When the open count reaches zero, the entry is removed. Files can be locked: a shared lock is like a reader lock and an exclusive lock is like a writer lock. Locking may be mandatory (the OS enforces it, as in Windows) or advisory (programs must check, as usual in UNIX).

Concepts in depth: access methods

  • Sequential: read next, write next and rewind, like a tape. The most common pattern (editors, compilers).
  • Direct (relative): the file is a numbered sequence of fixed-length logical records; read n or write n in any order. Databases need it.
  • Indexed: an index (for example, sorted keys) points to records; large files may use a multi-level index, as in IBM’s ISAM.

Concepts in depth: directory structures

StructureIdeaLimitation
Single-levelOne directory for everyoneName clashes; no grouping
Two-levelA master directory with one user directory per userUsers are isolated; sharing is awkward
Tree-structuredArbitrary subdirectories, absolute and relative path namesNo sharing of a file between two directories
Acyclic graphShared files or subdirectories through links (hard or symbolic)A file has several names; deletion needs reference counts
General graphLinks may form cyclesTraversal may loop; garbage collection needed to reclaim cycles

UNIX avoids general graphs by forbidding hard links to directories. A symbolic link stores a path and can dangle after the target is deleted. A hard link adds a directory entry to the same inode, and the inode keeps a link count.

Concepts in depth: allocation methods

Contiguous allocation. The directory stores (start, length). Block i of the file is start + i, so direct access is trivial and sequential access needs minimal seeks. The costs: external fragmentation (first/best fit again), and files that are hard to grow. Extents (contiguous chunks linked together) are the modern compromise.

Linked allocation. The directory stores the first and last block, and every block stores a pointer to the next. There is no external fragmentation and files grow freely. Costs: direct access is O(i), pointers eat space (a 4-byte pointer in a 512-byte block leaves 508 bytes of data, 0.78% overhead) and one damaged pointer loses the rest of the file. Clusters of blocks reduce the pointer overhead. The FAT (file-allocation table, MS-DOS and FAT32) moves all the next-pointers into one table at the start of the volume, indexed by block number. It can be cached in memory, which makes random access much faster.

Indexed allocation. Each file has an index block, an array of block addresses; entry i points to block i. Direct access is fast and there is no external fragmentation, but a small file wastes most of its index block. Large files use a linked scheme (chained index blocks), a multi-level index, or the combined scheme of the UNIX inode.

The UNIX inode. An inode holds some direct pointers (often 12) plus one single indirect pointer (to a block of pointers), one double indirect pointer and one triple indirect pointer. With block size B and pointer size p, each index block holds k = B ÷ p pointers, and:

max blocks = direct + k + k^2 + k^3
max size   = max blocks x B

Small files are reached with no extra disk reads; huge files with at most three extra index reads (assuming the inode is already in memory).

Concepts in depth: free-space management

  • Bit vector (bitmap): one bit per block. In the textbook convention, 1 = free and 0 = allocated. Finding the first free block: skip whole words that are 0, then find the first 1 bit. Block number = (bits per word) × (number of zero words) + offset of the first 1 bit. Size = number of blocks ÷ 8 bytes. Simple, but it must be kept in memory to be fast.
  • Linked list: free blocks point to each other. No wasted space, but traversal is slow (rarely needed, since any free block will do).
  • Grouping: the first free block stores the addresses of n free blocks, the last of which stores the next n.
  • Counting: store (first free block, count of contiguous free blocks) pairs. Good when space is freed in runs.

Performance tools: a unified buffer cache for file pages and memory-mapped pages, free-behind and read-ahead for sequential access, and journaling (log-structured metadata updates) for fast crash recovery.

Concepts in depth: disk structure and access time

A magnetic disk has platters; each surface has concentric tracks divided into sectors. The set of tracks at one arm position across all surfaces is a cylinder. The disk is addressed as a one-dimensional array of logical blocks, mapped onto sectors cylinder by cylinder.

  • Capacity = surfaces × tracks per surface × sectors per track × bytes per sector.
  • Access time = seek time + rotational latency + transfer time.
  • Rotation time = 60 ÷ RPM seconds. Average rotational latency = half of that. At 7,200 RPM, a rotation takes 8.33 ms and the average latency is 4.17 ms.
  • Transfer rate (bytes per second) = bytes per track × rotations per second.

Seek time dominates, which is why the OS reorders requests. SSDs have no seek, so they usually use FCFS or a simple request-merging scheduler.

Concepts in depth: disk-scheduling algorithms

AlgorithmRuleProperty
FCFSArrival orderFair, no starvation, usually the most movement
SSTFNearest pending request nextLow movement; can starve far requests; not optimal
SCAN (elevator)Sweep in one direction to the disk end, then reverseNo starvation; middle cylinders get better service
C-SCANSweep one way to the end, jump back to the other end without servicing, sweep againMore uniform waiting time
LOOKLike SCAN, but reverse at the last requestSaves the empty trip to the end
C-LOOKLike C-SCAN, but go only as far as the last request, then jump to the lowest pending requestThe practical form of C-SCAN
Conventions to read in every question: the disk range (for example 0–199), the current direction, and whether the return jump of C-SCAN or C-LOOK counts as head movement. Textbooks and answer keys differ on the last point. This course states the convention in every question and gives both totals in the examples.

Concepts in depth: RAID

LevelMethodUsable capacity (n disks of size D)Survives
0Block striping, no redundancynDNo failure
1MirroringnD ÷ 2One disk per mirrored pair
2Bit striping with Hamming-code ECCLess than nDOne disk (obsolete)
3Bit or byte striping, one parity disk(n − 1)DOne disk
4Block striping, one dedicated parity disk(n − 1)DOne disk; the parity disk is a write bottleneck
5Block striping, parity distributed over all disks(n − 1)DOne disk (needs n ≥ 3)
6Like 5 with two independent parities (P + Q)(n − 2)DAny two disks (needs n ≥ 4)
1+0 / 10Stripe across mirrored pairsnD ÷ 2One disk in each pair

RAID protects against disk failure, not against deleted files or software bugs, so it does not replace backups.

Concepts in depth: I/O systems

  • Polling (busy waiting): the CPU repeatedly reads the device’s status register. Fine for fast devices, wasteful for slow ones.
  • Interrupt-driven I/O: the device raises an interrupt when ready. The CPU saves state and runs the handler found through the interrupt vector. Maskable and non-maskable interrupts; priority levels.
  • DMA: for large transfers, the CPU gives the DMA controller the source, destination and count. The controller moves the data directly between device and memory (stealing memory cycles) and interrupts once at the end.
  • Application I/O interface: devices differ (block vs character, sequential vs random, synchronous vs asynchronous, sharable vs dedicated), and device drivers hide these differences behind a few standard interfaces.
  • Blocking calls suspend the process until the I/O completes. Non-blocking calls return at once with whatever is available. Asynchronous calls return at once and signal completion later.
  • Kernel I/O subsystem: I/O scheduling; buffering (to absorb speed mismatch, adapt transfer sizes and support copy semantics; double buffering lets one buffer fill while the other empties); caching (a fast copy of data that exists elsewhere); spooling (a buffer that holds output for a device such as a printer that cannot interleave jobs); device reservation; error handling; and protection (all I/O instructions are privileged).
  • A read request travels: system call → kernel I/O subsystem (check the cache) → device driver → device controller → interrupt on completion → driver → kernel → the process is woken up.

Worked examples

Example 1: all six disk-scheduling algorithms. Cylinders 0–199, head at 70 moving towards higher cylinders. Queue: 120, 25, 160, 88, 10, 185, 55, 135. Sorted: 10 25 55 [70] 88 120 135 160 185.

  • FCFS: 70→120→25→160→88→10→185→55→135: 50 + 95 + 135 + 72 + 78 + 175 + 130 + 80 = 815.
  • SSTF: 70→55 (15)→25 (30)→10 (15)→88 (78)→120 (32)→135 (15)→160 (25)→185 (25) = 235. The first move goes down, because 55 is 15 away and 88 is 18 away.
  • SCAN (up): 70→185 (115), on to the end 199 (14), then reverse to 10 (189): 318.
  • LOOK (up): 70→185 (115), reverse to 10 (175): 290.
  • C-SCAN (up): 70→199 (129), jump 199→0 (199), 0→55 (55): 383 counting the jump, 184 without it.
  • C-LOOK (up): 70→185 (115), jump 185→10 (175), 10→55 (45): 335 counting the jump, 160 without it.
LOOK from 70
up:   88 120 135 160 185
down: 55 25 10

If the head were moving down instead, SCAN would give 70→0 (70) then 0→185 (185) = 255, and LOOK would give 60 + 175 = 235.

Example 2: inode maximum file size. 12 direct pointers, 1 single, 1 double and 1 triple indirect; 4 KB blocks; 4-byte pointers.

  • k = 4096 ÷ 4 = 1,024 pointers per index block.
  • Blocks = 12 + 1,024 + 1,024² + 1,024³ = 12 + 1,024 + 1,048,576 + 1,073,741,824 = 1,074,791,436.
  • Size = 1,074,791,436 × 4 KB = 48 KB + 4 MB + 4 GB + 4 TB, which is just over 4 TB. The triple indirect pointer dominates.
  • Where does byte offset 5,000,000 live? Block number = ⌊5,000,000 ÷ 4,096⌋ = 1,220. Direct pointers cover blocks 0–11 and the single indirect covers 12–1,035, so block 1,220 is reached through the double indirect pointer. With the inode in memory, reading it takes 3 disk reads: the double indirect block, a single indirect block and the data block.

Example 3: disk capacity and access time.

  • A disk has 16 surfaces, 2,048 tracks per surface, 256 sectors per track and 512 bytes per sector. Capacity = 16 × 2,048 × 256 × 512 = 24+11+8+9 = 232 bytes = 4 GB. A sector address needs 32 − 9 = 23 bits.
  • At 7,200 RPM, one rotation takes 60,000 ÷ 7,200 = 8.33 ms, so the average latency is 4.17 ms. One track holds 256 × 512 = 131,072 bytes and the disk makes 120 rotations per second, so the transfer rate is about 15.7 MB/s.
  • A disk at 6,000 RPM with a 4 ms average seek and 500 sectors per track: rotation 10 ms, average latency 5 ms, time to read one sector 10 ÷ 500 = 0.02 ms. Average time to read one random sector = 4 + 5 + 0.02 = 9.02 ms.

Example 4: free space and FAT.

  • Bit vector for a 1 TB disk with 4 KB blocks: 240 ÷ 212 = 228 blocks, so 228 bits = 225 bytes = 32 MB.
  • With 1 = free and 8-bit words, the bitmap 00000000 00000000 00011010 … has two zero words, and the first 1 in the third word is at offset 3. First free block = 8 × 2 + 3 = 19.
  • FAT32-style table for an 8 GB volume with 4 KB clusters and 4-byte entries: 233 ÷ 212 = 221 entries × 4 B = 8 MB.

Example 5: RAID capacity. Six 2 TB disks.

LevelUsableWhy
RAID 012 TBAll space holds data
RAID 1 / 106 TBEvery block is stored twice
RAID 510 TBOne disk’s worth of parity
RAID 68 TBTwo disks’ worth of parity

File-system structure and implementation

A file system is built in layers, each using the services of the one below:

application programs
logical file system        metadata: directories, FCBs (inodes), protection
file-organisation module   logical block -> physical block, free-space manager
basic file system          generic "read block 123" commands, buffers and caches
I/O control                device drivers and interrupt handlers
devices

Layering reduces duplicated code (several file systems can share one basic file system and I/O control), at the cost of some overhead per layer.

On-disk structures. A boot control block (per volume; the first block, empty if the volume holds no OS; the UFS boot block, the NTFS partition boot sector); a volume control block with the number and size of blocks, the free-block count and pointers, and the free-FCB count (the UFS superblock, the NTFS master file table); a directory structure; and one FCB per file (the inode in UNIX; a row of the MFT in NTFS).

In-memory structures, loaded at mount time and discarded at dismount: the mount table (one entry per mounted volume), a directory-structure cache of recently used directories, the system-wide open-file table (a copy of each open file’s FCB), the per-process open-file table (a pointer into the system-wide table, the file position and the access mode), and buffers for blocks being read or written.

Creating a file: the application calls the logical file system, which allocates a new FCB (or takes a free one), reads the directory into memory, adds the new name and FCB, and writes the directory back. open() searches the system-wide table first; if another process already has the file open, only a per-process entry is created. UNIX treats a directory as a file with a type field; Windows has separate system calls for files and directories.

Directory implementation

  • Linear list of file names with pointers to the data blocks. Simple to program, but slow: finding a file needs a linear search, and creating a file first requires searching to make sure the name is not already used. Deletion can mark the entry unused, copy the last entry into the hole, or use a linked list. A sorted list allows binary search but must be kept sorted; a balanced tree (B-tree) is the usual answer for large directories.
  • Hash table: a linear list plus a hash table that takes a value computed from the name and returns a pointer into the list. Lookup time drops sharply, but collisions (two names hashing to the same slot) must be handled, and a fixed-size table must be rehashed when it fills (for example from 64 to 128 slots, which changes the hash function). A chained-overflow hash table makes each slot a linked list, so collisions just lengthen a chain.

Example 6: searching a directory. A directory holds 1,000 entries. As an unsorted linear list, a successful search compares on average (n + 1) ÷ 2 = 500.5 names, and an unsuccessful one (which every create needs) compares all 1,000. With a chained-overflow hash table of 64 slots and a uniform hash, the average chain holds 1,000 ÷ 64 = 15.625 entries, so an unsuccessful lookup examines about 15.6 names.

File-system mounting

Just as a file must be opened before use, a file system must be mounted before its files are available to processes. The OS is given the device name and a mount point, the place in the existing directory tree where the new file system is attached (typically an empty directory). The OS checks that the device holds a valid file system of the expected format (reading its superblock), then records the mount in the mount table. Path-name traversal that reaches the mount point switches to the root of the mounted file system.

  • If the mount point is not empty, its old contents are hidden (not deleted) until the file system is unmounted.
  • UNIX can mount at any directory; the root file system is mounted at boot, and others are listed in a configuration file (/etc/fstab on Linux) or mounted on demand (automount). Unmounting fails while a file on it is in use.
  • Windows traditionally gives each volume a drive letter (C:, D:), a separate name space; since Windows 2000 a volume can also be mounted at a directory. macOS mounts new devices under /Volumes.
  • Some systems forbid mounting at a directory that has files, or mounting the same file system twice. Remote mounting (NFS) attaches a server’s directory to a local mount point, which is the basis of file sharing across machines.

File sharing and consistency semantics

With multiple users, the system keeps an owner (user ID) and a group (group ID) for each file; the owner can change the attributes and grant access, and group members get a subset of the owner’s rights (the permission bits of cs37). Sharing across machines uses FTP-style explicit transfer, a distributed file system (remote directories mounted locally), or the web. Remote sharing uses the client–server model, and adds new failure modes: a network or server failure can leave a client’s request unanswered. A stateless protocol (NFSv3) lets the client simply retry; a stateful one must rebuild its state after a crash.

Consistency semantics say when one user’s writes become visible to others sharing the file: UNIX semantics (immediately; users may even share the file pointer), session semantics (only to sessions opened after the file is closed, as in AFS), and immutable shared files (a shared file can never change). cs38 covers distributed file systems in more detail.

Efficiency, performance and recovery

Efficiency depends on the allocation and directory algorithms and on what is kept in each FCB. Examples: UNIX preallocates inodes across the volume and keeps a file’s data blocks near its inode to cut seek time; clusters of varying size cut internal fragmentation; keeping a "last access" date means a directory write on every read; wider pointers (64-bit) allow larger files but use more space.

Performance. A buffer cache holds disk blocks; a page cache holds file data as virtual-memory pages. Without integration, a memory-mapped file is cached twice (double caching); a unified buffer cache uses the page cache for both mapped I/O and read()/write(). Synchronous writes wait until the data reach the disk (needed for metadata and databases); asynchronous writes (the usual case) return once the data are in the cache. For sequential access, LRU is a poor replacement choice: free-behind removes a page from the buffer as soon as the next page is requested, and read-ahead fetches the requested page and several following ones together.

Recovery. A crash can leave metadata inconsistent (for example a block marked free but used by a file).

  • Consistency checking: a program such as fsck (UNIX) or chkdsk (Windows) compares the directory structure and other metadata with the data blocks and repairs what it can. It can take a long time on a large volume.
  • Log-structured (journaling) file systems (ext4, NTFS, XFS) write every metadata change to a log as a transaction first; once the transaction is in the log it is committed and the system call can return. The changes are then applied to the real structures, and completed transactions are removed from the log. After a crash, committed but unapplied transactions are replayed and uncommitted ones are undone, so recovery is fast and needs no full scan.
  • Other approaches: copy-on-write designs never overwrite blocks in place (WAFL, ZFS, Btrfs), which also makes snapshots cheap.
  • Backup and restore. A full backup copies everything; an incremental backup copies only what changed since the previous backup. A typical cycle is a full backup on day 1, then an incremental each day. A restore needs the last full backup plus every incremental since it.

Example 7: restoring from a backup cycle. A full backup is taken on day 1 and an incremental backup (changes since the previous backup) on each of days 2 to 7. The disk fails after the day 7 backup. The restore needs the full backup and the incrementals of days 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, applied in that order: 7 backup sets. (With differential backups, each holding all changes since the last full backup, only 2 would be needed: the full backup and the day 7 differential.)

Disk management and swap-space management

  • Low-level (physical) formatting, usually done at the factory, divides the disk into sectors, each with a header and a trailer (sector number and an error-correcting code, ECC) around a data area (typically 512 bytes or 4 KB).
  • The OS then partitions the disk into one or more groups of cylinders and does logical formatting: it writes the initial file-system structures (free-space maps and an empty root directory). Some applications (databases) use a raw partition with no file system.
  • Boot block. The tiny bootstrap in ROM loads a full bootstrap program from the boot blocks at a fixed location on the disk (the MBR sector 0 on a PC; see cs32).
  • Bad blocks. Old disks had bad blocks marked by hand (format, chkdsk). SCSI-style controllers keep a list of bad blocks and a set of spare sectors: sector sparing (forwarding) logically replaces a bad sector with a spare, ideally on the same cylinder; sector slipping shifts the following sectors down one place to free the sector next to the bad one. Soft errors may be repaired from the ECC; hard errors lose data, which must be restored from backup.
  • Swap-space management. Swap space can be a large file in the normal file system (easy, but directory and allocation overhead make it slow) or a separate raw swap partition managed by a swap-space manager optimised for speed rather than space (some internal fragmentation is acceptable because swap data live briefly). Linux supports both and keeps a swap map: an array of counters, one per page slot, where 0 means free and a value above 0 counts how many processes map that page. Modern systems swap pages, not whole processes, and do not write unmodified code pages to swap at all (they are reread from the executable).

Application I/O interface, kernel I/O subsystem and request handling in depth

Device characteristics that the kernel hides behind a few interfaces: data-transfer mode (character or block), access (sequential or random), transfer schedule (synchronous or asynchronous), sharing (sharable or dedicated), speed, and direction (read only, write only, read–write).

InterfaceOperationsExamples
Block deviceread(), write(), seek(); raw or direct I/O; memory mappingDisks
Character streamget(), put() one character at a time; line editing on topKeyboard, mouse, serial port
Network socketcreate, connect, listen, send, receive; select() to see which sockets have dataNetwork interface
Clocks and timerscurrent time, elapsed time, set a timer (programmable interval timer)Time slicing, disk flushing

An ioctl() system call is the escape that passes device-specific commands to a driver. Vectored I/O (readv(), writev(), "scatter–gather") moves data between several buffers with one system call.

Kernel I/O subsystem, in more detail. Buffering is done for three reasons: a speed mismatch between producer and consumer, a transfer-size mismatch (network packets reassembled into messages) and copy semantics (write() copies the data to a kernel buffer at call time, so later changes to the user buffer do not affect what is written). Caching keeps a copy of data held elsewhere; spooling queues output for a device that can serve only one job at a time; error handling returns an error code (errno in UNIX) and may retry; I/O protection makes all I/O instructions privileged, so users must go through system calls. The kernel keeps state in data structures such as the open-file table, and many kernels (UNIX) use an object-oriented style in which a file descriptor’s operations dispatch to the right routine for files, raw devices or sockets.

Example 8: why double buffering helps. A process reads blocks and computes on each. Let T = 10 ms be the time to input a block, C = 6 ms the computation time per block and M = 1 ms the time to move a block from a system buffer to the user area. Time per block: no buffering T + C = 16 ms; single buffering max(C, T) + M = 11 ms (the next block is read while the current one is processed); double buffering max(C, T) = 10 ms (one buffer fills while the other empties, so the slower of input and computation sets the pace).

Transforming I/O requests to hardware operations. The OS must connect a file name to a device controller. MS-DOS uses the part before the colon (C:) to pick the device. UNIX looks up the longest matching prefix in the mount table to find the device name; the device name is itself a special file whose inode holds a <major, minor> device number. The major number selects the device driver and the minor number is passed to the driver to select the unit. Then the life cycle runs: system call → kernel checks the cache → driver issues commands to the controller → the controller transfers the data (often by DMA) and interrupts → the handler wakes the driver → the kernel copies the data and moves the process back to the ready queue. System V UNIX (and Solaris) also provide STREAMS: a full-duplex channel from a stream head (interfacing with the user process) through optional modules to a driver end, with message queues between them.

NTA traps

  • SCAN stopping at the last request. That is LOOK. SCAN goes all the way to the disk end (0 or the maximum cylinder) before reversing.
  • The return jump. C-SCAN and C-LOOK totals change by hundreds depending on whether the jump counts. Read the question; compute both if unsure and see which appears in the options.
  • Direction. SCAN and LOOK totals depend on the initial direction. If none is given, look for a hint such as the previous head position; otherwise compute both directions and see which total appears in the options.
  • SSTF is optimal. It is greedy and can be beaten; it can also starve requests.
  • Inode arithmetic. k = block size ÷ pointer size, not block size itself. A double indirect pointer covers k², not 2k.
  • Bitmap bits vs bytes. Divide by 8.
  • RAID 4 vs RAID 5. RAID 4 has a dedicated parity disk; RAID 5 spreads parity. Both give (n − 1) disks of capacity.
  • Linked allocation and direct access. It is poor at direct access. FAT improves this only because the table can be cached.
  • Buffering, caching and spooling. A buffer may hold the only copy of data; a cache always holds a copy of data stored elsewhere; a spool queues whole jobs for a non-sharable device.

How NTA asks this

  • Head-movement numericals: give the queue, head and direction; ask for one algorithm’s total. Sort the queue, then use the shortcut formulas for SCAN and LOOK.
  • Inode or index numericals: maximum file size, or how many disk reads for a given byte offset.
  • Match the List: allocation method ↔ property, directory structure ↔ limitation, RAID level ↔ method, I/O technique ↔ description.
  • Statement I/II and Assertion–Reason: fragmentation of allocation methods, starvation in SSTF, RAID 5 parity, DMA.
  • Order: layers of the file system, or the life of an I/O request.

Mini-example (Statement I/II). I: C-SCAN provides more uniform waiting time than SCAN. II: LOOK always gives a smaller total head movement than SCAN. Statement I is true: C-SCAN treats the disk as circular. Statement II is false as worded: LOOK is never worse than SCAN in the same direction, but it is equal (not smaller) when a request sits at the disk end. The answer is "Statement I is true but Statement II is false".

Watch out: when options contain both the "with jump" and "without jump" totals for C-SCAN or C-LOOK, the question wording decides. Never assume.

terms.definition: The per-file structure holding attributes: owner, permissions, size, timestamps and the location of the data blocks. In UNIX it is the inode.
Kernel tables of currently open files: a system-wide table (FCB copy, open count) and a per-process table (current position, access mode).
Each file occupies consecutive blocks. Fast sequential and direct access, but external fragmentation and hard file growth.
Each block holds a pointer to the next. No external fragmentation, but direct access needs a walk along the chain. FAT keeps the chain in a table.
All block pointers of a file are kept in an index block. The UNIX inode combines direct, single, double and triple indirect pointers.
Free-space map with one bit per block. Its size in bytes is (number of blocks) ÷ 8.
Seek: moving the arm to the cylinder. Latency: waiting for the sector to rotate under the head; on average half a rotation.
SCAN (elevator) sweeps to one end, then reverses. C-SCAN sweeps one way, returns to the start without servicing, and sweeps again, giving more uniform waiting time.
Like SCAN and C-SCAN, but the arm turns at the last request instead of travelling to the disk end.
Redundant array of independent disks: striping (RAID 0), mirroring (RAID 1), block striping with distributed parity (RAID 5) or double parity (RAID 6).

lessons.examTip: For every disk-scheduling question, first sort the queue and mark the head position on a number line. Then read the direction and whether the arm goes to the disk end (SCAN, C-SCAN) or only to the last request (LOOK, C-LOOK), and whether the return jump is counted.

quiz.question: A disk has cylinders 0–199. The head is at cylinder 60. The request queue is 30, 110, 75, 15, 180, 95, 140. What is the total head movement under SSTF?
quiz.explanation: From 60 the nearest is 75 (15), then 95 (20), 110 (15), 140 (30), 180 (40). Now 30 is nearer than anything else: 180 → 30 is 150, then 30 → 15 is 15. Total = 15 + 20 + 15 + 30 + 40 + 150 + 15 = 285. 500 is FCFS, 323 is SCAN upward and 300 is C-LOOK counting the jump.

quiz.question: An inode has 10 direct block pointers, 1 single indirect pointer and 1 double indirect pointer. The block size is 1 KB and a block pointer takes 4 bytes. What is the maximum file size?
quiz.explanation: One block holds 1024 ÷ 4 = 256 pointers. Blocks = 10 + 256 + 256² = 10 + 256 + 65,536 = 65,802. Size = 65,802 × 1 KB = 65,802 KB (about 64.3 MB). Option 2 counts only the double indirect part. Option 4 would need a triple indirect pointer too.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: FCFS: arrival order (A-II). SSTF: shortest seek, may starve (B-I). SCAN: the elevator (C-IV). C-SCAN: one-way service with a return sweep (D-III). Option 4 swaps SCAN and C-SCAN.

b: I. Can starve requests far from the head
II. Services in arrival order; fair but no optimisation
III. Returns to the start without servicing, giving more uniform waiting times
IV. Elevator algorithm that reverses at the disk end

quiz.question: A disk has cylinders 0–199. The head is at 60 and moving towards higher cylinders. The queue is 30, 110, 75, 15, 180, 95, 140. What is the total head movement under C-LOOK if the jump from the last request back to the lowest request is counted?

quiz.question: Six disks of 2 TB each are combined into a RAID 5 array. What is the usable capacity?
quiz.explanation: RAID 5 spends the equivalent of one disk on parity: (6 − 1) × 2 = 10 TB. RAID 0 would give 12 TB, RAID 6 8 TB and RAID 1 (or 10) 6 TB.

quiz.question: A 1 TB disk uses 4 KB blocks, and free space is tracked with a bit vector (one bit per block). How large is the bit vector?
quiz.explanation: Blocks = 2⁴⁰ ÷ 2¹² = 2²⁸. Bits = 2²⁸, bytes = 2²⁸ ÷ 8 = 2²⁵ = 32 MB. 256 MB forgets to divide by 8.

lessons.title: Security, protection and virtual machines
lessons.summaryHtml: Protection is the set of mechanisms inside the OS that control which process may touch which resource. Security is the wider job of defending the system against attackers, both inside and outside. Protection is described with domains and the access matrix, which is stored as access lists (per object) or capability lists (per domain). Security covers malware (virus, worm, trojan, logic bomb, rootkit), program attacks such as the buffer overflow, authentication (passwords with salt, biometrics, multi-factor), and the basic cryptography an OS uses. The lesson ends with virtual machines: Type 1 and Type 2 hypervisors, trap-and-emulate, binary translation, paravirtualisation and hardware support, and containers, which share the host kernel.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Think of a large office building. Protection is the lock-and-key system inside: which employee’s badge opens which room. It assumes everyone follows the rules and only stops honest mistakes and overreach. Security is the whole defence of the building: guards, cameras, checks on visitors, and plans for burglars who pick locks. In an OS, protection is the internal mechanism (domains, access rights, permission bits), and security is protection plus defence against attackers (malware, stolen passwords, network attacks).

A virtual machine is a second, fake building inside the first: software that makes one physical computer look like several separate computers. It is part of this unit because isolation between virtual machines is itself a protection mechanism.

Why it matters for NET

This topic usually gives one to three questions in Paper 2, and it overlaps with Unit 9 (network security). The favourite sub-topics are the access matrix and its implementations (ACL versus capability list), malware definitions, Bell–LaPadula versus Biba, Type 1 versus Type 2 hypervisors, and UNIX permission bits. Most questions are conceptual, often in Match, Statement I/II or Assertion–Reason form. A few are small numericals: key counts, permission octals, password search spaces and toy RSA.

Goals and principles of protection

  • Principle of least privilege: give each program, user and system component only the rights it needs for its task, and only while it needs them. Damage from a bug or a break-in stays small.
  • Need-to-know: at any time a process should access only the objects it currently needs. It is least privilege applied over time.
  • Separate policy from mechanism: the mechanism (how access is checked) should be general, so different policies (who may do what) can be set without changing the kernel.
  • Compartmentalisation and defence in depth: several independent layers, so one failure does not open everything.

Protection domains and rings

A domain is a set of access rights, each an ordered pair <object, rights-set>. A process executes in one domain at a time. Domains can be static (fixed for the process’s life, which breaks need-to-know) or dynamic (the process can switch domain). In UNIX a domain is tied to the user ID. Switching happens through the setuid bit: when a setuid program runs, its effective user ID becomes the file owner’s ID. The passwd program is setuid root, so an ordinary user can update the password file through it and nothing else.

MULTICS organised domains as concentric rings numbered 0 to 7. Ring 0 is the most privileged (the kernel), and an inner ring has every privilege of the outer rings. Modern CPUs keep the idea: x86 has rings 0–3 and ordinary OSs use ring 0 (kernel) and ring 3 (user).

The access matrix

The access matrix is the general model of protection. Rows are domains, columns are objects, and entry access(i, j) is the set of operations a process in domain Di may perform on object Oj. Domains can also be columns, so switching domains is itself a controlled right.

DomainF1F2PrinterD2 (as object)
D1read, write*owner, read–switch
D2read–print–
D3–executeprint–

Special rights let the matrix itself change in a controlled way:

  • copy (written with an asterisk, as in write*): a domain holding R* on an object may copy R into another domain’s entry in the same column. Variants are transfer (copy, then remove it from yourself) and limited copy (copy R without the asterisk, so it cannot spread further).
  • owner: the owner of an object may add and remove any right in that object’s column.
  • control: applies to domain objects; a domain with control over Dj may remove rights from Dj’s row.
  • switch: a process in Di may move to Dj if switch ∈ access(i, Dj).

Most cells are empty, so nobody stores the matrix as a 2-D array. The four implementations are a favourite comparison:

ImplementationWhat is storedStrengthWeakness
Global tableTriples <domain, object, rights>SimpleHuge; hard to keep in memory; cannot group objects
Access list (ACL)Per object: the column, <domain, rights> pairsMatches user thinking (“who may use my file?”); easy revocationChecking needs a search on every access
Capability listPer domain: the row, protected object pointers with rightsFast checking: holding the capability is the proofRevocation is hard; capabilities are scattered
Lock–keyObjects have locks (bit patterns); domains have keysA compromise: revocation by changing a lockKeys must be managed by the OS

Capabilities must be unforgeable. The OS keeps them in protected memory, or tags them in hardware so user code cannot change them (Hydra and the Cambridge CAP system are the classic capability systems). Real systems combine the two: UNIX checks the ACL (permission bits) at open(), then gives the process a file descriptor, which acts like a capability for later reads and writes.

Revocation questions ask whether it is immediate or delayed, selective or general, partial or total, and temporary or permanent. For capabilities the four schemes are reacquisition (delete them periodically and make processes ask again), back-pointers (the object points to all its capabilities), indirection (capabilities point to a global table entry that can be deleted) and keys (each capability carries a key compared with the object’s master key; changing the master key revokes all).

Security models and evaluation classes

Multilevel security gives every subject a clearance and every object a classification (for example Unclassified < Confidential < Secret < Top Secret).

  • Bell–LaPadula (confidentiality): the simple security property means no read up; the *-property means no write down. Secrets can flow only upward.
  • Biba (integrity) is the mirror image: no read down (do not trust dirtier data) and no write up (do not contaminate cleaner data).

The US TCSEC (“Orange Book”) graded systems as D (minimal), C1 and C2 (discretionary protection; C2 adds auditing and per-user accountability), B1, B2 and B3 (mandatory protection with labels) and A1 (verified design). The Common Criteria (ISO 15408) with levels EAL1–EAL7 replaced it.

Security threats

Silberschatz lists five kinds of security violation: breach of confidentiality, breach of integrity, breach of availability, theft of service and denial of service. Common methods are masquerading (pretending to be someone else), replay attacks, message modification, man-in-the-middle and session hijacking.

MalwareKey idea

Other classic program threats are the time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) race, where a file is checked and then swapped before use, and code injection.

The buffer overflow attack

C functions such as gets(), strcpy() and sprintf() copy without checking the destination size. If a local array on the stack receives more bytes than it holds, the extra bytes overwrite whatever lies above it: the saved frame pointer and then the return address.

high addresses
+--------------------+
| caller's frame     |
+--------------------+
| return address     |  <- overwritten with the address of the attack code
+--------------------+
| saved frame ptr    |
+--------------------+
| char buf[16]       |  <- strcpy(buf, input) writes upward from here
+--------------------+
low addresses

The attacker sends input that contains machine code (shellcode) and a new return address pointing into it. When the function returns, the CPU jumps into the shellcode, which runs with the victim program’s privileges. If that program is setuid root, the attacker gets a root shell. Defences: bounds-checked functions (fgets, snprintf, strncpy used carefully), stack canaries (a random value placed before the return address and checked before return), a non-executable stack (NX bit, DEP), ASLR (random memory layout), and compiling with safe languages or checks.

Authentication

Authentication proves identity with something you know (password, PIN), something you have (smart card, phone, hardware token) or something you are (fingerprint, face, iris; typing rhythm is a behavioural trait). Using two different factors is two-factor or multi-factor authentication.

  • Stored passwords are never kept in plain text. The OS stores hash(salt + password) and the salt. The hash is one-way, and the salt makes each user’s hash unique, so one precomputed (rainbow) table cannot attack all users. An n-bit salt multiplies the attacker’s precomputation by 2n.
  • Search space for a password of length L over an alphabet of size N is NL, and its strength in bits is L × log2 N.
  • One-time passwords (challenge–response, time-based codes) defeat replay because each value is used once.
  • Biometrics are judged by FAR (false acceptance rate: impostors accepted ÷ impostor attempts) and FRR (false rejection rate: genuine users rejected ÷ genuine attempts). Raising the threshold lowers FAR but raises FRR; the point where they are equal is the equal error rate (EER).

Cryptography basics for the OS

  • Symmetric encryption uses one shared key (DES with a 56-bit key, 3DES, AES with 128/192/256-bit keys). It is fast, but keys must be shared securely: n users who all talk in pairs need n(n − 1)/2 keys.
  • Asymmetric (public-key) encryption uses a key pair: encrypt with the receiver’s public key, decrypt with the private key (RSA). n users need only n pairs, 2n keys in all.
  • Hash functions (SHA-256 gives 256 bits; MD5 gives 128 bits and is broken) give a fixed-size digest; they store passwords and check integrity.
  • Digital signature: sign with the sender’s private key (usually on the hash of the message), verify with the sender’s public key. It gives authentication, integrity and non-repudiation. Certificates from a certificate authority bind a public key to an identity.

RSA in one line: choose primes p and q, n = pq, φ(n) = (p − 1)(q − 1), choose e with gcd(e, φ) = 1, find d with e × d ≡ 1 (mod φ). Encryption C = Me mod n, decryption M = Cd mod n.

Virtual machines

A virtual machine monitor (VMM) or hypervisor creates the illusion that each guest OS owns a whole computer. Popek and Goldberg (1974) set three requirements: fidelity (a program behaves as on real hardware), performance (most instructions run directly, without the VMM stepping in) and safety (the VMM keeps full control of resources). Their theorem: an architecture can be virtualised by trap-and-emulate if every sensitive instruction (one that reads or changes machine state) is also privileged (traps when run in user mode). The guest kernel runs in user mode; each privileged instruction traps to the VMM, which emulates it on the guest’s virtual state.

Classic x86 broke this rule. Some sensitive instructions, such as POPF, silently behave differently in user mode instead of trapping. Three fixes followed:

  • Binary translation (early VMware): the VMM scans guest kernel code and rewrites the troublesome instructions on the fly; user code runs natively.
  • Paravirtualisation (Xen): the guest OS is modified to call the hypervisor directly through hypercalls. It is fast, but the guest source must be changed.
  • Hardware-assisted virtualisation (Intel VT-x, AMD-V): a new root mode for the VMM and non-root mode for guests, with automatic VM exits. Nested (extended) page tables remove most shadow page table work.
KindWhere it runsExamples
Type 0In firmware; hardware partitionsIBM LPARs, Oracle LDOMs
Type 1 (bare metal)Directly on hardware; it is a small OS itselfVMware ESXi, Xen, Microsoft Hyper-V, KVM (turns Linux into the hypervisor)

Benefits: isolation between guests (a crashed or infected guest does not hurt others), server consolidation (many lightly used servers on one host), snapshots and cloning, running several OSs for testing, and live migration. In pre-copy live migration the destination reserves resources, all memory pages are copied while the VM keeps running, pages dirtied meanwhile are recopied in rounds, and finally the VM pauses briefly while the last dirty pages and CPU state are copied, then resumes on the destination. Memory tricks include overcommitment, a balloon driver inside the guest that frees pages on request, and sharing identical pages between guests.

Containers

A container virtualises the operating system, not the hardware. All containers on a host share one kernel. Linux builds them from namespaces (separate views of process IDs, network, mounts, hostname, IPC and users) and control groups (cgroups), which limit CPU, memory and I/O. Images are layered file systems. Docker packages and runs containers, and Kubernetes orchestrates many of them. Ancestors are chroot, FreeBSD jails and Solaris zones.

Worked examples

Example 1: Reading an access matrix. Using the matrix above, answer: (a) What is the ACL of F1? (b) What is the capability list of D3? (c) Can a process in D1 give D3 write access to F1? (d) Can D2 print after switching from D1?

  1. (a) The ACL is the F1 column: <D1, {read, write*}>, <D2, {read}>.
  2. (b) The capability list is the D3 row: <F2, {execute}>, <Printer, {print}>.
  3. (c) Yes. D1 holds write* on F1, and the asterisk is the copy right, so D1 may add write (or write* under unrestricted copy) to access(D3, F1).
  4. (d) D1 has switch on D2, so a process in D1 can move into D2. Once in D2, it gets D2’s rights, which include print on the printer. It loses D1’s rights while in D2.

Example 2: umask and special bits. The umask is 027. (a) What mode does a new file get if the program asks for 0666? (b) A new directory, asked for 0777? (c) What does ls show for mode 4755 and for 4644?

  1. Rule: final mode = requested & ~umask. ~027 clears the group write bit and all “others” bits.
  2. (a) 0666 & ~0027 = 0640, shown as rw-r-----.
  3. (b) 0777 & ~0027 = 0750, shown as rwxr-x---.
  4. (c) The leading 4 is the setuid bit, shown in the owner’s execute position. 4755 gives rwsr-xr-x (lowercase s: setuid and execute). 4644 gives rwSr--r-- (capital S: setuid set but the owner has no execute, so it is useless). Similarly 2 is setgid (s in the group position) and 1 is the sticky bit (t in the others position, as on /tmp: rwxrwxrwt, where only a file’s owner may delete it).

Verified by a real C program: after umask(027), open(..., O_CREAT, 0666) gives mode 640.

Example 3: Password strength and salt. Passwords have 8 characters over 62 symbols, and the attacker tries 10⁹ hashes per second. (a) Search space and bits? (b) Worst-case and average time? (c) The system adds a 12-bit salt. What does this change?

  1. (a) 62⁸ = 218,340,105,584,896 ≈ 2.18 × 10¹⁴. In bits: 8 × log₂ 62 = 8 × 5.954 ≈ 47.6 bits.
  2. (b) Worst case = 2.18 × 10¹⁴ ÷ 10⁹ ≈ 218,340 s ≈ 60.7 hours. Average = half of that, about 30.3 hours.
  3. (c) Salt does not make one guessed password harder: an attacker attacking one user reads the salt from the file and still needs about 2.18 × 10¹⁴ tries. What it defeats is precomputation. A single precomputed table no longer serves everyone; the attacker needs 2¹² = 4096 tables, one per salt value, and equal passwords no longer have equal hashes.

Example 4: Toy RSA and key counts. Take p = 5, q = 11, e = 3. Find d, encrypt M = 9, and count keys for 100 users.

  1. n = 55 and φ(n) = 4 × 10 = 40. gcd(3, 40) = 1, so e = 3 is valid.
  2. d = 3⁻¹ mod 40. Since 3 × 27 = 81 = 2 × 40 + 1, d = 27.
  3. C = 9³ mod 55 = 729 mod 55 = 729 − 13 × 55 = 14.
  4. Check: 14²⁷ mod 55 = 9. Decryption recovers M.
  5. Symmetric keys for 100 users talking in pairs: 100 × 99 ÷ 2 = 4950. Public-key: 100 pairs = 200 keys.

Example 5: Bell–LaPadula and Biba decisions. Levels are U < C < S < TS. Subject X is cleared at S. For objects at C and TS, which operations are allowed?

ObjectBLP readBLP writeBiba readBiba write
C (below)Yes (read down)No (no write down)No (no read down)Yes (write down)
TS (above)No (no read up)Yes (write up)Yes (read up)No (no write up)

Memory hook: BLP keeps secrets from leaking down; Biba keeps dirt from flowing up. Each rule of one model is the reverse of the other.

Example 6: Server consolidation. Twelve identical physical servers each average 8% CPU. The team will virtualise them onto hosts of the same capacity and keep each host at or below 80%. How many hosts are needed?

  1. Total load = 12 × 8% = 96% of one server.
  2. Hosts = ⌈96 ÷ 80⌉ = ⌈1.2⌉ = 2.
  3. Ten physical machines are freed. This saving, and not speed, is the main business case for virtualisation.

Access control and role-based access control

The access matrix is a model; access control is how real systems apply it. Three styles appear in exam options:

  • Discretionary access control (DAC): the owner of an object decides who may use it, through ACLs or permission bits (UNIX, Windows file ACLs).
  • Mandatory access control (MAC): a system-wide policy, which users cannot override, decides access from security labels (Bell–LaPadula levels, SELinux).
  • Role-based access control (RBAC): rights are attached to roles, and users are assigned roles. Solaris 10 is the textbook case. A privilege is the right to execute a system call or to use an option within one (for example, opening a file with write access). Privileges can be assigned to processes, limiting them to exactly the access they need; roles carry sets of privileges and programs; a user takes a role by entering the role’s password, or the role is assigned to the user. Because privileges are fine grained and are held only while needed, RBAC implements the principle of least privilege far better than the all-or-nothing root account, and it reduces the risk of a superuser or setuid program being abused. Administration is also easier: when someone changes job, only their role assignment changes.

Windows uses DAC through ACLs on objects, plus privileges (such as "back up files") held in the access token of each process.

Revocation of access rights: a closer look

Revoking a right can be described along four dimensions:

QuestionOptions
When?Immediate or delayed (and if delayed, can we know when it takes effect?)
Whom?Selective (a chosen group of users) or general (everyone who holds the right)
How much?Partial (a subset of the rights on the object) or total (all rights)
How long?Temporary (the right can be regained) or permanent

With an access list, revocation is easy: search the object’s list for the right(s) and delete them. It is immediate and can be general or selective, total or partial, permanent or temporary.

With capabilities it is hard, because the capabilities are spread through the system and must first be found. The four schemes compare as follows:

SchemeHow it worksSelective?Cost or catch
ReacquisitionCapabilities are deleted from each domain periodically; a process that still needs one must reacquire it and is refused if its right was revokedYesRevocation is delayed until the next sweep
Back-pointersEach object keeps a list of pointers to all its capabilities, which can be followed and changed (MULTICS)YesCostly to maintain
IndirectionCapabilities point to an entry in a global table, which points to the object; revoking deletes the table entry, and the freed entry can be reusedNoCannot revoke selectively
KeysEach capability carries a key; the object has a master key; access succeeds only if they match. Changing the master key (with a set-key operation, allowed only to the owner) revokes all existing capabilitiesOnly if a list of keys is kept per objectA single master key gives general revocation only

Example 7: choosing a revocation scheme. An object has 5 capabilities held by domains D1–D5, and the owner wants to revoke only D2’s. Indirection fails: all 5 capabilities may share one global-table entry, and deleting it revokes all 5. A single master key also fails: changing it invalidates all 5. Back-pointers succeed: follow the object’s pointer to D2’s capability and delete it (selective, immediate). Reacquisition also works, but only after the next periodic sweep (selective, delayed). With a list of keys per object, giving D2 a key of its own lets the owner delete just that key.

System and network threats

Program threats (above) attack through a program; system and network threats abuse services and network connections, creating a situation in which system resources and user files are misused. The more open a system is (more services enabled), the larger its attack surface, which is why systems are shipped "secure by default".

  • Worms spawn copies of themselves over the network, using up resources. The 1988 Morris worm used a grappling hook (bootstrap) program and three routes: rsh trust between hosts, a buffer overflow in finger, and the debug option of sendmail.
  • Port scanning is not an attack in itself but a way to find vulnerabilities: a tool such as nmap tries to connect to a range of ports on a host (or many hosts) to learn which services are listening, what software and version they run and which OS the host uses. Attackers often scan from compromised zombie systems to hide their origin.
  • Denial of service (DoS) disrupts legitimate use rather than stealing information. It either consumes resources (for example, a web page or applet that forks without limit) or disrupts the network: in a SYN flood the attacker sends TCP connection requests (SYN) but never completes the handshake, filling the server’s table of half-open connections. A distributed DoS (DDoS) is launched from many zombies at once and is hard to block. Even an authentication rule such as "lock the account after 3 failed attempts" can be abused to deny service.

Implementing security defences

No single defence suffices, so systems use defence in depth: many layers.

  • Security policy: a written statement of what is being secured (for example, "all externally accessible applications must pass a code review"). Without it, nobody can decide what is allowed.
  • Vulnerability assessment: a risk assessment of assets, followed by penetration tests and scans. A scan looks for short or easy passwords, unauthorised privileged (setuid) programs, unauthorised programs in system directories, unexpectedly long-running processes, improper directory protections, dangerous search paths (a Trojan in the current directory), changes to system programs (detected by comparing checksums, as Tripwire does) and unexpected network daemons.
  • Intrusion detection systems (IDS) raise an alarm; intrusion prevention systems (IPS) also block. They may be host based or network based. Signature-based detection looks for known attack patterns (it cannot catch new attacks); anomaly detection looks for behaviour that differs from the normal profile (it can catch zero-day attacks but gives more false alarms). Because intrusions are rare, even a small false-alarm rate can bury the real alarms.
  • Virus protection: antivirus programs search for signatures, decompress files before checking, and may run suspect code in a sandbox. Users can help by avoiding untrusted software and macros.
  • Auditing, accounting and logging record security-relevant events (failed logins, privilege use), both to detect attacks and to trace them afterwards.
  • Firewalls sit between trusted and untrusted networks and filter traffic by address, port or connection. A DMZ (demilitarised zone) holds public servers: the Internet may reach the DMZ, and the DMZ may not reach the internal network. Variants: personal firewalls (a software layer on one host), application proxy firewalls (understand one protocol, such as SMTP), XML firewalls and system-call firewalls (between applications and the kernel). A firewall cannot stop attacks inside the protocols it allows (tunnelling, buffer overflows in an allowed service) or spoofing.

Example 8: why false alarms matter. A network sees 100,050 connection attempts in a day; 50 are intrusions. An IDS detects 80% of intrusions and falsely flags 0.2% of normal attempts. True alarms = 0.8 × 50 = 40. False alarms = 0.002 × 100,000 = 200. So only 40 ÷ 240 = 1/6 ≈ 16.7% of alarms are real, and an administrator facing 240 alarms a day may start ignoring them. This base-rate effect is why lowering the false-alarm rate matters as much as raising the detection rate.

NTA traps

  • Virus versus worm. Wrong: “a worm attaches to files”. Fix: a virus needs a host; a worm is standalone and spreads over the network by itself.
  • ACL versus capability revocation. Wrong: “capabilities make revocation easy because each domain has its own list”. Fix: capabilities are scattered across domains, so revocation is hard; ACLs keep the object’s rights in one place.
  • Row versus column. Wrong: “an ACL is a row of the access matrix”. Fix: the ACL is the object’s column; the capability list is the domain’s row.
  • BLP versus Biba. Wrong: “Bell–LaPadula forbids writing up”. Fix: BLP forbids write down (leaking secrets); Biba forbids write up.
  • What salt does. Wrong: “salt makes each guess slower” or “salt makes the hash reversible”. Fix: salt defeats precomputed tables and hides equal passwords; it adds no work to a search on one known-salt hash.
  • snprintf return value. Wrong: “it returns the characters stored”. Fix: it returns the length the full output would have needed; truncation happened if the return value ≥ size.
  • Hypervisor types. Wrong: “VirtualBox is bare metal” or “Type 2 is faster”. Fix: hosted Type 2 hypervisors sit on a host OS and add a layer; Type 1 run on hardware.
  • Paravirtualisation. Wrong: “no change to the guest”. Fix: the guest OS is modified to use hypercalls; full virtualisation (binary translation or hardware assist) runs unmodified guests.
  • Containers. Wrong: “each container has its own kernel”. Fix: they share the host kernel, which is why they are light and why isolation is weaker.
  • umask. Wrong: subtracting digits (6 − 7 gives a negative) or adding execute bits. Fix: use bitwise AND with NOT umask; files requested as 666 never get x.

How NTA asks this

  • Match the lists: malware to behaviour, hypervisor product to type, access-matrix implementation to property, authentication factor to example, cipher to category. Memorise the malware table and the hypervisor examples.
  • Statement I/II and Assertion–Reason: ACL versus capability revocation, the salt purpose, why x86 needed binary translation, containers sharing the kernel.
  • Numericals: key counts, password search space, umask or octal permissions, toy RSA, FAR/FRR.
  • Order: TCSEC classes, steps of a buffer-overflow attack, phases of live migration.

Mini-example (Assertion–Reason). A: Classic x86 could not be virtualised by pure trap-and-emulate. R: Some sensitive x86 instructions do not trap when executed in user mode.

Both are true. Trap-and-emulate needs every sensitive instruction to trap; the ones that do not trap are exactly why it fails. So R explains A: option 1.

Elimination tricks: in a malware match, first fix the worm (the only one that spreads by itself over a network), then the logic bomb (the only one with a trigger); usually only one option survives. In BLP/Biba questions, write the four arrows before reading the options. In hypervisor matches, anything installed “on Windows or macOS” is Type 2.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: A virus needs a host program (III). A worm is standalone and spreads itself over the network (I). A trojan horse pretends to be useful (IV). A logic bomb waits for a trigger condition (II). The option A-I, B-III swaps virus and worm, the most common trap.

b: I. A standalone program that copies itself across a network without needing a host file
II. Hidden code that does harm only when a condition, such as a date, becomes true
III. Code that attaches itself to a host program and runs when the host runs
IV. A program that looks useful but secretly performs a harmful action

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: With ACLs the OS searches one list (the object’s column) and deletes the right, so revocation is immediate, selective or general. That is easy exactly because all rights for the object are in one place, so R explains A. Capability lists scatter the rights across domains, which is why revocation is hard there.

stmts: Assertion (A): Revoking a right on an object from every domain is easy when the access matrix is stored as access lists.
Reason (R): An access list keeps all the rights for one object in a single place.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Statement I is the definition of a bare-metal (Type 1) hypervisor, such as VMware ESXi, Xen or Hyper-V. VirtualBox is installed as an application on Windows, Linux or macOS, so it is a hosted (Type 2) hypervisor. Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the hardware without a host operating system.
Statement II: Oracle VirtualBox is an example of a Type 1 hypervisor.

quiz.question: Which of the following help defend against stack-based buffer overflow attacks?
options: A, B, C and E only
B, C, D and E only
A, B, C, D and E
quiz.explanation: Canaries detect a smashed return address, NX stops injected code from running on the stack, ASLR makes target addresses hard to guess, and bounds-checked functions stop the overflow in the first place. gets() has no length limit, so it causes overflows rather than preventing them.

stmts: A. Placing a canary value before the return address and checking it before the function returns
B. Marking the stack as non-executable (NX / DEP)
C. Address space layout randomisation (ASLR)
D. Reading input with gets()
E. Using bounds-checked functions such as fgets() and snprintf()
