quiz.question: What is the output of this C program?
quiz.explanation: snprintf writes at most sizeof buf − 1 = 7 characters plus the terminating null, so buf holds "overflo" and strlen is 7. Its return value is the length the full output would have had, 11, not the number of characters stored. No overflow happens, which is why snprintf is the safe choice. (Verified with gcc.)

quiz.question: A password is exactly 8 characters long, and each character is one of 62 letters and digits (A–Z, a–z, 0–9). An attacker can test 10⁹ passwords per second offline. Approximately how long does an exhaustive search take in the worst case?
quiz.explanation: Search space = 62⁸ = 218,340,105,584,896 ≈ 2.18 × 10¹⁴. Time = 2.18 × 10¹⁴ ÷ 10⁹ = 218,340 s ≈ 60.7 hours (about 2.5 days). About 3.5 minutes is what 26⁸ (lowercase only) gives, and 70.6 days is 94⁸ (all printable characters). On average the password is found in half the time, about 30 hours.

quiz.question: On a Linux system the umask is 027. A program creates a regular file, asking for mode 0666. What permission string does the new file get?
quiz.explanation: Final mode = requested mode AND NOT umask = 0666 & ~0027 = 0640. 6 = rw-, 4 = r--, 0 = ---, so the file is rw-r-----. rwxr-x--- (0750) is what a directory created with 0777 would get. The umask never adds bits; it only removes them.

quiz.question: Under the Bell–LaPadula model, a subject cleared at Secret wants to access an object classified Top Secret. Which access is permitted?
quiz.explanation: Bell–LaPadula protects confidentiality. The simple security property forbids reading up, so Secret cannot read Top Secret. The *-property forbids writing down but allows writing up, so blind write (append) to the higher level is permitted: information flows upward only.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a container from a virtual machine?
options: A container includes its own guest kernel; a VM shares the host kernel
A container shares the host kernel; each VM boots its own guest OS kernel
Both share the host kernel but VMs use cgroups
Neither uses a kernel; both run on firmware directly
quiz.explanation: Containers are OS-level virtualisation: processes isolated by namespaces and limited by cgroups, all running on one host kernel. A VM virtualises hardware, so each VM boots a complete guest OS with its own kernel. That is why containers start in milliseconds to seconds and VMs take longer.

lessons.title: Operating system case studies and distributed systems
lessons.summaryHtml: This lesson has two halves. The case studies cover how real systems apply the OS theory: Linux (a monolithic kernel with loadable modules, fork/exec, the CFS scheduler, buddy and slab allocators, VFS and inodes, and everyday commands), Windows (the NT hybrid kernel with HAL, executive and 32 priority levels, NTFS), Android (Linux kernel, HAL, ART, Binder) and iOS (the XNU kernel and its four layers). The distributed systems half covers types, goals and transparency, distributed file systems (NFS, AFS, GFS), clock synchronisation (Cristian, Berkeley, NTP), logical clocks (Lamport and vector clocks), distributed mutual exclusion with message counts, and election algorithms (bully and ring). Lamport and vector clock numericals and fork-counting programs are the most frequently tested patterns.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

The first half of this lesson looks at four real operating systems and asks: how did they apply the ideas from the earlier OS lessons? Linux, Windows, Android and iOS each made different design choices for the kernel, scheduling, memory and files. The second half moves from one computer to many. A distributed system is a set of independent computers that appears to its users as one coherent system. With no shared memory and no shared clock, even simple questions become hard: “what time is it?”, “which event happened first?”, “who may enter the critical section?” and “who is in charge?”.

Why it matters for NET

This topic usually gives one to three Paper 2 questions. Distributed-systems questions favour Lamport and vector clock numericals, mutual exclusion message counts, transparency types and the bully algorithm. Case-study questions ask about Linux commands and permissions, fork counting, kernel types (monolithic, hybrid, microkernel) and the layers of Android and iOS. Statement I/II and Match formats are common.

Linux

Kernel structure. Linux is a monolithic kernel: scheduling, memory management, file systems, networking and drivers all run in one kernel address space for speed. It stays flexible through loadable kernel modules (lsmod, insmod, modprobe, rmmod). User programs enter the kernel through system calls.

Processes. Each process or thread is a task_struct. fork() creates a child that is a copy of the parent (pages are shared copy-on-write); it returns 0 in the child and the child’s PID in the parent. exec() replaces the program image, and wait() collects a child’s exit status. A process that has exited but not been waited for is a zombie; a child whose parent exits is an orphan and is adopted by PID 1. Linux threads are made with clone(), which chooses what to share, so the kernel treats threads and processes alike. States include running/runnable, interruptible sleep, uninterruptible sleep, stopped and zombie.

Fork counting. n unconditional fork() calls in sequence give 2n processes (2n − 1 new). With && and || the short-circuit rule decides who forks again. Remember also that printf output sits in a user-space buffer, and fork() copies that buffer.

Scheduling. The Completely Fair Scheduler (since kernel 2.6.23) gives each task a share of CPU weighted by its nice value, from −20 (highest priority) to +19 (lowest). Runnable tasks sit in a red-black tree ordered by virtual runtime, and the leftmost task (smallest vruntime) runs next, so selection is O(1) from a cached pointer and insertion is O(log n). Real-time policies SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR use static priorities 1–99 and always beat normal tasks.

Memory. Demand paging with multi-level page tables, a buddy allocator for physical page frames (blocks of 2k pages that split and merge), a slab allocator (SLUB today) for small kernel objects, a unified page cache, swap space, and an out-of-memory (OOM) killer as the last resort.

Files. The Virtual File System (VFS) gives one interface over ext4, XFS, Btrfs, FAT, NFS and others through four objects: superblock, inode, dentry and file. “Everything is a file”: devices appear under /dev, and kernel data under /proc and /sys. A hard link is another directory entry for the same inode (it cannot cross file systems or link directories); a symbolic link is a separate file holding a path and can dangle. ext4 adds journaling and extents.

CommandPurposeCommandPurpose
ls -lList files with permissions, link count, owner, sizeps, topShow processes
chmod 750 fSet mode rwxr-x---kill -9 PIDSend SIGKILL (cannot be caught)
chown user fChange ownergrep pat fPrint lines matching a pattern
find / -name xSearch the directory treewc -lCount lines
df -h / du -shFree space per file system / space used by a directorysort | uniqSort, then remove adjacent duplicates
ln / ln -sHard link / symbolic linkmanManual pages

Signals to remember on x86 Linux: SIGINT = 2 (Ctrl+C), SIGKILL = 9, SIGTERM = 15 (the default for kill), SIGSTOP = 19 and SIGTSTP = 20 (Ctrl+Z). SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught or ignored.

Windows

Windows NT (and so Windows 10 and 11) has a hybrid kernel. From the bottom: the Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) hides chipset differences; the kernel handles thread scheduling, interrupts and synchronisation; the executive contains the object manager, process and thread manager, virtual memory manager, I/O manager, cache manager, security reference monitor and configuration manager (the registry). Environment subsystems (mainly Win32) and applications run in user mode.

The unit of scheduling is the thread. Windows uses 32 priority levels: 16–31 is the real-time class, 1–15 the variable class (priorities are boosted after I/O and decay back), and 0 is reserved for the zero-page thread. Scheduling is preemptive, priority-based, with round robin within a level. Memory uses demand paging with clustering and per-process working sets. NTFS stores everything as files described in the Master File Table (MFT); it supports journaling, ACLs, compression, encryption and large volumes.

Android

Android’s stack, from the bottom: the Linux kernel (drivers, power management, memory, security); the Hardware Abstraction Layer; the Android Runtime (ART) together with native C/C++ libraries such as libc, SQLite, OpenGL ES and WebKit; the Java API framework (activity manager, package manager, content providers, notification manager, view system); and the apps. ART replaced the Dalvik virtual machine (it became the default in Android 5.0) and compiles DEX bytecode ahead of time and just in time. Apps are packaged as APKs, and each runs in its own process under its own Linux user ID, which sandboxes it. Components are activities, services, broadcast receivers and content providers; they talk through intents and the Binder IPC driver.

iOS

iOS runs on the XNU kernel shared with macOS: a hybrid of the Mach microkernel (tasks, threads, IPC, virtual memory) and BSD (processes, POSIX, networking, file systems), together called Darwin. Its layers, from the top: Cocoa Touch (UIKit, touch events, notifications), Media (graphics, audio, video), Core Services (Foundation, Core Data, networking) and Core OS (kernel, drivers, security). Apps are signed, sandboxed and distributed through the App Store; the file system is APFS.

Distributed systems: types and goals

Types: distributed computing systems (clusters, grids, clouds), distributed information systems (transaction processing, enterprise integration) and pervasive systems (mobile, sensor networks, IoT). Architectures are client–server, multi-tier, and peer-to-peer; middleware (RPC, message queues, distributed objects) sits between the OS and applications. Goals: resource sharing, openness (standard interfaces), scalability (in size, geography and administration), fault tolerance, and transparency.

TransparencyHides
AccessDifferences in data representation and how a resource is accessed
LocationWhere a resource is
MigrationThat a resource may move to another location
RelocationThat a resource may move while in use
ReplicationThat several copies exist
ConcurrencyThat other users share the resource
FailureThe failure and recovery of a component

Distributed file systems

A DFS lets clients use remote files as if they were local. Key ideas: naming (location transparency: the name does not reveal the server; location independence: the name need not change when the file moves), caching at the client with a consistency policy, and replication for availability. Sharing semantics differ: UNIX semantics (a write is seen at once by all), session semantics (changes are visible to others only after close, as in AFS) and immutable files.

  • NFS (Sun): remote mounting through RPC. NFSv3 servers are stateless, so requests are idempotent and crash recovery is simple; NFSv4 became stateful, with open and lock state.
  • AFS (Andrew): whole-file caching on the client’s disk, with server callbacks that tell clients when their cached copy is out of date. It scales to thousands of clients.
  • GFS / HDFS: one master (NameNode) keeps metadata; files are split into large chunks (64 MB in GFS, 128 MB by default in HDFS), each replicated (3 copies by default) on chunk servers (DataNodes).

With replication, quorum rules keep reads consistent: with N copies, a read quorum R and a write quorum W must satisfy R + W > N (every read sees the latest write) and W > N/2 (no two writes at once).

Physical clock synchronisation

Crystal clocks drift. If the maximum drift rate is ρ, two clocks can move apart by 2ρ per second, so to keep them within δ they must resynchronise every δ/(2ρ) seconds.

  • Cristian’s algorithm: a client asks a time server; the reply time Ts is adjusted by half the round trip: new time = Ts + RTT/2 (or (RTT − server processing time)/2).
  • Berkeley algorithm: an active master polls all machines, averages the times (ignoring outliers), and sends each machine the adjustment it needs. No machine needs a UTC receiver; the group agrees internally.
  • NTP: a hierarchy of strata (stratum 1 servers are attached to reference clocks such as GPS or atomic clocks). From four timestamps it computes offset θ = ((T2 − T1) + (T3 − T4))/2 and delay δ = (T4 − T1) − (T3 − T2).

Clocks are never set backwards abruptly; they are slowed down or sped up gradually, so time never runs backwards for programs.

Logical clocks: Lamport and vector

Often we only need the order of events. Lamport’s happened-before relation: a → b if a comes before b in the same process, or a is the sending of a message and b its receipt, or there is a chain a → c → b. If neither a → b nor b → a, the events are concurrent (a ∥ b).

Lamport clock rules: (1) increment the counter before each event; (2) a send carries the current value; (3) on receive, set C = max(C, tmsg) + 1. This gives the clock condition: a → b ⇒ C(a) < C(b). The converse fails. For a total order, break ties with the process ID: (C, pid).

Vector clock rules: each process Pi keeps Vi[1..N]. Before each event Vi[i] += 1; a send carries Vi; on receive, Vi[k] = max(Vi[k], t[k]) for every k, then Vi[i] += 1. Compare: V ≤ W if every entry of V is ≤ the matching entry of W. Then a → b if and only if V(a) ≤ V(b) and V(a) ≠ V(b); if neither vector is ≤ the other, the events are concurrent.

Distributed mutual exclusion

AlgorithmMessages per entryIdea and weakness
Centralised3 (request, grant, release)A coordinator queues requests; single point of failure
Lamport (1978)3(N − 1)Timestamped request, reply and release to all; FIFO channels
Ricart–Agrawala2(N − 1)Request to all; a process replies at once unless it is inside, or wants in with an earlier (timestamp, id); deferred replies are sent on exit. Any of N processes failing blocks it
Token ring1 to ∞Only the token holder may enter; token loss must be detected
Maekawa3√N (up to 5√N)Each process asks only its quorum of about √N members
Suzuki–KasamiN, or 0 if it holds the tokenBroadcast request; token carries a queue

Election algorithms

  • Bully (Garcia-Molina): a process that notices the coordinator is down sends ELECTION to every process with a higher ID. If none answers, it wins and sends COORDINATOR to all. If one answers OK, that process takes over the election. The live process with the highest ID always wins. Worst case O(n²) messages, when the lowest-ID process starts.
  • Ring: processes are ordered in a logical ring. The initiator sends an ELECTION message with its ID; each live process appends its own ID and passes it on. When the message returns to the initiator, the highest ID in the list is the coordinator, and a COORDINATOR message goes round once more.

Worked examples

Example 1: Lamport clocks. Three processes, clocks start at 0. P1: a (internal), b (send m1 to P2), c (receive m3), d (internal). P2: e (receive m1), f (send m2 to P3), g (internal). P3: h (internal), i (receive m2), j (send m3 to P1).

P1:  a(1) --- b(2) ------------------------ c(7) --- d(8)
               \ m1 (ts 2)                  ^ m3 (ts 6)
P2:            e(3) --- f(4) --- g(5)       |
                         \ m2 (ts 4)        |
P3:  h(1) -------------- i(5) ------------- j(6)
  1. P1: a = 1, b = 2. m1 carries 2.
  2. P2: e = max(0, 2) + 1 = 3, f = 4 (m2 carries 4), g = 5.
  3. P3: h = 1, i = max(1, 4) + 1 = 5, j = 6 (m3 carries 6).
  4. P1: c = max(2, 6) + 1 = 7, d = 8.
  5. Total order with ties broken by process number (P1 < P2 < P3): a(1,1), h(1,3), b(2,1), e(3,2), f(4,2), g(5,2), i(5,3), j(6,3), c(7,1), d(8,1).

Example 2: Vector clocks on the same system.

EventVectorEventVector
a(1,0,0)f(2,2,0)
b(2,0,0)g(2,3,0)
c(3,2,3)h(0,0,1)
d(4,2,3)i(2,2,2)
e(2,1,0)j(2,2,3)
  1. e: receive m1 with (2,0,0): max((0,0,0), (2,0,0)) = (2,0,0), then P2’s entry +1 gives (2,1,0).
  2. i: receive m2 with (2,2,0) at (0,0,1): max gives (2,2,1), then +1 gives (2,2,2).
  3. c: receive m3 with (2,2,3) at (2,0,0): max gives (2,2,3), then P1’s entry +1 gives (3,2,3).
  4. Is h → c? (0,0,1) ≤ (3,2,3) and they differ, so yes (h → i → j → c).
  5. g and c: (2,3,0) vs (3,2,3). Neither is ≤ the other, so g ∥ c, even though the Lamport values are 5 < 7. Also g ∥ i, g ∥ j, and h is concurrent with a, b, e, f and g. That makes 9 concurrent pairs in total.

Example 3: Berkeley and resynchronisation. The master reads 10:00; two slaves read 10:12 and 9:57 (ignore message delays). Then: clocks drift at most ρ = 10⁻⁵ s per second; how often must they resynchronise to stay within 1 ms of each other?

  1. Differences from the master: 0, +12, −3 minutes. Average = (0 + 12 − 3) ÷ 3 = +3 minutes, so the agreed time is 10:03.
  2. Adjustments sent: master +3, slave 1 −9, slave 2 +6 minutes. The master sends adjustments, not the time, so message delay matters less.
  3. Resynchronisation interval = δ ÷ (2ρ) = 10⁻³ ÷ (2 × 10⁻⁵) = 50 seconds.

Example 4: Message counts. For N = 10 processes, count messages per critical-section entry.

  1. Centralised: 3. Lamport: 3 × 9 = 27. Ricart–Agrawala: 2 × 9 = 18. Token ring: 1 to ∞.
  2. Maekawa with N = 16: √16 = 4, so about 3 × 4 = 12 messages.
  3. Quorum check: N = 12 replicas and W = 10. The smallest R with R + W > N is R = 3. W = 10 > 6 also satisfies W > N/2.

Example 5: Counting fork() output. Each program below prints only x characters (no newline). Count them.

(i)   fork(); fork(); fork(); printf("x");
(ii)  if (fork() || fork()) printf("x");
(iii) for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { fork(); printf("x"); }
  1. (i) Three unconditional forks: 2³ = 8 processes, 8 x.
  2. (ii) Parent: first fork non-zero, so || is true at once and it prints. Child 1: first fork is 0, so it calls the second fork; child 1 gets non-zero and prints, and its child gets 0 and prints nothing. Three processes, 2 x.
  3. (iii) The trap is the stdio buffer. Without a newline or fflush, each x stays in the buffer, and fork copies the buffer. After the loop there are 8 processes, and each buffer holds 3 x (one per loop iteration in its history). Total = 8 × 3 = 24 x, not 2 + 4 + 8 = 14.

All three were compiled and run with gcc on Linux; the counts match.

Example 6: NTP and Cristian. NTP timestamps T1 = 10, T2 = 25, T3 = 27, T4 = 20 (ms). Offset θ = ((25 − 10) + (27 − 20)) ÷ 2 = (15 + 7) ÷ 2 = 11 ms. Delay δ = (20 − 10) − (27 − 25) = 8 ms. For Cristian: RTT = 40 ms, server time 10:00:02.500, server processing time 10 ms; new time = 10:00:02.500 + (40 − 10) ÷ 2 ms = 10:00:02.515.

Linux design principles and kernel modules

Linux is a multiuser, multitasking system with a full set of UNIX-compatible tools, designed to comply with POSIX. Its early aims were speed, efficiency and standardisation. A Linux system has three main bodies of code:

  • The kernel, which provides the core abstractions (virtual memory, processes). All kernel code runs in kernel mode with full access to the hardware, in one address space, so no context switch is needed when one part of the kernel calls another (a monolithic design for performance).
  • The system libraries (glibc), which define the standard functions applications use. They run in user mode; many simply wrap system calls, others (sorting, string handling) need no kernel privilege at all.
  • The system utilities: programs for individual management tasks, some run once (initialising a device), others permanently as daemons (network services, logging).

Kernel modules are sections of kernel code that can be compiled, loaded and unloaded independently of the rest of the kernel. A module typically implements a device driver, a file system or a networking protocol. Modules run in kernel mode with full privileges. They let a small base kernel be extended at run time, let third parties distribute drivers (even under non-GPL licences), and let a developer test a new driver without rebuilding and rebooting. Module support has four parts:

  • The module-management system loads module code into kernel memory and resolves its references to kernel symbols, using a kernel symbol table in which only explicitly exported symbols appear. It then calls the module’s start-up routine; on unload it calls the clean-up routine. The kernel can also request a module on demand when it needs one (request_module()).
  • The module loader and unloader: user-mode utilities (insmod, rmmod, lsmod, and modprobe, which also loads the modules the requested one depends on) that work with the module-management system.
  • The driver-registration system: a module tells the kernel which new drivers it provides (device drivers, file systems, network protocols, binary formats), and the kernel adds them to its tables.
  • A conflict-resolution mechanism: modules reserve hardware resources (I/O ports, interrupt lines, DMA channels) so that two drivers do not grab the same resource; the reservations are visible in /proc (for example /proc/ioports).

Linux input and output, and interprocess communication

Devices appear as files under /dev, identified by major and minor numbers. Linux splits them into three classes:

  • Block devices (disks, flash drives) allow random access to fixed-size blocks. Requests pass through the block buffer cache (merged with the page cache), then a request manager and an I/O scheduler. The classic deadline scheduler keeps a sorted queue plus separate read and write FIFO queues with deadlines (0.5 s for reads, 5 s for writes), favouring reads because a process usually blocks waiting for them. The completely fair queueing (CFQ) scheduler kept a queue per process; current kernels use multi-queue schedulers (mq-deadline, BFQ, Kyber, or none for fast SSDs).
  • Character devices are most other devices (mice, keyboards, sound cards); they have no block structure and requests go straight to the driver. Terminals add a line discipline, an interpreter that, for example, handles line editing for a tty.
  • Network devices are handled differently: user programs reach them through the networking subsystem and sockets, not through /dev files.

Interprocess communication. Signals tell a process that an event occurred; they carry no data except the signal number, and inside the kernel Linux uses wait queues and scheduling states instead of signals. For passing data Linux offers pipes (a child inherits a channel from its parent; a pipe is a special inode in the VFS with a pair of wait queues), shared memory (the fastest way to pass large or small amounts of data, because no copy is needed, but it provides no synchronisation, so it is combined with semaphores), and System V and POSIX message queues and semaphores, plus UNIX-domain sockets.

Linux network structure

Linux supports the standard Internet protocols and BSD-style sockets. Networking is implemented in three layers:

  1. The socket interface, a superset of BSD sockets, through which user programs make requests.
  2. Protocol drivers (TCP, UDP, IP, and others), which handle each protocol and pass data up or down.
  3. Network-device drivers, which talk to the interface hardware.

Data move between the layers in socket buffers (sk_buff), which can grow at the front or back so that headers are added or removed without copying. The IP layer does routing (using a forwarding information base and a cache of recent decisions), fragmentation and reassembly, and packet filtering: netfilter (configured with iptables or nftables) applies firewall chains to incoming, outgoing and forwarded packets.

Windows design principles, terminal services and fast user switching

Microsoft’s stated design goals for Windows are: security (ACLs, auditing, certified evaluations), reliability (the system should not crash because of a buggy application; driver verification), Windows and POSIX application compatibility (environment subsystems), high performance (preemptive threads, fast message passing), extensibility (a layered, modular design with subsystems that can be added), portability (written mostly in C and C++, with the HAL isolating hardware dependencies, so it runs on x86-64 and ARM), international support (Unicode and the national-language-support API), energy efficiency and dynamic device support (plug and play).

Terminal services and fast user switching. Windows lets several users use one machine at the same time through sessions. The session manager creates a session for each logged-on user, with its own session space (including its own copy of the kernel-mode windowing driver, win32k.sys), its own desktop and its own processes; system services run in session 0, isolated from interactive users since Vista.

  • Fast user switching (introduced with Windows XP): several users can be logged on at the same console. One user can lock the screen and another can log on; the first user’s session and applications keep running in the background, and each user can switch back without logging off or closing programs.
  • Terminal services (now Remote Desktop Services) use the same session mechanism for remote users. Applications run on the server; the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) sends screen updates to the client and keyboard and mouse input back. This supports thin clients and central administration, and Remote Assistance lets a helper view or control a user’s session.

Windows networking

  • Protocols: TCP/IP (the main protocol suite); SMB (Server Message Block, also called CIFS) for sharing files and printers and sending messages between systems; PPTP for virtual private networks; HTTP and WebDAV.
  • Driver interfaces: NDIS (Network Device Interface Specification) separates network adapters from transport protocols, so either can change without affecting the other; TDI (Transport Driver Interface) was the older interface to the transport layer.
  • Distributed-processing mechanisms: NetBIOS; named pipes (connection-oriented messaging, possibly between machines); mailslots (connectionless, unreliable broadcast messages); Winsock (the sockets API); and RPC (with an interface definition language, the basis of DCOM).
  • Redirectors and servers: a redirector is a client-side file-system driver that forwards I/O requests for remote files to the server (for example over SMB), so remote files look local.
  • Domains and Active Directory: a domain is a group of machines that share a common security policy and user database, managed by domain controllers. Active Directory is Windows’ LDAP-based directory service; it stores information about users, groups, computers and resources, and authenticates users with Kerberos.

Network-based operating systems

There are two general types of network-oriented OS.

In a network operating system, users are aware of the multiplicity of machines and access remote resources explicitly: by remote login (ssh, telnet) to the appropriate machine, or by remote file transfer (FTP, or cloud storage accessed through a browser). Each machine runs its own OS; the network OS adds these facilities.

In a distributed operating system, users access remote resources in the same way as local ones; the OS moves data and processes between sites:

  • Data migration: transfer the data to the site that needs them, either the whole file or only the portions needed at the moment (demand paging of files, as NFS does).
  • Computation migration: transfer the computation, not the data: invoke a procedure at the remote site (RPC) or send a message asking a remote process to do the work, and receive only the result. This wins when moving the data costs more than running the command remotely.
  • Process migration: an entire process, or parts of it, runs at different sites. Reasons: load balancing, computation speedup (subprocesses run concurrently at several sites), hardware preference (a specialised processor), software preference (software available only at one site) and data access (run where the data are).

Example 7: data migration versus computation migration. A user at site A needs a summary of a 40 MB file stored at site B. Sending the query costs 2 KB and the summary 6 KB. Data migration of the whole file moves 40 MB = 40,960 KB; computation migration moves 2 + 6 = 8 KB, which is 40,960 ÷ 8 = 5,120 times less. If the user then edits many parts of the file, data migration of just the needed portions may win instead.

Network structure and communication protocols

Network structure. A local-area network (LAN) covers a small area (a building or campus) with high speed and low error rates, usually Ethernet or Wi-Fi. A wide-area network (WAN) links sites across a country or the world through routers and slower, costlier, less reliable links; the Internet is a WAN of WANs. (Unit 9 covers topologies and protocols in detail.)

Designing communication in a distributed system raises five questions:

  • Naming and name resolution: how do two processes find each other? A process is identified by a pair <host name, identifier>; host names are mapped to network addresses by a name-resolution service, on the Internet the hierarchical DNS.
  • Routing strategies: fixed routing (the path from A to B is set in advance and changes only on hardware failure; messages arrive in order); virtual routing (a path is fixed for the duration of one session, as with virtual circuits); dynamic routing (the path is chosen only when a message is sent, so messages may arrive out of order and need sequence numbers).
  • Packet strategies: fixed-length packets or frames; connectionless (datagram, unreliable) or connection-oriented (reliable) delivery.
  • Connection strategies: circuit switching (a permanent physical link for the whole conversation, like a telephone call); message switching (a temporary link for the duration of one message, like the post); packet switching (each packet is sent separately and may take a different route; the message is reassembled at the destination).
  • Contention: when several sites want a shared link at once, CSMA/CD (listen, transmit, detect a collision, back off), token passing (only the holder of the token sends) or message slots (fixed-length slots circulate on a ring).

The protocols themselves are layered (the OSI model and the TCP/IP suite of Unit 9); names are resolved and messages routed by these layers.

Robustness of distributed systems

A distributed system can suffer hardware failures (a link or a site), software failures and lost or corrupted messages. To be robust it must detect failures, reconfigure so work can continue, and recover when the failure is repaired.

  • Failure detection uses handshaking (heartbeats). Sites A and B send each other an I-am-up message every T time units. If B receives none within T, it assumes something failed and sends A an are-you-up? message, then waits a further timeout. If no reply arrives, B cannot tell whether A is down, the link is down, or a message was lost; it can try another route to distinguish a link failure from a site failure, but it can never be completely certain.
  • Reconfiguration: if a link has failed, the failure is broadcast so that routing tables are updated; if a site has failed, every site is notified so that it stops using that site’s services. If the failed site was a central coordinator (for example for mutual exclusion or deadlock detection), a new coordinator must be elected (see the election algorithms above).
  • Recovery from failure: when the link or site is repaired, it must be integrated back smoothly: a repaired link is announced by handshaking and the tables updated; a repaired site must learn what happened while it was down (for example, fetch updated replicas).
  • Fault tolerance: the system should keep working, perhaps in a degraded form (graceful degradation), when components fail. This needs redundancy: replicated data and services, multiple paths and hot standbys. The replica-availability formula in the fact sheet shows how quickly availability grows with the number of copies.

Example 8: detecting a failure. Site A sends I-am-up every T = 4 s; B waits T after the last message, then sends are-you-up? and waits 3 s for a reply. A’s last message reaches B at t = 40 s, and A crashes at t = 41 s. At t = 44 s nothing has arrived, so B sends are-you-up?. No reply comes, so at t = 44 + 3 = 47 s B concludes that A (or the link to A) has failed, and starts reconfiguration: 7 s after the last message and 6 s after the actual crash.

NTA traps

  • The converse of the clock condition. Wrong: “C(a) < C(b), so a happened before b”. Fix: only a → b ⇒ C(a) < C(b). Use vector clocks to detect concurrency.
  • Forgetting the +1 on receive. Wrong: c = max(2, 6) = 6. Fix: max, then add 1, so c = 7.
  • Vector receive rule. Wrong: copying only the sender’s entry from the message, or forgetting to increment your own entry after the merge. Fix: take the maximum of every entry (the message also carries what the sender knew about third processes), then add 1 to your own entry.
  • Ricart–Agrawala count. Wrong: 3(N − 1). Fix: that is Lamport’s algorithm; Ricart–Agrawala has no release message, so 2(N − 1).
  • Bully winner. Wrong: “the process that started the election wins” or “the lowest ID wins”. Fix: the highest live ID wins.
  • Fork with printf. Wrong: counting only printf calls. Fix: count processes, apply short-circuit rules for && and ||, and remember that unflushed buffers are copied by fork.
  • Kernel types. Wrong: “Windows is a microkernel” or “Linux is a microkernel because it has modules”. Fix: Linux is monolithic with modules; Windows NT and XNU are hybrids; MINIX 3 and QNX are true microkernels.
  • nice values. Wrong: “nice 19 is the highest priority”. Fix: lower nice means higher priority; −20 is the most favoured.
  • NFS state. Wrong: “NFS servers keep open-file tables”. Fix: NFSv3 is stateless; AFS keeps callback state; NFSv4 added state.
  • Berkeley. Wrong: “the master sets everyone to its own time”. Fix: it averages all clocks and sends adjustments; no external UTC source is needed.

How NTA asks this

  • Numericals: a timeline with messages asking for a Lamport value or a vector; NTP offset and delay; Cristian’s adjusted time; Berkeley adjustments; message counts; fork counts.
  • Match the lists: transparency type to what it hides; mutual exclusion algorithm to message count; DFS to feature; OS to kernel type; Linux command to purpose; clock algorithm to description.
  • Statement I/II and Assertion–Reason: the clock condition and its converse, bully winner, NFS statelessness, Windows priority classes, Android’s Binder and ART.
  • Order: Linux boot stages, Android layers, the steps of Ricart–Agrawala.

Mini-example (Match). A. Centralised, B. Lamport, C. Ricart–Agrawala, D. Token ring against I. 2(N − 1), II. 3, III. 3(N − 1), IV. 1 to ∞.

Fix the easy ends first: centralised = 3 (II) and token ring = 1 to ∞ (IV). Only options with A-II and D-IV survive. Then Lamport has the extra release round, so B-III and C-I.

Elimination tricks: in any clock question, if an option shows a receive event with a smaller value than the send, discard it at once. In vector questions, check only one entry at a time: if a has a larger entry in one place and b a larger entry in another, they are concurrent. For fork programs, draw the process tree; never multiply printf calls blindly.

terms.definition: Linux design: all core services run in one kernel address space, and drivers can be loaded or removed at run time as modules.
Linux scheduler that keeps runnable tasks in a red-black tree ordered by virtual runtime and always runs the task with the smallest vruntime.
A kernel with a microkernel-like structure that still runs most services in kernel mode, as in Windows NT and Apple XNU.
Android’s kernel-supported inter-process communication mechanism, used for calls between apps and system services.
Lamport’s relation: a → b if they are in the same process with a first, if a is a send and b the matching receive, or by transitivity.
A counter per process: increment before each event, send the value with messages, and on receive set C = max(C, t) + 1. If a → b then C(a) < C(b), but not the reverse.
An array of N counters per process. It captures causality exactly: a → b if and only if V(a) < V(b); otherwise the events are concurrent.
Distributed mutual exclusion that uses 2(N − 1) messages per entry: a timestamped request to all, and a reply from each.
Election algorithm in which the live process with the highest ID always becomes coordinator.
Hiding the fact that resources are distributed: access, location, migration, relocation, replication, concurrency and failure transparency.

lessons.examTip: For a Lamport clock question, draw the timeline and apply only two rules: +1 on every event, and on receive take max(own, message) + 1. Then remember the one-way implication: a → b gives C(a) < C(b), but C(a) < C(b) does not prove a → b. Only vector clocks can show that two events are concurrent.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For the clock problems, draw the process timelines before computing.
Check with solutions.md and write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (for example “took C(a) < C(b) to mean a → b”).
Redo problem 3 by computing the vector clocks for every event, then list all concurrent pairs.
Compile and run the fork programs from the lesson with gcc, and check that the number of characters printed matches your count.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.

quiz.question:
Three processes use Lamport clocks that start at 0. Every event adds 1, and a receive sets the clock to max(local, timestamp) + 1.
P1: a (internal), b (send m1 to P2), c (receive m3), d (internal)
P2: e (receive m1), f (send m2 to P3), g (internal)
P3: h (internal), i (receive m2), j (send m3 to P1)
What is the Lamport timestamp of event c?
quiz.explanation: P1: a = 1, b = 2 (m1 carries 2). P2: e = max(0, 2) + 1 = 3, f = 4 (m2 carries 4), g = 5. P3: h = 1, i = max(1, 4) + 1 = 5, j = 6 (m3 carries 6). P1: c = max(2, 6) + 1 = 7, then d = 8. Answering 3 ignores the message; 6 forgets the +1 on receive.

quiz.question: For the same three-process system (P1: a, b send m1, c receive m3, d; P2: e receive m1, f send m2, g; P3: h, i receive m2, j send m3), vector clocks are used. Which pair of events is concurrent?
quiz.explanation: Vector clocks: a = (1,0,0), b = (2,0,0), c = (3,2,3), d = (4,2,3); e = (2,1,0), f = (2,2,0), g = (2,3,0); h = (0,0,1), i = (2,2,2), j = (2,2,3). g = (2,3,0) and c = (3,2,3): g has a larger P2 entry and c has larger P1 and P3 entries, so neither is ≤ the other: concurrent. b → e (send/receive), f → j (via m2), a → d (same process). Note that Lamport gives g = 5 < c = 7, yet they are concurrent.

quiz.question: What is the output of this C program? Assume every fork() succeeds and count all characters printed by all processes.
quiz.explanation: The first fork gives the parent a non-zero value and the child 0. The child short-circuits &&, so it does not fork again. The parent runs the second fork: its new child gets 0 (condition false), and the parent gets non-zero, so it forks a third time. Processes: parent, 3 children = 4, and each prints one x: xxxx. quiz.question: A client using NTP records T1 = 100 ms (request sent, client clock), T2 = 150 ms (request received, server clock), T3 = 152 ms (reply sent, server clock) and T4 = 110 ms (reply received, client clock). What are the estimated clock offset θ and round-trip delay δ?
quiz.explanation: θ = ((T2 − T1) + (T3 − T4)) ÷ 2 = (50 + 42) ÷ 2 = 46 ms: the server is about 46 ms ahead. δ = (T4 − T1) − (T3 − T2) = 10 − 2 = 8 ms. Using 10 ms forgets to subtract the server’s processing time.

quiz.question: A client using Cristian’s algorithm sends a request at local time 10:00:00.000 and receives the reply at local time 10:00:00.040. The reply says the server time is 10:00:02.500. To what time should the client set its clock?
quiz.explanation: Assume the reply took half the round trip: RTT = 40 ms, so add 20 ms. New time = 10:00:02.500 + 0.020 = 10:00:02.520. Using the server value as-is ignores the transit delay; adding the full RTT double-counts it.

lessons.title: Software process models
lessons.summaryHtml: A software process model is the plan for the order in which a team does communication, planning, modelling, construction and deployment. The waterfall (linear sequential) model does these once, in strict order; the V-model pairs every development phase with a test phase. The incremental and RAD models deliver the product in working pieces, while prototyping and the risk-driven spiral model (Boehm) are evolutionary. The Unified Process runs iterations through four phases: inception, elaboration, construction and transition. Agile methods such as Scrum and XP value working software, customer collaboration and response to change, and they deliver in short time-boxes. Choosing a model means matching it to how stable the requirements are, how big the risks are and how soon the customer needs something working.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Building software is like building a house. You could draw every plan, then lay the foundation, then build walls, then roof it, and only then let the owner in. Or you could build one liveable room first, let the family move in, and add rooms one by one. Or you could first build a cardboard model so the owner can say what they really want. Each approach is a process model: an ordered plan of activities, with rules for when to move on and when to go back.

No model is best in general. The right one depends on how well the requirements are understood, how risky the project is, how fast the customer needs something working, and how big and skilled the team is. The NET exam tests whether you know each model’s shape, strengths, weaknesses and ideal situation.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 6 (Software Engineering) is one of the ten Paper 2 units, and process models are a steady source of questions in it. These questions are almost always conceptual: “which model is risk-driven”, “match the model with its feature”, “arrange the UP phases”, “Assertion: waterfall is unsuitable when requirements change”. Agile (Scrum and XP practices, the manifesto) has become a favourite. Small numericals can appear through risk exposure, team communication paths and velocity-based planning. Because the facts are few and stable, this is a scoring area if you memorise the pairs exactly.

Software engineering, layers and the generic framework

IEEE defines software engineering as the application of a systematic, disciplined, quantifiable approach to the development, operation and maintenance of software. Pressman describes it as a layered technology. From the bottom: a quality focus (the bedrock), then process (the glue that holds the layers together), then methods (the technical how-to), then tools (automated support).

Pressman’s generic process framework has five framework activities, in this order: communication, planning, modelling, construction (code generation and testing) and deployment. These are supported throughout by umbrella activities: software project tracking and control, risk management, software quality assurance, technical reviews, measurement, software configuration management, reusability management, and work product preparation and production. A common trap is to list “construction” or “testing” as an umbrella activity; they are framework activities.

The process flow describes how the framework activities are arranged in time: linear (one after another), iterative (repeat one or more activities before moving on), evolutionary (circular, each circuit producing a more complete version) and parallel (activities run at the same time).

The SDLC and the classical waterfall

The software development life cycle names the phases every product passes through. In the form most Indian texts use (Rajib Mall), the classical waterfall phases are: feasibility study, requirements analysis and specification, design, coding and unit testing, integration and system testing, and maintenance. The feasibility study checks technical feasibility (can we build it with our technology and skills), economic feasibility (do benefits exceed costs), operational feasibility (will the users and the organisation actually use it) and often schedule and legal feasibility.

Winston Royce’s 1970 paper is credited with the waterfall. Its idea is that each phase ends with a reviewed document (a milestone), and the next phase starts from that document. Maintenance usually takes the largest share of life-cycle effort.

  • Strengths: simple, easy to manage, clear milestones and documents, good when requirements are well understood and stable (for example, a new version of a well-known payroll system).
  • Weaknesses: the customer sees working software only at the end; real projects rarely follow a strict sequence; errors made early are found late and cost the most to fix; it does not handle changing requirements or risk.

The classical waterfall is idealised: it has no feedback paths. The iterative waterfall adds feedback paths from every phase to earlier phases so that errors can be corrected where they were made. There is no feedback path to the feasibility study, because once a project is accepted it is not normally abandoned by the development team.

The V-model

The V-model bends the waterfall into a V. The left arm goes down through the development phases (verification); the right arm goes up through the test phases (validation); coding sits at the bottom point. Each left phase produces the test plan for its partner on the right:

Development phase (left)Matching test phase (right)
Requirements analysis (user requirements)Acceptance testing
System design (system specification)System testing
Architectural (high-level) designIntegration testing
Module (detailed / low-level) designUnit testing

Because test planning starts early, defects in the requirements and design are exposed early. The V-model is still sequential, so it suits well-understood, often safety-critical systems, but it shares the waterfall’s rigidity.

Incremental and RAD models

The incremental model applies linear sequences in a staggered way as calendar time passes. Each sequence produces a deliverable increment. The first increment is usually the core product: the basic requirements, with supplementary features left for later. For example, a word processor might ship basic editing first, then spelling and grammar, then advanced layout. The customer gets something useful early, early increments help find requirement errors, and fewer staff are needed at the start. The requirements for the whole system must still be broadly known to plan the increments.

The RAD (Rapid Application Development) model is a “high-speed” adaptation of the linear sequential model that achieves speed through component-based construction and several teams working in parallel. Pressman quotes a typical full cycle of about 60 to 90 days. The older Pressman phases are business modelling, data modelling, process modelling, application generation, and testing and turnover. RAD’s limits are exam favourites: large projects need enough people for several RAD teams; developers and customers must commit to the rapid-fire pace; the system must be modularisable; it is risky when high performance must be tuned into interfaces or when technical risks are high (new technology).

Prototyping

Prototyping is used when the customer cannot state detailed input, processing or output requirements, or when the developer is unsure of an algorithm’s efficiency, an operating system’s suitability or the right form of human-computer interaction. The cycle is: communication, quick plan, quick design (focused on what the user sees), construction of the prototype, delivery and feedback, and repeat.

  • Throwaway (rapid) prototype: built only to learn the requirements, then discarded; the real system is built properly.
  • Evolutionary prototype: refined step by step until it becomes the final system.
  • Horizontal prototypes show the whole interface with little behind it; vertical prototypes implement one slice of functionality through all layers.

Pressman’s warnings: the customer sees a working version and wants it shipped with a few fixes, not realising it was held together with shortcuts; and developers make implementation compromises (a convenient language, an inefficient algorithm) that later become permanent.

The spiral model

Barry Boehm’s spiral model (1986, published widely in 1988) is an evolutionary, risk-driven model. Each loop of the spiral is one phase of the process. Each loop passes through four quadrants:

  1. Determine objectives, alternatives and constraints.
  2. Evaluate alternatives; identify and resolve risks (often by prototyping, simulation or benchmarking).
  3. Develop and verify the next-level product.
  4. Plan the next phase (review, and commit to the next loop).

The radial dimension (distance from the centre) represents cumulative cost; the angular dimension represents progress through the loop. The number of loops is not fixed; the project manager decides it according to the remaining risk. Because each loop can look like a waterfall step, a prototype or an incremental build, the spiral is called a meta-model. Boehm later added anchor-point milestones: life-cycle objectives, life-cycle architecture and initial operational capability. The spiral suits large, expensive, high-risk projects. Its weaknesses are the need for real risk-assessment expertise and the difficulty of convincing customers (especially in fixed-price contracts) that the evolution is controllable.

Risk is quantified by risk exposure, RE = P × L, where P is the probability that the risk occurs and L is the loss (cost) if it does. Risks are ranked by RE. Boehm’s risk reduction leverage, RRL = (REbefore − REafter) ÷ cost of the risk-reduction step, tells you which mitigation gives the most reduction per rupee.

Concurrent, component-based and formal models

The concurrent model (Pressman) shows each activity as a set of states, such as inactive, under development, awaiting changes, under review, under revision, baselined and done. Events trigger transitions, so all activities exist at the same time in different states. It is useful when several teams engineer different parts at once.

Component-based development (CBSE) builds the system from pre-packaged components, including commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) components. Its steps: research and evaluate available components for the domain, consider integration issues, design an architecture that accommodates the components, integrate them, and test comprehensively. It raises reuse and can cut cycle time and cost; integration testing is still essential.

The formal methods model uses mathematical specification, development and verification; the cleanroom approach is a variant aimed at defect-free software through correctness verification and statistical usage testing. It is costly and needs specialist skills, so it is used mainly for safety-critical systems.

The Unified Process (UP / RUP)

The Unified Process, from Jacobson, Booch and Rumbaugh (the Rational Unified Process is its commercial form), is use-case driven, architecture-centric, and iterative and incremental. It uses UML throughout. Time is divided into four phases, each made of one or more iterations and ending in a milestone:

PhaseMain workMilestone at the end
InceptionBusiness case, scope, key use cases, rough estimates, main risksLife-cycle objectives
ElaborationMost use cases, architecture baseline (executable), plan for constructionLife-cycle architecture
ConstructionBuild and test the components; complete the product for releaseInitial operational capability
TransitionBeta testing, user feedback, training, deliveryProduct release

Pressman adds a fifth, production, phase for ongoing use and support. Across the phases run disciplines (workflows) such as business modelling, requirements, analysis and design, implementation, test and deployment. The effort in each discipline rises and falls across the phases, which is drawn as the RUP “hump chart”.

Agile development

The Manifesto for Agile Software Development (2001) states four values: individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; and responding to change over following a plan. The items on the right still matter; the items on the left matter more. Among its twelve principles: satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery; welcome changing requirements, even late; deliver working software frequently; face-to-face conversation is the most efficient way to convey information; working software is the primary measure of progress; sustainable pace; simplicity (maximising the work not done); self-organising teams; and regular reflection to become more effective.

Extreme Programming (XP), by Kent Beck, has the values communication, simplicity, feedback, courage and respect. Pressman describes its activities as planning, design, coding and testing. Key practices: user stories and the planning game; small releases; simple design (keep it simple) with CRC cards; spike solutions (a quick throwaway prototype for a hard design problem); refactoring; test-first development (unit tests before code); pair programming; continuous integration; collective code ownership; coding standards; an on-site customer; and a sustainable pace (the 40-hour week). XP’s project velocity is the number of stories (or points) completed in the previous iteration, used to plan the next.

Scrum organises work in sprints, fixed time-boxes of one month or less. The Scrum Guide (2020) has three accountabilities: Product Owner (maximises value, manages the product backlog), Scrum Master (a servant leader who helps the team use Scrum, removes impediments; not a task-assigning manager) and Developers. Its three artifacts are the product backlog, the sprint backlog and the increment, with the commitments product goal, sprint goal and definition of done. Its events are the sprint itself, sprint planning, the daily scrum (15 minutes), the sprint review (inspect the product with stakeholders) and the sprint retrospective (inspect the team’s process). Burndown charts and velocity are common tools, but they are not official Scrum artifacts.

Other agile methods you should recognise: ASD (Adaptive Software Development, Highsmith: speculation, collaboration, learning); DSDM (time-boxing and MoSCoW prioritisation: must have, should have, could have, won’t have this time); FDD (Feature Driven Development: small client-valued features, plan, design and build by feature); Crystal (a family of methods scaled by team size and criticality); and Kanban (visualise work on a board and limit work in progress).

Choosing a model

SituationBest fit
Requirements clear and stable, familiar domain, short projectWaterfall
Stable requirements and a strong need for planned verification (safety-critical)V-model
Core functions needed early; staff limited at startIncremental
Modular business application, tight deadline, reusable components, enough peopleRAD
Customer unsure of requirements, or user interface is the main unknownPrototyping
Large, costly, high-risk, new technologySpiral
Requirements changing often; customer available; small co-located teamAgile (Scrum / XP)
Large object-oriented project needing an architecture baseline and UMLUnified Process

Worked examples

Example 1: ranking risks in a spiral loop. A team lists three risks (loss in ₹ thousand): R1 with P = 0.40 and L = 500; R2 with P = 0.25 and L = 1200; R3 with P = 0.10 and L = 800. Rank them, and find the RRL of a mitigation for R2 that costs 60 and lowers its probability to 0.05.

  1. RE(R1) = 0.40 × 500 = 200. RE(R2) = 0.25 × 1200 = 300. RE(R3) = 0.10 × 800 = 80.
  2. Ranking by RE: R2 (300), R1 (200), R3 (80). Total exposure = 580. Note that R1 has the highest probability but is not the top risk.
  3. After mitigation, RE(R2) = 0.05 × 1200 = 60.
  4. RRL = (300 − 60) ÷ 60 = 240 ÷ 60 = 4.0. Each rupee spent removes four rupees of exposure, so the mitigation is worth doing (any RRL above 1 pays for itself).

Example 2: planning sprints from velocity. A product backlog holds 210 story points. The team’s last three sprints delivered 24, 28 and 26 points. Sprints are two weeks long. How many sprints and weeks are needed?

  1. Average velocity = (24 + 28 + 26) ÷ 3 = 78 ÷ 3 = 26 points per sprint.
  2. Sprints = ⌈210 ÷ 26⌉ = ⌈8.08⌉ = 9 sprints. You cannot run 0.08 of a sprint; the leftover work needs a whole sprint.
  3. Calendar time = 9 × 2 = 18 weeks.

Example 3: why adding people slows a late project. A team of 7 is late, and management adds 3 more developers. How do the communication paths change?

  1. With n people, the number of pairwise paths is n(n − 1) ÷ 2.
  2. Before: 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21 paths. After: 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = 45 paths.
  3. Staff rose by about 43%, but paths rose by 24 (more than double). New people must also be trained by the existing ones. This is Brooks’s law: adding manpower to a late software project makes it later. It is also why Scrum keeps teams small.

Example 4: staggered increments. Each increment takes 12 weeks from communication to deployment, and a new increment starts every 6 weeks. When are the first and the fourth increments delivered, and how does this compare with building the four increments one after another?

  1. Increment k starts at 6(k − 1) weeks and is delivered 12 weeks later.
  2. First delivery: 0 + 12 = 12 weeks. Fourth delivery: 6 × 3 + 12 = 30 weeks.
  3. Strictly one after another: 4 × 12 = 48 weeks. The staggering saves 18 weeks, and the customer has a working core product at week 12 instead of week 48 (a single waterfall delivery).

Example 5: picking the model. (a) A bank wants a new interest module identical in structure to three it already runs; the rules are fixed by regulation. Waterfall: stable, well-understood requirements. (b) A start-up wants a food-ordering app, will change features every two weeks based on user feedback, and its founder sits with the team. Scrum/XP. (c) A defence project uses a new sensor whose behaviour is uncertain and a failure would be very costly. Spiral. (d) A hospital cannot describe what its doctors want on screen. Prototyping (throwaway, then build properly).

Task sets, process patterns and process assessment

The generic framework says what is done (communication, planning, modelling, construction, deployment). Each framework activity is carried out by a set of software engineering actions, and each action is described by a task set: the work tasks, the work products to be produced, the quality assurance points and the milestones needed to finish that action. The team picks the task set that fits the project, so the same activity can look very different. For a small, simple project, requirements gathering might be: list the stakeholders, hold one informal meeting, ask each person for the features they need, discuss them, and agree a prioritised list. For a large, complex project the same action grows into distinct tasks: facilitated elicitation sessions, usage scenarios, elaboration, negotiation and formal validation of the requirements. The activity is the same; only the task set changes.

A process pattern (Scott Ambler, 1998, building on Coplien) describes a problem that comes up during software work, the environment in which it appears, and one or more proven solutions. It gives a team a vocabulary for building a process out of tested pieces. Pressman’s template for describing a pattern has these fields: pattern name; forces (the environment and the issues that make the problem visible); type; initial context (what must already be true before the pattern can be applied); problem; solution; resulting context (what is true after the pattern has been applied successfully); related patterns; and known uses and examples. Ambler’s three pattern types:

TypeProblem it describesExample
Stage patternA problem tied to a whole framework activity; it usually contains several task patternsEstablishingCommunication
Task patternA problem tied to one software engineering action or work taskRequirementsGathering
Phase patternThe sequence of framework activities within the process, even when the flow is iterativeSpiralModel, Prototyping

A process is only useful if it actually works, so it should be assessed. Pressman lists these assessment approaches: SCAMPI (Standard CMMI Assessment Method for Process Improvement, a five-step model: initiating, diagnosing, establishing, acting and learning); CBA IPI (CMM-Based Appraisal for Internal Process Improvement); SPICE (ISO/IEC 15504, a standard that defines requirements for process assessment); and ISO 9001:2000 for software. At the level of individuals and teams, Watts Humphrey’s PSP (Personal Software Process: planning, high-level design, high-level design review, development, postmortem) and TSP (Team Software Process) bring measurement and self-direction to engineers.

NTA trap: “initial context” is the precondition of a pattern and “resulting context” is its postcondition; options often swap them. And a stage pattern is about a framework activity, a task pattern about one action, a phase pattern about the order of activities.

Project management: the four Ps, W5HH and team structures

Pressman says effective project management focuses on the four Ps: people, product, process and project, in that order. People come first: the stakeholders are senior managers, project (technical) managers, practitioners, customers and end users, and the SEI’s People-CMM is a maturity model for developing them. The product is understood through its scope (context, information objectives, function and performance) and problem decomposition. The process is the framework plus the task sets chosen for this project. The project is the planned, controlled work itself.

Weinberg’s MOI model of leadership asks a team leader for Motivation, Organisation and Ideas (innovation). Mantei described three generic team organisations:

  • Democratic decentralised (DD): no permanent leader; task coordinators are appointed for short periods; decisions are made by group consensus; communication is horizontal.
  • Controlled decentralised (CD): a defined leader coordinates tasks, with secondary leaders for subtasks; problem solving is a group activity, but implementation is split among subgroups; communication is horizontal among peers and vertical along the hierarchy.
  • Controlled centralised (CC): the team leader does top-level problem solving and internal coordination; communication between leader and members is vertical. The chief programmer team (Baker and Mills) is the classic CC team.

Constantine adds four organisational paradigms: closed (traditional hierarchy), random (loose, depends on individual initiative), open (mix of control and innovation) and synchronous (natural compartmentalisation with little communication between parts). Boehm’s W5HH principle gives seven questions that any project plan must answer: Why is the system being developed? What will be done? When will it be done? Who is responsible for a function? Where are they located organisationally? How will the job be done technically and managerially? How much of each resource is needed?

Aspect-oriented software development

A concern is any requirement, property or area of interest in a system: “transfer money”, “log every transaction”, “check that the user is authorised”. Ordinary decomposition (functions, classes) handles core concerns well, but some concerns are crosscutting: their code cannot be placed in one module because it is needed in many. Security checks, logging, transaction management, error handling, caching and persistence are the textbook examples. Crosscutting shows two symptoms:

  • Scattering: the code for one concern is spread over many modules (logging calls in forty methods).
  • Tangling: one module contains code for several concerns mixed together (a transfer method that also logs, checks authorisation and manages the transaction).

Aspect-oriented software development (AOSD; aspect-oriented programming was introduced by Gregor Kiczales and colleagues at Xerox PARC in 1997) packages each crosscutting concern into a separate unit called an aspect. The vocabulary, as used in AspectJ (the aspect-oriented extension of Java):

TermMeaning
Join pointA well-defined point in the execution of the program: a method call or execution, a field access, an exception handler
PointcutAn expression that selects a set of join points
AdviceThe code that runs at the selected join points: before, after or around them
AspectThe module that bundles pointcuts and advice (and possibly inter-type declarations)
WeavingCombining aspects with the base code, at compile time, load time or run time, done by a weaver
aspect AuditLog {
  pointcut transfers(): execution(* Bank.transfer(..));
  before(): transfers() { log.write("transfer started"); }
}

Here one aspect replaces logging calls that would otherwise be scattered through every transfer method. At the requirements level, aspect-oriented requirements engineering identifies “aspectual requirements” that cut across many functional requirements. Pressman notes that a distinct aspect-oriented process is still maturing and would probably borrow the characteristics of evolutionary and concurrent models, because aspects are identified and engineered alongside the localised components.

Formal methods and cleanroom in more depth

The formal methods model specifies, develops and verifies software using mathematical notation. Informal (natural-language) specifications suffer from contradictions, ambiguities, vagueness, incompleteness and mixed levels of abstraction; a formal specification can be checked for consistency and completeness, and a design can be proved to meet it. A formal specification language has three parts: a syntax, a semantics and a set of relations (rules for deciding which objects satisfy the specification). The core ideas are the data invariant (a condition that stays true throughout the execution of the system), the state (the stored data), and each operation described by a precondition (what must hold before it is invoked) and a postcondition (what is guaranteed after it completes). Well-known notations: Z (schemas built on typed set theory and first-order predicate logic), VDM, the B method, OCL (the Object Constraint Language of UML), Larch, and CSP for concurrent systems.

The drawbacks explain why formal methods are used mainly for safety-critical and security-critical systems: they are slow and expensive, few developers are trained in them, and the notation is hard to use for communicating with customers. Bowen and Hinchey’s “ten commandments” advise, among other things: choose the right notation, formalise but do not over-formalise, estimate costs, keep a formal-methods expert on call, do not abandon traditional methods, document sufficiently, do not compromise quality standards, and test, test and test again.

Cleanroom software engineering (Harlan Mills, IBM) applies these ideas to aim for defect prevention rather than defect removal. Its features: incremental development; specification with box structures, refined in three steps: the black box (external behaviour as responses to stimuli), the state box (the state data and services, much like an object) and the clear box (the procedural design of the state box’s transition functions); correctness verification by the development team in place of unit testing (in pure cleanroom, developers do not execute their own code); and statistical use testing by a separate certification team, with test cases drawn from the expected usage probability distribution, so the measured reliability (for example MTTF) can be certified.

ASD, DSDM, FDD and Crystal in more depth

Adaptive Software Development (ASD), by Jim Highsmith, is aimed at complex systems and rests on self-organising teams and collaboration. Its life cycle has three phases. Speculation starts the project and plans adaptive cycles from the mission statement, constraints and basic requirements; the word signals that the plan is expected to change. Collaboration relies on motivated people who trust one another and pool their talent. Learning uses focus groups (customer feedback on increments), technical reviews and project postmortems to correct the course. ASD cycles are mission-focused, feature-based, iterative, time-boxed, risk-driven and change-tolerant.

DSDM (Dynamic Systems Development Method, from the UK DSDM Consortium, now the Agile Business Consortium) grew out of RAD. It follows a Pareto idea: about 80% of an application can be delivered in 20% of the time needed for the complete application. Its life cycle starts with a feasibility study and a business study, followed by three iterative cycles: functional model iteration, design and build iteration, and implementation. Its principles include active user involvement, empowered teams, frequent delivery, iterative and incremental development, reversible changes, requirements baselined at a high level, testing throughout, and time-boxes with MoSCoW prioritisation. DSDM can be combined with XP.

Feature Driven Development (FDD) was created by Peter Coad and Jeff De Luca (1997) and extended by Palmer and Felsing. A feature is a small client-valued function that can be built in two weeks or less, named with the template “<action> the <result> <by | for | of | to> a(n) <object>”, for example “Calculate the total of a sale”. Features are grouped into feature sets and business areas. FDD has five processes: develop an overall model, build a features list, plan by feature, design by feature and build by feature. It puts more stress on design and on chief programmers and class owners than other agile methods, and it tracks each feature through six weighted milestones: domain walkthrough 1%, design 40%, design inspection 3%, code 45%, code inspection 10% and promote to build 1%.

Crystal, by Alistair Cockburn, is a family of methods. Its premise is that each project needs a slightly different set of policies and conventions, so a method is chosen by team size and by criticality (what a failure costs: comfort, discretionary money, essential money or life). The members are named by colour: Crystal Clear for small teams (up to about 8 people), then Yellow, Orange and Red for progressively larger teams; a darker colour means a larger team and a heavier method. Crystal Clear’s properties include frequent delivery, reflective improvement, osmotic communication (the team sits together), personal safety, focus, easy access to expert users, and automated tests with frequent integration.

Example 6: tracking an FDD feature. A feature has passed its domain walkthrough, design, design inspection and coding, but not code inspection or promotion to build. How complete is it?

  1. Completed milestone weights: 1 + 40 + 3 + 45 = 89.
  2. So the feature is 89% complete. Only code inspection (10%) and promote to build (1%) remain, and 89 + 10 + 1 = 100.

Web engineering

Web engineering (WebE) applies sound engineering principles to web-based systems and applications (WebApps). Pressman lists the attributes that make WebApps different: network intensiveness, concurrency (many users at once), unpredictable load (users can jump from hundreds to thousands in a day), performance (users leave if they wait), availability (users expect 24/7 access), data driven (much of the job is presenting data from databases), content sensitive (quality and look of content matter), continuous evolution (content can change minute by minute), immediacy (very short time to market), security and aesthetics.

Because of immediacy and continuous evolution, WebE uses an incremental, agile process built on the generic framework, with short delivery cycles. It starts with formulation, which identifies the goals: informational goals (the content and information the user will get) and applicative goals (the tasks the WebApp will let the user perform), plus user profiles. Analysis then builds a content model, an interaction model, a functional model and a configuration model.

Pressman’s design pyramid for WebApps, from the top (closest to the user) down to the base: interface design, aesthetic design, content design, navigation design, architecture design and component design, all resting on technology. Content architectures may be linear, grid, hierarchical or networked, and the application architecture is often Model–View–Controller.

WebApp quality (Olsina’s quality tree) covers usability, functionality, reliability, efficiency and maintainability. Testing a WebApp includes content testing (errors in text, images and other content), interface testing, navigation testing (every link and navigation path leads where it should), component testing, configuration testing (different browsers, operating systems, devices and server set-ups), security testing, and performance testing, including load and stress tests as the number of concurrent users grows.

NTA trap: in the WebApp design pyramid, interface design is at the top and component design at the base; aesthetic (graphic) design sits just below the interface, and content design sits above navigation design.

NTA traps

  • “Spiral has four loops.” Wrong: it has four quadrants per loop; the number of loops varies with risk.
  • “Radial dimension = progress.” Wrong: radial is cumulative cost; angular is progress.
  • “Incremental and iterative are the same thing.” Incremental adds new pieces of function; iterative reworks and refines the same parts. UP and agile methods are both.
  • “An evolutionary prototype is thrown away.” That is the throwaway prototype. The evolutionary one grows into the product.
  • “In the V-model, testing starts after coding.” Test execution does, but test planning starts on the left arm; that is the point of the model.
  • “The Scrum Master is the project manager who assigns tasks.” Developers self-organise; the Scrum Master coaches and removes impediments.
  • “Burndown chart is a Scrum artifact.” The official artifacts are product backlog, sprint backlog and increment.
  • “Agile means no documentation or no planning.” Agile values working software more than documentation and responding to change more than following a plan; both still exist.
  • Rounding down sprints. 8.08 sprints means 9 sprints.
  • Author swaps. Waterfall: Royce. Spiral: Boehm. XP: Beck. UP: Jacobson, Booch, Rumbaugh. ASD: Highsmith.

How NTA asks this

  • Match the model with its feature or situation (the most common). Memorise the one-word identity of each model, then fix the pair you are surest of and eliminate options.
  • Order questions: UP phases, waterfall phases, spiral quadrants, Pressman’s framework activities, Scrum events in a sprint.
  • Assertion–Reason on why a model fits a situation. Check A and R separately first, then ask “does R cause A?”.
  • Multiple statements on agile values, XP practices, spiral facts.
  • Small numericals: RE = P × L, velocity-based sprint counts, n(n − 1)/2.

Mini A–R. A: The waterfall model is unsuitable when requirements are likely to change. R: In the waterfall model a phase starts only after the previous phase is complete and signed off. Both are true. Does R explain A? Yes: because phases are frozen in sequence, a late change forces rework of every completed phase. Answer: option 1.

Elimination trick: in a match on models, “risk” always pairs with spiral, “fuzzy/unclear requirements” with prototyping, “60–90 days / reuse / parallel teams” with RAD, and “testing phase for every development phase” with the V-model. Two sure pairs usually leave only one option.

terms.definition: The application of a systematic, disciplined, quantifiable approach to the development, operation and maintenance of software.
Linear sequential model (Royce, 1970): feasibility, requirements, design, coding, testing and maintenance done one after another.
Waterfall variant in which each development phase on the left has a matching test phase on the right, e.g. requirements with acceptance testing.
Delivers the system as a series of increments; the first increment is usually the core product.
Boehm’s risk-driven evolutionary meta-model. Each loop is a phase with four quadrants, and risk analysis is done in every loop.
Use-case driven, architecture-centric, iterative and incremental process with phases inception, elaboration, construction and transition.
RE = probability of the risk × loss if it occurs. Used to rank risks in the spiral model.
A fixed time-box of one month or less in Scrum, in which a usable increment is produced.
Story points a team completes per sprint or iteration. Used to forecast how many sprints a backlog needs.
Changing the internal structure of code without changing its external behaviour, a core XP practice.

lessons.examTip: Anchor each model to its one-word identity: waterfall = sequence, V = testing pairs, incremental = core first, RAD = speed through reuse, prototyping = unclear requirements, spiral = risk, UP = four phases, agile = change. Most NET options are eliminated by that word alone.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For the numericals, write the formula (RE = P × L, sprints = ⌈backlog ÷ velocity⌉) before substituting.
Check with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (for example “thought the spiral has a fixed number of loops”).
Draw the V-model from memory with all four test pairs, then the UP phases with their four milestones.
Write the four Agile Manifesto values and the three Scrum roles, artifacts and five events on one card.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.

All 15 finished within 24 minutes

The option that swaps B and C is the usual trap: RAD is about speed, not risk.
