quiz.question: A Scrum team has 190 story points left in its product backlog. Its velocities in the last three sprints were 21, 25 and 23 points. Using the average velocity, how many more sprints will the backlog need?
quiz.explanation: Average velocity = (21 + 25 + 23) ÷ 3 = 69 ÷ 3 = 23 points per sprint. Sprints = ⌈190 ÷ 23⌉ = ⌈8.26⌉ = 9. A partial sprint still takes a whole sprint, so 8 (rounding down) is wrong. 10 comes from using the lowest velocity 21 (190 ÷ 21 = 9.05, so 10).

quiz.question: During risk analysis in a spiral loop, a team estimates that a key third-party library has a 35% chance of being withdrawn, and that replacing it would cost ₹80,000. What is the risk exposure?
quiz.explanation: Risk exposure RE = P × L = 0.35 × ₹80,000 = ₹28,000. ₹80,000 is the loss alone and ignores probability. ₹52,000 is (1 − 0.35) × 80,000, the probability that the risk does not happen. ₹2,800 is a decimal slip.

quiz.question: Which process model is often called a meta-model because, depending on the risks, it can take the form of other models such as waterfall or prototyping in its loops?
quiz.explanation: Boehm’s spiral model is risk-driven: in a loop where user-interface risk dominates it behaves like prototyping, and where requirements are well known it behaves like the waterfall. That flexibility is why it is called a meta-model. RAD, V and incremental models each fix one shape.

Sprint Planning sets what and how for the sprint (II). Review (product) versus retrospective (process) is the swap NTA builds on.

b: I. The team inspects how the last sprint went for people, interactions, processes and tools, and plans improvements
II. Decides what can be delivered in the coming sprint and how that work will be done

lessons.title: Software requirements
lessons.summaryHtml: Requirements say what a system must do (functional) and how well it must do it, or under what limits (non-functional: performance, security, usability, reliability, standards, laws). Requirements engineering runs through inception, elicitation, elaboration, negotiation, specification, validation and management. Elicitation uses interviews, questionnaires, observation, JAD/FAST sessions, QFD, scenarios and prototypes. Analysis models the requirements with DFDs (context diagram and levelled, balanced diagrams), a data dictionary, decision tables and trees, and UML use case, activity and state machine diagrams. The result is the SRS; IEEE 830 says a good SRS is correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, ranked, verifiable, modifiable and traceable. Validation (reviews, prototyping, test-case generation) checks that the SRS describes the system the customer really wants.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Before you build a house, the owner tells you how many rooms they want (what the house does) and also that it must stay cool in summer, cost under a budget and follow the building code (how well, and under what limits). Software is the same. Requirements are the owner’s wishes, written precisely enough that the builder, the tester and the owner all understand the same thing. Most failed projects fail here: the team built the wrong thing well.

This lesson covers the kinds of requirements, how we find them (elicitation), how we model them (DFDs, data dictionary, decision tables, use cases and UML behaviour diagrams), how we write them down (the SRS) and how we check them (validation).

Why it matters for NET

Requirements questions appear in most cycles and are mainly conceptual. The favourites are functional versus non-functional classification, DFD rules and levels, balancing, data dictionary symbols, IEEE 830 characteristics of a good SRS, include versus extend, and which UML diagrams are behavioural. They come in match, multiple-statement and Assertion–Reason form. Small numericals can appear on decision-table rule counts and on Pressman’s specification-quality metrics.

What a requirement is, and its kinds

IEEE defines a requirement as a condition or capability needed by a user to solve a problem or achieve an objective, or one that a system must meet to satisfy a contract, standard or other formally imposed document. Sommerville separates user requirements (natural-language statements and diagrams for customers) from system requirements (detailed, precise descriptions of functions, services and constraints, often part of the contract).

  • Functional requirements say what services the system provides, how it reacts to inputs and how it behaves in given situations. “A member can reserve a book that is currently issued.”
  • Non-functional requirements (NFRs) constrain the services or the development: speed, reliability, security, usability, portability, standards and laws. They often apply to the system as a whole, so failing one can make the whole system unusable.
  • Domain requirements come from the application domain, for example a banking rule on interest calculation.

Sommerville classifies NFRs into three groups: product requirements (usability, efficiency covering performance and space, dependability, security), organisational requirements (environmental, operational, development process such as a mandated language or standard) and external requirements (regulatory, ethical, legislative such as accounting or safety law). Another common scheme is FURPS+: functionality, usability, reliability, performance, supportability, plus constraints.

A good NFR is measurable. “The system shall be user friendly” cannot be tested. Rewrite it as “A trained clerk shall be able to issue a book in under 30 seconds after 2 hours of training.” Typical metrics: transactions per second and response time (speed), memory or disk size (size), training time and number of help screens (ease of use), MTTF, availability and rate of failure occurrence (reliability), time to restart after failure (robustness), and percentage of target-dependent code (portability).

The requirements engineering process

Pressman lists seven tasks: inception (establish a basic understanding of the problem, the stakeholders and the nature of the solution), elicitation (draw out the requirements), elaboration (refine them into an analysis model), negotiation (reconcile conflicts and set priorities), specification (write them down: document, models, prototype), validation (check quality) and requirements management (track changes throughout the project). Sommerville’s simpler view: feasibility study, elicitation and analysis, specification, validation.

Elicitation is hard because of problems of scope (the boundary is ill-defined, or customers give unnecessary technical detail), problems of understanding (customers are unsure what they need, or omit “obvious” facts) and volatility (requirements change over time).

Elicitation techniques

TechniqueIdeaGood for / limits
Interviews (closed and open)Question stakeholders one to oneUnderstanding goals and problems; people may not mention tacit domain knowledge
Questionnaires / surveysWritten questions to many peopleLarge, spread-out user groups; poor for exploring vague needs
Observation / ethnographyWatch people doing their real workDiscovers the actual (not the official) process; weak for brand-new features
BrainstormingGroup generates ideas without criticismNew ideas; needs later filtering
JAD / FAST (collaborative requirements gathering)Facilitated joint meeting of customers and developers with an agenda and rulesFast agreement, shared ownership
QFDTranslate customer needs into technical requirementsMaximising customer satisfaction
Scenarios and use casesStories of how users interact with the systemConcrete behaviour, easy for users
PrototypingLet users try a modelUnclear interfaces; risk of the prototype being kept
Document / domain analysisStudy forms, manuals, existing systems, lawsDomain rules and data

Quality function deployment (QFD) identifies three kinds of requirement. Normal requirements are the goals the customer states in meetings; meeting them brings satisfaction. Expected requirements are so basic the customer does not state them, but their absence causes great dissatisfaction (ease of installation, for example). Exciting requirements go beyond the customer’s expectations and delight when present.

Requirements analysis: the models

Pressman’s analysis (requirements) model has four kinds of element: scenario-based (use cases, activity diagrams), class-based (class diagrams, CRC cards), behavioural (state diagrams, sequence diagrams) and flow-oriented (DFDs, control flow diagrams, data dictionary, process specifications). Classical structured analysis uses the last group plus ER diagrams and state transition diagrams.

Data flow diagrams

A DFD (also called a bubble chart) shows how data moves through a system and is transformed. Yourdon–DeMarco notation uses four symbols:

SymbolMeaningNaming
Circle (bubble)Process that transforms dataVerb phrase: “Validate order”
Labelled arrowData flow (data in motion)Noun: “order-details”
Two parallel lines (open box)Data store (data at rest)Noun: “Orders”
RectangleExternal entity (source or sink, terminator)Noun: “Customer”

Gane–Sarson notation draws processes as rounded rectangles and stores as open-ended rectangles, but the meaning is the same.

Rules. Every flow must begin or end at a process: there are no flows directly between two entities, two stores, or an entity and a store. A process must have at least one input and at least one output. A process with inputs but no outputs is a black hole; one with outputs but no inputs is a miracle; one whose inputs cannot produce its outputs is a grey hole. A DFD shows no control: no loops, decisions or timing. Those belong to flowcharts, activity diagrams and, for real-time systems, control flow diagrams (Ward–Mellor and Hatley–Pirbhai extensions).

Levels. The context diagram (level 0) shows the whole system as one bubble with its external entities; it shows no data stores. The level-1 DFD breaks that bubble into major processes, usually 3 to 7, numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on. The child diagram of process 3 has processes 3.1, 3.2, …, and the child of 3.2 has 3.2.1, 3.2.2, …. Each refinement adds detail until each bubble is simple enough to be described by a short process specification (a “functional primitive”). Note that some books call the context diagram “level 0” and others call the first decomposition “level 0”; in the Pressman and Rajib Mall convention, followed here, the context diagram is level 0.

Balancing. When a process is decomposed, the data flows entering and leaving the child diagram as a whole must be the same as those entering and leaving the parent process. An unbalanced DFD has a flow that appears at one level and disappears at the other.

Context (level 0)            Level 1
Customer --order--> (0 Order     (1 Validate) --> (2 Check stock) --> (3 Bill)
Customer <-invoice-- System)      Inputs at the boundary: order; outputs: invoice
                                  = balanced with level 0

Data dictionary and process specifications

The data dictionary holds a precise definition of every data flow, store and element: its name, aliases, where and how it is used, its content and format. Pressman’s content notation:

SymbolMeaningExample
=is composed ofname = first-name + last-name
+andaddress = street + city + pin
[ | ]either–or (select one)payment = [cash | card | UPI]
{ }n or m{ }nn repetitions, or between m and n repetitionspin = 6{digit}6
( )optionalname = first + (middle) + last
* … *comment* in rupees *

Each primitive process is described by a process specification (PSPEC): structured English, pseudocode, a decision table or a decision tree.

Decision tables and decision trees

A decision table has four quadrants: the condition stub (top left, the conditions), the condition entries (top right, values in each rule), the action stub (bottom left, possible actions) and the action entries (bottom right, which actions each rule fires). Each column is a rule.

  • Limited entry: conditions are Y/N. With n conditions there are 2n rules.
  • Extended entry: a condition has several values. The rule count is the product of the number of values of each condition.
  • Don’t care (–): a dash in a limited-entry rule means the condition does not matter, so the rule covers 2 combinations; d dashes cover 2d combinations. A table is complete when the covered combinations add up to 2n with no overlap. Two rules with the same condition entries but different actions are a contradiction.

A decision tree shows the same logic as branches; it is easier to read when the conditions are tested in a natural order, while a decision table is better for checking completeness.

The SRS and IEEE 830

The Software Requirements Specification is the agreed statement of what the software must do. It is used by customers (to confirm needs), developers (to design), testers (to write acceptance tests), managers (to estimate) and maintainers. IEEE Std 830-1998 is the classic reference; it has since been superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, but NET still asks about 830. A good SRS is:

  1. Correct: every requirement is one the software must meet.
  2. Unambiguous: every requirement has only one interpretation.
  3. Complete: all significant requirements, responses to all inputs (valid and invalid), labels and references are present; no “TBD” left.
  4. Consistent: no subset of requirements conflicts.
  5. Ranked for importance and/or stability.
  6. Verifiable: a finite, cost-effective process can check that the software meets each requirement.
  7. Modifiable: its structure lets changes be made easily and consistently (no redundancy, good organisation).
  8. Traceable: the origin of each requirement is clear (backward traceability) and each can be referenced by later documents (forward traceability).

The IEEE 830 outline: 1 Introduction (purpose, scope, definitions and acronyms, references, overview); 2 Overall description (product perspective, product functions, user characteristics, constraints, assumptions and dependencies); 3 Specific requirements (external interfaces, functions, performance, logical database requirements, design constraints, software system attributes); then appendixes and index.

Bertrand Meyer’s “seven sins” of specifiers are a useful checklist: noise (text that carries no information), silence (a feature not covered by any text), over-specification (describing the solution rather than the problem), contradiction, ambiguity, forward reference (using a feature not yet defined) and wishful thinking (a feature that cannot realistically be validated).

Pressman quotes Davis’s specification quality metrics. With nr = nf + nnf requirements: specificity Q1 = nui ÷ nr, where nui is the number of requirements every reviewer interpreted identically; completeness of functional requirements Q2 = nu ÷ (ni × ns), where nu is the number of unique functional requirements, ni the number of inputs and ns the number of states; degree of validation Q3 = nc ÷ (nc + nnv), where nc requirements are validated as correct and nnv are not yet validated.

Use cases and UML behavioural diagrams

A use case describes one goal an actor achieves by interacting with the system. An actor is a role (a person, device or external system) outside the system boundary; the primary actor starts the use case to reach a goal, and a secondary actor supports it. A use case description usually gives the primary actor, goal, preconditions, trigger, main success scenario, alternative and exception flows, and postconditions.

  • «include»: the base use case always performs the included behaviour (for example “Withdraw cash” includes “Authenticate user”). The dashed arrow points from the base to the included use case.
  • «extend»: optional behaviour inserted at an extension point when a condition holds (“Print receipt” extends “Withdraw cash”). The dashed arrow points from the extending use case to the base.
  • Generalisation: between actors or between use cases (a “Premium member” is a kind of “Member”).

UML 2 has 14 diagram types: seven structure diagrams (class, object, component, composite structure, package, deployment, profile) and seven behaviour diagrams (use case, activity, state machine, and four interaction diagrams: sequence, communication, interaction overview and timing).

An activity diagram models workflow: an initial node (filled circle), actions (rounded rectangles), decision and merge nodes (diamonds with guards), fork and join bars for concurrency, swimlanes (partitions) showing who does each action, and a final node. A state machine diagram shows the states of one object and the transitions between them, labelled event [guard] / action; states can have entry, exit and do activities, and can be composite.

Validation and management

Validation asks whether the requirements define the system the customer really wants. Sommerville’s checks: validity (does it meet real needs), consistency, completeness, realism (can it be built with the budget and technology) and verifiability (can tests be written). Techniques: requirements reviews (formal inspections or informal walkthroughs), prototyping, test-case generation (a requirement for which no test can be designed is suspect) and automated consistency analysis. Boehm’s one-liners: verification asks “are we building the product right?”; validation asks “are we building the right product?”.

Requirements management handles change. Each requirement gets an identifier, and traceability tables link it to features, sources, dependencies, subsystems and interfaces. A traceability matrix linking requirements to test cases shows coverage at a glance.

Worked examples

Example 1: building and checking a decision table. A loan rule uses C1 = income ≥ ₹6 lakh, C2 = credit score ≥ 700, C3 = existing customer. Actions: approve, refer to manager, reject.

  1. Limited entry with 3 conditions: 23 = 8 combinations.
  2. Simplified rules: R1 (Y, Y, –) approve; R2 (Y, N, Y) refer; R3 (Y, N, N) reject; R4 (N, –, –) reject.
  3. Coverage: R1 has one dash, 21 = 2; R2 and R3 cover 1 each; R4 has two dashes, 22 = 4. Total = 2 + 1 + 1 + 4 = 8 = 23, and no two rules overlap, so the table is complete and free of contradictions.
  4. If a fourth condition “loan type” with 3 values (home, car, personal) is added, the full table has 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 24 rules.

Example 2: checking DFD balancing. Parent process 3 “Process order” has inputs order-details and stock-status and outputs invoice and dispatch-note. Its child diagram (3.1 Validate, 3.2 Check stock, 3.3 Prepare invoice) receives order-details, stock-status and customer-credit from outside, and sends out invoice and dispatch-note.

  1. Inputs: child minus parent = {customer-credit}; parent minus child = {}.
  2. Outputs: identical sets {invoice, dispatch-note}.
  3. So the diagrams are not balanced: customer-credit appears only at the child level. Fix it by adding customer-credit as an input to process 3 in the parent (and its source entity or store), or by reading it from a store that is internal to process 3.

Example 3: specification quality metrics. An SRS has 48 functional and 16 non-functional requirements. Reviewers agreed on the interpretation of 52. Its 48 functional requirements contain 40 unique ones (the rest repeat earlier ones), and it defines 8 inputs and 10 states. 50 requirements have been validated as correct and 14 are not yet validated.

  1. nr = 48 + 16 = 64. Specificity Q1 = 52 ÷ 64 = 0.8125.
  2. Completeness Q2 = 40 ÷ (8 × 10) = 40 ÷ 80 = 0.5.
  3. Degree of validation Q3 = 50 ÷ (50 + 14) = 50 ÷ 64 = 0.78125, about 0.78.

Example 4: counting values from a data dictionary. roll-no = 2{digit}2 + dept-code + 3{digit}3, and dept-code = [CS | EC | ME]. How many distinct roll numbers exist?

  1. 2{digit}2 is exactly 2 digits: 102 = 100 choices.
  2. dept-code selects one of 3 alternatives.
  3. 3{digit}3 is exactly 3 digits: 103 = 1000 choices.
  4. The + means “and”, so multiply: 100 × 3 × 1000 = 300,000. If it were 3{digit}5 (3 to 5 digits), that part would give 103 + 104 + 105 = 111,000 choices, because the lengths are alternatives and are added.

Example 5: a use case with include and extend. ATM, use case “Withdraw cash”. Primary actor: customer; secondary actor: bank system. Precondition: card inserted. Main flow: 1. «include» Authenticate user (PIN). 2. Customer selects amount. 3. System checks balance with the bank. 4. Cash dispensed; account debited. Extension point after step 4: «extend» Print receipt, if the customer asks for one. Alternative flow 3a: insufficient balance, show message, return to step 2. Postcondition: balance reduced by the amount. Authentication is include because it always happens; the receipt is extend because it is conditional.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFact
Pressman RE tasksInception, elicitation, elaboration, negotiation, specification, validation, management
Sommerville NFR groupsProduct, organisational, external
QFD requirement typesNormal, expected, exciting
DFD symbolsBubble = process, arrow = flow, parallel lines = store, rectangle = external entity
DFD golden ruleEvery flow starts or ends at a process
DFD numberingContext (level 0) → 1, 2, 3 (level 1) → 3.1, 3.2 (level 2) → 3.2.1 (level 3)
Data dictionary= composed of, + and, [ | ] one of, { } repetition, ( ) optional, * * comment
Decision table rules2n (limited entry); product of value counts (extended); a rule with d dashes covers 2d
IEEE 830 good SRSCorrect, unambiguous, complete, consistent, ranked, verifiable, modifiable, traceable
Davis metricsQ1 = nui/nr; Q2 = nu/(ni × ns); Q3 = nc/(nc + nnv)
UML 2 diagrams14 = 7 structure + 7 behaviour (of which 4 interaction)
include / extendinclude: always, arrow base → included; extend: conditional, arrow extension → base
Validation checksValidity, consistency, completeness, realism, verifiability

NTA traps

  • “Response time under 2 seconds” marked functional. It constrains how well a service performs, so it is non-functional (product, efficiency).
  • Data stores in the context diagram. The context diagram shows only the single system bubble, external entities and flows.
  • “A DFD shows the sequence of processing.” It never does; no control flow at all.
  • Entity-to-store flows. Look for a flow that skips a process; that option is wrong.
  • Counting a dash as one rule. A dash covers two combinations.
  • Swapping include and extend. Include = mandatory, extend = optional. Also watch the arrow direction.
  • “SRS should specify the algorithms.” That is over-specification; the SRS says what, not how.
  • “Complete” versus “consistent”. Complete means nothing is missing; consistent means nothing conflicts.
  • Verification versus validation. Right product = validation; product right = verification.
  • Class diagram as a behaviour diagram. Class, object, component, package and deployment diagrams are structure diagrams.

How NTA asks this

  • Match: requirement statement with its type; DFD symbol with meaning; data dictionary symbol with meaning; IEEE 830 characteristic with definition; elicitation technique with description.
  • Multiple statements: which DFD flows are legal; which are NFRs; which are IEEE 830 characteristics; which UML diagrams are behavioural.
  • Order: Pressman’s RE tasks, the IEEE 830 outline, DFD levels.
  • A–R and Statement I/II: DFD has no control flow; balancing; include versus extend.
  • Numericals: decision-table rule counts; Davis metrics.

Mini match. A. Noise, B. Silence, C. Over-specification, D. Wishful thinking with I. describes the solution instead of the problem, II. a feature that cannot realistically be validated, III. text carrying no relevant information, IV. a feature not covered by any text. Sure pairs: noise–III and silence–IV. That already leaves over-specification–I and wishful thinking–II, giving A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

Elimination trick: in an NFR classification question, first mark anything with a number about speed, size, availability or time as a product requirement, anything mandated by the developer’s own company as organisational, and anything from law or regulation as external. Only then look at the options.

terms.definition: A statement of a service the system must provide: how it reacts to particular inputs and behaves in particular situations.
A constraint on the system’s services or qualities, such as response time, reliability, security, usability or a required standard.
Software Requirements Specification: the agreed statement of what the system must do, written without prescribing how (a black-box view).
Level-0 DFD: the whole system as one process, with its external entities and the data flows between them and the system.
Rule that the data flows entering and leaving a process must match the flows entering and leaving its child DFD.
An organised list of every data element in the system with a precise definition, using notation such as =, +, [ | ], { } and ( ).
A table of conditions and actions in four quadrants; each column (rule) is one combination of condition values and the actions it triggers.
A use case relationship in which the base use case always incorporates the behaviour of the included use case.
A use case relationship in which optional behaviour is inserted into a base use case at an extension point when a condition holds.
The ability to follow a requirement backward to its source and forward to the design, code and tests that realise it.

lessons.examTip: For DFD questions, remember one rule that kills most wrong options: every data flow must start or end at a process. No flow ever goes directly between two entities, two stores, or an entity and a store.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For decision tables, write 2ⁿ (or the product of the value counts) before counting rules.
Check with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (for example “counted a dash as one rule instead of two”).
Draw a context diagram and a balanced level-1 DFD for a library system from memory, then check every flow touches a process.
Write the eight IEEE 830 SRS characteristics and Pressman’s seven requirements engineering tasks on one card, in order.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct on the first attempt
Problems 3–7 (decision tables, data dictionary, metrics, balancing) all correct
All 15 finished within 24 minutes
Every DFD-legality question answered using the “touches a process” rule in under 45 seconds

quiz.question: A decision table has three limited-entry (Yes/No) conditions and one extended-entry condition that can take 3 values. How many rules does the complete table have before any simplification?
quiz.explanation: Rules = product of the number of values of each condition = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 24. 16 is 2⁴ (treating every condition as binary). 9 is 2³ + 1 and 12 is 2² × 3; both miscount the conditions.

quiz.question: An SRS contains 42 functional and 18 non-functional requirements. In a review, all reviewers gave an identical interpretation for 45 of the requirements. What is the specificity (lack of ambiguity) Q1 = n_ui ÷ n_r, as defined by Davis and used in Pressman?

quiz.question: In a use case diagram, which relationship shows optional behaviour that is inserted into a base use case at an extension point only when a certain condition holds?
quiz.explanation: «extend» adds conditional behaviour at an extension point; the base use case is complete without it, and the arrow points from the extending use case to the base. «include» is unconditional: the base always performs the included behaviour. Association links an actor to a use case.

lessons.title: Software design
lessons.summaryHtml: Design turns the requirements model into a blueprint: data/class design, architectural design, interface design and component-level design. Its core concepts are abstraction, stepwise refinement, modularity, information hiding and functional independence, which is measured by cohesion (how strongly a module’s parts belong together) and coupling (how strongly modules depend on each other). Cohesion from worst to best is coincidental, logical, temporal, procedural, communicational, sequential, functional; coupling from best to worst is data, stamp, control, external, common, content. Architecture is chosen from styles such as pipe-and-filter, repository, layered, call-and-return, object-oriented, client–server and MVC. Structured design maps DFDs to structure charts by transform or transaction analysis; object-oriented design uses UML class, sequence and state diagrams, SOLID principles and GoF design patterns; user interface design follows golden rules such as keeping the user in control.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Requirements say what to build; design says how it will be built. A good design is like a well-planned kitchen: each drawer holds one kind of thing (high cohesion), you can replace the fridge without rebuilding the cupboards (low coupling), and the layout follows a known plan (an architectural style) that any cook recognises. Design decisions are cheap to change on paper and very expensive to change in code, which is why this stage gets so much attention.

Why it matters for NET

Design is one of the most tested parts of Unit 6. The most frequent item by far is the ordering of cohesion and coupling types, asked as order, match, A–R and statement questions. Next come the design concepts (abstraction, information hiding, modularity, refinement), architectural styles, UML class and sequence diagram notation, design patterns (GoF categories), and user interface golden rules. Numericals are rare, but Pressman’s architectural metrics (fan-in, fan-out, Card–Glass complexity) and object-oriented metrics (DIT, NOC, LCOM) can appear.

The design model

Pressman maps the analysis model onto four design elements, drawn as a pyramid. From the base to the top: data/class design (data structures and classes), architectural design (major structural elements and their relationships), interface design (how the software talks to users, other systems and devices) and component-level design (the procedural detail of each component). Deployment-level design then places components on hardware. A good design implements every explicit requirement and the implicit ones the customer wants, is readable for coders and testers, and gives a complete picture of data, function and behaviour. Quality attributes are summarised as FURPS: functionality, usability, reliability, performance, supportability.

Fundamental design concepts

  • Abstraction. At the highest level the solution is stated in problem-domain terms; lower levels add detail. Procedural abstraction names a sequence of instructions with a limited function (“open door”); data abstraction names a collection of data that describes an object (“door”, with attributes).
  • Stepwise refinement (Niklaus Wirth, 1971) is the top-down strategy that elaborates an abstraction step by step. Abstraction and refinement are complementary: one suppresses detail, the other reveals it.
  • Architecture: the overall structure of the components and the way they interact.
  • Patterns: proven solutions to recurring problems.
  • Separation of concerns: a complex problem is easier to solve when divided into pieces that can be handled independently.
  • Modularity. Software is divided into separately named, addressable modules. As the number of modules rises, the cost of developing each one falls but the cost of integrating them rises, so total cost has a minimum in a middle region: neither under- nor over-modularise. Meyer gives five criteria for a modular method: decomposability, composability, understandability, continuity (small changes in requirements cause changes in few modules) and protection (errors stay within a module).
  • Information hiding (David Parnas, 1972): each module hides a design decision, such as a data structure or algorithm, and other modules use only its interface. Changes and errors stay local.
  • Functional independence: each module addresses one specific subset of requirements and has a simple interface. It is judged by cohesion and coupling.
  • Refactoring: reorganising a design (or code) to make it simpler without changing its external behaviour.
  • Aspects: crosscutting concerns, such as logging or security, that affect many modules.

Cohesion: the seven types, worst to best

Cohesion measures how closely the elements of one module are related. The classical scale comes from Yourdon and Constantine and is used by Pressman and by Indian texts such as Rajib Mall. From lowest (worst) to highest (best):

RankCohesionElements are grouped because…Example
1 (worst)CoincidentalNo meaningful relation; they just ended up togetherA “Utilities” module that prints a report, validates a date and sorts an array
2LogicalThey do logically similar things; a flag chooses which one runsReadInput(flag) that reads from keyboard, file or network depending on the flag
3TemporalThey run at the same timeInitialise(): open files, reset counters, clear the screen
4ProceduralThey follow one another in a fixed sequence of control, but work on different dataRead a student record, then print the page header
5CommunicationalThey operate on the same input data or produce the same outputFrom one employee record, compute gross pay and also update leave balance
6SequentialThe output of one element is the input of the nextRead raw data → validate it → format the valid record
7 (best)FunctionalAll elements contribute to a single, well-defined taskComputeSquareRoot(x); CalculateNetSalary(emp)

A quick test for functional cohesion is to describe the module in one sentence with one verb and one object. If the sentence needs “and”, the module is at best sequential or communicational; if it needs “first … then”, it is procedural or temporal; if it needs “either … or” selected by a flag, it is logical. When a module has several kinds of relation, it is classified by the lowest (weakest) one that holds.

Coupling: the types, best to worst

Coupling measures how much one module depends on another. From lowest (best) to highest (worst), as in Pressman’s classical coupling spectrum and in Myers, Yourdon and Constantine:

RankCouplingModules are connected by…
0 (best)No direct couplingNothing; they are unrelated or only share a caller
1DataElementary data items passed as parameters (only what is needed)
2StampA composite data structure (a record) passed as a parameter, of which only part is used
3ControlA control flag passed so that the caller decides the callee’s logic
4ExternalDependence on something outside the software: a device, a communication protocol, an externally imposed data format
5CommonShared global data (a global variable or common block)
6 (worst)ContentOne module uses or changes data or code inside another, or branches into its middle
/* data coupling: only the values needed are passed          */
double interest(double principal, double rate, int years);
/* stamp coupling: whole record passed, only one field used    */
int age(struct Student s);            /* uses s.dob only       */
/* control coupling: the flag steers the callee's logic        */
void print(struct Report r, int mode); /* mode 1 = PDF, 2 = CSV */
/* common coupling: both functions read and write a global     */
int total;  void add(int x) { total += x; }  void reset(void) { total = 0; }

Two memory aids. Cohesion climbs C-L-T-P-C-S-F (coincidental, logical, temporal, procedural, communicational, sequential, functional). Coupling climbs D-S-C-E-C-C (data, stamp, control, external, common, content). Some texts (Rajib Mall, for example) list only five coupling types and omit external; the relative order of the others is the same. Later editions of Pressman add class-level categories from Lethbridge and Laganière (such as layer cohesion and routine-call, type-use and inclusion coupling), but NET keys follow the classical scales above.

Architectural design and styles

Software architecture is the structure of the system: its components, their externally visible properties and the relationships among them. Pressman describes a style by its components, connectors, constraints and semantic models. The main styles:

StyleIdeaExample / note
Data-centred (repository, blackboard)A central data store accessed by independent clients; a blackboard notifies clients when data of interest changesCASE tools, IDE symbol tables, AI blackboard systems
Data-flow (pipe and filter; batch sequential)Filters transform input to output and pass it along pipes; filters do not know their neighboursUnix pipelines, compiler phases; poor for interactive systems
Call and return (main program/subprogram; remote procedure call)A control hierarchy of callsClassic structured programs; RPC across machines
Object-orientedComponents encapsulate data and operations; communicate by messagesMost modern applications
LayeredEach layer serves the layer above and uses the layer belowOSI and TCP/IP stacks, OS kernel/utility/application layers
Client–server, N-tierClients request services from serversWeb applications
Event-based (implicit invocation, publish–subscribe)Components announce events; registered handlers runGUIs, message brokers
MVCModel (data and rules), View (presentation), Controller (handles input and updates the model)Web frameworks
Microservices / SOASmall independently deployable services communicating over the networkCloud systems

Architectural design starts with an architectural context diagram showing the system with its superordinate systems (that use it), subordinate systems (that it uses), peer-level systems and actors. Archetypes (core abstractions) are then refined into components. Alternatives are compared with methods such as ATAM (architecture trade-off analysis method), which evaluates quality attributes and finds sensitivity and trade-off points.

Structured design: from DFD to structure chart

Structured design maps a DFD to a structure chart, a tree of modules showing the call hierarchy (not the sequence of execution). Notation: a rectangle is a module; a double-sided rectangle is a library (predefined) module; an arrow is a call; a small arrow with an empty circle is a data couple; one with a filled circle is a control couple (flag); a diamond at the base of a module shows a conditional call; a curved arrow over calls shows a loop.

Transform analysis applies when the DFD has transform flow: data comes in (afferent, incoming flow), is transformed at the transform centre, and goes out (efferent, outgoing flow). Pressman’s steps: review the fundamental system model; review and refine the DFDs; decide whether the flow is transform or transaction; isolate the transform centre by marking the incoming and outgoing flow boundaries; perform first-level factoring (a main controller with an input controller, a transform controller and an output controller); perform second-level factoring (map each bubble to a module under those controllers); refine the first-iteration structure with design heuristics.

Transaction analysis applies when one input item (a transaction) triggers one of several action paths. The DFD has a transaction centre; the structure chart gets a reception path and a dispatcher module that calls one action-path controller per transaction type (think of a menu-driven ATM).

Design heuristics: improve functional independence; keep fan-out moderate (a common guideline is at most about 7); increase fan-in as depth increases (reuse of utility modules); keep the scope of effect of a decision within its scope of control; reduce interface complexity; build modules whose behaviour is predictable; avoid pathological connections (branches into the middle of a module). High-level modules should make decisions (factoring: decision-makers on top, workers at the bottom).

Pressman’s architectural metrics: structural complexity S(i) = fout(i)2; data complexity D(i) = v(i) ÷ (fout(i) + 1), where v(i) is the number of input and output variables of module i; system complexity C(i) = S(i) + D(i) (Card and Glass). Henry and Kafura’s information-flow complexity is length × (fan-in × fan-out)2. Morphology metrics: size = n + a (nodes plus arcs), arc-to-node ratio r = a ÷ n, and width (the maximum number of nodes at any level).

Object-oriented design

OO design refines analysis classes into design classes (user interface, business domain, process, persistence and system classes) and adds implementation detail. Well-formed design classes are complete and sufficient, primitive, highly cohesive and loosely coupled. The widely taught SOLID principles (popularised by Robert C. Martin; Pressman’s component-level design chapter covers OCP, LSP, DIP and ISP, plus the package principles) are:

  • SRP (single responsibility): a class should have one reason to change.
  • OCP (open–closed): open for extension, closed for modification.
  • LSP (Liskov substitution): subclasses must be substitutable for their base classes.
  • ISP (interface segregation): many client-specific interfaces are better than one general interface.
  • DIP (dependency inversion): depend on abstractions, not on concretions.
  • Package principles: release reuse equivalency, common closure, common reuse.

The Chidamber–Kemerer (CK) metrics measure OO designs: WMC (weighted methods per class), DIT (depth of inheritance tree: longest path from the class to the root), NOC (number of immediate children), CBO (coupling between object classes), RFC (response for a class) and LCOM (lack of cohesion in methods). In the original CK definition, take every pair of methods: P is the number of pairs that share no instance variable and Q the number that share at least one; LCOM = P − Q if P > Q, otherwise 0.

UML for design: class, sequence and state diagrams

A class box has three compartments: name, attributes, operations. Visibility: + public, − private, # protected, ~ package. Multiplicity is written at association ends (1, 0..1, *, 1..*).

RelationshipNotationMeaning
DependencyDashed line, open arrowheadOne element uses another briefly (a parameter type)
AssociationSolid line (arrow for navigability)A structural link between objects
AggregationSolid line, hollow diamond at the wholeWhole–part; the part can exist on its own and be shared
CompositionSolid line, filled diamond at the wholeStrong whole–part; the part lives and dies with the whole
GeneralisationSolid line, hollow triangle at the superclass“is-a” inheritance
RealisationDashed line, hollow triangle at the interfaceA class implements an interface

By strength of the link between classes: dependency, association, aggregation, composition (weakest to strongest).

A sequence diagram shows objects as lifelines (dashed vertical lines), time running downward, activation bars (thin rectangles) where an object is executing, synchronous messages (solid line, filled arrowhead; the sender waits), asynchronous messages (solid line, open arrowhead), return messages (dashed line), object creation, destruction (an X at the end of a lifeline) and combined fragments (alt for if–else, opt for optional, loop, par for parallel, ref for a reference to another diagram). A communication diagram shows the same messages numbered (1, 1.1, 2) on links between objects; the two are semantically equivalent views. A state machine diagram shows the life of one object: states, transitions labelled event [guard] / action, entry and exit actions, composite states.

User interface design

Theo Mandel’s three golden rules (quoted by Pressman): place the user in control (no forced modes, interruptible and undoable interaction, hide technical internals), reduce the user’s memory load (meaningful defaults, intuitive shortcuts, real-world metaphors, progressive disclosure) and make the interface consistent (across screens and across a family of applications). Shneiderman’s eight golden rules add: strive for consistency, enable shortcuts, offer informative feedback, design dialogues to yield closure, prevent errors and offer simple error handling, permit easy reversal of actions, support internal locus of control, and reduce short-term memory load.

Pressman’s UI design process is a spiral of four activities: interface analysis and modelling (users, tasks, content, environment), interface design, interface construction (implementation, often a prototype first) and interface validation. Design issues to address: response time (length and variability), help facilities, error handling, menu and command labelling, application accessibility and internationalisation. Interaction styles include command language, menus, form fill-in and direct manipulation.

Design patterns

A pattern names a recurring problem, its context, a solution and its consequences. The “Gang of Four” (Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides, 1994) catalogue has 23 patterns in three groups:

GroupPurposePatterns
Creational (5)How objects are createdAbstract Factory, Builder, Factory Method, Prototype, Singleton
Structural (7)How classes and objects are composedAdapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy
Behavioural (11)How objects interact and share responsibilityChain of Responsibility, Command, Interpreter, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Observer, State, Strategy, Template Method, Visitor

Intents worth memorising: Adapter converts one interface into another that clients expect; Decorator adds responsibilities dynamically; Facade gives one simple interface to a subsystem; Proxy is a placeholder controlling access; Composite treats part–whole trees uniformly; Observer notifies all dependants when one object changes (the basis of MVC views); Strategy makes a family of algorithms interchangeable; Iterator gives sequential access without exposing representation; Template Method fixes an algorithm’s skeleton and lets subclasses fill steps. Architectural patterns (MVC, layers, broker) work at a larger scale; idioms work at the language level.

Worked examples

Example 1: classifying cohesion. Name the cohesion of each module.

  1. StartUp(): open log file, set counters to zero, display splash screen. All happen at start time → temporal.
  2. ProcessRecord(): read record → validate it → write the valid record to the output file, each step feeding the next → sequential.
  3. CustomerSummary(): from the same customer record, compute total purchases and also find the last order date → communicational.
  4. AllOutputs(code): print, e-mail or fax a document depending on the code → logical.
  5. ComputeGST(amount, rate) → one task → functional.

Ranked worst to best: logical (4), temporal (1), communicational (3), sequential (2), functional (5).

Example 2: classifying coupling. (a) Area(length, breadth) receives two numbers → data. (b) PrintAddress(customer) receives the whole customer record but prints only the address → stamp. (c) Sort(list, order) where order = 1 means ascending and 2 descending → control. (d) Two modules both read and write a global stockLevel → common. (e) A module that jumps into the middle of another module’s code or edits its private table → content. (f) Two modules that must both follow a fixed printer protocol → external. From best to worst: a, b, c, f, d, e.

Example 3: Card–Glass complexity of a structure chart. Main calls GetInput, Process and Output; Process calls Validate and Compute. The input/output variable counts v are Main 2, GetInput 3, Process 5, Validate 2, Compute 4, Output 3.

ModulefoutvS = fout2D = v ÷ (fout + 1)C = S + D
Main3290.59.5
GetInput03033
Process2541.675.67
Validate02022
Compute04044
Output03033

Main has the highest system complexity (9.5) because of its fan-out. Morphology: n = 6 nodes, a = 5 arcs, so size = 11 and r = 5 ÷ 6 ≈ 0.83; width = 3 (the three modules on the second level). A tree always has a = n − 1.

Example 4: information flow and CK metrics. (a) A module has 40 lines of code, fan-in 2 and fan-out 3. Henry–Kafura complexity = 40 × (2 × 3)2 = 40 × 36 = 1440. (b) A class has four methods using instance variables M1 {a, b}, M2 {b, c}, M3 {d}, M4 {d, e}. Of the 6 method pairs, (M1, M2) share b and (M3, M4) share d, so Q = 2 and P = 4. LCOM = P − Q = 2, showing the class really holds two separate responsibilities and could be split. (c) In a hierarchy where Vehicle has children Car, Bus and Truck, and Car has child SportsCar, DIT(SportsCar) = 2 and NOC(Vehicle) = 3.

Example 5: transform mapping. A payroll DFD: read timesheet → validate hours → compute pay → format payslip → print payslip. Incoming flow boundary after “validate hours”; outgoing flow boundary before “format payslip”; transform centre: “compute pay”. First-level factoring gives a Payroll main module with three subordinates: Get valid hours (input controller), Compute pay (transform controller) and Produce payslip (output controller). Second-level factoring puts “read timesheet” and “validate hours” under the input controller and “format” and “print” under the output controller.

Separation of concerns and data design

Separation of concerns (the phrase is Dijkstra’s) says that any complex problem is easier to handle if it is divided into pieces that can each be solved or optimised independently. A concern is a feature or behaviour stated in the requirements model. Pressman gives the argument in terms of perceived complexity C and effort E. For two problems p1 and p2: if C(p1) > C(p2) then E(p1) > E(p2); and the perceived complexity of the combined problem is often greater than the sum of the parts, C(p1 + p2) > C(p1) + C(p2). It follows that E(p1 + p2) > E(p1) + E(p2): solving the pieces separately takes less total effort. Modularity, functional independence, refinement and aspects are all ways of putting separation of concerns into practice. The argument has a limit, which is why modularity has an optimum: split too finely and integration cost rises. Concerns that refuse to be separated by ordinary modules are the crosscutting concerns handled by aspects.

Data design (the data/class element at the base of the design pyramid) turns the data objects of the analysis model into data structures and classes. It starts with a model of the data at a high level of abstraction (the user’s view) and refines it into progressively more implementation-specific representations. At the architectural level it means designing databases and, for business intelligence, a data warehouse: a separate store that is subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile (data are added, not overwritten). At the component level it means choosing the data structures and the algorithms that operate on them. Wasserman’s principles for data specification, quoted by Pressman:

  1. The systematic analysis principles applied to function and behaviour should also be applied to data.
  2. All data structures and the operations to be performed on each should be identified.
  3. A data dictionary should be established and used to define both data and program design.
  4. Low-level data design decisions should be deferred until late in the design process.
  5. The representation of a data structure should be known only to those modules that must use the data directly (information hiding).
  6. A library of useful data structures and the operations that may be applied to them should be developed.
  7. A software design and programming language should support the specification and realisation of abstract data types.
NTA trap: low-level data decisions are made late, not early, and a data warehouse is non-volatile.

NTA traps

  • Reversed scales. An order question may ask “highest to lowest”. Read the direction twice before you pick.
  • Logical versus temporal. Logical (flag-selected similar tasks) is below temporal.
  • Communicational versus sequential. Sequential (output feeds input) is above communicational (same data).
  • Control versus stamp. Control coupling is worse than stamp coupling.
  • Common versus content. Global data is bad (common); reaching into another module’s internals is worse (content).
  • “Low cohesion, high coupling is the aim.” The aim is the opposite.
  • Aggregation versus composition. Filled diamond = composition = the part dies with the whole.
  • Diamond position. The diamond sits at the whole, not the part; the triangle sits at the superclass.
  • Pattern groups. Adapter, Facade, Decorator, Proxy, Composite are structural; Observer, Strategy, Iterator, Command are behavioural; Singleton, Builder, Prototype, Factory Method, Abstract Factory are creational.
  • Structure chart shows sequence. It shows the call hierarchy, not the order of execution.

How NTA asks this

  • Order: cohesion or coupling ranking (either direction), design pyramid, transform-mapping steps, UI design process.
  • Match: cohesion or coupling type with description; architectural style with example; pattern with intent or group; UML notation with meaning.
  • A–R: why high cohesion and low coupling; why content coupling is the worst; information hiding and maintainability.
  • Multiple statements: creational patterns, CK metrics, design concepts, Mandel’s rules.
  • Numericals: Card–Glass, Henry–Kafura, DIT/NOC, LCOM.

Mini order question. Arrange from highest to lowest coupling: A. Stamp B. Content C. External D. Data E. Control. Write the scale D-S-C-E-C-C, reverse it (content, common, external, control, stamp, data), drop common, and read off the letters: B, C, E, A, D.

Elimination trick: in any cohesion or coupling order question, check only the two ends first. Functional must be last in a worst-to-best cohesion list and content must be last in a best-to-worst coupling list. That usually removes two options; then check the logical–temporal or stamp–control pair to finish.

terms.definition: Focusing on the essential features at one level while suppressing detail; procedural abstraction names a sequence of steps, data abstraction names a collection of data.
Parnas’s principle that each module hides its design decisions (data structures, algorithms) from other modules and exposes only an interface.
Designing modules that each do one clearly defined job and interact little with others: high cohesion and low coupling.
The degree to which the elements inside one module belong together. Best: functional. Worst: coincidental.
The degree of interdependence between modules. Best: data (or no direct) coupling. Worst: content coupling.
Fan-out is the number of modules a module directly calls; fan-in is the number of modules that directly call it.
Structured-design strategy that splits a DFD into incoming (afferent), transform-centre and outgoing (efferent) flow to derive a structure chart.
A family of systems described by its components, connectors, constraints and semantic model, e.g. pipe-and-filter or layered.
A strong whole–part association shown by a filled diamond at the whole; the part cannot exist independently of the whole.
A named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem in a context, described by its name, problem, solution and consequences.

lessons.examTip: Write both scales on your rough sheet before reading any design question: cohesion C-L-T-P-C-S-F (“Can Lazy Teachers Prepare Clear Structured Files”) from worst to best, and coupling D-S-C-E-C-C (data, stamp, control, external, common, content) from best to worst. Most order and A-R questions are then mechanical.

lessons.title: Software quality
lessons.summaryHtml: Software quality means meeting stated requirements and the implicit expectations of users, such as being reliable, usable and maintainable. Quality models (McCall, ISO/IEC 9126 and its successor ISO/IEC 25010) break quality into measurable factors. Quality is assured by process: SQA activities, reviews and inspections, and process maturity frameworks such as CMM/CMMI, ISO 9001 and Six Sigma. Reliability is measured with MTTF, MTTR, MTBF and availability, and predicted with growth models such as Musa’s. After delivery, software changes through corrective, adaptive, perfective and preventive maintenance, supported by reengineering and configuration management. Every numerical answer in this lesson was checked by a program.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A piece of software has quality when it does what the requirements say and also what users reasonably expect without being told: it does not crash, it is easy to use, it runs fast enough, it keeps data safe, and it can be changed without breaking. Because "good" is vague, software engineering splits quality into named factors (reliability, maintainability, portability and so on) and tries to measure each one.

Quality is not tested into a product at the end. It is built in by a disciplined process: standards, reviews, inspections, audits and measurement. That is why this topic also covers process frameworks (CMM/CMMI, ISO 9001, Six Sigma). Finally, software lives for years after release, so the lesson ends with maintenance, reengineering and configuration management, the activities that keep quality from decaying over time.

Why it matters for NET

Software engineering is one of the ten units of Paper 2, and software quality is one of its most reliably tested areas. NET questions here are mostly factual, which makes them quick marks if you memorise the lists exactly: the McCall groups, the ISO characteristics, and the CMM and CMMI level names and their key process areas. The numerical part is small but predictable: availability, MTBF, series and parallel reliability, and occasionally Musa’s reliability growth model or Boehm’s annual change traffic. Match-the-following and ordering questions on levels, maintenance types and reengineering steps are very common.

Concepts in depth

1. Quality models

McCall’s model (1977) looks at the product from three viewpoints and lists eleven factors. Learn it as a table, because NTA asks which group a factor belongs to.

Group (viewpoint)Question it answersFactors
Product operationHow well does it run?Correctness, reliability, efficiency, integrity, usability
Product revisionHow easily can it be changed?Maintainability, flexibility, testability
Product transitionHow easily can it move to a new environment?Portability, reusability, interoperability

McCall’s factors are measured through lower-level criteria (such as simplicity, modularity and self-descriptiveness), which in turn are measured by metrics. This factor–criteria–metric tree is the idea behind all later models. Boehm’s model (1978) is similar but hierarchical, with "general utility" split into as-is utility, maintainability and portability.

ISO/IEC 9126 (1991, revised 2001) standardised six characteristics, each with sub-characteristics:

ISO 9126 characteristicSub-characteristics
FunctionalitySuitability, accuracy, interoperability, security, compliance
ReliabilityMaturity, fault tolerance, recoverability
UsabilityUnderstandability, learnability, operability, attractiveness
EfficiencyTime behaviour, resource utilisation
MaintainabilityAnalysability, changeability, stability, testability
PortabilityAdaptability, installability, co-existence, replaceability

ISO/IEC 25010:2011 (part of the SQuaRE series) replaced 9126. Its product quality model has eight characteristics: functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability and portability. Security and compatibility were promoted from sub-characteristics to full characteristics. It also defines a separate quality-in-use model (effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction, freedom from risk, context coverage). A 2023 revision of 25010 reorganised the model again (for example adding safety); if an option set clearly follows the eight-characteristic list, answer from the 2011 edition, which is what textbooks teach.

2. Software quality assurance, reviews and inspections

Quality control checks products (testing, inspection of work products). Quality assurance checks that the process is followed and is capable of producing quality. An SQA group prepares the SQA plan, takes part in defining the process, reviews activities for compliance, audits work products, records non-compliance and reports to management. The cost of quality splits into prevention costs (planning, training, standards), appraisal costs (reviews, inspections, testing) and failure costs, both internal (rework before release) and external (complaints, warranty, patches after release). Spending on prevention and appraisal is worthwhile because the cost of fixing a defect rises steeply the later it is found.

Reviews range from informal desk checks to formal technical reviews (FTR). Two forms are always contrasted:

  • A walkthrough is led by the author, who walks the team through the product. It is relatively informal and is also used for knowledge sharing.
  • An inspection (Michael Fagan, IBM, 1976) is the most formal review. It has defined roles (moderator, author, reader, recorder, inspectors), entry and exit criteria, checklists and collected metrics. Its steps are planning, overview, individual preparation, the inspection meeting, rework and follow-up. The meeting only finds and logs defects; it does not fix them.

A standard measure of review and test effectiveness is defect removal efficiency: DRE = E ÷ (E + D), where E is the number of errors found before delivery and D the number of defects found after delivery.

3. Process maturity: CMM, CMMI, ISO 9001 and Six Sigma

The SEI Capability Maturity Model (CMM) rates an organisation’s software process on five levels. Each level above 1 is defined by key process areas (KPAs) that must be in place.

LevelCMM nameCMMI (staged) nameTypical KPAs / focus
1InitialInitialAd hoc, success depends on individual heroes
2RepeatableManagedRequirements management, project planning, project tracking and oversight, subcontract management, SQA, configuration management
3DefinedDefinedOrganisation process focus and definition, training, integrated software management, product engineering, intergroup coordination, peer reviews
4ManagedQuantitatively ManagedQuantitative process management, software quality management (statistical control)
5OptimizingOptimizingDefect prevention, technology change management, process change management

CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) merged several CMMs. It has two representations: staged (maturity levels 1–5 for the whole organisation, as above) and continuous (capability levels for each process area separately; in CMMI v1.3 these are 0 Incomplete, 1 Performed, 2 Managed, 3 Defined).

ISO 9001 is a generic standard for a quality management system, applicable to any organisation (a factory, a hospital or a software house). It requires documented processes, management responsibility, resource management, product realisation, and measurement, analysis and improvement, following the Plan–Do–Check–Act cycle. Certification says the process is documented and followed; it does not by itself guarantee a good product. ISO 90003 gives guidance for applying ISO 9001 to software. Unlike CMM, ISO 9001 is pass/fail rather than a ladder of levels.

Six Sigma (from Motorola) uses statistics to reduce variation. A "six sigma" process produces at most 3.4 defects per million opportunities (DPMO); this figure assumes the process mean drifts by 1.5σ in the long term, leaving 4.5σ to the nearest specification limit. DPMO = defects × 10⁶ ÷ (units × opportunities per unit). Existing processes are improved with DMAIC (Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control); new processes are designed with DMADV (Define, Measure, Analyse, Design, Verify).

4. Reliability, availability and their numericals

Reliability is the probability of failure-free operation for a specified time in a specified environment. A failure is a deviation of observed behaviour from the requirement; a fault (bug) is its cause in the code. The time-based measures fit together on one time line:

  working (MTTF)          repair (MTTR)   working (MTTF) ...
|========================|~~~~~~~~~~~~~|========================|
^ restart           failure^      restart^
|<--------------- one cycle = MTBF --------------->|

So MTBF = MTTF + MTTR and Availability = MTTF ÷ (MTTF + MTTR) = MTTF ÷ MTBF. Availability is a long-run fraction of time; it rewards both rare failures and fast repair.

Other reliability metrics: ROCOF (rate of occurrence of failures, for example 2 failures per 1000 operating hours), POFOD (probability of failure on demand, for example 3 failed requests in 1000 gives 0.003, used for systems that are called on occasionally, like a safety shutdown), and failure rate λ. If failures occur at a constant rate λ, the time to failure is exponential: R(t) = e−λt and MTTF = 1 ÷ λ.

For systems of independent components:

  • Series (all must work): R = R₁ × R₂ × … × Rₙ. The result is below the weakest component.
  • Parallel (redundant; one working copy is enough): R = 1 − (1 − R₁)(1 − R₂)…(1 − Rₙ). The result is above the best component.
  • The same rules apply to availabilities of independent components.

Nines of availability: a year has 8760 hours. Downtime per year = (1 − A) × 8760 h. So 99% allows 87.6 h, 99.9% allows 8.76 h, 99.99% about 52.6 minutes and 99.999% about 5.26 minutes.

5. Reliability growth: Musa’s models

As testers find and fix faults, the failure intensity λ (failures per CPU hour) falls. Musa’s basic execution-time model assumes each fixed fault reduces λ by the same amount. With λ₀ the initial failure intensity, ν₀ the total failures expected in infinite time, and μ the failures experienced so far:

  • λ(μ) = λ₀ (1 − μ ÷ ν₀), a straight line from λ₀ down to 0 at μ = ν₀.
  • Extra failures to go from a present intensity λP to a target λF: Δμ = (ν₀ ÷ λ₀)(λP − λF).
  • Extra execution time needed: Δτ = (ν₀ ÷ λ₀) ln(λP ÷ λF).

The logarithmic Poisson model assumes early fixes remove more failure intensity than later ones: λ(μ) = λ₀ e−θμ, where θ is the failure-intensity decay parameter. Then Δμ = (1 ÷ θ) ln(λP ÷ λF) and Δτ = (1 ÷ θ)(1 ÷ λF − 1 ÷ λP).

6. Maintenance, reengineering and configuration management

Maintenance is any change after delivery. The four types (Lientz and Swanson, extended by IEEE):

  • Corrective: fix defects reported after release.
  • Adaptive: fit a changed environment, such as a new OS, database, hardware or tax rule.
  • Perfective: add features or improve performance or usability at the users’ request. Studies consistently find this is the largest share of maintenance effort.
  • Preventive: restructure or document the software to make future maintenance easier, before problems appear.

Lehman’s laws of software evolution explain why this never ends: a used system must keep changing (continuing change) and, unless work is done to reduce it, its complexity keeps increasing. Boehm estimated yearly maintenance effort with the annual change traffic (ACT), the fraction of the code added or modified in a year: annual maintenance effort = ACT × development effort.

Reengineering rebuilds a legacy system into a better form. Pressman’s software reengineering process model has six activities, usually applied in this order and cyclically: inventory analysis, document restructuring, reverse engineering (recover design and specification from code), code restructuring, data restructuring and forward engineering (rebuild with modern methods using the recovered information). Reverse engineering alone changes nothing; it only extracts information.

Software configuration management (SCM) controls change across the life cycle. A software configuration item (SCI) is any work product placed under control (SRS, design, code, test plan). Once reviewed and approved, it becomes part of a baseline, and later changes go through formal change control. Pressman lists five SCM tasks: identification, version control, change control (change request, evaluation by a change control board, engineering change order, check-out and check-in), configuration audit (did we make the approved change correctly?) and status reporting (who changed what, when).

Worked examples

Example 1: availability from MTBF (the classic trap). A payment gateway has MTBF = 500 h and MTTR = 20 h. Find its availability and yearly downtime.

  1. MTBF already includes the repair, so MTTF = MTBF − MTTR = 500 − 20 = 480 h.
  2. Availability = MTTF ÷ MTBF = 480 ÷ 500 = 0.96 = 96%.
  3. Yearly downtime = (1 − 0.96) × 8760 = 350.4 h.
  4. The wrong option 500 ÷ 520 = 96.15% comes from using MTBF as if it were MTTF.

Reverse problem: to reach 99.9% with MTTR = 2 h, solve MTTF ÷ (MTTF + 2) = 0.999, giving MTTF = 0.999 × 2 ÷ 0.001 = 1998 h.

Example 2: series and parallel components. A request goes through a load balancer (R = 0.99), then to one of two identical application servers (each R = 0.9, either one is enough), then to a database (R = 0.95). Components fail independently.

  1. Parallel servers: 1 − (1 − 0.9)(1 − 0.9) = 1 − 0.01 = 0.99.
  2. Whole chain in series: 0.99 × 0.99 × 0.95 = 0.931095, about 0.931.
  3. Without the load balancer, the servers-plus-database part alone is 0.99 × 0.95 = 0.9405.
  4. Check the intuition: with a single server instead of two, the chain would be 0.99 × 0.9 × 0.95 = 0.846. Redundancy lifted reliability by more than 8 percentage points.

Example 3: exponential reliability and the nines. A module fails at a constant rate λ = 0.002 failures per hour.

  1. MTTF = 1 ÷ λ = 500 h.
  2. Probability of running 100 h without failure: R(100) = e−0.002 × 100 = e−0.2 = 0.8187.
  3. Probability of surviving the full MTTF: R(500) = e−1 ≈ 0.368. So "MTTF = 500 h" does not mean it will usually last 500 hours; only about 37% of runs do.
  4. A service promising 99.95% availability may be down (1 − 0.9995) × 8760 = 4.38 h per year.

Example 4: Musa’s basic model. Initial failure intensity λ₀ = 20 failures per CPU hour, total expected failures ν₀ = 200. So far μ = 100 failures have been experienced.

  1. Present intensity: λ = 20 × (1 − 100 ÷ 200) = 10 failures per CPU hour.
  2. The objective is λF = 5. Extra failures to experience: Δμ = (200 ÷ 20)(10 − 5) = 50.
  3. Extra execution time: Δτ = (200 ÷ 20) × ln(10 ÷ 5) = 10 × 0.6931 = 6.93 CPU hours.
  4. Compare the logarithmic Poisson model with λ₀ = 10 and θ = 0.02 per failure: after 50 failures λ = 10 e−1 = 3.68; going from 10 to 5 needs ln 2 ÷ 0.02 = 34.66 failures and (1 ÷ 0.02)(1 ÷ 5 − 1 ÷ 10) = 5 CPU hours.

Example 5: maintenance effort, DRE and DPMO.

  1. A 50 KLOC system has 5 KLOC added and 2.5 KLOC modified each year. ACT = 7.5 ÷ 50 = 0.15. It took 600 person-months to develop, so annual maintenance effort = 0.15 × 600 = 90 person-months.
  2. Reviews and testing found 45 errors before release and users reported 5 defects after release. DRE = 45 ÷ (45 + 5) = 0.9.
  3. An audit finds 17 defects in 500 forms, each with 10 fields that could be wrong. DPMO = 17 × 10⁶ ÷ (500 × 10) = 3400. A six sigma process would allow only 3.4, a thousand times fewer.

7. Quality control versus quality assurance

The two terms are paired in the syllabus and often confused in options. Quality control (QC) is the series of inspections, reviews and tests used throughout the process to make sure each work product meets its requirements. It is product-oriented and detective: it finds defects in what has been built, and it works as a feedback loop (measure the product, compare with the specification, correct). Testing a module, inspecting a design and checking an SRS against a checklist are QC.

Quality assurance (QA) is the auditing and reporting that tells management whether the QC activities and the defined process are effective and are being followed. It is process-oriented and preventive: it aims to stop defects from being made. Writing the SQA plan, defining standards, auditing whether reviews were held as required, and reporting non-compliance are QA. In short: QC checks the product, QA checks the process that makes the product; QC is usually done by the people who build and test, while QA is often done by an independent SQA group. Both feed quality management, together with quality planning and improvement.

Quality controlQuality assurance
FocusProduct (work products)Process
NatureDetective, correctivePreventive
Typical activitiesTesting, inspections, reviews of work productsSQA plan, standards, process audits, reporting to management

8. Change control and version control in depth

Version control manages the different versions of configuration objects. Three words must be kept apart. A new version (revision) supersedes the previous one after a change, as in 1.1 → 1.2. Variants are versions that exist side by side for different platforms or configurations (a Windows build and a Linux build of the same release). A release is a version distributed to customers. The history of an object is drawn as an evolution graph, whose nodes are versions and whose branches are variants or parallel lines of work. Tools save space by storing deltas (differences between versions) instead of full copies. Early tools (SCCS, RCS) and centralised systems (CVS, Subversion) keep one master repository; distributed systems such as Git and Mercurial give every developer a full copy of the repository and its history.

Change control combines human procedures and tools. Pressman’s sequence for a change to a baselined item is:

  1. A change request is submitted and evaluated for technical merit, possible side effects, overall impact on other configuration objects and system functions, and cost; the result is a change report.
  2. The change control authority (CCA, or change control board) decides. If the change is approved, an engineering change order (ECO) is issued, describing the change, the constraints and the review and audit criteria.
  3. The object is checked out of the project database, the change is made and appropriate SQA activities are applied.
  4. The change is reviewed (audited) and the object is checked in.
  5. A testing baseline is established, the change is promoted for inclusion in the next release, the software is rebuilt and distributed.

Check-out and check-in give access control (who may change which object) and synchronisation control (a lock, so two people cannot overwrite each other’s parallel changes). Before a baseline, only informal change control applies; after it, the formal procedure is used.

IEEE Std 982.1 measures how stable a product has become with the software maturity index: SMI = [MT − (Fa + Fc + Fd)] ÷ MT, where MT is the number of modules in the current release and Fa, Fc, Fd are the modules added, changed and deleted relative to the previous release. As SMI approaches 1.0 the product begins to stabilise.

Example 6: software maturity index. Release 5 of a product has 620 modules. Compared with release 4, 25 modules were added, 48 changed and 9 deleted. Find SMI.

  1. Modules affected = 25 + 48 + 9 = 82.
  2. SMI = (620 − 82) ÷ 620 = 538 ÷ 620 = 0.868 (to three decimals).
  3. The value is fairly close to 1, so the product is stabilising. Forgetting the deleted modules gives (620 − 73) ÷ 620 = 0.882, a common slip.

9. Software reuse

Almost any software artifact can be reused: code components, designs and design patterns, architectures, requirements, test cases and test data, documentation, plans and even estimates. Sommerville describes reuse at three scales: application system reuse (a whole system, configured or incorporated), component reuse (subsystems or single objects) and object and function reuse (library routines). Approaches that support reuse include design patterns, component-based development, application frameworks, legacy system wrapping, service-oriented systems, software product lines (a family of applications built on a common architecture), COTS and ERP integration, program libraries, program generators and aspect-oriented development.

Benefits: increased dependability (reused software has been tried and tested), reduced process risk (the cost of existing software is already known), effective use of specialists, standards compliance, and faster development. Problems: increased maintenance costs if the source code is not available, lack of tool support, the “not-invented-here” syndrome, the cost of creating and maintaining a component library, and the effort of finding, understanding and adapting components.

Systematic reuse is organised by domain engineering (domain analysis, construction and dissemination: find, build and catalogue the reusable components of an application domain). In component-based development each candidate component goes through qualification (does it do the needed job and fit the architecture?), adaptation (remove conflicts, often by wrapping: white-box, grey-box or black-box wrapping) and composition (assemble the components into the architecture).

Example 7: effort saved by reuse. A system is estimated at 80 KLOC. Of this, 30 KLOC can be reused, but adapting and integrating it costs 20% of the effort of writing it new. Productivity is 700 LOC per person-month. Compare the effort with and without reuse.

  1. Equivalent new code = 50 + 0.20 × 30 = 50 + 6 = 56 KLOC.
  2. Effort with reuse = 56,000 ÷ 700 = 80 person-months.
  3. Without reuse = 80,000 ÷ 700 = 114.29 person-months, so reuse saves about 34.29 person-months.

10. Reverse engineering in depth

Reverse engineering is the process of analysing a program to create a representation of it at a higher level of abstraction than source code. It is a process of design recovery: it extracts data, architectural and procedural design information, but it does not change the system. (Chikofsky and Cross also name redocumentation as its simplest form.) Pressman describes a reverse engineering process by four properties:

  • Abstraction level: the sophistication of the design information that can be extracted, from procedural design, through program and data structure information and data/control-flow models, up to entity–relationship or UML models. Higher is better.
  • Completeness: the level of detail provided at a given abstraction level. Completeness decreases as the abstraction level increases.
  • Interactivity: the degree to which the human is integrated with the automated tools. As the abstraction level rises, interactivity must rise, or completeness suffers.
  • Directionality: one-way means all extracted information goes to the maintenance engineer; two-way means it is also fed to a reengineering tool that tries to restructure or regenerate the program.

The process first restructures “dirty” source code (often automatically) so that it is easier to read, then extracts abstractions to produce an initial specification, which is refined and simplified into a final specification. Reverse engineering is applied to understand processing (what the code does), data (internal data structures and the database schema) and user interfaces. It is followed, in a reengineering project, by restructuring (code or data, same abstraction level, same function) and forward engineering (building the improved system from the recovered design).
