NTA traps

  • MTBF in the numerator. Wrong: A = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR). Fix: MTBF already contains MTTR; A = (MTBF − MTTR) ÷ MTBF.
  • Adding series reliabilities or averaging them. Wrong: 0.9, 0.95, 0.99 in series give about 0.95. Fix: multiply; a chain is weaker than its weakest link.
  • Mixing CMM and CMMI names. Level 2 is Repeatable in CMM but Managed in CMMI; level 4 is Managed in CMM but Quantitatively Managed in CMMI. Read which model the question names.
  • Placing KPAs one level off. Peer reviews are level 3, not 2. SQA and configuration management are level 2. Defect prevention is level 5, not 4.
  • Corrective versus perfective. Fixing a reported bug is corrective. Perfective is improvement requested by users. Preventive is done before any failure, to ease future change.
  • Reverse engineering equals reengineering. Wrong. Reverse engineering only recovers design information; reengineering also restructures and forward-engineers.
  • MTTF as a guarantee. With a constant failure rate, only e−1 ≈ 37% of runs survive to the MTTF.
  • ISO 9001 as a product standard. It certifies a quality management system (the process), for any industry. Product quality characteristics come from ISO 9126 and 25010.

How NTA asks this

  • Match the following: CMM level with name or KPA; McCall factor with group; ISO 9126 characteristic with sub-characteristic; maintenance type with example; cost-of-quality category with example.
  • Assertion–Reason and two statements: about availability depending on MTTR, walkthrough versus inspection, ISO 9001 scope, or what reengineering includes.
  • Ordering: CMMI levels, Fagan inspection steps, reengineering activities, DMAIC phases.
  • Numericals: availability (often with the MTBF trap), series and parallel reliability, downtime for a number of nines, Musa’s basic model, DRE, ACT.
Mini-example (match): List I: A. Reliability, B. Maintainability, C. Portability, D. Efficiency. List II: I. Installability, II. Time behaviour, III. Fault tolerance, IV. Analysability. Anchor the pair you are surest of: fault tolerance belongs to reliability (A-III). That alone removes every option without A-III. Then time behaviour is clearly efficiency (D-II). Usually one option is left: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.
Mini-example (A–R): A: In Pressman’s reengineering process model, reverse engineering comes before code restructuring. R: Reverse engineering changes the code into a better structure. A is true (the design must be recovered before the code is restructured). R is false (reverse engineering only extracts information; restructuring is a separate activity), so the answer is "(A) is true but (R) is false". Always test R on its own before asking whether it explains A.
Elimination trick: in availability questions, the correct value is always less than 1 and closer to 1 when MTTR is small. If an option equals MTTR ÷ MTBF, it is the unavailability, not the availability.

terms.definition: A planned set of activities (standards, reviews, audits, testing, measurement) that gives confidence that the process and product meet quality requirements.
Eleven quality factors in three groups: product operation, product revision and product transition.
The product quality model that replaced ISO/IEC 9126. The 2011 edition has eight characteristics, including security and compatibility.
Five stages of process maturity. CMM: Initial, Repeatable, Defined, Managed, Optimizing. CMMI staged: Initial, Managed, Defined, Quantitatively Managed, Optimizing.
Mean time to failure: the average operating time from a repair (or start) until the next failure.
Mean time to repair: the average time to detect, fix and restore service after a failure.
Mean time between failures: MTTF + MTTR, the average length of one full failure–repair cycle.
The fraction of time a system is working: MTTF ÷ (MTTF + MTTR).
A data-driven quality method that aims at no more than 3.4 defects per million opportunities, using DMAIC for existing processes.
Controlling change: identifying configuration items, versioning, change control, configuration audit and status reporting, around approved baselines.

lessons.examTip: Availability uses MTTF on top and MTTF + MTTR (= MTBF) below. If the question gives MTBF, first subtract MTTR to get MTTF; putting MTBF on top is the classic wrong option.

steps: Attempt problems 1–11 in 15 minutes without notes (about 80 seconds each, close to real exam pace). Write the formula first, then substitute.
Attempt problems 12–15 in 5 minutes. For the match question, fix the pair you are surest of and eliminate options.
Check with solutions.md. Write every mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (MTBF as MTTF, series versus parallel, CMM versus CMMI names).
Redo problem 5 with three servers in parallel and problem 7 with λ₀ = 30. Predict the direction of change before you compute.
Write the CMM KPAs for levels 2–5 from memory and compare them with the lesson table.
Redo every wrong problem after 24 hours without looking at the solution.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct
Problems 1–11 finished within 15 minutes
No MTBF-as-MTTF or series-versus-parallel mistakes
All five CMM and CMMI level names written correctly from memory

quiz.question: A web service runs for an average of 990 hours between the end of one repair and its next failure. Each repair takes 10 hours on average. What is its steady-state availability?
quiz.explanation: MTTF = 990 h and MTTR = 10 h. Availability = MTTF ÷ (MTTF + MTTR) = 990 ÷ 1000 = 0.99 = 99%. 98.99% comes from dividing by (MTTF + 2 × MTTR); 1% is the unavailability; 99.9% ignores the repair time scale.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: In the original SEI CMM the levels are 1 Initial, 2 Repeatable, 3 Defined, 4 Managed and 5 Optimizing, so A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II. Option 1 swaps Defined and Managed. Option 2 swaps levels 2 and 3. Option 4 swaps levels 4 and 5. Note that CMMI renames level 2 as Managed and level 4 as Quantitatively Managed, which is exactly what the distractors exploit.

b: I. Defined
II. Optimizing
III. Repeatable
IV. Managed

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Availability = MTTF ÷ (MTTF + MTTR). If MTTR is also very large (say MTTF = 10,000 h but each repair takes 10,000 h), availability is only 50%. So A is true, R is true, and R is exactly why A holds.

stmts: Assertion (A): A system with a very large MTTF can still have poor availability.
Reason (R): Availability depends on the mean time to repair as well as on the mean time to failure.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: A transaction passes through three independent components in series with reliabilities 0.9, 0.95 and 0.99. What is the reliability of the whole path (to three decimal places)?
quiz.explanation: In series every component must work, so multiply: 0.9 × 0.95 × 0.99 = 0.84645 ≈ 0.846. A series system is always less reliable than its weakest part (0.9). 0.947 is the average of the three; 0.990 wrongly uses the best component.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Adapting to a changed environment (new OS, hardware, law, database) is adaptive maintenance, so Statement I is true. Fixing a reported defect is corrective maintenance; perfective maintenance adds or improves features and performance on user request. So Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: Modifying an application so that it runs on a new version of the operating system is adaptive maintenance.
Statement II: Fixing a defect that a user reported after release is perfective maintenance.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: In McCall’s quality model, which of the following factors belong to the product revision group?
options: A, B, C and D only
quiz.explanation: Product revision (the ability to change the product) contains maintainability, flexibility and testability. Portability, reusability and interoperability form product transition. Correctness, reliability, efficiency, integrity and usability form product operation.

stmts: A. Maintainability
B. Flexibility
C. Testability
D. Portability
E. Reusability

quiz.question: Under Musa’s basic execution-time model, a program starts with a failure intensity of 20 failures per CPU hour, and the total number of failures expected over infinite time is 200. What is the failure intensity after 100 failures have been experienced?
quiz.explanation: Basic model: λ(μ) = λ₀(1 − μ/ν₀) = 20 × (1 − 100/200) = 10 failures per CPU hour. Failure intensity falls linearly with failures experienced. 7.36 is 20 × e⁻¹, the logarithmic Poisson form, which is a different model.

quiz.question: Arrange the following steps of a Fagan-style software inspection in the correct order.
quiz.explanation: The moderator plans the inspection (and an overview may be given), each inspector prepares individually, defects are logged in the meeting, the author reworks the product and the moderator follows up to check the fixes: C, B, E, A, D. Preparation must come before the meeting, and follow-up checks the rework, so it comes last.

stmts: A. Rework
B. Individual preparation
C. Planning
D. Follow-up

quiz.question: In software configuration management, what is a baseline?
options: Any version of a file stored in the repository
The first prototype shown to the customer
A work product that has been formally reviewed and agreed on, and that can be changed only through formal change control
The minimum set of test cases that every build must pass
quiz.explanation: A baseline is a reviewed and approved specification or product that serves as the basis for further development and is changed only through the formal change-control procedure. Ordinary versions are not baselines until they pass review; the other options describe prototypes and smoke tests.

quiz.question: A server has a mean time between failures (MTBF) of 500 hours and a mean time to repair of 20 hours. What is its availability?
quiz.explanation: MTBF = MTTF + MTTR, so MTTF = 500 − 20 = 480 h. Availability = MTTF ÷ MTBF = 480 ÷ 500 = 0.96 = 96%. The trap 96.15% treats 500 as MTTF: 500 ÷ 520. 4% is the unavailability.

lessons.title: Estimation and scheduling of software projects
lessons.summaryHtml: Before a project starts, a manager must estimate how big the software is, how much effort and time it needs, and how many people to put on it. Size is measured in lines of code (LOC) or, independent of language, in function points (FP). Effort and duration then come from empirical models: Boehm’s COCOMO (basic, intermediate, and COCOMO II) and Putnam’s SLIM model. The work is scheduled as a network of activities, and PERT/CPM finds the critical path, the floats and the probability of finishing on time. Progress is tracked with earned value, and risks are managed by identifying, analysing, planning for and monitoring them. Every numerical answer in this lesson was checked by a program.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A client asks: "How much will it cost, and when will it be ready?" To answer, a project manager needs three numbers. The first is size: how much software must be built, measured in lines of code or function points. The second is effort: how many person-months of work that size needs. The third is duration: how many calendar months, given that people cannot all work in parallel. Estimation models turn size into effort and duration using formulas fitted to data from many past projects.

Once the work is estimated, it is split into activities with dependencies and scheduled. PERT and CPM find which chain of activities decides the finish date (the critical path) and how much slack every other activity has. While the project runs, earned value tells the manager whether it is ahead or behind in time and money, and risk management deals with what might go wrong.

Why it matters for NET

This is the most numerical lesson in the software engineering unit. NET papers regularly contain a COCOMO calculation, a function point calculation, or a critical path or float question, and the formulas are fixed, so these are marks you should never lose. Around them come factual questions on the COCOMO modes and cost drivers, the five FP components and their weights, Putnam’s model, earned value terms and the risk management process, often in match-the-following form.

Concepts in depth

1. Size metrics: LOC, Halstead and function points

Lines of code (LOC, KLOC) is the simplest size measure. It is easy to count after the fact, but it depends on the language and coding style, is hard to estimate before design, and penalises high-level languages: the same feature in fewer lines looks like lower productivity. Productivity in LOC is expressed as LOC per person-month. A common way to estimate LOC before coding is the three-point (beta) estimate: S = (Sopt + 4Sm + Spess) ÷ 6.

Halstead’s software science measures a program by its operators and operands: n₁ distinct operators, n₂ distinct operands, N₁ total operators and N₂ total operands. Vocabulary n = n₁ + n₂, length N = N₁ + N₂, volume V = N log₂ n (bits), estimated length N̂ = n₁ log₂ n₁ + n₂ log₂ n₂, difficulty D = (n₁ ÷ 2)(N₂ ÷ n₂), and effort E = D × V.

Function point analysis (Albrecht, IBM, 1979; now standardised by IFPUG) measures functionality from the user’s point of view, so it is language independent and can be counted from the requirements. There are five function types, each rated simple, average or complex:

Function typeKindSimpleAverageComplex
External input (EI)Transactional346
External output (EO)Transactional457
External inquiry (EQ)Transactional346
Internal logical file (ILF)Data71015
External interface file (EIF)Data5710

The weighted sum is the unadjusted function points (UFP). Then 14 general system characteristics (data communications, distributed processing, performance, heavily used configuration, transaction rate, online data entry, end-user efficiency, online update, complex processing, reusability, installation ease, operational ease, multiple sites, facilitate change) are each rated 0 (no influence) to 5 (essential). The value adjustment factor VAF = 0.65 + 0.01 × ΣFᵢ lies between 0.65 and 1.35, and FP = UFP × VAF. FP can then be converted to LOC with a language-specific LOC-per-FP figure, or used directly for productivity (FP per person-month) and cost.

2. COCOMO (Boehm, 1981)

COCOMO classifies a project into one of three modes:

  • Organic: a small team with good experience of similar systems, familiar environment, flexible requirements (for example a payroll system in-house).
  • Semi-detached: a mix of experienced and new people, some unfamiliar aspects (for example a new DBMS or a compiler).
  • Embedded: tight hardware, software and operational constraints, such as real-time avionics or telecom switching software.

Basic COCOMO: effort E = a(KLOC)b person-months and development time D = c(E)d months. The average staff size is E ÷ D and productivity is KLOC ÷ E.

ModeBasic effort (a, b)Schedule (c, d)Intermediate a
Organic2.4, 1.052.5, 0.383.2
Semi-detached3.0, 1.122.5, 0.353.0
Embedded3.6, 1.202.5, 0.322.8

These are Boehm’s standard coefficients. Note two patterns: the exponent b is above 1 in every mode (effort grows faster than size, a diseconomy of scale caused by communication and integration), and it rises from organic to embedded. The schedule exponent d falls, so duration grows slowly with effort.

Intermediate COCOMO multiplies a nominal effort by an effort adjustment factor: E = a(KLOC)b × EAF, with the intermediate a values from the last column of that table (the exponents b are unchanged). EAF is the product of 15 cost-driver multipliers in four groups. The standard multipliers (very low, low, nominal, high, very high, extra high) are shown below. The driver codes mean: RELY required reliability, DATA database size, CPLX product complexity, TIME execution time constraint, STOR main storage constraint, VIRT virtual machine volatility, TURN turnaround time, ACAP analyst capability, AEXP applications experience, PCAP programmer capability, VEXP virtual machine experience, LEXP language experience, MODP modern practices, TOOL software tools, SCED required schedule.

DriverGroupVL / L / N / H / VH / XH
RELYProduct0.75 / 0.88 / 1.00 / 1.15 / 1.40 / –
DATAProduct– / 0.94 / 1.00 / 1.08 / 1.16 / –
CPLXProduct0.70 / 0.85 / 1.00 / 1.15 / 1.30 / 1.65
TIMEComputer– / – / 1.00 / 1.11 / 1.30 / 1.66
STORComputer– / – / 1.00 / 1.06 / 1.21 / 1.56
VIRTComputer– / 0.87 / 1.00 / 1.15 / 1.30 / –
TURNComputer– / 0.87 / 1.00 / 1.07 / 1.15 / –
ACAPPersonnel1.46 / 1.19 / 1.00 / 0.86 / 0.71 / –
AEXPPersonnel1.29 / 1.13 / 1.00 / 0.91 / 0.82 / –
PCAPPersonnel1.42 / 1.17 / 1.00 / 0.86 / 0.70 / –
VEXPPersonnel1.21 / 1.10 / 1.00 / 0.90 / – / –
LEXPPersonnel1.14 / 1.07 / 1.00 / 0.95 / – / –
MODPProject1.24 / 1.10 / 1.00 / 0.91 / 0.82 / –
TOOLProject1.24 / 1.10 / 1.00 / 0.91 / 0.83 / –
SCEDProject1.23 / 1.08 / 1.00 / 1.04 / 1.10 / –

Read the direction: product and computer drivers raise effort as the rating rises (more reliability costs more), while personnel and most project drivers lower it (better people and tools save effort). Detailed COCOMO goes further, with phase-sensitive multipliers and estimates for each module, subsystem and system.

COCOMO II (2000) has three sub-models suited to project stages: application composition (object points), early design and post-architecture. Its effort equation is PM = A × SizeE × ΠEMᵢ with A = 2.94 and E = B + 0.01 × ΣSFⱼ, where B = 0.91 and five scale factors (precedentedness, development flexibility, architecture/risk resolution, team cohesion, process maturity) set the exponent. So in COCOMO II the diseconomy of scale is computed for each project, not fixed by the mode.

3. Putnam’s model (SLIM)

Putnam fitted the Norden–Rayleigh staffing curve to large projects and derived the software equation Size = Cₖ K1/3 td4/3, where K is total effort, td the development time and Cₖ a technology constant. For a fixed size, K × td4 is constant, so effort ∝ 1 ÷ td4. Compressing the schedule to 90% multiplies effort by 1 ÷ 0.9⁴ ≈ 1.52. This is the numerical form of the rule that squeezing a schedule is extremely expensive (and below about 75% of nominal, often impossible).

4. Project scheduling: WBS, Gantt charts, CPM and PERT

The work breakdown structure (WBS) splits the project into tasks; a Gantt chart draws them as bars on a calendar, and an activity network shows their dependencies. CPM (critical path method) assumes each duration is known:

  1. Forward pass: ES = maximum EF of the predecessors (0 at the start), EF = ES + duration. The project length T is the largest EF.
  2. Backward pass: LF = minimum LS of the successors (T at the end), LS = LF − duration.
  3. Total float TF = LS − ES = LF − EF. Free float FF = (minimum ES of the successors) − EF. Always 0 ≤ FF ≤ TF.
  4. Activities with TF = 0 form the critical path, the longest path. There can be more than one.

PERT (program evaluation and review technique) handles uncertain durations with three estimates per activity: optimistic a, most likely m, pessimistic b, assuming a beta distribution. Then tₑ = (a + 4m + b) ÷ 6 and σ² = ((b − a) ÷ 6)². The critical path is found with the tₑ values. By the central limit theorem, the project time is taken as normal with mean Tₑ = Σtₑ and variance Σσ² along the critical path only. The probability of finishing by a target T is Φ(Z) with Z = (T − Tₑ) ÷ σ. CPM is also used for time–cost trade-off (crashing), while PERT is used for probability of completion.

5. Earned value analysis

Three numbers at a status date: PV (planned value, BCWS: budget of work scheduled so far), EV (earned value, BCWP: budget of work actually done) and AC (actual cost, ACWP). From them: SV = EV − PV and SPI = EV ÷ PV (schedule), CV = EV − AC and CPI = EV ÷ AC (cost). A negative variance or an index below 1 is bad news. With the budget at completion BAC, the estimate at completion is EAC = BAC ÷ CPI (if current cost efficiency continues), the estimate to complete ETC = EAC − AC and the variance at completion VAC = BAC − EAC.

6. Risk management

A risk is an uncertain event that would cause loss. Pressman classifies risks as project risks (schedule, budget, staffing, resources), technical risks (design, implementation, interface, verification problems) and business risks (market risk: nobody wants the product; strategic risk: it no longer fits the company’s strategy; sales, management and budget risks). Risks are also known, predictable or unpredictable. Reactive strategies wait for trouble; proactive strategies plan ahead.

Boehm’s process splits into risk assessment (identification, analysis, prioritisation) and risk control (management planning, resolution, monitoring). Prioritise by risk exposure RE = P × C (probability × cost of loss). A mitigation is worth doing if its risk reduction leverage RRL = (REbefore − REafter) ÷ cost of the mitigation is well above 1. Pressman records all this in a risk table and an RMMM plan (risk mitigation, monitoring and management).

Worked examples

Example 1: function points. A system has 12 simple and 8 average EIs, 10 average and 4 complex EOs, 6 simple EQs, 5 average ILFs and 3 simple EIFs. Each of the 14 characteristics is rated 3.

  1. UFP = 12×3 + 8×4 + 10×5 + 4×7 + 6×3 + 5×10 + 3×5 = 36 + 32 + 50 + 28 + 18 + 50 + 15 = 229.
  2. ΣFᵢ = 14 × 3 = 42, so VAF = 0.65 + 0.42 = 1.07.
  3. FP = 229 × 1.07 = 245.03.
  4. At 60 LOC per FP this is about 14,702 LOC; at a productivity of 8 FP per person-month the effort is 245.03 ÷ 8 ≈ 30.63 person-months.

Example 2: basic COCOMO. An organic project of 32 KLOC.

  1. E = 2.4 × 321.05 = 91.33 person-months.
  2. D = 2.5 × 91.330.38 = 13.90 months.
  3. Average staff = E ÷ D = 91.33 ÷ 13.90 = 6.57, so about 7 people.
  4. Productivity = 32,000 ÷ 91.33 ≈ 350 LOC per person-month.
  5. For comparison, a 50 KLOC semi-detached project needs E = 3.0 × 501.12 = 239.87 person-months and D = 2.5 × 239.870.35 = 17.02 months.

Example 3: intermediate COCOMO. A 40 KLOC semi-detached project needs high reliability (RELY H = 1.15) and has high complexity (CPLX H = 1.15), but has highly capable analysts (ACAP H = 0.86). All other drivers are nominal.

  1. EAF = 1.15 × 1.15 × 0.86 = 1.137 (to three decimals).
  2. Nominal effort = 3.0 × 401.12 = 186.82 person-months.
  3. Adjusted effort = 186.82 × 1.13735 = 212.48 person-months.
  4. D = 2.5 × 212.480.35 = 16.31 months.

Example 4: PERT and probability of completion. Times in weeks (a, m, b):

ActivityPredecessorsa, m, btₑσ²
A–2, 4, 640.444
B–3, 5, 1362.778
CA4, 6, 860.444
DA1, 2, 320.111
EB, D4, 6, 1472.778
FC3, 4, 540.111
GE, F2, 3, 430.111
  1. Paths: A-C-F-G = 4 + 6 + 4 + 3 = 17; A-D-E-G = 16; B-E-G = 16. The critical path is A-C-F-G, 17 weeks.
  2. Variance along it = 0.444 + 0.444 + 0.111 + 0.111 = 1.111, so σ = 1.054.
  3. P(finish within 18 weeks) = Φ((18 − 17) ÷ 1.054) = Φ(0.95) ≈ 0.829.
  4. Caution: the path B-E-G is only one week shorter but has variance 5.667. Its own chance of finishing within 18 weeks is Φ(2 ÷ 2.38) ≈ 0.80, lower than the critical path’s. Standard PERT ignores such near-critical paths, so its probability is optimistic.

Example 5: CPM floats. Durations in days: A 3 (start), B 4 (start), C 1 (after A), D 5 (after A), E 3 (after B and C), F 4 (after D and E).

Act  Dur   ES  EF   LS  LF   TF  FF
A     3     0   3    0   3    0   0
B     4     0   4    1   5    1   0
C     1     3   4    4   5    1   0
D     5     3   8    3   8    0   0
E     3     4   7    5   8    1   1
F     4     8  12    8  12    0   0
  1. Forward pass: E starts at max(4, 4) = 4; F starts at max(8, 7) = 8; T = 12 days.
  2. Critical path: A-D-F (all with zero total float).
  3. B has total float 1 but free float 0: delaying B by a day does not delay the project, but it does delay E’s earliest start. E has free float 1, because F waits for D anyway.

Example 6: earned value and risk exposure. BAC = ₹200 lakh. At the review date PV = 100, EV = 80, AC = 90 (₹ lakh).

  1. SV = 80 − 100 = −20, SPI = 0.8: behind schedule.
  2. CV = 80 − 90 = −10, CPI = 0.889: over budget.
  3. EAC = 200 ÷ 0.889 = 225; ETC = 225 − 90 = 135; VAC = 200 − 225 = −25.
  4. A risk with probability 0.3 and loss ₹5 lakh has RE = ₹1.5 lakh. If a ₹0.4 lakh mitigation cuts RE to ₹0.3 lakh, RRL = (1.5 − 0.3) ÷ 0.4 = 3, so it is worth doing.
  5. Halstead check for a small module with n₁ = 10, n₂ = 15, N₁ = 40, N₂ = 60: V = 100 log₂ 25 = 464.39 bits, D = 5 × 4 = 20, E = 9287.71.

7. LOC-based and FP-based (problem-based) estimation

Pressman calls LOC and FP estimation problem-based estimation, because both start from the problem, not from the process. The steps are:

  1. Start from a bounded statement of software scope.
  2. Decompose the software into functions (or information domain values, for FP) small enough to be estimated individually.
  3. Estimate the size (LOC or FP) of each function. Because a single guess is unreliable, use three values, optimistic, most likely and pessimistic, and take the expected value S = (sopt + 4sm + spess) ÷ 6.
  4. Add the function sizes, then divide by a historical productivity figure (LOC per person-month or FP per person-month) to get effort.
  5. Multiply effort by the labour rate (or size by the cost per LOC or per FP) to get cost.

LOC-based estimation needs decomposition down to fairly fine functions, because LOC can only be guessed for small pieces. FP-based estimation decomposes less finely: it estimates the information domain values (inputs, outputs, inquiries, files, interfaces) and the adjustment factor, which can be done from the requirements. The productivity figures must come from similar past projects in the same organisation; that is the weak point of both methods.

Process-based estimation is the alternative: the process is broken into its framework activities, and effort is estimated for each activity applied to each function (a function × activity table). Pressman advises using at least two techniques and reconciling them. If the estimates are close, they can be trusted; widely divergent estimates usually mean that the scope has been misunderstood or that the productivity data are unsuitable for this project.

Example 7: problem-based estimation. A system has three functions with LOC estimates (optimistic, most likely, pessimistic): F1 (2000, 2400, 3400), F2 (4000, 5200, 7000), F3 (1500, 1900, 2900). Historical productivity is 700 LOC per person-month and the labour rate is ₹80,000 per person-month. Separately, the system is sized at 250 FP and the organisation delivers 10 FP per person-month. Find the LOC-based effort and cost and the FP-based effort.

  1. F1 = (2000 + 4 × 2400 + 3400) ÷ 6 = 15,000 ÷ 6 = 2500 LOC. F2 = (4000 + 20,800 + 7000) ÷ 6 = 31,800 ÷ 6 = 5300 LOC. F3 = (1500 + 7600 + 2900) ÷ 6 = 12,000 ÷ 6 = 2000 LOC.
  2. Total size = 2500 + 5300 + 2000 = 9800 LOC.
  3. Effort = 9800 ÷ 700 = 14 person-months. Cost = 14 × ₹80,000 = ₹11,20,000, about ₹114.29 per LOC.
  4. FP-based effort = 250 ÷ 10 = 25 person-months. The two estimates differ a lot, so the team should check the scope and whether the productivity data suit this project before committing.

8. Scheduling principles, effort distribution, time-line charts and staffing

Pressman’s basic scheduling principles: compartmentalisation (divide the project into manageable activities and tasks), interdependency (find which tasks depend on others and which can run in parallel), time allocation (each task gets a start date, a duration and an amount of effort), effort validation (make sure no more people are allocated than are available at any time), defined responsibilities (every task has an owner), defined outcomes (every task produces a work product) and defined milestones (each group of tasks ends in a reviewed milestone).

Effort distribution. The 40–20–40 rule says roughly 40% of the effort goes to front-end analysis and design, 20% to coding and 40% to back-end testing. Pressman treats it only as a guideline; his more detailed ranges are about 2–3% for planning, 10–25% for requirements analysis, 20–25% for design, 15–20% for coding and 30–40% for testing and debugging.

Time-line charts. A time-line chart (Gantt chart) is generated from the task network once each task has its effort, duration, start date and owner. Tasks (and subtasks) are listed in the left column; horizontal bars show each task’s duration on a calendar; bars that overlap in time are concurrent tasks; milestones are drawn as diamonds. It can be drawn for the whole project or separately for each function or person. Alongside it, scheduling tools produce a project table, which lists every task with its planned and actual start and end dates, the effort assigned and notes; it is the main instrument for tracking. The time-line chart shows when and how long clearly, but dependencies and the critical path are shown more clearly by the activity network. Tracking uses status meetings, review results, milestone dates, comparison of actual and planned start dates, informal contacts and earned value.

Staffing. Effort and people are not interchangeable (Brooks’s law). The Putnam–Norden–Rayleigh (PNR) curve shows how staff should build up: few people at the start, a rise to a peak near the planned delivery time td, then a tail into maintenance. In Putnam’s form, the staffing rate is m(t) = (K ÷ td2) · t · e−t²/(2td²), where K is the total life-cycle effort. The peak is at t = td, where m(td) = (K ÷ td) e−1/2 ≈ 0.6065 K ÷ td, and the effort spent up to td is K(1 − e−1/2) ≈ 0.3935 K. The curve also shows why compressing a schedule is so costly: effort rises steeply as the delivery date is pulled in.

Example 8: effort distribution, effort validation and the Rayleigh peak. (a) A project needs 60 person-months. Apply the 40–20–40 rule. (b) A team of 3 works a 5-day week; one week’s tasks in the time-line chart need 17 person-days. (c) A project has life-cycle effort K = 200 person-months and delivery at td = 10 months. Find the peak staffing and the effort spent by delivery.

  1. (a) Analysis and design 0.40 × 60 = 24, coding 0.20 × 60 = 12, testing 0.40 × 60 = 24 person-months.
  2. (b) Capacity = 3 × 5 = 15 person-days, so the week is over-allocated by 17 − 15 = 2 person-days; effort validation fails and tasks must be moved or people added.
  3. (c) Peak = (200 ÷ 10) × e−0.5 = 20 × 0.6065 = 12.13 people, reached at month 10. Effort by delivery = 200 × (1 − e−0.5) = 200 × 0.3935 = 78.69 person-months.

9. Risk projection and the RMMM plan

Risk projection (risk estimation) rates each risk in two ways: the likelihood that it is real, and the consequences if it occurs. Pressman’s four steps: establish a scale for likelihood, describe the consequences, estimate the impact on the project and product, and assess the accuracy of the projection. Risks are recorded in a risk table with columns for the risk, its category (for example product size, business impact, staff, technology), its probability, its impact and a pointer to its RMMM entry. Impact is coded 1 = catastrophic, 2 = critical, 3 = marginal, 4 = negligible, judged over four risk components: performance, cost, support and schedule. The table is sorted by probability and impact, and a cut-off line is drawn: risks above it get first-order attention, those below are re-evaluated later. The Pareto observation applies: about 80% of the overall project risk usually comes from about 20% of the identified risks.

Each managed risk then gets three kinds of treatment, collected in the RMMM plan (risk mitigation, monitoring and management):

  • Mitigation (avoidance): proactive steps to reduce the probability. For high staff turnover: find out why people leave and deal with the causes, cross-train, set documentation standards, assign backup staff, hold peer reviews so that more than one person knows each part.
  • Monitoring: watch the factors that show whether the risk is becoming more or less likely (for turnover: team morale, relationships, the job market), and check whether the mitigation steps are working.
  • Management and contingency planning: assumes mitigation has failed and the risk has occurred, and puts the backup plan into action (for turnover: reassign work, bring new people up to speed using the documentation).

The RMMM plan can be a separate document or part of the project plan; many teams keep a risk information sheet (RIS) for each risk, with its description, context, mitigation, monitoring and management steps, and current status. RMMM costs effort itself, which is another reason to manage only the risks above the cut-off line in detail.

Example 9: risk exposure from a component-reuse risk. The plan assumes 15 reusable components will be available; there is an 80% chance they will not be, and each would then have to be built new at about 100 LOC and ₹250 per LOC. Find the cost C and the risk exposure RE.

  1. C = 15 × 100 × ₹250 = ₹3,75,000.
  2. RE = P × C = 0.80 × ₹3,75,000 = ₹3,00,000. This figure is added to the risk table and compared with the project’s cost estimate.

NTA traps

  • Mixing the mode coefficients. Using 2.4 with exponent 1.12, or the intermediate a = 3.2 in a basic question. Fix: memorise the (a, b) pairs as a unit, and note that only a changes in intermediate COCOMO.
  • Effort versus time. E is in person-months, D in months. An option equal to D is offered as the effort and vice versa.
  • Forgetting VAF, or using the average weights for everything. Read the complexity of each count, and check whether the question wants UFP or adjusted FP.
  • Language dependence. FP is language independent; LOC is not. Only the FP-to-LOC conversion depends on the language.
  • PERT variance. Wrong: add the standard deviations, or add variances of all activities. Fix: add variances of the critical-path activities only, then take the square root.
  • Critical path as the shortest path. It is the longest path, and it fixes the minimum project duration.
  • Total versus free float. FF ≤ TF always. An activity can have total float but zero free float, as B does in Example 5.
  • Putnam direction. Compressing the schedule increases effort by the fourth power, not linearly.
  • SPI above 1. An index above 1 is good (ahead of schedule or under budget); a negative variance is bad.

How NTA asks this

  • Numericals: basic or intermediate COCOMO effort, time and staff; FP from counts and GSCs; PERT expected time, variance and probability; critical path length and floats; Putnam compression; EVM indices.
  • Match the following: COCOMO mode with coefficients; FP component with weight; EVM measure with formula; estimation model with its author (COCOMO–Boehm, FP–Albrecht, SLIM–Putnam, software science–Halstead); risk type with example.
  • Assertion–Reason and two statements: Brooks’ law, the language independence of FP, the uniqueness of the critical path, what COCOMO II changes.
  • Multiple statements and ordering: which drivers are personnel attributes; steps of FP counting, CPM or risk management.
Mini-example (match): List I: A. Organic, B. Semi-detached, C. Embedded, D. Intermediate organic. List II: I. a = 3.6, b = 1.20; II. a = 3.2, b = 1.05; III. a = 2.4, b = 1.05; IV. a = 3.0, b = 1.12. Between the two b = 1.05 pairs, the basic organic a is 2.4 (A-III) and the intermediate one is 3.2 (D-II).
Mini-example (A–R): A: A project can have more than one critical path. R: A critical activity always has zero free float but may have positive total float. A is true: a network can have two paths of equal, maximum length (the quiz network with P-S-U and P-R-T-U, both 12 days, is one). R is false: on the critical path total float is zero, and free float can never exceed total float. Answer: (A) is true but (R) is false.
Elimination trick: in COCOMO questions, first estimate roughly. For 10–50 KLOC, organic effort is about 2.7 to 2.9 person-months per KLOC and embedded effort about 5.7 to 7.9. Any option below a × KLOC must be wrong, because b > 1.

quiz.question: A project has these activities (duration in days; predecessors in brackets): P 4 (none), Q 6 (none), R 3 (P), S 5 (P), T 2 (Q, R), U 3 (S, T). What is the minimum project duration, and what is the total float of Q?

lessons.title: Software testing
lessons.summaryHtml: Testing runs a program with chosen inputs in order to find defects. It is one part of verification ("are we building the product right?") and validation ("are we building the right product?"). Testing proceeds in levels: unit, integration, system and acceptance, including alpha and beta testing, with regression testing after every change. Black-box techniques (equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision tables, cause–effect graphs) derive tests from the specification. White-box techniques (statement, branch, condition and path coverage, basis path testing with cyclomatic complexity) derive them from the code. Mutation testing and defect seeding measure how good a test suite is, and debugging locates and removes the faults that tests reveal. Every numerical answer and program output in this lesson was checked by a program.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Testing is running a program on purpose to make it fail. A test that finds a defect is a successful test. Myers defined testing as "the process of executing a program with the intent of finding errors", and Dijkstra added the limit: testing can show the presence of bugs, never their absence. Because we can never try every input, the craft of testing is choosing a small set of tests with a high chance of exposing faults.

Some words are used precisely. A mistake (error) by a person puts a fault (defect, bug) into the code; when that code runs, it may cause a failure, an observable wrong behaviour. Debugging starts after a failure is seen: it finds the fault and removes it. Testing finds failures; debugging finds faults.

Why it matters for NET

Software testing is among the most frequently tested parts of the software engineering unit. Almost every paper has something on cyclomatic complexity (from a flow graph or from code), boundary value counts, black-box versus white-box classification, integration strategies (stubs and drivers), or verification versus validation. The numericals are short and formula-based; the conceptual questions come as match-the-following, assertion–reason and statement pairs that turn on one precise word.

Concepts in depth

1. Verification, validation and static testing

Boehm’s phrasing is the one NTA uses: verification asks "are we building the product right?" (does each phase’s output match its specification?) and validation asks "are we building the right product?" (does the final product meet the user’s real needs?). Verification includes static techniques that do not execute code: reviews, walkthroughs, inspections and static analysis tools. Validation is mostly dynamic: executing the software, ending in acceptance testing. The V-model pairs each development phase with a test level: requirements with acceptance testing, system design with system testing, architectural design with integration testing, and module design with unit testing.

2. Levels of testing

  • Unit testing checks one module in isolation, usually by the developer, using white-box and black-box tests. Because the module calls or is called by others, it needs scaffolding: a driver (a main program that feeds test data to the unit and prints results) and stubs (dummy versions of modules the unit calls).
  • Integration testing combines modules and tests their interfaces.
    • Big bang: combine everything at once. It is fast to set up, but failures are hard to localise.
    • Top-down: start at the main module and add modules below it, depth-first or breadth-first. It needs stubs. It shows a working skeleton early and tests the major control points early, but low-level processing is tested late.
    • Bottom-up: start with the leaf modules grouped into clusters (builds). It needs drivers. There is no need for stubs, but there is no working program until the last module is added.
    • Sandwich (hybrid): top-down for the upper layers and bottom-up for the lower layers, meeting in the middle.
  • System testing tests the complete system against the SRS, including non-functional tests: performance, load and stress, security, recovery and configuration testing.
  • Acceptance testing is done by or for the customer to decide whether to accept the system. Alpha testing is done by users at the developer’s site, with developers watching. Beta testing is done by real users at their own sites, without developers present, and they report problems back.

Regression testing re-runs earlier tests after any change (a fix, an enhancement, a new environment) to catch side effects. Smoke testing is a quick check of each daily build’s critical functions, to decide whether it is stable enough for deeper testing.

3. Black-box techniques

Black-box (functional, behavioural) testing uses only the specification. It finds missing or wrong functions, interface errors, and initialisation and termination errors.

Equivalence class partitioning splits each input’s domain into classes that the program should process identically, with valid and invalid classes. For a range (say 18 ≤ age ≤ 60) there are three classes: below, within, above. With several inputs, Jorgensen distinguishes weak normal testing (one value from each class, so as many tests as the input with the most valid classes) from strong normal testing (the Cartesian product of the valid classes).

Boundary value analysis exists because programmers often get the edges wrong (< instead of ≤, off-by-one loops). For each input with range [min, max], the basic values are min, min+ (just above), nominal, max− (just below) and max. Under the single-fault assumption only one variable takes a boundary value at a time, the others staying nominal. The counts, for n variables:

VariantValues per variableTest casesn = 2n = 3
Basic BVA5 (min, min+, nom, max−, max)4n + 1913
Robustness7 (adds min−, max+)6n + 11319
Worst-case5, all combinations5ⁿ25125
Robust worst-case7, all combinations7ⁿ49343

Decision table testing lists conditions and actions; each column (rule) is one combination of conditions. With n binary conditions, a full limited-entry table has 2ⁿ rules; a condition with k values multiplies the count by k. Rules whose actions are the same can be merged with don’t-care entries (a rule with d don’t-cares covers 2ᵈ combinations). Cause–effect graphing draws causes (input conditions) and effects (outputs) linked by AND, OR and NOT, with constraints, then converts the graph into a decision table, one test per column.

4. White-box techniques and coverage

White-box (structural, glass-box) testing uses the code. The main coverage criteria, from weakest to strongest:

  • Statement coverage: every statement runs at least once.
  • Branch (decision) coverage: every decision takes both its true and false outcomes. It subsumes statement coverage.
  • Condition coverage: every simple condition inside a decision takes both values. On its own it does not guarantee branch coverage; condition/decision coverage requires both.
  • MC/DC: in addition, each condition is shown to change the decision’s outcome independently. For n conditions it needs at least n + 1 tests, far fewer than the 2ⁿ of multiple condition coverage, which tries every combination.
  • Path coverage: every complete path runs. With loops this is usually infinite, so we use basis path testing instead.

Data flow testing selects paths from each definition of a variable to its uses (all-defs, all-uses, all-du-paths). Loop testing tests a simple loop with 0, 1, 2, m (typical) and n−1, n, n+1 passes, and handles nested loops starting from the innermost.

5. Cyclomatic complexity and basis path testing

McCabe represents the code as a flow graph: nodes are statements or blocks of sequential statements, edges are transfers of control. A predicate node is one with two or more outgoing edges. A compound condition such as a && b is split into one predicate node per simple condition, because each can send control elsewhere. The cyclomatic complexity V(G) can be computed three ways, which must agree:

  • V(G) = E − N + 2P, with E edges, N nodes and P connected components (P = 1 for one function; for a program with a main and k separately drawn procedures, P = k + 1).
  • V(G) = number of predicate nodes + 1 (a switch with k branches counts as k − 1 predicates).
  • V(G) = number of regions of the planar flow graph, counting the outer region.

V(G) is the number of linearly independent paths in a basis set: each new path adds at least one edge not used before. Testing each basis path guarantees that every statement and every branch runs at least once, so V(G) is an upper bound on the number of tests needed for branch coverage. It is not the total number of paths: two if statements in sequence have V(G) = 3 but 4 complete paths. As a design guideline, McCabe suggested keeping V(G) of a module at 10 or below, because risk and testing effort rise with it.

6. Measuring test adequacy: mutation and seeding

Mutation testing is a fault-based technique that tests the tests. A tool makes many mutants, each with one small change (replace > by ≥, + by −, a variable by a constant). A test suite kills a mutant if some test gives a different output. An equivalent mutant produces the same output as the original for every input, so it can never be killed and is excluded: mutation score = killed ÷ (total − equivalent). A live, non-equivalent mutant tells you which test is missing.

Defect seeding (Mills) inserts S known defects. If testing finds s of them and n original defects, the estimated total of original defects is N = n × S ÷ s, and N − n are estimated to remain. The estimate assumes seeded and real defects are equally hard to find.

7. Debugging

Pressman lists three debugging strategies. Brute force uses memory dumps, traces and print statements everywhere; it is the most common and least efficient. Backtracking starts where the symptom appears and traces the code backwards to the cause; it works for small programs. Cause elimination forms hypotheses about the cause (induction or deduction) and designs tests to prove or eliminate each one; binary partitioning of the input data belongs here. After a fix, run regression tests, because a fix can introduce new faults.

Worked examples

Example 1: generating BVA tests. A function takes x in [1, 100] and y in [18, 60]. Nominal values are the midpoints (rounded down): x = 50, y = 39.

  1. Vary x with y nominal: (1, 39), (2, 39), (99, 39), (100, 39).
  2. Vary y with x nominal: (50, 18), (50, 19), (50, 59), (50, 60).
  3. Add the all-nominal case (50, 39). Total = 4 × 2 + 1 = 9 tests.
  4. Robustness testing adds (0, 39), (101, 39), (50, 17), (50, 61): 6 × 2 + 1 = 13 tests. Worst-case testing takes all 5 × 5 = 25 combinations.

Example 2: equivalence classes and decision tables. A NextDate-style function has valid classes month ∈ {30-day months, 31-day months, February} (3), day ∈ {1–28, 29, 30, 31} (4) and year ∈ {2000, other leap years, common years} (3).

  1. Weak normal testing needs as many tests as the largest class count: 4.
  2. Strong normal testing takes the product: 3 × 4 × 3 = 36.
  3. A decision table with two yes/no conditions and one three-valued condition has 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 rules before any merging.

Example 3: cyclomatic complexity of the grade function. The code is the one in the quiz: if (m >= 40 && att >= 75) g = 1; else if (m >= 35) g = 2; while (m > 90) { g = g + 10; m = m - 5; } return g;

 1: g = 0
 2: m >= 40 ?      T -> 3   F -> 5
 3: att >= 75 ?    T -> 4   F -> 5
 4: g = 1          -> 7
 5: m >= 35 ?      T -> 6   F -> 7
 6: g = 2          -> 7
 7: m > 90 ?       T -> 8   F -> 9
 8: g = g + 10     -> 8b
8b: m = m - 5      -> 7
 9: return g
  1. Nodes N = 10, edges E = 13, so V(G) = 13 − 10 + 2 = 5.
  2. Predicate nodes: 2, 3, 5 and 7, so V(G) = 4 + 1 = 5.
  3. A basis set of 5 independent paths, with inputs (checked by running the code):
    • 1-2-5-7-9: m = 20, att = 0 gives g = 0.
    • 1-2-3-4-7-9: m = 50, att = 80 gives g = 1.
    • 1-2-3-5-6-7-9: m = 50, att = 60 gives g = 2.
    • 1-2-5-6-7-9: m = 37, att = 0 gives g = 2.
    • 1-2-3-4-7-8-8b-7-9: m = 95, att = 80 gives g = 11.
  4. Each path adds a new edge, and the path–edge matrix has rank 5, so the paths are independent.

Example 4: coverage is not the same as correctness.

int g(int a, int b) {
    int r = 0;
    if (a > 10) r = r + 1;
    if (b < 0)  r = r - 1;
    else        r = r * 2;
    return r;
}
  1. Tests g(15, 5) and g(3, 7) return 2 and 0. The first if takes both outcomes; the second takes only false.
  2. Branch coverage = 3 of 4 outcomes = 75% (gcov reports the same), and the statement r = r - 1 never runs.
  3. V(G) = 2 + 1 = 3, but there are 4 complete paths (T/F × T/F). Three basis paths suffice for branch coverage; covering all four paths is path coverage.

Example 5: mutation score, seeding and MC/DC.

  1. 50 mutants, 5 equivalent, 36 killed: score = 36 ÷ 45 = 80%.
  2. Replacing b > m by b >= m in a max-of-three function gives an equivalent mutant: when b equals m, assigning m = b changes nothing. No test can kill it.
  3. Seeding 20 defects and finding 16 of them plus 40 original ones: estimated original total = 40 × 20 ÷ 16 = 50, so 10 remain.
  4. MC/DC for A && B && C: (T,T,T) with (F,T,T), (T,F,T), (T,T,F) = 4 tests (n + 1). Each false test differs from TTT in one condition and flips the outcome. Multiple condition coverage would need 2³ = 8.

8. Error, fault, bug and failure: the exact terms

IEEE terminology (Std 610.12, carried into later standards) separates cause from effect. An error or mistake is a human action that produces an incorrect result (IEEE also uses “error” for the difference between a computed and a correct value). It leaves a fault (also called a defect or, informally, a bug): an incorrect step, process or data definition in the program. When faulty code executes under the right conditions, it may cause a failure: the system does not perform a required function within the specified requirements, an externally observable wrong behaviour. The chain is mistake → fault → failure. A fault need not cause a failure: the faulty statement may never run, or its effect may be masked. One fault can cause many failures, and testing sees failures while debugging looks for faults. Pressman uses a further convention: an error is a quality problem found before the software is released, a defect one found after release.

9. Control structure testing: condition, data flow and loop testing

Basis path testing is one white-box technique; Pressman groups three more under control structure testing, which broadens coverage and improves quality.

Condition testing exercises the logical conditions in a module. A simple condition is a Boolean variable or a relational expression; a compound condition joins simple ones with AND, OR and NOT. The errors it targets are Boolean operator errors, Boolean variable errors, parenthesis errors, relational operator errors and arithmetic expression errors. Branch testing of each condition, domain testing of each relational expression (values just below, equal to and just above the boundary) and, at the top end, all 2n combinations of n simple conditions are its forms.

Data flow testing selects paths according to where variables are defined and used. For a statement S, DEF(S) is the set of variables defined (assigned) in S and USE(S) the set of variables used in S. A definition-use (DU) chain is written [X, S, S′], where X is defined in S, used in S′, and not redefined on some path from S to S′ (a definition-clear path). The all-DU-paths strategy requires every DU chain to be covered at least once. Data flow testing is useful when a module has nested if statements and loops; the weaker criteria all-defs and all-uses were described in section 4.

Loop testing focuses on the validity of loop constructs. There are four classes:

  • Simple loops, with at most n passes: skip the loop entirely; one pass; two passes; m passes where m < n; n − 1, n and n + 1 passes.
  • Nested loops: testing every combination explodes, so start at the innermost loop and set all other loops to their minimum values; run the simple-loop tests on the innermost loop while holding the outer loops at minimum iteration values, adding tests for out-of-range values; work outward, keeping the other outer loops at minimum and the inner loops at typical values; continue until all loops are tested.
  • Concatenated loops: if the loops are independent, test each as a simple loop; if the counter of loop 1 is used as the initial value of loop 2, the loops are not independent and are tested as nested loops.
  • Unstructured loops: redesign them to reflect structured programming constructs, then test.

Graph matrices make basis path testing mechanical. A graph matrix is a square matrix whose size is the number of nodes in the flow graph; the entry in row i, column j is non-empty when there is an edge from node i to node j. With every link weight set to 1 it is a connection matrix. Then V(G) = Σ over the rows that have connections of (connections in the row − 1), plus 1. Link weights can also hold the probability that an edge is taken, its processing time or the memory it needs.

Example 6: DU chains, loop tests and a connection matrix. (a) For the fragment S1: read(a); S2: b = a * 2; S3: if (b > 10) S4: a = b − 10; S5: c = a + b; list the DU chains. (b) A simple loop may run at most 20 times; list the pass counts to test. (c) A flow graph has edges 1→2, 2→3, 2→4, 3→5, 4→5, 5→2, 5→6. Find V(G) from its connection matrix.

  1. (a) a is defined in S1 and S4. From S1: used in S2, and in S5 along the path where S3 is false (no redefinition), so [a, S1, S2] and [a, S1, S5]. From S4: [a, S4, S5]. b is defined in S2 and used in S3, S4 and S5: [b, S2, S3], [b, S2, S4], [b, S2, S5]. Total 6 DU chains.
  2. (b) Pass counts 0, 1, 2, a typical m such as 10, 19, 20 and 21: 7 tests.
  3. (c) Row connections: node 1 → 1, node 2 → 2, node 3 → 1, node 4 → 1, node 5 → 2, node 6 → 0. Σ(connections − 1) over non-empty rows = 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 2, so V(G) = 2 + 1 = 3. Check: E − N + 2 = 7 − 6 + 2 = 3.

10. Performance, stress and the other system tests

System testing puts the complete, integrated system through tests that no unit test can do. Pressman’s list:

  • Recovery testing forces the software to fail in various ways and verifies that recovery is properly performed. If recovery is automatic, re-initialisation, checkpointing, data recovery and restart are checked; if it needs people, the mean time to repair (MTTR) is evaluated.
  • Security testing verifies that the protection mechanisms will protect the system from improper penetration; the tester plays the role of an attacker.
  • Stress testing executes the system in a way that demands resources in abnormal quantity, frequency or volume: ten interrupts per second when one or two is normal, input data rates raised by an order of magnitude, maximum-memory test cases, cases that cause thrashing or excessive disk hunting. It deliberately goes beyond the specified limits to find where and how the system breaks, and whether it fails gracefully and recovers. Sensitivity testing is a variant that looks for a narrow range of valid data that causes extreme or erroneous processing.
  • Performance testing tests the run-time performance of the software within the context of the integrated system. It happens at every level, but true performance can only be judged when everything is integrated. It is often coupled with stress testing and needs hardware and software instrumentation to measure resource use (processor cycles, response times, throughput).
  • Deployment (configuration) testing exercises the software in each environment in which it must run, including installation procedures.

Industry adds finer names: load testing checks behaviour at the expected (peak) load; volume testing feeds very large amounts of data; soak (endurance) testing keeps a normal load for a long time to expose memory leaks and slow degradation; spike testing applies sudden jumps in load. A handy relation for performance numbers is Little’s law: the average number of requests in the system N = throughput X × average response time R.

Example 7: sizing a load test. A service must handle 120 requests per second with an average response time of 0.25 s. How many requests are in progress at once, and what does a stress test do beyond this?

  1. N = X × R = 120 × 0.25 = 30 concurrent requests on average; the load test drives the system at this level (and at the expected peak).
  2. The stress test keeps increasing the arrival rate beyond 120 per second (for example to 1200 per second, an order of magnitude) until response time collapses or errors appear, then checks that the system degrades gracefully and recovers.

NTA traps

  • Compound conditions counted once. Wrong: if (a && b) adds 1 to V(G). Fix: each simple condition is its own predicate node, so it adds 2.
  • Stubs and drivers swapped. Top-down lacks the lower modules, so it needs stubs; bottom-up lacks the callers, so it needs drivers.
  • 5n instead of 4n + 1. The all-nominal test is shared by every variable; count it once.
  • Robust worst-case as 5ⁿ or 6n + 1. Robust adds two values per variable (7 in all); worst-case means all combinations: 7ⁿ.
  • V(G) as the number of paths. It is the number of independent paths in a basis set. Total paths can be much larger, even infinite with loops.
  • Statement coverage implies branch coverage. It is the other way round: an if with no else can run every statement while never taking the false branch.
  • Alpha versus beta sites. Alpha is at the developer’s site; beta is at the customer’s site with no developer present.
  • Equivalent mutants in the denominator. Exclude them; they cannot be killed by any test.
  • Verification versus validation reversed. "Product right" is verification; "right product" is validation.

How NTA asks this

  • Numericals: V(G) from a flow graph (E, N, P), from code, or from regions; BVA counts; equivalence class counts; decision table rules; mutation score; defect seeding.
  • Code questions: "What is the cyclomatic complexity of this function?" or the output of a small test harness. Count simple conditions carefully.
  • Match the following: technique with category or description; integration strategy with scaffolding; test type (alpha, beta, regression, smoke) with its description; testing level with what it checks.
  • Assertion–Reason and statements: exhaustive testing, coverage subsumption, what V(G) guarantees, stubs versus drivers, verification versus validation.
  • Ordering: testing levels; coverage criteria from weakest to strongest.
Mini-example (match): List I: A. Alpha testing, B. Beta testing, C. Regression testing, D. Smoke testing. List II: I. quick check of a new build’s critical functions; II. re-running old tests after a change; III. by users at the developer’s site; IV. by users at their own sites without developers. Anchor on regression (C-II), then alpha versus beta by site: A-III, B-IV, D-I.
Mini-example (A–R): A: Top-down integration testing needs stubs. R: When a module is integrated top-down, the lower-level modules it calls may not have been integrated yet. Check each statement alone first: both are true. Then ask "because?": stubs are needed precisely because the called modules are missing, so R explains A. Compare: "R: Top-down integration shows a working skeleton early" is also true but does not explain the need for stubs.
Elimination trick: for V(G) from code, the correct option is usually one more than the option that treats compound conditions as single decisions. Count the operators && and || separately from the keywords if, while, for and case, then add 1.

terms.definition: Verification checks that each phase’s output meets its specification ("building the product right"). Validation checks that the product meets the user’s real needs ("building the right product").
Dividing the input domain into classes whose members the program should treat the same way, then testing one value from each class.
Testing at and next to the edges of each input range (min, min+, nominal, max−, max). For n variables, basic BVA needs 4n + 1 tests.
E − N + 2P for a flow graph. It equals the number of decision (predicate) nodes + 1 and the number of regions, and gives the size of a basis set of independent paths.
McCabe’s white-box method: draw the flow graph, compute V(G), find V(G) linearly independent paths and write one test for each.
A stub replaces a called module that is not ready yet (top-down integration). A driver calls the module under test (bottom-up integration).
Re-running selected earlier tests after a change, to check that nothing that used to work is now broken.
Making small changes (mutants) to the program and checking whether the tests detect them. Mutation score = killed ÷ (total − equivalent).
Alpha: users test at the developer’s site under the developer’s eye. Beta: real users test at their own sites without the developer present.
Modified condition/decision coverage: each simple condition must be shown to affect the decision on its own. It needs at least n + 1 tests for n conditions.

lessons.examTip: For cyclomatic complexity from code, count every simple condition: each if, while, for, case label and each extra && or || adds one. V(G) = that count + 1. The option that counts a compound condition as one decision is always there as a trap.

steps: Attempt problems 1–9 in 14 minutes without notes, about 90 seconds each. Draw a flow graph for every cyclomatic complexity problem instead of guessing.
Attempt problems 10–15 in 8 minutes. For problem 10, trace each value by hand before looking at the specification.

Check with solutions.md. Write every mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (compound conditions counted once, 5n instead of 4n + 1, stubs and drivers swapped, equivalent mutants left in the denominator).
For the function in problem 6, write the five basis paths and one input for each, then trace each input to confirm its path.
Write the BVA table of problem 2 again for robustness testing (13 tests) and for worst-case testing (25 tests) and check the counts against the formulas.
Redo every wrong problem after 24 hours without looking at the solution.

quiz.question: A function takes three integer inputs, each with a valid range. How many test cases does basic boundary value analysis (single-fault assumption, values min, min+, nominal, max−, max) generate?
quiz.explanation: Basic BVA holds all but one variable at its nominal value and gives the remaining one its four boundary values (min, min+, max−, max), plus one test with everything nominal: 4n + 1 = 4 × 3 + 1 = 13. 15 counts the all-nominal test three times (5n); 19 is robustness testing (6n + 1); 125 is worst-case testing (5ⁿ).

quiz.question: What is the cyclomatic complexity of the following C function?
quiz.explanation: Count the simple conditions: m >= 40, att >= 75 (the && creates a second decision node), m >= 35 and m > 90. That is 4 predicates, so V(G) = 4 + 1 = 5. In the flow graph there are 10 nodes and 13 edges: 13 − 10 + 2 = 5. The option 4 treats the compound condition as a single decision.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Top-down starts with the main module and uses stubs for what it calls (A-III). Bottom-up starts with leaf modules and uses drivers to call them (B-II). Sandwich (hybrid) works from both ends towards a middle layer (C-IV). Big bang integrates everything at once, which makes faults hard to locate (D-I). Option 2 swaps stubs and drivers, the most common confusion.

b: I. All modules are combined at once and tested together
II. Needs drivers to call the low-level modules under test
III. Needs stubs to stand in for lower-level modules that are not yet integrated
IV. Combines top-down and bottom-up, meeting at a middle layer

quiz.question: A mutation testing tool generates 50 mutants of a program. Analysis shows that 5 of them are equivalent to the original program. The test suite kills 36 mutants. What is the mutation score?
quiz.explanation: Equivalent mutants behave exactly like the original, so no test can kill them; they are removed from the denominator. Mutation score = killed ÷ (total − equivalent) = 36 ÷ (50 − 5) = 36 ÷ 45 = 80%. 72% = 36 ÷ 50 forgets to exclude them.

quiz.question: What is the output of the following C program?
quiz.explanation: (1, 1, 1): no side is ≥ the sum of the other two, and all are equal, so Equilateral. (1, 2, 3): 3 ≥ 1 + 2, a degenerate boundary case, so NotTriangle. (2, 2, 3): valid, two equal sides, Isosceles. (100, 99, 2): 100 < 99 + 2 = 101, so it is a valid (very thin) triangle with all sides different: Scalene. These are typical boundary tests: (1, 2, 3) sits exactly on the triangle-inequality boundary and (100, 99, 2) just inside it. Output verified with gcc.

quiz.question: To estimate how many defects remain in a program, a team deliberately seeds 20 known defects. Testing then finds 16 of the seeded defects and 40 original (non-seeded) defects. Using Mills’ defect-seeding estimate, how many original defects are estimated to remain undetected?
quiz.explanation: The tests found 16 ÷ 20 = 80% of the seeded defects. Assuming they find the same fraction of original defects, the estimated total of original defects = 40 × 20 ÷ 16 = 50. Remaining = 50 − 40 = 10. 50 is the estimated total, not what remains; 4 is the number of seeded defects still hidden.

lessons.title: Arrays, stacks, queues and linked lists
lessons.summaryHtml: This lesson covers the four linear data structures that every other algorithm is built on. An array stores elements in consecutive memory, so the address of any element comes from one formula (row-major or column-major). A stack is last-in-first-out and drives expression conversion (infix to postfix/prefix), expression evaluation and recursion. A queue is first-in-first-out; the circular queue, the deque and the priority queue are its exam favourites. A linked list trades random access for cheap insertion and deletion, and NTA tests it through pointer-update order and C output questions. Master the address formulas and the conversion trace table: they are pure marks.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A data structure is a way of laying data out in memory so that the operations you need are cheap. The four structures in this lesson are all linear: their elements have a first, a next and a last. An array is a row of equal-sized boxes in consecutive memory, so the computer can jump straight to box i with arithmetic. A stack is a pile of plates: you add and remove only at the top (LIFO). A queue is a ticket counter line: you join at the rear and leave from the front (FIFO). A linked list is a chain of separate nodes, each holding a pointer to the next one; you can splice nodes in and out cheaply, but you must walk the chain to reach the k-th node.

Almost every numerical question in this topic reduces to one of three skills: counting how many elements come before a target (address calculation), running a stack by hand (expression conversion and evaluation), and tracking two indices or a few pointers correctly (queues and lists).

Why it matters for NET

Unit 7 is one of the heaviest units of Paper 2, and this lesson is its most mechanical part. A typical paper has at least one or two questions from here, and they are among the fastest marks available. The sub-topics that dominate are: row-major and column-major address calculation (often with non-zero lower bounds), infix-to-postfix or prefix conversion, postfix evaluation, stack-permutation questions, circular queue full/empty conditions and element counts, and linked-list pointer manipulation shown as C code. Recursion appears as C output questions. Because there is no negative marking, a careful trace is always worth the ninety seconds it costs.

Concepts in depth: arrays and address calculation

An array occupies one contiguous block. If the first element is at address B (the base) and every element takes w bytes, the element with k elements before it lives at B + k × w. Every address formula is this single idea; only the way you count k changes.

One dimension. For A[L..U], the number of elements is U − L + 1, and A[i] has i − L elements before it: address = B + (i − L) × w.

Two dimensions. Let A[L1..U1][L2..U2] have R = U1 − L1 + 1 rows and C = U2 − L2 + 1 columns.

  • Row-major (C, C++, Java, Python lists of lists): all of row L1, then all of row L1+1, and so on. Before A[i][j] there are (i − L1) complete rows of C elements, plus (j − L2) elements of row i. Address = B + [(i − L1) × C + (j − L2)] × w.
  • Column-major (Fortran, MATLAB): whole columns one after another. Address = B + [(j − L2) × R + (i − L1)] × w.

Notice the pattern: in row-major you multiply the row offset by the number of columns; in column-major you multiply the column offset by the number of rows. Mixing these up is the single most common error.

Three or more dimensions. For A[L1..U1][L2..U2][L3..U3] with sizes D1, D2, D3, row-major means the last index changes fastest: k = (i − L1)·D2·D3 + (j − L2)·D3 + (l − L3). Column-major means the first index changes fastest: k = (l − L3)·D1·D2 + (j − L2)·D1 + (i − L1). The general row-major rule is Horner-like: k = ((i1′·D2 + i2′)·D3 + i3′)·D4 + …, where i′ are the zero-based offsets.

Back-solving. NTA sometimes gives two addresses and asks for the base, the width or a dimension. Subtract the two addresses: the difference divided by w is the difference in their k values, which gives an equation in the unknown dimension.

Concepts in depth: special and sparse matrices

Storing zeros wastes space, so matrices with a known zero pattern are packed into a 1-D array.

  • Lower triangular (A[i][j] = 0 when j > i), n × n, 1-based. Non-zero count = n(n+1)/2. Row-major: rows 1..i−1 contain 1 + 2 + … + (i−1) = i(i−1)/2 entries, so A[i][j] sits at 0-based index i(i−1)/2 + (j − 1). Column-major: column c holds n − c + 1 entries, so the index is (j−1)·n − (j−1)(j−2)/2 + (i − j).
  • Upper triangular (zero when j < i). Row-major index = (i−1)·n − (i−1)(i−2)/2 + (j − i); column-major index = j(j−1)/2 + (i − 1). Each is the mirror of a lower-triangular formula.
  • Symmetric matrices need only one triangle; A[i][j] with i < j is read from A[j][i].
  • Tridiagonal (non-zero only when |i − j| ≤ 1): 3n − 2 entries. Row 1 has 2 entries and every later row (except the last) has 3, so the row-major index is 2i + j − 3 (1-based i, j; 0-based result).

A sparse matrix has few non-zeros. The triplet (coordinate) form stores one row per non-zero as (row, column, value), plus a header row (number of rows, columns, non-zeros). With t non-zeros it takes 3(t + 1) words, so it saves space over an m × n array only when 3(t + 1) < mn. The fast transpose of a triplet matrix counts the entries per column first and runs in O(columns + t). Linked representations (orthogonal lists) are used when the matrix changes often.

Concepts in depth: stacks

A stack supports push, pop and peek (top), each O(1). In an array implementation, top starts at −1; push does top = top + 1 then stores; pop reads then decrements. Overflow is a push when top = n − 1; underflow is a pop when top = −1. A linked-list stack pushes and pops at the head and overflows only when memory runs out.

Applications: function calls and recursion (each call pushes an activation record), expression conversion and evaluation, bracket matching, undo/redo, backtracking and depth-first search, and converting recursion to iteration.

Notations. Infix puts the operator between operands (A + B) and needs precedence, associativity and brackets. Postfix (Reverse Polish) puts it after (A B +); prefix (Polish) before (+ A B). Neither postfix nor prefix needs brackets or precedence: the position of each operator already fixes the order of evaluation. The order of the operands never changes across the three notations; only the operators move.

Infix to postfix (the operator-stack method). Scan left to right.

  1. Operand: write it to the output.
  2. "(": push it.
  3. ")": pop and output until "(" is on top; discard the "(".
  4. Operator op: while the top is an operator with higher precedence, or with equal precedence and op is left-associative, pop it to the output. Then push op. For a right-associative operator such as ^, an equal-precedence top is not popped.
  5. At the end, pop everything left.

The standard precedence is ^ (highest, right-associative), then * / % (left), then + − (left). The maximum depth the operator stack reaches is itself a frequently asked number.

Infix to prefix. The safest method in an exam is to fully bracket the expression and move each operator to the front of its bracket. The mechanical method is: reverse the infix string, swap "(" and ")", convert to postfix (with the associativity rule mirrored), and reverse the result. Building the expression tree and reading it in preorder gives the same answer and avoids associativity slips.

Evaluating postfix. Scan left to right with an operand stack. On an operand, push it. On an operator, pop the right operand first, then the left, compute left op right, and push the result. At the end one value remains. Evaluating prefix is the mirror: scan right to left, and the first value popped is the left operand.

Stack permutations. If 1, 2, …, n are pushed in order and pops may happen at any time, the number of distinct output sequences is the Catalan number Cn = (2n)! / ((n+1)! n!): 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132 for n = 1..6. A sequence is impossible exactly when it contains the "3-1-2" pattern: some x, later a smaller y, and later still a z with y < z < x (for example 4 … 2 … 3). Put simply, once a larger number has been popped, the smaller numbers still inside must come out in decreasing order.

Concepts in depth: recursion

A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input and stops at a base case. Each active call has its own activation record on the run-time stack, holding its parameters, local variables and return address. So recursion depth d costs O(d) stack space even if each call does O(1) work. Tail recursion (the recursive call is the very last action) can be turned into a loop by a compiler, but the C standard does not require it. Standard counts worth remembering: the Tower of Hanoi with n discs needs 2n − 1 moves, and a naive recursive Fibonacci makes 2F(n+1) − 1 calls when the base case is n ≤ 1.

Concepts in depth: queues, deques and priority queues

A queue inserts at the rear and deletes from the front. A plain array queue wastes the space freed at the front, so real implementations use a circular queue, where indices wrap with mod n. Two conventions appear in textbooks, and NTA states which one it means:

  • One empty slot: front points one position before the first element and rear points at the last. Empty: front == rear. Full: (rear + 1) mod n == front. Capacity n − 1.
  • Count variable: front points at the first element and a separate count tracks the size, so all n slots can be used.

In the one-empty-slot form, the number of elements is (rear − front + n) mod n. Enqueue: rear = (rear + 1) mod n, then store. Dequeue: front = (front + 1) mod n, then read.

A deque allows insertion and deletion at both ends. An input-restricted deque inserts at one end only but deletes at both; an output-restricted deque inserts at both ends but deletes at one. With input 1, 2, 3, 4, each restricted deque can produce 22 of the 24 permutations: 4213 and 4231 are impossible for the input-restricted one, and 4132 and 4231 for the output-restricted one.

A priority queue removes the highest-priority element regardless of arrival. Unsorted array or list: insert O(1), delete-min O(n). Sorted array or list: insert O(n), delete-min O(1). Binary heap: both O(log n), which is why heaps (next lesson) are the standard choice.

Queue from two stacks. Enqueue pushes on S1. Dequeue pops S2; if S2 is empty, first pour all of S1 into S2. Every element is pushed and popped at most twice, so the amortised cost is O(1) even though one dequeue can cost O(n). A stack from two queues is also possible, but one of its operations costs O(n).

Concepts in depth: linked lists

A node holds data and a pointer. In a singly linked list you can only move forward; a doubly linked list adds a prev pointer; a circular list links the last node back to the first. Keeping a pointer to the last node of a circular singly list gives O(1) insertion at both the front and the end, because last->next is the front.

OperationArraySingly linkedDoubly linked
Access k-th elementO(1)O(k)O(k)
Insert at frontO(n) (shift)O(1)O(1)
Insert after a given nodeO(n)O(1)O(1)
Delete a given node (pointer to it only)O(n)O(n) in generalO(1)
Delete last node (with tail pointer)O(1)O(n)O(1)
Binary search on sorted dataO(log n)O(n)O(n)

Three pointer techniques cover most C questions. Reversal walks the list with prev, cur and next pointers, flipping each cur->next to prev: O(n) time, O(1) space. Slow and fast pointers find the middle (slow moves one step, fast two; for an even length the loop "while (fast && fast->next)" stops at the second middle) and detect a cycle (Floyd’s method: they meet inside the cycle). A pointer to a pointer (struct node **pp) deletes nodes without special-casing the head.

For insertion after P in a doubly linked list, four pointers change, and P->next must be read before it is overwritten. Deleting a middle node X changes two: X->prev->next and X->next->prev.

Worked examples

Example 1: 2-D address with negative lower bounds. A[−3..6][4..12] holds 4-byte integers from base 1200. Find the address of A[2][7] in row-major and in column-major order.

Rows R = 6 − (−3) + 1 = 10. Columns C = 12 − 4 + 1 = 9. Row offset = 2 − (−3) = 5; column offset = 7 − 4 = 3.

Row-major: k = 5 × 9 + 3 = 48, so the address is 1200 + 48 × 4 = 1392.

Column-major: k = 3 × 10 + 5 = 35, so the address is 1200 + 35 × 4 = 1340.

Example 2: 3-D address. A[1..4][1..5][1..6] of 2-byte elements, base 500. Find A[3][2][5].

Offsets: 2, 1, 4. Sizes: 4, 5, 6.

Row-major (last index fastest): k = 2 × (5 × 6) + 1 × 6 + 4 = 60 + 6 + 4 = 70, address = 500 + 140 = 640.

Column-major (first index fastest): k = 4 × (4 × 5) + 1 × 4 + 2 = 80 + 4 + 2 = 86, address = 500 + 172 = 672.

Example 3: lower-triangular packing. A 100 × 100 lower-triangular matrix of 4-byte values is packed from address 3000. Find A[20][15] in row-major and column-major packing.

Row-major: rows 1..19 hold 19 × 20 / 2 = 190 entries, and 14 entries of row 20 precede column 15: k = 204. Address = 3000 + 204 × 4 = 3816.

Column-major: columns 1..14 hold 100 + 99 + … + 87 = 14 × 100 − 14 × 13 / 2 = 1400 − 91 = 1309 entries. Column 15 starts at row 15, so 5 entries precede row 20: k = 1314. Address = 3000 + 1314 × 4 = 8256.
