Example 6: circular queue trace. An array of N = 5 slots uses the one-empty-slot convention with front = rear = 0 at the start. Enqueue 1..6 (a failed enqueue is ignored), then dequeue twice, then enqueue 7 and 8.

  • Enqueue 1, 2, 3, 4 go to slots 1, 2, 3, 4 (rear = 4). Enqueue 5 fails because (4 + 1) mod 5 = 0 = front; so does 6. Four succeed.
  • Two dequeues return 1 and 2; front = 2.
  • Enqueue 7: rear = 0. Enqueue 8: (0 + 1) mod 5 = 1 ≠ 2, so rear = 1.
  • Final front = 2, rear = 1, count = (1 − 2 + 5) mod 5 = 4 (elements 3, 4, 7, 8). The queue is full again.

Example 7: is 4 2 3 1 5 a stack permutation of 1..5? To output 4 first, push 1, 2, 3, 4 and pop 4. The stack now holds 1 2 3 with 3 on top. The next output must be 3 or a new push; 2 is buried under 3. So the sequence is impossible. By contrast, 3 2 5 4 1 works: push 1–3, pop 3, 2; push 4, 5, pop 5, 4, 1.

NTA traps

  • Swapping R and C. Wrong: "column-major, so multiply by the number of columns". Fix: in column-major you skip whole columns, and each column has R elements, so multiply by R.
  • Ignoring lower bounds. Wrong: using i and j directly for A[−3..6]. Fix: always subtract the lower bound first; with L = −3, the offset of index 2 is 5.
  • Forgetting the element size. The option that is exactly B + k (not B + k·w) is always there. Multiply by w last.
  • ^ associativity. Wrong: A^B^C → AB^C^. Fix: ^ is right-associative, so A^B^C = A^(B^C) → ABC^^. When ^ meets ^ on the stack, push; do not pop.
  • Operand order in evaluation. Wrong: popping x then y and computing x − y. Fix: in postfix the first value popped is the right operand; compute y − x. In prefix the first popped is the left operand.
  • Circular queue conventions. An array of 8 slots does not always hold 8 items. Read whether the question uses a count variable or the one-empty-slot rule.
  • "Tail pointer makes delete-last O(1)". Only in a doubly linked list. In a singly list you still need the predecessor.
  • Binary search on a linked list. It is not O(log n): finding the middle element costs O(n), so the whole search is O(n).
  • Pointer order. Overwriting P->next before using it breaks the list; always attach the new node first, then relink the old ones.

How NTA asks this

  • Numerical: address of an element with given bounds, base and size; index in a packed triangular or tridiagonal matrix; value of a postfix or prefix expression; count of elements in a circular queue; Catalan counts.
  • Direct MCQ: the postfix or prefix form of an infix expression. Eliminate fast: operand order never changes, so reject any option that reorders letters; then check the position of the operator you are least sure about (usually ^).
  • Code output: a stack, queue or linked-list routine in C. Draw the boxes and arrows, and update them line by line.
  • Match the following: structures with applications, or operations with complexities.
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: circular queue capacity, O(1) claims about list operations, recursion stack space.

Mini A–R. (A) Binary search is not efficient on a singly linked list. (R) A singly linked list can be traversed in only one direction.

Both are true, but the real reason is the lack of random access: reaching the middle costs O(n) even in a doubly linked list, which can move both ways. So the answer is "Both true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A". Test every A–R by asking: "If R were false, would A still hold?" If yes, R is not the explanation.

Remember: in a stack-permutation "which is possible" question, simulate from the left. The moment the required number is buried under a larger one still on the stack, the sequence is impossible.

terms.definition: Elements of a row are stored next to each other; the last index changes fastest. C uses it.
Elements of a column are stored next to each other; the first index changes fastest. Fortran uses it.
Operator written after its operands, e.g. AB+; needs no brackets and no precedence rules to evaluate.
An output order obtainable by pushing 1..n in order and popping at any time; there are Catalan(n) of them.
Array queue whose indices wrap with mod n; the one-empty-slot version holds at most n−1 items.
Double-ended queue: insert and delete at both ends. Input-restricted allows insertion at one end only; output-restricted allows deletion at one end only.
A matrix with mostly zero entries, stored as (row, column, value) triplets to save space.
The stack frame for one function call: parameters, locals, return address and saved registers.
Each node has prev and next pointers, so a known node can be deleted in O(1).

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 11 minutes. For 4–6 write a full trace table (symbol, stack, output or value).

For every address problem, redo it by writing "elements before the target" first, then multiplying by the size.
Compile problems 12 and 13 with gcc and compare the real output with your prediction.
Redo the wrong ones after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.

quiz.question: An array A[−2..7][3..10] of 2-byte integers is stored in column-major order starting at address 5000. What is the address of A[4][6]?
quiz.explanation: Rows = 7−(−2)+1 = 10, columns = 10−3+1 = 8. Column-major: elements before A[4][6] = (6−3)×10 + (4−(−2)) = 30+6 = 36. Address = 5000 + 36×2 = 5072. 5102 is the row-major answer ((4+2)×8 + 3 = 51, 5000+102). 5070 is one element short; 5036 forgets to multiply by the element size.

quiz.question: What is the output of this C program?
quiz.explanation: Stack after pushes: 4 7 2. a = 2, push 6 → 4 7 6. b = 6, c = 7, push 6−7 = −1 → 4 −1. r = −1 and the stack is left with only 4, so top = 0. Output: -1 0. "1 0" reverses b−c; "-1 1" forgets that r was popped.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Bracket matching is the classic stack use (A-II). BFS explores level by level, which is FIFO (B-III). Dijkstra repeatedly extracts the minimum-distance vertex (C-I). Removing a known node in O(1) needs its predecessor, which a doubly linked list gives through prev (D-IV).

b: I. Picking the nearest unvisited vertex in Dijkstra’s algorithm
II. Checking that brackets in an expression are balanced
III. Holding the frontier in breadth-first search
IV. LRU cache list where any node, given a pointer to it, is removed in O(1)

options: A, C, D and E only
quiz.explanation: Simulate: A pushes 1,2,3, pops 3,2, pushes 4,5, pops 5,4,1: possible. B: after popping 4 the stack holds 1 2 3 with 3 on top, so 2 cannot come next: impossible. C: pop 1; push 2,3 pop 3; push 4,5 pop 5,4,2: possible. D: after 5 is popped, the top is 4, then 3 must precede 1: impossible. E: push 1,2 pop 2; push 3 pop 3,1; push 4,5 pop 5,4: possible. lessons.title: Trees and heaps
lessons.summaryHtml: Trees organise data in levels, so a search can discard a whole subtree at each step. This lesson covers binary-tree counting facts (n0 = n2 + 1, node and height bounds), the four traversals and how to rebuild a tree from two of them, binary search trees (insert, delete, search in O(h)), and the balanced trees that keep h = O(log n): AVL trees with their four rotations, red–black trees, and the multiway B-trees and B+ trees used by databases. It ends with binary heaps (build-heap in O(n), insert and delete in O(log n)), tries, and the Catalan numbers that count binary trees and BSTs. NET asks for traces here: a final preorder after AVL inserts, a B-tree after splits, a heap array after build-heap. Compute them step by step.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A tree is a hierarchy: one root, and every other node has exactly one parent. In a binary tree each node has at most two children, called left and right. Trees matter because they let you throw away large parts of the data at each step: in a balanced search tree of a million keys, a search looks at only about twenty nodes. A heap is a different kind of tree that does not keep everything sorted; it only guarantees that the largest (or smallest) item is on top, which is exactly what a priority queue needs.

Most NET questions in this lesson are traces. You are given a sequence of insertions and asked for the final shape, a traversal, a height, or an array. The winning habit is to draw the tree after every single operation, never several at once.

Why it matters for NET

Trees are one of the most frequently tested topics in Unit 7, and they also reappear in Unit 4 (B and B+ tree indexes) and Unit 8 (parse and expression trees). Expect questions on counting properties (leaves versus internal nodes, maximum and minimum height), traversal reconstruction, BST insertion and deletion, AVL rotations, B-tree splits, heap construction, and Catalan counts. Statement-type questions often test the exact definitions: complete versus full, the height convention, and what a B-tree of order m allows.

Concepts in depth: binary tree facts

Terms. The depth of a node is the number of edges from the root; the height of a tree is the largest depth. This lesson uses the edge convention (a single node has height 0). Some books count levels (a single node has height 1); every formula then shifts by one, so always check.

  • Level i holds at most 2i nodes. A tree of height h has at most 2h+1 − 1 nodes and at least h + 1.
  • With n nodes, the height is at least ⌈log2(n+1)⌉ − 1 and at most n − 1 (a chain, also called a skewed tree).
  • n0 = n2 + 1. Proof: count edges two ways. Every node except the root has one parent edge, so edges = n − 1. Every node sends out edges to its children, so edges = n1 + 2n2. With n = n0 + n1 + n2, equating gives n0 = n2 + 1.
  • A binary tree with n nodes has 2n pointer fields of which n − 1 are used, so it has n + 1 NULL links. Threaded binary trees reuse these NULLs as pointers to inorder predecessors and successors.
  • A full (strictly binary) tree has every node with 0 or 2 children, so n = 2n0 − 1. A perfect tree has all leaves at the same level. A complete tree fills every level except possibly the last, which is filled from the left. Some Indian texts use "full" to mean perfect; read the definition given in the question.
  • A complete binary tree with n nodes has height ⌊log2 n⌋ and ⌈n/2⌉ leaves.
  • For a full k-ary tree with i internal nodes: n = ki + 1 and leaves = (k − 1)i + 1.

Concepts in depth: traversals and reconstruction

The depth-first traversals differ only in when the root is visited: preorder (root, left, right), inorder (left, root, right) and postorder (left, right, root). Level order visits level by level using a queue. All four take O(n) time; the recursive ones use O(h) stack space.

Reconstruction. Preorder (or postorder, or level order) tells you which node is the root; inorder tells you which nodes lie to its left and right. So preorder + inorder, postorder + inorder, and level order + inorder each fix a unique tree when keys are distinct. Preorder + postorder does not in general: a node with one child could have it on either side. It is unique only for full binary trees. For a BST, preorder alone is enough, because sorting the keys gives the inorder.

Expression trees. Operators are internal nodes and operands are leaves. Preorder gives prefix, postorder gives postfix, and inorder gives infix (with brackets needed to restore precedence).

Concepts in depth: binary search trees

A BST keeps smaller keys in the left subtree and larger keys in the right subtree of every node, so an inorder traversal prints the keys in sorted order. Search, insert and delete each follow one root-to-leaf path: O(h) time, which is O(log n) when the tree is balanced and O(n) when it degenerates into a chain (for example, inserting keys in sorted order).

Insertion always adds a new leaf. Deletion has three cases: a leaf is simply removed; a node with one child is replaced by that child; a node with two children takes the key of its inorder successor (the smallest key in its right subtree) or of its inorder predecessor (the largest in its left subtree), and that successor or predecessor node, which has at most one child, is then deleted. The successor is the usual convention, but NTA sometimes names the predecessor, and the two give different trees.

Concepts in depth: AVL trees

An AVL tree is a BST in which every node has balance factor (height of left subtree − height of right subtree) in {−1, 0, +1}. After an ordinary BST insertion, walk back up toward the root. At the first node Z whose balance becomes ±2, look at the first two steps from Z toward the new key:

CaseNew key went intoFix
LLleft subtree of Z’s left childsingle right rotation at Z
RRright subtree of Z’s right childsingle left rotation at Z
LRright subtree of Z’s left childleft rotation at the child, then right rotation at Z
RLleft subtree of Z’s right childright rotation at the child, then left rotation at Z

After an insertion, one single or double rotation restores balance everywhere, because the rotated subtree gets back its old height. A deletion may need a rotation at every level, so O(log n) rotations.

Height bound. Let N(h) be the fewest nodes an AVL tree of height h can have. The sparsest tree has one subtree of height h − 1 and one of height h − 2, so N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1 with N(0) = 1 and N(1) = 2: 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, 54, 88. This grows like the Fibonacci numbers, so the height is at most about 1.44 log2 n. To find the maximum height possible with n nodes, take the largest h with N(h) ≤ n.

Concepts in depth: red–black trees

A red–black tree is a BST whose nodes are coloured red or black so that: (1) the root is black; (2) the NULL leaves are black; (3) a red node has only black children; (4) every path from a node down to a NULL leaf has the same number of black nodes (its black-height). These rules force the longest path to be at most twice the shortest, so the height is at most 2 log2(n + 1). Insertion needs at most 2 rotations plus recolouring; deletion needs at most 3 rotations. That is why red–black trees are preferred when updates are frequent (C++ std::map, Java TreeMap), while AVL trees, being more strictly balanced, give slightly faster lookups. Every AVL tree can be coloured as a red–black tree, but not every red–black tree is an AVL tree.

Concepts in depth: B-trees and B+ trees

Disk reads are slow, so database indexes use short, wide trees whose nodes fill a disk block. A B-tree of order m satisfies: every node has at most m children and m − 1 keys; every internal node except the root has at least ⌈m/2⌉ children (so at least ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 keys); the root has at least 2 children unless it is a leaf; all leaves are at the same level; keys inside a node are sorted and separate the key ranges of its children.

Insertion goes into the correct leaf. If the leaf now has m keys, it splits: the median key moves up into the parent, and the keys on either side form two nodes. A split can cascade up; if the root splits, a new root is created and the height grows by one. This is why a B-tree grows at the top and all leaves stay on one level. With an odd m the median is unique. With an even m, a question must say whether the left or right middle key goes up. (Cormen’s version, defined by a minimum degree t, splits full nodes on the way down, which can give a different tree; use the convention the question states.)

Height bounds (t = ⌈m/2⌉, height h counted in edges): the fewest keys a B-tree of height h can hold is 2th − 1, and the most is mh+1 − 1. So h ≤ logt((n + 1)/2).

A B+ tree keeps every record pointer in the leaves, and the leaves are chained left to right, so range queries scan the leaf level. Internal nodes hold only separator keys (copies of leaf keys), so more keys fit per block and the tree is usually shallower. The order of a B+ tree node follows from the block size: an internal node with p pointers needs p·P + (p − 1)·K ≤ block size, and a leaf with q keys needs q·(K + Precord) + P ≤ block size (the extra P is the next-leaf pointer).

Concepts in depth: binary heaps

A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array. With 1-based indexing, the children of i are 2i and 2i + 1 and its parent is ⌊i/2⌋. With 0-based indexing, the children are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 and the parent is ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋. In a max-heap every parent is at least as large as its children, so the maximum is at the root. A sorted (descending) array is always a max-heap, but a heap is not sorted.

  • Insert: place the key in the next free slot and sift it up while it beats its parent. O(log n).
  • Delete-max: remove the root, move the last element to the root, and sift it down, swapping with the larger child. O(log n).
  • Build-heap (Floyd): call sift-down on nodes ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1. It is O(n), because a node at height h costs at most h swaps and there are at most ⌈n/2h+1⌉ such nodes. Building by n repeated insertions costs O(n log n) in the worst case and usually gives a different array.
  • In a max-heap the minimum is in a leaf (positions ⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n), so finding it takes O(n). The second largest is one of the root’s children.
  • The number of distinct max-heaps on n distinct keys follows H(n) = C(n − 1, L)·H(L)·H(n − 1 − L), where L is the size of the left subtree of the complete tree: 1, 1, 2, 3, 8, 20, 80 for n = 1..7.

Concepts in depth: tries and counting trees

A trie stores strings character by character; each node represents a prefix, and a flag marks where a word ends. Search and insertion cost O(L) for a word of length L, independent of how many words are stored. The number of nodes equals the number of distinct prefixes plus one for the root.

Counting. The number of binary tree shapes with n nodes, the number of BSTs on n distinct keys, and the number of binary trees with a given preorder are all the Catalan number Cn = (2n)!/((n+1)!·n!) = 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, 429. It satisfies Cn = Σ Ci·Cn−1−i: choose the root, then shapes for the left and right subtrees. With n labelled nodes (any arrangement allowed), the count is n!·Cn; for n = 3 that is 30.

Worked examples

Example 1: all four traversals.

        A
      /   \
     B     C
    / \   /
   D   E F
    \   / \
     G H   I

Preorder: A B D G E C F H I. Inorder: D G B E A H F I C. Postorder: G D E B H I F C A. Level order: A B C D E F G H I. Height 3, 4 leaves (G, E, H, I), 3 nodes with two children (A, B, F): n0 = n2 + 1 holds.

Example 2: rebuild from preorder and inorder. Preorder M K D B F L R Q T S, inorder B D F K L M Q R S T.

  1. Root M. Inorder left of M: B D F K L; right: Q R S T.
  2. Left part, preorder K D B F L: root K; inorder left B D F, right L.
  3. B D F with preorder D B F: root D with children B and F.
  4. Right part, preorder R Q T S: root R; left Q; right S T with preorder T S, so T has left child S.

Postorder: B F D L K Q S T R M. Level order: M K R D L Q T B F S.

Example 3: BST insertion and deletion. Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, 35, 45, 65.

            50
          /    \
        30      70
       /  \    /  \
     20   40  60   80
         /  \   \
        35  45   65

Preorder 50 30 20 40 35 45 70 60 65 80; postorder 20 35 45 40 30 65 60 80 70 50; height 3; 5 leaves. Delete 50 using the inorder successor: the smallest key in the right subtree is 60; copy 60 into the root and delete the old 60 (it has only the right child 65, which moves up). New preorder: 60 30 20 40 35 45 70 65 80. With the predecessor (45) instead, the preorder is 45 30 20 40 35 70 60 65 80.

Build-heap result 15 12 8 10 1 3 4 5 after 5 swaps. Inserting the keys one by one into an empty heap gives 15 12 10 5 1 3 8 4 after 6 swaps: a different, equally valid heap. A delete-max on the build-heap result moves 5 to the root and sifts it down: 12 10 8 5 1 3 4.

Forests and their binary-tree representation

A forest is an ordered collection of zero or more disjoint trees. Deleting the root of a tree leaves a forest of its subtrees, and adding one new root above a forest gives a tree. A forest with n nodes and k trees has exactly n − k edges, because every node except the k roots has one parent edge.

General trees and forests are stored as binary trees with the left-child right-sibling (first-child, next-sibling) rule. Each node keeps two pointers: left points to its first child and right points to its next sibling. The roots of the trees of a forest are treated as siblings. Formally, for a forest F = (T₁, T₂, …, Tₖ), the binary tree B(F) is empty if k = 0; otherwise its root is the root of T₁, its left subtree is B(subtrees of T₁’s root) and its right subtree is B(T₂, …, Tₖ). A single general tree therefore always becomes a binary tree whose root has an empty right subtree.

Counting links: in the binary form, a node has an empty left pointer exactly when it is a leaf of the forest, and an empty right pointer exactly when it is the last child of its parent or the last root. So empty left pointers = number of leaves, and empty right pointers = number of internal nodes + 1. The two add up to n + 1, as for any binary tree.

Traversals carry over as follows:

Forest traversalDefinitionEquals, in B(F)
Preorderroot of T₁, preorder of T₁’s subtrees, then preorder of T₂ … Tₖpreorder
Children-before-root order (Knuth: postorder; Horowitz–Sahni: forest inorder)T₁’s subtrees, then root of T₁, then T₂ … Tₖinorder
Horowitz–Sahni forest postorderT₁’s subtrees, then T₂ … Tₖ, then root of T₁postorder (no natural meaning in the forest)

Example 7: converting a forest. T₁: A with children B, C, D, where C has children E, F. T₂: G with child H. T₃: I with children J, K. That is 11 nodes, 3 trees and 11 − 3 = 8 edges.

A.left = B   B.right = C   C.left = E   E.right = F   C.right = D
A.right = G  G.left = H    G.right = I  I.left = J    J.right = K

Binary preorder: A B C E F D G H I J K, the forest preorder. Binary inorder: B E F C D A H G J K I, which lists every node after all its children, tree by tree. Binary postorder: F E D C B H K J I G A. Empty left pointers: 7 (the leaves B, E, F, D, H, J, K). Empty right pointers: 5 (internal A, C, G, I, plus 1). Total 12 = n + 1.

NTA trap: the forest order that lists children before the parent is called “postorder” by Knuth but “inorder” by Horowitz–Sahni. Either way it equals the inorder of the binary representation, not its postorder.

Threaded binary trees

A binary tree with n nodes has n + 1 NULL links. A threaded binary tree (Perlis and Thornton) puts them to work. In an inorder-threaded tree, an empty left link is replaced by a pointer to the node’s inorder predecessor and an empty right link by a pointer to its inorder successor. These extra pointers are the threads. Each node gets two tag bits (LTHREAD, RTHREAD) so that a thread can be told apart from a real child pointer. A one-way (right) threaded tree keeps only the successor threads; a two-way (fully) threaded tree keeps both.

Two threads have nowhere to point: the left thread of the first node in inorder and the right thread of the last. Horowitz–Sahni add a header node whose left child is the real root, and those two threads point to the header. The number of threads is still n + 1.

Inorder successor without a stack. If RTHREAD(x) is set, the successor is x.right. Otherwise, go to x.right and then follow left child links as far as possible. An inorder traversal starts at the leftmost node and applies this rule repeatedly: O(n) time, O(1) extra space, with no recursion and no stack. Predecessors work symmetrically. Inserting a node r as the right child of s: r takes over s’s right link and its tag, r’s left thread points to s, and s.right becomes a real child pointer to r. If r now has a real right subtree, the leftmost node of that subtree gets its left thread changed to r.

Example 8: threads of a small BST. Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 80, 75. Inorder: 20 30 40 50 70 75 80. The 7 nodes have 8 NULL links, which become threads:

NodeLeft thread → predecessorRight thread → successor
20header30
403050
7050(real child 80)
757080
80(real child 75)header

Successor of 70: its right link is real, so go to 80 and then left as far as possible, reaching 75. Successor of 75: its right link is a thread, so it is 80 directly.

B* trees

A B-tree guarantees only that non-root nodes are at least half full. Knuth’s B*-tree raises this to two-thirds full, which gives better storage use and a slightly shorter tree for the same keys. Two changes to insertion achieve it:

  1. Redistribution first. When a node overflows, it passes keys to an adjacent sibling that has room, rotating them through the separating key in the parent (the separator changes). No new node is created.
  2. 2-to-3 split. Only when that sibling is also full are the two nodes split into three. With order m, the two full nodes hold 2(m − 1) keys; add the new key and the parent separator to get 2m keys. Two of them go up as separators and the other 2m − 2 are shared among three nodes, so each holds about (2m − 2)/3 keys, two-thirds of the maximum m − 1. The parent gains one key net (two separators replace one).

Deletion is the mirror image: redistribute with siblings where possible and merge three nodes into two when they fall below two-thirds. The cost is more complex code and extra sibling reads during insertion; the benefit is fewer splits, better space use and fewer levels. The root is exempt from the two-thirds rule.

Example 9: B*-tree insertion, order 4 (at most 3 keys). Leaves [10 20 30] and [50 60] with separator 40 in the parent.

  • Insert 25: the left leaf would hold 10 20 25 30. The right sibling has room, so redistribute the 7 keys 10 20 25 30 | 40 | 50 60: left [10 20 25], new separator 30, right [40 50 60]. No split.
  • Insert 35: it goes right, giving 35 40 50 60. Its sibling [10 20 25] is full, so do a 2-to-3 split of the 2m = 8 keys 10 20 25 30 35 40 50 60: nodes [10 20], [30 35], [50 60] with separators 25 and 40 going up. Each leaf holds 2 of 3 keys, exactly two-thirds full.

NTA trap: B* is not B+. B+ trees move every record to linked leaves; B* trees keep nodes two-thirds full with redistribution and 2-to-3 splits. A few older texts loosely use “B*-tree” for the B+ tree, but in NET the two-thirds variant is meant.

Data structures for sets: disjoint sets and union–find

Sets are stored in different ways for different operations. A bit vector over a small universe gives O(1) membership and word-parallel union and intersection. Sorted lists or balanced trees support ordered-set operations. The syllabus item that NTA tests most is the disjoint-set (union–find) structure. It keeps a partition of n elements and supports MakeSet(x), Find(x), which returns the representative of x’s set, and Union(x, y), which merges two sets.

  • Quick-find: an array of set ids. Find is O(1), but Union relabels a whole set: O(n).
  • Forest (quick-union): each set is a tree of parent pointers whose root is the representative. Union links one root under the other in O(1) after the two Finds. Find walks to the root, which is O(n) in the worst case when the trees become chains.
  • Weighted union (union by size, or union by rank). The root of the smaller tree becomes a child of the root of the larger. A node’s depth grows only when its tree at least doubles in size, so every tree has height ≤ ⌊log₂ n⌋ and Find is O(log n). Horowitz–Sahni store −(size) in the root’s parent entry, so one array holds both parents and sizes.
  • Collapsing find (path compression). After a Find, every node on the path is pointed straight at the root.
  • Weighted union and path compression together cost O(m α(n)) for m operations, where α is the inverse Ackermann function. α(n) ≤ 4 for every n of practical size, so each operation is effectively constant. Neither rule alone achieves this.

Uses include Kruskal’s MST (an edge is rejected when both ends have the same root), connected components, cycle detection in undirected graphs, equivalence classes and job sequencing with deadlines.

Example 10: weighted union. Elements 1..8, all singletons (parent −1). The union rule: the root of the larger set becomes the parent, and on a tie the first argument’s root wins. Perform U(1,2), U(3,4), U(5,6), U(7,8), U(1,3), U(5,7), U(1,5).

i12345678
parent[i]−81131557

The tree has height 3 = log₂ 8, the worst case for weighted union. Find(8) walks 8 → 7 → 5 → 1. With collapsing find, 8 and 7 are then both pointed directly at 1, so a later Find(8) takes one step.

NTA trap: “union by rank alone gives O(1) Find” is false; it gives O(log n). The near-constant α(n) bound needs both union by rank (or size) and path compression, and it is an amortised bound, not a per-operation worst case.

NTA traps

  • Height convention. Wrong: "height of a single node is 1" when the question counts edges. Fix: check the base case; the N(h) and 2h+1 − 1 formulas above use edges.
  • Wrong rotation node. Wrong: rotating at the root because the root is unbalanced too. Fix: fix the lowest unbalanced ancestor of the new node; after that the ancestors are balanced again.
  • LR versus RL. Name the case from the unbalanced node Z, not from the new key’s parent: first step from Z, then second step.
  • Successor versus predecessor. BST deletion with two children gives different trees; use the one the question names (successor by default).
  • B-tree order. "Order m" in most Indian texts means at most m children (m − 1 keys). Cormen’s minimum degree t means at most 2t children. Convert before computing.
  • Root minimum. The ⌈m/2⌉ minimum does not apply to the root, which may have 2 children.
  • Build-heap is O(n log n). False: bottom-up build-heap is O(n). Repeated insertion is O(n log n).
  • Preorder + postorder. They do not fix a unique tree unless it is full.
  • Catalan confusion. BSTs on n keys = unlabelled shapes = Cn; labelled binary trees = n!·Cn.

How NTA asks this

  • Numerical: nodes from n0 = n2 + 1, minimum AVL nodes of height h, B-tree key bounds, B+ tree order from block size, Catalan counts, number of heaps.
  • Trace MCQ: final preorder after AVL inserts, root keys after B-tree inserts, heap array after build-heap or delete-max, postorder from preorder + inorder. Eliminate options by checking one easy fact first: the root (AVL), the first element (heap is the maximum), or the last postorder element (the root).
  • Code output: recursive functions on trees (leaf count, height, level sums, mixed traversals).
  • Match: structures with invariants, rotation cases with fixes, counts with values.
  • A–R and Statement I/II: build-heap complexity, AVL versus red–black, B-tree minimums, reconstruction uniqueness.

Mini match. A. LL imbalance, B. RR imbalance, C. LR imbalance, D. RL imbalance; I. right rotation at child then left at node, II. single right rotation, III. single left rotation, IV. left rotation at child then right at node. Answer: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I. Trick: a single rotation goes in the direction opposite to the heavy side (LL → right); a double rotation first straightens the zig-zag at the child.

Remember: heap first element = maximum, AVL/BST inorder = sorted keys, postorder last element = root. Use these to strike out options before doing a full trace.

lessons.title: Searching, sorting and hashing
lessons.summaryHtml: This lesson covers the three ways to find or arrange data. Searching: linear search works on anything in O(n); binary search needs a sorted array with random access and takes at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons. Sorting: the comparison sorts (bubble, selection, insertion, merge, quick, heap) cannot beat Ω(n log n) in the worst case, while counting, radix and bucket sort escape that bound by using key values. For each algorithm, know its best/average/worst time, whether it is stable and in-place, and how the array looks after each pass. Hashing maps keys to slots in O(1) expected time; collisions are handled by chaining or by open addressing (linear, quadratic, double hashing), and the load factor α sets the expected number of probes.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Searching asks "is this key here, and where?". Sorting puts keys in order so that later searches, merges and duplicate checks become cheap. Hashing skips order altogether: it computes a slot number straight from the key, so a lookup usually takes a constant number of steps. Each approach has a price. Binary search needs sorted data with random access. Fast sorts either give up stability or need extra memory. Hashing loses order and slows down as the table fills.

NET tests this lesson in two ways: facts (complexities, stability, in-place, clustering) and traces (the array after k passes, the table after a sequence of insertions). Both are fast marks if you have the fact table memorised and trace one step at a time.

Why it matters for NET

Sorting and hashing are among the most regular sources of questions in Unit 7. Typical items: which algorithm is stable or in-place; best and worst cases (especially quick sort and insertion sort); the array after a given number of passes of bubble, selection or insertion sort; the result of one quick-sort partition; radix-sort passes; the number of comparisons in binary search or merging; the final hash table after linear, quadratic or double hashing; and expected probe counts in terms of α. Lower-bound questions (⌈log₂ n!⌉, the 3n/2 min–max trick) appear as quick numericals.

Concepts in depth: searching

Linear search checks elements one by one. Worst case n comparisons; for a key that is present and equally likely to be anywhere, the average is (n + 1)/2. It works on unsorted data and linked lists.

Binary search compares the key with the middle element mid = ⌊(lo + hi)/2⌋ of a sorted array and discards half the range. Its comparisons form a decision tree of height ⌊log₂ n⌋, so the worst case is ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons (counting each equal/less/greater test as one). For n = 2k − 1 the tree is perfect: level i holds 2i keys found with i + 1 comparisons, so for n = 15 the total is 1·1 + 2·2 + 4·3 + 8·4 = 49 and the average successful search takes 49/15 ≈ 3.27 comparisons. Binary search is O(log n) only with random access; on a linked list, reaching the middle costs O(n). In C, writing mid = lo + (hi − lo)/2 avoids integer overflow for very large indices. Interpolation search guesses the position from the key value and averages O(log log n) on uniformly distributed keys, but its worst case is O(n).

Concepts in depth: the simple quadratic sorts

Bubble sort compares adjacent pairs left to right and swaps when they are out of order. After pass i, the i largest keys are in their final places at the end. The number of swaps equals the number of inversions. With an early-exit flag (stop when a pass makes no swap), the best case on sorted input is one pass: n − 1 comparisons, O(n). Worst and average: O(n²). Stable and in-place.

Selection sort finds the minimum of the unsorted part and swaps it into position i. It always makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, even on sorted input, but at most n − 1 swaps, which makes it attractive when writes are expensive. It is in-place but not stable: a long-distance swap can jump over an equal key.

Insertion sort takes the next key and shifts larger keys in the sorted prefix one place right until the key fits. The number of shifts equals the number of inversions. Best case (sorted) O(n) with n − 1 comparisons; worst case (reverse sorted) n(n − 1)/2 comparisons; average about n²/4. Stable, in-place, online (can sort data as it arrives) and very fast on small or nearly sorted arrays, which is why library sorts switch to it for small subarrays. Shell sort runs insertion sort on elements a gap apart and shrinks the gap; its complexity depends on the gap sequence (about O(n1.5) for common ones), and it is not stable.

Pass conventions. A "pass" of bubble sort is one sweep; a pass of selection sort places one element; a pass of insertion sort inserts one element (pass i handles a[i]). NET options often show the array after pass k of one algorithm next to pass k of another, so identify the algorithm by its footprint: bubble grows a sorted suffix of maxima, selection a sorted prefix of minima, and insertion a sorted prefix of the first k + 1 elements (not the smallest ones).

Concepts in depth: merge sort and quick sort

Merge sort splits the array into halves, sorts each recursively and merges them. Merging runs of sizes m and n takes at most m + n − 1 comparisons (at least min(m, n)). The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) gives Θ(n log n) in every case. The worst-case number of comparisons is W(n) = W(⌊n/2⌋) + W(⌈n/2⌉) + n − 1, which gives 17 for n = 8. It needs an O(n) auxiliary array for arrays (not in-place), is stable when ties are taken from the left run, and sorts linked lists with O(1) extra space by relinking nodes. The bottom-up version merges runs of size 1, then 2, then 4, and so on; each "pass" doubles the run length.

Quick sort partitions around a pivot, which lands in its final position, and recurses on the two sides. Two partition schemes are common:

  • Lomuto: pivot = last element; one index i marks the end of the "≤ pivot" zone; scan j from left to right, swapping small keys into the zone; finally swap the pivot into position i + 1. Uses n − 1 comparisons per partition.
  • Hoare-style (pivot = first element): i moves right past smaller keys, j moves left past larger keys, out-of-place pairs are swapped, and when the indices cross, the pivot is swapped with a[j].

The two schemes give different intermediate arrays, so a trace question must state its scheme. Best and average case Θ(n log n) (about 1.39 n log₂ n comparisons on average); worst case Θ(n²), reached when every pivot is the smallest or largest key, for example on sorted input with a first- or last-element pivot. Randomised pivots or median-of-three make the worst case unlikely but not impossible. Quick sort is in-place (O(log n) stack if the smaller side is recursed first) and not stable. It is usually the fastest comparison sort in practice because of its tight inner loop and good cache behaviour.

Concepts in depth: heap sort and the lower bound

Heap sort builds a max-heap in O(n) (previous lesson), then repeatedly swaps the root with the last element of the heap, shrinks the heap by one and sifts down: O(n log n) in every case, in-place, not stable.

Lower bound. A comparison sort is a binary decision tree whose leaves are the n! possible orders. A binary tree with n! leaves has height at least ⌈log₂ n!⌉, and log₂ n! = Θ(n log n) by Stirling’s formula. So every comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case; merge sort and heap sort are asymptotically optimal. Concrete values: ⌈log₂ 5!⌉ = ⌈log₂ 120⌉ = 7 and ⌈log₂ 10!⌉ = 22. Related selection results: finding the maximum needs n − 1 comparisons; finding both the minimum and maximum needs only ⌈3n/2⌉ − 2 (compare elements in pairs first); finding the second largest needs n + ⌈log₂ n⌉ − 2 (a knockout tournament).

Concepts in depth: linear-time sorts

  • Counting sort (integer keys 0..k): count each key, turn the counts into cumulative counts (the cumulative count of v is one more than the last position where v belongs), then scan the input from right to left, placing each key at position count − 1 and decrementing. The right-to-left scan makes it stable. Θ(n + k) time and space; worthwhile when k = O(n).
  • Radix sort (LSD): sort by the least significant digit first, then the next, and so on, using a stable sort (usually counting sort) for each digit. With d digits in base b: Θ(d(n + b)). Stability of each pass is essential; without it, the order from earlier digits is destroyed. MSD radix sort works from the most significant digit and recurses into buckets.
  • Bucket sort: for keys spread uniformly over [0, 1), put key x in bucket ⌊n·x⌋, sort each bucket with insertion sort, and concatenate. Expected Θ(n); worst case Θ(n²) if everything lands in one bucket.

Concepts in depth: hashing

A hash function maps a key to a slot 0..m − 1. Common functions: division h(k) = k mod m (choose m prime, not close to a power of 2); multiplication h(k) = ⌊m·(kA mod 1)⌋ with 0 < A < 1 (Knuth suggests A ≈ (√5 − 1)/2 ≈ 0.618), where m may be a power of 2; mid-square (square the key and take middle digits); and folding (split the key into parts and add them). A good hash spreads keys uniformly and is cheap to compute. Two keys with the same slot collide; with n keys and m slots, the expected number of colliding pairs under uniform hashing is n(n − 1)/(2m).

Separate chaining keeps a linked list per slot. The load factor α = n/m may exceed 1. Under simple uniform hashing, an unsuccessful search examines α keys on average (Θ(1 + α) time including the hash), and a successful search examines about 1 + α/2 keys. Deletion is easy.

Open addressing stores every key in the table itself (α ≤ 1) and follows a probe sequence h(k, 0), h(k, 1), … until it finds an empty slot:

MethodProbe sequenceDistinct sequencesWeakness
Linear probing(h(k) + i) mod mmprimary clustering
Quadratic probing(h(k) + c₁i + c₂i²) mod mmsecondary clustering; may miss slots
Double hashing(h₁(k) + i·h₂(k)) mod mabout m²h₂(k) must never be 0 and must be coprime to m

Linear probing visits every slot, but long runs of occupied slots grow faster: an empty slot right after a run of length r is filled next with probability (r + 1)/m. Quadratic probing with i² and m prime reaches only (m + 1)/2 slots, so success is guaranteed only when α ≤ 1/2. Double hashing behaves almost like ideal uniform hashing. Deletion in open addressing must leave a "deleted" marker (tombstone), otherwise later searches would stop early at the hole.

Expected probes (α = n/m < 1):

SchemeUnsuccessful search / insertSuccessful search
Uniform hashing (ideal; double hashing is close)1/(1 − α)(1/α)·ln(1/(1 − α))
Linear probing (Knuth)½(1 + 1/(1 − α)²)½(1 + 1/(1 − α))
Separate chaining (keys examined)α1 + α/2

At α = 0.75: uniform hashing needs 4 probes for an unsuccessful search and about 1.85 for a successful one; linear probing needs 8.5 and 2.5. As α approaches 1, open addressing explodes, which is why tables are resized (rehashed) at around α = 0.5 to 0.75.

Example 1: three quadratic sorts on [29, 10, 14, 37, 13, 5].

The array has 10 inversions, so bubble sort makes 10 swaps and insertion sort 10 shifts. Bubble sort makes 15 comparisons, selection sort 15 comparisons but only 4 swaps (pass 2 needs none), and insertion sort 13 comparisons.

Example 2: Lomuto partition. Partition [44, 17, 62, 8, 35, 91, 23, 50] with pivot 50.

  • j = 44, 17: both ≤ 50, so i advances to 0 and 1 (they swap with themselves).
  • j = 62: larger, skip. j = 8: i = 2, swap 62 and 8 → 44 17 8 62 35 91 23 50.
  • j = 35: i = 3, swap 62 and 35 → 44 17 8 35 62 91 23 50. j = 91: skip.
  • j = 23: i = 4, swap 62 and 23 → 44 17 8 35 23 91 62 50.
  • Swap the pivot with a[5] = 91 → 44 17 8 35 23 50 62 91; pivot index 5, 7 comparisons.

The next pivots are 23, 8, 44 and 91. With the Hoare-style scheme (pivot = first element 44) the first partition instead gives 35 17 23 8 44 91 62 50.

Example 3: bottom-up merge sort and LSD radix sort.

Merge sort on [44, 17, 62, 8, 35, 91, 23, 50]: runs of 2 → 17 44 | 8 62 | 35 91 | 23 50; runs of 4 → 8 17 44 62 | 23 35 50 91; final → 8 17 23 35 44 50 62 91. Comparisons 4 + 6 + 7 = 17, which here equals the worst case W(8).

Counts for 0..4: 1, 2, 0, 3, 2. Cumulative: 1, 3, 3, 6, 8. Scanning from the right: the last 3 goes to position 5, the 1 to position 2, the 4 to position 7, and so on. Output: 0 1 1 3 3 3 4 4, with equal keys in their original order.

Example 5: binary search trace. Array 3, 6, 9, …, 45 (15 elements, indices 0..14).

Search 39: mid 7 (24) → go right; mid 11 (36) → right; mid 13 (42) → left; mid 12 (39) → found in 4 comparisons. Search 20: 24, 12, 18, 21, then the range is empty: unsuccessful after 4 comparisons. Average successful comparisons = 49/15 ≈ 3.27.

Example 6: open addressing, three ways. m = 11, h(k) = k mod 11, keys 22, 1, 13, 11, 24, 33, 18, 42, 31.

Slot012345678910
Linear22113112433–18–4231
Quadratic (h + i²)221132411––18–3342

Linear probing: 11 needs 4 probes, 24 needs 3, 33 needs 6; total 20 probes for 9 keys. Quadratic probing: 11 probes 0, 1, 4; 33 probes 0, 1, 4, 9; and 31 cannot be inserted: its sequence 9, 10, 2, 7, 3, 1 (i = 0..5) repeats and never reaches the free slots 5, 6, 8.

Double hashing, m = 13, h₁ = k mod 13, h₂ = 7 − (k mod 7), keys 27, 53, 40, 14, 66, 19, 92 (all but 19 have home slot 1): 27→1; 53 step 3 → 4; 40 step 2 → 3; 14 step 7 → 8; 66 step 4 → 5; 19→6; 92 step 6 → 7. The key-dependent step spreads the colliding keys immediately.

Lower bound theory: comparison trees, adversaries and reductions

An upper bound comes from an algorithm. A lower bound is a statement about every algorithm for a problem, within a stated model of computation. When the two meet, the algorithm is optimal. Horowitz–Sahni give three standard tools.

1. Comparison trees. In the comparison model, an algorithm learns about its input only by comparing keys. Its behaviour on inputs of size n unfolds as a binary comparison (decision) tree: each internal node is a test such as xᵢ : xⱼ, each leaf is an outcome, and the worst-case number of comparisons is the height of the tree. A binary tree with L leaves has height at least ⌈log₂ L⌉, so counting the outcomes gives a bound:

  • Searching a sorted list of n keys must distinguish n “found at position i” outcomes and at least one “not found” outcome. That is n + 1 outcomes, so any algorithm needs ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉ comparisons in the worst case, and binary search is optimal.
  • Sorting n keys has n! outcomes, giving ⌈log₂ n!⌉ = Ω(n log n).
  • Merging sorted lists of sizes m and n has C(m + n, n) possible interleavings, giving ⌈log₂ C(m + n, n)⌉.

2. Oracles and adversary arguments. An adversary answers each comparison so as to keep as many inputs consistent as possible and forces the algorithm to keep working. For merging two lists of n keys each, the adversary makes the answer a₁ < b₁ < a₂ < b₂ < … < aₙ < bₙ. Every adjacent pair in that chain must be compared directly, or swapping the pair would give another consistent input with a different answer. That is 2n − 1 comparisons, so the ordinary merge is optimal. The information bound is weaker: for n = 8 it gives only ⌈log₂ 12870⌉ = 14, against the true 15. The results for the maximum (n − 1), for min and max together (⌈3n/2⌉ − 2) and for the second largest (n + ⌈log₂ n⌉ − 2) are proved the same way.

3. Lower bounds through reductions. Suppose problem A is known to need Ω(L(n)) time, and any instance of A can be transformed into an instance of B, solved by B, and the answer transformed back, all in τ(n) = o(L(n)) extra time. Then B also needs Ω(L(n)); otherwise the detour through B would solve A too fast. The known-hard problem is always reduced to the new problem.

  • Sorting → convex hull. Map each key x to the point (x, x²). All points lie on a parabola, so every point is a hull vertex, and reading the hull from its leftmost point gives the keys in sorted order. The transformation is O(n), so convex hull needs Ω(n log n).
  • Element uniqueness → closest pair. The keys are distinct exactly when the closest pair is at distance greater than 0. Element uniqueness needs Ω(n log n) in the algebraic decision-tree model, so closest pair does too.
  • Matrix multiplication → matrix squaring. To multiply n × n matrices A and B, square the 2n × 2n block matrix M = [[0, A], [B, 0]]. Then M² = [[AB, 0], [0, BA]]. So squaring cannot be asymptotically easier than multiplication.

Example 7: three bounds in one go.

  • Search 100 sorted keys: ⌈log₂ 101⌉ = 7 comparisons are needed, and binary search’s ⌊log₂ 100⌋ + 1 = 7 achieves it.
  • Sort 8 keys: ⌈log₂ 8!⌉ = ⌈log₂ 40320⌉ = 16.
  • Merge 4 + 4 keys: ⌈log₂ C(8, 4)⌉ = ⌈log₂ 70⌉ = 7 = 2·4 − 1, so here the two methods agree. For 8 + 8 keys they give 14 and 15.
  • Reduction check: the keys 3, −1, 2 become (3, 9), (−1, 1), (2, 4). The hull from the leftmost point, along the lower chain, is (−1, 1), (2, 4), (3, 9), which reads off the sorted order −1, 2, 3.

NTA trap: reversing the reduction. “Reduce convex hull to sorting” only shows that hull is no harder than sorting (an upper bound). A lower bound for hull needs sorting reduced to hull.

NTA traps

  • "Quick sort is O(n log n)." Only on average; its worst case is O(n²), and sorted input with a first- or last-element pivot triggers it.
  • Selection sort best case. Wrong: O(n) on sorted input. Fix: it always scans the whole unsorted part, so it is Θ(n²) comparisons in every case; only its swaps drop.
  • Insertion sort prefix. After k passes the first k + 1 elements are sorted among themselves, not the k + 1 smallest of the array. Selection sort is the one that places the smallest keys first.
  • Stability of selection sort. The array version with swaps is unstable, even though it is "simple".
  • Radix sort with an unstable inner sort. It gives a wrong result, not just a slower one.
  • Binary search count. ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1, not ⌈log₂ n⌉: for n = 1000 both give 10, but for n = 1024, ⌈log₂ n⌉ = 10 while the true worst case is 11.
  • α formulas. Do not mix successful and unsuccessful, or linear probing and uniform hashing. Write the formula first, then substitute.
  • Quadratic probing always succeeds while the table has space. False; with i² and prime m only half the slots are guaranteed reachable.
  • Deleting in open addressing. Emptying a slot breaks later searches; use a deleted marker.

How NTA asks this

  • Trace MCQ: the array after pass k, after one partition, or after one radix pass; the final hash table. Eliminate by footprint: bubble has the maxima at the end, selection the minima at the front, insertion a sorted prefix of the original first elements.
  • Numerical: binary-search comparisons, merge comparisons, lower bounds, number of swaps (count inversions), expected probes from α.
  • Match: algorithms with complexities or properties; collision methods with their weaknesses.
  • Multiple select: which sorts are stable, in-place, adaptive or comparison-based.
  • Code output: short C loops for bubble, insertion, selection, partition, merge and linear probing.

Mini A–R. (A) Radix sort must use a stable sort for each digit. (R) Counting sort runs in Θ(n + k) time.

Both statements are true, but the speed of counting sort is not why stability is needed. The real reason is that ties on the current digit must keep the order fixed by the earlier (less significant) digits. Answer: both true, R is NOT the correct explanation.

Watch out: when a trace question does not state the partition scheme or probe formula, work out which standard convention makes one of the options appear. If two conventions both appear among the options, prefer the one the question’s wording describes (for example "pivot is the last element" means Lomuto).

terms.definition: Keeps equal keys in their original relative order; needed when sorting on one field after another (as in radix sort).
Uses only O(1) extra memory apart from the input (quick sort is usually counted in-place despite its O(log n) recursion stack).
A pair (i, j) with i < j but a[i] > a[j]; bubble and insertion sort do one swap or shift per inversion.
Quick sort picks a pivot and rearranges the array so smaller keys are on its left and larger on its right; the pivot is then in its final place.
n/m: keys stored divided by table slots. Open addressing needs α ≤ 1; chaining allows α > 1.
In linear probing, occupied slots form long runs, and any key hashing into a run lengthens it.
In quadratic probing, keys with the same home slot follow the same probe sequence.
Probe sequence h₁(k) + i·h₂(k) mod m; the step depends on the key, so it avoids both kinds of clustering.
Any comparison sort needs at least ⌈log₂ n!⌉ comparisons in the worst case, which is Ω(n log n).

lessons.title: Performance analysis and recurrences
lessons.summaryHtml: Performance analysis measures how the running time and memory of an algorithm grow as the input size n grows. We describe that growth with asymptotic notations: O (upper bound), Ω (lower bound), Θ (tight bound), and the strict versions o and ω. Loops are analysed by counting how many times the innermost statement runs, and recursive algorithms give recurrences such as T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. You solve these with substitution, a recursion tree or the master theorem. Amortised analysis gives the average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence, and space complexity counts extra memory, including the recursion stack. NET asks this unit as growth-rate ordering, recurrence-to-answer matching, loop-count programs and true/false statements on the notations.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Two programs can both be correct and still differ hugely in speed. Performance analysis answers one question: as the input gets bigger, how fast does the cost grow? We do not care whether a loop takes 3 ns or 5 ns per step, because that depends on the machine. We care whether doubling the input doubles the work, quadruples it or squares it. That is the order of growth, and the asymptotic notations O, Ω, Θ, o and ω are the language for it.

Recursive algorithms describe their own cost with a recurrence: merge sort on n items does two sorts of n/2 items plus n work to merge, so T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. Solving recurrences is the second half of this lesson. The third half (the lesson is generous) is amortised analysis, which averages cost over a sequence of operations, and space complexity.

Why it matters for NET

This topic feeds every other algorithm question: sorting, graph algorithms and dynamic programming options are all written in Θ notation. On its own it regularly supplies a few questions per paper. The dominant sub-topics are: master-theorem recurrences, ordering a list of functions by growth rate, finding the complexity (or the exact count) of a loop nest, and true/false statements about the properties of the notations. Amortised analysis and space complexity appear less often, usually as a single conceptual question.

Asymptotic notations: the definitions

All five notations compare f(n) with a simpler g(n) for large n, ignoring constant factors.

  • O (big-O), upper bound: f(n) = O(g(n)) if there exist constants c > 0 and n₀ such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. Example: 3n² + 10n = O(n²) with c = 4 and n₀ = 10, because 10n ≤ n² once n ≥ 10.
  • Ω (big-Omega), lower bound: f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀.
  • Θ (big-Theta), tight bound: c₁g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₂g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. Equivalently f = O(g) and f = Ω(g).
  • o (little-o), strictly smaller: for every c > 0 there is an n₀ with f(n) < c·g(n). Example: n = o(n²), but 2n² ≠ o(n²).
  • ω (little-omega), strictly larger: for every c > 0, f(n) > c·g(n) eventually.

Note that big-O says “for some c”, while little-o says “for every c”. That one word is the whole difference. Also note that f(n) = O(g(n)) is a statement about sets: it really means f ∈ O(g). So n = O(n²) is true, even though it is not a tight bound. Many students mark it false because they read O as “exactly”.

The limit test

When both functions are positive, compute L = lim (n→∞) f(n)/g(n):

Limit LConclusion
L = 0f = o(g), hence also f = O(g); f is not Ω(g)
0 < L < ∞f = Θ(g)
L = ∞f = ω(g), hence also f = Ω(g); f is not O(g)

If the limit does not exist, the test is silent, and you go back to the definitions. L’Hôpital’s rule helps with logs: lim (log n)/n^ε = 0 for every ε > 0, so any power of n beats any power of log n.

Properties you must know

  • Transitivity holds for all five: f = O(g) and g = O(h) give f = O(h).
  • Reflexivity holds for O, Ω and Θ (f = Θ(f)), but not for o and ω (f is never o(f)).
  • Symmetry holds only for Θ: f = Θ(g) if and only if g = Θ(f).
  • Transpose symmetry: f = O(g) ⇔ g = Ω(f), and f = o(g) ⇔ g = ω(f).
  • Sum rule: f + g = Θ(max(f, g)). Product rule: O(f)·O(g) = O(f·g).
  • No trichotomy. Unlike numbers, two functions need not be comparable. The classic pair is f(n) = n and g(n) = n^(1 + sin n): the exponent swings between 0 and 2, so neither f = O(g) nor f = Ω(g).

Comparing growth rates

The standard ladder, slowest first:

1 < log log n < log n < (log n)^k < n^ε (0<ε<1) < n < n log n < n^(1+ε)
  < n^2 < n^3 < ... < n^(log n) < 2^n < 3^n < n! < n^n

Three tools settle almost every ordering question:

  1. Take logarithms. If log f grows strictly faster than log g by more than a constant, then f grows faster. n^(log n) has log (log n)², while 2^n has log n, so n^(log n) = o(2^n). Be careful: log f = Θ(log g) does not give f = Θ(g). For example, log n² = 2 log n = Θ(log n), yet n² ≠ Θ(n).
  2. Rewrite powers with a common base. 2^(log₂ n) = n, 4^(log₂ n) = n², n^(log₂ 3) = 3^(log₂ n). Bases of logarithms do not matter (log₂ n = Θ(log₁₀ n)) but bases of exponentials do (2^n = o(3^n)).
  3. Remember standard sums and Stirling. 1 + 2 + … + n = Θ(n²), Σ i^k = Θ(n^(k+1)), 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n = Θ(log n), 1 + r + r² + … + r^k = Θ(r^k) for r > 1, log(n!) = Θ(n log n), and n! = o(n^n) but n! = ω(2^n).

Loop complexity

Count how many times the innermost statement runs. Write it as a sum, then simplify. The shape of the loop is a hint, never a proof.

Loop patternCountOrder
i = 1 to n, j = 1 to nn²Θ(n²)
i = 1 to n, j = 1 to in(n+1)/2Θ(n²)
i = n; i > 0; i = i/2⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1Θ(log n)
i = 1; i*i ≤ n; i++⌊√n⌋Θ(√n)
i = 1 to n, j = 1; j ≤ n; j = j*2n(⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1)Θ(n log n)
i = 1; i ≤ n; i = i*2, j = 1 to i1 + 2 + 4 + … ≤ 2n − 1Θ(n)
i = 1 to n, j = 1; j ≤ n; j = j + iΣ ⌈n/i⌉Θ(n log n) (harmonic)
i = 2; i ≤ n; i = i*iabout log log nΘ(log log n)
s = s + i with i = 1, 2, 3, … while s ≤ nabout √(2n)Θ(√n)

The fourth-last row is the favourite trap: the outer loop runs log n times, the inner loop is “up to i”, and students multiply to get n log n. The real total is a geometric series dominated by its last term, so it is Θ(n).

Recurrences: substitution method

Guess the form of the answer, then prove it by induction. To show T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n is O(n log n), assume T(k) ≤ c·k log k for all k < n. Then T(n) ≤ 2c(n/2)log(n/2) + n = c·n log n − c·n + n ≤ c·n log n whenever c ≥ 1. A common pitfall: proving T(n) ≤ cn + n and calling it O(n). The induction hypothesis must be reproduced with the same constant c, so this proof fails. When a guess “almost” works, subtract a lower-order term from it (guess T(n) ≤ cn − d instead of cn).

Iterating (unrolling) is the informal twin: T(n) = T(n−1) + n = T(n−2) + (n−1) + n = … = 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2.

Recurrences: recursion tree

Draw the calls level by level. At level i of T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) there are a^i nodes, each costing f(n/b^i). The tree has log_b n levels and a^(log_b n) = n^(log_b a) leaves. Add up the levels:

  • If the level sums shrink geometrically, the root dominates: T(n) = Θ(f(n)).
  • If they are all about equal, multiply one level by the number of levels: Θ(f(n) log n).
  • If they grow geometrically, the leaves dominate: Θ(n^(log_b a)).

The recursion tree also handles unequal splits, which the master theorem cannot. For T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n, every full level costs n. The shortest root-to-leaf path has log₃ n levels and the longest has log_(3/2) n levels, so T(n) is between n·log₃ n and n·log_(3/2) n, that is Θ(n log n).

The master theorem

For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) with constants a ≥ 1, b > 1 and f(n) asymptotically positive, compare f(n) with the watershed function n^(log_b a):

CaseConditionSolution
1f(n) = O(n^(log_b a − ε)) for some ε > 0Θ(n^(log_b a))
2f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log^k n), k ≥ 0Θ(n^(log_b a) · log^(k+1) n)
3f(n) = Ω(n^(log_b a + ε)) and a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n) for some c < 1Θ(f(n))

The basic textbook version (Cormen) states case 2 only for k = 0. The extended form above, with log factors, is widely used and is safe for NET. A further extension handles k = −1: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n/log n = Θ(n log log n). For k < −1 the leaves dominate and T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)).

When the master theorem does not apply: a is not a constant (T(n) = 2^n T(n/2) + n); a < 1 (T(n) = 0.5T(n/2) + n); f(n) is not positive (T(n) = 64T(n/8) − n² log n); the subproblems are unequal (T(n/3) + T(2n/3)); the problem shrinks by subtraction (T(n−1)); or f falls in a gap, bigger than the watershed only by a log factor but not polynomially, as in T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n in the basic version. The basic version cannot solve that last one, but the extended case 2 gives Θ(n log² n).

Change of variable and subtract-and-conquer

For recurrences with √n, put n = 2^m. For example, T(n) = 2T(√n) + 1 becomes S(m) = 2S(m/2) + 1 = Θ(m), so T(n) = Θ(log n). Similarly T(n) = √n·T(√n) + n gives Θ(n log log n): divide by n and put S(m) = T(2^m)/2^m, which gives S(m) = S(m/2) + 1.

For T(n) = aT(n − b) + f(n) (“decrease and conquer”), unroll: with a = 1 the costs add up (T(n) = T(n−1) + 1 is Θ(n), T(n) = T(n−1) + n is Θ(n²), T(n) = T(n−1) + log n is Θ(n log n)); with a > 1 the tree explodes (T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1 = 2^n − 1 when T(1) = 1, so Θ(2^n), the Tower of Hanoi recurrence).

Amortised analysis

Amortised analysis bounds the total cost of any sequence of n operations, then divides by n. No probability is involved: it is a worst-case guarantee on the average. There are three methods.

  • Aggregate method: compute the total T(n) directly and divide by n. Binary counter: bit 0 flips on every increment, bit 1 on every second, bit k on every 2^k-th. Total flips for n increments is at most n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n, so Θ(1) amortised, even though a single increment can flip log n bits.
  • Accounting method: charge each operation a fixed fee. The surplus is stored as credit on the data structure and pays for expensive operations later. Charge 2 per increment: 1 pays for setting a bit to 1, and 1 stays on that bit to pay for resetting it to 0 later.
  • Potential method: define Φ(state) ≥ 0 with Φ(initial) = 0. Then the amortised cost is ĉ = c + Φ(after) − Φ(before). For the counter, take Φ = number of 1-bits. An increment that resets t bits costs t + 1 and changes Φ by 1 − t, so ĉ = 2.

The standard examples are the multipop stack (n operations cost O(n) in total, because each element is popped at most once), the binary counter and the doubling dynamic array (Θ(1) amortised per append). Two more are the union–find structure with union by rank and path compression, where m operations cost O(m α(n)) with α the inverse Ackermann function, and splay trees, with O(log n) amortised per operation.

Space complexity

Space complexity counts memory as a function of n. Usually we quote auxiliary space, the extra memory beyond the input. The recursion stack counts. Recursive factorial uses Θ(n) stack; the loop version uses Θ(1). Binary search is Θ(1) iteratively but Θ(log n) recursively. Merge sort needs Θ(n) for the merge buffer. Quick sort uses Θ(log n) stack if it always recurses into the smaller part first, but a naive version uses Θ(n) in the worst case. Heap sort is in place with Θ(1). Memoised dynamic programming often trades space for time, for example an n × m LCS table.

Worked examples

Example 1: an exact loop count

for (i = 1; i <= n; i++)
    for (j = 1; j <= n; j = j + i)
        count++;

Step 1. For a fixed i, j takes 1, 1 + i, 1 + 2i, … up to n, which is ⌈n/i⌉ values.

Step 2. Total = Σ (i = 1 to n) ⌈n/i⌉. For n = 12: 12 + 6 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 41.

Step 3. In general the sum is about n(1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n) = n·H(n) ≈ n ln n, so the loop is Θ(n log n).

Answer: 41 for n = 12; Θ(n log n) in general. (Checked by running the loop.)

Example 2: three master-theorem cases side by side

All three have a = 4 and b = 2, so the watershed is n^(log₂ 4) = n².

  1. T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n. f(n) = n = O(n^(2−1)). Case 1 → Θ(n²).
  2. T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n². f(n) = Θ(n² log⁰ n). Case 2 with k = 0 → Θ(n² log n).
  3. T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n³. f(n) = Ω(n^(2+1)). Check regularity: 4(n/2)³ = n³/2 ≤ (1/2)·n³, so c = 1/2 < 1. Case 3 → Θ(n³).

Two more to memorise: T(n) = 7T(n/2) + n² (Strassen) → n^(log₂ 7) ≈ n^2.81; T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n (Karatsuba) → n^(log₂ 3) ≈ n^1.585.

Example 3: exact solution of the merge-sort recurrence

Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, T(1) = 1, for n = 2^k.

Step 1. Unroll: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n = 4T(n/4) + 2n = 8T(n/8) + 3n = … = 2^i T(n/2^i) + i·n.

Step 2. Stop at i = k = log₂ n: T(n) = n·T(1) + n log₂ n = n log₂ n + n.

Step 3. Check with n = 1024: 1024 × 10 + 1024 = 11,264. Direct computation of the recurrence also gives 11,264.

Answer: T(n) = n log₂ n + n = Θ(n log n).

Example 4: a recurrence outside the master theorem

Solve T(n) = 2T(√n) + log n.

Step 1. Let n = 2^m, so √n = 2^(m/2) and log₂ n = m. Then T(2^m) = 2T(2^(m/2)) + m.

Step 2. Put S(m) = T(2^m): S(m) = 2S(m/2) + m. The watershed is m^(log₂ 2) = m, equal to f(m), so case 2 gives S(m) = Θ(m log m).

Step 3. Substitute back m = log n: T(n) = Θ(log n · log log n).

Example 5: amortised cost of a doubling array

An array starts with capacity 1. When it is full, the next append allocates double the capacity and copies every element. Find the total cost of 17 appends, counting 1 per element written and 1 per element copied.

Step 1. Expansions happen when the array holds 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 elements, so the copies are 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31.

Step 2. Writes = 17. Total = 17 + 31 = 48, and the final capacity is 32.

Step 3. In general, copies < 2n, so total < 3n: the amortised cost per append is Θ(1), although the 17th append alone costs 17.

Example 6: ordering by taking logarithms

Order n², 2^(log₂ n), n^(log₂ n), 2^n and log(n!) from slowest to fastest.

Step 1. Simplify: 2^(log₂ n) = n, and log(n!) = Θ(n log n).

Step 2. Compare n^(log₂ n) and 2^n by taking log₂: (log₂ n)² versus n. Since (log n)² = o(n), n^(log₂ n) = o(2^n).

Answer: 2^(log₂ n) < log(n!) < n² < n^(log₂ n) < 2^n.

NTA traps

  • “O means tight.” Wrong: n = O(n³) is true. If an option asks for the “best” or “tightest” bound, pick Θ; otherwise any valid upper bound is correct.
  • Constants in exponents. 2^(n+1) = O(2^n) is true, but 2^(2n) = O(2^n) is false. Likewise 4^(log₂ n) = n², not n.
  • Equal logs, different functions. log(n²) = Θ(log n) is true, but that does not make n² = Θ(n). Taking logs only proves an ordering when the gap between the logs is unbounded.
  • Doubling outer loop with “j ≤ i” inner loop. The count is 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n ≈ 2n, which is Θ(n), not Θ(n log n).
  • Forcing the master theorem. It does not apply to T(n−1), to T(n/3) + T(2n/3), to a < 1, or to f(n) = n/log n in the basic version. Look for a recursion tree or unrolling instead.
  • Forgetting the regularity condition in case 3. For f(n) = n^(log_b a + ε) it holds automatically, so NET rarely makes you check it, but a statement question may say “case 3 needs no extra condition”, which is false.
  • Amortised = average case. Wrong. Average-case analysis assumes a probability distribution on inputs. Amortised analysis gives a worst-case bound on a sequence.
  • Ignoring the recursion stack. A recursive algorithm with no arrays still uses Θ(depth) space.

How NTA asks this

Formats. Match the recurrence to its Θ solution (the most common); order four or five functions by growth; statement pairs on notation properties (symmetry, transitivity, o vs O); Assertion–Reason on “why” a bound holds; loop programs (“what is printed?” or “what is the time complexity?”); and single numericals from the master theorem.

Mini-example (match). List I: A. T(n) = 3T(n/3) + n, B. T(n) = 9T(n/3) + n, C. T(n) = T(2n/3) + 1, D. T(n) = 2T(n/4) + √n. Work: A: n^1 = f, case 2 → n log n. B: n² vs n, case 1 → n². C: a = 1, b = 3/2, n⁰ = 1 = f, case 2 → log n. D: n^(1/2) = f, case 2 → √n log n. Scan the options for the one with A → n log n and B → n². Usually only one or two survive, and D settles it.

Mini-example (A–R). (A) Binary search is Θ(log n). (R) Its recurrence is T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Both are true, and R explains A, so option 1.

Elimination tricks.

  • For growth ordering, find the extreme ends first: the slowest function (a log or constant) and the fastest (factorial or exponential). This usually eliminates two or three options immediately.
  • For a recurrence match, compute the watershed n^(log_b a) for every row before reading the options.
  • For loop code, run the loop mentally for a tiny n (such as n = 8) and compare with the options’ formulas.
  • For statement questions, test a concrete pair such as f = n and g = n² against each claimed property.

terms.definition: f(n) = O(g(n)) if there are constants c > 0 and n₀ with 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. An upper bound, not necessarily tight.
f(n) = Ω(g(n)) if there are c > 0 and n₀ with f(n) ≥ c·g(n) ≥ 0 for all n ≥ n₀. A lower bound.
f(n) = Θ(g(n)) if f is both O(g) and Ω(g): sandwiched between c₁g(n) and c₂g(n) for large n.
f = o(g) means f grows strictly slower than g (lim f/g = 0). f = ω(g) means strictly faster (lim f/g = ∞).
An equation that defines T(n) in terms of T on smaller inputs, for example T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n for merge sort.
For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) with a ≥ 1, b > 1: compare f(n) with n^(log_b a). Smaller → Θ(n^(log_b a)); equal (up to logᵏ) → multiply by one more log; larger (with the regularity condition) → Θ(f(n)).
A drawing of the cost at each level of the recursion. Total cost = sum over all levels.
Total cost of a worst-case sequence of n operations divided by n. It is a guarantee, not an expectation over random inputs.
Amortised cost = actual cost + ΔΦ, where Φ is a non-negative potential stored in the data structure.
Extra memory used by the algorithm beyond the input, including the recursion stack.

lessons.examTip: For any aT(n/b) + f(n) recurrence, first write n^(log_b a) next to f(n). The whole question is decided by which one is bigger, and whether it is bigger by a polynomial factor or only by logs.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For every recurrence, write n^(log_b a) beside f(n) before choosing a case.
For each loop problem, write the exact count as a sum first, then simplify. Do not guess from the loop shape.
Check with solutions.md and write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (for example: “applied master theorem when f(n) = n/log n”).
Type the loops from problems 4 and 12 into a C compiler, print the count for n = 32, 64, 128 and 256, and confirm that it grows the way your Θ bound predicts.
Redo the wrong ones after 24 hours, then take the lesson quiz.

quiz.question: What is the solution of T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n², T(1) = 1?
quiz.explanation: a = 8, b = 2, so n^(log₂ 8) = n³. f(n) = n² = O(n^(3−ε)) with ε = 1, so case 1 applies and T(n) = Θ(n³). Θ(n² log n) would need f(n) = Θ(n³) (case 2). Θ(n²) forgets that the leaves dominate.
