quiz.question: Arrange the following steps in the correct order to prove that a new problem X is NP-complete.
quiz.explanation: Membership first (A), then pick the known NP-complete source Y (B), build the polynomial transformation Y → X (C), prove it preserves yes/no answers in both directions (D), and conclude (E). Options 1 and 4 build f before Y has been chosen, which is impossible because f maps instances of Y. Option 2 proves correctness before f exists.

stmts: A. Show that X ∈ NP by giving a polynomial-time verifier for a certificate
B. Choose a problem Y already known to be NP-complete
C. Construct a function f that maps every instance of Y to an instance of X in polynomial time
D. Prove that y is a yes-instance of Y if and only if f(y) is a yes-instance of X
E. Conclude that X is NP-hard and, with step A, NP-complete
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: In the standard reduction from SAT to 3-SAT, a single clause with 7 literals is replaced by how many 3-literal clauses, and how many new variables are introduced?
quiz.explanation: A clause (l₁ ∨ … ∨ lₖ) with k > 3 becomes (l₁ ∨ l₂ ∨ y₁)(¬y₁ ∨ l₃ ∨ y₂)…(¬yₖ₋₃ ∨ lₖ₋₁ ∨ lₖ): k − 2 clauses and k − 3 new variables. For k = 7: 5 clauses and 4 new variables. Option 3 swaps the two counts.

quiz.question: Problem Q is a new problem. Which reduction, if found in polynomial time, proves that Q is NP-hard?
quiz.explanation: Hardness flows along the arrow: if a known NP-complete problem (3-SAT) reduces to Q, then Q is at least as hard, so Q is NP-hard. Q ≤p SAT only shows Q is no harder than SAT (it gives Q ∈ NP). Reducing Q to 2-SAT or to a P problem would put Q in P.

quiz.question: Which statement about approximating the travelling salesman problem (TSP) is correct, assuming P ≠ NP?
options: General TSP (arbitrary distances) has a polynomial-time 2-approximation
Metric TSP has a polynomial-time 3/2-approximation (Christofides), but general TSP has no constant-factor polynomial-time approximation
Metric TSP can be solved exactly in polynomial time
No NP-hard problem has any constant-factor approximation
quiz.explanation: With the triangle inequality, the MST-doubling method gives ratio 2 and Christofides gives 3/2. Without it, a constant-factor approximation would decide Hamiltonian cycle (give non-edges huge weight), so none exists unless P = NP. Metric TSP is still NP-hard, and vertex cover (NP-hard) has a 2-approximation, so option 4 is false.

lessons.title: Advanced algorithms
lessons.summaryHtml: This lesson covers five families of algorithms that NET tests with short numericals. Parallel algorithms run on the PRAM model (EREW, CREW, CRCW). There, n numbers are summed or prefix-summed in O(log n) steps, and speedup, efficiency and cost measure the gain. Randomized algorithms are either Las Vegas (always correct, random time, e.g. randomized quicksort) or Monte Carlo (fixed time, small error, e.g. Miller–Rabin). String matching covers the naive method, Rabin–Karp’s rolling hash with its spurious hits, and KMP’s prefix function, which gives O(n + m). Number-theoretic algorithms include Euclid’s GCD, the modular inverse, fast modular exponentiation and RSA. Approximation algorithms give provable ratios: 2 for vertex cover and 2 (MST) or 3/2 (Christofides) for metric TSP.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

The earlier lessons of this unit taught the classic techniques. This one collects five “advanced” families that the syllabus lists together.

  • Parallel algorithms ask how fast a job finishes when many processors work at once.
  • Randomized algorithms flip coins to avoid bad cases or to answer fast with a tiny, controlled chance of error.
  • String matching finds a pattern inside a text, as a search box or a DNA tool does.
  • Number-theoretic algorithms (GCD, modular powers, inverses) are the machinery behind RSA and secure websites.
  • Approximation algorithms give answers to NP-hard problems that are guaranteed to be close to the best.

Each family has one or two ideas worth understanding deeply. Once you have them, the exam numericals become mechanical.

Why it matters for NET

This topic mixes theory and quick numericals, which suits the NTA format. KMP prefix functions, Rabin–Karp spurious hits, RSA key and ciphertext calculations and modular exponentiation appear often. RSA also appears in the network-security unit, so one method earns marks in two places. PRAM model definitions, Las Vegas versus Monte Carlo, and approximation ratios are common in match-the-list and statement questions. The numericals are short but unforgiving: off-by-one shifts, reducing modulo n instead of φ(n), and forgetting the KMP fallback are the usual ways marks are lost.

Concepts in depth

Parallel algorithms and the PRAM model

A PRAM has p processors that run in lock-step and share one memory. Each step takes unit time. The variants differ in how processors may access the same memory cell in the same step:

ModelConcurrent readConcurrent write
EREWNoNo
CREWYesNo
ERCW (rarely used)NoYes
CRCWYesYes, resolved by a rule: common (all write the same value), arbitrary (any one wins), priority (the lowest-index processor wins)

By power, EREW ≤ CREW ≤ CRCW-common ≤ CRCW-arbitrary ≤ CRCW-priority. For example, a common-CRCW PRAM computes the OR of n bits in O(1) time. Each processor holding a 1 writes 1 into a result cell initialised to 0, and all writers write the same value. On EREW the same task needs Θ(log n).

Measures. Let T₁ be the best sequential time and Tₚ the parallel time on p processors.

  • Speedup S = T₁/Tₚ, efficiency E = S/p, cost = p·Tₚ.
  • An algorithm is cost-optimal if its cost is Θ(T₁).
  • Work W is the total number of operations and depth D is the longest chain of dependent steps.
  • Brent’s theorem: Tₚ ≤ W/p + D.

Parallel sum (reduction). Pair up neighbours and add. Each round halves the number of values, so n values take ⌈log₂ n⌉ rounds on EREW with n/2 processors. The cost is (n/2)·log n = Θ(n log n), which is not cost-optimal against the sequential n − 1 additions. The fix is to use p = n/log n processors. Each first adds a block of log n numbers sequentially, and then the p partial sums are combined in a tree. The time stays O(log n) and the cost becomes Θ(n).

Parallel prefix (scan). The goal is yᵢ = x₁ + … + xᵢ for all i. The Hillis–Steele method runs log₂ n rounds. In the round with offset k = 1, 2, 4, …, every position i ≥ k adds the value k places to its left, using the values from the previous round. It takes n·log₂ n − (n − 1) additions, so it is not work-efficient. The Blelloch (work-efficient) scan uses an up-sweep and a down-sweep over a balanced tree. It does Θ(n) work in O(log n) depth. Prefix sums are a building block for parallel radix sort, compaction and carry-lookahead addition.

Randomized algorithms

Las VegasMonte Carlo
AnswerAlways correctCorrect with high probability
Running timeRandom (bounded in expectation)Bounded (deterministic bound)
ExamplesRandomized quicksort, randomized select, universal hashingMiller–Rabin and Fermat primality tests, Karger min-cut, Freivalds’ matrix check

A Las Vegas algorithm can be turned into a Monte Carlo one: stop after, say, twice the expected time and output “don’t know” or a guess. By Markov’s inequality this fails with probability at most 1/2. If a Las Vegas trial succeeds with probability p, the number of trials is geometric with expectation 1/p.

Randomized quicksort. Choose the pivot uniformly at random. Let z₁ < z₂ < … < zₙ be the sorted order. Elements zᵢ and zⱼ are compared only if one of them is the first pivot chosen from zᵢ … zⱼ. That block has j − i + 1 elements, so the probability is 2/(j − i + 1). Adding over all pairs gives E[comparisons] = 2(n + 1)Hₙ − 4n ≈ 1.39 n log₂ n = O(n log n) for every input. Randomisation moves the risk from the input to the coin flips. The worst case is still Θ(n²), but it is very unlikely.

Primality tests. The Fermat test checks aⁿ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod n). It is fooled by Carmichael numbers such as 561 = 3·11·17, which pass for every base coprime to them. Miller–Rabin adds a square-root check. A composite passes one round with probability at most 1/4, so k rounds err with probability at most 4⁻ᵏ. The error is one-sided: a “composite” answer is always correct.

Karger’s min-cut. Contract uniformly random edges until two super-vertices remain. One run finds a particular minimum cut with probability at least 2/(n(n − 1)). Repeating about n² ln n times makes failure unlikely. Freivalds checks whether A·B = C by testing A(Br) = Cr for a random 0/1 vector r. Each test costs O(n²) and errs with probability at most 1/2.

String matching

Text T has length n and pattern P has length m. A shift s is valid if T[s+1 .. s+m] = P (0 ≤ s ≤ n − m).

Naive: try all n − m + 1 shifts and compare left to right. It needs no preprocessing and takes O((n − m + 1)m) in the worst case, for example T = aⁿ and P = aᵐ⁻¹b.

Rabin–Karp: treat each m-character window as an m-digit number in radix d and compare hashes modulo a prime q. Let h = dᵐ⁻¹ mod q. The window hash rolls in O(1):

t(s+1) = ( d * ( t(s) - T[s+1]*h ) + T[s+m+1] ) mod q

Equal hashes are only a candidate. The window must be verified character by character, and a failure is a spurious hit. Preprocessing takes Θ(m). The worst case is O((n − m + 1)m), when hashes collide at every shift. The expected time is O(n + m) when q is large and there are few valid shifts. A bigger q means fewer spurious hits. Rabin–Karp extends easily to searching for many patterns and 2-D patterns.

Knuth–Morris–Pratt: after a mismatch, a naive search forgets what it matched. KMP instead reuses the prefix function: π[q] is the length of the longest proper prefix of P[1..q] that is also a suffix of it (a “border”). If q characters matched and the next one fails, the next useful comparison is at π[q]. The text pointer never moves back. The algorithm computing π is:

pi[1] = 0; k = 0
for q = 2 to m:
    while k > 0 and P[k+1] != P[q]:
        k = pi[k]          // fall back to a shorter border
    if P[k+1] == P[q]:
        k = k + 1
    pi[q] = k

The amortised argument is that k rises by at most 1 per step and every fallback lowers it, so computing π takes Θ(m) and matching takes Θ(n). The total is O(n + m), with at most 2n character comparisons during matching. The finite-automaton matcher also matches in Θ(n), but building its transition table takes O(m·|Σ|). Boyer–Moore scans the pattern right to left with bad-character and good-suffix shifts, and in practice it is often sublinear.

Number-theoretic algorithms

Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), and gcd(a, 0) = a. Each two steps at least halve the larger number, so it runs in O(log min(a, b)) steps. Consecutive Fibonacci numbers are the worst case (Lamé’s theorem: at most 5 times the number of decimal digits of the smaller number). Extended Euclid also returns x, y with ax + by = gcd(a, b). When gcd(a, m) = 1, x mod m is the modular inverse a⁻¹.

Modular rules: (a + b) mod m and (a·b) mod m can be reduced term by term. Division means multiplying by an inverse, which exists only if the divisor is coprime to m.

  • Fermat: ap−1 ≡ 1 (mod p) for prime p with p ∤ a.
  • Euler: aφ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n) when gcd(a, n) = 1. Here φ(pq) = (p − 1)(q − 1) for distinct primes, and φ(pᵏ) = pᵏ − pᵏ⁻¹.
  • Chinese remainder theorem: for pairwise coprime moduli the system x ≡ aᵢ (mod mᵢ) has a unique solution modulo ∏mᵢ.

Fast modular exponentiation (square-and-multiply): scan the bits of e. Squaring once per bit and multiplying by a for each 1-bit gives ⌊log₂ e⌋ squarings and (number of 1-bits − 1) multiplications, left to right. That is O(log e) multiplications of O(β²) bit cost each for β-bit numbers.

RSA:

  1. Choose primes p and q.
  2. Compute n = pq and φ(n) = (p − 1)(q − 1).
  3. Pick e with gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1.
  4. Compute d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n).
  5. The public key is (e, n) and the private key is (d, n). Encrypt with C = Mᵉ mod n (M < n) and decrypt with M = Cᵈ mod n.

It works because ed = 1 + kφ(n), so Med = M·(Mφ(n))ᵏ ≡ M (mod n) by Euler, with a CRT argument covering M not coprime to n. A signature is S = Mᵈ mod n, verified by Sᵉ mod n. Security rests on the difficulty of factoring n.

Approximation algorithms

  • Vertex cover, ratio 2: take both ends of each edge of a maximal matching. Any cover needs one distinct endpoint per matching edge.
  • Metric TSP, ratio 2: build an MST, walk it in preorder and shortcut repeated vertices. The full walk costs 2·MST, shortcuts never increase cost under the triangle inequality, and OPT ≥ MST (remove one tour edge to get a spanning tree).
  • Christofides, ratio 3/2: MST plus a minimum-weight perfect matching on the odd-degree vertices gives an Euler tour, which is then shortcut.
  • General TSP: no constant ratio unless P = NP.
  • Greedy set cover: ratio H(max set size) ≤ ln n + 1.
  • Bin packing: Next Fit uses at most 2·OPT bins, and First Fit uses about 1.7·OPT.

Worked examples

Example 1: KMP prefix function and a matching run

Pattern P = abacabab. Compute π, then search T = abacabacabab.

q12345678
P[q]abacabab
π[q]00101232
  1. q = 3: P[1] = a = P[3], so k = 1. q = 4: c differs from P[2] = b, fall back to k = π[1] = 0; c ≠ a, so π = 0.
  2. q = 5, 6, 7: the matches a, ab, aba grow, so k = 1, 2, 3.
  3. q = 8: P[k + 1] = P[4] = c ≠ b, so fall back to k = π[3] = 1. P[2] = b matches, so π[8] = 2.
  4. Matching: T[1..7] = abacaba matches P[1..7] (q = 7). At T[8] = c, P[8] = b fails. Fall back to q = π[7] = 3 (“aba” is still matched). P[4] = c matches T[8], so q = 4.
  5. T[9..12] = abab matches P[5..8]. The match ends at position 12, so the valid shift is s = 4 (the match starts at position 5). There were 13 character comparisons in all. The text pointer never moved back.

Example 2: Rabin–Karp with a spurious hit

d = 10, q = 7, T = 4172839465 (n = 10), P = 283 (m = 3).

  1. Pattern hash p = 283 mod 7 = 3, and h = 10² mod 7 = 2.
  2. First window 417 mod 7 = 4. Roll to the next window: t = (10 × (4 − 4 × 2) + 2) mod 7 = (−38) mod 7 = 4, which matches 172 mod 7 = 4.
  3. Hashes of the 8 windows: 417→4, 172→4, 728→0, 283→3, 839→6, 394→2, 946→1, 465→3.
  4. Hash equals 3 at shifts 3 and 7. Verification: shift 3 (283) is a valid match, and shift 7 (465) is a spurious hit. Answer: 2 hash hits, 1 valid, 1 spurious.

Example 3: Euclid, extended Euclid and an inverse

gcd(1386, 595): 1386 = 2·595 + 196; 595 = 3·196 + 7; 196 = 28·7 + 0. So gcd = 7 in 3 division steps.

17⁻¹ mod 43: 43 = 2·17 + 9; 17 = 1·9 + 8; 9 = 1·8 + 1. Back-substitute:

  • 1 = 9 − 8 = 9 − (17 − 9) = 2·9 − 17
  • = 2(43 − 2·17) − 17 = 2·43 − 5·17

So 17 × (−5) ≡ 1, and the inverse is −5 + 43 = 38. Check: 17 × 38 = 646 = 15 × 43 + 1.

Example 4: square-and-multiply for 3⁴⁵ mod 7

45 = 101101₂. Scan left to right. Start with r = 3 for the leading 1. For each later bit, square r, and multiply by 3 if the bit is 1.

BitSquareMultiplyr
1 (lead)––3
09 mod 7 = 2–2
144·3 = 12 mod 7 = 55
125 mod 7 = 412 mod 7 = 55
025 mod 7 = 4–4
116 mod 7 = 266

So 3⁴⁵ mod 7 = 6, using 5 squarings + 3 multiplications = 8 modular multiplications. There is a shortcut: 3⁶ ≡ 1 (Fermat) and 45 mod 6 = 3, so 3³ = 27 ≡ 6.

Example 5: complete RSA round trip

  1. p = 7, q = 11, so n = 77 and φ = 60. Take e = 7 (gcd(7, 60) = 1). Then d = 43, since 7·43 = 301 = 5·60 + 1.
  2. Encrypt M = 8: 8² = 64, 8⁴ = 64² = 4096 ≡ 15 (mod 77). 8⁷ = 8⁴·8²·8 ≡ 15·64·8 = 7680 ≡ 7680 − 99·77 = 57.
  3. Decrypt C = 57 by CRT. Mod 7: 57 ≡ 1, so 1⁴³ = 1. Mod 11: 57 ≡ 2, and 2¹⁰ ≡ 1, so 2⁴³ ≡ 2³ = 8. Solve M ≡ 1 (mod 7), M ≡ 8 (mod 11), giving M = 8. The message is recovered.

Example 6: parallel sum and prefix

Sum 16 numbers on an EREW PRAM with 8 processors: log₂ 16 = 4 steps, against T₁ = 15 additions. Speedup = 15/4 = 3.75, efficiency = 3.75/8 ≈ 0.469, and cost = 8 × 4 = 32 > 15, so it is not cost-optimal.

Now sum n = 1024 numbers on p = 32 processors. Each processor first adds its 32 numbers (31 steps), then a tree combines the 32 partial sums (5 steps). That is 36 steps in total, with cost 32 × 36 = 1152 = Θ(n).

Hillis–Steele scan of x = [2, 5, 1, 4, 3, 6, 2, 1]:

k=1: [2, 7, 6, 5, 7, 9, 8, 3]
k=2: [2, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14, 15, 12]
k=4: [2, 7, 8, 12, 15, 21, 23, 24]

That is 7 + 6 + 4 = 17 additions (n log₂ n − (n − 1) = 24 − 7), compared with 7 sequential additions.

Example 7: MST-based 2-approximation for metric TSP

The distances are AB = 4, AC = 6, AD = 5, BC = 3, BD = 7, CD = 8. They satisfy the triangle inequality.

  1. MST by Prim from A: BC 3, AB 4, AD 5, total weight 12.
  2. Preorder walk from A (children in alphabetical order) gives A, B, C, D. The tour A–B–C–D–A costs 4 + 3 + 8 + 5 = 20.
  3. Guarantee: tour ≤ 2 × 12 = 24, and OPT ≥ MST = 12. The three distinct tours cost 20, 25 and 21, so the optimum is 20 and the approximation happens to be optimal here.

Polynomial arithmetic and the fast Fourier transform

Representations. A polynomial A(x) = a₀ + a₁x + … + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ of degree-bound n can be stored in three ways:

  • as a coefficient array (dense form);
  • as a linked list of (coefficient, exponent) terms sorted by exponent (sparse form, the classic linked-list application);
  • in point-value form {(x₀, A(x₀)), …, (xₙ₋₁, A(xₙ₋₁))} at n distinct points, which determines A uniquely.

Basic operations. Adding dense polynomials is Θ(n). Adding sparse lists with m and n terms is a merge on exponents, O(m + n): equal exponents are added, and a term whose sum is 0 is dropped. Horner’s rule evaluates A(x₀) = (…(aₙ₋₁x₀ + aₙ₋₂)x₀ + …)x₀ + a₀ with n − 1 multiplications and n − 1 additions for degree n − 1, which is optimal for general polynomials. Schoolbook multiplication forms every product aᵢbⱼ, which is Θ(n²). Karatsuba’s trick needs only three half-size products, (A₀ + A₁)(B₀ + B₁), A₀B₀ and A₁B₁, giving T(n) = 3T(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n^log₂3) ≈ Θ(n^1.585).

The idea behind FFT multiplication. In point-value form, multiplication is just pointwise multiplication, Θ(n), provided both factors are sampled at the same points. The product C = AB has degree-bound 2n − 1, so 2n points are needed. Evaluating at 2n arbitrary points costs Θ(n²) with Horner, but the FFT picks the complex roots of unity ω = e^(2πi/N), ω², …, ω^N = 1, where both evaluation and interpolation take Θ(N log N). The pipeline is:

  1. pad both coefficient vectors with zeros to length N, a power of 2 with N ≥ 2n;
  2. evaluate both by FFT (the DFT: yₖ = Σⱼ aⱼ ω^(jk));
  3. multiply the point values pointwise;
  4. interpolate by the inverse FFT: aⱼ = (1/N) Σₖ yₖ ω^(−jk).

The total is Θ(n log n).

Why the FFT is fast. Split A into even- and odd-indexed coefficients: A(x) = A_even(x²) + x·A_odd(x²). By the halving lemma, the squares of the N N-th roots of unity are the N/2 (N/2)-th roots of unity, each appearing twice. So two half-size DFTs suffice. They are combined by butterflies: y[k] = e[k] + ωᵏ·o[k] and y[k + N/2] = e[k] − ωᵏ·o[k], where e and o are the two half-size DFTs. The recurrence T(N) = 2T(N/2) + Θ(N) gives Θ(N log N). The radix-2 FFT has log₂ N stages of N/2 butterflies each: (N/2) log₂ N twiddle multiplications and N log₂ N complex additions. The iterative (Cooley–Tukey) version first permutes the input into bit-reversed order; for N = 8 that is a₀ a₄ a₂ a₆ a₁ a₅ a₃ a₇.

Example 8: multiplying (1 + 2x)(3 + x) with a 4-point FFT

The product has degree-bound 3, so N = 4 and ω = e^(2πi/4) = i. Padded vectors: a = (1, 2, 0, 0) and b = (3, 1, 0, 0).

  1. DFT(a) = (A(1), A(i), A(−1), A(−i)) = (3, 1 + 2i, −1, 1 − 2i).
  2. DFT(b) = (4, 3 + i, 2, 3 − i).
  3. Pointwise products: (12, 1 + 7i, −2, 1 − 7i).
  4. Inverse DFT (use ω⁻¹ = −i and divide by 4): c = (3, 7, 2, 0).

So the product is 3 + 7x + 2x², which schoolbook multiplication confirms. As a smaller check, the DFT of (1, 2, 3, 4) with ω = i is (10, −2 − 2i, −2, −2 + 2i).

NTA traps: (1) Sampling the product at only n points. The product needs 2n − 1 or more, so pad to 2n. (2) Sign convention. Cormen uses ω = e^(+2πi/N) for the DFT, while numpy and most engineering texts use e^(−2πi/N). The DFT of (1, 2, 3, 4) is then (10, −2 + 2i, −2, −2 − 2i), with the middle terms conjugated. Use the convention the question states.

Parallel algorithms for searching, merging and sorting

Searching. With p processors on a CREW PRAM, a sorted array of n keys can be probed at p equally spaced positions in one step. All processors read the key concurrently, and the comparisons cut the range into p + 1 parts. So the search takes ⌈log(n + 1)/log(p + 1)⌉ steps, which is Θ(log n / log p) and optimal on CREW (Snir). With p = 1 this is ordinary binary search, ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉. Searching an unsorted array of n keys with n processors takes O(1) on CRCW (the processor that finds the key writes the answer) but Θ(log n) on EREW, where even broadcasting the key costs log n steps.

Merging by ranking. For sorted arrays A and B with distinct keys, assign one processor per element. The processor for aᵢ binary-searches B for rank_B(aᵢ), the number of B-keys smaller than aᵢ, and writes aᵢ to output position i + rank_B(aᵢ), using 1-based i. B’s elements are handled symmetrically. Concurrent reads are needed because many processors search the same array (CREW). The time is O(log n) with 2n processors, but the work is O(n log n), so this is not cost-optimal. Splitting both arrays into blocks of size log n first gives an optimal O(log n)-time merge with n/log n processors. Batcher’s odd–even merge is the network form: it merges two sorted sequences of n keys each in depth log₂(2n).

Sorting.

  • Odd–even transposition sort on a linear array of n processors alternates compare-exchanges of pairs (1,2)(3,4)… and (2,3)(4,5)…. It always finishes within n phases, so it takes O(n) time with cost O(n²).
  • Bitonic sort (Batcher), for n = 2ᵏ, sorts bitonic sequences recursively. It has k(k + 1)/2 comparator stages of n/2 comparators each: depth O(log² n) and (n/4)·k(k + 1) comparators in total. For n = 8 that is 6 stages and 24 comparators.
  • Parallel merge sort with the O(log n) parallel merge takes O(log² n) time. Cole’s pipelined merge sort reaches O(log n) time with n processors on CREW (and EREW). The AKS network also has O(log n) depth, but with an impractically large constant.
  • Enumeration (rank) sort computes rank(xᵢ) = |{j : xⱼ < xᵢ}| with n² processors. This is O(1) on a CRCW PRAM whose concurrent writes add their values, and O(log n) on CREW, where the counts are summed in a tree.

Correctness of sorting networks is usually proved with the 0–1 principle: a comparator network that sorts every input of 0s and 1s sorts every input.

Example 9: parallel search, merge ranks and transposition phases

  • Search 80 sorted keys with p = 8 processors on CREW. Each step leaves at most 1/9 of the range, so ⌈log₉ 81⌉ = 2 steps are needed, against ⌈log₂ 81⌉ = 7 for binary search.
  • Merge A = (2, 7, 11, 15) and B = (3, 5, 12, 20). For 11: i = 3 and rank_B(11) = 2 (the keys 3 and 5), so 11 goes to position 5. The merged output 2 3 5 7 11 12 15 20 confirms it.
  • Odd–even transposition on (4, 3, 2, 1): after the odd phase 3 4 1 2, then 3 1 4 2, then 1 3 2 4, then 1 2 3 4. That is 4 = n phases.

NTA trap: O(log n) time does not mean cost-optimal. Merging by ranking with 2n processors has cost Θ(n log n) against Θ(n) sequentially. Cost-optimality needs p·Tₚ = Θ(T₁).

NTA traps

  • d modulo n. Wrong: “d = e⁻¹ mod 77.” The fix is d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n) = mod 60.
  • Choosing e not coprime to φ(n). e = 9 with φ = 60 has no inverse. Check the gcd first.
  • KMP without fallback. Wrong: “abacabab → last value 4” (extending the border blindly). The fix is to fall back through π until a match or 0.
  • 0-based versus 1-based shifts. Cormen’s shift s means a match starting at position s + 1. Read which one the question asks for.
  • Counting the valid match as spurious. Spurious hits are hash matches that fail verification only.
  • “Monte Carlo is always correct.” No: that is Las Vegas. Remember “Las Vegas never lies, Monte Carlo is always on time.”
  • “Randomized quicksort has worst case O(n log n).” Its expected time is O(n log n) for every input. Its worst case is still O(n²).
  • CREW reversed. CREW = concurrent read, exclusive write, not the other way.
  • Applying Fermat with a non-prime modulus. Use Euler’s φ(n) instead, and only when gcd(a, n) = 1.
  • TSP ratio without metric. The 2 and 3/2 bounds need the triangle inequality.

How NTA asks this

  • Numericals: the π array of a pattern, spurious-hit counts, RSA d or C, aᵇ mod m, GCD or inverse. Verify each candidate option instead of solving from scratch. For example, test e × d mod φ = 1, or check that 17 × 38 mod 43 = 1.
  • Match the lists: algorithm to complexity, PRAM model to its access rule, randomized algorithm to its type.
  • Statements and A-R: Las Vegas versus Monte Carlo, the RSA inverse modulus, the worst case of Rabin–Karp.
  • Code: short C loops implementing modular power, the prefix function or recursive GCD.

Mini A-R example

(A): Rabin–Karp runs in O((n − m + 1)m) time in the worst case. (R): Every hash match must be verified character by character, and a hash match can occur at every shift. Both are true and R explains A, so the answer is option 1.

Mini match example

Match: A. EREW, B. CREW, C. CRCW-common, D. CRCW-priority with I. lowest-index writer wins, II. no concurrent access, III. concurrent writers must agree, IV. only reads may be concurrent. Answer: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I. Fix the EREW row first, then use the word “common” to place C.

Remember: in π questions the first entry is always 0 and each entry is at most one more than the previous one (π[q + 1] ≤ π[q] + 1). Use these two facts to strike out options in seconds.

Public-key scheme: n = pq, φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1), public e with gcd(e, φ) = 1, private d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n); C = Mᵉ mod n, M = Cᵈ mod n.

quiz.question: What is the KMP prefix (failure) function π for the pattern P = abacabab? (Positions 1 to 8.)
quiz.explanation: π[q] is the longest proper border of P[1..q]. a:0, ab:0, aba:1 (a), abac:0, abaca:1 (a), abacab:2 (ab), abacaba:3 (aba). For abacabab: extending aba needs P[4] = c ≠ b, so fall back to π[3] = 1; P[2] = b matches, giving 2 (ab). So 0 0 1 0 1 2 3 2. Option 1 forgets the fallback.

quiz.question: In RSA, p = 7, q = 11 and the public exponent is e = 7. What is the private exponent d?
quiz.explanation: n = 77, φ(n) = 6 × 10 = 60. d = 7⁻¹ mod 60. Extended Euclid gives 60 = 8·7 + 4, 7 = 1·4 + 3, 4 = 1·3 + 1, so 1 = 2·60 − 17·7 and d ≡ −17 ≡ 43. Check: 7 × 43 = 301 = 5 × 60 + 1. The inverse is taken modulo φ(n) = 60, not n = 77.

lessons.title: Regular languages and finite automata
lessons.summaryHtml: A finite automaton reads a string one symbol at a time using a fixed, finite number of states. The languages it accepts are the regular languages. DFAs, NFAs, ε-NFAs, regular expressions and regular grammars all describe exactly this class. Subset construction turns an NFA into a DFA (at most 2n states). Partition refinement and Myhill–Nerode give the unique minimal DFA, which is the source of most "how many states" numericals. Arden's theorem (R = Q + RP ⇒ R = QP*) converts automata to regular expressions. Moore machines print n + 1 outputs and Mealy machines print n. Closure properties and the pumping lemma decide which languages are regular.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A finite automaton is a machine with a fixed, finite memory. It reads a string one symbol at a time, moves from state to state, and at the end says "accept" or "reject". It cannot count without limit and it cannot go back. The set of strings it accepts is a regular language. Regular expressions, DFAs, NFAs, ε-NFAs and regular grammars are five different ways of writing down exactly the same class of languages.

Think of a turnstile or a vending machine. It only needs to remember "which situation am I in now", never the whole history. That is the finite-state idea, and it is also how a compiler's lexical analyser recognises identifiers and numbers.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 8 is one of the heavier units in Paper 2, and finite automata are its most reliable source of marks. Expect questions on the number of states in a minimal DFA, which regular expressions are equivalent, which languages are regular, closure properties, subset construction and the output of Moore and Mealy machines. These questions are short to state and quick to solve once you know the standard patterns, so they are marks you should not lose.

Concepts in depth

1. Alphabets, strings and languages

  • An alphabet Σ is a finite, non-empty set of symbols, for example {0, 1}.
  • A string is a finite sequence of symbols. ε is the empty string, with |ε| = 0. Σk is the set of strings of length k, and it has |Σ|k members. Σ* is the set of all strings, including ε. Σ+ = Σ* − {ε}.
  • A language is any subset of Σ*. The empty language ∅ has no strings. The language {ε} has one string. They are different, and options often confuse them.
  • A string of length n has n + 1 prefixes and n + 1 suffixes (both counts include ε and the string itself). If all its symbols are distinct, it has n(n + 1)/2 non-empty substrings, plus ε.

2. Deterministic finite automata (DFA)

A DFA is a 5-tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F). Q is a finite set of states, δ : Q × Σ → Q is the transition function, q0 is the start state and F ⊆ Q is the set of final (accepting) states. From every state there is exactly one move on every symbol. A DFA in which some moves are missing is called partial; adding one non-accepting dead (trap) state makes it complete. Unless a question says otherwise, NET counts the states of a complete minimal DFA, so the dead state is counted.

Counting DFAs. With n states, an alphabet of m symbols and a fixed start state, each of the n·m transitions can go to any of n states, and any subset of states can be final. So there are nnm · 2n such DFAs. If the start state may also be chosen, multiply by n.

3. NFA and ε-NFA

In an NFA, δ : Q × Σ → 2Q. A state may have zero, one or many moves on a symbol. The NFA accepts a string if at least one path ends in a final state. An ε-NFA also allows moves on ε, without reading input. The ε-closure of a state is the set of states reachable from it using ε-moves only, including the state itself.

All three models accept exactly the regular languages. Nondeterminism adds convenience and can save states (exponentially), but it adds no power at this level. An ε-NFA converts to an NFA without ε-moves with the same number of states: the new δ'(q, a) is the ε-closure of the states reachable from ε-closure(q) on a, and a state becomes final if its ε-closure contains a final state.

4. Subset construction (NFA to DFA)

Each DFA state is a set of NFA states: all the places the NFA could be at that moment. Start with ε-closure(q0). For each new set S and each symbol a, the next set is the ε-closure of all moves from S on a. Keep only the sets you actually reach. A set is final if it contains at least one NFA final state. An NFA with n states gives a DFA with at most 2n states. The blow-up really is exponential. For "the k-th symbol from the right is a", the NFA has k + 1 states, while the minimal DFA needs 2k states because it must remember the last k symbols. That is half of the 2k+1 bound, but still exponential. (Other NFA families reach the full 2n.)

5. Minimising a DFA

Two states p and q are equivalent if, for every string w, δ*(p, w) is final exactly when δ*(q, w) is final. The minimal DFA merges each group of equivalent states. It is unique up to renaming of states. Minimal NFAs are not unique.

  1. Delete states that cannot be reached from the start state.
  2. 0-equivalence: split the states into two groups, final and non-final.
  3. k-equivalence: two states stay in the same group only if, on every symbol, they move into the same group of the previous partition.
  4. Repeat until a round makes no new split. Each final group is one state of the minimal DFA.

The table-filling (Myhill) method is the same idea written as a triangular table of pairs: first mark every (final, non-final) pair, then mark a pair whenever some symbol leads it to a marked pair. Unmarked pairs are equivalent.

6. Myhill–Nerode theorem

For a language L, say x ≡L y when, for every string z, xz ∈ L exactly when yz ∈ L. The theorem says: L is regular if and only if ≡L has finitely many classes, and the number of classes equals the number of states of the minimal complete DFA. This is the cleanest way to count states: list the different "situations" a prefix can be in. For "strings over {0, 1} ending in 00" the situations are: does not end in 0, ends in exactly one 0, ends in 00. That gives 3 classes, so 3 states. For {anbn}, the prefixes a, aa, aaa, … are pairwise distinguishable (aibi ∈ L but ajbi ∉ L), so there are infinitely many classes and the language is not regular.

7. Regular expressions

The base cases are ∅, ε and each symbol a. If r and s are regular expressions, then so are r + s (union), rs (concatenation) and r* (Kleene star). Precedence from high to low: star, concatenation, union. Useful identities:

  • ∅* = ε, ε* = ε, ∅r = r∅ = ∅, r + ∅ = r, εr = r.
  • r*r* = r*, (r*)* = r*, ε + rr* = r*, r(sr)* = (rs)*r.
  • (a + b)* = (a*b*)* = (a* + b*)* = a*(ba*)* = (a*b)*a* = (a + b*)*.
  • But a*b* ≠ (a + b)* and a* + b* ≠ (a + b)*: neither contains ba.

Conversions. Regex to ε-NFA uses Thompson's construction: a small fragment for each symbol, joined with ε-moves for union, concatenation and star. It uses at most 2k states for an expression with k symbols and operators. DFA to regex uses state elimination or Arden's theorem.

8. Arden's theorem

If P and Q are regular expressions and P does not contain ε, then the equation R = Q + RP has the unique solution R = QP*. Intuition: R is "Q followed by any number of P". To use it, write one equation per state: a state's expression is the sum of (predecessor state)(symbol), plus ε for the start state. Solve by substitution and take the sum of the final states' expressions. If P contains ε, the solution is no longer unique.

9. Moore and Mealy machines

These are finite automata with output and no final states. In a Moore machine the output depends on the state only (λ : Q → Δ). The start state prints before any input is read, so an input of length n gives n + 1 outputs. In a Mealy machine the output is attached to transitions (λ : Q × Σ → Δ), so an input of length n gives n outputs. They are equivalent if you ignore the Moore machine's first output. Moore to Mealy needs no extra states. Mealy to Moore may split a state into one copy for each different output with which the state can be entered, so the Moore machine can need up to |Q| × |Δ| states.

10. Closure properties and the pumping lemma

Regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement, difference, concatenation, Kleene star, reversal, homomorphism, inverse homomorphism, quotient, prefix and suffix. For complement, make the DFA complete and swap final and non-final states. This does not work directly on an NFA. For intersection, the product construction runs both DFAs together. With m and n states it needs at most m·n states. They are not closed under infinite union (every {aibi} is finite, but their union is anbn) and not under taking subsets (anbn ⊆ a*b*).

Pumping lemma. If L is regular, there is a p ≥ 1 such that every w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p can be split as w = xyz with |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1, and xyiz ∈ L for all i ≥ 0. It is a necessary condition only. You use it to prove a language is not regular, never to prove that it is. Languages that fail it include anbn, wwR, balanced parentheses, ap with p prime, an² and {w : #a(w) = #b(w)}.

Worked examples

Example 1: binary numbers divisible by 3

Read a binary number from the most significant bit. If the value so far is v with remainder r = v mod 3, reading bit b gives 2v + b. So the new remainder is (2r + b) mod 3, and the remainder is all we need to remember.

State (remainder)on 0on 1
→ * r0r0r1
r1r2r0
r2r1r2

Check 110 (six): r0 → r1 → r0 → r0, accepted. The minimal DFA has 3 states when ε is treated as the number 0 and accepted. Watch the convention: if ε must be rejected, the start state can no longer be final and the minimal DFA has 4 states. For divisor k, the count is k when k is odd. It can be smaller when k is even: divisible by 4 needs only 3 states (look at the last two bits), divisible by 6 needs 4, and divisible by 8 needs 4.

Example 2: subset construction

NFA for "second symbol from the right is 1" over {0, 1}: q0 loops on 0 and 1, q0 goes to q1 on 1, q1 goes to q2 on 0 or 1, and q2 is final.

DFA stateon 0on 1final?

C = {q0,q2}{q0} = A{q0,q1} = Byes
D = {q0,q1,q2}{q0,q2} = C{q0,q1,q2} = Dyes

4 reachable sets out of 23 = 8 possible. The DFA is already minimal: A, B, C and D stand for the last two symbols being 00, 01, 10 and 11. For "k-th symbol from the right", the same construction gives 2k states.

Example 3: minimisation by partition refinement

Start P; final states R, S, T; alphabet {0, 1}.

State01
→PQR

  1. V is unreachable, so delete it.
  2. 0-equivalence: {P, Q, U} and {R, S, T}.
  3. 1-equivalence: P and Q go to the non-final group on 0 and the final group on 1, but U goes to the non-final group on 1, so U splits off. R, S and T all go to T on 0 and to U on 1, so they stay together. The partition is {P, Q}, {U}, {R, S, T}.
  4. 2-equivalence: no new split, so we stop.

The minimal DFA has 3 states. It accepts "exactly one 1": {P, Q} means no 1 seen yet, {R, S, T} means exactly one 1, and U is the dead state.

Example 4: Arden's theorem

DFA over {a, b} for an even number of a's. q0 is the start state and the only final state. q0 goes to q1 on a and stays on b. q1 goes back to q0 on a and stays on b.

q0 = ε + q0 b + q1 a
q1 = q0 a + q1 b          → Arden (R = Q + RP): q1 = q0 a b*
q0 = ε + q0 b + q0 a b* a = ε + q0 (b + a b* a)
q0 = ε (b + a b* a)*      → answer (b + ab*a)*

b*(ab*ab*)* is an equivalent answer. The tempting b*(ab*a)*b* is wrong: it rejects aabaa, which has four a's. Brute-force checking of all strings up to length 12 confirms both claims.

Example 5: Moore versus Mealy output

A Moore machine whose state is the remainder mod 3 of the binary number read so far (Example 1), printing that remainder. Input 1101:

Prefixε1111101101
Value013613
Output01001

The Moore output is 0 1 0 0 1: five symbols for four inputs. The equivalent Mealy machine prints 1 0 0 1.

Example 6: counting states with Myhill–Nerode

L = strings over {a, b} with #a ≡ 0 (mod 3) and #b ≡ 0 (mod 2). A prefix is described by the pair (#a mod 3, #b mod 2). All 3 × 2 = 6 pairs are reachable and pairwise distinguishable, so the minimal DFA has 6 states. This matches the product construction bound m·n = 3·2. Changing "and" to "or" still gives 6 states: only the set of final states changes.

11. Regular grammars

A grammar is right-linear if every production has the form A → wB or A → w, where w is a string of terminals (possibly ε) and B is a single variable at the right end. It is left-linear if every production has the form A → Bw or A → w. A regular grammar (Chomsky Type 3) is either kind. The strict textbook form allows only A → aB, A → a, and S → ε when S never appears on a right side; every right-linear grammar can be brought into it.

Right-linear grammar to finite automaton. Make one state per variable plus one extra final state F. The start state is S.

  • A → aB gives a transition from A to B on a.
  • A → a gives a transition from A to F on a.
  • A → ε makes A a final state.

The result is an NFA with at most |V| + 1 states that accepts exactly L(G). Each derivation step corresponds to one move. In the strict form, a string of length n has a derivation of n steps, or n + 1 if it ends with an A → ε rule.

Finite automaton to right-linear grammar. Make one variable per state. For each move δ(p, a) = q write p → aq, and for each final state q write q → ε. The start variable is the start state. So right-linear grammars generate exactly the regular languages.

Left-linear grammars. Reverse every right side. A left-linear grammar for L becomes a right-linear grammar for LR. Build its automaton, then reverse the automaton (swap start and final, reverse every arrow). Since regular languages are closed under reversal, left-linear grammars also generate exactly the regular languages.

NTA trap. A grammar that mixes left-linear and right-linear rules is only a linear grammar, and it can generate a non-regular language: S → aA, A → Sb | b is a mix of the two forms and generates {anbn | n ≥ 1}. The opposite trap also appears: a grammar that is not regular in form, such as S → aSa | aSb | bSa | bSb | a | b, can still generate a regular language (here, all strings of odd length).

Example 7: from a right-linear grammar to an NFA

G: S → aS | bA, A → aA | bS | ε.

  1. States S (start) and A. A → ε makes A final. No rule of the form X → a exists, so the extra state F is not needed.
  2. Moves: S –a→ S, S –b→ A, A –a→ A, A –b→ S.
  3. Reading a leaves the state unchanged, and reading b toggles between S and A. The machine is in A exactly when it has read an odd number of b's.

So L(G) = {w ∈ {a, b}* | w has an odd number of b's}, and the automaton is already a complete 2-state DFA. For a left-linear example, G': S → Ab | Sb, A → Aa | a generates a+b+: A produces a+, and S appends one or more b's on the right.

NTA traps

  • Forgetting the dead state. "Strings of length exactly 2" looks like 3 states. The complete DFA needs 4, because longer strings need a trap state. Unless partial DFAs are allowed, count the trap.
  • The ε convention for divisibility. For "divisible by 3", the answer is 3 if ε counts as 0 and 4 if ε must be rejected. Read the wording.
  • 2n is a bound, not the answer. Subset construction usually reaches far fewer than 2n sets. Only count the sets you actually reach.
  • Complementing an NFA by swapping final states. This is wrong. Convert to a complete DFA first.
  • a* + b* or a*b* taken as (a + b)*. Test with ba. Neither contains it.
  • Using the pumping lemma to prove regularity. The lemma is only necessary. To show a language is regular, build a DFA or a regex, or use closure properties.
  • "Every subset of a regular language is regular." False: every language over Σ is a subset of Σ*.
  • Moore output length. The answer is n + 1, not n, because the start state prints before any input is read.
  • Non-regular looking languages that are regular. {w : #ab(w) = #ba(w)} looks like it needs counting. It is regular: it is exactly ε plus the strings that start and end with the same symbol.

How NTA asks this

  • Numerical: "minimum number of states in a DFA accepting …". Name the Myhill–Nerode situations, add the dead state, and check against the fact sheet.
  • Match the list: regular expressions against language descriptions, or languages against state counts. Test each expression on two or three short strings (ε, a single symbol, ba).
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: NFA versus DFA equivalence, uniqueness of the minimal DFA, closure under complement, the pumping lemma being necessary but not sufficient.
  • Multiple statements: "which of the following are regular?" or "which expressions equal (a + b)*?".
Mini example (A–R): A: "Regular languages are closed under complement." R: "In a complete DFA, swapping final and non-final states accepts exactly the complement." Both are true, and R is the proof of A, so the answer is option 1. If R had said "in an NFA", R would be false, and the answer would be option 3.
Elimination trick: for "which regex equals X", reject any option that fails on ε, on a one-symbol string, or on ba or ab. That usually leaves one option within 30 seconds.

terms.definition: A 5-tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) with exactly one transition from each state on each symbol.
An automaton whose transition function returns a set of states. It accepts if at least one path ends in a final state. Same power as a DFA.
The set of states reachable from a state using only ε-moves, including the state itself.
NFA to DFA conversion in which each DFA state is a set of NFA states. It gives at most 2^n states.
A non-final state that loops to itself on every symbol. It makes a DFA complete and is counted in minimal-DFA state counts.
L is regular if and only if the relation "x and y have the same future in L" has finitely many classes. The number of classes equals the number of states of the minimal DFA.
If ε ∉ P, the equation R = Q + RP has the unique solution R = QP*.
A finite-state transducer whose output depends on the state only. An input of length n gives n + 1 outputs.
A finite-state transducer whose output depends on the state and the input symbol. An input of length n gives n outputs.
Every long enough string in a regular language splits as xyz with |xy| ≤ p and |y| ≥ 1, and xy^i z stays in L for all i ≥ 0. It is a necessary condition only.

lessons.examTip: For any "minimum states" question, list the distinct situations a prefix can be in (Myhill–Nerode) and add the dead state. The k-th symbol from the right needs 2^k states, and the k-th from the left needs k + 2.

steps: Open practice-set.md and solve problems 1–8 in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
For problems 1–5 and 14–15, write the Myhill–Nerode situations in words before counting states, and add the dead state where one exists.
Solve problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For the Moore and Mealy problems, write the output under each input symbol.
Check with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (dead state, ε convention, 2^n bound, product not fully distinguishable, Moore n + 1).
Redo problem 5 by partition refinement on paper, showing the 0-, 1- and 2-equivalence partitions.
Redo every wrong problem after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.

Every state count justified by listing the equivalence classes

quiz.question: Strings over {0, 1} are read as binary numbers with the most significant bit first (ε is taken as the number 0). What is the number of states in the minimal complete DFA that accepts exactly the strings whose value is divisible by 5?
quiz.explanation: Track the remainder r = value mod 5. Reading bit b gives (2r + b) mod 5, so the states are r = 0…4. All five remainders are reachable and pairwise distinguishable, because each remainder needs a different continuation to reach 0. The answer is 5. 6 would be right only if ε had to be rejected (then the start state splits from remainder 0). 32 = 2^5 confuses this with the k-th-from-right pattern.

quiz.question: What is the number of states in the minimal complete DFA over {a, b} that accepts all strings whose 4th symbol from the right end is a?
quiz.explanation: The DFA must remember the last 4 symbols, because any of them may become the 4th from the right later. All 2^4 = 16 windows are distinguishable. The answer is 16. 6 = k + 2 is the answer for the 4th symbol from the left. An NFA needs only 5 states (k + 1), which is the 5 trap.

quiz.explanation: A: lengths 0, 1, 2, 3, plus a dead state for longer strings, gives 3 + 2 = 5 (II). B: we need "no progress", "seen a" and "found ab", which is 3 (I). C: the pairs (#a mod 3, #b mod 2) give 3 × 2 = 6 (III). D: 3rd from the right needs 2^3 = 8 (IV). So A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV. Option 2 swaps C and D.

quiz.explanation: Equal counts need an unbounded counter. The prefixes a, aa, aaa, … are pairwise distinguishable, so there are infinitely many Myhill–Nerode classes. Option 1 is finite, so it is regular. Option 2 is a*b*. Option 4 is (aa)*.

lessons.title: Context-free languages and pushdown automata
lessons.summaryHtml: A context-free grammar rewrites single variables, A → α, and describes nested structure such as aⁿbⁿ and balanced brackets. The matching machine is the pushdown automaton, a finite automaton with a stack. A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two parse trees. Grammars are simplified in the order ε, unit, useless. In CNF (A → BC | a) a string of length n needs exactly 2n − 1 derivation steps, and in GNF (A → aα) it needs n. NPDAs accept the same class by final state or by empty stack, but DPDAs are weaker and define the DCFLs. CYK decides membership in O(n³). CFLs are closed under union, concatenation and star but not under intersection or complement. DCFLs are the reverse on complement and union.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A finite automaton cannot match an opening bracket with its closing bracket, because it has no memory that grows with the input. A context-free grammar (CFG) describes such nested structure with rewriting rules, such as S → aSb | ε. The matching machine is a pushdown automaton (PDA): a finite automaton plus a stack. Every programming language's syntax (nested blocks, balanced parentheses, arithmetic expressions) is described mainly by a CFG, which is why this chapter leads straight into parsing in compilers.

Why it matters for NET

Context-free languages give a steady set of questions in Unit 8. The favourites are: which class a given language belongs to (regular, DCFL, CFL or not CFL), CNF and GNF derivation lengths, ambiguity and counting parse trees, closure and decision properties of CFLs and DCFLs, PDA acceptance modes, the CYK algorithm, and the pumping lemma for CFLs. Many of these come as Match the List or Statement I/II questions that test one precise fact each.

Concepts in depth

1. Grammars, derivations and parse trees

A CFG is a 4-tuple G = (V, T, P, S). V is a set of variables (non-terminals), T is a set of terminals, P is a set of productions of the form A → α with A ∈ V and α ∈ (V ∪ T)*, and S is the start variable. "Context-free" means that the left side is a single variable, so it can be rewritten wherever it appears.

  • A derivation applies one production per step. In a leftmost derivation the leftmost variable is always replaced. In a rightmost one, the rightmost variable is replaced. Every string in (V ∪ T)* reachable from S is a sentential form.
  • A parse tree has S at the root, variables at internal nodes and terminals (or ε) at the leaves. Its yield is the string of leaves read left to right. Parse trees, leftmost derivations and rightmost derivations are in one-to-one correspondence.

2. Ambiguity

A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two different parse trees. Equivalently, it has two leftmost derivations, or two rightmost derivations. For example, E → E + E | E * E | id gives two trees for id + id * id. With k operators, the number of trees is the Catalan number Ck = (2k)! / ((k + 1)! k!): 1, 2, 5, 14, 42 for k = 1…5. The ambiguity can be removed by encoding precedence and associativity: E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → (E) | id.

Some languages are inherently ambiguous: every grammar for them is ambiguous. The standard example is {aibjck | i = j or j = k}, because strings with i = j = k must have two trees. Deciding whether an arbitrary CFG is ambiguous is undecidable.

3. Simplifying a grammar

  1. Remove ε-productions. Find the nullable variables (A is nullable if A ⇒* ε). For each production, add every version with some nullable occurrences dropped, but never add A → ε. Only ε itself is lost from the language. If ε ∈ L, keep S → ε with a new start symbol that does not appear on any right side.
  2. Remove unit productions A → B. For every unit pair (A, B) with A ⇒* B through unit rules, copy B's non-unit productions to A.
  3. Remove useless symbols. First remove the non-generating ones (they derive no terminal string). Then remove the unreachable ones. The order matters: doing reachability first can leave useless symbols behind.

The safe overall order is ε, then unit, then useless. Removing ε-productions can create unit productions, and removing unit productions can make symbols unreachable.

4. Chomsky normal form (CNF)

Every production has the form A → BC (two variables) or A → a (one terminal). S → ε is allowed only when ε ∈ L and S does not appear on any right side. To convert: simplify, replace terminals inside long bodies by new variables (Aa → a), and break bodies longer than two into a chain of binary rules.

  • A string of length n ≥ 1 takes exactly 2n − 1 derivation steps: n − 1 steps of the form A → BC (each adds one variable) and n steps of the form A → a (each turns a variable into a terminal).
  • The parse tree has n leaves and 2n − 1 variable nodes. Its part made of binary rules is a full binary tree with n leaves. So the tree height, counted in edges down to the terminals, is at least ⌈log2 n⌉ + 1 and at most n.
  • CNF enables the CYK algorithm and the pumping lemma proof. If the longest path has k variables, the yield has length at most 2k−1.

5. Greibach normal form (GNF)

Every production has the form A → aα, where a is a terminal and α is a (possibly empty) string of variables. Each step produces exactly one terminal, so a string of length n takes exactly n steps. Conversion requires removing left recursion (A → Aα | β becomes A → βA', A' → αA' | ε, and then ε is eliminated). GNF is the grammar form that maps directly onto a PDA with no ε-moves on input, which reads one symbol per move.

6. Pushdown automata

A PDA is a 7-tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, Z0, F) with δ : Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) × Γ → finite subsets of Q × Γ*. A move reads one input symbol or ε, pops the stack top, and pushes a string. An instantaneous description is (state, remaining input, stack).

  • Acceptance by final state: the input is consumed and the PDA is in a state of F. Acceptance by empty stack: the input is consumed and the stack is empty. For nondeterministic PDAs these two modes accept the same class, the CFLs, and each mode can simulate the other.
  • A DPDA has at most one choice in every situation, including no conflict between an ε-move and an input move. DPDAs accepting by final state define the DCFLs. DPDAs accepting by empty stack accept only DCFLs with the prefix property (no string in L is a proper prefix of another). So for DPDAs, empty-stack acceptance is strictly weaker.
  • Regular ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL, and both inclusions are proper. {wcwR} is a DCFL, because the centre marker c tells the DPDA when to switch from pushing to popping. {wwR} is a CFL but not a DCFL, because the machine must guess the middle. Every DCFL has an unambiguous grammar (in fact an LR(1) grammar), but some unambiguous CFLs, including wwR, are not DCFLs.
  • CFG ↔ PDA: every CFG has an equivalent one-state PDA that simulates leftmost derivations on the stack, and every PDA has an equivalent CFG (the triple construction [pXq]).

7. The CYK algorithm

For a grammar in CNF and a string w of length n, CYK fills a triangular table. Cell (i, l) holds every variable that derives the substring starting at position i with length l. Length-1 cells come from the rules A → a. A longer cell tries every split into two shorter pieces and adds A whenever A → BC matches the two pieces. There are n(n + 1)/2 cells, and each tries up to n − 1 splits, so the running time is O(n3 · |G|). w ∈ L exactly when S is in the top cell. CYK is the standard proof that membership for CFLs is decidable.

8. Closure and decision properties

OperationCFLDCFL
UnionYesNo
IntersectionNoNo
ComplementNoYes
Concatenation, Kleene starYesNo
ReversalYesNo
Intersection with a regular languageYesYes
HomomorphismYesNo
Inverse homomorphismYesYes
Difference L − R, with R regularYesYes

Why CFLs fail intersection: L1 = {anbncm} and L2 = {ambncn} are both CFLs, but L1 ∩ L2 = {anbncn} is not. Complement then fails too, because union plus complement would give intersection by De Morgan's law. DCFLs are the reverse: complement works (a DPDA can be made to always finish reading its input, and then its final states are swapped), so union must fail.

Decidable for CFGs: membership (CYK), emptiness (is S generating?), finiteness (after simplification, is there a cycle in the variable dependency graph?). Undecidable for CFGs: ambiguity, equivalence of two CFGs, L(G) = Σ*, L(G1) ∩ L(G2) = ∅, L(G1) ⊆ L(G2), and whether L(G) is regular. For DCFLs, equivalence is decidable (Sénizergues, 1997), and so is L = Σ* (by complement closure).

9. Pumping lemma for CFLs

If L is context-free, there is a p such that every z ∈ L with |z| ≥ p can be written as z = uvwxy with |vwx| ≤ p, |vx| ≥ 1, and uviwxiy ∈ L for all i ≥ 0. The proof takes a CNF parse tree tall enough that some variable repeats on a path. For {anbncn}, take z = apbpcp. Since |vwx| ≤ p, the window vwx touches at most two of the three blocks, so pumping changes at most two of the counts. Standard non-CFLs are anbncn, ww, an², ap (p prime) and anbmcndm. Every CFL over a one-letter alphabet is regular (a consequence of Parikh's theorem). That is why an² fails at once.

Worked examples

Example 1: CNF conversion and derivation length

Grammar: S → aSb | ab. Replace terminals by variables, A → a and B → b, which gives S → ASB | AB. Break the length-3 body using C → SB:

S → AC | AB      C → SB      A → a      B → b

Derive aaabbb (n = 6). The leftmost derivation is S ⇒ AC ⇒ aC ⇒ aSB ⇒ aACB ⇒ aaCB ⇒ aaSBB ⇒ aaABBB ⇒ aaaBBB ⇒ aaabBB ⇒ aaabbB ⇒ aaabbb. That is 11 = 2 × 6 − 1 steps: 5 binary steps and 6 terminal steps. Exhaustive search over all leftmost derivations confirms 11 is the only possible length. The converted grammar generates exactly {anbn | n ≥ 1}, checked up to length 10.

Example 2: CYK on aabb

Using the CNF grammar of Example 1. Row l lists the cells for substrings of length l, starting at positions 1, 2, …

LengthCells (left to right)
1{A} a, {A} a, {B} b, {B} b
2∅ (aa), {S} (ab), ∅ (bb)
3∅ (aab), {C} (abb: S·B from ab + b)
4{S} (aabb: A·C from a + abb)

S is in the top cell, so aabb ∈ L. For abab, the length-3 and length-4 cells are all empty, so it is rejected.

Example 3: counting parse trees

Grammar E → E + E | E * E | id.

  • id + id * id: the top operator can be + or *, which gives 2 trees.
  • id + id + id + id and id * id + id * id: 3 operators give C3 = 5 trees each.
  • Grammar S → SS | a on an: 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42 trees for n = 1…6, that is Cn−1.

All counts were computed by dynamic programming over all splits.

Example 4: simplification in the right order

S → AB | D      A → aA | ε      B → bB | b      C → c      D → Da
  1. ε: only A is nullable. We get S → AB | B | D and A → aA | a.
  2. Unit: S → B and S → D are unit rules. Copy their bodies: S → AB | bB | b | Da.
  3. Useless: D never produces a terminal string (D → Da loops), so remove D and S → Da. C is unreachable, so remove it.
S → AB | bB | b      A → aA | a      B → bB | b          (language a*b⁺)

Example 5: PDA for aⁿbⁿ and counting moves

The PDA pushes X for each a, switches state at the first b and pops one X per b, then pops Z0 on ε and accepts by empty stack. On a4b4 it makes 4 push moves, 4 pop moves and 1 final ε-move: 9 = 2n + 1 moves. The stack reaches its maximum height of 5 (Z0 plus four X's) after the last a.

Example 6: pumping lemma for aⁿbⁿcⁿ

Assume the language is a CFL with constant p, and pick z = apbpcp. Since |vwx| ≤ p, vwx lies inside a*b* or inside b*c*. It cannot contain both a's and c's. Pumping with i = 2 increases at most two of the three counts, and |vx| ≥ 1 means at least one count changes. So uv2wx2y has unequal counts (or symbols out of order). This is a contradiction, so the language is not context-free.

10. PDA and CFG are equivalent: the two constructions

CFG to PDA. Given G = (V, T, P, S), build a PDA with a single state q that accepts by empty stack. The stack starts with S.

  • For each production A → α: δ(q, ε, A) contains (q, α). This expands the variable on top of the stack.
  • For each terminal a: δ(q, a, a) = {(q, ε)}. This matches an input symbol against the stack top and pops it.

The stack always holds the unmatched part of a leftmost sentential form, so the PDA guesses a leftmost derivation. An accepting run makes one expand move per derivation step and one match move per input symbol. For a grammar in CNF, a string of length n has a (2n − 1)-step derivation, so the run takes (2n − 1) + n = 3n − 1 moves. If G is in GNF, every production A → aα becomes the single move δ(q, a, A) ∋ (q, α), which reads a symbol at every step, so the run takes exactly n moves.

PDA to CFG (the triple construction). Assume the PDA accepts by empty stack. For every pair of states p, r and every stack symbol X, make a variable [pXr]. It generates exactly the inputs that take the PDA from state p with X on top to state r with X popped (and nothing below X touched). A move δ(p, a, X) ∋ (q, Y1…Yk) gives the productions [pXrk] → a[qY1r1][r1Y2r2]…[rk−1Ykrk] for every choice of states r1, …, rk. Add S → [q0Z0r] for every state r. With |Q| states and |Γ| stack symbols there are |Q|2 · |Γ| triple variables plus S.

Example 7: sizes of the two constructions

(a) A PDA with 2 states and 3 stack symbols gives 22 × 3 = 12 triple variables, and 13 variables with the new start symbol.

(b) CNF grammar S → AS | a, A → a, input aaaaa (n = 5). The leftmost derivation uses S → AS four times, A → a four times and S → a once: 9 = 2 × 5 − 1 steps. The one-state PDA therefore makes 9 expand moves and 5 match moves: 14 = 3n − 1 moves.

11. Unsolvable problems for context-free languages

The undecidable CFG questions are not arbitrary. They come from two reductions.

From PCP. Take a PCP instance with lists A = (x1, …, xk) and B = (y1, …, yk). Add k new index symbols 1, …, k and build

G_A:  S_A → x_i S_A i  |  x_i i     (i = 1 … k)
G_B:  S_B → y_i S_B i  |  y_i i

Each grammar is unambiguous, because the index symbols at the end spell out, in reverse, which rule was used. A string lies in both languages exactly when xi1…xim = yi1…yim for the same index sequence, that is, when the instance has a solution. Hence:

  • "Is L(G1) ∩ L(G2) = ∅?" is undecidable.
  • "Is G ambiguous?" is undecidable: take S → SA | SB. A string has two parse trees exactly when it is in both languages.

From computation histories. For a TM M, the set of strings that are not valid accepting computations of M (written with every second configuration reversed) is a CFL: a PDA can guess and check one local error. It equals Σ* exactly when M accepts nothing. So "Is L(G) = Σ*?" is undecidable. It follows that equivalence L(G1) = L(G2) (compare with a grammar for Σ*), inclusion L(G1) ⊆ L(G2), "Is L(G) regular?", "Is the complement of L(G) context-free?" and "Is L(G) inherently ambiguous?" are undecidable too.

What stays decidable: membership (CYK), emptiness, finiteness, removing useless symbols, and "Is L(G) ∩ R = ∅?" for a regular R. The last holds because L(G) ∩ R is again a CFL whose grammar can be built, and CFL emptiness is decidable.

NTA trap. Wrong: "intersection emptiness is undecidable for CFGs, so it is undecidable when one of them is regular." Fix: CFL ∩ regular is a CFL, so emptiness of L(G) ∩ R is decidable. Only CFL ∩ CFL is the PCP case.

Example 8: a PCP instance as an ambiguous grammar

A = (bab, aa, b), B = (ab, a, abb). The sequence 2, 1, 3 is a solution: aa·bab·b = aababb and a·ab·abb = aababb. In S → SA | SB, the string aababb312 (the solution string followed by the indices in reverse) is derived once through SA and once through SB, so it has 2 parse trees, while GA alone gives it exactly 1. An algorithm that decided ambiguity would therefore decide PCP.

NTA traps

  • 2n instead of 2n − 1. In CNF there are n terminal steps and only n − 1 binary steps. A binary tree with n leaves has n − 1 internal nodes.
  • Treating ambiguity as a property of the language. Ambiguity belongs to a grammar. A language is inherently ambiguous only when every grammar for it is ambiguous.
  • "CFLs are closed under intersection." False. They are closed only under intersection with a regular language. This is the most common Statement I/II trap.
  • Mixing up CFL and DCFL closure. DCFLs are closed under complement but not union. CFLs are the opposite.
  • "Final state and empty stack are always equivalent." This holds for NPDAs only. For DPDAs, empty stack is weaker.
  • "Unambiguous implies deterministic." False: wwᴿ has an unambiguous grammar but is not a DCFL. The true direction is DCFL ⇒ unambiguous.
  • Removing unreachable symbols before non-generating ones. This can leave useless symbols. Remove non-generating symbols first.
  • Using the regular pumping lemma for CFLs. The CFL version pumps two pieces, v and x, together, with |vwx| ≤ p.

How NTA asks this

  • Numerical: derivation steps in CNF or GNF, number of parse trees, CYK cell contents, PDA move counts.
  • Match the list: languages against classes (regular, DCFL, CFL, not CFL), or problems against decidable/undecidable.
  • Statement I/II and A–R: closure under intersection or complement, NPDA versus DPDA acceptance, inherent ambiguity.
  • Multiple statements: "which of the following are context-free?" or "which problems are decidable for CFGs?".
Mini example (Statement I/II): I: "CFLs are closed under intersection." II: "The intersection of a CFL with a regular language is a CFL." I is false (the aⁿbⁿcⁿ counterexample) and II is true (run the PDA and the DFA together). So the answer is option 4.
Elimination trick: to classify a language, ask how many independent counters it needs. One matching (aⁿbⁿ) means CFL. Two interleaved or crossing matchings (aⁿbⁿcⁿ, aⁿbᵐcⁿdᵐ, ww) mean not CFL. If the matching point must be guessed (wwᴿ), the language is not a DCFL.

terms.definition: A 4-tuple (V, T, P, S) whose productions have a single variable on the left side.
A grammar in which some string has two or more parse trees (equivalently, two leftmost derivations).
A CFL for which every grammar is ambiguous, e.g. {aⁱbʲcᵏ | i = j or j = k}.
Every production is A → BC or A → a. A string of length n takes 2n − 1 derivation steps.
Every production is A → aα with α a string of variables. A string of length n takes n derivation steps.
A variable that can derive ε. It is found first when removing ε-productions.
A finite automaton with a stack: (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, Z0, F). It accepts by final state or by empty stack.
A language accepted by a deterministic PDA by final state. It is closed under complement, always has an unambiguous grammar, and lies strictly between the regular languages and the CFLs.
Dynamic-programming membership test for a CNF grammar. It fills n(n + 1)/2 cells in O(n³·|G|) time.
Every long enough z in a CFL splits as uvwxy with |vwx| ≤ p and |vx| ≥ 1, and uvⁱwxⁱy stays in L for all i ≥ 0.

lessons.examTip: Memorise three numbers and two asymmetries: CNF needs 2n − 1 steps, GNF needs n steps, and CYK runs in O(n³). CFLs are closed under union but not complement, while DCFLs are closed under complement but not union. Both are closed under intersection with a regular language.

quiz.question: A context-free grammar G is in Chomsky normal form and has no ε-productions. How many steps does any derivation of a string of length 10 in G take?
quiz.explanation: Each rule A → BC adds one variable, and each rule A → a turns one variable into a terminal. Going from 1 variable to 10 variables needs 9 binary steps, and then 10 terminal steps are needed: 9 + 10 = 19 = 2n − 1. 20 is the 2n trap.

quiz.question: A grammar G is in Greibach normal form. How many steps does a leftmost derivation of a string of length 10 take?
quiz.explanation: Every GNF production A → aα produces exactly one terminal, and terminals are never produced otherwise. So a string of length n needs exactly n steps: 10. 19 is the CNF answer.

b: I. Regular
II. DCFL but not regular
