lessons.title: Turing machines and computability
lessons.summaryHtml: A Turing machine is a finite control with an unbounded read–write tape. Multi-tape, nondeterministic and two-stack variants all have the same power, and the Church–Turing thesis identifies TMs with algorithms. The Chomsky hierarchy pairs grammars with machines: type 0 with TMs, type 1 (context-sensitive) with LBAs, type 2 with PDAs, and type 3 with finite automata. A language is recursive if a TM always halts on it, and RE if a TM accepts exactly it. L is recursive if and only if both L and its complement are RE. The halting problem is RE but undecidable, and its complement is not RE. Reductions carry undecidability from a known problem to a new one. Rice's theorem makes every non-trivial property of L(M) undecidable. PCP is undecidable and is used to prove results about CFGs.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A Turing machine (TM) is a finite control with an unbounded tape that it can read, write and move over in both directions. It is the simplest model that can compute everything any real computer can, and it is the formal meaning of "algorithm". Once we have it, we can ask the deepest question of the unit: are there problems that no algorithm can ever solve? The answer is yes. The halting problem, Post's correspondence problem and every non-trivial question about what a program's language is (Rice's theorem) are all undecidable.

Why it matters for NET

This topic yields conceptual questions almost every cycle. The common ones are: the Chomsky hierarchy (grammar, machine, example), recursive versus recursively enumerable languages, decidable versus undecidable problems, Rice's theorem, reductions, PCP, and the big closure and decision tables across all language classes. Numerical questions are rarer: TM traces and step counts, PCP solutions, and LBA configuration counts. Match the List and multi-statement questions dominate here, so exact facts matter.

Concepts in depth

1. The Turing machine

A TM is a 7-tuple M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, B, F). Σ ⊂ Γ is the input alphabet, Γ is the tape alphabet, B ∈ Γ − Σ is the blank, and δ : Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R} is a partial function. In one move the machine reads the cell under the head, writes a symbol, moves one cell, and changes state. A configuration (instantaneous description) is written as the tape contents with the state placed just before the scanned symbol, for example 10q111. On an input, a TM can accept (halt in a final state), reject (halt in a non-final state), or loop forever. That third outcome is the source of all undecidability.

A TM can also compute a function (a transducer): the output is what is left on the tape when it halts. Standard constructions are binary increment, unary addition, copying, and marking symbols (X/Y) to compare counts.

2. Variants, all equal in power

VariantSimulation by a standard TM
Two-way infinite tape, stay option, semi-infinite tapeSame power, constant-factor overhead
Multi-tape TM (k tapes)Same power; a machine running t(n) steps is simulated in O(t(n)2)
Multi-head, multi-track, multi-dimensional tapeSame power, polynomial overhead
Nondeterministic TMSame power (breadth-first search over computations); the known simulation is exponential in time
PDA with two stacks, machine with two countersSame power as a TM
Enumerator (prints the strings of L)Enumerates exactly the RE languages

A universal TM U takes an encoding ⟨M, w⟩ and simulates M on w. The Church–Turing thesis says that every effectively computable function is TM-computable. It is a thesis, not a theorem, because "effectively computable" is informal. A PDA with one stack, an LBA and a finite automaton are all weaker than a TM.

3. Context-sensitive languages and the LBA

A context-sensitive grammar has productions α → β with |α| ≤ |β| (non-contracting), optionally with S → ε when S is not on any right side. Equivalently, it has rules of the form αAβ → αγβ with γ ≠ ε. A linear bounded automaton is a nondeterministic TM that never leaves the cells holding its input (between end-markers). The CSLs are exactly the languages accepted by LBAs. On an input of length n, an LBA with state set Q and tape alphabet Γ has at most |Q| · n · |Γ|n configurations. That number is finite, so a run that goes on longer must repeat a configuration and loop. This is why membership for CSLs is decidable and every CSL is recursive. Emptiness for CSLs is undecidable. CSLs are closed under complement (Immerman–Szelepcsényi, 1988). Whether deterministic LBAs are as powerful as nondeterministic ones (the "LBA problem") is still open. Examples: anbncn, ww, an², a2ⁿ.

4. The Chomsky hierarchy

TypeGrammar (productions)MachineLanguage class
0Unrestricted α → β (α contains a variable)Turing machineRecursively enumerable
1Context-sensitive, |α| ≤ |β|Linear bounded automatonContext-sensitive
2Context-free, A → γPushdown automaton (nondeterministic)Context-free
3Regular (right- or left-linear), A → aB | aFinite automatonRegular

The full chain is Regular ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL ⊂ CSL ⊂ Recursive ⊂ RE ⊂ all languages, and every inclusion is proper. The recursive languages have no grammar type of their own in the hierarchy.

5. Recursive and recursively enumerable languages

  • L is recursive (decidable) if some TM halts on every input and accepts exactly L. Such a TM is a decider or total TM.
  • L is recursively enumerable (RE, semi-decidable, Turing-recognisable) if some TM accepts exactly L. On strings not in L, that TM may reject or loop.
  • Key theorem: L is recursive if and only if both L and its complement L̄ are RE. To decide, run the two recognisers in parallel. One of them must accept.
  • So if L is RE but not recursive, L̄ is not RE. This is the standard way to prove that a language is not even recognisable.
  • Recursive languages are closed under complement. RE languages are closed under union and intersection but not complement.
  • Counting argument: TMs can be encoded as finite strings, so there are countably many of them. There are uncountably many languages over Σ (the power set of the countable set Σ*). So most languages are not RE. The diagonal language Ld = {⟨M⟩ | M does not accept ⟨M⟩} is a concrete example of a language that is not RE.

6. The halting problem

HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ | M halts on input w} and ATM = {⟨M, w⟩ | M accepts w} are both RE but not recursive. They are RE because the universal TM simulates M on w and accepts if the simulation accepts (or halts). They are undecidable by diagonalisation. Suppose a decider H existed. Build D, which on input ⟨M⟩ runs H on ⟨M, ⟨M⟩⟩ and does the opposite: it loops if H says "halts" and halts if H says "loops". Running D on ⟨D⟩ gives a contradiction either way. Therefore the complements of HALT and ATM are not RE.

7. Reductions

A many-one reduction A ≤m B is a computable function f with w ∈ A ⇔ f(w) ∈ B. Knowledge flows in two directions:

  • If B is decidable (or RE), then A is decidable (or RE). Information flows down the arrow.
  • If A is undecidable (or not RE), then B is undecidable (or not RE). Hardness flows up the arrow.

To prove P undecidable, reduce a known undecidable problem (HALT, ATM, PCP) to P, never the other way round. Reducing P to HALT only shows that P is no harder than HALT.

8. Rice's theorem

Every non-trivial property of the language recognised by a TM is undecidable. "Non-trivial" means that some RE languages have the property and some do not. "Property of the language" means that two TMs with the same language must agree on it. So these are all undecidable: is L(M) empty? finite? regular? context-free? equal to Σ*? does it contain 101? These are not covered by Rice, because they are properties of the machine, not of its language: does M have 7 states? does M halt within 100 steps on w? does M ever move left on blank input? Such questions may be decidable, and these three are.

A stronger version (Rice–Shapiro) says that a property can be RE only if it is determined by finite pieces of the language. So {⟨M⟩ | L(M) ≠ ∅} is RE (search for any accepted string by dovetailing), but {⟨M⟩ | L(M) = ∅}, {⟨M⟩ | L(M) is finite} and {⟨M⟩ | L(M) = Σ*} are not RE.

9. Post's correspondence problem (PCP)

An instance is a list of pairs (x1, y1), …, (xk, yk) of non-empty strings. A solution is a non-empty sequence of indices i1 … im, repeats allowed, such that xi1…xim = yi1…yim. PCP is undecidable in general, but it is semi-decidable: enumerate the sequences by length and stop if one works. The modified PCP (MPCP) forces the solution to start with pair 1 and is also undecidable. PCP is decidable when the alphabet has only one symbol, and when the instance has only two pairs. Because PCP reduces to them, ambiguity of CFGs and emptiness of the intersection of two CFLs are undecidable.

10. Closure table for all language classes

OperationREGDCFLCFLCSLRECRE
UnionYNYYYY
IntersectionYNNYYY
ComplementYYNYYN
ConcatenationYNYYYY
Kleene starYNYYYY
ReversalYNYYYY
Intersection with regularYYYYYY
Homomorphism (erasing allowed)YNYNNY
ε-free homomorphismYNYYYY
Inverse homomorphismYYYYYY
Difference L1 − L2YNNYYN

Cross-checks that help you rebuild the table: union plus complement forces intersection (De Morgan). Intersection plus complement forces difference. Closure under difference forces complement, since L̄ = Σ* − L. Every RE language is an (erasing) homomorphic image of some CSL, which is why CSL and REC fail under general homomorphism while RE is closed.

11. Decision table

ProblemREGDCFLCFLCSLRECRE
Membership w ∈ LDDDDDU
Emptiness L = ∅DDDUUU
FinitenessDDDUUU
Equivalence L1 = L2DDUUUU
Universality L = Σ*DDUUUU
Inclusion L1 ⊆ L2DUUUUU

D means decidable and U means undecidable. For REC and RE the languages are given by TMs (for REC, by deciders). Membership for RE is semi-decidable only.

Worked examples

Example 1: binary increment TM, step count

q0: 0 → 0,R   1 → 1,R   B → B,L, go to q1      (run to the right end)
q1: 1 → 0,L   (carry moves left)
    0 → 1,S, accept      B → 1,S, accept

Input 1011: 4 moves right, 1 move back onto the last 1, then 1 → 0 twice, then 0 → 1 and accept. That is 8 moves, and the tape holds 1100 (11 + 1 = 12). For 111, the carry runs off the left end and the blank becomes 1: the result is 1000, also in 8 moves. For 1111 the result is 10000 in 10 moves. In general, n + 1 moves reach the last symbol, plus one move per carry position, plus one final write.

Example 2: the X/Y marking machine for aⁿbⁿ

The machine repeatedly marks the leftmost a as X, runs right to the first b and marks it Y, then returns to the leftmost unmarked a. When no a is left, it checks that only Y's remain. The move counts by simulation are 5, 13, 25 and 41 for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, which fit 2n2 + 2n + 1. So the running time is Θ(n2), which is typical for single-tape comparisons. On aabb the machine makes 13 moves and the final tape is XXYY. It rejects aab after 7 moves, and abab after 4.

Example 3: solving a PCP instance

The pairs are 1 = (a, ba), 2 = (aa, a), 3 = (b, aa). The start must be a pair where one string is a prefix of the other. Pairs 1 (a against b) and 3 (b against a) fail at the first symbol, so start with pair 2: top aa, bottom a. Choose 2 again: top aaaa, bottom aa. Choose 3: top aaaab, bottom aaaa. Choose 1: top aaaaba, bottom aaaaba. Equal. So 2, 2, 3, 1 is a solution. A breadth-first search over all sequences confirms that no sequence of length 3 or less works. By contrast, in the instance (ab, a), (bba, bb), every top string is longer than its bottom string, so no sequence can ever balance, and that instance has no solution.

Example 4: classifying problems

ProblemStatusReason
Does DFA A accept w?Decidablesimulate |w| steps
Is L(G) = ∅ for a CFG G?Decidablegenerating-symbols test
Does TM M halt on w within 500 steps?Decidablebounded simulation (not about the language)
Does M have exactly 12 states?Decidableread the encoding
Is L(M) regular?Undecidable, not RERice, and not monotone
Is L(M) ≠ ∅?RE, not recursiveRice for undecidability; dovetailing shows it is RE
Is L(M) = ∅?Not REcomplement of the previous row
Does M halt on blank tape?RE, not recursiveHALT ≤m it

Example 5: LBA configurations

An LBA with |Q| = 5 states and |Γ| = 3 tape symbols, on an input of length n = 4, has at most 5 × 4 × 34 = 1620 configurations (state × head position × tape contents; here the head is counted on the n input cells). If it runs for more than 1620 moves, it has repeated a configuration and will loop forever. So a decider can simulate for 1620 moves and reject if the LBA has not accepted by then.

Example 6: the right direction of a reduction

Claim: ETM = {⟨M⟩ | L(M) = ∅} is undecidable. Reduce ATM to its complement. Given ⟨M, w⟩, build M' that ignores its own input x and runs M on w, accepting if M accepts. Then L(M') = Σ* if M accepts w, and L(M') = ∅ otherwise. So ⟨M, w⟩ ∈ ATM ⇔ ⟨M'⟩ ∉ ETM. A decider for ETM would give a decider for ATM, which is impossible.

12. Non-computational problems, the diagonal argument and Russell's paradox

Countable and uncountable. A set is countable if its members can be listed as a first, second, third and so on. Σ* is countable: list the strings by length, then alphabetically (ε, 0, 1, 00, 01, …). Every Turing machine is a finite string over a fixed alphabet, so the set of TMs is countable too, and so is the set of all programs in any language.

Cantor's diagonal argument. Suppose the languages over Σ could be listed as L1, L2, L3, … and let w1, w2, w3, … be the strings in order. Build D = {wi | wi ∉ Li}. D disagrees with Li about the string wi, for every i, so D is not in the list. Hence the set of all languages (the power set of Σ*) is uncountable. The same argument shows that the functions from ℕ to {0, 1} are uncountable, and in general that |P(S)| > |S| for every set S.

Non-computational problems. Countably many machines cannot cover uncountably many languages or functions. So most problems have no algorithm at all: they are non-computational (not computable, not even RE). Concrete examples are the diagonal language Ld, the complement of the halting problem, the busy beaver function Σ(n) (the largest number of 1s an n-state TM can leave before halting; it eventually exceeds every computable function), Kolmogorov complexity, Hilbert's tenth problem (does a polynomial equation have an integer solution?), the word problem for semigroups and the tiling problem.

Russell's paradox. In naive set theory any property defines a set. Take R = {x | x ∉ x}, the set of all sets that are not members of themselves. If R ∈ R, then by its definition R ∉ R. If R ∉ R, then R satisfies the property, so R ∈ R. Either way we get a contradiction. So unrestricted comprehension is inconsistent. Axiomatic set theory (Zermelo–Fraenkel) avoids it by allowing a property to select members only from an existing set (the axiom of separation). The barber who shaves exactly those who do not shave themselves is the everyday version.

One idea, three results. Russell's set, Cantor's D and the halting proof are the same trick: an object defined by disagreeing with itself on the diagonal. Ld = {⟨M⟩ | ⟨M⟩ ∉ L(M)} is Cantor's D with TMs in place of the listed sets, and the machine D of the halting proof does the opposite of what H predicts about D run on itself.

NTA trap. Wrong: "the set of Turing machines is uncountable, because a TM can have any number of states." Fix: each TM is a finite string, so there are countably many; it is the set of languages that is uncountable.

Example 7: running the diagonal

Strings in order: w1 = ε, w2 = 0, w3 = 1, w4 = 00. Row i shows whether each string is in Li (1 = member).

ε0100
L11010
L20011
L31110
L40100

The diagonal reads 1, 0, 1, 0. Flipping it gives 0, 1, 0, 1, so D contains exactly the strings 0 and 00. D differs from L1 on ε, from L2 on 0, from L3 on 1 and from L4 on 00: it is none of the listed languages.

13. Universal Turing machines, models of computation and the Church–Turing thesis

Encoding a TM. Number the states q1, q2, … (q1 the start), the tape symbols X1, X2, … and the directions D1 = L, D2 = R. The move δ(qi, Xj) = (qk, Xl, Dm) is written as 0i10j10k10l10m. Codes of different moves are separated by 11, and 111 separates the machine from its input. No move code contains 11, because every block of 0s is non-empty.

The universal TM U takes ⟨M, w⟩ and simulates M on w. A convenient version has three tapes: one holds ⟨M⟩, one holds M's tape, and one holds M's current state. For each step, U looks up the matching move code and updates the other two tapes. U accepts exactly when M accepts w, so L(U) = Lu = {⟨M, w⟩ | M accepts w}, which is RE but not recursive. U is not a decider: if M loops, U loops. U is the theoretical model of the stored-program computer, where the program is data.

Models of computation. Many independent definitions of "algorithm" compute exactly the same functions as the TM: Church's λ-calculus, the μ-recursive functions of Gödel and Kleene, Post systems, Markov algorithms, unrestricted grammars, two-counter and register machines, two-stack PDAs, and the random-access machine. The primitive recursive functions are strictly weaker: the Ackermann function is total and computable but not primitive recursive.

The Church–Turing thesis says that every function computable by an effective procedure is computable by a Turing machine. It is a thesis, not a theorem: "effective procedure" is informal, so it cannot be proved. The agreement of all the models above is the evidence for it. The extended (complexity-theoretic) thesis adds that reasonable models simulate each other with polynomial overhead. Quantum computers may challenge the extended thesis, but not the original one: they compute no function that a TM cannot.

Unrestricted (Type 0) grammars have productions α → β, where α contains at least one variable and β is any string, even ε. They generate exactly the RE languages. A TM can enumerate derivations, and a grammar can simulate a TM's moves as string rewriting. So membership for Type 0 grammars is undecidable, while for Type 1 grammars (|α| ≤ |β|) it is decidable, because sentential forms never shrink.

Example 8: encoding length

δ(q1, X2) = (q3, X1, D2) is coded as 0 1 00 1 000 1 0 1 00 = 0100100010100: 1 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 2 = 9 zeros and 4 ones, 13 symbols. δ(q3, X2) = (q1, X3, D1) is 00010010100010: 3 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 10 zeros and 4 ones, 14 symbols. A machine with just these two moves is coded as 0100100010100 11 00010010100010, of length 13 + 2 + 14 = 29. In general a move costs (i + j + k + l + m) + 4 symbols.

14. Measuring and classifying complexity: tractable and intractable problems

Measuring. For a TM that halts on every input, the time complexity t(n) is the largest number of moves on any input of length n, and the space complexity s(n) is the largest number of tape cells scanned. The classes are DTIME(t(n)), NTIME(t(n)), DSPACE(s(n)) and NSPACE(s(n)). The model matters only polynomially: a k-tape machine running in t(n) is simulated by a one-tape machine in O(t(n)2). So "polynomial time" means the same thing on every reasonable deterministic model, which is why polynomial time is used as the dividing line.

Classifying. P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME. The time hierarchy theorem gives P ≠ EXPTIME, so at least one of these inclusions is proper, but no one knows which. Savitch's theorem, NSPACE(s) ⊆ DSPACE(s2), gives PSPACE = NPSPACE. A machine running in time t(n) scans at most t(n) + 1 cells, so time bounds space.

Tractable problems are those solvable in polynomial time (class P): sorting, shortest paths, Euler circuits, 2-SAT, primality (AKS, 2002), linear programming. Intractable problems have no polynomial-time algorithm. Two kinds appear in questions:

  • Provably intractable: EXPTIME-complete problems such as generalised chess or checkers on an n × n board, and EXPSPACE-complete problems such as equivalence of regular expressions with a squaring operator. The hierarchy theorems prove they are not in P.
  • Believed intractable: NP-complete problems (SAT, 3-SAT, Hamiltonian cycle, TSP decision, 0/1 knapsack decision). None has a known polynomial algorithm, but no proof exists that none can have one; that is the P versus NP question.

Undecidable problems lie beyond both: no algorithm exists at any cost. Watch for near-twins across the line: Euler circuit (P) against Hamiltonian cycle (NP-complete), shortest path (P) against longest simple path (NP-hard), 2-SAT (P) against 3-SAT (NP-complete). The O(nW) dynamic program for knapsack is only pseudo-polynomial, since W is exponential in the number of bits used to write it.

Example 9: why the line is drawn at polynomial time

At 109 steps per second, n3 steps for n = 50 take 125,000 steps, about 0.000125 s. 2n steps for n = 50 take about 1.13 × 1015 steps, about 13 days. For n = 60 they take about 36.5 years.

Buying a machine 1000 times faster multiplies the size solvable in a fixed time by 10001/3 = 10 for an n3 algorithm, but only adds log2 1000 ≈ 10 to it for a 2n algorithm.

NTA traps

  • Applying Rice's theorem to machine properties. "Does M have 5 states?" and "does M halt within k steps?" are decidable. Rice covers only properties of L(M).
  • Reversing the reduction. To show P is undecidable, reduce the known undecidable problem to P.
  • "RE is closed under complement." False. If it were, every RE language would be recursive.
  • "Every recursive language is context-sensitive." False. CSL ⊂ Recursive properly.
  • "CSL emptiness is decidable because CSL membership is." Membership is decidable, but emptiness is not.
  • "A nondeterministic TM is more powerful." It is not. It is at most exponentially faster, as far as is known.
  • Semi-decidable versus undecidable. HALT is undecidable yet semi-decidable (RE). Its complement is not even semi-decidable. Options often offer "not RE" for HALT itself.
  • Homomorphism. CSLs and recursive languages are closed under ε-free homomorphism but not under erasing homomorphism. RE is closed under both.

How NTA asks this

  • Match the list: Chomsky types against machines, or problems against decidable / RE / not RE.
  • Multiple statements: "which of the following problems are decidable?", mixing Rice-type and machine-type questions.
  • A–R: "HALT is undecidable" with reasons about RE, diagonalisation or reductions. Check whether the reason is true, and whether it actually proves the assertion.
  • Numerical: TM traces (moves, final tape), PCP solutions, LBA configuration counts.
Mini example (A–R): A: "The halting problem is undecidable." R: "The halting problem is recursively enumerable." Both are true, but being RE does not explain undecidability (every recursive language is also RE). So the answer is option 2. If R were "assuming a decider leads to a contradiction by diagonalisation", the answer would be option 1.
Elimination trick: for "which are decidable", first strike every question about L(M) for a general TM (Rice). Then keep the questions about DFAs, CFG emptiness, finiteness and membership, CSL membership, and bounded-step simulations.

terms.definition: A 7-tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, B, F) with an infinite tape. It reads, writes and moves L or R each step, and may accept, reject or loop.
A nondeterministic TM restricted to the tape cells holding its input. It accepts exactly the context-sensitive languages.
A language decided by a TM that halts on every input. It is closed under complement.
A language accepted by some TM, which may loop on strings not in the language. It is not closed under complement.
Given ⟨M, w⟩, does M halt on w? It is RE but undecidable, and its complement is not RE.
A computable f with w ∈ A ⇔ f(w) ∈ B, written A ≤m B. It transfers decidability down and undecidability up.
Every non-trivial property of the language recognised by a TM is undecidable.
Given pairs (xi, yi), is there an index sequence with equal top and bottom concatenations? Undecidable but semi-decidable.
Every effectively computable function can be computed by a Turing machine. It is a thesis, not a provable theorem.
A TM that takes ⟨M, w⟩ and simulates M on w.

lessons.examTip: Sort every problem into one of three boxes. Recursive: a TM always halts. RE but not recursive: HALT, A_TM, L(M) ≠ ∅, PCP. Not RE: the complements of these, and L(M) = ∅. Rice applies only to properties of L(M), never to properties of the machine itself.

steps: Open practice-set.md and solve problems 1–8 in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
For the TM traces (problems 1–3), write each configuration on its own line and number the moves.
Solve problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. Before answering, label each problem Recursive, RE-not-recursive or not-RE.
Check with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (Rice misapplied, reduction reversed, RE complement, CSL emptiness).
Rewrite the closure table for all six classes and the decision table from memory, and check both against the lesson.
Redo every wrong problem after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.

quiz.explanation: 4 moves right, over 1, 0, 1, 1, to reach the blank. 1 move left onto the last 1. Two carries (1 → 0, left) take 2 moves. Then 0 → 1 and halt takes 1 move. Total 4 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 8, and the tape holds 1100, which is 11 + 1 = 12. Confirmed by simulation.

quiz.explanation: HALT is RE. If its complement were also RE, HALT would be recursive, which is false. So the complement is not RE: no TM can even semi-decide "never halts".

lessons.title: Compilers: lexical and syntax analysis
lessons.summaryHtml: A compiler works in phases. The lexical analyser turns characters into tokens, using regular expressions and longest match. The syntax analyser checks the token stream against a context-free grammar and builds a parse tree. Top-down LL(1) parsers need a grammar without left recursion or common prefixes, and they fill their table from FIRST and FOLLOW sets. Bottom-up shift–reduce parsers use LR item sets: LR(0) and SLR(1) share one collection of states, CLR(1) adds lookaheads and has more states, and LALR(1) merges CLR states with equal cores. NET asks you to count tokens, compute FIRST/FOLLOW, test LL(1), count states and spot conflicts.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A compiler reads a program written for people and produces a program the machine can run. It works in stages. The front end understands the source: it breaks the text into words (lexical analysis), checks that the words form valid sentences (syntax analysis), and checks meaning such as types (semantic analysis). The back end produces intermediate code, improves it and generates target code. This lesson covers the first two stages. The next lesson (8.5) covers the rest.

Think of reading an English sentence. First you see the words, then you check the grammar, then you understand the meaning. A scanner does the first job. A parser does the second, and it builds a parse tree that later stages walk.

Why it matters for NET

Compiler design is a steady source of questions in Unit 8, alongside automata theory. Most papers carry a small cluster of compiler questions, and the front end supplies most of them. The favourites are: counting tokens in a C fragment, FIRST and FOLLOW sets, whether a grammar is LL(1), the number of LR(0) or LR(1) states, which parser (LR(0), SLR, LALR, CLR) accepts a grammar, and which conflicts appear. Matching questions pair phases with their outputs or errors, and parsers with their table types. These are mechanical questions. Once the method is drilled they are quick marks.

Concepts in depth

1. The phases of a compiler

PhaseInput → outputTypical error it catches
Lexical analysis (scanner)character stream → token streamillegal character, unterminated string or comment, badly formed number
Syntax analysis (parser)tokens → parse tree / syntax treemissing semicolon, unbalanced parentheses, misplaced keyword
Semantic analysissyntax tree → annotated treetype mismatch, undeclared variable, wrong number of arguments, lvalue required
Intermediate code generationannotated tree → three-address code–
Code optimisationIR → better IR–
Code generationIR → target (assembly or machine) code–

Two components serve every phase: the symbol table (names with their type, scope, size and address) and the error handler. Phases 1 to 3 form the analysis part; phases 4 to 6 form the synthesis part. The front end depends on the source language, and the back end depends on the target machine. So with m languages and n machines you need m front ends and n back ends, not m × n compilers. A pass is one reading of the whole program (or its IR); several phases can be grouped into one pass. A cross compiler runs on one machine and produces code for another. Bootstrapping writes a compiler in the language it compiles; T-diagrams show the source language, target language and implementation language of each compiler.

2. Lexical analysis: tokens, lexemes and patterns

  • A token is a category, such as identifier, keyword, number, operator or punctuation. It is usually a pair: token name and an attribute (often a pointer to the symbol table entry).
  • A lexeme is the actual character sequence in the source that matches, for example count or >=.
  • A pattern is the rule, usually a regular expression, that describes the lexemes of a token, for example letter (letter | digit)*.

Tokens are described by regular expressions and recognised by a DFA. That is why the scanner needs only regular languages. Nested structure such as balanced parentheses needs a CFG, so it is the parser’s job.

Two rules decide which lexeme is taken when several patterns match:

  1. Longest match (maximal munch). Read the longest prefix that forms a valid token. So a+++b is a ++ + b, and x---y is x -- - y.
  2. Rule priority. If two patterns match the same longest lexeme, the rule listed first wins. This is why keyword patterns are written before the identifier pattern in LEX: if matches both, and the keyword rule comes first.

The scanner also removes white space and comments. They never become tokens, and a comment behaves like a separator. Scanners read input through a two-buffer scheme with sentinels: an eof marker at the end of each half means one test per character instead of two. Lookahead is needed because you cannot decide that > is complete until you see whether = follows.

Counting tokens in C, the rules NTA follows:

  • Each keyword, identifier, constant, operator and punctuator is one token: int, main, (, ), {, ;, ,.
  • A whole string literal "sum=%d" is one token, whatever is inside it, including spaces, %d and &. A character constant like '\n' is one token.
  • Multi-character operators are one token: ++ -- >= << -> += && ||.
  • Comments and white space are not tokens.
  • Preprocessor lines such as #include <stdio.h> are handled before scanning, so questions usually exclude them. Read the question’s convention.

3. Grammars for parsing: left recursion and left factoring

A context-free grammar (CFG) G = (V, T, P, S) describes the syntax. A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost non-terminal; top-down parsers trace it. A rightmost derivation always expands the rightmost non-terminal; bottom-up parsers trace it in reverse. A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two parse trees (equivalently, two leftmost derivations). No ambiguous grammar is LL(k) or LR(k).

Left recursion (A ⇒+ Aα) sends a top-down parser into an infinite loop, because expanding A leads straight back to A without consuming input. Remove immediate left recursion like this:

A → Aα1 | Aα2 | β1 | β2        (no βi starts with A)
becomes
A  → β1 A' | β2 A'
A' → α1 A' | α2 A' | ε

For indirect left recursion (S → Aa, A → Sd), order the non-terminals A1 … An. For each Ai, substitute the bodies of earlier Aj (j < i) into productions of the form Ai → Ajγ, then remove the immediate left recursion of Ai. The algorithm assumes no ε-cycles; it still works for the classic textbook example with A → ε, as the worked example below shows. The language never changes; only the shape of the parse trees changes. Left-associative operators become right-leaning trees, so semantic actions must compensate.

Left factoring handles two alternatives that share a prefix, such as A → αβ1 | αβ2. The parser cannot choose between them on one lookahead symbol, so factor the common prefix out: A → αA', A' → β1 | β2. Left factoring does not remove ambiguity. The dangling-else grammar stays non-LL(1) after factoring.

4. FIRST and FOLLOW

FIRST(α) is the set of terminals that can begin a string derived from α, plus ε if α ⇒* ε.

  1. If a is a terminal, FIRST(a) = {a}.
  2. For X → Y1 Y2 … Yk: add FIRST(Y1) − {ε}. If Y1 can derive ε, also add FIRST(Y2) − {ε}, and so on. Add ε only if all Yi can derive ε.
  3. If X → ε, add ε.

FOLLOW(A) is the set of terminals that can appear immediately to the right of A in some sentential form. It never contains ε.

  1. Put $ in FOLLOW(S) for the start symbol S.
  2. For B → αAβ: add FIRST(β) − {ε} to FOLLOW(A).
  3. For B → αA, or B → αAβ where β ⇒* ε: add all of FOLLOW(B) to FOLLOW(A).

Repeat the rules until no set changes; FOLLOW needs this fixed-point loop because rule 3 copies sets between non-terminals.

5. LL(1) parsing

LL(1) means: scan Left to right, produce a Leftmost derivation, using 1 symbol of lookahead. The parser is a stack plus a table M[A, a]. For each production A → α:

  • for each terminal a in FIRST(α), put A → α in M[A, a];
  • if ε ∈ FIRST(α), put A → α in M[A, b] for each b in FOLLOW(A), including $.

The grammar is LL(1) exactly when no cell gets two productions. For every pair of alternatives A → α | β this means: FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅; at most one of them derives ε; and if β ⇒* ε, then FIRST(α) ∩ FOLLOW(A) = ∅. A left-recursive or ambiguous grammar is never LL(1), and a grammar that needs left factoring is not LL(1) as written. Recursive-descent parsing is the hand-written form of the same idea: one procedure per non-terminal. It needs backtracking unless the grammar is LL(1), in which case it is predictive.

6. Bottom-up parsing: shift–reduce

A bottom-up parser starts from the input and reduces it to the start symbol, tracing a rightmost derivation in reverse. It has four actions: shift (push the next token), reduce (replace a handle on top of the stack by its non-terminal), accept and error. A handle is the substring that matches a production body and whose reduction is one step back along the rightmost derivation. The handle always appears on top of the stack, never buried inside it. A viable prefix is any prefix of a right-sentential form that does not extend past the handle, so viable prefixes are exactly the possible stack contents. The set of viable prefixes is a regular language, which is why a DFA of item sets can drive the parser.

A shift–reduce conflict occurs when the parser can both shift and reduce. A reduce–reduce conflict occurs when two different reductions are possible. There is no such thing as a shift–shift conflict: shifting a symbol leads to exactly one state.

Operator precedence parsing works for operator grammars, which have no ε-productions and no two adjacent non-terminals. It uses precedence relations ⋖, ≐ and ⋗ between terminals. It is simple, but it handles only a small class of grammars. For example, it cannot handle unary minus cleanly.

7. LR(0) items and the canonical collection

An LR(0) item is a production with a dot marking how much has been seen: A → X•YZ. First add the augmented production S' → S. CLOSURE(I) adds B → •γ for every item A → α•Bβ, repeatedly. GOTO(I, X) moves the dot over X in every item that allows it, then takes the closure. Starting from CLOSURE({S' → •S}), apply GOTO over all grammar symbols until no new sets appear. The result is the canonical LR(0) collection: the states of the DFA.

  • LR(0) table: a completed item A → α• means reduce in every column. A conflict exists if a state has a completed item together with another completed item (R/R) or with a shift item on a terminal (S/R).
  • SLR(1): same states. Reduce A → α• only on terminals in FOLLOW(A). A conflict remains if two completed items have overlapping FOLLOW sets, or if a shift terminal lies in FOLLOW(A).
  • CLR(1) (canonical LR(1)): items carry a lookahead, [A → α•β, a]. In the closure of [A → α•Bβ, a], add [B → •γ, b] for every b in FIRST(βa). Reduce only on the item’s own lookahead. It is the most powerful, but it has the most states.
  • LALR(1): merge the CLR(1) states that have the same core (the same LR(0) items), taking the union of the lookaheads. The number of states equals the LR(0)/SLR count. Merging can create new reduce–reduce conflicts, but never a new shift–reduce conflict. A shift depends only on the core, so if a merged state had an S/R conflict, one of the original CLR states already had it.

8. Parser power and state counts

RelationWhat it means
LR(0) ⊂ SLR(1) ⊂ LALR(1) ⊂ CLR(1) (grammars)each class strictly contains the previous one
LL(1) ⊂ CLR(1)every LL(1) grammar is LR(1)
LL(1) vs SLR(1), LALR(1)incomparable: some LL(1) grammars are not SLR(1), and some are not even LALR(1)
States: LR(0) = SLR = LALR ≤ CLRfor the textbook expression grammar: 12 LR(0)/SLR/LALR states, 22 CLR states
LanguagesLR(1) languages = LR(k) languages = deterministic CFLs; LR(0) languages = DCFLs with the prefix property
Ambiguous grammarnot LL(k) and not LR(k) for any k (conflicts are resolved by precedence rules in YACC)

9. LEX and YACC basics

A LEX (or flex) file has three parts separated by %%: definitions, rules (pattern plus action) and user code. LEX builds a DFA-based scanner yylex(). The matched text is in yytext and its length in yyleng. It uses longest match first and then the earliest rule. YACC (or bison) takes a grammar with actions and produces an LALR(1) parser yyparse() that calls yylex() for tokens. By default YACC resolves a shift–reduce conflict in favour of shift (which gives the usual dangling-else behaviour), and a reduce–reduce conflict in favour of the production listed first. %left, %right and %nonassoc declare associativity; declarations lower in the file have higher precedence. $$ is the value of the head, and $1, $2 are the values of the body symbols.

Worked examples

Example 1: counting tokens

Count the tokens in: int main(){int a=10,b=20;printf("sum=%d",a+b);return 0;}

Split into lexemes: int, main, (, ), {, int, a, =, 10, ",", b, =, 20, ; (14 so far); printf, (, "sum=%d", ",", a, +, b, ), ; (9 more, 23); return, 0, ;, } (4 more). Total 27. The string literal is one token even though it contains = and %d.

Maximal munch: x = a+++b; has 7 tokens (x, =, a, ++, +, b, ;). while(n--) total += n % 10; has 11 tokens. a = b/*c*/ + d; // done has 6 tokens, because both comments disappear.

Example 2: removing indirect left recursion

S → Aa | b
A → Ac | Sd | ε

Order S, A. S has no immediate left recursion. For A, substitute S into A → Sd: A → Aad | bd. Now A → Ac | Aad | bd | ε. Remove the immediate left recursion (the α’s are c and ad; the β’s are bd and ε):

S  → Aa | b
A  → bdA' | A'
A' → cA' | adA' | ε

A script that enumerates every string up to length 9 from both grammars finds the same 122 strings, so the language is unchanged.

Example 3: FIRST, FOLLOW and the LL(1) table for expressions

E  → T E'          E' → + T E' | ε
T  → F T'          T' → * F T' | ε
F  → ( E ) | id
Non-terminalFIRSTFOLLOW
E{ (, id }{ ), $ }
E'{ +, ε }{ ), $ }
T{ (, id }{ +, ), $ }
T'{ *, ε }{ +, ), $ }
F{ (, id }{ *, +, ), $ }

Why FOLLOW(T) has +: in E → T E', T is followed by E', and FIRST(E') − {ε} = {+}. E' can vanish, so FOLLOW(E) = { ), $ } is also copied into FOLLOW(T).

M    | id      | +        | *        | (       | )     | $
-----+---------+----------+----------+---------+-------+------
E    | E→TE'   |          |          | E→TE'   |       |
E'   |         | E'→+TE'  |          |         | E'→ε  | E'→ε
T    | T→FT'   |          |          | T→FT'   |       |
T'   |         | T'→ε     | T'→*FT'  |         | T'→ε  | T'→ε
F    | F→id    |          |          | F→(E)   |       |

There are 13 filled cells and none holds two entries, so the grammar is LL(1). Parsing id + id * id takes 17 steps (moves) including the final accept: every expansion or match is one step.

Example 4: LR(0) states and the SLR conflict test for S → CC

S' → S      S → C C      C → c C | d
StateItemsTransitions
I0S'→•S, S→•CC, C→•cC, C→•dS→I1, C→I2, c→I3, d→I4
I1S'→S•accept on $
I2S→C•C, C→•cC, C→•dC→I5, c→I3, d→I4
I3C→c•C, C→•cC, C→•dC→I6, c→I3, d→I4
I4C→d•reduce
I5S→CC•reduce
I6C→cC•reduce

There are 7 states. No state mixes a completed item with a shift or with another completed item, so the grammar is LR(0), and therefore also SLR, LALR and CLR. The canonical LR(1) collection has 10 states: I3, I4 and I6 each split into a copy with lookahead c/d and a copy with lookahead $. Merging those pairs gives back 7 LALR states.

Example 5: not SLR but LALR, the L = R grammar

S → L = R | R      L → * R | id      R → L

The LR(0) collection has 10 states. One of them is I2 = { S → L•=R, R → L• }. SLR reduces R → L on FOLLOW(R) = { =, $ } (= enters FOLLOW(L) through S → L=R, and FOLLOW(L) is copied into FOLLOW(R) through L → *R). But the state also shifts on =, which gives a shift–reduce conflict on =. The grammar is not SLR(1).

In CLR(1), the item in that state is [R → L•, $]: this state is reached from I0 on L, and the only R → L• item there comes from S → •R, which is followed only by $ (the = belongs to the other item, S → L•=R). So there is no conflict. The CLR collection has 14 states; merging by core gives 10 LALR states, still with no conflict. So the grammar is LALR(1) but not SLR(1).

Example 6: LALR fails where CLR succeeds

S → A a | b A c | B c | b B a      A → d      B → d

After reading d at the start, CLR has a state {[A→d•, a], [B→d•, c]}. After reading b d it has {[A→d•, c], [B→d•, a]}. Neither state has a conflict, and CLR has 13 states. The two states have the same core, so LALR merges them into {[A→d•, a/c], [B→d•, a/c]}: a reduce–reduce conflict on both a and c. The grammar is LR(1) but not LALR(1). This is the standard proof that merging creates only R/R conflicts.

Example 7: counting the moves of an SLR parse

Parse id * id + id with the SLR table for E → E+T | T, T → T*F | F, F → (E) | id. The parser makes 5 shifts, one for each token. It makes 8 reductions: F→id, T→F, F→id, T→T*F, E→T, F→id, T→F and E→E+T. Then it accepts. The reductions, read in reverse, give the rightmost derivation.

10. Precedence, associativity and recursive-descent predictive parsing

Encoding precedence and associativity in a grammar. Give each precedence level its own variable. The level nearest the start symbol holds the operator with the lowest precedence, because it is applied last, at the top of the tree. Associativity comes from the direction of recursion:

  • E → E + T | T is left-recursive, so + is left-associative: a + b + c groups as (a + b) + c.
  • P → F ^ P | F is right-recursive, so ^ is right-associative: a ^ b ^ c groups as a ^ (b ^ c).
  • C → E < E | E is non-associative: a < b < c has no parse at all.

An ambiguous grammar such as E → E + E | E * E | id can be kept, and the parser told how to choose. YACC's %left, %right and %nonassoc do this, and an operator-precedence table does the same with the relations ⋖, ≐, ⋗.

Recursive descent. Write one procedure per variable. The procedure for A chooses one of A's productions and processes its body left to right: it calls the procedure for each variable and matches each terminal against the next token. If it chooses by trying productions in turn and backing up on failure, it is backtracking recursive descent, which can take exponential time. If the grammar is LL(1), the next token alone selects the production (it must be in FIRST of the body, or in FOLLOW(A) for an ε-body), and the parser never backtracks. That is predictive recursive descent. It is the hand-written form of the LL(1) table: the table-driven parser replaces the recursion with an explicit stack.

E()  { T(); E'(); }
E'() { if (look == '+') { match('+'); T(); E'(); } }   /* else choose E' → ε */
T()  { F(); T'(); }
T'() { if (look == '*') { match('*'); F(); T'(); } }
F()  { if (look == '(') { match('('); E(); match(')'); } else match(id); }

A left-recursive rule E → E + T would make E() call itself before consuming anything, an infinite loop. That is why left recursion is removed first. The rewritten grammar leans the tree to the right, so a translator restores left associativity with an inherited attribute, or by coding E' as a while loop, E → T { + T }.

NTA trap. Wrong: "removing left recursion changes the language, or makes − right-associative in the result." Fix: the language is unchanged and the value computed is unchanged if the semantic actions pass the running value down (inherited attribute). Only the shape of the parse tree changes.

Example 8: counting procedure calls

With the procedures above, every variable node of the parse tree is exactly one call. For id + id * id the tree has E, T, F, T'(ε), E', T, F, T', F, T'(ε), E'(ε): 11 calls, and the deepest nesting is E → E' → T → T' → T'. For id alone it is E, T, F, T', E': 5 calls. For ( id + id ) * id the count is 16, because the bracketed E contributes its own 9 calls.

NTA traps

  • Counting a string literal as many tokens. Wrong: "sum = %d" has 4 tokens. Fix: a string literal is exactly one token.
  • Counting comments. Wrong: /* x */ gives 3 tokens. Fix: the scanner discards it completely.
  • Splitting operators. Wrong: >= is two tokens. Fix: maximal munch makes it one; a+++b is a ++ + b.
  • Putting ε in FOLLOW. Fix: FOLLOW holds terminals and $ only.
  • Forgetting the vanishing case. For B → αAβ with β ⇒* ε, FOLLOW(B) must also go into FOLLOW(A). Most wrong FOLLOW options come from missing this.
  • "Unambiguous means LL(1)." Wrong. E → E+T | T is unambiguous but left-recursive, so it is not LL(1).
  • "Every LL(1) grammar is SLR(1)." Wrong. S → AaAb | BbBa, A → ε, B → ε is LL(1), but its first state has a reduce–reduce conflict under SLR. (It is LR(1) and even LALR(1).)
  • "LALR has more states than SLR." Wrong. LALR, SLR and LR(0) have the same number of states; only CLR has more.
  • "Merging LR(1) states can create shift–reduce conflicts." Wrong. Only reduce–reduce conflicts can appear.
  • Left factoring does not fix ambiguity. The dangling-else grammar, even when left-factored, has two entries in M[S', else].
  • Top-down tracing. Top-down parsers give a leftmost derivation; bottom-up parsers give a rightmost derivation in reverse. Swapping these is a classic distractor.

How NTA asks this

  • Numerical (count): the number of tokens in a C line; the number of LR(0) states; the number of filled LL(1) cells; the number of reductions while parsing a string.
  • Set questions: "FOLLOW(A) is …" with four sets. Eliminate by checking $ (it must be in FOLLOW of the start symbol and of anything at a right end) and ε (it can never be in FOLLOW).
  • Classification: "The grammar is: LL(1) but not LR(0) / SLR but not LR(0) / LALR but not SLR / CLR but not LALR." Test from the weakest class upward.
  • Match: phases with outputs, parsers with their table or lookahead, errors with phases.
  • A-R and Statement I/II: the power hierarchy, conflict types after merging, YACC defaults.

Mini-example (match). List I: A. LR(0), B. SLR(1), C. CLR(1), D. LALR(1). List II: I. reduce on the item’s lookahead, II. reduce in every column, III. merged cores, IV. reduce on FOLLOW. Answer: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III. The distractors swap one pair, usually SLR/LALR or CLR/LALR. Anchor on LR(0) = every column first, then use "merge" to fix LALR.

Mini-example (A-R). A: An LALR(1) parser may report a reduce–reduce conflict for a grammar that is CLR(1). R: LALR(1) merges states with identical LR(0) cores. Both are true, and R explains A: merging is exactly what brings the two lookaheads together.

Remember: for any "which parser" question, first check for ambiguity and left recursion (neither is allowed for LL(1)). Then build only the state that contains a completed item: its FOLLOW or lookahead decides SLR versus LALR/CLR.

The actual character sequence in the source that matches a token’s pattern.
Lexer rule: always take the longest prefix that forms a token, so a+++b is a ++ + b.
Terminals that can begin a string derived from α, plus ε if α can derive ε.
Terminals (and $) that can appear immediately after A in a sentential form; never contains ε.
A grammar whose predictive parsing table has at most one production in every cell.
The production body on top of the stack whose reduction is one step of the rightmost derivation in reverse.
A production with a dot showing how much of its body has been seen, e.g. A → X•YZ.
Parser built by merging canonical LR(1) states with the same core; same state count as SLR, can gain only reduce–reduce conflicts.
A prefix of a right-sentential form that does not extend past the handle; the possible stack contents of an LR parser.

lessons.examTip: For any “which parser accepts this grammar” question, look only at states that contain a completed item A → α•: compare its reduce lookahead (every column, FOLLOW(A), or the item’s own lookahead) with the shift symbols in that state.

B → c C
C → b C | ε

lessons.title: Compilers: semantic analysis, runtime and code generation
lessons.summaryHtml: After parsing, a compiler attaches attributes to the parse tree using syntax-directed definitions. S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes and suit LR parsers; L-attributed ones also allow inherited attributes that flow from the parent and left siblings. The runtime environment places data in static memory, on the stack (in activation records with control and access links) or on the heap. Intermediate code is usually three-address code, stored as quadruples, triples or indirect triples, or in SSA form. Code is split into basic blocks, optimised (folding, CSE, dead code, loop optimisations, peephole) using DAGs and data-flow analysis, and finally mapped to registers and instructions.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Once the parser has a tree, the compiler must give it meaning and turn it into fast machine code. Semantic analysis attaches attributes such as values, types and code to tree nodes, and checks the types. The runtime environment decides where each variable lives while the program runs: in static memory, on the stack in an activation record, or on the heap. The compiler then produces intermediate code, usually three-address code. It splits that code into basic blocks, optimises it, allocates registers and emits target instructions.

An analogy: a translator first marks every sentence with its grammatical role and meaning (attributes). She then writes a simple, literal draft (three-address code). Next she removes repetition and dead phrases (optimisation). Finally she fits the text into the page layout of the target language (code generation).

Why it matters for NET

This half of compiler design gives a different mix of questions from the front end. Expect SDT evaluation questions ("what is the value computed / what is printed"), counts (quadruples, triples, DAG nodes, basic blocks, registers), and matching optimisations with their examples. Assertion–reason items test S- versus L-attributed definitions, static versus stack allocation, and quadruples versus triples. Most of these are quick once you know the definitions precisely, and each question hinges on one convention, which this lesson states explicitly.

Concepts in depth

1. Syntax-directed definitions (SDD)

An SDD is a CFG in which every grammar symbol has attributes and every production has semantic rules that compute them.

  • A synthesized attribute of a node is computed from the attributes of its children (and itself). Information flows up the tree, for example E.val = E1.val + T.val.
  • An inherited attribute of a node is computed from its parent and/or siblings. Information flows down or sideways, for example passing a declared type along a list of identifiers.
  • Terminals have only synthesized attributes, supplied by the lexer (such as num.lexval).

A dependency graph has an edge from each attribute to every attribute computed from it. Any topological order of this graph is a valid evaluation order. A cycle means the SDD cannot be evaluated. The parse tree with all attribute values filled in is the annotated parse tree.

ClassRuleEvaluated naturally by
S-attributedonly synthesized attributesbottom-up (LR) parsing: compute at each reduction, a post-order traversal
L-attributedin A → X1 … Xn, an inherited attribute of Xi may use only A’s inherited attributes and attributes of X1 … Xi−1 (siblings to its left); synthesized attributes are unrestrictedtop-down (LL / recursive descent) in one left-to-right depth-first pass

Every S-attributed SDD is L-attributed, but not the other way round. The standard L-attributed example is declarations: D → T L {L.inh = T.type}, L → L1 , id {L1.inh = L.inh; addtype(id.entry, L.inh)}, L → id {addtype(id.entry, L.inh)}. The rule L.inh = T.type copies information from the left sibling T, which L-attribution allows. A rule such as B.i = C.s in A → B C breaks L-attribution, because B would need a value from a sibling on its right.

2. Syntax-directed translation schemes (SDT)

An SDT places actions inside production bodies, for example E → E1 + T { print('+') }. An action runs when the parser reaches its position. A postfix SDT has every action at the right end, and the action runs at the moment of the reduction. That gives the golden rule for "what is printed" questions:

Remember: with actions at the end of productions, the output order is the order of reductions. The deepest (innermost, rightmost in a right-recursive list) production reduces first. So for S → aS {print 1} | bS {print 2} | c {print 3}, the input abac prints 3121, and the letters come out reversed.

To evaluate an unusual grammar, work out the precedence and associativity from the grammar’s shape, not from the symbols. An operator introduced closer to the start symbol has lower precedence. A left-recursive rule (E → E op T) is left-associative, and a right-recursive rule (T → F op T) is right-associative. Then apply the semantic rules, whatever they say (a rule may even define # as multiplication).

For LR parsing, an action in the middle of a body is replaced by a marker non-terminal M → ε whose reduction performs the action. For LL parsing, the left recursion is removed and the attributes are rewritten as inherited plus synthesized (for example E’ gets an inherited running total).

3. Type checking

  • A type expression is a basic type (int, float, char, boolean, void, type_error) or a type built with constructors: array(n, T), pointer(T), T1 × T2 (product), record(…), and function types D → R.
  • Static checking happens at compile time, and dynamic checking at run time, for example array bounds in Java. A strongly typed language guarantees that accepted programs run without type errors. A sound type system makes dynamic checks unnecessary.
  • Structural equivalence: two types are equal if they are built the same way. Name equivalence: they are equal only if they have the same name. Under name equivalence, two typedefs with identical bodies are different.
  • Coercion is an implicit conversion inserted by the compiler, usually widening (int → float → double), as in 7/2.0. An explicit conversion is a cast.
  • Overloading means one symbol has different meanings resolved by context (+ on int and float). Polymorphism means one piece of code works for many types; type inference finds the types using unification.

4. Runtime environments

A typical memory layout is: code, then static data, then the heap growing up, then free memory, then the stack growing down. Each call of a procedure is an activation. Calls form an activation tree, and the live activations at any moment are the path from the root to the current node. That path is exactly what the control stack holds.

Staticcompile time, fixed addressNo: one copy of locals per procedureglobals, C static variables, all of Fortran 77
Stackat call, freed on returnYeslocals, parameters, temporaries of C, Java, Pascal
Heapany time, explicit or garbage-collectedYesdata that must outlive the call: malloc/new, closures, objects

An activation record (frame) usually holds: actual parameters, the returned value, the control link (dynamic link, pointing to the caller’s frame), the access link (static link, pointing to the frame of the lexically enclosing procedure, used for non-local names in nested procedures), saved machine status (return address and registers), local data and temporaries. A display is an array of pointers, one per nesting depth, that replaces a chain of access links with a single lookup. Under static scope, a non-local name resolves through the access links; under dynamic scope, it resolves through the control links (deep access), or through a central table (shallow access).

The calling sequence works like this. The caller evaluates the actual parameters and stores them, then stores the return address and the old stack top in the callee’s frame and jumps. The callee saves registers, sets up its locals and runs. The return sequence places the return value, restores the registers and stack top, and jumps back. A dangling reference is a pointer to storage that has been freed, such as returning the address of a local. Garbage collection reclaims unreachable heap objects. The main methods are reference counting (cannot free cycles), mark-and-sweep, and copying collectors.

5. Intermediate code

Front ends produce syntax trees, DAGs (trees with common sub-expressions shared), postfix notation, or most often three-address code (TAC). In TAC each instruction has at most one operator on the right: x = y op z, x = op y, x = y, goto L, if x relop y goto L, param x / call p, n / return y, x = y[i], x[i] = y, x = &y, x = *y, *x = y.

RepresentationFieldsTemporaries named?Moving instructions
Quadruplesop, arg1, arg2, resultYes, explicit result fieldeasy: results are referenced by name
Triplesop, arg1, arg2No: a result is referred to by the triple’s positionhard: moving one changes the references
Indirect triplesa list of pointers to triplesNoeasy: reorder the pointer list only

Static single assignment (SSA): every variable is assigned exactly once, so each assignment creates a new version (x1, x2, …). Where control paths join, a φ-function selects the version from the path actually taken: x3 = φ(x1, x2). SSA makes def-use chains explicit and simplifies constant propagation and dead-code elimination.

6. Basic blocks and flow graphs

A basic block is a maximal sequence of instructions entered only at the first and left only at the last. Find the leaders: (1) the first instruction; (2) every target of a jump; (3) every instruction immediately after a jump (conditional or unconditional). Each block runs from one leader up to the next. A flow graph has an edge B → C if C can follow B, either by a jump or by falling through when B does not end in an unconditional goto.

Node d dominates n if every path from the entry to n passes through d. An edge n → d where d dominates n is a back edge. Its natural loop is d plus all nodes that can reach n without passing through d. Inside one block, a DAG gives local optimisation: identical operations on the same operand nodes share a node (common sub-expression), and an assignment just re-labels a node.

Live variables: IN[B] = use[B] ∪ (OUT[B] − def[B]), with OUT[B] = the union of IN over the successors. Reaching definitions: OUT[B] = gen[B] ∪ (IN[B] − kill[B]).

8. Register allocation and code generation

The code generator must choose instructions (instruction selection), choose which values stay in registers (register allocation and assignment), and choose the evaluation order. The simple code generator of Aho and Ullman keeps a register descriptor (what each register holds) and an address descriptor (where each variable’s current value is). It uses next-use information to free a register whose value is dead.

Graph-colouring allocation (Chaitin): build an interference graph, with one node per variable and an edge when two variables are live at the same time. Colour it with k colours, one per register. If that is impossible, spill a variable to memory. In straight-line code, the minimum number of registers without spilling equals the maximum number of variables live at one point.

Sethi–Ullman labelling gives the minimum number of registers needed to evaluate an expression tree without storing to memory. With register–memory instructions, a leaf that is a left child gets 1 and a leaf that is a right child gets 0 (it can be a memory operand). An interior node whose children have labels l1 ≠ l2 gets max(l1, l2); if l1 = l2, it gets l1 + 1. Evaluate the child with the larger label first. On a load–store machine every leaf gets 1. Check which convention a question uses.

Worked examples

Example 1: evaluating an SDT with unusual operators

E → E1 # T   { E.val = E1.val × T.val }
E → T        { E.val = T.val }
T → T1 & F   { T.val = T1.val + F.val }
T → F        { T.val = F.val }
F → num      { F.val = num.lexval }

Evaluate 2 # 3 & 5 # 6 & 4. # is introduced nearer the start symbol, so it has lower precedence than &, and both are left-associative. Group the input as 2 # (3 & 5) # (6 & 4). By the rules, & adds and # multiplies: 3 & 5 = 8 and 6 & 4 = 10, then 2 × 8 = 16 and 16 × 10 = 160. A reader who assumes the usual meaning of the symbols gets a different number, and that is the trap.

Example 2: what does the translation scheme print?

Scheme 1: S → a S {print 1} | b S {print 2} | c {print 3}, input abac. The reductions happen innermost first: S → c prints 3, then the S built from the third symbol a prints 1, then b prints 2, then the first a prints 1. Output: 3121.

Scheme 2: expr → expr + term {print '+'} | expr − term {print '−'} | term, and term → digit {print digit}, input 7 − 3 − 2 + 4. The grammar is left-recursive, so each operator prints after its right operand: 73−2−4+, the postfix form.

Example 3: TAC, quadruples, triples and DAG for a = b * −c + b * −c

Three-address code        Quadruples (op, arg1, arg2, result)   Triples
t1 = minus c              (0) minus  c        -     t1            (0) minus c    -
t2 = b * t1               (1) *      b        t1    t2            (1) *     b    (0)
t3 = minus c              (2) minus  c        -     t3            (2) minus c    -
t4 = b * t3               (3) *      b        t3    t4            (3) *     b    (2)
t5 = t2 + t4              (4) +      t2       t4    t5            (4) +     (1)  (3)
a  = t5                   (5) =      t5       -     a             (5) =     a    (4)

The tree form needs 6 quadruples, 6 triples and 5 temporaries. The DAG shares minus c and b * t1. It has leaves b and c and interior nodes minus, * and +: 5 nodes, with a attached as a label of the + node. From the DAG the code shrinks to t1 = minus c; t2 = b * t1; t3 = t2 + t2; a = t3.

Example 4: the DAG of a basic block

a = b + c
b = a - d
c = b + c
d = a - d

Leaves: b0, c0, d0. Node n1 = + (b0, c0), labelled a. Node n2 = − (n1, d0), labelled b. The third statement uses the new b (n2) and the old c0, so it creates n3 = + (n2, c0), labelled c. The fourth statement, a − d, is again − (n1, d0), which is the same as n2, so d is attached to n2. The DAG has 3 leaves and 3 interior nodes, 6 nodes in all. The last statement becomes d = b, a copy.

Example 5: leaders, blocks and loops

(1)  x = 0
(2)  i = 0
(3)  if i >= 10 goto (11)
(4)  t1 = i % 2
(5)  if t1 == 0 goto (8)
(6)  x = x - i
(7)  goto (9)
(8)  x = x + i
(9)  i = i + 1
(10) goto (3)
(11) y = x * 2

The leaders are: 1 (first instruction); 3, 8, 9 and 11 (jump targets); and 4 and 6 (after the jumps in 3 and 5). Instruction 8 is also the one after the goto in 7, and 11 the one after the goto in 10. Sorted: 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11, giving 7 basic blocks. The flow graph has 8 edges: B1→B2, B2→B3, B2→B7, B3→B4, B3→B5, B4→B6, B5→B6 and B6→B2. The single back edge B6→B2 defines a natural loop of 5 blocks (B2 to B6).

Example 6: registers by liveness and by Sethi–Ullman

Straight-line code, with only f live at the exit: a = p + q; b = a + q; c = a + b; d = c + p; e = d + b; f = e + d. Work backwards. The live sets between the statements are {p,q}, {a,p,q}, {a,b,p}, {b,c,p}, {b,d}, {d,e}, {f}. The largest set has 3 variables, so 3 registers suffice with no spill.

Expression a / (b + c) − d * (e + f), with register–memory labels. b + c gets max(1, 0) = 1. In a / (b + c), the left leaf a is 1 and the right child is 1, so it gets 2. In the same way e + f is 1 and d * (e + f) is 2. The root has two children labelled 2, so it gets 3. Under the all-leaves-1 convention the answer is also 3, so this question is safe under either convention.

Example 7: activation records for recursion

For int f(n) { return n < 2 ? n : f(n−1) + f(n−2); }, the call f(5) creates one activation per node of the activation tree: 15 activations. The deepest root-to-leaf path is f(5), f(4), f(3), f(2), f(1), so at most 5 frames are on the stack at once. Static allocation cannot run this function at all, because each activation needs its own copy of n.

9. Dependency graphs and evaluation order

For a given parse tree, the dependency graph has one node for each attribute of each tree node. If a semantic rule computes b from c, draw an edge c → b. A rule that is only a side effect, such as addtype(id.entry, L.inh), is given a dummy synthesized attribute of its node so that it also appears in the graph.

An evaluation order is any ordering in which every attribute comes after all the attributes it depends on, that is, a topological sort of the graph. If the graph has a cycle, there is no such order and the SDD is circular for that tree. Compilers avoid building the graph at run time in three ways:

  • Parse-tree method: build the graph for each tree and sort it topologically (fails on a cycle).
  • Rule-based method: the order is fixed when the compiler is built, by analysing the rules.
  • Oblivious method: a fixed order, such as the parser's own order. It works for S-attributed definitions (post-order, at each LR reduction) and L-attributed ones (depth-first, left to right: a child's inherited attributes before visiting it, the node's synthesized attributes after all its children).

NTA trap. Wrong: "the order in which the rules are written is the evaluation order." Fix: only the dependencies matter. Several topological orders are usually valid, and a rule written first may have to run last.

Example 8: the dependency graph of a declaration

SDD: D → T L { L.inh = T.type }, T → int { T.type = integer }, L → L1 , id { L1.inh = L.inh; addtype(id.entry, L.inh) }, L → id { addtype(id.entry, L.inh) }. For int a, b, c the tree has three L nodes. The nodes of the graph are T.type (1), L.inh for each L (3), id.entry for each id (3) and one dummy attribute for each addtype (3): 10 nodes. The edges are T.type → top L.inh, then top L.inh → middle L.inh → bottom L.inh (3 edges in this chain), each L.inh → its dummy (3) and each id.entry → its dummy (3): 9 edges. In general, n identifiers give 3n + 1 nodes and 3n edges. One valid order: T.type, the three L.inh from the top down, then each dummy after its id.entry.

10. Parameter-passing mechanisms

MechanismWhat the callee receivesEffect on the caller
Call by valuea copy of the actual’s value (C, Java primitives)none
Call by referencethe actual’s address (l-value); the formal is an aliasevery assignment is immediate
Call by value-result (copy-restore)a copy; on return the final value is copied back to the actual’s address, computed at the callonly at return

For a plain variable passed once, reference, value-result and name agree. They differ when there is aliasing (the same variable passed twice, or a global also passed as an argument) and when the argument contains an expression whose parts change inside the callee, such as a[i] with i modified.

NTA trap. Wrong: "value-result is the same as reference." Fix: with aliasing it is not. In q(n, n) the two copies are written back one after the other, and the last copy-back wins.

Example 9: one call, four answers

int n = 5;
void q(int x, int y) { x = x + 1; y = y + 10; }
q(n, n);

Value: n stays 5. Reference: x and y are both n, so n = 6, then 16: 16. Value-result: x = 6 and y = 15 locally; copying back left to right stores 6 and then 15, so n = 15. Name: every use of x and y means n: 16.

int i = 1; int a[3] = {10, 20, 30};
void p(int x) { i = 2; x = x + 5; }
p(a[i]);

Value: a unchanged. Reference and value-result: the address of a[1] is fixed at the call, so a[1] = 25. Name: x means a[i] and i is now 2, so a[2] = 35 and a[1] stays 20.

11. Symbol tables

The symbol table records every name with its attributes: kind (variable, constant, array, procedure, type, label), type, scope level, width and offset (storage address), for arrays the dimensions and bounds, and for procedures the number and types of parameters and the return type. Every phase uses it:

  • The lexer enters identifiers (or looks them up) and puts a pointer to the entry in the token.
  • The parser and semantic analyser add declarations, detect redeclaration and undeclared names, and check type compatibility and argument counts.
  • Intermediate and target code generation use the offsets for storage allocation and addressing.
  • The error handler enters an undeclared name once, so the same error is not reported at every use.

Organisation. The operations are insert and lookup (plus entering and leaving a scope).

StructureLookup cost for n entriesRemarks
Unsorted linear listO(n); on average (n + 1)/2 comparisons for a successful searchsimple; n insertions and e lookups cost O(n(n + e))
Sorted array / binary searchO(log n)insertion is O(n)
Search treeO(log n) on averageO(n) if it degenerates
Hash table (chaining)O(1) on averagethe usual choice in compilers

Scopes. Block-structured languages keep one table per scope, chained to the table of the enclosing scope, or one hash table whose chains keep the newest entry first together with a stack of scopes. A lookup searches the innermost scope first and moves outwards, so the most closely nested declaration wins (static scope). Leaving a block discards its table or its entries.

Example 10: resolving names through nested scopes

int x = 1;                           /* global table: x → 1 */
void show(void) { printf("%d ", x); }
int main(void) {
    int x = 2;                       /* main's table: x → 2 */
    { int x = 3;                     /* block's table: x → 3 */
      show(); printf("%d ", x); }
    printf("%d", x);
}

show is declared at global level, so its x is found in the global table: 1. Inside the block, x resolves to the block's own entry: 3. After the block its table is gone, and x is main's: 2. The program prints 1 3 2.

12. Translating declarations, assignments, Boolean expressions, control flow and calls

Declarations. A counter, offset, starts at 0 for each procedure. For each declaration T id, the translation enters (id, T.type, offset) in the symbol table and adds T.width to offset. Types are built as type expressions: int[2][3] is array(2, array(3, integer)), of width 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 bytes when an int takes 4 bytes. Nested procedures and records save the current offset, start a new table at 0, and restore the old values afterwards.

Example 11: offsets (int 4, float 8, char 1 bytes; no alignment padding)

int x; float y; int a[5]; char c;

x at 0, then offset 4. y at 4, then 12. a at 12 (width 5 × 4 = 20), then 32. c at 32, then 33. The procedure needs 33 bytes of local storage.

Assignments and array references. Each operator produces one three-address instruction into a new temporary. For a row-major array A[n1][n2] of elements of width w, A[i][j] is at base + (i × n2 + j) × w. For int a[2][3], x = a[i][j] becomes t1 = i * 12; t2 = j * 4; t3 = t1 + t2; x = a[t3].

Boolean expressions are translated either numerically (1 or 0 into a temporary) or as jumping code, where the value is the place control reaches. Jumping code gives short-circuit evaluation: for B1 || B2, if B1 is true, B2 is never tested. In one pass the jump targets are not known yet, so backpatching keeps lists of incomplete jumps: B.truelist, B.falselist and S.nextlist. A relational test emits two instructions, "if x relop y goto _" and "goto _". For B → B1 || M B2, the parser backpatches B1.falselist to M.instr (the start of B2), and B.truelist = B1.truelist ∪ B2.truelist, B.falselist = B2.falselist. For &&, B1.truelist is backpatched to B2, and the false lists are merged.

Control flow. if (B) S1 else S2 becomes the code for B, with B.true at S1 and B.false at S2, and a goto after S1 that skips S2. while (B) S becomes begin: the code for B, S, goto begin, with B.false leading out of the loop.

Procedure calls. For p(e1, …, en), evaluate every argument into a temporary first, then emit param t1, …, param tn, then call p, n, where n is the number of parameters. Emitting all the param instructions together keeps nested calls such as p(q(x), y) from interleaving their parameters.

Example 12: backpatching a < b || c < d

100: if a < b goto _
101: goto 102          (B1.falselist backpatched to B2's start)
102: if c < d goto _
103: goto _

B.truelist = {100, 102} and B.falselist = {103}. These three holes are filled when the enclosing if or while statement knows where the true and false exits go.

13. Data-flow analysis worked through

Local optimisation works inside one basic block. Global optimisation (constant propagation, global common sub-expressions, dead-code elimination and code motion across blocks) needs facts that hold at block boundaries. Data-flow analysis computes them by solving the equations for every block until nothing changes (a fixed point). Reaching definitions starts from IN = ∅ and uses union at join points. Live variables works backwards from the exit.

Example 13: reaching definitions and liveness on a loop

B1: d1: x = 5
    d2: y = 1
B2: if x <= 1 goto B4
B3: d3: y = y * x
    d4: x = x - 1
    goto B2
B4: d5: z = y + x          (z is used after the exit)
Edges: B1→B2, B2→B3, B2→B4, B3→B2

Reaching definitions: gen[B1] = {d1, d2}, kill[B1] = {d3, d4}; gen[B3] = {d3, d4}, kill[B3] = {d1, d2}. After iteration, IN[B2] = OUT[B1] ∪ OUT[B3] = {d1, d2} ∪ {d3, d4} = {d1, d2, d3, d4}. So at B2 the value of x may come from d1 or d4, and constant propagation cannot replace x by 5 there.

Live variables: use[B3] = {x, y}, def[B3] = {x, y}; use[B4] = {x, y}; use[B2] = {x}. Working backwards, IN[B4] = {x, y}, IN[B2] = {x} ∪ OUT[B2] = {x, y}, OUT[B1] = {x, y} and IN[B1] = ∅. Both x and y are live on every loop edge, so they need registers throughout the loop.

14. Peephole optimisation in more depth

A peephole optimiser slides a small window (a few instructions) over the target code or the intermediate code and replaces a pattern by a shorter or faster one. One replacement often creates another, so it makes repeated passes. The standard transformations are:

  • Redundant load and store elimination: in MOV R0, a followed by MOV a, R0, the second instruction is deleted (if it carries no label).
  • Unreachable code elimination: an unlabelled instruction right after an unconditional jump is removed. "if debug == 1 goto L1; goto L2; L1: print" becomes "if debug != 1 goto L2; print", and if debug is the constant 0 the whole test disappears.
  • Flow-of-control optimisation: jumps to jumps are short-circuited: goto L1 … L1: goto L2 becomes goto L2.
  • Algebraic simplification and strength reduction: x = x + 0 and x = x * 1 are deleted, x * 2 becomes x + x or a left shift, x2 becomes x * x.
  • Use of machine idioms: x = x + 1 becomes a single INC or an auto-increment addressing mode.

Peephole optimisation is machine-dependent when applied to target code, is local to the window, and needs no data-flow analysis.

15. Instruction scheduling

On a pipelined processor, an instruction that needs the result of a slow instruction (a load, a multiply) must wait for it. Instruction scheduling reorders instructions so that independent work fills those waiting cycles, without changing the program's meaning. Three dependences constrain the order:

  • True (flow, RAW): I2 reads what I1 writes. It can never be removed.
  • Anti (WAR): I2 writes what I1 reads.
  • Output (WAW): I2 writes what I1 writes.

Anti and output dependences come only from reusing a name, so renaming registers removes them. Inside a basic block, the dependences form a DAG whose edges are weighted by latency. List scheduling repeatedly issues, from the instructions whose operands are ready, the one with the highest priority. The usual priority is the length of the latency-weighted longest path from the instruction to the end of the block (the critical path). Scheduling and register allocation pull against each other: scheduling first raises register pressure, and allocating first introduces reuse of registers, which adds anti and output dependences. Beyond one block there are global techniques (trace and superblock scheduling) and, for loops, software pipelining, which overlaps successive iterations. Compilers for VLIW and in-order processors rely on scheduling most; out-of-order processors also reorder in hardware.

Example 14: filling load delays

One instruction issues per cycle. A dependent instruction may issue 3 cycles after a load, 2 after a multiply and 1 after an add.

1: r1 = load a      2: r2 = r1 + 1      3: r3 = load b
4: r4 = r3 * 2      5: r5 = r2 + r4     6: store c, r5

In the given order the issue cycles are 1, 4, 5, 8, 10, 11: the block takes 11 cycles, with 5 stall cycles. The critical-path priorities are 7 for instruction 3 (load 3 + mul 2 + add 1 + store 1), 6 for instruction 1, 4, 3, 2 and 1 for the rest. List scheduling issues 3, 1, 4, 2, 5, 6 at cycles 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7: 7 cycles, the minimum over all legal orders.
