NTA traps

  • Reading operators by their usual meaning. Wrong: in an SDT, # means "some operator" and you assume its usual precedence. Fix: read both precedence and meaning from the grammar and the semantic rules only.
  • Printing in input order. Wrong: S → aS {print 1} on "aac…" prints 1 first. Fix: actions at the end run at reduction, innermost first, so the output is reversed.
  • "Every L-attributed SDD is S-attributed." It is the reverse: S-attributed ⊂ L-attributed.
  • Counting DAG nodes with repeated sub-expressions. Each distinct (operator, operand nodes) pair is one node. Remember to use the current node of a variable after it is reassigned.
  • Leaders. Forgetting the instruction after a conditional jump is the most common slip. Jump targets and fall-throughs both count.
  • Control link versus access link. The control link points to the caller (dynamic); the access link points to the enclosing scope (static). Options swap these.
  • Triples versus quadruples. Triples save the result field but make code motion hard. Indirect triples fix that. Quadruples are not the option with "no temporary names".
  • Constant folding versus constant propagation. Folding evaluates constant expressions; propagation substitutes a known constant value for a variable.
  • Data-flow directions. Live variables and very busy expressions go backward; reaching definitions and available expressions go forward. Only available and very busy expressions use intersection.

How NTA asks this

  • SDT evaluation: "the value of the expression" or "the output printed". Group the input by the grammar first, then apply the rules.
  • Counts: the number of quadruples, triples, temporaries, DAG nodes, basic blocks, flow-graph edges or registers. State the convention in your head (is the assignment counted? which Sethi–Ullman labelling?) and check that it matches the options.
  • Match: optimisations with examples, data-flow problems with directions, storage classes with allocation, IR forms with properties.
  • A-R and Statement I/II: "static allocation cannot support recursion because …"; "the LR parser evaluates S-attributed definitions because …".
  • Code questions: C programs about static versus automatic storage, recursion depth and short-circuit evaluation. Trace the storage class carefully.

Mini-example (match). List I: A. x = y; z = x + 1 → z = y + 1, B. t = 4 * i → t = t + 4, C. x = 2 * 8 → x = 16, D. move n − 2 out of a loop. List II: I. constant folding, II. copy propagation, III. strength reduction, IV. code motion. Answer: A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV. Eliminate by fixing C (only folding evaluates at compile time) and B (only strength reduction replaces * with +).

Mini-example (A-R). A: Fortran 77-style static allocation cannot support recursive procedures. R: With static allocation each procedure’s local data has one fixed address for the whole run. Both are true, and R is the correct explanation: a second activation would overwrite the first one’s locals.

quiz.explanation: @ appears lower in the grammar, so it binds tighter than $. $ is left-associative (E → E $ T). So the input groups as (3 $ (4 @ 2)) $ 1. By the rules, @ multiplies and $ subtracts: 4 × 2 = 8, 3 − 8 = −5, −5 − 1 = −6. Evaluating strictly left to right gives ((3 − 4) × 2) − 1 = −3, which is not an option. 4 and 13 come from treating the symbols as other operators.

b: I. MOV R0, a followed by MOV a, R0: the second instruction is deleted
II. t1 = a*b; … t2 = a*b becomes t2 = t1
III. x = y + 1 is deleted because x is never used afterwards
IV. The loop body is written twice so the loop test runs half as often

lessons.title: Data communication fundamentals
lessons.summaryHtml: Data communication moves bits between devices through a medium under a protocol. Bits first become a signal, and the channel limits how fast that can happen. Nyquist (C = 2B log2 L) gives the limit for a noiseless channel, and Shannon (C = B log2(1 + SNR)) gives the hard ceiling for a noisy one. Signals weaken and pick up noise, which we measure in decibels. Line codes (NRZ, Manchester, differential Manchester, AMI) and modulation (ASK, FSK, PSK, QAM) turn bits into waveforms. Multiplexing (FDM, TDM, WDM) and switching (circuit, message, packet) let many users share the links.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices over some transmission medium. Five components are always present: the message, the sender, the receiver, the medium and the protocol (the agreed rules). Data flow can be simplex (one way only, like a keyboard to a computer), half-duplex (both ways but one at a time, like a walkie-talkie) or full-duplex (both ways at once, like a telephone call).

Before bits can travel, they must become a signal: a voltage on a wire, light in a fibre or a radio wave. This lesson is about that physical step. How many bits per second can a channel carry? How much weaker is the signal after a long cable? How is a 1 or a 0 drawn as a voltage pattern? How do several users share one link? Think of a highway. Bandwidth is its width, noise is the fog, line coding is the traffic rule for each car, and multiplexing is the lane system.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 9 usually gives a steady share of Paper 2, and this lesson is its most formula-driven part. The favourite items are Nyquist and Shannon capacity numericals, decibel conversions, bit rate versus baud rate with QAM, and "draw or identify the line code" questions. Matching questions pair modulation types, media or multiplexing methods with their properties, and statement questions test switching. These questions are short, and each hinges on one formula or one convention, so they are easy marks if you know them exactly.

Concepts in depth

1. Analog and digital signals, periodic signals and bandwidth

An analog signal takes infinitely many values over a range. A digital signal takes a limited number of levels. A periodic sine wave is described by its peak amplitude, frequency f (cycles per second, in hertz) and phase. Period T = 1/f, and wavelength λ = propagation speed / f. In air, a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi wave has λ = 3×108 / 2.4×109 = 0.125 m.

By Fourier analysis, any composite signal is a sum of sine waves. The bandwidth of a composite signal is the width of its frequency range: highest frequency minus lowest frequency. A signal made of 150, 450, 750 and 1050 Hz components has a bandwidth of 1050 − 150 = 900 Hz. A digital signal is in theory a composite with infinite bandwidth. In practice we keep enough harmonics to recover the bits.

The word "bandwidth" has two meanings, and NET options mix them up. Bandwidth in hertz is the range of frequencies a channel passes. Bandwidth in bits per second is the data rate a link supports. The capacity formulas below connect the two.

2. Bit rate, baud rate and the r factor

Bit rate N is the number of data bits sent per second. Baud rate S (signal rate, modulation rate) is the number of signal elements per second. If each signal element carries r bits, then S = N / r, and r = log2 L, where L is the number of distinct signal elements (levels or constellation points).

  • Binary NRZ: L = 2, r = 1, so S = N.
  • 16-QAM: L = 16, r = 4, so 9600 bps needs only 2400 baud.
  • Manchester: each bit uses two half-bit levels, so r = 1/2 and the signal rate can reach 2N. That is why Manchester needs about twice the bandwidth of NRZ.

Baud rate is what the channel bandwidth limits. More bits per symbol raise the bit rate without raising the baud rate. That is the whole idea of multilevel modulation.

3. Channel capacity: Nyquist and Shannon

Nyquist bit rate (noiseless channel): C = 2 × B × log2 L bits per second. A channel of bandwidth B can carry at most 2B signal elements per second without inter-symbol interference, and each element carries log2 L bits. On a noiseless channel, more levels always give a higher rate.

Shannon capacity (noisy channel): C = B × log2(1 + SNR), where SNR is a power ratio, not decibels. It is an upper limit that no coding or number of levels can beat. With more levels, the levels get closer together, and noise then causes errors. The practical recipe is:

  1. Use Shannon to find the ceiling.
  2. Pick a working rate below the ceiling.
  3. Use Nyquist to find how many levels that rate needs.

Two extremes to remember. If SNR = 0, the capacity is 0 whatever the bandwidth. For a high SNR, log2(1 + SNR) ≈ SNRdB / 3.01. So a 30 dB line gives about 10 bits per hertz.

4. Transmission impairments and decibels

Three impairments degrade a signal:

  • Attenuation is loss of energy with distance. Amplifiers compensate for it.
  • Distortion is a change of shape, because different frequency components travel at different speeds (delay distortion).
  • Noise comes in several kinds: thermal, induced, crosstalk and impulse.

The decibel measures relative power: dB = 10 log10(P2/P1). For voltages it is 20 log10(V2/V1), because power ∝ V2. A loss gives a negative number: halving the power is −3.01 dB. The great convenience is that the dB values of cascaded stages simply add. dBm is power relative to 1 mW: PdBm = 10 log10(P / 1 mW). So 0 dBm = 1 mW, 20 dBm = 100 mW and −30 dBm = 1 μW. Cable loss is often quoted in dB/km: multiply by the length, then add.

SNR = average signal power / average noise power, and SNRdB = 10 log10 SNR. A signal of 10 mW over 1 μW of noise has SNR = 10,000, which is 40 dB.

5. Performance: delay, throughput and bandwidth-delay product

Transmission delay = L / R (packet length / link rate). Propagation delay = distance / propagation speed. In copper and fibre, take the speed as about 2×108 m/s. Latency = transmission + propagation + queuing + processing delay. The bandwidth-delay product R × delay is the number of bits "in flight" that fill the pipe. It returns in the next lesson as the window size needed for full link use.

6. Line coding (digital data to digital signal)

Line coding maps bits to voltage patterns. The designer cares about three things: the DC component, self-synchronisation (enough transitions for the receiver clock) and the signal rate. Conventions differ between textbooks, so an exam question should state its convention. The ones used here, with H = high and L = low, are:

SchemeRuleNotes
NRZ-L (unipolar/polar)level shows the bit (here 1 = H, 0 = L; Forouzan draws the reverse)long runs of 1s or 0s give no transitions, so sync is lost
NRZ-Iinvert the level at the start of a 1; no change for a 0long runs of 0s still cause trouble; used with 4B/5B
RZsignal returns to zero in the middle of each bitthree levels, two changes per bit; rarely used now
Manchester (IEEE 802.3)mid-bit transition: 0 = H→L, 1 = L→Hself-clocking, no DC; 10 Mbps Ethernet. G. E. Thomas uses the opposite
Differential Manchestermid-bit transition always; transition at the start of a 0, none at the start of a 1polarity-independent; IEEE 802.5 Token Ring
AMI (bipolar)0 = zero volts; 1s alternate + and −no DC; B8ZS/HDB3 scrambling fixes long 0 runs
Pseudoternary1 = zero volts; 0s alternate + and −mirror image of AMI

Block coding adds redundancy for synchronisation. 4B/5B maps each 4 bits to a 5-bit code with no more than one leading and two trailing zeros, so 100 Mbps of data becomes 125 Mbps on the line (100BASE-TX, together with MLT-3). 8B/10B (Gigabit Ethernet) has a 25% overhead too.

Analog to digital: Pulse Code Modulation (PCM) goes through four steps. First a low-pass filter band-limits the signal. Then it is sampled at the Nyquist sampling rate of at least 2 × fmax. Each sample is quantised to one of L levels, and each level is encoded in n = log2 L bits. So the bit rate = sampling rate × n. For voice (4 kHz, 8 bits), that is 8000 × 8 = 64 kbps. Delta modulation sends only one bit per sample (up or down).

7. Modulation (digital data to analog signal)

  • ASK varies the amplitude. Bandwidth B = (1 + d) × S, where 0 ≤ d ≤ 1 depends on the filtering. It is sensitive to noise.
  • FSK varies the frequency. For binary FSK, B = (1 + d) × S + 2Δf, where 2Δf is the gap between the two carrier frequencies.
  • PSK varies the phase. BPSK has 2 phases and QPSK has 4 (2 bits per symbol). PSK resists noise better than ASK.
  • QAM varies amplitude and phase together. An M-point constellation carries log2 M bits per symbol: 16-QAM carries 4 bits, 64-QAM 6 and 256-QAM 8.

Analog-to-analog modulation (AM, FM, PM) is used for radio broadcasting. A standard AM station needs 2 × the audio bandwidth, and FM needs about 10 ×.

8. Multiplexing

  • FDM is analog. Each signal gets its own frequency band, with guard bands between neighbours. Total bandwidth = sum of channel bandwidths + guard bands between them.
  • WDM is FDM for light in optical fibre, done with a prism-like multiplexer. DWDM packs the wavelengths closely.
  • Synchronous TDM is digital. Each source owns a fixed slot in every frame, even when it has nothing to send, which wastes capacity. Frame rate = source rate / bits per slot. Link rate = frame rate × bits per frame, and framing bits count too.
  • Statistical TDM gives slots only to active sources, so each slot must carry an address.
  • The T-carrier hierarchy: T1 = 24 channels × 8 bits + 1 framing bit = 193 bits per frame at 8000 frames/s, which is 1.544 Mbps. E1 = 32 × 8 × 8000 = 2.048 Mbps.
  • Spread spectrum (FHSS, DSSS) deliberately widens the band for security and noise resistance.

9. Transmission media

  • Guided media:
    • Twisted pair (UTP/STP; Cat 5e, 6, 6a). The twisting cancels noise and crosstalk. RJ-45 connectors, 100 m segments.
    • Coaxial cable. A central conductor inside a braided shield. Cable TV and the old 10BASE5/10BASE2 Ethernet. BNC connectors.
    • Optical fibre. Light is guided by total internal reflection because the core has a higher refractive index than the cladding. Multimode step-index, multimode graded-index and single-mode (the thinnest core, lowest dispersion, longest reach). Fibre is immune to electromagnetic interference and has the highest bandwidth.
  • Unguided media: radio waves (omnidirectional, 3 kHz–1 GHz), microwaves (1–300 GHz, unidirectional, line of sight, satellite and cellular) and infrared (300 GHz–400 THz, short range, blocked by walls).

10. Switching

  • Circuit switching (telephone network) has three phases: setup, data transfer and teardown. It reserves resources, so the delay is constant but capacity is wasted in silences. It is done at the physical layer.
  • Message switching is store-and-forward of the whole message at every node.
  • Packet switching splits the message into packets. In datagram networks there is no setup, each packet is routed independently, and packets may arrive out of order. In virtual-circuit networks there is a setup phase, all packets follow the same path and carry a VC identifier (as in ATM and Frame Relay).

Store-and-forward delay over k links at rate R, ignoring propagation: a whole message of M bits takes k × M/R. Split into n packets of P bits, it takes (k + n − 1) × P/R, because packets overlap in the pipeline.

Worked examples

Example 1: Shannon then Nyquist

A channel has B = 2 MHz and SNR = 255 (a ratio). Find the capacity, and the number of levels needed to send at 12 Mbps.

  1. Shannon: C = 2×106 × log2(1 + 255) = 2×106 × 8 = 16 Mbps.
  2. Choose 12 Mbps (below the ceiling). Nyquist: 12×106 = 2 × 2×106 × log2 L, so log2 L = 3 and L = 8 levels.

Example 2: SNR given in decibels

A telephone line has B = 3000 Hz and SNR = 30 dB. Find the Shannon capacity.

  1. Convert first: 30 dB means SNR = 1030/10 = 1000.
  2. C = 3000 × log2(1001) = 3000 × 9.967 ≈ 29.9 kbps.
  3. The trap answer 3000 × 30 = 90 kbps puts decibels straight into the formula.

Example 3: cascaded gains and losses

A 5 mW signal passes a cable (−4 dB), an amplifier (+10 dB) and a second cable (−3 dB). Find the output power.

  1. Net gain = −4 + 10 − 3 = +3 dB.
  2. Pout = 5 × 100.3 = 5 × 1.995 ≈ 9.98 mW, which is about double, since +3 dB ≈ ×2.

Example 4: drawing line codes as sequences

Bits 1 0 0 1. Manchester (IEEE: 0 = HL, 1 = LH) gives LH HL HL LH.

Bits 0 1 1 0 in differential Manchester, with the previous level low:

  1. Bit 0: transition at the start (L→H), then mid-bit to L: HL.
  2. Bit 1: no start transition (stays L), mid-bit to H: LH.
  3. Bit 1: stays H, then goes to L: HL.
  4. Bit 0: start transition L→H, then H→L: HL.

Result: HL LH HL HL.

NRZ-I for 1 1 0 1 0 0 1, starting low: H L L H H H L. The level flips on each 1 and holds on each 0.

Example 5: synchronous TDM

Five sources of 2 kbps each are multiplexed. Each slot carries 2 bits, and every frame has 1 framing bit.

  1. Frame rate = 2000 / 2 = 1000 frames/s, so each frame lasts 1 ms.
  2. Bits per frame = 5 × 2 + 1 = 11.
  3. Link rate = 1000 × 11 = 11 kbps.

Example 6: message versus packet switching

A 12,000-bit message crosses 3 links of 1 Mbps (ignore propagation and headers).

  1. As one message: 3 × 12 ms = 36 ms.
  2. As 4 packets of 3000 bits: (3 + 4 − 1) × 3 ms = 18 ms. Pipelining halves the delay.

11. Data flow modes in more depth

The direction of data flow between two devices is a property of the link, and the syllabus names three modes.

ModeWhat happensCapacity useExamples
SimplexOne direction only; one device always sends, the other always receivesThe whole capacity flows one wayKeyboard to computer, computer to monitor, broadcast radio and TV
Half-duplexBoth directions, but only one at a time; the stations take turnsThe whole capacity goes to whichever station is sendingWalkie-talkie, CB radio, classic hub-based Ethernet (CSMA/CD), a Wi-Fi radio channel
Full-duplex (duplex)Both directions at the same timeShared: either two separate paths (two wire pairs or two fibres) or the bandwidth split into two bandsTelephone call, switched Ethernet port, a fibre pair

A 100 Mbps link in full-duplex mode can carry 100 Mbps each way, so up to 200 Mbps of traffic in total. In half-duplex mode the same link carries at most 100 Mbps in total, and it also loses time to turn-arounds (and to collisions on a shared medium). This is why switched, full-duplex Ethernet does not need CSMA/CD at all.

12. Baseband and broadband transmission

Baseband transmission puts the digital signal on the channel as it is, without moving it onto a carrier. Line coding (NRZ, Manchester and so on) produces the signal. Baseband needs a low-pass channel, one whose bandwidth starts at 0 Hz. The signal occupies the whole bandwidth of the medium, so only one signal is on the wire at a time, and stations share it in time (TDM or a MAC protocol). Ethernet is baseband: the "BASE" in 10BASE-T, 100BASE-TX or 1000BASE-T says exactly that.

How much bandwidth does a baseband signal of bit rate N need? The hardest pattern, 0101…, is a square wave of frequency N/2, and each extra odd harmonic adds more bandwidth. Forouzan's approximations:

ApproximationHarmonics keptMinimum bandwidth
Rough1st onlyB = N/2 (so a channel of bandwidth B carries about 2B bps)
Better1st and 3rdB = 3N/2
Best1st, 3rd and 5thB = 5N/2

Broadband transmission (also called passband or bandpass transmission) uses modulation. The data changes an analog carrier (ASK, FSK, PSK, QAM), which shifts the signal into a band-pass channel, one that does not start at 0 Hz. Each signal keeps to its own band, so many signals can share the medium at once by FDM. Cable TV, cable modems (DOCSIS), DSL (voice below 4 kHz, data above it), radio links and the old 10BROAD36 Ethernet are broadband. A broadband cable system usually carries upstream and downstream traffic in separate frequency bands through a head-end.

PropertyBasebandBroadband
SignalDigital, not modulated (line coded)Analog carrier, modulated
Channel neededLow-pass (starts at 0 Hz)Band-pass
Signals at onceOne; shared in timeMany; shared in frequency (FDM)
Signal boostingRepeaters regenerate the bitsAmplifiers boost the analog signal
Examples10BASE-T, 100BASE-TX, 1000BASE-TCable TV and cable modems, DSL, 10BROAD36

Example 7 (baseband bandwidth). A 1 Mbps signal is sent by baseband transmission. What bandwidth does it need?

  1. Rough (first harmonic only): B = N/2 = 500 kHz.
  2. Better (1st and 3rd harmonics): B = 3N/2 = 1.5 MHz.
  3. Best (up to the 5th harmonic): B = 5N/2 = 2.5 MHz.

Going the other way, a low-pass channel of 4 kHz carries about 2 × 4 = 8 kbps by the rough rule.

NTA trap: "broadband" in this syllabus sense does not just mean "fast Internet", and "baseband" does not mean slow. Baseband means unmodulated over a low-pass channel (Gigabit Ethernet is baseband); broadband means modulated, band-pass and usually many channels by FDM.

Formula and fact sheet

QuantityFormula or fact
Nyquist (noiseless)C = 2B log2 L
Shannon (noisy)C = B log2(1 + SNR), with SNR as a ratio
SNR in dB10 log10(Ps/Pn); 3 dB ≈ ×2, 10 dB = ×10, 30 dB = ×1000
Power / voltage dB10 log10(P2/P1) / 20 log10(V2/V1)
dBm10 log10(P / 1 mW); 0 dBm = 1 mW
Baud rateS = N / r, r = log2 L
ASK / BFSK bandwidth(1 + d)S / (1 + d)S + 2Δf
PCM bit rate2 fmax × log2 L
DelaysTt = L/R, Tp = d/v; bandwidth-delay product = R × delay
Wavelengthλ = v / f
T1 / E11.544 Mbps (24 ch) / 2.048 Mbps (32 ch)
Store-and-forwardmessage: kM/R; n packets: (k + n − 1)P/R
4B/5B, 8B/10Bline rate = 5/4 or 10/8 of the data rate
Data flowSimplex one way; half-duplex both ways in turns; full-duplex both ways at once (100 Mbps full-duplex = 200 Mbps total)
Baseband bandwidthB ≈ N/2 (rough), 3N/2 (better), 5N/2 (best); low-pass channel, one signal
BroadbandModulated carrier, band-pass channel, many channels by FDM (cable TV, DSL)

NTA traps

  • Putting decibels into Shannon. The wrong step is C = B log2(1 + 30) for "30 dB". Fix: convert first, SNR = 10dB/10.
  • Treating Nyquist as a noisy-channel limit. The wrong belief is that more levels always give more speed. Fix: on a noisy channel, Shannon caps the rate whatever L is.
  • Mixing up bit rate and baud rate. The wrong belief is "baud ≤ bit rate always". Fix: in Manchester the baud can be twice the bit rate. In QAM it is lower.
  • Using 20 log for power. Fix: 10 log for power, 20 log for voltage or current.
  • Forgetting guard bands or framing bits. In FDM, n channels have n − 1 guard bands. In TDM, add the framing bits to every frame.
  • Getting the Manchester direction wrong. Check which convention the question states. IEEE 802.3 is 0 = high-to-low, and G. E. Thomas is the reverse.
  • Getting the differential Manchester rule wrong. The bit is set by whether there is a transition at the start of the bit, not by the direction of the mid-bit transition.
  • Getting the fibre modes wrong. Single-mode has the smallest core and the longest reach. Multimode has a larger core.

How NTA asks this

  • Numericals. Nyquist, Shannon, dB and baud rate. Memorise the four formulas and three dB anchors (3, 10 and 30 dB). If the numbers are powers of two, the answer is usually exact.
  • Match the following. Modulation to the parameter it varies, media to their property, multiplexing to its domain, and line code to its rule.
  • Assertion–reason and statement questions. Manchester bandwidth, differential Manchester and polarity, and circuit versus packet switching.
  • Order questions. The PCM steps and the electromagnetic spectrum.

Mini-example: A–R

A: Manchester coding needs about twice the bandwidth of NRZ at the same bit rate. R: Manchester has a transition in the middle of every bit.

Both are true, and the mid-bit transition is exactly why the signal rate doubles. So the answer is option 1: (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

Elimination trick: in a capacity question, first check whether the question says noiseless or noisy. That tells you Nyquist or Shannon, and it removes two options at once. Then check whether SNR is in dB.

terms.definition: Number of signal elements per second; equals bit rate ÷ bits per signal element.
Maximum rate on a noiseless channel: 2B log₂ L, where L is the number of signal levels.
Maximum error-free rate on a noisy channel: B log₂(1 + SNR), with SNR as a power ratio.
10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁): the relative gain (+) or loss (−) of power; dB values of cascaded stages add.
Every bit has a mid-bit transition; in IEEE 802.3, 0 is high-to-low and 1 is low-to-high.
Mid-bit transition always; a transition at the start of the bit means 0, none means 1.
Modulation that varies amplitude and phase together; an M-point constellation carries log₂ M bits per symbol.
Each source owns a fixed time slot in every frame, even when idle.
Unused frequency strip between adjacent FDM channels to prevent interference.
Packet switching without setup; each packet is routed independently and may arrive out of order.

lessons.examTip: Decide first: noiseless → Nyquist (levels matter), noisy → Shannon (levels do not). Convert dB to a ratio before using Shannon.

Attempt problems 9–12, 14 and 15 (match, A–R, statements, multi-select and order) in 8 minutes.
Check every answer against solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for, for example putting dB straight into Shannon or forgetting a guard band.

Write the formula sheet (Nyquist, Shannon, dB, dBm, baud, ASK/FSK bandwidth, PCM, TDM, T1/E1) from memory and compare it with the lesson table.

quiz.question: A noiseless channel has a bandwidth of 4 kHz and uses 8 signal levels. What is the maximum bit rate?
quiz.explanation: Nyquist: C = 2B log₂ L = 2 × 4000 × log₂ 8 = 8000 × 3 = 24 kbps. 12 kbps forgets the factor 2. 32 kbps uses 8000 × 4, and 48 kbps doubles twice.

quiz.question: A channel has a bandwidth of 2 MHz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 255 (a power ratio, not in dB). What is its Shannon capacity?
quiz.explanation: C = B log₂(1 + SNR) = 2×10⁶ × log₂ 256 = 2×10⁶ × 8 = 16 Mbps. 32 Mbps wrongly uses the Nyquist factor 2B. 510 Mbps multiplies B by SNR directly. 8 Mbps takes log₂ 256 as 4.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: NRZ-L: the level itself is the bit (A-III). NRZ-I: invert on 1 (B-I). Manchester: the direction of the mid-bit transition is the bit (C-IV). Differential Manchester: always a mid-bit transition, and the presence of a transition at the start marks a 0 (D-II). The distractors swap one or two of these pairs.

b: I. The level is inverted at the start of a bit for a 1; no change for a 0
II. A mid-bit transition always; a transition at the start of the bit means 0
III. The signal level alone represents the bit
IV. A mid-bit transition whose direction gives the bit value

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Each bit is split into two half-bit levels, so up to two signal changes happen per bit: r = 1/2 and S can reach 2N. The higher signal rate is exactly why the bandwidth doubles. R explains A.

stmts: Assertion (A): For the same bit rate, Manchester encoding needs about twice the bandwidth of NRZ encoding.
Reason (R): Manchester encoding has a transition in the middle of every bit, so its signal rate can be up to twice the bit rate.

quiz.question: A 5 mW signal passes through a cable with 4 dB loss, then an amplifier with 10 dB gain, then another cable with 3 dB loss. What is the output power (approximately)?
quiz.explanation: dB values add: −4 + 10 − 3 = +3 dB. P_out = 5 × 10^(3/10) = 5 × 1.995 ≈ 9.98 mW. 15 mW adds the dB numbers to the milliwatts. 1.5 mW uses 5 × 3/10. 5.3 mW treats 3 dB as a small percentage.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Statement I is false: in Manchester coding, r = 1/2, so the baud rate can be twice the bit rate. Statement II is true: log₂ 16 = 4 bits per symbol.

stmts: Statement I: The baud rate of a digital signal is always less than or equal to its bit rate.
Statement II: In 16-QAM, each signal element carries 4 bits.

quiz.question: A modem must send 36 kbps using 64-QAM. What baud rate is needed?
quiz.explanation: 64-QAM carries log₂ 64 = 6 bits per symbol, so S = N / r = 36,000 / 6 = 6000 baud. 12,000 uses 3 bits per symbol. 2304 = 36,000 × 64 / 1000 is meaningless. 36,000 treats each symbol as one bit.

quiz.question: Which of the following statements about switching are correct?
quiz.explanation: A is true (resources are reserved from setup until teardown). B is true (datagrams are routed independently). C is false: a virtual circuit is set up first, then all packets follow it. D is true. E is false: queuing makes packet delays vary.

stmts: A. Circuit switching reserves link resources for the whole duration of the connection.
B. In a datagram network, packets of one message may take different paths and arrive out of order.
C. A virtual-circuit network needs no setup phase before data transfer.
D. Message switching stores and forwards the whole message at every node.
E. Packet switching guarantees the same delay for every packet.

quiz.question: Five sources, each of 2 kbps, are multiplexed by synchronous TDM. Each slot carries 2 bits from one source, and one framing bit is added to every frame. What is the data rate of the link?
quiz.explanation: Frame rate = source rate / bits per slot = 2000 / 2 = 1000 frames per second. Each frame has 5 × 2 + 1 = 11 bits. Link rate = 1000 × 11 = 11 kbps. 10 kbps ignores the framing bit. 12 kbps adds one framing bit per source.

quiz.question: Arrange the steps of Pulse Code Modulation (PCM) in the correct order.
quiz.explanation: PCM first filters the signal to limit its bandwidth (D). Then it samples at the Nyquist sampling rate (B), quantises the samples (C) and encodes the levels as bits (A). Quantising before sampling is impossible, because there are no samples yet.

stmts: A. Encode each quantised level as a group of bits
B. Sample the signal at a rate of at least 2 × f(max)
C. Round each sample to the nearest quantisation level
D. Band-limit the analog signal with a low-pass filter

lessons.title: Network models and the physical view
lessons.summaryHtml: Networks are classified by size (PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN) and by topology (mesh, star, bus, ring, hybrid). A full mesh of n devices needs n(n − 1)/2 links. The OSI model splits networking into seven layers, from physical up to application. The TCP/IP suite uses four or five layers, and its application layer covers OSI’s session and presentation layers. Each layer has its own address: MAC (48 bits, data link), IP (32 or 128 bits, network) and port (16 bits, transport). Hubs and repeaters work at layer 1, bridges and switches at layer 2 (one collision domain per port), and routers at layer 3 (they split broadcast domains). Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) frames are 64–1518 bytes long, and wireless LANs (802.11) use CSMA/CA.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A computer network is a set of devices (nodes) connected by links so that they can share data and resources. Sending a web page from a server to your phone involves many separate jobs:

  • putting bits on a wire;
  • getting a frame to the next box;
  • finding a route across many networks;
  • delivering the data to the right program;
  • making sure nothing is lost.

A layered model gives each job to one layer. Each layer uses the service of the layer below and offers a service to the layer above. Think of posting a parcel. You write the letter (application), put it in an envelope with an address (network), the post office bags it for the next van (data link), and the van drives the road (physical). Each helper only needs to understand its own label.

This lesson builds that picture: network types and topologies, the OSI and TCP/IP models, the four kinds of addresses, the devices that work at each layer, Ethernet and the IEEE 802 family, and the basics of wireless LANs.

Why it matters for NET

This is the most "matching-friendly" topic in Unit 9. NTA regularly asks you to match layers with their functions, devices with layers, IEEE standards with technologies, or addresses with their sizes. It also asks you to order the OSI layers or the encapsulation steps. The numericals are light but frequent: links in a mesh, collision and broadcast domains, header overhead and Ethernet frame limits. Precise definitions win these marks, and so do the classic confusions (hub versus switch versus router, OSI versus TCP/IP layer counts).

Concepts in depth

1. Network types and topologies

Networks are classified by size:

  • PAN: a few metres, such as Bluetooth.
  • LAN: a building or campus, privately owned, high speed.
  • MAN: a city.
  • WAN: a country or the globe, often leased lines. The Internet is a network of networks joined by routers.

Connections are point-to-point (a dedicated link between two devices) or multipoint (a shared link).

TopologyLinks for n devicesStrengthWeakness
Mesh (full)n(n − 1)/2 duplex links; n − 1 ports per devicerobust, private, no traffic sharingcostly cabling and ports
Starn links to a central hub or switcheasy to install; one link failure affects one devicethe hub is a single point of failure
Busone backbone + n drop linesleast cablea break in the backbone stops everything; hard fault isolation
Ringn point-to-point links, each device joined to two neighbourseasy to add a device; a signal travels one way through repeatersone break can disable the ring (dual rings help)
Hybrid / treecombinationsscalesmore complex

For example, a full mesh of 10 devices needs 10 × 9 / 2 = 45 links, and each device needs 9 ports. Going the other way, 66 links means n(n − 1) = 132, so n = 12.

2. The OSI reference model

The ISO's Open Systems Interconnection model has seven layers. A mnemonic from the bottom up is "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away".

#LayerKey responsibilitiesPDU
7Applicationservices to the user: file transfer, mail, directory, remote accessmessage / data
6Presentationtranslation (syntax), encryption, compressiondata
5Sessiondialog control (half/full duplex), synchronisation points (checkpoints)data
4Transportprocess-to-process delivery (port addresses), segmentation and reassembly, end-to-end flow and error control, connection controlsegment (TCP) / datagram (UDP)
3Networksource-to-destination (host-to-host) delivery across networks, logical addressing, routingpacket / datagram
2Data linknode-to-node (hop-to-hop) delivery, framing, physical addressing, flow and error control on a link, access controlframe
1Physicalbits to signals, the medium, data rate, bit synchronisation, line configuration, topology, transmission modebits

On the way down, each layer adds its own header (the data link layer also adds a trailer, the CRC). This is called encapsulation, and the receiver removes the headers in reverse order. Peer layers on two machines talk "virtually" through their headers, while the real data moves down, across and up. The peers follow a protocol. Adjacent layers in one machine meet at an interface, through service access points.

3. The TCP/IP protocol suite

TCP/IP came before OSI and runs the Internet. Textbooks draw it with four layers (application, transport, internet, host-to-network/link) or five (application, transport, network, data link, physical, as in Forouzan). Its application layer covers OSI's session, presentation and application layers. Protocols by layer:

  • application: HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS, SNMP, TELNET;
  • transport: TCP (connection-oriented, reliable), UDP (connectionless) and SCTP;
  • network: IP, with ICMP, IGMP and ARP;
  • data link and physical: Ethernet, Wi-Fi and so on.

OSI and TCP/IP differ in several ways:

  • OSI came as a model before its protocols; TCP/IP came as protocols first and the model was fitted later.
  • OSI clearly separates service, interface and protocol.
  • OSI's network layer supports both connectionless and connection-oriented service, but its transport layer is connection-oriented only. TCP/IP is the reverse: connectionless (IP) at the network layer, and both options (TCP/UDP) at the transport layer.

4. Addressing

AddressLayerSize and exampleScope
Physical (MAC)data link48 bits, e.g. 3D:1A:07:22:5C:90local link; changes at every hop
Logical (IP)network32 bits (IPv4) or 128 bits (IPv6)global, unchanged end to end (without NAT)
Porttransport16 bits, 0–65535; well-known 0–1023identifies the process
SpecificapplicationURL, e-mail addressuser-friendly names

A MAC address has a 24-bit OUI (the vendor ID) and a 24-bit device part, so one OUI covers 224 = 16,777,216 interfaces. The least significant bit of the first byte is the I/G bit: 0 means unicast (individual), 1 means multicast (group). FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF is the broadcast address. For example, 3D = 0011 1101 ends in 1, so 3D:… is multicast, while 5A = 0101 1010 ends in 0, so it is unicast.

5. Connecting devices

DeviceLayerWhat it doesCollision domainsBroadcast domains
Repeater1regenerates (not amplifies) the bit pattern, extends a segmentdoes not splitdoes not split
Hub1multiport repeater; sends every bit out of all portsdoes not splitdoes not split
Bridge2filters and forwards frames using a MAC table; learns addressesone per portdoes not split
Layer-2 switch2multiport bridge, full duplex per port, can build VLANsone per portone (per VLAN)
Router3forwards packets using IP addresses and routing tablesone per interfaceone per interface
Gatewayup to 7translates between different protocol suites––

A learning switch (or bridge) starts with an empty table. For each frame, it records source MAC → incoming port. It then forwards to the known port of the destination, or floods the frame out of every other port if the destination is unknown or broadcast. Loops between bridges are prevented by the Spanning Tree Protocol (IEEE 802.1D). VLANs (IEEE 802.1Q) split one switch into several broadcast domains.

6. Ethernet and IEEE 802

IEEE project 802 splits the data link layer into LLC (802.2, flow and error control shared by all LANs) and MAC (access method, specific to each LAN). The main members are:

  • 802.1: bridging, STP and VLANs;
  • 802.3: Ethernet (CSMA/CD);
  • 802.4: token bus;
  • 802.5: token ring;
  • 802.11: wireless LAN;
  • 802.15: WPAN (802.15.1 is Bluetooth, 802.15.4 is the base of Zigbee);
  • 802.16: WiMAX.

The Ethernet frame fields, in order: preamble (7 bytes) and SFD (1 byte), then destination address (6), source address (6), type/length (2), data (46–1500), CRC (4).

  • The preamble and SFD are added by the physical layer and are not counted in the frame length.
  • So the minimum frame is 6 + 6 + 2 + 46 + 4 = 64 bytes and the maximum is 1518 bytes.
  • Payloads below 46 bytes are padded.
  • The destination comes first so that a station can start filtering early.
  • The minimum size exists so that a collision is detected while the sender is still transmitting (next lesson). At 10 Mbps, the slot time is 512 bit times = 51.2 μs.
StandardMediumMax segmentEncoding
10BASE5thick coax (bus)500 mManchester
10BASE2thin coax (bus)185 mManchester
10BASE-TUTP to a hub (star)100 mManchester
10BASE-Ffibre2000 mManchester
100BASE-TX / FXCat 5 UTP / fibre100 m / 2 km4B/5B + MLT-3 / 4B/5B + NRZ-I
1000BASE-SX, LX, Tmultimode fibre, single-mode fibre, Cat 5e550 m, 5 km, 100 m8B/10B (fibre), 4D-PAM5 (T)

In the name "10BASE-T", 10 is the rate in Mbps, BASE means baseband signalling, and 5 or 2 is roughly the segment length in hundreds of metres. Switched full-duplex Ethernet has no collisions, so CSMA/CD is not used there.

7. Wireless LANs (IEEE 802.11) basics

An 802.11 network has two modes:

  • A BSS (basic service set) is either ad hoc (stations only) or infrastructure (with an access point, AP).
  • Several BSSs joined through a distribution system form an ESS.

A wireless station cannot listen while it transmits, and it may not hear distant stations. This gives the hidden-station problem (two stations that cannot hear each other both send to the AP) and the exposed-station problem. So 802.11 uses CSMA/CA with inter-frame spaces (DIFS, SIFS), random backoff, positive ACKs and an optional RTS/CTS handshake. The NAV timer implements virtual carrier sensing. An 802.11 data frame can carry up to four address fields.

VariantBandPeak rate
802.11b2.4 GHz11 Mbps
802.11a5 GHz54 Mbps
802.11g2.4 GHz54 Mbps
802.11n (Wi-Fi 4)2.4 / 5 GHz, MIMOup to 600 Mbps
802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5)5 GHzmulti-gigabit
802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6/6E)2.4 / 5 (/6) GHz, OFDMAmulti-gigabit

Worked examples

Example 1: collision and broadcast domains

Router R has two interfaces. Interface 1 goes to switch S1, which has 4 hosts and also hub H1 (with 3 hosts) attached. Interface 2 goes to hub H2 with 5 hosts.

  1. S1 side: each switch port is its own collision domain. That gives the R–S1 link (1), the 4 hosts (4), and the H1 port together with everything on H1 (1): 6 domains.
  2. H2 side: a hub does not split anything, so R, H2 and its 5 hosts share 1 domain.
  3. Collision domains = 6 + 1 = 7. Broadcast domains = the router interfaces = 2.

Example 2: header overhead

A 1400-byte application message gets a 20-byte TCP header, a 20-byte IP header and 18 bytes of Ethernet header plus trailer.

  1. Total = 1400 + 20 + 20 + 18 = 1458 bytes.
  2. Efficiency = 1400 / 1458 = 96.02%, so the overhead is about 3.98%.

Example 3: a learning switch

Hosts A, B, C and D sit on ports 1–4. The table starts empty. The frames are A→C, C→A, B→C, D→B, and then B→broadcast.

  1. A→C: learn A on port 1; C is unknown, so the frame is flooded.
  2. C→A: learn C on port 3; A is known, so it is forwarded to port 1.
  3. B→C: learn B on port 2; forwarded to port 3.
  4. D→B: learn D on port 4; forwarded to port 2.
  5. B→broadcast: always flooded.

Frames flooded = 2. The final table has all 4 entries.

Example 4: Ethernet limits

A 10-byte payload needs 46 − 10 = 36 bytes of padding. A full frame carries 1500 payload bytes in 1518 bytes, and on the wire you also pay 8 bytes of preamble/SFD and a 12-byte inter-frame gap. So the efficiency = 1500 / 1538 = 97.53%. At 100 Mbps, a 1518-byte frame takes 1518 × 8 / 108 = 121.44 μs.

8. Backbone networks and the structure of the Internet

A backbone network joins several LANs. Its "stations" are not end hosts but the connecting devices of the LANs: bridges, switches or routers. It normally runs faster than the LANs it joins (10/40/100 Gigabit Ethernet over fibre). Forouzan describes three architectures.

  • Bus backbone. The backbone is a shared, bus-like medium, and each LAN's bridge or router attaches to it. It suits a distributed backbone that runs through a building, floor by floor.
  • Star backbone (also called a collapsed or switched backbone). The backbone is a single high-speed switch, and each LAN connects to it. It is the common design inside a building today. The central switch is a single point of failure, so large sites duplicate it.
  • Connecting remote LANs. A point-to-point link (a leased line, fibre or a WAN service) joins two remote bridges or routers, and the link itself acts as the backbone.

Campus networks are usually built in three tiers: the access layer (switches where hosts plug in), the distribution layer (which aggregates access switches and applies policy, often with routing between VLANs) and the core layer (the fast backbone that joins the distribution blocks). Whether the backbone joins the LANs into one broadcast domain depends on the device: a backbone switch leaves one broadcast domain for the whole site (unless VLANs split it), while a backbone router gives one broadcast domain per interface.

The Internet is a network of networks with a loose hierarchy of Internet service providers. Tier-1 ISPs run global backbones and reach every other network by peering, without paying anyone for transit. Tier-2 (regional) ISPs buy transit from tier-1 networks and peer with each other. Access (tier-3) ISPs connect homes and offices. Networks meet at IXPs (Internet exchange points), where many of them interconnect and exchange traffic, and each provider has points of presence (PoPs) where customers connect. Large content providers run their own private networks close to users. Coordination is shared: the IETF writes the standards (published as RFCs), ICANN/IANA coordinates the root of the domain name system and the global pools of addresses and protocol numbers, and five regional Internet registries allocate address blocks (APNIC serves the Asia-Pacific region, including India).

9. Virtual LANs (VLANs)

A VLAN is a LAN defined by software rather than by wiring. The switch groups ports or stations into logical broadcast domains, wherever the stations physically sit. A broadcast in one VLAN reaches only the members of that VLAN. The benefits are less broadcast traffic, better security (groups are isolated at layer 2), cheaper moves (a person who changes desk is moved by configuration, not by recabling) and virtual workgroups that span floors.

Membership can be decided by any of these characteristics:

  • Port number (static, the most common): ports 1–8 in VLAN 10, for example.
  • MAC address: the 48-bit hardware address decides, so a station keeps its VLAN when it moves.
  • IP address (layer-3 based): the station's logical address decides.
  • IP multicast: a station joins a VLAN by joining a multicast group.
  • A combination of these.

Configuration is manual, semi-automatic or automatic. Switches tell one another about membership by table maintenance, by time-division multiplexing of the trunk among VLANs, or, in practice, by frame tagging, standardised as IEEE 802.1Q. The 802.1Q tag is 4 bytes inserted after the source MAC address:

FieldBitsMeaning
TPID160x8100, marks the frame as tagged
PCP3Priority (802.1p), 8 levels
DEI1Drop eligible indicator
VID12VLAN identifier: 4096 values, of which 0 and 4095 are reserved, leaving 4094 usable VLANs

So the largest tagged Ethernet frame is 1518 + 4 = 1522 bytes. A trunk link between switches carries frames of many VLANs, tagged. An access port carries one VLAN, untagged. The tag does not change the MAC addresses, and a frame never leaves its VLAN at layer 2. Traffic between VLANs needs a router (for example "router on a stick" over one trunk) or a layer-3 switch.

Example 5 (VLANs and broadcast domains). Three switches are joined by 802.1Q trunks and carry VLANs 10, 20, 30 and 40, each with hosts on all three switches. How many broadcast domains are there, and how does a host in VLAN 10 reach a host in VLAN 20?

A VLAN is one broadcast domain however many switches it spans, so there are 4 broadcast domains (not 3 switches, not 12 switch–VLAN pairs). A broadcast in VLAN 10 crosses the trunks tagged with VID 10 and reaches only VLAN 10 ports. Traffic from VLAN 10 to VLAN 20 must go through a router or a layer-3 switch. If the same site instead joined 6 switched LANs (no VLANs) through a backbone router with one interface per LAN, there would be 6 broadcast domains; through a backbone switch, just 1.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFact

NTA traps

  • "TCP/IP has seven layers." The wrong reasoning copies OSI. Fix: TCP/IP has 4 or 5 layers, and its application layer absorbs session and presentation.
  • "A switch separates broadcast domains." The wrong reasoning is "a switch splits everything". Fix: a switch splits collision domains only (unless you use VLANs). Routers split broadcast domains.
  • "A repeater amplifies." Fix: it regenerates the bit pattern, so noise is not amplified. It works only at layer 1.
  • Counting the preamble in the frame length. Fix: the 64 and 1518 byte limits exclude the preamble and SFD.
  • Routing belongs to the network layer, not transport. Also, encryption and compression belong to the presentation layer, and dialog control to the session layer.
  • Mixing up the kinds of delivery. Hop-to-hop is the data link layer, not the network layer. Process-to-process is the transport layer.
  • Reading the wrong bit for multicast. Fix: check the least significant bit of the first byte, not the last byte.

How NTA asks this

  • Match. Layer ↔ function, device ↔ layer, IEEE number ↔ technology, address ↔ size, Ethernet variant ↔ medium.
  • Order. The OSI layers, the encapsulation data units (message → segment → packet → frame → bits) and the Ethernet frame fields.
  • Numericals. Mesh links, domain counts, overhead percentage and padding.
  • A–R and statements. Hub versus switch versus router behaviour, and OSI versus TCP/IP.

Mini-example: match

Match Repeater, Bridge, Router and Gateway with Physical, Data link, Network and All layers.

The answer is Repeater–Physical, Bridge–Data link, Router–Network, Gateway–All layers. Distractors usually swap the bridge and the router. Eliminate any option that puts a hub or repeater above layer 1.

Elimination trick: for domain counting, first mark every router interface: that gives the broadcast count at once. Then count one collision domain per switch or bridge port, and treat everything behind a hub as a single domain.

terms.definition: Each layer adds its header (and the data link layer a trailer) to the data from the layer above before passing it down.
The transport layer’s job: delivering data to the correct program using port numbers.
The data link layer’s job: moving a frame from one node to the next node on the same link.
Part of a network where two simultaneous transmissions collide; split by switch, bridge and router ports.
Set of devices that receive each other’s broadcast frames; split only by routers (or VLANs).
48-bit physical address; 24-bit OUI plus 24-bit device part; LSB of the first byte = 1 means multicast.
Records source MAC → port for each frame, forwards to known destinations and floods unknown or broadcast ones.
IEEE 802 split of the data link layer: 802.2 LLC common to all LANs, MAC specific to each LAN type.
Two wireless stations that cannot hear each other both transmit to the same AP; eased by RTS/CTS.

lessons.examTip: For domain counting: broadcast domains = router interfaces; collision domains = one per switch/bridge/router port, and a hub with everything behind it is one.

steps: Download practice-set.md. Attempt problems 1–4, 9, 11 and 14 (the counting problems) in 11 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).

Check every answer against solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for, for example counting hub hosts as separate collision domains or learning from the destination address.

lessons.title: Data link layer
lessons.summaryHtml: The data link layer turns a noisy bit pipe into a reliable node-to-node link. It frames the bits (character count, byte stuffing, or bit stuffing with the flag 01111110). It detects errors with parity, checksums or CRC (modulo-2 division), and it can correct them with Hamming codes (2r ≥ m + r + 1). It runs flow control and ARQ: stop-and-wait has η = 1/(1 + 2a), and Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat allow windows of 2k − 1 and 2k−1. HDLC and PPP are the classic link protocols. On shared media, the MAC sublayer decides access. Pure ALOHA peaks at 18.4% and slotted ALOHA at 36.8%. CSMA/CD needs frames of at least 2TpR bits, and CSMA/CA and token passing avoid collisions altogether.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

The physical layer delivers a raw stream of bits that may contain errors. The data link layer turns that stream into a reliable link between two neighbouring nodes. It does four jobs:

  • It cuts the stream into frames.
  • It adds redundancy so the receiver can detect or correct errors.
  • It paces the sender (flow control) and retransmits lost frames (ARQ).
  • When many stations share one medium, its MAC sublayer decides who may transmit (ALOHA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA, token passing).

Picture a courier between two offices. He packs documents into numbered envelopes (framing), adds a checksum seal (error detection), waits for receipts (ARQ), and on a shared corridor follows a rule for who walks first (MAC).

Why it matters for NET

This is the most numerical lesson of Unit 9, and a frequently tested area. The favourites are:

  • CRC remainders by modulo-2 division;
  • Hamming distance and the number of Hamming check bits;
  • stop-and-wait efficiency, Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat window sizes and sequence-number bits;
  • ALOHA throughput;
  • the CSMA/CD minimum frame size or maximum cable length.

Statement and matching questions test bit stuffing, HDLC frame types and the MAC protocols. Every numerical here follows one fixed formula, so practise the formulas until they are automatic.

Concepts in depth

1. Framing

The receiver must find where each frame begins and ends. There are four ways:

  • Character count. A header field gives the frame length. One corrupted count loses synchronisation for all later frames.
  • Byte stuffing. Special FLAG bytes mark the boundaries. If a FLAG or ESC byte appears in the data, an ESC is inserted before it. PPP uses flag 0x7E and escape 0x7D, and the escaped byte is XORed with 0x20. So 7E 41 7D 20 becomes 7D 5E 41 7D 5D 20.
  • Bit stuffing. HDLC's flag is 01111110. Inside the frame, after every five consecutive 1s the sender inserts a 0, and the receiver removes a 0 that follows five 1s. So the flag pattern can never appear in the data. For example, 0111111111100 becomes 011111011111000.
  • Physical-layer coding violations. Invalid code symbols mark frame boundaries.

2. Error detection

Errors come as single-bit errors or burst errors. The length of a burst is counted from the first corrupted bit to the last.

  • Simple (even) parity. One bit makes the number of 1s even. It detects every odd number of flipped bits, but no even number.
  • Two-dimensional parity. There is a parity bit for every row and every column. It detects all 1-, 2- and 3-bit errors and corrects any single-bit error (the failing row and column meet at the bad bit). Some 4-bit rectangular patterns go undetected.
  • Checksum. The Internet checksum used by IP, TCP and UDP works like this. Add the data as 16-bit words in one's complement arithmetic, wrapping every carry back into the low bits. Then complement the sum. The receiver adds everything, including the checksum, and must get all 1s, whose complement is 0.
  • CRC (cyclic redundancy check). Choose a generator polynomial G(x) of degree r, written as r + 1 bits. Append r zeros to the data and divide by G using modulo-2 arithmetic, where subtraction is XOR and there are no borrows. The r-bit remainder is the CRC, and it replaces the zeros. The receiver divides the whole codeword by G: a zero remainder means "accept".

The CRC guarantees are:

  • all single-bit errors are detected if G has at least two terms;
  • all burst errors of length ≤ r are detected;
  • all odd numbers of errors are detected if (x + 1) is a factor of G;
  • longer bursts slip through with probability about (1/2)r.

CRC-32 (Ethernet) has r = 32.

3. Error correction: Hamming distance and Hamming code

The Hamming distance d(x, y) is the number of positions in which two equal-length words differ: count the 1s in x XOR y. The minimum distance dmin of a code is the smallest distance between any two codewords. The key results are:

  • to detect up to s errors, you need dmin ≥ s + 1;
  • to correct up to t errors, you need dmin ≥ 2t + 1.

So a code with dmin = 5 detects 4 errors and corrects 2.

The Hamming code corrects single-bit errors. For m data bits it needs r check bits, where r is the smallest number with 2r ≥ m + r + 1. The r bits must be able to name every one of the m + r positions, plus "no error". Check bits sit at the power-of-two positions 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on. The check bit at position p covers every position whose binary index has bit p set. With even parity, the receiver XORs the indices of all positions holding 1. This syndrome is 0 for a valid word, or else it is the position of the flipped bit.

Data bits m471112265758
Check bits r3445567

4. Flow control and ARQ

Let Tt = frame transmission time (L/R) and Tp = one-way propagation delay. Define a = Tp / Tt. The sender needs 1 + 2a frame times to send a frame and receive its ACK, if ACK transmission time is neglected.

  • Stop-and-wait ARQ sends one frame and waits for its ACK. Efficiency η = Tt / (Tt + 2Tp) = 1 / (1 + 2a). Throughput = η × R. A 1-bit sequence number (0/1) is enough to catch duplicates when an ACK is lost.
  • Sliding window keeps up to W frames outstanding. Efficiency η = min(1, W / (1 + 2a)). The window needed for full use is W ≥ 1 + 2a, which is the bandwidth-delay product in frames.
  • Go-Back-N: the sender window is at most 2k − 1 with k-bit sequence numbers, and the receiver window is 1. The receiver discards out-of-order frames and sends cumulative ACKs. On a timeout or NAK, the sender resends the lost frame and every frame after it.
  • Selective Repeat: the sender and receiver windows are at most 2k−1. The receiver buffers out-of-order frames, and only the lost frame is resent. The window is half the sequence space so that, after a wrap-around, a retransmitted old frame can never be mistaken for a new one.
  • Piggybacking sends the ACK inside a data frame going the other way.

With a frame error probability p, stop-and-wait needs on average 1/(1 − p) transmissions per frame.

5. HDLC and PPP

HDLC is a bit-oriented protocol. Its frame is: flag 01111110, address, control, information, FCS (CRC), flag.

  • Frame types. I-frames carry user data and piggybacked ACKs (N(S), N(R)). S-frames carry control only: RR, RNR, REJ (go-back-N) and SREJ (selective). U-frames manage the link: SABM, DISC, UA and so on.
  • Modes. NRM (normal response, primary and secondary stations), ABM (asynchronous balanced, where combined stations are peers) and ARM.
  • Sequence numbers. 3 bits (modulo 8), or 7 bits (modulo 128) in extended mode.

PPP is byte-oriented and is used on point-to-point links such as dial-up and DSL. Its frame is: flag 0x7E, address 0xFF, control 0x03, protocol, data, FCS, flag. It uses LCP to set up the link, the PAP/CHAP protocols to authenticate, and NCPs (such as IPCP) for each network protocol. PPP detects errors but has no flow control and no retransmission.

6. Multiple access: ALOHA

Let Tfr be the frame time and G the average number of frames generated per frame time (all stations, including retransmissions). Throughput S is the average number of successful frames per frame time.

  • Pure ALOHA: send whenever there is a frame. The vulnerable time is 2Tfr, so S = G e−2G. The maximum is 1/(2e) ≈ 0.184 at G = 0.5.
  • Slotted ALOHA: send only at slot boundaries. The vulnerable time is Tfr, so S = G e−G. The maximum is 1/e ≈ 0.368 at G = 1.
  • With N stations, each sending in a slot with probability p, the chance that one station succeeds is N p (1 − p)N−1. This is largest at p = 1/N.

7. CSMA, CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA

CSMA means "listen before talking". There are three persistence strategies: 1-persistent (send as soon as the line is idle), non-persistent (wait a random time, then sense again) and p-persistent (in slotted channels, send with probability p). Collisions still happen, because a signal takes time to propagate.

CSMA/CD (classic Ethernet) listens while it transmits, sends a jam signal on a collision, and then backs off. To detect a collision before it finishes sending, a station must still be transmitting when the collision news comes back: Tt ≥ 2Tp. This gives the key formula:

minimum frame size Lmin = 2 × Tp × R = 2 × (d / v) × R

At 10 Mbps, Ethernet's 512-bit (64-byte) minimum with a 51.2 μs slot time comes from this rule. Binary exponential backoff: after the n-th collision, the station picks K at random from 0 … 2min(n,10) − 1 and waits K slot times. It gives up after 16 attempts. Throughput improves as a becomes smaller.

CSMA/CA (802.11) avoids collisions rather than detecting them. It uses inter-frame spaces (DIFS, SIFS), a random backoff counter that freezes while the channel is busy, positive ACKs, and optional RTS/CTS with the NAV timer.

Controlled access is the alternative: reservation, polling, or token passing. In a token ring (IEEE 802.5, differential Manchester), a station may send only while it holds the token. So there are no collisions, and the delay is bounded. The token holding time limits each station's turn.

Worked examples

Example 1: CRC

Data 1101101, generator 1011 (x3 + x + 1, r = 3).

  1. Append three zeros: 1101101000.
  2. Divide by 1011 using XOR at every step where the leading bit is 1.
  3. The remainder is 111, so the transmitted codeword is 1101101111.
  4. Check: dividing 1101101111 by 1011 leaves 000.
Dividend 1101101000, divisor 1011
Each step: XOR the 4-bit window with 1011 if it starts with 1,
drop the leading bit, bring down the next dividend bit.
1101 XOR 1011 = 0110
1101 XOR 1011 = 0110
1100 XOR 1011 = 0111
1111 XOR 1011 = 0100
1000 XOR 1011 = 0011
0110 leading 0, no XOR
1100 XOR 1011 = 0111
Remainder = last 3 bits = 111

Example 2: Hamming(7,4)

Data 1101 goes into positions 3, 5, 6, 7 (d3 = 1, d5 = 1, d6 = 0, d7 = 1), with even parity.

  1. p1 covers 3, 5, 7: 1 + 1 + 1, so p1 = 1.
  2. p2 covers 3, 6, 7: 1 + 0 + 1, so p2 = 0.
  3. p4 covers 5, 6, 7: 1 + 0 + 1, so p4 = 0.

The codeword is 1010101. Suppose 1011101 is received. The 1s are at positions 1, 3, 4, 5 and 7, and 1 ⊕ 3 ⊕ 4 ⊕ 5 ⊕ 7 = 4. So bit 4 is flipped, and correcting it gives 1010101.

Example 3: stop-and-wait and sliding windows

Take R = 4 Mbps, L = 2000 bits and Tp = 2 ms.

  1. Tt = 0.5 ms, so a = 4.
  2. Stop-and-wait η = 1/(1 + 8) = 1/9 ≈ 11.1%, so the throughput is about 444 kbps.
  3. A window of W ≥ 1 + 2a = 9 frames would fill the link.

Now take Tt = 1 ms and Tp = 12 ms.

  1. 1 + 2a = 25 frames are needed.
  2. Go-Back-N needs 2k − 1 ≥ 25, so k = 5.
  3. Selective Repeat needs 2k−1 ≥ 25, so k = 6.

With W = 7 and a = 5, η = 7/11 ≈ 63.6%.

Example 4: ALOHA

A 100 kbps channel carries 500-bit frames, so Tfr = 5 ms. All stations together produce 100 frames/s, so G = 100 × 0.005 = 0.5.

  1. Pure ALOHA: S = 0.5 e−1 = 0.184, which is about 18.4 frames/s succeeding (the maximum possible).
  2. Slotted ALOHA with the same G: S = 0.5 e−0.5 = 0.303, which is about 30.3 frames/s.

Example 5: CSMA/CD

A 100 Mbps bus is 1 km long, with v = 2×108 m/s.

  1. Tp = 5 μs.
  2. Lmin = 2 × 5 μs × 108 = 1000 bits (125 bytes).

Going the other way, Gigabit Ethernet with a 512-byte (4096-bit) minimum frame gives Tt = 4.096 μs. So Tp ≤ 2.048 μs, and d ≤ 409.6 m.

8. Controlled access: reservation, polling and token passing

In controlled access the stations consult one another to decide who may send, and a station transmits only when it has been authorised. There are no collisions, and the delay is bounded.

Reservation. Time is divided into intervals. Each interval starts with a reservation frame that has one minislot per station. A station that wants to send puts a bit in its own minislot, and the stations that reserved then send their data frames in minislot order. With N stations, a minislot of m bits, frames of F bits and k stations reserving, the efficiency is k·F / (k·F + N·m). The reservation frame is overhead whether or not stations have data.

Polling. One device is the primary and the others are secondaries. All data exchange goes through the primary, which controls the link. It uses two functions:

  • Select: the primary has data for a secondary. It sends a SEL frame naming the secondary, waits for an ACK saying the secondary is ready, and then sends the data, which the secondary acknowledges.
  • Poll: the primary asks secondaries in turn whether they have data to send. A secondary with nothing to send answers NAK; one with data sends it, and the primary acknowledges.

Polling wastes time on polls to idle stations, and the whole link fails if the primary fails. HDLC's normal response mode, a Bluetooth piconet (the master polls the slaves) and the 802.11 point coordination function are polling schemes.

Token passing. The stations form a logical ring: each has a predecessor and a successor. A special frame, the token, gives the right to send. A station holding it may transmit until its token-holding time (THT) runs out, and then it passes the token on. Token management must detect a lost or duplicated token and may assign priorities. The logical ring can sit on a physical ring (IEEE 802.5 Token Ring, FDDI's dual ring), on a bus (802.4 token bus) or on a star (a hub or MAU wired as a ring). The ring latency is the time for a bit to go once round: the propagation delay plus the delay each station adds. In the worst case a station waits N × THT plus the ring latency for the token. With early token release a station passes the token as soon as it finishes sending; with delayed release it waits for its frame to come back round.

Example 6 (reservation, ring latency and THT).

  1. Reservation with N = 10 stations, 8-bit minislots (an 80-bit reservation frame) and 1000-bit data frames. If all 10 stations reserve: 10 000 / 10 080 ≈ 99.2%. If only 5 reserve: 5000 / 5080 ≈ 98.4%.
  2. A 1 km token ring at 10 Mbps with propagation speed 2 × 108 m/s has 50 stations, each adding a 1-bit delay. Propagation takes 1000 / (2 × 108) = 5 μs. The stations add 50 bits = 5 μs. The ring latency is 10 μs, or 100 bit times.
  3. At 16 Mbps with THT = 10 ms, a station can send at most 16 × 106 × 0.01 / 8 = 20 000 bytes per turn.

9. Channelization: FDMA, TDMA and CDMA

Channelization (channel partitioning) shares the bandwidth of a link among stations by frequency, by time or by code.

  • FDMA divides the available bandwidth into frequency bands, and each station keeps its band for as long as it is active. Each station band-pass filters its signal into its band, and guard bands separate neighbours. FDMA is a data-link access method; FDM is the physical-layer technique that combines signals, which is why Forouzan keeps the two apart. The first-generation AMPS system used 30 kHz channels: an operator with 12.5 MHz in each direction had 12.5 MHz ÷ 30 kHz = 416 channels.
  • TDMA lets stations share the whole bandwidth in time: each gets its own time slot in every frame. The stations must be synchronised, and guard times and preambles in each burst absorb propagation differences. In GSM a burst lasts 156.25 bit periods, of which 114 carry data, so only about 73% of the slot is payload. TDMA (an access method) is to TDM (a physical-layer technique) as FDMA is to FDM.
  • CDMA lets every station use the whole band all the time. Stations are separated by orthogonal codes (chip sequences). A station sends its code for 1, the negated code for 0 and nothing when idle. The receiver multiplies the sum by a station's code and divides by the code length (the decoding is worked in lesson 9.7). The chip rate is the bit rate times the code length. IS-95 sends 1.2288 Mcps with 64-chip Walsh codes, so each code channel carries 1.2288 × 106 / 64 = 19.2 kbps.

Walsh tables. The codes come from a recursive construction. W1 = [+1], and W2N is built from WN as the block matrix [WN WN; WN −WN]. The number of codes, and so the number of stations, must be a power of 2. Any two rows are orthogonal.

W2 = | +1 +1 |        W4 = | +1 +1 +1 +1 |   row 0
     | +1 -1 |             | +1 -1 +1 -1 |   row 1
                           | +1 +1 -1 -1 |   row 2
                           | +1 -1 -1 +1 |   row 3

OFDMA, used in the 4G LTE downlink, Wi-Fi 6 and 5G, is a refinement of FDMA: users get sets of closely spaced orthogonal subcarriers that overlap in frequency without interfering.

NTA trap: in a match question, "divides by time" is TDMA, "divides by frequency" is FDMA and "everyone at once, separated by codes" is CDMA. Do not match CDMA with "frequency hopping". That is FHSS, as in classic Bluetooth.

NTA traps

  • Getting the Hamming check bits wrong for 12 data bits. The wrong reasoning uses 2r ≥ m, which gives 4. Fix: 2r ≥ m + r + 1. For r = 4, 16 ≥ 17 fails, so r = 5.
  • Getting detection and correction the wrong way round. dmin = 4 detects 3 errors and corrects only 1, not 2.
  • Taking the SR window as 2k − 1. Fix: SR allows only 2k−1. GBN allows 2k − 1.
  • Using a CRC remainder with too few bits. The remainder always has exactly r bits (one fewer than the generator), leading zeros included, and you append r zeros before dividing.
  • Using 1 + a instead of 1 + 2a. The ACK must travel back, so the round trip counts twice. Check whether the question gives the one-way delay or the RTT.
  • ALOHA G in frames per second. Fix: G is per frame time. Multiply frames per second by Tfr first.
  • CSMA/CD with the one-way delay. Fix: Lmin uses 2Tp (the round trip), not Tp.
  • "PPP does flow control." It does not. HDLC S-frames (RR/RNR) do.

How NTA asks this

  • Numericals. CRC remainder, Hamming bits, syndrome, dmin, η, window and sequence bits, ALOHA S, and Lmin or maximum distance.
  • Match. Protocol ↔ window size, ALOHA quantity ↔ value, HDLC frame ↔ purpose, and technique ↔ definition.
  • A–R and statements. Slotted versus pure ALOHA, CSMA/CD in wireless, and SR window limits.
  • Order. The CSMA/CD steps and the CRC generation steps.

Mini-example: A–R

A: Slotted ALOHA has twice the maximum throughput of pure ALOHA. R: Slotting halves the vulnerable period to one frame time.

Both are true, and R explains A: 1/e versus 1/(2e). The answer is option 1.

Elimination trick: in a window question, compute 1 + 2a first. Then the GBN bits are ⌈log2(W + 1)⌉ and the SR bits are ⌈log2(2W)⌉. The two answers differ by at most one bit, and options often list both.

terms.definition: Inserting a 0 after every five consecutive 1s in the data so the flag 01111110 never appears inside a frame.
Cyclic redundancy check: the remainder of modulo-2 division of the data (with r zeros appended) by an (r+1)-bit generator.
Number of bit positions in which two codewords differ; d(min) ≥ s+1 detects s errors, d(min) ≥ 2t+1 corrects t.
In a Hamming code, the XOR of the positions of all 1 bits; 0 means no error, otherwise it is the position of the flipped bit.
T(p) / T(t): propagation delay divided by frame transmission time.
Sliding-window ARQ, sender window ≤ 2ᵏ − 1, receiver window 1; resends the lost frame and all after it.
Sliding-window ARQ with windows ≤ 2ᵏ⁻¹ at both ends; the receiver buffers and only lost frames are resent.
Interval in which another transmission would collide with a frame: 2T(fr) in pure ALOHA, T(fr) in slotted ALOHA.
After the n-th collision, wait K slot times with K random in 0 … 2^min(n,10) − 1.
Carrying an acknowledgement inside a data frame travelling in the reverse direction.

lessons.examTip: Compute a = T(p)/T(t) first. Everything else follows: η = 1/(1+2a) for stop-and-wait, W = 1+2a for full use, GBN needs 2ᵏ−1 ≥ W and SR needs 2ᵏ⁻¹ ≥ W.

Attempt problems 6–11 (ARQ, ALOHA and CSMA/CD) in 9 minutes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace). Write a = T(p)/T(t) before anything else.
Attempt problems 12, 13 and 15 in 4 minutes.

Check every answer against solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for, for example 1 + a instead of 1 + 2a, 2ᵏ − 1 used for SR, or a dropped leading 0 in a CRC remainder.
Redo problems 8 and 9 as a timeline of transmission numbers, marking the lost ones, until the GBN and SR counts come out without hesitation.
Redo the problems you got wrong after 24 hours, without looking at the solutions.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct on the first attempt.
Problems 6–11 finished within 9 minutes.
Both CRC divisions (problems 1–2) and the Hamming syndrome (problem 5) correct.
You can write the ALOHA, stop-and-wait, window and CSMA/CD formulas from memory.

quiz.question: The data 1101101 is sent using CRC with the generator polynomial x³ + x + 1. What is the CRC (remainder) appended to the data?
quiz.explanation: The generator is 1011 (r = 3). Append three zeros, 1101101000, and divide modulo 2. The steps give remainder 111, so the codeword is 1101101111. Check: 1101101111 ÷ 1011 leaves 000. The other options come from arithmetic slips, such as dividing without the appended zeros.

quiz.question: A 4 Mbps link sends 2000-bit frames using stop-and-wait. The one-way propagation delay is 2 ms. Ignoring ACK size and processing, what is the link efficiency?
quiz.explanation: T(t) = 2000 / 4×10⁶ = 0.5 ms, so a = T(p)/T(t) = 4. η = 1/(1 + 2a) = 1/9 ≈ 11.1%. 20% uses 1/(1 + a). 25% is T(t)/T(p) with the ratio turned upside down.

quiz.question: The frame transmission time is 1 ms, and the one-way propagation delay is 12 ms. What is the minimum number of sequence-number bits Selective Repeat needs to keep the link fully utilised?
quiz.explanation: Full utilisation needs W ≥ 1 + 2a = 1 + 2 × 12 = 25 frames. Selective Repeat requires W ≤ 2ᵏ⁻¹, so 2ᵏ⁻¹ ≥ 25 gives k − 1 = 5 and k = 6. 5 bits is the Go-Back-N answer (2⁵ − 1 = 31 ≥ 25).

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Hamming distance counts the differing bit positions (A-III). CRC is modulo-2 polynomial division (B-IV). Bit stuffing inserts a 0 after five 1s (C-I). Piggybacking puts ACKs inside reverse data frames (D-II).

b: I. Inserting a 0 after five consecutive 1s
II. Carrying an acknowledgement in a data frame
III. Number of positions in which two codewords differ
IV. Polynomial division using modulo-2 arithmetic

quiz.question: A pure ALOHA channel runs at 100 kbps with 500-bit frames. All stations together generate 100 frames per second (including retransmissions). About how many frames per second succeed?
quiz.explanation: T(fr) = 500 / 10⁵ = 5 ms, so G = 100 × 0.005 = 0.5 frames per frame time. S = G e^(−2G) = 0.5 e^(−1) ≈ 0.184, and 0.184 × 100 ≈ 18.4 frames/s. This is the maximum for pure ALOHA. 30.3 is the slotted ALOHA value at G = 0.5. 13.5 is pure ALOHA at G = 1.

quiz.question: A CSMA/CD network runs at 100 Mbps over a 1 km cable, with a signal speed of 2×10⁸ m/s. What is the minimum frame size needed so that collisions are always detected?
quiz.explanation: T(p) = 1000 / 2×10⁸ = 5 μs. The frame must last at least 2T(p) = 10 μs: L = 10⁻⁵ × 10⁸ = 1000 bits (125 bytes). 500 bits uses T(p) instead of 2T(p). 125 is the answer in bytes, not bits.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Pure ALOHA: S = Ge^(−2G), max 1/(2e) ≈ 0.184. Slotted: S = Ge^(−G), max 1/e ≈ 0.368. That is exactly double, and the reason is that the vulnerable period is halved.

Reason (R): In slotted ALOHA, the vulnerable period is reduced from two frame times to one frame time.

quiz.question: How many check bits does a single-error-correcting Hamming code need for 12 data bits?
quiz.explanation: You need the smallest r with 2ʳ ≥ m + r + 1 = 13 + r. r = 4: 16 ≥ 17 fails. r = 5: 32 ≥ 18 holds. So r = 5. Answering 4 comes from checking only 2ʳ ≥ m.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Correcting t errors needs d(min) ≥ 2t + 1, so 5 ≥ 5 gives t = 2 (Statement I is true). Detecting s errors needs d(min) ≥ s + 1, so s = 4, not 5 (Statement II is false). Five errors can turn one codeword into another.
