lessons.title: Network security
lessons.summaryHtml: Network security protects data in transit. It keeps data secret (confidentiality), unchanged (integrity) and available, and it proves who sent it (authentication, non-repudiation). Classical ciphers (Caesar, Vigenère, Playfair, rail fence) are the source of small hand-computation questions. DES (56-bit key, 16 Feistel rounds) and AES (128-bit block, 10/12/14 rounds) are the symmetric workhorses. RSA and Diffie–Hellman are the public-key numericals: find d with e × d ≡ 1 mod φ(n), and find the shared key gab mod p. Hashes, MACs, digital signatures and X.509 certificates build trust. Firewalls, IPSec (AH/ESP, transport/tunnel), SSL/TLS and VPNs apply all of this at different layers.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Network security is about sending data over a network that you do not control, while making sure nobody can read it, change it or pretend to be you. Cryptography gives the tools. A cipher scrambles a message with a key. A hash gives a short fingerprint of a message. A digital signature proves who wrote it. On top of these tools sit protocols and devices: certificates tell you whose public key you hold, firewalls filter traffic, and IPSec, SSL/TLS and VPNs protect traffic at different layers.

An everyday picture helps. Symmetric encryption is a locked box where both people hold copies of the same key. Public-key encryption is a letterbox: anyone can drop a letter in through the slot (the public key), but only the owner has the key that opens the back (the private key).

Why it matters for NET

Network security is the last topic of Unit 9 and usually gives a few questions per paper. It also overlaps with the security part of Unit 5. Three kinds of question dominate. The first is small numericals: RSA (find d, encrypt, decrypt, sign), Diffie–Hellman (find the shared key), classical ciphers (Caesar, Vigenère, Playfair, rail fence) and key counts for n users. The second is fact matching: key and block sizes of DES and AES, digest sizes of MD5 and SHA, AH versus ESP, and firewall types. The third is concept statements: which key signs, which key encrypts, and which service a mechanism gives. All three can be answered in under a minute if you know the fact sheet below.

Security goals, services and attacks

The core goals are the CIA triad:

  • Confidentiality: only the intended people can read the data. It is provided by encryption.
  • Integrity: the data has not been changed. It is provided by hashes, MACs and signatures.
  • Availability: the service stays usable. Denial of service attacks target it.

ITU-T X.800 adds authentication (you are talking to the right party), access control (only permitted actions), and non-repudiation (the sender cannot later deny having sent the message).

Attacks are split into two groups. A passive attack only listens, so it is hard to detect and the defence is prevention (encryption). An active attack changes the data stream, so the aim is to detect it and recover.

Passive attacksActive attacks
Release of message contents (eavesdropping)Masquerade: pretending to be another entity
Traffic analysis: studying who talks to whom, how often and how much, even when the contents are encryptedReplay: capturing a valid message and resending it later
Modification of messages: altering, delaying or reordering them
Denial of service: flooding or disabling a service (DDoS uses many machines)

Other names you should know: man-in-the-middle (the attacker sits between two parties and relays or changes traffic), spoofing (a forged source address), phishing (tricking a user into giving credentials), and SYN flooding (half-open TCP connections exhaust the server’s table).

Classical ciphers

Classical ciphers work on letters (A = 0 to Z = 25). They are of two kinds. A substitution cipher replaces each letter. A transposition cipher keeps the letters but changes their positions.

  • Caesar (shift) cipher: C = (P + k) mod 26 and P = (C − k) mod 26. There are only 25 useful keys, so brute force breaks it at once. ROT13 is k = 13, which is its own inverse.
  • Monoalphabetic substitution: any permutation of the alphabet is the key, so there are 26! ≈ 4 × 1026 keys (about 288). It still falls to frequency analysis, because each plaintext letter always maps to the same ciphertext letter (E is the most common letter in English).
  • Playfair: a 5 × 5 square built from a keyword (I and J share a cell). The plaintext is split into pairs. If a pair has the same letter twice, a filler X goes between them, and an odd last letter also gets an X. Rules: same row → take the letter to the right of each; same column → the letter below each; otherwise → the letters at the other two corners of the rectangle, each staying in its own row. It hides single-letter frequencies but not digram frequencies.
  • Vigenère: a keyword is repeated along the plaintext, and each letter is shifted by the matching key letter: Ci = (Pi + Ki mod m) mod 26. It is polyalphabetic: the same plaintext letter can become different ciphertext letters. The Kasiski test finds the key length m from repeated fragments.
  • One-time pad: a truly random key as long as the message, used only once. It is the only cipher with perfect secrecy (Shannon), but the key is hard to distribute.
  • Rail fence: write the plaintext in a zig-zag over k rails and read row by row. Columnar transposition: write the plaintext in rows under a key, then read the columns in the order the key gives. Letter frequencies are unchanged, which is how a transposition is recognised.

Modern symmetric ciphers

A block cipher encrypts a fixed-size block (DES 64 bits, AES 128 bits). A stream cipher XORs the data with a keystream, one bit or byte at a time (RC4, ChaCha20). Shannon’s two design ideas are confusion (the link between key and ciphertext is complex, done with substitution) and diffusion (one plaintext bit affects many ciphertext bits, done with permutation).

A Feistel network splits the block into halves L and R. Each round computes Li = Ri−1 and Ri = Li−1 ⊕ F(Ri−1, Ki). Decryption is the same circuit with the round keys in reverse order, so F need not be invertible.

DES is a Feistel cipher. It has a 64-bit block and a 64-bit key, of which 8 bits are parity, so the effective key is 56 bits. It runs 16 rounds with 48-bit round keys. The F function expands 32 bits to 48, XORs the round key, and passes the result through 8 S-boxes, each mapping 6 bits to 4. An initial and a final permutation wrap the rounds. A 256 key space is now too small for brute force.

Double DES uses two keys (112 bits) but falls to the meet-in-the-middle attack. The attacker encrypts forward from the plaintext and decrypts backward from the ciphertext, then matches in the middle. This takes 256 encryptions plus 256 decryptions, about 257 operations (with a large table), not 2112. Triple DES (encrypt–decrypt–encrypt) with two keys has a 112-bit key, and with three keys a 168-bit key with about 112 bits of effective security. If all three keys are equal, EDE reduces to single DES, which gives backward compatibility.

AES (Rijndael) is not a Feistel cipher. It is a substitution–permutation network working on a 4 × 4 byte state. The block is always 128 bits. Keys are 128, 192 or 256 bits, with 10, 12 or 14 rounds. Each round has four steps in this order: SubBytes (S-box), ShiftRows, MixColumns and AddRoundKey. The last round omits MixColumns, and an extra AddRoundKey comes before round 1, so there are rounds + 1 round keys (11 for AES-128).

Modes of operation say how a block cipher handles a long message:

ModeIdeaKey point for exams
ECBEach block encrypted independentlyEqual plaintext blocks give equal ciphertext blocks, so patterns leak
CBCCi = E(Pi ⊕ Ci−1), with an IVEncryption is sequential. A one-bit error in Ci garbles Pi and flips one bit of Pi+1
CFBEncrypts the previous ciphertext to make the keystreamBehaves like a self-synchronising stream cipher
OFBKeystream made by encrypting the previous outputBit errors do not spread
CTRKeystream = E(nonce ∥ counter)Fully parallel, with random access to any block

Other symmetric algorithms that appear in options are IDEA (64-bit block, 128-bit key), Blowfish (64-bit block, variable key) and RC4 (a stream cipher, now deprecated).

Public-key cryptography: RSA and Diffie–Hellman

Each user has a public key that everyone may know and a private key kept secret. To send a secret, encrypt with the receiver’s public key. To sign, use the sender’s private key, and anyone can verify with the sender’s public key.

RSA key generation:

  1. Choose two large primes p and q, and compute n = p × q.
  2. Compute φ(n) = (p − 1)(q − 1).
  3. Choose e with 1 < e < φ(n) and gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1.
  4. Compute d = e−1 mod φ(n), so that e × d ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)). The extended Euclidean algorithm finds it.
  5. The public key is (e, n) and the private key is (d, n).

Encryption is C = Me mod n and decryption is M = Cd mod n, with M < n. It works because of Euler’s theorem: Med = M1 + kφ(n) ≡ M (mod n). Security rests on the difficulty of factoring n. Anyone who finds p and q can compute φ(n) and then d. Compute large powers by square-and-multiply: write the exponent in binary, square repeatedly, and multiply the needed squares, reducing mod n at every step.

Diffie–Hellman key exchange lets two people agree a shared secret over a public channel. It is a key agreement, not an encryption method.

  1. Public values: a prime p and a generator g (a primitive root mod p).
  2. Alice picks a secret a and sends A = ga mod p. Bob picks a secret b and sends B = gb mod p.
  3. Alice computes K = Ba mod p, and Bob computes K = Ab mod p. Both equal gab mod p.

Security rests on the discrete logarithm problem. Basic DH has no authentication, so a man-in-the-middle can run one exchange with each side. Signed or certificate-based DH fixes this. Elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC) gives the same security as RSA with much shorter keys.

Key counts. With symmetric keys, every pair of n users needs its own key: n(n − 1)/2 keys. With public-key cryptography, each user needs one key pair: n pairs, or 2n keys in total.

Hash functions, MACs and digital signatures

A cryptographic hash H maps a message of any length to a fixed-length digest. It must be quick to compute and have three properties:

  • Preimage resistance (one-way): given h, it is hard to find M with H(M) = h.
  • Second-preimage resistance (weak collision resistance): given M, it is hard to find another M′ with the same hash.
  • Collision resistance (strong): it is hard to find any pair with the same hash.

The birthday paradox means a collision on an n-bit hash appears after about 2n/2 tries, so a 128-bit digest gives only about 264 collision security. A hash alone gives no authentication, because an attacker can change the message and recompute the hash. A MAC mixes in a secret key. HMAC computes H((K ⊕ opad) ∥ H((K ⊕ ipad) ∥ M)). A MAC gives integrity and authentication but not non-repudiation, because both sides share the key.

A digital signature signs the hash of the message with the sender’s private key. In RSA: S = H(M)d mod n, and the receiver checks Se mod n = H(M). It gives integrity, authentication and non-repudiation, but not confidentiality. DSA and ECDSA are signature-only schemes.

Certificates, PKI and Kerberos

A public key is only useful if you know whose it is. A certificate (X.509) binds a subject name to a public key. It holds the version, serial number, signature algorithm, issuer, validity period, subject, the subject’s public key and extensions (v3), and it is signed with the CA’s private key. A Certification Authority (CA) issues certificates, and a Registration Authority checks identities for it. Browsers trust a set of root CAs, and a server certificate is checked along a chain of trust up to a root. A certificate withdrawn before its expiry appears on a CRL (Certificate Revocation List), or can be checked online with OCSP.

Kerberos is a symmetric-key authentication service. A Key Distribution Centre has an Authentication Server (AS), which issues a Ticket-Granting Ticket, and a Ticket-Granting Server (TGS), which issues service tickets. The user logs in once and uses tickets afterwards. Timestamps in the authenticators stop replay.

Firewalls

TypeWorks onNotes
Packet-filtering (stateless)Network and transport headers: IP addresses, protocol, portsFast, but each packet is judged alone and it cannot see content
Stateful inspectionThe same headers plus a connection-state tableAllows replies only for connections started from inside
Application-level gateway (proxy)The application layerCan filter by URL, command or content, needs one proxy per service, and is slower
Circuit-level gatewayThe session layer: it relays TCP connections (SOCKS)Checks the handshake, then copies bytes without inspecting them

A DMZ (screened subnet) holds public servers between an outer and an inner firewall. A bastion host is a hardened machine exposed to attack. Firewalls cannot stop attacks that bypass them, such as a dial-up link or an insider.

IPSec, SSL/TLS and VPNs

IPSec protects IP packets at the network layer, so every application above is protected without change.

  • AH (Authentication Header, IP protocol 51) gives integrity, data-origin authentication and anti-replay. It gives no confidentiality. It also covers the unchanging fields of the outer IP header, which is why it breaks with NAT.
  • ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload, protocol 50) gives confidentiality, with optional integrity and authentication.
  • Transport mode protects only the payload and keeps the original IP header. It is used host to host.
  • Tunnel mode encapsulates the whole original packet inside a new IP header. It is used gateway to gateway, as in site-to-site VPNs.
  • A Security Association (SA) is one-way and is identified by the SPI, the destination address and the protocol. A two-way link needs two SAs. IKE (over UDP port 500) negotiates SAs and keys.

SSL/TLS sits between TCP and the application. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS on port 443. It has two layers. The Record protocol fragments, (optionally) compresses, adds a MAC and encrypts. Above it run the Handshake, Change Cipher Spec and Alert protocols. In the classic (TLS 1.2) full handshake the order is: ClientHello → ServerHello → server Certificate → ServerHelloDone → ClientKeyExchange → ChangeCipherSpec → Finished. Public-key cryptography is used only to agree a session key, and bulk data then uses fast symmetric encryption. TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) shortens the handshake to one round trip and keeps only forward-secret (ephemeral Diffie–Hellman) key exchange.

A VPN builds a private, encrypted tunnel across a public network. A site-to-site VPN usually uses IPSec tunnel mode between gateways. A remote-access VPN connects a single user, using IPSec or an SSL/TLS VPN. Older protocols are PPTP and L2TP (L2TP is usually run with IPSec). For email, PGP and S/MIME give confidentiality and signatures.

Worked examples

Example 1 (Caesar and Vigenère). (a) Encrypt NETWORK with a Caesar shift of 3. (b) Encrypt PROTOCOL with the Vigenère key NET.

(a) Add 3 to each letter: N(13)→16 Q, E(4)→7 H, T(19)→22 W, W(22)→25 Z, O(14)→17 R, R(17)→20 U, K(10)→13 N. The ciphertext is QHWZRUN.

(b) Repeat the key: N E T N E T N E, which is 13, 4, 19, 13, 4, 19, 13, 4.

P 15 + 13 = 28 mod 26 =  2  C
R 17 +  4 = 21           V
O 14 + 19 = 33 mod 26 =  7  H
T 19 + 13 = 32 mod 26 =  6  G
O 14 +  4 = 18           S
C  2 + 19 = 21           V
O 14 + 13 = 27 mod 26 =  1  B
L 11 +  4 = 15           P

The ciphertext is CVHGSVBP. The three O’s became H, S and B. That is the polyalphabetic effect.

Example 2 (Playfair). Keyword NETWORK. Encrypt TAKE BALL.

N E T W O
R K A B C
D F G H I
L M P Q S
U V X Y Z

Pairs: TA KE BA LL. The pair LL has a double letter, so it becomes LX, leaving a lone L, which becomes LX. So the pairs are TA KE BA LX LX.

  • TA: T and A are in the same column, so take the letter below each: T→A and A→G, giving AG.
  • KE: same column, so K→F and E→K, giving FK.
  • BA: same row, so take the letter to the right: B→C and A→B, giving CB.
  • LX: L is in row 4, column 1 and X is in row 5, column 3. Use the rectangle corners, each in its own row: L→P and X→U, giving PU.

The ciphertext is AG FK CB PU PU.

Example 3 (rail fence). Encrypt NETWORKSECURITY with 3 rails.

N . . . O . . . E . . . I . .
. E . W . R . S . C . R . T .
. . T . . . K . . . U . . . Y

Read the rails in order: NOEI + EWRSCRT + TKUY = NOEIEWRSCRTTKUY. Rail 1 holds positions 1, 5, 9 and 13, because the zig-zag period is 2(k − 1) = 4.

Example 4 (full RSA). p = 7, q = 11 and e = 7. Find d, encrypt M = 5, and check the decryption.

n = 77 and φ(n) = 6 × 10 = 60. gcd(7, 60) = 1, so e is valid. Extended Euclid gives the inverse of 7 mod 60:

60 = 8 × 7 + 4
 7 = 1 × 4 + 3
 4 = 1 × 3 + 1
back-substitute: 1 = 4 − 3 = 2 × 4 − 7
               = 2 × (60 − 8 × 7) − 7 = 2 × 60 − 17 × 7
so 7 × (−17) ≡ 1, and d = −17 + 60 = 43.
Check: 7 × 43 = 301 = 5 × 60 + 1

Encryption by square-and-multiply, with 7 = 4 + 2 + 1: 51 = 5, 52 = 25, 54 = 625 mod 77 = 9. So C = 9 × 25 × 5 = 1125 mod 77 = 47. Decryption: 4743 mod 77 = 5, which is the original message.

Example 5 (Diffie–Hellman). p = 29 and g = 2. Alice’s secret is a = 5 and Bob’s is b = 11. Find the exchanged values and the shared key.

A = 25 mod 29 = 32 mod 29 = 3. B = 211 mod 29 = 2048 mod 29 = 18, since 29 × 70 = 2030. Alice computes 185 mod 29 and Bob computes 311 mod 29. Both give K = 15, which equals 255 mod 29. An eavesdropper sees 29, 2, 3 and 18, and would need a discrete logarithm to find 5 or 11.

Example 6 (key counts and the birthday bound). A company has 100 employees who must all talk privately in pairs.

Symmetric keys: 100 × 99 ÷ 2 = 4950 keys. Public-key cryptography: 100 key pairs, or 200 keys. For a 160-bit hash (SHA-1), a birthday collision search needs about 280 hashes, not 2160.

Malware

Malware (malicious software) is any program written to harm a system or its users. The classes differ in whether they need a host program and whether they copy themselves.

TypeNeeds a host?Self-replicates?What it does
VirusYes (a program, a boot sector or a document)Yes, when the host runsInserts copies of itself into other programs or files
WormNo, a standalone programYes, over the network, without user actionExploits network services to spread (the Morris worm of 1988; WannaCry in 2017 spread through an SMB flaw)
Trojan horsePoses as a useful programNoHides a malicious function behind an attractive one
RansomwareOften arrives as a Trojan or a wormVariesEncrypts the victim's files and demands payment for the key
Spyware, keylogger, adwareUsually installed with other softwareNoCollects information or keystrokes secretly, or pushes advertisements
RootkitInstalled after a break-inNoHides the attacker's presence at the OS or kernel level and keeps privileged access
Backdoor (trapdoor)Part of a programNoA secret entry point that bypasses authentication
Logic bombPart of a programNoRuns its payload when a condition is met (a date, a deleted employee record)
Bot (zombie)Installed by other malwareOftenObeys a remote command-and-control server; many bots form a botnet, used for DDoS and spam

A virus goes through four phases: dormant (idle, waiting), propagation (copying itself into other programs or disk areas), triggering (activated by an event) and execution (the payload runs). By target, viruses are boot-sector, file-infector or macro viruses (in documents such as spreadsheets). By concealment, a stealth virus hides its changes from antivirus software, a polymorphic virus changes its encrypted form in every copy (so no fixed signature exists), and a metamorphic virus rewrites its whole code in every copy. Defences are antivirus scanning (signature, heuristic and behaviour-based), patching, least privilege, sandboxing, e-mail filtering, offline backups against ransomware, and user awareness.

Steganography

Steganography ("covered writing") hides the existence of a message by embedding it in an innocent carrier. Cryptography hides the meaning of a message, but everyone can see that a secret message exists. The two combine well: encrypt the message first, then embed the ciphertext, so that even a discovered message cannot be read. Historical examples are invisible ink, microdots and messages under the wax of writing tablets.

  • The cover object is the innocent carrier (an image, audio, video, text or network traffic). Embedding the secret message gives the stego object. A shared stego key can decide where the bits go, so only the key holder can extract them.
  • The goals are imperceptibility (the stego object looks and sounds normal), capacity (how much can be hidden) and robustness (surviving processing). Steganalysis is the art of detecting hidden data.
  • LSB substitution in images replaces the least significant bit of each colour byte with a message bit. The intensity changes by at most 1 in 256, which the eye cannot see. Capacity = width × height × channels × bits used per channel.
  • Lossy JPEG recompression destroys LSB data, so JPEG steganography hides bits in the DCT coefficients instead. Audio methods include LSB coding, echo hiding and phase coding. Text methods use spacing, word choice or null ciphers. Network steganography hides bits in unused header fields or in packet timing (covert channels).
  • Digital watermarking uses the same embedding ideas to mark ownership. Its priority is robustness, and the presence of the mark is often known; steganography's priority is secrecy.

Worked example (LSB capacity and embedding). An 800 × 600 image with 24-bit colour (3 bytes per pixel) hides 1 bit in the LSB of each colour byte.

  1. Capacity = 800 × 600 × 3 = 1 440 000 bits = 180 000 bytes. Using only one channel per pixel would give 480 000 bits = 60 000 bytes.
  2. A colour byte 10110100 (180) hides the bit 1: it becomes 10110101 = 181. Hiding the bit 0 leaves it at 180, unchanged.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemValue or formula
CaesarC = (P + k) mod 26 (25 useful keys)
Monoalphabetic key space26! ≈ 4 × 1026 ≈ 288
VigenèreCi = (Pi + Ki mod m) mod 26
DES64-bit block, 56-bit key, 16 rounds, 48-bit subkeys, 8 S-boxes (6→4), Feistel
2DES / 3DES2DES ≈ 257 (meet-in-the-middle); 3DES keys of 112 or 168 bits
AES128-bit block; 128/192/256-bit keys → 10/12/14 rounds; SPN, not Feistel
RSAn = pq, φ = (p−1)(q−1), ed ≡ 1 mod φ, C = Me mod n, M = Cd mod n
Diffie–HellmanA = ga, B = gb, K = Ba = Ab = gab (mod p)
Key countsSymmetric n(n−1)/2; public-key 2n keys (n pairs)
Digest sizesMD5 128; SHA-1 160; SHA-256 256; SHA-512 512 bits
Birthday boundAbout 2n/2 tries for a collision on an n-bit hash
SignatureSign with the sender’s private key, verify with the sender’s public key
IPSecAH = protocol 51 (no confidentiality); ESP = 50; IKE on UDP 500

Virus vs worm vs TrojanVirus needs a host and spreads when it runs; worm is standalone and spreads over the network by itself; Trojan poses as useful and does not replicate

NTA traps

  • Signing with the public key. Wrong: “the sender signs with the receiver’s public key.” Fix: encrypt with the receiver’s public key, sign with the sender’s private key.
  • φ(n) against n. Wrong: taking d as the inverse of e mod n. Fix: the inverse is taken mod φ(n) = (p − 1)(q − 1).
  • DES key is 64 bits. Wrong: the key input is 64 bits, but 8 of them are parity. The effective key is 56 bits.
  • Double DES gives 112-bit security. Wrong: meet-in-the-middle cuts it to about 257.
  • AES is a Feistel cipher. Wrong: DES is Feistel, and AES is a substitution–permutation network.
  • AH encrypts. Wrong: AH only authenticates, and ESP is the protocol that encrypts.
  • A hash gives authentication. Wrong: anyone can recompute a plain hash. You need a key (MAC) or a signature.
  • A MAC gives non-repudiation. Wrong: both sides hold the MAC key. Only a digital signature gives non-repudiation.
  • Playfair filler. Wrong: pairing LL as it stands. Fix: insert X between the double letters and re-pair the rest. I and J share a cell.
  • Traffic analysis is active. Wrong: it only observes, so it is a passive attack.

How NTA asks this

  • Direct numerical: “p = …, q = …, e = … . Find d” or “find the shared key.” Check each option: e × d mod φ must equal 1. That takes seconds and needs no extended Euclid.
  • Match the list: algorithm to key, block or digest size; attack to category; IPSec element to function. Fix one pair you are sure of (AES block 128, SHA-1 160), then eliminate options.
  • Assertion–Reason: signatures and non-repudiation, DH and man-in-the-middle, ECB and pattern leakage.
  • Arrange in order: AES round steps, TLS handshake messages, RSA key-generation steps, Kerberos exchanges.

Mini A-R. A: Basic Diffie–Hellman is vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle attack. R: The values ga and gb are sent without authentication. Both are true, and R explains A, because the attacker can substitute its own values unnoticed. The answer is option 1.

Remember: for an RSA option check, multiply e by each candidate d and reduce mod φ(n). Only the true d gives 1. For DH, gab mod p is a quick cross-check when the exponents are small.

terms.definition: Confidentiality, integrity and availability, the three core security goals.
A passive attack only observes (eavesdropping, traffic analysis). An active attack alters the data stream (masquerade, replay, modification, denial of service).
A digraph substitution on a 5 × 5 keyword square (I/J share a cell). Same row: take the letter to the right. Same column: take the letter below. Otherwise: swap the rectangle corners.
A round structure L_i = R_(i−1), R_i = L_(i−1) ⊕ F(R_(i−1), K_i). DES uses it, and decryption reuses the same circuit with the keys reversed.
n = pq, φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1), e × d ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)). C = M^e mod n and M = C^d mod n. Security rests on factoring.
Key agreement: A = g^a mod p, B = g^b mod p, K = g^(ab) mod p. Security rests on discrete logarithms. Unauthenticated DH is open to man-in-the-middle.
The hash of a message signed with the sender’s private key and verified with the sender’s public key. It gives integrity, authentication and non-repudiation.
A document binding a subject name to a public key, signed by a Certification Authority’s private key. It is revoked through a CRL or OCSP.
IPSec Authentication Header (protocol 51) gives integrity and authentication only. ESP (protocol 50) adds confidentiality.
Transport mode protects only the IP payload. Tunnel mode wraps the whole original packet in a new IP header, as in site-to-site VPNs.

lessons.examTip: For any RSA option, multiply e by the candidate d and reduce mod φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1). Only the right d gives 1. Remember: encrypt with the receiver’s public key, sign with the sender’s private key.

steps: Open practice-set.md and solve problems 1–8 in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
For every RSA or Diffie–Hellman problem, write the square-and-multiply table (powers 1, 2, 4, 8 …) instead of computing the whole power.
Solve problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For match and A-R problems, lock one pair or statement you are sure of before reading the options.
Check with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (mod n vs mod φ(n), wrong key for signing, AH vs ESP, Playfair filler, 2DES security).
Redraw the Playfair square and the rail fence zig-zag for problems 3 and 4 from memory and re-encrypt.
Redo every wrong problem after 24 hours without looking at the solutions.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct on the first attempt
Problems 9–15 solved within 12 minutes
Every RSA d checked by multiplying e × d mod φ(n)
No sign/encrypt key mix-ups on the redo

quiz.question: In an RSA system, p = 5, q = 13 and the public exponent e = 5. What is the private exponent d?
quiz.explanation: n = 65 and φ(n) = 4 × 12 = 48. We need 5d ≡ 1 (mod 48). 5 × 29 = 145 = 3 × 48 + 1, so d = 29. Checking the others: 5 × 19 = 95 ≡ 47, 5 × 23 = 115 ≡ 19 and 5 × 41 = 205 ≡ 13 (mod 48). The inverse is taken mod φ(n), not mod n = 65.

quiz.question: In a Diffie–Hellman exchange, the public prime is p = 29 and the generator is g = 2. Alice’s secret is a = 5 and Bob’s secret is b = 11. What is the shared secret key?
quiz.explanation: Alice sends A = 2^5 mod 29 = 32 mod 29 = 3. Bob sends B = 2^11 mod 29 = 2048 mod 29 = 18. Alice computes 18^5 mod 29 = 15 and Bob computes 3^11 mod 29 = 15. Both equal 2^55 mod 29 = 15. The values 3 and 18 are the public values that are exchanged, not the key.

quiz.question: The plaintext NETWORK is encrypted with the Vigenère cipher using the key KEY (A = 0, …, Z = 25). What is the ciphertext?
quiz.explanation: The repeated key KEYKEYK gives shifts 10, 4, 24, 10, 4, 24, 10. N(13)+10 = 23 X, E(4)+4 = 8 I, T(19)+24 = 43 mod 26 = 17 R, W(22)+10 = 32 mod 26 = 6 G, O(14)+4 = 18 S, R(17)+24 = 41 mod 26 = 15 P, K(10)+10 = 20 U. So the ciphertext is XIRGSPU. DAVMKTA comes from subtracting the key (decryption), and WHQFROT uses shifts that are one too small.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: The DES key is 64 bits with 8 parity bits, so it is 56 effective (III). The AES block is always 128 bits, whatever the key size (IV). SHA-1 gives 160 bits (I) and SHA-512 gives 512 bits (II). So A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II. Option 2 swaps the DES key with the AES block, which is a common slip.

a: A. Effective key length of DES
b: III. 56

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Only the holder of the private key could have produced a signature that verifies with the matching public key. So the sender cannot later deny it. R is exactly why A holds. By contrast, a MAC uses a shared key and cannot give non-repudiation.

stmts: Assertion (A): A digital signature provides non-repudiation of origin.
Reason (R): The signature is created with the sender’s private key, which only the sender holds.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Statement I is correct: transport mode inserts the IPSec header after the original IP header and protects the payload. Statement II is wrong: AH gives integrity, data-origin authentication and anti-replay but no encryption. ESP is the protocol that gives confidentiality.

Statement II: The IPSec Authentication Header (AH) provides confidentiality by encrypting the payload.

options: A, C, D and E only
quiz.explanation: Active attacks change or inject traffic: masquerade, replay, modification and denial of service. Traffic analysis and release of message contents only observe, so they are passive. So A, C and D only.

B. Traffic analysis
C. Replay

quiz.question: A group of 50 people want every pair to be able to communicate secretly using symmetric-key cryptography. How many distinct secret keys are needed?
quiz.explanation: Each unordered pair needs its own key: n(n − 1)/2 = 50 × 49 ÷ 2 = 1225. 2450 counts each pair twice. 100 is the public-key count (50 key pairs, 2n keys).

quiz.question: Which type of firewall can allow HTTP traffic but block requests for particular URLs or file types?
options: Screening router using only port numbers
quiz.explanation: URLs and file types live in the application-layer payload. Only an application-level gateway (proxy) parses the HTTP request. Packet filters and screening routers see only IP and port headers. A circuit-level gateway relays TCP connections without inspecting their content.

lessons.title: Mobile technology, cloud computing and IoT
lessons.summaryHtml: Cellular networks reuse frequencies across clusters of N = i² + ij + j² cells, with reuse ratio D/R = √(3N). The generations moved from analog FDMA (1G) to GSM TDMA and IS-95 CDMA (2G), then WCDMA (3G), then all-IP LTE with OFDMA (4G), and then 5G NR with eMBB, URLLC, mMTC and network slicing. Mobile IP keeps a home address, using a home agent that tunnels packets to a care-of address. Bluetooth forms piconets of 1 master and 7 active slaves in the 2.4 GHz band, and Wi-Fi runs from 802.11b to Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) using CSMA/CA. Cloud computing follows NIST: 5 characteristics, 3 service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) and 4 deployment models, built on virtualisation. IoT links perception, network and application layers with MQTT (TCP publish/subscribe), CoAP (UDP REST), Zigbee (802.15.4) and RFID.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

This lesson covers three ways computing has left the desk. Mobile technology connects moving users. A cellular network divides an area into cells, each served by a base station. Frequencies are reused in cells far enough apart, and calls are handed over as users move. Mobile IP keeps a laptop’s IP address the same when it changes networks, and Bluetooth and Wi-Fi give short-range wireless links. Cloud computing rents computing like electricity: you use servers, platforms or whole applications over the network and pay for what you use. The Internet of Things (IoT) connects sensors and actuators, such as a soil-moisture probe or a smart meter, using light protocols such as MQTT and CoAP over low-power radios such as Zigbee.

Why it matters for NET

This topic mostly yields fact and matching questions, with a few formula numericals. The typical items are: match a generation to its access technology, match a service model to its example, list the NIST cloud characteristics, match a Wi-Fi amendment to its band or generation name, and match an IoT protocol to its transport. The numericals are cellular cluster size and reuse ratio, channels per cell, CDMA chip decoding, and availability and downtime. Paper 1’s ICT unit also asks about cloud and IoT basics, so the effort pays off twice.

Cellular concepts

A cellular system covers an area with many low-power base stations. Each cell gets a set of channels, and a cluster of N cells shares the whole spectrum. The same set is then reused in the next cluster. For hexagonal cells, the valid cluster sizes are

N = i2 + ij + j2 (i, j non-negative integers), which gives 1, 3, 4, 7, 9, 12, 13, 16, 19, 21 …

The co-channel reuse ratio is Q = D/R = √(3N), where D is the distance between co-channel cells and R is the cell radius. A larger N means co-channel cells are further apart, so there is less interference, but fewer channels per cell. With path-loss exponent n and six first-tier interferers, the signal-to-interference ratio is S/I ≈ (√(3N))n ÷ 6. Capacity is raised by cell splitting (smaller cells), sectoring (directional antennas, 120° or 60°) and reuse.

A handoff (handover) moves a call to a new cell. A hard handoff is break-before-make and is used in FDMA/TDMA systems such as GSM. A soft handoff is make-before-break: in CDMA, neighbouring cells use the same frequency, so the phone can talk to two base stations at once.

There are three multiple-access methods. FDMA splits the spectrum into frequency slices. TDMA splits a carrier into time slots. CDMA lets everyone share the same band at the same time, separated by orthogonal chip codes (such as Walsh codes). A station sends its chip sequence for bit 1 and the negated sequence for bit 0. The receiver takes the normalised inner product of the received sum with a station’s code. The result is +1 for bit 1, −1 for bit 0 and 0 if that station was silent. This works because distinct codes are orthogonal: their inner product is 0.

GSM architecture has three parts. The mobile station is the handset plus its SIM. The BSS is made of BTS units (radio transceivers, one per cell) controlled by a BSC. The network subsystem has the MSC (switching, call routing, handover between BSCs), the HLR (the permanent subscriber database), the VLR (a temporary copy for subscribers roaming in an MSC area), the AuC (authentication keys) and the EIR (a register of handset IMEIs). GSM-900 has 25 MHz in each direction. At 200 kHz spacing that gives 124 usable carrier pairs, and each carrier has 8 TDMA slots. A TDMA frame lasts about 4.615 ms, so a slot lasts about 577 µs.

LTE schedules a time–frequency grid. A resource block is 12 subcarriers × 15 kHz = 180 kHz wide. A 1 ms subframe holds 14 OFDM symbols (normal cyclic prefix), and a 10 ms frame holds 10 subframes. A 20 MHz carrier has 100 resource blocks. 5G NR generalises this with numerology μ. The subcarrier spacing is 15 × 2μ kHz, and a 14-symbol slot lasts 1/2μ ms, so wider spacing gives shorter slots and lower latency. 5G can run non-standalone (NSA: an NR radio anchored on an LTE core) or standalone (SA: with the 5G core).

Mobile IP

An IP address says where a host is attached. If a laptop moves to another network, connections would break. Mobile IP (IPv4) solves this with two addresses and two agents.

  • Home address: the permanent address that correspondents use.
  • Care-of address (CoA): a temporary address in the visited network. It is either the foreign agent’s address (FA CoA) or a co-located CoA that the mobile node obtains for itself, for example by DHCP.
  • Home agent (HA): a router on the home network that intercepts packets for the absent host and tunnels them (IP-in-IP, which adds a 20-byte outer header) to the CoA.
  • Foreign agent (FA): a router on the visited network that detunnels packets and delivers them.

Operation has three steps. In agent discovery, agents send advertisements (extensions of ICMP router discovery), or the mobile node solicits them. In registration, the mobile node sends its CoA to the HA, via the FA, on UDP port 434, and the HA replies. In tunnelling, the HA forwards packets to the CoA. Replies from the mobile node can go straight to the correspondent. This path shape is called triangular routing, and it is inefficient. Route optimisation tells the correspondent the CoA directly. Mobile IPv6 has no foreign agents and builds in route optimisation.

Bluetooth

Bluetooth (originally IEEE 802.15.1) is a short-range WPAN in the 2.4 GHz ISM band. Classic Bluetooth (BR/EDR) uses frequency-hopping spread spectrum over 79 channels of 1 MHz, at 1600 hops per second, which gives 625 µs time slots. A piconet has one master (central) and up to 7 active slaves, and more devices can be parked. Overlapping piconets that share a device form a scatternet. Bluetooth Low Energy (from version 4.0) uses 40 channels of 2 MHz, of which 3 are advertising channels, and is designed for coin-cell devices. Bluetooth 5 (2016) added a 2 Mbps LE mode and a long-range coded mode. Bluetooth Core 6.0 (2024) added Channel Sounding for distance measurement. The protocol stack includes the radio, baseband, L2CAP, RFCOMM (serial-port emulation), SDP (service discovery), and the ATT/GATT layers for BLE.

The 802.11 MAC uses CSMA/CA, not CSMA/CD. A radio cannot listen while it transmits, and it may not hear a hidden terminal, so collisions are avoided rather than detected. In the DCF, a station senses the medium, waits DIFS plus a random backoff, sends, and waits for an ACK. The inter-frame spaces satisfy SIFS < PIFS < DIFS, so ACKs and CTS frames (after SIFS) win priority. An optional RTS/CTS exchange reserves the medium and sets every neighbour’s NAV timer, which solves the hidden-terminal problem. The exposed terminal problem is the opposite case: a station stays quiet when it did not need to. In the 2.4 GHz band, channel centres are 5 MHz apart (2412 MHz for channel 1), so only channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap. Security has improved through WEP (RC4, broken), WPA (TKIP), WPA2 (802.11i, AES-CCMP) and WPA3 (SAE handshake).

Cloud computing

The NIST definition (SP 800-145) is the one exams follow. Cloud computing is on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable resources that can be provisioned and released quickly with minimal management effort. It has five essential characteristics:

  1. On-demand self-service: you get resources without a human at the provider.
  2. Broad network access: resources are reached over the network from any device.
  3. Resource pooling: resources are multi-tenant and location-independent.
  4. Rapid elasticity: resources scale out and in, and appear unlimited.
  5. Measured service: usage is metered, and you pay per use.
Service modelConsumer managesProvider managesExamples
IaaSOS, runtime, applications, dataHardware, virtualisation, network, storageAmazon EC2, Google Compute Engine, Azure VMs
PaaSApplications and dataEverything up to the runtime and middlewareGoogle App Engine, Heroku, Azure App Service
SaaSOnly settings and dataThe whole application stackGmail, Salesforce, Microsoft 365 web apps

Serverless computing, or FaaS (such as AWS Lambda), runs individual functions on events and bills per invocation. It is often placed between PaaS and SaaS. The four deployment models are public (open to anyone, run by the provider), private (for one organisation, on or off its premises), community (shared by organisations with common concerns) and hybrid (two or more clouds joined so that data and applications can move between them, as in cloud bursting).

Virtualisation is the enabling technology. A hypervisor (VMM) runs several virtual machines on one host.

  • A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on the hardware: VMware ESXi, Xen, Microsoft Hyper-V, KVM. It is used in data centres.
  • A Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor runs as an application on a host OS: Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation.
  • Full virtualisation runs an unmodified guest OS (with binary translation or hardware help). Paravirtualisation modifies the guest to make hypercalls (the classic Xen approach). Hardware-assisted virtualisation uses CPU extensions such as Intel VT-x and AMD-V.
  • Containers (Docker) share the host kernel and isolate processes, so they are lighter and start faster than VMs. Kubernetes orchestrates them.

Benefits of virtualisation are server consolidation, isolation, live migration, snapshots and fast provisioning. Cloud concerns include security and privacy, vendor lock-in and dependence on the network. The shared responsibility model says the provider secures the cloud and the customer secures what they put in it. The provider’s share grows from IaaS to SaaS. An SLA states the promised availability, and availability is where the numericals come from.

Internet of Things

IoT connects physical “things” with sensors and actuators to the Internet, so that data can be collected and acted on. The simple three-layer architecture is: perception (sensors, actuators, RFID tags), network (moving data through gateways, Wi-Fi, cellular, Zigbee) and application (smart home, health, agriculture). The five-layer version is perception, transport, processing (middleware: storage and analytics), application and business (models, management). Edge and fog computing process data near the devices to cut latency and bandwidth, and the cloud does the heavy analytics.

  • MQTT is a light publish/subscribe protocol that runs over TCP (port 1883, or 8883 with TLS). Clients publish to hierarchical topics such as home/kitchen/temp on a broker, which forwards the messages to subscribers. The wildcard + matches exactly one level, and # matches any number of levels, including zero (it must come last). QoS 0 is at most once (PUBLISH only). QoS 1 is at least once (PUBLISH, PUBACK). QoS 2 is exactly once (PUBLISH, PUBREC, PUBREL, PUBCOMP). A retained message is stored and sent to new subscribers, and a Last Will message is published if a client drops unexpectedly. Versions 3.1.1 (OASIS 2014, ISO/IEC 20922) and 5.0 (2019) are the standards.
  • CoAP (RFC 7252) is a RESTful request/response protocol for constrained devices over UDP (port 5683, or 5684 with DTLS). It has GET, POST, PUT and DELETE, a 4-byte fixed header and four message types: Confirmable, Non-confirmable, Acknowledgement and Reset. The Observe option (RFC 7641) pushes updates, and proxies map CoAP to HTTP easily.
  • IEEE 802.15.4 is the low-rate WPAN PHY/MAC: 250 kbps in 2.4 GHz with 16 channels, and a maximum frame of 127 bytes. Zigbee builds network and application layers on it. It supports star, tree and mesh topologies, with a coordinator, routers and end devices. 6LoWPAN fits IPv6 (minimum MTU 1280 bytes) into 127-byte frames by header compression and fragmentation.
  • RFID has a reader and tags. Passive tags have no battery: the reader’s field powers them and they reply by backscatter. Active tags carry a battery and reach further. The bands are LF (125–134 kHz), HF (13.56 MHz) and UHF (860–960 MHz). NFC is a 13.56 MHz HF technology for a few centimetres. It supports card emulation, reader/writer and peer-to-peer modes.
  • For long range and low power there are the LPWAN technologies: LoRaWAN (unlicensed spectrum) and NB-IoT (licensed cellular).

Worked examples

Example 1 (cluster size, reuse ratio, S/I). In a hexagonal layout, co-channel cells are reached by moving i = 2 cells, turning 60° and moving j = 1 cell. Find N, D/R and S/I for a path-loss exponent of 4 with six interferers.

N = 22 + 2 × 1 + 12 = 7. D/R = √(3 × 7) = √21 ≈ 4.58. S/I = (√21)4 ÷ 6 = 441 ÷ 6 = 73.5, and 10 log10 73.5 ≈ 18.66 dB. With N = 4, S/I is only 144 ÷ 6 = 24, or about 13.8 dB. With N = 12, D/R = 6 exactly.

Example 2 (channels per cell). An operator has 20 MHz of spectrum. Each simplex channel is 25 kHz, and a duplex channel needs two. How many duplex channels does each cell get with N = 7 and with N = 4?

A duplex channel takes 2 × 25 = 50 kHz, so there are 20 000 ÷ 50 = 400 duplex channels. With N = 7: 400 ÷ 7 = 57.1, so 57 per cell (with a few cells getting one extra). With N = 4: 100 per cell. A smaller cluster gives more capacity per cell but a worse S/I.

Example 3 (CDMA decoding). The chip codes are A = (+1 +1 +1 +1), B = (+1 −1 +1 −1), C = (+1 +1 −1 −1) and D = (+1 −1 −1 +1). A and D send bit 1, B sends bit 0, and C is silent.

−B       = (−1 +1 −1 +1)
D        = (+1 −1 −1 +1)
sum S    = (+1 +1 −1 +3)
S·A / 4 = (1 + 1 − 1 + 3)/4 = +1  → A sent 1
S·B / 4 = (1 − 1 − 1 − 3)/4 = −1  → B sent 0

Example 4 (availability). (a) How much downtime per year does a 99.9% SLA allow? (b) A web tier with 99.9% availability depends on a database with 99.5%. What is the overall availability? (c) Two independent 99% servers run in parallel. What is their availability?

(a) 0.001 × 365 × 24 × 60 = 525.6 minutes, about 8.76 hours. At 99.99% it is 52.56 minutes, and at 99.999% it is about 5.26 minutes. (b) Components in series multiply: 0.999 × 0.995 = 0.994005, about 99.4%, which is lower than either part. (c) The pair fails only if both fail: 1 − 0.012 = 0.9999, or 99.99%.

Example 5 (LTE and NR grid). (a) How wide is an LTE resource block, and how many resource elements does it hold per 1 ms subframe? (b) What are the subcarrier spacing and slot length of NR with μ = 2?

(a) 12 × 15 kHz = 180 kHz. 12 subcarriers × 14 symbols = 168 resource elements. 100 RBs × 180 kHz = 18 MHz of a 20 MHz carrier, and the rest is guard band. (b) 15 × 22 = 60 kHz, and the slot is 1/22 = 0.25 ms.

Example 6 (MQTT topic filters). Which topics match the filter sensors/+/temp, and which match sensors/#?

sensors/+/temp matches sensors/lab1/temp, but not sensors/lab1/room2/temp, because + is exactly one level. sensors/# matches sensors itself (# may match zero levels) and also sensors/lab1/room2/temp. sensors/+ does not match sensors/lab1/temp, which has one level too many.

Mobile computing, middleware and gateways

Mobile computing is computing while on the move: portable devices, wireless communication and software that copes with both. Its constraints shape every design: limited battery energy, processing power, memory, small screens and awkward input; variable, low and intermittent bandwidth, including disconnection; a network address that changes as the device moves; greater security risk (radio can be overheard, and devices are lost or stolen); and location-dependent behaviour. Mobile applications are usually built in three tiers: presentation on the device, application logic (with middleware) on servers, and a data tier.

Middleware sits between the operating system and network below and the applications above. It hides the differences between devices and networks and handles disconnection. The main kinds for mobile computing are:

  • Message-oriented middleware: asynchronous queues with store-and-forward, so a sender and a receiver need not be connected at the same moment. It suits intermittent links better than synchronous RPC or object middleware (CORBA, Java RMI).
  • Transaction-processing middleware (TP monitors), which keeps multi-step operations consistent.
  • Data synchronisation and database middleware: replicas on the device that are reconciled later. The Coda file system's disconnected operation has three phases: hoarding (caching files while connected), emulation (working on the cache while disconnected) and reintegration (sending changes back and resolving conflicts). SyncML was a standard for such synchronisation.
  • Adaptation (transcoding) middleware, which reformats content for small screens and slow links, and context-aware middleware, which adapts to location and resources.
  • Mobile agents: code that migrates to the server, works there while the device is disconnected, and returns the result.

A gateway joins networks that use different protocols and translates between them. The classic example is the WAP gateway. WAP (Wireless Application Protocol) gave early phones a light protocol stack: WAE (the application environment, with WML pages and WMLScript), WSP (the session layer, a compact binary form of HTTP), WTP (reliable request/response transactions), WTLS (security) and WDP (datagrams, over UDP where IP is available or over bearers such as SMS). The WAP gateway sits between the phone and ordinary web servers. It converts WSP/WTP requests into HTTP over TCP/IP and encodes the replies (WML into binary WBXML, WMLScript into bytecode) for the phone. Other gateways are the SMS gateway (between applications and the operator's SMS centre, often over SMPP), the voice gateway (speech and IVR to web content) and the GPRS GGSN (between the mobile network and the Internet).

Mobile communication protocols include Mobile IP (above) and WAP, and also TCP variants for wireless links. Standard TCP reads every loss as congestion and slows down, even when a radio error caused the loss. Indirect TCP (I-TCP) splits the connection at the access point into a wired part and a wireless part, which loses end-to-end semantics. Snooping TCP caches segments at the base station and retransmits them locally, keeping end-to-end semantics. M-TCP freezes the sender by advertising a zero window while the mobile is disconnected.

GSM services, GPRS and SMS

GSM offers three kinds of service. Bearer services carry data between user–network interfaces at a given rate (circuit-switched data at up to 9.6 kbps in original GSM). Teleservices are complete end-user services: telephony, emergency calls (112), SMS and fax. Supplementary services modify or add to a basic teleservice and cannot be offered on their own: call forwarding, call barring, call waiting and hold, caller line identification (CLIP) and conference calls.

GPRS (General Packet Radio Service, 2.5G) adds packet switching to the GSM network. Users hold a radio channel only while sending, so they can be "always on" and pay for the volume sent rather than the time connected. It adds a PCU (packet control unit, at the BSC, which separates packet traffic from circuit traffic) and two core nodes joined by an IP backbone with GTP tunnels:

  • SGSN (serving GPRS support node): serves the mobiles in its area. It handles mobility management, authentication, ciphering and the routing of packets to and from them, the packet counterpart of the MSC.
  • GGSN (gateway GPRS support node): the gateway to external packet data networks such as the Internet. It assigns IP addresses and acts as a router.

A phone that wants data activates a PDP context, which gives it an IP address and a tunnel through the SGSN to the GGSN. The HLR stores the GPRS subscription too. GPRS can bundle several of the 8 time slots, and each slot's rate depends on the coding scheme: CS-1 9.05, CS-2 13.4, CS-3 15.6 and CS-4 21.4 kbps. The theoretical maximum is 8 × 21.4 = 171.2 kbps, though real phones used a few slots and got a few tens of kbps. EDGE later raised the rate with 8-PSK.

SMS is a store-and-forward teleservice. A message goes from the phone to the operator's SMS centre (SMSC), which stores it and forwards it when the receiver is reachable. SMS travels on the signalling channels, so it works even during a call. One SMS carries 140 octets of user data: 140 × 8 / 7 = 160 characters in the GSM 7-bit alphabet, 140 in 8-bit data, or 140 × 8 / 16 = 70 in UCS-2 (Unicode, needed for Indian scripts). A longer text is sent as a concatenated SMS. A 6-octet user data header numbers the parts, which leaves 134 octets per part: 153 7-bit characters, 134 8-bit characters or 67 UCS-2 characters.

Worked example (SMS segments). A 310-character message in the GSM 7-bit alphabet needs ⌈310 / 153⌉ = 3 parts, not ⌈310 / 160⌉ = 2, because each part loses 7 characters to the header. A 140-character message in Hindi (UCS-2) needs ⌈140 / 67⌉ = 3 parts, although 140 / 70 = 2 might suggest otherwise.

Communication satellites

A communication satellite is a radio relay in orbit. It receives on an uplink frequency, changes the frequency and retransmits on a downlink, using a transponder. The area it covers is its footprint. The uplink uses the higher frequency of each pair, because the satellite's transmitter power is limited and lower frequencies suffer less attenuation on the way down. Common bands are L (about 1–2 GHz: GPS and mobile satellite phones), C (6 GHz up, 4 GHz down), Ku (14 GHz up, about 11–12 GHz down: direct-to-home TV) and Ka (about 30 GHz up, 20 GHz down).

The orbital period follows Kepler's third law, T = 2π√(a3/μ), where a is the distance from the Earth's centre (Earth radius 6378 km + altitude) and μ = 398 600 km3/s2. Forouzan gives the shortcut T ≈ (1/100) × a1.5 seconds with a in km, which is close enough for exam options.

Mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs)

A MANET is a temporary network of mobile nodes that organises itself without any infrastructure: no access point, no base station, no central server. Every node is both a host and a router, forwarding packets for others, so paths are multi-hop. The topology changes as nodes move, links are wireless (limited bandwidth, hidden and exposed terminals), nodes run on batteries, and security is hard because there is no central authority. Uses include battlefields, disaster relief, vehicular networks (VANETs) and sensor fields.

Routing protocols fall into three families:

  • Proactive (table-driven): every node keeps routes to all destinations at all times, by periodic updates. DSDV is distance vector (Bellman–Ford) with destination sequence numbers that prevent loops and count-to-infinity. OLSR is link state, cutting the flooding cost by letting only chosen multipoint relays (MPRs) forward updates. Routes are ready at once, but the control traffic flows even when nobody sends data.
  • Reactive (on-demand): routes are found only when a source needs one. In AODV, the source floods a route request (RREQ); each node records the reverse path; the destination, or a node with a fresh enough route, unicasts a route reply (RREP) back along it; a route error (RERR) reports a broken link. Destination sequence numbers keep routes loop-free and fresh, and tables hold only the next hop. DSR uses source routing: the full route travels in each packet header, and nodes keep a route cache. Overhead is low, but the first packet of a new flow waits for route discovery.
  • Hybrid: ZRP (zone routing protocol) is proactive inside a zone of radius ρ hops around each node and reactive between zones.

Flooding cost is easy to count. If every node except the destination rebroadcasts an RREQ exactly once, a 25-node network carries 25 − 1 = 24 RREQ transmissions (the source's broadcast plus 23 rebroadcasts).

Wireless geolocation

Wireless geolocation finds the position of a mobile device from radio measurements, for emergency calls (E911/E112), navigation, fleet tracking and location-based services. The measurements are:

  • Cell-ID (cell of origin): the position of the serving cell is the estimate. It needs no extra hardware, and its accuracy is the cell size (a hundred metres to several km).
  • RSSI (received signal strength): a path-loss model converts power into distance. P(d) = P(d0) − 10 n log10(d/d0), so d = d0 × 10(P(d0) − P(d)) / (10n). Fading makes it coarse.
  • TOA (time of arrival): distance = c × travel time, which puts the device on a circle round each reference. A 2-D fix by trilateration needs three references, and all clocks must be synchronised. Every 1 μs of timing error means 300 m of range error.
  • TDOA (time difference of arrival): the difference in arrival times at two synchronised receivers puts the device on a hyperbola. The handset's clock need not be synchronised, and three base stations (two hyperbolas) give a 2-D fix.
  • AOA (angle of arrival): antenna arrays measure the direction of the incoming signal. In 2-D, two base stations suffice (two lines cross), but the error grows with distance.
  • Fingerprinting: the device's pattern of signal strengths is matched against a survey database (common for Wi-Fi positioning indoors).
  • GNSS (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou and India's regional NavIC) is satellite TOA. A receiver needs four satellites for a 3-D fix, because it solves for x, y, z and its own clock bias. Assisted GPS (A-GPS) receives satellite data through the cellular network, which cuts the time to the first fix.

Worked example (geolocation numericals).

  1. TOA: a signal takes 10 μs, so d = 3 × 108 × 10 × 10−6 = 3 km.
  2. RSSI: P(1 m) = −40 dBm, measured −70 dBm, n = 3. d = 1030/30 = 10 m. (With n = 2 and −80 dBm, d = 1040/20 = 100 m.)
  3. Trilateration: references at (0, 0), (10, 0) and (0, 10) measure distances 5, √65 and √45. From x2 + y2 = 25 and (x − 10)2 + y2 = 65, subtracting gives −20x + 100 = 40, so x = 3. From x2 + (y − 10)2 = 45, subtracting gives −20y + 100 = 20, so y = 4. The device is at (3, 4).

Cloud storage and database storage

Clouds offer storage in several forms.

KindHow it is usedExamples
Block storageRaw volumes attached to one virtual server, used like a disk (for an OS or a database); low latencyAmazon EBS, Azure Managed Disks
File storageA shared hierarchical file system mounted over NFS or SMB by many serversAmazon EFS, Azure Files
Object storageA flat namespace of buckets holding objects (data + metadata + a unique key), read and written whole over HTTP REST (PUT, GET); massively scalable; for backups, media and data lakesAmazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage
Archive storageVery cheap, for data rarely read; retrieval takes minutes to hoursS3 Glacier, Azure Archive

Durability comes from replication (typically 3 copies, so usable capacity is a third of the raw capacity) or erasure coding: data is cut into k fragments plus m parity fragments, any k of which rebuild it. The storage overhead is (k + m)/k and any m fragments can be lost. For example, 300 TB of raw capacity gives 100 TB usable with 3-way replication, but 300 × 6/9 = 200 TB with a (6, 3) code, which still survives any 3 lost fragments. Going the other way, storing 40 TB of customer data with 3 replicas needs 3 × 40 = 120 TB of raw disk.

Database storage in the cloud is usually DBaaS (database as a service): the provider installs, patches, backs up and replicates the database engine, and the customer handles the schema, queries and access rights. Offerings include managed relational databases (Amazon RDS, Azure SQL Database, Google Cloud SQL), cloud-native distributed SQL (Aurora, Spanner), NoSQL stores (DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, Bigtable) and warehouses (Redshift, BigQuery). Read replicas scale reads, sharding (horizontal partitioning) spreads data and writes over many servers, and synchronous replicas in another availability zone give fail-over.

Resource management, virtual servers and SLAs

A virtual server (a VM instance) is a slice of a physical host created by the hypervisor, with its own vCPUs, memory, virtual disks and IP address. Providers sell fixed instance types, and a VPS is the same idea sold by hosting companies. Cloud resource management decides how the pool is shared:

  • Provisioning: static (sized in advance for the peak) or dynamic (on demand, as load changes).
  • Placement and scheduling: choosing a host for each VM, a bin-packing problem often solved with first-fit style heuristics. Admission control refuses requests that would break existing commitments, and over-commitment sells more vCPUs than there are physical cores. For example, a host with 32 physical cores over-committed at 4:1 offers 128 vCPUs, enough for 128 / 8 = 16 virtual servers of 8 vCPUs each (if memory allows).
  • Load balancing: spreading incoming requests over several instances.
  • Scaling: vertical (scale up: a bigger VM, limited by the largest host and often needing a restart) or horizontal (scale out and in: more or fewer instances, which is what elasticity means). Auto-scaling rules add instances when a metric passes a threshold, or track a target such as 60% CPU.
  • Live migration moves a running VM to another host with negligible downtime, and consolidation packs VMs onto fewer hosts so that idle hosts can be switched off to save energy.
  • Monitoring and metering feed both the scaling decisions and the bill.

For example, a service receives 1800 requests/s, one VM can handle 250 requests/s, and the auto-scaler keeps each VM at 60% of capacity. Each VM then takes 150 requests/s, so ⌈1800 / 150⌉ = 12 VMs are needed, not the 8 that full load would suggest.

A service level agreement (SLA) is the contract between provider and customer. It contains the service description; the service level objectives (SLOs), which are targets such as 99.95% monthly availability or a 200 ms response time; the service level indicators (SLIs), which are the measured quantities; the measurement method and period; responsibilities; exclusions (scheduled maintenance, force majeure); and remedies, usually service credits (a percentage of the monthly bill refunded when a target is missed). An SLA has a life cycle: negotiation, implementation, monitoring, enforcement and renewal or termination. Availability arithmetic is the common numerical. Components in series multiply (A1 × A2). Redundant components in parallel give 1 − (1 − A1)(1 − A2). The downtime allowed in a 30-day month is (1 − A) × 43 200 minutes.

Worked example (SLA arithmetic).

  1. Two web servers, each 99% available, run in parallel behind a load balancer that is 99.9% available. Servers: 1 − 0.012 = 0.9999. Whole service: 0.999 × 0.9999 = 0.9989, about 99.89%. The redundant pair is better than the balancer, which now limits the service.
  2. An SLA of 99.5% monthly uptime allows (1 − 0.995) × 43 200 = 216 minutes (3.6 hours) of downtime in a 30-day month. 99.9% allows only 43.2 minutes.
  3. An SLA refunds 10% of the monthly bill for availability from 99.0% up to (but not including) 99.9%, and 25% from 95.0% up to 99.0%. A month measured at 99.5% on a bill of ₹50 000 earns a credit of ₹5000.

NTA traps

  • Any N is a valid cluster. Wrong: N must equal i² + ij + j². So 5, 6, 8, 10 and 11 are impossible for hexagonal cells.
  • D/R = √N. Wrong: the reuse ratio is √(3N).
  • GSM is pure TDMA. Wrong: GSM uses FDMA to create 200 kHz carriers and TDMA within each carrier.
  • Soft handoff in GSM. Wrong: soft handoff is a CDMA feature, and GSM uses hard handoff.
  • The care-of address always belongs to the FA. Wrong: a co-located CoA belongs to the mobile node itself.
  • A Bluetooth piconet has 8 slaves. Wrong: it has 8 active devices in total, meaning 1 master and 7 slaves.
  • Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CD. Wrong: 802.11 uses CSMA/CA, and classic Ethernet uses CSMA/CD.
  • In SaaS, the customer patches the OS. Wrong: in SaaS the provider runs everything. The customer handles the OS only in IaaS.
  • Type 2 hypervisors are faster. Wrong: Type 1 runs on bare metal and is the data-centre choice.
  • MQTT runs over UDP. Wrong: MQTT runs over TCP, and CoAP is the UDP protocol. (MQTT-SN is a separate variant for non-TCP networks.)
  • # in the middle of a filter. Wrong: # must be the last level. home/#/temp is invalid.

How NTA asks this

  • Match the list: generation to access method, Wi-Fi amendment to name or band, cloud model to example, IoT protocol to transport, GSM entity to role. Anchor on the pair you know best, such as SaaS with Gmail or MQTT with the broker.
  • Which are correct (multi): NIST characteristics (watch for “vendor lock-in” or “unlimited free storage” as distractors), 5G usage scenarios, protocols that run over UDP.
  • Chronological order: AMPS → GSM → UMTS → LTE → NR; 802.11b → n → ac → ax → be.
  • Small numericals: N from (i, j), D/R, channels per cell, CDMA decode, downtime.

Mini A-R. A: A packet sent to a mobile host that is away from home first reaches its home network. R: The correspondent knows only the home address, and the home agent tunnels the packet to the care-of address. Both are true and R explains A, so the answer is option 1. If R had said “the correspondent knows the care-of address”, it would be false for basic Mobile IPv4.

Remember: the cloud is “5-3-4” (characteristics, service models, deployment models). MQTT is TCP publish/subscribe with a broker. CoAP is UDP and REST. Zigbee sits on 802.15.4.

terms.definition: The number of cells that share the whole spectrum once. For hexagons N = i² + ij + j² (1, 3, 4, 7, 9, 12 …), and the reuse ratio D/R = √(3N).
Hard handoff is break-before-make (GSM). Soft handoff is make-before-break, possible in CDMA because neighbouring cells use the same frequency.
An orthogonal ±1 sequence per station. Sending the code means 1 and its negation means 0. The receiver decodes with a normalised inner product.
The temporary address of a mobile node in a foreign network: the foreign agent’s address or a co-located address. The home agent tunnels packets to it.
A Bluetooth network of one master and up to seven active slaves. Linked piconets form a scatternet.
The 802.11 medium access method: sense, wait DIFS plus a random backoff, send, and wait for an ACK. Optional RTS/CTS handles hidden terminals.
Rented infrastructure (you manage the OS upward), a platform (you manage the app and data), or finished software (you manage only settings and data).
Bare-metal (ESXi, Xen, Hyper-V, KVM) against hosted on an OS (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation).
A publish/subscribe IoT protocol over TCP through a broker. QoS 0/1/2 give at most once, at least once and exactly once. The wildcards are + (one level) and # (many levels).
A RESTful IoT protocol over UDP (RFC 7252) with confirmable and non-confirmable messages, and DTLS for security.

quiz.question: In a hexagonal cellular layout, the nearest co-channel cell is reached by moving i = 2 cells, turning 60° and moving j = 1 cell. What are the cluster size N and the co-channel reuse ratio D/R?
quiz.explanation: N = i² + ij + j² = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7, and D/R = √(3N) = √21 ≈ 4.58. The option 2.65 is √7, which wrongly uses √N. N = 5 would come from i² + j², and 5 is not a valid hexagonal cluster size.

quiz.question: Four CDMA stations use the chip codes A = (+1 +1 +1 +1), B = (+1 −1 +1 −1), C = (+1 +1 −1 −1) and D = (+1 −1 −1 +1). The receiver gets the sum S = (+1 −3 −1 −1). Which conclusion is correct?
options: A sent 1, B sent 0, C was silent, D sent 1
A sent 0, B sent 1, C was silent, D sent 1
A sent 0, B sent 1, C sent 1, D sent 1
A sent 0, B sent 1, C sent 0, D was silent
quiz.explanation: Divide each inner product by 4. S·A = 1 − 3 − 1 − 1 = −4, giving −1, so A sent 0. S·B = 1 + 3 − 1 + 1 = 4, giving +1, so B sent 1. S·C = 1 − 3 + 1 + 1 = 0, so C was silent. S·D = 1 + 3 + 1 − 1 = 4, giving +1, so D sent 1. Check: −A + B + D = (1, −3, −1, −1).

quiz.question: A cloud provider promises 99.99% availability over a 365-day year. What is the maximum downtime allowed?
quiz.explanation: Downtime = (1 − 0.9999) × 365 × 24 × 60 = 0.0001 × 525600 = 52.56 minutes. 8.76 hours is the figure for 99.9%, 4.38 hours is for 99.95%, and 5.26 minutes is for 99.999%.

quiz.question: An IoT designer needs a RESTful request/response protocol with GET and PUT methods that runs over UDP on constrained devices. Which protocol fits?
quiz.explanation: CoAP (RFC 7252) is REST for constrained nodes over UDP, with confirmable messages for reliability. MQTT is publish/subscribe over TCP. Zigbee is a network stack on IEEE 802.15.4, not a REST protocol. RFID is a tagging technology.

quiz.question: The GSM-900 band gives 25 MHz in each direction. With 200 kHz carrier spacing, 124 carrier pairs are usable, and each carrier has 8 TDMA time slots. How many full-rate traffic channels (slots) does the band provide in total?
quiz.explanation: 124 carriers × 8 slots = 992. 25 MHz ÷ 200 kHz = 125, and one carrier is lost to guard bands, which leaves 124. 1000 wrongly uses 125 carriers. 124 ignores TDMA.
