domains.blurb: Search, knowledge representation, planning, NLP, fuzzy logic, genetic algorithms and neural networks.

lessons.title: AI approaches and search
lessons.summaryHtml: AI builds rational agents that perceive an environment (described by PEAS) and act to maximise expected performance. Many AI tasks become search through a state space defined by an initial state, actions, a transition model, a goal test and a path cost. Uninformed methods (BFS, DFS, UCS, IDS, bidirectional) differ only in which frontier node they expand next. Informed methods use a heuristic h(n): greedy search expands the lowest h, and A* the lowest g + h, which is optimal when h is admissible (tree search) or consistent (graph search). Local search (hill climbing, simulated annealing) and CSP techniques (backtracking, MRV, forward checking, arc consistency) handle optimisation and constraint problems. Minimax with alpha–beta pruning solves two-player games and returns the same value as plain minimax with less work. NET asks for complexity tables, heuristic properties, expansion orders and alpha–beta pruning counts.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Artificial intelligence is the study of programs that choose sensible actions. The standard view in Russell and Norvig is the rational agent: something that perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators, choosing the action expected to do best by some performance measure. Many AI problems reduce to search. You describe the start situation, the moves allowed and the goal, and the program explores the space of possible situations until it finds a route to the goal. Uninformed search explores blindly. Informed search uses a heuristic guess of the distance to the goal. Local search improves one state at a time. Adversarial search plans against an opponent who is trying to make you lose.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 10 is a full unit of the Paper 2 syllabus, and this lesson is its most computational part. Questions come in three families. First, definitions and matching: approaches to AI, the Turing test, agent types, PEAS and environment properties. Second, property questions on search algorithms: which one is complete, which is optimal, what its time and space complexity is, and what admissible and consistent heuristics guarantee. Third, traces: the order in which BFS, DFS, UCS or A* expands the nodes of a small graph, the minimax value of a game tree and the number of leaves alpha–beta prunes. The traces are quick marks if you fix your conventions in advance, so this lesson states them clearly.

Concepts in depth

1. What is AI? Four approaches and the Turing test

HumanlyRationally
ThinkingCognitive modelling: build programs that think the way people do (compare with psychology experiments).Laws of thought: correct inference in logic, from Aristotle’s syllogisms onwards.
ActingThe Turing test approach: behave so that a person cannot tell the machine from a human.The rational agent approach: act to achieve the best expected outcome. This is the modern textbook approach.

Alan Turing proposed the imitation game in his 1950 paper “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”. A human interrogator exchanges typed messages with a hidden human and a hidden machine. The machine passes if the interrogator cannot reliably tell which is which. To pass, a machine needs natural language processing, knowledge representation, automated reasoning and machine learning. The total Turing test adds a video signal and object passing, so it also needs computer vision and robotics. John Searle’s Chinese room argument (1980) claims that passing such a test through symbol manipulation does not prove understanding. The term “artificial intelligence” was coined by John McCarthy for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.

2. Agents, PEAS and environments

An agent function maps the percept sequence to an action; the agent program implements it. A rational agent picks the action that maximises the expected performance measure, given its percepts and built-in knowledge. Rational is not omniscient: it maximises expected, not actual, outcome. The task environment is specified by PEAS: Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors. For an automated taxi: P = safe, fast, legal, comfortable trip; E = roads, traffic, pedestrians; A = steering, accelerator, brake, horn; S = cameras, GPS, speedometer, sonar.

PropertyMeaningExample
Fully vs partially observableDo sensors give the complete relevant state?Chess is fully observable; poker is partially observable.
Deterministic vs stochasticIs the next state fixed by the current state and action?Crossword is deterministic; taxi driving is stochastic.
Episodic vs sequentialDoes the current decision affect future ones?Defect detection on an assembly line is episodic; chess is sequential.
Static vs dynamic (semi-dynamic)Can the world change while the agent thinks? Semi-dynamic: the world stays, but the score changes with time.Crossword is static; chess with a clock is semi-dynamic; driving is dynamic.
Discrete vs continuousFinite distinct states, percepts and actions?Chess is discrete; driving is continuous.
Single vs multi-agentOther agents whose goals interact?Solitaire is single-agent; chess is competitive multi-agent.

The five agent programs, from simplest to richest, are: simple reflex (condition–action rules on the current percept only; works only when the environment is fully observable), model-based reflex (keeps an internal state that tracks the unseen parts of the world), goal-based (plans actions that reach a goal), utility-based (compares states by a utility function, so it can trade off conflicting goals and uncertainty), and the learning agent. A learning agent has four parts: the performance element, the critic, the learning element and the problem generator.

Interactive solver

Enter any problem, including the ones in your practice set, and the solver works it out step by step with the conventions stated. Use it to check your answers, not to replace doing them by hand: the exam gives you no solver.

Interactive solver: Minimax, alpha–beta and A* solver

The solver runs in your browser. Turn on JavaScript to use it.

3. Problem formulation and state spaces

A search problem has five parts: the initial state, the actions available in each state, the transition model (the result of an action), the goal test and the path cost. Together they define a state space. A solution is a path from the initial state to a goal state, and an optimal solution has the lowest path cost. Classic formulations are the 8-puzzle (9!/2 = 181,440 reachable states), the n-queens problem, the water-jug problem and missionaries and cannibals. The older Indian syllabus texts (Rich and Knight) also use production systems: a set of rules, a database and a control strategy. They also describe weak methods: generate-and-test, means–ends analysis (reduce the difference between the current state and the goal, as in GPS) and problem reduction with AND–OR graphs, solved by the AO* algorithm.

Two kinds of search algorithm matter for traces. Tree search may revisit states. Graph search keeps an explored (closed) set and never expands a state twice. Every algorithm keeps a frontier (open list) of generated but unexpanded nodes. The algorithms differ only in which frontier node they pick next.

4. Uninformed search

  • Breadth-first search (BFS) uses a FIFO queue, so it expands the shallowest node first. It finds the path with the fewest edges, which is optimal only when every step costs the same.
  • Uniform-cost search (UCS) uses a priority queue ordered by the path cost g(n). It is Dijkstra’s algorithm with an early stop, and it is optimal for any step costs of at least some ε > 0. It must test for the goal when a node is expanded, not when it is generated, because a cheaper path may still be on the frontier.
  • Depth-first search (DFS) uses a LIFO stack or recursion, so it expands the deepest node first. It needs only O(bm) memory. It is not optimal, and tree-search DFS is incomplete when paths are infinite or contain loops.
  • Depth-limited search is DFS that stops at depth l. It is incomplete if l < d. Iterative deepening search (IDS) runs depth-limited search with l = 0, 1, 2, … until it finds a goal. It combines the O(bd) memory of DFS with the completeness of BFS. The repeated work is small: nodes at depth i are generated (d + 1 − i) times, so the total is (d+1)·1 + d·b + (d−1)·b² + … + 1·bd. For b = 10 and d = 4 that is 12,345 against 11,111 for BFS.
  • Bidirectional search runs one search forward from the start and one backward from the goal. It stops when the two frontiers meet: 2·bd/2 is far smaller than bd. It needs reversible actions and an explicit goal state.
AlgorithmComplete?Optimal?TimeSpace
BFSYes (b finite)Yes, if all step costs are equalO(bd)O(bd)
UCSYes, if step cost ≥ ε > 0YesO(b1+⌊C*/ε⌋)O(b1+⌊C*/ε⌋)
DFSNo (yes in finite graph search)NoO(bm)O(bm)
Depth-limited (l)No (yes if l ≥ d)NoO(bl)O(bl)
IDSYesYes, if all step costs are equalO(bd)O(bd)
BidirectionalYes (BFS both ways)Yes, if all step costs are equalO(bd/2)O(bd/2)

Here b is the branching factor, d the depth of the shallowest goal, m the maximum depth, and C* the optimal cost.

5. Informed search: greedy best-first and A*

A heuristic h(n) estimates the cheapest cost from n to a goal, with h(goal) = 0. Greedy best-first expands the node with the smallest h(n). It is often fast, but it is not optimal, and tree-search greedy can loop forever. A* expands the node with the smallest f(n) = g(n) + h(n), the estimated cost of the cheapest solution through n. UCS is A* with h = 0, and greedy search ignores g.

  • h is admissible if it never overestimates: h(n) ≤ h*(n), where h* is the true cost to the goal. With an admissible h, A* tree search is optimal.
  • h is consistent (monotone) if h(n) ≤ c(n, n′) + h(n′) for every edge. This is the triangle inequality. Consistent implies admissible (given h(goal) = 0), and then f never decreases along a path. So A* graph search expands nodes in non-decreasing f order and is optimal without reopening closed nodes. An admissible but inconsistent h can make graph search A* suboptimal unless closed nodes can be reopened.
  • If h₂(n) ≥ h₁(n) for all n and both are admissible, h₂ dominates h₁. A* with h₂ never expands more nodes. For the 8-puzzle, Manhattan distance dominates the misplaced-tiles count.
  • A* expands every node with f(n) < C*. It is optimally efficient among such algorithms, but it keeps every generated node in memory. IDA*, RBFS and SMA* are the memory-bounded versions.

The trace convention used in this course is: graph search, successors taken in alphabetical order, ties in the priority queue broken alphabetically, and the goal test applied when a node is expanded. For BFS we also show what changes if the goal test is applied when a node is generated.

6. Local search

Local search keeps one current state (or a few) and moves to neighbours. It uses constant memory and suits optimisation problems where the path does not matter, such as n-queens. Hill climbing (steepest ascent) moves to the best neighbour and stops when no neighbour is better. It gets stuck at local maxima, on ridges and on plateaus (flat areas; a shoulder is a plateau from which progress is still possible). The fixes are sideways moves, stochastic hill climbing, first-choice hill climbing and random-restart hill climbing. Simulated annealing picks a random neighbour. It always accepts an improvement, and it accepts a worse move with probability e−ΔE/T, where ΔE > 0 is how much worse the move is and T is the temperature. As T falls, bad moves become rare. With a slow enough schedule it finds a global optimum with probability approaching 1. Local beam search keeps k states and chooses the k best successors of all of them together. Genetic algorithms are covered in lesson 10.5.

7. Constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs)

A CSP has variables Xi, domains Di and constraints. A solution is a complete, consistent assignment. Map colouring, n-queens, Sudoku, scheduling and cryptarithmetic are standard CSPs. Backtracking search assigns one variable at a time and backtracks on a violation. It is improved by three heuristics. MRV (minimum remaining values, “fail first”) chooses the variable with the fewest legal values. The degree heuristic breaks ties by choosing the variable in the most constraints with unassigned variables. LCV (least constraining value) chooses the value that rules out the fewest options for neighbours. Forward checking deletes inconsistent values from neighbours’ domains after each assignment. Arc consistency (AC-3) makes every arc X→Y consistent: every value of X has some supporting value in Y. AC-3 runs in O(cd³) for c binary constraints and domain size d. A tree-structured CSP is solvable in O(nd²). Min-conflicts is a local search for CSPs that solves even million-queens problems quickly.

8. Adversarial search

For a two-player, zero-sum game with perfect information, minimax assumes both players play optimally. MAX takes the maximum of its children’s values and MIN the minimum, working up from the terminal utilities. It is a DFS: time O(bm), space O(bm). Alpha–beta pruning returns the same root value but skips branches that cannot matter. Here α is the best value MAX can guarantee so far on the current path, and β is the best (lowest) value MIN can guarantee. A MIN node stops as soon as its value is ≤ α. A MAX node stops as soon as its value is ≥ β. In general, prune when α ≥ β. With perfect move ordering, alpha–beta examines about O(bm/2) nodes, so it can search twice as deep in the same time. With random ordering it examines about O(b3m/4). Real programs cut off at a depth limit and apply an evaluation function, typically a weighted linear sum of features. Cutting off creates the horizon effect, which is reduced by quiescence search. For games with dice, expectiminimax adds chance nodes whose value is the probability-weighted average of their children.

Worked examples

Examples 1 and 2 use this undirected graph. The start is S and the goal is G.

Edges (cost):  S–A 1   S–B 6   A–C 3   A–D 6   B–D 2
               B–E 5   C–D 1   C–G 9   D–G 4   E–G 2
Heuristic h:   S 7   A 6   B 5   C 4   D 3   E 2   G 0
True cost h*:  S 9   A 8   B 6   C 5   D 4   E 2   G 0

Every h(n) ≤ h*(n), so h is admissible. Checking all ten edges shows h(n) ≤ c + h(n′) in both directions, so h is also consistent.

Example 1: BFS, DFS and IDS

BFS (FIFO queue, goal test on expansion):

  1. Expand S. Add A and B to the queue.
  2. Expand A. Add C and D.
  3. Expand B. D is already queued, so only E is added.
  4. Expand C. Add G. Then expand D and E, which add nothing new, and finally G.

Expansion order: S, A, B, C, D, E, G. The path is S–A–C–G, with 3 edges and cost 1 + 3 + 9 = 13. If the goal test is done when a node is generated, BFS stops while expanding C, after expanding only S, A, B and C.

DFS (recursive, alphabetical): S → A → C (from C, A is visited, so try D before G) → D → B → E → G. The order is S, A, C, D, B, E, G. The path found is S–A–C–D–B–E–G, with cost 1 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 5 + 2 = 14. DFS finds a goal, but a long and costly one.

IDS (no repeated states on the current path):

  • Limit 0: S.
  • Limit 1: S, A, B.
  • Limit 2: S, A, C, D, B, D, E.
  • Limit 3: S, A, C, D, G, and the goal is found at depth 3.

That is 1 + 3 + 7 + 5 = 16 node visits. IDS finds the same shallowest path as BFS, S–A–C–G.

Example 2: UCS, greedy best-first and A*

UCS (order by g):

StepExpand (g)Frontier after the step
1S (0)A 1, B 6
2A (1)C 4, B 6, D 7
3C (4)D 5 (improved from 7), B 6, G 13
4D (5)B 6, G 9 (improved from 13)
5B (6)G 9, E 11
6G (9)goal

The UCS order is S, A, C, D, B, G, and the path is S–A–C–D–G with cost 9, which is optimal. G was generated with cost 13 at step 3, but stopping then would give a wrong answer. That is why the goal test waits for expansion.

Greedy (order by h): from S, B (h 5) beats A (h 6). From B, E (h 2) beats D (h 3). From E, G is chosen. The path is S–B–E–G with cost 6 + 5 + 2 = 13, which is not optimal.

A* (order by f = g + h):

StepExpand (f)Frontier after the step (f)
1S (7)A 1+6=7, B 6+5=11
2A (7)C 4+4=8, D 7+3=10, B 11
3C (8)D 5+3=8, B 11, G 13+0=13
4D (8)G 9+0=9, B 11
5G (9)goal

A* expands 5 nodes (S, A, C, D, G), one fewer than UCS, because B’s f = 11 exceeds C* = 9. It finds the same optimal cost of 9. The f values along the chosen path are 7, 7, 8, 8, 9, which never decrease, as a consistent h guarantees.

Example 3: minimax and alpha–beta on a three-ply tree

                 MAX  root
            /                 \
        MIN B                 MIN C
       /     \               /     \
   MAX D    MAX E        MAX F    MAX G
   4   8    9   3        2   1    6   7

Minimax: D = 8, E = 9, F = 2, G = 7. Then B = min(8, 9) = 8 and C = min(2, 7) = 2. The root is max(8, 2) = 8.

Alpha–beta, left to right:

  1. D sees 4 and then 8, so D = 8. B now has β = 8.
  2. E sees 9, so E ≥ 9 ≥ β = 8. MIN at B will never choose E, so leaf 3 is pruned.
  3. B = 8, so the root has α = 8.
  4. Under C, F sees 2 and 1, so F = 2 and C has β = 2 ≤ α = 8. The whole of G (leaves 6 and 7) is pruned.

The root value is 8, the same as minimax. The algorithm evaluates 5 leaves and prunes 3.

Example 4: alpha–beta on a two-ply tree

MAX has four MIN children with leaves (5, 8, 6), (3, 9, 7), (2, 10, 4) and (6, 2, 1), searched left to right.

  1. The first MIN node is min(5, 8, 6) = 5, so α = 5 at the root.
  2. The second MIN node sees 3 ≤ 5, so 9 and 7 are pruned.
  3. The third MIN node sees 2 ≤ 5, so 10 and 4 are pruned.
  4. The fourth MIN node sees 6 (still > 5), then 2 ≤ 5, so 1 is pruned.

The root is 5. The algorithm evaluates 7 of the 12 leaves and prunes 5. The best MIN child comes first here, which is the ordering that lets the root prune the most. Inside each later MIN node, pruning also depends on how early a value ≤ α appears: the fourth node had to look at two leaves because its first leaf, 6, was not low enough.

Example 5: water jug, heuristics and simulated annealing

Water jug. You have jugs of 4 L and 3 L and must get exactly 2 L in the 4 L jug. Write states as (x, y). BFS finds the shortest solution, with 6 moves: (0,0) → (0,3) → (3,0) → (3,3) → (4,2) → (0,2) → (2,0). Note that 2 L first appears in the 3 L jug after 4 moves. Questions that do not say which jug contains the 2 L therefore have a different answer.

8-puzzle heuristics. Take the state 4 1 3 / 7 2 6 / _ 5 8 and the goal 1 2 3 / 4 5 6 / 7 8 _.

  • Misplaced tiles: 4, 1, 7, 2, 5 and 8 are out of place, so h₁ = 6.
  • Manhattan distance: each of those six tiles is exactly one move from home, so h₂ = 6.

Here the two are equal, but h₂ ≥ h₁ always holds.

Simulated annealing. A move that is worse by ΔE = 4 at temperature T = 2 is accepted with probability e−2 ≈ 0.135. At T = 10, a worse move with ΔE = 3 is accepted with probability e−0.3 ≈ 0.741.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFact
Nodes BFS generates (to depth d)1 + b + b² + … + bd = (bd+1 − 1)/(b − 1)
Nodes IDS generates(d+1) + d·b + (d−1)·b² + … + bd; for b = 10 and d = 4 it is 12,345
A* evaluationf(n) = g(n) + h(n); UCS is h = 0; greedy is f = h
Admissibleh(n) ≤ h*(n) for all n; gives optimal A* tree search
Consistenth(n) ≤ c(n, n′) + h(n′); implies admissible; gives optimal A* graph search, and f is non-decreasing
Dominanceh₂ ≥ h₁ (both admissible) means h₂ expands no more nodes

NTA traps

  • “BFS is always optimal.” Wrong: BFS minimises the number of edges. It is optimal only when all step costs are equal. For weighted graphs, use UCS or A*.
  • “UCS may stop when the goal is generated.” Wrong: in Example 2, G was generated with cost 13 before the cost-9 path was known. UCS and A* test for the goal when they expand a node.
  • “Consistent follows from admissible.” Reversed. Consistent implies admissible, but not the other way round. For instance, h(C) = 5 and h(D) = 1 are both admissible in the graph above, yet h(C) = 5 > c(C, D) + h(D) = 2.
  • “Alpha–beta may change the minimax value.” Wrong: it returns exactly the minimax value at the root. Only the amount of work depends on the move ordering.
  • “Pruning happens when α < β.” The cut-off condition is α ≥ β. At a MIN node: prune when its value ≤ α. At a MAX node: prune when its value ≥ β.
  • “IDS wastes a lot of time.” It wastes only about 11% extra for b = 10 (12,345 against 11,111 nodes). It is the preferred uninformed method when the search space is large and the depth is unknown.
  • “DFS space is O(bm).” The time is O(bm); the space is only O(bm).
  • “Simple reflex agents work in partially observable worlds.” They need full observability. With partial observability you need a model-based agent, and randomisation can help escape loops.

How NTA asks this

  • Trace questions: “In which order are the nodes expanded?” or “What path does A* return and at what cost?” Write the frontier after each step, as in the tables above, and state your tie-break. The options often differ only in the position of one node.
  • Alpha–beta counts: “How many leaf nodes are pruned?” Mark α and β as you move left to right. A MIN child is cut as soon as it goes to α or below. Count the pruned leaves at the end.
  • Match the following: algorithm to data structure, or algorithm to complexity. Mini-example: BFS–FIFO queue, DFS–stack, UCS–priority queue on g, A*–priority queue on g + h. In the options, check the item you are surest of first (for example BFS–queue), and eliminate every option that disagrees with it.
  • Assertion–Reason: for example, A: “A* with a consistent heuristic never reopens a closed node.” R: “With a consistent heuristic, f is non-decreasing along any path.” Both are true and R explains A. Check whether R is the cause of A, not just a true fact.
  • Environment and PEAS matching: memorise one example for each property (chess with a clock is semi-dynamic, poker is partially observable, image classification is episodic).

The set of generated but not yet expanded nodes (the open list); the algorithm’s choice from it defines the strategy.
Expands the frontier node with the smallest path cost g(n); optimal for step costs ≥ ε > 0.
Depth-limited DFS repeated with limits 0, 1, 2, …; complete, optimal for unit costs, O(b^d) time and O(bd) space.
h(n) ≤ h*(n) for every node: it never overestimates the true cost to the goal.

lessons.examTip: Before any trace question, fix three conventions and write them down: the order of successors (usually alphabetical), how ties are broken, and whether the goal test is applied at generation or at expansion. UCS and A* must test at expansion.

steps: Download practice-set.md. Write the three trace conventions (alphabetical successors, alphabetical tie-break, goal test on expansion) at the top of your sheet.
Attempt problems 1, 2, 5, 6 and 9 to 15 in 15 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Do the traces (problems 3, 4, 7 and 8) in 12 minutes. Draw a frontier table for UCS and A*, and mark α and β beside each node of the game trees.
Check every answer against solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for, for example stopping UCS when the goal was only generated.
Re-run problems 3 and 4 with the goal test at generation and note exactly where the answer changes.
Redo the problems you got wrong after 24 hours, without looking at the solutions.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct on the first attempt.
Problems 1, 2, 5, 6 and 9 to 15 finished within 15 minutes.
Your UCS and A* frontier tables match the solutions row by row.
You can explain in one sentence why alpha–beta prunes nothing in problem 8.

quiz.question: A directed graph has these edges (cost): S→A 2, S→B 4, A→C 4, A→D 1, B→D 2, B→E 4, C→G 2, D→C 2, D→G 6, E→G 1. What is the cost of the path returned by uniform-cost search from S to G?

The path is S→A→D→C→G = 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 7. 8 is the BFS/DFS path S→A→C→G, 9 is the greedy path S→B→E→G, and 6 is not the cost of any S–G path.

quiz.question: A game tree has a MAX root with three MIN children. The leaves, from left to right, are (4, 7, 2), (9, 1, 6) and (3, 8, 5). Using alpha–beta pruning left to right, what is the root value and how many leaves are pruned?

quiz.question: In simulated annealing, the current state has value 20 and a randomly chosen neighbour has value 14 (we are maximising). The temperature is T = 3. What is the probability that the move is accepted?
quiz.explanation: The move is worse by ΔE = 20 − 14 = 6. A worse move is accepted with probability e^(−ΔE/T) = e^(−6/3) = e^(−2) ≈ 0.135. e^(−6) forgets to divide by T. Probability 1 applies only to improving moves.

quiz.question: Iterative deepening search is run on a uniform tree with branching factor b = 3 and the shallowest goal at depth d = 3. How many nodes does it generate in total, counting every repeated generation (the goal is the last node at depth 3)?
quiz.explanation: Nodes at depth i are generated (d + 1 − i) times: 4·1 + 3·3 + 2·9 + 1·27 = 4 + 9 + 18 + 27 = 58. BFS would generate 1 + 3 + 9 + 27 = 40, so the overhead is about 45% for b = 3. It shrinks as b grows. 27 counts only the last level.

lessons.title: Knowledge representation and reasoning
lessons.summaryHtml: Knowledge representation chooses the language in which an agent stores what it knows. Reasoning derives what follows from it. Propositional and first-order logic give precise meaning. Resolution on clauses (after CNF conversion and Skolemisation), with unification to match terms, is a refutation-complete proof method. Forward chaining (data-driven) and backward chaining (goal-driven) run rule-based expert systems. Semantic networks, frames, scripts and conceptual dependency structure knowledge around objects, stereotyped events and primitive acts. For uncertainty, AI uses Bayes’ rule and Bayesian networks, whose joint distribution is the product of local conditional tables, MYCIN’s certainty factors, and Dempster–Shafer belief and plausibility. NET asks for MGUs, resolution steps, chaining traces, CD primitives and exact probability calculations.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

An intelligent program must store what it knows and draw new conclusions from it. Knowledge representation is the choice of language for that store. Reasoning is the procedure that derives what follows. Logic gives precise languages: propositional logic for simple facts, and first-order logic (FOL) for objects, relations and quantifiers. Resolution with unification is the classic mechanical proof method. Structured schemes such as semantic networks, frames, scripts and conceptual dependency organise knowledge the way people seem to. Rule-based expert systems chain if–then rules forwards or backwards. The real world is uncertain, so AI also reasons with numbers: probabilities and Bayesian networks, MYCIN’s certainty factors, and Dempster–Shafer belief functions.

Why it matters for NET

This topic produces a steady set of questions in Unit 10, and it overlaps with Unit 1 (logic, Bayes’ theorem). The favourites are: finding the most general unifier of two literals (or showing that none exists), converting to CNF and Skolemising, resolution proofs, forward versus backward chaining, and matching the structured representations (frames with slots, scripts with scenes, CD primitives). The uncertainty questions ask for a Bayes posterior, a probability from a small Bayesian network, a combined certainty factor, or a Dempster–Shafer combination. Each of these is a short, exact calculation.

Concepts in depth

1. Logic as a representation language

A knowledge base (KB) is a set of sentences. KB entails α (KB ⊨ α) if α is true in every model where KB is true. An inference procedure is sound if it derives only entailed sentences, and complete if it can derive every entailed sentence. Propositional entailment is decidable, since you can check every model. It is co-NP-complete in general, but for Horn clauses it takes linear time. FOL adds constants, variables, functions, predicates and the quantifiers ∀ and ∃. FOL entailment is only semi-decidable: a proof procedure finds a proof if one exists, but it may run forever when the sentence is not entailed.

The key inference rules are as follows.

  • Modus ponens: from α → β and α, infer β.
  • Modus tollens: from α → β and ¬β, infer ¬α.
  • And-elimination: from α ∧ β, infer α.
  • Resolution: from (α ∨ β) and (¬β ∨ γ), infer (α ∨ γ).
  • Universal instantiation: from ∀x P(x), infer P(t) for any ground term t.
  • Existential instantiation: from ∃x P(x), infer P(C) for a new constant C.
  • Generalised modus ponens: modus ponens with unification. From p₁′, …, pₙ′ and (p₁ ∧ … ∧ pₙ → q), infer qθ, where θ unifies each pᵢ′ with pᵢ.

Resolution is refutation-complete. If KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable, resolution will eventually derive the empty clause □.

2. Converting to clause form (CNF)

Resolution works on clauses, which are disjunctions of literals. The conversion has eight steps, in this order:

  1. Eliminate ↔ and →: α → β becomes ¬α ∨ β.
  2. Move ¬ inwards, using De Morgan’s laws together with ¬∀x P ≡ ∃x ¬P and ¬∃x P ≡ ∀x ¬P.
  3. Standardise variables apart, so that each quantifier uses a different variable name.
  4. Skolemise: remove each ∃ by replacing its variable with a Skolem function of the ∀ variables that enclose it. For example, ∀x ∃y Loves(x, y) becomes Loves(x, F(x)). If no ∀ encloses the ∃, use a Skolem constant: ∃x ∀y P(x, y) becomes P(C, y).
  5. Drop the universal quantifiers; every remaining variable is implicitly universal.
  6. Distribute ∨ over ∧.
  7. Split the conjunction into separate clauses.
  8. Rename the variables in each clause.

A Horn clause has at most one positive literal. A definite clause has exactly one, which makes it a rule or a fact. A goal clause has none. Prolog programs are sets of definite clauses.

3. Unification

Unification finds a substitution θ that makes two expressions identical. The most general unifier (MGU) is the one that commits to as little as possible. Every other unifier is an instance of it. Robinson’s algorithm compares the two expressions from left to right, as follows.

  • A variable meets a term: bind the variable to the term, unless the variable occurs inside that term. This is the occurs check, so x cannot unify with f(x).
  • Two compound terms: they must have the same function symbol and the same number of arguments. Then unify the arguments in pairs, applying the substitution found so far before each comparison.
  • Two different constants, or different function symbols, cannot be unified: this is a clash.

Once the MGU is found, it is the same whatever order the argument pairs are processed in (up to renaming of variables).

4. Forward and backward chaining; rule-based systems

Forward chaining is data-driven. It starts from the known facts, fires every rule whose premises are satisfied and adds the conclusions, and it repeats until nothing new appears or the goal is reached. It suits monitoring and configuration; XCON (R1) and OPS5 work this way. Backward chaining is goal-driven. It starts from the query and looks for rules that conclude it, then tries to prove their premises as subgoals, working depth first. It suits diagnosis and question answering; Prolog and MYCIN work this way. Both are sound and complete for definite clauses.

A production system has three parts: a rule base (long-term memory), working memory (the facts), and an inference engine that runs the recognise–act cycle (match, conflict resolution, act). When several rules match, conflict resolution picks one. The usual strategies are:

  • Refraction: do not fire the same rule on the same data twice.
  • Recency: prefer rules that match the newest facts.
  • Specificity: prefer the rule with more conditions.
  • Priority: rules carry explicit priorities.

The Rete algorithm speeds up matching by compiling the rule conditions into a network that remembers partial matches between cycles. An expert system adds a knowledge-acquisition interface and an explanation facility. The explanation facility answers “why?” (why is the system asking this question) and “how?” (how was this conclusion reached). Classic systems: MYCIN (diagnosing blood infections; backward chaining with certainty factors), DENDRAL (inferring molecular structure), PROSPECTOR (mineral exploration) and XCON (configuring computers).

5. Structured representations

SchemeKey ideaVocabulary NTA uses
Semantic network (Quillian)A graph whose nodes are concepts and whose labelled arcs are relationsIS-A (subclass), INSTANCE-OF, HAS-PART; property inheritance along IS-A links
Frames (Minsky, 1975)A record-like structure for a stereotyped object or situationSlots with facets (value, default, type, range); procedural attachments or demons (if-needed, if-added, if-removed); inheritance
Scripts (Schank and Abelson)A frame for a stereotyped sequence of events, such as eating at a restaurantEntry conditions, props, roles, track, scenes, results
Conceptual dependency (Schank)Represents the meaning of sentences with a small set of primitive acts, independent of the languageATRANS (transfer of possession), PTRANS (physical transfer), MTRANS (mental transfer), MBUILD, PROPEL, MOVE, GRASP, INGEST, EXPEL, SPEAK, ATTEND

Inheritance in semantic nets and frames is usually default inheritance: a more specific node can override an inherited value. For example, a penguin IS-A bird, but its can-fly slot says no. This makes the reasoning non-monotonic, because adding knowledge can withdraw a conclusion. Non-monotonic reasoning also includes default logic, circumscription and the closed-world assumption (what cannot be proved is taken as false, as in Prolog’s negation as failure). Truth maintenance systems (JTMS, ATMS) record why each belief is held, so they can retract its consequences when the belief is withdrawn.

6. Probability, Bayes and Bayesian networks

Bayes’ rule: P(H | E) = P(E | H) P(H) / P(E), where P(E) = Σh P(E | h) P(h). It turns the causal direction, P(symptom | disease), into the diagnostic one, P(disease | symptom). A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph in which each node holds a conditional probability table (CPT), P(X | Parents(X)). The network encodes the joint distribution compactly:

P(x1, …, xn) = Π P(xi | parents(Xi))

A Boolean node with k Boolean parents needs 2k independent numbers, while the full joint over n Boolean variables needs 2n − 1. Each node is conditionally independent of its non-descendants given its parents. Read independence from the three connection patterns (d-separation):

  • Chain A → B → C: A and C are independent given B.
  • Common cause A ← B → C: A and C are independent given B.
  • Common effect (v-structure) A → B ← C: A and C are independent when B is not observed. They become dependent once B (or a descendant of B) is observed. This is explaining away.

Exact inference is by enumeration (sum the joint over the hidden variables) or variable elimination. It is NP-hard in general but linear for polytrees. Approximate inference uses sampling: rejection sampling, likelihood weighting or Gibbs sampling (MCMC). A naive Bayes classifier is the special network where the class is the only parent of every feature.

7. Certainty factors and Dempster–Shafer theory

MYCIN attaches a certainty factor CF ∈ [−1, 1] to each rule and conclusion. CF = MB − MD, the measure of belief minus the measure of disbelief. The rules of combination are:

  • For a conjunction of premises, use the minimum of their CFs. For a disjunction, use the maximum.
  • For a rule, CF(conclusion) = CF(rule) × CF(premise), applied when the premise CF is above a threshold (usually 0.2).
  • For two rules supporting the same conclusion:
    • both positive: CF = CF₁ + CF₂(1 − CF₁);
    • both negative: CF = CF₁ + CF₂(1 + CF₁);
    • mixed signs: CF = (CF₁ + CF₂) / (1 − min(|CF₁|, |CF₂|)).

Dempster–Shafer theory assigns a mass m to subsets of the frame of discernment Θ, rather than to single outcomes, with Σ m(A) = 1 and m(∅) = 0. Mass on Θ represents ignorance. From the masses you get:

  • Belief: Bel(A) = Σ m(B) over B ⊆ A, the lower bound.
  • Plausibility: Pl(A) = Σ m(B) over B ∩ A ≠ ∅, the upper bound. Pl(A) = 1 − Bel(¬A), so Bel(A) ≤ P(A) ≤ Pl(A).

Dempster’s rule combines two independent bodies of evidence: m(C) = ΣA∩B=C m₁(A)m₂(B) / (1 − K), where K = ΣA∩B=∅ m₁(A)m₂(B) is the conflict.

Worked examples

Example 1: propositional resolution

KB: P → Q, Q → R and P. Prove R.

  1. Convert to clauses: (1) ¬P ∨ Q, (2) ¬Q ∨ R, (3) P. Add the negated goal: (4) ¬R.
  2. Resolve (2) with (4): ¬Q.
  3. Resolve that with (1): ¬P.
  4. Resolve that with (3): □.

The empty clause means that KB ∧ ¬R is unsatisfiable, so KB ⊨ R. Three resolution steps were used.

CNF conversion. A ↔ B becomes (¬A ∨ B) ∧ (A ∨ ¬B), which is 2 clauses. ¬(A ∧ (B ∨ C)) becomes ¬A ∨ (¬B ∧ ¬C), and then (¬A ∨ ¬B) ∧ (¬A ∨ ¬C).

Example 2: most general unifiers

Here x, y, z, u and v are variables, and a, b and John are constants.

PairMGU or failure
Knows(John, x) and Knows(y, Mother(y)){y/John, x/Mother(John)}
P(x, f(y), z) and P(a, f(g(z)), b){x/a, z/b, y/g(b)}. Note that y is bound to g(z), and z later becomes b.
P(x, g(x), g(f(a))) and P(f(u), v, v)x/f(u), then v/g(f(u)); finally g(f(u)) against g(f(a)) gives u/a. So the MGU is {x/f(a), v/g(f(a)), u/a}.
P(x, x) and P(f(y), y)Fails: x/f(y), and then f(y) must equal y, which the occurs check rejects.
Q(f(a), g(x)) and Q(y, y)Fails: y/f(a), and then f(a) must equal g(x), which is a function-symbol clash.

Example 3: first-order resolution with Skolemisation

The facts: every student who studies passes, everyone who passes is happy, and Ravi is a student who studies. Prove Happy(Ravi).

  1. Clause 1: ¬Student(x) ∨ ¬Studies(x) ∨ Passes(x).
  2. Clause 2: ¬Passes(y) ∨ Happy(y).
  3. Clause 3: Student(Ravi). Clause 4: Studies(Ravi). Clause 5 (the negated goal): ¬Happy(Ravi).
  4. Resolve 5 with 2, using {y/Ravi}: ¬Passes(Ravi).
  5. Resolve that with 1, using {x/Ravi}: ¬Student(Ravi) ∨ ¬Studies(Ravi).
  6. Resolve with 3: ¬Studies(Ravi). Resolve with 4: □.

Four resolution steps prove Happy(Ravi).

Skolemisation. ∀x [Person(x) → ∃y Mother(y, x)] becomes ¬Person(x) ∨ Mother(M(x), x), where M is a Skolem function because the ∃ lies inside ∀x. The sentence ∃y ∀x Likes(x, y) (“someone is liked by everyone”) becomes Likes(x, C), with a Skolem constant C.

Example 4: forward versus backward chaining

The rules are R1: A ∧ B → C, R2: C → D, R3: D ∧ E → F and R4: A → E. The facts are A and B, and the goal is F. Conflict resolution: fire the lowest-numbered applicable rule that has not fired yet.

  • Forward:
    • Cycle 1: R1 and R4 match; R1 fires, giving C.
    • Cycle 2: R2 and R4 match; R2 fires, giving D.
    • Cycle 3: only R4 matches; it fires, giving E.
    • Cycle 4: R3 fires, giving F.
    That is 4 rule firings, in the order R1, R2, R4, R3.
  • Backward: the goal F is concluded by R3, so the subgoals are D and E. D comes from R2, with subgoal C. C comes from R1, whose subgoals A and B are facts. E comes from R4, whose subgoal A is a fact. Backward chaining touches only the rules relevant to F. With a larger rule base, that is its advantage.

Example 5: a Bayesian network, computed exactly

Heavy rain M causes flooding F and a traffic jam T, and F and T together affect L (being late). The structure is M → F, M → T, and F, T → L.

P(M) = 1/5
P(F | M) = 1/2     P(F | ¬M) = 1/20
P(T | M) = 3/5     P(T | ¬M) = 1/5
P(L | F,T) = 9/10  P(L | F,¬T) = 7/10  P(L | ¬F,T) = 1/2  P(L | ¬F,¬T) = 1/10
  • Parameters. The network needs 1 + 2 + 2 + 4 = 9 numbers. The full joint table would need 24 − 1 = 15.
  • A joint entry. P(M, F, ¬T, L) = 1/5 × 1/2 × 2/5 × 7/10 = 7/250 = 0.028.
  • P(F). P(F) = 1/5 × 1/2 + 4/5 × 1/20 = 1/10 + 1/25 = 7/50.
  • Diagnosis. P(M | F) = (1/10) / (7/50) = 5/7 ≈ 0.714.
  • By enumeration. P(L) = 353/1250 = 0.2824, and P(M | L) = 145/353 ≈ 0.411.
  • Explaining away. P(F | L) = 279/706 ≈ 0.395. Once we also learn T, P(F | L, T) = 153/418 ≈ 0.366. The traffic jam partly explains the lateness, so flooding becomes less likely.

Example 6: Bayes’ rule, certainty factors and Dempster–Shafer

Bayes. A disease has prevalence 1%. The test detects it 90% of the time and gives a false positive 5% of the time. Then P(D | +) = (0.01 × 0.9) / (0.01 × 0.9 + 0.99 × 0.05) = 0.009 / 0.0585 = 2/13 ≈ 0.154. The rare prior dominates.

CF. Two rules support H with CF 0.6 and 0.5, which combine to 0.6 + 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.8. If a third rule gives CF −0.4 against a current CF of 0.7, the result is (0.7 − 0.4) / (1 − 0.4) = 0.5. If a rule with CF 0.8 has premises with CFs 0.9 and 0.6 joined by AND, then CF = 0.8 × min(0.9, 0.6) = 0.48.

Dempster–Shafer. Let Θ = {Flu, Cold, Allergy}.

  • Evidence 1: m₁({Flu}) = 0.6 and m₁(Θ) = 0.4. Evidence 2: m₂({Cold}) = 0.5 and m₂(Θ) = 0.5.
  • The conflict is K = m₁({Flu}) × m₂({Cold}) = 0.3.
  • After dividing by 1 − K = 0.7: m({Flu}) = 0.3/0.7 = 3/7, m({Cold}) = 0.2/0.7 = 2/7 and m(Θ) = 0.2/0.7 = 2/7.
  • So Bel(Flu) = 3/7 ≈ 0.43 and Pl(Flu) = 3/7 + 2/7 = 5/7 ≈ 0.71.

8. Ontologies

Gruber (1993) defined an ontology as “an explicit specification of a conceptualisation”. Studer and colleagues later sharpened this to a formal, explicit specification of a shared conceptualisation. A conceptualisation is the set of objects, concepts and relations that we assume exist in a domain. Writing it down formally gives people, programs and agents a common vocabulary with an agreed meaning, so that knowledge can be shared and reused instead of being rebuilt for every system.

An ontology has five kinds of building blocks:

  • Classes (concepts): Patient, Doctor, Hospital. They are arranged in a taxonomy by subclass (IS-A) links.
  • Individuals (instances): particular members, such as Dr Meena or KIMS Hospital.
  • Properties (relations, slots): an object property links two individuals (treats, worksAt); a datatype property links an individual to a value (age = 42).
  • Axioms (constraints): rules that restrict interpretation, such as “Doctor and Patient are disjoint”, a domain and range for a property, or “every patient has at least one doctor” (a cardinality restriction).
  • Vocabulary and documentation: the names and their human-readable definitions.

In description logic, the formal basis of OWL, the class-level axioms form the TBox (terminological box) and the facts about individuals form the ABox (assertional box). A reasoner can then classify classes (work out the hierarchy), check consistency and infer class membership.

By generality, there are upper (top-level) ontologies such as Cyc, SUMO, DOLCE and BFO, which describe very general notions (object, event, time); domain ontologies such as the Gene Ontology or SNOMED CT for medicine; and task and application ontologies. WordNet is a lexical ontology: it groups synonyms into synsets and links them by hypernymy (IS-A), hyponymy and meronymy (part-of). Ontology languages include KIF and Ontolingua (the early knowledge-sharing work), RDF Schema, and the W3C’s OWL (2004; OWL 2 in 2009). OWL came in three species, OWL Lite ⊂ OWL DL ⊂ OWL Full, in increasing expressiveness; OWL DL is decidable, and OWL Full is not. Protégé (Stanford) is the most widely used ontology editor.

Semantic networks and frames are the ancestors of ontologies: an OWL class plays the role of a frame, and its properties play the role of slots. The difference is that an ontology is formal, shareable and machine-checkable. Noy and McGuinness give seven steps for building one: determine the domain and scope, consider reusing existing ontologies, enumerate the important terms, define the classes and the class hierarchy, define the properties (slots), define the facets of the slots, and create instances.

NTA trap: open versus closed world. Wrong: “the ontology does not say Ravi is a doctor, so Ravi is not a doctor.” Fix: OWL and the semantic web make the open-world assumption, where a missing fact is simply unknown. Databases and Prolog make the closed-world assumption, where what cannot be proved is false.

9. Expert systems in depth

An expert system is a program that solves problems in a narrow domain at the level of a human expert, by applying a large body of domain knowledge (facts and heuristics) through an inference mechanism. Feigenbaum’s slogan “knowledge is power” sums up the idea: the strength comes from the knowledge, not from a clever general algorithm. The architecture has six parts:

ComponentRole
Knowledge baseLong-term domain knowledge: facts and IF–THEN rules (or frames, or cases)
Working memoryThe facts of the current case, and the intermediate conclusions
Inference engineChooses and fires rules (forward or backward chaining, conflict resolution)
Explanation facilityAnswers “why?” (why a question is asked) and “how?” (how a conclusion was reached)
Knowledge acquisition facilityHelps the knowledge engineer or expert add, test and refine rules
User interfaceDialogue with the end user

The people involved are the domain expert, the knowledge engineer (who elicits the expertise and encodes it) and the end user. The key design principle is the separation of knowledge from control: the knowledge base is kept apart from the inference engine. Remove the knowledge base and what remains is an expert system shell, ready to be filled for a new domain. EMYCIN (“Essential MYCIN”) was MYCIN with its medical rules removed. CLIPS (NASA, written in C), Jess (Java), OPS5 and EXSYS are other shells.

Buchanan and colleagues describe five stages of development: identification (the problem, participants and resources), conceptualisation (the key concepts and relations), formalisation (choosing the representation and the inference method), implementation (writing the rules in the chosen tool) and testing (evaluating the prototype against expert judgement). The process loops back when testing exposes gaps.

Knowledge acquisition is the slowest and hardest step, the knowledge acquisition bottleneck. Experts often cannot state their heuristics, because the knowledge has become compiled and intuitive. Techniques include structured interviews, protocol analysis (the expert thinks aloud while solving cases), repertory grids, observation, and machine learning (rule induction from examples). Compared with a conventional program, an expert system is heuristic rather than algorithmic, keeps knowledge separate from control, can explain itself, tolerates uncertain or incomplete data (as with MYCIN’s certainty factors), and is changed by editing rules rather than rewriting code. Its weaknesses are brittleness (performance collapses just outside its narrow domain), a lack of common sense, and the cost of maintaining a large rule base. Hayes-Roth’s task categories are interpretation, prediction, diagnosis, design, planning, monitoring, debugging, repair, instruction and control.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFact
Resolution(α ∨ β), (¬β ∨ γ) ⊢ (α ∨ γ); refutation-complete; □ means the premises are contradictory
DecidabilityPropositional logic: decidable (Horn: linear time). FOL: semi-decidable.
Skolemisation∃ inside ∀x₁…∀xₙ becomes F(x₁,…,xₙ); an outermost ∃ becomes a constant

NTA traps

  • “P(x, x) and P(f(y), y) unify with x = f(y).” Then f(y) must equal y, which the occurs check forbids. There is no unifier.
  • Stopping the MGU too early. In P(x, f(y), z) against P(a, f(g(z)), b), the answer is y/g(b), not y/g(z). Always apply the final substitution to every binding.
  • Skolemising with a constant when the ∃ is inside a ∀. ∀x ∃y Loves(x, y) needs Loves(x, F(x)). Writing Loves(x, C) would claim that everyone loves the same C.
  • “Forward chaining is goal-driven.” Reversed. Forward chaining is data-driven; backward chaining is goal-driven. MYCIN is backward; XCON is forward.
  • Confusing P(E | H) with P(H | E). A test that is 90% sensitive gives only a 2/13 posterior when the prevalence is 1%.
  • Explaining away. Two causes of a common effect are independent until the effect is observed. Observing the effect makes them dependent.
  • Using the both-positive CF formula for mixed signs. For 0.7 and −0.4, the answer is (0.7 − 0.4)/(1 − 0.4) = 0.5, not 0.7 + (−0.4)(1 − 0.7) = 0.58.
  • “Bel(A) + Bel(¬A) = 1.” In Dempster–Shafer, Bel(A) + Bel(¬A) ≤ 1. The gap is the ignorance, Pl(A) − Bel(A).
  • ATRANS and PTRANS. “John gave Mary a book” is ATRANS (possession changes). “John went to Delhi” is PTRANS (physical location changes). “John told Mary” is MTRANS.

How NTA asks this

  • MGU questions: four candidate substitutions. Apply each one to both literals and check that they become identical. Then choose the most general one. Eliminate any option that binds a variable to a term containing itself.
  • Match the following: CD primitives to verbs, representation schemes to their parts, or expert systems to their domains. Mini-example: MYCIN–medical diagnosis, DENDRAL–chemical structure, XCON–computer configuration, PROSPECTOR–mineral exploration. Fix the pair you are surest of (MYCIN) and eliminate.
  • Assertion–Reason: for example, A: “Resolution refutation can establish KB ⊨ α for every FOL sentence α that KB entails.” R: “Resolution is refutation-complete.” Both are true, and R explains A. (Resolution is not complete for deriving α directly; it proves α by refuting KB ∧ ¬α.)
  • Numerical: a Bayes posterior, a joint entry from CPTs, the parameter count of a network, a combined CF, or a Dempster–Shafer mass. Work in fractions to avoid rounding errors between options.
  • Statement pairs on decidability, on Horn clauses and on non-monotonic reasoning. Watch for the words “always” and “every”.

terms.definition: The least committed substitution that makes two expressions identical; every other unifier is an instance of it.
The unification test that refuses to bind a variable to a term containing that variable, such as x to f(x).
Removing ∃ by replacing its variable with a new function of the enclosing ∀ variables (or a new constant if there are none).
Proving KB ⊨ α by adding ¬α to the clauses of KB and deriving the empty clause.
A clause with at most one positive literal; entailment for Horn clauses takes linear time with forward or backward chaining.
A slot-and-filler structure for a stereotyped object, with default values, facets and procedural attachments (if-needed, if-added).
A frame for a stereotyped event sequence, with entry conditions, props, roles, track, scenes and results (Schank and Abelson).
A DAG whose nodes carry P(X | parents); the joint probability is the product of these local tables.
MYCIN’s measure CF = MB − MD in [−1, 1], combined by fixed formulas for AND, OR and multiple rules.
Dempster–Shafer lower and upper bounds on the probability of a set: Bel(A) ≤ P(A) ≤ Pl(A) = 1 − Bel(¬A).

lessons.examTip: For an MGU question, apply each candidate substitution to both expressions and check that they become identical, then prefer the least specific one. Reject any option that binds a variable to a term containing it (occurs check).

steps: Download practice-set.md. Attempt problems 1, 2, 3, 9, 10, 13 and 14 in 11 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Do problems 4, 5 and 6 (resolution and chaining) in 7 minutes. Number every clause and write the substitution beside each resolution step.
Do problems 7, 8, 11, 12 and 15 (the numericals) in 12 minutes. Keep every probability as a fraction until the last line.
Check every answer against solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for, for example Skolemising a variable that was really universal.
For problem 8, rebuild the full joint table of 16 rows once, and confirm that it sums to 1 and gives the same P(L).
Redo the problems you got wrong after 24 hours, without looking at the solutions.
check: At least 12 of 15 correct on the first attempt.
All four MGUs in problem 1 correct, including the occurs-check failure.
Problems 7, 8, 11 and 12 answered as exact fractions or decimals that match the solutions.
You can state from memory which of the chain, fork and collider patterns is opened by observing the middle node.

quiz.question: Here x, y and z are variables, and a and b are constants. What is the most general unifier of P(x, f(y), z) and P(a, f(g(z)), b)?
quiz.explanation: Unify pairwise from left to right: x/a; then f(y) with f(g(z)) gives y/g(z); then z/b. Apply the final substitution to every binding: y becomes g(b). So the MGU is {x/a, y/g(b), z/b}. {x/a, y/g(z), z/b} is not fully applied: after applying it, the second arguments are f(g(z)) and f(g(b)), which are not identical.

quiz.question: In MYCIN, the current certainty factor of hypothesis H is 0.7. A new rule concludes H with CF = −0.4. What is the combined certainty factor?
quiz.explanation: The signs differ, so CF = (CF₁ + CF₂)/(1 − min(|CF₁|, |CF₂|)) = (0.7 − 0.4)/(1 − 0.4) = 0.3/0.6 = 0.5. 0.3 is the plain sum. 0.58 wrongly applies the both-positive formula: 0.7 + (−0.4)(1 − 0.7).

quiz.question: The frame is Θ = {Flu, Cold, Allergy}. Evidence 1 gives m₁({Flu}) = 0.6 and m₁(Θ) = 0.4. Evidence 2 gives m₂({Cold}) = 0.5 and m₂(Θ) = 0.5. After Dempster’s rule of combination, what are Bel({Flu}) and Pl({Flu})?
quiz.explanation: The conflict is K = 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.3 ({Flu} ∩ {Cold} = ∅). The unnormalised masses are {Flu} 0.3, {Cold} 0.2 and Θ 0.2. Divide by 1 − K = 0.7 to get 3/7, 2/7 and 2/7. Bel(Flu) = m({Flu}) = 3/7. Pl(Flu) = m({Flu}) + m(Θ) = 5/7. The option 0.3 and 0.5 forgets to normalise.

lessons.title: Planning, natural language processing and multi-agent systems
lessons.summaryHtml: Planning finds a sequence or partial order of actions that turns the initial state into a goal state. STRIPS describes each action by a precondition, an add list and a delete list, so the new state is (s − DEL) ∪ ADD. Planners search forwards (progression), backwards through relevant actions (regression), in plan space with causal links and threats (partial-order planning), in a planning graph (GraphPlan) or by refining high-level tasks (HTN). NLP works through levels from phonology and morphology to syntax, semantics, discourse and pragmatics, and it must resolve ambiguity at each level; parsing uses grammars and chart algorithms such as CYK, and information retrieval ranks documents with TF-IDF and cosine similarity. Multi-agent systems use BDI, reactive and hybrid architectures, communicate with speech-act languages (KQML, FIPA-ACL), cooperate through protocols such as the contract net, and negotiate using auctions, voting and game theory.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

This lesson covers three things an intelligent agent does beyond basic search and inference. Planning means working out a sequence (or a partial order) of actions that turns the current situation into a goal situation. The actions are described in a structured language such as STRIPS, so the planner can reason about what each action needs and changes. Natural language processing (NLP) means understanding and generating human language. It works through levels, from words to sentence structure, meaning, context and intention, and it must resolve ambiguity at every level. Information retrieval, finding relevant documents for a query, is its most widely used application. Multi-agent systems (MAS) study many autonomous agents that must communicate, cooperate, compete and negotiate with each other.

Why it matters for NET

These three topics complete the core AI part of Unit 10. The questions are mostly conceptual, with a few crisp numericals. From planning, NTA asks about STRIPS action schemas (precondition, add and delete lists), the result of applying actions, the Sussman anomaly, progression against regression, partial-order planning (causal links, threats, promotion and demotion), GraphPlan mutexes and HTN planning. From NLP, it asks you to order the levels of analysis, identify the type of ambiguity, compare grammars (ATN, case grammar, transformational grammar), count parses with CYK, and compute an n-gram probability, a TF-IDF weight or precision and recall. From MAS, it asks about BDI and subsumption architectures, KQML and FIPA-ACL performatives, speech acts, the contract net protocol, auctions, voting and game-theoretic negotiation (Nash equilibrium, Pareto optimality).

Concepts in depth

1. Classical planning and STRIPS

Classical planning assumes a world that is fully observable, deterministic, static and discrete. STRIPS (Fikes and Nilsson, 1971) describes a state as a set of ground atoms. Under the closed-world assumption, anything not listed is false. An action schema has three parts:

  • the precondition: atoms that must hold before the action;
  • the add list: atoms the action makes true;
  • the delete list: atoms the action makes false.

The result of an action is (state − delete list) ∪ add list. Every atom not mentioned stays as it was. This STRIPS assumption is how STRIPS avoids the frame problem, the difficulty of stating everything an action does not change. ADL and PDDL extend STRIPS with negative preconditions, disjunctive goals, conditional effects, typed variables and equality.

Unstack(x, y)  PRE: On(x,y), Clear(x), HandEmpty
               ADD: Holding(x), Clear(y)
               DEL: On(x,y), Clear(x), HandEmpty
Stack(x, y)    PRE: Holding(x), Clear(y)
               ADD: On(x,y), Clear(x), HandEmpty
               DEL: Holding(x), Clear(y)
Pickup(x)      PRE: Clear(x), OnTable(x), HandEmpty
               ADD: Holding(x)
               DEL: Clear(x), OnTable(x), HandEmpty
Putdown(x)     PRE: Holding(x)
               ADD: Clear(x), OnTable(x), HandEmpty
               DEL: Holding(x)

With n blocks there are n Pickup, n Putdown, n(n − 1) Stack and n(n − 1) Unstack ground actions, which is 2n² in all. For 3 blocks that is 18.

2. State-space planning: progression and regression

  • Progression (forward) planning searches from the initial state, applying every action whose precondition holds. It is simple, but it considers many irrelevant actions.
  • Regression (backward) planning starts from the goal and chooses only relevant actions: those that add some goal atom and delete none. Regressing a goal g through an action a gives (g − ADD(a)) ∪ PRE(a). The branching factor is smaller, but regression works on sets of states.

Good domain-independent heuristics come from relaxed problems. Ignore preconditions gives roughly the number of unsatisfied goals. Ignore delete lists gives the heuristic behind the FF planner. Goal-stack planning (STRIPS itself, and Rich and Knight’s presentation) solves one goal at a time using a stack. The Sussman anomaly shows the weakness of this. The start is C on A, with A and B on the table, and the goal is On(A, B) ∧ On(B, C). Achieving either goal first and then the other forces you to undo the first. The shortest plan interleaves the goals: Unstack(C, A), Putdown(C), Pickup(B), Stack(B, C), Pickup(A), Stack(A, B), which is 6 actions. A planner that insists on finishing one subgoal before starting the next is called non-interleaved (or linear), and it cannot find this plan without undoing work.

3. Plan-space (partial-order) planning

A partial-order planner (POP) searches the space of plans, not states. A plan has four parts:

  • a set of actions, including the dummy actions Start (whose effects are the initial state) and Finish (whose preconditions are the goal);
  • ordering constraints A ≺ B;
  • causal links A →p B, meaning that A achieves the precondition p of B;
  • a set of open preconditions.

The planner repeatedly chooses an open precondition and supports it with a new or an existing action. When an action C could delete p between A and B, C is a threat to the link A →p B. A threat is resolved by demotion (C ≺ A) or promotion (B ≺ C). The plan is complete when no preconditions are open and there are no threats. It follows the least-commitment principle: it orders steps only when it must. Any linearisation (topological order) of the final plan is a valid total-order plan. For example, two independent chains of two actions each have C(4, 2) = 6 linearisations.

4. GraphPlan and hierarchical planning

GraphPlan builds a planning graph of alternating literal levels and action levels, with persistence (no-op) actions carrying literals forward. It records mutex (mutually exclusive) pairs. Two actions are mutex in three cases:

  • inconsistent effects: one deletes an effect of the other;
  • interference: one deletes a precondition of the other;
  • competing needs: their preconditions are mutex at the previous level.

Two literals are mutex if one is the negation of the other, or if they have inconsistent support: every pair of actions that could achieve them is mutex. The graph grows in polynomial time. The level at which all the goals first appear with no mutex between them is an admissible estimate of plan length, and GraphPlan extracts a plan by backward search from that level. Hierarchical task network (HTN) planning starts from high-level tasks, such as “build house”, and refines them step by step into primitive actions, using a library of methods. ABSTRIPS was an early hierarchical planner that ignored low-criticality preconditions at the higher levels. Real planners also use conditional (contingency) planning for nondeterministic worlds, and execution monitoring and replanning when things go wrong.
