lessons.title: Artificial neural networks and machine learning basics
lessons.summaryHtml: An artificial neuron computes net = Σwᵢxᵢ + b and outputs f(net) through an activation function (step, sigmoid, tanh, ReLU). The perceptron learns with w ← w + η(t − y)x and converges when the data are linearly separable; it cannot learn XOR, which needs a hidden layer. Multilayer networks are trained by backpropagation: a forward pass, deltas δ = (t − o)o(1 − o) at the output, deltas passed back to the hidden units, then gradient-descent updates. Other models: Hebbian learning (Δw = ηxy), Hopfield associative memory (symmetric weights, energy minimisation) and Kohonen SOM (competitive, unsupervised). Machine learning is supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement learning.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

An artificial neural network (ANN) is a large set of very simple units, called neurons, joined by weighted links. Each neuron adds up its weighted inputs, applies an activation function and passes the result on. The network is not programmed with rules. It learns by adjusting its weights from examples until its outputs are good. This is the core idea of machine learning: improve at a task through experience instead of explicit instructions.

The field grew in steps. McCulloch and Pitts proposed a threshold neuron in 1943, Hebb gave a learning principle in 1949, and Rosenblatt built the perceptron in 1958. Minsky and Papert then showed its limits in 1969. Hopfield and Kohonen revived interest in 1982, and backpropagation, popularised by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams in 1986, made multilayer networks practical. Modern deep learning is built on the same pieces.

Why it matters for NET

Neural networks and learning basics usually give one to three questions in Unit 10. The usual numericals are a perceptron weight update, the output of a neuron with a sigmoid or step activation, the weights from Hebbian learning, and sometimes one backpropagation delta. The theory questions ask why a single perceptron cannot learn XOR, the formulas of the learning rules, the features of Hopfield networks and Kohonen maps, the ranges and derivatives of activation functions, and the difference between supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. Match-the-following on "rule ↔ formula" and "network ↔ inventor" appears often.

Concepts in depth

Biological and artificial neurons

Biological neuronArtificial neuron
Dendrites receive signalsInputs x1, …, xn
Synapse strengthWeights w1, …, wn
Soma (cell body) sums the signalsNet input net = Σ wixi + b
Firing thresholdBias b (or threshold θ = −b) and activation f
Axon carries the outputOutput y = f(net)

The brain has around 1011 neurons working slowly but massively in parallel. An ANN copies only the broad structure: many simple units, adaptive connection strengths and distributed storage of knowledge.

The McCulloch–Pitts neuron

The McCulloch–Pitts (M-P) neuron has binary inputs and a binary output. It fires (y = 1) when the weighted sum reaches a threshold θ. Excitatory weights are positive, and an active inhibitory input can block firing. Weights and thresholds are fixed by hand; the model does not learn. With weights 1 and 1, θ = 2 gives AND and θ = 1 gives OR. NOT uses one inhibitory input. For n inputs with weight 1, θ = k fires when at least k inputs are on, so θ = 2 with three inputs is the majority function. Any Boolean function can be built from networks of M-P neurons, but no single one computes XOR.

Activation functions

FunctionFormulaRangeDerivative
Binary step1 if net ≥ θ, else 0{0, 1}0 (undefined at θ)
Bipolar step (sign)+1 if net ≥ θ, else −1{−1, +1}0 (undefined at θ)
Linear (identity)net(−∞, ∞)1
Sigmoid (logistic)σ(z) = 1/(1 + e−z)(0, 1)σ(1 − σ), maximum 0.25 at z = 0
tanh (bipolar sigmoid)(ez − e−z)/(ez + e−z)(−1, 1)1 − tanh², maximum 1 at z = 0
ReLUmax(0, z)[0, ∞)0 for z < 0, 1 for z > 0
Softmax (output layer)ezᵢ/Σ ezⱼ(0, 1), outputs add to 1used with cross-entropy

Backpropagation needs a differentiable activation, so it uses sigmoid, tanh or ReLU, not the step. The sigmoid derivative is at most 0.25. Multiplying many such factors through deep layers makes gradients tiny: the vanishing gradient problem that ReLU reduces. A network with only linear activations, however deep, collapses to one linear map, so hidden layers need non-linear activations.

The perceptron and linear separability

Rosenblatt’s perceptron is a single layer of threshold units with adjustable weights. For input x with target t and output y = step(w·x + b), the perceptron learning rule is:

w ← w + η(t − y)x, b ← b + η(t − y)

η is the learning rate. When the output is correct, t − y = 0 and nothing changes. When a positive example is missed, the weights move towards x; when a negative example fires wrongly, they move away from x. The perceptron convergence theorem says that if the training data are linearly separable, the rule finds a separating set of weights in a finite number of updates. If they are not separable, the weights never settle.

A single perceptron draws a decision boundary w1x1 + w2x2 + b = 0, which is a straight line in 2-D and a hyperplane in general. XOR needs (0,1) and (1,0) on one side and (0,0) and (1,1) on the other, and no single line does that. Minsky and Papert’s 1969 book Perceptrons made this limit famous. Of the 16 Boolean functions of two inputs, 14 are linearly separable; only XOR and XNOR are not. For three inputs, 104 of the 256 functions are separable. The fix is a hidden layer: for example h1 = OR(x1, x2), h2 = AND(x1, x2) and y = h1 AND NOT h2 computes XOR.

ADALINE and the delta rule

Widrow and Hoff’s ADALINE (1960) uses the same neuron, but it learns from the linear output net, before thresholding. Its delta (LMS, Widrow–Hoff) rule is Δw = η(t − net)x. This is gradient descent on the squared error E = ½(t − net)², so it keeps adjusting even when the thresholded output is already right. It converges to the least-squares solution when the data are not separable. MADALINE combines several ADALINEs. The generalised delta rule for non-linear units is backpropagation.

Hebbian learning

Hebb’s principle, from 1949, is "cells that fire together wire together". The weight between two units grows when both are active together: Δwi = η·xi·y. In the supervised form, y is the target t. There is no error term, so Hebbian learning is correlation-based, and it can be supervised or unsupervised. With binary 0/1 data it fails: when x = 0 or y = 0 nothing is learnt. That is why it is usually shown with bipolar (±1) data. Plain Hebbian weights can grow without limit; Oja’s rule adds normalisation.

Multilayer networks and backpropagation

A multilayer perceptron (MLP) has an input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer, with full connections between adjacent layers in a feedforward network. A layer of n inputs feeding m units has n·m weights plus m biases, (n + 1)·m parameters in all. By the universal approximation theorem, one hidden layer with enough non-linear units can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region to any accuracy.

Backpropagation trains an MLP by gradient descent on E = ½ Σ (tk − ok)². For sigmoid units, one training step is:

  1. Forward pass: compute every hidden output hj and every output ok.
  2. Output deltas: δk = (tk − ok)·ok(1 − ok).
  3. Hidden deltas (back-propagate): δj = hj(1 − hj)·Σk wjkδk, using the old output weights.
  4. Weight updates: Δwjk = η·δk·hj and Δwij = η·δj·xi, with biases updated as weights on a constant input 1.

One pass over the whole training set is an epoch. Updating after every example is stochastic (online) learning; after a group of examples it is mini-batch learning; after the whole set it is batch learning. Practical issues are local minima and plateaus, the choice of η (too large oscillates, too small is slow), momentum (Δw(t) = −η∂E/∂w + αΔw(t − 1)) to smooth and speed up descent, vanishing gradients, and overfitting. Overfitting is controlled by early stopping on a validation set, weight decay (regularisation), dropout or more data.

Hopfield networks

A Hopfield network (1982) is a single layer of bipolar units, each connected to every other unit. It is a recurrent network with symmetric weights (wij = wji) and no self-connections (wii = 0). It works as an associative (content-addressable) memory. To store bipolar patterns x(1), …, x(p) it uses the Hebbian outer-product rule W = Σ x xT − pI. To recall, start from a noisy probe and update units one at a time (asynchronously): si ← sign(Σj wijsj). The energy E = −½ ΣiΣj wijsisj never increases under asynchronous updates, so the network settles in a minimum, ideally a stored pattern. The capacity is about 0.138N random patterns for N units. Beyond that, recall fails and spurious states (such as mixtures of stored patterns) appear. Hopfield networks are also used for optimisation problems such as TSP. The Boltzmann machine is a stochastic relative.

Kohonen self-organising maps

A self-organising map (SOM), by Kohonen (1982), learns without targets. Output units sit on a 1-D or 2-D grid, and each has a weight vector the same size as the input. For each input x:

  1. Find the winner (best matching unit): the unit whose weight vector is closest to x, usually by Euclidean distance.
  2. Update the winner and its grid neighbours: w ← w + η(x − w).
  3. Shrink the learning rate and the neighbourhood radius over time.

This is competitive (winner-take-all) learning. The map preserves topology: inputs that are similar end up on nearby units. SOMs are used for clustering, visualising high-dimensional data and vector quantisation. Related models include LVQ (a supervised variant), ART (Grossberg and Carpenter, which tackles the stability–plasticity dilemma) and RBF networks.

Machine learning basics

  • Supervised learning: learn from labelled pairs (x, t). Classification predicts a category (spam or not); regression predicts a number (house price). Examples: perceptron, MLP with backprop, decision trees, k-NN, SVM, naive Bayes.
  • Unsupervised learning: find structure in unlabelled data, as in clustering (k-means, SOM), dimensionality reduction (PCA) and association rules.
  • Reinforcement learning: an agent acts in an environment, receives rewards, and learns a policy that maximises the long-term return. Q-learning updates Q(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α[r + γ maxa′ Q(s′, a′) − Q(s, a)], with learning rate α and discount factor γ. It must balance exploration and exploitation (for example ε-greedy).
  • Semi-supervised learning uses a few labelled and many unlabelled examples.

Data are split into training, validation and test sets; k-fold cross-validation rotates the held-out part. Underfitting (high bias) gives poor results even on training data. Overfitting (high variance) gives low training error but high test error. For classifiers, the confusion matrix gives accuracy = (TP + TN)/total, precision = TP/(TP + FP), recall = TP/(TP + FN) and F1 = 2PR/(P + R). k-means repeats two steps: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its points, until nothing changes.

Worked examples

Example 1: Perceptron learning of AND

Binary inputs, targets AND = 0, 0, 0, 1. Start with w1 = w2 = b = 0 and η = 1. The output is y = 1 if net > 0, else 0. The inputs are shown in the order (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1).

EpochInputtnetyw1, w2, b after
1(0,0)0000, 0, 0
1(0,1)0000, 0, 0
1(1,0)0000, 0, 0
1(1,1)1001, 1, 1
2(0,0)0111, 1, 0
2(0,1)0111, 0, −1
2(1,0)0001, 0, −1
2(1,1)1002, 1, 0

Continuing in the same way, the weights at the end of epochs 3, 4 and 5 are (2, 1, −1), (2, 2, −1) and (2, 1, −2). Epoch 6 makes no error, so training stops with w1 = 2, w2 = 1, b = −2. Check: net = 2x1 + x2 − 2 is > 0 only for (1, 1). The boundary 2x1 + x2 = 2 cuts the x1 axis at 1 and the x2 axis at 2.

A single update with real numbers: w = (0.2, −0.5), b = 0.1, η = 0.5, x = (1, 1), t = 1, y = 1 if net ≥ 0. net = 0.2 − 0.5 + 0.1 = −0.2, so y = 0 and t − y = 1. New w = (0.2 + 0.5, −0.5 + 0.5) = (0.7, 0) and b = 0.6.

Example 2: One backpropagation step (2-2-1 network, sigmoid)

Input x = (1, 0), target t = 1, η = 0.5. Hidden unit h1 has weights (0.3, −0.2) and bias 0.1; h2 has (0.4, 0.1) and bias −0.1. The output unit has weights (0.5, −0.4) from h1 and h2, and bias 0.2.

  1. Forward: neth1 = 0.3 + 0.1 = 0.4, so h1 = σ(0.4) = 0.5987. neth2 = 0.4 − 0.1 = 0.3, so h2 = σ(0.3) = 0.5744. neto = 0.5 × 0.5987 − 0.4 × 0.5744 + 0.2 = 0.2696, so o = 0.5670. E = ½(1 − 0.5670)² = 0.0938.
  2. Output delta: δo = (1 − 0.5670) × 0.5670 × 0.4330 = 0.1063.
  3. Hidden deltas (old weights): δh1 = 0.5987 × 0.4013 × 0.5 × 0.1063 = 0.01277; δh2 = 0.5744 × 0.4256 × (−0.4) × 0.1063 = −0.01040.
  4. Updates: wh1→o = 0.5 + 0.5 × 0.1063 × 0.5987 = 0.5318; wh2→o = −0.4 + 0.5 × 0.1063 × 0.5744 = −0.3695; bo = 0.2 + 0.5 × 0.1063 = 0.2532. wx1→h1 = 0.3 + 0.5 × 0.01277 × 1 = 0.3064; wx1→h2 = 0.4 − 0.0052 = 0.3948. The weights from x2 do not change, because x2 = 0.

Example 3: Hebbian learning of AND (bipolar)

Inputs (1,1), (1,−1), (−1,1), (−1,−1) with targets 1, −1, −1, −1 and a bias input of 1. With η = 1, each weight is the sum of xi·t over the four examples:

  • w1 = 1 − 1 + 1 + 1 = 2; w2 = 1 + 1 − 1 + 1 = 2; b = 1 − 1 − 1 − 1 = −2.

Check: net = 2x1 + 2x2 − 2 is 2 for (1,1) and −2 or −6 for the others, so sign(net) reproduces AND. With binary 0/1 data the same rule fails, because every example with t = 0 contributes nothing.

Example 4: Hopfield storage and recall

Store p = (1, −1, 1, −1) in a 4-unit network. W = p pT − I:

W = |  0  -1   1  -1 |
    | -1   0  -1   1 |
    |  1  -1   0  -1 |
    | -1   1  -1   0 |

Probe s = (1, 1, 1, −1), with unit 2 corrupted. Update unit 2: net = −1(1) + 0 − 1(1) + 1(−1) = −3, so s2 = −1 and the stored pattern comes back. Energies: E(s) = −½ sTWs = 0 for the probe and −6 for the stored pattern. Recall slides downhill in energy.

Example 5: Kohonen winner and update

Three units have weights w1 = (0.2, 0.6), w2 = (0.5, 0.3), w3 = (0.9, 0.8). Input x = (0.3, 0.5), η = 0.5, and only the winner is updated.

  • Squared distances: 0.01 + 0.01 = 0.02; 0.04 + 0.04 = 0.08; 0.36 + 0.09 = 0.45. The winner is unit 1.
  • w1 ← (0.2, 0.6) + 0.5 × ((0.3, 0.5) − (0.2, 0.6)) = (0.25, 0.55). It moves halfway towards x.

Example 6: Classifier metrics and a Q-learning update

A classifier gives TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 30. Accuracy = 70/100 = 0.7. Precision = 40/50 = 0.8. Recall = 40/60 = 0.6667. F1 = 2 × 0.8 × 0.6667/(0.8 + 0.6667) = 0.7273.

Q-learning with Q(s, a) = 2, α = 0.5, reward r = 1, γ = 0.9 and maxa′ Q(s′, a′) = 4: Q ← 2 + 0.5 × (1 + 0.9 × 4 − 2) = 2 + 0.5 × 2.6 = 3.3.

Reinforcement learning in depth

In reinforcement learning (RL), an agent learns by trial and error. At each step it observes a state st, takes an action at, and receives a scalar reward rt+1 and a new state st+1. Nobody tells it the correct action; the feedback is only evaluative (how good), never instructive (what was right). This is what separates RL from supervised learning. Rewards may also be delayed, so the agent must work out which earlier actions deserve the credit (the credit assignment problem).

The problem is modelled as a Markov decision process (MDP) ⟨S, A, P, R, γ⟩. S is the set of states and A the set of actions. P(s′ | s, a) gives the transition probabilities and R the rewards. γ ∈ [0, 1] is the discount factor. The Markov property says that the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on the history. The main quantities are these:

  • Policy π(a | s): the agent’s behaviour, a mapping from states to actions.
  • Return Gt = rt+1 + γrt+2 + γ²rt+3 + … = Σ γkrt+k+1. With γ < 1 an endless stream of reward r has the finite value r/(1 − γ). γ near 0 makes the agent short-sighted, and γ near 1 makes it far-sighted.
  • Value functions: Vπ(s) is the expected return starting from s and following π. Qπ(s, a) is the expected return after taking a in s and following π afterwards.
  • Bellman equations: Vπ(s) = Σa π(a | s) Σs′ P(s′ | s, a)[R + γVπ(s′)]. The optimality form is V*(s) = maxa Σs′ P(s′ | s, a)[R + γV*(s′)]. Acting greedily with respect to Q* is optimal.
  • Model: the agent’s own prediction of P and R, if it has one.

The solution methods fall into two groups:

MethodNeeds a model?Update
Dynamic programming (value iteration, policy iteration)Yes (P and R known)Sweeps of the Bellman equation over all states
Monte CarloNoWaits until the episode ends, then uses the actual return G
TD(0)NoV(s) ← V(s) + α[r + γV(s′) − V(s)]; it bootstraps from the estimate V(s′)
SARSA (on-policy)NoQ(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α[r + γQ(s′, a′) − Q(s, a)], where a′ is the action actually taken next
Q-learning (off-policy)NoQ(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α[r + γ maxa′ Q(s′, a′) − Q(s, a)]

SARSA is on-policy: it evaluates the policy it is actually following, exploration included. Q-learning is off-policy: it learns the greedy (optimal) policy while behaving exploratorily. The term in square brackets is the TD error. The agent must balance exploration (trying actions to learn about them) against exploitation (using the best known action). With ε-greedy selection, it picks a random action with probability ε and the greedy action otherwise. With k actions, the greedy action is therefore chosen with probability 1 − ε + ε/k, and each other action with probability ε/k. Softmax (Boltzmann) selection is the smooth alternative. Well-known successes are TD-Gammon (backgammon), and AlphaGo, which combines RL with deep networks. Policy-gradient and actor–critic methods learn the policy directly.

Example 7: return, TD(0), SARSA versus Q-learning, and ε-greedy

  • Return. The rewards 2, 0 and 4 end an episode, and γ = 0.5. G = 2 + 0.5 × 0 + 0.25 × 4 = 3. A constant reward of 1 forever with γ = 0.9 is worth 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10.
  • TD(0). V(s) = 5, r = 2, V(s′) = 4, α = 0.1, γ = 0.9. The TD error is 2 + 3.6 − 5 = 0.6, so V(s) becomes 5 + 0.06 = 5.06.
  • SARSA versus Q-learning. Q(s, a) = 1, r = 0, α = 0.5, γ = 0.9. In s′, Q(s′, up) = 2 and Q(s′, down) = 6, and the ε-greedy policy happens to choose up.
    • SARSA: 1 + 0.5 × (0 + 0.9 × 2 − 1) = 1.4.
    • Q-learning uses the max: 1 + 0.5 × (0 + 0.9 × 6 − 1) = 3.2.
  • ε-greedy. With ε = 0.2 and 4 actions, the greedy action is chosen with probability 0.8 + 0.05 = 0.85, and each other action with probability 0.05.

NTA traps

  • Perceptron vs delta rule. Wrong: using net in the perceptron rule, or y in the delta rule. Fix: perceptron uses the thresholded y; ADALINE uses the linear net.
  • Threshold convention. Wrong: assuming y = 1 at net = 0 when the stem says net > 0. Fix: read whether the step uses ≥ or >; the answer often depends on it.
  • Forgetting the bias. Wrong: updating w but not b. Fix: b is a weight on a constant input 1, so Δb = η(t − y).
  • XOR claims. Wrong: "a perceptron learns XOR with enough epochs or a smaller η". Fix: no single-layer perceptron can, ever; it needs a hidden layer.
  • Sigmoid derivative. Wrong: writing σ′ = σ(1 + σ) or using net in place of σ. Fix: σ′ = o(1 − o) with the output o; its maximum is 0.25.
  • Hidden deltas with new weights. Wrong: back-propagating through weights you have just updated. Fix: compute every delta first with the old weights, then update.
  • Hopfield facts. Wrong: "trained by backprop", "self-connections equal 1", "unlimited capacity". Fix: Hebbian outer product, zero diagonal, symmetric weights, about 0.138N patterns.
  • SOM is unsupervised. Wrong: listing SOM or k-means as supervised. Fix: both learn without labels; LVQ is the supervised cousin.
  • Precision vs recall. Wrong: dividing TP by (TP + FN) for precision. Fix: precision looks at predicted positives (TP + FP); recall at actual positives (TP + FN).

How NTA asks this

Numericals: "find the new weights after one perceptron step", "output of a neuron with sigmoid activation", "weights after Hebbian training of AND", "δ of the output unit". Write net first, then the activation, then the rule. Watch for bipolar or binary data and for the threshold convention.

Match the following: rules to formulas (Hebb ηxy, perceptron η(t − y)x, delta η(t − net)x, Kohonen η(x − w)), or networks to people (McCulloch–Pitts: threshold neuron; Rosenblatt: perceptron; Hopfield: associative memory; Kohonen: SOM). Mini-example: A. Sigmoid, B. tanh, C. ReLU, D. Step with I. (−1, 1), II. {0, 1}, III. (0, 1), IV. [0, ∞). Answer: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

Assertion–Reason mini-example. A: A single-layer perceptron cannot implement XOR. R: The XOR classes cannot be separated by one straight line. Both are true and R explains A. A variant pairs a true A with a true R that does not explain it, for example R: "the perceptron uses a step activation".

Order questions list the backprop steps (forward pass, output error, output deltas, hidden deltas, weight update) or the history in time order. Multi-statement questions mix facts such as "Hopfield weights are symmetric" (true), "k-means needs labels" (false) and "sigmoid is differentiable everywhere" (true). Strike out any option that gives a perceptron XOR, or gives Hopfield or SOM a teacher signal.

quiz.question: A perceptron has weights w = (0.4, −0.3), bias b = −0.2 and learning rate η = 0.2. Its output is y = 1 if net ≥ 0, else 0. For the input x = (1, 1) with target t = 1, what are the weights and bias after one application of the perceptron learning rule?
quiz.explanation: net = 0.4 − 0.3 − 0.2 = −0.1 < 0, so y = 0 and t − y = 1. w ← w + 0.2 × 1 × (1, 1) = (0.6, −0.1); b ← −0.2 + 0.2 = 0.0. The third option forgets the bias. The last subtracts, which would be right only for t = 0, y = 1.

quiz.question: A neuron with the logistic sigmoid activation has inputs x = (1, 0.5), weights w = (0.4, −0.6) and bias 0.3. What is its output (to 4 decimal places)?

With b = 0, net = x1 + x2 > 0 exactly for OR. 1 1 0 3 forgets that the epoch counter is incremented for the error-free epoch too.

quiz.question: In a network trained with backpropagation, an output unit uses the sigmoid activation. For one training example its output is o = 0.6 and its target is t = 1. What is its delta δ = (t − o)·o·(1 − o)?
quiz.explanation: δ = (1 − 0.6) × 0.6 × (1 − 0.6) = 0.4 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.096. 0.4 is only the error t − o. 0.24 is only the derivative o(1 − o). 0.144 = 0.4 × 0.6² wrongly uses o² in place of the sigmoid derivative o(1 − o).

quiz.question: A fully connected feedforward network has 4 inputs, one hidden layer of 5 units and 3 output units. Every hidden and output unit has a bias. How many trainable parameters (weights plus biases) does it have?
quiz.explanation: Input → hidden: (4 + 1) × 5 = 25. Hidden → output: (5 + 1) × 3 = 18. Total = 43. 35 = 4 × 5 + 5 × 3 counts the weights but not the 8 biases. 60 = 4 × 5 × 3 multiplies the layer sizes.

questionBank.question: Which of the following formulas is a contradiction?
questionBank.explanation: (p ∧ ¬q) ∧ (p → q): p = T and q = F make p → q false, so the conjunction is false in every row. (p → q) ∧ (q → p) is p ↔ q, a contingency; (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬p is true at p = F, q = T; and p ↔ ¬¬p is a tautology.

questionBank.question: How many of the 16 binary connectives (truth functions f(p, q) of two variables) are commutative, that is, satisfy f(p, q) = f(q, p) for all values?
questionBank.explanation: Commutativity only forces f(T, F) = f(F, T). So the function is fixed by three free values: f(T, T), f(F, F) and the common value of the mixed rows. 2³ = 8 connectives are commutative (for example ∧, ∨, ⊕, ↔, NAND, NOR and the two constants); → is not.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: At p = F, q = F, r = F: (p → q) → r = T → F = F, but p → (q → r) = T. So → is not associative and Statement I is false. Statement II is the exportation law: both sides equal ¬p ∨ ¬q ∨ r, so it is true.

stmts: Statement I: (p → q) → r is logically equivalent to p → (q → r).
Statement II: (p ∧ q) → r is logically equivalent to p → (q → r).
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: The argument has the form p → q, q ⊢ p, the fallacy of affirming the consequent. R gives the counterexample row that proves it invalid, so R explains A.

stmts: Assertion (A): The argument “If it rains, the ground is wet. The ground is wet. Therefore, it rained.” is invalid.
Reason (R): From p → q and q one cannot validly conclude p, because p = F, q = T makes both premises true and the conclusion false.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Which of the following sets of connectives are functionally complete? (F denotes the constant false.)
options: A, B, C and D only
A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: NAND alone is complete (¬p = p ↑ p, p ∧ q = ¬(p ↑ q)). {¬, →} is complete since p ∨ q ≡ ¬p → q. {→, F} gives ¬p ≡ p → F and then everything. {∧, ∨} only builds monotone functions and cannot make ¬. {↔, ¬} only builds linear (XOR-type) functions and cannot make ∧.

stmts: A. {NAND}
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q (II). p ↔ q is true when both agree (III). p ⊕ q is true when they differ (IV). NOR, “neither”, is ¬p ∧ ¬q (I). The first distractor swaps ↔ and ⊕, the classic confusion.

b: I. ¬p ∧ ¬q
II. ¬p ∨ q
III. (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q)

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Taking the variable order p, q, r (p most significant), which is the sum-of-minterms (PDNF) form of (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ r)?
questionBank.explanation: p ∧ q is true in rows 110 (6) and 111 (7). ¬p ∧ r is true in rows 001 (1) and 011 (3). So the formula is Σm(1, 3, 6, 7). Σm(0, 2, 4, 5) is the complement (the PCNF indices).

questionBank.question: How many maxterms appear in the principal conjunctive normal form (PCNF) of p → (q ∨ r)?
questionBank.explanation: The PCNF has one maxterm per false row. p → (q ∨ r) is false only when p = T and q ∨ r = F, that is at p = T, q = F, r = F. So the PCNF is the single maxterm (¬p ∨ q ∨ r). Its PDNF has the other 7 rows.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: The PDNF and PCNF built from the truth table always exist, so Statement I is true. A CNF is true in every row only if every clause is; a clause (an OR of literals) is always true exactly when it contains some x and ¬x, so Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: Every propositional formula is logically equivalent to some formula in CNF and to some formula in DNF.
Statement II: A formula in CNF is a tautology if and only if every one of its clauses contains a complementary pair of literals.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: If one x works for every y, then for each y that same x is a witness, so A is valid. R is false: over the integers ∀y∃x (x + y = 0) is true while ∃x∀y (x + y = 0) is false.

stmts: Assertion (A): ∃x∀y P(x, y) → ∀y∃x P(x, y) is valid for every predicate P.
Reason (R): Changing the order of an existential and a universal quantifier never changes the meaning of a formula.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Which of the following is NOT valid for all predicates P and Q over every non-empty domain?
questionBank.explanation: Counterexample for option 4: domain {1, 2}, P true only at 1 and Q true only at 2. Then P ∨ Q holds everywhere, but neither ∀x P(x) nor ∀x Q(x) holds. Options 1 and 2 are the two genuine distribution laws, and option 3 is the valid one-way implication.

questionBank.question: Which of the following are equivalent to “p only if q”?
options: A, C, D and E only
A, B, C and D only
questionBank.explanation: “p only if q” means p cannot hold without q: p → q (A). Its contrapositive (C) and the disjunction form ¬p ∨ q (D) are equivalent, and “q is necessary for p” is another reading of p → q (E). q → p (B) is the converse, which reads “p if q”.

stmts: A. p → q
B. q → p
C. ¬q → ¬p
D. ¬p ∨ q
E. q is necessary for p
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: An argument has premises p → q, q → r and ¬r. In how many of the 8 truth assignments to p, q, r are all three premises true?
questionBank.explanation: ¬r forces r = F. Then q → r forces q = F, and p → q forces p = F. Only p = q = r = F satisfies all premises, so ¬p (and ¬q) follows validly: this is modus tollens applied twice.

questionBank.question: From the premises p ∨ q and ¬p ∨ r, the conclusion q ∨ r follows by which rule of inference?
questionBank.explanation: Resolution cancels the complementary pair p and ¬p and joins what is left: q ∨ r. Disjunctive syllogism needs a lone ¬p; constructive dilemma needs two conditionals; hypothetical syllogism chains conditionals.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: Universal statements pair ∀ with →: “All” is IV and “No” is II. Existential statements pair ∃ with ∧: “Some” is III and “Not every” (some S is not P) is I. The first distractor swaps “No” with “Not every”, the most common confusion.

a: D. Not every S is P
b: II. ∀x (S(x) → ¬P(x))
III. ∃x (S(x) ∧ P(x))
IV. ∀x (S(x) → P(x))

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: (p ∧ q) → p is simplification: to falsify it we would need p ∧ q true and p false, which is impossible, so A is true. R (the law of excluded middle) is also true, but A does not follow from it; A holds because a conjunction implies each conjunct.

stmts: Assertion (A): (p ∧ q) → p is a tautology.
Reason (R): p ∨ ¬p is a tautology.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: The converse q → p differs from p → q at p = F, q = T, so A is false. The contrapositive ¬q → ¬p ≡ q ∨ ¬p ≡ p → q, so R is true.

stmts: Assertion (A): The converse of a conditional statement is logically equivalent to the conditional.
Reason (R): The contrapositive of a conditional statement is logically equivalent to the conditional.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: The correct laws swap the connectives: (p ∨ q) → r ≡ (p → r) ∧ (q → r) and (p ∧ q) → r ≡ (p → r) ∨ (q → r). Counterexamples: at p = T, q = F, r = F, Statement I’s left side is F but its right side is T; at the same row Statement II’s left side is T but its right side is F. Both are false.

stmts: Statement I: (p ∨ q) → r is logically equivalent to (p → r) ∨ (q → r).
Statement II: (p ∧ q) → r is logically equivalent to (p → r) ∧ (q → r).
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question:
Let the domain be {1, 2, 3} and L(x, y) mean x < y. How many of the following statements are true?
(i) ∀x∃y L(x, y)
(ii) ∃x∀y (x ≠ y → L(x, y))
(iii) ∀y∃x (L(x, y) ∨ x = y)
(iv) ∃y∀x ¬L(y, x)
questionBank.explanation: (i) is false: for x = 3 no y in the domain is larger. (ii) is true with x = 1, which is below every other element. (iii) is true: take x = y. (iv) is true with y = 3, which is below nothing. So 3 statements are true.

questionBank.question: Which formula is equivalent to ¬∃x∀y P(x, y)?
questionBank.explanation: Move ¬ right, flipping each quantifier: ¬∃x∀y P = ∀x ¬∀y P = ∀x∃y ¬P(x, y). The other options either do not flip both quantifiers or change their order.

questionBank.question: Which of the following formulas are tautologies?
options: A, B, D and E only
A, B, C and D only
A, B, C, D and E
questionBank.explanation: A is addition. B: when p and q are both true they are equal, so the implication never fails. D is disjunctive syllogism. E: if q is true, p → q is true; if q is false, q → p is true. C is denying the antecedent: p = F, q = T makes the left side true and ¬q false.

stmts: A. p → (p ∨ q)
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: What is the output of this C program?
questionBank.explanation: The loop visits all 8 rows. f = (p → q) ∧ (q → r) is true at pqr = 000, 001, 011 and 111, so sat = 4. taut checks whether f → (p → r) holds in every row; it does (hypothetical syllogism), so taut stays 1. Output: 4 1 (verified with gcc).

questionBank.question: What is the dual of (p ∧ T) ∨ (q ∧ ¬r)?
questionBank.explanation: The dual swaps ∧ with ∨ and T with F, but leaves the literals (including ¬r) unchanged: (p ∨ F) ∧ (q ∨ ¬r). Option 2 also negates the variables, which gives the negation of the formula, not its dual.

questionBank.question: Let G: “I go out” and R: “it rains”. Which formula expresses “I go out unless it rains”?
questionBank.explanation: “G unless R” means “if not R, then G”: ¬R → G ≡ R ∨ G. It makes no promise about what happens when it does rain, so R → ¬G adds a claim that is not in the sentence.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements (x does not occur free in Q):
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Rewrite P(x) → Q as ¬P(x) ∨ Q. Then ∃x (¬P(x) ∨ Q) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) ∨ Q ≡ ¬∀x P(x) ∨ Q ≡ ∀x P(x) → Q, and ∀x (¬P(x) ∨ Q) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x) ∨ Q ≡ ¬∃x P(x) ∨ Q ≡ ∃x P(x) → Q. A quantifier moved out of an antecedent flips, so both statements are true.

stmts: Statement I: ∃x (P(x) → Q) is logically equivalent to ∀x P(x) → Q.
Statement II: ∀x (P(x) → Q) is logically equivalent to ∃x P(x) → Q.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Arrange the following steps of a proof by resolution (refutation) in the correct order.
questionBank.explanation: Refutation starts by assuming the conclusion is false (B). Everything is then put in clause form (C), clauses are resolved (A), and reaching the empty clause (D) shows that the premises plus ¬conclusion are unsatisfiable, so the conclusion follows.

stmts: A. Repeatedly resolve pairs of clauses that contain complementary literals
B. Negate the conclusion and add it to the premises
C. Convert every premise and the negated conclusion to clause form (CNF)
D. Stop when the empty clause is derived: the conclusion follows
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: How many of the 16 truth assignments to p, q, r, s satisfy (p ↔ q) ∧ (r ⊕ s)?
questionBank.explanation: The two conjuncts use disjoint variables. p ↔ q holds in 2 of the 4 (p, q) rows (both T or both F), and r ⊕ s holds in 2 of the 4 (r, s) rows. 2 × 2 = 4 assignments.

questionBank.question: From “∀x (Human(x) → Mortal(x))” and “Human(Socrates)”, the conclusion “Mortal(Socrates)” is obtained by:
options: Universal instantiation followed by modus ponens
Existential generalisation followed by modus tollens
Universal generalisation followed by modus ponens
Existential instantiation followed by hypothetical syllogism
questionBank.explanation: Universal instantiation gives Human(Socrates) → Mortal(Socrates); modus ponens with Human(Socrates) gives the conclusion. Together they are often called universal modus ponens. Generalisation rules go the other way (from instances to quantified statements).

questionBank.question: A formula A is satisfiable but not a tautology. Which of the following must be true of ¬A?
options: ¬A is satisfiable and not a tautology
questionBank.explanation: A is a contingency: it is true in some rows and false in others. ¬A flips every row, so it is also true in some rows and false in others, a contingency. ¬A would be a contradiction only if A were a tautology.

questionBank.question: An argument has the premises p → q, ¬q and p. Which of the following is correct?
options: The argument is invalid for every conclusion
The argument is valid only if the conclusion is p ∧ ¬q
The argument is valid whatever the conclusion is
The argument is valid only if the conclusion is a tautology
questionBank.explanation: p and p → q give q, which contradicts ¬q, so no row makes all premises true. A valid argument only requires that the conclusion is true in every row where all premises are true; with no such rows, every conclusion follows (vacuously). This is why inconsistent premises are useless in practice.

questionBank.question: How many one-to-one (injective) functions are there from a 3-element set to a 5-element set?
questionBank.explanation: The first element has 5 possible images, the second 4, the third 3: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 = 5!/2!. 125 = 5³ counts all functions and 10 = C(5, 3) counts image sets, not functions.

questionBank.question: How many functions are there from a set A with 4 elements to a set B with 3 elements?
questionBank.explanation: Each of the 4 elements of A independently picks one of 3 images: 3⁴ = 81. 4³ = 64 counts functions from B to A.

questionBank.question: If |A| = m and |B| = n, how many relations are there from A to B?
questionBank.explanation: A relation from A to B is any subset of A × B, which has mn elements, so there are 2^(mn) relations. n^m counts functions from A to B.

questionBank.question: How many relations on a 4-element set are both reflexive and antisymmetric?
questionBank.explanation: Reflexive fixes all 4 diagonal cells. There are C(4, 2) = 6 off-diagonal pairs, and antisymmetry allows 3 states for each (neither, one direction, the other): 3⁶ = 729.

questionBank.question: How many equivalence relations on a 5-element set have exactly two equivalence classes?
questionBank.explanation: This is S(5, 2) = 2⁴ − 1 = 15. Choose which elements go with element 1: any subset of the other 4, except all of them (then there would be one class), giving 2⁴ − 1 = 15. 31 = 2⁵ − 1 forgets that the two classes are unordered.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: An asymmetric relation has an all-zero diagonal and at most one direction in each off-diagonal pair, so there are 3^(n(n−1)/2): Statement I is true. Statement II is false: the identity relation {(a, a)} is antisymmetric, but it is not asymmetric because it contains loops. (Every asymmetric relation is antisymmetric, not the other way round.)

stmts: Statement I: The number of asymmetric relations on an n-element set is 3^(n(n−1)/2).
Statement II: Every antisymmetric relation is asymmetric.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: A is true: reflexivity demands (a, a) for every a, and the empty relation has none. R is also true (vacuous truth). But R talks about symmetry and transitivity; it does not explain why reflexivity fails.

stmts: Assertion (A): The empty relation on a non-empty set is not reflexive.
Reason (R): The empty relation is symmetric and transitive, because it contains no pairs that could violate these properties.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Define R on ℤ by a R b if and only if a − b is divisible by 5. Which of the following statements are correct?
options: A, B, C and D only
A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: Congruence modulo 5 is reflexive (a − a = 0), symmetric and transitive (sum of multiples of 5), so it is an equivalence relation with classes [0], [1], [2], [3], [4] (C), and 7 − 2 = 5 puts 2 and 7 in the same class (E). It is not antisymmetric: 2 R 7 and 7 R 2 but 2 ≠ 7.

stmts: A. R is reflexive.
B. R is antisymmetric.
C. R has exactly 5 equivalence classes.
D. R is transitive.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Which of the following posets is a lattice?
questionBank.explanation: {1, 2, 3, 6} is D6: every pair has lcm and gcd inside the set. In {1, 2, 3}, 2 and 3 have no upper bound. In {2, 3, 4, 6}, 2 and 3 have no lower bound (1 is missing) and 4 and 6 have no upper bound. In {1, 2, 3, 6, 9}, 6 and 9 have no upper bound (18 is missing).

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II (all functions are from ℤ to ℤ)
questionBank.explanation: 2x is one-to-one but misses every odd number (III). ⌊x/2⌋ hits every integer k (from 2k) but sends 2k and 2k + 1 to the same value (IV). x + 3 has inverse x − 3 (I). x² sends 1 and −1 to 1 and never gives a negative number (II).

b: I. Bijective
II. Neither injective nor surjective
III. Injective but not surjective
IV. Surjective but not injective

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: How many functions from {1, 2, 3, 4} to {a, b, c} are NOT onto?
questionBank.explanation: All functions: 3⁴ = 81. Onto functions: 81 − 3·2⁴ + 3·1⁴ = 81 − 48 + 3 = 36. Not onto: 81 − 36 = 45. Choosing 36 answers the opposite question.

questionBank.question: Let R = {(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)} on {1, 2, 3, 4}. How many ordered pairs does the transitive closure of R contain?
questionBank.explanation: Add every pair joined by a path: (1, 3), (2, 4) and (1, 4). R⁺ = {(1,2), (2,3), (3,4), (1,3), (2,4), (1,4)}: 6 pairs. 10 would be the reflexive-transitive closure, which also adds the four loops.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: The symmetric difference is the elements in exactly one set, which is the union minus the intersection: Statement I is true. The three pieces “only A”, “only B” and “both” partition A ∪ B: Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: A ⊕ B = (A ∪ B) − (A ∩ B).
Statement II: (A − B) ∪ (B − A) ∪ (A ∩ B) = A ∪ B.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: If |A| = 10, |B| = 15 and |A ∩ B| = 4, what is |A ⊕ B| (symmetric difference)?
questionBank.explanation: |A ⊕ B| = |A| + |B| − 2|A ∩ B| = 10 + 15 − 8 = 17. The common intersection is removed from both sets. 21 is |A ∪ B|, which keeps the intersection once.

questionBank.question: Which of the following set identities hold for all sets A, B and C?
options: A, B, C and E only
A, B, C, D and E
questionBank.explanation: A is absorption. B is De Morgan for differences. C: Cartesian product distributes over union. E: a set is inside A ∩ B exactly when it is inside both. D is wrong: A − (B ∩ C) = (A − B) ∪ (A − C); with A = {1}, B = {1}, C = ∅ the left side is {1} and the right side is ∅.

stmts: A. A ∪ (A ∩ B) = A
E. P(A ∩ B) = P(A) ∩ P(B)
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: 30 = 2·3·5. Each divisor a has the complement 30/a (gcd 1, lcm 30), and D30 ≅ P({2, 3, 5}). Being distributive, it cannot have two complements for one element. R gives both existence and uniqueness, so it explains A.

stmts: Assertion (A): In the lattice (D30, |), every element has a unique complement.
Reason (R): D30 is a Boolean algebra, because 30 is square-free, and in a distributive lattice complements are unique when they exist.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Which of the following posets is a totally ordered set (chain)?
questionBank.explanation: Any two integers are comparable under ≤. In P({1, 2}), {1} and {2} are incomparable; under divisibility 2 and 3 are incomparable (in ℤ⁺ and in {1, 2, 3, 6}).

questionBank.question: How many relations on a 4-element set are both reflexive and symmetric?
questionBank.explanation: The diagonal is fixed (reflexive). Each of the C(4, 2) = 6 off-diagonal pairs is either both in or both out (symmetric): 2⁶ = 64. 1024 = 2^10 counts symmetric relations without the reflexive condition.

questionBank.question: How many partial order relations are there on a set with 3 elements?
questionBank.explanation: Count by the shape of the Hasse diagram on labelled elements: antichain 1; one edge plus an isolated point 6; a chain of 3, 6; a “V” (one element below two) 3; a “Λ” (two below one) 3. Total 1 + 6 + 6 + 3 + 3 = 19. 6 counts only the total orders.

questionBank.question: What is the inverse of f : ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = 3x + 2?
questionBank.explanation: Solve y = 3x + 2 for x: x = (y − 2)/3, so f⁻¹(x) = (x − 2)/3. Check: f((x − 2)/3) = x − 2 + 2 = x. x/3 − 2 undoes the steps in the wrong order.

questionBank.question: Let f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x on ℝ. What are (f ∘ g)(3) and (g ∘ f)(3)?
questionBank.explanation: (f ∘ g)(3) = f(g(3)) = f(6) = 7. (g ∘ f)(3) = g(f(3)) = g(4) = 8. Composition is not commutative; f ∘ g applies g first.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following numbers in increasing order.
questionBank.explanation: C: 2⁴ − 2 = 14. A: B₄ = 15. B: 19. E: 4! = 24. D: 2⁶ = 64. Increasing: C, A, B, E, D.

stmts: A. Equivalence relations on a 4-element set
B. Partial orders on a 3-element set
C. Onto functions from a 4-element set to a 2-element set

questionBank.question: In the poset ({2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12}, |), which are the minimal and the maximal elements?
questionBank.explanation: Minimal: no other element divides it; 2 and 3 qualify (4, 6, 8, 9, 12 all have a divisor in the set). Maximal: it divides no other element; 8, 9 and 12 qualify. With three maximal elements there is no greatest element, and with two minimal ones there is no least element.

questionBank.question: How many equivalence relations on {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} put 1 and 2 in the same class?
questionBank.explanation: Glue 1 and 2 into one item; the partitions of {12, 3, 4, 5} correspond one-to-one to the required partitions, so the count is B₄ = 15. 52 = B₅ counts all equivalence relations on 5 elements.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: If f and g are onto, every c equals g(b) for some b, and b = f(a) for some a, so g ∘ f is onto: Statement I is false. For |A| = |B| = n finite, n distinct images fill B, and covering B with n inputs forces distinct images: Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: The composition of two surjective functions need not be surjective.
Statement II: A function between two finite sets of the same size is injective if and only if it is surjective.

questionBank.question: In the lattice (D60, |), what are the least upper bound and the greatest lower bound of 12 and 15?
questionBank.explanation: In Dn the join is the lcm and the meet is the gcd. lcm(12, 15) = 60 and gcd(12, 15) = 3. 180 is 12 × 15, which is not even in D60.

questionBank.question: What is the output of this C program?
questionBank.explanation: The program treats each of the 2⁹ = 512 bit masks as a relation matrix on a 3-element set. Reflexive: 2^(9−3) = 64. Symmetric: 2^(3·4/2) = 64. Both: the diagonal is fixed and each of the 3 off-diagonal pairs is in or out, 2³ = 8. Output: 64 64 8 (verified with gcc).

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: 1 ≤ 2 but not 2 ≤ 1, so ≤ is not symmetric (it is antisymmetric): Statement I is false. Divisibility is a partial order in which 2 and 3 are incomparable, so it is not total: Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: The relation ≤ on ℤ is symmetric.
Statement II: Every partial order is a total order.

questionBank.question: Which of the following sets is uncountable?
options: The set of all finite binary strings
questionBank.explanation: By Cantor’s theorem there is no surjection from ℕ onto P(ℕ), so P(ℕ) is uncountable (it has the size of ℝ). ℤ × ℤ and ℚ can be listed by a diagonal walk, and finite strings can be listed by length, so they are countable.

questionBank.question: Consider the poset (P({a, b, c}), ⊆). Which of the following statements are correct?
options: A, B, C and E only
A, B, C, D and E
questionBank.explanation: There are 2³ = 8 subsets, and the Hasse diagram is a cube: each subset of size k has 3 − k covers above it, giving 3 + 6 + 3 = 12 edges. Join is ∪ and meet is ∩, so it is a lattice, and the complement of X is {a, b, c} − X. D is false: {a, b, c} is the only maximal element (it is the greatest element).

stmts: A. Its Hasse diagram has 8 vertices.
B. Its Hasse diagram has 12 edges.
C. It is a lattice.
D. It has 3 maximal elements.
E. It is a complemented lattice.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: If |A| = n, an injection gives n distinct images inside a set of size n, so every element is hit: A is true. R is false: f(n) = n + 1 on ℕ is injective but never takes the value 0. Finite and infinite sets behave differently here.

stmts: Assertion (A): Every injective function from a finite set A to itself is also surjective.
Reason (R): Every injective function from ℕ to ℕ is surjective.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: ≤ on ℤ is a total order (IV). Congruence mod 3 is an equivalence (II). Proper subset is never reflexive and is transitive (III). |a − b| ≤ 1 is reflexive and symmetric, but 1 R 2 and 2 R 3 while 1 and 3 differ by 2, so it is not transitive (I).

questionBank.question: In how many ways can 7 people be seated around a round table, if seatings that differ only by a rotation are the same?
questionBank.explanation: Fix one person’s seat to remove rotations; the other 6 can be arranged in 6! = 720 ways. 5040 = 7! counts rotations as different; 360 would also identify mirror images, which is only right for necklaces.

questionBank.question: How many 5-card hands from a standard 52-card deck contain exactly 2 aces?
questionBank.explanation: Choose 2 of the 4 aces, C(4, 2) = 6, and 3 of the 48 non-aces, C(48, 3) = 17296. Product rule: 6 × 17296 = 103776. 2598960 is the number of all 5-card hands.

questionBank.question: A class is graded A, B, C or D. What is the minimum number of students needed to guarantee that at least 5 of them get the same grade?
questionBank.explanation: With 4 grades (boxes) and 4 students per grade, 16 students can avoid 5 of a kind. One more forces a fifth: 4(5 − 1) + 1 = 17. 20 = 4 × 5 is the most common off-by-one error.

questionBank.question: The number of moves for the Tower of Hanoi satisfies aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ + 1 with a₁ = 1. What is a₁₀?
questionBank.explanation: The closed form is aₙ = 2ⁿ − 1 (check: a₁ = 1, a₂ = 3, a₃ = 7). So a₁₀ = 1024 − 1 = 1023.

questionBank.question: The solution of aₙ = 4aₙ₋₁ − 4aₙ₋₂ with a₀ = 1 and a₁ = 4 is:
questionBank.explanation: r² − 4r + 4 = (r − 2)² has the double root 2, so aₙ = (α + βn)2ⁿ. a₀ = α = 1; a₁ = 2(1 + β) = 4 gives β = 1. So aₙ = (1 + n)2ⁿ. n·2ⁿ fails a₀ = 1, 2ⁿ⁺¹ − 1 fails a₁ = 4, and (1 + 2n)2ⁿ gives a₁ = 6.

questionBank.question: How many binary strings of length 8 contain no two consecutive 0s?
questionBank.explanation: Let bₙ count such strings. A valid string ends in 1 (after any valid string of length n − 1) or in 10 (after any valid string of length n − 2): bₙ = bₙ₋₁ + bₙ₋₂ with b₁ = 2, b₂ = 3. Then 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55: b₈ = 55.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is the standard closed form. For Statement II, a binary tree with n nodes is a root with a left subtree of i nodes and a right subtree of n − 1 − i nodes, giving the Catalan recurrence with C₀ = 1. Both are true: for example, 3 nodes give C₃ = 5 trees.

stmts: Statement I: The n-th Catalan number is Cₙ = C(2n, n)/(n + 1).
Statement II: Cₙ counts the structurally different binary trees with n nodes.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: A is true: element 1 goes to some position k (n − 1 choices); either k goes to 1 (derange the remaining n − 2: Dₙ₋₂) or it does not (an effective derangement of n − 1 items: Dₙ₋₁). Check D₅ = 4(9 + 2) = 44. R is true because Dₙ/n! = Σ(−1)^k/k!, a partial sum of the series for e⁻¹. But the limit does not explain the exact recurrence.

stmts: Assertion (A): Dₙ = (n − 1)[Dₙ₋₁ + Dₙ₋₂] for n ≥ 3, where Dₙ is the number of derangements of n objects.
Reason (R): Dₙ/n! approaches 1/e as n grows.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: 1/(1 − x) = 1 + x + x² + … (IV). Squaring it gives coefficients n + 1 (III). 1/(1 − 2x) = Σ(2x)ⁿ (II). If F(x) = Σ Fₙxⁿ, then F(x)(1 − x − x²) = x from the Fibonacci recurrence (I).

b: I. Fibonacci number Fₙ (F₀ = 0, F₁ = 1)
II. 2ⁿ
III. n + 1
IV. 1 for every n

questionBank.question: How many permutations of {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} have exactly 2 fixed points?
questionBank.explanation: Choose the 2 fixed points, C(6, 2) = 15, and derange the remaining 4, D₄ = 9: 15 × 9 = 135. 265 = D₆ counts permutations with no fixed point.

questionBank.question: For the recurrence aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ + 2ⁿ, which is a particular solution?
questionBank.explanation: 2 is not a root of r − 3 = 0, so try C·2ⁿ: C·2ⁿ = 3C·2ⁿ⁻¹ + 2ⁿ. Dividing by 2ⁿ⁻¹ gives 2C = 3C + 2, so C = −2 and the particular solution is −2·2ⁿ = −2ⁿ⁺¹. Check: 3(−2ⁿ) + 2ⁿ = −2ⁿ⁺¹. The n·2ⁿ form is only needed when 2 is a characteristic root.

questionBank.question: In how many ways can a convex octagon be divided into triangles by non-crossing diagonals?
questionBank.explanation: A convex (n + 2)-gon has Cₙ triangulations. An octagon has 8 = 6 + 2 sides, so the answer is C₆ = C(12, 6)/7 = 924/7 = 132. 429 = C₇ and 42 = C₅ are off-by-one indices.

questionBank.question: How many lattice paths from (0, 0) to (5, 5), using unit steps right (R) and up (U), never go above the line y = x?
questionBank.explanation: All paths: C(10, 5) = 252. By the reflection principle, the paths that cross the diagonal correspond to paths to (4, 6), C(10, 6) = 210. Good paths: 252 − 210 = 42 = C₅.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Each round-table seating appears n times among the n! linear orders (once per rotation), so the count is (n − 1)!: Statement I is false. A necklace can also be flipped, which pairs up arrangements when n ≥ 3: (n − 1)!/2. Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: The number of ways to arrange n distinct people around a round table is n!.
Statement II: The number of ways to make a necklace from n distinct beads (n ≥ 3), where rotations and reflections count as the same, is (n − 1)!/2.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Which of the following are equal to 2ⁿ for every n ≥ 1?
options: A, B, C and D only
A, B, C, D and E
questionBank.explanation: A is (1 + 1)ⁿ by the binomial theorem. B, C and D are the same count in three forms: a subset is its characteristic function, which is a binary string. E is the central binomial coefficient: C(2, 1) = 2 but C(4, 2) = 6 ≠ 4.

stmts: B. The number of subsets of an n-element set
C. The number of binary strings of length n
D. The number of functions from an n-element set to {0, 1}
E. C(2n, n)
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: What is the coefficient of x³y⁴ in the expansion of (2x − y)⁷?
questionBank.explanation: The term is C(7, 3)(2x)³(−y)⁴ = 35 × 8 × 1 × x³y⁴ = 280x³y⁴. The sign is positive because (−y) is raised to an even power; 35 forgets the factor 2³.

questionBank.question: Which is the solution of T(n) = T(n − 1) + n with T(0) = 0?
questionBank.explanation: Unrolling: T(n) = n + (n − 1) + … + 1 + T(0) = n(n + 1)/2. Check T(1) = 1 and T(2) = 3. n(n − 1)/2 gives T(1) = 0.

questionBank.question: What is the minimum number of integers that must be chosen from {1, 2, …, 20} to guarantee that two of them add up to 21?
questionBank.explanation: Form the 10 pairs {1, 20}, {2, 19}, …, {10, 11}; each sums to 21. Choosing one from each pair (10 numbers, such as 1 to 10) avoids a sum of 21. An 11th number must complete a pair, so 11 are needed.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: R is the negative binomial expansion; it counts the ways to write n as an ordered sum of k non-negative parts. With k = 3 it gives C(n + 2, 2), which is A. So R explains A.

stmts: Assertion (A): The generating function of the sequence aₙ = C(n + 2, 2) is 1/(1 − x)³.
Reason (R): For every k ≥ 1, 1/(1 − x)^k = Σₙ C(n + k − 1, k − 1)xⁿ.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: The order is the gap between aₙ and the earliest term it uses. aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ uses only aₙ₋₁, so it has order 1: A is false. The Fibonacci recurrence goes back two steps and has no constant term, so it is linear homogeneous of order 2: R is true.

stmts: Assertion (A): The recurrence aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ is a linear homogeneous recurrence of order 2.
Reason (R): The recurrence aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂ is a linear homogeneous recurrence of order 2.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: 24 × (1/2 − 1/6 + 1/24) = 12 − 4 + 1 = 9, so D₄ = 9 and A is true. R uses the right formula but states the wrong value (12 is only the first term), so R is false as written.

stmts: Assertion (A): The number of derangements of 4 objects is 9.

questionBank.question: In how many ways can 3 books be chosen from 10 books standing in a row on a shelf, so that no two chosen books are next to each other?
questionBank.explanation: Place the 7 unchosen books first; they create 8 gaps (including both ends). Choose 3 different gaps for the chosen books: C(8, 3) = 56. In general C(n − k + 1, k). 120 = C(10, 3) ignores the condition.

questionBank.question: How many 4-digit strings (digits 0–9, leading zeros allowed) contain at least one repeated digit?
questionBank.explanation: All strings: 10⁴ = 10000. Strings with all digits different: 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5040. At least one repeat: 10000 − 5040 = 4960. 5040 is the complement you subtract.

questionBank.question: How many integers from 1 to 500 are divisible by 3 or 7?
questionBank.explanation: ⌊500/3⌋ = 166, ⌊500/7⌋ = 71, ⌊500/21⌋ = 23. By inclusion–exclusion, 166 + 71 − 23 = 214. 237 forgets to subtract the multiples of 21.

questionBank.question: n straight lines are drawn in a plane so that no two are parallel and no three meet at a point. The number of regions satisfies Rₙ = Rₙ₋₁ + n with R₀ = 1. How many regions do 10 such lines make?
questionBank.explanation: The n-th line crosses the n − 1 earlier lines at n − 1 points, so it passes through n regions and splits each one. Unrolling, Rₙ = 1 + (1 + 2 + … + n) = 1 + n(n + 1)/2. R₁₀ = 1 + 55 = 56. 55 forgets the initial region.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II (selecting r objects from n distinct types or objects)
questionBank.explanation: Ordered without repetition is P(n, r) (III); ordered with repetition is n^r (I); unordered without repetition is C(n, r) (IV); unordered with repetition is stars and bars C(n + r − 1, r) (II).

questionBank.question: What is the output of this C program?
questionBank.explanation: The loop applies Dₙ = (n − 1)(Dₙ₋₁ + Dₙ₋₂): 2, 9, 44, 265, 1854, 14833, 133496, 1334961. So d[6] = 265 and d[10] = 1334961 (about 10!/e). The values fit easily in a long. Output: 265 1334961 (verified with gcc).

questionBank.question: What is the output of this C program?
questionBank.explanation: The inner loop is the Catalan recurrence Cₙ = Σ CᵢCₙ₋₁₋ᵢ with C₀ = 1: 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, 429, 1430, 4862. So c[5] = 42 and c[9] = 4862. Output: 42 4862 (verified with gcc).

questionBank.question: Which of the following are counted by the Catalan number Cₙ?

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:

questionBank.explanation: Positive solutions number C(10 − 1, 3 − 1) = C(9, 2) = 36; C(12, 2) = 66 counts non-negative solutions, so Statement I is false. The coefficient of x² is C(10, 2) = 45; 90 = 10 × 9 forgets to divide by 2!, so Statement II is false.

questionBank.question: How many distinct arrangements of the letters of MISSISSIPPI are there?
questionBank.explanation: 11 letters with M × 1, I × 4, S × 4, P × 2: 11!/(1!·4!·4!·2!) = 39916800/1152 = 34650. 39916800 = 11! ignores the repeats; 69300 forgets the 2! for the P’s.

questionBank.question: What is the coefficient of x⁶ in (1 + x + x²)⁴?
questionBank.explanation: We need the number of ways to pick an exponent 0, 1 or 2 from each of 4 factors with sum 6. By symmetry (the coefficients read 1, 4, 10, 16, 19, 16, 10, 4, 1), the x⁶ coefficient equals the x² coefficient. For x²: one factor gives 2 (4 ways) or two factors give 1 (C(4, 2) = 6 ways), total 10. 19 is the middle coefficient (x⁴).

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: Adding 3 each step gives an arithmetic sequence 3n + 2 (II). Multiplying by 3 gives 2·3ⁿ (III). Adding n gives the triangular numbers n(n + 1)/2 (IV). Hanoi gives 2ⁿ − 1 (I). Check each at n = 0 and n = 1.

III. 2·3ⁿ

questionBank.question: A family has two children. Given that at least one of them is a boy, what is the probability that both are boys? (Assume boy and girl are equally likely and independent.)
questionBank.explanation: Sample space {BB, BG, GB, GG}. “At least one boy” leaves {BB, BG, GB}, three equally likely outcomes, one of which is BB: 1/3. The tempting 1/2 answers a different question (“the older child is a boy”), which leaves {BB, BG}.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: The base case (one horse) is fine. The step removes a different horse to form two groups of k and uses a common horse to link their colours. For k + 1 = 2, the two groups of size 1 share no horse, so P(1) → P(2) fails and the whole chain collapses. R pinpoints why A is true.

stmts: Assertion (A): The inductive “proof” that all horses in any group have the same colour is invalid.
Reason (R): Its inductive step relies on two groups of k horses overlapping, which fails when going from k = 1 to k + 1 = 2.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Geometric: mean 1/p, variance (1 − p)/p². Variance < mean would need (1 − p)/p < 1, i.e. p > ½. With p = ¼ the mean is 4 and the variance is 12, so Statement I is false. Statement II is the defining property of the Poisson distribution (both equal λ).

stmts: Statement I: For a geometric random variable (number of trials up to the first success), the variance is always less than the mean.
Statement II: For a Poisson random variable, the mean equals the variance.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: The number of requests arriving at a server in one second follows a Poisson distribution with mean 2. What is the probability of at least 2 requests in a second? (e^−2 ≈ 0.1353)
A fair die is rolled repeatedly. What is the probability that the first six appears on the third roll?
questionBank.explanation: Geometric: two failures then a success, (5/6)² × (1/6) = 25/216 ≈ 0.116. 1/216 = (1/6)³ is three sixes in a row. 1/18 = 3 × 1/54 has no basis.

questionBank.question: A box holds 10 bulbs of which 4 are defective. Three bulbs are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that exactly one is defective?
questionBank.explanation: Hypergeometric: C(4,1)·C(6,2)/C(10,3) = 4 × 15/120 = 60/120 = 1/2. 54/125 = C(3,1)(0.4)(0.6)² is the binomial answer, valid only with replacement.

questionBank.question: The 10 letters of a mailing are put into their 10 addressed envelopes completely at random, one per envelope. What is the expected number of letters that land in their correct envelope?
questionBank.explanation: Let Iᵢ = 1 if letter i is in its own envelope; E[Iᵢ] = 1/10. By linearity (the Iᵢ are dependent, but linearity does not care), E[Σ Iᵢ] = 10 × 1/10 = 1. The answer is 1 for every n. 1/e is (approximately) the probability that no letter is correct, a derangement.

questionBank.question: A fair die is rolled until every face has appeared at least once. What is the expected number of rolls?
questionBank.explanation: When j faces are still missing, each roll finds a new face with probability j/6, so the wait is geometric with mean 6/j. Total = 6/6 + 6/5 + 6/4 + 6/3 + 6/2 + 6/1 = 6 × (1 + ½ + ⅓ + ¼ + ⅕ + ⅙) = 6 × 49/20 = 14.7. 6 would be the expectation to see one particular face.

questionBank.question: Which of the following are correct for random variables X and Y with finite means and variances, and constants a and b?
options: A, C, D and E only
A, B, C and D only
B, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A: linearity needs no independence. C: the product rule holds under independence. D: shifting does not change spread and scaling squares it. E: the computational formula. B needs independence (or zero covariance): with Y = X, Var(2X) = 4Var(X), not 2Var(X).

stmts: A. E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] for all X and Y
B. Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) for all X and Y
C. E[XY] = E[X]·E[Y] when X and Y are independent
D. Var(aX + b) = a²·Var(X)
E. Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])²

questionBank.question: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 1/2 and P(B) = 1/3. What is P(A ∪ B)?
questionBank.explanation: P(A ∩ B) = ½ × ⅓ = 1/6 by independence. P(A ∪ B) = ½ + ⅓ − 1/6 = 2/3. Check: 1 − P(Ā)P(B̄) = 1 − ½ × ⅔ = 2/3. 5/6 forgets to subtract the overlap (treats them as exclusive).

options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: R is a true counterexample: each event has probability ½, each pairwise intersection has probability ¼ = ½ × ½, but all three happen only on HH, with probability ¼ ≠ ⅛. That same example shows A is false.

stmts: Assertion (A): If each pair among three events A, B, C is independent, then A, B and C are mutually independent.

Reason (R): For two fair coin tosses, the events “first is heads”, “second is heads” and “both tosses show the same face” are pairwise independent, yet P(all three) ≠ the product of their probabilities.

questionBank.question: Three fair dice are rolled. What is the expected value of the sum of the numbers shown?
questionBank.explanation: Each die has mean 7/2, so by linearity the sum has mean 3 × 7/2 = 21/2 = 10.5. 21 is the sum of the faces of one die; 9 and 18 are not supported by any calculation.

questionBank.question: X follows a binomial distribution with n = 20 and p = 1/4. What are its mean and variance?
questionBank.explanation: Mean = np = 20 × ¼ = 5. Variance = np(1 − p) = 5 × ¾ = 15/4 = 3.75. The variance of a binomial with 0 < p < 1 is always below its mean; 5 and 5 would be a Poisson.

questionBank.question: What is the output of this C program?
questionBank.explanation: The 8 values of m are the 8 outcomes of three tosses (bit = 1 for heads). At least two heads: exactly two (3 outcomes: 011, 101, 110) plus three (111): 4 outcomes. The program prints 4/8 = 0.50 (verified with gcc). 3/8 counts only “exactly two”; 7/8 is “at least one”.

questionBank.question: Postage stamps of 4 units and 5 units are available in unlimited supply. What is the largest amount that cannot be paid exactly?
questionBank.explanation: Amounts 12, 13, 14 and 15 are payable (4+4+4, 4+4+5, 4+5+5, 5+5+5), and from there adding a 4 covers everything (strong induction with four base cases). 11 is not payable (11 − 4 = 7, 11 − 8 = 3, 11 − 5 = 6, 11 − 10 = 1 are all not multiples of the other stamp). For coprime a, b the largest unpayable amount is ab − a − b = 20 − 9 = 11.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is the well-ordering principle. Statement II fails: {1, ½, ⅓, …} (or the set of all positive rationals) has no least element, because below any element there is a smaller one. This is why induction works on ℕ but not on ℚ⁺.

stmts: Statement I: Every non-empty set of positive integers has a least element.
Statement II: Every non-empty set of positive rational numbers has a least element.

questionBank.question: A random permutation of 4 distinct numbers is generated, all 24 orders being equally likely. What is the expected number of inversions (pairs i < j with the larger number in position i)?
questionBank.explanation: Each of the C(4, 2) = 6 pairs is inverted with probability ½, so by linearity the expectation is 6 × ½ = 3 = n(n − 1)/4. 6 is the maximum number of inversions, not the mean. This is also the average number of swaps made by bubble sort or insertion sort on random input.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: Weak induction uses only the previous case (III); strong induction uses all earlier cases (IV); well-ordering is about least elements (I); structural induction works over recursively built objects such as trees and strings (II).

questionBank.question: In a group of 23 people (ignore leap years; all 365 birthdays equally likely), the probability that at least two share a birthday is closest to:
questionBank.explanation: P(all different) = (365 × 364 × … × 343)/365²³ ≈ 0.4927, so P(some shared birthday) ≈ 0.5073. 0.063 = 23/365 wrongly compares with one fixed birthday. The same idea gives the birthday bound for hash collisions: about √m keys for m slots.

questionBank.question: Which of the following define valid probability mass functions?
options: A, B, C and E only
questionBank.explanation: A: (1+2+3+4)/10 = 1, all non-negative. B: ½ + ¼ + … = 1. C: (1+2+3)/6 = 1. D: sums to (−1+0+1+2+3)/5 = 1, but p(1) = −1/5 < 0, so it is invalid. E: sums to 4/5 ≠ 1.

stmts: C. p(x) = x/6 for x = 1, 2, 3

questionBank.question: In a multiple-choice test with 4 options per question, a student knows the answer with probability 3/4 and otherwise guesses at random. Given that the student answered a question correctly, what is the probability that the student knew the answer?
questionBank.explanation: P(correct) = ¾ × 1 + ¼ × ¼ = 13/16. P(knew | correct) = (3/4)/(13/16) = 12/13 ≈ 0.923. 3/4 is the prior; 13/16 is P(correct); 1/13 is P(guessed | correct).

Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Both are standard results. Statement I is the law of rare events that justifies the Poisson approximation (for example, 100 bits with error rate 0.02 ≈ Poisson(2)). Statement II: independent Poisson counts over disjoint intervals merge into one Poisson count with the rates added.

stmts: Statement I: The Poisson distribution with parameter λ is the limit of Binomial(n, p) as n → ∞ with np = λ held fixed.
Statement II: The sum of two independent Poisson random variables with parameters λ₁ and λ₂ is Poisson with parameter λ₁ + λ₂.

questionBank.explanation: Statement I: independence gives P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) > 0, so they are definitely not exclusive. Statement II is the definition of independence, not a law for all events: for a die, A = even and B = {2}, P(A ∩ B) = 1/6 but P(A)P(B) = 1/12.

stmts: Statement I: If A and B are independent events with positive probabilities, then A and B are mutually exclusive.
Statement II: For any two events, P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B).

questionBank.explanation: A is the definition of conditional probability. R is false: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) and P(B | A) = P(A ∩ B)/P(A), which differ whenever P(A) ≠ P(B). In the medical-test example, P(+ | D) = 0.99 but P(D | +) = 1/6.

questionBank.question: What is the smallest integer n₀ such that 2ⁿ > n² holds for every n ≥ n₀?
questionBank.explanation: Check small n: n = 1: 2 > 1 (true); n = 2: 4 > 4 false; n = 3: 8 > 9 false; n = 4: 16 > 16 false; n = 5: 32 > 25 true. From 5 on it stays true: if 2ᵏ > k² then 2ᵏ⁺¹ > 2k² ≥ (k + 1)² for k ≥ 3 (since k² ≥ 2k + 1). So n₀ = 5. Option 1 (3) is wrong because 2³ = 8 < 9.

questionBank.explanation: A is false: n = 40 gives 1600 + 40 + 41 = 1681 = 41². R is a true statement of what an inductive proof requires, and it is exactly why A’s reasoning is invalid.

stmts: Assertion (A): Because n² + n + 41 is prime for n = 0, 1, 2, …, 39, it is prime for every non-negative integer n.
Reason (R): A proof by induction needs a base case and an inductive step valid for every k; checking finitely many cases is not a proof.

questionBank.question: If Var(X) = 4, what is Var(3X − 2)?
questionBank.explanation: Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X) = 9 × 4 = 36. The constant −2 shifts the distribution but does not change its spread. 12 multiplies by a instead of a²; 10 and 34 wrongly bring the constant in.

questionBank.question: X takes the values 0, 1 and 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3. What is the standard deviation of X?
questionBank.explanation: E[X] = 0.5 + 0.6 = 1.1; E[X²] = 0.5 + 1.2 = 1.7; Var = 1.7 − 1.21 = 0.49; standard deviation = √0.49 = 0.7. 0.49 is the variance; 1.1 is the mean; 1.7 is E[X²].

questionBank.question: H = {0, 4, 8} is a subgroup of (ℤ₁₂, +₁₂). How many distinct cosets of H are there in ℤ₁₂?
questionBank.explanation: Index = |G|/|H| = 12/3 = 4. The cosets are {0, 4, 8}, {1, 5, 9}, {2, 6, 10} and {3, 7, 11}: they partition ℤ₁₂ into equal blocks. 3 is |H|, not the number of cosets.

questionBank.question: How many elements of order 8 are there in the cyclic group (ℤ₂₄, +₂₄)?
questionBank.explanation: In a cyclic group of order n, for each divisor d of n there are φ(d) elements of order d. φ(8) = 4. In ℤ₂₄ they are 3, 9, 15 and 21 (each has 24 / gcd(24, k) = 8).

questionBank.question: On the set of positive rational numbers ℚ⁺, define a * b = ab/2. (ℚ⁺, *) is a group. What is the inverse of 8?
questionBank.explanation: Identity: ae/2 = a ⟹ e = 2. Inverse of a: ab/2 = 2 ⟹ b = 4/a. For a = 8, b = 4/8 = 1/2. Check: 8 * ½ = 4/2 = 2 = e. 1/8 is the ordinary reciprocal, which would give 8 * ⅛ = ½ ≠ 2.

questionBank.question: How many subgroups does the symmetric group S₃ have (including {e} and S₃)?
questionBank.explanation: {e}; three subgroups of order 2, one for each transposition; A₃ of order 3; and S₃. Total 6. S₃ is not cyclic, so the “one subgroup per divisor” rule does not apply: it has three subgroups of order 2. 3 is the number of normal subgroups.

questionBank.question: In the group U(10) = {1, 3, 7, 9} under multiplication modulo 10, what is the order of the element 3?
questionBank.explanation: 3¹ = 3, 3² = 9, 3³ = 27 ≡ 7, 3⁴ = 81 ≡ 1 (mod 10). So o(3) = 4 = |U(10)|, and 3 generates U(10), which is therefore cyclic. 9 has order 2.

questionBank.question: Which of the following groups are cyclic?
