questionBank.question: Which of the following propositional formulas are tautologies?
options: A, B, C and E only
questionBank.explanation: Check each formula over all 4 rows of p, q. A: if p → q is false then p = T, q = F, and then q → p is true, so A is never false: tautology. B: an implication implies its contrapositive (they are equivalent): tautology. C: this is disjunctive syllogism; the antecedent is true only when p = F and q = T, and then q is true: tautology. D: p = F, q = T makes p → q true but q → p false: not a tautology (the converse is not implied). E: p = T, q = T makes the antecedent true and ¬q false: not a tautology (it is modus ponens with the wrong conclusion). So A, B and C only.

questionBank.question: How many binary relations on a set with 4 elements are antisymmetric?
questionBank.explanation: For antisymmetry, each of the n diagonal pairs (a, a) is free: 2ⁿ ways. Each of the n(n − 1)/2 unordered pairs {a, b} with a ≠ b has 3 allowed choices: neither (a, b) nor (b, a), only (a, b), or only (b, a). Count = 2ⁿ × 3^(n(n−1)/2) = 2⁴ × 3⁶ = 16 × 729 = 11664. 4096 = 2¹² counts relations with the diagonal fixed; 729 = 3⁶ forgets the diagonal; 1296 = 6⁴ has no basis. (Checked by brute force over all 2¹⁶ relations.)

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: the 3 diagonal pairs are forced in, the other 9 − 3 = 6 pairs are free: 2⁶ = 64 (II). B: equivalence relations correspond to partitions; the Bell number B₃ = 5 (III). C: onto maps 4 → 3 = 3⁴ − 3·2⁴ + 3·1⁴ = 81 − 48 + 3 = 36 (I). D: one-one maps 3 → 4 = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 (IV). So A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV. The tempting swap C-IV/D-I mixes up onto and one-one counts.

a: A. Reflexive relations on a 3-element set
B. Equivalence relations on a 3-element set
C. Onto functions from a 4-element set to a 3-element set
D. One-one functions from a 3-element set to a 4-element set
b: II. 64
III. 5
IV. 24

questionBank.question: How many integers from 1 to 1000 (inclusive) are divisible by none of 2, 3 and 5?
questionBank.explanation: Count those divisible by at least one: |2| + |3| + |5| − |6| − |10| − |15| + |30| = 500 + 333 + 200 − 166 − 100 − 66 + 33 = 734. None of them: 1000 − 734 = 266. 734 is the complement (a classic trap), and 300 or 234 come from wrong floors or dropping the |30| term.

questionBank.question: A sequence satisfies aₙ = 5aₙ₋₁ − 6aₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 2, with a₀ = 1 and a₁ = 4. What is a₅?
questionBank.explanation: Characteristic equation r² − 5r + 6 = 0 gives r = 2, 3, so aₙ = c₁2ⁿ + c₂3ⁿ. From a₀: c₁ + c₂ = 1; from a₁: 2c₁ + 3c₂ = 4, so c₂ = 2, c₁ = −1. aₙ = 2·3ⁿ − 2ⁿ, and a₅ = 2 × 243 − 32 = 454. Iterating also gives 1, 4, 14, 46, 146, 454. 146 is a₄ and 1394 is a₆ (off-by-one indexing).

questionBank.question: How many solutions in non-negative integers does x₁ + x₂ + x₃ + x₄ = 12 have when x₁ ≤ 3?
questionBank.explanation: Without the bound, the count is C(12 + 3, 3) = C(15, 3) = 455. Remove the solutions with x₁ ≥ 4: put y₁ = x₁ − 4, then y₁ + x₂ + x₃ + x₄ = 8 has C(11, 3) = 165 solutions. Answer = 455 − 165 = 290. 455 ignores the bound and 165 is the subtracted part.

questionBank.question: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test detects it in 95% of people who have it and gives a false positive for 5% of people who do not. A randomly chosen person tests positive. The probability that the person has the disease is closest to
questionBank.explanation: P(D | +) = P(+ | D)P(D) / [P(+ | D)P(D) + P(+ | ¬D)P(¬D)] = (0.95 × 0.01) / (0.95 × 0.01 + 0.05 × 0.99) = 0.0095 / 0.059 ≈ 0.161. The trap 0.95 confuses P(+ | D) with P(D | +); the low prior makes most positives false positives.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I: the generators of ℤₙ are the k with gcd(k, n) = 1, so there are φ(36) = 36 × (1 − 1/2)(1 − 1/3) = 12 of them. True. Statement II: in ℤₙ the order of k is n / gcd(k, n) = 12 / gcd(8, 12) = 12 / 4 = 3; indeed 8 + 8 + 8 = 24 ≡ 0 (mod 12). True. So both statements are true.

stmts: Statement I: The cyclic group (ℤ₃₆, +) has exactly 12 generators.
Statement II: In the group (ℤ₁₂, +), the element 8 has order 3.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: The graph G is obtained from the complete graph K₄ by deleting one edge. How many spanning trees does G have?
questionBank.explanation: K₄ has 4⁴⁻² = 16 spanning trees (Cayley). Each edge of K₄ lies in the same number of spanning trees: 16 trees × 3 edges / 6 edges = 8. Deleting one edge removes those 8 trees, leaving 16 − 8 = 8. (Kirchhoff’s matrix-tree theorem on G gives the same value.) 16 is K₄ itself; 12 assumes only a quarter is lost.

questionBank.question: A connected planar simple graph has 10 vertices and every vertex has degree 3. How many faces (regions, including the outer face) does every planar drawing of it have?
questionBank.explanation: Handshake lemma: 2e = sum of degrees = 10 × 3 = 30, so e = 15. Euler’s formula for a connected planar graph: v − e + f = 2, so f = 2 − 10 + 15 = 7. (The Petersen graph is 3-regular on 10 vertices but non-planar; a planar example is the pentagonal prism, which has 7 faces.) 15 is the edge count and 5 forgets the outer face correction.

questionBank.question: The minimal sum-of-products form of F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15) is
questionBank.explanation: Minterms 0, 2, 8, 10 are the four corners of the K-map (B = 0, D = 0), giving the quad B′D′. Minterms 5, 7, 13, 15 form the centre quad (B = 1, D = 1), giving BD. All 8 minterms are covered by these two prime implicants, so F = BD + B′D′ (the XNOR of B and D). B ⊕ D is its complement; the extra A′C′ term is redundant; the 3-literal terms do not cover all minterms.

questionBank.question: Maximise Z = 3x + 5y subject to x + 2y ≤ 8, 3x + 2y ≤ 12, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. The optimal value of Z is
questionBank.explanation: Corner points of the feasible region: (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 4) and the intersection of x + 2y = 8 with 3x + 2y = 12. Subtracting gives 2x = 4, so x = 2, y = 3. Z values: 0, 12, 20 and 3(2) + 5(3) = 21. The maximum is 21 at (2, 3). 20 is the corner (0, 4), a trap for students who stop at the intercepts.

questionBank.question: A 5-bit ripple (asynchronous) counter is built from flip-flops that each have a propagation delay of 10 ns. Ignoring other delays, the maximum clock frequency at which it can be used reliably is
questionBank.explanation: In a ripple counter the clock ripples through all n flip-flops, so the worst-case settling time is n × t_pd = 5 × 10 ns = 50 ns. f_max = 1 / 50 ns = 20 MHz. 100 MHz is the synchronous-counter answer (one flip-flop delay), the classic trap.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: JK: sets when J = 1 and Q = 0, holds when K = 0 and Q = 1, so Q⁺ = JQ′ + K′Q (III). T: toggles when T = 1, Q⁺ = T ⊕ Q (IV). SR: Q⁺ = S + R′Q with SR = 0 (I). D: Q⁺ = D (II). The distractors swap the JK and SR equations, which look alike.

b: I. S + R′Q
II. D
III. JQ′ + K′Q
IV. T ⊕ Q

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: The IEEE 754 single-precision representation of −13.625, written in hexadecimal, is
The minimum number of check (parity) bits needed by a single-error-correcting Hamming code for 26 data bits is
questionBank.explanation: We need 2ʳ ≥ m + r + 1. With m = 26: r = 4 gives 16 ≥ 31, false; r = 5 gives 32 ≥ 32, true. So 5 check bits (a 31-bit codeword). 6 would be needed only for SEC-DED (one extra overall parity bit).

questionBank.question:
A two-word instruction is stored at addresses 250 and 251. Its address field is 400. Register R1 holds 150, the index register XR holds 60, and memory word 400 holds 720.
Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A (indirect): EA = M[400] = 720 (II). B (relative): after fetching both words PC = 252, so EA = 252 + 400 = 652 (IV). C (indexed): EA = 400 + XR = 460 (I). D (register indirect): EA = R1 = 150 (III). The trap in B is using PC = 250 or 251 instead of the updated PC.

b: III. 150

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A 5-stage instruction pipeline has stage delays of 12, 8, 10, 15 and 10 ns, and each pipeline latch adds 1 ns. The non-pipelined processor takes the sum of the stage delays (55 ns) per instruction. For 200 instructions with no stalls, the speedup of the pipeline is closest to
questionBank.explanation: Pipeline clock = slowest stage + latch = 15 + 1 = 16 ns. Pipelined time = (k + n − 1) × clock = (5 + 199) × 16 = 3264 ns. Non-pipelined time = 200 × 55 = 11000 ns. Speedup = 11000 / 3264 ≈ 3.37. 5.00 is the ideal k-stage speedup; 3.44 = 55/16 is the limit as n → ∞, not the 200-instruction value.

questionBank.question: In a pipelined processor with an ideal CPI of 1, 20% of instructions are conditional branches and 60% of branches are taken. The processor predicts every branch as not taken, and a misprediction costs 3 stall cycles. The effective CPI is
questionBank.explanation: Stalls occur only for taken branches (mispredicted). Stall cycles per instruction = 0.20 × 0.60 × 3 = 0.36, so CPI = 1 + 0.36 = 1.36. 1.60 charges every branch; 1.24 uses the not-taken fraction (0.4).

questionBank.question: A disk transfers data to memory by DMA in cycle-stealing mode at 4 MB/s. Each DMA transfer moves one 4-byte word and steals the bus for 40 ns. Take 1 MB = 10⁶ bytes. What percentage of the time is the CPU denied the bus?
questionBank.explanation: Words per second = 4 × 10⁶ / 4 = 10⁶. Bus time stolen per second = 10⁶ × 40 ns = 0.04 s, so 4% of the time. 16% forgets to divide bytes by the word size; 1% divides twice.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I: offset = log₂ 32 = 5 bits; number of sets = 64 KB / (32 B × 4) = 512, so index = 9 bits; tag = 32 − 9 − 5 = 18 bits, not 17. False. Statement II: AMAT = 2 + 0.1 × (10 + 0.2 × 100) = 2 + 0.1 × 30 = 5 ns. True. So Statement I is false and Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: For a 64 KB, 4-way set-associative cache with 32-byte blocks and 32-bit byte addresses, the tag field is 17 bits.
Statement II: With an L1 hit time of 2 ns and miss rate 0.1, an L2 hit time of 10 ns and local miss rate 0.2, and a memory access time of 100 ns, the average memory access time is 5 ns.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A system uses a TLB with a 10 ns lookup and a single-level page table in main memory; a memory access takes 100 ns. The TLB hit ratio is 90%. Assuming the TLB is searched before memory and there are no page faults, the effective memory access time is
questionBank.explanation: Hit: 10 + 100 = 110 ns. Miss: 10 + 100 (page table) + 100 (data) = 210 ns. EAT = 0.9 × 110 + 0.1 × 210 = 99 + 21 = 120 ns. 110 ns ignores misses; 130 ns charges the TLB twice on a miss.

questionBank.question: 80% of a program can be parallelised perfectly and the rest is strictly serial. By Amdahl’s law, the speedup on 8 processors is closest to
questionBank.explanation: Speedup = 1 / [(1 − f) + f/p] = 1 / (0.2 + 0.8/8) = 1 / (0.2 + 0.1) = 1 / 0.3 ≈ 3.33. 6.40 = 0.8 × 8 is the naive scaled answer; 5.00 is the limit 1/0.2 with infinitely many processors.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Static scoping: the x inside g always means the global x, so both calls print 5: output 5 5. Statement I is true. Dynamic scoping: g looks up the most recent active binding of x. Called from h, the most recent binding is h’s local x = 9, so it prints 9; called directly from main, only the global x = 5 exists, so it prints 5. Output 9 5, so Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement II: For the same pseudo-code, dynamic scoping prints 9 9.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: What is the output of this C program?
questionBank.explanation: s is static, so one copy is shared by all calls. The calls f(4), f(3), f(2), f(1) add 4, 3, 2, 1: s becomes 10 before any call returns. f(1) returns s = 10. Each outer call reads s after its recursive call returns, so it also sees 10: f(2) = 10 + 10 = 20, f(3) = 20 + 10 = 30, f(4) = 30 + 10 = 40. Output: 40 (checked with gcc). 20 assumes each frame sees the value s had when it was entered.

questionBank.question: What is the output of this C program?
questionBank.explanation: p points to a[1] = 20, so *p + 2 = 22 (dereference first, then add; 30 would be *(p + 2) style thinking). *(p + 2) is a[3] = 40. q − p = 4 − 1 = 3 elements: pointer subtraction counts elements, not bytes (12 is the byte difference with 4-byte int). Output: 22 40 3 (checked with gcc).

questionBank.question: What is the output of this C program?
questionBank.explanation: Macros are textual. SQ(3 + 2) becomes 3 + 2 * 3 + 2 = 3 + 6 + 2 = 11. 100 / SQ(5) becomes 100 / 5 * 5; / and * have equal precedence and associate left to right, so (100 / 5) * 5 = 100. Output: 11 100 (checked with gcc). 25 and 4 are what a correctly parenthesised macro ((x) * (x)) would give.

questionBank.question: What is the output of this C++ program?
questionBank.explanation: Constructing B runs the base constructor first: A then B. p->f() is virtual, so B::f runs and prints 2. The destructor of A is virtual, so delete p runs ~B then ~A: b then a. Output: AB2ba (checked with g++). AB2a is what happens if ~A were not virtual (only the base destructor runs, which is in fact undefined behaviour); AB1ba ignores dynamic binding.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about XML are correct?
options: A, B, C and E only
questionBank.explanation: A: true, one root element is a well-formedness rule. B: true, validity (conforming to a DTD or schema) presupposes well-formedness. C: false, a well-formed document need not follow any DTD/schema. D: false, XML is case-sensitive, so <Book> … </book> is not well-formed. E: true, unquoted attribute values are an error in XML (unlike old HTML). Hence A, B and E only.

stmts: A. A well-formed XML document has exactly one root element.
B. Every valid XML document is also well-formed.
C. Every well-formed XML document is also valid.
D. XML element names are case-insensitive, so <Book> can be closed by </book>.
E. Attribute values must be enclosed in quotes.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A raster display has a resolution of 1280 × 1024 and uses 24 bits per pixel. The frame buffer size needed is (1 MB = 2²⁰ bytes)
questionBank.explanation: Size = 1280 × 1024 × 24 bits = 31,457,280 bits = 3,932,160 bytes = 3,932,160 / 1,048,576 MB = 3.75 MB. 30 MB forgets to divide by 8 (it is 30 Mbit); 1.25 MB is 8 bits per pixel.

questionBank.question: Bresenham’s line algorithm is used to draw the line from (20, 10) to (30, 18). The initial decision parameter p₀ and the pixel plotted immediately after (20, 10) are
questionBank.explanation: Δx = 10, Δy = 8, slope 0.8 < 1, so x steps by 1. p₀ = 2Δy − Δx = 16 − 10 = 6. Since p₀ ≥ 0, y also increments: the next pixel is (21, 11), and p₁ = p₀ + 2Δy − 2Δx = 6 − 4 = 2. (21, 10) would be chosen only if p₀ < 0; 16 is 2Δy alone.

questionBank.question: The point (4, 2) is rotated by 90° anticlockwise about the pivot point (1, 1). Its new position is
questionBank.explanation: Translate the pivot to the origin: (4 − 1, 2 − 1) = (3, 1). Rotate 90° anticlockwise: (x, y) → (−y, x) = (−1, 3). Translate back: (−1 + 1, 3 + 1) = (0, 4). The composite matrix is T(1, 1)·R(90°)·T(−1, −1). (−2, 4) rotates about the origin; (−1, 3) forgets the last translation; (2, 0) rotates clockwise.

questionBank.question: A cubic Bézier curve has control points P₀ = (0, 0), P₁ = (2, 4), P₂ = (6, 4) and P₃ = (8, 0). The point on the curve at t = 0.5 is
questionBank.explanation: At t = 0.5 the Bernstein weights are (1 − t)³ = 0.125, 3t(1 − t)² = 0.375, 3t²(1 − t) = 0.375 and t³ = 0.125. x = 0.125(0) + 0.375(2) + 0.375(6) + 0.125(8) = 0 + 0.75 + 2.25 + 1 = 4. y = 0 + 0.375(4) + 0.375(4) + 0 = 3. Point (4, 3). (4, 4) assumes the curve passes through the inner control points, which a Bézier curve generally does not.

questionBank.question: An ER diagram has strong entity sets DEPT, EMP and PROJECT. EMP and PROJECT are related by the many-to-many relationship WORKS_ON, which has the attribute hours. DEPT and EMP are related one-to-many (each EMP belongs to exactly one DEPT, total participation). DEPENDENT is a weak entity set identified by EMP. What is the minimum number of relational tables needed?
questionBank.explanation: Tables needed: DEPT, EMP, PROJECT (one per strong entity) = 3. WORKS_ON is M:N, so it needs its own table (keys of EMP and PROJECT plus hours) = 4. The 1:N DEPT–EMP relationship is absorbed into EMP as a foreign key (no extra table). The weak entity DEPENDENT gets its own table with EMP’s key as part of its key; the identifying relationship needs no table = 5. 6 wrongly gives the 1:N relationship a table; 4 forgets that a weak entity needs a table.

questionBank.question: Relation Enrol(sid, cid) contains the tuples (s1, c1), (s1, c2), (s1, c3), (s2, c1), (s2, c3), (s3, c2), (s3, c3), (s4, c1), (s4, c2), (s4, c3). Relation Core(cid) contains c1 and c3. How many tuples are in Enrol ÷ Core?
questionBank.explanation: Enrol ÷ Core returns the students enrolled in every course of Core, that is in both c1 and c3. s1 has c1 and c3: yes. s2 has c1 and c3: yes. s3 has c3 but not c1: no. s4 has c1 and c3: yes. Result {s1, s2, s4}: 3 tuples. 2 would be “students with exactly the Core courses”, which is not what division means.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I: every R tuple has a non-null B that matches exactly one S tuple (B is a key of S), so each of the 100 R tuples joins with exactly one S tuple: 100 tuples. True. Statement II: the Cartesian product has |R| × |S| = 100 × 50 = 5000 tuples, whatever the keys. True. Both statements are true.

stmts: Statement I: R(A, B) has 100 tuples and S(B, C) has 50 tuples, where B is the primary key of S and R.B is a NOT NULL foreign key referencing S. Then R ⋈ S has exactly 100 tuples.
Statement II: For the same relations, R × S has 5000 tuples.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question:
Table Emp(eid, dept, salary) holds (1, CS, 50), (2, CS, 70), (3, EE, 40), (4, EE, 60), (5, EE, 80), (6, ME, 45), (7, ME, 55), (8, CE, 90). How many rows does this query return?
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM Emp WHERE salary > 45 GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary) > 55;
questionBank.explanation: WHERE runs first and removes rows 3 (40) and 6 (45). Groups: CS {50, 70}, average 60; EE {60, 80}, average 70; ME {55}, average 55; CE {90}, average 90. HAVING AVG > 55 keeps CS, EE and CE (ME’s 55 is not > 55). 3 rows (verified with SQLite). 4 counts ME by treating > as ≥; 2 or 1 come from applying HAVING to rows that WHERE has already removed, or from filtering groups before grouping. Remember the order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT.

questionBank.question:
Table Staff(id, bonus) has 5 rows with bonus values 100, NULL, 200, NULL, 300. What does this query return?
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(bonus), AVG(bonus), SUM(bonus) / COUNT(*) FROM Staff;
questionBank.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows: 5. COUNT(bonus) skips NULLs: 3. AVG(bonus) = (100 + 200 + 300) / 3 = 200 (NULLs ignored, not treated as 0). SUM(bonus) / COUNT(*) = 600 / 5 = 120, which is what AVG would be only if NULL meant 0. Verified with SQLite.

questionBank.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) has the functional dependencies AB → C, C → D, D → B, D → E. How many candidate keys does R have?
questionBank.explanation: A never appears on a right-hand side, so every key contains A. A⁺ = {A}. Try pairs with A: AB⁺ = ABCDE (AB → C → D → E); AC⁺ = ACDBE (C → D → B, E); AD⁺ = ADBEC (D → B, E, then AB → C); AE⁺ = AE. So AB, AC and AD are keys, and any other superkey contains one of them. 3 candidate keys. 1 is the usual answer of students who stop after finding AB.

questionBank.question: For the same relation R(A, B, C, D, E) with AB → C, C → D, D → B, D → E (candidate keys AB, AC, AD), the highest normal form R satisfies is
questionBank.explanation: Prime attributes: A, B, C, D. The only non-prime attribute is E. D → E: D is a proper subset of the candidate key AD and E is non-prime, so E is partially dependent on a key. That violates 2NF, so R is only in 1NF. The trap is to check only C → D and D → B (both have prime right-hand sides, which 3NF allows) and wrongly answer 3NF.

questionBank.question: A B⁺-tree is stored on disk with a block size of 1024 bytes. A search key is 9 bytes and a block pointer is 7 bytes. The maximum order p (the maximum number of child pointers) of an internal node is
questionBank.explanation: An internal node holds p pointers and p − 1 keys: 7p + 9(p − 1) ≤ 1024, so 16p ≤ 1033 and p ≤ 64.56. p = 64 (7 × 64 + 9 × 63 = 448 + 567 = 1015 ≤ 1024). 63 is the leaf capacity if each leaf holds (key, record pointer) pairs plus one next-leaf pointer: 16q + 7 ≤ 1024; 65 does not fit.

questionBank.question: Consider the schedule S: R1(X), R3(Y), W2(X), W4(Y), R1(Z), R3(Z). How many serial schedules are conflict-equivalent to S?
questionBank.explanation: Conflicting pairs (same item, different transactions, at least one write): R1(X) before W2(X) gives T1 → T2; R3(Y) before W4(Y) gives T3 → T4. R1(Z) and R3(Z) are both reads, so no conflict. The precedence graph is acyclic with two independent chains T1 → T2 and T3 → T4. Each topological order is a conflict-equivalent serial schedule: choose the 2 positions for T1, T2 among 4 = C(4, 2) = 6. 24 ignores the edges; 2 treats the chains as blocks.

questionBank.question: Five transactions contain the items {A, B, C}, {A, C}, {A, D}, {B, C, E} and {A, B, C, E}. The support and confidence of the rule {B, C} → {E} are
questionBank.explanation: Support of the rule = fraction of transactions with B, C and E = 2/5 = 40% (transactions 4 and 5). Confidence = support(BCE) / support(BC) = 2/3 ≈ 66.7%, since B and C appear together in transactions 1, 4 and 5. 60% is the support of {B, C} alone; 100% would be the confidence of {E} → {B, C}.

questionBank.question:
Consider this assembly program. Each instruction and each DC occupies one word; DS n reserves n words; LTORG places pending literals at the current location.
      START 200
L1    MOVER AREG, ='5'
X     DS    5
Y     DC    '3'
L2    ADD   AREG, Y
      LTORG
      END
After pass 1, the addresses of L2 and of the literal ='5' are
questionBank.explanation: Location counter: L1 = 200 (1 word), X = 201 (DS 5 takes 201–205), Y = 206 (1 word), L2 = 207 (1 word). LTORG then places the literal ='5' at 208. 203 treats DS 5 as one word; 206/207 forgets that X itself is at 201.

questionBank.question: Processes P1–P4 arrive at times 0, 1, 3 and 6 with CPU bursts 8, 5, 2 and 4 respectively. Using SRTF (preemptive SJF), the average waiting time is
questionBank.explanation: Gantt chart: P1 0–1 | P2 1–3 | P3 3–5 | P2 5–8 | P4 8–12 | P1 12–19. At t = 1, P2 (5) beats P1’s remaining 7. At t = 3, P3 (2) beats P2’s remaining 3. At t = 5, P2 (3) runs; at t = 6, P4 (4) does not beat P2’s remaining 2. Completion: P1 19, P2 8, P3 5, P4 12. Waiting = TAT − burst: P1 19 − 8 = 11, P2 7 − 5 = 2, P3 2 − 2 = 0, P4 6 − 4 = 2. Average = 15/4 = 3.75.

questionBank.question: Processes P1–P4 arrive at times 0, 1, 2 and 4 with CPU bursts 6, 4, 7 and 3. Using Round Robin with time quantum 3 (a newly arriving process joins the queue before a preempted one), the average turnaround time is
questionBank.explanation: Gantt chart: P1 0–3 | P2 3–6 | P3 6–9 | P1 9–12 | P4 12–15 | P2 15–16 | P3 16–20. Queue at t = 3: P2, P3, P1. At t = 6 (P4 arrived at 4): P3, P1, P4, P2. Completion: P1 12, P2 16, P3 20, P4 15. TAT = CT − AT: 12, 15, 18, 11. Average = 56/4 = 14. 9 is the average waiting time.

questionBank.question:
A system has resource types R1, R2, R3 and five processes. Available = (1, 1, 2).
Allocation: P1 (1, 0, 2), P2 (2, 1, 0), P3 (1, 1, 1), P4 (0, 2, 0), P5 (1, 0, 1).
Max: P1 (4, 2, 3), P2 (3, 2, 2), P3 (5, 3, 2), P4 (2, 4, 2), P5 (3, 1, 4).
Which of the following is a safe sequence under the Banker’s algorithm?
questionBank.explanation: Need = Max − Allocation: P1 (3, 2, 1), P2 (1, 1, 2), P3 (4, 2, 1), P4 (2, 2, 2), P5 (2, 1, 3). With Work = (1, 1, 2), only P2 fits; Work becomes (3, 2, 2). Now P1 (3, 2, 1) fits: Work (4, 2, 4). P3 (4, 2, 1) fits: Work (5, 3, 5). P4 fits: (5, 5, 5). P5 fits: (6, 5, 6). So P2, P1, P3, P4, P5 is safe. P1 cannot start first; after P2, neither P3 (needs 4 of R1) nor P5 (needs 3 of R3) fits.

questionBank.question: Four processes share identical units of one resource type. Each process may need up to 3 units at the same time. What is the minimum number of units that guarantees deadlock can never occur?
questionBank.explanation: Worst case: each process holds one less than its maximum, 4 × (3 − 1) = 8 units, and all wait. One more unit lets some process finish and release its units: 8 + 1 = 9. With 8 units deadlock is possible; 12 is enough but not minimum.

questionBank.question: A system uses 32-bit virtual addresses, 4 KB pages and a single-level page table with 4-byte entries. The page table of one process occupies
questionBank.explanation: Offset = log₂ 4096 = 12 bits, so there are 2³²⁻¹² = 2²⁰ pages. Page table size = 2²⁰ × 4 bytes = 4 MB. 1 MB counts entries, not bytes; this size is why multilevel paging is used.

questionBank.question:
The page reference string 1, 3, 0, 3, 5, 6, 3, 1, 6, 0, 5, 4, 3, 6, 0 is run with demand paging starting from empty frames.
Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: Simulating each policy (verified by program): FIFO with 3 frames gives 13 faults (IV); LRU with 3 frames gives 12 (II); Optimal with 3 frames gives 9 (I); Optimal with 4 frames gives 7 (III). Optimal is always the lowest for a given frame count, and more frames never increase faults for Optimal or LRU (stack algorithms). So A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III.

b: II. 12
III. 7
IV. 13

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: A: FIFO gives 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 with 4 frames (verified by simulation), so A is true: this is Belady’s anomaly. R: true, and it is exactly why the anomaly can happen. Stack algorithms (LRU, Optimal) satisfy the inclusion property and can never show it. So both are true and R explains A.

stmts: Assertion (A): For the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, FIFO replacement causes more page faults with 4 frames than with 3 frames.
Reason (R): FIFO is not a stack algorithm, so the set of pages it holds with n frames is not always a subset of the set it holds with n + 1 frames.

questionBank.question: A software system has a mean time to failure (MTTF) of 950 hours and a mean time to repair (MTTR) of 50 hours. Its MTBF and availability are
questionBank.explanation: MTBF = MTTF + MTTR = 950 + 50 = 1000 hours. Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) = 950 / 1000 = 0.95 = 95%. 94.7% comes from (950 − 50)/950; 900 h subtracts MTTR instead of adding it.

questionBank.question: Using basic COCOMO in organic mode (a = 2.4, b = 1.05, c = 2.5, d = 0.38), the effort and development time for a 32 KLOC project are closest to
questionBank.explanation: Effort E = a × KLOC^b = 2.4 × 32^1.05 ≈ 2.4 × 38.05 ≈ 91.3 person-months. Time D = c × E^d = 2.5 × 91.3^0.38 ≈ 2.5 × 5.56 ≈ 13.9 months. 77 = 2.4 × 32 ignores the exponent; 6.5 months does not come from the time equation D = 2.5E^0.38; about 146 person-months is what the semi-detached constants (3.0, 1.12) would give.

questionBank.explanation: Path lengths: A–D–F = 3 + 6 + 2 = 11; A–C–E–F = 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 10; B–E–F = 4 + 3 + 2 = 9. The critical path is the longest: A–D–F, 11 days (earliest finish of F = max(EF of D = 9, EF of E = 8) + 2 = 11).

There are three binary decisions: the while condition, the if and the else-if. V(G) = number of decisions + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4. Equivalently V(G) = E − N + 2 for its flow graph, or the number of bounded regions + 1. 3 forgets the +1; 5 counts the else as a decision.

questionBank.question: An array A[−5 … 10][3 … 12] of 4-byte integers is stored in row-major order starting at address 1000. The address of A[2][7] is
questionBank.explanation: Rows −5…10 (16 rows); columns 3…12, so 10 columns per row. Offset in elements = (2 − (−5)) × 10 + (7 − 3) = 70 + 4 = 74. Address = 1000 + 74 × 4 = 1296. 1316 uses column-major style counting; 1136 forgets that the lower row bound is negative.

questionBank.question: The bottom-up build-heap procedure is applied to the array [4, 10, 3, 5, 1, 15, 8] (index 0 first) to build a max-heap. The resulting array is
questionBank.explanation: Heapify from the last internal node (index 2) back to the root. Index 2 (3): children 15, 8, swap with 15 → [4, 10, 15, 5, 1, 3, 8]. Index 1 (10): children 5, 1, no change. Index 0 (4): larger child 15, swap → [15, 10, 4, 5, 1, 3, 8]; continue sifting 4 at index 2: children 3, 8, swap with 8 → [15, 10, 8, 5, 1, 3, 4]. questionBank.question: Keys 12, 18, 13, 2, 3, 23, 5, 15 are inserted in this order into an empty hash table of size 10 using h(k) = k mod 10 and linear probing. In which slot does key 15 end up?
questionBank.explanation: 12 → 2; 18 → 8; 13 → 3; 2 → 2 taken, 3 taken, goes to 4; 3 → 3, 4 taken, goes to 5; 23 → 3, 4, 5 taken, goes to 6; 5 → 5, 6 taken, goes to 7; 15 → 5, 6, 7, 8 all taken, goes to 9. Final table: [–, –, 12, 13, 2, 3, 23, 5, 18, 15]. Slot 9. Primary clustering is what makes the probe sequence so long.

questionBank.question: Characters a, b, c, d, e, f, g occur 10, 15, 12, 3, 4, 13 and 1 times in a message. Using Huffman coding, the total number of bits needed to encode the message is
questionBank.explanation: Merge the two smallest each time: g1 + d3 = 4; 4 + e4 = 8; 8 + a10 = 18; c12 + f13 = 25; b15 + 18 = 33; 25 + 33 = 58. Code lengths: b, c, f = 2; a = 3; e = 4; d, g = 5. Total = 15×2 + 12×2 + 13×2 + 10×3 + 4×4 + 3×5 + 1×5 = 30 + 24 + 26 + 30 + 16 + 15 + 5 = 146 bits (58 characters, about 2.52 bits each). A fixed 3-bit code would need 174 bits.

questionBank.question: The KMP prefix (failure) function π for the pattern “abacabab” is
questionBank.explanation: π[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[1..i] that is also a suffix. a: 0; ab: 0; aba: 1 (a); abac: 0; abaca: 1; abacab: 2 (ab); abacaba: 3 (aba); abacabab: the next character b ≠ c, so fall back from 3 to π[3] = 1, then compare b with pattern[2] = b: match, so 2. questionBank.question: A context-free grammar in Chomsky normal form and another in Greibach normal form both generate a string w of length 7 (and neither has ε-productions). The number of derivation steps for w is
questionBank.explanation: In CNF each A → BC step adds one non-terminal (n − 1 such steps to reach n non-terminals) and each A → a step turns one into a terminal (n steps): 2n − 1 = 13. In GNF every step A → aα produces exactly one terminal, so n = 7 steps. Swapping the two is the classic slip.

Statement II is false: DPDAs accept only the deterministic CFLs, a proper subset; for example, even-length palindromes {wwᴿ} need nondeterminism. Both statements are false.

questionBank.question: Which of the following problems are decidable for context-free grammars G, G₁ and G₂?
options: A, B, C and E only
A, B, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A (membership) is decidable, for example with the CYK algorithm in O(n³). B (emptiness) is decidable by checking whether the start symbol is generating. E (finiteness) is decidable: in the simplified CNF grammar, check for a cycle in the variable graph. C (equivalence) and D (ambiguity) are undecidable for CFGs (both reduce from the Post correspondence problem). So A, B and E only.

stmts: A. Is a given string w in L(G)?
B. Is L(G) empty?
C. Is L(G₁) = L(G₂)?

questionBank.question:
How many tokens does a C lexical analyser produce for the statement
printf("x=%d", a+++b);
questionBank.explanation: The lexer uses maximal munch, so a+++b is split as a, ++, +, b. Tokens: printf | ( | "x=%d" | , | a | ++ | + | b | ) | ; = 10. The string literal is one token (its contents are not split). 11 splits +++ as +, +, + or counts the format specifier separately; 9 merges ++ and + incorrectly.

questionBank.question:
Consider the grammar
S → A a B | B b
A → c A | ε
B → d B | ε
where S is the start symbol. Which option is correct?
options: FIRST(S) = {a, c, d, ε} and FOLLOW(B) = {a, b, $}
FIRST(S) = {a, b, c, d} and FOLLOW(B) = {b, $}
FIRST(S) = {a, b, c, d} and FOLLOW(B) = {$}
questionBank.explanation: FIRST(A) = {c, ε} and FIRST(B) = {d, ε}. FIRST(A a B) = {c} ∪ {a} (A can vanish) = {a, c}; FIRST(B b) = {d, b}. So FIRST(S) = {a, b, c, d}, and ε ∉ FIRST(S) because both alternatives end in a terminal or need a. FOLLOW(B): from S → A a B, FOLLOW(B) ⊇ FOLLOW(S) = {$}; from S → B b, b ∈ FOLLOW(B); from B → d B nothing new. FOLLOW(B) = {b, $}. Forgetting that A and B are nullable gives {c, d}.

questionBank.explanation: LR(0) ⊂ SLR(1) ⊂ LALR(1) ⊂ CLR(1) (canonical LR(1)). SLR adds FOLLOW-set lookaheads to LR(0) items; LALR merges CLR(1) states with the same core, so it can introduce reduce–reduce conflicts that CLR avoids, making it weaker than CLR but stronger than SLR. Order: B, D, C, A.

stmts: A. CLR(1)
B. LR(0)
C. LALR(1)
D. SLR(1)

questionBank.explanation: In the grammar, & is lower in the tree (T is inside E), so & binds tighter than #, and both are left-associative. The parse is (2 # (3 & 5)) # 4. Values: 3 & 5 = 3 + 5 = 8; 2 # 8 = 16; 16 # 4 = 64. 44 evaluates left to right ignoring precedence ((2 × 3 + 5) × 4); 30 treats # as + and & as ×.

questionBank.question:
How many basic blocks does this three-address code have?
1. s = 0
2. i = 0
3. if i >= n goto 9
4. t1 = 4 * i
5. t2 = a[t1]
6. s = s + t2
7. i = i + 1
8. goto 3
9. print s
questionBank.explanation: Leaders: statement 1 (the first), statements 3 and 9 (targets of jumps), statement 4 (follows the conditional jump in 3) and statement 9 again (follows the goto in 8). Leaders {1, 3, 4, 9} give 4 blocks: {1, 2}, {3}, {4–8}, {9}. 3 misses that the jump target 3 starts its own block.

questionBank.question: A channel has a bandwidth of 4 kHz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 63 (linear). Its Shannon capacity, and the number of signal levels a noiseless Nyquist channel of the same bandwidth would need to carry that rate, are
questionBank.explanation: Shannon: C = B log₂(1 + SNR) = 4000 × log₂ 64 = 4000 × 6 = 24 kbps. Nyquist: bit rate = 2B log₂ L, so 24000 = 8000 log₂ L, log₂ L = 3, L = 8. 64 levels confuses 1 + SNR with L; 48 kbps forgets that Shannon has no factor 2.

questionBank.question: The message 101110101 is sent using CRC with generator polynomial x³ + x² + 1. The transmitted frame is
questionBank.explanation: Generator bits 1101 (degree 3), so append three 0s: 101110101000. Divide by 1101 using XOR (modulo-2) long division; the remainder is 110. Transmitted frame = message followed by the remainder = 101110101110. 101110101000 sends the padded message without the CRC; the other two use a wrong remainder.

questionBank.question: A 1 Mbps link has a one-way propagation delay of 20 ms and uses 1000-bit frames. What is the minimum number of sequence-number bits needed for Selective Repeat ARQ to keep the link fully busy?
questionBank.explanation: Transmission time = 1000 / 10⁶ = 1 ms, so a = propagation / transmission = 20. A full pipe needs a window of 1 + 2a = 41 frames. Selective Repeat requires window ≤ 2ᵏ / 2, so 2ᵏ ≥ 82 and k = 7. 6 bits (64) would be enough for Go-Back-N (window ≤ 2ᵏ − 1 = 63), which is the trap.

questionBank.explanation: A: one-way delay = 2500 / (2 × 10⁸) = 12.5 µs; the frame must last one round trip, 25 µs, so 10⁷ × 25 × 10⁻⁶ = 250 bits (III). B: S = G e^(−2G) peaks at G = 0.5: 1/(2e) ≈ 18.4% (IV). C: S = G e^(−G) peaks at G = 1: 1/e ≈ 36.8% (I). D: a = 20, efficiency = 1 / (1 + 2a) = 1/41 ≈ 2.44% (II).

B. Maximum throughput of pure ALOHA

questionBank.question: An IPv4 datagram of total length 4000 bytes (20-byte header, no options) must pass through a link with MTU 1500 bytes. For the third fragment, the fragment offset field and the total length are
questionBank.explanation: Data to send = 4000 − 20 = 3980 bytes. Each fragment can carry at most 1500 − 20 = 1480 data bytes, a multiple of 8. Fragments carry 1480, 1480 and 1020 bytes. questionBank.question: An organisation owns a /22 block and wants to split it into equal subnets with at least 50 usable hosts each. The maximum number of subnets it can create is
questionBank.explanation: 50 usable hosts need h host bits with 2ʰ − 2 ≥ 50, so h = 6 (62 hosts); the prefix becomes /26. Subnet bits borrowed = 26 − 22 = 4, giving 2⁴ = 16 subnets. 32 would allow only 30 hosts each (/27); 8 wastes a bit.

questionBank.question: A TCP connection starts in slow start with cwnd = 1 MSS and ssthresh = 12 MSS. In slow start cwnd doubles every RTT but never jumps past ssthresh (it is set to min(2 × cwnd, ssthresh)); from ssthresh onwards it grows by 1 MSS per RTT. With no loss, cwnd at the start of the 8th RTT is
questionBank.explanation: RTT 1: 1, RTT 2: 2, RTT 3: 4, RTT 4: 8, RTT 5: min(16, 12) = 12 (ssthresh reached), then congestion avoidance: RTT 6: 13, RTT 7: 14, RTT 8: 15 MSS. 16 lets slow start overshoot to 16; 128 = 2⁷ ignores ssthresh.

questionBank.question: In RSA, p = 11, q = 13 and the public exponent e = 7. The private exponent d and the ciphertext for the message M = 9 are
In Diffie–Hellman key exchange, the public values are p = 29 and g = 2. Alice picks the secret a = 5 and Bob picks b = 9. The shared secret key is
questionBank.explanation: Alice sends A = 2⁵ mod 29 = 32 mod 29 = 3. Bob sends B = 2⁹ mod 29 = 512 mod 29 = 19. Alice computes B^a = 19⁵ mod 29 = 21; Bob computes A^b = 3⁹ mod 29 = 21. Key = 21. 3 and 19 are the public values, not the key; 28 is g^(a+b) mod 29 = 2¹⁴ mod 29, which uses the sum of the secrets instead of the product.

questionBank.question: A two-ply game tree has a MAX root with three MIN children. The leaf values under the MIN nodes, left to right, are [5, 9, 4], [3, 8, 6] and [7, 2, 10]. With alpha–beta pruning (children examined left to right), the minimax value of the root and the number of leaves pruned are
questionBank.explanation: First MIN node: all three leaves are seen, value min(5, 9, 4) = 4, so α = 4 at the root. Second MIN node: its first leaf 3 ≤ α, so its value is at most 3 and the leaves 8 and 6 are pruned (2 leaves). Third MIN node: 7 > 4, keep going; 2 ≤ 4, so leaf 10 is pruned (1 leaf). Root = 4 and 3 leaves are pruned. 7 is the maximum of the first leaves, not a minimax value.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: this is the definition of admissibility and the standard optimality result for A* tree search. Statement II is false: the implication goes the other way. A consistent heuristic (h(n) ≤ c(n, n′) + h(n′), with h(goal) = 0) is always admissible, but an admissible heuristic can violate the triangle inequality on some edge. So Statement I is true and Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: A heuristic is admissible if it never overestimates the true cost to reach a goal, and A* tree search with an admissible heuristic returns an optimal solution.
Statement II: Every admissible heuristic is also consistent (monotone).

Fuzzy relations R and S are given by the matrices R = [[0.3, 0.8], [0.6, 0.4]] and S = [[0.5, 0.9], [0.7, 0.2]] (rows listed in order). The max–min composition T = R ∘ S is
The output fuzzy set of a controller is {10/0.2, 20/0.6, 30/1.0, 40/0.4} (value/membership). The crisp output by the (discrete) centroid method is closest to
questionBank.explanation: Centroid = Σ xμ(x) / Σ μ(x) = (10 × 0.2 + 20 × 0.6 + 30 × 1.0 + 40 × 0.4) / (0.2 + 0.6 + 1.0 + 0.4) = (2 + 12 + 30 + 16) / 2.2 = 60 / 2.2 ≈ 27.27. 30 is the mean-of-maximum (the peak); 25 is the plain average of the x values.

questionBank.question: For the fuzzy set A = {x1/0.2, x2/0.5, x3/0.8, x4/1.0, x5/0.4}, which option correctly gives the α-cut at α = 0.5, the strong α-cut at α = 0.5, and the core of A?
questionBank.explanation: The α-cut keeps elements with μ ≥ 0.5: x2 (0.5), x3, x4. The strong α-cut uses μ > 0.5: x3, x4. The core is {x : μ = 1} = {x4}. The set of all five elements is the support (μ > 0), not the core; including x5 (0.4) in the α-cut is wrong.

questionBank.question: A GA population has four chromosomes with fitness values 5, 12, 20 and 9. Using roulette-wheel selection, the probability of choosing the chromosome with fitness 12 in one spin, and its expected number of copies when 4 parents are selected, are closest to
questionBank.explanation: Total fitness = 5 + 12 + 20 + 9 = 46. Probability = 12 / 46 ≈ 0.261. Expected copies = N × p = 4 × 12/46 ≈ 1.04, which is also f / f̄ = 12 / 11.5. 0.25 assumes equal slices; 0.12 divides by 100.

questionBank.question: A perceptron with a step activation (output 1 if net ≥ 0, else 0) has weights w = (0.2, −0.4), bias b = 0.1 and learning rate η = 0.5. It receives input x = (1, 1) with target t = 1. After one application of the perceptron learning rule, the new weights and bias are

Leaving the weights unchanged ignores the error; forgetting the bias gives b = 0.1; the negative option applies the correction with the wrong sign.

questionBank.explanation: Think of the n × n relation matrix. A (reflexive): the n diagonal entries are forced to 1 and the other n² − n entries are free, so 2^(n² − n) (III). B (symmetric): the n diagonal entries are free and each of the n(n−1)/2 off-diagonal pairs {(i,j),(j,i)} is either both in or both out, so 2^n · 2^(n(n−1)/2) = 2^(n(n+1)/2) (IV). C (antisymmetric): diagonal free (2^n) and each off-diagonal pair has 3 legal states (neither, only (i,j), only (j,i)), so 2^n · 3^(n(n−1)/2) (I). D (reflexive and symmetric): diagonal forced, each off-diagonal pair has 2 states, so 2^(n(n−1)/2) (II). Check with n = 3: 64, 64, 216 and 8 relations respectively, confirmed by brute force over all 512 relations. The trap options swap B and D, which differ only in whether the diagonal is free.

questionBank.question: Five letters are placed at random into five addressed envelopes, one letter per envelope. In how many ways can this be done so that no letter goes into its correct envelope?
questionBank.explanation: This is the derangement number D₅ = 5! (1 − 1/1! + 1/2! − 1/3! + 1/4! − 1/5!) = 120 − 120 + 60 − 20 + 5 − 1 = 44. Check with the recurrence Dₙ = (n − 1)(Dₙ₋₁ + Dₙ₋₂): D₃ = 2, D₄ = 9, D₅ = 4 × (9 + 2) = 44. 120 counts all arrangements with no restriction, and 45 comes from rounding 120/e ≈ 44.15 up instead of to the nearest integer (Dₙ is always the integer nearest to n!/e).

So Statement I is true and Statement II is false.

questionBank.question: Which of the following sets of Boolean operators are functionally complete?
options: A, C, D and E only
A, B, C and E only
questionBank.explanation: A and E: NAND and NOR are each universal on their own. C: ¬ with → gives OR (p ∨ q ≡ ¬p → q) and then AND by De Morgan, so {→, ¬} is complete. B: AND and OR can only build monotone functions, so NOT cannot be made. D: XOR and AND both map (0, 0) to 0 (they preserve 0), so any composition of them also outputs 0 on the all-zero input and the constant 1 or NOT cannot be built; {XOR, AND, 1} would be complete, but {XOR, AND} is not. So A, C and E only. (Verified by computing the closure of each set over all 3-variable Boolean functions.)

stmts: A. {NAND}
B. {AND, OR}
C. {→, ¬} (implication and negation)
D. {XOR, AND}
E. {NOR}

questionBank.question: A disease affects 2% of a population. A test detects it in 95% of people who have it (sensitivity) and gives a negative result for 90% of people who do not have it (specificity). A randomly chosen person tests positive. The probability that the person has the disease is closest to:
questionBank.explanation: Let D be "has the disease" and + be "tests positive". P(+ | D) P(D) = 0.95 × 0.02 = 0.019. P(+ | not D) P(not D) = 0.10 × 0.98 = 0.098. By Bayes’ theorem P(D | +) = 0.019 / (0.019 + 0.098) = 0.019 / 0.117 ≈ 0.162, about 16.2%. The trap answer 95% confuses P(+ | D) with P(D | +); 19.0% forgets to multiply the false-positive rate by 0.98; 2% ignores the evidence.

questionBank.explanation: R is true: the non-pipelined unit takes n·k·t_p (each task takes k stage times) while the pipeline takes (k + n − 1)·t_p (k cycles to fill, then one completion per cycle), so S = nk / (k + n − 1). A is false: from R, S < k for every finite n because k + n − 1 > n whenever k > 1; S only approaches k as n → ∞. For example k = 4, n = 10 gives 40/13 ≈ 3.08, not 4. So A is false but R is true.

stmts: Assertion (A): An ideal k-stage pipeline achieves a speedup of exactly k over a non-pipelined unit for any finite number of tasks.
Reason (R): For n tasks on an ideal k-stage pipeline with equal stage delays, the speedup over the equivalent non-pipelined unit is nk / (k + n − 1).

questionBank.question: A byte-addressable machine uses 32-bit physical addresses. It has a 64 KB, 4-way set-associative cache with 32-byte blocks. How many bits are in the tag field?
questionBank.explanation: Offset bits = log₂ 32 = 5. Number of blocks = 64 KB / 32 B = 2¹⁶ / 2⁵ = 2048. Number of sets = 2048 / 4 = 512 = 2⁹, so the index (set) field is 9 bits. Tag = 32 − 9 − 5 = 18 bits. The trap answer 16 treats the cache as direct-mapped (index = 11 bits); 17 comes from treating it as 2-way (1024 sets, 10 index bits) and 19 from 8-way (256 sets, 8 index bits).

Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: the single-precision exponent field has 8 bits and a bias of 2⁸⁻¹ − 1 = 127 (double precision uses 1023). Statement II is false: 8-bit two’s complement represents −2⁷ to 2⁷ − 1, that is −128 to +127. The range −127 to +127 belongs to sign-magnitude and one’s complement, which waste a pattern on −0. So both statements are false.

stmts: Statement I: In IEEE 754 single precision, the exponent is stored with a bias of 128.
Statement II: The range of integers that can be represented in 8-bit two’s complement is −127 to +127.

questionBank.question: In Mano’s basic computer, arrange the following micro-steps of the instruction cycle in the order in which they occur.
questionBank.explanation: The fetch–decode sequence in the basic computer is: T0: AR ← PC (C). T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1 (B). T2: decode IR(12–14) into D0–D7, AR ← IR(0–11), I ← IR(15) (A). T3: for a memory-reference instruction with I = 1, AR ← M[AR] to get the effective address (D). T4 onward: execute (E). The address must reach AR before memory can be read, which is why C precedes B, and indirection cannot be checked until the instruction is decoded, which is why A precedes D.

stmts: A. Decode the operation code and transfer bit 15 of IR to flip-flop I
B. Read the instruction from memory into IR and increment PC
C. Transfer the contents of PC to AR
D. If the instruction is memory-reference and indirect, read the effective address from memory into AR
E. Execute the instruction

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about pipeline hazards are correct?
options: A, B, C, D and E
A, B, C and E only
questionBank.explanation: A true: forwarding sends the ALU result straight to the next instruction’s input, removing most RAW stalls (a load followed by use may still need one). B true: predicting the branch lets the pipeline continue fetching instead of waiting. C true: e.g. a single memory port used by instruction fetch and a data access in the same cycle. D false: in a simple in-order pipeline every instruction reads its operands (stage 2) before any later instruction can write (stage 5), so WAR and WAW hazards cannot occur; they appear with out-of-order execution. E true: this is the delay-slot idea. So A, B, C and E only.

stmts: A. Operand forwarding (bypassing) reduces the stalls caused by read-after-write data dependences.
B. Branch prediction is a technique to reduce the penalty of control hazards.
C. Structural hazards arise when two instructions need the same hardware resource in the same clock cycle.
D. Write-after-read (WAR) hazards occur frequently in a simple in-order five-stage pipeline where every instruction reads registers in stage 2 and writes in stage 5.
E. In a delayed branch, the compiler tries to fill the slot after the branch with a useful instruction that executes regardless of the branch outcome.

questionBank.question: A program spends 80% of its execution time in a part that can be perfectly parallelised; the rest is strictly sequential. According to Amdahl’s law, what is the speedup on 8 processors?
questionBank.explanation: Amdahl’s law: S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/p) with f = 0.8 and p = 8. S = 1 / (0.2 + 0.8/8) = 1 / (0.2 + 0.1) = 1 / 0.3 ≈ 3.33. The maximum speedup even with infinitely many processors is 1/0.2 = 5. The option 6.40 is 0.8 × 8 (scaling only the parallel part), and 8 is the ideal linear speedup that ignores the sequential 20%.

questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: in a daisy chain the interrupt-acknowledge signal travels from the CPU through the devices in series, and the first requesting device it reaches (the one nearest the CPU) blocks it from going further, so the nearest device has the highest priority. Statement II is true: burst (block) transfer holds the bus for the whole block, while cycle stealing takes the bus for one word at a time and returns it to the CPU between words. So Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: In a daisy-chain priority interrupt scheme, the device electrically farthest from the CPU has the highest priority.
Statement II: In burst-mode DMA, the DMA controller keeps control of the system bus until the whole block of data has been transferred.

A is false for exactly that reason: a hardwired unit generates the signals with fixed logic (decoders, gates, sequence counter), and changing the instruction set means redesigning that logic. Hardwired control wins on speed, not on flexibility. So A is false but R is true.

stmts: Assertion (A): Hardwired control units are easier to modify than microprogrammed control units when the instruction set changes.
Reason (R): In a microprogrammed control unit, many instruction-set changes need only new contents in the control memory.

questionBank.question: What is the output of this C program?
questionBank.explanation: A static local variable is initialised once and keeps its value between calls. The calls return ++c * 2 with c becoming 1, 2 and 3, so they return 2, 4 and 6, and s = 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 (output verified with gcc). questionBank.question: A raster display has a resolution of 1024 × 768 pixels and stores 24 bits of colour per pixel. What is the minimum size of its frame buffer? (1 MB = 2²⁰ bytes)
questionBank.explanation: Bits = 1024 × 768 × 24. Bytes = 1024 × 768 × 3 = 2,359,296. In megabytes: 2,359,296 / 1,048,576 = 2.25 MB. The option 0.75 MB forgets that 24 bits is 3 bytes (uses 1 byte per pixel); 1.5 MB uses 2 bytes per pixel; 3 MB uses 4 bytes per pixel (32-bit colour).

questionBank.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) has the functional dependencies AB → C, C → D, D → E and E → A. How many candidate keys does R have?

questionBank.question:
Four processes arrive as follows (times in ms):
P1: arrival 0, burst 5
P2: arrival 1, burst 3
P3: arrival 2, burst 1
P4: arrival 3, burst 2
They are scheduled by round robin with a time quantum of 2 ms. A process that arrives at the same instant as another is pre-empted joins the ready queue before the pre-empted process. Context-switch time is negligible. What is the average waiting time?
questionBank.explanation: Gantt chart: 0–2 P1 (P2 and P3 arrive, then P1 re-joins: queue P2, P3, P1); 2–4 P2 (P4 arrives at 3, then P2 re-joins: queue P3, P1, P4, P2); 4–5 P3 finishes; 5–7 P1 (queue P4, P2, P1); 7–9 P4 finishes; 9–10 P2 finishes; 10–11 P1 finishes. Completion: P1 11, P2 10, P3 5, P4 9. Turnaround = completion − arrival: 11, 9, 3, 6. Waiting = turnaround − burst: 6, 6, 2, 4. Average = 18 / 4 = 4.5 ms (checked by simulation). Getting the tie at t = 2 wrong (putting P1 before P3) changes the whole chart, which is why the question states the rule.

questionBank.question: Three processes share identical units of a single resource type. Each process may need up to 4 units at the same time, and acquires them one at a time. What is the minimum number of units that guarantees the system can never deadlock?

One extra unit lets some process reach its maximum of 4, finish and release its units, after which the others can finish too. Keeping only the listed keys: 20 (C), 40 (D), 30 (B), 70 (E), 50 (A). The trap "C, B, D, …" is the inorder pattern; in postorder the root of every subtree comes after both its children.

questionBank.question: What is the solution of the recurrence T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n², with T(1) = 1?
questionBank.explanation: Here a = 4, b = 2, so n^(log_b a) = n^(log₂ 4) = n². The driving function f(n) = n² is Θ(n^(log_b a)), which is case 2 of the master theorem: T(n) = Θ(n² log n). Intuitively, each of the log₂ n levels of the recursion tree does n² total work (level i has 4ⁱ subproblems of cost (n/2ⁱ)² each). Θ(n²) is the trap of looking only at f(n).

A, B, C, D and E
questionBank.explanation: A false: Dijkstra finalises a vertex when it is extracted, assuming no later path can be shorter; a negative edge found later can break that, even without a negative cycle. B true: if a (V)-th relaxation round still improves some distance, a negative cycle is reachable. C true: three nested loops over V. D true: union–find checks in near-constant time whether an edge would create a cycle. E true: BFS explores in order of distance in edges. So B, C, D and E only.

B. The Bellman–Ford algorithm can detect a negative-weight cycle reachable from the source.
C. The Floyd–Warshall algorithm runs in O(V³) time.
D. Kruskal’s algorithm is usually implemented with a disjoint-set (union–find) structure.
E. BFS finds shortest paths (by number of edges) from the source in an unweighted graph.

questionBank.question: Keys 12, 22, 32, 42, 5 and 15 are inserted in that order into an initially empty hash table of size 10 with h(k) = k mod 10 and linear probing. In which slot does the key 15 end up?

This shows primary clustering: keys with different home slots (5 and 15 hash to 5, but the run started at 2) join one long run.

questionBank.question: Let L be the set of all strings over {a, b} whose third symbol from the right end is a. How many states does the minimal DFA for L have?
questionBank.explanation: An NFA needs only 4 states (guess the position of the a, then read exactly two more symbols), but a DFA must remember the last three symbols read, because any two different 3-symbol suffixes can be distinguished: if they differ at position j from the right, appending j − 1 more symbols brings that position to the third place from the end. So there are 2³ = 8 Myhill–Nerode classes, and the minimal DFA has 8 states (confirmed by counting distinct residual languages by program). In general "n-th symbol from the end is a" needs 2ⁿ DFA states, the standard example of exponential blow-up in subset construction.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: A is true: it is proved with the pumping lemma for CFLs (the pumped part vxy can touch at most two of the three blocks, so the counts become unequal). R is true: {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} and {aᵐbⁿcⁿ} are both context-free but their intersection is {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}. Note that R is usually proved using A, not the other way round; the non-closure does not by itself show that this particular language is not context-free. So both are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

stmts: Assertion (A): The language {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 1} is not context-free.
Reason (R): The class of context-free languages is not closed under intersection.

questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: a universal TM can simulate M on w and accept if it halts, so HALT is recursively enumerable; Turing’s diagonal argument shows it is not recursive. Statement II is false: if both L and its complement were r.e., L would be recursive (run both recognisers in parallel). Since HALT is r.e. but not recursive, its complement is not r.e. So Statement I is true and Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: The halting problem for Turing machines is undecidable, but the set of (machine, input) pairs on which the machine halts is recursively enumerable.
Statement II: The complement of every recursively enumerable language is also recursively enumerable.

questionBank.question: Which of the following languages are regular?
options: A, B, C and E only
A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A regular: it is a*b*. B not regular: a DFA cannot count an unbounded number of a’s (pumping lemma). C regular: the counts of 01 and 10 can differ by at most 1, and they are equal exactly when the string is empty or starts and ends with the same symbol, which a small DFA checks. D not regular: the gaps between consecutive squares grow without bound, which contradicts pumping. E regular: a 3-state DFA counts length mod 3. So A, C and E only. Language C is the classic trap: it looks like a counting language but is regular.

stmts: A. {aⁿbᵐ | n, m ≥ 0}
B. {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0}
C. {w ∈ {0, 1}* | w contains equally many occurrences of the substrings 01 and 10}
D. {aᵏ | k is a perfect square}
E. {w ∈ {a, b}* | the length of w is divisible by 3}

questionBank.question: Arrange the following phases of a compiler in the order in which they are applied to a source program.
questionBank.explanation: The front end reads characters and groups them into tokens (lexical analysis, B), builds a parse tree from the tokens (syntax analysis, A) and checks types and declarations (semantic analysis, D). It then produces an intermediate representation such as three-address code (C), which is optimised (E) before target code generation. So B, A, D, C, E. The symbol table and error handler interact with all phases.

B. Lexical analysis
C. Intermediate code generation
D. Semantic analysis
E. Code optimisation

questionBank.question:
How many tokens does a C lexical analyser produce for the following statement?
printf("x=%d", x+++1);
questionBank.explanation: The lexer uses maximal munch, so x+++1 is split as x, ++, +, 1. Tokens: printf, (, "x=%d", comma, x, ++, +, 1, ), ; which is 10 tokens (checked with a maximal-munch tokenizer). The string literal is one token no matter what it contains (so %d and = inside it do not count). Counting + + + as three tokens gives 11; splitting the literal gives even more.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A. LL(1) is top-down, predicts with FIRST/FOLLOW and needs a grammar without left recursion or common prefixes (II). B. SLR(1) builds LR(0) item sets and puts a reduce by A → α in the columns of FOLLOW(A) (I). C. LALR(1) merges LR(1) states that have the same core, giving as many states as SLR with more precise lookaheads; YACC/Bison generate LALR(1) parsers (IV). D. CLR(1) uses the full LR(1) items and is the most powerful of the four, at the cost of many more states (III).

II. Top-down predictive parser that uses FIRST and FOLLOW sets and cannot handle left recursion
III. Uses full LR(1) item sets and usually has the largest number of states
IV. Merges LR(1) states with identical cores; the method used by YACC

Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: A is true: L-attributed definitions restrict only the inherited attributes (they may depend on the parent’s inherited attributes and on left siblings). An S-attributed definition has no inherited attributes at all, so it meets the restriction trivially. R is also true: that is exactly why the L restriction exists. But R states an evaluation property of L-attributed definitions; it does not explain why S-attributed ones are included. The explanation of A is that S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes. So both are true and R is not the explanation.

stmts: Assertion (A): Every S-attributed definition is also L-attributed.
Reason (R): An L-attributed definition can be evaluated in a single depth-first, left-to-right traversal of the parse tree.

questionBank.question:
For the assignment
a = (b + c) * (b + c) − (b + c) / d
what is the minimum number of three-address instructions (each with at most one operator on the right-hand side, the last one assigning to a) obtained after common-subexpression elimination using a DAG?
questionBank.explanation: The DAG has one node for b + c, shared by all three occurrences. The interior nodes are +, *, / and −, so the code is: t1 = b + c; t2 = t1 * t1; t3 = t1 / d; a = t2 − t3. That is 4 instructions (counted from the DAG by program). Without eliminating the common subexpression, b + c would be computed three times, giving 6 instructions.

questionBank.question: A telephone channel has a bandwidth of 3 kHz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 30 dB. Its Shannon capacity is approximately:
questionBank.explanation: Convert dB to a ratio: 30 dB = 10^(30/10) = 1000. C = B log₂(1 + SNR) = 3000 × log₂ 1001 ≈ 3000 × 9.967 ≈ 29,902 bps ≈ 29.9 kbps. The trap 90 kbps uses 30 (the dB value) as if it were log₂(1 + SNR); 9.97 kbps forgets to multiply by the bandwidth in kHz properly (uses 1 kHz).

questionBank.question: A host has the IP address 192.168.10.100 with prefix /26. What is the broadcast address of its subnet?
questionBank.explanation: A /26 mask is 255.255.255.192, so each subnet has 2⁶ = 64 addresses in the last octet: blocks 0–63, 64–127, 128–191, 192–255. 100 falls in 64–127, so the network address is 192.168.10.64 and the broadcast address is 192.168.10.127 (verified with Python’s ipaddress module). The subnet has 62 usable hosts, 65 to 126. 192.168.10.255 is the broadcast of the /24, and .128 is the next subnet’s network address.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both are true. Example with m = 2 and window 4: frames 0, 1, 2, 3 arrive and the receiver now expects 0 again. If all ACKs are lost, the sender times out and resends frame 0, which the receiver wrongly accepts as a new frame 0. With window 2ᵐ − 1 = 3, the receiver would be expecting 3 while the resent frame is 0, so the duplicate is rejected. R is exactly the reason for the bound in A, so R explains A. (Selective Repeat needs the stricter bound 2ᵐ⁻¹.)

stmts: Assertion (A): In Go-Back-N ARQ with m-bit sequence numbers, the sender window size can be at most 2ᵐ − 1.
Reason (R): With a window of 2ᵐ, if all acknowledgements of a full window are lost, the receiver cannot tell the retransmitted frames from new frames with the same sequence numbers.

questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: UDP is connectionless and provides no ordering, acknowledgement, retransmission or flow control; applications that need order must handle it themselves. Statement II is false: the TCP header is 20 bytes without options, but options (maximum segment size, window scale, SACK, timestamps) can extend it to 60 bytes; the 4-bit data offset (header length) field gives the length in 32-bit words, 5 to 15. So both statements are false.

stmts: Statement I: UDP guarantees that datagrams are delivered to the application in the order they were sent.
Statement II: The TCP header always has a fixed length of 20 bytes because TCP does not support header options.

questionBank.question: Alice and Bob run the Diffie–Hellman key exchange with the public prime p = 29 and generator g = 2. Alice’s secret is a = 5 and Bob’s secret is b = 9. What is the shared secret key?
questionBank.explanation: Alice sends A = gᵃ mod p = 2⁵ mod 29 = 32 mod 29 = 3. Bob sends B = gᵇ mod p = 2⁹ mod 29 = 512 mod 29 = 19 (29 × 17 = 493). Alice computes Bᵃ mod p = 19⁵ mod 29: 19² = 361 ≡ 13, 19⁴ ≡ 13² = 169 ≡ 24, 19⁵ ≡ 24 × 19 = 456 ≡ 21. Bob computes Aᵇ mod p = 3⁹ mod 29: 3³ = 27 ≡ −2, so 3⁹ ≡ (−2)³ = −8 ≡ 21. Both get g^(ab) mod p = 2⁴⁵ mod 29 = 21 (checked with pow). The trap 28 multiplies the public values (3 × 19 = 57 ≡ 28, which is g^(a+b)); 3 and 19 are just the public values A and B, which an eavesdropper already sees.

questionBank.question: A slotted ALOHA channel has a data rate of 100 kbps and all frames are 1000 bits long, so one slot carries one frame. If the offered load is G = 1 frame per slot, what is the throughput in successful frames per second (to one decimal place)?
questionBank.explanation: There are 100,000 / 1000 = 100 slots per second. For slotted ALOHA the throughput per slot is S = G e^(−G); with G = 1, S = e^(−1) ≈ 0.368 frames per slot, which is the maximum. So the throughput is 100 × 0.368 ≈ 36.8 frames per second. 18.4 comes from the pure-ALOHA formula S = G e^(−2G) at G = 0.5, and 100 ignores collisions.

IDS repeats depth-limited DFS with limits 0, 1, 2, …, combining DFS memory with BFS completeness and optimality for unit costs (IV). D. A* expands the node with the lowest f(n) = g(n) + h(n) (III).

questionBank.question: A two-ply game tree has a MAX root with three MIN children. Reading left to right, the leaves below them are (5, 9, 7), (4, 11, 3) and (8, 6, 10). What is the minimax value of the root, and how many leaves are not evaluated by alpha–beta pruning with left-to-right ordering?
questionBank.explanation: MIN values: min(5, 9, 7) = 5, min(4, 11, 3) = 3, min(8, 6, 10) = 6. The root takes max(5, 3, 6) = 6. Alpha–beta: after the first child, α = 5 at the root. At the second child the first leaf 4 makes that MIN node’s value ≤ 4 < α, so leaves 11 and 3 are pruned (2 leaves). At the third child, 8 and 6 are both above α = 5, so no cut is possible and 10 must also be examined. Result: value 6 with 2 leaves pruned (checked by running minimax and alpha–beta).

questionBank.question: A population has four chromosomes with fitness values 10, 20, 30 and 40. Roulette-wheel selection is used to fill a mating pool of size 4. What is the expected number of copies of the chromosome with fitness 30 in the pool?
questionBank.explanation: Total fitness = 10 + 20 + 30 + 40 = 100, so the selection probability of the chromosome with fitness 30 is 30/100 = 0.3. With 4 independent spins, the expected count is 4 × 0.3 = 1.2. Equivalently, expected count = fᵢ / f̄ = 30 / 25 = 1.2. The option 0.3 is the probability for one spin, not the expected count.

Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: XOR is not linearly separable; (0,0) and (1,1) give 0 while (0,1) and (1,0) give 1, and no single line separates the two classes, so at least one hidden layer is needed. Statement II is true: this is the perceptron convergence theorem (Rosenblatt; Novikoff’s bound on the number of updates). So Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: A single-layer perceptron can learn the XOR function of two inputs.
Statement II: The perceptron learning rule converges in a finite number of steps if the training data are linearly separable.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following stages of natural language understanding in the order in which they are usually applied.
questionBank.explanation: The standard sequence (as in Rich and Knight) is: morphological analysis splits words into morphemes (B); syntactic analysis parses the word sequence into a structure (D); semantic analysis assigns meanings (A); discourse integration relates the sentence to the ones around it, for example resolving pronouns (E); pragmatic analysis reinterprets the meaning in context to find what was actually intended (C). So B, D, A, E, C.

stmts: A. Semantic analysis
B. Morphological analysis
C. Pragmatic analysis
D. Syntactic analysis
E. Discourse integration

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation:
Statement I is true. If one y₀ works for every x, then for each x we can pick that same y₀, so ∀x ∃y P(x, y) holds. (The converse ∀x ∃y → ∃y ∀x is NOT valid: on the integers, “for every x there is a larger y” is true but “some y is larger than every x” is false.)
Statement II is false. Take p = F, r = F (q anything): (p → q) → r = T → F = F, but p → (q → r) = T because the premise p is false. Implication is not associative.
So Statement I is true and Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: For every predicate P(x, y) over every domain, ∃y ∀x P(x, y) → ∀x ∃y P(x, y) is valid.
Statement II: (p → q) → r is logically equivalent to p → (q → r).

questionBank.question:
Match List I with List II
Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4}. List I describes a kind of binary relation on A and List II gives how many such relations exist.
questionBank.explanation:
n = 4, so there are n² = 16 ordered pairs, 4 diagonal and 12 off-diagonal (6 unordered pairs {i, j}).
A. Reflexive: all 4 diagonal pairs forced in, the 12 others free: 2¹² = 4096 (IV).
B. Symmetric: diagonal free (2⁴) and each of the 6 pairs {i, j} is in or out together (2⁶): 2¹⁰ = 1024 (III).
C. Antisymmetric: diagonal free (2⁴); each of the 6 pairs has 3 choices (neither, only (i, j), only (j, i)): 2⁴·3⁶ = 16 × 729 = 11664 (I).
D. Total 2¹⁶ = 65536; reflexive 4096; irreflexive 4096; none is both (n ≥ 1). Neither = 65536 − 8192 = 57344 (II).
Answer: A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II. The trap options swap the symmetric and antisymmetric counts.

a: D. Relations that are neither reflexive nor irreflexive
