questionBank.question: In the group U(15) = {1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14} under multiplication modulo 15, what is the order of the element 7?
questionBank.explanation: The order of g is the least k ≥ 1 with gᵏ ≡ 1 (mod 15). 7¹ = 7; 7² = 49 ≡ 4; 7³ = 28 ≡ 13; 7⁴ = 91 ≡ 1. So the order is 4. By Lagrange, it must divide |U(15)| = φ(15) = 8, and 4 does. 8 is the order of the group, not of the element (U(15) is not cyclic, so no element has order 8); 7 confuses the element with its order; 2 is the order of 4, 11 and 14.

questionBank.question: A university enrols students from all 12 months of birth. What is the minimum number of students that must be admitted to guarantee that at least 5 of them share a birth month?
questionBank.explanation: Generalised pigeonhole: with 12 boxes, N objects force some box to hold at least ⌈N/12⌉ objects. We need ⌈N/12⌉ ≥ 5, i.e. N > 4 × 12 = 48, so N = 49. With 48 students it is possible to have exactly 4 per month, so 48 does not guarantee it. 60 = 5 × 12 is the number that fills every month to 5, which is not what is asked; 61 has no basis.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: K₂,ₙ is planar for every n. Place the two vertices of the small side above and below a horizontal line and the n others along the line; every edge goes straight up or down without crossing. Only K₃,₃ and K₅ (and their subdivisions) are the Kuratowski obstructions. Statement II is false: a connected simple planar graph with v ≥ 3 has e ≤ 3v − 6 = 3 × 10 − 6 = 24 edges, so 25 edges is impossible.

stmts: Statement I: The complete bipartite graph K₂,₅ is non-planar.
Statement II: A connected simple planar graph with 10 vertices can have 25 edges.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question:
A project has the activities below (durations in days).
A: 3, no predecessor
B: 4, no predecessor
C: 2, after A
D: 4, after A
E: 6, after B and C
F: 3, after D and E
What are the project completion time and the total float of activity D?
questionBank.explanation: Forward pass (earliest finish): A = 3, B = 4, C = 3 + 2 = 5, D = 3 + 4 = 7, E starts at max(4, 5) = 5 and finishes at 11, F starts at max(7, 11) = 11 and finishes at 14. Project time = 14 days. Paths: A–C–E–F = 3 + 2 + 6 + 3 = 14 (critical), B–E–F = 13, A–D–F = 10. Backward pass for D: F must start by 14 − 3 = 11, so D’s latest finish is 11 and latest start 7; earliest start is 3. Total float = 7 − 3 = 4 days. 13 days is the B–E–F path; 10 days is the A–D–F path; a float of 0 would put D on the critical path, which it is not.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: D: the output simply copies D at the clock edge, Q⁺ = D (III). T: toggles when T = 1 and holds when T = 0, Q⁺ = T ⊕ Q (IV). JK: sets with J, resets with K, toggles with J = K = 1: Q⁺ = JQ′ + K′Q (I). SR: sets with S, holds when both are 0, and S = R = 1 is forbidden: Q⁺ = S + R′Q with SR = 0 (II). So A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II. Options that swap C and D confuse the JK and SR equations, which look alike.

h: List II (characteristic equation, Q⁺ = next state)
b: I. Q⁺ = JQ′ + K′Q
II. Q⁺ = S + R′Q
III. Q⁺ = D
IV. Q⁺ = T ⊕ Q

questionBank.question: How many valid states do a 5-bit Johnson (twisted-ring) counter and a 5-bit ring counter have, respectively?
questionBank.explanation: A ring counter circulates a single 1 through n flip-flops, so it has n = 5 states. A Johnson counter feeds the complement of the last flip-flop back to the first; it fills with 1s and then empties, giving 2n = 10 states (00000, 10000, 11000, 11100, 11110, 11111, 01111, 00111, 00011, 00001). 32 = 2⁵ is the state count of a 5-bit binary counter; the remaining 22 patterns of a Johnson counter are invalid (unused) states.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements are correct?
options: A, B, C and E only
A, B, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A: a tree of 2-to-1 MUXes needs 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 31 units (in general n − 1 for n inputs): correct. B: one 2-to-4 decoder drives the enables of four more 2-to-4 decoders: 5 decoders, 16 outputs: correct. C: the decoder produces all 8 minterms, and an OR of the chosen minterms gives any SOP: correct. D: 8 inputs need only log₂ 8 = 3 output lines: incorrect. E: use three variables on the select lines; for each select combination the function of the fourth variable is 0, 1, x or x′, which is fed to that data input: correct. So A, B, C and E only.

stmts: A. A 32-to-1 multiplexer can be built from 31 multiplexers of type 2-to-1.
B. A 4-to-16 decoder can be built from five 2-to-4 decoders that have enable inputs.
C. A 3-to-8 decoder together with OR gates can implement any Boolean function of 3 variables.
D. An 8-input priority encoder needs 4 output lines to encode the index of the active input (excluding the valid bit).
E. An 8-to-1 multiplexer can realise any 4-variable Boolean function if the fourth variable, its complement and the constants 0 and 1 are available at the data inputs.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Two 8-bit two’s complement numbers 10110110 and 11001100 are added. What is the 8-bit result and is there an overflow?
questionBank.explanation: 10110110 = −(01001010) = −74 and 11001100 = −(00110100) = −52. Binary addition: 10110110 + 11001100 = 1 10000010; the carry out of bit 7 is discarded, leaving 10000010 = −126. The true sum −126 lies within the 8-bit range −128 … 127, so there is no overflow. Check with the rule: overflow happens only when two numbers of the same sign give a result of the opposite sign; here both operands and the result are negative. The carry out of the MSB (which is 1 here) is not the overflow flag in two’s complement: that is the trap.

questionBank.question: What decimal value does the IEEE 754 single-precision bit pattern with hexadecimal representation C1440000 hold?
questionBank.explanation: C1440000 = 1100 0001 0100 0100 0000 … in binary. Sign bit = 1 (negative). Exponent field = 1000 0010 = 130, so the true exponent is 130 − 127 = 3. Fraction = 100 0100 0…, so the significand is 1.10001₂ = 1 + 0.5 + 0.03125 = 1.53125. Value = −1.53125 × 2³ = −12.25. −6.125 and −24.5 come from using bias 128 or 126 (an exponent off by one); +12.25 ignores the sign bit.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I: binary to Gray keeps the MSB and XORs each pair of adjacent bits: g₃ = 1, g₂ = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1, g₁ = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1, g₀ = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0, giving 1110: true. Statement II: a code is self-complementing if the code of 9 − d is the bitwise complement of the code of d. In excess-3, 0 = 0011 and 9 = 1100, 1 = 0100 and 8 = 1011, and so on: true. In 8421 BCD, 0 = 0000 but 9 = 1001, not 1111, so BCD is not self-complementing. Both true.

stmts: Statement I: The Gray code of the binary number 1011 is 1110.
Statement II: Excess-3 code is self-complementing, whereas 8421 BCD is not.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Booth’s algorithm multiplies two 8-bit two’s complement numbers, with the multiplier 00111100. Scanning bit pairs (Qᵢ, Qᵢ₋₁) from the least significant end with Q₋₁ = 0, how many add or subtract operations of the multiplicand are performed in total?
questionBank.explanation: Booth’s rule: pair 10 means subtract the multiplicand, 01 means add it, 00 and 11 mean shift only. The multiplier bits from Q₀ to Q₇ are 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0. Pairs (Qᵢ, Qᵢ₋₁): i = 0: (0, 0) none; i = 1: (0, 0) none; i = 2: (1, 0) subtract; i = 3, 4, 5: (1, 1) none; i = 6: (0, 1) add; i = 7: (0, 0) none. Total = 1 subtraction + 1 addition = 2. This is why Booth’s method is efficient for a run of 1s: 00111100 = 64 − 4, one add and one subtract. 4 counts the 1 bits, as the ordinary shift-and-add method would; 8 counts every step.

questionBank.question: A 4-way set-associative cache of 32 KB uses 64-byte blocks. The processor issues 32-bit byte addresses. How many bits does the tag field have?
questionBank.explanation: Number of blocks = 32 KB / 64 B = 2¹⁵ / 2⁶ = 2⁹ = 512. With 4 blocks per set, number of sets = 512 / 4 = 128 = 2⁷, so the set index has 7 bits. The block offset needs log₂ 64 = 6 bits. Tag = 32 − 7 − 6 = 19 bits. 17 is the tag for a direct-mapped cache (9 index bits); 21 is for 16-way; 15 is a distractor.

questionBank.question: A 5-stage pipeline has stage delays of 150, 120, 180, 160 and 140 ps, and each pipeline register adds 20 ps. The non-pipelined version takes the sum of the stage delays per instruction. What is the speedup of the pipeline for 1000 instructions, ignoring hazards?
questionBank.explanation: Pipeline clock = slowest stage + latch = 180 + 20 = 200 ps. Pipelined time for n = 1000 instructions on k = 5 stages = (k + n − 1) × 200 = 1004 × 200 = 200,800 ps. Non-pipelined time = 1000 × (150 + 120 + 180 + 160 + 140) = 1000 × 750 = 750,000 ps. Speedup = 750,000 / 200,800 ≈ 3.74. 3.75 = 750/200 is the limit as n → ∞ (it ignores the 4 fill cycles); 4.17 = 750/180 forgets the latch delay; 5.00 is the ideal k-stage speedup that assumes equal stages.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following steps of a DMA block transfer in the correct order.
questionBank.explanation: The CPU first programs the controller through its registers (A). When the device is ready, the controller requests the bus (B); the CPU grants it after the current bus cycle and puts its bus lines in the high-impedance state (C). The controller then moves the block directly between the device and memory (D), and when the count reaches zero it gives back the bus and informs the CPU with an interrupt (E). So A, B, C, D, E. The CPU cannot grant a bus that has not been requested (so C never precedes B), and the transfer cannot start before the controller has been initialised.

stmts: A. The CPU loads the DMA controller with the starting memory address, the word count and the direction of transfer.
B. The DMA controller raises the bus request (BR) signal.
C. The CPU finishes its current bus cycle, releases the buses and asserts bus grant (BG).
D. The DMA controller transfers the data words directly between the device and memory, decrementing the word count.
E. When the word count reaches zero, the DMA controller releases the bus and interrupts the CPU.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.explanation: (i) By reference, x and y are both aliases of a. x = x + 1 makes a = 3; y = y * x makes a = 3 × 3 = 9. Printed: 9. (ii) By value-result, x and y are local copies initialised to 2. x = 3; y = 2 × 3 = 6. On return the values are copied back left to right: a = x = 3, then a = y = 6, so the last copy wins: 6. Option “9 and 3” assumes a right-to-left copy-back (y first, then x); “3 and 6” forgets the aliasing under call by reference. Call by value would print 2.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: which operation a symbol denotes is fixed when the language is designed (III). B: C leaves the size of int to each compiler and platform, so its range is fixed at language implementation time (IV). C: Java is statically typed; the declaration binds the type when the program is compiled (II). D: an automatic variable gets a cell on the stack each time the function is called, i.e. at run time (I). So A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I. Swapping A and B (design vs implementation) is the standard trap.

a: A. The symbol * bound to the multiplication operation in C
B. The range of values of the type int in C
C. A variable bound to its type in a Java program
D. A local (non-static) variable of a C function bound to a memory cell
b: I. Run time
II. Compile time
III. Language design time
IV. Language implementation time

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: (A) is the definition of dynamic scoping: the binding of a free name depends on the calling sequence, found by walking back through the active activation records (the most recent binding wins). (R) is false: because the declaration that a non-local name refers to is not known until run time, a compiler cannot statically determine its type. This is one of the main arguments against dynamic scoping; static (lexical) scoping is the one that permits compile-time checking. So (A) true, (R) false.

stmts: Assertion (A): Under dynamic scoping, a non-local variable referenced in a procedure is resolved by searching the chain of active procedure calls at run time.
Reason (R): Dynamic scoping makes it easier for a compiler to type-check non-local references statically.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: translating the whole program to machine code before running it is what a compiler does. A pure interpreter decodes and executes the source statement by statement, with no separate machine-code translation of the whole program. Statement II is true: javac produces platform-independent bytecode (an intermediate form), and the JVM executes it by interpretation and JIT compilation, the textbook hybrid model.

stmts: Statement I: A pure interpreter translates the entire source program into machine code before any statement is executed.
Statement II: Java uses a hybrid implementation: source code is compiled to bytecode, which the JVM then interprets or compiles just-in-time.

questionBank.question: What is the output of the following C program?
questionBank.explanation: p starts at a[1]. x = *p++: postfix ++ binds tighter than *, but it yields the old pointer, so x = a[1] = 20 and p moves to a[2]. y = *++p: p first moves to a[3], then y = 40. z = ++*p: this increments the pointed-to value, a[3] becomes 41, and z = 41. p still points to a[3], so a[3] prints 41. Output: 20 40 41 41. “20 40 41 40” forgets that ++*p changes the array element itself; “20 30 31 40” treats *++p as if it did not move p before the read.

questionBank.question: What is the output of the following C program?
questionBank.explanation: s is static: it is initialised once and shared by every call. f(3): s = 3, calls f(2): s = 5, calls f(1): s = 6, returns 6. Back in f(2): r = 6, returns 6 + s = 6 + 6 = 12 (s is now 6, not 5). Back in f(3): r = 12, returns 12 + 6 = 18. The second call f(1) does not reset s: s = 6 + 1 = 7 and it returns 7. Output: 18, then 7. “12” uses the value of s at the time of each call; “1” forgets that a static local keeps its value between calls.

questionBank.question:
The C program below is compiled to an executable and run from the shell as: ./prog alpha beta
What does it print?
questionBank.explanation: argc counts the program name too: argv[0] = "./prog", argv[1] = "alpha", argv[2] = "beta", so argc = 3. argv[argc − 1] = argv[2] = "beta" and its character at index 1 is e. argv[0] + 2 is a pointer two characters into "./prog", so %s prints "prog". Output: 3 e prog. Options with 2 forget that argv[0] is the program name; “b” uses index 0 of the string instead of index 1.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about file handling in C are correct?
questionBank.explanation: A is correct: "r+" requires the file to exist and keeps its contents. B is correct: "w" creates the file or truncates it. C is correct: append mode forces every write to the current end of file, whatever the file position was set to. D is wrong: "r" fails and returns NULL if the file does not exist. E is wrong: the end-of-file indicator is set only after a read operation has tried to go past the end, which is why loops of the form while (!feof(fp)) run one iteration too many. So A, B and C only.

stmts: A. fopen(name, "r+") opens an existing file for both reading and writing without truncating it.
B. fopen(name, "w") truncates an existing file to zero length.
C. In a file opened with mode "a", every write goes to the end of the file, even after an fseek() to an earlier position.
D. fopen(name, "r") creates the file if it does not exist.
E. For an empty file, feof() returns true immediately after fopen(), before any read is attempted.

questionBank.question: What is the output of the following C++ program?
questionBank.explanation: Construction of obj: members are constructed in declaration order before the body of C() runs. m (type A) prints A. n (type B) first constructs its base A, printing A, then B. Then C’s body prints C: “AABC”. Destruction is the exact reverse: C’s body prints c, then members in reverse order: n is destroyed as B then its base A (“ba”), then m (“a”): “cbaa”. Output: AABCcbaa. “CAAB…” runs the body before the members; “…aabc” destroys in construction order instead of reverse.

questionBank.question: A window with corners (10, 20) and (60, 70) is mapped to a viewport with corners (0, 0) and (200, 100). To which viewport point is the window point (35, 45) mapped?
questionBank.explanation: Window-to-viewport mapping: xv = xvmin + (xw − xwmin) × sx with sx = (xvmax − xvmin)/(xwmax − xwmin) = 200/50 = 4, and yv = yvmin + (yw − ywmin) × sy with sy = 100/50 = 2. xv = 0 + (35 − 10) × 4 = 100; yv = 0 + (45 − 20) × 2 = 50. The point is (100, 50), the centre of the viewport, as expected for the centre of the window. (140, 90) forgets to subtract the window minimum (35 × 4, 45 × 2); (50, 100) swaps the scale factors.

questionBank.question: An ER diagram has strong entity sets E1, E2 and E3 with simple attributes, except that E1 also has one multivalued attribute. Relationship R1 between E1 and E2 is one-to-many (E1 on the “one” side), R2 between E2 and E3 is many-to-many, and E4 is a weak entity set identified through E3. What is the minimum number of relational tables needed?
questionBank.explanation: One table each for E1, E2 and E3 (3). The multivalued attribute of E1 needs its own table (E1’s key, value): 4. R1 is 1:N, so it is absorbed into E2 by adding E1’s key as a foreign key: no extra table. R2 is M:N and needs its own table with both keys: 5. The weak entity E4 gets a table whose key is E3’s key plus E4’s partial key, and its identifying relationship is absorbed: 6. Total = 6. 5 forgets the multivalued attribute; 7 wrongly gives R1 its own table; 8 also adds a table for the identifying relationship.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: In the three-schema architecture, logical data independence is the ability to change the conceptual schema (for example, add an attribute) without rewriting external schemas or programs (A-II). Physical data independence is the ability to change the internal schema (file organisation, indexes) without affecting the conceptual schema (B-IV). The external level holds user views (C-III) and the internal level describes storage structures and access paths (D-I). So A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I. Swapping A and B is the most common error; logical independence is the harder one to achieve.

b: I. Describes the physical storage structures and access paths
II. Changing the conceptual schema without changing external schemas or application programs
III. A view of the database for a particular user group
IV. Changing the internal schema without changing the conceptual schema

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: (R) is true: a weak entity set (for example, Dependent of Employee) has only a partial key (the dependent’s name), which is unique only within one owner. (A) is true: because every weak entity needs its owner’s key to be identified, no weak entity can exist without being related to an owner, so its participation in the identifying relationship is total (double line in the ER diagram). The need for the owner’s key is exactly why participation must be total, so (R) explains (A).

stmts: Assertion (A): A weak entity set always participates totally in its identifying relationship.
Reason (R): A weak entity set has no key of its own; its partial key identifies an entity only together with the key of its owner entity.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: with 1:1 cardinality and total participation on both sides, every entity of one set is paired with exactly one entity of the other, so merging them (the “merged relation” option in ER-to-relational mapping) creates no NULLs and no redundancy. Statement II is false: a derived attribute can be computed when needed (in a view or query) and is usually not stored, because storing it creates update anomalies (Age changes every year). So I true, II false.

stmts: Statement I: If a one-to-one relationship has total participation on both sides, the two entity sets and the relationship can be mapped into a single relation.
Statement II: A derived attribute, such as Age computed from DateOfBirth, must always be stored as a column in the relational schema.

questionBank.question: Relation Enrol(Student, Course) contains the tuples (s1, c1), (s1, c2), (s1, c3), (s2, c1), (s2, c3), (s3, c2), (s3, c3), (s4, c1), (s4, c2), (s4, c3). Relation Core(Course) contains c1 and c3. What is the result of Enrol ÷ Core?
questionBank.explanation: Division returns the students enrolled in every course of Core, i.e. both c1 and c3. s1 has c1 and c3 (and c2, which does not matter): yes. s2 has c1 and c3: yes. s3 has c2 and c3 but not c1: no. s4 has c1, c2, c3: yes. Result = {s1, s2, s4}. {s1, s4} wrongly requires all three courses; {s2} requires exactly the Core courses and nothing else; {s1, s2, s3, s4} is a projection, which requires only some Core course.

questionBank.question: A relation R(A, B, C, D, E) has exactly two candidate keys: {A} and {B, C}. How many superkeys does R have?
questionBank.explanation: A superkey is any superset of a candidate key. Supersets of {A}: A must be present and each of B, C, D, E is free: 2⁴ = 16. Supersets of {B, C}: B and C present, A, D, E free: 2³ = 8. Supersets of both, i.e. containing A, B and C: D and E free: 2² = 4. By inclusion–exclusion: 16 + 8 − 4 = 20. 24 double-counts the 4 common sets; 16 counts only the supersets of {A}.

questionBank.question: Which of the following relational algebra equivalences and claims are correct?
options: A, B, C and D only
questionBank.explanation: A: cascading selections combine into one selection with ∧: correct. B: a cascade of projections keeps only the last (outermost) one, provided its attributes are in the inner one: correct. C: selection distributes over set difference: correct. D: projection does not distribute over difference. Counterexample: R = {(1, 2)}, S = {(1, 3)}: π_A(R − S) = {1}, but π_A(R) − π_A(S) = {1} − {1} = ∅. Incorrect. E: {t | ¬(t ∈ R)} describes infinitely many tuples (everything not in R), so it is unsafe. Answer: A, B and C only.

stmts: B. π_A(π_A,B(R)) = π_A(R)
C. σ_c(R − S) = σ_c(R) − σ_c(S)
D. π_A(R − S) = π_A(R) − π_A(S) for all R and S with the same schema
E. The tuple relational calculus expression {t | ¬(t ∈ R)} is safe.

questionBank.question:
Table Emp(id, dept, sal) holds the rows (1, D1, 60), (2, D1, NULL), (3, D2, 70), (4, D2, 40), (5, D2, 80), (6, D3, NULL), (7, D3, 90). What does the following query return?
SELECT dept, COUNT(*), COUNT(sal) FROM Emp GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(sal) > 60;
questionBank.explanation: Aggregates other than COUNT(*) ignore NULLs. D1: AVG(sal) = 60/1 = 60 (the NULL is skipped, not treated as 0), and 60 > 60 is false, so D1 is dropped. D2: AVG = (70 + 40 + 80)/3 = 63.33 > 60, kept, COUNT(*) = 3, COUNT(sal) = 3. D3: AVG = 90/1 = 90 > 60, kept, COUNT(*) = 2 (both rows) but COUNT(sal) = 1. Result: (D2, 3, 3) and (D3, 2, 1). (D3, 2, 2) treats COUNT(sal) like COUNT(*); including D1 misreads > as ≥; “Only (D3, 2, 1)” comes from miscomputing D2’s average.

questionBank.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) has the functional dependencies A → B, BC → D, D → E and E → A. How many candidate keys does R have, and what is its highest normal form?
questionBank.explanation: C appears on no right-hand side, so every key contains C, and C⁺ = {C} is not enough. Try pairs: AC⁺ = {A, C, B, D, E}; BC⁺ = {B, C, D, E, A}; CD⁺ = {C, D, E, A, B}; CE⁺ = {C, E, A, B, D}. All four are keys and each is minimal (C alone is not), so there are 4 candidate keys: AC, BC, CD, CE. Every attribute appears in some key, so all attributes are prime and every FD has a prime right-hand side: R is in 3NF. It is not in BCNF because in A → B (and D → E, E → A) the left side is not a superkey. Answer: 4; 3NF.

questionBank.question: A login page builds its SQL query by concatenating user input into the string. Which measure is the most effective primary defence against SQL injection?
options: Using prepared statements with bound parameters so that input is always treated as data
Hiding database error messages from the user
Encrypting the password column in the database
Allowing only POST requests from the login form
questionBank.explanation: SQL injection works because input such as  x’ OR ’1’=’1  becomes part of the SQL text and changes the query’s structure. Prepared (parameterised) statements send the query structure and the values separately, so the input can never be parsed as SQL: this removes the vulnerability at its root. Hiding error messages only makes attacks harder to tune (blind injection still works); encrypting passwords protects stored data but not the query; POST versus GET makes no difference to injection. Least-privilege database accounts and input validation are useful extra layers.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: Pass 1 scans the source, advances the location counter and records every label’s address in the symbol table (A-II). Pass 2 uses the opcode table and the completed symbol table to produce the object code (B-IV). A relocating loader adjusts the address fields marked by the relocation bits or modification records when the program is loaded somewhere other than its assembled origin (C-III). A linkage editor combines object modules and resolves their external (EXTRN/ENTRY) references into one load module (D-I). So A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I.

a: A. Pass 1 of a two-pass assembler
B. Pass 2 of a two-pass assembler
b: I. Resolves external references between separately assembled modules and produces a single load module
II. Assigns addresses to labels using the location counter and builds the symbol table
III. Modifies address-dependent words of a program, using relocation information, when it is placed at a new load address
IV. Translates opcodes and substitutes symbol addresses to generate the object code

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: (A) is true: when a one-pass assembler meets JMP LOOP before LOOP is defined, the address is unknown, so it records the reference (in a forward-reference list or the table of incomplete instructions) and patches it when the label appears. (R) is also true: pass 1 of a two-pass assembler defines all symbols. But (R) describes the other design; the reason (A) is needed is that a one-pass assembler has no earlier pass to collect the addresses. So both are true, but (R) does not explain (A).

stmts: Assertion (A): A one-pass assembler must handle forward references, for example by leaving the address field blank and back-patching it once the label is defined.
Reason (R): In a two-pass assembler, the symbol table is built during the first pass.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about macros and subroutines are correct?
options: A, B, C and E only
questionBank.explanation: A: expansion is done by the macro processor before or during assembly: correct. B: every call inserts a full copy of the body, whereas a subroutine exists once: correct. C: a subroutine needs a call instruction, a return and saving/restoring the return address at run time; an expanded macro is straight-line code: correct. D is wrong: macros routinely take positional or keyword parameters that are substituted during expansion. E: conditional assembly (AIF/AGO-style) and macro calls inside macro definitions are standard features: correct. So A, B, C and E only.

stmts: A. A macro call is expanded at assembly (or preprocessing) time, not at run time.
B. When a macro is called many times, the object code is usually larger than with an equivalent subroutine.
C. A subroutine call has run-time linkage overhead (call, return, saving the return address) that an expanded macro does not have.
D. Macros cannot take parameters.
E. Many macro processors support conditional expansion and nested macro calls.

questionBank.question: A counting semaphore S is initialised to 4. Its value may become negative, in which case the magnitude equals the number of blocked processes. Twelve wait (P) operations and five signal (V) operations are then performed on S. What is the final value of S?
questionBank.explanation: Each wait decrements S by 1 and each signal increments it by 1, whatever the order, so the final value is 4 − 12 + 5 = −3. With this (Silberschatz-style) implementation, −3 means three processes are blocked on S. 3 is the number of blocked processes, not the value; 1 and −1 come from arithmetic slips.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: Peterson’s algorithm uses one turn variable and two flags and is proved correct for two processes; extending it to n processes needs a different construction (for example the filter algorithm or Lamport’s bakery algorithm). Statement II is false: on a uniprocessor, a process spinning on a lock wastes its whole time slice, because the lock holder cannot run until the spinner is preempted. Spinlocks pay off on multiprocessors when locks are held briefly. Both false.

stmts: Statement I: Peterson’s algorithm, exactly as written for two processes, guarantees mutual exclusion for any number of processes.
Statement II: On a single-processor system, a spinlock (busy-waiting semaphore) is always preferable to a blocking semaphore.

questionBank.question: In a bounded-buffer producer–consumer solution with semaphores mutex = 1, empty = n and full = 0, the producer is changed to execute wait(mutex) BEFORE wait(empty), while the consumer is unchanged (wait(full), then wait(mutex)). What can happen?
options: Nothing changes, since both orders are equivalent
A consumer may read an empty slot
Deadlock, when the producer holds mutex and blocks on empty because the buffer is full
Two producers may write into the same slot
questionBank.explanation: If the buffer is full (empty = 0), the producer acquires mutex and then blocks on wait(empty) while still holding mutex. The consumer, which is the only process that could signal empty, first passes wait(full) and then blocks on wait(mutex). Each waits for the other: deadlock. The correct order is to wait on the counting semaphore (empty/full) first and on mutex second. Mutual exclusion itself is not broken, so the “same slot” and “empty slot” options are wrong.

questionBank.question: How many times is the character 1 printed by the following program? (Assume every fork() succeeds.)
questionBank.explanation: Let the original process be P. The first fork() creates C1. In P it returns a non-zero PID, so || short-circuits, the condition is true, and P forks again, creating C2: both P and C2 print. In C1 the first fork() returned 0, so C1 evaluates the second fork(), creating C3. In C1 that call returns non-zero, so the condition is true and C1 forks C4: C1 and C4 print. In C3 the second fork() returned 0, so the condition is false and C3 just prints. Printers: P, C2, C1, C4, C3 = 5 processes, so 1 is printed 5 times. 6 ignores the short-circuit; 4 forgets C3.

questionBank.question: Four processes arrive as follows (arrival time, CPU burst in ms): P1 (0, 5), P2 (1, 3), P3 (2, 6), P4 (4, 2). They are scheduled with Round Robin, quantum = 2 ms. A newly arrived process joins the ready queue before a preempted process that is re-queued at the same instant. What is the average waiting time?
questionBank.explanation: Gantt chart: P1 0–2, P2 2–4, P3 4–6, P1 6–8, P4 8–10, P2 10–11, P3 11–13, P1 13–14, P3 14–16. (At t = 2, P3 arrives and is queued before the preempted P1; at t = 4, P4 arrives before the preempted P2.) Completion times: P1 = 14, P2 = 11, P3 = 16, P4 = 10. Turnaround = completion − arrival: 14, 10, 14, 6. Waiting = turnaround − burst: 9, 7, 8, 4, total 28, average 28/4 = 7.0 ms. 11.0 ms is the average turnaround time; the others come from queuing the preempted process first.

questionBank.question: A system uses 32-bit logical addresses, a page size of 8 KB and single-level page tables with 4-byte entries. What is the size of the page table of one process?
questionBank.explanation: Page size 8 KB = 2¹³ bytes, so the offset takes 13 bits and the page number 32 − 13 = 19 bits. The page table has 2¹⁹ entries × 4 bytes = 2²¹ bytes = 2 MB. 4 MB comes from a 4 KB page (2²⁰ entries); 1 MB from 2-byte entries; 512 KB from a 32 KB page.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements about three periodic real-time tasks with (execution time, period) = (1, 4), (2, 6) and (3, 12), where the deadline equals the period.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Utilisation U = 1/4 + 2/6 + 3/12 = 0.25 + 0.333 + 0.25 = 0.833. Statement I is true: EDF schedules any such set with U ≤ 1. Statement II is false: the Liu–Layland bound n(2^(1/n) − 1) = 3(2^(1/3) − 1) ≈ 0.780 is only a sufficient condition. U = 0.833 exceeds it, so the test is inconclusive, not a proof of failure. Exact response-time analysis shows RM succeeds: task 3 (lowest priority) has response time R = 3 + ⌈R/4⌉·1 + ⌈R/6⌉·2, iterating 6 → 7 → 9 → 10 → 10, and 10 ≤ 12. So I true, II false.

stmts: Statement I: The task set is schedulable under Earliest Deadline First (EDF).
Statement II: The total utilisation exceeds the Liu–Layland bound for three tasks, so the set cannot be scheduled by Rate Monotonic (RM) scheduling.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: XP is known for its engineering practices: pair programming, test-first coding, refactoring, small releases (A-III). Scrum is a management framework: sprints, product and sprint backlogs, daily Scrum (B-I). ASD, from Highsmith, replaces plan–design–build with the speculate, collaborate and learn phases of adaptive cycles (C-IV). DSDM, the Dynamic Systems Development Method, grew out of RAD and uses time-boxing and MoSCoW (must, should, could, won’t) prioritisation (D-II). So A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

II. MoSCoW prioritisation within fixed time-boxes, evolved from RAD
III. Pair programming, test-first development and continuous refactoring
IV. A speculate–collaborate–learn life cycle driven by mission and time-boxed adaptive cycles

questionBank.question: According to IEEE 830, which of the following are characteristics of a good Software Requirements Specification (SRS)?

A, B, D and E only

questionBank.question: In a data flow diagram (DFD), which of the following connections is NOT allowed?
options: A process reading from a data store
An external entity sending data to a process
A data flow going directly from one data store to another data store
A process sending data to another process
questionBank.explanation: In a DFD every data flow must begin or end at a process, because data can only be moved or transformed by a process. A flow directly from one data store to another (or from an external entity straight into a data store, or between two external entities) is therefore illegal: some process must perform the transfer. The other three connections are all legal.

questionBank.question: The control-flow graph of a module (a single connected component) has 13 nodes and 17 edges. What is its cyclomatic complexity, and hence the number of independent paths in a basis set?
questionBank.explanation: McCabe’s cyclomatic complexity V(G) = E − N + 2P = 17 − 13 + 2 × 1 = 6. It equals the number of linearly independent paths in a basis set, i.e. the minimum number of test cases for basis path testing, and it also equals the number of regions of the planar flow graph, and the number of binary predicate nodes + 1. 4 uses E − N; 5 uses E − N + 1; 30 adds E and N.

questionBank.question: A system has the following function counts, all of average complexity (weights in brackets): 10 external inputs (4), 8 external outputs (5), 5 external inquiries (4), 4 internal logical files (10) and 2 external interface files (7). The sum of the 14 value adjustment factors is 42. What is the adjusted function point count?
questionBank.explanation: Unadjusted FP = 10×4 + 8×5 + 5×4 + 4×10 + 2×7 = 40 + 40 + 20 + 40 + 14 = 154. Value adjustment factor VAF = 0.65 + 0.01 × ΣFᵢ = 0.65 + 0.42 = 1.07. FP = 154 × 1.07 = 164.78. 154 is the unadjusted count; 144.76 uses 0.94 (1.36 − 0.42) as the factor; 169.40 uses a factor of 1.10.

questionBank.question: In the RMMM (Risk Mitigation, Monitoring and Management) approach, what is the purpose of risk monitoring?
options: To buy insurance against every identified risk
To track whether predicted risks actually occur, check that the planned aversion steps are being applied, and gather information for future risk analysis
To remove all risks from the project before coding starts
To assign the blame for a risk that has occurred to a team member
questionBank.explanation: Pressman describes three objectives of risk monitoring: assess whether a predicted risk does in fact occur, ensure that the risk aversion (mitigation) steps defined for it are being properly applied, and collect information that can be used for future risk analysis (and determine which problems were caused by which risks). Mitigation is the proactive avoidance plan; management and contingency planning handle a risk that has become real. No plan can remove all risks, and blame assignment is not a goal.

questionBank.question: An array is declared as A[−3 … 6][4 … 13] with 4-byte elements, stored in column-major order from base address 2000. What is the address of A[2][7]?
questionBank.explanation: Rows run from −3 to 6 (10 rows) and columns from 4 to 13 (10 columns). In column-major order, whole columns are stored one after another, so the element offset = (j − 4) × (number of rows) + (i − (−3)) = (7 − 4) × 10 + (2 + 3) = 30 + 5 = 35. Address = 2000 + 35 × 4 = 2140. 2212 is the row-major answer ((2 + 3) × 10 + 3 = 53 elements); 2136 and 2208 come from forgetting the negative lower bound (using i = 2 or losing one element).

questionBank.question: What is the value of the postfix expression 8 3 4 * + 6 2 / − 2 ^ (where ^ denotes exponentiation)?
questionBank.explanation: Scan left to right with a stack. Push 8, 3, 4. * pops 4 and 3, pushes 12. + pops 12 and 8, pushes 20. Push 6, 2. / pops 2 and 6, pushes 6/2 = 3 (the first popped value is the right operand). − pops 3 and 20, pushes 17. Push 2. ^ pops 2 and 17, pushes 17² = 289. Result 289. 17 stops before the last operator; 324 = 18² and 256 = 16² come from getting the order of operands wrong in the / or − step.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: * has higher precedence, so b * c is done first and then added to a: a b c * + (III). B: the parentheses force a + b first: a b + c * (I). C: b + c first, then multiplied by a: a b c + * (IV). D: a * b first, then + c: a b * c + (II). So A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II. Operand order never changes in infix-to-postfix conversion; only operator positions move, which is a quick way to eliminate options.

b: I. a b + c *
II. a b * c +
III. a b c * +
IV. a b c + *

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: with the “one empty slot” convention, the queue is full when (rear + 1) mod n = front, so it holds at most n − 1 elements. Statement II is true: push onto an in-stack; to dequeue, pop from an out-stack, and when it is empty move all elements of the in-stack into it. Each element is pushed and popped at most twice in total, so the amortised cost per operation is O(1), even though one dequeue may cost O(n).

stmts: Statement I: A circular queue implemented in an array of size n, which keeps one slot empty to distinguish full from empty, can hold n elements.
Statement II: A queue can be implemented using two stacks so that each enqueue and dequeue takes O(1) amortised time.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A binary heap (a complete binary tree) contains 100 nodes. What are its height (root at depth 0) and its number of leaves?
questionBank.explanation: Height of a complete binary tree with n nodes = ⌊log₂ n⌋ = ⌊log₂ 100⌋ = 6 (since 2⁶ = 64 ≤ 100 < 128). In array form, the nodes with indices ⌊n/2⌋ + 1 … n are leaves, so leaves = n − ⌊n/2⌋ = 100 − 50 = 50. 7 counts levels instead of edges on the longest path; 51 is ⌈n/2⌉ + 1, a slip in the leaf formula.

questionBank.question: The keys 42, 17, 63, 8, 29, 51, 77, 23, 35, 70 are inserted in this order into an initially empty binary search tree. What is the postorder traversal of the tree?
questionBank.explanation: Build the tree: 42 is the root; 17 left, 63 right; 8 is left of 17; 29 right of 17; 51 left of 63; 77 right of 63; 23 left of 29; 35 right of 29; 70 left of 77. Postorder (left, right, root): left subtree of 42 gives 8, 23, 35, 29, 17; right subtree gives 51, 70, 77, 63; then 42. Answer: 8, 23, 35, 29, 17, 51, 70, 77, 63, 42. The sorted sequence is the inorder traversal; the sequence beginning with 42 is the preorder; the third option swaps 23 and 35, children of 29.

questionBank.question: The keys 30, 20, 10, 25, 28 are inserted in this order into an initially empty AVL tree, with rebalancing after each insertion. What is the preorder traversal of the final tree?
questionBank.explanation: Insert 30, 20, 10: a left-left case at 30, so a single right rotation makes 20 the root with children 10 and 30. Insert 25: it goes left of 30; balanced. Insert 28: it goes right of 25. Now 30 has balance +2 with its left child 25 leaning right: a left-right case. Rotate left at 25, then right at 30, making 28 the parent of 25 and 30. Final tree: 20 (10, 28 (25, 30)). Preorder: 20, 10, 28, 25, 30. The second option is the unbalanced BST without the double rotation.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements are correct?
options: A, B, C and E only
A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A: the minimum-occupancy rule of a B-tree: correct. B: the defining feature of a B+ tree: correct. C: a B* tree delays splits by redistributing keys to a sibling and splits two full nodes into three, so nodes stay at least 2/3 full: correct. D is wrong: in a right in-threaded tree, the NULL right pointer points to the inorder successor (left threads point to the predecessor). E: there are 2n pointer fields and n − 1 of them are used by edges, leaving 2n − (n − 1) = n + 1 NULLs, which is exactly what threading reuses: correct. So A, B, C and E only.

stmts: A. In a B-tree of order m, every internal node other than the root has at least ⌈m/2⌉ children.
B. In a B+ tree, all data pointers are stored in the leaves, and the leaves are linked to support sequential access.
C. A B* tree requires every non-root node to be at least two-thirds full, using redistribution between siblings before splitting.
D. In a right in-threaded binary tree, a NULL right pointer is replaced by a thread to the node’s inorder predecessor.
E. A binary tree with n nodes, stored with two child pointers per node, has exactly n + 1 NULL pointers.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A hash table of size 11 uses h(k) = k mod 11 with linear probing. The keys 43, 21, 32, 17, 28, 54 are inserted in this order into an empty table. In which slot is 54 stored, and how many probes (slots examined, including the final one) does its insertion take?
questionBank.explanation: 43 mod 11 = 10 → slot 10. 21 mod 11 = 10, taken, so slot 0 (wrap-around). 32 mod 11 = 10, taken; slot 0 taken; slot 1. 17 mod 11 = 6 → slot 6. 28 mod 11 = 6, taken → slot 7. 54 mod 11 = 10: slot 10 taken, slot 0 taken, slot 1 taken, slot 2 free. So 54 goes to slot 2 after examining 4 slots (10, 0, 1, 2). Forgetting the wrap-around from slot 10 to slot 0 is the usual slip; “3 probes” counts only the collisions.

questionBank.question: An algorithm must find both the maximum and the minimum of 100 distinct numbers using only comparisons. What is the minimum number of comparisons needed in the worst case?
questionBank.explanation: Compare the elements in pairs: 50 comparisons split them into 50 “winners” and 50 “losers”. The maximum is among the winners (49 comparisons) and the minimum among the losers (49 comparisons). Total = 50 + 49 + 49 = 148 = ⌈3n/2⌉ − 2. An adversary argument shows no algorithm can do better, so 148 is also the lower bound. 198 = 2(n − 1) finds the maximum and minimum separately; 150 = 3n/2 forgets the −2; 99 = n − 1 finds only one of them.

questionBank.question: How many states does the minimal DFA have for the language of all strings over {a, b} in which the number of a’s is divisible by 3 and the number of b’s is even?
questionBank.explanation: Track (number of a’s mod 3, number of b’s mod 2): 3 × 2 = 6 combinations, the product of the two component DFAs. All 6 are reachable and pairwise distinguishable: from states (i, j) and (i′, j′), the suffix aᵏ bˡ that returns (i, j) to (0, 0) leaves the other state outside (0, 0). The start state (0, 0) is the only accepting one. So the minimal DFA has 6 states. 5 = 3 + 2 adds the component sizes instead of multiplying them; 8 = 2³ is a distractor.

questionBank.question: Let L be the set of binary strings whose 4th symbol from the right end is 1. What are the numbers of states in the minimal DFA and in a minimal NFA for L, respectively?
questionBank.explanation: NFA: guess the position: a start state loops on 0 and 1 and moves to a new state on 1; then three more states read any symbol; the last one accepts. That is 1 + 4 = 5 states (n + 1 for the n-th symbol from the right). DFA: it must remember the last 4 symbols read, since any of them may turn out to be the 4th from the end. All 2⁴ = 16 windows are pairwise distinguishable, so the minimal DFA has 16 states. This is the standard example of the exponential blow-up of the subset construction. 8 and 4 would be for the 3rd symbol from the right; 4 forgets the NFA’s start state.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: any prefix followed by the fixed suffix abb (III). B: an a followed by exactly two arbitrary symbols at the end, so the a is third from the right (IV). C: after the leading b*, each repetition adds exactly two a’s with any b’s around them, so the number of a’s is even (I). D: blocks of exactly two symbols, so the length is even (II). So A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II. C and D are the pair to watch: “even number of a’s” and “even length” are easy to swap.

b: I. Strings with an even number of a’s
II. Strings of even length
III. Strings ending in abb
IV. Strings whose third symbol from the right is a

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: (A) is false: if L were regular, then L ∩ a*b* = {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0} would be regular (regular languages are closed under intersection), but the pumping lemma shows aⁿbⁿ is not: pumping inside the leading a’s of aᵖbᵖ unbalances the counts. A DFA cannot keep an unbounded difference count. (R) is true: swap the accepting and non-accepting states of a complete DFA. So (A) false, (R) true.

stmts: Assertion (A): The language L = {w ∈ {a, b}* | w has equal numbers of a’s and b’s} is regular.
Reason (R): The complement of a regular language is regular.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: a Moore machine’s output is attached to states, and it visits n + 1 states for n input symbols (the start state included), so it emits n + 1 symbols. A Mealy machine’s output is attached to transitions, giving n symbols. Statement II is true: the two models are equivalent (ignoring the Moore machine’s initial output). Mealy → Moore may need more states (a state is split for each distinct output on its incoming transitions); Moore → Mealy keeps the same number of states. Both true.

stmts: Statement I: For an input string of length n, a Moore machine produces an output string of length n + 1 (counting the output of the start state).
Statement II: For every Mealy machine there is an equivalent Moore machine, and for every Moore machine there is an equivalent Mealy machine.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A string w of length 8 is generated by a grammar in Chomsky Normal Form and also by a grammar in Greibach Normal Form. How many steps does a derivation of w take in each grammar?
questionBank.explanation: CNF: rules are A → BC or A → a. Growing from 1 variable to 8 variables needs 7 applications of A → BC, and each of the 8 variables then needs one A → a step: 7 + 8 = 15 = 2n − 1. GNF: every rule is A → a α and puts exactly one terminal in place, so the derivation takes exactly n = 8 steps. 16 = 2n and 7 = n − 1 are off-by-one slips; “8 and 15” swaps the two.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements are correct?
options: A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A: correct; for example the palindromes over {a, b} are context-free but need non-determinism. B is wrong: {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} ∩ {aᵐbⁿcⁿ} = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}, which is not context-free. C: correct; run a PDA and a DFA in parallel (product construction). D: correct; mark the generating variables and check whether the start symbol is generating. E is wrong: ambiguity of CFGs is undecidable (by reduction from PCP). So A, C and D only.

stmts: A. Deterministic PDAs accept exactly the deterministic context-free languages, a proper subset of the context-free languages.
B. The class of context-free languages is closed under intersection.
C. The intersection of a context-free language with a regular language is context-free.
D. It is decidable whether the language of a given context-free grammar is empty.
E. It is decidable whether a given context-free grammar is ambiguous.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Consider the grammar S → aS | Sa | a. How many distinct parse trees does the string aaa have?
questionBank.explanation: Let T(n) be the number of parse trees of aⁿ from S. For n = 1 only S → a applies: T(1) = 1. For n ≥ 2 the root is either S → aS (the rest aⁿ⁻¹ comes from S) or S → Sa (again aⁿ⁻¹ from S), and S → a is impossible. So T(n) = 2 T(n − 1), T(2) = 2 and T(3) = 4. The four trees correspond to choosing, at each of the two upper levels, whether the extra a is added on the left or the right. More than one tree for the same string means the grammar is ambiguous.

questionBank.question:
Consider the grammar (ε is the empty string):
S → X Y z | Y w
X → x X | ε
Y → y | ε
What are FIRST(S) and FOLLOW(X)?
questionBank.explanation: FIRST(X) = {x, ε} and FIRST(Y) = {y, ε}. For S → X Y z: X can vanish and then Y can vanish, so FIRST(X Y z) = {x, y, z}. For S → Y w: FIRST = {y, w}. FIRST(S) = {x, y, z, w}. FOLLOW(X): X appears only in S → X Y z (and in X → x X, which adds FOLLOW(X) to itself). What follows X is FIRST(Y z) = {y} ∪ {z} (because Y ⇒ ε). $ is not included, since X is never at the end of a right-hand side of S. FOLLOW(X) = {y, z}.

questionBank.question: Which of the following is NOT normally performed as a peephole optimisation?
options: Removing a redundant load that follows a store to the same location
Replacing x * 1 or x + 0 by x (algebraic simplification)
Loop-invariant code motion across the basic blocks of a loop
Replacing a jump to an unconditional jump by a direct jump to the final target
questionBank.explanation: Peephole optimisation looks at a small sliding window of consecutive target instructions and applies local rewrites: redundant load/store elimination, algebraic simplification and strength reduction, flow-of-control optimisation (jumps to jumps), and removal of unreachable code. Moving loop-invariant computations out of a loop needs global data-flow analysis over the loop’s flow graph (reaching definitions, loop detection), so it is a loop (global) optimisation, not a peephole one.

questionBank.question: A telephone-grade channel has a bandwidth of 4 kHz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 30 dB. A designer wants to send data using 16 signal levels. What is the maximum achievable bit rate?
questionBank.explanation: Shannon gives the channel’s upper limit: SNR = 10^(30/10) = 1000, so C = B log₂(1 + SNR) = 4000 × log₂ 1001 ≈ 39.9 kbps. Nyquist gives the limit for a given number of levels: 2B log₂ L = 2 × 4000 × log₂ 16 = 32 kbps. The achievable rate is the smaller of the two: 32 kbps (16 levels is below what the channel could support). 39.9 kbps is the Shannon capacity, which these 16 levels cannot reach; 16 kbps forgets the factor 2; 64 kbps uses 16 as the bits per symbol.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: NRZ-I (non-return-to-zero, invert) encodes a 1 as a change of level and a 0 as no change (A-III). Manchester always changes in mid-bit and the direction of the change is the data (B-IV). Differential Manchester also always changes in mid-bit, for clocking, but the data is carried by the presence (0) or absence (1) of a transition at the start of the bit (C-I). AMI uses zero volts for 0 and alternating polarity for 1s, so there is no DC component (D-II). So A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II. B and C are the usual swap.

b: I. Always a transition in the middle of the bit; an extra transition at the start of the bit means 0
II. Binary 0 is zero voltage; successive 1s alternate between positive and negative voltage
III. The signal level is inverted at the start of a bit if the bit is 1 and kept if it is 0
IV. Always a transition in the middle of the bit, and its direction (low-to-high or high-to-low) gives the bit value

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A modem uses 64-QAM and transmits data at 30 kbps. What is its baud (signal element) rate?
questionBank.explanation: 64-QAM has 64 distinct signal elements, so each carries log₂ 64 = 6 bits. Baud rate = bit rate / bits per element = 30000 / 6 = 5000 baud. 30000 treats one bit per element; 469 ≈ 30000/64 divides by the number of levels instead of the bits per level; 10000 assumes 3 bits per element (8-level).

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: (A) is true: in baseband transmission the digital signal is sent as it is, without modulating a carrier, and a digital signal has components down to (or near) zero frequency, so it needs a low-pass channel. (R) is also true: Manchester coding always has a mid-bit transition, which provides self-clocking. But (R) is about the synchronisation property of one line code and does not explain why baseband needs a low-pass channel. Both true, (R) not the explanation.

stmts: Assertion (A): Baseband transmission of a digital signal requires a low-pass channel, ideally with a bandwidth starting from zero frequency.
Reason (R): Manchester encoding has a transition in the middle of every bit.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A signal of power 2 mW passes through an amplifier with a gain of 20 dB and then through two cable segments with losses of 7 dB and 5 dB. What is the output power (approximately)?
questionBank.explanation: Decibels add along a path: net gain = +20 − 7 − 5 = +8 dB. Power ratio = 10^(8/10) = 10^0.8 ≈ 6.31. Output = 2 mW × 6.31 ≈ 12.62 mW. 6.31 mW forgets to multiply by the input power; 16 mW treats 8 dB as a factor of 8; 5.02 mW uses 10^(8/20), the voltage-ratio formula, for a power ratio.

questionBank.question: Arrange the units of data, as a message passes down the TCP/IP stack at the sender, in the correct order.
questionBank.explanation: The application layer produces a message (C). The transport layer adds a TCP/UDP header to form a segment (B; a user datagram for UDP). The network layer adds the IP header to form a datagram or packet (D). The data link layer adds a header and trailer to form a frame (A). The physical layer transmits the frame as bits (E). So C, B, D, A, E. Swapping the segment and the datagram is the most common error.

stmts: A. Frame
B. Segment
C. Message (application data)
D. Datagram (packet)
E. Bits on the medium
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A hub only regenerates and repeats bits: physical layer (A-II). A bridge or layer-2 switch filters and forwards frames using MAC addresses: data link layer (B-IV). A router forwards datagrams using IP addresses and routing tables: network layer (C-I). A gateway translates between different protocol suites and may work at all layers up to the application (D-III). So A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

h: List II (highest layer at which it operates)
b: I. Network layer
II. Physical layer
III. Up to the application layer (all layers)
IV. Data link layer

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about virtual LANs (VLANs) are correct?
options: A, B, C and D only
questionBank.explanation: A: VLANs group stations logically; a broadcast in one VLAN does not reach the others: correct. B: 802.1Q adds a 4-byte tag (TPID plus priority and a 12-bit VLAN ID) between the source address and the type field: correct. C: different VLANs are different broadcast domains (and usually different IP subnets), so inter-VLAN traffic needs routing: correct. D is wrong: trunk links carrying tagged frames let a VLAN span several switches. E is wrong: all ports of a hub share one collision domain. So A, B and C only.

stmts: A. VLANs divide a single physical switched LAN into several separate broadcast domains.
B. IEEE 802.1Q identifies a frame’s VLAN by inserting a 4-byte tag into the Ethernet frame.
C. Traffic between two different VLANs must pass through a layer-3 device such as a router or a layer-3 switch.
D. All members of a VLAN must be connected to the same physical switch.
E. A hub, like a switch, creates a separate collision domain for each port.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: The data bits 1101011 are sent using CRC with the generator polynomial x³ + x + 1. What is the transmitted codeword?
questionBank.explanation: The generator x³ + x + 1 is 1011 (degree 3), so append 3 zeros to the data: 1101011000. Divide this by 1011 using modulo-2 (XOR) long division, ignoring the quotient. The successive partial remainders are 110, 111, 100, 010, 100, 011, 110, and the final 3-bit remainder is 110. The transmitted codeword is the data followed by the remainder: 1101011 110 = 1101011110. Check: dividing 1101011110 by 1011 leaves remainder 000, so the receiver accepts it. 1101011000 is the padded dividend before the remainder is added; 011 and 101 are wrong remainders from subtracting in ordinary arithmetic or dropping a step.

questionBank.question: A host has the IP address 172.20.137.45/21. What are its network address and directed broadcast address?
questionBank.explanation: /21 means the mask 255.255.248.0: the third octet keeps its top 5 bits, so blocks are 8 wide (0, 8, …, 128, 136, 144, …). 137 lies in the block 136–143. Network address = 172.20.136.0; broadcast = the last address in the block = 172.20.143.255. 172.20.137.0/.255 treats it as a /24; 172.20.128.0 uses a /20 block start but a /21 end; .151.255 uses a block of 16.

questionBank.question: A game tree has a MAX root with three MIN children B, C and D, evaluated left to right. The leaf values are B: 6, 11, 4; C: 9, 3, 12; D: 2, 8, 10. With alpha–beta pruning, what is the minimax value of the root and how many leaves are NOT evaluated?
questionBank.explanation: B: all three leaves are needed; B = min(6, 11, 4) = 4, so α = 4 at the root. C: first leaf 9 (β = 9 > α); second leaf 3 makes β = 3 ≤ α = 4, so C is cut off: leaf 12 is not evaluated. D: first leaf 2 makes β = 2 ≤ 4, so leaves 8 and 10 are not evaluated. Root value = max(4, ≤ 3, ≤ 2) = 4. Leaves not evaluated = 1 + 2 = 3. “4 and 2” misses one of D’s pruned leaves; 6 is the maximum leaf of B, not its MIN value.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: BFS is complete and optimal when all steps cost the same, but it keeps the whole frontier: O(bᵈ) space (A-IV). DFS stores only one path and its siblings, O(bm) space, but can run down an infinite branch (B-II). IDS repeats depth-limited DFS with growing limits: it has BFS’s completeness and optimality with DFS’s linear O(bd) space (C-III). Bidirectional search runs a forward and a backward search and stops when the frontiers meet; since b^(d/2) + b^(d/2) is far smaller than bᵈ, it saves time and space, but it needs an explicit goal and invertible actions (D-I). So A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I.

b: I. Runs two searches, from the start and from the goal, that meet in the middle, needing about O(b^(d/2)) time and space
II. Space O(bm), but not complete in infinite-depth spaces
III. Complete and optimal for unit step costs with only O(bd) space
IV. Complete and optimal for unit step costs, but needs O(bᵈ) space

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: admissibility (h never overestimates) does not imply h(n) ≤ c(n, n′) + h(n′) on every edge. For example, with S → A cost 1 and A → G cost 5, the values h(S) = 6, h(A) = 2, h(G) = 0 are admissible (true costs 6 and 5) but not consistent, since h(S) = 6 > 1 + 2. Statement II is true: summing the consistency inequality along an optimal path from n to the goal gives h(n) ≤ h*(n). So I false, II true.

stmts: Statement I: Every admissible heuristic is consistent (monotone).
Statement II: Every consistent heuristic with h(goal) = 0 is admissible.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A* search is run from S to goal G on an undirected graph with edge costs S–A 1, S–B 4, A–B 2, A–C 5, B–C 1, B–G 7, C–G 3 and heuristic values h(S) = 6, h(A) = 5, h(B) = 3, h(C) = 2, h(G) = 0. In what order are nodes expanded, and what is the cost of the path found?
options: S, A, B, C, G; cost 7
questionBank.explanation: f = g + h. Expand S (f = 6): A has g = 1, f = 6; B has g = 4, f = 7. Expand A (f = 6): B improves to g = 3, f = 6; C gets g = 6, f = 8. Expand B (f = 6): C improves to g = 4, f = 6; G gets g = 10, f = 10. Expand C (f = 6): G improves to g = 7, f = 7. Expand G (f = 7): goal. Order S, A, B, C, G; path S–A–B–C–G with cost 1 + 2 + 1 + 3 = 7. The heuristic is admissible (true costs to G: S 7, A 6, B 4, C 3), so 7 is optimal. The other options stop at the first path found to G, which A* never does.

questionBank.question: What is the most general unifier (MGU) of P(x, f(y), z) and P(g(w), f(a), w), where x, y, z, w are variables and a is a constant?
questionBank.explanation: Unify argument by argument. First: x with g(w), giving x/g(w) (the occurs check passes). Second: f(y) with f(a), giving y/a. Third: z with w, giving z/w. The MGU is {x/g(w), y/a, z/w}. {x/g(a), y/a, z/a} is a unifier but not the most general, since it needlessly binds w to a. Binding both w/z and z/w is circular and not a valid substitution. The terms are unifiable, so the last option is wrong.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: Minsky’s frames organise knowledge about an object or situation as slots and fillers, with defaults and procedures such as if-needed (A-II). Schank and Abelson’s scripts describe stereotyped event sequences, the restaurant script being the classic one (B-III). Schank’s conceptual dependency reduces sentences to primitive acts such as PTRANS (physical transfer) and ATRANS (transfer of possession) (C-IV). Semantic networks are graphs of concepts with labelled relations and inheritance along IS-A links (D-I). So A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

b: I. Nodes for concepts linked by labelled arcs such as IS-A and HAS-PART, with inheritance
II. Slots and fillers with default values and attached procedures
III. A stereotyped sequence of events for a familiar situation, such as eating at a restaurant
IV. Meaning expressed with a small set of primitive acts such as PTRANS and ATRANS

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: In a MYCIN-style expert system, two independent rules both support the same hypothesis H, with certainty factors 0.6 and 0.5. What is the combined certainty factor of H?
questionBank.explanation: For two positive certainty factors the combination rule is CF = CF₁ + CF₂ (1 − CF₁) = 0.6 + 0.5 × (1 − 0.6) = 0.6 + 0.2 = 0.8. The result stays below 1 and grows with each supporting piece of evidence. 1.1 simply adds them (a CF cannot exceed 1); 0.3 multiplies them; 0.55 averages them.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about inference are correct?
options: A, B, C and D only
A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A and B are the standard definitions: correct. C: Prolog uses SLD resolution, i.e. backward chaining, exploring clauses depth-first and left to right: correct. D: resolution is refutation-complete; showing KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable (derives the empty clause) proves KB ⊨ α: correct. E is wrong: forward (and backward) chaining with generalised modus ponens is complete only for definite (Horn) clauses; general clauses need resolution. So A, B, C and D only.

stmts: A. Forward chaining is data-driven: it starts from known facts and applies rules to derive new facts.
B. Backward chaining is goal-driven: it starts from the query and works back to known facts.
C. Prolog answers queries using backward chaining with depth-first search.
D. Resolution refutation proves KB ⊨ α by deriving the empty clause from KB ∧ ¬α.
E. Forward chaining with modus ponens is complete for arbitrary first-order clauses, not only Horn clauses.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: (R) is true: goal stack planning is linear; it pushes the goals and solves them one after another. (A) is true: in the Sussman anomaly (C on A initially, goal A on B and B on C), whichever subgoal is solved first gets undone while solving the second, so the planner has to re-achieve it and produces a longer plan than necessary. The interference between subgoals described in (R) is exactly the cause of (A). Non-linear (partial-order) planning avoids this by interleaving steps.

stmts: Assertion (A): Goal stack planning in the STRIPS style can produce non-optimal plans, for example on the Sussman anomaly in the blocks world.
Reason (R): A linear planner works on one subgoal at a time and may undo a subgoal it has already achieved while achieving the next one.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A k-nearest-neighbour classifier (Euclidean distance) has the training points (1, 1) A, (2, 1) A, (3, 2) A, (4, 4) B and (5, 3) B. What class does it assign to the query point (3, 3) with k = 1 and with k = 3, respectively?
questionBank.explanation: Distances from (3, 3): to (3, 2) = 1; to (4, 4) = √2 ≈ 1.41; to (5, 3) = 2; to (2, 1) = √5 ≈ 2.24; to (1, 1) = √8 ≈ 2.83. k = 1: the nearest point (3, 2) is class A. k = 3: the three nearest are (3, 2) A, (4, 4) B, (5, 3) B; the majority is B. So A and B. This shows how the choice of k changes a KNN decision: a small k follows single noisy points, a larger k smooths the decision boundary.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation:
Statement I is true. This is the exportation law: both sides are false only when p = T, q = T and r = F.
Statement II is false. p → (q ∨ r) is false only when p = T, q = F, r = F. But (p → q) ∧ (p → r) is also false when p = T, q = T, r = F (the second conjunct fails), while p → (q ∨ r) is true there. The correct equivalence is p → (q ∨ r) ≡ (p → q) ∨ (p → r); with ∧ on the right it would be p → (q ∧ r).
So Statement I is true and Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: (p ∧ q) → r is logically equivalent to p → (q → r).
Statement II: p → (q ∨ r) is logically equivalent to (p → q) ∧ (p → r).
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: How many binary relations on a set with 5 elements are both reflexive and antisymmetric?
questionBank.explanation:
n = 5 gives 25 ordered pairs: 5 diagonal pairs and 20 off-diagonal pairs forming 10 unordered pairs {i, j}.
Reflexive: all 5 diagonal pairs must be present (1 way).
Antisymmetric: for each unordered pair {i, j} there are 3 choices: neither, only (i, j), or only (j, i). That is 3¹⁰.
Total = 3¹⁰ = 59049.
Traps: 2²⁰ = 1048576 counts all reflexive relations (off-diagonal pairs free); 2¹⁰ = 1024 counts reflexive and symmetric relations; 3⁵ = 243 applies the 3 choices per element instead of per pair.

questionBank.question:
Match List I with List II
All relations are on the set {1, 2, 3}.
questionBank.explanation:
A: contains every (x, x), so reflexive; (1,2) without (2,1), so antisymmetric; the only chains are (1,1)(1,2) and (1,2)(2,2), both giving (1,2), so transitive. A partial order (II).
B: symmetric, but (1,2) and (2,1) force (1,1) for transitivity, and (1,1) is missing. Symmetric but not transitive (III).
C: reflexive, symmetric, and transitive (its classes are {1, 2} and {3}). An equivalence relation (I).
D: no pair and its reverse, so antisymmetric; (1,2), (2,3) need (1,3), which is missing. Antisymmetric but not transitive (IV).
Answer: A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV.

b: I. An equivalence relation
II. A partial order
III. Symmetric but not transitive
IV. Antisymmetric but not transitive
