questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: by weak duality every feasible dual solution bounds the primal objective, so if the primal objective is unbounded, no dual feasible solution can exist (the dual is infeasible). The converse is not guaranteed: an infeasible dual can also go with an infeasible primal. Statement II is true: resource levelling (smoothing) moves only non-critical activities within their available float to reduce peaks and valleys in resource usage; the critical path, and hence the project duration, is unaffected as long as no activity is delayed beyond its float. So both statements are true.

stmts: Statement I: If the primal linear programming problem has an unbounded objective, then its dual has no feasible solution.
Statement II: Resource levelling shifts non-critical activities within their float to smooth the day-to-day resource requirement; when the float is sufficient, the project duration does not change.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A single-accumulator computer uses 32-bit instructions. Each instruction has one indirect-addressing mode bit, an operation-code field, and an address field large enough to address a memory of 2²⁰ words directly. What is the maximum number of distinct operation codes?
questionBank.explanation: Address field: 2²⁰ words need 20 bits. Mode (I) bit: 1 bit. Opcode bits = 32 − 20 − 1 = 11, so there can be 2¹¹ = 2048 distinct opcodes. 4096 (2¹²) forgets the mode bit; 1024 (2¹⁰) subtracts one bit too many; 512 would be a 9-bit opcode.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: In Mano’s treatment of logic microoperations, B acts as a pattern that selects bits of A. OR with B sets the bits of A where B has 1s: selective set (A-II). XOR with B complements those bits: selective complement (B-IV). AND with B′ clears the bits of A where B has 1s: selective clear (C-III). AND with B keeps only the bits where B has 1s and clears the rest: the mask operation (D-I). So A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I.

b: I. Mask operation
II. Selective set
III. Selective clear
IV. Selective complement

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: In Mano’s basic computer, arrange the following register transfers for a memory-reference instruction with indirect addressing in the order in which they occur.
questionBank.explanation: The instruction cycle is driven by the timing signals. T₀: AR ← PC (C) puts the instruction address in AR. T₁: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1 (E) fetches the instruction. T₂: decode the opcode, copy the address part to AR and the mode bit to I (A). T₃: because I = 1 (indirect), AR ← M[AR] (B) fetches the effective address. T₄ onwards: execute (D). So C, E, A, B, D. Fetching the effective address before decoding (C, E, B, A, D) is impossible, because the control does not know it is indirect until IR(15) is copied into I.

stmts: A. D₀…D₇ ← decode IR(12–14), AR ← IR(0–11), I ← IR(15)
B. AR ← M[AR]
C. AR ← PC
D. Execute the memory-reference microoperations of the decoded instruction
E. IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both statements are true. The interrupt cycle is RT₀: AR ← 0, TR ← PC; RT₁: M[AR] ← TR, PC ← 0; RT₂: PC ← PC + 1, IEN ← 0, R ← 0, SC ← 0. So the return address is saved at location 0 and control goes to location 1 (A is true), and IEN is cleared (R is true). But clearing IEN does not explain where the return address is stored or where control branches; it explains why the service routine is not itself interrupted. So (R) is not the explanation of (A).

stmts: Assertion (A): In Mano’s basic computer, the interrupt cycle stores the return address in memory location 0 and then branches to memory location 1.
Reason (R): During the interrupt cycle the interrupt-enable flip-flop IEN is cleared, so no further interrupts are accepted until the service routine executes ION.

questionBank.question: A microprogrammed control unit has a control memory of 1024 words. Each microinstruction holds 48 control bits (one bit per control signal), a condition-select field that picks one of 16 status conditions, and a branch-address field. What is the width of a microinstruction?
questionBank.explanation: Branch-address field: 1024 words need log₂ 1024 = 10 bits. Condition select: 16 conditions need log₂ 16 = 4 bits. Control field: 48 bits (horizontal, one bit per signal). Width = 48 + 4 + 10 = 62 bits. 58 drops the 4 condition bits; 74 uses a 16-bit one-hot condition field instead of an encoded one; 52 forgets the branch-address field.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: the first pass only builds the address symbol table (by counting locations with the location counter). A forward reference cannot be resolved while that pass is still running, because the symbol has not been seen yet; the second pass translates the instructions using the completed table, and that is where forward references are resolved. Statement II is false: changing a hardwired control unit means redesigning gates and wiring, while a microprogrammed unit is changed by rewriting control memory. Microprogrammed control is the flexible one; hardwired control is the faster one. Both statements are false.

stmts: Statement I: In a two-pass assembler, forward references are resolved during the first pass, because the address symbol table is complete during that pass.
Statement II: Hardwired control units are generally easier to modify than microprogrammed control units when new instructions are added to the instruction set.

questionBank.question: In the microprogrammed control of Mano’s basic computer, an instruction’s 4-bit operation code is mapped into a 7-bit control-memory address by the rule 0 xxxx 00 (a 0, then the opcode bits, then two 0s). What control-memory address (in decimal) does the opcode 1011 map to?
questionBank.explanation: Apply the mapping: 0 1011 00 = 0101100₂ = 32 + 8 + 4 = 44. Each opcode therefore gets a block of four consecutive microinstructions (addresses 44–47 here). 11 is the opcode itself, ignoring the two appended 0s; 22 appends only one 0; 88 appends three 0s (a shift by 3).

questionBank.question: A 64 KB, 2-way set-associative cache uses 32-byte blocks, and the processor generates 32-bit byte addresses. How many bits are there in the tag, set-index and block-offset fields respectively?
questionBank.explanation: Offset: 32-byte blocks need log₂ 32 = 5 bits. Number of blocks = 64 KB / 32 B = 2048; with 2 blocks per set there are 1024 sets, so the index has log₂ 1024 = 10 bits. Tag = 32 − 10 − 5 = 17 bits. “16, 11, 5” treats the cache as direct-mapped (2048 lines, 11 index bits); “18, 9, 5” uses 4-way sets; “17, 11, 4” miscounts the offset.

questionBank.question: A non-pipelined processor takes 700 ps per instruction. It is split into a 5-stage pipeline with stage delays 150, 120, 160, 140 and 130 ps, and each pipeline register adds 10 ps. Ignoring hazards, how long does the pipeline take to execute 200 instructions?
questionBank.explanation: The clock must fit the slowest stage plus the latch: cycle = 160 + 10 = 170 ps. For k = 5 stages and n = 200 instructions the time is (k + n − 1) × cycle = (5 + 199) × 170 = 204 × 170 = 34 680 ps = 34.68 ns. 34.00 ns counts only n × cycle and forgets the 4 fill cycles; 32.64 ns forgets the 10 ps latch delay (204 × 160); 140.00 ns is the non-pipelined time 200 × 700 ps. (Speedup ≈ 140 000 / 34 680 ≈ 4.04.)

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about computer arithmetic algorithms are correct?
options: B, C, D and E only
A, B, C and E only
questionBank.explanation: A is correct: (1, 0) marks the start of a run of 1s, so the multiplicand is subtracted; (0, 1) marks the end of a run and causes an addition. B is correct: Booth’s recoding works directly on two’s-complement operands, which is one of its main advantages. C is correct: restoring division subtracts the divisor and, if the result goes negative, adds it back (restores) before the next shift. D is false: non-restoring division may end with a negative remainder, and then one final addition of the divisor is needed to correct it. E is correct: two positive operands cannot give a negative sum, so a sign bit of 1 signals overflow. So A, B, C and E only.

stmts: A. In Booth’s multiplication algorithm, the bit pair (Q₀, Q₋₁) = (1, 0) causes the multiplicand to be subtracted from the partial product.
B. Booth’s algorithm handles a negative two’s-complement multiplier without any separate sign correction.
C. In restoring division, the divisor is added back whenever the partial remainder becomes negative.
D. Non-restoring division never needs a final correction step on the remainder.
E. When two positive numbers are added in two’s complement and the result’s sign bit is 1, an overflow has occurred.

questionBank.question: Using homogeneous coordinates, the point Q(5, 3) is rotated through 90° anticlockwise about the fixed point (2, 1). Where does Q end up?
questionBank.explanation: The composite matrix is T(2, 1) · R(90°) · T(−2, −1): translate the fixed point to the origin, rotate, translate back. Q − (2, 1) = (3, 2). A 90° anticlockwise rotation maps (x, y) to (−y, x): (3, 2) → (−2, 3). Translate back: (−2 + 2, 3 + 1) = (0, 4). (−3, 5) rotates about the origin instead of the fixed point; (4, −2) rotates clockwise ((3, 2) → (2, −3), then + (2, 1)); (−2, 3) forgets the final translation back.

questionBank.question: A window with corners (10, 20) and (50, 60) is mapped to a viewport with corners (0, 0) and (200, 100). What are the viewport coordinates of the window point (30, 50)?
questionBank.explanation: Window-to-viewport mapping: xv = xvmin + (xw − xwmin) × sx with sx = (200 − 0)/(50 − 10) = 5, and yv = yvmin + (yw − ywmin) × sy with sy = (100 − 0)/(60 − 20) = 2.5. xv = 0 + (30 − 10) × 5 = 100; yv = 0 + (50 − 20) × 2.5 = 75. So (100, 75). (100, 150) uses the x-scale for y; (150, 75) forgets to subtract xwmin (30 × 5); (75, 100) swaps the coordinates.

options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both are true. Because all projectors pass through one centre of projection (R), a set of parallel lines that is not parallel to the projection plane projects to lines that meet at a vanishing point, so parallelism is lost (A). A parallel projection, whose projectors are parallel to each other, preserves parallel lines. The converging projectors are exactly why perspective views shrink distant objects and bend parallels to vanishing points, so (R) explains (A).

stmts: Assertion (A): A perspective projection does not, in general, keep parallel lines parallel.
Reason (R): In a perspective projection the projectors converge to a single centre of projection.

questionBank.question: A colour is specified as (R, G, B) = (0.2, 0.7, 0.4), with each component in [0, 1]. What is the same colour in the CMY model?
questionBank.explanation: CMY is the subtractive complement of RGB: (C, M, Y) = (1 − R, 1 − G, 1 − B) = (1 − 0.2, 1 − 0.7, 1 − 0.4) = (0.8, 0.3, 0.6). Cyan absorbs red, magenta absorbs green and yellow absorbs blue. (0.4, 0.7, 0.2) just reverses the triple; (0.8, 0.6, 0.3) complements correctly but swaps M and Y; (0.2, 0.7, 0.4) is the RGB value unchanged.

(i) Call by reference: x and y are both aliases of a. x := x + 1 makes a = 6; y := y * 2 makes a = 12. (ii) Call by value-result: x and y are local copies initialised to 5. x becomes 6 and y becomes 10. On return, x is copied back (a = 6) and then y is copied back (a = 10), so the last copy wins: a = 10. “12, 6” copies back in the wrong order; “11, 10” doubles before incrementing; “10, 12” swaps the two mechanisms. Aliasing is the classic case where reference and value-result differ.

questionBank.explanation: Static scoping: the free x inside h refers to the x visible where h is defined, the global x. h sets global x = 15 and prints 15; g prints its own local x = 3; main prints the global x = 15. questionBank.question: What is the output of the following C program?
questionBank.explanation: Macros are expanded textually before compilation. SQ(a+1) becomes a+1*a+1 = 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 (not 16), because the parameter is not parenthesised. CUBE(a-1) is fully parenthesised: ((2)*(2)*(2)) = 8. So b = 7 + 8 = 15. SQ(2)/SQ(2) becomes 2*2/2*2, evaluated left to right as ((2*2)/2)*2 = 4, not 1. Output: 15 4. Every valid document is well-formed, but not the other way round. Statement II is true: the servlet container loads and initialises a servlet once (init), then serves each request by invoking service (doGet/doPost) on a thread, and calls destroy when unloading it. This is why servlets scale better than CGI, which starts a new process per request.

questionBank.question: A B⁺-tree is stored on disk blocks of 1024 bytes. A search-key value takes 12 bytes, a block pointer 8 bytes and a record pointer 10 bytes. What is the order p of an internal node (the maximum number of block pointers it can hold)?
questionBank.explanation: An internal node with p pointers holds p − 1 keys: 8p + 12(p − 1) ≤ 1024, so 20p ≤ 1036 and p ≤ 51.8, giving p = 51. 46 is the leaf order: a leaf holds p_leaf (key, record-pointer) pairs plus one next-leaf block pointer, 22 p_leaf + 8 ≤ 1024, p_leaf = 46. 52 rounds 51.8 up; 85 = ⌊1024/12⌋ counts only the keys and ignores the pointers.

questionBank.question: Consider the schedule S: r2(A), r1(B), w2(A), r3(A), w1(B), w3(A), r3(B). To which serial schedules is S conflict-equivalent?
options: Both T1 → T2 → T3 and T2 → T1 → T3
questionBank.explanation: Build the precedence graph from conflicting pairs (same item, different transactions, at least one write). On A: r2(A) before w3(A), w2(A) before r3(A) and w2(A) before w3(A) all give T2 → T3. On B: w1(B) before r3(B) gives T1 → T3; r1(B) before w1(B) is the same transaction. T1 and T2 touch different items, so there is no edge between them. The graph has edges T2 → T3 and T1 → T3 and no cycle, so S is conflict-serializable, and every topological order is an equivalent serial schedule: T1, T2, T3 and T2, T1, T3. Picking only one of them misses that T1 and T2 are unordered.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: strict 2PL keeps every exclusive (write) lock until the transaction commits or aborts, so no one reads uncommitted data and schedules are strict and cascadeless (IV). B: conservative 2PL predeclares and acquires all locks at the start; a transaction never waits while holding locks, so deadlock cannot occur (III). C: in timestamp ordering, Thomas’ write rule ignores a write whose value has already been overwritten by a younger transaction, instead of aborting (II). D: in wound–wait, an older requester “wounds” (aborts) the younger holder; a younger requester waits (I). So A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I.

b: I. An older transaction requesting a lock held by a younger one forces the younger to roll back
II. An obsolete write is ignored instead of rolling back the writer
III. All locks are declared and obtained before the transaction begins, so it is deadlock-free
IV. Exclusive locks are held until commit or abort, avoiding cascading rollback

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both are true. A schedule is cascadeless if transactions read only committed data; it is strict if they neither read nor overwrite uncommitted data (R is the definition of strict). Since strictness forbids reading uncommitted data, it implies cascadelessness, so (A) follows directly from (R). The hierarchy is strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable.

stmts: Assertion (A): Every strict schedule is cascadeless.
Reason (R): In a strict schedule, no transaction reads or writes a data item until the transaction that last wrote it has committed or aborted.

questionBank.question:
A stationery shop records eight transactions:
T1 {pen, notebook, stapler}; T2 {notebook, ink}; T3 {pen, notebook, ink}; T4 {pen, stapler}; T5 {notebook, stapler}; T6 {pen, notebook, ink, stapler}; T7 {pen, notebook}; T8 {ink, stapler}.
What are the support and confidence of the rule {pen, notebook} → {ink}?
questionBank.explanation: Support of the rule = fraction of all transactions containing {pen, notebook, ink}: T3 and T6, so 2/8 = 25%. Confidence = support({pen, notebook, ink}) / support({pen, notebook}). {pen, notebook} appears in T1, T3, T6 and T7, so 4 transactions; confidence = 2/4 = 50%. “Support 50%, confidence 25%” swaps the two (50% is the support of the antecedent); 40% divides by 5 by miscounting the antecedent.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about data warehousing and OLAP are correct?
options: A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A is correct: roll-up moves up a hierarchy (city → state → country) or removes a dimension, aggregating the measures. B is false: drill-down is the reverse of roll-up and increases detail (e.g. quarter → month). C is correct: slice fixes one dimension to a value (e.g. year = 2025) and gives a sub-cube; dice selects on two or more dimensions. D is false: normalising dimensions into several tables is what makes a snowflake schema; a star schema has one denormalised table per dimension. E is correct: this is the standard OLTP vs OLAP contrast. So A, C and E only.

stmts: A. Roll-up aggregates data by climbing up a concept hierarchy, for example from city to state.
B. Drill-down reduces the level of detail of the data being viewed.
C. A slice selects a single value on one dimension and yields a sub-cube.
D. In a star schema, each dimension is normalised into several tables.
E. OLTP workloads consist mostly of short update transactions, while OLAP workloads consist of complex, read-mostly analytical queries.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: once a site votes ready, it has promised to commit if told to, so it enters the prepared (in-doubt) state and cannot decide alone. This is why 2PC blocks if the coordinator fails at that point. Statement II is false: it describes vertical fragmentation (projections on column subsets that keep the key, rebuilt by join). Horizontal fragmentation splits a relation into subsets of rows (selections) and rebuilds it by union.

stmts: Statement I: In the two-phase commit protocol, a participant that has voted “ready” (yes) cannot abort on its own and must wait for the coordinator’s decision.
Statement II: Horizontal fragmentation divides a relation into subsets of columns, each of which keeps the primary key so that the relation can be rebuilt by a join.

questionBank.question: A relation R(A, B, C, D, E) has the functional dependencies F = {A → B, BC → D, D → A}. How many candidate keys does R have, and what is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questionBank.explanation: C and E never appear on a right-hand side, so every key contains CE. CE⁺ = {C, E} is not enough. Try adding one attribute: ACE⁺: A → B, then BC → D: all five attributes. BCE⁺: BC → D, D → A: all. CDE⁺: D → A, A → B: all. So ACE, BCE and CDE are the candidate keys (3), and every attribute is prime. BCNF fails because A → B has a left side that is not a superkey. But 3NF only requires, for each non-trivial X → Y, that X is a superkey or Y is prime; B, D and A are all prime, so R is in 3NF. Hence 3 candidate keys, highest form 3NF.

COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of NULLs: 5. COUNT(sal) ignores NULL salaries: 4. COUNT(DISTINCT dept) ignores the NULL department: {A, B} = 2. AVG(sal) ignores NULLs: (100 + 200 + 300 + 50) / 4 = 650 / 4 = 162.5, not 650 / 5 = 130. The options with 130 treat NULL as 0; the one with 3 counts NULL as a distinct department.

questionBank.question:
A system has five processes P0–P4 and three resource types R1, R2, R3. The currently available vector is (1, 2, 1).
Allocation: P0 (1, 1, 2), P1 (2, 0, 1), P2 (3, 1, 1), P3 (0, 2, 1), P4 (1, 0, 0)
Max: P0 (4, 3, 3), P1 (3, 2, 2), P2 (5, 1, 3), P3 (2, 4, 2), P4 (2, 2, 1)
Using the Banker’s algorithm, which of the following is a safe sequence?
questionBank.explanation: Need = Max − Allocation: P0 (3, 2, 1), P1 (1, 2, 1), P2 (2, 0, 2), P3 (2, 2, 1), P4 (1, 2, 1). With Available (1, 2, 1) only P1 or P4 can run first. P1 runs: Available = (1, 2, 1) + (2, 0, 1) = (3, 2, 2). P4 (1, 2, 1) runs: (4, 2, 2). P0 (3, 2, 1) runs: (5, 3, 4). P2 (2, 0, 2) runs: (8, 4, 5). P3 (2, 2, 1) runs: (8, 6, 6). All finish, so P1, P4, P0, P2, P3 is safe. The other sequences fail at their first step: P0 needs 3 of R1, P2 needs 2 of R1 and 2 of R3, and P3 needs 2 of R1, but only 1 of R1 is available.

questionBank.question: Four processes share a single resource type with identical instances. Their maximum needs are 3, 4, 5 and 6 instances, and each process holds its instances until it finishes. What is the minimum number of instances that guarantees the system can never deadlock?
questionBank.explanation: The worst case is every process holding one instance less than its maximum and waiting for one more: (3 − 1) + (4 − 1) + (5 − 1) + (6 − 1) = 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 14 instances, all allocated, and everyone waiting: deadlock. One more instance lets some process complete and release everything, so the minimum is 14 + 1 = 15. 14 is exactly the deadlock-prone allocation; 18 is the sum of maxima; 19 is that sum plus one.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about deadlocks are correct?
questionBank.explanation: A is correct: a total order on resource requests makes a circular chain of waits impossible. B is correct: with single-instance resources, a cycle is necessary and sufficient for deadlock. C is false: with multiple instances a cycle is necessary but not sufficient, because another instance may be released by a process outside the cycle. D is false: the Banker’s algorithm is deadlock avoidance; it grants requests only if the state stays safe, rather than negating one of the four conditions. E is false: unsafe means deadlock is possible, not certain. So A and B only.

stmts: A. Numbering all resource types and requiring every process to request them in increasing order prevents circular wait.
B. If every resource type has a single instance, a cycle in the resource-allocation graph implies a deadlock.
C. If resource types have several instances, a cycle in the resource-allocation graph always implies a deadlock.
D. The Banker’s algorithm is a deadlock-prevention technique.
E. A system in an unsafe state is necessarily deadlocked.

questionBank.question: A system has a 36-bit virtual address space, a page size of 8 KB and page-table entries of 8 bytes. It uses multilevel paging in which every page table at every level must fit in a single page. What is the minimum number of levels?
questionBank.explanation: Offset = log₂ 8K = 13 bits, so the virtual page number has 36 − 13 = 23 bits. One page holds 8192 / 8 = 1024 entries, so each level can resolve log₂ 1024 = 10 bits of the page number. Levels = ⌈23 / 10⌉ = 3 (split as 3 + 10 + 10 bits). Two levels would resolve only 20 bits; 4 or 5 levels are more than needed.

questionBank.question: A paged system has a TLB access time of 10 ns and a main-memory access time of 80 ns, and uses a single-level page table kept in memory. The TLB hit ratio is 90%. What is the effective memory access time? (Assume the TLB is looked up first, and that on a miss the page table is read from memory.)
questionBank.explanation: Hit: TLB lookup + memory access = 10 + 80 = 90 ns. Miss: TLB lookup + page-table access + memory access = 10 + 80 + 80 = 170 ns. EAT = 0.9 × 90 + 0.1 × 170 = 81 + 17 = 98 ns. 90 ns ignores misses; 97 ns forgets the TLB lookup on a miss (0.9 × 90 + 0.1 × 160); 88 ns ignores the TLB time altogether (0.9 × 80 + 0.1 × 160).

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both are true. With FIFO, adding a frame can increase the number of faults for some reference strings (Belady’s anomaly), so (A) is true. LRU and optimal are stack algorithms: the pages held with n frames are always a subset of those held with n + 1 frames, so more frames can never cause more faults, so (R) is true. But (R) says why other algorithms are immune; it does not explain why FIFO shows the anomaly. The explanation for (A) is that FIFO is not a stack algorithm. So (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

Reason (R): LRU and optimal page replacement never exhibit Belady’s anomaly.

questionBank.question: A disk has cylinders 0–199. The head is at cylinder 50, and the queue holds requests for cylinders 82, 170, 43, 140, 24, 16 and 190. What is the total head movement (in cylinders) under SSTF scheduling?
questionBank.explanation: SSTF always serves the nearest pending request. From 50: 43 (7), then 24 (19; nearer than 82, which is 39 away), then 16 (8), then 82 (66), 140 (58), 170 (30) and 190 (20). Total = 7 + 19 + 8 + 66 + 58 + 30 + 20 = 208. 341 is C-LOOK moving upwards first (140 up to 190, the 174-cylinder return to 16, then 27 up to 43). 314 is LOOK moving upwards first (140 up to 190, then 174 down to 16). 642 is FCFS in the given queue order. SSTF is greedy and can starve far requests, but here it gives the smallest total.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following steps in the order in which they are applied when a C source program is turned into a running process.

questionBank.question: A function contains one while loop. Inside the loop body there is an if–else statement. After the loop comes a switch statement with three case labels and a default, each ending in break. All conditions are simple (no && or ||). What is the cyclomatic complexity of the function?
questionBank.explanation: For a single-entry, single-exit structured program, V(G) = number of binary decision points + 1. The while condition gives 1 decision and the if gives 1. A switch with k outcomes contributes k − 1 decisions; here there are 4 outcomes (3 cases + default), so 3. V(G) = 1 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 6. The same value comes from E − N + 2 on the flow graph or from counting regions. 5 counts the switch as 2 decisions (ignoring the default); 7 counts it as 4 (one per outcome).

questionBank.question: A function takes two independent integer inputs, x in the range 10–60 and y in the range 1–5. How many test cases does robust boundary value analysis (single-fault assumption) generate?
questionBank.explanation: Robust BVA tests, for each variable, the values min − 1, min, min + 1, nominal, max − 1, max, max + 1 while the other variable stays at its nominal value. That gives 6 non-nominal values per variable plus one all-nominal case: 6n + 1 = 6 × 2 + 1 = 13. 9 = 4n + 1 is normal BVA; 25 = 5ⁿ is worst-case BVA; 49 = 7ⁿ is robust worst-case BVA.

questionBank.question: A system has the following function counts, all of average complexity: 20 external inputs (weight 4), 12 external outputs (weight 5), 10 external inquiries (weight 4), 6 internal logical files (weight 10) and 4 external interface files (weight 7). questionBank.question: A software component has a mean time to failure of 480 hours and a mean time to repair of 20 hours. What is its steady-state availability?
questionBank.explanation: MTBF = MTTF + MTTR = 480 + 20 = 500 hours. Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) = 480 / 500 = 0.96 = 96%. 4% is the unavailability; 95.83% computes 1 − MTTR/MTTF = 1 − 20/480; 92% subtracts twice the repair fraction.

questionBank.question: What is the solution of the recurrence T(n) = 9T(n/3) + n² log n?
questionBank.explanation: Here a = 9, b = 3, so n^(log_b a) = n^(log₃ 9) = n². f(n) = n² log n is larger than n² only by a log factor, so case 3 of the basic master theorem does not apply (it needs a polynomial gap). The extended case 2 applies: if f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) logᵏ n) with k ≥ 0, then T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) logᵏ⁺¹ n). With k = 1 this gives Θ(n² log² n). Θ(n² log n) wrongly treats the log factor as case 3 dominance; Θ(n²) ignores f(n); Θ(n³) has no basis.

questionBank.question: Six characters occur in a file with these frequencies: p 7, q 3, r 12, s 10, t 18, u 2 (52 characters in all). How many bits does a Huffman code need to encode the whole file?
questionBank.explanation: Build the tree by repeatedly merging the two smallest weights: 2 + 3 = 5; 5 + 7 = 12; 10 + 12 = 22; 12 + 18 = 30; 22 + 30 = 52. The total encoded length equals the sum of the weights of all merged (internal) nodes: 5 + 12 + 22 + 30 + 52 = 121 bits. One valid code gives lengths t 2, r 2, s 2, p 3, q 4, u 4: 18×2 + 12×2 + 10×2 + 7×3 + 3×4 + 2×4 = 36 + 24 + 20 + 21 + 12 + 8 = 121. Ties may give different codes but always the same total. 156 is a fixed 3-bit code (52 × 3).

questionBank.question: A 0/1 knapsack has capacity 10. The items (weight, value) are I1 (3, 40), I2 (4, 50), I3 (5, 60), I4 (2, 25) and I5 (6, 65). What is the maximum total value?
questionBank.explanation: Checking the feasible subsets (or running the DP table), the best is I1 + I3 + I4: weight 3 + 5 + 2 = 10, value 40 + 60 + 25 = 125. Alternatives: I2 + I5 = 115 (weight 10); I1 + I2 + I4 = 115 (weight 9); I2 + I3 = 110. 115 is also what greedy-by-ratio gives (ratios 13.3, 12.5, 12, 12.5, 10.8 pick I1, I2, I4, then nothing else fits), showing that greedy is not optimal for 0/1 knapsack. 127 is the fractional-knapsack optimum (I1, I2, I4 plus 1/5 of I3), which is not allowed here.

For 0/1 knapsack, a high-ratio item can waste capacity (the previous question shows greedy getting 115 against an optimum of 125). (R) is false: 0/1 knapsack does have optimal substructure, which is why dynamic programming solves it in O(nW); what it lacks is the greedy-choice property.

stmts: Assertion (A): Taking items in decreasing order of value-to-weight ratio gives an optimal solution to the fractional knapsack problem but not always to the 0/1 knapsack problem.
Reason (R): The 0/1 knapsack problem does not have the optimal substructure property.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about threaded binary trees is correct?
options: In a right in-threaded binary tree, every null right-child pointer is replaced by a pointer to the node’s in-order predecessor.
In-order traversal of a fully threaded binary tree still needs an explicit stack.
In a right in-threaded binary tree, every null right-child pointer is replaced by a pointer to the node’s in-order successor.
A binary tree with n nodes has n − 1 null links available for threads.
questionBank.explanation: Threads reuse null links. In a right in-threaded tree, a null right link points to the in-order successor, so in-order traversal can follow threads without recursion or a stack; in a fully (double) threaded tree, null left links point to the in-order predecessor. A binary tree with n nodes has 2n links of which n − 1 are used by edges, so n + 1 links are null and available for threads, not n − 1. A flag bit per link distinguishes a thread from a real child pointer.

questionBank.question: What is the minimum number of comparisons that any comparison-based algorithm needs in the worst case to sort 5 distinct elements, according to the decision-tree lower bound?
questionBank.explanation: A comparison sort is a binary decision tree whose leaves must include all 5! = 120 orderings. A binary tree of height h has at most 2ʰ leaves, so 2ʰ ≥ 120 and h ≥ ⌈log₂ 120⌉ = 7 (2⁶ = 64 < 120 ≤ 128 = 2⁷). Seven comparisons are also achievable for 5 elements (merge insertion), so the bound is tight here. 6 forgets the ceiling; 8 is what plain merge sort uses in the worst case; 10 = 5 × 4 / 2 is the bubble-sort count.

questionBank.question: A context-free grammar is in Chomsky normal form and generates no ε. How many steps does any derivation of a string of length 12 take?
questionBank.explanation: In CNF every production is A → BC or A → a. Growing from one variable to 12 variables takes 11 applications of A → BC, and turning 12 variables into 12 terminals takes 12 applications of A → a. Total = 11 + 12 = 2n − 1 = 23. 24 is 2n; 12 is the GNF count (each GNF step emits exactly one terminal); 11 counts only the A → BC steps.

questionBank.question: Context-free languages are closed under which of the following operations?

C: closed; run the PDA and the DFA in parallel (product construction), which still needs only one stack. D: not closed; otherwise closure under union and complement would give closure under intersection by De Morgan’s law. E: closed; add S → S S₁ | ε. So A, C and E only.

questionBank.question: What does the diagonal argument establish in the theory of computation?
options: Every context-free language is decidable, because a CYK table can be filled diagonally.
There are languages over {0, 1} that no Turing machine accepts, because there are uncountably many languages but only countably many Turing machines.
The set of all Turing machines is uncountable, so some machines cannot be encoded as strings.
The halting problem is NP-hard, because diagonal reductions take polynomial time.
questionBank.explanation: Cantor’s diagonal argument shows that the power set of a countable set is uncountable. Every Turing machine has a finite description, so there are only countably many TMs, while the set of all languages over {0, 1} (subsets of Σ*) is uncountable; hence some languages are not recognised by any TM. The same diagonal construction gives the non-RE diagonal language and the undecidability of halting. CFLs are indeed decidable, but not because of diagonalisation; the set of TMs is countable, not uncountable; and NP-hardness is about polynomial reductions, unrelated to this argument.

questionBank.question:
How many tokens does a C lexical analyser produce for the following statement?
  printf("x=%d", a[i] += 2);
questionBank.explanation: The tokens are: printf, (, "x=%d", ,, a, [, i, ], +=, 2, ), ; which is 12. A string literal is a single token, whatever it contains (so the % and = inside it are not separate tokens). += is one compound-assignment operator, not two tokens. 13 splits += into + and =; 11 forgets the semicolon or treats the string as part of printf; 10 misses both.

questionBank.question: Which of the following are peephole optimisations?
options: A, B, C and D only
questionBank.explanation: Peephole optimisation looks at a short sliding window of target (or intermediate) instructions and replaces patterns locally. A (redundant load/store elimination), B (flow-of-control optimisation, jump to jump) and C (algebraic simplification and strength reduction on one instruction) are classic peephole transformations. D is global register allocation, which needs liveness information for the whole procedure. E is loop-invariant code motion, a global (loop) optimisation that needs data-flow analysis. So A, B and C only.

stmts: A. Deleting the load in “MOV R0, a” immediately followed by “MOV a, R0”, when the second instruction has no label
B. Replacing a jump to an instruction that is itself an unconditional jump by a direct jump to the final target
C. Replacing x * 2 by x + x or by a left shift
D. Assigning registers to variables across a whole procedure by graph colouring
E. Moving a loop-invariant computation out of a loop that spans several basic blocks

questionBank.explanation: The grammar fixes precedence and associativity: & is generated lower in the tree (at the T level), so it binds tighter than #, and both operators are left-associative. The input parses as (2 # (3 & 4)) # 5. With the semantic rules, 3 & 4 = 3 + 4 = 7, then 2 # 7 = 2 × 7 = 14, then 14 # 5 = 14 × 5 = 70. 50 evaluates strictly left to right, ((2 × 3) + 4) × 5, ignoring the precedence built into the grammar. 26 gives # the higher precedence: (2 × 3) + (4 × 5). 19 swaps the semantic actions, reading # as + and & as ×: 2 + (3 × 4) + 5.

questionBank.question: A TCP connection starts with cwnd = 1 MSS in transmission round 1 and ssthresh = 32 MSS. In slow start cwnd doubles each round, but if doubling would exceed ssthresh it is set to ssthresh; at or above ssthresh, congestion avoidance adds 1 MSS per round. A timeout occurs during round 9; then ssthresh becomes ⌊cwnd/2⌋ and cwnd is 1 MSS in round 10. What is cwnd in round 16?
questionBank.explanation: Rounds 1–6: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 (slow start reaches ssthresh = 32). Rounds 7–9: 33, 34, 35 (congestion avoidance). Timeout in round 9 with cwnd = 35: ssthresh = ⌊35/2⌋ = 17, cwnd = 1. Rounds 10–14: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Round 15: doubling 16 would give 32 > 17, so cwnd = 17. Round 16: congestion avoidance, 17 + 1 = 18 MSS. 17 stops one round early; 32 keeps doubling past the new threshold; 19 starts additive increase a round too soon.

questionBank.question: A TCP connection runs over a 1 Gbps link. Using the 32-bit sequence-number field, how long does it take for the byte sequence numbers to wrap around at full speed?
questionBank.explanation: TCP numbers bytes, so the sequence space is 2³² bytes = 4 294 967 296 bytes. The link carries 10⁹ / 8 = 1.25 × 10⁸ bytes per second. Wrap-around time = 2³² / 1.25 × 10⁸ ≈ 34.36 s. 4.3 s treats the sequence numbers as counting bits (2³² / 10⁹); 275 s multiplies by 8 instead of dividing; 17.2 s uses only half the space (2³¹). Since this is shorter than common maximum segment lifetimes on fast links, TCP uses the timestamp option (PAWS) at high speeds.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: SMTP, used to send and relay mail between servers, listens on TCP 25 (A-II). DNS uses port 53, mostly over UDP for queries and TCP for zone transfers and large responses (B-IV). POP3, which downloads mail to a client, uses 110 (C-III). IMAP, which manages mail on the server, uses 143 (D-I). So A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I.

b: II. 25
III. 110
IV. 53

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: SCTP supports multistreaming (several independent streams in one association, so loss in one stream does not block the others) and multihoming (an endpoint may have several IP addresses). Statement II is true: association setup is INIT, INIT-ACK (carrying a signed state cookie), COOKIE-ECHO and COOKIE-ACK. The server keeps no state until the cookie comes back, which defeats the half-open-connection flooding that affects TCP’s three-way handshake.

stmts: Statement I: SCTP, like TCP, carries only a single stream of data in each connection.
Statement II: SCTP sets up an association with a four-way handshake that uses a state cookie, which protects the server against SYN-flooding-style attacks.

questionBank.question: In an RSA system, p = 7, q = 19 and the public exponent is e = 5. What is the private exponent d?
questionBank.explanation: n = 7 × 19 = 133 and φ(n) = (7 − 1)(19 − 1) = 6 × 18 = 108. d is the inverse of e modulo φ(n): 5d ≡ 1 (mod 108). Since 5 × 65 = 325 = 3 × 108 + 1, d = 65. Check with m = 4: c = 4⁵ mod 133 = 1024 mod 133 = 93, and 93⁶⁵ mod 133 = 4. The other values fail 5d ≡ 1 (mod 108): 5 × 43 = 215 ≡ 107, 5 × 29 = 145 ≡ 37 and 5 × 77 = 385 ≡ 61. A common slip is to invert e modulo n instead of φ(n).

questionBank.question: Two users run the Diffie–Hellman key exchange with prime q = 29 and primitive root g = 2. User A picks the private key 5 and user B picks 8. What is the shared secret key?
questionBank.explanation: A sends Y_A = 2⁵ mod 29 = 32 mod 29 = 3. B sends Y_B = 2⁸ mod 29 = 256 mod 29 = 24. A computes Y_B⁵ mod 29 = 24⁵ mod 29 = 7, and B computes Y_A⁸ mod 29 = 3⁸ mod 29 = 6561 mod 29 = 7. Both get K = 7 (= 2⁴⁰ mod 29). 3 and 24 are the public values Y_A and Y_B, which travel in the clear and are not the key.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about network security are correct?
options: A, B, C and E only
A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A is correct: signing uses the private key, so anyone with the public key can verify origin and integrity. B is correct: steganography conceals that a message exists (e.g. in image bits), whereas cryptography makes it unreadable. C is correct: AES (Rijndael) has a fixed 128-bit block with 10, 12 or 14 rounds for 128-, 192- and 256-bit keys. D is false: a packet filter decides on header fields (addresses, ports, protocol); payload inspection needs an application-level gateway or proxy. E is correct: tunnel mode protects the entire original packet and adds a new outer header, which is why it is used between VPN gateways; transport mode protects only the payload. So A, B, C and E only.

stmts: A. A digital signature is created with the sender’s private key and verified with the sender’s public key.
B. Steganography hides the existence of a message, while cryptography hides its meaning.
C. AES works on 128-bit blocks with key sizes of 128, 192 or 256 bits.
D. A packet-filtering firewall inspects application-layer payloads to block malicious SQL statements.
E. In IPSec tunnel mode, the whole original IP packet, including its header, is encapsulated inside a new IP packet.

questionBank.question: The data bits 1101011 are sent using CRC with generator polynomial x³ + x + 1. What check bits (the remainder) are appended?
questionBank.explanation: The generator x³ + x + 1 is 1011 (degree 3), so append three 0s: 1101011000. Divide by 1011 using XOR (mod-2) division: the remainder is 110. The transmitted frame is 1101011 110, and it leaves remainder 000 when divided by 1011 at the receiver. The distractors come from appending the wrong number of zeros or from ordinary (non-XOR) subtraction.

questionBank.question: The network 172.20.0.0/16 is to be divided into equal-size subnets, each of which must hold at least 500 hosts. What is the maximum number of such subnets?
questionBank.explanation: A subnet needs h host bits with 2ʰ − 2 ≥ 500, so h = 9 (510 usable hosts); 8 bits give only 254. Prefix length = 32 − 9 = 23. Subnet bits borrowed from the /16 = 23 − 16 = 7, giving 2⁷ = 128 subnets. 64 uses 10 host bits; 256 uses 8 host bits, which is too small; 126 applies the obsolete rule of discarding the all-zeros and all-ones subnets, which CIDR does not need.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: GPRS adds packet switching to GSM; the Serving GPRS Support Node tracks the mobile and the Gateway GPRS Support Node connects to external packet networks (III). B: SMS messages go through the SMSC, which stores and forwards them, using the GSM signalling channels (II). C: a mobile ad hoc network has no base stations; nodes relay for each other using protocols such as AODV or DSR (IV). D: in cloud computing, an SLA is the agreement between provider and customer on service levels, e.g. 99.9% availability, with credits if missed (I). So A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I.

b: I. A contract that fixes measurable targets such as uptime and response time, with penalties
II. Short messages carried by a store-and-forward centre over the signalling channels
III. Packet-switched data added to GSM through SGSN and GGSN nodes
IV. An infrastructure-less multi-hop network that uses on-demand routing such as AODV

questionBank.question: A perceptron with a step activation (output 1 if net ≥ 0, else 0) has weights w = (0.2, −0.4) and bias b = 0.1. The learning rate is η = 0.5. It is shown the input x = (1, 1) with target t = 1. What are the weights and bias after one application of the perceptron learning rule?
questionBank.explanation: net = 0.2 × 1 + (−0.4) × 1 + 0.1 = −0.1 < 0, so the output y = 0 and the error t − y = 1. Update: wᵢ ← wᵢ + η (t − y) xᵢ and b ← b + η (t − y). w₁ = 0.2 + 0.5 = 0.7, w₂ = −0.4 + 0.5 = 0.1, b = 0.1 + 0.5 = 0.6. Leaving the bias unchanged is a common slip; subtracting the update uses the wrong sign of the error; leaving everything unchanged assumes the output was already correct.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: a Hopfield network has symmetric recurrent connections; each asynchronous update lowers an energy function, so the network settles into stored patterns (associative memory) (II). B: a SOM uses competitive, unsupervised learning; the best-matching unit and its neighbourhood move towards the input, preserving topology (III). C: backpropagation is supervised gradient descent for multilayer perceptrons using the chain rule (IV). D: Q-learning is reinforcement learning from rewards (I). So A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

b: I. Learns action values from a scalar reward signal
II. A recurrent network with an energy function, used as content-addressable memory
III. Updates a winning neuron and its neighbours to form a topology-preserving map
IV. Propagates the output error backwards with the chain rule to adjust hidden-layer weights

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both are true, and (R) explains (A). A single-layer perceptron computes a linear threshold, so it can only separate classes with a straight line (hyperplane). The XOR points (0,0), (1,1) (output 0) and (0,1), (1,0) (output 1) cannot be split by any line: the four constraints on w₁, w₂ and b are contradictory. Adding a hidden layer (a multilayer perceptron) removes the limitation.

stmts: Assertion (A): A single-layer perceptron cannot learn the XOR function.
Reason (R): The XOR function’s two classes are not linearly separable in the input space.

questionBank.question: A neuron uses the sigmoid activation σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ). Its inputs are (1, 0, 1), its weights are (0.5, −0.3, 0.25) and its bias is −0.75. What is its output?
questionBank.explanation: z = 0.5 × 1 + (−0.3) × 0 + 0.25 × 1 + (−0.75) = 0.5 + 0 + 0.25 − 0.75 = 0. σ(0) = 1 / (1 + e⁰) = 1/2 = 0.5. 0 and 1 are what a step function might give at the threshold, not a sigmoid; 0.73 ≈ σ(1) forgets the bias.

questionBank.question: A game tree has a MAX root with three MIN children B, C and D, explored left to right. The leaves are B: 5, 8, 6; C: 4, 9, 7; D: 7, 3, 10. With alpha–beta pruning, what is the minimax value of the root, and how many leaves are pruned?
questionBank.explanation: B is evaluated fully: min(5, 8, 6) = 5, so α = 5 at the root. C: the first leaf 4 makes C ≤ 4 ≤ α, so the remaining leaves 9 and 7 are pruned (2 leaves). D: the first leaf 7 gives D ≤ 7, which is still above α, so continue; the next leaf 3 makes D ≤ 3 ≤ α, so the leaf 10 is pruned (1 leaf). Root = max(5, ≤4, ≤3) = 5, with 2 + 1 = 3 leaves pruned. “2 pruned” misses the cut in D; 7 takes the max of the first leaves.

questionBank.question: A search tree has a uniform branching factor of 3 and the shallowest goal is at depth 4. Counting every node generated except the root, and assuming the goal is the last node at depth 4, how many nodes does iterative deepening search generate?
questionBank.explanation: In IDS the nodes at depth i are generated once in each iteration with limit ≥ i, that is (d + 1 − i) times. Total = 4 × 3 + 3 × 9 + 2 × 27 + 1 × 81 = 12 + 27 + 54 + 81 = 174. BFS generates each level once: 3 + 9 + 27 + 81 = 120. So the repeated work of IDS costs only about 45% extra here, while it uses O(bd) memory instead of O(bᵈ). 363 = 3⁰ + … + 3⁵ counts an extra level; 179 also counts the root, which IDS regenerates in each of the 5 iterations.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about search strategies are correct?
options: A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A is correct: UCS expands nodes in order of path cost g(n), so the first goal expanded is cheapest when costs are positive. B is false: greedy best-first uses only h(n) and ignores the cost already paid, so it can return a costlier path even with an admissible h. C is correct: with h(n) ≤ h*(n), A* tree search never expands a suboptimal goal before the optimal one. D is correct: consistency h(n) ≤ c(n, n′) + h(n′), applied along an optimal path to the goal, gives h(n) ≤ h*(n). E is false: hill climbing can get stuck at local maxima, plateaus and ridges. So A, C and D only.

stmts: A. Uniform-cost search is optimal when every step cost is positive.
B. Greedy best-first search is optimal whenever its heuristic is admissible.
C. A* tree search is optimal when its heuristic is admissible.
D. A consistent heuristic with h(goal) = 0 is also admissible.
E. Steepest-ascent hill climbing is complete.

questionBank.question: An aggregated fuzzy output set is defined on the points x = 10, 20, 30, 40 with membership grades 0.2, 0.6, 1.0 and 0.4 respectively. What is the crisp output by the (discrete) centroid method?
questionBank.explanation: Centroid = Σ μ(x)·x / Σ μ(x) = (0.2 × 10 + 0.6 × 20 + 1.0 × 30 + 0.4 × 40) / (0.2 + 0.6 + 1.0 + 0.4) = (2 + 12 + 30 + 16) / 2.2 = 60 / 2.2 ≈ 27.27. 30 is the max-membership (height) method; 25 is the plain average of the four x values; 15 divides Σ μ(x)·x by the number of points (60/4) instead of by Σ μ(x).

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: goal stack planning works on one goal at a time with a stack, assuming subgoals can be solved in sequence (linear planning). With interacting goals, as in the Sussman anomaly with blocks, solving one goal undoes another, giving longer plans; non-linear (partial-order) planners handle such cases better. Statement II is true: in the semantic-web layer cake, RDF gives subject–predicate–object triples, RDFS adds classes and properties, and OWL adds richer ontology constructs (cardinality, equivalence, disjointness) that multi-agent systems use for knowledge sharing.

stmts: Statement I: Goal stack planning, as used with STRIPS operators, is a linear planner and can produce non-optimal plans or get stuck on interacting subgoals, as in the Sussman anomaly.
Statement II: In the semantic web, OWL builds on RDF and RDF Schema to describe ontologies that software agents can share.

questionBank.question: In a genetic algorithm, the population of 5 chromosomes has fitness values 12, 28, 5, 35 and 20. Using roulette-wheel selection to fill a mating pool of 5, what is the expected number of copies of the fittest chromosome?
questionBank.explanation: Total fitness = 12 + 28 + 5 + 35 + 20 = 100. The fittest has fitness 35, so its selection probability is 35/100 = 0.35. Expected copies in 5 spins = 5 × 0.35 = 1.75 (equivalently fᵢ / f̄ = 35 / 20). 0.35 is the probability of one spin, not the expected count; 2 rounds the expectation; 1.4 = 28/20 is the second-fittest.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false. Multiplication of non-zero integers is closed and associative and 1 is the identity, but inverses fail: the inverse of 2 would be 1/2, which is not an integer. Only 1 and −1 have inverses, so (ℤ∖{0}, ×) is a commutative monoid, not a group. Statement II is true. If x² = e for every x, then every element is its own inverse. For any a, b: ab = (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹ = ba, so G is abelian. (The Klein four-group is the standard example.) So Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: The set of non-zero integers is a group under ordinary multiplication.
Statement II: If every element x of a group G satisfies x ∘ x = e, then G is abelian.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Let the domain of x and y be the set of all integers ℤ. Which of the following statements is FALSE?
questionBank.explanation: ∀x ∃y (x + y = 0) is true: for each x choose y = −x. ∃y ∀x (x + y = x) is true: y = 0 works for every x (one fixed y is enough, so the ∃ can stand outside). ∀x ∃y (y < x) is true: for each x choose y = x − 1. ∃x ∀y (x ≤ y) says ℤ has a least element; there is none, because for any candidate x the integer y = x − 1 is smaller. So this statement is false. The trap is that the same formula is true over ℕ, where 0 is the least element: the truth of a quantified statement depends on the domain and on the order of the quantifiers.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: addition on the non-negative integers is closed and associative with identity 0, but no element except 0 has an additive inverse inside the set: a commutative monoid, not a group (IV). B: (ℤ, +) has identity 0 and inverse −a for every a, and addition is commutative: an abelian group (II). C: concatenation of strings is associative and the empty string ε is the identity, but ab ≠ ba, so it is a non-commutative monoid, the free monoid on Σ (III). D: subtraction is closed on ℤ but not associative: (5 − 3) − 1 = 1 while 5 − (3 − 1) = 3. So (ℤ, −) is only a groupoid (magma), not even a semigroup (I).

b: I. Closed binary operation, but not a semigroup
II. Abelian group
III. Non-commutative monoid
IV. Commutative monoid that is not a group

questionBank.question: The map f : (ℤ, +) → (ℤ₆, +₆) is defined by f(x) = x mod 6. Which of the following is the kernel of f?
questionBank.explanation: f is a homomorphism because (x + y) mod 6 = (x mod 6) +₆ (y mod 6). The kernel is the set of elements mapped to the identity 0 of ℤ₆, i.e. all x with x mod 6 = 0: the multiples of 6, 6ℤ. {0} would mean f is one-to-one, which it is not (0 and 6 both map to 0). ℤ would mean f is trivial, which it is not (f(1) = 1). 3ℤ is wrong because f(3) = 3 ≠ 0. By the first isomorphism theorem, ℤ/6ℤ ≅ ℤ₆, since f is onto.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements are correct?
options: A, B, C and D only
questionBank.explanation: A is correct: a tree is connected and acyclic, and by induction (remove a leaf) it has n − 1 edges. B is correct: this is Euler’s theorem; entering and leaving each vertex uses edges in pairs, so all degrees must be even, and in a connected graph that condition is also sufficient. C is incorrect: K₃,₃ is one of Kuratowski’s two basic non-planar graphs (with K₅). D is correct: this is König’s characterisation of bipartite graphs. E is incorrect: every pair of vertices of K₅ is adjacent, so all 5 vertices need different colours and χ(K₅) = 5. So A, B and D only.

stmts: A. Every tree with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges.
B. A connected multigraph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree.
C. The complete bipartite graph K₃,₃ is planar.
D. A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no cycle of odd length.
E. The chromatic number of the complete graph K₅ is 4.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A connected simple planar graph has 12 vertices, and every vertex has degree 3. How many faces (regions, including the outer face) does any planar drawing of it have?
questionBank.explanation: By the handshake lemma, 2e = sum of degrees = 12 × 3 = 36, so e = 18. Euler’s formula for a connected planar graph gives v − e + f = 2, so f = 2 − v + e = 2 − 12 + 18 = 8. (The truncated tetrahedron is a graph of this kind.) 6 comes from using v − e + f = 0; 20 comes from taking e = 36, forgetting to halve the degree sum; 10 is 2 + 8, an arithmetic slip.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both statements are true, and R explains A. R: in a planar drawing of a triangle-free simple graph, every face is bounded by at least 4 edges and each edge borders at most 2 faces, so 4f ≤ 2e. Substituting f = 2 − v + e into Euler’s formula gives e ≤ 2v − 4. A: K₃,₃ is bipartite, so it has no triangle, with v = 6 and e = 9. R would require 9 ≤ 2 × 6 − 4 = 8, which is false, so K₃,₃ cannot be planar. The general bound e ≤ 3v − 6 (9 ≤ 12) is satisfied and does not decide the question, which is the usual trap.

stmts: Assertion (A): The complete bipartite graph K₃,₃ is not planar.
Reason (R): Every simple planar graph with at least 3 vertices and no triangle satisfies e ≤ 2v − 4.

questionBank.question: Which of the following sets of binary codewords is a prefix code?
questionBank.explanation: In a prefix code no codeword is a prefix of another, so every codeword is a leaf of the binary code tree and decoding is instantaneous. {0, 10, 110, 111}: 0 is not a prefix of any word starting with 1; 10 is not a prefix of 110 or 111 (they begin 11). This is a prefix code (it is a Huffman-type tree). {0, 01, 11, 111}: 0 is a prefix of 01, and 11 of 111. {1, 10, 100, 000}: 1 is a prefix of 10 and 100. {00, 01, 0, 11}: 0 is a prefix of 00 and 01.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following steps of the Critical Path Method (CPM) in the order in which they are carried out.
questionBank.explanation: CPM starts with the activity list, durations and predecessors (C). The network is drawn from those precedences (B). The forward pass computes earliest start and finish times, which gives the project duration (E). The backward pass starts from that duration and computes latest times (A); it needs the forward pass result, so E comes before A. Finally total float = LS − ES (or LF − EF) is computed, and activities with zero float form the critical path (D). Order: C, B, E, A, D.

stmts: A. Compute the latest start and finish times by a backward pass from the project end
B. Draw the activity network (arrow or node diagram) from the precedence relations
C. List all activities with their durations and immediate predecessors
D. Compute total float for each activity and mark the zero-float activities as the critical path
E. Compute the earliest start and finish times by a forward pass from the project start

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true. Levelling first uses the floats of non-critical activities, but when a resource limit is tight, some activities must be delayed beyond their float and the project finishes later. (Resource smoothing, by contrast, keeps the duration fixed and works only within the float.) Statement II is false. The project duration equals the length of the critical path. Shortening a non-critical activity only increases its float and leaves the critical path unchanged, so the duration does not fall. Crashing pays off only on critical activities, choosing the one with the least cost slope first. So Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: Resource levelling, which shifts activities to remove peaks in resource demand under a resource limit, may lengthen the project duration.
Statement II: Crashing an activity that is not on the critical path always shortens the project duration.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: a horizontal microinstruction dedicates one bit to each control signal. The word is long, but many micro-operations can be issued in the same cycle with no decoding delay (III). B: a vertical microinstruction encodes mutually exclusive signals into short fields, so each field must be decoded. The word is short but less parallel (II). C: nanoprogramming uses two levels. The control memory holds short microinstructions that index a nanomemory of wide words carrying the actual signals, which saves control-store space when many microinstructions repeat the same signal patterns (IV). D: a hardwired control unit has no control memory; gates, flip-flops, decoders and a sequence counter generate the signals directly (I). It is faster but harder to modify.

b: I. Control signals are produced by combinational logic from the decoded opcode and the timing signals
II. Encoded control fields; each field needs a decoder, so the word is short
III. One bit per control signal; a wide word allowing maximum parallelism
IV. Two-level control store: a short microword points to a wider nanoword that holds the signals

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true. A label can be used before it is defined (a forward reference), so pass 1 scans the program with a location counter and records every label and its address in the symbol table. Pass 2 then translates each instruction, looking up symbolic addresses in that table. Statement II is false on both counts. Microprogrammed control needs a control-memory read for each micro-step, so it is usually slower than hardwired logic; its advantage is flexibility, which suits large CISC instruction sets. RISC designs have simple, uniform instructions and generally use hardwired control for speed. So Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: In a two-pass assembler, the first pass assigns addresses to labels and builds the symbol table, and the second pass uses the table to produce the machine code.
Statement II: Microprogrammed control units are generally faster than hardwired control units, which is why most RISC processors use microprogramming.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: A is false and R is true. Branch and Save return Address (BSA) does not use AC. Its micro-operations are D5T4: M[AR] ← PC, AR ← AR + 1, then D5T5: PC ← AR. So BSA 135 writes the return address into memory word 135, and the subroutine body starts at 136. The subroutine returns with an indirect branch, BUN 135 I, which loads PC from word 135. Keeping AC untouched is what lets the calling program pass a value to the subroutine in AC. So (A) is false but (R) is true.

stmts: Assertion (A): In Mano’s basic computer, executing BSA 135 stores the return address in the accumulator (AC) and then branches to address 135.
Reason (R): BSA stores the address of the next instruction (the current PC) in the memory word at the effective address and then sets PC to the effective address plus one.

questionBank.question: A two-word instruction is stored at memory addresses 300 and 301, and its address field (the second word) holds 450. Register R1 contains 200. The PC is incremented after each word is fetched. What is the effective address if the addressing mode is PC-relative?
questionBank.explanation: Both words are fetched before the operand address is computed, so PC = 302 when execution starts. In relative mode EA = PC + address field = 302 + 450 = 752. 750 is the trap of adding the address field to the instruction’s own address (300). 650 is the index/base-register result, R1 + 450. 452 wrongly uses 2 (the instruction length) as the PC value.
questionBank.topic: Effective address: relative and indexed modes

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: in immediate mode the operand itself is in the address field, which suits constants such as ADD R1, #5 (II). B: in register indirect mode the register holds the memory address of the operand, i.e. it acts as a pointer (IV). C: autoincrement uses the register as a pointer and then advances it by the operand size, so a loop can walk through an array without a separate increment instruction (III). The usual confusion is between B and C: both use a register pointer, but only C updates it.

D: multi-cycle microcoded complex instructions are the defining feature of CISC, not RISC; RISC aims at about one instruction per cycle with hardwired control. E: a large register file (sometimes with overlapping register windows) reduces memory traffic: characteristic. So A, B, C and E only.

questionBank.question: A processor has 24-bit instructions. Each instruction contains two register fields that can address any of 32 general-purpose registers, and a 6-bit immediate field. The rest of the instruction is the opcode. What is the maximum number of distinct opcodes?
questionBank.explanation: Each register field must select one of 32 registers, which needs log₂ 32 = 5 bits, so two fields take 10 bits. The immediate field takes 6 bits. Opcode bits = 24 − 10 − 6 = 8, so at most 2⁸ = 256 opcodes. 128 comes from using 6 bits per register field (an off-by-one in log₂); 64 from forgetting that there are two register fields and subtracting 6 + 6 + 6; 512 from giving the opcode 9 bits.

questionBank.question: Booth’s algorithm is used to multiply two 8-bit signed numbers, with 01110110 as the multiplier. Scanning the multiplier bit pairs (Qᵢ, Qᵢ₋₁) from the least significant end, with Q₋₁ = 0 initially, how many add or subtract operations of the multiplicand are performed in total?
questionBank.explanation: Booth’s rule: pair (1, 0) means subtract the multiplicand, (0, 1) means add it, and (0, 0) or (1, 1) means only shift. The multiplier bits from LSB to MSB are 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0. The pairs (Qᵢ, Qᵢ₋₁) are: (0,0) shift; (1,0) subtract; (1,1) shift; (0,1) add; (1,0) subtract; (1,1) shift; (1,1) shift; (0,1) add. That is 2 subtractions + 2 additions = 4 operations. Each run of 1s costs just two operations, one at each end, which is why Booth recoding helps. 5 counts the number of 1 bits, the operation count of plain shift-and-add multiplication.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:

questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true. If two cores cache the same block and one writes to it, the other core’s copy becomes stale. Snooping or directory protocols such as MESI invalidate or update the other copies. Statement II is false. Exclusive means that only this cache holds the line and that it is clean, i.e. identical to memory. The dirty exclusive state is Modified (M). The benefit of E is that a write to an E line can move it silently to M without a bus transaction. So Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: In a multicore processor where each core has a private L1 data cache, a cache coherence protocol such as MESI is needed so that cores do not read stale copies of shared data.
Statement II: In the MESI protocol, a cache line in the Exclusive (E) state is dirty, meaning its contents differ from main memory.

questionBank.explanation: Both are true, and R explains A. A control hazard occurs because the instruction after a branch is fetched before the branch outcome is known. With a delayed branch, the architecture always executes the instruction in the delay slot. The compiler moves an independent instruction from before the branch into that slot (or inserts a NOP if none is available). The cycle that would have been a stall is therefore used productively, which is exactly why the penalty falls.

stmts: Assertion (A): Delayed branching can reduce the penalty caused by control hazards in an instruction pipeline.

Reason (R): In delayed branching, the compiler fills the slot after the branch with an instruction that must execute whether or not the branch is taken, so the pipeline does useful work while the branch is resolved.

Under dynamic scoping, a non-local name is resolved through the chain of active calls, using the most recent declaration still alive. First call h(): h declares a local x = 2 and calls g. questionBank.question: What is the output of this C program?
questionBank.explanation: p starts at a[1]. x = *p++: postfix ++ binds tighter than *, but it yields the old pointer, so x = a[1] = 9 and p moves to a[2]. y = *++p: p first moves to a[3], then it is dereferenced, so y = 25. z = ++*p: this increments the pointed-to value, so a[3] becomes 26 and z = 26; p stays at a[3]. &a[4] − p = 4 − 3 = 1 element. The C program below is compiled to an executable named prog and run from the shell as: ./prog red green blue

questionBank.question: Which fopen() mode opens a file for both reading and writing, creates the file if it does not exist, and truncates it to zero length if it already exists?
questionBank.explanation: "w+" opens for update (read and write); the file is created if absent and truncated if present. "r+" also opens for reading and writing, but the file must already exist and it is not truncated. "a+" opens for reading and appending; it creates the file if needed, but it never truncates it, and every write goes to the end. "rw" is not a valid mode string in standard C.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:

Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Both statements are false. Statement I: a class with at least one pure virtual function (virtual void f() = 0;) is abstract, and the compiler rejects any attempt to create an object of it, whether or not f is ever called. It can only be used as a base class or through pointers and references. Statement II: constructors cannot be virtual. Dynamic dispatch uses the object’s virtual table pointer, which is only set up by the constructor, and when an object is created its exact type is always known. Destructors, on the other hand, can and usually should be virtual in a polymorphic base class. So both Statement I and Statement II are false.

Statement II: In C++, a constructor can be declared virtual so that the correct derived-class constructor is selected at run time.

Likewise sy = 200/40 = 5. xv = 0 + (60 − 20) × 5 = 200, and yv = 0 + (30 − 10) × 5 = 100. The point is at the centre of the window, so it maps to the centre of the viewport: (200, 100). (240, 120) divides by the window’s maximum coordinates (400/100 and 200/50) instead of its width and height, and ignores the window origin; (300, 150) scales 60 and 30 by 5 without subtracting the origin; (200, 150) subtracts the origin in x only.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about a Bezier curve defined by n + 1 control points are correct?

Every Bernstein polynomial is non-zero on the whole open interval (0, 1), so moving any control point changes the entire curve. Local control is a property of B-splines. E: B′(0) = n(P₁ − P₀), so the curve starts in the direction of P₀P₁: correct. So A, B, C and E only.

B. The curve lies inside the convex hull of its control points.

B: vertical fragments are projections, and the key is needed in each to reconstruct the relation by a lossless join: correct. C: incorrect. After voting YES, a participant enters the prepared (uncertain) state and must wait for the coordinator’s global commit or abort decision; this is why 2PC can block. D: incorrect. Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both are true, and R explains A. The CAP theorem (Brewer’s conjecture, proved by Gilbert and Lynch) says that during a partition a system must choose between C and A. R gives the reason: a replica cut off from the others cannot know the latest write, so it can either wait or refuse (CP, as in HBase) or reply with what it has (AP, as in Cassandra with low consistency levels). Since partitions cannot be ruled out in a real network, the practical choice is between CP and AP behaviour.

stmts: Assertion (A): A distributed data store cannot guarantee consistency, availability and partition tolerance all at the same time.

Reason (R): When the network is partitioned, a node that cannot reach the other replicas must either refuse the request, giving up availability, or answer with possibly stale data, giving up consistency.

questionBank.question: A 700 MB file is stored in HDFS with a block size of 128 MB and a replication factor of 3. How many block replicas are stored across the DataNodes in total?
questionBank.explanation: Number of blocks = ⌈700/128⌉ = 6: five full 128 MB blocks (640 MB) and one final block of 60 MB. Each block is replicated 3 times, so 6 × 3 = 18 block replicas. The disk space used is 700 × 3 = 2,100 MB, not 6 × 128 × 3 = 2,304 MB, because the last block occupies only 60 MB. 6 forgets replication; 15 uses ⌊700/128⌋ = 5 blocks; 21 uses 7 blocks.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following stages of a Hadoop MapReduce job in the order in which they occur.
questionBank.explanation: The input is first split (B), so that each split can be given to one map task, ideally on the node that holds the data. Map tasks emit intermediate (key, value) pairs (E). The framework then partitions these by key, transfers them to the reducers and sorts them (C), so that each reducer sees all values of a key together. Reducers aggregate the values (A), and their output is written to HDFS (D). Order: B, E, C, A, D. Shuffle and sort always sit between map and reduce, which is what the distractors disturb.

stmts: A. Reduce tasks aggregate all values for each key
B. The input file in HDFS is divided into input splits
C. Intermediate key–value pairs are partitioned, shuffled and sorted by key
D. The final output is written back to HDFS
E. Map tasks process each split and emit intermediate key–value pairs

questionBank.question: A web application builds the query "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "'" from text typed by the user. Which measure most effectively prevents SQL injection in this code?

Checking the input with JavaScript in the browser before it is submitted
Adding DISTINCT to the SELECT clause
Storing passwords in the users table as salted hashes
questionBank.explanation: SQL injection happens because user text is concatenated into the SQL string, so an input such as x' OR '1'='1 changes the query’s structure. With a parameterised query, the statement is compiled first and the input is sent separately as data, so it can never be parsed as SQL: this is the primary defence. Browser-side JavaScript checks are easily bypassed by sending the request directly. DISTINCT only removes duplicate rows. Hashing passwords protects stored credentials if they leak, but does not stop the query from being altered.

questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true. Applying σ before a join shrinks the operands, so the join handles fewer tuples; pushing projections down similarly removes unneeded attributes. Statement II is false. A Cartesian product of R and S produces |R| × |S| tuples, which is the most expensive operation. The heuristic is the opposite: combine a Cartesian product with a following selection into a join, and order joins so that the most restrictive ones run first. So Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questionBank.question: A system uses 32-bit virtual addresses, a page size of 4 KB and single-level paging. Each page table entry is 4 bytes. What is the size of the page table of one process?
questionBank.explanation: Page offset = log₂(4 KB) = 12 bits, so the page number has 32 − 12 = 20 bits and there are 2²⁰ pages. Page table size = 2²⁰ entries × 4 bytes = 2²² bytes = 4 MB. 1 MB forgets the 4-byte entry size (it counts entries); 4 KB confuses the table with one page; 16 MB multiplies by 16. A 4 MB table per process is exactly why multilevel and inverted page tables exist.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:

Both Statement I and Statement II are false

questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true. After mmap(), the first access to a page causes a page fault that brings the file block in through demand paging; later reads and writes are ordinary loads and stores, and dirty pages are written back to the file. Statement II is false. Several processes can map the same file, and the OS can map the same physical frames into each address space. This is a standard way of sharing memory between processes, and it is how Windows implements shared memory. So Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: Memory-mapped file I/O associates disk blocks of a file with pages of a process’s virtual address space, so that the file can be read and written with ordinary memory accesses.
Statement II: Two processes can never map the same file at the same time, because each mapped page must belong to exactly one process.

questionBank.explanation: Both are true, and R explains A. Belady’s anomaly is when adding frames increases the number of page faults, which can happen with FIFO. For a stack algorithm, the n most recently used pages are always among the n + 1 most recently used pages, so any reference that hits with n frames also hits with n + 1 frames. Faults can therefore never increase when frames are added. LRU and Optimal are both stack algorithms; FIFO is not, which is why FIFO can show the anomaly.

stmts: Assertion (A): The LRU page-replacement algorithm never exhibits Belady’s anomaly.
Reason (R): LRU is a stack algorithm: for any reference string, the set of pages in memory with n frames is always a subset of the set that would be in memory with n + 1 frames.
