questionBank.question:
A process has 3 page frames, all initially empty. It references pages in this order:
2, 5, 1, 2, 6, 5, 2, 7, 1, 5, 6, 2
How many page faults occur with LRU replacement?
questionBank.explanation: Trace, writing the resident pages from least to most recently used (F = fault): 2 F [2]; 5 F [2 5]; 1 F [2 5 1]; 2 hit [5 1 2]; 6 F, evict 5 [1 2 6]; 5 F, evict 1 [2 6 5]; 2 hit [6 5 2]; 7 F, evict 6 [5 2 7]; 1 F, evict 5 [2 7 1]; 5 F, evict 2 [7 1 5]; 6 F, evict 7 [1 5 6]; 2 F, evict 1 [5 6 2]. There are only 2 hits in 12 references, so LRU gives 10 faults. 7 is the count for Optimal replacement on the same string (the minimum possible); 9 comes from treating page 5 at reference 10 as still resident (it was evicted at reference 9), and 11 from missing one of the two hits. FIFO happens to give 10 faults on this string too, so only a careful trace, not a guess about which policy is better, settles the answer.

Both Statement I and Statement II are false

questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false. Rate-monotonic (RM) scheduling gives the highest static priority to the task with the shortest period, i.e. the highest rate; priority is inversely related to the period. Statement II is true. EDF assigns priorities dynamically by the nearest absolute deadline and is optimal on a single processor for such task sets: they can be scheduled if and only if Σ Cᵢ/Tᵢ ≤ 1. RM, by contrast, guarantees schedulability only up to the bound n(2^(1/n) − 1), about 69% for large n. So Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: Rate-monotonic scheduling assigns a higher static priority to a periodic task with a longer period.

Statement II: Under preemptive earliest-deadline-first (EDF) scheduling on one processor, a set of independent periodic tasks whose deadlines equal their periods is schedulable if its total CPU utilisation is at most 1.

questionBank.question: Five processes share identical units of a single resource type. Each process may need up to 4 units, and a process releases its units only after it finishes. What is the minimum number of units that guarantees that a deadlock can never occur?
questionBank.explanation: The worst case is when every process holds one unit less than its maximum and waits for one more: 5 × (4 − 1) = 15 units are then allocated and nobody can proceed if there are only 15. With one more unit, at least one process can reach its maximum of 4, finish and release its units, and the others can then finish in turn. Minimum = 5 × 3 + 1 = 16. 15 is exactly the deadlock-prone count, and 20 (5 × 4) is sufficient but not the minimum.

questionBank.question: Which of the following is a Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor?
questionBank.explanation: A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the hardware and hosts guest operating systems without a host OS underneath; VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, Xen and KVM (which turns the Linux kernel itself into the hypervisor) are the usual examples. VirtualBox, VMware Workstation and Parallels Desktop are Type 2 (hosted) hypervisors: they run as applications on a host operating system such as Windows, Linux or macOS, which adds a layer between the guests and the hardware.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: XP (Kent Beck) is known for its engineering practices: pair programming, unit tests written before the code, continuous refactoring and small releases (II). B: ASD (Jim Highsmith) replaces plan–build–revise with speculation, collaboration and learning cycles (III). C: DSDM uses time boxes and MoSCoW prioritisation (must, should, could, won’t), and holds that about 80% of an application can be delivered in 20% of the time a full application would take (IV). D: FDD (Coad and De Luca) organises the work around a feature list, with plan-by-feature, design-by-feature and build-by-feature steps (I).

b: I. Work is planned, designed and built by client-valued features, each small enough to deliver in about two weeks
II. Pair programming, test-first development, refactoring and small frequent releases
III. A life cycle of speculation, collaboration and learning
IV. Time-boxed iterations with MoSCoW prioritisation, following the 80/20 principle

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Both statements are false. Statement I: the spiral model (Boehm) is risk-driven. Every loop includes risk analysis and often prototyping, which makes it suitable for large, complex, high-risk projects with evolving requirements. Its overhead is not justified for small, well-understood projects, which suit the waterfall model. Statement II: in the waterfall model, phases run strictly in sequence, so working software appears only near the end, after coding and testing; this late visibility is its best-known weakness. So both Statement I and Statement II are false.

stmts: Statement I: The spiral model is best suited to small projects whose requirements are fixed and fully understood at the start.
Statement II: In the waterfall model, a working version of the software is available to the customer early in the life cycle.

questionBank.question: Arrange the phases of the Unified Process, as described by Pressman, in the order in which they occur.
questionBank.explanation: Inception (C) establishes the business case, the scope and the initial use cases. Elaboration (E) refines the use-case model and baselines the architecture. Construction (A) builds and tests the software components. Transition (B) delivers the software to users for beta testing and feedback and produces the release. Production (D) covers ongoing use, monitoring and support. Order: C, E, A, B, D. (The RUP variant has only the first four phases.)

stmts: A. Construction
B. Transition
C. Inception
D. Production
E. Elaboration

questionBank.question: According to IEEE Std 830, which of the following are characteristics of a good software requirements specification (SRS)?
options: A, B, C and D only
A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: IEEE 830 lists eight qualities of a good SRS: correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, ranked for importance and/or stability, verifiable, modifiable and traceable. A, C and D match verifiable, traceable and unambiguous. B is wrong: an SRS states what the system must do, not how it will be designed; design detail belongs in the design document. E is wrong for the same reason: implementation choices are design constraints only if the customer imposes them, and they are not a quality of a good SRS. So A, C and D only.

stmts: A. Every requirement is verifiable by some finite, cost-effective process.
B. It describes in detail how each module will be designed and coded.
C. The origin of each requirement is clear and it can be referenced in later documents (traceable).
D. Every requirement has only one interpretation (unambiguous).
E. It fixes the programming language and the database product to be used.

questionBank.explanation: A: QFD focuses on maximising customer satisfaction and classifies requirements as normal (stated), expected (implicit, whose absence causes dissatisfaction) and exciting (beyond expectations) (III). B: a use case describes, from an actor’s point of view, the sequence of interactions with the system for one goal (IV). C: FAST (Joint Application Development is a similar technique) brings stakeholders together in a structured meeting with a facilitator and an agenda (II). D: a throwaway prototype is built quickly to settle unclear requirements and then discarded (I).

b: I. A partial working model built to clarify requirements that users cannot state precisely, and discarded afterwards
II. A joint meeting of customers and developers, run by a neutral facilitator, to identify the problem and propose solution elements
III. Translates customer needs into technical requirements, classifying them as normal, expected and exciting
IV. A scenario describing how an actor interacts with the system to achieve a goal

questionBank.explanation: A is true: the requirement states a performance constraint on how well the system does something, i.e. a quality attribute. That makes it non-functional (like reliability, security or usability requirements). R is false: providing services and reacting to particular inputs is the definition of functional requirements. Non-functional requirements are constraints on those services, such as timing, throughput, standards and qualities. So (A) is true but (R) is false.

Reason (R): Non-functional requirements specify the services the system must provide and how it must react to particular inputs.

questionBank.question: A project plans to reuse 120 software components. The team estimates a 60% probability that 30% of them will not integrate and will have to be written from scratch. Each such component averages 150 LOC, and the cost is $10 per LOC. What is the risk exposure (RE) for this risk?
questionBank.explanation: Risk exposure RE = P × C, where P is the probability of the risk and C is the cost to the project if it occurs. Components that must be rebuilt = 30% of 120 = 36. C = 36 × 150 LOC × $10 = $54,000. RE = 0.6 × $54,000 = $32,400. $54,000 is C alone (P is forgotten); $21,600 uses 1 − P = 0.4; $108,000 multiplies 120 components by 150 × 10 and 0.6. RE values of all risks are compared to decide where the mitigation, monitoring and management (RMMM) effort should go.

questionBank.question: The control flow graph of a module is connected, has 11 nodes and 14 edges, and contains 4 predicate (decision) nodes, each with two outgoing edges. What is its cyclomatic complexity V(G), i.e. the number of independent paths in a basis set?
questionBank.explanation: McCabe’s formula gives V(G) = E − N + 2P = 14 − 11 + 2 × 1 = 5. The predicate-node formula gives the same value: V(G) = number of binary decisions + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5. (For a planar flow graph it also equals the number of regions, including the outer region.) So basis path testing needs 5 test cases. 4 counts only the decisions; 6 uses E − N + 3; 3 uses E − N.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following types of module cohesion from the lowest (worst) to the highest (best).
questionBank.explanation: The standard scale runs coincidental < logical < temporal < procedural < communicational < sequential < functional. Coincidental (B): unrelated tasks grouped together. Logical (D): similar kinds of tasks selected by a flag, for example all input routines. Temporal (C): tasks that run at the same time, such as initialisation. Procedural (E): steps that follow a fixed order of control. Communicational (A): tasks that work on the same data. Order: B, D, C, E, A. The most common slip is swapping logical and temporal.

stmts: A. Communicational cohesion
B. Coincidental cohesion
C. Temporal cohesion
D. Logical cohesion
E. Procedural cohesion
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true. In each failure–repair cycle the system is up for MTTF on average and down for MTTR, and MTBF = MTTF + MTTR, so availability = MTTF/MTBF. For example, MTTF = 480 h and MTTR = 20 h give 480/500 = 96%. Statement II is true. Perfective maintenance enhances the software (new functions, better performance or usability). Corrective maintenance fixes faults, adaptive maintenance adapts the software to a changed environment, and preventive maintenance improves future maintainability. So both statements are true.

stmts: Statement I: Steady-state availability of a system can be computed as MTTF/(MTTF + MTTR).
Statement II: Perfective maintenance modifies software to add new features or improve performance in response to user requests.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: Huffman coding repeatedly merges the two least frequent trees, a locally optimal choice that is provably globally optimal: greedy (III). B: Floyd–Warshall builds dᵏ[i][j] = min(dᵏ⁻¹[i][j], dᵏ⁻¹[i][k] + dᵏ⁻¹[k][j]) from a table of subproblem solutions: dynamic programming (IV). C: Strassen splits the matrices into quadrants and uses 7 recursive multiplications instead of 8, giving Θ(n^2.81): divide and conquer (I). D: LC search expands the live node with the least estimated cost ĉ(x) and uses bounds to discard nodes: branch and bound (II).

b: I. Divide and conquer
II. Branch and bound
III. Greedy method
IV. Dynamic programming

questionBank.question: A knapsack has capacity 10. Four items have (weight, value) = (5, 40), (4, 30), (6, 50) and (3, 24). Each item is either taken whole or left out. What is the maximum total value that fits?
questionBank.explanation: Check the feasible combinations of at least two items (weight ≤ 10): (5,40)+(4,30) = 70 at weight 9; (5,40)+(3,24) = 64 at weight 8; (4,30)+(6,50) = 80 at weight 10; (4,30)+(3,24) = 54 at weight 7; (6,50)+(3,24) = 74 at weight 9. Any three items weigh at least 12, which is too much. The optimum is 80 (items 2 and 3); a DP table V[i][w] gives the same result. 74 is the greedy-by-ratio answer (take 50/6 ≈ 8.33 first, then a ratio-8 item that fits); 82 is the fractional-knapsack optimum (50 + 4/5 of 40), which is not allowed in the 0/1 version.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false. The value-density greedy rule is optimal for the fractional knapsack problem, but for 0/1 knapsack it can leave unused capacity that a different combination would fill better. (In the previous question it gives 74 instead of 80.) Statement II is true. Optimal substructure means that an optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems; overlapping subproblems means that the same subproblems recur, so storing their solutions (memoisation or a table) pays off. Without overlap, plain divide and conquer is enough. So Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: Choosing items in decreasing order of value per unit weight always gives an optimal solution to the 0/1 knapsack problem.
Statement II: Dynamic programming is applicable when a problem has optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Six symbols have the frequencies p: 8, q: 3, r: 14, s: 20, t: 5, u: 50 (out of 100). What is the average code length, in bits per symbol, of a Huffman code for them?
questionBank.explanation: Merge the two smallest weights each time: 3 + 5 = 8; 8 + 8 = 16; 14 + 16 = 30; 20 + 30 = 50; 50 + 50 = 100. Code lengths: u 1 bit, s 2, r 3, p 4, q and t 5 each. Weighted length = 50×1 + 20×2 + 14×3 + 8×4 + 3×5 + 5×5 = 50 + 40 + 42 + 32 + 15 + 25 = 204, so the average is 204/100 = 2.04 bits. As a shortcut, the total equals the sum of the merged weights: 8 + 16 + 30 + 50 + 100 = 204. The ties (two weights of 8 and two of 50) can change individual codes but not the average. 3.00 is a fixed-length code (⌈log₂ 6⌉ = 3).

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements are correct?
options: A, C, D and E only
A, B, C and D only
B, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A: Dijkstra finalises a vertex once it is extracted with the smallest tentative distance; a later negative edge could lower that distance, so its answers can be wrong: correct. B: after |V| − 1 rounds of relaxation, any edge that can still be relaxed reveals a reachable negative cycle: correct. C: Kruskal adds edges in increasing weight order and uses union–find to reject edges whose ends are already in the same component: correct. D: BFS explores in layers of increasing edge count, so it gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs: correct. E: incorrect. Prim’s algorithm finds a minimum spanning tree of a connected, undirected, weighted graph; spanning trees are not defined in this sense for directed graphs. So A, B, C and D only.

stmts: A. Dijkstra’s algorithm may give wrong shortest-path distances when some edge weights are negative.
B. The Bellman–Ford algorithm can detect a negative-weight cycle reachable from the source.
C. Kruskal’s algorithm is usually implemented with a disjoint-set (union–find) structure to test whether an edge would form a cycle.
D. Breadth-first search from a vertex s finds the minimum number of edges from s to every reachable vertex.
E. Prim’s algorithm can be applied only to directed acyclic graphs.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: An undirected weighted graph has vertices A–F and the edges A–B 7, A–C 4, B–C 6, B–D 2, C–D 8, C–E 5, D–E 9, D–F 3, E–F 10 and B–E 11. What is the total weight of its minimum spanning tree?
questionBank.explanation: Kruskal’s algorithm takes edges in increasing order of weight and skips any edge that would form a cycle. B–D 2 (take), D–F 3 (take), A–C 4 (take), C–E 5 (take), B–C 6 (take: it joins {A, C, E} with {B, D, F}). That makes 5 edges for 6 vertices, so the tree is complete. Weight = 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 20. Prim’s algorithm from any vertex gives the same total. 21 comes from choosing A–B 7 instead of B–C 6 to join the two parts; 18 omits one edge.

questionBank.question: During a depth-first search of a directed graph, u and v have discovery and finishing times with d[u] < d[v] < f[v] < f[u], and (u, v) is an edge that is not a tree edge. What kind of edge is (u, v)?
options: Tree edge whose discovery was delayed
questionBank.explanation: The interval of v lies inside the interval of u, so v is a descendant of u in the DFS forest (parenthesis theorem). A non-tree edge from an ancestor to a proper descendant is a forward edge. A back edge goes the other way, from a descendant to an ancestor (d[v] < d[u] < f[u] < f[v]); back edges are exactly what signals a cycle. A cross edge joins vertices whose intervals do not overlap, with v finished before u is discovered (d[v] < f[v] < d[u] < f[u]). The question says the edge is not a tree edge, so the last option is ruled out.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: Compare f(n) with n^(log_b a). A: n^(log₃ 3) = n = f(n), case 2: Θ(n log n) (III). B: n^(log₃ 9) = n², which is polynomially larger than f(n) = n, case 1: Θ(n²) (IV). C: n^(log₄ 2) = n^(1/2) = √n = f(n), case 2: Θ(√n log n) (II). D: n^(log₂ 2) = n, and f(n) = n³ is polynomially larger; the regularity condition holds because 2(n/2)³ = n³/4 ≤ c·n³ with c = 1/4 < 1, so case 3 gives Θ(n³) (I). The usual slip is to compare f(n) with a or with b instead of with n^(log_b a).

b: I. Θ(n³)
II. Θ(√n log n)
III. Θ(n log n)
IV. Θ(n²)

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Both statements are false. Statement I: in an in-threaded binary tree, a null right pointer is replaced by a thread to the inorder successor, and a null left pointer by a thread to the inorder predecessor. The right threads make inorder traversal possible without a stack or recursion. Statement II: a B* tree tightens the B-tree rule. When a node overflows, keys are first shared with a sibling, and a split turns two full nodes into three, so every non-root node is at least about two-thirds full. This gives better space use and fewer splits. So both Statement I and Statement II are false.

stmts: Statement I: In a right in-threaded binary tree, each null right-child pointer is replaced by a thread to the node’s inorder predecessor.
Statement II: In a B* tree, every non-root node is required to be only at least half full, exactly as in a B-tree.

questionBank.topic: Threaded binary trees and B* trees

questionBank.question: Using the decision-tree (comparison-tree) argument, what is the lower bound on the number of comparisons that any comparison-based algorithm needs, in the worst case, to sort 5 distinct elements?
questionBank.explanation: A comparison sort is a binary decision tree whose leaves must include all n! orderings of the input. A binary tree of height h has at most 2ʰ leaves, so 2ʰ ≥ n!, i.e. h ≥ ⌈log₂ n!⌉. For n = 5: 5! = 120, and 2⁶ = 64 < 120 ≤ 128 = 2⁷, so h ≥ 7. (Merge insertion actually sorts 5 elements in 7 comparisons, so the bound is tight here.) 10 = C(5, 2) is the number of pairs; 12 ≈ 5 log₂ 5 is the asymptotic n log n estimate, not the exact bound; 6 is ⌊log₂ 120⌋, which rounds the wrong way.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: unrestricted (Type 0) grammars generate exactly the recursively enumerable languages, the languages accepted by Turing machines (III). B: non-contracting productions (|α| ≤ |β|) define the context-sensitive (Type 1) grammars, equivalent to linear bounded automata, i.e. TMs that may use only the tape cells holding the input (II). C: a single variable on the left makes the grammar context-free (Type 2); these languages are exactly those accepted by non-deterministic PDAs, while deterministic PDAs accept only the smaller class of DCFLs (IV). D: right-linear productions give regular (Type 3) grammars, equivalent to finite automata (I). The trap is pairing context-free grammars with deterministic PDAs.

a: A. α → β, where α contains at least one variable and there is no other restriction
C. A → γ, with a single variable on the left and any string γ on the right
D. A → aB or A → a, where A and B are variables and a is a terminal
b: I. Finite automaton
II. Linear bounded automaton
III. Turing machine
IV. Non-deterministic pushdown automaton

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false. The halting language H = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w} is RE, but its complement is not RE; otherwise H would be decidable (by Statement II). RE languages are not closed under complementation. Statement II is true. Run a recogniser for L and a recogniser for its complement in parallel (alternating steps). Every string is in exactly one of the two languages, so one of them accepts, and the combined machine always halts with the right answer. So Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: The complement of every recursively enumerable language is recursively enumerable.
Statement II: If a language L and its complement are both recursively enumerable, then L is recursive.

questionBank.question: Which of the following problems are decidable?
options: A, B, C and E only
A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A: decidable; mark the generating (useful) variables and check whether the start symbol is among them. B: undecidable; equivalence of CFGs is a classic undecidable problem (only equivalence of DFAs or regular expressions is decidable). C: decidable; context-sensitive grammars are non-contracting, so only finitely many sentential forms of length ≤ |w| need to be tried (an LBA always halts on such a check). D: undecidable (Post, 1946); it is the standard tool for proving CFG ambiguity undecidable. E: decidable; L(M) is infinite if and only if M accepts some string of length between n and 2n − 1, where n is the number of states (equivalently, a cycle lies on some path from the start state to a final state). So A, C and E only.

stmts: A. Whether the language generated by a given context-free grammar is empty
B. Whether two given context-free grammars generate the same language
C. Whether a given string belongs to the language of a given context-sensitive grammar
D. Whether a given instance of the Post correspondence problem has a solution
E. Whether a given deterministic finite automaton accepts an infinite language
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. A follows from Cantor’s diagonal argument: Σ* is countably infinite, and a language is any subset of Σ*, so the languages form the power set of a countable set. If they could be listed as L₁, L₂, …, the language D = {wᵢ : wᵢ ∉ Lᵢ} would differ from every Lᵢ, a contradiction. R is true: encodings are finite strings, and the set of finite strings is countable. But R concerns machines, not languages. Taken together with A, R shows that some languages are not recursively enumerable, which is a consequence rather than the explanation of A. So both are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.

stmts: Assertion (A): The set of all languages over the alphabet {0, 1} is uncountable.
Reason (R): The set of all Turing machines over {0, 1} is countable, because every Turing machine can be encoded as a finite binary string.

questionBank.question: For a Turing machine M, which of the following questions is decidable?
options: Does L(M) contain the string ab?
Does M have more than 10 states?
questionBank.explanation: Rice’s theorem says that every non-trivial property of the language recognised by a TM is undecidable. Emptiness, regularity and membership of ab are all non-trivial properties of L(M) (some TMs have them and some do not), so each is undecidable. “Does M have more than 10 states?” is a property of the machine’s description, not of its language; it is decided by reading the encoding ⟨M⟩ and counting its states. Rice’s theorem does not apply to such syntactic properties.

questionBank.question:
Consider the grammar (ε is the empty string; S is the start symbol):
S → A B c | d
A → a A | ε
B → b | ε
What is FOLLOW(A)?
questionBank.explanation: A appears on the right-hand side in S → A B c and in A → a A. From S → A B c: FOLLOW(A) contains FIRST(B c). FIRST(B) = {b, ε}, and because B can vanish, FIRST(c) is added too: FIRST(B c) = {b, c}. From A → a A: A is at the right end, so FOLLOW(A) contains FOLLOW(A), which adds nothing new. So FOLLOW(A) = {b, c}. $ is not included because A is never at the right end of an S-production (c always follows). {b} forgets that B is nullable, and {a, b, c} wrongly adds FIRST(A).

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: an LR(0) parser reduces whenever a state contains a complete item, with no lookahead, so any state with a complete item and another item conflicts (II). B: SLR(1) uses the same LR(0) automaton but reduces only on symbols in FOLLOW(A), which removes many conflicts (IV). C: LALR(1) merges LR(1) states with the same core. It has the LR(0) number of states, can introduce reduce–reduce but never shift–reduce conflicts, and is what YACC/Bison build (I). D: canonical LR(1) keeps the exact lookahead in every item. It is the most powerful of the four but has the largest tables (III). Power: LR(0) ⊂ SLR(1) ⊂ LALR(1) ⊂ LR(1).

b: I. Merges LR(1) states that have identical cores, so it has as many states as LR(0)
II. Reduces by a completed item without looking at the next input symbol
III. Uses full LR(1) items with individual lookaheads and usually has the most states
IV. Reduces by A → α only when the next input symbol is in FOLLOW(A)

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true. With A → Aα | β, every string derived from Aα starts with a string derived from β as well, so FIRST(Aα) and FIRST(β) overlap, the LL(1) table gets two entries in one cell, and a predictive parser would loop. Left recursion must be removed first (A → βA′, A′ → αA′ | ε). Statement II is true. An LL(1) parser must choose a production after seeing only the first symbol of its expansion, while an LR(1) parser decides after seeing the whole right-hand side plus one symbol. It has strictly more information, so LL(1) ⊂ LR(1). (LL(1) is not contained in LALR(1) in general.) So both statements are true.

stmts: Statement I: A grammar that is left-recursive cannot be LL(1).
Statement II: Every LL(1) grammar is also an LR(1) grammar.

questionBank.question: A compiler’s peephole optimiser examines only a short sliding window of consecutive target instructions. Which of the following transformations is outside the scope of such an optimiser?
options: Moving a loop-invariant computation out of the loop body
Deleting a load of a value that was just stored from the same register to the same location
Replacing x × 2 by x + x or a left shift
Removing unreachable instructions that follow an unconditional jump
questionBank.explanation: Peephole optimisation looks at a small sliding window of consecutive target instructions and replaces patterns locally. Typical examples: redundant load/store elimination (MOV R0, a followed by MOV a, R0), algebraic simplification and strength reduction (x × 2 → x + x or a shift), removing unreachable code after an unconditional jump, flow-of-control optimisation (a jump to a jump), and using machine idioms such as INC. Loop-invariant code motion needs loop detection and data-flow analysis over the whole loop, which is a global (loop) optimisation, not a peephole one.

questionBank.question: A DFA reads a binary number, most significant bit first (the empty string counts as 0), and accepts exactly the strings whose value is divisible by 6. What is the number of states of the minimal such DFA?
questionBank.explanation: The obvious DFA tracks the remainder r ∈ {0, …, 5}, with the transition r → (2r + bit) mod 6: 6 states. Now minimise. After reading at least one more bit, the new remainder depends only on 2r mod 6, which depends only on r mod 3. So r and r + 3 behave the same on every non-empty suffix. They differ on the empty suffix only if one of them is 0 (accepting). Hence 1 ≡ 4 and 2 ≡ 5, but 0 and 3 must stay apart. The minimal DFA has the 4 states {0}, {3}, {1, 4} and {2, 5}. The trap answer 6 is the unminimised remainder automaton; 3 is the answer for divisibility by 3.

questionBank.question: In an RSA system, p = 17, q = 19 and the public exponent is e = 5. What is the private exponent d?
questionBank.explanation: n = pq = 323 and φ(n) = (p − 1)(q − 1) = 16 × 18 = 288. d is the inverse of e modulo φ(n): 5d ≡ 1 (mod 288). The extended Euclidean algorithm gives 288 = 57 × 5 + 3, 5 = 1 × 3 + 2, 3 = 1 × 2 + 1, and back-substitution gives d = 173. Check: 5 × 173 = 865 = 3 × 288 + 1. 194 is the inverse of 5 modulo n = 323 (the trap of using n instead of φ(n)); 115 satisfies 5 × 115 ≡ −1 (mod 288), a sign slip.

questionBank.question: Alice and Bob use Diffie–Hellman key exchange with the public prime p = 29 and generator g = 2. Alice’s secret is a = 5 and Bob’s secret is b = 9. What is the shared secret key?
questionBank.explanation: Alice sends A = gᵃ mod p = 2⁵ mod 29 = 32 mod 29 = 3. Bob sends B = gᵇ mod p = 2⁹ mod 29 = 512 mod 29 = 19. Alice computes Bᵃ = 19⁵ mod 29 and Bob computes Aᵇ = 3⁹ mod 29; both equal g^(ab) = 2⁴⁵ mod 29 = 21. 3 and 19 are the public values exchanged over the channel, not the key. Since an eavesdropper sees A and B but not a or b, recovering the key requires solving a discrete logarithm.

questionBank.explanation: A: steganography conceals that a message exists at all, for example in the low-order bits of an image. Cryptography, by contrast, hides only the content (III). B: a digital signature is created with the sender’s private key and checked with the public key, so it proves origin and prevents the sender from denying it later (IV). C: a hash such as SHA-256 maps a message to a fixed-size digest; any change to the message changes the digest (I). D: a firewall (packet filter, stateful or application gateway) allows or blocks traffic at a network boundary according to rules (II).

Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false. AES (Rijndael) is a substitution–permutation network: every round (SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, AddRoundKey) transforms the whole 128-bit state, with 10, 12 or 14 rounds for 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys. DES is the classic Feistel cipher. Statement II is true. DES takes 64-bit blocks and a 64-bit key of which 8 bits are parity, leaving 56 effective key bits, and runs 16 Feistel rounds. So Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

Statement II: DES operates on 64-bit blocks with a 56-bit effective key and uses 16 rounds.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements are correct?
options: A, B, D and E only
B, C, D and E only
A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A: incorrect. In SaaS (for example web e-mail), the provider runs and maintains everything, including the application; the consumer only uses it and configures settings. B: correct. IaaS supplies virtual servers, storage and networks, and the consumer installs and manages the OS, middleware and applications. C: correct. An SLA defines metrics such as uptime percentage and response time, how they are measured, and the penalties or service credits for violations. D: correct: that is the definition of a hybrid cloud (cloud bursting is a common use). E: correct. In PaaS (for example Google App Engine), the provider manages the platform and the consumer controls only its deployed code and data. So B, C, D and E only.

B. In IaaS, the consumer manages the operating system and applications running on the provider’s virtual machines.
C. A service level agreement (SLA) states measurable service commitments, such as availability, and the remedies if they are not met.
D. A hybrid cloud combines private and public cloud infrastructure, with workloads able to move between them.
E. In PaaS, the provider manages the operating system and runtime, and the consumer deploys its own applications.

Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both are true, and R explains A. MQTT decouples senders and receivers through a broker: a sensor publishes to a topic and any number of subscribers receive the message. Its minimal 2-byte fixed header, small code footprint and three QoS levels (0, 1, 2) keep bandwidth and power use low, which is exactly why it suits constrained devices and poor links. MQTT runs over TCP; CoAP is the comparable protocol that runs over UDP.

questionBank.question: Which transport-layer protocol supports both multihoming (one association using several IP addresses per endpoint) and multistreaming (several independent message streams within one association)?
questionBank.explanation: SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol, RFC 9260) is message-oriented like UDP but reliable and congestion-controlled like TCP. It adds multistreaming, so loss on one stream does not block delivery on the others (no head-of-line blocking across streams), and multihoming, so an association can fail over to another address. It also uses a four-way handshake with a cookie to resist SYN-flooding. TCP has one byte stream between a single pair of addresses; UDP is unreliable and connectionless; RTP is an application-level protocol usually carried over UDP.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true. VLAN membership is configured in software (by port, MAC address or protocol), so stations on different switches can share a broadcast domain, and moving a station does not require rewiring. Statement II is false. The 802.1Q tag is 4 bytes: a 2-byte TPID (0x8100) and 2 bytes of tag control information, which hold a 3-bit priority, a 1-bit DEI and a 12-bit VLAN ID. The trap is the “12”: it is the width of the VLAN ID in bits, allowing 4,094 usable VLANs, not the size of the tag in bytes. So Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: A VLAN groups stations into one logical broadcast domain regardless of their physical location on the switches.
Statement II: IEEE 802.1Q identifies the VLAN of a frame by inserting a 12-byte tag into the Ethernet header.

questionBank.question: Which of the following is a controlled-access method, in which stations take turns and only a station holding the right to transmit may send?
questionBank.explanation: Multiple access protocols fall into three families. Random access (ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA): any station may try to send, and collisions are avoided or resolved. Controlled access (reservation, polling, token passing): stations consult one another, and only the station that holds the token, has been polled by the primary, or has reserved a slot may send, so collisions do not occur. Channelisation (FDMA, TDMA, CDMA): the bandwidth is divided by frequency, time or code. Token passing is therefore the controlled-access method.

questionBank.question:
A game tree has a MAX root with three MIN children. The leaves under the MIN children, in left-to-right order, are:
MIN₁: 6, 9, 7
MIN₂: 8, 2, 11
MIN₃: 5, 12, 4
If alpha–beta pruning examines the nodes from left to right, how many leaves are NOT evaluated?
questionBank.explanation: MIN₁: all three leaves are evaluated (there is no bound yet), giving value 6, so α = 6 at the root. MIN₂: the leaf 8 gives β = 8 > α. Then 2 gives β = 2 ≤ α = 6, so MIN₂ is worth at most 2 and MAX will not choose it: leaf 11 is pruned (1 leaf). MIN₃: the first leaf 5 ≤ α = 6, so 12 and 4 are pruned (2 leaves). Total pruned = 3, and the root’s minimax value is 6, the same as without pruning. 2 misses the cut after leaf 2 in MIN₂; 4 also prunes a leaf of MIN₁, although no bound exists while the first child is being searched; 0 ignores pruning altogether.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: BFS finds the shallowest goal, so it is optimal when all steps cost the same, but it stores the whole frontier: O(b^d) time and space (III). B: DFS keeps only the current path and its siblings, O(bm) space, but it can go down an infinite branch forever and is not optimal (IV). C: IDS runs depth-limited DFS with limits 0, 1, 2, …, combining BFS’s completeness and optimality with DFS’s O(bd) space; the repeated work only changes the constant (I). D: with an admissible heuristic (never overestimating), A* tree search returns an optimal solution; graph search needs a consistent heuristic for the same guarantee (II).

a: D. A* search with an admissible heuristic (tree search)
b: I. Complete, and optimal for unit step costs, while using only O(bd) memory
II. Optimal: the first goal selected for expansion is a cheapest solution
III. Complete and optimal for unit step costs, but needs O(b^d) memory
IV. Needs only O(bm) memory, but is not complete in infinite state spaces

Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true. Consistency means h(n) ≤ c(n, n′) + h(n′) for every successor n′, with h(goal) = 0. Summing this inequality along an optimal path from n to the goal gives h(n) ≤ h*(n), which is admissibility. (The converse fails: admissible heuristics need not be consistent.) Statement II is false. Hill climbing moves only to a better neighbour and stops when none exists, so it can get stuck on a local maximum, a plateau or a ridge. Random restarts or simulated annealing are used to escape. So Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: Every consistent (monotone) heuristic is also admissible.
Statement II: Steepest-ascent hill climbing is guaranteed to reach the global maximum of the objective function.

questionBank.question: For an automated taxi driver working in city traffic, which of the following descriptions of the task environment are correct?
options: A, C, D and E only
A, B, C and E only
B, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A: correct. The sensors cannot see everything, for example what other drivers intend or what is behind a truck. B: correct. The outcome of an action is uncertain (tyres skid, other drivers react unpredictably). C: correct. Other drivers and pedestrians are agents whose behaviour affects the taxi’s performance. D: incorrect. Speed, position and steering angle vary continuously, so the environment is continuous. E: correct. The world changes while the agent is deliberating. Russell and Norvig use taxi driving as the example of the hardest combination: partially observable, stochastic, multi-agent, sequential, dynamic and continuous. So A, B, C and E only.

stmts: A. Partially observable
B. Stochastic
C. Multi-agent
D. Discrete
E. Dynamic

B: a semantic network is a graph of concepts with labelled relations; properties are inherited along IS-A links (III). The usual confusion is between frames (a static object description) and scripts (an event sequence).

questionBank.question: A disease affects 2% of a population. A test detects it in 90% of people who have it, and gives a false positive for 5% of people who do not have it. A randomly chosen person tests positive. What is the probability, to two decimal places, that the person has the disease?
questionBank.explanation: Let D = has the disease and + = tests positive. P(D) = 0.02, P(+|D) = 0.9 and P(+|¬D) = 0.05. Total probability: P(+) = 0.9 × 0.02 + 0.05 × 0.98 = 0.018 + 0.049 = 0.067. Bayes’ theorem: P(D|+) = 0.018/0.067 ≈ 0.2687 ≈ 0.27. 0.90 confuses P(D|+) with the sensitivity P(+|D), the classic base-rate fallacy; 0.02 ignores the test result. The answer is low because the healthy group is so large that its 5% of false positives outnumber the true positives.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both are true, and R explains A. Forward chaining is called data-driven precisely because it works from the available data (facts) towards conclusions, as R describes; production systems such as OPS5 and CLIPS work this way. Backward chaining, used in Prolog, is goal-driven: it starts from the query and works back to find supporting facts. For Horn clauses, both methods are sound and complete.

stmts: Assertion (A): Forward chaining is described as a data-driven inference method.

Reason (R): Forward chaining starts from the known facts and repeatedly fires rules whose premises are satisfied, adding their conclusions as new facts until the goal is derived or nothing new can be added.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements are correct?
options: A, C, D and E only
A, B, C and E only
B, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A: correct. A STRIPS operator lists the preconditions that must hold, the facts it makes true (add list) and the facts it makes false (delete list). B: correct. Goal stack planning pushes the goal conjunction and its components, and solves the goal on top first; it is the standard linear planner. C: correct. In the Sussman anomaly (a three-block problem), either order of the two subgoals forces the planner to undo the one it achieved first, which motivates non-linear planning. D: incorrect. Partial-order planning follows the least-commitment principle and orders actions only when a constraint requires it. E: correct. OWL (Web Ontology Language) builds on RDF and RDF Schema to define classes, properties and axioms that agents can share. So A, B, C and E only.

stmts: A. In STRIPS, an action schema is described by its preconditions, an add list and a delete list.
B. Goal stack planning is a linear planner that works on one goal at a time, keeping goals and operators on a stack.
C. The Sussman anomaly shows that achieving subgoals one after another may undo a subgoal that was achieved earlier.
D. Partial-order planning commits to a total order of all actions as early as possible.
E. On the semantic web, ontologies are commonly written in OWL, built on RDF.

questionBank.question: In a fuzzy controller, the aggregated output fuzzy set over the output variable z has the discrete membership values μ(10) = 0.2, μ(20) = 0.6, μ(30) = 0.8 and μ(40) = 0.4. What crisp output does the centroid (centre of gravity) method give?
questionBank.explanation: The discrete centroid is z* = Σ μ(z)·z / Σ μ(z). Numerator = 0.2×10 + 0.6×20 + 0.8×30 + 0.4×40 = 2 + 12 + 24 + 16 = 54. Denominator = 0.2 + 0.6 + 0.8 + 0.4 = 2.0. z* = 54/2 = 27. 30 is the mean-of-maximum (or first-of-maxima) answer, the z with the largest membership; 25 is the plain average of the four z values, which ignores the memberships; 13.5 divides by 4 instead of by Σ μ.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false. A single perceptron draws one straight line (hyperplane) through the input space, and XOR’s positive points (0,1) and (1,0) cannot be separated from (0,0) and (1,1) by any line. The perceptron convergence theorem applies only to linearly separable data. A hidden layer, i.e. a multilayer perceptron, is needed. Statement II is true. A SOM has no target outputs; for each input, the neuron whose weight vector is closest wins, and it and its topological neighbours move towards the input, which produces a topology-preserving map. So Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: A single-layer perceptron can be trained to compute the XOR of two binary inputs.
Statement II: A Kohonen self-organising map learns by unsupervised competitive learning, updating the winning neuron and its neighbours.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation:
Statement I is false. Take the domain {1, 2} with P true only at 1 and Q true only at 2. Every element satisfies P ∨ Q, so the premise is true, but neither ∀x P(x) nor ∀x Q(x) holds, so the conclusion is false. (∀ distributes over ∧, not over ∨; the converse (∀x P ∨ ∀x Q) → ∀x (P ∨ Q) is the valid direction.)
Statement II is true. With B = ∀y Q(y) not containing x, (∃x P(x)) → B ≡ ∀x (P(x) → B): pulling an ∃ out of the antecedent of an implication turns it into ∀. Then P(x) → ∀y Q(y) ≡ ∀y (P(x) → Q(y)) because P(x) contains no y.
So Statement I is false and Statement II is true. Trap: treating “∃ in the antecedent” as ∃ after prenexing.

stmts: Statement I: For all predicates P and Q over every non-empty domain, ∀x (P(x) ∨ Q(x)) → (∀x P(x) ∨ ∀x Q(x)) is valid.
Statement II: (∃x P(x)) → ∀y Q(y) is logically equivalent to ∀x ∀y (P(x) → Q(y)).

questionBank.question: How many equivalence relations on A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} have exactly three equivalence classes and place 1 and 2 in the same class?
questionBank.explanation:
Equivalence relations with k classes correspond to partitions into k blocks, counted by the Stirling number S(n, k).
Forcing 1 and 2 into the same block is the same as gluing them into one object, which leaves 5 objects to split into 3 blocks: S(5, 3).
S(5, 3) = S(4, 2) + 3·S(4, 3) = 7 + 3·6 = 25.
Check: S(6, 3) = 90 partitions in all, and 90 − 25 = 65 of them separate 1 and 2.
Traps: 90 ignores the condition, 65 counts the complement, 15 = S(5, 2) uses the wrong number of blocks.

questionBank.question: A connected simple planar graph G is 4-regular and has 12 vertices. In a plane embedding of G, every face (including the outer face) is bounded by either 3 or 4 edges. How many faces are triangles?
questionBank.explanation:
Handshake: E = 12 × 4 / 2 = 24.
Euler’s formula: F = 2 − V + E = 2 − 12 + 24 = 14.
Let t triangles and q quadrilaterals. Counting face–edge incidences, each edge borders two faces: 3t + 4q = 2E = 48, and t + q = 14.
Subtracting 3 × (t + q) = 42 gives q = 6, so t = 8. (G is the cuboctahedron.)
Traps: 6 is the number of quadrilaterals, 14 is the total number of faces, and 16 = 2E/3 assumes that every face is a triangle.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation:
A. The rim is an odd cycle (C₇), which needs 3 colours; the hub is adjacent to every rim vertex and needs a 4th colour: 4 (II).
B. For even n, Kₙ has chromatic index n − 1 (a round-robin schedule splits its edges into n − 1 perfect matchings): K₈ needs 7 (IV).
C. The Petersen graph contains 5-cycles, so it needs at least 3 colours, and a 3-colouring exists: 3 (I).
D. For odd n, a colour class in Kₙ has at most (n − 1)/2 edges. K₅ has 10 edges and each class has at most 2, so at least 5 colours are needed, and 5 suffice: 5 (III).
Answer: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III. Traps: the rule “χ′(Kₙ) = n − 1” holds only for even n, and the Petersen graph’s chromatic index (4) is not its chromatic number (3).

a: A. Chromatic number of the wheel with 8 vertices (a hub joined to every vertex of a 7-cycle)
B. Chromatic index (edge chromatic number) of K₈
C. Chromatic number of the Petersen graph
b: II. 4
III. 5
IV. 7

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation:
(A) is true. With parts {a₁, a₂, a₃} and {b₁, b₂, b₃}, the cycle a₁ b₁ a₂ b₂ a₃ b₃ a₁ visits all 6 vertices. K₃,₄ has 7 vertices and no Hamiltonian cycle.
(R) is true. Every edge joins the two parts, so a cycle alternates between them and uses equally many vertices from each. A Hamiltonian cycle would have to use all 3 + 4 vertices, which is impossible when the parts differ in size.
(R) is exactly why K₃,₄ fails while K₃,₃ succeeds, so (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

stmts: Assertion (A): The complete bipartite graph K₃,₃ has a Hamiltonian cycle, but K₃,₄ does not.
Reason (R): Every cycle in a bipartite graph alternates between the two parts, so a bipartite graph whose parts have unequal sizes cannot have a Hamiltonian cycle.

questionBank.question: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15). How many prime implicants does F have, how many of them are essential, and how many literals does a minimal sum-of-products form of F contain (in that order)?
questionBank.explanation:
Prime implicants (from the K-map or Quine–McCluskey):
B′D′ = m(0, 2, 8, 10); BD = m(5, 7, 13, 15); A′B′C = m(2, 3); A′CD = m(3, 7); A′C′D′ = m(0, 4); A′BC′ = m(4, 5). That is 6 prime implicants.
Essential: B′D′ is the only one covering m8 and m10; BD is the only one covering m13. So 2 are essential.
After B′D′ + BD, minterms 3 and 4 remain. m3 is covered by A′B′C or A′CD, and m4 by A′C′D′ or A′BC′. No single term covers both, so two 3-literal terms are needed, e.g. F = B′D′ + BD + A′B′C + A′C′D′: 2 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 10 literals (there are four equally minimal forms).
Traps: 4 “essential” counts the cyclic choices as essential; 8 assumes one 2-literal cube covers m3 and m4; 12 adds a redundant term.

questionBank.question: Which of the following sets of operations are functionally complete? (0 denotes the constant-0 function.)
options: A, B, C and E only
questionBank.explanation:
Post’s criterion: a set is complete iff, for each of the five classes (0-preserving, 1-preserving, self-dual, monotone, affine), it contains a function outside that class.
A. Complete: ¬x = x → 0, and x ∨ y = ¬x → y, giving {¬, ∨}.
B. Not complete: ∧, ∨ and ⊕ all map (0, 0) to 0, so every composition is 0-preserving and ¬ can never be built.
C. Complete: NAND alone gives ¬x = x ↑ x and x ∧ y = ¬(x ↑ y).
D. Not complete: M and ¬ are both self-dual, and compositions of self-dual functions stay self-dual, so for example x ∧ y (not self-dual) cannot be built.
E. Complete: x → x = 1, x ⊕ 1 = ¬x, and ¬x → y = x ∨ y.
Correct: A, C and E only.

stmts: C. {↑} (NAND)
D. {M, ¬}, where M(x, y, z) is the majority function

questionBank.question: Seven students hand in their lab-record books, and the books are returned to them at random, one book per student. What is the probability that exactly two students get their own books back?
questionBank.explanation:
Choose the 2 students who get their own books: C(7, 2) = 21 ways. The other 5 must all get wrong books: a derangement, D₅ = 44.
Favourable = 21 × 44 = 924; total = 7! = 5040.
P = 924/5040 = 11/60 ≈ 0.183.
(D₅ = 5!(1 − 1 + 1/2 − 1/6 + 1/24 − 1/120) = 120 − 120 + 60 − 20 + 5 − 1 = 44.)
Traps: 11/30 = D₅/5! is the probability that 5 books are all wrong; 1/2 = 21 × 5!/7! lets the other 5 books fall anywhere; 103/280 = D₇/7! is the probability that nobody gets their own book.

questionBank.question:
A project has the activities below (optimistic a, most likely m, pessimistic b, in weeks):
1–2: (2, 4, 6)
1–3: (3, 5, 13)
2–4: (4, 6, 8)
3–4: (1, 3, 5)
2–5: (5, 8, 17)
4–5: (2, 5, 8)
Using PERT with tₑ = (a + 4m + b)/6 and σ² = ((b − a)/6)², what are the expected project duration and the variance of the critical path?
questionBank.explanation:
Expected times: 1–2: (2 + 16 + 6)/6 = 4; 1–3: (3 + 20 + 13)/6 = 6; 2–4: 6; 3–4: 3; 2–5: (5 + 32 + 17)/6 = 9; 4–5: 5.
Paths: 1–2–5 = 4 + 9 = 13; 1–2–4–5 = 4 + 6 + 5 = 15; 1–3–4–5 = 6 + 3 + 5 = 14.
The critical path is 1–2–4–5 with expected duration 15 weeks.
Variance along it: (4/6)² + (4/6)² + (6/6)² = 0.444 + 0.444 + 1 = 1.89.
Traps: 4.22 is the variance of 1–3–4–5 (2.778 + 0.444 + 1), and 4.44 is the variance of 1–2–5 (0.444 + 4). The project variance is taken along the critical path, not the path with the largest variance.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation:
Statement I is true. A cyclic group of order n has φ(n) generators; φ(36) = 36 × (1 − 1/2)(1 − 1/3) = 12.
Statement II is false. The element orders in U(15) are: 1 → 1; 2 → 4 (2, 4, 8, 1); 4 → 2; 7 → 4; 8 → 4; 11 → 2; 13 → 4; 14 → 2. No element has order 8 = |U(15)|, so the group is not cyclic (it is isomorphic to ℤ₂ × ℤ₄).
Trap: U(n) is cyclic only for n = 1, 2, 4, pᵏ and 2pᵏ (p an odd prime); 15 = 3 × 5 is not of this form.

stmts: Statement I: A cyclic group of order 36 has exactly 12 generators.
Statement II: The group U(15) = {1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14} under multiplication modulo 15 is cyclic.

questionBank.question: A 6-bit ripple (asynchronous) up-counter is built from flip-flops that each have a propagation delay of 12 ns. The counter outputs drive a decoding AND gate with a delay of 8 ns. For the decoded output to settle within every clock period, the maximum clock frequency is
questionBank.explanation:
In a ripple counter each flip-flop is clocked by the previous one, so in the worst case (for example 011111 → 100000) the change ripples through all 6 stages: 6 × 12 = 72 ns.
The decoding gate adds 8 ns, so the clock period must be at least 72 + 8 = 80 ns.
f_max = 1 / 80 ns = 12.5 MHz.
Traps: 83.3 MHz = 1/12 ns treats it as a synchronous counter; 13.9 MHz = 1/72 ns forgets the decoder; 50 MHz = 1/(12 + 8) ns counts only one stage.

questionBank.question: Booth’s algorithm multiplies a multiplicand M by the 8-bit two’s-complement multiplier Q = 0101 1101. The bit pairs (Qᵢ, Qᵢ₋₁) are scanned from i = 0 with Q₋₁ = 0. How many times is M added to, and subtracted from, the partial product?
questionBank.explanation:
Booth rule: (1, 0) → subtract M; (0, 1) → add M; (0, 0) or (1, 1) → shift only.
Q₇…Q₀ = 0 1 0 1 1 1 0 1, with Q₋₁ = 0:
i = 0: (1, 0) subtract; i = 1: (0, 1) add; i = 2: (1, 0) subtract; i = 3: (1, 1) none; i = 4: (1, 1) none; i = 5: (0, 1) add; i = 6: (1, 0) subtract; i = 7: (0, 1) add.
Total: 3 additions and 3 subtractions.
Check with the recoded digits: −1 + 2 − 4 + 32 − 64 + 128 = 93 = 0101 1101₂. ✓
Trap: 5 additions is the plain shift-and-add count (one addition per 1 bit). Booth only acts at the ends of runs of 1s.

questionBank.question:
Match List I with List II
A two-word instruction occupies addresses 400 and 401; its address field (the second word) holds 500. After the fetch, PC = 402. The index register XR = 120 and the processor register R1 = 700. Memory holds M[500] = 800, M[620] = 350, M[700] = 900 and M[902] = 150. List I gives an addressing mode; List II gives the effective address.
questionBank.explanation:
A. Indirect: the address field points to the address, so EA = M[500] = 800 (II).
B. Relative: EA = PC + address field = 402 + 500 = 902 (IV). PC has already moved past both words of the instruction.
C. Indexed: EA = address field + XR = 500 + 120 = 620 (I).
D. Register indirect: EA = contents of R1 = 700 (III).
Answer: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.
Traps: using PC = 400 for relative mode gives 900; confusing the EA with the operand gives 350 (indexed), 900 (register indirect) or 150 (relative).

b: III. 700

questionBank.question: A CPU has 24-bit instructions and 64 registers. Two-address instructions have the format opcode | register (6 bits) | memory address (12 bits). The designers implement 50 two-address instructions and use an expanding opcode for one-address instructions with the format opcode | memory address (12 bits). What is the maximum number of one-address instructions?
questionBank.explanation:
Two-address format: opcode = 24 − 6 − 12 = 6 bits, so 2⁶ = 64 opcodes. 50 are used, leaving 14 free.
One-address format: opcode = 24 − 12 = 12 bits. Each unused 6-bit prefix can be extended by the 6 bits that the register field used to occupy: 2⁶ = 64 codes per prefix.
Maximum = 14 × 64 = 896. (Equivalently, 2¹² − 50 × 2⁶ = 4096 − 3200 = 896.)
Traps: 14 forgets to extend the prefixes; 3584 = 14 × 256 assumes 8 extra bits; 1024 is not tied to the free prefixes.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation:
(A) is true. RISC designs use simple, fixed-length instructions and a load/store architecture, so every instruction flows through the same pipeline stages and one instruction can complete per cycle in the ideal case.
(R) is true. RISC machines typically have 32 or more general-purpose registers (and some use register windows) to reduce memory traffic.
But (R) does not explain (A). A CPI near 1 comes from pipelining that is made easy by uniform, simple instructions, not from the size of the register file. So both are true, and (R) is NOT the correct explanation.

stmts: Assertion (A): RISC processors can approach an average CPI close to 1.
Reason (R): RISC processors usually provide a larger set of general-purpose registers than typical CISC processors.

questionBank.question: A 5-stage instruction pipeline has stage delays of 180, 220, 200, 240 and 160 ps, and each pipeline register adds 20 ps. 20% of instructions are branches with a 2-cycle penalty; 30% are loads, and half of these are immediately followed by a dependent instruction that stalls for 1 cycle. Compared with a non-pipelined design whose instruction time equals the sum of the stage delays, the speedup is closest to
questionBank.explanation:
Non-pipelined time per instruction = 180 + 220 + 200 + 240 + 160 = 1000 ps.
Pipelined clock = slowest stage + latch = 240 + 20 = 260 ps.
CPI = 1 + (0.20 × 2) + (0.30 × 0.5 × 1) = 1 + 0.40 + 0.15 = 1.55.
Pipelined time per instruction = 1.55 × 260 = 403 ps.
Speedup = 1000 / 403 ≈ 2.48.
Traps: 3.85 = 1000/260 ignores stalls; 4.17 = 1000/240 ignores both stalls and the latch; 2.69 = 1000/(1.55 × 240) forgets the latch delay.

questionBank.question: A 6-stage linear pipeline (one clock per stage, no stalls) processes n independent tasks. What is the smallest n for which the pipeline efficiency is at least 99%?
questionBank.explanation:
Time for n tasks = (k + n − 1) cycles with k = 6. Efficiency = speedup / k = n / (k + n − 1) = n / (n + 5).
n / (n + 5) ≥ 0.99 ⇒ n ≥ 0.99n + 4.95 ⇒ 0.01n ≥ 4.95 ⇒ n ≥ 495.
Check: 495 / 500 = 0.99 exactly; 494 / 499 ≈ 0.98998 < 0.99.
Traps: 500 is the cycle count k + n − 1 for n = 495; 594 and 99 come from confusing efficiency with speedup.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation:
Statement I is true. One instruction stream is broadcast by a single control unit to many processing elements that each work on their own data: single instruction, multiple data.
Statement II is false. Flynn’s taxonomy counts instruction streams and data streams, not how many instructions overlap. A pipelined uniprocessor still fetches one instruction stream and works on one data stream, so it is SISD. Pipelining is parallelism within a single stream; MIMD needs several independent processors with their own programs.

stmts: Statement I: An array processor, in which many processing elements execute the same instruction on different data under one control unit, is an SIMD machine in Flynn’s taxonomy.
Statement II: A pipelined uniprocessor is an MIMD machine in Flynn’s taxonomy, because several instructions are in execution at the same time.

questionBank.question: A byte-addressable machine with 32-bit addresses has a 256 KB, 8-way set-associative cache with 64-byte blocks. Each cache line stores its tag, one valid bit and one dirty bit. What is the total size of this per-line metadata (tag + valid + dirty) for the whole cache?
questionBank.explanation:
Lines = 256 KB / 64 B = 4096. Sets = 4096 / 8 = 512, so the index has 9 bits.
Offset = log₂ 64 = 6 bits. Tag = 32 − 9 − 6 = 17 bits.
Per line: 17 + 1 + 1 = 19 bits. Total = 4096 × 19 = 77824 bits (9.5 KB).
Traps: 69632 = 4096 × 17 counts the tag only; 65536 = 4096 × 16 uses a direct-mapped tag (32 − 12 − 6 = 14 bits) + 2; 81920 = 4096 × 20 takes the tag as 18 bits by using 8 index bits.

questionBank.question: A program spends 80% of its single-core execution time in code that parallelises perfectly on a multicore processor; the rest is strictly serial. According to Amdahl’s law, what is the minimum number of cores needed for a speedup of at least 4?
questionBank.explanation:
Amdahl: S(n) = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/n) with f = 0.8.
S(n) ≥ 4 ⇒ 0.2 + 0.8/n ≤ 0.25 ⇒ 0.8/n ≤ 0.05 ⇒ n ≥ 16.
Check: S(16) = 1 / (0.2 + 0.05) = 4; S(15) = 1 / (0.2 + 0.0533) ≈ 3.95.
Traps: 5 is the limit of S(n) as n → ∞ (1/0.2), not a core count; 8 cores give only 1/(0.2 + 0.1) ≈ 3.33; 20 cores also exceed 4 (S ≈ 4.17) but are not the minimum.

A. By value: a = b = 3 are copies. The body changes only the copies, then x = x + 1 = 4. Prints 4 (II).
B. By reference: a, b and x are all the same cell. a = a + b = 6 (x = 6); b = a × 2 = 12 (x = 12); x = x + 1 = 13. Prints 13 (IV).
C. Value-result: a = b = 3 on entry. a = 6, b = 12, and the global x becomes 4. On return a is copied to x (x = 6), then b is copied to x (x = 12). Prints 12 (I).
D. Same, but b is copied first (x = 12) and then a (x = 6). Prints 6 (III).
Answer: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III. The key traps are aliasing under call by reference and the order of copy-back under value-result.

a: C. Call by value-result, copied back left to right (a, then b)
D. Call by value-result, copied back right to left (b, then a)
b: II. 4
III. 6
IV. 13

questionBank.question: What is the output of the following C program?
questionBank.explanation:
p has type “pointer to an array of 4 ints” and points to row a[1].
**p = a[1][0] = 5. p + 1 points to row a[2], so *(*(p + 1) + 2) = a[2][2] = 11. The sum is 16.
q = a[1] + 1 points to a[1][1] = 6, so *(q + 2) = a[1][3] = 8.
sizeof(*p) is the size of a whole row (4 ints) and sizeof(**p) is one int, so the quotient is 4.
Output: 16 8 4 (checked with gcc).
Traps: 9 takes q as pointing at a[1][2]; 8 as the first number treats p as a (row 0): 1 + 7; 1 for the last number assumes *p is a pointer rather than an array.

questionBank.question:
The program below is compiled to a.out and run as:  ./a.out net jrf 2026
What does it print?
questionBank.explanation:
argv[0] = "./a.out", argv[1] = "net", argv[2] = "jrf", argv[3] = "2026", so argc = 4 (the program name counts).
s = 3 × 1 + 3 × 2 + 4 × 3 = 3 + 6 + 12 = 21, so argc + s = 25.
*argv[argc − 1] is the character '2'; adding 1 gives '3', which %c prints as 3.
argv[1] + 1 points to the second character of "net", so %s prints et.
Output: 25 3 et (checked with gcc).
Traps: 24 takes argc as 3 (forgetting argv[0]); 21 prints s alone; 2 and net ignore the + 1 on a char and on a char pointer.

questionBank.question: What is the output of the following C program?
questionBank.explanation:
Macros are textual substitutions.
SQ(i + 1) expands to i + 1 * i + 1 = 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 (not 16, because the argument is not parenthesised).
MAX(i, j − 1) = ((3) > (4) ? (3) : (4)) = 4. So k = 7 + 4 = 11.
36 / SQ(3) expands to 36 / 3 * 3; / and * have equal precedence and group left to right: (36 / 3) * 3 = 36.
Output: 11 36 (checked with gcc).
Traps: 20 assumes SQ(i + 1) = 16; 4 assumes 36 / (3 × 3). The fix is #define SQ(x) ((x) * (x)).

questionBank.question: What is the output of the following C++ program?
questionBank.explanation:
new Derived runs Base() first. While the Base constructor runs, the object is still a Base, so the virtual call show() inside it runs Base::show: prints B then b.
Then Derived() runs: prints D, and show() now resolves to Derived::show: d.
ptr->show() is a virtual call on a Derived object: d.
delete ptr: the destructor is virtual, so ~Derived runs first (~D) and then ~Base (~B).
Output: BbDdd~D~B (checked with g++).
Traps: “Bd…” assumes virtual dispatch reaches the derived class during base construction; “…~B” alone assumes a non-virtual destructor; “BbDbd…” thinks the constructor call in Derived still uses Base::show.

questionBank.question: What is the output of the following C++ program when compiled as C++17 (where copy elision of prvalues is guaranteed)?
questionBank.explanation:
C a(1), b(2): two constructor calls, so n = 2.
a + b calls a.operator+(b). The parameter o is passed by value, so it is copy-constructed from b: o.v = 2 + 10 = 12 and n = 4.
return C(v + o.v) constructs C(1 + 12) = C(13): n = 5. In C++17 this prvalue initialises c directly (guaranteed elision), so no further copy is made.
Output: 13 5 (checked with g++ -std=c++17).
Traps: 3 forgets that the by-value parameter uses the modified copy constructor; 7 adds a copy for the return value, which C++17 elides.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about C++ are correct?
options: A, B, C and D only
questionBank.explanation:
A. Correct: a class with a pure virtual function is abstract; you can have pointers and references to it, but not objects.
B. Incorrect: constructors cannot be virtual (the vtable pointer is set up by the constructor itself). Virtual destructors are allowed and are often necessary.
C. Correct: a friend is a non-member granted access; friendship is neither inherited nor transitive.
D. Correct: with virtual inheritance only one shared sub-object of the common base exists, which removes the ambiguity.
E. Incorrect: a static member function has no this pointer, so it cannot touch non-static members without an object.
Correct: A, C and D only.

stmts: A. A class that has at least one pure virtual function cannot be instantiated.
B. A constructor can be declared virtual so that the right derived-class constructor is chosen at run time.
C. A friend function of a class is not a member of the class, and friendship is not inherited.
D. In multiple inheritance, the diamond problem is resolved by declaring the common base as a virtual base class.
E. A static member function can access non-static data members directly through the this pointer.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation:
Statement I is false. It reverses the relation: a valid document is well-formed AND conforms to its DTD or schema. A well-formed document only follows XML syntax rules (one root, properly nested and closed tags, quoted attributes) and need not be valid.
Statement II is false. init() runs once, when the container loads the servlet; service() (and so doGet/doPost) runs for every request; destroy() runs once before the servlet is unloaded.
So both statements are false.

stmts: Statement I: Every well-formed XML document is valid, because well-formedness includes conformance to the document’s DTD.
Statement II: In the servlet life cycle, init() is called once for every client request, just before service().

questionBank.question: A window with corners (20, 10) and (100, 50) is mapped to a viewport with corners (100, 50) and (300, 250). To which viewport point does the window point (60, 40) map?
questionBank.explanation:
Scale factors: sx = (300 − 100)/(100 − 20) = 200/80 = 2.5; sy = (250 − 50)/(50 − 10) = 200/40 = 5.
xv = xvmin + (xw − xwmin) × sx = 100 + (60 − 20) × 2.5 = 200.
yv = yvmin + (yw − ywmin) × sy = 50 + (40 − 10) × 5 = 200.
The point maps to (200, 200). Because sx ≠ sy, shapes are stretched (the aspect ratio is not preserved).
Traps: (200, 125) uses sx for both axes; (250, 250) forgets to subtract the window minimum; (150, 200) uses a viewport width of 100 instead of 200.

questionBank.question: The point (5, 4) is rotated by 90° anticlockwise about the point (2, 3), and the result is then reflected about the line y = x. The final point is
questionBank.explanation:
Rotation about a pivot = translate the pivot to the origin, rotate, translate back.
Translate by (−2, −3): (5, 4) → (3, 1).
Rotate 90° anticlockwise, (x, y) → (−y, x): (3, 1) → (−1, 3).
Translate back by (2, 3): (1, 6).
Reflect about y = x, (x, y) → (y, x): (6, 1).
Traps: (1, 6) stops before the reflection; (5, −4) rotates about the origin ((5, 4) → (−4, 5)) and then reflects; (0, 3) rotates clockwise ((3, 1) → (1, −3) → (3, 0)) and then reflects.

1. HOSPITAL.
2. DOCTOR, with hospital_id as a foreign key. WORKS_IN is many-to-one with total participation, so it is absorbed into DOCTOR (hospital_id NOT NULL).
3. PATIENT. The composite address is flattened into simple columns; it needs no table.
4. WARD(hospital_id, ward_no, …): the weak entity takes the owner’s key plus its partial key, and the identifying relationship HAS is absorbed.
5. TREATS(doctor_id, patient_id, visit_date): M:N always needs its own table.
6. PATIENT_PHONE(patient_id, phone): a multivalued attribute needs its own table.
Total = 6.
Traps: 7 makes WORKS_IN a separate table; 8 also makes HAS a table; 5 forgets the multivalued attribute.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation:
A. A weak entity set has no key of its own; it is identified by the owner’s key plus its partial key (III). It is drawn as a double rectangle.
B. Total participation (every entity takes part in the relationship) is shown by a double line (I).
C. A derived attribute (for example age from date_of_birth) is shown as a dashed ellipse (II).
D. Specialisation is the top-down process of defining subclasses (IV); generalisation is the bottom-up counterpart.
Answer: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV.

questionBank.question:
Relations: WORKS(emp, proj) = {(e1, p1), (e1, p2), (e1, p3), (e2, p1), (e2, p3), (e3, p2), (e3, p3), (e3, p1), (e4, p3)} and NEED(proj) = {(p1), (p3)}.
What is the result of  π_emp(WORKS) − π_emp((π_emp(WORKS) × NEED) − WORKS)?
questionBank.explanation:
This expression is the standard definition of WORKS ÷ NEED: the employees who work on every project in NEED.
π_emp(WORKS) = {e1, e2, e3, e4}.
π_emp(WORKS) × NEED = all 8 (employee, p1/p3) pairs.
Removing the pairs present in WORKS leaves only (e4, p1), because e1, e2 and e3 each have both p1 and p3, and e4 has only p3.
π_emp of that = {e4}. Result = {e1, e2, e3, e4} − {e4} = {e1, e2, e3}.
Traps: {e4} is the intermediate “disqualified” set; {e1, e3} wrongly requires p2 as well; the full set forgets the subtraction.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation:
Statement I is true. The query becomes  … WHERE name = 'u' AND pw = '' OR '1'='1'. AND has higher precedence, so this is (name = 'u' AND pw = '') OR '1' = '1', which is true for every row. This is classic SQL injection.
Statement II is true. With a prepared statement the SQL text is compiled first with placeholders (?), and the user’s input is bound later as a value. However many quotes it contains, it can never change the query’s structure.
So both statements are true.

stmts: Statement I: An application builds the query "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + u + "' AND pw = '" + p + "'" by string concatenation. If a user enters p = ' OR '1'='1 (with any u), the WHERE clause becomes true for every row, because AND binds more tightly than OR.
Statement II: Using a prepared statement with bound parameters defeats this attack, because the bound value is treated as data and is never parsed as SQL.

questionBank.question: R(A, B, C, D, E, F) has the functional dependencies AB → C, C → D, D → A, BE → F and F → E. How many candidate keys does R have, and what is the highest normal form that R satisfies?
questionBank.explanation:
B never appears on a right-hand side, so B is in every key; B⁺ = {B}.
The attributes A, C, D form a cycle given B: AB → C → D → A. So AB⁺, BC⁺ (C → D → A) and BD⁺ (D → A, AB → C) all equal {A, B, C, D}.
E and F determine each other given B: BE → F and F → E.
So a key needs B, one of {A, C, D} and one of {E, F}: ABE, ABF, BCE, BCF, BDE, BDF, which gives 6 candidate keys (each is minimal).
Every attribute appears in some key, so every attribute is prime. 3NF only requires each FD’s right side to be prime or its left side to be a superkey, so R is in 3NF.
BCNF fails: in C → D, C is not a superkey. Highest form: 3NF.
Traps: BCNF ignores C → D; “2NF” forgets that prime right-hand sides satisfy 3NF.

questionBank.question: A B+ tree index is built on a 12-byte key. The block size is 4096 bytes, and a tree pointer and a record pointer are 8 bytes each. An internal node holds p tree pointers and p − 1 keys; a leaf holds q (key, record pointer) pairs and one next-leaf pointer. If every node is completely full, what is the internal order p, and how many levels (root to leaf, leaves included) are needed to index 10,000,000 records with one leaf entry per record?
questionBank.explanation:
Internal node: 8p + 12(p − 1) ≤ 4096 ⇒ 20p ≤ 4108 ⇒ p = 205.
Leaf: 20q + 8 ≤ 4096 ⇒ q = 204.
Leaves needed: ⌈10,000,000 / 204⌉ = 49,020.
Level above: ⌈49,020 / 205⌉ = 240; next: ⌈240 / 205⌉ = 2; root: 1.
Levels = leaf + 3 internal levels = 4.
Check: 3 levels can hold at most 205 × 205 × 204 = 8,573,100 records < 10⁷, so 3 is not enough.
Traps: 204 is the leaf capacity, not the internal order; 3 levels forgets the capacity check.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about data mining are correct?
questionBank.explanation:
A. Correct: the SVM maximises the margin; points away from the margin could be removed without changing the solution.
B. Correct: k-NN only stores the training data and computes distances when a query arrives.
C. Incorrect: summing over all paths is the Forward algorithm. Viterbi takes a maximum at each step and finds the single most likely state sequence.
D. Incorrect: k-means is unsupervised clustering.
E. Correct: support is anti-monotone, which is why Apriori prunes candidates that have an infrequent subset.
Correct: A, B and E only.

stmts: A. A support vector machine chooses the separating hyperplane with the maximum margin, and only the support vectors determine it.
B. k-nearest neighbour is a lazy learner: it builds no explicit model during training and does its work at classification time.
C. In a hidden Markov model, the Viterbi algorithm computes the total probability of an observation sequence by summing over all state paths.
D. k-means is a supervised classification method that needs labelled training data.
E. By the Apriori property, every non-empty subset of a frequent itemset is also frequent.
