questionBank.question: Three periodic real-time tasks have (execution time, period) = (1, 4), (2, 6) and (1, 8). What is their total CPU utilisation, and what does the Liu–Layland bound say about rate-monotonic (RM) scheduling?
options: 0.708; schedulable under RM, since it is below the bound of about 0.780
0.708; not guaranteed, since it exceeds the bound of about 0.693
questionBank.explanation: U = 1/4 + 2/6 + 1/8 = 0.250 + 0.333 + 0.125 ≈ 0.708. The Liu–Layland bound for n = 3 tasks is n(2^(1/n) − 1) = 3(2^(1/3) − 1) ≈ 0.780. Since 0.708 ≤ 0.780, RM is guaranteed to meet all deadlines. 0.693 (ln 2) is the limit as n → ∞, not the bound for 3 tasks, and using it here would be wrong anyway because 0.708 is above it; 0.625 and 0.833 are arithmetic slips.

questionBank.question: A system uses 36-bit virtual addresses, 16 KB pages and 8-byte page-table entries. What is the size of a single-level page table for one process?
questionBank.explanation: Page offset = log₂(16 K) = 14 bits, so the page number has 36 − 14 = 22 bits and there are 2²² pages. Page table size = 2²² × 8 bytes = 2²⁵ bytes = 32 MB. 16 MB uses 4-byte entries; 64 MB uses 8 KB pages; 4 MB drops the entry size.

questionBank.question: Three processes share identical units of one resource. Their maximum needs are 3, 5 and 6 units. What is the minimum number of units that guarantees the system can never deadlock?
questionBank.explanation: The worst case is each process holding one unit less than its maximum and waiting for one more: (3 − 1) + (5 − 1) + (6 − 1) = 2 + 4 + 5 = 11 units allocated with everyone blocked. One extra unit lets some process finish and release its units, after which the others can finish too. Minimum = 11 + 1 = 12. 11 is exactly the deadlock-prone total; 14 = sum of maxima is sufficient but not minimal.

questionBank.question: The disk head is at cylinder 58 and moving towards higher cylinder numbers. The request queue is 22, 91, 140, 37, 120, 12, 65. Using C-LOOK, and counting the return seek from the highest request to the lowest request as head movement, what is the total head movement?
questionBank.explanation: C-LOOK serves requests in one direction only, up to the highest request, then jumps to the lowest pending request and continues upwards. Order: 58 → 65 → 91 → 120 → 140 (movement 140 − 58 = 82), jump 140 → 12 (128), then 12 → 22 → 37 (25). Total = 82 + 128 + 25 = 235. 107 leaves out the return seek, which this question counts. 210 is LOOK (58 → 140, then back down through 37 and 22 to 12: 82 + 128). 259 jumps to cylinder 0 instead of the lowest request and then climbs to 37 (82 + 140 + 37).

questionBank.question: Arrange the following types of cohesion from the worst (least desirable) to the best (most desirable).
questionBank.explanation: The standard scale from worst to best is: coincidental (unrelated tasks thrown together) → logical (tasks of the same general kind, selected by a flag) → temporal (tasks that happen at the same time, such as initialisation) → procedural (steps in a fixed order of execution) → communicational (tasks working on the same data) → sequential → functional. So B, E, D, A, C. The usual slips are swapping logical and temporal, or swapping procedural and communicational.

stmts: A. Procedural cohesion
B. Coincidental cohesion
C. Communicational cohesion
D. Temporal cohesion
E. Logical cohesion

Adapter (structural) wraps a class to present the interface a client expects (I). Factory Method (creational) defers the choice of concrete class to subclasses (III). So A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

Statement II is true: data coupling, passing only the elementary values that are needed, is the loosest and most desirable.

Statement II: Data coupling, in which modules communicate only through elementary data parameters, is the most desirable form of coupling.

questionBank.question: A server has a mean time to failure (MTTF) of 480 hours and a mean time to repair (MTTR) of 20 hours. What are its MTBF and availability?
questionBank.explanation: MTBF = MTTF + MTTR = 480 + 20 = 500 hours. Availability = MTTF / MTBF = 480 / 500 = 0.96 = 96%. 95.8% is 460/480 (subtracting MTTR from MTTF); 480 hours treats MTBF as the same as MTTF.

Product revision (the ability to change the product): maintainability, flexibility, testability. Product transition (adapting to new environments): portability, reusability, interoperability. So A, C and D only. Portability is a transition factor and integrity an operation factor.

questionBank.explanation: V(G) = E − N + 2P = 12 − 10 + 2 × 1 = 4. Check with decision nodes: node 2 (to 3 or 4), node 6 (to 7 or 8) and node 8 (to 9 or 10) each have two successors, so V(G) = 3 + 1 = 4. questionBank.question: Which of the following statements are correct?

questionBank.explanation: A is true: every NP problem reduces to any NP-complete problem, so a polynomial algorithm for one gives one for all. B is false: NP-hard problems need not be in NP at all (the halting problem is undecidable). C is true: 2-SAT is solved in linear time using the implication graph and strongly connected components. D is true: SAT reduces to the halting problem (build a program that halts iff it finds a satisfying assignment), so it is NP-hard, but not in NP. E is false: the reduction must go the other way, from a known NP-complete problem to X, and X must also be shown to be in NP. So A, C and D only.

Therefore the DP gives no polynomial-time algorithm for the (NP-complete) decision version of knapsack, and nothing follows about P versus NP: (A) is false.

questionBank.question: What is the KMP prefix (failure) function π for the pattern “abacabab” (positions 1 to 8)?
questionBank.explanation: π[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[1..i] that is also a suffix of it. a: 0. ab: 0. aba: “a” → 1. abac: 0. abaca: “a” → 1. abacab: “ab” → 2. abacaba: “aba” → 3. abacabab: extending “aba” would need the character after it (c) to match b, which fails; fall back to π[3] = 1, and the character after “a” is b, which matches, so π = 2. Result: 0 0 1 0 1 2 3 2. “… 3 4” extends without checking the mismatch.

questionBank.question: Rabin–Karp is run on the digit string T = 2718281828 with the pattern P = 18, using the hash h(x) = x mod 7 on each 2-digit window. How many valid matches and how many spurious hits occur?
questionBank.explanation: h(P) = 18 mod 7 = 4. The nine windows and their hashes: 27 → 6, 71 → 1, 18 → 4, 82 → 5, 28 → 0, 81 → 4, 18 → 4, 82 → 5, 28 → 0. The hash equals 4 for windows 18 (position 3), 81 (position 6) and 18 (position 7). Checking character by character, 18 matches twice (valid) and 81 does not: 1 spurious hit. Answer: 2 valid, 1 spurious.

Summing n numbers as a balanced binary tree with n/2 processors takes ⌈log₂ n⌉ parallel steps (I). Taking both endpoints of every edge in a maximal matching gives a vertex cover at most twice the optimum (III). So A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

D. Vertex cover from a maximal matching

questionBank.question: In RSA with p = 5, q = 17 and public exponent e = 5, what is the private exponent d, and what is the ciphertext for the message M = 2?
questionBank.explanation: n = 5 × 17 = 85 and φ(n) = 4 × 16 = 64. d is the inverse of e modulo φ(n): 5d ≡ 1 (mod 64). 5 × 13 = 65 = 64 + 1, so d = 13. Encryption: C = M^e mod n = 2⁵ mod 85 = 32. Check: 32¹³ mod 85 = 2, the original message. d = 29 would be an inverse mod a wrong φ; C = 10 is 2 × 5 (multiplying instead of exponentiating).

questionBank.question: What is the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height 5? (A tree with a single node has height 0.)
questionBank.explanation: The sparsest AVL tree of height h has a root with subtrees of heights h − 1 and h − 2, each also sparsest: N(h) = N(h − 1) + N(h − 2) + 1, with N(0) = 1 and N(1) = 2. N(2) = 4, N(3) = 7, N(4) = 12, N(5) = 20. 12 is N(4); 32 and 33 are counts for complete or full binary trees, not the AVL minimum.

questionBank.question: What is the asymptotic solution of the recurrence T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n³ log n?
questionBank.explanation: a = 8, b = 2, so n^(log_b a) = n^(log₂ 8) = n³. f(n) = n³ log n = Θ(n^(log_b a) logᵏ n) with k = 1. By the extended case 2 of the master theorem, T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) log^(k+1) n) = Θ(n³ log² n): each of the log₂ n levels of the recursion tree costs about n³ log(n/2ⁱ), and these sum to Θ(n³ log² n). Θ(n³ log n) forgets the extra log factor from the recursion depth; Θ(n³) would need f to be polynomially smaller than n³; Θ(n⁴) wrongly applies case 3, but n³ log n is not polynomially larger than n³.

questionBank.question: A weighted undirected graph has the edges A–B 4, A–C 3, B–C 2, B–D 5, C–D 7, C–E 8, D–E 6, D–F 3, E–F 1. What is the weight of its minimum spanning tree?
questionBank.explanation: Kruskal: sort the edges: E–F 1, B–C 2, A–C 3, D–F 3, A–B 4, B–D 5, D–E 6, C–D 7, C–E 8. Take E–F (1), B–C (2), A–C (3), D–F (3). A–B (4) would close the cycle A–B–C: reject. B–D (5) joins {A, B, C} to {D, E, F}: take it. Five edges for six vertices, done. Weight = 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 5 = 14. Taking D–E (6) instead of B–D gives 15; using A–B instead of A–C gives 15.

questionBank.question: The keys 12, 23, 45, 34, 7, 18 are inserted in that order into an empty hash table of size 11 with h(k) = k mod 11 and quadratic probing (probe sequence h(k), h(k) + 1², h(k) + 2², … mod 11). In which slot is 34 stored?
questionBank.explanation: 12 → 1. 23 → 1 is taken, 1 + 1 = 2: slot 2. 45 → 1 taken, 2 taken, 1 + 4 = 5: slot 5. 34 → 1 taken, 2 taken, 5 taken, 1 + 9 = 10: slot 10. (Then 7 → 7, and 18 → 7 taken, 8: slot 8.) Linear probing would put 34 in slot 4 (1, 2, 3 is free for 45, then 4), which is the trap answer.

questionBank.question: L is the set of strings over {a, b} in which the number of a’s is congruent to 1 modulo 3 and the number of b’s is even. How many states does the minimal DFA for L have?
questionBank.explanation: The DFA must track (number of a’s mod 3, number of b’s mod 2): 3 × 2 = 6 combinations, with exactly one accepting state (1, 0). Any two different pairs are distinguishable: from pair (i, j) the suffix aᵐbⁿ that reaches (1, 0) is unique, so it leads one state to acceptance and the other not. Hence no states merge and there is no dead state: 6. 5 = 3 + 2 adds the counters instead of multiplying; 7 adds an unnecessary trap state.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about regular languages are correct?
options: A, B, C and D only
questionBank.explanation: A: swap the accepting and non-accepting states of a complete DFA: true. B: the product construction gives a DFA for the intersection: true. C is false: {aⁿbⁿ} is a subset of the regular a*b* but is not regular. D: reverse every edge of an NFA and swap start and final states: true. E is false: every language is a union of (possibly infinitely many) singleton languages, each regular, so {aⁿbⁿ} = ∪{aⁿbⁿ} would be regular. Closure holds only for finite unions. So A, B and D only.

stmts: A. Regular languages are closed under complement.
B. Regular languages are closed under intersection.
C. Every subset of a regular language is regular.
D. Regular languages are closed under reversal.
E. The union of infinitely many regular languages is always regular.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A: anything followed by abb: strings ending in abb (III). B: all a’s come before all b’s, so an a never follows a b (IV). C: repeated blocks of exactly two symbols: all even-length strings, including ε (I). D: b’s, then an a, then b’s, then a second a, then anything: at least two a’s (II). So A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

b: I. Strings of even length
II. Strings with at least two a’s
III. Strings ending in abb
IV. Strings in which no a comes after a b

questionBank.question: A DAG is built for the basic-block statement a = (b + c) * (b + c) − d / e, with common subexpressions shared. How many interior (operator) nodes does the DAG have?
questionBank.explanation: Leaves: b, c, d, e. Interior nodes: one + node for b + c (shared by both operands of *, because it is a common subexpression), the * node, the / node for d / e, and the − node (to which the label a is attached). That is 4 interior nodes. A syntax tree without sharing would have 5 (two separate + nodes); 3 forgets the node for d / e; 6 counts the assignment as a separate node.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: an S-attributed definition uses only synthesised attributes, and L-attributed definitions allow synthesised attributes plus restricted inherited ones, so S-attributed ⊂ L-attributed. Statement II is false: L-attributed definitions may have inherited attributes (taken from the parent or from siblings on the left). They fit naturally into a depth-first, top-down (LL) evaluation; in a bottom-up parser they need extra work such as marker non-terminals.

stmts: Statement I: Every S-attributed definition is also L-attributed.
Statement II: Any L-attributed definition can be evaluated during a bottom-up (LR) parse without modification, because all its attributes are synthesised.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: Constant folding evaluates expressions with constant operands at compile time (II). Strength reduction replaces an expensive operation with a cheaper one, typically an induction-variable multiplication by an addition (I). Loop-invariant code motion hoists a computation whose value does not change inside the loop (III). Peephole optimisation looks at a short sliding window of target code and removes redundant loads and stores, jumps to jumps and the like (IV). So A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV.

a: B. Strength reduction on induction variables
D. Peephole optimisation of target code
b: I. Replacing i * 4 inside a loop by an addition to a running value
II. Replacing 3 * 60 by 180 at compile time
III. Moving t = x * y, whose operands do not change in the loop, to before the loop
IV. Removing a redundant LOAD R1, a that follows STORE a, R1 by scanning a small window of target instructions

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question:
How many basic blocks does the following three-address code contain?
(1) i = 1
(2) t1 = 4 * i
(3) t2 = a[t1]
(4) if t2 > 50 goto (7)
(5) s = s + t2
(6) goto (8)
(7) c = c + 1
(8) i = i + 1
(9) if i <= 20 goto (2)
(10) print s
questionBank.explanation: Leaders: (1), the first statement; (2), the target of the jump in (9); (5), which follows the conditional jump (4); (7), the target of (4); (8), the target of (6) and also the statement after the jump (6); (10), which follows the jump (9). Six leaders give six basic blocks: {1}, {2–4}, {5–6}, {7}, {8–9}, {10}. 5 misses that (2) is a jump target; 7 wrongly makes (3) a leader.

questionBank.question: For the grammar S → A B c | d, A → a A | ε, B → b | ε, what is FOLLOW(A)?
questionBank.explanation: A appears in S → A B c, followed by B c. FIRST(B c) = FIRST(B) − {ε} ∪ FIRST(c) (since B can derive ε) = {b} ∪ {c} = {b, c}. In A → a A, A is at the end, so FOLLOW(A) ⊇ FOLLOW(A), which adds nothing. $ is not included because A is never at the end of a sentential form derived from S (c always follows). FOLLOW(A) = {b, c}. {b} forgets that B is nullable; {a, b, c} confuses FIRST(A) with FOLLOW(A).

questionBank.question: A context-free grammar is in Chomsky normal form (and has no ε-productions). How many steps does every derivation of a string of length 7 take?
questionBank.explanation: In CNF each production is either A → BC or A → a. To build a string of length n we need n − 1 applications of A → BC (each increases the number of symbols by one, from 1 to n) and n applications of A → a (one per terminal). Total = 2n − 1 = 2 × 7 − 1 = 13. 7 counts only the terminal rules; 14 = 2n overcounts by one.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: (A) is true: the standard proof assumes a decider H for halting and builds a machine that does the opposite of what H predicts about itself, a contradiction (a diagonal argument). (R) is also true: TMs can be encoded as finite strings, so they are countable, while the power set of Σ* is uncountable (Cantor’s diagonal argument). But (R) only shows that some language is not recognised by any TM; it does not show that the particular halting language is undecidable. So (R) is not the explanation of (A).

stmts: Assertion (A): The halting problem for Turing machines is undecidable.
Reason (R): The set of all languages over an alphabet is uncountable, whereas the set of all Turing machines is countable.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A channel has a bandwidth of 2 MHz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 63. What is its Shannon capacity, and how many signal levels does the Nyquist formula require to reach this rate?
questionBank.explanation: Shannon: C = B log₂(1 + SNR) = 2 × 10⁶ × log₂ 64 = 2 × 10⁶ × 6 = 12 Mbps. Nyquist: bit rate = 2B log₂ L, so 12 × 10⁶ = 2 × 2 × 10⁶ × log₂ L → log₂ L = 3 → L = 8 levels. 64 levels confuses 1 + SNR with L; 6 Mbps forgets the factor 2 in Nyquist when working backwards; 24 Mbps uses 2B in Shannon’s formula.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: NRZ-I (inverted) signals a 1 by a change of level and a 0 by no change (II). Manchester always has a mid-bit transition, and its direction (low-to-high or high-to-low) encodes the bit (I). Differential Manchester also always has the mid-bit transition for clocking, but the bit is given by the presence (0) or absence (1) of a transition at the start of the bit (III). AMI uses zero for 0 and alternating +/− pulses for 1, which gives no DC component (IV). So A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV.

b: I. A transition in the middle of every bit, whose direction gives the bit value
II. The level is inverted for a 1 and unchanged for a 0
III. A transition in the middle of every bit; a 0 has an extra transition at the start of the bit, a 1 does not
IV. Zero voltage for 0; 1s are sent as alternating positive and negative pulses

questionBank.question: A modem using 64-QAM transmits at a bit rate of 36 kbps. What is its baud (signal element) rate?
questionBank.explanation: 64-QAM has 64 signal elements, so each carries log₂ 64 = 6 bits. Baud rate = bit rate / bits per element = 36000 / 6 = 6000 baud. 12000 assumes 3 bits per element (8-QAM); 4500 uses 8 bits; 2304 is not a meaningful result (36 × 64).

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: circuit switching sets up a dedicated path with reserved resources for the whole call, and the data flows along it as a continuous stream; independent routing of packets is datagram switching. Statement II is false: in a datagram network each packet is routed on its own and may take a different path, so packets can arrive out of order, be duplicated or be lost; ordering is left to a higher layer such as TCP.

stmts: Statement I: In circuit switching, data is broken into packets that are routed independently through the network.
Statement II: A datagram packet-switched network guarantees that packets are delivered in the order in which they were sent.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Arrange the following OSI layers from the lowest to the highest.
questionBank.explanation: The OSI stack from bottom to top is Physical (1), Data link (2), Network (3), Transport (4), Session (5), Presentation (6), Application (7). So B, D, A, C, E. The two distractors swap Network with Transport or Transport with Session.

stmts: A. Network layer
B. Physical layer
C. Transport layer
D. Data link layer
E. Session layer

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A hub only regenerates and repeats bits: physical layer (II). A bridge or layer-2 switch forwards frames using MAC addresses: data link layer (III). A router forwards packets using IP addresses: network layer (I). A gateway (protocol converter) can translate between different protocol suites up to the application layer (IV). So A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV.

h: List II (highest OSI layer at which it operates)
b: I. Network layer
II. Physical layer
III. Data link layer
IV. Up to the application layer

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about addressing in the TCP/IP model are correct?
options: B, C, D and E only
A, B, C and D only
questionBank.explanation: A: port numbers (16 bits) identify processes: true. B: MAC addresses are 48 bits (6 bytes): true. C: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits: true. D: each link has its own frame with the MAC addresses of that hop, while the IP source and destination stay fixed (ignoring NAT): true. E is false: a layer-2 switch uses the destination MAC address; routers look at IP addresses. So A, B, C and D only.

stmts: A. A port address identifies a particular process on a host.
B. An Ethernet MAC address is 48 bits long.
C. An IPv4 address is 32 bits long.
D. As a packet travels, the physical (MAC) addresses change at every hop, while the logical (IP) addresses normally stay the same end to end.
E. A layer-2 switch forwards frames by looking at the destination IP address.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: The message 1101011 is sent using CRC with the generator polynomial x³ + x + 1 (1011). What is the transmitted frame?
questionBank.explanation: Append 3 zeros (the degree of the generator): 1101011000. Divide by 1011 using XOR (mod-2) long division: 1101 ⊕ 1011 = 110; bring down 0: 1100 ⊕ 1011 = 111; bring down 1: 1111 ⊕ 1011 = 100; bring down 1: 1001 ⊕ 1011 = 010; bring down 0: 0100 starts with 0, so XOR with 0000: 100; bring down 0: 1000 ⊕ 1011 = 011; bring down the last 0: 0110 starts with 0: remainder 110. Transmitted frame = message followed by the remainder: 1101011110. Check: 1101011110 divided by 1011 leaves remainder 000. 1101011000 just appends zeros without dividing.

questionBank.question: An organisation is given the block 200.40.16.0/20 and divides it into 8 equal subnets. What is the network address of the third subnet, and how many usable host addresses does each subnet have?
questionBank.explanation: 8 subnets need 3 extra bits: /20 → /23. Each /23 has 2³² ⁻ ²³ = 2⁹ = 512 addresses, of which 510 are usable (network and broadcast removed). The third octet steps by 2: 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30. The first subnet is 200.40.16.0/23, the second 200.40.18.0/23, the third 200.40.20.0/23. 512 forgets to remove the two special addresses; 18.0 is the second subnet; 24.0 is the fifth.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) is message-oriented and allows several independent streams in one association, so loss in one stream does not block the others (no head-of-line blocking across streams), and multi-homing gives fault tolerance. Statement II is true: VLANs group stations by software configuration rather than by cable; a broadcast reaches only the members of the same VLAN, and inter-VLAN traffic needs a router or a layer-3 switch.

stmts: Statement I: SCTP supports multi-streaming within one association and multi-homing (an endpoint can use several IP addresses).
Statement II: A VLAN divides the ports of a switched LAN into separate logical broadcast domains, independent of the physical location of the stations.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Fuzzy sets on X = {x1, x2, x3} are A = {0.3/x1, 0.8/x2, 0.5/x3} and B = {0.6/x1, 0.4/x2, 0.9/x3}. Using the standard (min) intersection, what is the scalar cardinality (sigma count) of A ∩ B?
questionBank.explanation: Standard intersection takes the minimum membership at each point: x1: min(0.3, 0.6) = 0.3; x2: min(0.8, 0.4) = 0.4; x3: min(0.5, 0.9) = 0.5. Scalar cardinality = 0.3 + 0.4 + 0.5 = 1.2. 2.3 is the sigma count of A ∪ B (0.6 + 0.8 + 0.9); 1.6 is |A|; 1.4 mixes one max into the minimums.

questionBank.question: Fuzzy relations R (on X × Y) and S (on Y × Z) have the matrices R = [[0.2, 0.7, 0.4], [0.9, 0.3, 0.6]] and S = [[0.5, 0.8], [0.6, 0.1], [0.3, 0.7]]. What is the max–min composition T = R ∘ S?
An aggregated fuzzy output has membership 0.2 at x = 10, 0.6 at x = 20, 0.8 at x = 30 and 0.4 at x = 40 (and 0 elsewhere). What is the crisp output using discrete centroid defuzzification?
questionBank.explanation: Centroid x* = Σ xμ(x) / Σ μ(x) = (10 × 0.2 + 20 × 0.6 + 30 × 0.8 + 40 × 0.4) / (0.2 + 0.6 + 0.8 + 0.4) = (2 + 12 + 24 + 16) / 2.0 = 54 / 2 = 27. 30 is the mean-of-maximum (the peak at 0.8); 25 is the plain average of the x values, ignoring the memberships.

questionBank.question: For the fuzzy set A = {0.2/a, 0.5/b, 0.7/c, 1.0/d, 0.4/e}, which of the following statements are correct?
options: A, B, C and D only
A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A: the α-cut keeps elements with μ ≥ 0.5: b (0.5), c (0.7), d (1.0): {b, c, d}: true. B: the strong α-cut uses μ > 0.5, which drops b: {c, d}: true. C: the support is every element with μ > 0; all five qualify: true. D: the core is the set with μ = 1: {d}: true. E is false: the height is the largest membership, 1.0, so A is a normal fuzzy set. So A, B, C and D only.

stmts: A. The 0.5-cut of A is {b, c, d}.
B. The strong 0.5-cut of A is {c, d}.
C. The support of A is {a, b, c, d, e}.
D. The core of A is {d}.
E. The height of A is 0.7.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: STRIPS represents states as sets of facts and actions by preconditions, add and delete lists (II). Partial-order (non-linear) planning keeps the plan as a partially ordered set of steps and commits to an order only when needed (III). Hierarchical planning (as in HTN planners) refines abstract tasks into subtasks (IV). Goal stack planning pushes the goal conjunction and subgoals onto a stack and works on the top one, a linear method that can fail on interacting goals such as the Sussman anomaly (I). So A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

b: I. Keeps goals and operators on a stack and solves one subgoal at a time (linear planning)
II. Describes each action by a precondition list, an add list and a delete list
III. Least-commitment planning: orders steps only when a constraint forces it
IV. Decomposes abstract high-level tasks into more concrete subtasks

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Arrange the following stages of natural language understanding in the order in which they are usually applied.
questionBank.explanation: Words are first broken into morphemes and tagged (A); the words are then parsed into a sentence structure (C); meaning is assigned to that structure (D); the sentence is related to the sentences around it, for example to resolve pronouns (E); finally the intended meaning in context is worked out (B). So A, C, D, E, B. Putting semantic analysis before syntax, or pragmatics before discourse, are the usual slips.

stmts: A. Morphological (lexical) analysis
B. Pragmatic analysis
C. Syntactic analysis
D. Semantic analysis
E. Discourse integration
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: KQML (Knowledge Query and Manipulation Language), like FIPA-ACL, is an agent communication language built on speech-act performatives such as ask-one and tell. Ontologies for the semantic web are written in RDF Schema or OWL. Statement II is true: “objects do it for free, agents do it because they want to”: invoking a method on an object always executes it, whereas an agent receiving a request can refuse, negotiate or delegate.

stmts: Statement I: KQML is an ontology language used to define class hierarchies and properties for the semantic web.
Statement II: Unlike passive objects, agents are autonomous: an agent can decide for itself whether to carry out an action that another agent requests.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A two-ply game tree has a MAX root with three MIN children. Their leaves, from left to right, are (5, 9, 7), (3, 11, 6) and (8, 4, 10). With alpha–beta pruning, evaluating left to right, what is the minimax value of the root and how many leaves are pruned?
questionBank.explanation: First MIN node: all three leaves are needed: min(5, 9, 7) = 5, so α = 5 at the root. Second MIN node: its first leaf is 3 ≤ α, so this node’s value will be at most 3 and can never beat 5: 11 and 6 are pruned (2 leaves). Third MIN node: 8 > 5, so continue; 4 ≤ 5, so prune 10 (1 leaf). Root = max(5, ≤3, ≤4) = 5, with 3 leaves pruned. “2 leaves” misses the cut in the third subtree.

questionBank.question: In a MYCIN-style rule-based system, two independent rules support the same hypothesis with certainty factors 0.7 and 0.4. What is the combined certainty factor?
questionBank.explanation: For two positive certainty factors, CF = CF1 + CF2 × (1 − CF1) = 0.7 + 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.7 + 0.12 = 0.82. The result is the same whichever rule is taken first (0.4 + 0.7 × 0.6 = 0.82), it stays below 1, and it grows with each new piece of supporting evidence. 1.10 simply adds; 0.28 multiplies (as for a conjunction of independent probabilities); 0.55 averages.

questionBank.question: A perceptron with a step activation (output 1 if net ≥ 0, else 0) has weights w = (0.2, −0.4), bias b = 0.1 and learning rate η = 0.5. It is shown the input x = (1, 1) with target t = 1. What are the weights and bias after one application of the perceptron learning rule?
questionBank.explanation: net = 0.2 × 1 + (−0.4) × 1 + 0.1 = −0.1 < 0, so the output o = 0, but the target is 1: an error of t − o = 1. Update: wᵢ ← wᵢ + η(t − o)xᵢ, so w1 = 0.2 + 0.5 = 0.7 and w2 = −0.4 + 0.5 = 0.1; b ← b + η(t − o) = 0.1 + 0.5 = 0.6. The first option would be correct only if the output were already right; the last one subtracts instead of adding; the third forgets to update the bias.

questionBank.question: Let P(x, y) mean “x has reviewed y”. Which of the following is logically equivalent to ¬∀x ∃y P(x, y)?
questionBank.explanation:
Push the negation inward one quantifier at a time, flipping each quantifier: ¬∀x ∃y P(x, y) ≡ ∃x ¬∃y P(x, y) ≡ ∃x ∀y ¬P(x, y). In words: “some x has reviewed nothing”.
Traps: ∀x ∀y ¬P flips only the first quantifier’s meaning (nobody reviewed anything, too strong); ∃x ∃y ¬P forgets to flip ∃y; ∀x ∃y ¬P forgets to flip ∀x.

questionBank.question: Which of the following propositional formulas are tautologies?
questionBank.explanation:
A. An implication and its contrapositive always agree: tautology.
B. Modus ponens written as one formula: whenever p and p → q are true, q is true. Tautology.
C. An implication does not imply its converse: p = F, q = T makes p → q true and q → p false. Not a tautology.
D. De Morgan’s law: tautology.
E. p = T, q = F makes p ∨ q true and p ∧ q false. Not a tautology.
So A, B and D only.

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation:
(A) is true: this is modus tollens. If p were true, p → q would force q to be true, contradicting ¬q.
(R) is true: p → q and ¬q → ¬p have identical truth tables.
(R) explains (A): rewriting p → q as ¬q → ¬p and applying modus ponens with ¬q gives ¬p. So both are true and (R) is the correct explanation.

stmts: Assertion (A): From the premises p → q and ¬q, the conclusion ¬p validly follows.
Reason (R): p → q is logically equivalent to its contrapositive ¬q → ¬p.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Maximize Z = 4x + 3y subject to x + y ≤ 8, 2x + y ≤ 12, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. What is the maximum value of Z?
questionBank.explanation:
Corner points of the feasible region: (0, 0), (6, 0) from 2x + y = 12 with y = 0, (0, 8) from x + y = 8 with x = 0, and the intersection of x + y = 8 and 2x + y = 12: subtracting gives x = 4, y = 4.
Z at the corners: 0, 24, 24 and 4(4) + 3(4) = 28. Maximum Z = 28 at (4, 4).
Traps: 24 stops at an axis corner; 32 uses (8, 0), which violates 2x + y ≤ 12; 30 comes from mixing the two intercepts.

questionBank.question: In PERT, an activity has optimistic time 3 days, most likely time 6 days and pessimistic time 15 days. What are its expected time and standard deviation?
questionBank.explanation:
Expected time tₑ = (a + 4m + b) / 6 = (3 + 24 + 15) / 6 = 42 / 6 = 7 days.
Standard deviation σ = (b − a) / 6 = (15 − 3) / 6 = 2 days (the variance is σ² = 4).
Traps: “7 and 4” gives the variance as σ; 8 is the plain average (3 + 6 + 15)/3; 6 is the most likely time.

questionBank.question: A project network has the activities (i–j, duration in days): A(1–2, 4), B(1–3, 6), C(2–4, 6), D(3–4, 2), E(2–3, 1), F(4–5, 4). What is the project duration and the critical path?
questionBank.explanation:
Forward pass (earliest event times): node 1 = 0; node 2 = 4; node 3 = max(0 + 6, 4 + 1) = 6; node 4 = max(4 + 6, 6 + 2) = 10; node 5 = 10 + 4 = 14.
The paths are A–C–F = 4 + 6 + 4 = 14, B–D–F = 6 + 2 + 4 = 12 and A–E–D–F = 4 + 1 + 2 + 4 = 11. The longest path is the critical path: A–C–F, 14 days.
Traps: 12 is the path with the largest first activity; picking the shortest path (11) confuses CPM with shortest-path routing.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation:
Statement I is true: this is the standard (symmetric) primal–dual pair: max cᵀx, Ax ≤ b, x ≥ 0 has the dual min bᵀy, Aᵀy ≥ c, y ≥ 0.
Statement II is false: by weak duality every dual-feasible value bounds the primal objective. If the primal is unbounded, no such bound exists, so the dual is infeasible.
So Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: The dual of a maximization LPP whose constraints are all of the ≤ type (with non-negative variables) is a minimization LPP with ≥ constraints and non-negative dual variables.
Statement II: If the primal LPP has an unbounded objective value, its dual has a finite optimal solution.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question:
Four jobs J1–J4 are to be assigned to four machines M1–M4, one job per machine. The cost matrix (rows J1–J4, columns M1–M4) is:
J1: 10  7 12  9
J2:  8 11  6 13
J3: 14  9 10  7
J4:  9 12 13  8
What is the minimum total assignment cost?
questionBank.explanation:
Hungarian method. Row reduction subtracts 7, 6, 7, 8: J1: 3 0 5 2; J2: 2 5 0 7; J3: 7 2 3 0; J4: 1 4 5 0.
Column reduction subtracts the column minima 1, 0, 0, 0: J1: 2 0 5 2; J2: 1 5 0 7; J3: 6 2 3 0; J4: 0 4 5 0.
Zeros allow an independent assignment: J1–M2, J2–M3, J3–M4, J4–M1.
Cost = 7 + 6 + 7 + 9 = 29, which equals the total reduction (7 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 1 = 29), confirming optimality.
Traps: 33 is the next-best assignment; taking each row’s minimum independently (7 + 6 + 7 + 8 = 28) ignores the one-job-per-machine rule and is infeasible.

questionBank.question: How many integers from 1 to 700 (inclusive) are divisible by neither 4 nor 6?
questionBank.explanation:
Divisible by 4: ⌊700/4⌋ = 175. Divisible by 6: ⌊700/6⌋ = 116. Divisible by both means divisible by lcm(4, 6) = 12: ⌊700/12⌋ = 58.
By inclusion–exclusion, divisible by 4 or 6: 175 + 116 − 58 = 233. Neither: 700 − 233 = 467.
Traps: 409 subtracts 175 + 116 without adding back 58; using 24 (4 × 6) instead of the lcm 12 gives a wrong overlap.

questionBank.question: Machine M1 makes 60% of a factory’s bolts and machine M2 makes 40%. 2% of M1’s bolts and 5% of M2’s bolts are defective. A bolt picked at random is defective. What is the probability that M2 made it?
questionBank.explanation:
P(defective) = 0.6 × 0.02 + 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032.
Bayes: P(M2 | defective) = 0.020 / 0.032 = 5/8 = 0.625.
Traps: 0.375 is P(M1 | defective); 0.40 is the prior P(M2); 0.05 is P(defective | M2), the reversed conditional.

questionBank.question: A byte-addressable machine has 32-bit addresses and a 64 KB direct-mapped cache with 32-byte blocks. How many bits are in the tag, line (index) and block-offset fields respectively?
questionBank.explanation:
Offset: 32-byte block → log₂ 32 = 5 bits.
Number of lines = 64 KB / 32 B = 2¹⁶ / 2⁵ = 2¹¹ = 2048 → 11 index bits.
Tag = 32 − 11 − 5 = 16 bits.
Traps: 15, 12, 5 counts 4096 lines (uses 128 KB); 4-bit offsets assume 16-byte blocks.

questionBank.question: A two-level cache has an L1 hit time of 1 ns and an L1 miss rate of 10%. L2 has a hit time of 8 ns and a local miss rate of 20%. Main memory access takes 100 ns. What is the average memory access time?
questionBank.explanation:
AMAT = L1 hit time + L1 miss rate × (L2 hit time + L2 local miss rate × memory time)
= 1 + 0.10 × (8 + 0.20 × 100) = 1 + 0.10 × 28 = 3.8 ns.
Traps: 2.8 forgets the L1 hit time; 3.0 ignores the L2 hit time (1 + 0.1 × 20); 21.8 applies the L2 miss rate to every access (1 + 0.1 × 8 + 0.2 × 100) instead of only to L1 misses.

questionBank.question: A paged system has a TLB with a 10 ns lookup and an 80% hit ratio. A memory access takes 90 ns and the page table is in main memory (single level). What is the effective memory access time?
questionBank.explanation:
TLB hit: 10 + 90 = 100 ns. TLB miss: 10 + 90 (page-table access) + 90 (data) = 190 ns.
EAT = 0.8 × 100 + 0.2 × 190 = 80 + 38 = 118 ns.
Traps: 100 ns ignores misses; 110 ns forgets the TLB time on a miss; 128 ns charges two extra memory accesses on a miss.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation:
A. Associative (content-addressable) memory is searched by content: II.
B. Write-through writes to cache and main memory together: IV.
C. Write-back marks the block dirty and writes it to memory only on replacement: I.
D. In a k-way set-associative cache, a block maps to one set and may occupy any of its k lines: III.
So A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

b: I. Main memory is updated only when a modified (dirty) block is replaced
II. Words are accessed by their content rather than by an address
III. A block can go into any line within one fixed set
IV. Main memory is updated on every write to the cache

questionBank.question: A device transfers data at 10 MB/s using DMA in cycle-stealing mode. Each DMA cycle transfers one 4-byte word and steals the bus for 40 ns. For what percentage of time is the CPU kept off the bus by this device?
questionBank.explanation:
Words per second = 10 × 10⁶ B/s ÷ 4 B = 2.5 × 10⁶ words/s.
Bus time stolen per second = 2.5 × 10⁶ × 40 ns = 0.1 s.
Fraction = 0.1 s / 1 s = 10%.
Traps: 40% moves only one byte per DMA cycle (10⁷ cycles × 40 ns); 25% divides 10 by 40; 4% forgets that each word costs a full 40 ns bus cycle.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about priority interrupts are correct?
questionBank.explanation:
A. True: the acknowledge signal passes through devices in series, so the first device in the chain wins.
B. False: daisy chaining is a hardware (serial) priority method; polling is the software method.
C. True: the first device tested that has a pending request is served first.
D. True: the mask register enables or disables each line and the encoder produces the vector of the highest-priority unmasked request.
E. False: in vectored interrupts the device supplies the vector (address), so no polling is needed.
So A, C and D only.

stmts: A. In daisy chaining, the device electrically closest to the CPU has the highest priority.
B. Daisy chaining is a software method in which the CPU polls each device.
C. In a polling scheme, priority is decided by the order in which the service routine tests the devices.
D. A parallel priority interrupt uses an interrupt register, a mask register and a priority encoder.
E. With vectored interrupts, the CPU has to poll all devices to identify the source.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Arrange the steps of a source-initiated asynchronous transfer using handshaking in the correct order.
questionBank.explanation:
Source-initiated handshaking: the source first puts the data on the bus (B) and then raises data valid (E). The destination latches the data and raises data accepted (D). Seeing this, the source drops data valid and invalidates the bus (C). Finally the destination drops data accepted (A), ready for the next transfer.
So B, E, D, C, A. The traps swap the last two steps or raise data valid before the data is on the bus.

stmts: A. Destination disables the data-accepted signal
B. Source places the data on the data bus
C. Source disables data valid and removes the data from the bus
D. Destination accepts the data and enables data accepted
E. Source enables the data-valid signal
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: An IEEE 754 single-precision number is stored as the hexadecimal pattern C1480000. What decimal value does it represent?
questionBank.explanation:
C1480000 = 1100 0001 0100 1000 0000 … in binary.
Sign = 1 (negative). Exponent = 1000 0010 = 130, so the true exponent is 130 − 127 = 3. Fraction = 1001 000…, so the significand is 1.1001₂ = 1 + 0.5 + 0.0625 = 1.5625.
Value = −1.5625 × 2³ = −12.5.
Traps: 12.5 drops the sign bit; −25.0 uses exponent 4 (bias 126); −6.25 uses exponent 2.

questionBank.question: A 5-bit ripple (asynchronous) counter uses flip-flops each with a propagation delay of 20 ns. What is the maximum clock frequency at which the counter can be operated safely?
questionBank.explanation:
In a ripple counter each flip-flop is clocked by the previous one, so the worst-case settling time is n × t_pd = 5 × 20 = 100 ns.
f_max = 1 / 100 ns = 10 MHz.
Trap: 50 MHz uses one flip-flop delay, which is the limit for a synchronous counter, not a ripple counter.

questionBank.question: On a multicore processor, 80% of a program’s execution time can be parallelised perfectly and the rest is serial. By Amdahl’s law, what is the speedup on 8 cores?
questionBank.explanation:
Speedup = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/p) = 1 / (0.2 + 0.8/8) = 1 / (0.2 + 0.1) = 1 / 0.3 ≈ 3.33.
Traps: 8 ignores the serial part; 6.4 multiplies 8 by 0.8; 4.00 uses 1 / (0.2 + 0.05).
Note the limit: even with infinite cores the speedup cannot exceed 1/0.2 = 5.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation:
Statement I is false: validity is checked on top of well-formedness. A document that breaks the basic syntax rules (unclosed tags, bad nesting) cannot even be parsed, so it cannot be valid. Every valid document is well-formed, but not the other way round.
Statement II is true: a single root element is one of the well-formedness rules, together with properly closed and nested tags, quoted attribute values and case-sensitive names.
So Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: An XML document that is valid against a DTD need not be well-formed.
Statement II: A well-formed XML document must have exactly one root element that encloses all other elements.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation:
A. A servlet runs in the web container on the server and responds to requests: II.
B. An applet runs on the client side, inside the browser (now obsolete): III.
C. A JSP page is HTML with Java scriptlets and tags; the container translates it into a servlet: IV.
D. A DTD defines the elements, attributes and nesting an XML document must follow: I.
So A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

b: I. Declares the legal elements and structure of an XML document
II. Server-side Java class that handles HTTP requests and builds responses
III. Java program downloaded and run inside the client’s browser
IV. HTML page with embedded Java code that is translated into a servlet

questionBank.question: Arrange the events in the life cycle of a Java servlet in the correct order.
questionBank.explanation:
The container first loads the servlet class (B) and creates one instance (E). It then calls init() once (D). Every request is handled by service() (A), which dispatches to doGet/doPost. When the servlet is taken out of service, destroy() is called (C).
So B, E, D, A, C. Trap: init() cannot run before an instance exists.

stmts: A. service() is called for each client request
B. The servlet class is loaded by the container
C. destroy() is called before the servlet is removed
D. init() is called once
E. An instance of the servlet is created

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about HTML, CSS and HTTP are correct?
questionBank.explanation:
A. True: specificity is inline > ID > class/attribute/pseudo-class > element.
B. False: an inline style overrides external and internal style sheet rules (unless !important is used there).
C. True: div starts on a new line and takes the full width; span flows inside text.
D. True: alt is the alternative text, also used by screen readers.
E. False: HTTP is stateless; cookies, sessions or tokens add state.
So A, C and D only.

stmts: A. In CSS, an ID selector has higher specificity than a class selector.
B. An inline style has lower priority than a rule in an external style sheet.
C. The div element is block-level while the span element is inline.
D. The alt attribute of the img element gives the text shown when the image cannot be displayed.
E. HTTP is a stateful protocol, so cookies are not needed to track sessions.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Bresenham’s line algorithm is used to draw the line from (10, 10) to (18, 14). With p₀ = 2Δy − Δx, the rule “if pₖ < 0 plot (xₖ + 1, yₖ) and add 2Δy; otherwise plot (xₖ + 1, yₖ + 1) and add 2Δy − 2Δx” is applied. What is the second pixel plotted and the decision parameter p₁?
questionBank.explanation:
Δx = 8, Δy = 4, so p₀ = 2(4) − 8 = 0.
p₀ is not negative, so the next pixel is (11, 11) and p₁ = p₀ + 2Δy − 2Δx = 0 + 8 − 16 = −8.
(The next step, with p₁ < 0, plots (12, 11).)
Traps: treating p₀ = 0 as “negative” gives (11, 10) and p₁ = 8.

questionBank.question: A raster display has a resolution of 1920 × 1080 and stores 24 bits per pixel. What is the minimum frame-buffer size?
questionBank.explanation:
Pixels = 1920 × 1080 = 2,073,600. Each pixel needs 24 bits = 3 bytes.
Frame buffer = 2,073,600 × 3 = 6,220,800 bytes (about 5.93 MB).
Traps: 2,073,600 is the pixel count (1 byte per pixel); 8,294,400 uses 32 bits per pixel; 49,766,400 is the size in bits.

questionBank.question: In Cohen–Sutherland line clipping, the clipping window is 10 ≤ x ≤ 50, 10 ≤ y ≤ 40, and region codes are written as the 4 bits Top, Bottom, Right, Left (in that order). For the line from P(60, 5) to Q(30, 45), what are the region codes and what does the algorithm decide in its first test?
options: P = 0110, Q = 1000; the line is trivially rejected
P = 0110, Q = 1000; the line needs further clipping
P = 1001, Q = 0100; the line is trivially rejected
P = 0101, Q = 1000; the line is trivially accepted
questionBank.explanation:
P(60, 5): x > 50 sets Right, y < 10 sets Bottom → T B R L = 0 1 1 0.
Q(30, 45): y > 40 sets Top → 1 0 0 0.
Trivial accept needs both codes 0000 (not the case). Trivial reject needs P AND Q ≠ 0000: 0110 AND 1000 = 0000, so it cannot be rejected either. The line must be clipped against the window edges.
Trap: seeing two non-zero codes and rejecting at once; the test is the bitwise AND, not whether each code is non-zero.

questionBank.question: The midpoint circle algorithm draws a circle of radius 8 centred at the origin, starting at (0, 8) with p₀ = 1 − r and moving along x in the first octant. Which are the first three pixels plotted?
questionBank.explanation:
p₀ = 1 − 8 = −7 < 0, so the next pixel keeps y: (1, 8), and p₁ = p₀ + 2x₁ + 1 = −7 + 3 = −4.
p₁ < 0 again, so the next pixel is (2, 8), and p₂ = −4 + 2(2) + 1 = 1.
(Only now p ≥ 0, so the fourth pixel drops to y = 7.)
So the first three pixels are (0, 8), (1, 8), (2, 8). Traps: decrementing y at the first step, or reading p₀ = −7 as “move diagonally”.

questionBank.question: What is the output of the following C program?
questionBank.explanation:
Output: 8 9.
“REVISION” has I at indexes 3 and 5 (R0 E1 V2 I3 S4 I5 O6 N7), so n = 3 + 5 = 8.
sizeof(s) counts the array, which includes the terminating ’\0’: 8 characters + 1 = 9.
Traps: 8 8 uses strlen instead of sizeof; 2 counts the I’s instead of adding their indexes.

questionBank.question: What is the output of the following C++ program?
questionBank.explanation:
Output: AB-ba.
Constructing a derived object runs the base constructor first (A), then the derived constructor (B). Then “-” is printed. When x goes out of scope at the end of main, destructors run in reverse order: derived first (b), then base (a).
Traps: AB-ab destroys in construction order; BA-… constructs the derived part first.

questionBank.question: Relation R(A, B) has the tuples (1, x), (2, y), (3, x), (4, z), (5, y). Relation S(B, C) has the tuples (x, 10), (x, 20), (y, 30), (w, 40). How many tuples are in the natural join R ⋈ S?
questionBank.explanation:
Join on the common attribute B, value by value:
B = x: 2 tuples in R × 2 in S = 4.
B = y: 2 in R × 1 in S = 2.
B = z and B = w have no partner.
Total = 4 + 2 = 6.
Traps: 20 is the Cartesian product 5 × 4; 5 assumes each R tuple matches exactly once.

questionBank.question: Enrolled(S, C) has the tuples (s1, c1), (s1, c2), (s2, c1), (s3, c1), (s3, c2), (s3, c3), (s4, c2). Courses(C) has the tuples c1 and c2. What is the result of Enrolled ÷ Courses?
questionBank.explanation:
Division returns the S values paired with every C value in Courses, that is, students enrolled in both c1 and c2.
s1: c1 and c2 → yes. s2: c1 only → no. s3: c1, c2 (and c3) → yes; extra courses do not matter. s4: c2 only → no.
Result {s1, s3}.
Traps: {s3} wrongly demands an exact match of the course set; the full set is the projection πS(Enrolled).

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation:
A. A super key is any identifying attribute set, minimal or not: II.
B. A candidate key is a minimal super key: I.
C. A foreign key references a primary key and enforces referential integrity: IV.
D. The primary key is the chosen candidate key and obeys entity integrity (no NULLs): III.
So A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

b: I. A super key with no proper subset that is also a super key
II. Any set of attributes whose values identify each tuple uniquely
III. The candidate key chosen by the designer, which cannot be NULL
IV. An attribute set that refers to the primary key of another (or the same) relation

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation:
Statement I is true: relational calculus specifies the properties of the result, whereas relational algebra gives a sequence of operations.
Statement II is false: “all tuples not in Student” is an infinite set (every possible tuple outside the relation). A safe expression must produce values only from the domain of the expression, so this one is unsafe.
So Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: Tuple relational calculus is a non-procedural language: a query says what to retrieve, not how.
Statement II: The expression {t | ¬(t ∈ Student)} is a safe expression.

questionBank.question:
Table Emp(name, dept, sal) has the rows (Anu, HR, 40000), (Binu, HR, 65000), (Chitra, IT, 70000), (Dev, IT, 52000), (Eshan, IT, 45000), (Fida, OPS, 30000), (Gopi, OPS, NULL). What is the output of:
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM Emp GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(sal) > 50000;
questionBank.explanation:
Group averages (AVG ignores NULL):
HR: (40000 + 65000) / 2 = 52500 > 50000 → kept, COUNT(*) = 2.
IT: (70000 + 52000 + 45000) / 3 ≈ 55667 > 50000 → kept, COUNT(*) = 3.
OPS: only 30000 is counted, so AVG = 30000 → removed.
Output: HR 2 and IT 3.
Traps: treating NULL as 0 would still drop OPS; COUNT(*) counts rows (it would be 2 for OPS), COUNT(sal) would be 1. “IT 3 only” wrongly uses the overall average.

questionBank.question:
Table T(x) holds the values 1, 2, 3, 4 and table U(y) holds the values 2 and NULL. How many rows does this query return?
SELECT x FROM T WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM U);
questionBank.explanation:
x NOT IN (2, NULL) means x <> 2 AND x <> NULL. The comparison x <> NULL is UNKNOWN for every x, so the condition is either FALSE (x = 2) or UNKNOWN (the rest). WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE, so no row qualifies: 0 rows.
Traps: 3 ignores the NULL (the usual expectation 1, 3, 4); 4 assumes NULL makes the subquery empty. Use NOT EXISTS, or filter y IS NOT NULL, to get the intended result.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about SQL are correct?
options: A, C, D and E only
A, B, C and D only
questionBank.explanation:
A. True: WHERE filters rows before grouping, so aggregates are not available there.
B. False: a view stores only its defining query; rows are produced when it is used (a materialized view is the exception).
C. True: TRUNCATE deallocates the table’s data and is treated as DDL (it usually cannot be rolled back row by row).
D. True: it refers to a column of the outer row, so conceptually it is re-run per outer row.
E. True.
So A, C, D and E only.

stmts: A. A condition with an aggregate function can be written in HAVING but not in WHERE.
B. An ordinary (non-materialized) view physically stores a copy of its rows.
C. TRUNCATE TABLE is classified as a DDL command.
D. A correlated subquery is, in principle, evaluated once for each row of the outer query.
E. UNION removes duplicate rows, while UNION ALL keeps them.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation:
(A) is true: with placeholders, the user input is bound as a data value, so text such as ' OR '1'='1 cannot change the structure of the query.
(R) is false: prepared statements do not encrypt anything. They work because the query is parsed first and the parameters are sent separately, never parsed as SQL.
So (A) is true but (R) is false.

stmts: Assertion (A): Using parameterised (prepared) statements is an effective defence against SQL injection.
Reason (R): A prepared statement encrypts the SQL text before it is sent to the database server.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) has the functional dependencies A → B, BC → D, D → E, E → A. How many candidate keys does R have?
questionBank.explanation:
C never appears on a right side, so every key contains C. C⁺ = {C}, so C alone is not a key.
AC⁺: A → B, then BC → D, D → E → {A, B, C, D, E}: key.
BC⁺: BC → D, D → E, E → A → all: key.
CD⁺: D → E, E → A, A → B → all: key.
CE⁺: E → A, A → B, BC → D → all: key.
All four are minimal (C alone fails), and any other set containing C includes one of them. So there are 4 candidate keys: AC, BC, CD, CE.
Traps: stopping at AC, or missing that the cycle A → B → D → E → A lets each of them pair with C.

questionBank.question: Consider the schedule S: r1(A), w2(A), r3(B), w1(B), r2(B), c1, c2, c3. Which serial order is S conflict-equivalent to?
questionBank.explanation:
Conflicting pairs (different transactions, same item, at least one write), in schedule order:
r1(A) before w2(A): edge T1 → T2.
r3(B) before w1(B): edge T3 → T1.
w1(B) before r2(B): edge T1 → T2.
(r3(B) and r2(B) are both reads, so no conflict.)
The precedence graph T3 → T1 → T2 has no cycle, so S is conflict serializable, equivalent to T3, T1, T2.
Trap: T1 → T2 → T3 just follows the order of first operations.

questionBank.question:
An assembler processes the program below. Every instruction and every WORD takes 3 bytes; RESW n reserves n words of 3 bytes; RESB n reserves n bytes.
      START 1000
      LDA   ALPHA
      ADD   BETA
      STA   GAMMA
ALPHA WORD  5
BETA  RESW  4
GAMMA RESB  10
      END
What are the symbol-table value of GAMMA and the program length (in bytes)?
questionBank.explanation:
Location counter in pass 1: LDA 1000, ADD 1003, STA 1006, ALPHA 1009 (WORD, 3 bytes), BETA 1012 (RESW 4 = 12 bytes), GAMMA 1024 (RESB 10 = 10 bytes), end at 1034.
GAMMA = 1024; length = 1034 − 1000 = 34 bytes.
Traps: 1016 and 26 count RESW 4 as 4 bytes; 1024 and 24 forgets GAMMA’s own 10 bytes.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation:
A. The loader brings the program into memory (allocation, relocation) and transfers control to it: III.
B. The linker joins separately assembled or compiled modules and resolves external symbols: II.
C. The macro processor expands macro calls (a textual substitution before translation): I.
D. The debugger supports breakpoints, tracing and inspection: IV.
So A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV.

b: I. Replaces each macro call with the body of its definition before assembly
II. Combines object modules and resolves external references
III. Places the executable in memory and prepares it for execution
IV. Lets the programmer set breakpoints and inspect variables during execution
